_childDocuments_.review: My wife and I played this and enjoyed it for the most part, but there were some pretty glaring problems:The absolute worst issue we had was, after four and a half hours of play time, near the end of the game, the game just disconnected from the session and booted us to the main menu. It did not crash to desktop; no errors, no nothing. However, this CORRUPTED our save. We were not able to get back into our session to finish the game, which really turned us off. We had to restart from the very beginning (where you can't skip the long music cutscene).The second-largest issue we had was the controls themselves. During dialog events you have to kind of "fight" the compass selector. At times, we had to constantly jiggle the right thumb stick to make sure we selected what we wanted. The game characters themselves get stuck on each other if they get too close. The flashlight control is horrendous. You control the flashlight and camera with the right thumbstick. However, the flashlight will move at a faster rate than the camera, so they are not synced up. This results in a constant fight to actually see what you want to look at. The flashlight will re-orient itself to the center of the camera, but it takes a full 5 seconds of not touching the controls for that to happen.The camera will often times change from a leashed camera to a fixed camera and, due do the 3D controls, our characters will suddenly go from the direction we were initially moving to a completely different direction, which will often result in them moving backwards, where the camera changes back to a leashed camera.Subtitles were broken for me (player 2), but not for my player partner (player 1). I enabled subtitles in the game options, but they only worked during pre-rendered cutscenes. The printed text when reading an inspect-able item would work sporadically for me (they worked about 20% of the time), but my partner got them every single time, so I often couldn't read the small print on the items.The pacing is sometimes FORCED by the NPC characters. In at least two parts of the game we are forced forward instead of being allowed to look around. In two specific instances I was able to spot an inspect-able object, but while my character was bending down to pick it up I was forced out, because my partner (who is not controlled) decided to move to a advancement trigger, which starts a cutscene and pulls me out.The ending of the game is rather lame, in my opinion, since it's very cliche. I was able to figure out what was truly going on just a couple hours into the game. I do like the subtle nuances that are in the game that hint toward what is really happening though. I think they're added in a well-done way.Overall, I don't think I can recommend this game in its current state since the buggy controls really take you out of the immersion. Because it's using the exact same system as the previous game (Man of Medan) they should have been able to iron out the bugs to smooth out gameplay. Honestly, I'd get a refund if I could. Perhaps they'll get it right next time?

_childDocuments_.review: I had a little fear that I would not like the setting of this game, like the other ones of the anthology, but boy, luckily I was wrong. The devs did good in Man of Medan, but in Little Hope, they raised the bar.The atmosphere of the little town, the old witch trials, the cozy 70's flashbacks... marvelous. There is so much thought and love put in this game, it just melts your heart.The five protagonists are carefully chosen, you see them as real people, not cheap archetypes, like in most horror flicks. The sounds, the music, the eerie fog, the sins, long forgotten, getting unearthed... man, this is what horror should be. Their decisions that you have to make for them are truly feeling like an anchor on your shoulder.Finally, the epilogue... wow. Mind blowing.Don't think, if it's on sale, buy it, play it, cherish it!

_childDocuments_.review: Long story short, it's okay. If you want to "play" a decent episode of Twilight Zone or Beyond Belief with substantial production quality with a couple QTEs here and there this is your game. Since it's about 4 years old as of now, won't be too much to handle for a modern mid-level system but will still look great nonetheless. If you want the long story however, just keep reading and expect minor .Let me start with the "Lethal" difficulty which I don't think is designed the best. More than half of it is fine; correct button pressing, button mashing and the stealth "rythm" sections all work. They can get plenty challenging, and that's what I expected and wanted out of the difficulty. But the "aiming" parts where you have to drag a reticule to a certain point on the screen are almost always bullsh*t I have to say. On other difficulties, where you need to aim is highlighted by a circle; with Lethal you only get the reticule and when you aim correctly it turns red. So far so good but when the correct spot to aim doesn't make any common sense, you feel you get ripped off. I mean I have a sledgehammer and I'm expected to hit a monster's hand of all things when its head is even closer to me? To me that's just nonsense. The whole thing just makes me feel like Lethal mode was designed just as a mode to be played when you compelete the game on easier difficulties, with prior knowledge of the QTEs you need to execute. I just would like that to be disclosed in some way on the menus. Don't get me wrong either since I'm not salty or anything because I couldn't save a character (I'm actually completely content with the ending I got), I just think this difficulty and this specific QTE could've been designed better with little context clues to ever so slightly help on the dot rather than having nothing and making it completely nonsensical guesswork because almost every time, that's what decides if a character lives or dies.And then comes the overall gameplay of the game, which ends up consisting of walking in a very slow speed, interacting with certain objects and trying to make the character you control pointing their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ flashlight or light source to where you actually want them towards. I don't get why anyone would hold their flashlight in pure darkness at the side of their body to only illuminate anywhere but where they are headed towards. Don't know for sure if that was an issue with gamepad controls but it sure was weird. Camera was also odd might I add, it just felt it was way too far back from the character that it made looking around a chore sometimes; just one movement of it and a tree branch obscures your view or even another character standing somewhere. And when you add the non-existent level design on top of it all -which turns most of the game into one long corridor where you walk in a painfully slow speed, trying to wrestle with the controls- I was shocked to see my entire playtime was somewhere around 5 to 6 hours, because I swear just walking from point A to B at any given time alone  like it took hours to me. I would even just take the characters to not have the agility of a fridge at that point and have everything else stay the same, because screw "realism" and give me a character that can at the very least "stroll" dang it!     It's a crying shame too, because I really liked the overall premise and much more than I expected I have to add. The whole "Curator" aspect was pulled off excellently; not too cheesy nor too serious, it just hits that sweet spot, almost to the point that I couldn't even wait to see him again. So props to both mocap, voice acting and writing for that. On the other hand, while not incredibly satisfying, the story is also decent as well. I just think writers play their cards too early with little subtlety to boot and that takes away the mystique of the whole situation away too quickly. If you are even a little observant, you understand where the story is going towards rather early on. But even with all these combined, I don't hate the game, however- I simply couldn't go without mentioning all its issues. Without those, I would play this many more times to see every ending, every secret and detail but as things stand that's not gonna happen anytime soon. It's almost the perfect embodiment of a "" game even though I'm not too fond of that scaling system.Thanks for reading this entire, unnecessarily long rant.

The main reason is the inescapable feeling that I am on rails through the whole story. I have replayed this game 4+ times hoping to have that experience of finding a new branch to the story, only to experience the same scenes no matter what. The dialogue gets nicer/angrier, the characters become more/less rational, but the scenes do not change. This in the echoes of Man of Medan's branching options () just does not compare. This is only amplified in the two player experience where Man of Medan really succeeded () and Little Hope barely registers. While it improved on ~atmosphere~ the scares themselves fell short (and I am a chicken). The repetitiveness of the jump scares got old quick. I acknowledge they were important to the story, but  have to happen the same way 6+ times?I wanted to love this game the same way I loved Man of Medan, but while the superficial elements improved (visuals, sound design, etc.) it lost its way in the actual game play. _childDocuments_.review: I preferred this over Man of Medan. The Witch Trials were pretty interesting and I felt pretty engaged throughout most of the experience. There's some things some characters do, which are questionable I won't go into too much detail, but Little Hope has a very similar ending to Man of Medan. How you get there is different and why it all happened is different as well but it's .What's pretty frustrating about all of this is that it's pretty obvious fairly early on that this what the conclusion to the game will be. Some might even be able to guess this from the opening scene, since you don't see the bus driver and the other characters together, at any point. Interactions with a certain other character make sense in hindsight but for me, the whole experience suffers for it. Others may like it, but from the start of the game, me and a friend were just hoping it would actually be super natural and wouldn't try to explain it all away with .Another thing I really wish they would stop doing is whenever something "spooky" happens, they really REALLY need to stop with the stupidly loud jump scare sounds. Whenever someone walks past in the shadows, grabs a characters arm or when a cat crosses the bloody road, there's a really loud and obnoxious noise in an attempt to startle a player. These games are not scary in the slightest and in my opinion, should stop trying to be with such cheap tricks that do not add to the experience. Any tension; however small, that's built up is quickly diminished by this nonsense. What's worse is that most of the time these jump scares are for the most part telegraphed in a really obvious way, which makes them completely pointless, other than to surprise a player who might not be paying that much attention.This may also be a bit more subjective, but the narrator himself adds absolutely nothing to the game. I find it dumb that we have to cut away from what's happening for a few minutes to listen to a guy tell us what's happened so far in this pretty short game, to give us his non-advice, which has always been "maybe you've made the right choice or not or maybe you have or not". This somewhat worked better in Until Dawn, since it was a longer game and a player was more likely to not finish the game in a single session so a little reminder for those who might need it can be seen as a good thing. In this series so far though, it's only frustrated me and without a shadow of a doubt if you play the next game in the series, you can call the narrators sections break time where you just leave the game running for a few minutes to get a drink, a sandwich or something. The narrator sucks and so does his stupid opening theme song.Graphically, it's pretty good. Voice acting is mostly good. I liked the characters and the setting more than what was on offer in Man of Medan (aside from the narrator). Some people may like the ending, which is fine but for me it's given me little hope that the third instalment will be anything other than military woman has ptsd and imagines things: the game. I might try the next game, but I'll be waiting for it to be heavily discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: Decent game if you are looking for a interactive horror narrative the length of a mini series but get it on discount.Firstly, this is an  game and should be assessed on this basis. If your intention is to buy a survival horror game or a combat focused horror themed game, then you should not purchase this game.This game offers an immersive experience that allows you to shape outcomes based on your choices and ability to pass the quick time events. The game focuses on exploration, conversation/conduct choices, quick time events and process where a portion of the plot and backstory is revealed to the player through observation. voice acting, excellent graphics and animation, good game world design and the ability to keep the player in suspense throughout the game which is a good point for a game within the horror genre. The game over-relies on jump scares. While some jump scares are required in order to keep the player in suspense, primary horror elements (e.g. fear, disturbance, shock, disgust etc.) should be conveyed by other means such as through the narrative itself. While the game utilizes other methods to deliver horror elements, jump scares in the game have been turned into a plot mechanic. In addition, the effect of each jump scare employed for use in the game decreases the impact of subsequent jump scares. The first negative point is the game's brevity. I completed the game in 5.5 hours. While brevity is not a necessarily a bad quality, a game that can be completed in 5.5 hours indicates that the game may not have offered sufficient content to justify the price currently charged on the Steam store (I paid about US$30).The second negative point is the game's abrupt ending. From my perspective, the narrative was still in the process of gathering momentum at the point the game ended. I was left with the impression that character development was not complete and there was a missed opportunity for a true climatic moment.

_childDocuments_.review: To be honest, I didn't really plan to write this review. I mean... what is there to say? It's the second game in 's horror anthology (a series of short spooky stories told in "choose your own adventure" way with some  elements) and I already wrote detailed review of  (which was the first one), so, like I said, what else is there to say? Surprisingly, it turned out that, even though the core mechanics here is almost identical to what we've seen in , the actual storytelling, the  of the game is pretty different and it does make it to feel... well... . So... here goes.First of all, unlike , this game allows you to re-play previous scenes at any point. In other words, you don't need to play through the entire thing to be able to return to the main menu and re-start from any place you've already visited. And you  want to do that. For two reasons. First –  play (way) bigger role now and it'll be easy to lose one of your characters pretty often. And second – unlike ,  heavily relies on the exploration. I mean, sure, you needed to do some exploration in  to get the full picture of what's going on, but in this game? The entire ending will depend on what you will discover on the way. This time we've got ourselves a witch story (you know,  kind of stuff) and technically speaking, you'll need to discover who put  in the  (if you know what I mean), otherwise, no one will be happy.And that's... quite an interesting thing. See, what we've got here is a multi-layered story. With tons of details, some of which will become clear only during the ending. Which is way,  more interesting than what we had in , in which things were pretty obvious since very beginning. But at the same exact time... it feels a little bit weird. Especially for those of us who play in either co-op or hotseat. Because yes, multiplayer mode is still the main dish in this game, with single player being only five-hours-long thing that, while being totally fine, can't really compete with what you'll get in a company. You see,  with its unique structure that used to make you question everything, was  funny in multiplayer exactly because of that. It was impossible to say what's real and what's not. People used to panic and therefore make a lot of stupid mistakes. And it was  exactly because of that. If you've ever seen horror movies before, you know exactly what I'm talking about. Remember all of those kids on the screen? Screaming and running like idiots and therefore ending up dying in some very stupid ways? That's exactly what  used to make you to do. Here? It's exactly different story (pun not intended). Together with your friends, you'll try to discover as many clues as possible and make some right decisions, while trying to survive all the  encounters. In other words, it's not about panicking anymore. It's about the exploration and  skills. And somehow... it's hard not to miss what we had in previous game.I'm not trying to say that  feels bad, or something like that. Quite the opposite. I'm a  fan of this kind of stories  I'm very glad that the amazing idea of people playing adventure games online that  brothers ( / ) had back in early s () is still alive and kicking. But at the same exact time, the new formula doesn't feel nearly as exciting as the one from  where it was easy to lose the character just because one of your friends panicked and made some really poor choices. Even in single player the new formula doesn't feel nearly as exciting. Just because... you know. After you learn the truth, the game starts to get boring and not only I didn't feel motivated enough to play through the alternative cut (an alternative mode that puts a different set of characters from your group into the spotlight and shows you about an hour of cutscenes you haven't seen before), I didn't even feel like I wanted to save everybody. Just because... but no, I won't spoil it to you. I already said that the story is more complicated this time, let's just say that there won't be nearly as much sense in saving everybody this time.So... yeah. I totally admire the fact that  didn't try to just copy / past things from their previous game. While using the same exact mechanics, they did their very best to make  to feel different. And it does. For both good and bad. I totally loved the story this time, the setting is very solid, the atmosphere is fantastic (as long as you love woods, fog, abandoned houses and stuff like that) and all in all, the game has quite a lot of things to surprise you during your first run. But at the same time, multiplayer mode (again, let's not forget that multiplayer is a main dish here) doesn't feel nearly as exciting. Just because the entire “don't trust your eyes” thing is gone and it's all about the  now. Also, the endgame development can feel a bit frustrating. Especially during your first try. For example, even if you'll be able to achieve the good ending, some of your characters will still be able to die. Just because of some choices you've made ages ago, without even knowing about the impact they'll have on the ending. It's like “Hey! We won! Yay!” and then BOOM! Some monster appears and one of your guys is dead. With no way for you to interfere. It's kinda... smart and when you'll look back and think about all that during your second run, it'll start making sense to you, but at the first time... no, seriously, it's a mess. Playing through the entire thing and then watching your guys dying? Doesn't feel right.I still do recommend this game, though. Heck, I think I'm turning into ' fan. Totally love the way they tell their stories. From  to  to . Can't really call any of those games perfect, but somehow,  never fail to create that certain feeling that makes you feel like you're actually diving into a movie. And I'm not even a big fan of the interactive movies. It's just... I dunno, with  it's always  to be a part of all that. To explore, to make the mistakes, to try and figure out what's going on... I always end up feeling like everything I see in the game is real. For whatever screwed up reason there is. And the multiplayer mode that  offers? I don't think you'll find anything else like that on the market. You have friends who love horror movies? You're in for a treat. Especially if those friends are living nearby. Because personally? I'm totally in love with the hotseat mode here. Just make sure to order enough pizza and the next five hours of your life will be awesome. I'd say, play  first, though. Because, even though story there isn't as cool as in , multiplayer-wise, it's the best one so far. Dixi.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Hope follows a group of survivors trapped in a fog-shrouded town haunted by eerie visions of the 17th-century witch trials. The narrative weaves psychological horror with supernatural elements, creating an unsettling atmosphere where reality blurs with nightmarish hallucinations.The story stands out with its chilling premise and themes of guilt and redemption, but it falters with repetitive scares and slow pacing. While choices play a significant role in determining the fates of characters, the impact of these decisions can feel inconsistent, and some twists in the plot may not resonate with everyone.Despite its flaws, Little Hope delivers a hauntingly mysterious experience with a tense, creepy ambiance, but it might leave you craving a more satisfying resolution.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Hope is the second story in the Dark Pictures horror anthology. Three college students and two teachers have been trapped in a small abandoned town, and the player must guide them to safety. As is usual for this type of narrative focused game, the primary gameplay mechanics involve making dialogue choices and performing QTEs during action scenes.After the first hour of establishing the story, I felt like the group was in constant danger, being attacked frequently by strange monsters, whose visual design is very creative. Any of the main characters can die if you make bad choices or mess up the QTEs, and while I wouldn’t say the game is scary, this certainly makes the action scenes feel intense. I kept everybody alive on my first attempt in Man of Medan, but I didn’t have the same success in Little Hope.The story was mostly well written and has an interesting sense of mystery, incorporating different time periods and themes of witchcraft, but the ending was kind of annoying. It makes sense, but it made me feel like ultimately nothing I did had any relevance. Its a shame, because until that final scene I really enjoyed playing Little Hope. It took me 4.7 hours to finish the story, which is almost an hour longer than Man of Medan, but still quite short.Voice acting is very good, although I have to mention one moment of unintentional comedy, when one of the group insists that another character spoke in a strange unrecognisable accent, as more evidence that weird stuff is happening in the town. Where I live, we call that accent “Yorkshire”. I guess they’ve never seen a Sean Bean film.Controls worked fine with my Xbox 360 controller, and I didn’t have any problems with bugs or framerate. However I’m disappointed that the developers insist on continuing their version of Telltale’s “x will remember this”, where pretty much every choice made or item collected flashes up a message in the top corner informing the player of “traits updated” or “bearing updated”. Its hard to be scared when you’re constantly being reminded that you’re playing a game.Little Hope is worth playing if you like horror stories, but I definitely advise waiting for a sale, because its short and the replay value is questionable.

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10Having now finished all of the games in The Dark Pictures Anthology, season 1, I now feel confident in giving the games a proper review. This game is alright, it has an interesting setting and an overall compelling story. However, the script is often terrible and the characters are very unlikeable. The horror mainly come from a TON of cheap jump-scares (which I absolutely hate) and gets annoying quickly. However, the ending is great and overall made up for the sub-par experience along the way.Being the second entry in The Dark Pictures Anthology, season 1, Little Hope puts you in the shoes of five survivors of a buss-crash. You alternate between controlling each of them as they venture from their wreck into the town of Little Hope to seek help. However, the town seems deserted except for a few odd inhabitants and a pack of monsters and spirits to help and hinder the survivors on their trip home. The gameplay consists of quicktime-events, freely exploring the town (one small area at a time) and making decisions for the characters that alter the story vastly. A choice could be the difference between life and death, so be careful.It is hard not to go into more detail when describing what is good and bad about Little Hope, as a lot of my opinions are rooted in the story, which I do not want to spoil. The "good" is mainly that as a Supermassive Games-game, it does the job. It also has a great ending. That is about it, the rest is meh or outright bad. The acting is nothing special, the writing is sometimes laughably bad and the constant use of cheap jump-scares makes me more angry than properly scared. I hate screamers that get up in your face and it happens at least 15 times throughout the short game.It is time to summarize:+ An overall interesting story with a great ending+ Fantastic visuals- Poor writing- Overuse of jump-scares- Mediocre acting at bestOverall, I only give this a 6/10 because of the ending. The game is so short that I do not feel robbed of my time, but this is not a step up from Man of Medan. If you have already started playing this series you are probably going to be playing this but if you just browse games made by Supermassive Games and have no experience with Until Dawn or The Quarry, you should 100% play thise instead of this series.

Note that it's still QTE fighting, but boy, are you glad you hit that button in time. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: After loving MAN OF MEDAN so hard (it's one of my favourite games), LITTLE HOPE was a letdown. I really wanted to like it, and some of it was very good. The creepiness factor was dialled way up, and the setting of a decaying old town haunted by its witch-trials past was the perfect setting for a horror game. I liked the experience of settling into a new cast of characters and learning their personalities and secrets. But the ending let me down.If you liked other games in the Dark Pictures Anthology, you might give LITTLE HOPE a try. You might like it. I had major issues with the story resolution, which might not be your experience. But if you're looking for a deep, internally consistent narrative like MAN OF MEDAN, I would skip this game and go on to HOUSE OF ASHES.Pros:-creepy, well-detailed setting-lots of jump scares (if you like them this is a pro, otherwise it's a con)-deep characters you can explore throughout the game-the same 'choices matter' style storytelling as other games in the franchiseCons:-a few, but let's just talk about the ending

_childDocuments_.review: Like Man of Medan, Little Hope is based to some extent on true events or legends and this time it's about the Salem witch trials of the late 17th century.With a great atmosphere, we are a group of college students and their professor on a school trip when the school bus has an accident.And things seem to escalate relatively quickly.The bus driver has disappeared from the scene of the accident and an impenetrable and mysterious fog makes the search for help one hell of a trip.We are inevitably stuck in Little Hope, where, it seems, time has stood still.Apart from the witch trials that took place here, the city was once a thriving business location. At least until the local textile factory closed and the residents gradually left.What remained was a ghost town that is now haunted by the past.And I can tell you this much:The resolution at the end is quite successful and whoever survives Little Hope's nightmare will be surprised. This is largely due to the fact that the story remains relatively unpredictable and delivers good moments of tension and comes along with a twist at the end., the game is again more like a movie than a classic game. Although you have the opportunity to move freely with the protagonists in the limited areas, Little Hope remains true to its roots and itself in a playful way.As usual, in the dialogues you have the choice between two conversation options that influence the future behavior of the character and, depending on the action, is a decision that can sooner or later affect the course of the story.In the more action-packed passages, some QTEs have to be passed again. In this part there are new small "pre-warnings" so that you don't get caught on the wrong foot like in Man of Medan.Different icons briefly show in advance whether you have to press a button or, for example, face a challenge in the form of aiming at your opponent.These QTEs are sometimes the most important when it comes to keeping all characters alive.Also important again are the secrets that are often found off the obvious path. These secrets give you information about what's really going on in Little Hope. And as usual, when exploring, you "stumble" over postcards or pictures that point to a possible, mostly fatal event in the future.But the same applies here: if you want to see everything, you have to play through the game several times.The game deliberately uses horror clichés in its narrative and offers a thoroughly exciting story. Still, like its predecessor, it's an absolute jumpscare-fest and spooky-wise the game is no picnic.The abandoned village, the mysterious opaque fog, the forests and the cemetery are almost too many horror clichés at once, but for no reason they are not represented in so many games and films.Coupled with the cruel witch trials, you know why you might get goosebumps while playing. But it only gets really disturbing when Mary, the little girl, appears.With every contact you experience memories from the time of the witch trials and in the form of the protagonists.Unfortunately, the whole horror is destroyed by too many jump scares, always the same and unfortunately predictable over time.A bunch of stupid teenagers: check ✓The cat running through the picture: check ✓A scary little girl: check ✓In his stylishly furnished library, he comments and evaluates the actions of the player and obviously enjoys teasing us with a few cryptic clues and tips packed in riddles. However, he does not have a direct influence on the story and what exactly the curator is all about remains a mystery so far.For me, the great thing about The Dark Pictures Anthology is that I can very well do without my unloved phrases like "the other was better". This is of course subjective, but I think that “the game is different” is much more accurate and does justice to each and every one of the games.. But that is due to the actual scenario with the foggy ambience and I personally found the characters more interesting.The plot with the little "time travel", the bizarre creatures and the mysterious doppelgangers remains quite exciting until the end, even if the "shock effects" wear off a bit over time.The tricky animations, respectively the facial expression transitions and the controls can certainly still be improved, but unlike in Man of Medan, the story in Little Hope is not only forward-looking, but a story that overlays several epochs, which actually makes the biggest difference.Little Hope isn't a psychological masterpiece of horror, nor is it a "continuous shocker". It's interactive cinema and anyone who can get involved in this way and can overlook the cinematic staging in terms of game depth, mechanics and length can expect an atmospheric and audiovisually successful and sometimes convincing horror experience.✅ Atmospheric environment and sound✅ oppressive mood✅ cinematic staging✅ Worthwhile co-op through more scenes✅ exciting story✅ Decisions affect the course of the story✅ Detailed locations✅ mysterious curator✅ different endings✅ alternate history✅ increasing level of difficulty✅ good tutorial❌relatively short❌minor technical defects❌unsympathetic pale characters❌Cracky animations❌ Consequences seem arbitrary❌Predictable jump scares❌End with open questions

_childDocuments_.review: I gotta say the narrative really crashed and burned for me during the last act.Which was fatal for me personally in a game that is nothing but the narrative, because the characters certainly aren't a factor since none of them actually exist. I was honestly atleast a little invested in the characters making it out alive. This was unfortunately detrimental to my experience.I gotta question if certain mechanics in this game, such as the relationship tracking decisions, are just for show since this seemed to have no bearing on the narrative, atleast in my playthrough. Maybe it does maybe it doesn't but me even questioning this is an issue to say the least.Technical issues all around with this one too. Weird out of place models, teleporting and disappearing NPCs the list goes on. The biggest offender has to be the pricing of this game. As of writing this game costs 30€ on Steam. However if you'd like to play with a friend your friend also has to buy the game, because the devs disabled the friend pass. So for the full coop experience you need to pay 60 bucks in total. Pretty steep for a 4 hour game. Of course multiple playtroughs are incentivised. For a one and done however this price is completley unreasonable and quite frankly disgusting.Lastly I'd like to mention something which players in english speaking countries might not even realise. The invitee in a coop lobby is forced to play with the native dub of his current country of residence. I currently reside in Germany. This forced me to endure the god awful german dub of this game, while my friend could enjoy the english voice acting, which was apparently pretty good.This game honestly made me appreciate the work of David Cage and I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate the work of David Cage let me tell ya.

The cut scenes also just jump all over the place and it doesn't feel fluid whatsoever.  Like two of my characters were at a store, i opened the door for my second character to come in, We then left the building? and then all of a sudden, cut, we are back on the road no where near the building we were just at.

_childDocuments_.review: Was kind of indecisive whether to upvote or downvote but I ended up going with downvote. The game isn't really that bad to be honest and it makes for a decent playthrough ... the first time around. The issue is that the ending kind of kills the replay value. Replay value is what makes these games shine and apart from the ending there is another problem that hinders the replay value of the game: the moment to moment choices don't really matter. There are set moments in the game that will decide whether a character will die or not based on their character traits. Like I was trying really hard to kill off Taylor by failing every QTE possible when she was in danger but since she wasn't meant to die yet I could not make her die until the "trait check" arrived. So in a way your decisions affect the long term outcome of the characters but that doesn't really feel that satisfying and kind of pigeonholes you certain decisions to ensure you get certain traits. It's kind of the opposite of Man of Medan when it comes to replay value.These games have basically no gameplay so they should lean heavily into the "your choices matter" aspect of interactive movies and the game really falls flat in that regard.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a fan.Spoilers Ahead.There's nothing I despise more than the "it was all a dream" plot twist. _childDocuments_.review: Do you remember the days when you’d take field trips in school. Loading into the bus with all your fellow miscreants, driving for an hour or two, then touring some historic place where Betty Boop, or Mr. Potatoe Head lived 450 years ago, walking through their boring house or historical sights, and wondering when it would be over. The boredom forcing you to rip out chunks of your hair.. Then after 3 or 4 hours, you scuttle back onto the bus, and drive another hour back home.. Imagine, if you will that trip back home gets detoured, and then your bus crashes…..  not the cool fiery crash you see on youtube videos, but the, that sucks I banged my head and scrapped my knee type of crashes..   Upon exiting the bus you find yourself trapped and unable to escape, being forced to travel towards an uncertain fate surrounded by bags from school that you probably hate..Well if you can imagine that scenario above then you’ll probably know what to expect in Dark Pictures Little Hope, the second entry into the Dark Pictures Anthology (Think they are calling it season 1, and it has four entries thus far, Man of Medan, Little Hope, House of Ashes and Devil Inside me)  If you’ve played any of the games you sort of get the idea how the game words,, for those who haven’t here goes.. The Curator, introduces you to himself, and proceeds to pull out a book, which he claims is unfinished and says you will be the one to write it.The Story – Four students and their teacher are returning from a field trip, their bus is detoured into little hope and eventually winds up crashing after the driver swerves to avoid hitting a little girl.  Lost, confused and with the Bus Driver no where to be found the Five lost adventurers start their quest to find the driver, find help or maybe even find themselves.Gameplay – If you’ve played any of the TellTale style adventure games you’ll get a good idea how these games work.  Third person exploration, with loads of cutscenes, some QTE’s, finding collectibles and making lots of choices, choices which unlike most of the later TellTale games actually matter in the grand scheme of things..Pros Tremendously interesting and engaging storyUniquely replay ableEasy achievementsBite Sized 4 hour adventureCons Poorly Optimized (was getting lag with my 4090)Minor Graphical and sound issuesCan’t skip cut scenes you’ve already seenRecommendation – Little hope set aside the atmospheric approach to horror that Man of Medan took and went with Jump scares, and since we’re in 2023, jump scares are kind of weak sauce..  With that said, Little hope tells a compelling story that blends elements of the past with the present to create a edge of your seat thrill ride up until the end.  The game is worth the price of admission for some of the gore, which was clearly ramped up from Man of Medan..  So I’d recommend picking this game up if you’re into Telltale Style action adventure games, the story is out of this world.. or dimension and you’ll be happy you did..

_childDocuments_.review: Little Hope - A Haunting Tale of Mystery and ChoicesLittle Hope is a captivating and atmospheric psychological thriller that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. From the creators of Until Dawn, this interactive horror experience delivers a chilling narrative filled with twists, turns, and moral dilemmas that will leave you questioning every decision you make.Set in the eerie town of Little Hope, the game's visuals are hauntingly beautiful, with a sense of foreboding that permeates every scene. The attention to detail in the environments and character design draws you into the story and enhances the feeling of isolation and dread.The story of Little Hope is a gripping blend of supernatural elements, psychological horror, and mystery. As you guide a group of characters through a series of terrifying events, you'll uncover the dark history of the town and its inhabitants, all while trying to survive the night and escape the malevolent forces at play.One of the standout features of Little Hope is its emphasis on player choice and consequence. Every decision you make, big or small, can have far-reaching effects on the story and the fate of the characters. This creates a sense of tension and urgency that keeps you invested in every moment, wondering what repercussions your choices will have down the line.The characters in Little Hope are well-developed and complex, each with their own fears, secrets, and motivations. The stellar voice acting brings them to life, making you care deeply about their fates and adding emotional weight to the unfolding events.Gameplay-wise, Little Hope offers a mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and quick-time events that keep the pace engaging and the tension high. The game's multiple endings and branching paths encourage replayability, as you strive to uncover all the secrets hidden within the town of Little Hope.In conclusion, Little Hope is a must-play for fans of narrative-driven horror games. With its atmospheric setting, compelling story, and impactful choices, it delivers a memorable and immersive experience that will stay with you long after the credits roll. Prepare to be scared, surprised, and thoroughly entertained as you unravel the mysteries of Little Hope.

_childDocuments_.review: The Dark Pictures Anthology: Little Hope is a story driven horror game, where 4 students and a professor suffer a bus accident around Little Hope and can't escape from the fog around them. They need to venture more into to stare into their dark fate.This review is based on Shared Play Online.One is definetly something I need to mention, is the gameplay. If you played Men of Medan or Until Dawn, it will be familiar. You get small areas to check, search for clues and moments, which give you hints about your future and making hard decision, which might save your characters... or kill them. What I liked about it, the game is straight forward playing. It's not too difficult at all. Also, playing with a friend through online is really fun in my opinion, because you can play both type of scenes, which makes the whole gameplay better. The game has Quick Time Events and they are not annoying at all, and got easier, because the game will show you in advance, where the button will appear and you can get prepare. It's not too easy either. You get difficult choices too, which can change the gameplay greatly. In short, gameplay is really sweet, but some people won't like the fact, the game is 6 hours long. Also, the game has some issues at online, like the infinite loading screens, which happens when you stop after loading times or sometimes mid cutscenes. You can try to fix it with loading back a previous checkpoint or if the other player can move, try to trigger a cutscene. With us, this problem occured 2 times, thankfully we were able to continue it. Really good gameplay, short playtime and few annoying or some gamebreaking bugs, but still a really good point so far.About the story itself... _childDocuments_.review: The theme of the game is a witch hunt that took place in the late 17th century in New England, in the north-east of the USA. Throughout the approximately five-hour adventure, one can find motifs from the Silent Hill series, as well as many cinematic images, such as The Witches of Salem, The Omen, The Messenger of Hell or The Witch. Most importantly, however, the new English game performs far better than the first episode of The Dark Pictures, improving on most of its predecessor's flaws. While the first game of the series was basically a disappointment, I thoroughly enjoyed this oneThe once prosperous New England town of Little Hope suffered decades ago from economic decline and the closure of its factories, and it was impossible to survive on tourism alone. Particularly as the town was reaping the rewards of its grim past, with tragic events mirroring those in Salem and Andover. People were drowned, burned at the stake and crushed, and the devilish energy born of blatant injustice, as you might guess, is back to take revenge on those who happen to be entangled in Little Hope. Our unlucky victims are the victims of a bus crash that overturned a block away from the boarded-up (and quite literally so) town. They are lost students straight out of a horror film about teenagers, their grumpy old friend and a professor trying to keep his head on straight, whose only hope, nomen omen, is to move on. And there is nowhere to go, because 'Little Hope' offers perhaps the greatest  area for exploration so far, usually empty, but nevertheless necessary to explore, as we learn the history of the cursed place from notes or newspapers discovered here and there. We can also find illustrations bearing prophecies of a possible future, always vague, but nevertheless successfully building up tension.The plot here is more complex than it appears at first glance. Suffice it to say that, plot-wise, Little Hope is by far Supermassive Games' strongest offering, but its effect is subordinated, for better or worse, to the finale. It does a good job of explaining the script's kinks, clarifying all the inconsistencies and wrapping things up, but on the other hand it doesn't encourage you to finish the game again. In other words, despite a good story, in terms of gameplay this is probably the least attractive part of the Dark Pictures Anthology (I also include Until Dawn in this collection out of convenience), both because of its poor replay value and low difficulty level. Encounters with creatures are great, it's still fun to play with someone next to you on the sofa or on the other side of the internet connection, and the whole thing is directed with aplomb and jump scares can give you sudden heart palpitations, but Little Hope struggles to generate tension during the numerous exploration scenes. There seems to have been too much subordination of the story - whose leitmotif is dealing with loss and guilt - to the pace of the gameplay, with the result that interactivity is relegated to the background, making us more of an observerNonetheless a successful game that did not disappoint and is worth trying out.

_childDocuments_.review: Of the three games released so far Man of Medan remains my favorite to play because of the diverse cast and branching storylines, but when it comes to actual story House of Ashes definitely wins for best narrative.  Set in 2003 we join a group of soldiers in the Gulf War searching for chemical weapons following the capture of Saddam Hussein, but not before a brief and terrifying prologue set 4,000 years prior where we play as a Sumerian temple guard defending against an invading army.  How these two events tie together will quickly be revealed.As expected, House of Ashes maintains that same level of cinematic quality with exciting locations, and a diverse cast of characters all expertly portrayed by actors lending their voices and motion-capture performances to create a truly interactive movie.  My only issue with the game was the character model for Rachel King (Ashly Tisdale) that goes well into “uncanny valley” territory.  Her voice performance was fine, but knowing what Ashly looks like in real-life and seeing this creepy recreation in the game was really distracting; not that having her drenched in Carrie post-prom blood for the final act of the game wasn’t already distracting.I really enjoyed House of Ashes.  It had some truly terrifying moments, great story reveals, interesting relationship building, and a cinematic quality that you don’t often get in horror adventure games.  A single pass through the story took me just over six hours and only earned me seven of the thirty possible achievements, so there is plenty of incentive to revisit this game in the future and definitely share it with friends. Read full review at First two hours of gameplay at More Steam reviews on our Curator page -

_childDocuments_.review: It was very hard to choose whether to recommend this game or not.Since I had a blast playing it all the way trough, I ultimately decided to recommend it, but god dang did the ending leave a sour taste in my mouth.This is the second game in the Dark Pictures Anthology and this was way better than it's predecessor, Man of Medan.-The characters were way more interesting-The story was way more exciting-A lot of the problems Man of Medan had were solved:--The QTE's sometimes came out of nowhere in Man of Medan, in Little Hope, there are warnings before a QTE, which is a very nice quality of life addition--The "Button Mash" QTE looked almost exactly the same as the normal QTE's in Man of Medan, resulting in some deaths because you didn't realise you had to press the button multiple times. In Little Hope, the button mash QTE is very distinct.-The Movie night gamemode was way better implemented. Movie night is a gamemode where everyone gets their owncharacters assigned and you pass the controlled when it's your turn to play your character.In Man of Medan, you were often responsible for the lives of other characters, making you feel like you didn't really have control over your own fate.In Little Hope you're usually in control over your own character during the crucial moments and one feature I especially liked was where the controls switched between characters during 1 scene. For example, when 2 characters have to run away and jump over a bunch of obstacles, then you'd first control the guy in the front and do the QTE's to jump over them and then the camera switches over to the character in the back and now it was their turn to do the QTE's.It was a very fun feature when playing with multiple people.So, after all those improvements. It shocks me that they still managed to screw up the ending.The game would literally been better if the game suddenly just stopped instead of showing that ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this game a positive review because I want the devs to make more, but this installment was disappointing.The ending is fine. I have no problems with the ending. BUT:THIS GAME IS SO LINEAR. This is Until Dawn levels of linear. Choices barely matter. The game tricks you into thinking traits can determine a character's death, when really it's just one dialogue choice you make that will result in a character surviving until the end or not (assuming you hit most QTEs).Andrew and John -- that is, 2 of the 5 protagonists -- are GUARANTEED to survive until the game is almost over. That's ridiculous. In Man of Medan, anyone can die before Act 3 (while there is a maximum of two deaths, those two deaths can be a variety of combinations). This game is so much more linear. Every chapter is guaranteed to happen, and while there is admittedly variety in who does what in those chapters and in the dialogue you get, the situations stay the same.The Bearings are not like Until Dawn or Man of Medan at all. They just update as things happen on screen, regardless of the choices you make. Guaranteed cutscenes while activate/update Bearings even though you didn't make a choice. Apparently the devs forgot how to their own Bearing system works.I guess the main pro is that it's longer, and the characters and plot are fine -- but it's barely a choice-based game. Until Dawn isn't, either. This and Until Dawn both have barely any variety in terms of situations and plot developments. Man of Medan is much better than Little Hope in this regard -- it doesn't give certain characters plot armor and it has branching gameplay.Supermassive, you did branching choice-based horror right with Man of Medan.. Until Dawn was not good when it came to its "butterfly effect" concept. Little Hope is not good when it comes to its "moral compass" concept, which is the same thing. Man of Medan got it right. Please do better than this in House of Ashes.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start with a warning. If it wasn't for the brilliant story I would not recommend this.The simple fact is that I did love this game. The visuals are great, the sound for the most part is too, but if it had directional audio I couldn't tell. The voice acting (or acting in general) was top notch and the whole vibe of the stories was perfect. There did seem to be odd scene changes at times though, as if something else was supposed to happen, but didn't. Perhaps these change depending on your choices and the reaction to them from the game world and it's characters.What nearly killed this for me was the bizarre choice of turning the game into a point and click with incredibly twitchy quick time events that caused many of characters to die off in ways that felt no fault of my own, unlike previous efforts where I just wasn't quick enough. Add to this a laborious camera that fought against you every inch of the way and you have a build up of dread for the mechanics instead of the story, which deserves to hold centre stage. Those game mechanics felt like such a bad choice for this. I don't mind the odd quick time event (after all, they are a staple of The Dark Pictures), but please get rid of the point and click style. They just didn't gel well together.Still, if you liked Supermassive Games' other stuff, you'll no doubt still get enjoyment from it. I look forward to the next one with excitement.

It's annoying, because a person is hoping for some additional information / additional inspection of the object, but he doesn't get anything◉ Your games often give the effect of uncanny valley, which is probably even more horror than the genre treatments themselves◉ Incomprehensible decisions with QTE events. Clicking specific keys gives potential for error, clicking the mouse in a specific place on the screen not necessarily. All the pressure is gone while its so hard to fail anything◉ It would be nice if you would go for some horror elements that are more integrated into the game (like something happening in the distance, something unpleasant to look at or anything that is psychically exhausting) rather than constant jumpscares that feels quite cheap while overused◉ The absurdity of decisions-making which forces you to chose more illogical options in order to achieve "better" ending is nuts. These are logical only from a perspective of a player that already knows the ending and can relate to that, but wouldn't really make much sense if approached without such knowledge◉ Situations where a group of characters is attacked by some enemy and no one can help or if they actually try to they do it in a very clumsy way looks ridiculous◉ Situations where the character randomly disappears from the scene even though he was standing next to it a moment ago◉ Situations where both players will approach some place that triggers cutscene, but when the scene is triggered only one character is there and the other is just approaching (I know that they are prerendered but it still can affect the experience a bit)◉ Showing at the end of each cutscene that something is following us was repetitive and lazy◉ Infinite loading screens that occured so many times that we actually thought about dropping the game◉ There was a chunk where part of the cutscene was played twice◉ You have to ask if someone sees the scene because its hard to tell whether we experience the same part of content or not➝ I didn't like the plot, but there are so many other things that went wrong and actually ruined my experience throughout the game, that me not liking the plot is the last problem that I should mention. Its actually riddiculous to see something like this in such story-driven project.--TLDR:It's quite freakin bad...

_childDocuments_.review: Silent Hill meets The Crucible. It's a straight to the point, CYOA styled, suspenseful, interactive movie game.. but it's a bit rough around the edges. SIMILAR GAMES: Silent Hill, Man of Medan, Until Dawn SIMILAR MOVIES: The Crucible, Blair Witch Project, Sleepy HollowFor those unfamiliar with Supermassive Games (the developer), they make interactive movie games (Until Dawn, Hidden Agenda, Man of Medan) much like David Cage (Detroit: Become Human, Beyond Two Souls, Heavy Rain). Those names right there should give you a fairly good idea about whether or not you'll be enjoying this game. In general, these movie games are heavily story driven and usually have minimalist gameplay. You'll explore some fairly linear environments, take control of a group of characters, learn the backstory to each character, find some collectibles, view some premonitions, make important split second decisions that can potentially kill off your character (CYOA approach), and encounter a bunch of quick time events that can also kill off your character. Everyone can live or everyone can die - that's what makes this genre so interesting. Yes they are a lot of QTEs and jump scares so if you don't like that, this game might not be for you. Additionally, if you want to do a lot of actual PLAYING, this might also not be for you. Little Hope is the second game in Supermassive's new video game horror anthology - The Dark Pictures. You don't need to play Man of Medan at all to enjoy this game. There is no relationship except the Curator who hosts this horror anthology.Without going into too much detail, Little Hope is set in a deserted New England town with an infamous history of witch hunting. Our five protagonists find themselves being forced to journey through this town after their bus crashes and they are stranded in the middle of nowhere. Pretty soon, weird horror stuff starts to happen and they'll quickly find out they share more connections with the town than previously believed. Going into any more detail would just give it away. However I will say this - the story is quite refreshing. It's slightly more supernatural in nature giving you a break from the usual zombies/demons/science experiment gone wrong. The graphics are fairly nice for 2020 - I had no trouble maxing it out - 1440p/ultra/120+fps on my 2070 Super. No major glitches, crashes or bugs that I encountered. The game took me 6 hours to beat on my first playthrough hence the $30 price tag. Furthermore, the game is meant to be replayed at least once or twice as there are multiple endings so you'll get your money's worth. Great overall performance from movie actor Will Poulter and a decent so-so performance from the supporting cast. The game can be played alone or in a group of 5 people (everyone gets a character to babysit but you have to take turns watching your friends play). Each character's segment is about 15-20 minutes long. You can also play online with a friend but I haven't tried that yet and I'm not sure how well it works. I also played on the XBOX ONE controller and everything worked perfectly. Now as for my biggest complaint - the QTE segments. I'm fairly neutral on QTE. I don't love em or hate em. They are fine in small doses - just be clear and concise what and when you want us to press especially if you gotta press it once or tap multiple times. This game doesn't do that. So during a button mash segment, you'll press it once and waste a second realizing you should have been tapping. By then, it's too late and you fail. Additionally, there's a segment where you have to press buttons in a rhythmic manner, like a heartbeat, and the timing has to be near perfect (can't be too early or too late). That was fine too BUT you gotta tell us WHICH segment is coming up. There ARE indications telling you a QTE is coming up but not WHICH QTE and it's hard to differentiate between the three. I thought a QTE quick press was coming up but it was a QTE rhythm thus I failed the entire segment because I pressed the button that I saw pop up. My girlfriend played with me and encountered the exact same problem. We failed the segment. When you do that - your character is at risk of dying.. and that's exactly what happened, a character died. But you eventually get use to it on your second playthrough. It's not too complicated but when it's the only gameplay mechanic, you really expect it to be perfect. Also don't bother jumping back to the main menu hoping to reload an old save and make an alternate decision, the game makes SUPER FREQUENT autosaves as soon as you press the button. Some other things - the game really wasn't all that scary but it really depends on your definition of scary. Suspenseful? Yes definitely. Engaging? For sure. Scary like Outlast, P.T., or Amnesia? Not really. It's primarily here just to put a cheap smile on your face and give you an interesting narration, not raise industry standards on horror or anything like that. Yes there are a bunch of cliche horror tropes like no cell phone coverage, arrogrant characters wanting to split up, and poor decisions resulting in ridiculous hung by own sweater deaths. Yes there are a BUNCH of jump scares - some love it, some hate it. I believe in moderation they definitely went overboad with them towards the end. That being said, I still enjoyed the game and I'm gonna replay it later tonight. It wasn't as good as Until Dawn (my favorite Supermassive game) but I liked it better than Man of Medan. For $10-20 it's definitely worth playing at least once or especially on Halloween.

_childDocuments_.review: First thing first, this is not a game but a rather expensive interactive movie with 3-8h content depending on your play speed.I would recommend to buy this "game" for 10 bucks or less, if you can snatch it on a discount.Like Man of Medan, this game throws QTEs (Quick Time Events) at you. But like in the previous game, those Events are neither meaningful, nor carry deep consequences. 80-90% of all QTEs are distractions for the player without any real impact on the story.The next issue with the QTEs are the design of them. You have one new type of QTE, where a prompt is displayed on your screen, and you have to click it in a given time frame. But, your mouse cursor is hidden until the point where the QTE starts, which means you need time to A. Find your Cursor and B. Move the cursor and Click the prompt on the screen. The game tries to position the QTE as fair as possible in relaiton to your cursor, but does not put into consideration, that you can move your hidden cursor after the QTE was placed. That leads to some situations, where your cursor is in the upper left corner of your screen and the QTE prompt is in the lower right half, which makes it very hard to succed in this QTE. A fix to this solution would be, make the cursor visible bevor the QTE is shown.I experienced a bug in coop where i choose the english voice over for the game, but after joining the coop session, the game switched to german voice over, with no way for me to set it back to english. Even as a native german speaker i would not recommend under any circumstances to play this game with german voice over, unless you want to switch the genre of the game from "horror" to "comedy". Like in many games, the german voice over is stiff, emotionless and pale.The story and the possible outcomes are extreemly hard to predict, the QTEs sometimes seem out of place, where you are not able to predict, what a possible outcome of an event would be. That leads into situations where you have to be a "very big brain" or think out of the box to accomplish hat you think would be best, otherwise it feels like rolling a dice every time you make a decision.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Hope is a story driven game so i'll try to keep out anything spoiler-ish.Little Hope manages to fix what problem's Man Of Medan had, mainly the story, tone and feel. Man Of Medan had an issue where it tried to have a ghost story but kept slamming clue's down your throat which told you otherwise and made it feel more like a long and tedious Scooby-Doo episode. It also had a harsh issue of saying "well something could of been said/happened here but you didn't look at this object or go down a certain path".Little Hope manage's to fix this, creating a decent mystery that is engaging and the writing is improved to avoid those  awkward "You missed something" point's.The picture mechanic, wow did i forget this was a thing. In Man Of Medan it was pretty much pointless, they show'd you event's that you really couldn't avoid or wouldn't see at all if you didn't take one path. In Little Hope, these feel more involved. If you see a picture you get a good sense of what you should be looking out for to avoid or gain those situation's.QTE's and Action sequence's have been greatly improved in several way's. They actually give you a decent warning of a certain action that will happen so your not caught off-guard and are handed an overly cheap death to an unseen QTE. The other change which i don't want to spoil is excellent and really make's the overall experience much more fun.Before moving on to the issue's. I played this game solo, after playing Man Of Medan with friends there wasn't much interest in doing another one as a group. However it's clear that they designed Little Hope a lot better and in term's of the multiplayer aspect, i can see it being very fun in a group session. So if you where looking/ want to/ can, play this with friends.Now for the issues i had. The biggest issue is the overuse of JUMPSCARES. I'm not sure why they thought more was better, but every transition is a literal "spooky face screaming up in your face" and it get's very old and annoying fast. These are for specific transition's as well, which clearly could have been done better in any other form.Moving on, the writing is somewhat questionable. The dialogue of the character's will take a dive at point's but is pretty much standard horror character flare for the rest as the mystery continues.The last issue is something i don't really have but can and will probably see a lot of people have.The ending, oh boy, i feel they did well with it. Heck i even called and then dismissed it part way through. It's an unpopular choice for mystery/horror but i do feel it was done well here. I bring this up because, well, when it comes to horror game's, especially where there's mystery and the story keep's it vague and encourage's the player to make sense of it, alot of people don't try or develop some idolized version and get blind-sided and feel ripped-off. Outlast 2 is a great example, player's were looking for something that was never really there as it wasn't the story being told and pretty much complained to high hell.So if you do play it, go in with an open perspective and don't go in with a pre-conceived concept that you want to cling to.Overall, 5 step's forward 1 and half back.

_childDocuments_.review: (Contains unmarked spoilers)In spite of the title, my hopes for this game were high. Man of Medan(MoM) wasn't exactly good, but I still enjoyed it a lot, in the same way I enjoy watching horror B-movies. It had the right amount of honest camp to it that made up for its shortcomings to me. Not a good game, but a fun one. As such, I expected to at least get that from this game, too.Sadly, I was disappointed.Compared to its direct predecessor, Little Hope goes for a much stronger start. While the opening seems confused in terms of pacing, the game quickly settles in for creepy imagery and a much slower buildup, which helps capture a tense atmosphere.As the plot progresses, the mysteries keep piling on. Where MoM struggled to engage due to its basic premise being so painfully obvious, this time around I wanted to learn the answers to the questions the game posed. The characters, though one-dimensional, were at least a big enough step up to make me care for them. Their lack of depth this time comes more from a lack of development rather than being one-note.Sadly, the game flip-flops on what to do with them. Instead of exploring the characters and their dynamics, which seem to be the focus for the first half of the game, buried under the mystery of their mysterious dopplegängers in the past, towards the end the game simply rushed for the "hidden test of character" for each of them. Demoting terrifying demons to mere metaphors for their own personal shortcomings could have been an intriguing concept had it been developed from the start. Instead it painfully contrasts with the buildup the game had done up to that point.The same is even more true for the main plot. After a lot of buildup, puzzling developments and hinting at a larger picture connecting it all, literally all of that is dropped for a last minute twist that reminds me of the worst days of M. Night Shamalayan: A twist for the twist's sake, even if it makes for a worse story. The "subverting expectations" meme in a nutshell.The ending throws out all the development, all the mystery and with it all the appeal of the setting and plot. Even more annoying, upon replaying the early parts of the game, it outright contradicts information given in the game's very opening, making it fail to live up to its own internal consistency. That the game dares to pat itself on a back with a "guess you missed all this foreshadowing" montage just adds insult to injury in light of that.Little Hope's plot could have been another fun B-movie horror romp and that would have been fine. Instead, the story flatlines on the last second, leaving a conclusion that is neither cheesy bad fun nor well-written good fun. It's just bad.No changes here. The same formula was carried over 1:1 from Until Dawn(UD) and MoM and remains just as serviceable as it was prior. The controls still feel wonky in exploration moments and the slow movement can get more frustrating than anything when the lack of hurry while trying to explore every nook and cranny of a level clashes with a supposed sense of urgency in the story.The personality trait and relationship system first seen in UD is also around again, but still just as an empty shell of what it could be. While there is a veneer of it having some actual relevance to the story early on, it quickly become apparent that none of it has any impact other than changing a line of dialogue here or there. The major consequences still are tied to singular decisions. There is potential here, as always, but while the game at least acknowledges the system more properly this time, there is a lot of work to be done in future installments of the Anthology before it becomes an actual feature.The rest of the gameplay works just fine, but is disappointing for a different reason: It is altogether too easy. You mileage may of course vary, but with the preceding two games as my frame of reference, this is by far the easiest of them all. MoM and UD weren't super difficult, but there were a few moments where I hit a wrong button, screwed up an input, failed to keep still. Little Hope never had me stressed over any QTEs and as a result the only way to really get something wrong was via a 'wrong' choice. It says a lot that this is the first of Supermassive's games that I completed without any deaths and missed QTEs on the first try.It's not the end of the world, but in a game that wants to be frightening, easing on the difficulty (and not providing the option to adjust it) feels like a step in the wrong direction.The production values are a step up from MoM, but seem less impressive at the same time. Most of this is due to the very limited scope and drowning the entire surroundings in fog. While part of the story, it means the graphics can never really shine.The animations are improved over MoM and the times where a person talking looks off are fewer in between. However, blending from one facial animation to another still looks very uncanny, often making "cuts" in the dialogue that are there to facilitate multiple outcomes of previous choices all the more apparent.For the first time in a Supermassive game, the music stood out to me, and in a mostly good way. While towards the beginning and the end, it tends to go overly dramatic, a lot of the tracks, especially during the flashbacks, proved very effective and are actually a decent listen on their own.UD and MoM never quite delivered "horror", but "terror". Chase scenes, scares, all to get your blood pumping. Never the sort of stuff that makes you deeply uncomfortable and afraid to turn the next corner.Little Hope had the opportunity to finally improve on that, as the setting and slower pacing in the beginning lends itself to that quite well. However, though the initial buildup starts off well, the game tries much too hard to present a sense of danger at the same time. It seems at almost every other corner the camera reveals a spooky presence creeping through the woods, or watching the characters unseen, often accompanied by a scare chord.It is this worry about losing the players attention, this lack of trust in its own atmosphere that makes it fall flat. When terror hits, it still hits decently, but for getting much closer to actual horror than the previous games, it makes the failure to actually achieve it, and for such a silly reasons, all the more disappointing.Any chance of tension building is further ruined by the game's insistence of "spicing up" its exposition heavy moments by starting them off with frankly silly jumpscares, instantly deflating any fear build up to that point. Whether the developers were trying to meet a certain quota of "scream worthy" moments or were unable to execute a more subtle and scary transition between scenes in the present and scenes in the past, I don't know. It's a damned shame either way.This was by far the most disappointing of Supermassive's games so far, which is a damn shame. It had potential like no other. It also seemed to by *trying* harder in some areas. But for various reasons, many of them unnecessary, it falls short of those ambitions and loses much of its fun camp factor in the process. The result neither works as something fun for how bad it is, nor fun for how good it is. It's simply not fun and not good.If there is anything nice to say about it, it's that there's indication that Supermassive is learning. Some parts are improved over MoM, and with a bit of luck, future installments of the Anthology could reach the potential that is there, either in a truly good sense, or in another fun B-movie horror style.But for now, massive flaws in the writing and an inconsequential approach to presentation make this the worst Dark Picture yet.One can only hope House of Ashes, which I am still looking forward to, will remedy this regrettable downturn.

The ending would be bad normally, but it is especially bad within the context of the game. Some people don't mind it (or even like it, somehow), others had it ruin the experience entirely. Personally I found it left a bitter taste in my mouth even though I went in knowing about it and trying to keep an open mind. IF you are the type that isn't bothered by a bad ending if the journey is good enough then this MIGHT be worth your time. But I wouldn't want to have spent full price on this game, and I can't recommend you do so even if bad endings don't bug you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looks great and runs great with my only complaint being some jittery animations here and there that seem a bit uncanny. With that out of the way the most important thing to look at with a game such as this is substance and this game is a very mixed bag in that regard. Almost everything that makes up this game is subjectively a good or bad thing depending upon what it is you want out of this experience. If you're looking for a terrifying horror game with a compelling narrative then I would tell you to look elsewhere. If you're looking for a b-movie tier plot with characters to match but has just enough charm to keep you entertained for reasons that may or may not have been the original developer's intent, then maybe continue reading.[possible minor non-specific spoilers ahead] If you've played Man of Medan then you should expect characters in almost the same vein as that game. Their dialogue is rough and sometimes completely mismatched with the mood. The voice acting is at times rather stiff but a step up from Man of Medan at least. I personally found it difficult to grow attached to any of the main cast, every time I caught myself rooting for them to succeed it was mostly due to the fact that their success was crucial to continue the game. There are many times the characters create a situation outside of your control that you must then navigate to the best outcome. Which if we're speaking horror movies is not an uncommon scenario, but it is still annoying to see it happen so frequently, especially in a game setting where you are meant to control the story. The story is nothing special. It is a complete package but so is a dollar menu burger, may not be the best thing out there but it gets the job done. The plot moves along without much sense of direction for the first half of the game. The air of mystery that Man of Medan had when exploring the ship is pretty much nonexistent and feels more like a tour rather than a journey. The main objective, to get out of the town, somehow doesn't feel as threatening or urgent as escaping the ship and the bad guys in Man of Medan. The scares are pretty much all jump scares, and almost all the same jump scare. The environmental scares and subtle changes in scenery that Man of Medan had are nowhere to be found in this game. The monster design is decent but nothing you haven't seen before and any sense of danger that these monsters could invoke is thrown out the window when your only interactions with them are through long and drawn out quick-time events. Which leaves us with the ending, the major point of contention amongst all the reviews I've seen. It, like Man of Medan, has a twist ending. A subversion of expectations finishes this narrative after all your choices have been made. It's nothing new, it's been done before and it's both been done badly and also executed well in the past. Little Hope's execution was decent enough. I can see how it could have been a major let down to people but it really didn't bug me that much. So with all that said, why am I still recommending it? I enjoyed my time with it. Simple as that. I do really feel like this game is best enjoyed with other people, just like watching a b-movie with friends. It's got plenty to laugh at, plenty to talk about while its going and in the end this is one of those experiences where the end result isn't where the entertainment comes from. If you've got some friends to enjoy it with and love campy horror movies then give it a shot. If you liked Man of Medan then you'll probably like this one too. If all the negatives I've outlined in this review don't sit well with you, then this game isn't for you.
