_childDocuments_.review: I was pleasantly surprised by the improvements that Supermassive Games made to Little Hope over Man of Medan. Where Man of Medan felt rushed Little Hope was very polished. Here are the pros and cons of this game in relation to Man of Medan. (Forewarning, I only played this game Co Op so I can't speak for the singleplayer or Movie Night experience.)-Graphics and Performance: The graphics have improved by a noticeable margin since Man of Medan. Textures are more detailed and the lighting is the best it's ever been. But the performance increase compared to Man of Medan is incredible. Somehow this game looks better, is far more open and detailed and runs extremely better. Man of Medan often struggled with poor performance no matter the graphics settings and frequent lag spikes. Little Hope simply doesn't have this issue. I ran the game on Ultra without issue, running the game better than I ever did Man of Medan. I only ever noticed one lag spike, it happened when my character picked up an item and lasted a fraction of a second, and my friend only noticed one as well, when he looked down the road behind us but it only lasted a second. -Lack of Glitches and Crashes/Freezes: Completed the game without any glitches. None at all. Judging by the other reviews I seem fortunate in this matter. Once again, this was an issue that plagued Man of Medan that I was very glad wasn't present in Little Hope. Only complaint I have is that the start up time for the game was very slow for me, everytime I launched the game I'd sit on a black screen for 40 seconds and if I clicked anything the game would freeze and never start. -Gameplay: The gameplay hasn't changed much since Man of Medan but all of the small improvements they've made are greatly appreciated and the mechanics that already existed seem to have been perfected. The addition of a 360 degree camera in most areas was a nice addition.-Story: The story this time around was far better written than that in Man of Medan. The story is very complex and full of twists and turns making the story very hard to predict while never having a plot twist out of nowhere. -Characters: The quality of the characters is better but not all are equal. Some characters are definitely written better than others, some can be quite shallow. But despite this, every character in this game has more depth and intrigue than any in Man of Medan. -Horror: There were a couple times the game gave me chills and a few times I was certified spooked but overall it's not incredibly scary. This was about on par with Man of Medan to be honest. One thing I'll give Man of Medan is that it didn't use the heartbeat mechanic as much. Not that I don't like the heartbeat mechanic, I want it to stay, but it was used a lot and when it's in use seeing the enemy is nearly impossible since you're staring at the heartbeat bar. I felt that this kinda detracted from the horror a bit. I found this game more stressful, not in a bad way, than scary.-Voice Acting/Dialogue: For my final point of discussion, the quality of the voice acting has been improved but its still not perfect. Man of Medan really struggled with its dialogue, every other line left me groaning from either cringe or from terrible voice acting (90% cringe, 10% bad voice acting. I don't blame most of the voice actors but some of them in Man of Medan were just terrible.) Little Hope though, while still having these issues a little bit, was solid. There were a couple lines during the beginning of the game that were cringy and one voice actor at the beginning let out a terribly performed line but overall I was impressed by the considerable increase in quality here. Conclusion: Where Man of Medan left me with dread for the future of the Dark Pictures Anthology, Little Hope leaves me with nothing but... Hope (yeah, I shuddered writing that lmao). Again, I was really impressed by the sheer amount of improvements they made and if they continue with this momentum into next year this will become a legendary series. Before I leave, there are a couple improvements I'd like Supermassive Games to make. First, please improve the quality of dialogue. Little Hope's was solid but definitely had room for improvement. Certain characters were very shallow, you know which ones, and if the characters next year get just a little bit more depth I'd be happy. Also, don't be afraid to dip into the supernatural a bit more like you did in Until Dawn. I know that wasn't the goal of this series but I don't think it would hurt it at all if done properly. Also, the price is a bit steep. $40 CAD for 4 hours of gameplay is a bit hard to justify sometimes. I think $30 CAD would be a bit more reasonable and possibly deter people from just watching a Youtube video.

name: Meet Your Maker
detailed_description: Sector 2: Shattered Peak SECTOR 2: SHATTERED PEAK — AVAILABLE NOW Deep in the desolate Arctic wasteland lies the Shattered Peak Sanctuary, home to the latest in lethal advancements in tech and cloning. Battered by suffocating snowstorms and facing endless isolation, fear and paranoia ensnared its residents, turning Custodian and Advisor against each other, and the former research facility into a blood-splattered nightmare. All Meet your Maker players gain instant access to a new environment and themed Deco Pack . A new Custodian and guard are also available, letting you harness the snowbound horrors that tore the Sanctuary apart. Meet Your Maker: Deluxe Edition Ready to Meet Your Maker? The Deluxe Edition includes the base game and the Scorched Necropolis Collection that expands your post-apocalyptic toolbox with a full set of ancient-Egyptian-inspired cosmetics. Combine myth and machine to build and raid in deadly new directions. Create post-apocalyptic pyramids and temples, or gear up with golden weaponry and Custodian Suits to take on other players’ creations. Deluxe Edition contents: Meet Your Maker Base Game  Scorched Necropolis Deco Pack 2 Blocks (each available in 3 shapes)  Limestone  Golden Age   2 Props  Winged Molding  Temple Light  1 Animated Prop  Spinning Enigma  8 Decals  1 Scorched Necropolis Weapon Skin: Sunclaw 2 Scorched Necropolis Custodian Skins: Desert Cyclops and Gilded Warrior *All items in Meet Your Maker can be mixed and matched freely when building an Outpost or creating a Raider loadout. About the Game You are the Custodian of the Chimera, a living experiment created as a last resort to save life on Earth. Enter a battle of skill and wits for the only remaining resource that matters and the key to your Chimera’s evolution: pure genetic material. Mine the darkest corners of your imagination to build and fortify deadly fortresses known as Outposts to extract and guard your Genmat. Infiltrate and survive other players’ Outposts to steal more. Adapt, upgrade, and evolve… or die. The world’s deadliest toolbox is at your fingertips. Combine a huge array of blocks, traps and guards to build a fortress that’s devious, cunning, and utterly without mercy. Enjoy complete control over your creation, modifying traps and recording custom patrol paths for guards, then share your Outpost and watch others try to survive it. Reap rewards from those who die, learn from those who live, and never lose progress by being raided. Put your will to the test raiding other players’ Outposts. Rely on your instinct, intellect, and reflexes in a do-or-die heist to steal the materials you need to fuel your next build. Choose the right loadout for each unique challenge, then get in, grab the Genmat and make it out alive mastering every Outpost that stands in your way. Keep your friends close and your enemies closer. Combine creativity and build with an ally or join forces to raid as a team of two. Use the replay system to watch Raiders challenge your Outposts. Grow your reputation with accolades left by others to reward your ingenuity. Easily find your friends and favorite Builders to play their Outposts at any time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is dog. A lot of bugs. My game crashed TWICE in a run of a single map. Evolving your Chimera is pointless, as there is no story or visual changes to her. There are like 5 different currencies, and getting a hang of them all takes hours. The tutorial doesn't help with anything.The concept of the game is awesome. The little splash art trailer at the beginning of the game/tutorial tells an interesting post apocalyptic story, but doesn't get elaborated on any further no matter how long you play. The maps you build cannot be saved or reused (They only stay for a limited amount of time) so you have to build a new base very often. Also, they cost currency to upkeep daily.The maps don't have enough variety and are either TOO EASY to cheese or TOO DIFFICULT to beat. (You don't have to play through your own map to complete it. You can just make a room full of deathtraps and enemies, then release it.)There is barely any progress (only a handful of weapons, three armor types, like 7 different traps and 3 mobs you can place.) and NO ENDGAME. You are not playing to get to a certain point. You just play.If the point of the game is to just play, there should NOT be any currencies and upgrades, as there is no plot or endgame that needs pacing. The way the game is at the moment, you'll be playing the game without the loadout you want for 20 hours, until you finally upgrade everything you need, at which point you've probably seen every type of map and the game gets boring.Also, there are like only 100 players online at any given time. That is laughably low, considering that the only content this game offers is player made. No player = No Content.I was hyped when I saw this game was free to play, but it's a massive let down. Don't waste your time or money.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, and it's worth the $30 imo, but my computer struggled a lot until I upgraded (was above min specs too), and that WILL stop people from playing (it stopped me). It isn't optimized enough honestly.Raiding is exciting, puzzles are fun to figure out; but if you don't participate in the discord then you will miss out on some of the best levels in the game.  That said, most levels are decent, not nearly as much trash as you might find in something like Mario Maker. You learn what maps to avoid picking or finishing after a little bit. Good or great maps feel amazing to stumble into. Creating maps is EXTREMELY satisfying. The replays system allows you to watch every raid on your base and its wonderful (if occasionally buggy). If game or level design is interesting to you, then you will love creating levels.Devs are fully invested in making the game better and better, and it has already improved from release with the free DLC (better traps = better maps) but certain things that will never change remain head-scratchers (the "economy" is messy for newbies). I have no problem recommending this game for people who enjoy creating and game design, but if you think you only want to play to raid and complete other bases then you will definitely be left wanting after some time. It might take some time before this game is up to par for people who *only* want one side of the coin (create vs play), but if you think you could enjoy both aspects of the game you will get a lot more out of it. And remember; you can always just leave crappy maps, the only thing lost is a bit of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: On paper, everything about this game seems great. The problems stem from the developers and their treatment of this game.The absolute worst choice was to make user levels temporary. I think your levels only last in the rotation for 2 weeks, with ways to extend that to maybe a month? Why not just keep them all in rotation, but decrease the odds of older maps? Oh right, because BHVR really like for their players to be forced to grind, see their other games. In this game, the only currency that you won't have a surplus of is Cells (the red one). Cells are needed to unlock new weapons/suits/guards/traps, upgrade anything mentioned in the previous point, and also if you want to activate a temporary buff to see statistics about maps on the worldmap (trap/guard count, top 2 most used traps/guards). Have Cell drop rates been improved much since launch? Not really: you can now get a slight amount from daily challenges + each map 'sector' will usually have 1 "free space" (worth about 1 map). Sadly, the latest weapons/suits/traps/guards (and their upgrades) added cost 2-3x the price of the older ones.Because the maps are in rotation for such a short amount of time, builders are encouraged to make very spammy bases to generate Cells. The most common spam bases you will find are either: a chokepoint leading into a large room filled with tons of ranged traps and guards ("kill boxes"), or a maze with the roof being acid cubes dripping all over the floor. The latter is more personally annoying, as you are forced to low-jump at all times to minimize your time on the floor.After a while you've seen a million of these and my solution was to just abandon them on sight, hoping to find a quality map. And there are some very, very cool maps. Very pretty ones, detailed or themed ones, or ones with a really fun idea/challenge to them. The problem is that most of the great ones are out of rotation by now, so playing them will earn you NOTHING.I should have learned my lesson from Deathgarden, BHVR's game before this that was killed within a year (like this one). It seems that any game that isn't a money printer (DBD) is just pumped and dumped. Take these last few 'season' updates: maybe a few sentences, and 1-4 lazy recolors.The developers gave up on this game after anniversary. There is no reason to buy this game at full price as there will be no new (actual) content.

_childDocuments_.review: How can this game has such high positive score with a active playerbase worldwide with 40 peoples via steam xD this game isnt good, it dosent got fixed or advanced. 6months only cosmetic updates :))) what a joke. Words from smarter guys- Bug patches are being released way too slowly, many bugs that have been actively ruining the players experience have been in the game since its release and it's been more than a month now. Usually developers prioritize fixing exploits and bugfixes, especially soon after release. Not BHVR.- Not enough new content to keep players hooked. A lot of people tried this game in the open or closed beta, and there's basically nothing different about the full version and the beta versions. People who already experienced the game for free don't have anything new to experience in the full paid release.- Lack of proper marketing. They did a streamer event and paid for a game awards ad and such, but that's still clearly not enough.- The roadmap tells us that any new substantial content will be released in two months from now. The trap mods they've been releasing so far aren't interesting enough to get players to return to the game.- An unfun meta has formed and the developers are fine with it, as evident with their recent blog post. Despite what a handful of pros might think, just because killboxes are technically possible doesn't mean they're fun to raid over and over again. Variety is the spice of life and all that. In fact, making fun levels in general is punished by the game itself. The game asks you to make unfun, hard levels.- Almost every player retention/player reward system in this game is done poorly, in fact most systems in the game are.Accolades and prestige are done poorly and lead to people losing their good outposts or having to refill them daily due to circumstances outside of their control.Difficulty calculation is done poorly and is very buggy, you can gain rank for adding a mod then delete the trap and still keep the extra difficulty. Normals can be as hard as brutals, brutals can be as simple as normals.Rank is done especially poorly and not just me but many others here have gone in detail as to why it's actively harming the game.The game feels early access despite not being labelled as such.

_childDocuments_.review: Building your own level, watching replays of people playing through it and making adjustments to it on the fly can be extremely addicting. Despite some needed limitations that can sometimes feel too constraining there's enough tools to make some really clever traps and level designs to outsmart raiders and (hopefully) make sure everyone has a good time, as you don't lose any resources if someone successfully raids your base. You get resources for every raider kill, but there's no upside to making players ragequit.The raiding part can be a mixed bag, as is expected from community generated content.Although there is a rating system that tries to incentivize making levels that are fun to play, it doesn't quite do enough to stop people from making levels that are simply as tedious and frustrating as possible. Still, there's plenty of fun levels to play out there for now, it remains to be seen how the meta will shift in the future and whether or not interesting maps will eventually disappear in favor of cheesing for resources

_childDocuments_.review: While so far i haven't found a single mythical 'killbox' as every level has been beatable. I do agree that there must be some kinda 'certified beatable' badge in some forms. i haven't play brutal map much. But from what i've seen in Dangerous level? they are certainly exists. I just haven't find it yet.Some creative level are out there and very high quality. i found one that basically is a labyrinth. the path at the beginning are designed to kill the worker that led you to genmats. and the rest is a 3-floor labyrinth and interwoven together. i think it took me almost 10 minutes just to find both tombs and genmats. And i enjoy every single minutes of that map. that was one of the most creative maps i ever played since launch. It's exactly the kind of potential we are having in our hands.Sadly we rarely find such maps. I know that this isn't Mario Maker and making killbox is kind of a point, But the fact that the game favor killing first and foremost, make most of the level design really boring. tight corridor, surprise trap, and blocky linear level. it gets old. Very quickly. The biggest culprit is that damn worker. I think that's why i found the labyrinth map so refreshing and creative. Their mere existance is exactly why the game is full of braindead design. It always led to shortest path to the genmats and you have no complete control over it. sure, people don't really follow him. But builder are still forced to having to make level design around letting him into the destination. He can't climb, jump or crawl around without proper platform, that means no multiple pathway to the genmats, no platforming-based level, no upper-verticality play (it's so stupid, you have grappling hook that can go pretty much any direction without cooldown, and then you have builder mode that forced you to create corridor map? absolutely baffling.) and the worst part? you can't change where the genmats should be. you are literally building a level inside a box. on a game that demand your creativity.... i have no words. The other reviews were right. You just can't play this game in a long session. The variety is just not there because of how the game reward you. The player are just too braindead to think of anything more creative than one-path linear trap galore or spamming 9 armored warmonger behind holocube as soon as you picked that genmats. Wow, such creative. Much fun.For now, i'm gonna go with thumbs down. The game core shooting and traversing mechanic is solid, but the way the game designed around specific things too much actually severely limit creativity in the game. Why not making forsaken tombs more valuable? why not reward players more based on accolades and not killing? So many questionable design led me to go with a no for now. I'll updated if there's any changes.

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant game! You have to get used to the game mechanics, because they are so different from what you know from other games. In this game, it doesn't really matter if you die. Quite the opposite, because it's part of the game. You have a limited amount of ammunition with which you can kill traps or guards on the way to the valuable genmat.  And you always have to get the ammunition back, because there is no new ammunition. This is dangerous because you have to grab the grappling hook to get the ammunition out of the ceiling.You think nothing bad and suddenly you are shot by a bolt and have to start all over again. _childDocuments_.review: Potential: 10/10Actual: 4/10Reason: This is inherently subjective, I have a very specific photosensitivity this game and no other triggers called Chromophobia. The game's UI and much of the game's common hub area feature a very highly saturated shade of green-yellow that, even over a period of 30 minutes, will make me very nauseous, distort my eyesight, and even cause dizziness.I seriously wish I didn't suffer from this, but unfortunately I do, and as a result, and with no ability to toggle an alternate coloring mode within the game, I have no choice but to not recommend.The one time I need an accessibility option, there isn't one.I used ReShade to fix the problem by taking the offending color into a hue affecting plugin and I desaturated that color to grey, have no problems after that.This is still a Not Recommend because I've recently made discoveries that makes Kernel-Level Anticheat a no-go for me. However as I am currently a low-value target, I will make a deal to the developers: Implement an accessibility option for my chromophobia to change the game's core palette color to a distinctly non-yellow-green color (preferably blue or red-dominant colors than yellow-dominant colors) and I will not only play the game and stream it, but I will also help with content creation, I will ignore the Kernel-Level Anticheat as a negative, turn this review positive and if at all advantageous to you, the developers, I'm willing to also produce fanart as my way of thanks.I don't consider this as a bribe, but a mutual arrangement, I highly value this game and loved my time playing it but...I want to play your game without using ReShade to make 70% of it greyscale.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is just fundamentally flawed. It has a cool concept, but the game designed in an unfun way and there isn't enough content to justify the $30 price tag. It will be in the Death Garden in no time.Reasons it's flawed:1. Bad performing bases are incentivized: You build a base. If that base does well in terms of kills and accolades, it eventually goes inactive and must be prestiged to the next level to reactivate it. Once you hit Prestige 10, your base can never be reactivated in the normal matchmaking pool again, it can only be put into "Social" mode. But there is no incentive to ever raid social mode bases because you don't get resources from doing it, and simply trying to browse social mode bases is a mess and basically broken unless you know the author/base you want to raid.However, if your base DOESN'T do well in terms of kills and accolades, then your base doesn't prestige, but it still goes inactive, but you can reactivate it and attempt to get enough prestige points again. So effectively, a base that performs poorly can exist in the matchmaking pool indefinitely compared to a good performing base. It's not that hard to get the resources required to reactivate a base through raiding, which brings me to my next point:2. The game punishes builders who don't want to raid. You don't get nearly enough resources from raiders dying to your base to afford all the upgrades. And you barely start with any traps/guards. I've seen multiple comments from people who were discouraged by the game because they were essentially forced to raid for resources. Personally I like raiding more than building, but that leads me to my next point:3. The lack of block types lead to uninteresting bases. Cube. Ramp. Corner block. That's all you get. I'm glad they're adding more decals and block textures, but the game really needs new geometry available. The more you play this game, the rarer it gets to see an interesting base. And that happens a bit too quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a thumbs up although I did not buy it after the free trial. I'll come back when it's $15. To me it's currently 7/10, but could be 10/10 with some improvements. Very fun core mechanics and pieces to build with. First of all though, add vaulting up onto blocks! Grappling *almost* high enough and falling, or grappling onto something further away and getting stuck on a block in front of you is very frustrating. Also with the grappling hook there is no way to deal with death pits that are full of mobs or acid.Most importantly, I agree with many players that you should have to play through your own outpost before you activate it and whenever some number of changes are made. Beating another player's outpost after 1-3 deaths is the sweet spot imo, and more brutal outposts and "kill boxes" are the worst part of the experience. They tried to award accolades more highly than base kills, but I think it's not enough. You should only get any rewards from someone raiding your base if they end up beating it - and you shouldn't be able to give accolades to outposts that you forfeit (unplayable bases get rewarded like this). Better metrics for builders would be amazing as well: "heat map" style outlines of paths all the recent players took and where they died, kill counters on individual traps/monsters, average number of accolades given to you per raid, etc.Alongside that, I think it needs more granular difficulty tiers, such as more advanced traps putting outposts straight into the Dangerous level so new players are unlikely to encounter them.The other issue as people are mentioning is the progression system. Everything simply costs currency which is hard to remember the names of, and unlocks aren't gated behind your level so it feels more like a grind than you're "leveling up" and becoming a better raider/builder. Maybe if suits/weapons/consumables were related to your "raider level" and guards/traps were related to your "builder level" they could more properly match raiders to the appropriate bases (I'm a level 5 raider, this base was made by a level 5 builder, etc). Alongside this, while trap and guard mods are fantastic (second wave is a blast), suit/gear/weapon mods are very lackluster. I was expecting more functional mods like: you can't hang on your grapple anymore but it launches you much farther / your grenades do less damage but split after throwing/launching them / your bolts fly slower but penetrate 1-2 targets, ricochet off surfaces, curve after firing, etc. Also, why are we feeding and leveling up the chimera? Is there nothing gated by your player level at all?Lastly, the advisor levels and boost system are pretty unsatisfying. You "level up" your advisors but it doesn't feel impactful at all, since they very slightly increase the duration of boosts which aren't worth their cost anyway - at least in my first 10 hours of playing. Some more meaningful level up rewards such as cheaper unlocks, cheaper boosts, a free boost at a certain level, or a random rotating discounted boost, would make it much more enticing to even open the boost menu. After a few hours, I ended up raiding any outposts that looked fun rather than aiming to level up any particular advisor.P.S. If you guys could crack crossplay raiding and building I would absolutely get this game to play with my console buddies.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game IS FUN! But it's only fun for so long before you start seeing it's faults, and these faults really take away a lot. This is a long review because I REALLY like the core concept for this game and want to recommend it, but there are several key things that I feel need to be changed or added to the game, otherwise I think it's at risk of an early death. #1: "killboxes"/unbeatable maps- You don't have to beat your own map before publishing it so players are encouraged to just stack a huge room full of traps that are near impossible to get through. 9/10 brutal maps I come across are killboxes and it makes me not want to play the higher difficulty maps, however the lower difficulty maps are too easy. Adding the requirement that the publisher has to beat their own map (or upload it socially for someone else to beat) to be able to add it to the main story roster feels like a necessary step to keep this game from dying. #2: Trap timings- The delay on trap activation is way too long. I can play almost any map and just speed run through it, and as long as I have a place to sidestep/backstep I can ALWAYS get out of the way of the trap. You should not have enough time to hear the trap activate, locate it, and then shoot a relatively slow moving arrow at it BEFORE it goes off. Traps need to be more punishing in their timing or at least a way to hide their visibility via upgrades or something to offset their insanely long buildup. #3: Lack of "triggers"- I have many trap ideas that are ineffective because there is no way to set their activation based on a trigger. I like to set AI to chase the players after a set amount of time via the patrol recording, however if a player steps off the main platform and doesn't enter the map the timing is completely ruined and the surprise is lost. I need a way to activate certain things when a player touches a specific spot. Balance wise you could set the trigger to only activate a single trap or a set number of traps so people can't just activate an entire room of flamethrowers when you get to the middle of it. It could also be made expensive to build so having a triggered trap costs 3x more than a standard visible trap. A trigger would also stop people from just corner peaking constantly and taking out every single thing.#4: Slow/Bad progression/currency earnings- I have so many levels on the AI characters in my main base and I have no idea what those levels are for. As far as I can tell, all unlocks are just stuck behind an earned currency paywall and currency is earned excruciatingly slow. Particularly the orange currency which is necessary for upgrading traps and creatures, as well as purchasing and prestiging your maps. The main problem comes down to having to use orange currency for everything useful, and how little you get outside of leveling up. On each map is a node that has a chance to drop currency and if you are able to find every node you may get up to 150 or more. However the map doesn't require that these nodes are accessible, and most players don't even realize those nodes are on their maps and don't design maps around them. The majority of the time the node is blocked off and I can't even get to them which means I get a whopping ZERO orange currency that run. And the only other decent way to get it (that I've found) is having players die on your map which leads me to my next and I feel most important aspect that ruins this game for me.#5: 24 hour map life- If you make a map it only stays in rotation for 24 hours before depleting and you have to spend ORANGE CURRENCY to prestige it and reupload it. That means double your investment just to have a CHANCE to earn your money back. I've had one map that I prestiged twice and when I first made it, about 8 different players tried it out, then I prestiged it and about the same amount of people played it, and I prestiged a third time and 1 person played it. 24 hours is not nearly enough time for a map to be active, and if you get especially unlucky you won't have a single person play it. I spent about 3 hours making a map that had zero players try it out likely because it was a monday. And when having players try your map is the main way to make decent money it's insane that you don't get to keep it for more than a day. The timer should at LEAST be based on how long players are on your map, otherwise you just get unlucky and nobody plays it, and then you can't afford to prestige it.Some small gripes: Why are boosts only active for like, 20 minutes? You spend 100+ of a currency for a chance at more of a different currency and it's only active for 1 or 2 runs? This especially doesn't make sense for currencies earned when players die on your map. If I only get one player over the course of 24 hours why would I ever spend money to have a small boost for 20 minutes that's almost guaranteed to be completely wasted. Leveling up the character makes the boost longer but my guys are like 10+ and it's still around the half hour mark. Not worth the money at all.The grappling hook should have weighted physics to it, or an alternate version that has physics. It would just be way more fun being able to swing around instead of ziplining straight forward. Replays are super laggy/glitchy. Half the fun of this game is watching people play your map for the first time but there's a lot of desync and visual glitches that hinder that experience a lot. I assume this will be fixed in a future patch but it's a pretty big deal. Having to load into your building mode to collect dropped loot from dead players is unnecessary. I feel like it's a holdover from a previous build that didn't have the replay system so you could see which traps were killing players but I already watched the replay so having to manually collect it is just tedious. The tombstones are helpful as reminders but just give me my loot. Upgrades are expensive and feel pretty worthless. I get 1 extra arrow and a shorter reload for the same currency that upgrades my traps which have a way higher return on investment so why bother with them. I haven't even bought the other suit yet because I can't see what it does and it's too expensive to throw money at just to try it out. The little guy that walks through the map makes sense in concept so that you're always guaranteed a path to the objective. It really stifles creativity though in terms of jump puzzles and verticality when you have a grappling hook for movement but everything needs to be wheelchair accessible. It also limits secret paths and mazes because you just watch where he goes and he leads you directly to it.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it good? Yes, but not for $30 dollars. It takes about 3 days till you unlock everything. Most bases you raid are too easy because of speed running or to hard because of kill boxes. The game has a few game breaking bugs that people abuse (2 phase cube bug). _childDocuments_.review: Played for a few hours via PS Plus before grabbing it on Steam.Short version: It's a solid foundation, already enjoyable as it is but also with the potential to become a proper little gem with attention and support.Long version: I really like what this game has going on.  Content is a bit bare-bones at the moment (there's something like half a dozen each of trap and guard types, two each of ranged and melee weapons, and two combat suits); however, the developer's stated their intention to start adding more early and often, so I'm not terribly worried about it.What's encouraging is what they've already gotten right.  Visible, obvious traps are easy for even a half-competent player to avoid or disable, so the game is in figuring out how to place them to catch raiders off guard--hidden spots, layered gauntlets, intentional funneling of movement and the like.  It feels like a proper battle of wits.(Yes, killboxing is occasionally an issue--however, in several hours of playtime I can only think of two outposts I ran across that actually felt unfair to the point that I wasn't sure if it was legitimately possible to complete them.  Thankfully the game gives you an option to pass on any given outpost that pops up on your map, so you're not stuck banging your head against a wall forever.)The onboarding experience is well designed; you'll need to do at least a few runs as a raider before getting the chance to build an outpost of your own, and if you're smart you'll be taking mental notes the whole time of which setups managed to get you so you can give them a shot yourself.  Your outposts will also not only tell you how many kills they got, but where and to what, so you have a record of what's working and what isn't.  Combined with the progressive unlocking of mods that tweak the functioning of your traps and guards, it feels like there's a lot of depth to be had in learning how to design a good, lethal outpost that will only get deeper as content is added.Overall I think it's pretty easy to get $30 worth of enjoyment out of this game even as it stands right now, and if the devs live up to their promises with content drops then I can see myself continuing to play this for a long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastically executed concept with a few minor issues. The core gameplay loop is FANTASTIC. Having user created maps makes the new content literally endless. The construction and traps systems is nearly perfect, and my only issue is the presence of the Genmat "gremlin" for level validation. The player has a much larger skill set when it comes to movement mechanics and being forced to make maps that this little box dude can navigate will feel like you're "dumbing down" the concepts you'd really like to execute. However, box dude's presence kinda makes a new playstyle, as some map makers will set alternate routes, hidden paths or trap setups based on the "guaranteed path", making it more dangerous to follow the gremlin or more rewarding to deviate. Plus it makes it so that no level is unwinnable. There's a good variety of enemy types, traps and player mechanics/abilities. All of those have a small catalog of mods that can radically change how the modded item behaves, adding tension for raiders and offering new strategies for map makers. The core movement and combat mechanics are nice and tight, and fit the game's atmosphere and pace well. However, I'd love wallrunning or at least walljumping (which you kinda have if you grapple hook good) at some point in later updates. One of the best features in here is the replay system. Not only can you replay your own attempts at storming people's bases, but all attempts on your bases are saved as well, for your viewing pleasure. You can learn the strengths and weaknesses of your design by watching how others navigate your deathtrap. Or at the least you can watch the player slowly descend into madness as the death room you built pushes their aim, patience and timing into the dirt.ALSO, the devs have outlined their DLC roadmap, and not only are they gonna be adding more content over the game's lifetime, but it seems like only cosmetic items will be purchase exclusive, everything else can be earned through gameplay (see: warframe).My only other gripe with this game is that, at least for me, it crashes a LOT. It never does it when im in the actual maps, but it really likes to crash when I enter/exit a menu in the main hub. Overall, I give this a 9/10, with a 10/10 if they change the level validator and fix the crashes. Buy this game, support this level of content quality, murder your friends and internet strangers with an egyptian pyramid filled with flamethrowers,

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime fan of BHVR's projects, I felt compelled to try this game, even though TO BE COMPLETELY CLEAR, it is not like BHVR's Magnum Opus, Dead by Daylight. With this said, there are elements of the gameplay that show the hallmarks of BHVR's creation-style, taking after the dystopian landscape that Deathgarden was excellent at portraying.For those completely unaware of "what" Meet your Maker is, a quick rundown. The levels are community made, designed by players with the express goal of catching/killing as many players as possible. So naturally, that creates two main playable parts of the game; building outposts, and raiding outposts. While building, you can buy your own "burial site" with it's own features that determine how much creating one can do, and how much "GenMat" can be harvested while it is active (GenMat is a resource gained passively by having bases active). With your burial sites, you are free to place/modify a variety of traps and guards while adding some personal cosmetic touches to make your outposts a blend of fun and challenging. While raiding, you undertake a mission to steal GenMat from other player's bases. To do this, you will enter armed with weapons, assisted by gadgets and perks and moving around with both a double-jump and a grappling hook at your disposal, turning this raiding experience into a dystopian parkour/temple looting experience. I suppose the big question is, has this very weird game concept worked out? Answer: definitely. MYM has a simple idea conceptually and allows the players to challenge each other within the bounds of some very simple rules that ensure that every raid is possible, even if it proves challenging. Personally I have much preferred the raiding side of the game (the prestiging system with the burial sites is slightly confusing, hence why I am not as big a fan of building).I will note that I have had some weird game crashes and I am not entirely sure why. But beyond that, I have had a great time and look forward to more content (and some small fixes to stop the crashes XD).Would defo recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker is a game that puts you in the role of both level designer and playtester. You can design outposts full of traps and monsters, and try to get through the outposts designed by other players.  If you want to build as a creative outlet, just to see all the variety of levels you can make, you will probably enjoy the game for a few days. The raiding is also pretty fun. Everything dies with one hit, including you, so raids tend to be a fun challenge and you have a grappling hook which makes things more exciting.  The aesthetic is cool and there are the beginnings of an interesting story, but then the game doesn't really expand on it, and what you do in the game doesn't really make sense for the story.However, the game has tons of problems with it.1. The UI is overly complicated. You have to press like six buttons to end a level, and you need to visit each base to collect resources from it, prestige it, or activate it, rather than being able to do this all from a main menu.2. The progression system is overly complicated. There are tons of different resources and progression mechanics: synthite, parts, cells, genmat, character experience, chimera experience, and experience levels for each individual advisor. You get most of them by doing the same things, some of them do nothing except give you the other ones, and the ones you can choose to focus on hardly make any difference. The game could easily get by with just one or two resources.3. The devs keep insisting that they don't want to force players to be good at both raiding and building, but at the same time, you cannot just be a builder, because you can't gain enough resources from your outposts to maintain them or buy new ones. Building a good outpost is a huge time commitment, and then you hardly get any reward from it.4. The game crashes a lot.5. It seems a bit expensive for a game that you'll likely get tired of pretty quickly.6. The forums are full of people giving feedback and suggestions to the devs on this game that's still pretty early in development, and I have yet to see a single developer response, which is disappointing.  7. I don't think many people are even playing this game any more. It needs a community of both builders and raiders in order to thrive, and doesn't have one.8. And what bothers me most about the game is that it has the foundation to be a really non-toxic multiplayer game, in that you can design challenging but solvable levels just for other people to enjoy, and yet you are not incentivized to do so. The game incentivizes builders to kill raiders as many times as possible, and incentivizes raiders to abandon raids and block builders if they don't like one of their bases. This is all toxic, and is a huge wasted opportunity to build a friendly community-based game.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your maker is a game where you build a map for other players to go through, or go through a map other players have built for you. If you are building, your objective is to not only kill the player, but make the player enjoy the map you have built. Building a map intended to be 'impossible', isn't favorable to a map that can be beaten, but is challenging and rewarding.The building system is entirely reliant on a grid-based system with blocks. This makes it easy to build whatever you want without sinking hours and hours into it, though if you're like me this will end up happening anyway.Along with the building system is a replay system, which allows you to look back on who raided your base, and where they, or your traps, failed.A complaint i see very frequently is the lack of trap variety. As of writing there are 9 (6 of which can kill) traps in the game.The Boltshot, which acts similar to a dart trap.The Bomb Ejector, which 'ejects' a large number of bombs in a path.The Corrosive Cube, which acts akin to any kill barrier in any other game. Think lava in minecraft.The Death Piston, which is a, well, piston, which continually expands and retracts, killing anyone if it squishes them against a wall.The Holocube, A fake block which can be used to hide traps.The Impaler, Which is simply a spike trap.The Incinerator, which spews flame in a long line.The Iron Claw, which is a grappling hook that grabs players and pulls them toward it.Lastly, the Plasma Sentinel, which acts as a turret.Each trap has a set of modifications that can be applied, individually, to each trap placed. These can make them faster, have longer reach, ect. It is important to note that the Holocube, Bomb Ejector, Boltshot, and Impaler will only activate once, then never work again unless given a mod that lets them activate more than once, of which only the Boltshot and Impaler have.A complaint i commonly see is that there are few traps. While i am somewhat confident more traps may be added in the future, the main way these traps are used interacts with eachother, not functioning individually. A single trap, or even a single mod for a trap, could very well make a combination of any set of traps very, very strong.Further reinforcing this, all traps, excepting the holocube and corrosion cube, all take at minimum one second to activate. Using one trap by itself will rarely get anyone. When they do, it is due to clever placement.In addition to the traps, the game has a set of enemies you can place in your maps.The Cannonback, which launches a single bomb at the player.The Enforcer, which launches a single bolt in a straight line at the player.The Hornet, which flies and fires a single, slow, homing projectile.And the Warmonger, which charges at the player with two swords.All of these enemies die in one hit from any weapon the player has, with one exception. A modifier can be put on them, just like any trap, which gives them armor. If given armor, they can only be be killed if hit in spots where the armor does not cover, or the player breaks the armor first with a heavy weapon. A personal gripe of mine is that there are only three blocks. A cube, A wedge, and a square corner. In addition to this, the way the game checks if a player can complete a level, is by having an npc that walks in a straight path to the objective of the map, then back out to the player spawn.This npc requires about one half block of space to either side, and one full block above it to reach the objective. This limits what kind of pathways you can make, and often results in players making long wedge paths that go up and down repeatedly. I would prefer to see this npc capable of going through smaller spaces, a bit larger than what the player can go through. This would enable players to make better looking, and more dangerous, corridors and rooms.In addition, i would like to see the list of blocks expanded upon from the existing three. Even a simple, normal corner piece, would be extremely appreciated, but some other frequently seen blocks in other block games such as ramp pieces and inverse corners would also be very nice to see, and would enable players to, yet again, make better looking outposts, rooms, and corridors, and give players going through the map a better challenge.Finally, i would like to see the game have a larger pool of decorative props to choose from. Currently, the list of props is acceptably large, but all of them can only go inside of a wall. Props that can go in the world space could add much needed detail to the standard 1x1 hallway often seen.Now for the part i'm sure most of you were waiting for, raiding.At first, raiding in the game is very daunting, as other players know much more than you do when you first start, and are likely to get you with the traps several times, especially if they are good with how they set them up. However, the small pool of traps and enemies lets you get used to them very quickly. The key things to learn are what sounds each one makes when they activate, and the range, as well as effect, of each one. Each enemy, trap, and even props in the game make noise. Often very distinct from eachother, and easy to hear. This gives you important information on how to handle each one before you see it, or if you've triggered it.After your first few raids into other players maps, you'll gain some of the resources in the game, which you can use to upgrade your equipment, or get new ones. This loop is continual, and feeds into building as-well, building acting as an idle component of this game. The better your base preforms, the more resources you will get out of it over time.There are four weapons, and one shield in the game. Two crossbows, two swords, and the 'arc shield', which i will explain soon.The crossbows are the 'Volt Lancer', and the 'Falconic Plasmabow', being a heavy and light variants of the crossbow respectively. The Volt Lancer can break traps, and armor on enemies, but only gets two to three shots. The Falconic Crossbow can only kill enemies, and won't break armor or traps, but gets between six to fifteen shots. The high ammo count of the Falconic Crossbow makes it desirable, but it is highly situational.The swords are the 'Sledgeblade', and the 'Fury's Edge', being the Heavy and Light variants of the sword respectively.Both swords can break traps, and most importantly,  Deflecting projectiles is a mechanic many newer players miss, but the swords can both deflect *any* projectile if you swing them as the projectile gets within range.The only difference between the two, is that the sledgeblade is slower, but can break armor, while Fury's Edge is faster, but cannot.The arc shield is a unique 'weapon', that acts much like a sword that can only deflect. The difference being that this deflect lasts a full second and a half, and makes you completely immortal for the duration.Of these weapons you can only equip two, so choose wisely.In addition to the weapon you have four 'utility' items, which are used up when you use them. These are the Grenade, Flash Barrier, Phoenix Pod, and Spike Drive. The Grenade is as it says on the tin, you throw it and it explodes. You get them from the start of the game, and they are always useful as they can disable traps around corners.The Flash Barrier acts much like the Bubble Shield from halo. It provides a dome, in which traps cannot hit you though. It can also break traps if the trap is inside the Bubble. Enemies cannot shoot through the bubble, but can walk inside.The Phoenix Pod acts as a respawn point you can place down.The Spike Drive makes you 20% faster, which doesn't sound like much, but this small boost lets you simply walk away from more or less any trap in the game due to the added speed.The game is as fast or slow as you make of it. If you want to go fast, try speedrunning, if not, go slow and check every corner.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: "Meet your maker," construct nefarious lairs of torment to safeguard the unholy artifact from the feeble grasp of lesser beings, and revel in their anguish as you witness their futile struggles within your malevolent fortress of despair. There is no pleasure more delectable than observing the helpless souls ensnared by your meticulously crafted snares, as they perish again and again in their pitiful endeavors to seize what is yours. Fortify your sanctum of suffering by unlocking new upgrades and traps, each imbued with the power to inflict exquisite agony upon any wretched fool who dares to trespass within the shadowy recesses of your wicked, twisted domain. As the bodies of your enemies accumulate, your reputation will grow, instilling dread in the hearts of those who hear whispers of your merciless cruelty. Let your reign of terror be unrelenting, as you continue to refine and expand your labyrinth of despair, ensuring that none shall ever escape the clutches of your ruthless mastery.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe you remember "the mighty quest for epic loot" before Ubisoft bought and ruined it. Meet your maker has the same premise but changes up a few things:Neutral Changes:-Meet your Maker is a fps rpg. Mighty quest was a hack and slay rpgPros:-Vertical movement. As a raider you are super agile with no-cooldown grappling hook and double jumps. The movement in general feels really smooth.-Everything deals 1 damage. Everything has 1 Hp. You. Traps. Guards. Everything. This makes the information that you have to process a lot simpler and the gameplay more dynamic.-Freedom of Building. You can get very creative with your outposts. (though some players don't use this potential)-Caring Devs, that already reacted to community feedback.Cons:-Gore. The guards are very distorted and killing them results in beheadings etc. If you like stuff like that, than thats a pro for you... I guess.-Limited Content. This term is relative. The game has only 4 different guards and 9 different traps. However, each of these do fundametally different things and can be equipped with 2 different mods each. There are 4-6 different Mods per trap and 7 Mods per Guard. I guess their use and diversity depends on the way they are positioned/set on patrol.-Slow Unlocks. The game is very grind intensive - especially at the start. Some say this is to increase the runtime due to the limited content. I am neutral to this. You should do some informed choices what to unlock first. But after you got the basic everything gets smoother and faster.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and addictive game! Most negative reviews here are complaining about "killbox" style bases, but I honestly enjoy trying to find a methodical way to take those on and I haven't found any base that's truly impossible. With every raid I complete, I feel like I'm learning new techniques to take back to my own builds.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I played the hell out of the beta, I'm so happy all my progress carried over! If you enjoy Super Mario Maker, you'll love this! Once I figured out there was a progression system, it changed everything and made the game really addicting! The Suit upgrades are really fun. Once you've maxed out a skill on that Suit, you can then unlock it for the other suit! Mix and matching skills is nice and I can't wait for BHVR to add even more! The editing mode is nice and simple. Took me a few minutes to get used to it, It does feel a bit clunky at first, but once I got used to it, I then realised they couldn't make it any more simple and easy to use! Watching people raid you base and watch them die over and over is extremely satisfying! I got this one guy who died 10 times, finally got to the end, just to die to a simple spike trap... Then I got another guy who sped through it in 30 seconds without dying! For the price, this game is a 9/10 for me. It's a nice, quick, simple game to kill time that is actually fun!
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I think the negative reviews are warranted. I really think that the game is great to play with friends and solo when you get a few mods(upgrades). The killboxes people talk about are not fun while playing solo but are a lot more manageable with a friend or two. I think that if they made the player SOLO their base/dungeon before it goes active it could prevent a lot of these "impossible killboxes". Currently the only thing you need to do is allow the robot/human to walk to the objective and back. This means you can't have any jump/vertical puzzles in the game. This is a disappointment just because they built such good mobility into the game. There would be no need for this robot-chicken-man IF you made the player solo their own dungeon from start to finish successfully. It would also allow for a lot more creativity in the map creation.I do think this game is great! The bones are solid and with time it will be an amazing niche game that you can't get anywhere else. Its worth the money as it is right now. But do remember that "Brutal" difficulty is just that, dying 10+ times to figure the map, then dying 10+ more times to get it done. Its a great game. Play it and bring a friend!

_childDocuments_.review: The Outpost Prestige system needs a re-work. Even with a high-kill outpost, it's a chore to keep outposts going. With your Outpost getting 12 hours of uptime, there's no guarentee you'll get more than 1 or 2 raiders. And you won't earn enough GenMat to Prestige. The game has a major issue rewarding both raiding and building. Based on their ranking system, they seem to expect people to raid for 2-3 hours a day as well. It's going to create a ton of burnout. and things could overall just be done better. It's not worth 30$. Maybe 20$ at most. Looking back on my purchase, I can't really recommend it. I had some fun. But, really it's a big missed opportunity IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like a lot of the negative reviews for this game boil down to "it's too hard for me, so I don't like it." This game is BRUTAL at times, but there's nothing forcing you to do any specific user's base. If you get stuck, you can take the L and find another target. Lot of fun, super innovative concept.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: We had a good thing going, but BHVR thought it would be a good idea to effectively abandon the game's development since "we had fully see the world that Meet Your Maker has to offer"... in reality they are too lazy to actually flush out this world and would rather just cash out while they have the chance.This game had massive potential but they threw it away early on.If you want a rough timeline of events, continue reading, if you dont care, just skip past...The game was riddled with bugs early on and the developers did too little too late to actually fix it. The Second Wave (augment) lets traps be activated once the Genmat was collected, but there was a bug that let other traps see the player and trigger through Corrosive Cubes (with the Second Wave augment) and potentially kill the player. It resulted in almost every base being full of traps that you had to waste crossbow bolts to destroy but could not actually retrieve the bolts.As a result players left the game. The developers took months to actually fix it.Content releases were slow, we received little to no communication or community support. The final straw was them effectively just releasing a battlepass while also not really addressing the community issues or adding content that was actually meaningful for both sides. It felt like the game was trying to cash out on whatever it could without actually trying to support the community in a slightest.To put it as bluntly as possible, the game did not earn the right to monetize itself further, and the community was pissed.Now here we are. Almost everyone left. BHVR is stopping development on the game. The official forums for Meet Your Maker got deleted by BHVR and instead just redirects you to the Steam page. Please, just avoid this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: On principle and for the first 3-4 hours this game has a satisfying loop. Beyond this, you soon get the sinking feeling that there's not a great deal there.2 classes for a game where you spend 90% of your time raiding as that class?7-9 traps (depending on your definition) in a game entirely reliant on traps. This game has two parts, building and raiding. Let's talk about raiding first.What is it?You get resources by attempting to steal X McGuffin from Y map. The "Y map" being one that is user created with traps and enemies designed to stop you.What's fun about it?What's not fun about it?What is it?You in turn build your own deathtrap dungeons for other users to attempt to raid. You get resources for each player you kill.What's fun about it?What's not fun about it?The developers are very focused on "creating a balanced player ecosystem". And the way they have gone about it almost seems like they're about to add microtransactions to buy resources at any moment. The whole game feels like it's squeezing you for resources. Forcing you to play as many levels as possible regardless of quality. And to a certain degree this makes sense, they need to maximize the ratio of level plays to levels, otherwise, builders wouldn't get plays on their levels.I would say I am more of a builder, and usually only sign on to replenish/prestige my levels and watch some replays. But now I think, what's the point? It's getting more and more expensive and I have to sink more and more time just to keep my level active for what, 6 hours?I don't want to build a kill box, I want to build something fair, fun, and pretty. Yet the current state of the game encourages maximum kill at the cost of all other features.I don't want to play the 100th "drop bombs on you from above on a ramp" level. I have seen it.I understand that the developers want to release with less, so it's easier to balance and maintain this "player ecosystem", but honestly I feel this game needed to release with 3x times the content. Whether or not you feel that this game has enough content, as it stands it's gone from an average peak of 3000 concurrent Steam players to 1000. 1/3rd in two weeks. That's 2000 less players that are part of the player ecosystem, playing levels, and giving builders resources. 2000 fewer players innovating and building interesting levels. If the developers really are cautiously trying to optimize the player economy, I'd say they may need to up the ante.The developers plan to release 1 more trap, class, gun, and map theme in June. I personally feel that's a plaster over a gaping wound.If that's the rate of content additions, then this game will be prime to pick up on sale after 5 years of content. Who can say if it will survive it that long.EDIT 18/10: After two "content updates" I signed in to see if things have improved. - 1 new trap which I can't afford without another 6 hours.- My outpost only got 4 plays before needing a refill. - Levelling up the prestige of your outpost still only allows you to add one upgraded trap.- Higher skill and more tools mean fair levels don't get kills, further encouraging killboxes.Developers.This type of game is made for me. But this game needs more than drip-feed of cosmetics.It needs doors, timers, traps, block pushers, rotators; .

_childDocuments_.review: Only complaints are graphical issues and stability:I get weird visual bugs and changing settings doesn't fix them nor does verifying game assets... They eventually lead to the game freezing and I need to open task manager to kill the game.On the up side, the game runs otherwise amazing, visuals are awesome, controls are tight, and the gameplay is very engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels early access, everything visually and mechanically works and seems to be bug free.It's the experience that feels Early Access.End of the day, dying constantly to traps cheap shotting you Or having a gun with 2 shots that have to be retrieved with nothing to help isn't fun. At first I found myself with intrigue going in and exploring these areas but then when i realized i would have to grind 100s of the easy no challenge dungeons to get stuff i want, and would probably always avoid the brutal and challenging ones until I get better gear. _childDocuments_.review: Quite fun. If you're up for challenging yourself and mastering a games skills there is a lot here. The game is split into two parts. Part One -Attacking bases for resources, Part Two -Making bases to collect resources. For most players I think part 1 is likely what you are getting the game for, so I'll spend a bit more time on this than part 2, largely because while you can play the game without making bases, but I don't think it is entirely realistic to try and play exclusively as a base builder, you will eventually need to attack at least a few bases. The Bases are split into 3 difficulties, Normal, Dangerous, and Brutal. The difficulty seems to be based partially on number of traps and enemies, with a multiplier based on how close they are to the pathway. Because of this some bases, particularly larger bases will try to lure you off the path where their dangers are cheaper for them to place down. The primary method of this is that maps will have between one and three locations on the map, marked by a fairly loud rumble, if you can make it to these locations they give you extra loot to collect. This is most likely to be used on Dangerous and Normal maps as the map creators are trying to keep their danger rating bellow a certain level. Do remember that all bases are made by players, so do expect even normal ones to be a decent challenge at time, though the low number of options means you should be through sooner than others, that just means that players have to make what traps they do have count.Your goal is to follow the path, reach the end, and then escape the base. Traps all have a wind up time and a warning indicator to tell you their direction to guarantee you have time to either back away to safety the way you came, or to instantly turn and destroy the threat. Because of this there are two obvious playstyles you may gravitate towards. 1 Spec Ops, making sure to sweep and clear out threats one by one, checking every corner, this will often get you extra resources as you will gain resources from destroyed traps. 2 Jedi, where you just rush on through trying to get ahead of the traps before they can even activate, relying on quick reflexes and skilled movement, often in combination with the sword or shield, to try and get in and out as quickly as possible. Now while you are likely to prefer one or the other, some maps will be designed specifically with one of these two styles in mind, sometimes having traps activate in long halls or with a homing property to reduce your ability to get ahead of them, or alternatively having a large room with multiple projectiles to try and make it more difficult for you to dodge everything, other bases might try to counter more methodical play by having guards with patrol paths to surprise you from behind or otherwise make the base less predictable and try to force you to hurry along faster and out of your comfort range. For bases that are designed to throw off your style it is recommended that you try to get used to both of them for when you need them. That said, while switching to other styles of play can make bases easier, it is still quite possible to win with either if you really want to force the issue, even the largest rooms filled with the most enemies will still just be firing and where you just were, so if you are quick enough, or willing to keep at it long enough you should be able to work out a path that lets you whittle down the enemy, or otherwise just ignore and get past them, the same with roaming guards, if you can figure out their path can always ambush them back, afterwards letting you get back to a calm sweep and clear. If you are looking for, or trying to avoid specific experiences you have some tools in game to learn what sort of traps or guards maps have before you even enter them, so if you want to play a Doom or Quake sort of level look for lots of enemies to fight.That's most of the important stuff on attacking the bases, there are of course bits of gear, upgrades and such you can get to make missions significantly easier, but they are fairly easy to understand once you get them, the only thing left to mention is that if you feel a base will take too long to beat, you can always hit escape and exit that level.Part 2 of the game is map creation, and there is only really a few things to mention here as it grants you a lot of freedom to make what you like and thus is a bit much to try and pin down to a few points. The main thing to know is just the threat rating mentioned above, that having traps on or very near the path multiplier their threat rating, pushing you towards Brutal more quickly, in addition to that, having guards within live of sight of the path also increases their threat, giving them any patrol paths at all increases their threat, and having that patrol bring them within line of sight of the path is is similar if not the same as having them start that way. Your best tool to improve your maps, besides raiding other peoples and copying what works, is watching players Replays as they run through your base, and noting what traps never work as is, and what traps seem very effective, then going in to experiment with new placements. Overall the game is, as I said at the start, quite fun. I've had to learn a lot of skills to get good at this, patience, get at least decent with the zipline, had to focus on my reaction time, but thus far, while I have had a few missions I didn't think were worth the time to finish, I've yet to run into one that seemed impossible, the most difficult and annoying one was a player using a current bug, and even that one I got eventually.

I can't trust that there is a way to beat some outposts, so I'm left wasting my time trying all sorts of trickery or speed run nonsense to try and make simple progression. _childDocuments_.review: Meet Your Maker is a building and raiding game that reminds me of Capture the Flag, Minecraft, Quake, Super Mario Maker, and The Mighty Quest for Epic Loot. While building you attempt to awaken the evil mastermind within you to build the various temples of doom filled with combinations of traps and guards. When raiding you let loose your inner vandal and enjoy a rougelite gameplay loop as you leave paths of destruction during your attempted heist to steal resources essential for your character development. During both elements of game-play you have the option to go solo or co-op with a partner.The raiding game-play loop is rougelite. Loops look something like being presented with a selection of levels, trying a level out and deciding if you want to stick with it or discard it from your presentation, making your way to the in-game objective while dying a few times, eventually grabbing the in-game objective, and getting out with the in-game objective while dying a few times. Both you and most of the environment one-hit-kill, and the Rougelite elements come into play with you respawning at the start of a level upon death with the information you have obtained from your last run and a chance to change equipment to prepare for the next run. All the levels you will raid are player-made, and the creativity I've witnessed is wonderful.As a builder your primary objective is to kill raiders by making effective use of the land you are building on, your guards and traps, and every twist, turn, and artistic choice you make. You do this on a grid-based system with build sites varying in size. You can take control of your guards to give them a patrol route in the same first-person view you control your character and have tools to see how traps will act along with a "test" option to make sure everything works as you want before you put your map live. There is no penalty for missing a weak-point by default but those confident in their constructs can turn on "overcharge mode" which gives the builder more per kill but subtracts from them if the raider(s) escape.Everything in the game can be unlocked with the standardized currency and raiding resources. This includes all of the DLC armor, consumables, guards, traps, and weapons. All of your armor, consumables, and weapons have standard "unlock" or "unlock and level" upgrade paths. Guards and Traps are unlocked, but then have augments upgrades you can buy and equip on them during the building process.After every raid attempt, whether you are the builder or the raider and whether or not the attempt was a failure or success, you get the option to watch a video copy of the attempt. You can watch either from the player's first-person perspective or in free-roam with a camera drone. This was the most fun part of the game for me; with my fondest memory of the game being of a player being so paranoid to walk on the floor of one of my constructs they shot every floor tile before stepping on it only to die and quit after a half-hour of making it to the in-game objective and falling through the floor thinking they were safe.At this time, I would not recommend this game. The developers recently announced they were moving the team they had working on this game to other projects. I feel the game itself was fun, but would have been great if it were wrapped in something more; maybe if this game-play loop had been for protecting a guild-hall while players were off exploring a PvE environment. I would have loved to go hunting for the resources needed to make and craft my traps or guards but sadly Meet Your Maker offered too little to capture and retain an audience large enough to be successful.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game. It’s Minecraft with an objective. However, when I-- a low level player with rotten FPS skills-- chooses one of the “easiest” rated dungeons in the game to raid and see a Prestige 10 on the runway (which isn’t known ahead of time) followed by a slew of traps and enemies that do not come with starter building tools-- in addition to the deathbox awaiting inside, I realized my own time with the game was coming to a close.This forces me to wonder if the dungeons' difficulty rating focuses on “number” of traps and guards rather than “deadliness” of traps and guards via their placement and add-ons. Either way…When two dungeons called “easy” have a cakewalk right next to a deathbox-- I realized rolling the dice on raiding wasn’t worth the fun of building. I’m not here to drown. I’m here to build. But with the currency needed to build mostly locked behind raiding, the rising water level I just faced was not one I want to repeat.Thank you for the hours spent. The idea is neat, and I really hope this game does well.

_childDocuments_.review: A game where you build a deathtrap base, and raid the deathtrap bases built by other players. My fear coming into this would be that players would create the most frustrating, impossible to overcome bases that they could, and I wasn't wrong. The lowest difficulty bases are short, usually have some neat tricks or challenges to them, and are often fun. Medium difficulty is a mix of fun, challenging bases, and borderline impossible killboxes with two dozen traps concentrated across a short hallway with some exploitative configurations like traps at the end of tight hallways that make retrieving your ammo impossible. The highest difficulty - forget about it. As a result I ended up grinding the lowest difficulty bases until it became tedious, occasionally dipping my toes into the higher difficulties but finding it too punishing and unfun to continue. I wish the game encouraged people to make maps that were challenging but fair rather than grueling, but it doesn't.  The base building aspect is fun at least.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is insanely fun. Its the game I never knew I wanted.A lot of other reviews can explain whats fun about it better then I can, but suffice to say, this game has serious long term enjoyment potential.I do want to address an issue other players keep bringing up: killbox bases.The thing is, there is nothing forcing you to try to beat a base. If you don't enjoy the style of a base, simply go play another. (You can abandon a run, which re-rolls it for a different one.) You can also use the suit advisor boost to tell what the main traps are, which helps if you reaally want to avoid a specific kind of base. Another thing: most of these complaints are from players jumping into bases on the highest difficulty level from the start. But you don't have to do that! The Normal difficulty bases will always be far easier in comparison, especially when you are starting out and don't have any equipment upgrades or experience dodging traps.Now that I've addressed the biggest concern, what are you waiting for? Give it try! Its fun!
