_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great concept and it's good enough for me to keep playing it, but it needs more time in the oven. When I started playing I really thought it was an early access release. For starters they LOVE loading screens,Every time you want to change an outpost status, collect resources from kills or prestige/reset an outpost you have to go into build mode, which requires a loading screen to get in and a loading screen to get out just to press one button. All of these options should be do-able from the hub. We're constantly changing maps to social so our friends can try them out, you have to then change it back to active after they're done, that's four loading screens. Loading is reasonably quick, but so unnecessary. There's usually very little reason to go back to the hub after a completing a map unless you want to upgrade or change to build mode, It'd be better if you were able to go into another map without loading back into the hub, there's no reason why you shouldn't be able to access the maps menu after I've finished the map.Watching a replay of someone playing your map is fun also requires loading into the replay and back to the hub, again no reason not to let us load into a different replay or a map to play. The Replay system also has a lot of issues, lot of lagging and freezing, especially when trying to jump forward or backwards.Going into a map to collect resources from your kills where the kills happen is cool but it gets pretty old fast, give us an option to collect all from the hub.There's currently four Accolades, they're fine but more would be better, especially negative ratings like "Boring" or "Long" I can guess the  reason for doing it this way but it feels bad to go into a ♥♥♥♥ map and the only option is to not play it and give no accolade. There's a LOT of really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ maps and no "This is a bad map" option.Having the little guide robot slowly lead the way and be able to be killed is really stupid, you can't have it both ways. Either don't show the path or show it all the time. You want people to be able to use the robot as a guide but you also want to slow down the pace of the game and make it boring.Being able to kill the little guide robot at the start of the map (or at all for that matter) shouldn't be possible, people do it and create boring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mazes with infinite paths and barely any traps, they take forever, they're not hard. It's just boring.Selling $20 DLC that give access to textures with the same colour as the traps is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weak ¯\_(ツ)_/¯The game is fun and I'll get a decent amount of hours out of it, it's a little pricey for what you get and there are a lot of other minor problems not important enough to mention, I dunno how much work they're gonna put into refining this game, but until they do I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun raiding and base building wise, but I simply cannot recommend people play this game as is. Lots of text ahead:Base building seems to have a large part of RNG to it. Layouts of the maps you get are seemingly randomly generated, which can make building a base you had in mind completely impossible, on top of this you don't get to choose where the end-goal (genmat) is, nor where any of the side-goals (tombs) are either. This can be extremely annoying, and can cause some builders to just either completely block off or ignore side-goals all together. Edit, this is sorta better since their matchmaking update, but the amount of raiders you get is still way too low on average.  Edit, after prestige and matchmaking reworks it's much easier and consistent to prestige your bases.Raiding can range from fun to infuriating. I've seen a lot of creative, inventive, and super fun bases while I've played, but on top of this I've also encountered a very large amount of the same type of base you've probably seen referenced in other reviews, killboxes.I've never found a killbox I couldn't beat, but that doesn't mean that killboxes are fine or even enjoyable. They're tedious, waste time, and waste your resources in the form of gear. Simply put, there is no base that can't be beat, but there are MANY bases that are extremely awful and boring to raid. Because of this, playing on harder difficulties only prove a challenge because of how much of your time they waste. The harder the difficulty, the less creative, inventive, and fun the bases get. Not because the bases are actually harder, but because there's a very clear cookie-cutter meta at the higher difficulties that cut out the creativity that is present at other difficulties where it's more difficult to fill rooms with traps: Death pistons with flamethrowers behind them, rooms full of plasma sentinels, armored cannonbacks that line the walls, acid cubes and grapples as far as the eye can see, and sometimes all of these are used and combined in the same raid, or even in the same room.Rant aside, raiding has potential to be fun, but steps need to be taken in order to ensure that it's fun for the raider to play the game, otherwise you're purposefully killing half of the gameplay loop. And no, I don't think that forcing builders to complete their own base is the solution, because the only road that'll lead down are hidden holo-blocks that allow the builder to easily complete the base while leaving the actual raider in the dark. (I think the quickest way to deal with the issue is to force trap uniqueness, making raiders only able to use so many of one type of trap, but this also comes with its own set of issues.) Edit, after roughly 65~ hours of gameplay (including time from the open beta), I have maxed out all advisors, armor, biolinks, weapons, equipment, guards, traps, and the chimera. tl;dr it takes about 65 hours to max everything outGame has lots of potential, can be really fun, but building has a surprising amount of RNG and raiding devolves into tedious time-wasters at higher difficulties.I'll change my review if any of the things I have talked about change in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Level creators don't have to actually beat their own stage before posting, and the game incentivizes you to create brutal stages because you get currency for every person you kill.  This results in any stage you try to play either being incredibly hard for no reason, downright unfair, or specifically created to waste your time.I've had stages with giant arenas with a ton of enemies slapped on it that takes around 20 minutes to fight through because the combat in this game is simplistic and clunky.  I've had stages that spawn-kill the NPC that walks from the start of the stage to the end so you have to walk through a gigantic maze with no guidance.  I've had literal walking sims where you spend 5-10 minutes walking to the goal, only for tons of traps to spring up on you and instantly kill you as soon as you grab the materials.  So you then have to do the beginning part all over again just to try again.Every single person is trying to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ kaizo mario level.  This isn't an enjoyable mario-maker style game where you can find fun, casual levels, challenging but fair levels, etc.  The levels are encouraged to be unfair, and as a result, it makes the game incredibly un-fun.Edit: Found out that the reasons the stages are like this is because the stage creator has needless limitations that essentially forces makers to create bland, uninspired stages.  There's an NPC called "The Harvester" that needs to have a clear path from start to finish in order to upload the map.  Issue is, the Harvester can't jump, and walks very slowly.  So despite having a double jump and grappling hook, EVERY SINGLE STAGE needs to be completable without jumping a single time. Needless to say, this limits what makers can do significantly, and forces them to spam traps or enemies and create actual horrible stages in order to compensate.  If they try to make a normal, fair level, you can actually run through the entire stage by just holding forward and running through the whole thing. I've tested this on around 20 different stages, and 18 of them were completable with this method.Would not recommend. It's a game that is entirely focused on user-generated content.  The user-generated content is bad and not fun to play, and the creation tools are so limited and hard to work with that it's hard to actually create anything fun or good.  It fails on both aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a really interesting concept. You build a base, or bases (or outposts, as they're called here) in a Minecraft fashion - all the items you can place are cubes. People can raid your base, with the objective of finding their way the the precious Genmat, which you have hopefully fiendishly hidden in your trap-filled maze. Most outposts end up looking quite like oldschool Doom levels, and there are some truly inventive designs out there already, even though the game has only just released.Of course, you should raid other bases too, because all the resources you manage to collect in someone's outpost are yours to keep and put towards upgrading your own outpost, or upgrading your traps and guards.Your character comes with a grappling hook, gun and sword as standard. Your weapons are for killing guards, and destroying traps. Traps are flat plains that you can stick to any surface of any cube, and they range from  spikes that shoot out on contact, or projectile traps that will shoot arrows or bombs at you (and a bunch of other devious things), depending on their configuration. Your weapons can be upgraded to have more ammo, or a faster lunge or swing with the sword, for example. Currently there are 2 different suits you can choose from - a more ranged type and a more melee type. Like everything else, the suits are upgradeable with perks.The absolute best feature about Meet your Maker is the replay system. Anyone who attempts a raid on your base has their run saved for your viewing pleasure, and it's a real thrill watching people trying to navigate your base, and seeing how some people obliviously pass by obvious areas where you've left easy access to resources for them (players stealing your resources doesn't subtract those resources from your stash - you lose nothing if someone beats your outpost (unless you opt for the ability to let your stuff be actually stolen, but the default settings loses you nothing).It's a great new morning ritual for me, to sit with a coffee and some of the devil's lettuce and watch people trying to raid my outpost.Since I also own Dead By Daylight, made by the same devs, I got a cool extra tileset of blocks with the DBD theme. Very nice touch.This game is already a firm favourite of mine, and by the looks of things there's a lot more cool stuff on the way. I bought this here on Steam, and then it went free on PS+, and I don't even care. It's worth the price and it's far more suited to mouse & keyboard than a controller. I've noticed that console players generally have a much tougher time, especially when trying to line up split-second panic shots against guards. But hey, if you don't feel like shelling out cash for this game, I'd say go grab it for your PS5. Meet your Maker is something that really has to be experienced, and seriously, the replay system is a stroke of genius.There is one gripe that many people have an issue with though, which is your outpost has an expiry date. While active it generates Genmats for you, but when they dry up the base goes offline. You can use some of your in-game currency (earned by playing, not bought with cash), and "prestige" your outpost, making it live for everyone else again. After 10 prestiges (which will take a while), your outpost is removed from circulation, but it's still not the end. If you're particularly fond of your outpost you can set it to "social" instead of simply "active", and it'll stay up for ever. Only thing is you won't generate any more resources from Social outposts, but at least you can technically keep it up and running purely for the enjoyment of other players.Solid 9/10 from me.Edit: Typos.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker is an asynchornous and synchronous multiplayer game wherein players create bases of various levels of complexity and hide "GenMat" deep within their territory. Players are then able to play these levels through random generation in an attempt to steal GenMat for themselves in a gameplay loop of build, steal, upgrade, repeat.While the game's mechanics build on top of themselves, the light guidance about where to go, the telegraphing of enemies and traps, and the general feel of a well-balanced game is very prevalent.Players who are familiar with Behaviour Interactive's other titles (Dead by Daylight, Hooked on You) will feel a little amiss in this new IP which strays from the DBD formula they are known for and doesn't interact akin to the Visual Novel of Hooked on You gameplay. However, players who ARE familiar with The Legend of Zelda's Dungeon maker mode on the switch, or Mario Maker, as well as PC players who play Satisfactory, Cities:Skylines or even First Person Shooters will feel as though this is a familiar departure with a bit of strategy sprinkled throughout. Players who were fond of Phantom Abyss will like the pseudo-random nature of the puzzles and bonus objectives scattered throughout levels made by players.If you're looking for a fun, puzzle-solver with a less-intense Doom atmosphere, You'll find this game fun. However if you come into this game looking to be challenged with intense gameplay, you'll be hard-pressed to find it without self-imposing challenges (I will beat this level in 0 deaths, I will beat this level in 5 minutes, etc.)A unique level sharing code or favorites system which would allow you to go back and challenge for significantly diminished rewards, or "difficulty modes" alongside this system for enhanced replayability would go a significant way to ensuring levels will continue to come for a substantial amount of time.Meet your Maker is a phenomenal attempt at making new IP in a genre-blending puzzle-making, looter-shooter with many avenues to tantilize players. The blank slate base building for puzzles, combined with excellently made tutorial levels and a currently rather easy level of challenge for learning the puzzles make this a great game to pickup, play one puzzle and set down while providing for that "just one more" itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of the beta so my hours here may not reflect that. Calling this a First Person Shooter is a stretch.  This is more of a player-generated puzzler played in a first person view where occasionally you may need to "shoot" something with a harpoon gun.  The entire point is that another player creates a building full out of different blocks, fills said building with traps and enemies, and places an "End" point somewhere inside of it.  Once you find the end point, a second layer of the building opens up which could potentially contain more traps, more enemies, or a more complex layout.  It's fairly simple but can get fairly addicting, and the premise of infinite user generated content makes the $30 very enticing.  The main issue you may run into on more difficult missions is people creating "killboxes" where the entire point is to immediately kill the player rather than provide a more unique challenge/puzzle to solve.  Besides that I'm having a great time finding unique and intricate maze with puzzles to solve and obstacles to overcome, with extra resources (used to unlock consumable items, permanent upgrades, and additional Tiles for your custom buildings) being available to pick up.  I'm curious how they'll expand upon this in the future, but for now it's a nice little thing to plug away at.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I go into this review:This game is being actively developed. Don't let my or any other review let you think this is the guaranteed final product, If you think this game could be worth it in the future, it's worth considering. The only reason I have my review as not recommended is the current state of the game being.... incomplete feeling. Which makes sense, the game isn't finished yet, and the devs haven't necessarily put everything they want in the game yet.Review:Admittedly, this game struggles to hold my attention. But not for a lack of effort. The game is the most fun when you aren't trying to optimize everything as a raider at the start. Some reviews miss the point of raiding, slowly going through bases rather than rushing and figuring out the layout through repetition, changing your load out in between deaths, and fun movement mechanics. The opposite can be said of the base building however. You have to be very careful about the choices you make and working around the restrictions placed on you. It's interesting and honestly I far prefer it over the raiding, which is ironic because most people seem to have the opposite opinion. There are content updates coming which will solve my main issue with the game: There's only so much to do. To comparing it to their other game dead by daylight, something I am loathing since they are so different, the amount of customization is sorely lacking compared to the perk and addon system simply because of how little there is in the game so far. I hope that the devs will add some non-Premium ways to get new traps and minions on the base building front, along with new suits and weapons for raiders. As it is now there isn't enough content to justify the 30 dollar price tag, along with the cost of dlc to make the game feel more robust. I only hope some of their future content updates focus on giving the player more to do at base without a hard monetary blocker. I want to love this game, but I've already unlocked a good portion of what is available and as you can see from this review I am not that far in. That doesn't mean I've run out of enjoyment for the game, but I feel like that enjoyment is on borrowed time right now.

_childDocuments_.review: I am glad to say that this game's devs have finally come around. On launch, this game had a few glaring issues with design and implementation of certain systems. I am glad to say that they have made the necessary changes for the game to be great. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes the idea of raiding player made bases, and maybe making your own to throw into the pile. Game is very snappy and responsive most of the time, and the movement is absolutely fantastic. Highly reccomendOLD REVIEW:I would absolutely love to recommend this game, as it's fun and super interesting of an idea.The problem lies with the devs and their decision to punish the playerbase for doing well.tl;dr if you make a good base, it inevitably becomes literally useless after a ton of work and resources have been poured into it. Good concept and gameplay, but kneecaps you for doing wellLong version:This game's bases have a level system called Prestige. Bases only stay active for up to 24 hours at a time (based on a randomly generated stat you can't change or upgrade) and every time they run out you have 2 choices. If your base did well, you HAVE TO prestige the base, which levels it up one, and fills it back up with time. If your base didn't do well, you have the "reset" button instead that refills the time without going up a level, but this is ONLY available if your base didn't do well at all. Both resetting and going up in prestige cost an ingame resource, with the cost going higher with level.Upon hitting rank 10 Prestige with any base, once it runs out of time that base becomes "retired", meaning that it CANNOT BE ACTIVATED EVER AGAIN besides social (friend only) raids. So our reward for making an ingenious and deadly base? Killing it with fire.I get that they want fresh bases for people to raid, but there are ways to accomplish that without kneecapping their players like this. There's even have the champion system, where a base that does exceptionally well becomes a champion base, and gives extra rewards to raiders in exchange for bringing a ton of extra raiders in. The caveat is if your base has to "reset" instead of prestige, you lose champion status. They could easily just make it so once you reach 10, you have to reset every time, so you can't become champion. Then all champion bases are fresh and interesting, and no one loses hours and hours of work + resources.

Added with the fact that the "champion" bases can be these kill boxes, really seems to hinder any kind of progression.To anyone wondering what a kill box base refers to, its shoving loads of ranged enemies in a a large room, usually armoured, paired with corrosive cubes and drops to trap your ammo. And a lot of traps to funnel you to the genmat, where your ammo cannot sustain to fight and progress normally, only forced to rush through hoping you won't get hit (everything is a one shot kill).TLDR: A lot of players are taking advantage of poor balancing and progression feels very slow. I would suggest to wait for a sale or at least a first balance patch, to try and reduce the amount and effectiveness of the "kill box" type bases.**EDIT** This review I amend slightly, while I still wouldn't recommend the game in its current state, I would say definitely wait for some updates like before. _childDocuments_.review: The game can't be played for more than 10 to 15 minutes at a time without crashing to desktop and it's a common occurrence across varied hardware specs. I'm on a 3070 with 64gb RAM and it took me 3 hours to build my first base because it kept crashing and then deleting all my base building changes.It's also overrun with cheaters already. Most of the replays you see in bases involve people with infinite ammo who can either see your traps with an ESP cheat, or who skip the formalities and simply phase through your walls to get in and out in less than a minute.More importantly, and not as easy to fix, the bases themselves are a waste of time to build. They grant you resources but theyre on a timer where at the end of it they have to be "prestiged" or go inactive. This means your base can run out entirely without ever seeing a raider if you're unlucky. Once it reaches prestige 10 the base is permanently taken offline and all your work is lost. All in all, you get about 1 week per base before it either goes inactive forever OR can be made a "social raid" which means you can share it with your friends and it does nothing besides.Leveling, upgrading, etc is all meaningless. Your progression system is tied to collecting "GenMat" and leveling your advisors (merchants who provide weapons, gear, traps, etc) but leveling them does nothing but slightly increase the duration of boosts they provide. These boosts however cost money each time you use them and are by and large useless so progression feels, for the most part, like a meaningless treadmill designed to send you on endless raids for no benefit. Not that endless raids are that difficult because there's such a startling lack of trap diversity that if you've played about 10 to 15 bases, you've seen every combination of them. Don't get me wrong, every 1 in 30 bases you'll find something truly unique but most often you'll see the exact same configuration of killbox over and over and over until beating them becomes second nature. Sadly this means that unless you play on the highest difficulty (Where people can spam as many ridiculous and unwieldy traps combinations as they want) you get maybe 3 hours of challenge out of the game before you realize that you can use the grappling hook to zoom past literally everything untouched.In fact, the difficulty system is meaningless in itself. It has nothing to do with how difficult a given base actually is, instead it's based purely on how many trap blocks are placed down. This means that some Normal (easy level) bases are filled with completely unavoidable death traps and some Brutal (hard level) bases are just bizarre open rooms filled with a seemingly random assortment of ill-placed traps that you can walk straight through.The game also seems to be catering to the worst kind of PvP player. Trolls who intentionally wall off resource nodes called "Tombs" in such a way that it prevents players from ever accessing them all. Others still will intentionally use the games "Second Wave" mechanic to turn the room in which you acquire the GenMat, the games raiding goal point, into an inescapable death trap. This isn't possible before you acquire the Genmat because the Harvester (an NPC that leads players to the Genmat through the maze of traps) has to have a clear path from entrance to GenMat, however once the GenMat is acquired all bets are off and they can more or less turn every surface of the room into a giant trap that fires all the same time and decimates the player......Unless of course you use the item called the "Arc Barrier" which gives you god mode and once upgraded can basically be used to waltz through almost any base completely unscathed unless you choose to intentionally step into a giant glowing orange acid cube. (They glow. You can literally see them from a mile away and there's no logical reason anyone would be killed by one.)Edit: Also if you own Dead by Daylight, you get a special cosmetic block in a Dead by Daylight style. The issue is that the blocks are intentionally designed to perfectly mimic the texture of the traps. This means that players who own Dead by Daylight are at a distinct advantage against any legitimate raider because their traps are almost completely camouflaged.The Harvester is also frequently a target for trolls who intentionally kill him as soon as they enter their base. The base itself is then made into a giant 4K+ piece box filled with endless mazes that lead nowhere and take players an hour to navigate only to encounter a final room that spells instant death, designed solely to waste peoples time and then collect resources from their corpse when they rage quit.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to recommend this game, i really do. but with a dying and complainy player base i cannot. I love this game, I love that it essentially puts you in charge of your own dungeon or you can raid other player's bases but this game has some issues, both from the dev side and community side. first, game wise. the game is grindy, like, in a very bad way. It costs materials to make a base public and depending on how many raids you get you might not get enough mats to even republish it. with a dwindling playerbase this issue is made a hell of a lot worse. so to make up that lose you have to go raid yourself, which is a good 5-15 raids before you can release the base....and that was only the base, to unlock other things like traps or weapon unlocks is a whole other grind. the community side of things, the vast majority of the people who left the game probably shared the same complaint when it came to player bases, specifically, kill boxes and wanting builders to beat their base themselves before publishing. firstly, kill boxes. I never understood the hate for them in this game purely because grenades exist. 2 well placed grenades either destroy or neuter the majority of all kill boxes.  1 thrown grenade might even be enough to open it up to where you could even just run through the box. I honestly believe the kill box hate on this game was overblown...when again, for 90% of them throwing a single grenade solved them or made them easier to manage. secondly, the game had an excellent system for authenticating if a base was beatable, adding onto that by forcing builders to complete their bases would not solve any perceived problem just because the complaining player cant beat "brutal" bases. if you did add that feature builders would just create a shortcut for themselves and call it a day, and if you think you'd somehow would be able to find it to cheese the base GOOD LUCK when all the outer walls of the base are magma cubes with only 1 out of 100 blocks being passable. but anyways, dying and grindy game. GG

_childDocuments_.review: Meet Your Maker is a good concept that has been tried many, many times, and it, like so many other games before it, fell prey to the same issues that plagued every other game. The game struggled to find a healthy balance making people want to play levels and create levels. They incentivized kill box designs that encouraged unsatisfying levels, because those were the most profitable, and in turn made it a hassle to play, meanwhile you were unable to create levels because of the miniscule amount of drops that you received which were necessary to create levels.The only successful game of this type was likely Mario Maker, and this game is unfortunately a far cry from it. There's fun to be had, the actual gameplay mechanics were solid, but unfortunately the developers were too blind, deaf or confident in their vision to budge to community demands, to the point where they've now decided to abandon ship.Do not buy the game, it's neither worth the money (even after the price drop), nor worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: "Internet access is required to access this content"Even in singleplayer, you need 24/7, completely uninterrupted access to the internet to access other peoples bases (ie, the "game" half of the game.) Even if you're computer has already loaded an entire base for you to raid, the moment your internet so much as flickers, you get kicked out.This isn't a game you pay for and get.  This is a "game as a service" that will die when the game devs (or whoever they sell the rights to) stop profiting from hosting this game.  If there are any plans to release the source code or hosting rights at the end of the games lifespan, I haven't seen them.That said, my purchase was worth it for my own entertainment.  Getting into the head of a dungeon maker and dungeon delver is fascinating.  I'm just not going to pretend my purchase was ethical. "Games as a service" is an inherently bad idea without a plan to release after the commercial lifetime of a product.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I actually like this game. That being said, I'd be a jerk recommending it to anyone in its current state. There are SO many great tools, both for raiding and building, but the game is structured around incentives that encourage players to use these tools in ONE way. It has been said and then echoed that switching to a mario-maker-style map verification system would improve most of the game's core issues. I'm not going to break from the pack on that one. There is the obvious upside of keeping people who are bad at the game from challenging the people who are the best at it. The unending tide of kill boxes would turn into a trickle, and each one would go from being an arresting speed bump in the gameplay loop to a seriously impressive feat by whoever made it. That would be nice—really nice—but there's a bit more of a benefit than that.The current way MYM determines whether or not a map is beatable is by checking if a small cargo guy can waddle across an uninterrupted path between the base's central goal and the outside. In a very literal sense, that works, but it causes bases to all follow the same claustrophobic theme as raiders are bound to the track of the NPC that cannot even jump. Juxtaposed against that, the raider has a double jump and grappling hook, allowing for a degree of fun and responsive mobility that you can only currently experience by hopping around the outside walls of the trap-laden labyrinth with its 1 by 1 corridors that you just loaded in to. A jumping puzzle map was one of my first ideas when I saw the trailers for this game, so while I'm disappointed on a personal level, the regimented nature of drawing a straight line to the goal flies in the face of potential level diversity as a whole. Conversely, opting for the 'mario maker' style of letting the map maker prove their map is beatable by doing it themselves would let builders embrace more unique level ideas and keep the game unpredictable and give people—and I mean me—a constant reason to come back. Clearly, though, that isn't currently the case. There's a very 'samey' feeling to nearly all bases, and while the current map verification is a contributor to that fact, it's not nearly the biggest.Before I mentioned the tools players are given in MYM. There's a small but actually really varied arsenal that raiders can get their hands on: High ammo guns that can only kill enemies, swords for deflecting bullets and swords for crushing enemies' armor, and an invulnerability shield that rewards you for perfect parrying instant death. You get to bring two of these in at a time which leads to interesting builds and fundamentally changes your relationship with the map you're on. One build I like is the samurai that just runs around dual wielding blades and slashing everything to pieces. It's the same on the builders' side: there are grapple traps that reposition raiders, hologram walls that drop raiders and let you do some seriously creative stuff with monster positioning. But for all of that, raiders get rewarded for doing one thing: escaping the map. And builders? They get rewarded for one thing: killing raiders. The current state of the game shows how in-game incentives warp a playerbase's actions.Now what I say next is just my experience. It's anecdotal, and doesn't exactly represent a perfect picture of the game. If anyone reading this wants to form their own opinion without sinking money into a game that might die before it has a chance to live, steam has refunds for a reason. With that said, personal experience is still the  kind of experience anyone is going to have with this game, and mine is the reason this review exists at all. That experience not only ends with the kill box but begins with it too.When I booted up the MYM beta a month ago, the first thing I did was try to build a base. I found the land plot purchasing menu and noticed they cost in-game currency. I just loaded up the game; of course it was going to be at zero. So I raided—went from level to level collecting orange boxes and ruby red cylinders—until I could afford my first map. When I got it, though, I was worried—worried that a map that flippantly followed my creative interests wouldn't kill enough players to earn me the points I needed for my second map. I think you can guess what I did, but I'll say it anyway. I made a kill box—a lazy, blocky, mess with uncountable traps and monsters all pointed at the entrance the players have no choice but to walk in to. The worst part is that I was right. My first map is about to expire for good, and it sits around 3700 player deaths. That map funded all the weird and wacky building I pulled off. I could afford my hologram wall because of it, I got the beefy guards that make close quarters combat exciting and terrifying. But when I make my creative maps now, there's that worry that I can't afford to keep it all running, and it literally costs currency JUST to keep a map running, if it wasn't deadly enough. So my maps are all a little aggravating—not as much as the first, which I'm actually glad is about to go offline, but there's a bit of my first in all of them now.My time as a raider was like Dante's Inferno. I truly think it was a very minor and almost comical microcosm of going to hell for my sins. Every map was a kill box. Every. Single. One. And in this I could only be frustrated with myself and the other builders for bending to the currents of digital currency. I didn't quit, however, I optimized my build instead. For the fun sucking, soul crushing kill box, there is an equally unfair and unbelievable raiders build. With a deflecting sword, invulnerability bubble, and a speed boost, you can race past the cramped and unimaginative dungeons faster than they were built. I didn't feel like I was missing something by crushing a person's base in a minute flat. You can take one look at the map you load into and see the stagnant lineage of every map that came before it. And when you know how that map will look and how it will play, the only thing left for a player to enjoy is winning, and I want you to remember how a raider wins:Imagine that. The two playstyle's simplistic and diametrically opposed incentives between keeping a raider as bogged down in your base and, as a raider, running through other players' bases so fast you couldn't remember what color the  were leaves us in a game state where the only fun—which is a word I am stretching to its limit—is when you are done playing. Meet Your Maker is so uncompromisingly geared towards results that there is no room for anything else.Now I can't really stomach playing much more. I know it says fifteen hours now, but I played the beta for ninety, and the game is very much unchanged since then. I only hope that MYM's dev team breaks with their mother-company's tradition of ignoring their players. Right now, this game doesn't even have the player base to survive that kind of belligerence. I've said it before—it's even my title—the community is right. They're giving advice and feedback freely after buying the game.I'd like to believe that the devs will implement at least some of the community's suggestions, but their hesitance to speak about it on AMAs and streams leaves me doubtful. And for everyone on the fence about buying this game, I say wishlist it. . If they structure their game around results and raw numbers, chances are they'll respond to them too.Anyway, i understand that was a massive wall of text. If you made it to the end, thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: I have greatly enjoyed playing this game and likely I'll continue to enjoy it for a while.It's great to see the deadly designs that other players have come up with, and it's crazy how different individual bases can feel. _childDocuments_.review: PROS:- Pretty unique gameplay, I don't think there's anything similar on the market at the moment.- Graphics look ok. Enemy designs are interesting.- Good sound design, can tell what traps are firing based off sound.- Combat and mobility feels good, although everything being a 1shot kill can take some time to get used to.- Co-op Rading is a blast with a friend, co-op building can also be fun.CONS:- The games progression system is extremely one sided. If you don't raid you'll not be able to get anywhere with progression, which is pretty unfortunate since I enjoy building the deathtraps a bit more then Raiding the deathtraps.- Resource gain feels too slow. I really hope they increase how much resources you get soon, especially Synthite. Parts are the only resource that feels about right.- The content feels a bit light, I feel like there should be many more enemy types, traps, suits and weapons to choose from. So it can feel a bit stale after a while.VERDICT:I think MYM has a lot of potential to go from a good game to a great game, it just needs more content and time to mature. If support is kept up and new content keeps coming, I think this will be a great game in a year or so. Would I recommend to buy it? Yes, but get it on sale if at all possible, the base price is a bit high for what you get in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing this game during the free to play period we were given has come up short on any reason to buy this game for the $30 price tag they have attached. Sure the game can be fun to mess around in especially if you have a friend in there with you but the limitations in building, a core mechanic of a game like this, is so stifling it is criminal. They are just teasing you with ideas utilizing mechanics they have but they can't actually be done because their other mechanics get in the way. Compound this with the low selection of weaponry and gadgets, an already low player base, and the deprecation system and you get repetitive gameplay, nothing to grind for, and a base you worked hard on getting thrown into a closet with no incentive for players to look at it anymore. If the devs make a few changes, this game can really be something but until then, wait for a significant sale or just play it for free within the next 15 hours of this review and see it for yourself.

There are some problems of balance and base visibility to other players, but they are not critical and the developers are listening to the community feedback and show will and wish to take care of the problems. I think that Meet Your Maker - one of the best games that came out recently, and it's definitely worth a try.

_childDocuments_.review: Like a mad-max themed rogue-like shooter with a large dose of Mario Maker. This game is very addictive and very fun. When raiding other bases, it's intense and punishing. One wrong move and you have to start over from the beginning. Every death you learn a bit more about the base and learn what tricks to expect. Beating a base is a very satisfying feeling, but what's more satisfying is the building. I built my first base the other night, and because I'm low level, it's not difficult, and it's small. However, one player who I'm assuming was also a bit newer based on how he was acting in the replays, died 3 times before clearing it, and all 3 of those deaths were fun to watch, like watching a movie you've seen, thinking "here comes the hidden trap he hasn't seen yet..." and seeing potential weaknesses in your base that could use touch-ups. It's overall a very enjoyable game, and I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just started playing this but i love it. The creative freedom that the developers give is amazing!This game is like a mix between Mario Maker and Doom, which is a weird combination but i think it really works! the combat can be fluid or methodical depending on your preferred style, and the maps! They're GREAT! i've seen people who build super challenging bases made to test you reaction time (and your memory) just to pass their levels while others will take the complete opposite approach and focus on spectacle big fights and fun! The developers really knew what they were doing when designing their system.see there's no penalty for dying or getting successfully raided when you set up a base you can get rewards 2 ways, killing lots of people and reaping the rewards or getting accolades for your great level design both of which allow you to prestige your bases and improve on them! This encourages all sorts of level design philosophys and I love seeing it. I've seen super creative uses of traps and amazing room design in just 4 hours and i would HIGHLY recommend this to anybody who likes these types of games!honestly the only things i'd really want is the ability to add comments and maybe more unlocks in the future though this game has only recently released so i'm sure it will be expanded upon at a later date. The one big issue is that the game frequently crashes randomly, you'll just be playing the game then it will freeze up.TLDR I HIGHLY recommend this game and i can see myself playing it a lot in the future

_childDocuments_.review: I happen to like this game a lot, despite the issues it has. It manages to scratch a particular itch I can't quite put my finger on. Most everyone compares this to Mario Maker, with good reason, but I never played that game so I can't really comment there. To me, it oddly reminds me of Trackmania online play. Trackmania is a racing game, but all the tracks were user-generated in the editor. While racing, the other players/racers where essentially ghosts. They couldn't directly hinder you. Instead, you were really trying to figure out the "puzzle" that was the track itself. How to take each turn to get the best time. You don't directly race other players in this game (though I'm sure the speed running community will do that eventually by posting their times and videos elsewhere). It's that "solving a puzzle" element that feels so prevalent in this game. Ultimately, you are trying to solve a puzzle designed by another player, or vice-versa when you build a base and post it. And, to be clear, there is no official time element in this game. You can play as fast or slow as you desire. Depending on how you like to play, you'll get some resources faster than others, but you'll get everything you need eventually.At the time of writing this (about 2 weeks after release), there are definitely some growing pains as the community figures out what works and doesn't, and the other systems in place that encourage certain play-styles over others. The "meta", and the drama, are ever shifting. Last week it was "killboxes are impossible!", now it seems to be "long mazes are annoying and not fun". Point being, user-generated content games are a dice-roll. Your mileage will vary. The saving grace here is that you are not at all prevented from making progress in the game itself by running into a map that you can't beat/don't like. Just leave and play a different one.All of that said, as much as I like the game, I find it hard to recommend at full price, especially this early. Maybe after a few big content drops. For right now though, I highly recommend doing research. Watch the trailers, then go watch a few different streamers play it. If you love everything you see, great. Still on the fence? Wait for a sale or a free weekend. (Or play it for free on Playstation if you have that option, but I think it's only free for the launch month April 2023).
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game about building your outposts with traps and guards so invaders would be killed, and raiding other players outposts to steal some resources.The game starts very fun.Raiding bases, when they aren't just a crappy kill-room build, is fun for a few hours. Then you get used to every trick and it becomes repetitive.Building outposts and watching players get killed by your carefully setup distractions and traps is hilarious, until you realise the map you have spent two or three hours building will only be online twelve hours, plus twelve hours for every time you "prestige" it (you have to pay resources for it).The killer here is that even if your outpost is online, there is no guarantee anyone will raid it before it goes offline again.Update 1 : there has been a patch allegedly fixing that specific issue. I've tried to play a bit more and to prestige a couple of times : the fix doesn't work.Update 2 : an additional issue is the ever-increasing amount of outposts exploiting some mechanic or building bug that hasn't been fixed yet since the Beta.My original conclusion stands:In its current state, this one is for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: The game only works on paper. I think with better execution it would still work and could be its own popular genre. From where Meet Your Maker is today I feel like a total overhaul is needed, but really more of a total do-over. *Building Bases*Building a base is slightly less than OK. Tools are simple. Everything basically fills a single block in a 3D grid. There are a few traps, but be careful- your own traps can destroy the other traps. There are no movement modifier blocks (like a grav-lift, launch pad, ladder, etc) you can't even build a platforming puzzle because in order to share your base this little robot dude has to be able to walk ON THE GROUND to the end. This dramatically limits what you can do with being creative and means all you can build is essentially a single walking path to the end. Needs so much more to be fun. The major issue is how you share your base- you should force someone to complete their base before sharing. Add movement modifiers- ladders, launch pads, elevators, grav lifts. After running a few bases they are the same slogs through hallways or kill box rooms.Don't make people spend hours crafting weapons. Let the level designer provide the weapons and items at the start. Since they have to use those items to complete it before sharing- it adds SO MUCH more to the design and play strategy not in the game today. There is also a level I played that REQUIRED you to have purchased and equipped the shield to complete- this is bad design. The proper tools to even have a chance at completing a mission should be provided. Maybe you can work to meta upgrade certain items if the level provides them (like the level gives you the shield, and you had crafted it to have +2 uses outside of the level so when you get it in the level it is upgraded) but you should never be forced to have unlocked an item before completing a mission. The 'gunplay' is bad. I wanted a level where you tear through a jumping puzzle with a shotgun and blast the baddies-- what I got was a slingshot that you pewpew while standing on the ground. OVER AND OVER AND OVER AND OVER. *Playing Bases*If building bases is as simple as I noted... why would you think playing them is any better? It gets old FAST. I got a chuckle seeing some of the creative uses of the extremely limited tools you have to choose from, but it's not fun. It's a quick snort out of my nose and tip of my hat to the maker and then I move on.

_childDocuments_.review: I told them the problems that would kill this game when it was in alpha, they didn't listen and now the game its dead!You spend hours and days making your bases, you do raid after raid for weeks to get the resources to buy and build them. Then when your bases does well and kills lots of people, when they hit level 10 they die and you lose everything. Or you spent hours or days building an amazing base, but because not enough raiders come so its dies.What a complete waste of time!!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game rules.A podcast (The Besties) described this game as "mario maker + doom" and it did not disappoint.  Most levels are engaging and feel hand-crafted, because they literally are.  Getting impaled by some spikes out of nowhere feels good, in an odd way.  It feels good because you know a real person put that spike there to catch you off-guard.  I find myself saying "oh, good one" a lot while playing.  If it's extra clever, I steal that idea for my own levels.  The cycle continues. I couldn't explain the story with a gun to my head but the aesthetic is cool.  Mad Max and Blade Runner 2049.  Everything is very dusty.Of course, there are plenty of troll/impossible levels that aren't fun.  I tag these "Brutal" and move on quickly.  There's little downside. _childDocuments_.review: Okay so, 5 hours in... Meet Your Maker is a fun combination of dungeon building and trap defence (similar to Orcs Must Die!) and raiding other players' bases. The game runs smoothly and all the features feel very intuitive - the developers have obviously looked at how other games do base building and have taken a lot of good features. After a player raids your base, you have the option to watch their replay to see where you outsmarted them... and where you need to do more work!It's a visually pleasing game - the grimy "Mad Max" aesthetic is done well and, alongside the near-constant paranoia of looking out for traps and monsters, you feel quite immersed in the universe of the game. Where this gets muddled though is in the progression. There's no "story" to speak of, only the grind for resources to improve your equipment, traps, base or buy new land to create new bases. The upgrades though feel overly-expensive and having glanced through most of them I find myself uninspired to pursue any of the different areas mentioned above. It feels like it's a technique to add longevity to the game, but it's over-extended and actually feels disheartening. Even the most minor of upgrades means a sizeable grind, or sacrificing buying that new plot of land you've been working towards. I'd like to see 10 times as many upgrades at half the cost, and upgrades which actually effect play style - as it is, almost everyone plays the same way because there's little you can do to TRULY change your load-out.Is it a AAA title? No. What it does, does it do well? Yes!It's important to remember that MYM has only just been released and personally I'm eager to see where this game goes.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game a thumbs up. I do; it does so many things right; the look, the feel, and the entire idea is fantastic, but there isn't enough content to justify the price. Unless I'm missing something, you have a single unlockable ranged weapon, a single unlockable melee weapon, a single unlockable suit, 5-6 unlockable mutants to guard your outposts, and a handful of traps. Sure, all of these things have their own upgrades to go with them, and when it comes to the mutants and traps, I'll admit there's a nice selection, but suit and weapon upgrades are dull at best, and suit upgrades can be ignored. Sure, they're nice, but due to the nature of the game, there aren't major walls to overcome that require upgrades. I would have rather had skins or more suits in general. One of the game's primary goals has you "evolve" the chimera, something I thought would have a significant impact on the status/look of the sanctuary, but nope, you press a button and listen while the Chimera yells one of the few, repetitive voice lines at you. Leveling up vendors does... Well, I'm not sure what it does besides pulling them into the floor for several seconds, rendering them unusable for that time. No visual changes to them, maybe changes to the level of upgrade you can buy. Evolving the Chimera is made to look like you're doing something. When in reality, you're just opening a box of bonus resources. Several other reviews have already covered the issue with Killboxes, so I wont bother with that here, but it is a huge issue that needs to be resolved if the devs want any longevity out of this game. Once again, I could be missing something. There could be more content I still have yet to discover. Still, as of now, I see no signs of any extra unlocks, unless you count day one DLC (included in the deluxe edition) as extra unlockables. I'll happily change my review once the raiding side of the game gets some much-needed support and is no longer a content desert. If you must try the game, I remind you to keep and eye on your play time, and keep in mind that what you see in the level 1 vendor will be the exact same thing you see eight hours later in a much higher leveled vendor.

_childDocuments_.review: Been having a lot of fun with this, really cool idea done for the most part very well.However a few things to bare in mind:- Does feel a bit "Early Access" still, only two load outs, one being far more viable than the other and had a few crashes.- Progression feels a bit artificial, every level up system just gives a bit of currency and after 15~20 hours i had most of the upgrades i wanted, everything else left is just horizontal progression like new traps to try etc.- I've not had too much of an issue, but the fact that makers don't need to complete their own outposts means there are some very cheesy strats or just plain boring... like i could spend 20 mins slowly taking apart this copy pasted room, or i could just try another outpost.- Because the currency to maintain your outposts is the same as unlocking new traps + making new outposts I've hit a bit of a rut where i do some raids not to unlock new traps/make new bases but just to keep my current ones running. I have 3 outposts and it takes about 3~4 hours each day just to get them back up and runningAll small things that hopefully with time will be tweaked or fixed but overall been having a blast and look forward to what they add next.Some things i'd love to see:- Secondary objectives, we have the tombs (Which are not explained well to new players) but if we had more directed "Side Dungeons" which gave both the raider and the maker more on completion would really make the outposts have more substance to them. Maybe even have a keycard system to get to the GenMat.- Checkpoints, some of the bigger outposts are a slog and dying after 20 mins to have to do it all again is depressing. Maybe have the raider spend currency at a checkpoint to activate it so they have to balance the risk/reward? and that would encourage the maker to place them as they potentially get more currency.- A better rating system, you can use a boost to get more info about a outpost but even then its not that helpful, just some sort of player rating to know before going in, even if its to see an outposts accolades beforehand. also be nice to see the highest rated outposts to give them a try for ideas for your own outposts.- Decorations on traps, Because you cant place props/decorations on traps, even if they are second wave it leads to some very bland base building since you can tell if you decorate all but certain tiles that oh there's going to be a trap there later. Its a minor gripe but it would be great to have more freedom in decoratingOverall been having a blast, I hope this game succeeds and i look forward to what they add in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, after playing this game for over 40 hours, I think that's plenty of time enough to write a pretty solid review on it. First off, I will start by saying completely ignore ALL negative reviews about it not requiring you to complete your map to make it playable for others. This is literally not the case as I've tested it on various outposts and not one would actually activate if there was no path that could win. That said, yes, some maps can be EXTREMELY tedious in trying to find a way to win, but there is always a way to do it. The overwhelming majority of players have constructed well thought out bases for fun and a hefty challenge. You will die...often times a lot in some cases lol. I've seen people die to obvious traps, well hidden traps, and even their own friends hehe, which is always fun to watch the panic ensue. I myself have also wound up dying to my own grenades before, so I'm not innocent to stupid deaths either lol it happens when you least expect it to. Don't beat yourself up if you can't beat a map, simply play other ones till the next day. The choices refresh everyday as to what outposts show up for you to raid so if you have troubles beating one, simply play others till it refreshes and changes to another that you might be able to beat. So I highly recommend this game, especially if you have friends or enjoy critical thinking like myself! it's a ton of fun and despite the negative reviews, much of the community is even nice enough to put arrows to the "tombs" without any traps by them (especially true in the harder maps as these players tend to realize their traps are difficult to escape lol). Most people will test their own maps before activating them, so do not sweat that at all. Every outpost I've raided there was always a way to win, and that's even with some extremely difficult ones too with only 1 way out lined with traps lol. If you upgrade your weapon and suit, you'll do just fine. If you fail the first time, simply take what you learned and try again. And often times I've found the shield and grenade to be extremely useful in getting out of really difficult situations, so it's worth using both depending on the situation. Lot of enemies, use the grenade to clear some out. Lot of traps near the genmat? Use the shield after grabbing it and destroy the immediate threats while it's active. It's not too difficult once you learn how to maneuver. And as a last resort, you can always place a respawn point at a safe spot then grab the genmat and leave even if you die so long as your quick to do so.Overall, pros:Fun every changing maps (no 2 are the same)Great to watch the replays of those who raid your outposts (some really fun moments like the one I saw where this guy very narrowly missed getting hit in the left eye by a spike! It was so close I could just see the guy's heart attack moment unfold lol, I was like "I don't think that could EVER be closer than that!" and I saved that replay as it's awesome! And he won after that so great job to him! But there's a lot of fun replays like that too!)Easy to learn the mechanics and controls are quite smoothEverything is one hit to kill unless it's an armored enemy (psst, use grenades on those or a really big sword!)Critical thinking required to excelGreat fun with a friend!Lots of challenges and various updatesGreat concept and great delivery on it tooTons of potential future additionsCONS:There are definitely a few unfair maps that are 1 in 1000 to win. These are more of a waste of time and not fun to enter. Just leave those when you find em, save your sanity! lol but it does feel great if you stick to it and win at one of em too though! Some of the blocks can easily disorient you since they can be rotated in odd waysEnemies can easily be an unfair disadvantage if a lot of them are in one big room against you where they all see you at once.A lot of players put tons of traps pointed at the genmat with no clear way to escape it unless you're very luckyBadly laid out outposts make designing nice looking ones difficult at timesLimited number of blocks to build with/outpost customizing is pretty limited for nowThe really neat blocks are locks behind paid DLC that is half the price of the base game (feels like these shoulda been base game to be honest)Limited number of potential outposts you can raid (if you're having troubles clearing them you can't refresh to new ones manually, making it impossible to progress sometimes if you're getting only bad outposts to raid)Keeping your outposts activated requires a LOT of raiding from yourself (best done wth a buff and even then it can take 10 raids to get enough coin to reactivate your own, which increases as you prestige up your own too)You die to anything with one hit. (This makes certain areas very difficult to survive such as a tight cooridor with 4 armored enemies rushing at you with nowhere for you to get away to....yup that situation sucks when they take up to 4 hits each and you die to one....would definitely be better with at least a free revive back to the spawn with all the traps cleared from previous life (but you'd have to go back and get the genmat again of course). Dying to the simplest of traps is inevitable, and it will happen lolKilling yourself is easier than you think, yes you Spider man imposter! Swinging around like that will eventually make you die to something you shoulda seen coming a mile away!Players aren't required to give a clear way to safety at the genmat location (yup, can be completely lined with traps all pointing at you from any direction you can potentially escape to. You're only way out is sheer luck custodian!)Resources feel lacking at times from players killed at your base, sometimes not giving anything at all.Coins are very difficult to get compared to the other materials (say about 25 or so per raid in most cases when an outpost activation starts at 600 for the smallest one and each upgrade takes anywhere from 250 to 800 and each outpost prestige starts at 650 for the next level or 600 to refill if it doesn't have enough prestige (more or less, this takes so long to replenish that by the time you do, your other outposts have farmed up all the materials while you were doing that so you have to repeat it in an endless grind)But anyway, take it as you will. I quite enjoy the game, will get it for my friend so she can play with me too cause I think she'll like it too! Playing together is definitely more fun than alone, but a lot less challenging if you're looking for the challenge. I'd say give Meet Your Maker a shot if you are looking for a great game with repetition but not endlessly grinding the same map over and over. Every raid will be different, guaranteed! I really hope the devs take this game even further and make it way more expanded on traps, suits, gadgets and just the overall potential that is already there being filled out more. They can do so much with it and I really hope they do! I bought the game thinking "welp I'm going to be terrible at this but hey I'll give it a chance" and wound up being pretty good overall, but still die a few times here and there. If you take your time, you're set for the most part! Hope you found my review helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics & Visual Style: The game's graphics may not be groundbreaking, but they convey a unique atmosphere reminiscent of Doom and Rage. The character models, in particular, showcase a level of creativity that helps distinguish Meet Your Maker from other FPS titles.Storyline & Characters: While the story centers around evolving a Chimera and collecting genetic material, it serves primarily as a backdrop for the gameplay. Although the narrative may not captivate players, it provides a context for the game's main focus: base-building and raiding.Gameplay: Meet Your Maker truly excels in its gameplay, offering an engaging experience where players both raid and build bases. This combination of creativity and competition sets it apart from other FPS games, providing a fresh alternative for fans who desire a break from typical multiplayer matches or battle royales.Soundtrack & Sound Design: The soundtrack is a solid accompaniment to the action on-screen, setting the tone without stealing the spotlight. While it may not be particularly memorable, it serves its purpose.Technical Aspects & Controls: Some bugs and quirky controls, such as the grappling gun, are present, but they do not significantly detract from the overall experience. Players can adapt to these quirks as they progress through the game.Difficulty & Learning Curve: Meet Your Maker strikes a balance between casual and hardcore gaming, catering to fans of the FPS genre who appreciate a challenge without feeling overwhelmed.Additional Features: The game's gore adds a visceral element to the experience that some players may find appealing. It's worth noting for those who appreciate or prefer to avoid such content.Considering its unique gameplay mechanics and overall engaging experience, Meet Your Maker earns a solid rating of 7.5 out of 10. It's a creative and gory spin on the FPS genre that's worth exploring for fans looking for a fresh approach.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fairly decent, don't get me wrong. Loading into other people's levels, seeing what unique twists, combos, and ways people design their bases is amazing.  The progression is worth the reward, and its fairly easy to get the resources you need to buy the upgrades for your attacker or base upgrades for defender. So, good job there.However, the deal breaker for me is the way the base design works. Just discovered that artistic map I made for an hour and half filled with traps, strategy, and a theme (some maps i was getting onwards of 6 kills so it was working) ran out of its map resource, making the map no longer accessible.  Having to constantly remake maps and spend my currencies on buying new land is a bit of a deal breaker for me.  I'm someone who likes map design, spending hours on Divinity's campaign makers, Far Cry 5's maps, Halo Forge (back in the day), so i'm someone who likes my creations to be permanent and repeatedly played on.If you're like me, and are heavily invested in the base building part, maybe think twice, as you'll be forced to remake your creations as they become irrelevant.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 - If you enjoy base building and/or raiding other player's bases, you will enjoy this game!At the time of writing, 24 April 2023, the game has just released and in all fairness, you can tell.There's a small bug here and there, some things need some smoothing out and the game has crashed several times for me.Other than these few minor issues, the game does feel like a finished game. There is plenty of content and diversity. You can build and play a lot of different base types. Some you will enjoy, others you won't, but you don't lose anything by just skipping the bases you don't like.The game offers several unique trap types and each trap has several mods to slightly adjust what it does.There are several weapons and play styles to choose from when raiding bases as well.What excites me most about this game is knowing that it's from the makers for Dead By Daylight. If they keep updating this game like they did DBD, we're going to have an AMAZING game in a few months that will only get better and better the coming years.To me this is mostly a single player game. You can build and raid with two players, but that sort of just breaks the game and removes all the challenge. Though a lot of people who have raided my bases seem to be enjoying doing it together.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid gameplay, satisfying gameplay loop with room for flexibility, and a unique approach to several genres simultaneously.If you were to take the base building from Dungeons and greatly expand on it, then combine that with Dark souls, you would get close to describing this. From making your base, to setting up traps, with full creative license, to the foul and devious sense of joy watching others fall to your careful planning and strategy. This game puts forth it's very best!Make raids on dungeons made by fellow players, dodge harrowing traps, defeat guards around every corner, grab the objective and make your escape! Sound fun? Good, because there's more! You get your chance to make your own beautiful and horrible labyrinths filled with danger, pitfalls, and dead ends. After each run, purchase upgrades to make yourself and your lair even more dangerous. Outsmart your adversary for bonus points and resources. Expand your arsenal to create a work of art to be proud of! The movement is fluid, the visuals are impressive, and best of all the bugs are minimal and quickly addressed by devs when bug reports are made. Definitely worth full-price! My only complaint isn't with the game at all, but y'all make some right nasty levels!

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and original concept BUT falls short of greatness on almost every aspects other than the core gameplay.Ressources and upgrades:To build a base and to upgrade your character/your traps and guard you need ressources. This, to me, is the biggest problem with this game. There are 3 types of ressources which I'll just call red orange and blue here but the difference between what they can be used to buy will only matter for the first few hours of you playing the game. You will quickly find yourself always lacking red and having an abundance of blue and orange. This is an issue because every traps/guards/character upgrades that you can buy always requires red + either blue or orange. Red can only be acquired by leveling your chimera(this is a long process that takes more or less 10 raids), completing daily challenges or by encountering reward nodes on the new expedition raiding system. Completing any of the above will typically only reward you with enough red to buy a single upgrade. Upgrades are very strong, very fun to use while raiding and building bases and should be rewarded to hard working players, but as it currently stands the process of obtaining upgrades is way to slow and repetitive. It completely breaks the flow of the game and will have you raid for hours before you can afford enough upgrades that you want to go back and rework existing bases or create new ones.Building bases:The controls of the base editor are pleasant and easy to use. There are several environment in which to build and they can have different weather conditions, sizes and flavor, providing players with a decent amount of choice to be creative with. A good palet of block styles and colors to choose from. Generally new environments and blocks are added with updates.Traps:While there isn't a massive selection of traps offered, They can all be customized with 2 upgrades that range from a simple rate of activation acceleration to fully altering the way in which they function. That being said some traps and upgrade are obviously a lot weaker than some others but the developers have made balance changes in the past.Guards:offer a wide variety of attack style and are in my opinion fun and interesting to fight against in raids. I will mention two things that I don't like about them: The upgrades for guards feel generic and unexciting, they are more or less the exact same on every types of guards with 1-2 actually gameplay changing mechanics included.The armor lack visual clarity especially from a distance. I think the armor upgrades provide interesting challenge but it's often hard to tell what part of the guard is being shielded when far away from them.Collecter/harvester/base generation:When building a base you have to create a valid path for the collector npc to walk from the spawn point of your base to the "objective" of the base. Bases are randomly generated but come with some amount of obligatory blocks that cannot be deleted. This along with the valid path restriction can often hinder creative freedom when making bases. Note that this was originally meant as a resctriction to keep the builder from making an impossible to complete base(validly so), but it's now become clear that such bases can exist even with this restriction which is mostly why I have a problem with it.Story/visual style/ambiance:I love the creepy dystopian wasteland in which the game takes place. I was very excited to explore the world when i first started playing. I wondered about what caused humanity to go nearly extinct, I was excited to meet/kill other player's chimeras, the advisor all seemed like they had interesting backstories and the player lobby seemed like it held secrets and upgrades that I would unlock along the way. All this potential is fully wasted, there is no story in this game, the player hub serves no purpose and could easily be replace with a menu and the NPCs constantly say the exact same lines adding nothing to a world that seemed like it was designed with a lot of taught and interest. I hope this will be expended upon at some point.Newly added expedition system:I personally think this brings little more or nothing more to the raid gameplay loop. You have to complete every raid in order to complete the expedition so why even add paths to the expedition? It's as if this was meant to give the palyer more agency on what raids they want to do and create a danger VS reward tension but at the end of the day it feels even more restricting than the old system.In short, Meet your maker is a game with a great concept and a fun and interesting core gameplay (raiding/building system) where every other system feels like incomplete fillers. It's truly a shame to see such potential being wasted.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, I can have fun in this game and I like the idea that they were going for. But I wouldn't recommend it, not even on sale, because it is a live service and its player count is barely 100 peak players on steam so at any point you could get the "I'm sorry" Jpeg from the dev's saying they're shutting down service on the game. Also the state of the game is piss poor. Again I like this game, but thats the bottom line.    I'll go further into my opinion below but I've had fun and I appreciate that the Dev's stuck to their vision despite the community voicing desire for changes to how maps dole out rewards and are considered for matchmaking.         Almost a year after release I don't think it was the right choice, people asked for changes for a reason. The system that existed led to the same map with the same goal and 0 creativity no matter what difficulty you were on.  Kill boxes, maps whose only goal was to kill a player as many time as possible with as small a chance of success for the one playing the map as possible. These maps were close to never fun to play against and crazy easy to make yourself because you never had to actually complete a map yourself, unlike in similar concept game Mario maker, leading to a feedback loop no one wanted which in turn led to the fore-mentioned requests from the community only to fall on disinterested ears. On top of 2-3 new items to unlock every 3 months some of which might be irrelevant to you because you just build, or just run maps. Itd kill anyone's motivation to keep playing.Playing now you don't see any kill rooms. Not because they don't work, they would if they were still made they never changed the system, but because the only people left playing are playing with the mentality of "If i die more than 2 times its not worth completing" and will leave long before a kill room has any chance to work. On top of that if your map takes too long people will also leave, because its just not worth it to complete it.  I am also guilty of this mentality because of how rewards are still doled out. it has nothing to do with time, or deaths in a level its all about completion. A flat reward upon completion. so spending 30 min trying to beat the map you died 60 times in rewards the same if not LESS than the map you completed in 30 seconds to 1 minute. Sure there are Vaults you can find in a level but sometimes a map creator will just block them off so is it really worth it to spend another 2 minutes looking on the off chance they have just for an extra 10-20 currency?     This thought is just permanently stuck in your mind while your making any gameplay decision because to make maps you need currency to buy them, which you get from running maps. To get new gear to run maps you need currency, so you have to run maps. To get new traps to put in your maps you need currency, so you have to run maps and so on.    Not to say that you cant get currency from deaths in your created maps but because of the mentality of efficiency that permeates the games systems at large anything you'd get from a map in 24 hours real time is outclassed by an hour of playing.  All that on top of 1-2 new traps or weapons every 6 months

_childDocuments_.review: When I first got into it I was expecting a lot of unfun bases that try their best to kill you through overwhelming you with quantity, but I was pleasantly surprised when I started playing. About 90% of bases are actually decently designed with plenty of unique designs that are fun to go through. The leftover 10% are ones that either put you in a death chamber at the end when you pick up the material or a mess of small corridors with multiple traps around every corner with the occasionall big room with 30+ traps aiming at every step you walk forward.Luckily there is a simple solution for both problems. For the death chambers at the end you can use the shield consumable to get your bearing and then play the map out normally as you head back. As for the bases that are unfun and try to make your life hell around every corner, you can abandon them! You do not lose anything for just leaving the map and abandoning it, look for greener pastures instead.Watching replays in the bases I am proud of building is also very fun. Watching how different people fall for different traps so you can fine tune it a bit to give them more breathing room or to adjust the traps or layout a bit to create different challenges feel very rewarding when you see the next runner go through.The main thing I wish that the game had would be emotes. It would be fun to see back in replays when people emote out of frustration or because they approve of a design. Perhaps with an emote icon in the timeline for replay watchers so they can see where the action is happening.Another interesting thing would be the ability for the attacker to put down a sign with a comment that you can see when you go into building mode and that would disappear once you leave building mode again similar to the death beacons they leave behind.
