_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game if you like fast paced dungeon running or building nefarious deathtraps.I see a looot of "killroom" complaints, and I think these are mostly frmo players not using most of the mechanics, people who are playing slowly and not using the parry, grapple speedboost etc, which are tools you're meant to use on harder levels. A lot of the easier levels lull you into "crawling" gameplay where you peak every corner slowly and methodically only use a gun to disarm traps one at a time, you just can't do this for all the levels, so people are suddenly experiencing a massive difficulty spike when snail gameplay doesn't work.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved playing this during beta and I like what it is. It's a fresh idea and in many ways, the kind of game I probably dreamed of having as a kid. Some changes to the core gameplay loop need to happen for me to recommend it to anyone though. As it stands now, it is not sustainable: It requires constant farming of materials just to keep your bases running - player-made bases are what keep the game going, and it forces you to farm for HOURS just to keep one of yours running for another day, leaving no time for enjoying the creative part or unlocking fun upgrades to make it more interesting (traps, etc. use the same resource) It's been out a short time and I already cannot keep up with this and I feel like it will kill the game without serious changes. I understand the need for a loop that encourages people to do both building and raiding, but most players aren't going to spend several hours "earning" the opportunity to do the thing they want to do. Reward creative builders and make it so I don't have to farm 1000 thingymabobs just to turn on one of the several bases we're encouraged to keep operating. Provide incentives for  raiding through other means and let people do what they enjoy and it will be fun. Otherwise it is a job that people will quit very soon and the rest of the game will erode as a result and people will have nothing to raid. (edited for clarity / length)

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some aspects to love on both ends.First off raiding is fun for those who like to explore as each base is crafted by other players meaning you always have to check every corner never knowing where traps are exactly or what the layout will be.Raiding is also for those who like a challenge, with the game being one hit and dead (outside of some tools that block damage) Building is fun in it's own way if you like being creative either in how it looks or trap placement. Checking replays later can be a mixed bag of laughing when things work or cheering for a struggling player (even tho it's a replay and you know they made it eventually).

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an insanely cool concept but a terribly unsuccessful implementation. It's fun to play, the asymmetry constantly forces you to switch between game modes. The builder allows you to construct genuinely beautiful structures, which challenges other players to figure out how to conquer the next peak. HOWEVER! The online experience is just dreadful. Firstly, to maintain 5 bases, you need, on average, about 3900 in-game currency, which is earned in approximately 1.5 hours by raiding other bases. That might not sound critical, as it opens up access to the third appealing aspect of the project - watching replays of other players raiding your base.Unfortunately, the online community is so negligible that you spend 2 hours farming every day (plus about 30 hours on construction, give or take a reasonable 5 bases). That's the minimum, but only about 10 unique individuals will see your base, if you're lucky.I'll give the game a plus in hopes of improvement, but if bhvr doesn't change their marketing strategy and methods of sustaining the online community, it'll be a big fat minus

_childDocuments_.review: Good concept and there's a game here that will be very fun with time, but the consensus right now is pretty clear: creative and fun bases are not incentivized enough, it's far easier and more successful mechanically to instead build huge rooms filled with guards and the same plasma trap over and over. Little care taken to planning, to crafting rooms or corridors with cleverly hidden traps; just throw a bunch of random nonsense in the same room and everyone will get overwhelmed. Also, unlike my experience in the betas, the game is crashing *constantly.* I haven't had crashes in a game this bad in some time. Needs time for rebalancing the game to promote better bases and fixing performance.EDIT: Apparently they're not gonna do any of the stuff I thought would be pretty obvious for a dev working on this game so this review should be a lot less hopeful than it is!

It is however really enjoyable to see tricks that others  have come up with and find your own way to mix techniques to make your own frustrating death trap. The one thing I will say as the most important would be that this game does lose its luster after awhile. _childDocuments_.review: Lots of potential, but ultimately a grindy waste of time.Avoid.In this game, you raid bases built by other players, and build yourself some bases.Doing so level up councellors, which in turn level up a chimera, which in turn gives you some ressources.There's three main ressources. All let you unlock some stuff, but : the red one is only used for unlocks and thus become irrelevant after a while, the blue one is used for consumables but is dropped quite frequently so you'll be swimming in it, and then there's the yellow one, called synth.Unlocking a level slot to build cost synth. Unlocking traps cost synths. Unlocking guards cost synth. UPKEEPING YOUR LEVELS cost synth too, and lots of it. Because there's a prestige system in this game : after a while (max 24 hours), you have to reactivate them by paying some more synth, an amount close to what it took to buy the slot at first, but it gets worse : depending on your outpost performances in killing players and gaining accolades, you may have to prestige it. Doing so allows you to put more stuff in your level, but it'll cost more and more synth each time. It's NOT optional, and eventually, a 24h activation become more expensive than the first time, for the same result.Best part being, after the outpost reaches level 10, it won't be reactivated again. After that it gets relegated to "social" raiding if you so choose, a mode where no one gains anything.You gain pitiful amounts of synth by killing raiders in your outpost, a little by raiding yourself destroying traps, and a bit more by leveling up the chimera. But even when using drop boosts, it's a slog to maintain levels running - and remember, it's also used for unlocking stuff, so you're making no progress on that front in the meantime.On top of that, while some outposts are fun to raid, the current meta is a glitchfest of traps hidden behind opaque cubes, or a good old overwhelming spam of traps in a killbox. Allegedly some people find that "fun". Current steam stats tell me there's not that many of them and they'll be enjoying a stale game pretty soon, as devs aren't showing any sign of changing anything. Maybe they're willing to keep the server on but even that isn't that sure.So yeah, don't buy it. Maybe give it a try if it goes F2P one day, but expect tedious grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker had such potential to be good but the game flopped real quick. One of my biggest complaints is the building in this game and how you can publish it without beating it. In most games like this, the player has to do a run and beat the level in order for it to be playable, games like Mario Maker. But this game is far from that. The building in this game is so frustrating and limiting and it's all because of one mechanic in the game. When building, you have a harvester and you have to be able to path the harvester to and from your objective and from. But here's the problem, the harvester can only walk, so if you're trying to create a path that requires you to jump, grapple, etc, good luck with that.Now let's talk about maps being published. There are a lot of times that people don't play your map and your map remains active for a certain amount of times before you have to spend points to be able to activate it again. I personally think it's stupid, why am I having to spend points in order to keep a map I spent a lot of time active?I had such high hopes for this game and as someone who loves to build in video games, I'm very disappointed. I understand Behaviour taking risks creating something new but I feel the execution was poor. Graphically it looks nice but gameplay just sucks. Behaviour, in their words, did a good job with the game so far. Might as well stick with Dead By Daylight

Thus you won't find yourself in a situation where you absolutely have to have a specific upgrade to progress.What the game does need though, is replays of the people raiding your dungeons. _childDocuments_.review: Went in thinking players killboxes would be the "be all end all" but the reality is you have a lot of power as the player with a grappling hook and movement. You can react to a lot of basic traps like spikes/arrow launchers really well. I've beat all the player levels I've played thus far on the three difficulties, and made one map that killed 22 times in 10 attempts, with only one person ragequitting. So most maps are pretty beatable, you will die, but you will eventually succeed. Theres some crazy ones though with really good setups ( 2x guards on each side, two arrow traps on the ceiling, orb launcher at the back, guards on on ramps and grenade launcher somewhere on the floor )Can be played in coop building and coop raids. Very interesting gameplay loop

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game.  Not Great.  For the price, the gameplay loop needs some work that it doesnt seem like the developers are going to put into the game.  The game lacks features to make maps truly unique once youve seen the tricks most people are using.  Currently, the game is great for the first 10 hours, then you fairly rapidly see the end of new content.The DLC pack is salt in the wound, as it allows players to make use of blocks very close in colour to the traps, which appears to be counter to the in game designs against letting you disguise your traps.  If you can pay money to get background blocks that look like traps, why cant I repaint the traps?  The lack of any way to distinguish between "fun and challenging" and "room of pain" makes finding maps to complete frustrating.  I have seen some really cool and unique levels that players have made, but there needs to be a way to "downvote" crappy content or move it to a difficulty beyond brutal.  If the developers make an effort to add more content to the game, then the pricing makes sense. As it is, it needs a reduction in price, or more content.  There are some other issues with the game that need visiting, -constant need to change locations resulting in revisiting the (reasonable, but frequent) load times.

_childDocuments_.review: I have more than a thousands hours on DbD, and when I saw this was Behavior behind this game, I was like "meh, will it be good ?" because let's face it, they're mostly famous thanks to DbD... But oh god, I don't regret buying this game a single second.The game is, honestly, quite addictive. It has a doom-like mood but all handmade by players, which is something I like.Additionally, I don't share the opinion of some other players saying "They need to make it so players need to succeed their base before publishing it". I think this is a good thing that it's not in the game, because it forces player to invest and use all the tools that are given to the players.Yes, some dungeons are, honestly, incredibly hard. But you can have an invulnerability shield, you can speed run, you can buy extra ammo, you can reflect projectiles (yes, it takes some skills & timing, but you can !) so no, honestly, I really think that all dungeons are possible. Some just take some extra thinking.And yes, some other are just "kill-boxes" without any hints of ingeniosity. But what if you give the player some resources ? Who cares, as you're not losing any if a bit of your time ?After all, that's why you can give a grade to the dungeon once you're done. You finished it but didn't like it ? Don't give it any grade, it's fine. No grade will punish him once the dungeon's timer has ran out.Overall, I think the game is great and very fun to play, of course there will always be people to complain, but the game is brand new and the developers already shared the "upcoming roadmap" which is great news.Bonus : You can actually skin your maps like DbD, which is awesome :D

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game and great concept. I am excited to see where this goes. Being able to play on player created levels make for a wide range of difficulty. _childDocuments_.review: You can build or raid; you aren't required to do both.The game has impressive polish and balance, especially for a new release.Don't let the negative reviews scare you away from a good time. Some maps require a lot of patience and practice to complete, but you can do it! It doesn't cost anything to keep trying.(Yes, there are consumables like grenades but they are purely for convenience and are never  required.)You have a grapple and a double jump, it rewards skilled movement and has a very responsive feel.It is satisfying to break traps and kill guards, you can find the game currency from destroying them.You can bring a friend with you for 2 player co-op if you enjoy more relaxing gameplay.Building is very intuitive and there are many quality-of-life features.Every time another player tries your map (even if you are offline), it will save a replay so you can see how they played it.When you go back to your map to edit it, you can pick up currency from the places where players died.The game feels very unique and I highly recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: Played the hell out of the beta and picked the full game up late last night (thought it was out the following day)I think I have built a "kill box" that people are complaining about but I've only played 1 map before that's kind of like mine. To build a "kill box" is hard. If you just put traps everywhere, when a trap is triggered it can destroy another trap or kill a guard. You need to watch the replays of how people beat your map and improve it. Because of the time I've put into building my base, I get alot of kills, but 9 out of 10 co op players complete it and 6 out of 10 solos complete it. They just die alot and that's the point of building a base. I've played some maps that have some amazing ideas, using traps in ways I didn't think possible. I wish there was a way to leave a message to the builder to say what you liked and thought about parts of it. The whole game is a action puzzle that you have to work out when to run and when to take it slow. The people complaining need to learn that. People who grappling hook though my base fast and non stop, do it in 2 or 3 life's. People  who move slow trying to take out all the traps do it in 20 30 40 life's. Every map requires you to change your play style and that's what the hook of the game is.

_childDocuments_.review: This game scratches some itches for me. I'm a big fan of base building and making puzzle traps. There are no other games where you get to do this against real players that I can think of other than Mario Maker. You get to outwit players and not some NPC zombie like on 7 Days to Die. I have came across some outposts that are nearly impossible to complete alone or they take an extra-ordinary amount of time and patience to complete. On top of that, you will earn a variety of equipment that can help you in tough situations.  The Harvester is enough as to determine if it can be a win as I've seen players just hold W through a raid even with 10 traps set off at once. I just wish they'd add Boss fights. That's all this game lacks is a boss fight.My number one issue, however, is that BHVR is not hyping this game as much as it should.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game. Puts level design in the player's hands, bringing out all kinds of devious ideas that are so fun to be challenged by, not to mention people coming up with all sorts of cool aesthetics and themes to their maps (Giant prison? Eerie tomb? Circus tent?). Gameplay is extremely satisfying. You have a grapple and double jump, cool katana, and electric rifle with limited ammo that challenges you to use your bullets, and your movement, strategically. Cyborg guards get split in half, bombs drop from the ceiling, you can slice through incoming arrows. It's really cool.Overall, I love it and I would recommend it to anyone who likes FPS-style building trapped up bases, watching people attempt them (the game has a replay feature for everyone who plays your map), and running through the gauntlet yourself to fly out of a trap-infested ruin like Indiana Jones.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR It's a fairly challenging and enjoyable game that has the potential to become really great. Feels like Doom meets Rust with a bit of Super Mario Maker and Portal mashed together. With updates, this is definitely capable of becoming a fantastic game and I highly recommend it.Heard a lot of people complaining about some aspects like absurd difficulty on some player creations, not having to actually beat your own creation to publish it, route pathing being limited to slops and planes, etc. There are some legitimate complaints there. The building types are rather limited and some trap placement is rather BS at times. I will say that very rarely have I found a base to be basically unraidable due to the difficulty.I think that progress is super slow, it definitely needs to be sped up and there needs to be more options of weapons, traps, enemies, expanded building options, etc. The game is still early in it's life and Behaviour has a very dedicated subsect of players who will complain about anything the dev team does or talks about; but I do hope this game gets attention and love from palyers and the devs. It really is special and has genuine potential.As of launch week: buff material acquisition rates, improve the AI pathing or allow players to custom/manually path, expand on the base building options, add more of everything (weapons, tools, blocks, traps, monsters, etc), force creator completion to publish, add a proper tutorial, etc.Behaviour will likely add most if not all these things that I and many others have mentioned in the coming weeks and months. Hopefully, this game will get serious content added down the line. What there is now definitely is a solid start, they've got a good foundation for the dev team to build off of.I look forwards to seeing where this game goes. _childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome! It's basically a mature mario maker extraction game focused on trap bases and shooting. You build bases and get rewards for them killing other people. You play other people's bases and get rewards for beating them. You use these rewards to buy new traps, new abilities and lots of stuff to upgrade your character and your base. It's a fun and rewarding gameplay loop. This is not a platforming game, it's about trying to maneuver through a kill house and escape with the treasure. You won't be doing pixel perfect jumps or crazy obstacle courses. You'll mostly be trying to figure out how to get past/destroy X trap without Y and Z trap killing you. Before any trap is triggered, you'll see a red alert flash and have about 1 second to react. For the most part, you can dodge or avoid almost every trap fairly easily. I'v seen people complain about traps in the back but you quickly learn to lookout for those and you still get a red alert to help you avoid them.More difficult bases will use a combination of traps to bait you into moving the wrong way or something and it can be fun to try and figure out the proper way to avoid the combination of traps A few of the higher difficulty maps can be extremely difficult but they are not impossible, especially once you have upgraded your character and abilities some. It's a great game and definitely worth a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it for a week or so, then realised how utterly shallow it is.You have three shapes/bricks/primitives to build out of; a cube, a slope, and a pyramid. No concave shapes at all. You place traps, which trigger when they see a player. That is it. Place enough traps to make a killbox or place traps aimed at traps, aimed at traps. Make a maze. Yay for a day or two. Oh and nomatter how good, your bases are removed from play after lvl 10, so try keeping enthusiasm while building your 30th base from scratch.The core concept of asynchronously raiding other player's bases is solid, and I look forward to more games inspired by MYM, But I don't think there's enough here to maintain a playerbase. It's neither complex nor rewarding enough.Edit: Uninstalled now. Sorry devs. Make it more.Edit #2: I feel compelled to edit again after the dev response. I want to get back in to it, because the game is beautiful and moody.. But as a builder there's nothing interesting to do beyond trying to distract raiders enough to walk into traps. As those raiders know they're raiders, they are expecting traps. Give us more SYSTEMS to mess with. Motion detector blocks linked to separate trap blocks, moving blocks, conveyor belt blocks, water/swimming/underwater traps and enemies, commander guards that make subordinate guards act as a team, Cube (movie) style laser guillotines running down tracks... There are so many places you could go with this whole asynchronous base raid thing but all a creative player can do is place block traps.

_childDocuments_.review: The builder and raider playstyles in Meet Your Maker are both highly enjoyable and virtually equally rewarding. The game is quite entertaining and addictive. Due to the repetitive nature of the game, I would say that this isn't the kind of game I would advocate playing for extended amounts of time; therefore, I would say that this is best enjoyed in short bursts, but to each their own.I appreciate the game and generally find it to be pretty enjoyable, despite the fact that I have listed more drawbacks than advantages. The scale of the player base and the fact that every map has been made by a player worry me because, if the player base ever dips low enough, there might not be enough fresh content to go around. I'd suggest this game to folks who like building lethal outposts or who like playing fast-paced, violent raider games. If the devs manage to handle this game properly, I see it holding enormous potential.After spending more time with the game, I've acquired more ideas about it, as well as additional negatives. The game is enjoyable and entertaining, but it has some fundamental flaws that make it unsatisfying, infuriating, and at times disheartening.Overall, I want this game to succeed since it strikes me as a very unique game that I can see myself playing for a long time provided some of the issues I've raised are solved.

_childDocuments_.review: (Review revised after 9 more hours of play.)Lets get the easy stuff out of the way first. The game is well presented and while the graphics won't win any awards the aesthetic is great. The sound design is on point and it needs to be, as the sound cues are important as you're working your way around a level. The UI is intuitive enough and the game plays just as well on K&M as it does on a controller, including the base building (though given the nature of the game, K&M is probably the preferred option).That's the pleasantries out of the way...Games like these live or die by their community and their creations. Being given away for "free" on PSN has given it a grace period as thousands of people can try the game without a dog in the fight, bring in fresh content and add more meat to the grinder (more on that later). Quite a shrewd move by Behavior. Though even 4 days after release its showing signs of dying within a couple of months.Every base you go into, you go into blind. Not in terms of it's content, that can be overcome by the abilities o f your "advisors", which will give you a rough idea of what you're up against once they're levelled enough. No, the problem is that you have no idea if you're going up against a boring labyrinth or a killbox (of which there are many). The game gives you four feedback options upon completion of a level, of which you can select two; "fun", "brutal", "artistic" and "ingenious". As oversimplified as these options are (God forbid we're able to leave a comment on a level) they're ultimately pointless, as you can't see the feedback a level has received prior to playing it. In an era where people are incapable of taking any form of criticism, there is no facility to leave any kind of negative feedback, so the only option available is to block the player, preventing them from viewing your replays or their maps appearing in your rotation.Even if your life depended on those little dopamine hits from your intricately designed Reddit post, it wouldn't matter. You are the only person who can see that feedback and it doesn't incentivise you to create a level that is challenging or good to look at, because the mechanics of the game are geared towards you killing players for their resources. Killbox it is then.Bases are not permanent. Once they have extracted their resources they are deactivated. To reactivate them requires one of the three resources (mobile game mechanics?) to "prestige" your base. Your base can go through 10 levels of prestige. Once you hit the 10th level, your base is disabled permanently and can only be played "socially" and won't net you any resources or XP (as far as I know). The gameplay loop here is that to maintain a base it has to operate as a meat grinder, as the easiest way to obtain the resources required to keep it running is by killing players. Am I the only one that can see the problem here long term? The plaudits you might receive are meaningless. Thumbs up don't maintain your base, resources do. Why create a fun, challenging aesthetically pleasing base? Head pats don't keep the lights on.The multiple types of resources should be a dead giveaway for what type of game this is. This kind of thing is a staple for F2P games. The three resources are cells, parts and synthite. Three levels of obfuscation. I won't go into detail, but once you realise that there are multiple levelling systems in this game you know what you're up against; its a treadmill. The same kind of mechanics can be found on any cash-grab mobile game.Once you've obtained all of the tangible stuff in the game (unlocked and upgraded all weapons, traps, mobs etc) theres very little on offer. You don't even get any kind of cosmetic alterations to your hub to signify any progress. Your hub will look the same on day one as it will a week from now.The one saving grace of this game is the level editor, but even this is flawed. Buying a location for your base doesn't come cheap and the price varies depending on the size of the plot and the resources on offer. The problem is you can't preview the location before you buy it. How is that a problem? Bedrock. The first location I purchased was terrible and didn't lend itself to making a decent level because of the positions of the genmat (the "goal") and the indestructible bedrock. A level cannot be activated until there is a clear path to the genmat (no jumping allowed!) and as you can't relocate the genmat you have to work your way around a randomised set of bedrock which can't be previewed before you commit your resources. There is no option for a blank slate, so that's another thing impeding your creativity. The tools to create your base are fine, the material you have to work with? Not so much.There are some serious and, more disappointing, intentional design decisions that will prevent this game from having any lasting appeal. The gameplay loop is very cynical and you can see the obvious gaps waiting to be filled with DLC/microtransactions. The basic premise is fantastic; an FPS version of Super Mario Maker, whats not to love? The execution has all of the worst aspects of gaming over the past decade or so. If this was more accessible to touch screen controls you would see it propping up the Google Play store.

_childDocuments_.review: I am not the best at expressing my thoughts and opinions, however I want to write an honest review on this game after playing it for some time.I bought this game solely because I spent more than 3000 hours playing Dead by Daylight, and as someone that enjoys the game a lot (despite it's toxic community and overall insane amount of bugs) I still enjoy the design of the game. _childDocuments_.review: I really hate to give this game a no, but right now this game just isn't in a good spot.Quick TL;DR For those who don't wanna read my whole review: Game is good, but lacks content and has some pretty poorly thought out mechanics in it's current state So then, i'll start by saying the concept of the game is AMAZING! Really love the idea of crafting your own bases for people to raid, it's a very fun concept. The issue that currently exists is the complete lack of content. You have four or five basic primitive shapes to craft your base with, about 7 traps (each with about two mods to slightly change how they work), and 3 minions. Once you have completed 10 or so enemy bases you've seen pretty much everything. This makes replay-ability piss poor in it's current state as everything feels kinda samey and boring. There's also only 4 total weapons to choose from, 2 combat suits, and 4? grenades/utility items to choose from, doesn't really allow for much movement in how you're clearing bases or offer any real difference in gameplay, not enough for me at least.Now onto the systems, currently the core gameplay loop is raid, get materials, build base, rinse and repeat. You earn rep/exp with your different advisors who you then can buff yourself temporarily in various ways either as a raider or to your base directly. This seems kinda pointless since the buffs don't feel that impactful or worth your while, especially when you need those mats to build and run your bases. There's also a chimera that you're upgrading constantly. Like every other raid you go in and press the button to upgrade it, and every so many upgrades you get a couple of mats... cool... I guess? Idk, it feels kinda pointless and the rewards are boring. There is a ranking system in this game, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is it a SLOG to rank up. You start at the bottom of bronze or iron or whatever and you need something like 4k Ranked points to go up a rank, at most you get 200 points for a perfect brutal level raid clear. Perfect meaning no deaths, which... good luck.This brings me to my last point, but like many others have said, why the ♥♥♥♥ do you not make people beat their raid before publishing it? The amount of raids where you go in, reach the end, then get insta killed by tens of traps all going off at the same time is infuriating. There is no way to beat some of these maps.IMO, before you purchase the game the following changes need to be made: +Add more content, specifically traps, guards, and building blocks for more interesting bases+Tidy up the gameplay loop and give us more interesting rewards. Cosmetics, upgrades, things we can work towards. +Make it so you HAVE to beat your own level before you are allowed to publish it. Seriously, it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this wasn't thought of. +Make the ranked system not as horrible to climb, or if you're going to, give rewards. Currently there's no reason to climb besides shiny symbol on your profile.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - crashes more than a Bethesda game. if you only want to build, skip this. if you only want to raid, you'll probably have fun.I would give this game a very mixed review. I truly enjoy the game sometimes, and others it's just dull, uninspiring, and irritating. I will very likely keep playing it, but only begrudgingly.General: One of the earliest things I encountered in this game was that the achievements weren't counting correctly. I had a level 12 advisor or something, but the achievement was only tracked at 5/10. I was able to keep playing and level that up and get the achievement eventually, but obviously a bug is fun for no one. The game also crashes A LOT. Sometimes I don't have this happen for hours, sometimes it'll crash every other raid; but it sure makes it harder and harder to press that "Play" button again. Scroll through some other reviews and you will see many, many people mention this.Raiding: I think raiding is mostly fun. There are definitely times--and countless other reviews will also mention--where you will run across "death boxes" or those nice "death tunnels" with exploding enemies. Most people say that the creators should have to beat their own levels before uploading, but I don't think that's necessarily something that needs to happen. There are counters for everything and I think this is where matchmaking comes in and (I hope it) doesn't match a base-kit player with a prestige 10 death box/tunnel. Social Raiding: Let me first start this section off by saying it is one of the worst decisions ever, but if you have a friend or someone in a stream who wants you to play a level they created, they have to go un-list their level from being active and turn it on to "social" mode in order for you to find it. I don't know why there isn't just a code you can give someone to play a map that you own. And on top of that, there isn't a way to open up the "social raid" screen and say "find maps made by my friends". You have to input their name and search for it.Building: If you want to be strictly a builder, don't buy this game. Skip past it, you cannot build without raiding*. You don't have a choice on who sees your map, but both building and raiding count toward your ranking. If you can see how this review and how this game is going though, I'm sure you can guess that it's much quicker and more effective to raise your rank through raiding. On a game based around killing, it doesn't feel rewarding for killing people. Sure it sounds great when you (re-)launch the game (after it crashes) to hear the chimera say "You have created a deathtrap, and raiders march to the slaughter", but then you only see +2 deaths next to your outpost and you get 5 synthite (of the 1000 you need to level it to prestige 10). And speaking of prestige, a gripe you will come across in nearly every review is that once you get to prestige 10 on an outpost, there is no way to re-activate it. At that point, you can only make it "Social" or delete it--or keep it there and look at the "Mastered" banner for no reason.*unless you're getting like thousands and thousands of kills on your outposts. maybe, probably. and which you probably won't be able to do on your first outpost.

_childDocuments_.review: I have enjoyed Meet Your Maker. There are two aspects to the game and as a player you will play both of them.The Good Part:1. The raiding game. The first part of the game has you raiding creations of other players. Working your way through their death trap filled mazes to steal the core of the maze and escape again. This portion of the game is fun and completing dungeons will give you materials to both upgrade your weapons & armor but also allows you to buy and upgrade traps and guards for the second part of the game.2. The death maze creation phase. This part of the game has you purchasing a plot of land using the materials you farmed from other players mazes and from leveling up your player character or custodian. Once you own a plot of land you can build your maze and fill it with traps. To me it feels like minecraft meets dungeon keeper.You can make mazes that will kill all but the best players but if you are excluding most of the player base. Dungeons that are beatable and rewarding are the way to go.3. Once your maze is built players will raid it and I really enjoy watching the replays of all the players who tried out my maze. I can see where they died, what areas are too tough for people, and how I can improve. You will see some reviews talking about massive rooms filled with all the traps but this is just one type of maze people make. You will see amazing mazes and you can incorporate their tricks into your design then watch people try to beat it. You will also be amazed at how experienced players breeze through portions of your maze with ease giving you both ideas on how to beat other mazes and ideas on how to change your own maze.4. Take a friend. Dungeons are much easier to raid with a friend. I think the game shines when played with another. You still die quite often but your friend can get you back on your feet and as long as one of you is up you can revive the other. The Bad part:While raiding your controls can be unresponsive at times. Button clicks are often not registered and there is nothing more annoying then getting through a tough portion of a maze to die to a simple trap because you couldn't attack and destroy the enemy creation. I have felt great accomplishment in this game at times when getting through a tricky part of a maze to have the experience robbed from me due to unresponsive controls.Conclusion:Even with the bad controls and sometimes insane dungeons I still find myself playing the game again and again. I would encourage new players to try the game out and if you ever need help you can join another play to raid dungeons together.

_childDocuments_.review: In short - Great ideas hamstrung by terrible negative reinforcement loop.The primary problem with this game right now is that the only sort of behavior that is rewarded in map design is kills.  In theory that would at least spur sadistic designs and kaizo traps.  In reality it breeds what every metrics driven system does: minimal effort, maximal output to try and get as many kills as possible.  Sure, you could develop an interesting, clever, themed level with multi-layered traps and routes that corral player movement.  But why would you do that when you can just dump the player into a featureless box with no cover and maxing out the build limit with lasers/plasma balls/spike infantry covering the walls?  The game gives the player some limited tools to deal with it, they're not impossible to complete.  It's just a tedious slog to get through them.  They're built to get maximum kills, not to trick people.  People don't even bother with stickers to spice things up most of the time, it's just spammed default blocks and projectile turrets.The problem isn't even that it's hard or that you're dying a lot - if you play this game, that's not really a concern.  The problem is that it breeds extremely boring and bland levels that aren't interesting to play.  I rarely get got by a clever trap anymore, I just fall into a big, open box and sigh as I hear the projectile turrets starting to spin up.  That's why the steam player count cratered after launch and is just limping along with 100-200 players.  People will say "just don't play brutal levels" or whatever, but limiting building freedom isn't going to fix anything.  Really all that needs to change is that map makers should get rewards only based off of accolades given by the player, not kills, and there should be a downvote function.  They could keep the game balance exactly as is, and all the trash kill farming levels would settle to the bottom where they belong instead of flooding your level selection screen.  There's good mechanics here.  It's a salvageable game.  It's just built to reward blenders and meat grinders over clever or thoughtfully themed designs.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Game, With a Few Caveats. MYM(Meet Your Maker) has a very simple game play loop; you raid another player's base and gain materials, you build a base for other players to raid and if they die in your base you collect more materials, rinse and repeat. This loop is appealing because it is all built around player made content, but this is also where the game falls flat. Some players build bases that are easy, some players build bases that are difficult, and other players build bases that look pretty. Many players consider raiding to be too easy while others see it as too challenging. Some players think the game should focus more on building and other players opt not to build at all. This game is what you make of it. One issue that stands out with this game is the price and the live service model. Every "season" of this game brings about new DLC that comes in 2 packs, a cosmetic pack, and a pack that features new items for players to use in raiding or building. If you do not buy these DLCs you may be at a disadvantage compared to other players depending on the strength of these seasonal offerings. Understanding this, the game is still very solid game that offers a new experience with every login but has an ever increasing "buy-in", waiting for a sale to pick this game up is more than a good idea.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. BUT the devs just don't seem to get how not being able to negative rate outposts hurts the games future. I was excited to play this game, and making my outpost was fun! whats not fun is doing three outposts in a row that are designed to NOT be winnable. I see the devs talked about WHY they don't force players to beat their own outposts.... and it wasn't really logical. When there is no downside to no win kill boxes AND no real way to warn other players that its just a kill box (and no, the brutal rating doesn't mean anything, no one minds a HARD outpost), then the games lifespan is limited. I'm giving it a few more goes but as is I'm probably returning it.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Takes a while to get used to how it wants you to play, but is amazing afterwards. Player created bases are often too easy though, as most people just spam traps without thinking too much about the placement. A validation system for the bases would be nice though, as it would be a nice incentive to create hidden paths and the likes, leading to more base variety. Currently it is very focused around creating a killbox as the base builder and figuring out how to beat the killbox as the raider. So far every single one was solvable though.The variety comes from different trap layouts players use. There are slow killboxes which require thinking to get through, as you need to use your limited resources wisely. On the other hand there are trap parkours which require movement, aiming and also the correct usage of your items. Sometimes both are combined, leading to the hardest bases as you need to figure out when to slow down.Unfortunately the game seems to suffer from a lot of people not understanding the gameplay and complain about "unsolvable bases", just because they are not good enough. No base is unsolvable. Some are harder, some are easier. But theres a reason the game provides you with 3 "Oh ♥♥♥♥!"-Buttons. A reusable shield, a shield to drop down and a literal revive.This is no game where you have to trick people into traps once. You need to kill them with your layout despite them knowing where the traps are. And as a raider you need to be able to switch tactics. Sometimes you need to think about a trap layout, other times its best to rush through and use shields as well as the ability to deflect traps. And not every level 1 player is supposed to be able to beat every base first try. The amount of level 1 players which attempt to raid my brutal base is astonishing.

_childDocuments_.review: 11/1 edit: 100% avoid. They're prepping to go F2P with it because average player count is sub 30. If you're interested: wait. Though they'll still have the same problem if they want to insist on gimping their editor and systems to make it so the only levels you see are the same three flavors of noob spam. The game had massive problems consistent across multiple beta runs and launch, feedback was pretty unanimous outside a couple sycophants, and instead of fixing them they doubled down on the awful design decisions creating the problems and got defensive about it when nobody liked these systems. Basically pissed off all of the people investing time into making good maps, and the rest of the players left when they found out the devs are committed to their "no variety" editor constraints.-----The game is fun, but I have a hard time recommending it due to longevity concerns. There's a couple design choices really holding it back. If they can address that: it could turn out to be one of the best map maker games out there, but it's pretty mid right now, and grows stale fast. The problem is a combination of an overly restrictive editor, and bad grind incentives that makes it so most maps you'll play are extremely similar to one another. It's also pretty needy with its resource grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Movement feels very bad.  Attacking traps initiates a lunge towards them, which can easily put you into danger;  for destroying a trap point-blank it's frequently better to just shoot it.  The grapple hook is jank - there is no course correction so a bad angle will leave you caught on geometry, double jumping/regrappling out of a hang feels inconsistent, and while grappling to a wall will let you hang for a time the duration is very short, shorter than the duration of some traps you may have been trying to avoid.  Targeting a body part in melee combat is inaccurate, unintuitive, and will often leave you dead; again, melee is not very useful.  Outpost upkeep is needy and tedious and feels like the game was meant for different monetization.  Additionally, progression is unsatisfying, building materials/shapes feel limiting, and the front-loaded story and NPC dialogue are all very "who cares."Lastly, though it need not be said, the outposts are made by other people.  In the Brutal category of outpost raids, expect at least one in every eight or so to be near-unwinnable death-traps.  The game not only makes this possible, but actively encourages it.The kinda-fun base building is hampered by every other system in the game feeling bad.Either see how the game develops or maybe wait for a sale. 6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Before any other point:The top review I see is ''You dont have to beat it yourself''. I understand this frustration if you're only going through Outposts which are one long corridor filled with Enforcers, Lava and boltshot/grapple... but this is simply not the game. There are so many outposts out there that are sick, innovative and leave you either refreshed or surprised! On top of this, THERE IS NO COST TO RETRYING, DYING OR ABANDONING. Either get better at the game -- you get good time per trap to react -- or stop whining with your 1.5hr playtime-ass. The game draws mainly from Dungeon Keeper, Mighty Quest for Epic Loot and Quake. A grimy, post-apoc setting and artstyle bring home the brutality of it and an easy to use base-builder make it a breeze to design outposts after your ideas. At time of writing 30$ with a roadmap planned with free-for-everyone content, an entirely new biome and several other additions. Currently in the game are several weapons to upgrade, traps, guards and boosts to unlock. Additionally it has crossplatform capability -- PSN's Gamepass has the game as well (Steam User Data is thus not representative of total players! The playerbase is much higher than indicated on just here).I give this game a worth-it/the price. Three hours of work on minimum wage will get you this game which has entertained me for many more!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great core concept of a game, with a few very odd design choices.I can understand the dev's reasoning behind not wanting level creators to have to re-play their levels over and over again just because they changed one block or decal. The flip side of this though is that creators can make and publish levels that are essentially impossible to beat, or at least impossible without having a very specific loadout of gear that isn't unlocked for newer players.The difference in difficulty between single players and multiplayer groups is also staggering. As a solo player, any damage at all will send you back to the start of the level, while a 2 player team can keep triggering traps, dying, and resurrecting each other with no limit to "lives" or anything. Seems to trivialize a lot of more challenging levels, even the well designed ones.As someone who primarily likes to build rather than raid, I feel like the 12 - 18 hour expiration on maps I've made is rather grindy and feels like I spend a lot of my time just raiding to try and get enough material to keep a level I made going for another half-day. Even a full 24 hours would feel like this game was less of a second job at times. I play test my own maps to make sure they are challenging, yet completely beatable and hopefully fun to play, so I don't wind up with the massive resource farm that a killbox map can generate.

_childDocuments_.review: This game can easily be summed up by 4 words. Mario Maker with Gore. I think the game plays extraordinarily well, although there is definitely room for improvement in many aspects, mostly quality of life stuff. When purchasing and building outposts, they come with a lot of pieces already placed, which contributes to the overall "building capacity" cap. This wouldn't be such a large issue, but with a lack of a "remove all" option, it becomes very tiresome trying to remove every single piece so you can start building with the maximum amount of traps/structural pieces. It also makes it very inconvenient for completely remodeling your outpost, as you have to remove each piece individually. I'm hoping to see something like this implemented in the future, though I'm not sure what the devs have in mind for future updates.The replay system for watching back the raids on your base is an excellent feature, which could also use some upgrades. Now this could totally just be on my end, as my computer is pretty outdated, but I've found that the replays tend to have a decent amount of lag/freezing while playing them. It's not a super large issue, as it doesn't interfere with my ability to see where my traps went wrong and how to fix them, but it does get annoying really quick. There also isn't a whole lot of explanation to a few things. Of course, I could also just be unobservant or maybe I skipped some dialogue/explanation boxes somewhere, but I've searched through many menus and still haven't been able to find what leveling up your advisors actually does. It doesn't change the prices of unlocking new things, nor does it change the cost of upgrading them either. It doesn't unlock new traps/weapons/guards, so I'm a little lost on why I should bother grinding for xp for any specific one of them. There is also potential that there is a "remove all" option for building, but I just can't find it anywhere in any sort of explanations/tutorials. I think the hardest part of the whole game is just being able to get people to raid your bases. They do run on a timer of sorts, in that they only generate you materials for a short time, before you have to prestige them to reset the timer. To prestige your base you need points from raider kills and accolades (basically like commendations) which can be difficult to get. There are some things you can do, like making your base fit within the "normal" or "dangerous" difficulty areas, which I feel get more player activity, but this does also require you to shoot yourself in the foot a little bit by holding back on how many traps you place. Not sure what improvements could be made to fix this issue, outside of increasing the active time of bases. Despite these criticisms, the game is a very fun one with a lot of replayability. Raiding bases made by other players means there's no shortage of new layouts and traps to explore and beat, and it keeps the gameplay fresh and exciting. Even though a lot of people seem to be complaining about killboxes, I have yet to find one I can't outwit in one way or another, and I have been spending a lot of time exclusively playing the highest difficulty bases (brutal). Are they difficult? Absolutely. Have there been bases where I racked up 10+ deaths and thought about calling it quits? Sure, but I still stuck it out and managed to beat it in the end. The gameplay takes a little getting used to, but once you've got it down, I'd say even some of the more elaborate killboxes are possible to beat. Of course, with only 17 hours in the game, I obviously haven't seen a large extent of what's possible, but I'd say that the best solution to these so-called "impossible" killboxes would just be to make it so that builders have to beat their own base before they can publish it. TLDR: This game is a very fun one with a lot of content to play with, but it could definitely use some improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: The game has the potential to be good, but right now it's probably not worth your time.  I'm pretty average at games in the FPS genre and I was able to beat player-made maps that were on the highest difficulty while only dying 2-3 times. One of the main reasons for this is that all defenses in the game have some sort of delay, there's nothing that will punish you instantly for stepping somewhere. Knowing this, you can full-speed run through almost every map and not have to worry about dying as long as you know where traps are coming from, which the game tells you with the heads-up display. I can imagine the game is much more challenging on controller/console, but that's because your movement is more restricted. There's also a huge lack of traps, guards, weapons, and mods to unlock. Genuinely, where is all the content? There are just not many ways to make creative and fun maps because map creators have such few tools at their disposal. There will be more content in these areas in future updates I'm sure, but as of right now there's really not much. You can probably unlock everything in less than a week of playing. Overall, fantastic concept, but the execution is evidently rushed and poor. It'll take some time for Meet Your Maker to shape up to the game it's meant to be.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a [Meh] or a [Neutral Opinion] option, but there isn't so i'll just have to go to the one I lean on the most.This game is great for a few hours, then you slowly start to realize a lot of the numbers are useless and don't go anywhere. Like most cookie cutter games of our time. This has a unique premise, but pretty stupidly executed.First the story is your basic apocalyptic mad-max with kill houses instead of regular houses, your boss is a giant fetus that everyone takes orders from because.... That's right. Because. The Chimera doesn't strike me as something that should lead an operation into humanities salvation, it strikes me as a science project that became self aware and started to build a savior complex.The game itself is pretty simple. You are a created thing, that goes into buildings made by other created things and then you create things to kill other things or protect you from things trying to kill you. I say things a lot because that is exactly what everything is. There is no overarching faction or enemy at large, it's just mutated things built from test-tubes or traps built from mutated test tube people.The fun factor varies. Do you like beating your head against a wall and trying to solve 1 map? Do you like killboxes?I've played this game a lot and did some metrics. I played 200ish raids, of those 200 every other one, was a killbox. A map that was less a level in Doom or some other forge-style game. And more of a; throw everything into a small room.But you know people are going to do that if killing nets you rewards, also the point of the game is tomb raiding and security needs to be tight? Well it's hard to be a locksmith in the era of plastic explosives, and the explosives used to crack most maps are.1) Shield2) Adrenaline3) Free Space.95% of the time you can just speed run a level that was meant to take 10-15 mins, just by popping a 3-4 second shield and some go-go juice then running through the map. Taking the prize, then doing the same exact thing out of it. Sure you might die 1-2 times while you get the feel of it. But you'd complete a lot of maps this way.Someone made an elaborate bomb puzzle? Rush through it. Warbringer Spam? Grenade as equipable, rush through the armor or even back-stabbing them through the front like a TF2 spy. Firewalls? Shield and rush through it.Gotta problem? Shield and rush through it.The traps take 1-2 seconds to trip, now I know that doesn't sound like a lot. But when you're actually walking through it the time gives you plenty of space to just waltz right through it. The fastest trap is a spike-trap that pierces you with sharpened rods and you can just go through it at default running pace. Tack on other traps that take 2-3 seconds LONGER to trip and you wonder why people aren't dying left and right to good positioned traps. Make the shield have limited uses so that the sword deflection is actually used on some traps and increase the AoE of grenades if you're only going to give out 3. Make mods for the equipment so grenades can glide ontop of acid too. If builders have mods for their stuff, why can't raiders?So if map makers can't reliably use the traps what do they do to get rewards via kills?Killboxes and spam. Oh i'm sorry you want your 2-3 hour thought out build to be up to speed with the meta of shield and speed? Don't care. Here is a room full of eyes that shoot the same damn AoE bolt, riddled with pistons that take 6 years to get through and flames instead.Oh you want your ammunition back after it was lost in an acid cube? Or perhaps it is too far away in the killbox for you to reliably get some? Too bad, guess you should use the Sword + shield meta and get the new suit ASAP so you aren't behind. The direction here is all over the place and easily fixable. Give raiders more equipment to mess around with [3 Equipables instead of 2], make traps proc faster and harder to spot around corners so it is a guessing game of whether or not what you are shooting is an actual trap and actually reward players for incorporating Lost Tombs in their maps. Give a mod for creatures so they can't friendly fire [Cannonball] and make some of the other traps more viable so we don't spam Bolt + Homing or Eye + Field. Allow trappers to tweak traps in different ways like proc-time [For bombs] and give like 30-50 points for free in the creator for cosmetic purposes.BHVR I know from looking at DBD that you're not exactly keen on Balancing, but I am begging you. This game is going to nose-dive fast if you don't make it [FUN]. Not everything has to be a competition, I'm going to reliably say that no one cares about what rank they are in a tomb-raider game alright?

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad saying that I don't recommend this game. Behaviour definitely showed a lot of care when making this game, but just made a bunch of stupid decisions on the way that slowly killed the game.My biggest problem with the game is that the only requirement to complete your base is if there's a straightforward path to your little flag at the end. This kills the opportunity for parkour maps, puzzle maps, things like that, making every map just the worlds worst rust base. Full of killboxes, trap spam, enemy spam. It was definitely one of the major reasons people dropped this game shortly after release. Another absolutely stupid thing is that your base will just stop working after about a day, give or take a few hours. You know that super cool base that you spent hours decorating, handcrafted every little detail on? Its going to go away, don't worry though, you can prestige the base which keeps it public for another day, it just costs in game currency that scales up in price everytime you do it, I don't know why they did this. They could have had the perfect rust mixed with mario maker game, but by trying to keep it competitive, and with decisions like this just to try and increase your engagement, it had the opposite effect, many people just stopped working on bases, or stopped playing the game overall.Despite this the games not all bad. The graphics and atmosphere are top notch, and some of the levels were genuinely fun, but with an average player count of 20 players, and Behaviours tendency to pull the plug on failed projects, I don't see this game lasting much longer.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game might have potential, but it is hamstrung by both the developers design philosophy, and the games lack of actual content.In short, the game is a simple community driven game divided into two main parts: raiding, and building. Builders create levels consisting of traps and a few basic enemies, while raiders play through levels for some minor resources and progression rewards. Meet Your Maker in concept is similar to a game like Mario Maker, but plays like a slower paced Doom title. This on paper sounds good, and if executed differently, it probably would be. So if the game is conceptually sound where do things go wrong?The biggest issue, is that all of the incentive and reward for building a level lies with how many people you kill. The developers even leaned into this in their marketing and trailers which for me is the most concerning part of it. This simple design concept snowballs into lots of other issues that I'll get into.Because builders from the get go are encouraged to kill the raiders above all else, it means that zero regard for player enjoyment is put in place. 95% of levels you will come across will be complete garbage, and there is no way to filter the quality of levels you play.So if every level is designed to be as miserable and unfair as possible, does this mean the raiding feels impossible and hopeless?Surprisingly, the answer is no.The developers knew that this would happen, but instead of changing the incentive and rewards for building, they made the building tools ineffective. The game puts many features in to protect the raiders from the atrocities getting thrown their way. The danger indicators are so overly generous, that traps are extremely trivial to avoid. Even the most effective traps are extremely one dimensional, and over half of the tiles and perks are completely useless.The second biggest issue with Meet Your Maker, is the games lack of content.As a raider, the tool and weapon variety is so scarce that they might as well not have custom loadouts to begin with. This doesn't pose too much of an issue, and clearly was done on purpose to make the game easier to balance.Building on the other hand, is unforgivably shallow. There is only four total enemies, and nine total trap tiles. Typing nine feels disingenuous because in reality you are only using five of these tiles. The tile and enemy perks, while interesting at a glance, barely add any depth to the gameplay, and less than half of them are effective in any way.The lack of content is exacerbated by the games horrible progression system. The developers were worried that players had nothing to work towards and the game would have no longevity, so you start off the game with about 10-20% of the games already limited tools. This means that the majority of the levels you are going to play through are going to have the exact same three trap tiles and basic ranged enemy with no perks. There is some irony to this, because by locking building tools behind a progression system, the levels as a result feel even more repetitive. This in turn is going to do more harm to player retention than not having a "DING DING LEVEL UP HERE'S YOUR PRIZE" style incentive.In conclusion, Meet Your Maker is a conceptually interesting game that doesn't live up to its potential. The games only content is what was created by the players/builders themselves, but the developers chopped off the builders arms, resulting in a monotonous gameplay loop. Good co-op fun for a day, but there's no meat on the game's bones to keep you coming for more.

_childDocuments_.review: CURRENTLY EXPERIENCING MULTIPLE CRASHES W/ NO RHYME OR REASON THAT FORCES A HARD RESTART ON MY PC.Enjoyed the open beta and the official release is the same. Important thing to point out is the necessary right mindset for this game. It's Super Meat Boy trial and error 1st. You will die over and over, so that demands patience, anticipation, and reflexes. You will creep around corners, fearing for what you can see and panicking what you can't see. You will frantically run, hook, and deflect in ground and aerial combat w/ enemies that may be fast, armored, or freaking explode upon death. There are levels that may have both! It really helps the game has a very simple control scheme: run, slash, shoot, and grapple. This makes playing almost wholly reliant on YOUR abilities and reflexes, and it feels fair 99% of the time.Essentially if you can gel w/ the process of either quickly figuring out a base's traps and defenses or carefully dissecting them 1-by-1, then the satisfaction of successfully escaping is repeating nice feeling; especially w/ some devious or straight-up brutal base designs.What's also great about raiding is even failed attempts slowly increases your EXP and resources, if you play smart enough. Always search the outside for free loot walls. Half the time, (respectable) builders will even help you out and designate where they are. To be fair, though, sometimes they'll also booby-trap them. I should know. I've done it every other base. When you attempt a raid, you get rewards/EXP for enemy you kill, trap you destroy, or even barely surviving either. Each raid attempt is essentially a farming opportunity, and the only consequence is your time and patience.The 2nd thing is the base-building, that's my favorite. When I acquire a new area, I'm always excited to test a new concept or theme around a new trap or upgrade. It's a really robust building system and works perfectly on M&K or controller.1 unfortunate MAJOR issue I'm having is the occasional HARD crash almost every other play session w/ no rhyme or reason. My PC hasn't been upgraded in 2yrs but I haven't had any similar issue in awhile so something is probably buggy w/ engine at the moment.Some nitpick complaints are the rare moments where an action doesn't respond in time because a few other things in the game got triggered at the same, killing me. And (for artistic building) applying colors is limited around and on traps, so artistry can conflict w/ hidden trap design occasionally. But those only come up every so often, and you can easily work around them.While I don't care for (or agree) w/ the $$$ of the DLC for only cosmetics (at least how relatively expensive they're starting out w/), the base game for $30 is well worth it. This game has become a nice daily/semi-daily loop of check my base kill progress, raid for resources, and build a new base.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun, polished game with very few bugs for a modern game. There are some negative reviews complaining about not having to raid your own base to verify it, but the developers explained that no outpost is impossible given all the (fully upgraded) tools available and at 37 hours, I have yet to prove them wrong.There were certainly times where I died many times attempting some brutal raids, but, I was able to solve all of them by coming back later with more experience, better gear, and the right consumables. The choice not to have to verify your own raid map is intentional as you are often required to modify and tinker with your map after watching replays or watching players succeed on your map, and having to validate it every time would be tedious as a lot of the modification is iterative. It also allows players who are not strong fps players to still compete in a meaningful way via their devious base building.You can also choose different difficulty maps and the devs have recently greatly improved the match making system to make it more fun overall. It is immensely satisfying watching replays of players die in your bases, and completing challenging raids yourself.It's worth noting that you can also do any raid co-op which makes it much easier.

_childDocuments_.review: After spending 26h in the game, my thoughts are as follows: In general the game will be worth buying after a few months provided some things will be addressed, namely:- Killboxes: it ruins the fun big time but can be easily dealt with, as other reviews pointed, the creator should be forced to complete his own map before allowing players to go through it. How this is not a feature right now is beyond me. Currently there are tons and tons of outposts created with sole purpose of providing you enough frustration to last for a decade.- Pathings: no sophisticated design is possible due to limitations connected with the robot that has 0 mobility, just walks straight down the shortest path. This should be changed as it severly limits and interesting designs- Lacking content in terms of traps/blocks to useI believe the gameplay loop is good, the idea is terrific and the game has tons of potential, just in it's current state, I would simply recommend waiting for sale or (hopefully) for devs addressing the core issues. I frankly am a bit disapointed at this moment but will track the progress and hope for things to improve.

_childDocuments_.review: (Original positive review at the bottom)NEGATIVE REVIEW:Late game sucks. I have a couple outposts that after building them and prestiging them once gained enough points to be max rank which is great because I don't have to worry about them not making it to prestige.However as you prestige the outpost and your outpost gets closer and closer to lvl 10 you need more and more yellow currency (synthite) this yellow currency is earned how? Primarily by raiding. This ruins the ability to jump into the game watch a couple funny replays and prestige your base and come back to it later. It forces you to either spend a couple hours doing normal or dangerous maps or at least a while doing Brutal maps.For reference all of my advisers are around lvl 50 at this point I need to do at least 2 brutal maps which give 3750 genmat (adviser xp) each which means I need 7500+ xp to level those advisers and I need to do that 5 times in order to get a chimera level which only gives you 250 synthite which means I need to level my chimera 3-4 times if my outpost is level 8-9 which all adds up to about 30-40 brutal raids or roughly 5x that in dangerous or roughly 8x that in normal raids. If they fix the late game then yes I will change it back to positive but right now I've hit 41 hours and I am kinda done playing unless you absolutely love raiding you will be too and even then I enjoy raiding and it gets repetitive after a while because there's only so much you can build and a lot of meta recycled designs.(Original positive review)I was skeptical at first about the not having to complete your own maps etc but I now see why the developers are not concerned with it. It is actually more beneficial to force people to have a walkable path than to complete their own because it would be too easy to make insanely hard parkour maps with massively long jumps etc without the little robot having to complete the course.As far as killboxes go yes there are lots of maps that are garbage killboxes for no reason that are basically impossible to complete, To those maps I say just don't play them. You get the choice of 15 maps that are sorted based on size and number of traps in Normal Hard or Brutal. Some of the Normal ones are killboxes. some of the Brutal ones are easy. It's not an exact science or difficulty scale but it helps AND if you know a map is a killbox then after going into the map and trying it even if you only go in and look and die once (not sure if you have to die or not) and say no this map isnt for me you can abandon it and go in your list of maps and delete it in the bottom left corner and it will give you a new map.It is lots of fun to make maps. It is lots of fun to work hard and die 20 times to a map and finally beat it and feel good that you beat it. It is also really rewarding watching people die to your maps.

_childDocuments_.review: Played since beta with about 20-50 hours in the beta alone. good concept but the level building is flawed. there is nothing to stop or de-incentivize players from making kill box bases flooded with corrosive cubes(which have the lowest cost of any trap and are indestructible). this results in any base on 'Brutal" difficulty just being extremely cheesy bases with little thought or creativity put into them. as a result the actual fun of the game is extremely short lived. the only reason to play on any base difficulty lower than "brutal" is so that you can learn the ropes (which only takes maybe an hour or two max) after that any lower difficulty bases is laughably easy to complete seeing as the builders literally do not have the base capacity to place enough traps/guards to be a threat beyond the first wave. The result is you either willingly play extremely easy bases or you play extremely cheesy bases on "brutal". It removes and sense of challenge or accomplishment from raiding. You can try to build your own fun base but there is no reason to when the META is just to use the cheap costing corrosive cubes as a means to deny ammo retrieval as well as create entire floors made of lava. this was already an major issue in the beta and wasn't addressed in anyway. Maybe like DBD it will get better with time but just like DBD it's first iteration is deeply flawed and easily exploited.TLDR: not worth buying in it's current state. the only options for raiding bases are basically baby's first base or a kill box spammed with lava cubes and tracking plasma eye traps in a large open room. No actual challenge, no sense of accomplishment, extremely slow and unrewarding progression system as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Its set in an interesting setting and has fun movement. That's pretty much it really. It does have base building and challenging other player bases but it makes two main mistakes in that. 1. It's completely dependant on other players to produce content. 2. It incentivises players to create bases that 'win' not necessarily bases that are fun. Why build an elaborate trap maze or interesting parkour challenge when a square room full of armoured enemies will do 30x better? You wouldn't, and neither would many other players. That and the complaints about the building system being somewhat flawed due to having to have an easy path to the finish for the drone. (See most other reviews.) That's my experience anyway, though I didn't get to see much as I only tried the free trial for an hour or two right before it ended. I actually enjoyed playing the game. I just can't recommend it when it was showing early red flags and has design decisions that seem like they result in poor creations. Even though it was fun for the first hour or few, I feel like it would quickly get boring. It's just the nature of player created content games.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - Game has a great look and vibe, but makes focusing on base building impractical and discourages fun at every turn by design.Behaviour, as usual, nails the aesthetic. Navigation and movement feels quick and responsive and there is certainly a lot of potential to this game. Sadly, that is where my praise for this game ends.The overwhelming focus on raiding rather than building kills this for me, though. The reason games like Super Mario Maker or King of Thieves can function is because there is adequate space for both people who enjoy building and people who enjoy playing/raiding. In Meet Your Maker, however, building is costly and time-consuming. In return, your base might get very few plays and is likely not to even return the resources you put into it. To add insult to injury, your creation won't even persist - it will eventually be rendered defunct and destroyed. Raiding is an absolute necessity to the game - even if you play the game primarily to make bases, raiding will take up a significant portion of your time. To make matters worse...The entire model seems to punish fun or artistic levels, instead encouraging builders to make tedious, boring, cruel bases that you then have to hope someone is bone-headed enough to die in a few dozen times. This, in turn, hurts the raiding experience - since the game doesn't reward making something people might actually want to play, most of the bases you raid will be of the same miserable, ghoulish design. This is great for the people who like that brutal difficulty, and I am glad that sort of experience is available, but making it the only profitable design is a misstep that sours both building and raiding for me.I continue to hope that some significant change down the road will fix this, at which point I will amend my review, but until then there are better games for making or challenging fun, creative designs.
