_childDocuments_.review: Kind of appalled by some of the design decisions here.First of all, there's no proper rating system in this game. You are forced to give any level you complete one of four compliments, no matter how bad you actually thought it was. Badly designed levels don't get filtered out as a result and players aren't encouraged to make good levels. Instead, the game rewards you only for killing as many people as possible in your levels and actually punishes you if players manage to complete your level, meaning players are encouraged to make infuriatingly unfair kill boxes instead of fun levels. The game also doesn't require you to playtest a level before publishing it, meaning as soon as impossible level combinations are discovered, people will flood the game with them so they can farm kills and not lose out from people finishing their levels. Now, say you want to actually make a good, fun level nonetheless. You'll be restricted in a major way, because while you don't have to playtest your level, you do have to make it possible for a certain NPC to pathfind its way to the goal and back. This NPC cannot jump like a player, so you have to build slopes everywhere and cannot make platforming sections. This NPC also cannot squeeze into certain tight sections a player could, meaning if you want to make certain passages you simply can't. This NPC always shows the shortest route to the goal, meaning there's no point in making any levels with mazes. This NPC also cannot choose a different path if the previous one it took closes up and another opens, so you can't craft a level that requires the player to take a different route when they get in and back out.It's so limiting it's a joke, but let's say you still manage to design a good level, having thought of everything in a player's arsenal to make sure a player cannot cheese your level and has to complete it in the intended way. Well too bad, because players that are further into the game than you are will have access to abilities that you don't, meaning you can't foolproof your level against them since you have no ability to test them out and gain an understanding of how they can affect your level. Have a section in your level where the players have to dodge multiple projectiles and traps? Some can just deflect them. Have a level where players have to navigate in-between a bunch of deadly acid blocks? Some can just walk through them. There's probably way more abilities I don't even know about yet, but basically this means you'll often be in a situation where you think you did a great job at a level, only for it to be cleared with ease by using abilities you were never even introduced to. You can also play levels in multiplayer, which breaks a few things as well. Normally, if a player dies, the whole level gets reset and you're back at the entrance, meaning you have to carefully navigate through levels to finish them. But in multiplayer, one player can just run head-first into a trap and kill themselves to deactivate it, then the second player comes in to revive them, all without the level resetting. This basically means you can endlessly kill yourself over and over and you progress through the level, requiring no care or strategy on the player's end and nullifying any clever design from the builder.So in conclusion, you're actively discouraged from making fair, fun levels & instead encouraged and able to make impossible levels, you're severely limited in designing creative & unique levels, and you are unable to craft a specific experience for the player since they may have abilities you can't test out in your levels & they can kill themselves over and over to cheese your levels.TLDR: Absolute disaster of a level creator game, do NOT buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: An amazingly unique game. Fast and precise movement and shooting mechanics with great building tools which lets you think up devious and clever traps to kill players that try to raid your outposts.The main issue I have of the game is its difficulty system, which does not accurately portray how hard an outpost is. A lot of current player frustration stems from the fact that many players are attempting the hardest difficulty outposts ("brutal" difficulty) with starter gear and perks, and playing these outposts can range from a walk in the park to something insanely hard and cannot possibly be beaten with starter gear. I think this large variance with difficulty should be looked at because the playerbase seems to expect to be able to beat every outpost without breaking a sweat, even ones that should be the hardest possible to run.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: It's been pretty fun for now. The game is kinda grindy at first, which limits the amount of traps and upgrades you'll have for your very first builds/raids, but after 10-20 hours, you'll likely have unlocked everything you want. I'm currently at 50 hours and have almost unlocked everything, although the grind will likely become worse when new options are released.There are quite a few performance/stability issues, but I've only had crashes because I play on a potato. The game is still playable and in a good state, I haven't seen any bug apart from the occasional crashes.Also, to the people complaining about "killboxes": stop sucking ♥♥♥♥♥. I can count on the fingers of a single hand the amount of hard maps I have played, and I've still cleared them. Pro tip: it's left shift to grapple, and if you just run forward and grapple for speed, you literally can't die to anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I really think this game is going a right direction, but I have one problem with it and it's how good levels are over shadowed by more "kill box" hodgepodge levels.  I think that a level that's hard, but is well designed, should be the main type of levels that players should experience as it best shows how good this game is.  I think, right now, the game rewards both deaths and accolades a little too evenly.  Because of this, it's more efficient to create a level that kills players over and over again forcing them to run the exact same loop than to create creative traps, that may or may not kill a player, giving the level accolades.  Quality or quantity should be the name of the game.  However, with the number of "kill box" type levels that I play, it seems it's just more efficient to go for kills.  Granted I play in "Brutal" difficulty and if that's just how that difficulty is then fine, but I still think that even Brutal levels can be creative and challenging.  If this changes, then I'll change this review to be a recommend.  Until then, accolade levels that make creative traps and try to fake you out rather than one large arena with the same three traps over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: Binged it for a weekend during the beta then got burned out as there's no content and the currency systems are a chore to keep up with. The community is also extremely small so the likelihood of getting your bases raided is starting to get really low. The game crashes every 2 or so levels, the textures are verrrryyy bugged, most levels are just spam because creators dont have to play their own maps, and there are so many exploits.please make a feature where creators can play their own maps to verify themedit: its gotten worse with paid dlc that gives advantages over people who still paid for base gameat this point only get this game if you love endless suffering and even then theres better options for that

_childDocuments_.review: I just wanna say, the more I play this game and the longer its out, the better its gonna get. _childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Meet Your Maker, In Two ways. Yours the first time, and well a lot of re meeting that same maker. Sums up about the 5 hours I just put in. Game Consists of Building Complex or not so Complex Trap Vaults to Protect your goodies, but your loose nothing if anyone steals your goodies, but you get goodies if you kill them. If you don't Kill them Meh. There is a Vault rating system after the attempt where you can pick "2" aspects you feel fit doing so helps Prestige to vault so it can be built bigger and deadlier. So that's part one.... Part two is by far one of the best experiences I have had at dieing over and over again to the same person in a video game. Kinda want to Keep going back in to get even farther into the madness to see how bad it really gets. Repeats don't hurt you, it's more a will to succeed at how many deaths you commit to attempting to steal the Goodies. 10/10 Should give it 11 cause that's my limit before giving up on a raid.Edited after a few more hours of game play... Yes there are Glitches. Mainly the Anticheat Failure  on game relaunches. Have to Verify files to get it to launch again.... Only Bad mark so far. Game has an issue with Super kill boxes, but there are guides out there for how to avoid them. Still Fun to Build and raid to better your build. And watch someone speed run one of your vaults on replay in and out in 40 seconds no shots fired

_childDocuments_.review: This game is seriously great. It's buggy and has flaws (as all new games do) but the concept is great and it's very fun to play, especially co-op. Ignore the people whining about kill boxes, they are just bad at the game. No base is impossible, this game takes practice, especially in your reaction time. It's rewarding to watch yourself get better. Great game and concept.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty cool puzzle game with a FPS, trap and objective twist.Editing my review as i play on a ROG Ally and i finally got a keyboard.This game has some really interesting puzzles all player created. I am having so much fun watching folks die in my own puzzle dungeons, but also i have learned to laugh at my own stupidity, when i die in obvious traps.I recommend this fully and hope the player base picks up so we can maybe in the future, get more content!
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying that I love the bones of this game so much.The building is fluid and fun for me. The raiding much the same.There are a lot of people who complain about build metas and stuff, but in my opinion that's all nonsense. It is impossible to make a base that cannot be conquered. If you don't have the right tools to beat a base, buy them, equip them, etc. Something that people neglect to mention in their reviews a lot about this game is that raiding is predominantly a game of memorization. If you fail, you just gotta remember the locations and patterns of the base and keep iterating until you succeed. Additionally, people whine and complain about killboxes nonstop. That is such a colossal misconception of how to approach those builds. Bring both guns. Stop using a sword. You don't have to be flashy or fast. Just make the effort to learn the timings and view distances of the traps and guards. As for the game itself, like I said before the bones are very strong but there are some needed improvements to keep the longevity of the game intact. Bump the maximum prestige level of bases to 15 before they become mastered, to quell the complaints about time spent building and iterating vs lifespan of a base. Additionally, allow for 7 bases to be active at once.For people who have perfected their base, allow for prestiging and activating the base to be done from the main hub. As well as collecting the drops by killed players.Allow for definable trigger mechanisms on traps, where you can tie a trap triggering to another trap being triggered. It's fine the way it is now, but people would have a much more increased level of innovation and freedom if I could make a holocube floor trigger underneath a person who is looking up to shoot at a bomb dropper that just triggered. Locking all of the traps to sightlines is very lateral and limited thinking. No doubt balancing would be tough, and perhaps these functions would be limited to a few less than lethal trap mechanisms, but it would create a lot of variance in build styles and generate more creative freedom.Lastly, the various currencies. I have well over 30k blue and over 10k red but the synthite or orange currency, while relatively easy to build up by prioritizing the tombs (which some people intentionally block off), is used disproportionately to the other two currencies. I would consider adding a synthite balancing mechanic in which if you raid a base faster or with fewer deaths than the average last 10 runs or so, that you get a bonus amount of the orange currency. Doesn't have to be a lot, maybe 50 or so. But I think that would incentivize people to actively try speed runs, which would also create interesting build variance.Altogether I think MYM is a solid game with strong foundations. With continued content updates and more tweaks, it could go down as a legendary game in the user generated content field of games.7/10 as is.10/10 in potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after a lot of inner deliberation after watching some friends play it. The second I did I immediately started feeling regret. I didn't have time to play it that night but I did boot it up to check the settings and see how it ran on my mid-tier GPU. It ran okay, but then I I took a look at the upgrades and things you can buy and my remorse increased a lot more.I woke up the next morning, and while I was taking my morning shower I started to get a vision of the future. What I saw was 300+ dollars in DLC, season passes, skins, and content that both should have been in the base game and will be almost necessary to survive in the world of Meet Your Maker. I know how Behavior does business, and I honestly don't know why I didn't realize that before I pulled the trigger.This game has a major issue. While it has a cool theme and idea, It has almost no content to speak of. 2 Classes which are essentially the exact same with a few tiny stay differences (We're talking like 10% faster move speed, stuff like that), 4 placeable enemies, 9 traps, 2 nearly identical guns, two nearly identical swords, etc. Behavior is outsourcing all their game development to the players, which is fine as that's literally what the game is about, but I would expect at least a few more things to actually play with.I would be STUNNED if they added a single more thing without it being a 15 dollar DLC pack. I've seen a few interesting uses for things, like splitting bombs into two places with a divider, but for the most part these have a single use and no synergy. Unlike MYMs contemporaries, there's no interesting interactions where things change behavior when placed near each other or can fill different roles when used creatively. For the most part, level design is to place a thing that shoots if the player doesn't notice it. In order to scale the difficulty of the levels, players for the most part just spam a million traps and enemies in a room. Sometimes, they do so to the point that the level becomes nearly impossible to beat.Players are not required to beat their own levels before they upload them. This is MYMs biggest mistake. Of the few brutal levels I joined, none of them were interesting and challenging gauntlets. All of them were a series of rooms with a trap on every wall and enemies blocking every platform. Beating these levels would be an exercise in slowly disarming 15-30 traps in a single room, slowly stepping inch my inch, only to get cheap shot by a bomb that just happened to bounce right into your face by chance and have to start all over. Not every level is like this, I've seen streamers play levels that look awesome. However, since Players are incentivized to kill you, not make fun levels for the fun of it, that is the rare exception.Because there is no comment or rating system in the game it's impossible to hunt for something fun. Even Nintendo allowed you to say a level sucked. All this game has is a useless set of buttons at the end of the level where you can pick 2 of 4 possible positive only "ratings" which as far as I can tell does nothing at all except let the creator know if you liked it.Finally, we have to get back to Behavior. In response to a lot of genuinely good feedback on some of the same stuff I'm saying here, Behavior has responded basically "Nah, ♥♥♥♥ you get good noob". This is classic Behavior... behavior. The problem isn't that I can't "get good" and beat the levels, the problem is that they are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BORING that I don't want to. They fundamentally misunderstand why people want these features added, and that couldn't be more Behavior if they tried.I want to like this game so bad that I purchased it despite knowing somewhere deep down that I was going to feel this way about it  and maybe it'll be better in the future, but right now it's extremely mid. There's fun to be had but I cant help but see the writing on the wall.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Hesitant to recommend, given this game is much like Super Mario Maker, meaning it needs a stable community to create interesting maps that you can raid. As long as players are active the game should be fine, but I don't imagine playing randomly generated maps for long would be fun. So hopefully a small number of dedicated players will continue playing, including the devs.The core experience is fun and well made and can easily be expanded on, my favorite feature is probably the Replay feature, I can watch other people raid my maps.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: A new entry into Behavior's catalog that I'm surprisingly hopeful for. Whether you enjoy running through death gauntlets or building them yourself, there's a few dozens of hours worth of entertainment currently in this package with free content drops coming this Summer. All bases require a straight forward path to be published and even if you manage to find a base that you find too cheesy to your liking, you can easily back out and re-roll your choices with no consequences. The game itself supports content sharing across multiple platforms (not crossplay, sadly) and PS+ users were given the game for free at launch. As long as Behavior sticks to a healthy update schedule and balances out any problematic metas that emerge, this game shouldn't have issue holding a healthy playerbase for the years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I first played this game during the free weekend on steam and I had never seen a game pull off player created levels as a core mechanic like this since little big planet, I’d go as far to say this does it better. The fact that this game rewards you for making a good level is something I haven’t seen in any other game before.𝙶𝚊𝚖𝚎𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚢: Fun to build levels and fun to die 100 times to a max difficulty level 10/10𝚂𝚝𝚘𝚛𝚢: Some lore included, not a selling point 7/10𝙳𝚒𝚏𝚏𝚒𝚌𝚞𝚕𝚝𝚢: Varies between levels, at medium difficulty it can be pretty damn hard𝙶𝚛𝚊𝚙𝚑𝚒𝚌𝚜: AAA level wasteland art style 9/10𝙿𝚛𝚒𝚌𝚎: Recent price change to $20 which is definitely worth it𝙻𝚎𝚗𝚐𝚝𝚑: Infinitely replay-able𝙰𝚞𝚍𝚒𝚎𝚗𝚌𝚎: 12+
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game but the devs have gone on record saying that they will not implement any style of making a base builder complete their own level first because, and I quote "Not all base builders are experienced raiders"...... This is going to kill your already low player count game faster than anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I waited a very long time for a game like this. Precisely since "awesome quest for epic loot" went down the drain if anyone knows this.Meet your Maker has a strong foundation and the potential for limitless fun, thanks to player made content. Because of this the experience varies from "wow a killbox... this ♥♥♥♥ gets old" to just "wow nice" if you can appreciate a well made level.Im enjoying it quite a lot and eventually for a long time.With a little bit of balancing and new content from time to time, this could be a self sustaining fun machine.And thats where im concerned.-04.04.2023 Meet your Maker released.-05.04.2023 First paid Skin pack DLC released.This is ridiculous.Right now there are only 6 Skin packs in the basegame. The other Skin pack is only available if you own "Dead by Daylight" which is conveniently the only skinpack with the same colorpalette as all the traps...   (This is an advantage btw)In my opinion this game needs broader content more than Behaviour Interactive needs more money.Without many options, excluding a part of the playerbase (which ultimately creates this game) cant be healthy.When this game gets the fair support it deserves ill change the recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game! Build an outpost from the ground up (can have 5 active outposts at a time), fill it with various traps and guards to protect your precious Genetic Material. Replay system allows for you to watch raids on your outpost, to show where you could improve your defenses. For example, I have a replay where a raider died 20 times and spent 19 minutes in my outpost BUT in the end they made it out with the 'Gen Mat". It is inspiring to see the determination of other raiders. Raiders can rate the outpost Fun, Ingenious, Brutal, and Artistic. These accolades, along with the kill count of your outpost, award prestige points which allow you to prestige your outpost. When you prestige, it expands the build limit for the outpost, allowing you to add or upgrade to the defenses. In between watching replays and collecting the dropped resources of fallen raiders, go out for a raid of your own and try to outmaneuver another's defenses.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Become the best builder, raider, both or neither.Just build for fun and run social raids if competition is not your thing. Build, raid, die, repeat. filler joke, relevant young person slang, cliche challenge to defeat my bases.After the first week of the game bases only get raided once a day, so make sure it is tempting enough to prestige off of one raid.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review:
You are the Custodian of the Chimera, a living experiment created as a last resort to save life on Earth. Enter a tactical battle for the planet's most coveted resource and the key to your Chimera's evolution: pure Genetic Material. Construct and fortify brutal Outposts to extract and guard your Genmat. Infiltrate and outsmart other players' Outposts to gather more.

Adapt, upgrade, and evolve... or die trying.

Meet Your Maker is a post-apocalyptic first-person building-and-raiding game where every level is designed by players. Switch between roles as you mastermind devious maze-like Outposts filled with traps and guards, then gear up for methodical fast-paced combat raiding other players' creations.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

name: Moncage
detailed_description: FOLLOW US We're a small team creating artistic games with dreamlike experiences for our players! Follow us here: Twitter: Discord: Awards About the Game Moncage is a stunning vignette puzzle adventure developed by Optillusion. The game takes place inside a mysterious cube, with each side of the cube housing a unique world: be it an old factory, a light tower, an amusement park, or a church, etc. At first sight, they may seem random and unrelated, but upon closer look, you will become mesmerized by the subtle and intricate ways of how these worlds connect…… 【Solve Puzzles with Mind-Boggling Optical Illusions】 Use your imagination and spare no brain cells to find the connection and pinpoint every possible interaction between different sides of the cube, then watch as the magic unfold in front of you. 【Collect All Photos to Unveil the Story】 Behind the puzzles, there lies a story with a surprising twist for the player to uncover. Collect the photos from obscure corners and angles to reveal the underlying story, one photo at a time. 【Get Unstuck with Thoughtful Hints】 There is a multitude of guidance systems to help prevent players from getting stuck. Focus can be activated to highlight the key items to the solution, while hint texts are available to provide further clarity. And, if all else fails, video walkthroughs can be unlocked as the ultimate safety plan. 【Prove Your Puzzle-Solving Skills with Medals】 There are a total of 15 achievements in the game, each corresponding with a Medal that has been crafted with a uniquely stunning design. A complete collection of the 15 Medals could be the perfect evidence to attest to your master puzzle-solving skills~

short_description: Moncage is a unique puzzle adventure game where you explore a fascinating world trapped inside a mysterious cube. With each face displaying a unique scene, you’ll have to leverage the illusions and discover the hidden links to solve the puzzle.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterfully crafted puzzle game that takes place on five sides of a cube as you piece together the story through interconnecting scenes.  is a relaxing perspective-based puzzle game with pleasant visuals, touching story told without words, and relaxing soundtrack. There is an alternate ending that requires players to find all hidden photos and replay the story a second time while keeping an eye out for ways "to think outside the cube".  About 2 to 5 hours to complete depending on how often you use the hint system or unlocking achievements.  A must try for puzzle enthusiast [10/10]
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzle games or sequences in games built around perspective and optical illusions are tricky to do well. You have to direct player view to the patterns you wish them to see, but without robbing them of the eureka moment of finding it, provide them with a goal without turning the process into just solving problems, keeping the joy of discovery intact. Antichamber, Gorogoa or even The Witness (for all of its countless issues) are great examples of titles that do that well, at least for the most part. Moncage isn’t. It’s not bad, but playing it isn’t particularly fun.The concept is pretty simple – you look at a cube where each of its 5 available sides can show a different scene. Elements of those scenes, however can be interacted with or even combined, if you look at them from a correct perspective. So, say, a ladder on one side and a grate of the same overall form and color on the other side might actually connect between the two sides and change something on the scene. It’s a very simple, but fun mechanic that provides some fun during the first ten or so minutes of the game.Then it stops being fun. Mostly because the game never provides any understandable goals or reasons for combining elements – you just randomly rotate the perspective, shifting between different zoomed in elements of the scenes, until randomly stumbling upon something that connects and you can proceed further. Most of the time I couldn’t understand why I did what I did even after doing it and understanding what visual story it’s trying to tell. The game also sometimes hides elements that can be interacted with under odd perspective angles with no clear reason as to why that’s there and why interacting should do anything, but until you do, you’re stuck.I had some fun during the opening moments of the game and it isn’t a terrible execution of the idea. But it’s extremely undercooked, often poorly handled and in the end there are simply far better and more exciting titles that explore similar, if maybe not exactly the same, ideas.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Moncage is a really neat spacial puzzle adventure, played out over 5 sides of a cube.  There's no text; the story is told through the visuals and animation only.  About 2-4 hours to complete, depending on how many hints you take.  Lot of replayability through the collectibles and achievements as well.  Worth checking out!
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing the demo a while ago, and I was really excited to see the full release! Unfortunately, my enthusiasm quickly faded. It's a beautiful game, beautifully crafted, clever, but not much fun. After a few puzzles, finding the proper connections felt more tedious than fun: there's not much more to the gameplay than rotating the cube over and over to find matching patterns. Luckily, the hint system allows you to quickly find what you missed.I'm not sure I'd recommend playing the game. I don't regret playing, but it feels like watching a full playthrough on YouTube would be more satisfying than playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: A clever puzzle game that relies on changing perspectives and connecting 2 or more scenes together to solve puzzles. Took me a good 2 hours to solve it the first time and 30 minutes when chasing after the "Completed the game under 45 minutes" achievement so it is not particularly long, but it has 2 different endings you can get at least (one can only be gotten on 2nd playthrough).There is an element of story added on top of it but it is pretty vague and I am not even sure I understood it correctly.Works without any issues on Linux with Proton (7.0-6).

_childDocuments_.review: To summarise briefly, Moncage is a point-and-click puzzle game the gameplay loop of which seems to be heavily inspired by Gorogoa: rotate a cube to seamlessly combine motifs in two adjacent images into new objects in order to advance the actions or to unlock new scenes. Since Moncage is 3D (rather than 2D as Gorogoa), it also has some flavours of Monument Valley.In terms of visuals, Moncage is absolutely stunning. However, sometimes the puzzles become rather obscure and unintuitive; the in-game highlight and hint system will come in handy. And some designs are questionable:- There is no manual save, no level selection after completion, no save slot, which is particularly annoying due to missable achievements and collectibles, on which the underlying story depends (not that it is a coherent one, anyway);- After getting all the collectibles, you need to play through it once more to unlock the true ending, with virtually no difference in gameplay;- To see either ending again, you need another playthrough;- There is a speedrun achievement. For a point-and-click puzzle game, seriously? Maybe a tribute to Gorogoa?As a result, you probably need three playthroughs to 100% complete the game; completionists should think twice before purchasing this title.All in all, it is an enjoyable journey, which feels more like playing with an exquisite and well-crafted toy than solving puzzles, hence my recommendation. If you are interested in this game, you should also take a look at Gorogoa and Monument Valley that I mentioned above. If you truly are a puzzle lover, I also strongly recommend getting the Brilliant Boxes Bundle: the other three titles from this bundle are all excellent puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Moncage is a beautifully designed and unique puzzle game. I finished the game in about 3.5 hours and then redid a run for the achievements I missed along the way which took another ~45 minutes. This game is similar to other titles such as Gorogoa (the developers said they were inspired by it) and Superlimiinal, where you play with perspective to solve puzzles and to move forward with the narrative. While I think the storyline is ambiguous, there is enough there to keep you interested even aside from the really great puzzles.I personally found the puzzles to be fair, though some of the solutions are on the harder end. The game has two separate and really solid hint systems. The first is the ability to highlight critical parts to the puzzle and the second is the ability to have three hints given to you, and finally, if you're really really stuck, a video of the solution. I used the hints probably 3-4 times and a video once for a puzzle I was completely lost on. The hints are nice in that they start out explaining a "what" aspect to the puzzle vs. a "how" solution to solve the puzzle (e.g. the first hint might be something along the lines of "A pressure plate is not activated" indicating you need to do something to the pressure plate, but how you actually activate it is left to you). The second and third hint for an area will become more explicit, allowing for players who are stuck to get the help they need, but without having the puzzles be easy (unless you want to watch a video solution to all areas, which is an option, just not a fun one lol). I think that because the develops incorporated the hint systems, the puzzles are challenging enough for those who want to work/think outside the box (cage?) for a solution.All in all, this is a really great pick if you're looking for a moderately challenging puzzle game against a moving, though implied, narrative. If you enjoyed Gorogoa or Superliminal, I suspect you'd enjoy this title too.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Moncage is a game I just found and had sitting in my library for a long time, but I finally got around to it and I will be blunt. I really enjoyed it. A lot of the puzzles are really solid and I think the game does a good job at showing most of the mechanics. The photos may be something you could miss some of, but they are simple collectibles that help tell the story of the game in a subtle way. I think it is a nice example of telling a story without needing to spell out anything to somebody trying to follow along. In this case you are walking through the events and learning what happened as you also try to solve the puzzles the game has for you to solve. In short, I loved it.

_childDocuments_.review: (Обзор на русском тут: )There's the cube where each side is a scene from one person's life. By rotating the camera, we can combine two objects from different sides of the cube – do a  – and then something will happen: an object will move, a mechanism will start working, or even another side will be changed.– The game is confusing. The usual logic doesn't apply here, because the player doesn't know the end goal or often even what will happen after combining objects.– Some items are hidden behind extreme camera angles – and then you're wondering what to do next.– I didn't like the controls. A single click is to apply/zoom in, and a double click is to zoom out. When you're trying to do something quickly, you click a lot, and the result isn't always what you need.= There is a highlighting of active objects. By default, you are brightly highlighted the next object, what looks more like a cheat.= Some of the non-story achievements are hidden — and it's unclear how the player has to get them, except to get accidentally (or look in the guide).After the first hour, I wanted to abandon the game, because I didn't understand what to do without using hints every minute. Then I calmed down – and accepted the rules of the game: now I carefully examine each scene and think about montage.+ Re-using mechanics. The game teaches you some tricks you'll encounter later. For example, that color is important to match objects. Or you will know a way to light a lamp.+ Collectables: there are hidden photos in tricky parts of scenes.+ Small details. If you look more closely at the locations, you can see both clues and additional story details.+ Variety as much as possible in a game like this: you can rotate valves, open/close crates, there are several time-based segments, and even a simple puzzle.+ Motivation to replay. To collect all the pictures, get achievements and find uses for some suspicious scenes.I passed the game three times. The first one took  because I was stupid. In the second one, I collected most achievements and all photos – 50 minutes. The third attempt was a speedrun and  – finished in 25 minutes.During 2nd walkthrough, I started putting the pieces of the story together – to get a pretty sad story. I have no regrets that I gave the second chance to the game.

However, it felt rather frustrating when I could see the end of the puzzle to move to a new location, but couldn't execute it because I haven't figured out some other step in between. _childDocuments_.review: Got this as a Christmas gift from my SO.This game is an experience, not only a puzzle game. Music, art, story, puzzles, everything screams care and attention to detail. Some of the puzzles are quite challenging, and you will find yourself banging your head at walls for quite some time if you are the type that does not peak at hints or walkthroughs for a helping hand at any cost. The hints. The hint system is nice, it gives you a timed window to pull your hair for each puzzle, then offers the option to ask for hints. There are 3 for each panel, and a video solution as the fourth hint if you REAAALLY dont get it. I'd say first playthrough may take you anywhere from 2 hours to 5-6 hours, depending on how skillful you are at optical puzzles and perspective vision. Subsequent playthroughs (for achievements, for eg.) can take as little as 20-25 minutes if you are clockwork. 30-35 min if you take your time to smell the roses.All in all, a wonderful experience. Totally worth the time and money. 10/10 would recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Fun little puzzlegame, interesting mechanics, a nice story.Good relaxing musicGood hint system if you are stuck.Too short, first playthrough in about 2.5 hours, altho I remembered the mechanics and some of the puzzles from the demo.graphics are nice too.As I said, it is short, but on the other hand, a game you can finish in an evening (or two)

_childDocuments_.review: mysterious box In front of you containing a story of someone. He lived his life, the good and the bad, and here you are trying to find out its details.The gameplay here is unique. It is a box with each side of it containing a story and a world and also a puzzle and you try to solve these puzzles by rotating this box to try to connect the items between two different worlds. You may even get to the point where you are trying to change something in one world and transfer it to another. the puzzle idea is very beautiful, especially with every progress the story reveals to you and what happens in it. Sometimes you may have difficulty solving puzzles (it only happened to me twice) but with the hint button you will find it as soon as possible.The story here is beautiful and the way it is told is even more gorgeous. The game never talks to you, but the events that take place in these worlds and the images that you may find scattered is the story. This type of storytelling I rarely come across and find it very interesting.The game pleases the viewers, I find it very simple and there are no details that might distract you. Usually the game details always focus on the box itself. What's around it are frames containing the photos you collect. As for the sounds, they are good and calm for the atmosphere of the game.- Although the game is fun, I find its price a little high with the time that we are given (about an hour and a half to finish it).- Everyone who watched me stream the game liked their system and said they would give it a try (I know they never will).I see the game perfect in its aspects and worth the experience, although it is short compared to the price in it.aaaaaaaaaand that it <3
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: "What am I thinking of?" if you like that kind of riddle, then you'll like Moncage.The game started out really interesting, but after playing it for a while the novelty wore off and I felt less embarrassed for using hints until I realized I stopped caring about the puzzles.Moncage doesn't make YOU feel clever, because you might have a ton of great ideas how to solve the puzzles, but only the developers' intended solution is accepted.What a shame.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe this one didn't grab me. I absolutely love puzzles games. And the overwhelmingly positive reviews on Steam! From the first time I saw the trailer I knew I would be buying it. Loved the concept. It's essentially Superliminal but in a cube form, not a 3D walkable environment. Instead of having "aha" moments when I figured something out they were "ugh, finally" though. I just found the process tedious which surprised me because again, the concept was fantastic. I'm still struggling to put into words why I couldn't bother playing anymore. It just made me wonder what other dynamics/theme to the same cube rotating design this game could have come up with. Because what's here just wasn't fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I like other puzzle box games like the Room, and Moncage is doing something very cool with the bleeding of elements between frames.  However, I found it to be mostly tedious and had to rely heavily on the focus / highlight mechanic, as the pieces that connect are not visually obvious.  This is made worse by some elements only connecting when the color temperature in a scene caused the connecting elements to match colors, and the use of reflections to find some objects.  The story is very understated, and there's not much reward for solving a puzzle.  This game might be a real hit for some people, but not for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: is a simple story about a father and son during a time of war. The mechanic of the game is simple to understand but can get highly complex, the hallmark of a good puzzle game. On a cube in front of you shows five scenes, and by adjusting your perspective, objects in different scenes can line up to activate machines or trigger events. The game should take you less than 2 hours in full, and there are a few achievements to go hunting for. I've played a game like this one time before, called  And after playing both games with a similar mechanic, I recommend  above this game. They are both priced at $15.00, and tell beautiful stories in their own right. But the story you are given in  is less satisfying, less thematic, and not as tightly constructed as  Often times I wondered, "What are we doing in this random location?" "What was the moral of the story?" "Who are these characters, why do I care about their relationship?" And finally, the game  no final conclusion, but repeats the story with a little Ouroboros icon. So what was the point? Without intrigue into the story, I couldn't bring myself to care. Go play  instead for the same price, and if you crave more of this type of game, buy  next.

_childDocuments_.review: I love puzzle games, and this one is beautiful, but it still hasn't been doing it for me. The solutions often seem arbitrary and frustrating, and the game trains you early on to look for glowing connections to proceed, and then later on, it starts breaking that convention, leaving me confused. When it comes to puzzle games about perspective, I preferred Gorogoa and Superliminal.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Moncage is a multi dimensional perception puzzle game with beautiful visuals, a text less story and a great ambient OST.The whole game revolves around a single cube, with each one of it's sides having a different scenery with multiple observation levels in which you can also change the position of certain objects. Our task is finding the right angles & properties for connecting multiple cube side's into a single scene that leads an optical illusion & each individuals side's solution. Difficulty is somewhere between mediocre & hard but you can solve any puzzle at your own pace since there is no time requirements, making it a very relaxing experience. There are also "hidden" photographs you can collect that leads to a different ending.Totally recommended to all puzzle junkies & not only !
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: A unique approach to "perspective" based games - each side of the cube is a different, manipulatable area.Pros:* Some moderately difficult puzzles.* Great music* Interesting take on perspective-based games.Cons:* Short.  Like, maybe 2-3 hrs max on your 1st playthru.  Like, has an achievement for finishing the game in 45 min - which ought to inform how short it is.* Plot is vague and forgettable.Meh:* Collectibles that are only rarely in a-hole'ish locations.* The game doesn't bother explaining that COLOR matters as much as SHAPE, for matching up sides on the cube.TL;DR: If you like puzzle games, it's worth buying - maybe on sale, but get it.  Otherwise, avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a somewhat similar gameplay design like Gorogoa; a pattern matching game where you need to locate said patterns in different, distinct areas next to each other. However, where Gorogoa tells a story (said story is a bit vague, but it's definitely there) here it seems like a series of puzzles with no discernible theme.Look, the pattern matching is all fine in and of itself, and if this is enough for you then definitely get this. For me it's lacking that extra something to make it memorable and I found I just didn't enjoy it as much as I hoped I would (I really liked Gorogoa, even if I still think the base price of that game was disproportionate to its length).
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another 'puzzle' game with hardly any actual puzzles. Most of this game is just 'find the interactable'. You can either play with the highlight function and trivialise that process, or drag it out to the point of tedium without it.The few actual puzzles are pretty good, but anyone buying should expect to go about twenty minutes between them.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Was looking for a neat game to play on Steam, so I decided to check out Steam awards to find out what's the highest rated games around on PC in 2021. Bunch of AAA and highly rated titles, and Moncage was one of the nominees for Most Innovative Gameplay. Haven't heard of this game before unlike the rest, so I check out the Steam Page to learn more, and sees overwhelmingly positive reviews.Decided to give it a try. It was nominated for most innovative gameplay, and have bunch of positive reviews, it gotta be good right? And yes indeed, the game features refreshing gameplay. Its a perspective puzzler title , where you have to solve puzzles that happen across the cube faces. You'll have to align key elements across 2 faces of the cube to get the game going, in addition you'll have to rotate around and explore (via trial and error) to see what you just solved and triggered.In the background you'll be collecting photos which depict a story as you solve the puzzles. It is a soothing game which gets your brain cells kicking, and is very, very good. Now I understand why it is getting so many positive reviews.More players should definitely check out this title. I clocked in at 3 hours gameplay time, so I guess the down side is that the game is kinda short. Still a great weekend game.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting idea and fantastic visually, but the puzzles and pretty weak. You solve the "puzzles" by lining up two different pictures from two sides of the cube. The big problem is that you often don't know what you are trying to achieve apart from lining up said images for the sake of it.This means that instead of having a test of logic to solve a problem, you are must mashing the button which highlights the features and seeing what fits. So the majority of the game is basically a very pretty 'spot the similarity' and then fiddling with the images until it lines up  the way the game wants it to. For some people, the good design will make up for the lacking puzzles and thats perfectly fine,
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Infuriating.I am a fan of puzzle games and was really hyped for this one. Such cool optical illusion / forced perspective mechanic I thought - this will be so much fun!Well, it's all just about as much fun as late-stage Sierra adventure games. There is no logic to the progress, no way of figuring it out organically. I ended up constantly waiting for hints to refresh and then realized "hey, I can just watch a walkthrough on YouTube" and quit playing.It could of course be me, but I am currently having a ton of fun with Talos Principle 2 which presents just the right level of challenge - so I guess maybe puzzle designs in Moncage are not the best.Sure looks like a game that was designed for mobile devices with a paid hint system.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game was going to be exactly the sort of thing I usually enjoy, but there was not much point to it. You just spin the box around finding pieces that fit together with no real story or purpose for what you're doing. Eventually you find some pieces that go together and one of the sides of the box changes so that you have a new room full of junk to try to fit together.It would have done well to have some sort of narrative or purpose the puzzles other than just 'can you find the crap that goes together so that you can move forward to the next stage'.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed Moncage! I would recommend it if you like puzzle games, with a recommendation multiplier depending on if you like or don't like puzzles that lean more towards observation and visual lateral thinking.Moncage had a very similar vibe to Gorogoa. If you liked Gorogoa then I think you would like Moncage.Mechanically the game consists of figuring out how to match up elements of different scenes visually. This is a 3D game and so you can rotate the perspective view any way that you want, and your task is to find a way to position the viewpoint such that two different things match up. Early in the game this is all that you do, and making a successful match triggers some event that allows you to find the next match. As the game progresses so does the complexity, but the focus is always on "how can I make two different scenes interact?" Not only did I love this as a mechanic, but I thought the game did a good job of utilizing the core idea in many different creative ways. It's a relatively short game (Steam says I played 3 hours), but it felt like exactly the right length to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I have fully completed the game and I have to say that I had a blast doing it. This game just brings so much satisfaction when get to match everything up and solve the puzzle. Some puzzles seemed a bit confusing but the focus feature proved to be a great solution to this problem. The hidden story within melts my heart. I loved watching these memories unfold in front of me telling a clear story without any dialogue but with subtle clues within game. Nonetheless, I would absolutely recommend this game if you are a hardcore puzzle enjoyer or are just getting started with puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Half of the time it's unclear what the goal is, then it's completely random why the solution works. I believe this game would feel much better if it was designed as a longer story focused puzzler where individual mechanics are introduced more gradually and established completely before demanding the use. Without careful design, it really does feel random. The premise of the game is combining elements on the edges of the cube, yet sometimes a puzzle step is contained within a side completely, so it's more of a camera perspective-only piece. "The moon is a source of light". Made no sense. And with the "cart over the bridge" puzzle, the hint video is the first ever place that explains a thing in the game is even possible! I must be super out of the loop with the genre? I had no issue playing "The room" series where similar mechanics are used.Overall, I can't really give this game a score or a recommendation, for or against. Other people seem to enjoy it, so ok on discount I guess?
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: If Steam had a "maybe" option I'd use that here.The game is unique and some of the puzzles are enjoyable, but a large number of them are finicky thanks to the controls, require things to happen off-screen, or otherwise just obtuse. They also don't change in complexity from start to finish, the game just conveyor belts them to you one after another until the abrupt end. I understand there's a secret ending that requires a 2nd playthrough, but the story is threadbare and puzzle games aren't a good fit for that repeat playthrough setup.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: After the initial wow factor, the puzzles settle into a boring "find which two pieces light up and match them together" pattern.  It quickly becomes clear these aren't logic puzzles: they're jigsaw puzzles, and that's all. Even worse, they're occasionally fussy jigsaw puzzles: do both scenes need to have the same lighting (etc) to connect? Sometimes yes, sometimes no. So you change a couple things, the puzzle completes, and you move on. It all feels disjointed and arbitrary.I wanted to like this game, but every puzzle was basically one step long: connect the two pieces, something moves or changes, and now rotate the cube and find the new pieces you have to connect. Yawn.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Very disappointed on this one. Maybe the reviews likening it to Gorogoa sets in up too much since Gorogoa is one of my favorite puzzle games of all time and I went into this game with high expectations.Unfortunately movement in this game is sluggish and sometimes there is no rhyme or reason to some puzzles. The gameplay gets real old since your actions is constrained around the cube (which Gorogoa does to be fair, but puzzles are actually good on that one). Good thing there was a nice and harrowing story and the game looks gorgeous so I was able to go through it.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game - it's a clever dimension puzzle with a comfy art style and relaxing music.The game has a good assist mode that includes focus mode, three text hints for each stage, and one video hint if you are stuck. So you'll never get confused in Monocage.I'd recommend it for anyone either seeking a good puzzle with interesting mechanics or just a slow-pace relaxing game.My score: 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: As a puzzle game lover, I surprisingly has lost my interest in this game quickly. It does not leave you a clear objective to achieve or a main puzzle to solve. All you see is pieces everywhere. Although it does provide hint if you need so, it feels so frustrated that you have ask for hint every time to make clear what are you looking for.Very disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: It's a clever and relaxing perspective-based puzzle game with pleasant visuals and interesting interactions.I tried to avoid using the explicit Hint system to avoid robbing myself of the playtime and satisfaction, but made fairly regular use of the "highlight" mechanic.  If you know what you're doing, it can be completed in under 30 minutes, though a typical first playthrough will probably take a couple of hours.Surprisingly, there's a story there that's deeper and darker than I expected.I'm particularly impressed with the way the story becomes more meaningful as you progress toward 100% of the collectibles and achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: A game worth playing twice, which says a lot. I found the story a little confused at some point, the pictures you add in the album not being in order and the events can be a bit depressing at times.The puzzles are interesting, using the same mechanic while at the same time being inovative.I still don't know what that boat underwater was supposed to be used for.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: A great little gem of a puzzle game. If you liked Gorogoa, Moncage is also for you. This has similar mechanics, just in 3D instead of 2D. I enjoyed the relaxing atmosphere and the creative puzzles very much, there was just one moment where a new mechanic was introduced that I found too unintuitive and obtuse (it involves a bridge and a railcart). Other than that, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game, especially if you're into innovative puzzle mechanics.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Moncage manages to achieve something that is extremely important in puzzle games - it makes you think, it challenges you - but it never gets too convoluted to become frustrating. It is a fresh, well-designed experience that I'd recommend to puzzle game aficionados who enjoyed anything on the scale from Gorogoa to The Room series.

_childDocuments_.review: A small but smart game based on connecting and functioning objects through the various perspectives, all viewed as the edges of a space-time cube. Each plane show and hold a memory of a war veteran and his journey from grief to redemption.A very beautiful story that tries to express itself through different planes of times and each withholding a distinct stages of the man.A beautiful yet melancholic experience, Moncage is worth exploring and finding 'new perspective' in life.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Innovative puzzle game concept that makes full use of 3 dimensional space and 5 subspaces with a short and sweet story. Unfortunately this work is heavily held down by it's clunky controls and clunky-ness of navigation. Puzzles are awkward as they don't snap in place intuitively, lack of jingles/snap feeling from solving a puzzles takes away part of the joy of solving it. Hints are intentionally spaced out with arbitrary timers akin to timers for mobile game ads. In fact, this is available on GooglePlay for a quarter of the price.Overall an interesting concept with a wonderful little story  that dampens itself from poor gameplay and quality of life  designs. Get it only on >75% off or on mobile.

_childDocuments_.review: A unique, involving, intriguing puzzle game where you have to move a 3-d cube around that itself has a world within each side.  The puzzle is finding how some piece of one scene fits into another - sometimes it's obvious (an arm of a desk lamp with the bottom part of a crane) and sometimes it's much harder.  The harder stuff is a satisfying effort, and sometimes you have to change perspective, lighting, or do something dynamic within one scene.  There a lot of times I asked myself how the creators were able to think up this or that thing, the answer is that they're very creative and smart.The game proceeds at your pace, with a zen-like musical backdrop.  It follows a loose story that you put together in your own head, in a non-linear way that is perfectly compatible with the way the puzzles are structured.   It's absolutely worth every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I'm getting old and dumb. but shouldn't puzzle games give you clue to investigate. rather than point and click randomly and see what sticks? and a lot of times you know something works, but the game just refuses to let you process, until certain point or certain angle. Which yet again, can only be achieved by random chance. This is the worst puzzle game I've played that has a Overwhelmingly Positive review score.I've previously played another perspective puzzle game, Superliminal. That's what I expected from this, but was very disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, super great game. It has the same level of puzzle complexity and environmental story telling as Gorogoa (which is to say, its top-tier-best-a-da-best *chef's kiss). The intimate art + atmosphere mixed with its steady pacing can result in some real impactful moments (SO IF YOU WANT A GAME THAT GIVE THE BIG CHILLS, THIS GAME WILL GIVE THE BIG CHILLS). The puzzles are greatly satisfying to complete, and the game does a really good job of providing hints to guide you along if you are stuck. If you were to play it, HIGHLY RECOMMEND 100% it. It's totally worth the little extra effort as it is a relatively short game (took me 5 hours to complete and 5.8 hrs to 100%). Judging from the credits the dev team is really quite small, and to pull this masterpiece off is really impressive (sheeesh pop off)

_childDocuments_.review: Well I do not like giving thumbs down really but that is how I feel about it. The Game itself it a very big thumbs up. Imaginative, original and intriguing type of game play.But, what is the point?I am quite new to gaming so maybe I do not have the skill set yet to get the most out of this sort of thing. But overall it was a tedious experience. How folk manage to make the visual link ups is beyond me and I virtually always needed the 'clues' and the videos to work out what the heck I was supposed to be doing. Perhaps developers who are so closely into what they are creating forget that us mortals come at these things from a different angle? There is also some narrative here but what? Scenes of warfare nestle along side a fairground - all very confusing. A similar game I have played is Gorogoa but I enjoyed that enormously. Moncage I found impenetrable and ultimately it is just not for me. To me what it 'looks like' has taken precedent over the coherence of the content. Sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: Runs really well on the Steam Deck. The puzzles can be a bit too subtle or hard to spot at times, and hints don't always give much useful information to actually point you down the right path. You can also find stuff out of order which makes getting stuck even easier as you wait for the next hint to be available.The biggest issue i have is complete lack of a full custom controller config. The game may be simple, but when its designed for computer it helps massively to have an OOTB controller config that binds the menu, hints, double-clicks, point of interest highlighting, etc. You can do it yourself on Steam Deck, but each game has slight differences to how it accepts inputs. So using Steam input to string together menu interactions doesn't always work the same and can take hours to get working. It improves gameplay a ton though once its setup to your liking, but some form of custom controller mapping from the devs would be preferred.Despite those shortfalls, its still a good creative puzzle game. Worth checking out on sale for sure. But be prepared for odd control scheme OOTB on Steam Deck.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well-made puzzle game.  I absolutely adore the setup of having to connect different objects across multiple faces of the puzzle to get the solution, though on occasion the solutions are a bit too obtuse (specifically ones that require specific colors to match up, which makes it unclear if you're matching items that aren't supposed to match or if you're just doing it at the wrong time).  Thankfully it has a good hint system built-in, and there's also a lot of collectibles hidden throughout and a ton of cool details in the levels.  Just be aware it's a bit short if you aren't going for 100%.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a great game, I struggled quite a bit until I finished the first playthrough. I usually really enjoy playing the likes of escape room games, The Room series, House of Da Vinci series etc but my brain just didn't want to work for this one for a lot of it ^^" Glad the hints were there. I often wanted to jump ahead and there is no clear indication of order until you get it, so I guess neurodivergents might struggle with it XD Take your time and think everything through or use the well-timed help. Once you understand all, you can then enjoy a re-run to find everything that you missed in the first attempt and it is really worth it!I enjoyed the imagery and themes in the game and the music was very relaxing. To me it also evoked Hemingway a bit, but that might just be me ^^" So if you like puzzle games with a twist and having to rethink perspective, I highly recommend it, just don't try to rush it.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to say that this game was a journey. I originally bought this because it was listed as a puzzle game, which is a genre of game i enjoy playing a lot. At the time of this review i have 3 hours played, which is how long it took me to beat it my first time around. This is not an ordinary puzzle game, this is a story. The soundtrack is outstanding the whole way through. The art is wonderful in its own way. This is a very visually appealing game to play. I had a lot of moments I was super stumped as well, which is what makes a great puzzle game great in my opinion. As you follow the story along and collect memories and actively think outside the box, you are constantly reminded that anything goes as long as you can connect it. In the end, I will be replaying this as I've missed several achievements. Hopefully though whoever may see this truly considers picking it up because THIS is one gem of a game for an outstanding price. I don't want to spoil what the deep meaningful story it will take you on is, you have to find that out for yourself :-)

_childDocuments_.review: A short, fun game with a cool concept. I think I got the gist of the story from playing through it, though it feels very left up to interpretation and imagination. If I have any complaints about the game, it would mainly be that missing anything means you need to replay the entire game again. It's relatively short, but with no way to make things move faster, I was getting impatient. If you're good and thorough, you can probably 100% the game in only 2 playthroughs, but I kept missing things due to my own impatience and mistakes, meaning I had to play through it at least 4 if not 5 times. Some kind of checkpoint or level select after you finish the game to make either getting the true ending or specific achievements (mainly the exhaustive method) would have been appreciated, but the game is short enough that I can't hold too much of a grudge. Overall I enjoyed it, but if you're going for 100%, be careful of replay frustration.

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like a clone of Gorogoa. It's slicker, but the puzzles are more obtuse and the story is even harder to follow than Gorogoa. It also doesn't feel like you are directing your journey as much. It does have a much better hint system though!So, if you loved Gorogoa, then you'll like this. If you haven't played Gorogoa then go play it. It's amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: Hmmm,Let's see. On one hand, it's a concept I love, a bit similar to Gorogora where all the game revolves around visual tricks to solve puzzles.The hint system is great to make your understand the few basic principles you can play with.It's incredible that this game is kinda unexplainable. It's quite difficult to predict what the level designer had in mind before you actually see it in one very specific angle and it's quite satisfying once you do.On the other hand, it took me 4 hours to complete the game including all achievements.4 or 5 play through. _childDocuments_.review: Moncage is an interesting perspective puzzle game. They did a great job of working the hints into the game through allowing you to highlight important pieces, and even receive small hints through the pause menu. The game is exceptionally beautiful and many of the stunning environments felt like tiny little worlds to look at and explore.In some puzzles I felt that in the eventual solution, there was little "connection" to the objects being linked or to the action being performed. Some puzzles felt very intuitive and satisfying but others were difficult because of sheer obscurity.Overall a great addition to the genre, 7.5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzle games do not typically attract me, but the visuals and mechanics of Moncage piqued my interest anyway. In my opinion, the game hits a balance that puzzle games often struggle with, being challenging enough to be satisfying to solve without being a constant irritation. The mechanic, rotating the camera around to match objects in adjacent faces of the cube, is creative and elegant, yet simple so one does not need to learn some complicated, unruly system, making it easy to pick up.The game is also somewhat short (likely just a couple hours) and I think being short and sweet in this way helps keep it from becoming tiresome.There is something a narrative, subtly told, that takes you through the life of the protagonist. However, I confess that I was not inclined to pay much attention to it nor was I extremely motivated to find the collectibles that really help tell it. This is not because that story is bad in any way, but simply because I was perfectly satisfied with solving the puzzles for their own sake.A nice, casual, interesting puzzle game worth a couple hours when you can spare them <3
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty good game, took me two and a half hours. There were plenty of parts that I got stuck on and had to use the hint function (which has an annoying timer). There were only a few parts that I thought were counter-intuitive, one part made you do the same thing three times in a row to progress, which completely stumped me because I thought "well I already did that, and it didn't work" so I didn't do it again much less two more times. There were a few parts that were tricky to align, to the point that I thought that I wasn't supposed to align them until I looked at the hint and saw that I actually was supposed to align them.The art and music are great though, and if you are clever enough to not be constantly having to use the hints then I could see how this game could be really good.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Kinda neat. My issue with this game is that since the puzzles are all based around the cube, the only continuous thread gameplay wise is the cube itself. This resulted in me holding the space bar to know how things are connected, but not piecing together the physics of it all and how they connect. I get that's the point, but it just wasn't fun to see the solution to the puzzle was one click away yet such an obscure element that I'd never have gotten it. Although it's very possible I'm just dumb.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting puzzle game with interesting mechanics using a combination of different schemes in a cube where you progress by interacting and matching scenes to achieve an outcome to move ahead.Good+ A unique take on a puzzle game, similar in some ways to Gorogoa.+ The premise of war and peace is interesting but not really fleshed out fully on the message it wishes to convey, but interesting nonetheless.+ Challenging but satisfying results when you get a solution right after a hard try.+ Lovely art style and design in their graphics.Cons- Frustrating at times at what the solution, they do have a multi tiered hint system which does help somewhat but it would be better if some of it was more intuitive.- The matching lock between puzzle pieces can be frustrating when you know its the solution but it doesn't align well enough or need such a precision that it becomes tedious or too difficult to just get it right in certain positions.- Some of the timing puzzles require too much precision. - Tedious, I really wish to like this but its really frustrating (yes i have used this word multiple times) that I just feel like giving up despite it being interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, as much as I would have loved to be able to recommend this game, I can’t.It was simply missing logic when trying to piece two things together and felt rather like random pattern matching.Don’t get me wrong, some puzzles were alright, where you knew what you were trying to accomplish but most of them just felt random. _childDocuments_.review: Moncage is built around a quaint yet enthralling puzzles, involved around making an object look like it crosses scenes. As this mechanic is fully explored, you are taken on a journey through a subtly compelling story. I played this game assuming it would be good, and was repeatedly surprised by how great it was.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful puzzle game that tells a tragic and bittersweet story about war in the background, how it changes us and the world around us, and how even after tragedy, there can still be beauty. A lot of the connections force you to think outside (or in this case, I suppose inside) the box. There was only once or twice where I used hints where I thought "how would I ever thought of that on my own?" But even in those cases, I wouldn't say it was the developer's fault for making a bad puzzle; instead, it was just that the solution was very clever and required more steps and more brain power. Highly recommend. One of the best puzzle games I've ever played, if not THE best one I've ever played. Extremely unique and simple. The diverse hint system allows for varying levels of difficulty depending on how much of a puzzle you want (and if you want an extremely challenging experience, I suggest never hitting the space bar).
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Highly Recommended. When people talk about games as art, Moncage should be an example, Minimalist art style, minimalist story telling, and yet it tells a powerful story with strong imagery. This is a puzzle solving game based on perspective, similar to Monument Valley and Maquette, and while not particularly groundbreaking the execution here is probably the best I've ever experience for this style of game. The puzzles had a good amount of brain strain, I was never stalled for long, and found I got a good sense of momentum and some "a-ha" moments where everything clicked and you could make good progression. The hint system was very well implemented in that it would give you multiple nudges in the right direction before showing you a video if you were truly stuck, letting you control just how much help you need.Give it a shot!
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: The hitboxes for where it wants you to line things up have a good chance of just not working, even when doing the very thing the video hints do. The achievements were also super buggy, where I had to beat the game 4 times in under 30min each to get the 'veteran' achievement, which only requires time under 45min. This was due to a couple things including not accepting a completion if all album cards weren't found and the final alignment before the credits playing but never starting the actual credits.Game is also quite short for the price buggy or not, with no replay value as the only way to do new runs of the game is to wipe all progress.

_childDocuments_.review: DNF - becomes a chore only way to complete is read the clues. This unfortunately means it becomes unenjoyable with no sense of achievement. There's a great game mechanic here - but too many issues in puzzle design to recommend it. The game fails due to it's locking together mechanism being immensely shonky, and also no real cohesion within the puzzles. With the locking mechanism sometimes you can be miles away and it will autocomplete, others you're fiddling for ages just to get it right on that spot.There's also a couple of Goat Puzzle moments where the game throws in new mechanics without any warning. Even after you've looked up the solution and found what you're trying to do is right your left fiddling for 10mins to get it to the exact mm of where it wants.This unfortunately ruins the entire game by removing all fun, as it's no longer logic or guess work but looking up the answer via the hints or the an online walkthough. And as I've mentioned them - the "online walkthrough players" with there "Oh I'm just gonna try this... " no, it's quite obvious you already know the solution.

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up only because I refunded this after fifteen minutes so a negative review didn't feel entirely fair. I wish there was a "Neutral" option. I found the game a little too focused on...how should I phrase this...Polish in place of Art (Heart). It had the flavor I might expect if a AAA developer tried to make a "point, click, rotate" puzzle game. And I just didn't feel the puzzle element; it felt much more like I-Spy, with a number of the connections relying a bit too much on blind flailing. Perhaps this would've changed if I played longer, but I think the first fifteen minutes set up exactly what the whole game will be. Also, the last "point and click" puzzle game I played was Gorogoa, and Moncage just didn't live up to it by comparison.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful puzzle game taking place in different scenes in the sides of a cube where the player has to line up different objects until they look connected between the scenes, causing some change to occur. There are plenty of puzzles that felt pretty easy to solve and plenty that made me scratch my head a bit and spin around the cube multiple times. Thankfully, there is a hint system in the game that seems to only be based on time, so you have a lot of time to try to solve the puzzles without being tempted to get a hint for something you could have solved with a little more thinking. The art style is beautiful and the game tells a story without words that mostly depends on the number of pictures you find throughout the game and put in your album. The story went in places I didn't expect and honestly made me tear up a bit at the end and I felt that I managed to get a good grip on what was going on both without words and without having found every single picture. The soundtrack was at times quietly minimalist and at times building up with the story beats and it could be quite sorrowful and beautiful. A truly enjoyable experience with depth beyond its face.

I manage to finished it in 2-3 hours.There is an underlying story hidden somewhere here about a PTSD war veteran and the cycle of generational trauma, but to be honest... I don't play this game because of its story. But hey, it's there if you want to dive deep into it.Overall, very nice game!

The hint system is good and nonintrusive & some of the puzzles can be a little finicky but it's not frustrating. Overall would definitely recommend on sale as it isn't even really a couple hours long unless you go for every collectible and achievement.

_childDocuments_.review: Though it was frustrating at times, I did have a good time playing this game. It was creative, interesting, colorful, and a lot of love clearly went into it. And considering it looks like it was made almost entirely by 2 people, I'm willing to be more lenient on it. The frustration mostly stemmed from the fact that some of the solutions can feel finicky, in the sense that I had actually solved the puzzle, I just hadn't gotten things in the exact right spot. The hint system was also not my favorite, but that's kind of a minor issue.Aside from all that, this is short, clever puzzle game that I think is worth your time, especially if you were intrigued by the screenshots. Also not too tough to 100%, though I do recommend using a guide, because some of them you only get one shot at per playthrough.
