_childDocuments_.review: Resident Evil Village is a first-person shooter survival horror developed by Capcom. The game is set in the present time, three years following the events of RE 7. Once again, the player assumes the role of Ethan Winters, who, after an unfortunate series of events, finds himself separated from his family and stranded in a remote Romanian village. Here, he will set himself on a journey to save his family and, at the same time, survive the dreadful and unforgiving place.By far, its story is my favorite in the entire series. The writers have surprisingly taken the Resident Evil narrative to a whole new level, and that’s something I didn’t think I’d ever say. Ethan’s arduous journey to rescue his family is convincing, immersive, and full of mysteries and twists, with memorable moments and characters — definitely an experience that will stick with me for a while. The game’s heavy, bleak, and terrifying atmosphere is remarkable. Wandering within the various bewildering and interconnected rooms of Castle Dimitrescu, exploring decrepit sheds, and running in the claustrophobic corridors of a colossal factory definitely felt like a dose of adrenaline. At all times, I couldn’t help but feel this eerie and disturbing feeling of vulnerability and anxiety — always expecting a jump scare or something of the sort at every turn and corner. Gameplay-wise, this title is beyond excellent. From frantic combat to exciting exploration, everything is fluid, well-crafted, and entertaining. Once again, Capcom opted to deviate a little from their last iteration and give Village a more significant focus on the action. At first, I was slightly skeptical about it, as the last thing I wanted was this to be just another mediocre title, with some cheap Michael Bay-style sort of action segments and uninspired gameplay — yes, I’m talking to you, RE 6. Though, to my surprise and satisfaction, it wasn’t anything like that. In Village, they flawlessly attained the precise equilibrium between action and horror, essentially creating the perfect incorporation of RE 4 and 7 into one. Hence, even if you are not fond of this slightly more action-focused turn the game took, you shouldn’t be all worried; because, in the end, the game still manages to be a true survival horror, truthful to its roots.The pleasant combat mechanic is one of the key features that made this title stand out the most. Whether gunning down a crowd of enemies who dare stand in your way, or just trying to protect yourself with a mere knife, Village’s combat plays fluidly and actually strives to keep the player engaged at all times. In order to stand your ground against the myriad of repulsive monstrosities, you can count on an immense and diversified arsenal that will help you send your foes to the other plane of existence. I’m really fond of the game’s large weapon assortment and how the guns work; each weapon in the game, from shotguns to hand cannons, is unique and feels totally authentic and pleasant to handle and shoot. And things don’t end there: during the journey, the player can additionally find a plethora of attachments to enhance their guns, these varying from extended magazines, barrels, foregrips, and even scopes.While the game indeed recycles some of its predecessor’s core gameplay mechanics, it also brings plenty of additional features to the table, as well as tweaks to pre-existing ones. One of my favorites is that Ethan can now parry basic enemy attacks in addition to blocking them — which can be pretty useful; it certainly saved my life countless times. The crafting system was also further improved, and it is much simpler and quicker to craft your items this time. Instead of the old mechanic of “combining items” present in pretty much all previous iterations, here, crafting has its own exclusive tab where you can quickly assemble your items by pressing one mere button. And, surprisingly enough, Village has a pretty interesting hunting and cooking mechanic — which works in a very simplified manner. Scattered throughout the map, you can find a variety of animals to hunt, ranging from pigs to fishes and even goats. Once you kill any of the animals, it will drop a piece of meat, which can be delivered to the merchant to brew your selected desired meal. Eating certain dishes will highly improve Ethan’s overall stats permanently, such as health, movement velocity, and even how much damage he can take in fights. This cooking mechanic is indeed a very welcomed feature; even with its simplicity, it still is one of the best additions to the title. One aspect that the RE series is well known for and nearly constantly delivers in great fashion is, definitely, the boss fights — and here, it’s no different. Village has some of the most charismatic bosses and thrilling battles of the series. Every boss encounter plays uniquely, with each one of them having their own distinctive move sets, attack patterns, and weak spots the player must exploit to prevail in the fight. Even though I didn’t find them very arduous opponents (besides the final one), standing your ground against all the daunting monsters on the hardest difficulty certainly made me break a sweat. To my surprise, the optional bosses are back in Village. There are five of them you can encounter as you progress in the narrative. Even though they aren’t as creative or their fights as unique as the main villains, I still had lots of fun facing them.The revamped level design is one of the best aspects of the game. Most areas are much more open now — with a surplus of broader sections to explore and secrets to unravel. This novel approach regarding the levels is excellent and also refreshing to the series. Though, what caught my attention the most, was the much more extensive exploration system. Fortunately, that mechanic is excellent, and very much worthwhile. Similar to various horror titles, exploring each part of the map is essential for your survival. Here, investigating and exploring the various intriguing and breathtaking areas in search of crafting resources, ammunition, and all sorts of supplies can be the only thing that determines whether you die or stay alive to fight another day.Throughout my multiple playthroughs, I, fortunately, had very few performance problems. I played the entire game on the max settings (RTX On) and had a pretty decent overall frame rate; it usually fluctuated around 85-100FPS with no stuttering. The only time where my PC struggled a bit was in a particular section with a bug swarm. Regarding the game’s performance with the RTX turned off, it ran smoothly, far above the 100FPS mark with no problems whatsoever. On the topic of bugs, I encountered few of them. Those I came upon were mere collision bugs that caused enemies to clip through environmental props. I also had this weird glitch where every time I’d alt-tab, the frame rate would lock at 20FPS; though it was fixable, however, by just setting the game to borderless.Resident Evil Village was, undoubtedly, my most delightful surprise this year thus far. I surely had a great time and have solely good things to say about the game — it absolutely has surpassed any expectations I had. Capcom did everything right this time, from the narrative and atmosphere to the gameplay mechanics; everything was made with the utmost care and attention. Therefore, with all that said, even at full price, I can’t recommend this game highly enough. Village is, without a shadow of a doubt, one of the best survival-horror experiences out there.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will hitch any time you make any progress toward unlocking an achievement and it is _emphatically_ caused by CAPCOM's unorthodox level of Denuvo protection I had some success jumping over the problematic anti-tamper triggers, but only an actual cracked executable will _safely_ undo CAPCOM's SteamAPI quantum entanglement. Pirates will definitely have a better PC experience than actual Steam customers unless CAPCOM patches this @#$%.Anti-tamper nightmare aside, there is something even stupider lurking under the hood to make the PC version run poorly. It is creating and destroying DXGI factories each and every frame to ask Windows for a list of resolutions your monitor supports and the amount of installed VRAM. Luckily this does not cause stutter, it has a  performance penalty (on the order of 3 ms of CPU time).Special K has worked around this baffling performance parachute (consult the #releases section on my Discord server).

name: Nexomon: Extinction
detailed_description: Nexomon: Extinction is a return to classic monster catching games, complete with a brand new story, eccentric characters and over 300 unique Nexomon to trap and tame. The world is on the brink of extinction as mighty Tyrant Nexomon fight for dominion over humans and monsters. Join the Tamer's guild and begin an epic journey to restore balance before all hope is lost… Begin Your Journey Leave the orphanage you grew up in, choose your first Nexomon and start your life as a Tamer. Explore a world teeming with Nexomon Trap and tame 381 Nexomon from nine elemental types, with powerful evolutions. Join the Fight Tyrant Nexomon roam free and the Tamer's Guild is stretched to the limit, can you change the tide of the battle? Battle Trainers and Tyrants Step up and take on would-be challengers and dangerous foes in beautifully animated turn-based battles. Discover Diverse Regions From arid deserts to freezing tundra, navigate challenging environments and manage their effects on your Nexomon. Immerse yourself in the world of Nexomon Uncover secrets, stumble upon side-quests and encounter a raft of eccentric characters. Train hard to become the greatest Dynamic difficulty will see the world around you get more challenging as you progress, as even defeated trainers come back stronger than before and ready to battle again!

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since I've finished a game and actually felt "achieved". It is extremely easy to make a path for players, do this, do that, bam, you completed the game! A lot of games fall into this trap where a player isn't really being given anything of substance for this. I worried this game might be the same but it blew me away from start to finish.Looking back on the Pokemon games I find them unplayable for me. Each gym battle practically forces you to do an aggravating amount of grinding with little to no reward for completing them, not to mention purposefully putting the odds against you to deplete your team before that point. There are only bare bone stories to keep you continuing and the characters are forgettable. I began to realize I love the idea of Pokemon, of collecting adorable/cool creatures and bonding with them, but not the execution. Why do I bring up Pokemon? Because, for the casual player, Nexomon does everything Pokemon did wrong Nexomon doesn't force a play style, and the game is beatable for those who just want to fill their team with cute/cool Nexomon or people who are super into strategy. As long as you continue to level up your team on the way and stay well stocked on supplies. The game actively rewards you for investing in your Nexomon with pretty great abilities. It's all thanks to the combat system. Instead of PP, Nexomon uses a system similar to a stamina or mana bar, so essentially you can use any moves as many times as you want, they simply will lower that bar. Just like health, the bar can be refilled with a potion. Having this be a bar makes it much easier to manage. Switching between Nexomon is also a wonderfully seamless and quick process, helping you spread out exp and manage health. It's easy and simple and, after some trail and error, I really got the hang of it. The wild Nexomon in the area are usually what you can pretty much expect from the bosses there, so you can get used to their abilities and counteracting their status effects. The level of wild Nexomon and those in trainer encounters also serve as a little hint at what level the game expects you to be at in that point in the game, so you know what to shoot for. This makes any "grinding" much easier, and you can actively feel the changes in your Nexomon as they level and evolve rather than it just feeling like a cosmetic change. The game doesn't want you to fail, it's not an up hill battle but a curve it does its best to lead you down without holding your hand. Trainers level up to match with where you should be as well. Add the addition of cores, items your Nexomon can hold to increase a variety of things, and you have a battle system that is fun but challenging in the right ways.Nexomon realizes fighting is part of the genre, but not the be all end all. It lets its story drive its fights, not the other way around. Whenever you are fighting, it is for a good reason. There are actual stakes to your fights, characters you care about are either cheering for you or on the line, and the story constantly intrigues you with shocking twists and turns. It also knows that if it is going to put its players through several battles, it needs to make it worth their while and reward them for it. After big fights, you are not only given big rewards, but also increase your ranking in the organization you are a part of. This gives you more access to materials, locations, and so on. The addition of side quest and treasure gives the player more to do as well.Now the story; Nexomon aims for an older audience, presenting a Pokemon like world with a dark spin. You see, creatures called Tyrants have been raging a war ever since their king died in search for another heir. Humans have been left in the crossfire of this, and what we're left with is a torn apart world. Its compelling and while it isn't a high graphics game, a lot of the places just look gorgeous honestly. The lore behind each location is definitely fun and imaginative. But I haven't even mentioned the player yet, and for once they actually have relevance instead of just being a completely blank slate. Nexomone recognizes that, in a game, it's fun to have importance  You feel like you are a part of this story rather than being an observer or willing participant, watching everything blow up around you. The twists are extremely well written, the story in inventive and spins the genre on its head, and your character is someone worth getting invested in. It's the type of story that blew me away and has to be experienced to fully appreciate it. The ending  I'm thrilled to see there is plenty of worthwhile after game content to explore.The characters are also very lovable, including Cocoa. He's supportive, yet makes funny comments along the way, and his sarcasm was pretty entertaining. The other characters have their own charm to keep dialogue interesting. The inside jokes based on your playthrough only make it better. Heck, even NPCs remember when you saved them and some of your other exploits. But dialogue is hardly forced down your throat and, with this and the teleportation system, you are freely allowed to explore the world in anyway you want.There are also a lot of fun, quality of life features. You're able to select your avatar and change this and your name whenever you want. You can collect followers, cute little Nexomon to follow you around. Cocoa always asks you if you're ready before fast traveling you somewhere else, and lots of other characters do this as well before a mission so you can make sure you are completely prepared. Even after starting a mission, you can sometimes still teleport away for materials and there is in-between time to heal your Nexomon or take a break. You can rebattle trainers to help get exp. There is plenty explanation of the story of the first game, so you don't have to play it to understand this one. The Nexomon designs are great! They're wonderfully creative with plenty to chose from. Even the humanoid ones, something I usually hate, just look really cool and cute. Finally, and my favorite features, there are crystals around the world that replenish your team without you having to use your resources, and they respawn after some time. They are great to use in a pinch or when battling trainers to level up.To summarize, Nexomon, in my opinion, is a very good game that goes above and beyond its genre. It's great for players that have always wanted to be a fan of Pokemon, but found the gameplay too grindy and unrewarding. It is also great for casual players and there is a lot for them to love here. That being said, if you struggle to grasp even the basic concepts of Pokemon, Nexomon is probably going to be too hard for you. If you like Pokemon, well, it just depends. Either way, I love this game and would highly recommend it. It's very underappreciated for how great its writing is and fun/smooth its gameplay is.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really really good game. Frankly it's fantastic with a few downpoints.+Extremely good monster designs! There's a few duds but overall some amazing designs with many to love+Stamina instead of PP as a system is a good balancer+Really really good STORY. who plays pokemon for the story? But I found I got really engaged in the plot. there were jokes I laughed at! Characters I enjoyed! I got really into the lore and mysteries. It's a sequel, I later learned, so there's characters from the first game... but because it takes place hundreds of years later, it doesn't feel too past-plot reliant. In fact, most old characters are ghosts now, adding to the atmosphere of it being post-apocalyptic+yes, that's right, this game has ATMOSPHERE. it takes place in a current-post apocalypse world and it feels quite spooky how you are exploring around bomb craters, old cars, ancient ruins of modern cities, and even a downed trainline. The plot and such matches this. It feels like the good happy days were in the past, and you're in this broken, struggling world. with cute monsters.+A challenge!! the game levels with you, so fights never get to the point of you being able to just slay easily. The last few fights are actually hard, and especially the final boss! I hated that prick so much!+Open world ish. You can very early on freely explore the world. The plot limits some areas, and you'll likely revisting places you've been before when you follow it, but it's nice how you can explore almost everywhere right away and catch a huge variety for your team.Downsides of note-There's no tutorial really. This is a plus in some ways, but also is frustrating when it comes to status effects and type advantages. You learn types eventually, but it's a lot to pick up without a guide. Status effects have no explanation anywhere, which is tricky. A lot of them overlap in strange ways (like puzzled VS confused)-If you want to 100%, as I did, it takes a while. I beat the game after 32 leisurely hours, but to 100% it took me 53. Most of that was grinding the nexomon database. The trick is that the encounter rate for mega rares is very very low, and for legendaries it's about 2%. it can take hours to find one. you will grind a lot. getting to level 99 is not hard when you consider the grinding you'll do to catch them all.-There's a place where the majority of rare nexomon are, and it's just a small island. This feels fun when you first explore it, as it's full of cool nexomon... but then when you go grinding you realize it's TOO MANY. Most zones have like 5 or 6 nexomon types, one patch on the island will have 12. Additionally, encounter rates in many places aren't based on screens, but on specific patches of grass- and in large patches, it'll be sides of parts of grass. This means if you're hunting in the right area, you still may not have any luck because you're on the wrong part of the grass.-When you try to fight every trainer (twice) there's no way to keep track of this, and it also means a lot of grinding.-basically, don't try to 100% unless you're ready to grind

_childDocuments_.review: Solid capture monster game. I know that all of these games are compared to Pokemon, but Nexomon: Extinction is a fantastic and distinct game. It is somewhat of a cross between Pokemon and Epic Battle Fantasy, with much more of the latter story and humour style. The Nexomon themselves are fantastically designed, with a good mix of abilities and types to provide different play styles and strategies. I am at the end game now, although I have grinded quite a bit. If you stick to the main story, and limit strolling through grass trying to capture any Nexomon you don't have, you can expect at least 30 hours of game play if you stick to the story.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon is... weird. As someone who's grown tired of Nintendo's inability of making an enjoyable Pokemon game, I started trying indie alternatives. I have to accept not one of them comes close to the undeniable charm of Gamefreak's creations, but most manage to be fun. This is one of them.Nexomon is a Pokemon rip-off, they're not even trying to hide it and that's OK. You know what to expect when you come here; find creatures in the tall grass, weakening them, throwing stuff to capture them, and then using them to rinse and repeat the cycle. Each Nexomon has an element which determines its strengths and weaknesses, you can only have 6 at a time, yadda yadda. You get the catch.Nexomon, however, manages to do stuff different enough to be its own different beast. First, this game is absolutely single-player focused, which means the challenges are crafted for PVE in mind and there's no Breeding/EVs/IVs; you catch your monster at its best, and that's how it is. It also means Nexomon have no gender so, name them whatever. Second, the catching method is much more involved; despite it being the classic "weaken them and throw trap", it also comes with other factors you can manipulate, such as giving the monster snacks that will make them like you more, and imputing key commands in a minigame as you try to catch them in order to up the possibilities of a successful capture. There's an MP system that replaces PP, meaning all powers you use consume Points from a pool rather than each move having its own number of uses, which means spamming powerful moves is usually not a good idea. There's more focus on items and resource management, as Nexomon hit VERY hard and even wild battles can prove to be lethal. Unlike newer Pokemon games, there's no XP share, meaning you have to grind old-school; speaking of which, each Nexomon has a series of slots you can equip with boosters that actually work like XP shares or give them other special abilities, they're much more customizable than Pokemon.The story is... special. This game doesn't takes itself seriously, it knows it's a Pokemon rip-off and constantly makes fun of itself and pet catching games with fourth wall breaking and meta commentary. Most of the times the humor misses, but when it hits, it hits hard. Now, even this game has its serious moments, but those are few and far between and it's much more focused on being a silly adventure game of monster catching.Lastly, the Nexomon designs are quite good when compared to other Indie Monster Catching games, some of them I could actually imagine in a Pokemon game, and there's a LARGE roster of critters roaming in the wilds waiting to be caught; and since IVs/EVs aren't a thing, it means you can more easily grab the ones you like and go wild!No game is perfect though. The UI is weird and was clearly designed for mobile gaming in mind. The constant attempts at being humorous can get tiring, there's little to no tutorials in-game, meaning you never really know which element is best against certain Nexomon and other stuff that goes unanswered. There's no map, no XP from capturing monsters, and the difficulty spikes are all over the place.I recommend Nexomon to those monster-catching enthusiasts that are looking for something else out there. As mentioned before, this isn't as fun or polished as Pokemon, but it's very enjoyable and close enough to justify a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: I went from playing the first Nexomon game to this one within a week. I really enjoyed the first game and put about 22 hours into it. While this game does have some improvements, there are also a lot of things I didn't like. I actually initially stopped playing and refunded this game because of the atrocious QoL changes it had from the first game. Luckily, I learned that custom mode existed, though I had to rely on a kind soul from the Steam community to provide a save file since they lock it behind game completion. The game feels much more playable by even simply doubling the XP rates to more closely match the first game.Pros:- The graphics are improved from the first game.- The music is very well done.- The combat interface is better.- The story and overall feel of the game are still great like the first Nexomon game.Cons:- This game removed many of the nice QoL features that the first game had.-- No more auto-run - not even a toggle. You have to hold the button. -- XP rates were nerfed into the ground so you have to kill like 4x more Nexmon to gain a level.-- You no longer restore HP and Stamina on leveling up.-- Exp share (early game) is now in multiple individual items which you have to manually add and remove to each Nexomon which feels very clunky.- Custom Mode is locked to completing the main game.- A lot of the gold-star and blue-star quests in-game are just pointless. I don't do most of the blue ones and only some of the gold ones. -- For the trade quests, why can they not just take from my box? Why do I have to have them in my inventory?I am enjoying the game with custom mode from the get-go, but man was it a rough transition from the first game. I feel they focused way too hard to customization and really missed the mark in many areas.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get right into the good and the badGOOD- 8 starters to pick from and something like 70 more Nexomon to capture nearby RIGHT at the start of the game. This meant I had a stacked team of Nexomon of varying types that I liked right off the bat. Lots of replayability concerning team variety.- The game is generous with ports. You gain access to this games version of "Fly" early on and it save a lot of time. They also port you back through the ends of caves instead of forcing you to backtrack which is welcomed.- Personally I like how many Nexomon there are and enjoy lots of their designs. There is something here for everyone.- The story is a breath of fresh air. It vaguely follows the pokemon tropes here and there but also has you doing stuff other than "Kill X Gym Leaders". Instead you are running all around the map doing quests. I also really enjoyed the side character "Coco" who is sort of the mouth piece for you being the mute protagonist. He acts as comic relief and his little comments often break the fourth wall but in a fun way. I like that he sort of took the piss out of story that doesn't need to take itself seriously.- Toooooons of post game quests and monster capturing. I have only competed the main story but there are A LOT of legendary esque creatures to capture in the post game if that's your kind of thing.THE BAD- Scaling. The game scales trainer and wild encounters with you at specific points when moving the story forward. This means that you aren't actually rewarded for having a balanced team of six compared to blasting through the game with one over power Nexomon. About half way through the game I was able to craft the equivalent of "EXP Share" for my whole party which greatly help mitigate this problem but it was still more of nuisance than a welcomed feature. Much of the community also seems to agree.- New moves are mostly garbage. It wasn't until late game I started replacing some of my early moves with upgraded attacks. A lot of them are buffs that are trivial or attacks with low chances to apply a debuff. Some of them might be great if Nexomon had an online VS feature. - Which bring me to the lack of an online battle system. Much of my drive to do post game capturing and training hinges on that feature alone personally. Without online battles there seems to be little point it "Catching them all" when there is no forum to show off your Nexomon.- Swapping Cores can be a pain. Later on when you do have a ton of EXP related Cores moving them around your team is a bit tiresome. The older less relevant ones also become useless and just sit in your inventory collecting dust. I also didn't end up using any of the stat related cores because simply levelling my Nexomon was just more effective. Another reason Online Battling would be useful

_childDocuments_.review: ❤ Audience ❤☐ Beginner☑ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☐ Expert☼ Graphics ☼☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☑ Beautiful☐ Fantastic♬ Music ♬☐ Bad☐ Alright☑ Good☐ Beautiful☐ Fantastic☠ Difficulty ☠☐ Easy☑ Average☑ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Hard☐ Unfair§ Bugs §☐ Bugs destroy the game☐ Lots of bugs☐ Few Bugs☑ Nothing encountered☯ Story ☯☐ There is none☐ Bad☐ Alright☑ Good☐ Fantastic⚔ Gameplay ⚔☐ Frustrating☐ Sleepy☐ Boring☑ Fun☐ Challenging۞ Game time / Length ۞☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☐ Few hours (10 - 20 hours)☑ Long (40-60 hours)☑ Very Long (61-100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)$ Price / Quality $☑ Full price☑ Wait for Sale☐ Don't buy☐ Refund it if you canI "beat" the game around 40 hours or so but there are still a lot of things that I need/want to do. If you want to catch every Nexomon or are only hunting for certain Legendary and/or Cosmic (the game's version of a "shiny") Nexomon then you will probably double or triple my playing time.One thing that everyone should do is make sure you level up multiple Nexomon and don't try to rely on only one to get you through the game. _childDocuments_.review: While there are some minor inconvenience to the game, i think the good FAR outweight the bad. Everyone claims it as a Pokemon clone, which is fairness it somewhat is, but it does enough to seperate itself from it.Pros:- Monsters are actually really good looking. Everyone has a charm of their own and it makes you wish you had a lot more room in your party.- The game doesn't really force you on one single path. The open-ness of the paths are really refreshing. Pokemon (especially the later games) always have you on a single track and you never feel like you get the mons you like until the game tells you you can. Here you can kinda go anywhere.- The story is really endearing. The writing has some quirky jokes that sometimes break the fourth wall. I enjoy it.- Quests are fun. They don't feel like chores and you can kind of get to them whenever. - The catching mechanic is a series of QTE which is really fun (but can get tedious after repeated misses)- While you can't customize your character, there's a lot of variety to choose your avatar so it still feels rich and unique.- I love that the game offers you a starter of whichever elements you want and that you can actually find them in the wild with enough searching.Cons:- The typing chart is pretty convoluted. It's hard to know what works against what and what's resisted by what. There's no answer flat out after a few hours in so you kind of have to figure it out past the obvious Water -> Fire deal.- The battle menu is a bit clunky. Running away always send you a prompt, or catching something requires some extra steps then just pressing A but overall those are rather minor inconvenience.- There's a severe lack of healing which adds to the challenge, which is nice but always get you to backtrack.- The game doesn't use a system of PP but rather Stamina, which is almost always empty. It can be annoying if it's your last monster and it's too tired to battle.All in all, I absolutely recommend the game if you enjoy the monster capture genre. It's well worth it's full price and I would recommend it to all my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Love it, probably one of my favorite games this year so far though there are some critiques:ProsStory: Quite good, certainly more interesting than the usual Pokemon formula of catch 'em all and beat the elite four, saving the world in those games always feels like a side objective. Nexomon Extinction despite looking just as cutesy is a bit darker of tone and your character's goal from the word go is to try to make the world a better place. Writing: Love it, the writing meant to get me invested in the story if good, but where the writing shines is the comedy. Maybe it's simply just cause I don't expect it in this type of game, but Nexomon got quite a few chuckles and a couple of hearty stints of laughter from me during the story.Exploration: A problem I've had for a while with Pokemon is that Exploration is important mostly if you want new pokemon, you can find a bit of supplies and occasionally some special items and level up candies. In Nexomon scattered throughout the world are plentiful, but small bonuses: +3% XP here, 10% more cash after battles, 3% easier to catch X type of Nexomon, and most all of these type of buffs stack with each duplicate you collect. Meaning taking the time to explore can give pretty significant boosts that make the trouble worth it.Equipment: Nexomon utilizes a "core" system wherein you can equip your Nexomon with specific cores to boost certain stats. These can prove immensely useful, though I mainly used it just to ensure my team levelled uniformly so I can't say how great an effect they can prove in certain combos. Designs: I think the designs are pretty good, don't have a great eye for this type of thing, but nothing ever screamed out as "this looks wrong", save for once or twice out of  400+ designs so I find that pretty good, though can't say I saw more than 350 of them.Cons:Puzzles: Hope you don't like puzzles cause I can only recall about 5 max puzzles through the game. Most of the challenges thrown against you will be combat oriented.Combat: It can run into the issue Pokemon does where it turns into slug fests and buffs, debuffs, and otherwise are detrimental to try to utilize. However there are certain buffs at least that proof valuable enough that it can give you a reason to use something other than your strongest punch, but it's not often.Catch 'Em All: The equivalent for the Pokedex for this game is quite lacking, while it records all Nexomon you've encountered there is no info whatsoever about where you can find a specific Nexomon. To be fair it's a Steam game and you can just look up a guide online, but c'mon. Secondly, while many tamers are willing to trade for your Nexomon, never are there offers to trade you a Nexomon.My final word is that overall I loved it and definitely looking forward to the next thing they release. Good job y'all.

_childDocuments_.review: i've really enjoyed playing this game so far: the graphics are so cute and colourful (which was what motivated me to get the game in the first place), the different areas are unique and fun to explore and so far the story has been very exciting to play through. grinding is also really easy due to rematchable tamers and battles are pretty simplehowever, i feel that the battling portion of the game feels a little dull, because despite the unique tamer models and dialogue before and after tamer battles, they don't really feel much different from one another. although this is really extra and probably won't be implemented, adding a unique trainer model (the existing models would be good enough) on the VS screen or even adding the names of the tamers as text would make each tamer more unique rather than just battling lots of different people over and over (this isn't much of an issue however, just that it may help to make the game even better by reducing the dullness of battles at times). other than that, i love the moving animations of the nexomons in battle and the different skills too! great game overall :)

_childDocuments_.review: edit: i think i reviewed this game too early. the story is 10/10, genuinely. and levelling becomes much less of a problem with the cores you acquire/craft yourself. overall i really enjoyed this game and i highly recommendif you're looking for a pokemon clone, this honestly isn't a bad one. the creature designs are good, the story is interesting with some humour sprinkled in. the battle system is extremely simplistic which i feel isn't necessarily good or bad, but it does make the game more accessible and less frustrating. however, i do feel like there are needlessly frustrating elements to the game. one of them being how slow it is to level up your nexomon. within the 14 hours i've played so far, my nexomon are only really averaging around level 26 or 27 or so. another frustrating thing is that, when your party faints, you teleport to the last place you healed... with half of your nexomon's health remaining. why not just have the nexomon restored to full health? it's extra steps that don't make the game more challenging, but more time consuming over the course of a playthrough and mildly infuriating.overall, i think it's an enjoyable pokemon clone with an appealing art style, pretty decent designs and a fun story. i also think it's nice to have the choice of what to do next, as you can select quests depending on what you feel like doing, something that i feel pokemon doesn't really have. the main cons are only really things that are mildly frustrating and don't totally ruin your experience, as long as you don't mind some grinding and travelling back and forth between places.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing, if you enjoy pokemon you will fall in love with this game. I feel bad comparing it to pokemon because honestly this game gets so much right that it deserves to be the gold standard from here on out. I will break down the pros and cons below.PROS:1) The humor is a breath of fresh air and quite funny, the whole game is a giant parody but at the same time delivers a nice sense of seriousness when it needs to. The dialogue made me actually want to talk to everyone and do things to get little hidden dialogues (like trying to open doors to houses in one part of the game that's supposed to be serious will net you a nice little laugh) 2) The game doesn't restrict your freedom too much, you can explore quite a bit in advance without following the main story 3) Art - The art is so beautiful, I actually want to catch almost every monster in this game (even though that isn't the main goal of this game) just for how pretty every monster is and the environments are quite pleasing as well.4) It doesn't try hard to be pokemon, this game stands on it's own and I hope it will be a continuing series.5) $20??? For the enjoyment you get from this game it's money very well spent.CONS:1) No exp share (bit of an annoyance when you catch low level monsters and have to keep swapping them out later in the game to level them)2) No way to create a set of cores (e.g leveling core set or battle core sets)3) Shards become so hard to farm early because of the low respawn time, I wish they buffed this a little bit to craft cores/etc.4) This one is a bit of a con and a bit of a pro. The game doesn't hold your hand, it encourages you to explore and learn about the world and everything you can do in it on your own. It points you in the right direction but ultimately you decide how much you engross in the world. All in all an amazing game, if the devs read steam comments Thank you for the amazing game, and I hope you'll continue the series. Shining light of 2020.Update: For anyone playing this game, items are extremely important in this. If you're like me and barely used items in pokemon and thought you could do it here, you will have a rough time.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are anything like me, you played Pokémon games in your childhood but never tried any other monster collector games. But truth be told, even though Pokémon is so nostalgic to me due to me growing up with it, I must admit that I prefer Nexomon.How did this happen? How did an indie company beat Game Freak at their own game? Let’s take a look.(Or you could take a really short peek at the TLDR at the bottom)The story in this game is very captivating and interesting. Sure, it might start off very generic with you being an orphan that has finally come of age to become a nexomon tamer that can now go to the nearby forest to capture your very first nexomon.But it doesn’t take long before the story pulls you in as you try to climb the ranks of the guild you are in and uncover secrets and lore about the interesting world that you find yourself in. More on that later.Every major event had me even more excited to see what would happen next, and there were a few twists and turns I could not predict.The characters also help make the story as memorable and interesting as it is. They just feel so... Alive, I guess? They are actually real characters with personalities, which is something I am not used to from Pokémon games at all.There are some comedy relief characters as well though, and these are very hit or miss for me. You have a sidekick called Coco that accompanies you through most of your journey and he cracks a joke almost every time he opens his mouth. Some of it is genuinely funny, while most of it is just annoying in my opinion.All these characters reside in a very beautiful world. There are varying biomes from lush forests, big cities, dry deserts, floating islands, tropical beaches, haunted woods, and even volcanic landscapes for you to explore.Every zone has its own beautiful soundtrack. NPCs in towns will often move around, they will throw you out if you enter their house unannounced, they will give you sidequests, they might tell you about their problems if you talk to them, their dialogue might change as you progress through the story, when you move around the world you leave behind little clouds of dust. The world and the people in it just feel so alive, which is once again not something I am used to from Pokémon games where everything feels so robotic in comparison.Okay so the story is good, there are cool characters and an interesting world. What else is there?Oh yeah, the nexomon!There is a crazy amount of nexomon in this game for you to find, fight, capture, and train. 427 of them to be exact. I captured all of them for a steam achievement so please take my word for it when I say there are a lot of them.They are found in the wild, but only in patches of grass that are moving. So if you don’t want to encounter any wild nexomon, just mind your step when you walk through grass and you won’t have to deal with it.The only exception to this is when you enter caves, you can be attacked at any time there, but the game gives you an infinite repel you can toggle on and off whenever you want sometime in the middle of the game, so it’s hardly a problem.Some of the designs for these nexomon are very interesting and instantly made me fall in love with them and use them in my party, while others made me question what the devs were smoking. I’ll show you what I mean.These are my personal two favorite nexomon designs:And here are my personal two least favorite nexomon designs:So, these cool looking (and not so cool looking) nexomon fight each other of course. It wouldn’t be a creature collector game without some dogfighting.The combat is a lot faster paced than any Pokémon game I have ever played. There are no drawn-out animations that you have to watch every time you make an attack, no sitting around waiting for the HP to slowly tick down, no XP slowly ticking in, and no unnecessary text asking you if you want to switch your nexomon after every nexomon you defeat. These are a few examples of how the combat is sped up. Thank you for not wasting my time, game.There are only 9 different types of nexomon in the game. Fire, water, grass, normal, ghost, psychic, electric, rock and flying. Some of the strengths and weaknesses are a little weird, such as rock being weak to flying, or psychic being weak to grass, but it just takes a little bit of memorization  and you’ll be fine.Fighting NPCs in this game is also quite engaging. They will constantly swap their active nexomon to try to get the type-advantage and keep you on your toes. They aren’t just punching bags that pose no threat to you. They will also want a rematch after 20-30 minutes, but only if you walk up and talk to them. A real godsend here is that the type of the nexomon you are up against is always displayed next to their name, so don’t worry about having to remember what typing the 427 nexomon have.Another thing worth mentioning here is that the game scales to you and the level of your party.Don’t think for a second that this will let you skip trainer battles. The story related events and boss battles have a set level that will absolutely cave your face in if you are not prepared for them. But due to trainers scaling to whatever level you are and being willing to rematch you, you can level up quite fast.Nexomon: Extinction really pulls through as a great monster collector game.Even through all the years and games of Pokémon I’ve played, I never actually completed the Pokédex. The largest reason for this is that I always felt like the game actively sabotaged me.Want another starter than the one you picked? Too bad, you can only get one per save file.Want these two specific Pokémon? Too bad, they are only in the other version of the game.Want the evolved version of this one? Are you dumb or something? It only evolves when you trade it!Come to think of it, many things are like that in those games.Like HMs, learning an old move, changing nickname of a Pokémon, getting running shoes, etc.Nexomon just gives you a quality gaming experience with none of that garbage.Want to change your character’s name whenever you want? Sure, go ahead.Want to change how your character looks and even your gender whenever you want? Why shouldn’t you?Changing the names of your nexomons? Whenever you want from the menu.Running shoes? From the moment you start the game.HM abilities to make you progress through the story? Not something you have to teach your nexomon.Forced to have a flying type in your party so you can fly between places? Nope, teleporters.The game is good.If you have ever played a Pokémon game and enjoyed that, you will probably enjoy this as well.If you have never played a Pokémon game before but are interested, test the waters with this game.Just play the game. Play it right the frick now. Or else, I will make you spill your juice and you will end up looking like Consider this a warning and a threat.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't praise this game and its devs enough. The devs are active within and listening to the community, the world is immense and open, and the writing is better than Pokemon ever has been.It's no Pokemon- Pokemon clones rarely are- and, while I hope they get improved upon later, there are a lot of things that lack the usual Nintendo shine/attention to detail. The database is lacking information on evolution trees/levels, there's no map system, there's no genuine move relearning system, and the storage box is inferior for various reasons (thankfully it at least serves its purpose as storage). Don't expect the Nintendo level of refinement, basically- and if you're expecting a fully balanced game, this isn't it. It's an imperfect title- it's an indie. It's also immensely enjoyable and great in its own right.This captures the heart of (non competitive) Pokemon. I would possibly even compare this to Gold/Silver and their remakes in terms of the feeling of not only exploration and openness- but just scale overall. The artstyle is beautiful and there's lots of content. There are some (reasonable) gripes about level scaling, etc.. but to my experience so far, it's nowhere near as bad as comments make it out to be, and it builds upon an already enjoyable gameplay loop.

_childDocuments_.review: When compared to the likes of Pokemon, Nexomon has a better, more interesting main story, hard(er) 'mon battles, and a massive variety of 'mons, side-quests and other content that really keep one going. However; the bug when using healing items is annoying and something I wish would be fixed; the typing's are varied but not that new or unique enough to warrant the amount and are thus repetitive; some parts are a slog to get through since an ass load of story is piled on at certain parts without much room for a break in between, and is something I wish was mitigated with more trainer battles; certain battles are an endurance run and therefore very boring / not fun, and are made worse by not having better healing points or flat-out not healing you after key battles that lead into another two or three key battles; and finally, there are typos sprinkled throughout the game but don't detract from the game to much that they are a major problem. Overall, I really loved my time with Nexomon, and plan to play the end-game content since I have enjoyed this game very much, but there are bugs that can be annoying and kind of game-breaking to deal with, endurance battles with very minimal or no healing checkpoints, and run-of-the-mill 'mon typing's drop this games score to a 7/10, but is definitely a massive improvement over the original title, Nexomon. Highly recommended to pick this up while on-sale or at full-price for a great creature collector / Pokemon-like with tens of hours of entertainment.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I think the game is fairly good. At the end of the day it's what you'd expect from Fakemon game, though some monsters are more Pokemon ripoffs than Pokemon-inspired. The combat is simpler than Pokemon's, but this causes a lack of diversity in its rather large monster lineup. It's worth trying out if it's on sale at least. Definitely not a BAD game, and it is competently made, but some creative choices leave me kinda puzzled. Before I get into that though, there are some things it does that I'm quite a fan of. The capture mechanics are slightly more detailed than Pokemon's, and wild monsters are level-scaled to you.It feels like there's plenty of passion and effort put into it, but perhaps having around 400 creatures was not to its benefit. The monster lineups of games like this (such as Coromon or TemTem) are generally composed of fakemon of mixed quality, and there are definitely some pretty good ones in there, but I feel like there's plenty of filler. And that's fair enough, but some of them are unrepentant ripoffs of existing Pokemon.There's a ghost that is just a Duskull but as a sheet ghost with the same eye gimmick, a blue Krokorok, but the most blatant one I've seen was literally just a worse Vikavolt. There was a cool little electric stag beetle, and then it evolved into a ripoff Vikavolt and I never felt so disappointed by a Fakemon game evolution. At least change the typing! It's just like... if you're gonna put effort into the game then at least also put in more effort with the creature design and don't just blatantly rip stuff off!On another note, mechanics-wise the game is simpler than Pokemon, with fewer stats, no dual-typing and no passive abilities, and this makes the ~400 monsters less distinct from each other, as they mostly vary by movesets. While the simplified combat may be welcome, I think it does not mesh well with the quantity of creatures. The lack of IV and EV equivalents is very welcome though, at least if you catch one monster you won't end up with the possibility of just having it be straight up worse than another one.Storywise it seems to at least want to go in a different direction than Pokemon and many games derivative of it. It's slightly edgier and darker, but not in the "hey dude what if someone just shot the pokemon??" kinda crude video-game parody way. It doesn't take itself too seriously most of the time, but also personally I think it's REALLY overdoing it with the 4th wall break humour. Actually a lot of the comedy is either just 4th wall breaks or trying to point out that something that's normal in a video game should be kind of absurd or messed up. It gets old pretty fast imo.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I am far from the end of the game yet, I think I can deliver a good enough review by this point.Once again, just like its prequel, this game is a solid if a bit flawed Pokemon alternative and I can recommend it for anyone looking for that specific type of game.The story is alright, so far, there are some good twists, funny characters. Most of the monster designs are either actually good or work well enough, I have only seen a handful of real misses so far.The music is on the weaker side of "rather meh" but nothing that would be genuinely annoying.The UI is... well, there were very little improvements compared to the prequel. You can't change the key binding, which genuinely should be a sin. You can't open the main menu during fights, another sin. In a menu when the option of "Accept or Cancel" comes up, the button that usually means "cancel" (L) in-game doesn't actually pick Cancel in this case, instead you have to move the cursor on the Cancel option and hit K, the "accept" button. Woefully terrible design. You can't scroll up or down continuously by holding the arrow keys, which is again a sin. There are other things, such as not having enough time to read (or even notice properly) what move the enemy is doing. There is no encyclopedia/codex/tutorial menu that would explain what certain status effects like "frail" or "rooted" do.Each such problem on its own wouldn't be a problem, but they add up quickly. A good UI is the one you do not notice at all, as the saying goes, and you will most CERTAINLY notice this UI, unfortunately.Still, overall, I'm having fun with the game. If you can live with a less-than-stellar UI design and meh music, I recommend this game to you. Happy hunting!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what's wrong with me. By all measures, Nexomon Extinction is probably one of the best creature collector games I've ever played. In both the first game and this one, the writing is so clever (especially the humor); the plots, while threadbare, are utilized to the fullest extent, the creature designs are cool, and the worldbuilding is adequate. Nexomon Extinction, however, is even more clever with its dialogue and humor than the first; the fact that the game takes place in the far future from the original is emphasized by creature designs that look evolved (in a Darwinian sense) from the first; and there are a bunch of additions that make the game both more complex and more fun.But.For whatever reason, I can't get into the Nexomon games. If I hadn't accidentally bought Extinction before the original, and only ever played the first, I probably never would've played this one... which, again, is a huge improvement from the likable and enjoyable first one. I think the biggest problem for me is that the visual aesthetics for the games are really unappealing. The 3-D cartoony world with chibi character sprites are a turn off for me, but if that were all, I doubt it'd be such a dealbreaker. But I'm hoping that by writing this positive review, I can get over myself and just enjoy this game for what it is. Because, again, it's one of the best I've played in its genre. I can't recommend it enough. But I'm so apathetic about it, and I don't want to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a monster catcher game with turn-based battles. It's best described as a pokemon clone which isn't a bad thing. Everyone who played pokemon before will feel right at home here. The tutorial is very short. Most of the game is self-explanatory. You can have up to 6 monsters with you. There are over 300 Nexomon in total.  There are 8 classes like fire, water, rock, ghost, etc. As you level up your monsters, they learn new attacks and can evolve. The story is more mature and funny than in any Pokemon game I played before. Most joked are based on the fourth wall and thus mature enough to be funny for adults. The story is still not a masterpiece but it doesn't need to be in this kind of game. Let's talk about different approaches to the genre. There are different ways to catch Nexomons. You need a Nexotrap to catch them. There are normal traps and one for each class, as well as special ones like Gold (99% chance to catch), etc. If you want to catch one, you select a trap and look at the stats. They show you how likable it is to really catch them. A hurt Nexomon is easier to catch, etc. You can also feed them to get a higher percentage. If you throw your trap, a quick-time event will appear. There's a timer to spice it up a bit. You can't see Nexomons moving around in the overworld but you can still see WHERE they are. The grass will move when a nexomon is there so you know to either avoid it or get into a fight. Who doesn't know the annoying feeling of constantly getting attacked when you just want to get somewhere? Easy to avoid in Nexomon. There's a mechanic called "cores". You can find cores or craft them in a labor. Equip Monsters with cores to make them stronger, give them EXP bonuses or a percentage of the total EXP after every fight, without them having to be in one. A good way to level up your monsters IMO. There are also no arenas instead there are bossed with special Nexomons you need to defeat for story purposes. Talking about the main quest, there are also many side quests around the world and other things to do. The main difference may be that the Monsters level scales with your level. There are pros and cons to this. Mainly there is less of a grind because of that but the feeling of accomplishment while getting stronger and stronger is mostly gone. TBH I am not a fan of level scaling but I still enjoy it after giving the game a chance. The game is over 20 hours long just doing main quests. With side-quests and extras, it's over 30 hours long (copied from howlongtobeat). In my playtime of a bit over 8 hours, I am not even halfway through the game (you'll know when playing, can't say more without spoiling anything). The sound and graphics are good enough, nothing special.One thing I don't like is the controls with the keyboard and mouse. It would be easy enough to make this game playable with just a mouse but it's not. You don't even need the mouse at all. I rather played with a controller which is more comfortable IMO.  All in all, Nexomon: Extinction is everything you want from a pokemon-like game. It's also more enjoyable than Temtem IMO. It's only 15€/USD on a sale and even at full price just 20€/USD. That's not really expensive for this amount of content. It feels high quality, I did not encounter any bugs at all. Mechanic-wise it does some things differently in a good way and the story is more mature and funny. Definitely recommended for everyone who is into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like people who have never played Pokemon trying to copy Pokemon. - All the nexomons have almost identical base stats on their final evolution- The move diversity is really bad. Many of the moves are completely useless except the damaging ones. - Expect to have only 4 moves per mon for the majority of your playthrough and even then you'll only ever use 2 -  Even mega or ultra rare nexomon will have pretty much the same potential as a common first route nexomon. - There are no abilities that would differentiate nexomons from each other- Nexomon can only be one type so even that small variation is gone- Many of the designs are actually pretty good but some are also pretty basic. There are about 5 evolutionary lines that are just cat + element, two are fire type. - There are 301 Nexomon but because of all of the above I struggle to see why you'd want to bother catching all of themIt's almost feels like a parody of how non-Pokemon fans see Pokemon, you just click the supereffective move and win. The core gameplay is extremely basic compared to the other Mon games I've played like Coromon and Temtem. The dialog heightens the feeling of parody as a lot of it is self-referential and fourth wall breaking making fun of the tropes of the genre or directly referencing the player. It's kind of hard to get immersed in a story that treats itself like a joke.

_childDocuments_.review: *I apologize if I repeat myself or ramble.the pros-before you complete the first story mission you can explore most of the map, but beware the waystones that are red mean you can't warp to the places you explore until you get access to them after the second or third sotry mission.- the system for catching nexomon is interesting, you have cxontrol over the percentage chance to catch them by feeding, inflicting damage or statud, finding items called elemental whistles which are a passive buff that increase your odds by 3% that stack. The downside to this is that it takes longer to catch nexomon than it does to catch pokemon, and a nexotrap(pokeball) cost about three times as much as food, meaning you want to make sure you have as much and varied types of food on you at all times.- Variety: there's a large variety of nexomon that are cool and and interestingthe cons- combat is fun, but pretty simple and any nexomon that has the move heal can cheese anything in the game and is basically unkillable, however I like the cores which are items that improve stats or give more exp, money or act as exp shares, and the way you get cores primarily is by making them with elemental shards- music kinda sucks, but that's just personal tasteConclusionThe game really encourages exploring and catching as many nexomon as possible, which is nice because you'll want to acquire friendship points by releasing your nexomon(sacrificing them to the magical talking tree ;) ) .It's a slower game, that can be as hard or easy as want depending on how you play, but if you like exploring catching stuff and can get over the combat system(the combat system isn't that bad, but is poorly balanced e.g. heal always goes first and heals 100hp and cost 25 stamina; natrure spirit fully heals you, always goes last and costs 70 stamina. One thing with the story though is that when progressing the level of enemies does increase throughtout but doesn't scale with your average level so you can still overlevel. You will notice this with trainer battles even as the same ones you fight will over time use different or evolved versions instead.Art: Love it. I really enjoyed the world design, character and nexomon design and at key story points they have a still image which I feel gives the story more impact at those times.UI: Could be better. Some UI glitches in menus that's annoying and could be more user friendly (Such as equipping cores to Nexomon - Would be nice to make sets to equip instead of doing each of the 4 slots manually)Combat: This is where it's similar to the 1st game where the rarity is what affects the Nexomon's stats. A "Common" is going to be infinitely worse compared to rarer ones so the best strat is capturing the rare ones earlier to use in combat. This is what I don't like since there's tons of Nexomon that people may like and want to use but if they're a lower rarity you're really hindering yourself. I'm going to compare this part to Coromon since each one can have a range of rarity so you can farm to get the rarer ones of a specific Coromon and use that. Another thing with combat is the stamina seems pretty tight (Maybe if you equip stamina cores) but you really drain it fast and would need to replenish it potentially after 1-2 trainer battles.Collecting (Items): There are some items to collect that increases some stats (Some for exp gain, coin gain or capture chance for a specific type as "whistles"). The whistle part I find can be misleading as the capture chance shows when attempting to catch a Nexomon (There is a breakdown where whistles falls under "Other"). The "Other" looks to be out of 100% however there are limited whistles in the game so you're really going to just have that as 9% or 12%. Also when exploring you (This is also more in focus at late game or post story completion) that you need to open some vaults. These vaults have some great items and some of them give key items that greatly helps some things...which is a shame because you could have used these items much earlier in the game which would be more appropriate if it was something to upgrade.Collecting (Nexomon): This is what drove me to write this review. There are 427 Nexomon to find and the rarity is pretty wide (Common/Uncommon/Rare/Ultra Rare/Mega Rare/Legendary). The chance of encountering some Nexomon is absurdly low and in very specific areas (Even a patch of bushes on a map vs the other one) that it just makes this game drag out and not fun - Taking 2+ hours to encounter a Nexomon for the chance of capturing it just takes the fun out of it. Also there doesn't appear to be any items that increases encounter rate which draws this out more (After completing the main story and DLC you do get an item that can boost the chance of a specific one to appear though you must have encountered it before which appears in the database). Because some Nexomon appear in very specific areas and there isn't anything ingame that references spawns you're just doing trial and error (Would be nice if the game had some information of where they may be local to).Overall this game is adequate. I would say Coromon is better. Once again I wish Steam had a better range of review ratings to leave which I would at least put it in the middle.

_childDocuments_.review: 2021-02-02Im normally not a kind of person that writes that much reviews but in that case I really really have to.First of all, I finished the whole game with all its achievements in around 60 hours. So I hopefully have enough overview/experience to write a useful review now. Very important to know -> I will compare that game with the biggest player in that kind of genre, "Pokemon" of course:Cons / against 1 & 2 you can just google:(1) World sometimes confusing: The ways you can go and the possibilities you have from the beginning are kinda overwelming. You sometimes feel lost in the world, dont know were you are. You have a storyline you can easily follow, but if you decide to explore around, the "openworld-like" until certains spots can confuse a lot.In case a developer will read this -> a map would be pretty useful :)(2) Nexomon locations: When you try to hunt all the available Nexomon you need a guide, otherwise you could only "guess" where they are located exactly. The ingame nexo-wiki with informations about the location would help here.(3) Nexomon of same Kind have the same stats at max level: Compared to Pokemon, Im missing EV (effort values), so additional "hidden" points you could get from slaying specific enemys. That would give the a little more complexity and more lategame hardcore gamer content. Same with IV (individual values)(4) No breeding: You dont need breeding that much when you havent EV and IV, but it would fun anyways. It would also be another possibility to get the cosmic nexomon without over and over search in gras.(5) No PvP: Maybe it changes at some point. I dont know how much Nexomon will develop in the future but until now, there is no PvP content available.Pro:(1) Humor: It is not only fun to play, its simply funny overall. Normally Im the kind of person the constandly skips dialogs, but here I didnt. The dialogs were funny and interesting to read.(2) Story: It is not "the best story Ive ever seen!". But it is a decent story. One of the worst things you have in Pokemon is a mostly lame story that is just focused on the medals you have to earn. In Nexomon there is a bunch of interesting, sometimes weird (in a good way^^) and funny dialogs that gets you closer into the story.(3) Easy to understand: Try to imagine, you would start pokemon from scratch now and know nothing about it. The newest games with all the new pokemons and doubled elements and so on - the complexity in the elementsystem is to overloaded in my opinion. Nexomon is keeping it more simple, like it was in the first pokemon generations.(4) Catch them all: One of the most annoying things was, for a casual player it was impossible to catch all pokemon listed in you pokedex. I played these games a lot but that annoying me over and over again. I like to collect, so in Nexomon i finally could collect all monsters in a single game!(5) Implemented RANDOMIZER: That is the most amazing feature they have implement with a patch. The possibility to randomize your game and change the game experience completly! That feature gives the game a very high replayability. Also -> you can modify the game you would like (without level cap, higher monster levels, more exp, more money) as you like to. Conclusion: A pretty good game and in my opinion even a much better pokemon. Im missing a few things mentioned in the cons, but overall it is much more fun than I thought in a first look. Sure, the animations and the style are "different" for people like me that just played the pokemon francise, but I gave it a chance and it catched me completly.Thumbs up from me!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a monster collecting RPG with a battle system that can be simple and/or complex if you need it. When compared to others in the genre, this one has come a long way when you learn of the past titles it's born from. Micromon was more simple compared to it's successors, but it had created the basis for what is to come for gameplay mechanics and story. The first Nexomon game polished mechanics further, and the style of the games become noticeable with the lively animations of the Nexomon and jokes peppered throughout the story. Nexomon Extinction then went further to build off what the others started, refining the battle system and continuing the story hundreds of years after the first Nexomon game concludes.One more thing I like about this game, is that it has a custom mode for when you complete the main story. Starting a new save allows you to create a game with randomized encounters/items/skills, nuzlocke rules, and more. Adding to the replay-ability of the game.Try it out if you like monster collecting RPGs, enjoy an assortment of puns, and/or like story/world-building (might have to look into the previously mentioned games).

_childDocuments_.review: I went in expecting a Pokemon knock-off. I looked at the reviews that praised the writing, design, and story. I bought the game on sale for half off. I regret the purchase.Nexomon Extinction would have been a decent game in a vacuum, but with Pokemon to compare it to it just falls short on almost every measure. The creature designs are passable, the writing self-derogatory, the combat system one gimmick (stamina instead of move points) from a copy of older Pokemon games, the world is constrained to a grid which even Pokemon has moved away from... I expected a Pokemon knock-off, and the game disappointed even that.

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR: This game is fantastic, i would highly recommend, funny and engaging story, and excellent game play that has challenging aspects.  Im not a great writer at all, the fact that ive taken the time to even do this should be a testiment to how good this game has been while the world has gone to ♥♥♥♥. This game is for the most part excellent, when comparing to other main stream "pocket monster" collection games, there are some definite differences, for one this game can actually challenge you.  Unlike the more popular monster games this will require actual work to win. The Gameplay - challenging and fun, you will need to swap in and out if you want your monsters to live, you will need to bit of thought into the moves you make and dont go challenging everyone you seen, you will come back with your tail in-between your legs. Classic turn based battle system, interesting and diverse monsters to find with great community and fan made info for getting monster locations if you like.The Story -  Is great, there actually is a plot that as you may expect, you save the world, or not its up to you :), just go adventureing everywhere you can, thats what i did, very fun. This game on more than one occasion has caused me to convulse with laughter, there is a large comedy element that usually plays as a straight man to the events in the game, making fun of the world and occasionally breaking the forth wall, this keeps the game very light and very easy to enjoy, this game out of all the "pocket monster" games i have played has been the most engaging. There are regular updates to the game with more features on the way, I am personally hoping for PVP and trading in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: Addictive, Challenging and most important of all Fun! Really surprised about this one, was recommended by word of mouth and I am so glad I gave it a shot. Monster design was great, only thing I could wish for would be more types. Some of the monsters definitely did not look like their typing, but that's a minor complaint. Is it like Pokemon? Only in parts of battle system and even less in the monster catching system. Story is way different, this one actually has a decent one. Overall I enjoyed Nexomon and had a lot of fun, It was definitely worth the asking price and I will be looking forward to the Sequel. I would definitely recommend it to Pokemon fans or really anyone who likes monster collection games, this ones a real diamond in the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: Great for casual play. Story is super cute, mechanics are refreshing and I see a lot of potential for complexity in the future. I enjoy the shard and mining aspect of this game, it gives purpose and more meaning to exploration. I also like the idea of basically moving stat points on whatever 'mon you want to. I also enjoy the feeding mechanic, I think they can expand on that in the future as well. The story is funny and entertaining with lots of anime-esque characters, but I think that brings a charm. Cons: The battles itself don't have a lot of depth but that's okay. This is the second game released in the series and it does not need to be that polished. The moves are very repetitive and offer little to no variety. The status are poorly explained, if at all. Due to the lack of abilities and held items, every mon seems like a reskinned version of each other. Lastly, some of the 'mons are a little over done and the design is kinda ugly.That being said, I see huge potential in the future. This game is still being improved and worked upon. I love how much effort and care they put into this game. If you like pokemon (casually), I highly suggest this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Had more fun with this (and Nexomon 1) than any game of the famous, established monster taming rpg franchise that I need not name here. The story and setting is great, it has genuinely hysterical fourth-wall breaking comedy at times. This game knows what it is, it knows what the player is here for and it delivers. The only thing it sorely could have used was a distinction between types of attack between of the special/magical variety and the physical one, which have allowed for more complex, layered team bulding and strategy in battles, but what is here is fantastic already.That being said, I'll never understand the decision to make Mons only learn mostly moves of their own type and Normal, unlike in Nexomon 1 where they could learn moves outside their own typing for coverage (or dual typings for mons!), and the "having to pay someone with currency to change and re-learn moves" thing is a genuine hassle compared to having them all available to be equipped and unequipped at the player's convenience like it was in Nexomon 1. I don't understand the vision behind said downgrades.For these reasons I say this is a solid 9/10 monster taming rpg for anyone who feels let down by the brain-dead, stale gameplay of a certain mainstream monster taming franchise that shall go without being named here. It's since been unseated by Cassette Beasts as my favorite monster taming rpg (the "Creature Collector" tag for this genre on steam is stupid imo), but it's still up there in second place with Monster Sanctuary, in my book.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game that has worked out many of its flaws. I'd give it a solid 6.5/10. The gameplay is a lot of fun, and the story is decent. The constant fourth wall breaks really brought the story down from what would have been an 8/10. I know many games have issues with silent protagonists, but this was one of the worst examples I've seen. However, if you're looking for a creature collector, then this game is for you. They patched in healing stones to fix the biggest issue that the negative reviewer was complaining about, and they have toned down the autoscaling. Originally, the wild Nexomon would scale to equal the level of your strongest Nexomon, however, the scaling is now gated behind different checkpoints in game. Those two adjustments address the issues that were (correctly) called out in the negative review that is on the front page. I recommend this game at $20. If you can get it on sale, even better. You're going to get 50-60 hours of play time out of it and it is a fun game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so this game is clearly trying to be a pokemon-like game and appeal to people who like pokemon and alike, hence, I'll use pokemon as a "standard" and compare to what this game did better or worse in comparison.Combat feels like a major step up from pokemon games. It's no longer x2 weakness / higher speed / 1HKO game. Combat is more engaging and last longer than just using that 1 move and KO the opponent directly. Weakness type only do a little bonus so type disadvantage is a more manageable. The stamina system also prevents you from spamming that 1 pet every fight.This is the part where the games tries too hard to be pokemon and becomes its flaw. As mentioned, combat last longer, that means your pet gets damaged every fight. And like a pokemon-like game, you run to a healing center but it becomes a terrible system combined with the combat system. I have to make trips to healing centers too frequently and it becomes a chore. It's also a pain to level up a low level pet because of this system in place and there's no exp share. It's good. The designs of Nexomons in this game are diverse and well-made. It does feel like some of the designs were just squeezed out from the artists to meet the quota but I could say the same for pokemon. The environment designs are also well-made. It has aesthetics of an older game like Maplestory. It's colorful and diverse.Overall, this game is pretty good. I'd score it around 8/10. None of the issues I've had with this game is too big of an issue.

_childDocuments_.review: It has a simplistic combat system like Gen 1 of Pokemon, the looks and feel of Gen 5 as well as a story that is as good as Gen 5, and the creature design is on par with some of the best Pokemon out there, combine this with its own unique spin on the genre, an open world, many actually enjoyable side quests to do, and cool areas that you wouldn't find in many other monster taming games and you get one of the best in the genre, rivaling some of the best Pokemon games and destroying newer Pokemon games like Sword and Shield. This review is full of comparisons to Pokemon, but thats because thats the best comparison out there, and most people playing this have played Pokemon, but even when not compared to Pokemon, this game is still great, def worth the asking price. This is also one of the only games I have seen that implements features in game that allow for nuzlockes, randomizers, NG+ and more, you get a lot more playtime than just the main story.
