_childDocuments_.review: I REALLY wanted to like this game and I put up with it till the end and finish the game. With that said there is too many cons/bad things in the game over the pros/good things.The Cons:- Having to heal after every 2 or 3 battles. Either you lose too much HP by trying to conserve your Stamina or you run out of Stamina by trying to defeat the enemies without taking too much DMG. Until you get to level 30-40 you will constantly have to use potion/ether or run all the way back to a heal point.- IF you are not 10+ levels above enemies they will 3 shot your Nexomon.- Feeding a Nexomon before catching means you lose a turn and would have to take DMG. Minor issue for me- Catching Nexomon early on is useless because there is no EXP share and its better to level up just 2 Nexomon. Since enemies level up base on your progress on the story, It's better to just catch higher level monster than grinding for hours trying to level up your low level Nexomon.- All you see from the start is all you get through out the game; Examples are skill set, Cores that upgrade your ATK, Def, etc- The game feels like an Early Access gamePros:- There is no Pokemon game or monster catching game like this out there on PC- Really basic and easy (For me it was)RATING 2/10I wouldn't recommend buying this game at full price. Wait for it on sale 50% or more. For me I would say the game is worth around $5-$10

_childDocuments_.review: Monster catching RPGs are a personal fave since these are usually lighthearted games that are easy to get into, and are usually a lot of fun. Nexomon Extinction caught my eye a few weeks ago, and I have definitely enjoyed this game quite a bit! Things you may like about the game are:- It's a very colorful 2d game with nice artwork and some great monster designs here and there.- It has a really good soundtrack. Seriously, some of these tracks are really good!- It takes inspiration from the earlier pokemon games so it's a more simplistic take when it comes to types and movesets, which is not really a bad thing since you'll get used to it quickly and no nexomon feels useless thanks to this.- Lots of customization options and some great QoL options that pokemon fans keep asking for pokemon games but we never get. Things such as multiple save slots (Thank goodness!), and being able to rematch trainers in the wild who keep improving their teams (Seriously, why this isn't a thing in the pokemon games?) among many others.- Features an epic story that, despite taking itself quite seriously at times, doesn't have any troubles with poking lots fun at itself and the genre quite often! (Coco and Atlas got quite a few laughs out of me, that's for sure!)- The game encourages you to consider type coverage when building your teams and training (grinding obviously!). Otherwise the game can and will get somewhat difficult if you don't!Things fans of these games may not like are:- At the moment, the game features no multiplayer content.- The game could use some extra things to do besides battling or fetching stuff to NPCs to add some variety. (Salem's little challenge early in the game was a fun little distraction, why isn't there any more of that for example?)After beating the main story, I can say with confidence I really liked this game a lot. If the more recent Pokemon games have let you down, this is a really nice alternative to consider!

_childDocuments_.review: I often leave negative reviews on games that I’m mostly meh about; this is for people searching the negative reviews who want info. When I first played I found some issues, researched through the forums, and then posted my review. As you can see a dev responded claiming what I said was wrong. Others had mentioned having trouble finding monsters; I’ve been unable to confirm.My opinion to anyone considering this is to check the forums. _childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent take on the traditional pocket monster formula. There is a lot of passion and great art here. I loved the story, it was well paced, well executed and had some great plot twists. And one really big plot twist that was a real mind bender for a moment. Fantastic use of deception. Also wow there are a lot of nexomon to catch, like seriously a tonne. I caught absolutely everything not nailed down and I ended my run catching HALF the roster! HALF! That's like 200 and something!? I also I really enjoyed the element typing here, in other games its usually a blender of random elements with weird super effective/ ineffective match ups. Here it was really intuitive and I learned most of the match-ups just through play.I only have a few issues. The food system is not good. It is easy to get 10 of every food and all it boils down to is navigating the feed popup until you find the food the nexomon you want to catch likes. Catch rates without setup suck for the most part so it often feels mandatory. And while powerful, many status effect moves have such low power and such low odds of being inflicted that strategy ends up being 'use big move till it dies'. There are a few exceptions of course. I used a Mara with max hp cores and the rooted buff combined with the dodge buff to become effectively invincible (15% dodge chance, heal 30 points every turn).Ultimately I enjoyed my time here and am looking forward to the sequel. It felt like a real adventure and I loved that, so thanks again nexomon team! One of the few games I watched the credits for.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. This is what I wish Pokemon currently was, and what I feel Pokemon used to be (at least, how Pokemon used to make me feel). I don't like typing out 5000 word reviews, so I'll try to keep this succint:Combat - Very fun. I think the stamina system is a 100% upgrade to the PP system (I am inevitably going to compare this to the most prolific series of the genre, sorry). There are some interesting abilities that allow for tactical choices in the combat, and not being able to sweep the entire enemy team with one of my Nexomon (assuming they are within ~10 levels of me) makes the play feel more engaging. I wish there were some more unique animations for abilities, but that's a very minor gripe. Typing is also a bit imbalanced, with some types feeling slightly stronger than others and normal type being pretty objectively the worst.Catching - This is just straight up better in every way than catching Pokemon in the core games. The ability to feed the wild Nexomon different food to increase your catch chance is neat, and the fact I can acquire a LOT of the 100% chance Nexotraps is great as a collector. I also personally enjoy the little typing minigame you do during the catch sequence, but I could see that being a downside for some people.Story - Honestly, very well put together. During my first 20 - 30 minutes of the game I felt the writing was going to be pretty weak, as it was primarily meta jokes and other sorts of humorous quips (I do enjoy the jokes, to be clear, I just assumed because of the early writing the actual story wouldn't be particularly interesting), but I was wrong. The story has plenty of awesome twists, the characters are all likable or interesting, there are some truly cool moments later on. Kudos to the writers!Travel - I like the Metroid inspired upgrades you get throughout the game (minor spoiler, sorry). It's fun to go back to places you've been before and explore new parts of them that were inaccessible before. I also like that you can tell exactly what patches of grass will trigger an encounter, so if you're just trying to get somewhere you can avoid all of the wild Nexomon. I was much less frustrated playing this game than I have been historically playing Pokemon.Items - One of my favorite parts about the game. I like that there are passive items that increase different stats or give much needed QOL features for this genre. One example is there is a stackable item that increases how much XP your Nexomon gain from battle; another is a stackable item that increases your chance of finding a shiny (called Cosmic Nexomon in this game). Story battles have also been difficult enough that I find myself using potions, revives, and elixirs frequently, causing money to have value even towards the end of the game.This review ended up being pretty wordy anyway, sorry about that!Overall personal score: 9.8/10 losing a small amount of score only for some balancing issues with typing.

_childDocuments_.review: This is what Pokemon in 2020 should be. With an actual good story. -------------------Pros: --Ever feel like it was weird that no one in Pokemon was acknowledging your badassery? This one strokes your hero boner harder than any game. You will constantly be praised for saving things, advancing your rank, and a host of other things as you progress through the game, a lot of times by NPC's you have already talked to who have updated dialogue every time you advance. --Lots of awesome Nexomon to choose from with designs that honestly are better than Pokemon in a lot of cases. I find myself wanting to swap mons out way more in this since I run into so many cool ones. --Gearing up Nexomon is fun--TONS of boss fights--The catching system is much more involved. --Collecting in general. There are so many ways to advance your ability to catch, buy, get money, and other things. --Scaling wilderness areas removes the need to level up super low level nexomon if you want to switch. You can just go back later and catch a higher level one. --Scaling trainers makes for a fun challenge later. Refighting any trainer after a short cooldown,--Challenge in general. It's so much better than Pokemon on that front. Instead of fighting 30 people in a row with 1 pidgey each, you fight 2 with 5 fully evolved beasts each. 100% improvement. Items are actually useful, and you will be restocking constantly to keep your mons healthy. They are also really cheap, so can use them freely and wild encounters drop gold. --Grinding is stupidly easy with EXP items. 2-4 kills a level. --The story is actually neat. Much more involved and epic than any of the recent Pokemon games. --Freedom. You can go pretty much anywhere early on, with tons of side areas to explore. More unlocks as you get abilities. --HM's don't need an HM slave. They are just part of your character. --Tons of side stuff throughout the game. Feels like Zelda almost with how often you get distracted with another side quest or path. --It's cheap--Coco. Coco is hilarious and best companion. -------------------Neutral: --No EXP share. Some like it. You don't really need it though with scaling mons.--No PVP. Honestly I never enjoyed rock-paper-scizzors pokemon PVP, but lots do. --Only one ATK stat, no special ATK. I don't really miss it, but the complexity is nice in Pokemon--No EV/IV/Natures. Every Loki is the same as every other Loki. Personally I've always hated the grind that was EV/IV/Natures, so I'm good with it. I know a lot of people love them though. -------------------Cons: --No online trading--Nexomon only have a single type (though some of them get a lot of abilities from another type, so your normal might get tons of rock abilities) --Not a ton of side game things like Safari Zone or game corner in Pokemon--Less systems in general than Pokemon. Nexomon can wear 4 pieces of gear, but the gear is basic stat stuff. No evolution stones. No special evolution. Just level based. --No TM system --No genders and breeding, but without IV/EV its kinda pointless anyway. -------------------All in all, it's a great game. Character designs are top notch. The art is beautiful. I really hope it does well so we can get more. Expanding on this formula will only do it well. If you are tired of easier and easier Pokemon every generation, this is the answer. You can't beat it for 20 bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: I have played the full campaign. I guess steam hasn't updated with the cloud yet because I have over 27 in-game hrs. LolI am only talking about the main campaign. Not the expansion or the post game:I've been making my way through the majority of so-called "Pokemon clones". I hate using this term because it often muddles genuine efforts like this game as a cheap knockoff when it's really not. Something sharing similar elements to another genre doesn't inherently make it cheap. The execution is what makes the game good.Compared to Nexomon 1, Nexomon: Extinction is a great two steps forward but it's flaws also make it take one step back. Positives:-The game is definitely a step up in terms of quality. The overall feel of the game is less "cheap" compared to the first. I know this might not be fair as Nexomon 1 (N1) was made for mobile users, but the devs really worked hard to make Extinction feel like it wasn't. The environments are more expansive and memorable, the characters have more personality with a nice amount of development, NPCs are abundant and well worth talking to, Nexomon have more variety with their designs than the first game, capture mechanics have been expanded upon greatly, and the music is a genuine improvement from the blander soundtrack of the first game.-The battle system is more refined with Nexomon no longer dying in just a hit or less after spamming your strongest move. Buffs/Debuffs got a nerf. No longer do you have the confusion spam that was present in the first game (thank goodness) meaning you can't just rely on cheese strats. Nexomon have less variety with their movepoolss in this game, but more than make up for it with a better variety of Nexomon to use. As most Nexomon can evolve in this game, you're no longer feeling like that Common Nexomon you caught feels pointless to raise. It's not a strong as a rare, but that's the point anyways. You can still use it and that's what matters.-The story. I won't spoil much but the story as a sequel is a great continuation to N1's light-hearted tone while also shifting to darker storyline. It really is a wild ride from start to finish and I do think it's best to go in blind to get the full experience of all the neat twists and turns.-Dungeons are much more expansive with a decent amount of puzzles to boot. I was pleasantly surprised by the amount of dungeons to explore, even if some were dead ends.  N1's dungeons left a lot more to be desired because of how linear they were (which was found in the post game). Here, I'm glad the devs took the feedback from that to make the world feel more explorative. You can explore the begining of the game to your hearts content and visit most places within the world without an issue rather early on. Levels scale so there's no fear of missing out on something or being in an area you don't want to be in yet. The game will give you plenty of hints if you're going in the right direction.-Cores add a nice layer of depth to Nexomon by giving passive buffs. You can have only 4 cores at a time, but the benefits are crucial to surviving in battles. I found myself picking up shards because I wanted to either make them into Cores to buff my Nexomon or trade them off during side-quests. The only downsides is that Cores are limited in what you can use them for. You have Attack, Defense, Stamina, HP, Immunity to status ailments, EXP, Money, and EXP share. That's it. I wish that there was more of a variety of options (like for speed) because by late game, you aren't going to need the EXP share or Money cores when you're drowning in collectibles aka. Shards to sell/trade for money.-The music. I'll be frank, N1's soundtrack was rather bland. So while this soundtrack is certainly not winning any awards any time soon, it is a major step up from N1. There's a better variety of music that doesn't just focus on "happy track, intense track". There are a variety of background tracks and battle tracks that set the mood just right.Negatives:-Ui is a step up from N1, but lacks the streamlining found from those menus. I understand N1 was a mobile game first and foremost, but the streamlining with the game worked well. Everything was clear and easy to access. Not so much in this game. While the general UI no longer looks cheap, how it functions is a different story. You can't move your Nexomon in your party freely. You have to "Set as Main" unless you're messing with the PC. I haven't encountered any other monster-taming game that's done something like this (for modern games) and it's such a bizarre decision because N1 allows you to freely move your party. I've tried messing with the controls on my Steam Deck to see if I missed something, but I couldn't find anything. (I'll edit this review if it's fixed and I'm just missing something. Lol). However, my complaints with the UI and visual consistency don't just end with that example. There are other tiny things that really start to pile up. Specific buttons are now tied to your actions in battle, but they never feel "right" to use. I know describing controls is hard to explain, but compared to N1's tight controls, it never felt comfortable using buttons compared to a simple touch ironically. In cutscenes, your character will be shown as the default MC despite changing your skin tone/appearance. I understand this working in N1 as you couldn't change your character but here it comes off as a little jarring for story-related scenes. Now, I'm definitely not saying for the devs to redraw every design they made for your MC customizations in the cutscenes, but when other cutscene CGs don't feature your character and still work, I have to wonder why those few CGs are so visually inconsistent.-The difficulty spikes. Other reviews have mentioned this but while N1 was grinder than this game, you could catch up in levels easily due to the EXP all for every party member. You even get the ability to double the EXP you earned in that game. The issue is that Nexomon Extinction's level curve is fixed. Meaning, whatever level you're at, other Nexomon will be around the same level. This works very well in the early/mid game when exploring but not so much in the later game in which simple random encounters will send you to the Healing Center real quick. Obviously, this is not as impossible as people make it out to be, but I absolutely agree with the overall criticisms of it originally being poorly implemented for the later half of the game. Thankfully, by that point you'll have more than enough resources to manage, but when you get to that first difficulty spike it is ROUGH. The inclusion of difficulty modes was added to alleviate this, but this is a fundamental problem with how the game is designed in itself. This is why I hope for the next game, that the devs take what they learned and make things more balanced from the start.-Catching Nexomon is a double-edged sword. Nexomon have more depth in how you capture them. But with a horrible catch, a mini game. Every time you want to capture ANYTHING in this game you have to play a boring catching mini game. Press the right buttons and capture the mon. It should be simple, but I found to be rather clunky in execution. Not only does it make capturing mons more tedious, it feels intrusive to other mechanics. Even if it does increase your chance of capture, it doesn't really add to the immersion of getting a Nexomon. I think the food mechanic already did a good job, but having the mini game just felt pointless. I wish there was an option to just skip it.-You need to capture 70 Nexomon AND RELEASE THEM in an obscure sidequest to get the Portable PC and Teleporter. Why wasn't this just a key item late game? It's so tedious to get.Overall while I do recommend this Nexomon Extinction as it IS a better game than N1 in every way, there are stipulations that come with that recommendation. I want to recommend it more as I did enjoy it but it's flaws are apparent.

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This is my first review, my first time playing any Nexomon game - I wasn't aware there was a prequel - therefore I'm a complete newbie both game/review wise, however it made a new fan in me and made me want to backtrack to it's prequel so I wrote this.If you love the handheld Pokémon games it is very likely you will enjoy Nexomon: Extinction as game-play wise it has similarities to Pokémon and could almost be called the meme version of Pokémon thanks to it's running commentary of fourth-wall jokes. However the two games are not the same as Nexomon: Extinction stands on it's own feet as a traditional RPG, and does so successfully, but happily flaunts that it was very likely inspired by Pokémon with it's critter catcher base. Instead I'd recommend people to try not to go in expecting it to be exactly the as Pokémon same mechanics wise, but instead to expect it to have similarities and give you some nostalgia - especially difficulty wise - whilst being an entirely different game.✔️ It's a game that is fairly cheap and overall will be smooth running game even for lower spec users like myself. (I do find when I boot up the game and use my first attack against an opponent in a battle it freezes for a short time, but it unfreezes pretty quick and runs perfectly fine after that so it's minor.)✔️ It's both colourful and visually appealing in all aspects. In particular I like the backgrounds over the Nexomon but the designs of the Nexomon are also well done. (And yes shiny ones are available and are called "cosmic".)✔️ The main story is fairly large (I completed it in about 30+ hours) and well paced. The world is also a nice size and very explorable as it's a semi open world from the get go. ✔️ All the characters are likeable and I love the silly fourth wall breaking humour. I have laughed at this game several times. However this will very much depends on the player though and will get old for some.✔️ Alongside your main slot there are 3 extra save slots for multiple playthroughs.✔️ It's fairly difficult and doesn't hand everything to you on a spoon. Be prepared for some grinding, buying potions, running back to the Nexostop (health centre) and the opponents switching out Nexomon strong against yours.✔️ Additional side quests are not only there but they don't feel forced into the game for no reason. There's also plenty of them as well which makes the game fairly playable even after finishing.✔️ All Nexomon, including starters, can be caught in the game and the game certainly makes it feel doable. No DLCs or anything of the sorts are needed. ✔️ Level scaling can be a make or break feature for some, but I personally enjoyed that the Nexomon and Tamers (who you can re-battle anytime) in world got tougher and it increased the difficulty nicely.✔️ Customisation is pretty good. You can customise your character whenever you want with a nice selection of sprite choices, find a few different Nexomon sprites that can follow you if you wish (and is entirely optional) and use a custom mode once you complete the game to change the game-play entirely.  ❌ No ability to change the keyboard mapping made it much more awkward for playing on a keyboard as did have odd controls. When I switched to controller I found it far easier for this game in particular. ❌ Whilst I enjoyed them at first and they're not terrible, some of the mechanisms got a bit repetitive for me. The mini game as you catch the Nexomon, the boulder smashing to farm shards and looking for higher percentages when throwing food at the Nexomon are some that just got repetitive after a while.❌ There was no tutorial about the type and status system so knowing what they did was pretty much a guessing game unless you googled it. An NPC or something explaining what the all types and status system are would've been really helpful for both old and new players.❌ Exploring is fun but without an on the go in-game map and no route names I found it hard to find/remember places sometimes (warpstones do help but you have to find it first). Maybe my sense of direction is bad though.❌ There just seemed like a lot of scrolling. Need to buy 50 potions? You're adding all of them 1 at a time. Same goes for things like throwing food at Nexomon and searching for a Nexomon in the Database. I personally think a bulk option and a few shortcuts would help out for some of it.❌ For those collecting them all there is no feature in the Database telling you where Nexomon was last seen/where to find them or any sort of hint. Right now it's a lot of wandering aimlessly and/or being reliant on online guides.❌ Move pool was fairly small but it felt even smaller since many of the non attacking moves just don't feel worth the slot they take up because the percentage of them hitting is just so low. Sadly this made the Nexomon kinda feel the same strategy wise for me since they also didn't have any unique abilities, stats and whatnot, then also all had similar move pools.❌ Minor but no selling items at the store was a shame. It would've been nice to be able to sell those excess Nexotraps I wasn't using for some money. All in all it very much embraces the fact it is Pokémon like but manages to change up those core features a just tad bit to make them feel different for both new and old players of the critter catcher genre. The game is most certainly not a masterpiece and could use with some things changing up a little, however considering how cheap it is and it's still receiving updates regularly I would most certainly recommend this game for anyone who loves critter catcher and RPG games or wants to play a Pokémon-esque game with a different take.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like if Neopets made a pokemon clone that poked fun at other games. The designs for a majority of the nexomon have potential to be really cool but then too often fall flat. After 14 hours of grinding out levels to try and see what all my nexomon look like evolved I gave up and looked up the dex on their website. Out of the 18 pages of nexomon only like 3 pages (the last 3) of them look really cool. Even so, when those cool ones are enlarged for cut scenes they really do not age well and just look so flat. Shading can go a long way.The writing is forgetable and the best of it is jokes from your cat companion breaking the 4th wall. The game is way more open than a pokemon game so you can go to a majority of areas before you need to for the story and farm materials and xp. Speaking of XP the game has scaling for enemies. Each zone has a minimum level starting but then scales based primarily on story progress with a little from the highest level nexomon in your party. There is exp share but you have to make it and it in the form of special orbs you can equip (4 per nexomon) and equip it to whoever is getting leveled. Need to swap them to a different nexomon? unequip all and then equip them on a new one one at a time. Tedious and and grind just to start grinding. Since they did this grid based layout that also means there is only up, down, left, right when moving around. It felt jarring for a while when not in grass moving around because you feel like diagonals should be possible. At first between the UI and the navigation handling I thought it felt like it should have been a mobile game instead. Turns out it was put out on mobile and the PC version feels like a mobile port. If the game is on sale for really cheap and after watching someone else play it looks like something you wanna put time into it you could do a lot worse. I think what is frustrating is how I can see a lot of potential and I want to like it more.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought it on a whim.Now?I like it more than I like Pokemon games.Designs are cool, the jokes are (in my opinion) pretty damn good, and I had a blast playing through the story. ~~~There is a point when you're meeting a certain enemy that you can actually just agree with their demand. Surprised, they congratulate you on your wisdom, essentially give you a Master Ball (1 use 100% catch rate) as a reward and then you just immediately turn around and beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of them.~~~My time in the game is a bit skewed, its really closer to 45 hours since I went at the game a very specific way the first time I played and just wore myself out. (I essentially was trying to do an all-Phantom type team, which was a pain in the ass later on when typing is a huge battle factor.)If I had to be realistic, you could probably finish it MUCH sooner than I did, but I really enjoyed the world and had a good bit of fun doing quests and searching for Vaults. I also ended up fighting the last battle with a team of Level 72 Nexomon, and it was a fair fight if I'm being pragmatic, so if you're worried about it being too easy or something, don't even sweat it; the game will challenge you enough.I won't lie though, I definitely abused a game mechanic to cheese some of the tougher fights, but I feel like that's part of what makes this game beautiful; the fact that you can slap 4 Level 3 Health Cores on a Foreer, first turn use Natural Healing (Ingrain) and then use Green Sphere (delayed Recover) every other turn as a strategy is absolutely amazing.~~~For those of you unaware of a majority of the game's mechanics, that's the setup for a health tank who has a massive health pool and heals 10% of it every turn, with an additional 30% every other turn if you're diligent with the move Green Sphere. It's probably my favorite stall mechanic because on the turns where you aren't setting up Green Sphere, you can attempt to Poison or Bind (Wrap) the enemy and they can't do anything about it other than hope that RNJesus is on their side.~~~That aside, it really is a fantastic game. Again, I bought this expecting to be disappointed. I most certainly was NOT disappointed. It truly is your loss if you end up ignoring this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I went in just wanting "sort of pokemon but on PC". I neither expected nor wanted more. I was blindsided by an absolutely fantastic writing and story. A mostly hilarious and friendly tone telling a tragic story in a way that just works. It's a tragicomedy that constantly breaks the fourth wall, amidst a pokemon-like experience. If you're a pokemon fan looking for something different, especially if, gen after gen you keep hoping for an actual good story and characters, this is it. If you're a pokemon fan, get it on those grounds alone.If you're not a pokemon fan, let's talk about the bad.The battle system is simplistic pokemon. The leveling moves are often nonsensical, you unlock worse moves as you progress, and pokemon only ever learn their own type and normal moves. (Or normal moves + another type if normal.) These make the experience feel both easier to read and less interesting to play. It's okay, nothing heinous by any means, but a missed opportunity. If they make a sequel, that's the part they should improve.That said, even with those cons, the battle system has some things that are absolutely great. Trainers switch on you constantly, keeping you on your toes instead of just standing there getting bashed super effectively. They do it just enough to be challenging but not enough to be annoying. The core system, while pretty shallow, is an interesting take. The game's big upside are bosses. They are actual bosses and feel difficult. Grandmaster tamers will absolutely dumpster you if you go there underleveled or carelessly, tyrants (legendaries) will eat your face off if you let them, overall a very pleasurably challenging experience that i wish pokemon games would copy.The world also scales with you at specific story triggers, keeping every trainer fight interesting and wild encounter relevant to your party. Overall, it is truly a great experience. It has flaws, of course, but it is a very enthusiastic recommendation from me.Play this !

_childDocuments_.review: Was sorta looking forward to this. This game goes against most rules of RPGs and not really in a good way and I dislike everyone's answer to this being pretty much, "Just play it in the way you don't usually play RPGs." No the community didn't say that specifically, but they simply said they have no problem with the game so nobody else should either. I didn't complete this game, and I know that's a stigma against game reviews, but a stigma against me as a player is that I don't wanna play a game that isn't fun just so that I'm allowed to tell people it isn't fun.Let's get into the nitty gritty of why I don't like this game. It's semi open world (some places needing story progression to access) which might seem like a good thing, but it means that levels have to be balanced differently. Every enemy in the game is scaled to your level based on story progression. The basic reward of playing an RPG is becoming stronger, but you'll never feel that unless you willingly avoid doing the story.Did I mention there's no IVs/EVs? Some people would clap at that fact, but they don't realize that makes every Nexomon you encounter no different from the ones in your party besides levels and the cores equipped. What does that mean? If you encounter the same Nexomon you have in the wild but of a higher level, it would be better to catch that one instead of keeping the one you raised yourself because cores are easily swapped over. It's very shallow. Your Nexomon is not your friend that helps you through thick and thin, your Nexomon is a tool. Maybe you're cool with that, I dunno. I like to be immersed within RPGs, but that's just me.Let's talk about battling. I'm all for high difficulty, but it's so artificial here. Every enemy you fight takes 3 hits and you take 3 hits unless you get randomly crited. There's no point in using status moves because the buffs and debuffs don't do ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Weakening the enemy? Cool, you'll still die in 3 hits so that's just a turn wasted. Buffing yourself? You take a hit and the damage you deal to them has little gain. Moves that inflict status aliments have 30% chance at success. Turn wasted once again. Wanna raise a weak Nexomon, but don't want him to die? Swap them out because there's no EXP Share and because all the enemies will probably be scaled to your highest level so it's not even a guarantee they'll survive to do it consistently. I like how the Healing Centers are super quick, but that's probably to account for the hundreds of times you'll backtrack to them in order to heal. Training is a hassle when the wild Nexomon scale alongside you. It would probably be fine if it were only the Trainers who scaled. An actual human with strategy should be difficult after all. I also hate that everyone who defends this game argues against EXP Share being an option. It's like saying people shouldn't drink coffee because they don't have problems waking up themselves. It's an option. You can turn it off if it's so bad.This open world high difficulty would probably be better if the game weren't a turn based RPG. There's never a moment where you feel powerful in this game. Even in Dark Souls it has small weak enemies so you can compare them to the bosses. In this game every battle is a struggle so you don't feel any progression. You feel no different fighting bosses from when you encountered your first few wild Nexomon. It's like a Pokemon Clone tried to evolve into its own identity, but it abandoned what made Pokemon great and went against the RPG Genre as a whole.Pokemon games suffered from giving you too much for easy mindless combat. This game suffers from giving you too little for balls to the walls difficult combat. If Pokemon weren't in a terrible state you probably wouldn't give this game a single glance unless you had no idea what Pokemon was.Pros:Every Nexomon is well designed and unique.Animations are nice and fluid.Comedy is nice. While I myself didn't laugh loudly I know others who will.Cons:Level scaling makes it feel like you aren't progressing or getting stronger.While battle animation is nice, you could swap most attacks with an attack of the same typing and see no difference.Sound design is pretty basic. I don't remember any tunes besides the battle theme.The overworld looks like a high res mobile game made in RPGMaker.Unsatisfying and shallow gameplay loop.CocoRatings:Graphics: 6/10Sound: 4/10Gameplay 3/10

_childDocuments_.review: So I've spent a few hours in the game so far, and while it presents a lot of interesting dynamics to the genre, I don't think I can quite recommend it yet.  First is the battle system- I think it's interesting, but limited. I really like the idea of having a single stamina pool rather than each move having it's own uses like in other games, but for at least the early game (as I'm only about 4 hours in so far), pretty much every single battle against an equally leveled opponent depletes nearly all of my stamina, which if I'm trying to train up that one monster to be more in line with the rest of my team, results in my running back and forth to a healer pretty much every battle, which is a big minus on my part. That, when accounting that it splits XP if multiple monsters participate and there is no EXP Share as far as I can tell, means that leveling up your nexomon is an incredible grind    The type system is pretty simple, with there only being 9 types total with each having 2 weaknesses and usually 2 or 3 resistances, but each monster only has a single type and that makes me wonder why there are so many Nexomon? There are really only 3 stats to worry about aside from HP and Stamina (Attack, defense, and speed), so none of the nexomon of the same type really feel all that different aside from their appearance. Like, once you find a rare nexomon of a certain type, there seems to be very little reason to ever use one of the common ones. Second, thus far the game has done an awful job of informing me of the game mechanics. There are these types, but after looking high and low for some in-game teacher (ala Trainer Schools in pokemon for example), there appears to be no one willing to explain the basic information you would need to know. What do the status effects do? Damned if I know, I can't find any explanation in-game. I get if you don't want to bog us down with a forced tutorial, but at least have like, an in-game manual or some NPCs that will explain mechanics for those of us that would rather do that than go to google. My 3rd complaint is really just personal preference, as I've seen in other reviews that other people love this so I'm in the minority but- I really hate the game's humor. The game presents the world as being in a bad way; the Nexomon Tamers are the only bastion against these Tyrant monsters, and humanity is on the brink of extinction, and the story has been touted as a main selling point... but then every other NPC breaks the 4th wall, if you walk into people's houses without being a high ranking tamer, they complain about protagonists breaking into people's homes, NPCs say there aren't that many towns because of lazy developers, that people are loitering around because it's expensive to draw them walking, etc. Just immediately takes me out of the world when every other interaction is a tongue-in-cheek joke on either the genre or games as a whole. Also, I really, really, very much so, HATE the companion we are forced to walk around, who also breaks the 4th wall constantly and doesn't seem to have a high opinion of your character. I would leave them behind in an instant if I were given the option.The art is good, I like the music and the stage design, the monster designs are cool and cute, but the things I listed above have annoyed me and lessened my enjoyment

_childDocuments_.review: Alright! Game Review Time!Nexomon: ExtinctionAfter spending 53 hours on this game, and fully completing the database, I can speak on it with confidence!Nexomon: Extinction is a monlike unlike any other. It has competent writing, an amazing story, a genuine world that doesn't hide how bad things really would be in a world with monsters everywhere. Its funny, and dark at times, and a little in-jokey and 4th-wall-breaking, but that only works in its favor. Its really cool.Graphics: 9/10Every single Nexomon has amazing art, seriously. I can't point to any and say 'it looks ugly', they are all awesome! And almost every NPC has a picture for when they have dialogue too! Its super awesome, the only thing it lacks in any sense is in the CGs (because cutscenes require CGs) only feature the default male or female avatar you can choose, based on, y'know, if you chose a male or female avatar. That knocks it down to the 9/10 that it isGameplay: 8/10Finally, a monlike that doesn't fall into the 'Everyone is a glass canon' trap! Battles may take a little longer, but they're genuinely fun and enjoyable, and you've got a fighting chance even 10 levels below your opponent! Unfortunately it does fall into the much harder to avoid pitfall of 'I'm just going to spam one move and win', and while that's fully doable for singular fights, the stamina system in the game really helps, and means you have to decide on what move you're going to spam, instead of always using the strongest one.Content: 9/10There is so much stuff, I've sunk 53 hours into the game and only completed the database 3 hours ago. There are 381 Nexomon to find and catch! And while hunting down the roaming legendaries can be annoying, its super rewarding and awesome! I'm still hunting down the last few tamers I haven't beaten so I can snag the last two achievements!Overall: 9/10Excellent game that is absolutely worth the 20 bucks it costs. Its super new and the devs are active too!

_childDocuments_.review: Is this a Pokemon clone?Yes.Is it better than Pokemon?Yes.(This comes from someone who has really only played Pokemon Firered FYI)Pros:-Random Grass encounters are significantly less annoying because in Nexomon you can see when the Nexomon are rustling in the tall grass and avoid them.(There is also a repel spray you can get in the late game that negates random encounters period.)-In Pokemon Firered you need to beat the first gym leader in order to gain the ability to run however in Nexomon you simply run as soon as the campaign starts-In **ALL** pokemon games you have 3 different choices to pick as your starter vs nexomon you get a choice of I believe 9 different Nexomon-Grinding doesn't feel as tedious or annoying in this game because it's alot easier to level up(In Firered you get the EXP share sometime in the mid-game if you catch about 50 pokemon but in the early game of Nexomon you can easily craft an EXP share)-In pokemon there are 18 different types vs Nexomon which has 9 types,it keeps things alot simplier with the rock paper scissors system-You can re-battle other trainers which is very fun and makes it more enjoyable for grinding-You can interact more with the overworld I'd like to say-Catching Nexomon is much more complex compared to Pokemon as you need to implement more strategy to it-Writing wise it's significantly funnier than pokemon although they aren't as limited to what they can say due to this being an indie game-Story wise it has a pretty thick lore and is not just 10 year old kid wakes up and goes out on a journey to become the champion of this regionCons:-It makes too many 4th wall jokes in my opinion not to the point where it's unbearable but to the point where I just don't laugh-I think it's easy get lost sometimes in certain areas-Sidequests aren't the most fun thing to do-More of a personal complaint but I do kinda prefer the 18 types of Pokemon vs the 9 of Nexomon

_childDocuments_.review: Pros- Great art- Self aware dialogue that gave me a few chuckles- Challenging, a bit too much at times, but it  feels right- Unique movesetsCons- Animations are fast but feel too fast at times which made it hard for me to grasp what was happening until I got used to it. I feel like a better battle log system would help with this especially because many moves have second abilities to them other than just damage. There is sort of a battle log system in the bottom left but it goes by way too fast to even read what is happening. I'll put this in here too but determining type advantages was pure trial and error which was a bit annoying if you're too used to Pokemon and I feel like a more advanced log system would help new players figure things out quicker.- Nexomon in the world scale rather than being a set range for the entire game (just an opinion and I recommend new players experience it first hand before judging off this review)- Stamina < Power PointsMy first hour was great. I was really into the art style, the music was catchy and relaxing, and the world/story felt new and interesting. I wanted to keep playing to discover more Nexomons and progress the story, so I did. Six hours later I'm finding myself kind of frustrated yet not at the same time. I think all of my years playing Pokemon have spoiled this "monster/pet battling" genre for me so this game felt like a chore to keep playing but I was also enjoying myself. It really is a huge leap in difficult from the hand holding recent Pokemon games give you. My biggest complaint is the leveling system. I progressed to the 2nd major fight using the same 2-3 Nexomons while switching them around to keep them at similar levels. This is similar to how I would approach Pokemon. Once I got to into the fight, I immediately felt useless and I barely won after spamming potions and ethers. Even lesser battles up to this point felt super difficult and, at times, unwinnable but I prevailed to the major fight. It felt like I was severely underleveled even though my levels matched (+1/-1) those of the opposition.I backtracked a bit to derail from the main story and catch some new Nexomon with different types to get some diversity in my team and see some new faces. However, was met with the tedious challenge of grinding any Nexomon that I caught to a similar level so it could compete. This game has world scaling levels. All wild Nexomon scale up as you progress. Grinding any new Nexomon you catch to a similar level of your main party absolutely sucked. I was barely winning 1v1s with my new Nexomon against wild Nexomons with type disadvantage at similar levels. I would fight 1 wild Nexomon, have to either backtrack and heal at a camp or use the potions I was saving for important battles, and repeat the process. Switch training doesn't really work in this game either as I rarely OHKO wild Nexomons and the experience gain from splitting is so very small. I enjoy this game's uniqueness especially after wishing Pokemon would evolve it's core for once but I personally feel that world scaling is the wrong approach.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. Pros:- Super adorable and fun Nexomon to catch!- The art is great and all of the zones are fun to play in.- The prices for stuff you need, like traps and potions etc., are fairly priced. - There are either towns or medics close enough where you don't have to stray too far with knocked out Nexomons and no one to fight with, but far enough where you still need to be strategic about your potion usage and 'mon catching.Cons: - None of the Nexomon from the first game are in this one which is a bummer because there were some from the first game I really loved and wanted on my team. - Some of the conversations can be a bit silly, since some of the characters just say ridiculous things at times. _childDocuments_.review: Now that I've gone through the main story I think I can give this a proper review.My TL/DR would be some of the other bad reviews are misleading, it has real flaws, but it has refreshing aspects for the mon-catch genre and I want to see how they improve and grow with the sequel. And Old Scientist boi better be in the sequel like he wanted.Gameplay: I'll start with the positives. Usually you choose when to fight wild mons and tamers, huge quality of life for these kinds of games before you have the ability to teleport around. You can get/make "cores" which can be slotted into mons to increase stats or exp/money gain, or share exp etc. You can get special items exploring or doing quests that stack benefits like catch rate, exp or money boosting, etc. You can also get QoL items like an infinite repel spray to turn off/on, or the ability to access your storage box from anywhere. You can also change nicknames freely at any time, easily get back old moves, and other little things that just make it nicer than Mon-catch games that try to follow too closely to pokemon. Also there are actual boss battles that feel good...or as good as they can be, given the simplicity of the game.As for the negatives, these will probably make or break your intentions to pick this game up if you only care about the gameplay and nothing else. Firstly, outside of combat (where all options are labeled) you are never told the controls, and never will be. WASD/arrow keys work for movement, Q/E switches columns in menus, i is menu, J/U/O has special menu effects which are -sometimes- labeled, K is your standard interaction and yes button, L is your standard cancel and no button. Again, you wont be told this so if you are going to play it, there you go. Then there is typing, movesets, and stats. I like the type matchups as they are, feels right for the most part, and certainly more balanced out than pokemon. But there are no dual types so there is no brain power use in your decision making, made all the worse by the movesets. The movesets are baffling. Mons almost never have damage types outside Normal and their own type (I believe I saw 2 mons with an off type elemental move). So it usually really is easiest to just switch to type advantage and spam attack.  There are a bunch of moves that are just worse speed/power/accuracy versions of other moves, with little sense in when they are distributed in a mon's lvls. Most of the non-attack moves are far too situational, like a series of "take less damage from [element] for x turns except they are only learned by mons of said element which means they already resist said element. There are mons that can pick up objectively best moves at lvl 10 (which you can always get back if they are missing from a higher level catch) making the choice between 2 mons you are considering painfully obvious when the other wont learn said move til lvl 61 (or never), made all the worse by the issue with stats. And That issue is: They aren't different enough to matter. At low lvls every mon is only 1 or 2 points different in any given stat. By the very late game you can finally start to feel that a mon has low defense or good speed, and at that point you are beating the end of the story (maybe sooner, if you don't do any side stuff and avoid battles and catching mons like the plague, since the game has adaptive difficulty scaling you can probably beat the end of the game at a lower level than I did.)Art/Music: I think the art is very good personally, and I even like a lot of the designs. Obviously these are highly subjective things so I suggest looking at the database (pokedex equivalent) yourself before buying. I can't comment on the music as it was turned off for my playthrough (played casually with podcasts and stuff in the background)Story: If you really don't like it and you aren't here for it, spamming K and L at the same time will BLAST through dialogue, so I wouldn't worry about that. If you do care about the story, then I'd say in my opinion its actually good. I didn't play the first game, which has impact on this, but that didn't stop me from getting what was going on. I think its got a good number of twists, can be funny, and its leagues better than a standard pokemon game.Beyond that praise though, I have to say: The writer for the dev has contempt for themselves, the people they work for, and the players, and they need to stop and get help. Make friends and touch grass. The number of meta jokes are too high, sure, but thats not my real issue here. The real issue is its clear someone working on this has been badly hurt by negative, non-constructive criticism and is constantly injecting put downs to the game, and to gripes players may have against it or perhaps the previous game. If there was something making the story bad, it was this. Stop attacking the reader. Stop attacking yourself. The game, you, and the players will be better for it.Previous Review for transparency:Still gonna play it for some mindless time kill listening to podcasts/streams. But I don't recommend.You can't lower the volume until you've entered the title screen, chosen a save slot, watched a long intro, picked your character avatar and name, watched a cutscene, and told where to go. THEN you can change settings. The gradient for change is like 8 steps or so, so the music was too loud on the lowest setting and I still had to regulate it via windows volume mixer.Speaking of settings. You also can't change the resolution. You can change between fullscreen or not fullscreen (after going through all the same hoops required to change sound settings). You can force a resolution change while in windowed mode by haphazardly squishing the box as it'll 'pop' into the closest resolution to that, but this just makes everything smaller, it does not balance UI elements for legibility.Finally the controls. I already read from other reviews that you can't change them. Its annoying and dumb, but they are a serviceable. The much more pressing matter with them is they aren't told to you. Ever. They you a non-standard IJKL with I being the equivalent of a "start" button, opening your menu of options. K is you standard interaction and yes button. L is your standard cancel action and no or back out button. Holding L also lets you run, ala pokemon running shoes etc. If you read this review and still want to play it, then this is the only time you'll be told. I repeat, the game will never tell you any of this. And whats more, some characters WILL mention buttons...But they just call them "action button". The characters want to complain with meta humor about not having budget? Maybe don't pay for that Loud intro and put a settings option at the main menu, and show the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls. Its borderline contempt for players.

_childDocuments_.review: Making a long story short: I totally recommend and loved this game. You don't need to wait for any sale. It's totally worth buying. But I liked so much that I bought the first one, and I'm probably gonna play it soon.The story is pretty good and well written. And for a monster-catching game, it's surprising (at least for me).I'm not giving any spoiler, but the way the story goes and develops its "villain" is amazing. One of the things I don't like at all in most stories is some sort of one-dimensional villain. And this game is not the case. Actually sometimes you are somehow considered a villain or the person doing things that are not suppose to be done. There's no ordinary dichotomy between evil and good, so all character's motivations are understandable.The story is also funny to follow, I liked the comedy and I enjoyed reading all the dialogues.Coco is the best character, he follows you and breaks the fourth wall all the time. It couldn't have done better.The mechanics are good for me and the variety of nexomons is very entertaining. The environment is one of the things I liked the most. _childDocuments_.review: This review is for those who are put off by the artwork.Even after 40+ hours, the cover art makes me want to load up a different game. The good news is once you start playing it's borderline addictive.Highlights- Interesting lore & story. My favorite games are usually JRPGS, and the writers did a good job with this. There are some genuine laugh-out-loud moments and a fun climax.- Combat is a decent challenge. There's an emphasis on type advantage and buffs/debuffs. Nexomon don't learn moves outside their type, so you're supposed do a little planning with your party to cover any weaknesses. The A.I will switch out to gain the advantage (quite a few times).- Quests & Exploration. There's a quest system that offers good rewards. You're even able to acquire multiple copies of the golden Nexotrap (which gives 100% catch rate). Exploration is fun; there are hidden areas, vaults to unlock, equipment/abilities that allow further exploration.- Continued game support. After launch the devs have listened to feedback and rebalanced bosses, added exp boost, and even added a custom mode! You can play the game with built in "Nuzlocke" rules, start a new game plus, remove the Nexomon level cap, randomize trainer battles, randomize wild Nexomon, randomize move sets, etc. This adds so much replay value.Room for Improvement- Nexomon customization. Currently the only thing we have is Synergy cores, which are gems that gives various buffs, and relearning old moves. There are no "min-maxing" options and Nexomon stats are very similar across the board. This allows you to play with whatever 'mons you think look the best, for better or for worse.- Filling out the Dex. For a single player game, this is way more time consuming than it should be. Everything in the world scales with your party (up to a point), which means stage 1 'mons are nearly impossible to find in the late game. There's no trading, breeding, or in-game ways to track where wild Nexomon are located. Don't get me started on the encounter rates for some of the Legendaries. As a completionist, this game is a bit of a nightmare.- Combat depth. Outside of type match-ups and your usual buffs/debuffs there's not a lot going on. If you want Radical Red levels of strategy, you'll have to stick to that game for now. There's a lot of potential with the synergy cores. But that's up for future iterations to improve on.SummaryBuy it! For 20 bucks it's one of the best creature collectors out there (in a genre the surprisingly sparse). The Nexomon designs are very hit or miss, but you'll find enough that look great. This games deserves more attention!

_childDocuments_.review: As with any game where you capture monsters, there is the inevitable comparison to the long standing nostalgia ogled franchise of . I'd be lying if I didn't grow up with the series, although I always enjoyed Dragon Quest Monsters far more. Tangents aside, Nexomon: Extinction is Pokemon for better and for worse.Personally, there's a lot I don't like about the  now-a-days. With the inclusion of all these sub-systems like held items, passive abilities, EVs, IVs, moves through breeding, etc, etc, the games have become . From a casual perspective, they're hard to enjoy. When I know that X  is objectively better than Y  because of an inherently better stat block/moveset/typing, it sort of takes the joy out of crafting a team. Nexomon: Extinction gets around this by basically making all Nexomon the same. Basically. There are minor differences in stats, but nothing so egregiously damning as to make any one Nexomon worthless. You can craft a team with any Nexomon you like and get through the game without worry. Some Nexomon do inherently have better movesets, but not to as large a degree as to create an optimal choice (outside of a select few Nexomon that can solo everything).This freedom to choose whatever team you like without being hampered by sub-optimal choices is great! Especially considering that you can catch a whole swath of Nexomon right from the beginning. The game has a far more open world dynamic than  ever did- and with 381 Nexomon to collect, there's a Nexomon for everyone's fancy. Right out the gate you have the choice of one starter from a choice of nine- one of each type.  the starters that you didn't choose can be found out in the wildly almost immediately. You never feel like you missed out on something, unlike in the  where you might not have the ability to ever catch the other starters you didn't choose.So that's the better, or at least a quick rundown, what about the worse?Nexomon: Extinction... Can be a bit boring. The story and combat are nothing to write home about. The writing is interesting in the sense that it finds humor in breaking the fourth wall by acknowledging common tropes in RPGs, but it's not something that's going to make you want to play more. It's just there. It's a backdrop. It serves the purpose. The combat is repetitive and can be grindy, but... Have you ever play ? Repetition is the name of the game.I think Nexomon: Extinction makes enough improvements on the monster catching genre to be worth a playthrough, if just to see the various Nexomon- there are some great things here. It does skew heavily toward the casual player, which is great for me but may frustrate someone looking for a challenge. I would say the game  worth the $20 price tag if you're looking for a casual monster catching game, and definitely worth a try if its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: *UPDATE: 70 HOURS LATER*Full cleared the game and 56/56 achievementsPROS:-A simplified Pokemon-style game with "Metroidvania"-lite elements that offers a solid story and gameplay without taking itself too seriously. (Catch, fight, evolve, win. Nine elements instead of forty or whatever Pokemon is up to now)-Great dry, sarcastic humor that kept things fresh and lively throughout. Coco is a breakout character that needs to reappear. He reminds me of Kazooie from Banjo & Kazooie. Videll was also hilarious and memorable.-You feel strong yet engaged/challenged from the start. It isn't two or three hours of spamming tackle and growl.-Nexomon designs were on point. Range from cute to cool, with some real standouts (Psychic Ghost, Electric-types were almost all homeruns). Animations were very well done for the art style.-Music was well done and didn't wear on the ears while farming an area. Some real bangers.-Leveling system is rewarding and doesn't feel like a grinding slog even at 90+ thanks to the core system.-The movement skills you unlock (similar to Surf, Strength, etc.) are perfect and adds the "Metroidvania" feel. I had a great time going back to previous areas with new powers to unlock secrets.-Zones are compact but don't feel rushed at all. Great level layout for the most part, feeding into that Metroidvania thing.-Tamers "level up" several times and allow you to challenge them again and again.CONS:Note: None of these ruined any aspect of the game for me. They're just my personal opinion on where I feel it could be improved.-Nexomon lack individuality and investment.In Pokemon you have things like IVs, EVs, Natures, Abilities, dual element monsters.I think Nexomon actually sold itself a bit short by not incorporating at least one version of their own.There is the core system that can boost attack, defense, HP, stamina, status resist. It doesn't go far enough though and the fact that you can remove cores from one Nexomon to give to another makes the monsters themselves expendable. You don't have any investment that you leveled a monster to 65 and don't want to replace it for one in the wild you find at 75 (I did this many times).Speaking to individuality, Nexomon of a given element all feel the same regardless of rarity and the stat spread is too tame. Common or Legendary, their stats don't differ enough to standout. There is no iconic bulky Chansey or super sweeper Alakazam. There is SO MUCH POTENTIAL here though. Seriously, when I saw Glunch or Blimpapa I thought "that's a big boi." and expected some massive HP to chew through, which wasn't the case. Everything dies in 2-3 hits on average assuming correct typing.Devs if you're reading this: The core system would be the perfect place to introduce "legendary cores" or "unique cores" that work only for a specific evolution line and give a special ability.Another remedy to this would be to add a slight variable on base stats akin to Pokemon IVs so more invested players can feel they caught a "good one" (without the insane rarity of it being cosmic/shiny).-Most Nexomon only learn abilities of their element or the neutral "Normal" type.Only Normal-types themselves and a legendary learn anything else. There is tons of potential here without breaking the game balance to give some Ghost-types a Psychic move, or a Fire-type a Mineral move (looking at you Meteor Shower)Maybe there can be some buyable or quested scrolls to teach cross-element abilities.-On the topic of learned abilities. The leveling progression for unlocking them is totally jumbled. A few times I've had my final ability, or even last few, be a lackluster weak normal move. -I'd love a multiplayer, but if not, at least include some post-game tamers you can challenge at level 99 in Cadium's stadium or something! There isn't much to do with your legendaries after you catch them or with a team you took the time to build in post-game.**MOST IMPORTANT: There needs to be Glunch and Zumble plushies for sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:The main draw of these types of games is the monsters. The Nexomon are generally well designed (honestly, the only ones I don't really care for are the legendaries which tend to look like giant monsters with lots of spikes).The story is engaging, the graphics are charming. Way better than any modern Pokemon game, imo. The game mechanics are really fun. I was surprised that I actually enjoyed the pickaxe mechanic, I thought it was going to get old really quick, but the payoffs are good and there's something really satisfying about popping some gemstones (maybe it's the sound fx?). I also enjoyed the scaling of all the monsters which means that over-levelling one huge monster does not solve the game.Negatives:I think the combat could be deeper. There's very little reason to use attacks that do not deal damage. Most status effects do very little. There is no real reason to play a monster over another of the same type and level other than the difference in stats. Meaning that all monsters will play the same role on a team. I know that not all games can go super deep on these type of stuff and it seems that the devs decided to spend their time making the casual play and the story more interesting which is fine.I do like that the weakness and resistance does not immediately mean win or loss and that it's very unlikely you're going to be one-shotted by some enemy monster.

_childDocuments_.review: TRUE VISUAL MASTERPIECE.Let me tell you why. You think think this is just another "mobile" port? Wrong. What's bad about typical mobile visual (HD + 2D) is they use 2D assets with skeletal animation that squeezes and stretches the assets, resulting in weird artistic output (bad). Some PC games do it too and the result is as expected: artistically weak. This game also use skeletal animation (if that is the right term) but it does it in a way that doesn't squeeze and stretch 2D assets like common mobile games, resulting in the output being closer to true realtime 3D rendering (on the characters, npc, monsters). Except you don't need fancy anti alias to make the edges looks smooth like in realtime 3D rendering coz the 2D assets already be smoothened like crazy. Basically like the characters in Harvest Moon: Back to Nature. Visually looks like sprite animation but based on actual 3D model. There is consistency that you would expect from 3D model. This game is just like that but with 2020 technology. Ain't that fancy.I am very glad to buy this game. HD 2D art in games should be either like this or classic sprite animation. Squeezing + stretching 2D assets in the fashion of many mobile games is weird man, nobody should ever do that.

_childDocuments_.review: I only played about 2 hours of it, but I didn't have any fun during those two hours.  People complain it is a tedious grindfest, and I tend to agree.    The biggest issue is the dynamic leveling system.  It is a risk that the devs took, and I appreciate them trying to bring something new.  I understand that it is suppose to be a challenge; however, having to heal after even a few fights with wild monsters so early in the game is incredibly annoying.  Back and forth running for heals after every fight or two is discouraging and feels like a waste of time.  I don't feel as if I am making progress.  Just leveling one or two nexomon takes forever.The devs are active and answer questions about the dynamic leveling, which I admire.  They state that there is a 1-3 level cap regarding opposing nexomon.  The devs continue saying that the game gets a bit easier the more you grind/progress the story; however, at least in the first 2 hours, I felt that my hard work of running back and forth for so many hours felt useless.  I was not rewarded for fighting wild monsters, and after two hours, that is discouraging enough for me to put down the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Warmly recommend this game.It successfully scratches the Pokemon itch, easily one of the best games of it's genre currently on steam both by price tag and content it offers.Story is interesting enough to hook you in with twists, turns and a little bit of 4th wall breaking.The grind i felt was self imposed, mostly due to previous experiences in other games. I found myself levels way above the opposition but after doing side activities the difficulty level picked up the pace and i found myself right back into the leveling curve. This game offers quality of life mechanics that are very much appreciated. (Tutorials for different mechanics feel a bit late compared to when you actually have access to them)Compared to other games, the rarity of 'mons do not influence their combat effectiveness, the stats are mostly the same with 1 maybe 2 points difference in rarity, this is barely noticeable given the weaknesses we're all too familiar with. My personal suggestion is to find the 'mons that please you aesthetically and roll with them. Do not be afraid to change your party, you might find yourself pleasantly surprised by some common,uncommon or rare ones that absolutely mop the floor with any opponent boss, legendary, you name it. (this game has some hidden gems, real diamonds in the dirt when it comes to its 'mons)All starters can be acquired in game some as early as the very start of the game after choosing your first.The map does feel a bit cramped, most areas you find yourself backtracking a lot, it felt as the game was about to end after basic exploration. Concerns aside, activities pop up after progression, areas that previously were inaccessible require certain elements to be unlocked as well as new 'mons that become available in previously explored patches of grass/caves.As a finishing note, both games, this and the previous one have different mons, some of them have made it into this game, as a flavor but most if not all are newly designed, that makes the work and dedication given very much appreciated as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't quite finished the game yet, but that is also precisely why i chose to write a review now. This game does a lot of things right, innovates on some things, but also struggles in other areas. Despite my review I will finish this game, although mainly to see where its going. Now hear me out on why:-  So far this game has a well written story, intriguing and funny. Unlike your traditional Pokemon title, you will find that some characters grow on you, you will be able to relate to them, while loathing other characters. The pacing is well done, unless you chose to actively grind/catch Nexomon. There are plot twists, some more obvious than others (even at this point in the game I am impressed by the story, which is why I will finish it).-  The music in this game is really good. It has individual tracks for areas, that fit the theme and set the mood. The battle themes are catchy and you will quickly find yourself humming along the tune.-  The art is quite breathtaking in my opinion. Its fairly unique from what games I've played so far in this genre, the animations are crisp and look cool. Every Nexomon really has a unique feel to it and evolutions make sense + you start to look forward to them.-  There are things other than music, story and artstyle that make this game different and one of the most interesting ones in my opinion, are "passive" items. There are also items called Cores, that boost the stats of your Mon, and you can equip more than 1 (4 in total). Throughout the game you will find items, that permanently increase money/EXP, or other things, you get. These are usually rewarded through side quests, which can often times be turned in immediatly when you arrive, or after a little bit of time investment, depending on how thoroughly you play through certain areas. I have probably invested about 1/4 of my time playing, trying to finish side quests and quite enjoyed it. Now despite all those points you might wonder, why I can't quite recommend this game. My main reason for that is the games actual main mechanic, the battle system. If you have played through other monster catching games, there are certain things you might have gotten used to, or grown to like. Nexomon, in my opinion, has a very shallow battle system, and heres why:-  As any other monster catching game, Nexomon also has types, with certain Weaknesses, or Strengths. Now oddly enough, I have not found information in the actual game, that tells you "hey, this is weak against that, while that is strong against this. I had to look it up on the "wiki". There are no multitype Nexomon either.Another thing that felt weird, was the actual amount of damage "effective" or "ineffective" moves did. Effective moves deal +25% damage, while ineffective moves deal 35% less damage and yes, that wasn't a typo, +25%/-35%.STAB (Same Type Attack Bonus) also seems to be a thing, albeit very minor, I could barely ever tell the difference.-  There are none. No Nexomon have any abilities, that can give them an advantage like causing rain, levitating etc..-  Nexomon have little base stats. Theres HP, ATT, DEF, Speed and "Stamina". This means a Mon with high base stats, can often win despite having a type disadvantage, while using a move that is ineffective. Mons of the same species also dont seem to have different stats (like IVs/EVs in Pokemon), meaning 2 Mon of the same species will have the same stats with an equel Level.On top of that, there are no Attack/Defense moves in the traditional sense. You can't buff your Mons attack to +6 like in Pokemon. While there are moves (like Barrier) that increase your DEF by 25%, nothing on the actual game screen, tells you that you have that buff, so better keep that in mind when you use it. You use it once during battle and its permanent (no clue if switching it in and out during one battle loses you that buff though, since the game just keeps it hidden from you). These things alone, cause battles to go one of 2 ways. You can chose to level a complete team, and will often find yourself looking for a type advantage on the field, OR, you will always fall back to that one Nexomon (most likely a Psychic type), that will quickly overlevel. In fact, you can  easily pick up a Mon called Divette early on, and sweep through everything in your path, if you have 10+ levels on the area you are in.Regardless of my negative review, this game has things to offer. In fact, maybe if you play monster catching games very casual, and haven't heard about deeper statistics (like EVs/IVs, SpD/SpA, abilites) and dont care about them, you might just enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: way better than the first game while still not being a masterpiece, it's very enjoyablevery similar to pokemon, and while not as good as the best ones, it's better than the recent gamesthe good:- 427 nexomon, might even be a little too much- the design of the monsters is generally pretty good- the musics are great- the story is nice, better than the first game, but having played the first before made me enjoy it a bit more- the stamina system is better than the PP if you compare it to pokemon, it's basically more like manathe improved from nexomon 1: - 2 more types, but still far behind the complexity of pokemon types (thus less interesting), no double type, no bonus for spell on your own type...- speed added, if you played the first one you know what i mean- the story is way better than nexomon 1, but there is still an annoying, 4th wall breaking npc always with you. he's less annoying than the one from the first game though- kinda "open world" as in you don't have to follow the story linearly to go where you want most of the time, which is pretty cool but it comes at the cost of having level scaling which I'll talk about belowthe bad:- while less linked to rarity than nexomon 1 (but still generally is), there are a lot of nexomon that are just bad and only here for the "catch them all" part, not usefull in a team- everything feels slow, opening and closing a menu, characters emoting in cutscenes and many other things, but it's a bit better than the first game- less spells from different type than your nexomon than pokemon, so you always have to switch to the type that works against what you have against you, very boring- 1v1 fight (at least 1 at a time) is very uninteresting, you won't be bothered if you only played pokemon but compared to a lot of RPGs, even old ones, the fights are too straight-forward- 4 spell maximum at a time for each nexomon, only to do exactly like pokémon but that's something they could have changed easily to make it better, the fights are already too straight forward as stated before- the spells are generally pretty boring, but that's to be expected from a turn based - 1 monster at a time game, but even comparing it to pokémon the spells are not as interesting- the level scaling, which negates the feeling of progression of power you want in an rpg, you can't win underleveled by playing well (the fights are not complexe enough anyway), you can't grind to feel powerful, the enemies level always follows you. if you want to add back an underleveled nexomon to your team, you can't level him in any other way than xp sharing since it scales to your highest level from what i understood, or you can catch a new one of that same nexomon that will have scaled from the level scalingI'd give it a 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a monster tamer game, but tired of Pokemon, this game is one of the best alternatives I have seen. The game play is simple which, I think, is perfect for its genre. The designs are great, some can be too similar to other games like pokemon, but that's only 2 or 3 monsters. What makes this game shine is it's story and humor. The story for a monster tamer is great, and the game isn't afraid to make fun of itself nor the genre it's apart of for the sake of comedy.Now, it is a budget game, so somethings maybe off and there isn't really an after game; however, I find these vary easy to look over all its charm.
_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed the Pokemon franchise for years, it feels like the series has focused on multiplayer battles at the expense of everything else.  Not so with Nexomon: Extinction, which has all the single-player charm of old-school Pokemon games, combined with great visuals, creative creature designs that blow newer Pokemon out of the water, fun characters, and some witty writing that had me chuckling. With that witty writing comes a story much better than its Pokemon equivalent, with less bland moralizing and forgettable side characters. I can't help but make so many comparisons to Pokemon, because the game feels like the designers were fed up with Pokemon's descent into laziness and wanted to show the jaded heads at Game Freak how it's done, and succeeded at doing so.Having played the first Nexomon game, I have to say that this game is decided improvement in every regard, and well worth the price tag.
