_childDocuments_.review: So you're telling me I can play "Almost Pokemon" without Nintendo threatening to sue me every time you play it?!A Pokémon-like that plays like a Souls? HELL YEAH. My wife’s boyfriend says it’s like Neopets and Digimon had a toxic relationship so Pokemon raised their kid.Extinction is far beyond Pokemon. It evolves every aspect of the game and makes Pokemon retroactively a worse experience. It was reminiscent of Pokemon, but it was it's own unique thing. I really liked the challenge. I loved everything about it. No hand holding, somewhat high difficulty, absolutely gorgeous world, brilliant characters and dialogue(the humor in particular is top notch) and there is so much content for only $20. The Nexomon designs are really impressive to me. I would be totally convinced if you told me they were new Pokemon. The game is self aware, it knows it's a game so it makes some of the dialogue very funny.  The story is interesting as well. It has some subtle set ups with some great pay offs.Nexomon is like a pure old fashioned Pokemon turn based game but with updated graphics (camera above looking down) and a better story than just becoming Pokemon Grand Master by going to all the Pokemon gyms in every city. The story is far more compelling than Pokémon's simple plot, and it has lore behind the character you play as, as well as almost everyone you encounter. Hell your main character in the game has more personality than frankly every Pokemon MC ever. I found myself wanting to learn more about the game's history after I was done with the main story because I was genuinely interested in the world they had built. It again made me laugh a lot, especially the talking cat sidekick Cocoa. And the ending was great. The gameplay is, overall, fairly similar to Pokémon, but simpler in just the right way.Nine types, with no dual-types, and nothing is outright immune to another type, which makes it easier to remember what's effective against what without needing a convoluted chart. The amount of debuffs is interesting also. With Pokémon, I mostly remember asleep, paralyzed, burned, poisoned. There might be frozen as well IIRC. But with Nexomon, there's also things like demotivated, provoked, nervous, frail, and sick, some of which make for interesting dynamic battles. I also liked that instead of having IV and EV stats, you just have base stats that can be modified by cores. Yeah, you mostly will probably use the HP, Stamina, Attack, and Defense cores, but it still provides some more interesting ways to set up your team without feeling too complicated.Haven't explored any of the post game yet, but I could totally see myself jumping back in to finish collecting all the Nexomon. If you are starting the game, don't worry about trying to collect ALL the Nexomon right away. You'll definitely want to explore and collect a variety of types in the beginning (fire, plant, electric, water, etc). But the game and wild areas level up with you. So if you caught a Nexomon at level 10 and its been sitting in storage and now you're at level 60, you could just go back to the area you found it in and catch one at level 52. I'm not sure if you'll be able to get all the same upgrades as you would if you raised it from level 10, but it could potentially save you from leveling any unnecessary Nexomon you wouldn't otherwise have to. Overall I'm thrilled with the game. Everything I dislike about current Pokemon games does not exist here and it's wonderful. It's a shame it's very unlikely to become popular. I know I'll be recommending it to everyone. For $20 it is a no-brainer. Even if you're happy with current Pokemon there are enough differences to make it worth playing.I wholeheartedly recommend the game to any Pokemon fan or people who have fun with Monster Collection RPG's in general. In my opinion, it is better than the recent Pokemon games and shows what can be done with less money, less developers and when someone has a fresh vision that is not blurred by $ signs. The game wears it's heart on it's sleeves and it shows in what love has been put into it. I seriously hope that the developers will make another game. I personally can't wait!10/10

_childDocuments_.review: The short summary is that this is a masterpiece of epic proportions. The long, well...Story. The start of the game is probably the weakest part of the entire plot. You live in an Orphanage, you head out, you encounter a woman with anger issues. A few minutes later, you got attacked by a Dragon, time suddenly stopped, you're forced to pick a Starter to fight for your life (and lose duh) before a Ghost saved you by opening a hole to a cave beneath a statue. I never understood why the Dragon just stood there and waited for your cat to drag you inside after going through the trouble to kick your ass, btw. I wouldn't go as far as to say that it's a bad impression, but it was a meh one for sure. The early meta jokes certainly didn't help to improve said impression either.  If some people quit the game, it must be within the first hour or so. Anyone who survives that basically gets hooked in until the end.That being said, the plot improved drastically once you're about an hour into the game, and it never stopped getting better until the very last moment. I won't spoil the overall plot, but suffice to say it can probably be sold as a movie trilogy and actually not flop. The writing is very strong, and the attention to detail is very appreciated, especially the part where opinions of you change as you clear a main story quest or ascend a Tamer rank. If I remember correctly, a generic guard can have up to 7 lines based commenting on your progress and achievements, and considering that there are hundreds of NPCs in the game, it's incredibly impressive.Gameplay. Gotta have to keep this short because there are so many things to talk about. Nexomon differs greatly from other Pokemon or Pokemon-like games in that you don't level up your Nexomon to play, or at least the method won't hold the more you progress the story. More specifically, you focus all the experience on one super powerful Nexomon that can 1 versus infinite like a super boss and then just keep changing the other 5 so they don't fall behind in levels due to dynamic difficulty. This is because the amount of experience you get for defeating a Nexomon that outlevels you by 10 is still piss poor, and it's faster to just capture a Nexomon in the wild anyway. I personally don't have problems with this, it's a refreshing change to the grind formula and one that I actually like.And no, I'm not telling you what Nexomon I'm using to 1 versus everything, dev. You ain't nerfing my main, and that's that.Money. You're always going to be short on money. Even if you can farm Elemental Shards to save money on Nexotraps, the need for consumables is still going to drain your money like a sink. Even if you grit your teeth and fight 10 trainers in a row, and THEN capture Nexomon in the wild to catch up in levels, you're still going to run out of cash very soon, so that's a problem. I'm pretty sure people hate dynamic difficulty because of this.Nexomon battles. Frankly, it doesn't have the complexity of a Pokemon game. Stats are extremely basic. In fact I think that most Nexomon share the same stats, only separated by their rarity. There are only like 10 real skills per Nexomon(?) and they loop again and again as you level up, although this is a good thing because this means you don't have to go to a relearner constantly. Also, they don't matter that much. There's a joke in the game that goes something like: "You only use one move over and over anyway!" and that's true for the the other 5 Nexomon you're constantly recapturing. In the end the goal is to kick the enemy's ass so a move that gets the job done is a move.Flow. Probably the best thing about the game besides the story. It's hard to describe, but I can feel the amount of hours the devs and the game testers put into the game to make the gameplay loop as fluid as possible. Things feel natural and intuitive, and once you shed your old Pokemon shackles and embrace the Nexomon formula you find it very, very pleasing. You take less overall damage if you just suck it up and feed the wild Nexomon, so just do it, idiot.Puzzles, or almost the lack thereof. There aren't many puzzles, and I appreciate that to hell and back because I HATE puzzles in a game like this. There were some Pokemon fangames that I adored but could never muster the strength to play again because their puzzles are as nightmarish as they are genius.Warpstones, or your equivalent of a world map. The exclusion of a mini map of sorts is definitely a risk the dev took, but it also made me memorize practically every location except the caves, so overall I believe it was the right move. I still want an Escape Rope/Smoke Bomb equivalent though, especially since everyone in the god dang world seem to have the ability to teleport to somewhere except you.Characters. This both a plus and a minus. If we just look at interaction with minor characters, then it's the most well done in an RPG game I've ever seen. You get a clear perception of how the people of each city function etc, and as mentioned both most of them have plenty of dialogue. The bad? Everyone's a minor character besides Coco and the miner girl, shockingly. You feel disconnected to pretty much everyone else, including your "rivals" because they just don't have much scenes. This also diminishes the feeling you get when a certain scene happen very near the end game. Even the Tyrants left a bigger impression than the rivals, and that's saying something. Flaws. The standout is obviously no "new game+", or more accurately no teleporting you back to the world after credits roll. Does it make story sense? Not really, but this is one part I feel like the game should just say ♥♥♥♥ it and let us enjoy whatever content we haven't cleared yet. The rest are very minor. Some I already mentioned above like almost simple battles and characters etc. There are hardly any bugs, although the one I remember was Renovate not clearing status conditions despite advertising so, and the middle trader in Lateria saying "Yes I can finally sell you my wares at a reasonable price!" and then the dialogue just ends there. For now I can't think of anything else but nitpicks so I guess I'll leave it here.All in all, absolutely don't regret my hours spent on this game. Easily the best single player Pokemon-like game I've ever played ever, so much so that I'm DEFINITELY not playing the first Nexomon because I'm almost certainly it would disappoint me and pollute my good feelings for Nexomon: Extinction. Also the rating for that game was pretty meh. But really, this game is great. Absolutely worth the money, time and energy I spent on.P.S. Oh, I remember one flaw now. You took away our attack on Parum, you should've at least let us drop Amelia in a pit of spikes or something, like come on.

_childDocuments_.review: This game title is an absolute blast given its extremely low retail price. I had been a fan of Pokemon since Red & Blue, and now playing Nexomon really brings back a lot of good memories in 2020. Instead of being a clone, Nexomon is a pure traditional RPG built on monster catching mechanics, but the pacing, QOL and story line is strong enough to make Nexomon worth a play. Below are the strongest points i felt Nexomon had delivered extremely well:[Story & Characters]The story writing, suspense and mystery is surprisingly funny and mature at the same time. Characters felt unique and held enough weight for players to actually care and remember. Even random NPC design in town area all look distinct and unique rather than generic makes the immersion of game world felt alive. Addition of CoCo as talking companion with the protagonist really makes it felt very different from traditional story telling.[Graphics]For 1/5 price of standard Pokemon, the 2D background couple with animation and bright coloring really blends and mesh well in overall presentation. Battle animation is flashy yet smooth and fast, makes the grinding a lot more fast pace and enjoyable. The character design are also very cute and funny at times, giving a very enjoyable feel throughout game play.[Music]It is smooth and soothing, yet creative enough for the ear to remember. [Quality of Life]There are so many improvement if you compare this to standard Pokemon. One example is healing center, instead of  making a pointless NPC dialogue and animation of laying down your monster on the healing pod, Nexomon reduces this whole process to around 3 seconds. Fighting is also much smooth as attack animation is fast and direct. Since players are expected to grind & repeat, healing and battle should be fast to facilitate it. The Developers are also very generous in providing free loot throughout the world, which makes exploration very encouraging.[Progression]This game certainly packs a punch, which is much welcome. Wild monsters and NPC will gain scaling and Bosses are actually tough to challenge. But because of the QoL, grinding is definitely not an issue, and players are encourage to prepare which is the essences of RPG. Scaling is also very welcome because players can now actually catch a higher level monster with less grind to reach next evolution stage instead of getting a level 5 monster when your main party is already 50s. Making the completion of dex much more manageable and players can also easily make line-up changes without having to re-grind the new member too much.There are also alot of interesting side quests (500++), lots of chest and loots that rewards players for exploration. The crafting system utilizing shards is also engaging and purposeful, which is motivating for players who puts in effort to collect and do everything the game has to offer.Highly recommended title!

_childDocuments_.review: I find it sad that people are actually complaining about difficulty - the newer Pokemon games suffer from just this - BEING WAY TOO EASY. Yet when something comes out with a little difficulty that requires common sense, people get upset because they cant mindlessly button press their way through the game anymore.  I see the complaint about level scaling as well and within 30 minutes I figured out an easy solution - DON'T LEVEL ONE SPECIFIC NEXOMON OTHERWISE THE OTHERS WILL BE LEFT IN THE DUST.  You need to level your team evenly or the wild Nexomon will end up being higher level than the ones you neglected.  In reality, that is your fault, yet people still complain.  You could just catch new Nexomon, yet people still complain.  Level your team evenly and the level scaling becomes unnoticeable.  Bought this game at 8 pm and it was 12:40 am before I even looked at the clock a second time and I wanted to keep playing but had to sleep for work. This is coming from someone who has played and beat every single pokemon game that has come out with the exception of ultra sun and moon and the newer atrocities they released as Pokemon games as well.  The mainstream games have no appeal anymore because they are obvious cash grabs with absolutely no difficulty or real thought put in.  This is a breath of fresh air.After beating the game at 34 hours I can say this is a must buy for anyone that is a fan of Pokemon or monster catching games - they have added more QoL improvements as well as other fixes which only makes the game more enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: There is this stigma that because something is inspired by something that came before it, that automatically makes it bad. That is completely untrue in the case of Nexomon: Extinction. You can't avoid drawing comparisons to Pokemon, no matter how hard you try. People just do it all the time, but in my humble opinion, Nexomon ups Pokemon in many ways. Story, Gameplay, and level design all come together beautifully in Nexomon to make a game that feels like a return to more classic Monster-catching games but also finds a way to outdo them. You will find new ways to traverse the environment as you progress through the story, allowing you to travel back to previous areas to explore new nooks and crannys.The game is also completely open from the moment you complete the small intro. You can go to almost any region that isn't 100% plot important. All wild battles scale with your level, so it is hard to be over or under leveled for anything. If you want a good challenge and story that remind you of the golden era of Monster Taming games, then give the game a shot. It has enough bang for your buck.

_childDocuments_.review: Very worthy sequel to an already excellent Pokemon-like game.Unfortunately Nexomons are still mono types, although they did introduce two more. They have more stat variety, but you'll end up using only the starters and legendaries, because they are the only ones that get the strongest damaging moves.Speaking of moves, status effects went from broken in the first game to almost useless here, low proc chance and no / very weak damage on the move itself. So there's almost no strategy, just use your strongest attack and hit your opponent weakness.The post-game is also imo a bit worse than in the first game, shorter and it's almost just a capture fest with very very low catch rates (but there are now ways to improve it).Overall though, the story is fun, soundtrack is great, graphics look good, plays perfectly on Steam Deck and I hope we get another sequel!

The open world is very nice, but once you that there are barely any differences between monsters of the same type, it loses its meaning.Moreover, this game does not try to be more than a shallow pokemon clone. It does not try to add anything new to the formula and has no redeeming qualities. It is just pokemon with fewer types and moves, a less intricate stat system, no abilities, no strategy, etc.Unfortunately, I only understood all this after playing other, more original monster catchers, e.g. Cassette Beasts or Disc Creatures. Even Coromon, which is also just a pokemon clone, is better than this, because it actually tries to be as good as pokemon once was. This game is just lacking in every way that matters, and I can not recommend it over any other monster catcher.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my wishlist for ages and recently finally got it. It looks like a cheap pokemon copy at the first glance but this thought ended up being far from the truth. The story was really impressive for the genre. I don't think I played any other monster catching game with such a nice story. I constantly wanted to know more about the characters and the world. The characters were not static and the story did have some turning points and plot twists. I even stopped after the first few hours and picked up the first game since many events and characters were referenced. It is worth playing the first game even though the first game is bad compared to this one. It is not required to play the first one though. It actually even spoils some twists. In addition to that you get to see some pretty dope artwork at certain key points during the story. The quality of those varies for some reason though. The artwork for getting your first Nexomon was one of the best for example. While the characters lines were usually well written and funny, they did force 4th wall breaking jokes a bit too often tbh.The fights were not really impressive imho.. you basically just spam the strongest move with type advantage you have against the current enemy. You can bring some strategy to fights in the form of healing your Nexomon but that's probably it. Maybe I am not "competetive" enough to rate the combat system though. Otherwise the gameplay was awesome though. TONS of quality of life features. Travelling is easy but not too easy, as in you can't just teleport everywhere from anywhere. Exp share is a thing but you have a lot of control over it, as in which Nexomon receives how much shared exp. In addition to that there are other QoL items in the game like a monster repel which stays active as long as you want it to stay active, allowing you to ignore random encounters entirely. If you do want to encounter monsters, however you don't want to fight all of them, there is an item that guarantees the flee options from battles. There is actually a quite decent post game in Nexomon. Except the generic "catch all Nexomon" thing you do unlock some post game quest lines and I even heard of an bigger upcoming update that is coming soon. Since there are over 300 Nexomon you can train you will have enough things to do anyways. You can battle trainers you have beaten again as often as you want and there is a lot to explore even after you are done with the main story line! Engaging story, tons of (mostly) interesting Nexomon to catch, impressive QoL features and decent post game. Totally worth the price if you like the genre or want to get into it!

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry for my english, its not my main language!In the first few hours this game was so tedious. But after my gold was not so limited anymore, i stocked up on healing items and i had a blast.Just a little story: At the beginning i went to an area i was not supposed to go yet and guards blocked my path. I got the option "Try to stop me!" or "Alright i go back...". I chose the first one, obliterated their mons and proceeded walking around, searching for cool mons to catch there. I think that was super fun and gave me a big feeling of freedom. Enemy-Levels scale with your story progress, so i didnt struggle too much by going off-road. Had a nice "open-world"-feeling!The story doesnt take itself very serious but at the same time it does. There is actually a good story in there and dialogue is very well written, while managing to ruin my immersion every few minutes by breaking the fourth wall. Its like a crazy rollercoaster, especially towards the end. Some plot-twists just came out of nowhere. I loved it!The graphics look clunky. Dont know how else to describe it. There is definitely room for improvements. I loved the battle-backgrounds though. Also, there are some reeeally cool mon designs! (And some really weird ones, i guess...)Music was a mixed bag for me, similar to the graphics. I hated it when it tried to be generic "Spooky-Music", "Beach-Music" and so on. I loved it when it tried to be original and unique.I will be honest, the mechanics could be better, but at least it works. Its very simple and there is not much depth. Nexomon with the same element are almost identical. Cores (equipment items) are a bit bland/grindy and equipping them to your mons is tedious, especially if you use more than 6 mons, like me. I liked the cores that helped me gain more Exp though! Its very fun to see your Exp-gain going crazy, also it safes a lot of time.Balancing is all over the place. For example, some of the mons learn Scratch (one of the weakest attacks) as their second-last move at Level 50 or so, while at the same time learning their already strongest move at Level 10. Its weird and almost feels randomly-generated.Forging your individual strategy felt unrewarding. Since the game is actually very unforgiving, you have little space to go "out of the meta" which is simply spamming your strongest attack. I had some success with Healing-focused strategies, to some degree. I tried really hard to make useful and interesting strategies, but it was unrewarding and just didnt work out. There are also not that many options to work with.I missed a in-battle status-check. I mean, you can check the stats of your Nexomon, but you cant check if your "This attack has a 30% chance to decrease opponents Defense" actually triggered or not. There is literally no feedback and some things you can only find out by tedious testing. I still dont know if buffs or debuffs stack. An in-game explanation for special-effects would also be very nice (what does "puzzled" even mean?!)I criticised a lot here, but in the end its crazy how much content and fun i got out of this, its a steal, especially when its on sale!A sequel is already announced and i hope they will look over the mechanics, gameplay and balancing a bit more this time. But only if that unique charm isnt lost in the process! Wouldnt be worth it.

I'd highly recommend giving this game a chance, if you haven't played the first one it's worth giving a shot but this version of Nexomon is a vast improvement. Item use has a nice quality control to it between battles and the idea of having certain Nexomon available after completing certain tasks helps the game progress gradually without it feeling too broken at the start with team building. Grinding levels has always been a thing for monster taming games so people can't really complain on that part because Pokemon has been the master of grinding levels for your team for years. With new features like modding the game is really fun and refreshing so every experience is different playing the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this one, it does a couple of things right and also a couple of things not so right.The good:-you can actually rematch trainers-and related to that, the levels scale to your team so you'll never end in underleveled fights.-Money is actually pretty easy to earn since you can actually get money from wild encounters.-You can actually tell at what level they evolve in the database.the bad:-Even though there is a large selection of Nexomon, every one of them is single--type and there are only 9 types so there isn't too much variation.-Adding to that, the nexomon can only learn moves of their own type and normal moves-Some of the type match-up is kinda weird, like rock being weak to wind and a bunch of others, i advice looking up a type-chart(for Extinction because it's slightly different from the first game)- This one might be a personal preference thing but when you use a potion during battle, it's always on the first Nexomon in your team by default, not on the one that you're currently fighting with and it can be a bit disorientingAll in all, as far as pokeclones go, this one was more enjoyable than Temtem

_childDocuments_.review: is a monster collecting RPG game that comes as the second entry in the series. It is not necessary to have played the first in order to jump into this game, even though there are some references back to the first game.It's a fairly standard monster-catching/taming/battling game where you take the role of a young Nexomon tamer and follow the storyline events, through the process you will earn money, find loot, fight and trap Nexomon, and fight against trainers and gradually progress. There are Tyrants to face on your journey as bosses. You will end up facing against the same trainers with increased difficulty later on. You will be able to take on side quests as well. There are different regions in the game that have effects on your monsters because of their types and you have to manage things to best suit the situations that you are in.I have a lot of experience playing  games and so with that also comes certain expectations for games that have a similar gameplay and even a similar name. I have not been able to really enjoy this game all that much because this game tries so hard to be  but just falls short a bit in several major ways.+ You can fight trainers multiple times, this allows you to earn some additional money when needed.+ The artwork looks really good, the creatures are designed well.+ There are many Nexomon to collect, over 300 (closer to 400 actually).+ You can find a lot of loot throughout the game.+ There are no game editions restricting specific monsters like you see in - Unfairness in battles,  unfair for the player. When you fight against another trainer you or the opposing trainer can switch out Nexomon accordingly. If you switch a monster, the opposing trainer can hurt your monster that turn. If the AI trainer does a switch, you cannot do the same to them. It just does not make sense to me and feels unfair. It leaves a sour taste in the mouth.- The monster catching process involves a bit of button mashing on the controller to increase your chances. I really do not like that at all. And in turn, you will likely need multiple traps to catch any one Nexomon.- The world is populated with too many NPCs that it feels quite overwhelming. I ended up skipping by most of them instead of trying to talk to them, to get their stories, etc.- No trading system.- No Nexomon breeding.- No shinies.- Overall the game just feels like it's trying to be  but it ends up falling short and leaves a bit of disappointment for a true  fan.The artwork is pretty good, and the battle screens/animations resemble the  styles, just not as good.These are very nice aspects of the game.This game is meant to be played with a controller, but it can also be played with a keyboard.It is 19.99 Euro/USD base price. It's double the price of the original in USD, but more than double in Euros because of lack of regional pricing for the EU.I did try to like  for what it is, but its flaws kept wearing away at my patience. Being a hardcore  fan, I was not very impressed. For people who enjoyed the first game, you will probably find a similar amount of enjoyment in this installment. For people who have never played  or maybe even dislike it, but still want a monster-taming adventure, this is perhaps a title to reach for.I cannot recommend it for people who, like me, have thoroughly enjoyed all of the  games. I was rather disappointed, and I think you might be too, in just some of the game aspects that have become integral to the monster-taming games. It just whet my appetite for the next actual  installment without offering any significant satisfaction in the gameplay. The battles in their unfair nature also left a bitter feel.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely phenomenal and I'm looking forward to its sequel.  In this review, I'm going to mention what this game excels at, some factors that could further amplify the game, as well as some suggestions of my own.  This is simply my opinion and it's entirely up to the incredible developers what to leave or take.+ As for what Nexomon excels at.  It an engaging story that pulls you in and keeps you on the edge of your seat, begging for more.  Where this truly shines is that it doesn't take the typical black/white approach of "we are good and they are evil," rather, it has the player questioning their OWN position in the story whether what they are doing is truly right - very much like how we live our own lives.  This is especially present when the "antagonist" is made clear and we are questioning our actions against them, as they haven't technically done something wrong.+  Compared to Pokemon, the functionality of Nexomon is astronomically simpler.  There are no EVs or IVs, there is only 1 defensive stat to track (just defense, no special defense), you can explore a large portion of the map before even beginning the story (it's not aggressively holding your hand), and the game scales in level (mapwide) as you progress the story.  Some combination of these factors can be unappealing to some, but ultimately simplifies the game, making it much more casual friendly, which I find is a huge plus, drawing in casual players by eliminating the "necessity" for micromanaging team-building.- As for what could be improved on.  I felt the many of the Nexomon were relatively bland, outside of appearances, specifically the learnsets and similar behavior of a plethora of the skills in the game.  For example, for the former, most plant-type Nexomon learn mostly the exact same moves, but at different levels (the learnsets).  That's not to say there weren't some signature moves (such as one for the mon that carried me through the story, Odiborg the lightning 'spider'), it just felt like most of the nexomon lacked uniqueness for their absence of signature moves (or abilities - which aren't in the game).  - On a lesser note, there are several moves that a blatantly useless.  For example, why would I use a move that deals no damage but has a 40% chance to confuse, when I could instead use a move that has 50 base-power with a 30% chance to confuse?  Similarly, why would I use an 75 base-power move with a 25% chance to crit and 80% accuracy, when I can use a 100 base-power move with a 5% chance to crit and 100% accuracy?  However, if the reason for this is to have players figure out what makes a better move to pick, then this is perfectly acceptable, as I fully understand the need for "new player's traps."~ As for what to challenge you with, I suggest focusing on the uniqueness factor of Nexomon (the monsters, not the game).  That was the main thing that bugged me the most, as many other monster catchers set their way of defining a unique creature is by having an ability that no other species can have, which might be something to consider.  If that deviates too much from Nexomon's intentions, then I would simply suggest signature moves for each Nexomon, preferably earlier in the game (if it learns them at 50+, then that means for 80%+ of the game, it isn't unique).  I'm aware this isn't easy to do, because to make 3 unique skills for each species, that's roughly 500 skills to come up with, which is no simple task.  Regardless of what Nexomon decides to change for its sequel, I am fully confident it will be the right decision, with another banger of a game to play once more.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Nexomon title and it was a blast. The monster designs are cool and the story is pretty good even though it isn't hard to predict most of it. I really like the jokes that make fun of general RPG / monster hunter mechanics, the previous game and even the potential sequel. I'd definitely recommend it if you're fine with emulator-style controls, because this game does nothing with the mouse despite being a PC version. The keys cannot be remapped, which might be a deal-breaker for some, but the WASD + IJKL setup didn't feel too bad to me.Below are some of the nitpicks I had with the game mechanics which aren't major enough to make me dislike it, but that I hope can improve in updates or the sequel.I didn't really like the capture circle, though the breakdown of factors like status, food and bonus items that aid with capture is awesome. The game didn't really explain how the circle affects the rate - is it the speed, fewer misclicks, both? The game never explicitly covered the type match-ups, but since there are only 9 it isn't too hard to figure it out or look up the Elemental Type Chart available online on the official website.The friend points system doesn't feel very integrated with the rest of the gameplay loop. The game never incentivizes capturing monsters for the sake of capture, so I never had extras that I wanted to release. Capturing a lot of Nexomon just to release them is tedious because of multiple steps and the wheel mechanic. It would also be better if portable storage and portable warpstone items are pointed out by someone, so the player knows to work towards them over the course of the entire game. I never went back to that location till a lot later, so I had no idea a shop opened there.

_childDocuments_.review: I like Pokemon, and I think this game has potential to be a good Pokemon-like, but if I had a time machine and had to tell myself whether or not to play it as it is currently, it would be a soft no. The game is an unambiguous Pokemon clone—I’ll just call the monsters pokemon from now on. It’s single player, so the core of the game is pokemon battles vs NPCs. Unfortunately, the battle system is cruder and less interesting than even Pokemon Gen I. There are fewer types, and no dual-typing, so the rock-paper-scissors mechanic is simple, even with the 6 mon party limit. Because creating a favorable type matchup is trivial, the devs are forced to set the effectiveness multipliers much lower than in Pokemon: +25% bonus for supereffective, -35% for non-effective. In Pokemon, consistently generating favorable matchups against different trainers with different mons requires knowledge of a complex type chart, careful team building, and thoughtful play. The reward is an explosive advantage over even much stronger enemies. In Nexomon, there’s no challenge in forcing a favorable matchup and the reward for doing so is barely worth it—if your enemy is a few levels above you they’ll still beat you 1-on-1.There are plenty of pokemon to catch, but there is little variety in how they play beyond type advantages. Nexomon drops the physical/special distinction, and base stats don’t vary that much. Nexomon also drops abilities, so mons are defined exclusively by their BST and movepool. EV spreads do have an equivalent in “cores”, which give you 4 slots to put stat buffs. Sadly the movepools are very small, and there is no analogue to TMs. Generally, mons get access to the a small set of moves from their typing, plus a few normal type moves for neutral coverage, making battles extremely predictable—enemies will hit you with normal moves if you have a type advantage and their own type otherwise. There are very few strategically interesting moves when compared to Pokemon. Most useful moves vary only in terms of base power, accuracy, crit chance, and mana cost. Status moves have very low proc chances, making them difficult to use outside of boss battles, which feature high HP, low damage enemies and therefore long fights that benefit from permanent status effects. Buffs and debuffs are generally quite weak, e.g. a move that decreases an opponent’s attack stat by 15%. Battles boil down to clicking your best attack until your enemy is dead and switching to an appropriate counter if your current mon can’t win 1-on-1. While Pokemon has experimented with a variety of single-player battle formats, Nexomon exclusively features the classic format-- 1-on-1 battles with 6 mon parties. The upshot of all this is that almost every battle you fight in Nexomon reduces to the mindless attack spamming and potion quaffing of the most basic JRPGs. There are also many QoL problems and other design oversights, but those are frequently mentioned in other reviews.This is all a shame, because Pokemon games have many shortcomings that could be addressed in an indie like this. Pokemon has always set the single-player difficulty to 0 in order to appeal to small children, and a pokemon-like that featured NPC trainers with a broad range of challenging strategies and creative moves and abilities that might be imbalanced in competitive play but fun and rewarding in single player could be a big step forward for the genre. Instead, Nexomon's method of upping the difficulty is to simply overlevel your opponents. A game with uninspired combat can still be good if it has a great setting and story, but NE has some shortcomings here, too. I said NE is a Pokemon clone, but it’s really halfway between an early gen Pokemon game and a generic 90’s JRPG. Many of the features that distinguished Pokemon from its JRPG forebears are rolled back here—Pokemon (at least initially) replaced warfare with a competitive sport and hopeless quests to avert apocalypse with what is essentially a sports story—rising to the top of your game. NE tries to present a more mature, grittier take on the classic kid’s game—this isn’t about having fun with your pokemon and being the very best, this is life and death!—but this inversion of the Pokemon formula is simply the generic portentous JRPG story that Pokemon itself inverted. This extends to gameplay—mana (in the form of stamina) replaces PP and RPG-style plot-based battles replace the structured gym challenges of Pokemon.Despite having a lot of JRPG boilerplate, the story has some interesting twists. However, the writing often falls short. Characters act in ways that serve to further the plot through its twists and to its climax but seem bizarre in the moment, only becoming rationalizable based on information the characters themselves learn later. The story is totally linear, so this includes your own choices, which often seem insane or evil when you’re making them. The story’s big shounen payoff moments—former enemies and old friends taking dramatic stands with you against the world—feel unearned, as most characters get little development or interaction with your silent protag. Besides your sassy narrator/silent-protag-interpreter Coco, only the last boss seems to have any real rapport with you—he rails off an endless stream of ponderous JRPG anti-villain dialogue during your final battle. In contrast, in this story your orphaned character finds out their mother is alive and has set the entire plot in motion—everything that happens to you, everything that you do—loses her again, and has the chance to get her back in the postgame. If you do, the resolution to the biggest thread in the story and the presumably most emotionally charged experience your character has is a single line of dialogue and a pokemon battle.Nexomon hedges its bet on the gritty story with plenty of humor, but its approach is quantity over quality. Characters constantly break the fourth wall and lampshade both the tropes of the genre and most of the shortcomings I’ve described above, but the jokes are very perfunctory—the lowest of low hanging fruit. E.g. “The game’s over, someone roll the credits!” “The developers didn’t have money to animate me properly lol”. There aren’t any laugh-out-loud moments or memorable punchlines. Nexomon Extinction is a simple and sometimes fun Pokemon-like that is frank about its own shortcomings, but wryly acknowledging those problems doesn't fix them.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun pokemon-alike, interesting mobs, but short of having to get your badge early on to access areas you pretty much can run around as much you want to hunt whatever nexomon type you want without waiting on the plot to let you (i went after ghost types extremely early and you can just hop a flight to dragon town). Only issue is the nexomon are quite a bit more squishy then pokemon, so expect them to run out of stamina and having to heal alot, so much the game has various methods for you to do this on the go, but you can expect to hear the low hp beep, or the faint animation alot if your just messing around in longer dungeons (or accidently blunder into a boss battle without gulping potions and ethers). Not so much game over but expect to have to hunt down a shiney rock (a full party heal that regenerates on maps) when your off type nexomon gets two shot on a crit hit from something you ran into the grass. Also while most nexomon are fairly balanced, there are a few legendary types and starters that are just plain better. Can be hard to give up a spot for an interesting nexomon when your samurai is taking face hits and slashing cause he's an uber rare, but your cute ghost pokemon dies to one fire blast. Most evolved states though can take a few hits, but early not evolved ones will likely be fairly weak (like a water type bird that did a whole five whopping damage, and died in one hit to anything it was weak too.)

_childDocuments_.review: I completed this game, but that doesn't mean I would recommend this game to anyone else.It is a creature taming/raising Pokemon-like game, so if you like Pokemon you might like this game.My biggest problem with this game is that stat up and/or down moves don't say if they do nothing so it's nearly impossible to tell if they do anything at all. Another problem is that there is no explanation what's the deal with the quick-time catch input. Something you might have heard about is all opponents get stronger as you progress. The main problem with this is that there is no explanation how or why this is. This part wouldn't be so bad if it only affected tamer battles. A big problem for me is shards, there are several types of these that you get randomly, you need these to get "permanent" buffs for your team that you can swap out also they are used for quests, again you get them randomly, so getting a specific one that you want is very difficult. Some things happen for no explanation other than that's how Pokemon does it. Nexomon that don't evolve are basically unusable. Also there are a few small, but noticable bugs.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good price point, great systems, non-stop entertaining. An amazing entry for the monster-trainer genre.A game where you set out to do a quest and get side tracked by new Mons, new quests, new areas, new mechanics, etc. on the way for an hour or two does something right.NPCs offering you trades and side-quests offers a lot to do. Battle animations are fast and snappy so they don't get old even after seeing them a hundred times.Big props to how type advantages are designed! If you min-max you can get a counter for any type with a team of just 4 out of 6 Nexomons. Which means that you have a lot of flexibility when building your team because type match-ups can overlap without leaving holes in your team. That's a really smart way to design your rock-paper-scissors table. It shifts the focus of teambuilding from "optimal and solved" to a matter of preference, how it should be in a game with so many Mons.What I definitely didn't like is that there are SO MANY completely useless moves. Especially status effect inducing skills are just horrible. Like a 30% chance to put the enemy to sleep. You could kill the enemy Mon in the time it might take you to even proc the sleep. Your choices when it comes to move sets are very limited because the vast majority of skills are so abhorrently bad that in reality most Nexomon only learn like 4 to 6 usable ones in total. I sometimes even found myself struggling to fill all 4 move slots because the choices were so bad. Sometimes Nexomon even learn a skill at higher levels that has just straight up worse numbers than a skill they already knew.The good thing is that you can switch moves at a move-trainer at any point for a small price. Additional means to traverse the environment are directly learned by the main character, not your Mons.The fact that Nexomon has level scaling is a bit unconventional but really not an issue. You can still overlevel and underlevel depending on your playstyle. And you can pick up any Mon at any level at any point and get it up to speed with the rest of your team in a reasonable amount of time thanks to XP share items.The humor is great! It's pretty rare to get more than a soft, short chuckle in media these days but Coco, the cat sidekick, has some absolute zingers that had me legitimately laughing. As do some other NPCs and quests.The story is nice, even offers moral ambiguity. And there are several moments where you have to do dubious things to achieve your goals, which is a nice touch for this genre.A bit barren. Would've loved additional info on where to find Nexomons in the wild that you already saw.If there ever is a Nexomon 3, I am here for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Good story, mechanically meh.First thing I'd like to note is this is a very slight thumbs down, I actually enjoyed the majority of my time with the game, but the game simply doesn't give me enough incentive to finish it.Nexomon is a heavily Pokemon inspired monster tamer RPG which has quite a few things going for it. It's main strength is that it has decent writing, a coherent somewhat unpredictable story and a large open world to explore from the get go.Your companion Coco is pretty hilarious and the game never takes itself to seriously, the whole "WHERE ARE YOUR PARENTS" common complaint is actually factored into the story and the world has a structure that makes sense in terms of broad strokes, tamers are organized, Nexomon are seen as dangerous animals and the world is in peril. NPCs update their dialog frequently when certain story beats happen. The story does become formulaic later on after you get a certain mcguffin but its never as simple and straightforward as "get the badges, elite four, win gaem".Side quests are interesting and varied considering the genre, the world is large and has varied locales from deserts, forests, mines, labs, vaults, multiple cities and just feels large and put together. The in battle animations and visuals are fantastic, with great animations on the movement of the Nexomon which is doubly impressive when you consider how many of them there are. Combat animations are also great, being short enough to not get repetitive but expressive and flash enough to be entertaining.So why didn't I finish it? Simply put, the meat and potatoes of the game,  monsters bopping each other, is under cooked. Catching monsters has some annoying fluff that doesn't really add anything to the experience. Most if not all the games mechanical hooks seem interesting at first glance, but are shallow and don't really pique your curiosity or have you theory crafting like other monster tamers.Firstly catching a monster means feeding it something it likes, OK, interesting concept, but what does that mean game-play wise? It means buying a bunch of stuff, scrolling through a menu until a higher percentage comes up and clicking on it... so its not really engaging and kinda just wastes time. Maybe if there was a way to figure out organically what monsters like or food had an actual effect on the battle such as causing status effects or healing the monster so you can get it fully restored after capturing it then maybe...but still kinda half baked.Then you need to do a button press minigame, which is interesting the first 3 times you do it, but quickly devolves into busywork because it never really changes that much. In a turn based RPG based on knowledge why have a twitch based timing puzzle? It seems so out of place.Then we get to the Nexomon themselves, they have no special quirks or unique abilities and their stats are so similar that using any Nexomon of the same type basically yields the same result, so why are there 381 of them? Once you have a strong water type all other water types are moot unless you like the different looking sprites, because they have the same stats, most likely the same movepool and catching them means you lose out on exp. There are no special evolutions, no item based evolutions, no location based ones, time based ones, quest based ones, special event based ones, combat based ones, moveset based ones, zip, nada, nill.Speaking of movepools the game is remarkably shallow, maybe my viewpoint is tainted because I used to be into competitive pokemon battling and love the Shin Megami Tensei battle systems but there just doesn't seem to be much there. Status effects aren't explained anywhere, moves that inflict status have about a 30% chance to proc, buffing stats does next to nothing, de-buffing also does next to nothing and your Nexomon can learn stronger moves earlier or not its completely random! Nexomon also only learn their base element with the exception of normal which learn normal and one extra element, so the basic rock-paper-scissors gameplay just means switching since type coverage isn't a thing. This means movepools require zero thought .The stamina system means you should swap out mons between fights before they become useless, or just take a turn off and use the extremely cheap ether to heal it up. This isn't necessarily a "bad" in theory, they just didn't use it in a strategic way, its just a meter that drains. Why not have really high costing stamina moves but have it completely heal on switch out or at the end of the battle, meaning you really have to plan your moves instead of just healing every now and then.The only interesting moves are healing and absolute barrier which makes you invincible for a couple of turns, there is a speed system which subs in for priority from pokemon, but it never matters because you never outspeed barrier or healing. These aren't even that interesting because you can just use items to substitute for them.The battle system is literally, learn the type chart, hit the guy, swap frequently because your mons can't cover more than one element and use healing/absolute barrier to cheese the simplistic AI, or just potion spam because there isn't much else to do. Bosses are also just big dudes, normal mons with more HP and stamina, no unqiue strategies, no buffing/de-buffing, no in battle conversations they are all the same.Why not some high dps glass cannon bosses, some tank bosses, some sneaky bosses, bosses that rely on status effects, stallers, sweepers, item abusers?There is an equipment system but its literally just flat boosts to exp/damage/defense/status resistance with the only interesting one being exp share, a huge missed opportunity, I know they didn't want to copy pokemons item system but if they were gonna go the raw stat equips why not sets of cores, with bonuses like special effects or even special stats? Use the cores costing a lot of stamina like a heal or burst of damage?The crafting system is also pretty basic, you mine rocks and make nexotraps and cores, that's it, it's always a rock that looks exactly the same, which makes it just seem like busywork, maybe having a nexomon harvest from different looking resources? Getting resources from beating certain types of nexomon (eg: grass mon drops sap, earth mon drops clay, water drops fish scales etc) which gives you an excuse to move around the environment but it just feels like it has nothing to do with taming or Nexomon at all.Items are also pretty boring, there is no TM system to teach moves, no berry or held item systems, no There are item trades that give things that reduce prices by a certain small percent, boost exp by a percent, give discounts or increase coin gain but the problem is tiny percent increases are just BORING, did anyone really think "YES 3 PERCENT MORE EXP, WORTH IT", NPCS also trade items that includes special type based nexo traps, food and other things but it highlights the fact that there are zero Nexomon based trades, but there really couldn't be because there isn't much special about the Nexomon.There isn't any PVP but honestly the battle system isn't deep enough to support PVP.Overall I'm more disappointed in Nexomon than anything, it's clear the developers put a lot of love into the product, they are listening to the community and patching things in at a quick pace and I honestly don't regret my purchase if only to fund Nexomon 3. I sincerely hope that they add more depth to the core game play because the story and novelty/world alone carried me through 20+ hours of gameplay, its just now that my mons are reaching lvl 40 and I've fought enough tamers and bosses to realize that I'm just going through the motions, there isn't really anything to look forward to besides more damage sponge bosses and statistically identical Nexomon.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER - Play the first game! I unfortunately doubted that there was a first game, but there is. go play that one first. You don't HAVE TO to enjoy the game but I think its better if you did.Yes. Yes. Yes. YESThis game is epic. If you have felt unhappy with the newer Pokemon games you will LOVE this. Mind you this isn't a Pokemon Clone or ripoff. This is a Monster Catching Game. It fits within a sub-genre of RPG similar to how "Battle Royal" is a sub-genre of shooters. The story, the mechanics and the strategies you use are going to be fairly different than in Pokemon. First off there is no power point system for each individual move. Nexomon have stamina and each move or skill they have requires a set amount of stamina. Many of these skills inflict damage but some inflict statuses as well. Some skills only inflict statuses while others change how damage is dealt. There is a type system that I believe is more balanced than Pokemon's MASSIVE list of all the different types. Nexomon have 7(?) types i believe. Fire, Water, Wind, Mineral, Lightening, Ghost and Psychic. I may have missed one there. But anyway, different strategies include - trying to outlast your enemy by exhausting all their stamina, this causes them to have to take a whole turn to recharge some of it. It may also render some skills useless as they'd need to wait 2 or even 3 turns (the latter being rare) to recharge enough stamina to use that skill effectively. Another strategy is letting a nexomon die to get a free switch in. Now this strategy has been seen in pokemon I will admit but, Nexomon health fells more precious. There are fewer skills to restore your health and the ones that do don't do it in large enough quantities to really make a huge difference or require a large chunk of your stamina to activate. So, at least in my experience, health is more valuable in Nexomon and deciding to sacrifice one near-death Nexomon to conserve health for another that might have type-advantage is a calculated loss. So the story, this story (about 15-20 hours in) honestly beats out any story of any Pokemon game I've been exposed to. Now I haven't played the mystery dungeon series or the Pokemon Ranger series but as far as the main games go? They don't ever come close to this. Pokemon Black and White had a grand story that is very good but it just doesn't match the scale of this one. I have yet to finish the game but so far I have gotten to the biggest plot twist and MY GOD that was wild. This game doesn't hold your hand either. Even if you are even leveled with type-advantage, RNG might be your doom. I make sure to grind all my Nexomon up to where they are all equal level and at least 2 levels above what I think the game will throw at me next.Lastly, If you don't like 4th wall humor, this game may not be your cup of tea. This game will break the 4th wall for a joke at the drop of a hat, at one point it will make fun of you for laughing at 4th wall breaks. I adore this game's incredibly sarcastic humor. It doesn't take itself too seriously but it still has an awesome tone to it and honestly? So far this is my best game of 2020.Now with all those pros there's gotta be some cons right? Yeah....- graphical glitches (rare)- 4th wall humor can get a little old but they typically try to space it out-  Wind Nexomon in particular seem just kinda weak in general.- I think when you lose a fight you should be punished more harshly than just being sent back to your last save with all Nexomon at half health and half stamina- the moves aren't big and flashy like you see in later stage Pokemon games like Black and White, not really something i think everyone cares about but its a personal gripe- Wild Nexomon scaling with you. i prefer how pokemon handles wild levelsIt was difficult for me to get into this game but.... just finish the first quest you get as a Bronze tamer. That's where I was hooked.PS: this game has samurai riding dragons in sky island japan. Pokemon does not have that. Checkmate.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros--------------Interesting story full of TONS of unexpected developments-Hundreds of creatures that all feet unique in design-Memorable characters with a good level of personality -Many battles actually feel challenging and tense -Gorgeous environments that all feet different from the last-Gives the PC lots of room to free roam early on, while still never leaving you lost on what's next-Optional exploration out the wazoo. Quality of life items, rare Nexomon, cosmetic companions, and plenty more. Including an entire region that's untouched by the main story.-Good balance of goofy humor thrown everywhere, while still having emotional tense moments throughout -Balanced money economy and level scaling-Plenty of optional quests, most of which are unique and interesting. There's also citizens all over that have useful rare items if you're willing to trade.-Unique Cores>Held Items system brings a nice bit of change to the usual system-Option to do a customized run after finishing the story (individual Nuzlocke mechanics, randomizer, no level cap, carry over a team from a used save, general easy/hardmode settings, etc.)-Each area is a habitat for new Nexomon. While some common ones show up in multiple areas, the majority are fresh, which makes exploring each new place feel worthwhile-Minimal hand-holding the PC through mechanics. Not every obvious system is expounded upon by a 5 minute NPC dialogue. -On that note, not once did I feel the need to spam through text boxes while slamming my head in a George Foreman. The game keeps a good pace throughout the whole story.-Enough good music variety to keep the adventure feeling fresh. Each area definitely has a vibe to match.-Smooth, quick animations. Combat related, cutscenes, screen transitions, idles, environment ambiance, etc. While nothing is elaborate per-say, nothing ever felt jarring, too robotic, or too slow.Cons--------------Maybe more of a personal gripe, but in order to fully enjoy it, I felt the need to trash my starter, and only use mons with varied rarities until I finished the main story. Some of the best designed monsters are of the lower rarities, and are still used on opponents' teams the entire game, so why not yours? "The rarer the better stats" system feels unbalanced when it's possible to get a full team of Mega Rares within the first couple hours with enough exploration.-Move variety/balance. The move list fell really flat for me. More often than not, when a move is learned while leveling: you'll skip it. Too many moves learned later on (across ALL rarities) that are just intrinsically worse than what was learned 20 levels back. A related aside: all but the occasional normal type mon will ONLY have attacking moves of their own type. No coverage moves, there's hardly any decent setup moves, and most status moves are too inaccurate/situational to feel worth keeping around. While battles were still fun, the lack of viable combat variety grew stale about halfway through my playthrough.Final Word-------------Definitely try it out if you like the genre! There's 20-30 hours of game here, depending on if you enjoy the exploration and sidequests or just beeline through the story. More with endgame. The engaging story, design, personality, and the creatures themselves shine through the negatives here. For the size of the team behind it, the polish and storytelling was worth every bit of time and money put into it. The first game I felt compelled to 100% in years :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game plays a lot like the pokemon franchise, but it's a lot harder. The battles can be unforgiving early-on due to the monsters not having decent attacks (type advantage is critical!). You can pretty much adventure from the get-go. Although it is best to progress at least past the first main quests to do so. This will unlock a few options for you which will aid you in the rest of your story. Whichever way you decide to adventure, keep in mind that you will have to follow the storyline eventually... Either to progress further or because the game becomes too easy. Be warned about the active level-scaling. The monsters scale upwards to about your level. Which keeps the game challenging, but a bit harder than most. The level-scaling depends on where you're at in the main story, so if you rush the game it will become real difficult real fast. The level scales up by 5 levels or so, each time. So early-on this might seem a bit drastic if you rush through. Keep in mind that there is (by my account) no exp-share item in this game, a monster needs to participate in a battle in order to gain experience. There is an alternative to this in the form of some exp-sharing cores (a core is an equipable item for your monsters). But if i'm not mistaken, this is something which is recently added to the game. At the very least, I just found out after about a full lvl 50 team and progressing pretty far in the main story.   All in all, I like this game and its challenges. It's a bit more difficult than most games of the genre, but its very much achievable if you keep certain things in mind. What keeps me playing the game is the way the story is written, it's not a typical 'pokemon clone' where you adventure to become the very best or to catch them all. No, this game has a few funny, intruiging and unexpected plot twists.EDIT: There have been some aditions to the game since writing my initial review. These include the resting option in combat, the synergy cores, tamers not automatically want a rematch after you already beat them once, these healing stones that spawn in certain areas. Having played for 6 whole hours with these aditions, I can already say this makes the game so much easier. Too easy even for me! It took some of the challenges out of the game... challenges I, myself, really enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: I have reviewed the original Nexomon game already, so for this review there will be a lot of comparison between Nexomon 1 and Nexomon Extinction.So let’s get into the review:Price & is it worth it?Nexomon Extinction is priced at £16.99, and despite being over double the price of the original Nexomon game, you are still getting your money’s worth and more with the £16.99 price tag. In comparison to the original Nexomon game, Nexomon Extinction has a LOT more content: a better in-depth story, more innovative Nexomon designs, side quests, lots of end-game content, the list can go on. You are paying for what you get, and with Nexomon Extinction, you get countless hours of fun monster taming content.Storyline & QuestsThe storyline is extremely enjoyable in Nexomon Extinction. Character backgrounds, character development, a diverse range of beautiful environments, Nexomon universe lore, this game has a lot to offer in terms of the story. Whilst Nexomon 1’s was quite basic and shallow, Nexomon Extinction’s storyline thrives and really keeps you intrigued. Especially with the multiple plot twists that happen throughout, everything links together in a clever way.Nexomon Extinction DesignsIn my opinion, the Nexomon’s designs in Extinction is a big step above the Nexomon’s designs in the original game. The design in Nexomon 1 had gotten quite repetitive and felt basic. It felt like quantity was prioritised over quality. However, Nexomon Extinction stepped up their game, and to me, each design felt more thought-out and interesting.Nexomon Extinction TypesIn additional to the original 7 types in Nexomon 1: Normal / Wind / Fire / Water / Electric / Plant / Mineral - Nexomon Extinction has added 2 additional types: Psychic and Ghost. I felt like this is a nice addition as it brings more diversity to the game and allows for more strategic gameplay. I also am a big fan ofthe ghost type Nexomon in particular, as they give a very cool, sleek and creepy appearance.Nexomon Extinction StartersWith the original Nexomon game featuring a starter for each type, Nexomon Extinction has followed in its footsteps and gives the option for 9 different starters, an additional 2 for the newly introduced types: Ghost and Psychic. Starters are catchable in the wild, and so I played through the game with 6/9 of the starters to really a get a feel for their use and capabilities. Overall, I can confidently say that VEWO Interactive did an amazing job with the starter evolutions lines. Each starter felt different, and most specialised in various altering playstyles. Each evolution also felt very refreshing in design and appearance.Nexomon Extinction’s Experience / Level Up / Stamina mechanicsNexomon Extinction’s mechanics has improved MASSIVELY compared to the original Nexomon game. Nexomon’s 1 experience was far too easy and quick to grind, making the levelling up incredibly fast, and the stamina system obsolete. Nexomon Extinction has improved on this by making the experience required per level-up higher, and scrapping the original system of regaining full health and stamina after each level up. Overall, Nexomon Extinction feels like more of a challenge and a finished product compared to Nexomon 1.Nexomon Boss BattlesIn my opinion, the boss battles in Nexomon Extinction has improved a lot in comparison to Nexomon 1. The boss battles felt more challenging, more diverse and a lot more enjoyable overall.End-game ContentNexomon Extinction’s end-game content is one of its strongest offerings. Unlike Nexomon 1, Nexomon Extinction offers a plethora of different content such as side quests to unlock important items, vaults to find high valued loot, findable companions that follow your in-game character around, additional post-game completion quests to unlock all of the Legendary Nexomon and a completely FREE DLC: Nexomon Abyssmal. Overall, there is a lot of content still available past post-game completion.Likes- Good character development and greater links to the overall plot of the story- Able to choose character design- A better introduction to the story than Nexomon 1- 9 starters to choose from, 2 more than Nexomon 1, including new Psychic and Ghost types- Great starter choices & evolution lines- Game soundtracks are very fitting and well suited- UI is a lot more neat, sleek and better in layout compared to Nexomon 1- Moves now display full statistics of power/accuracy/stamina/speed and crit chance- Moves are more diverse- Nexomon’s stats are better displayed in battle (HP/Stamina) on display compared to Nexomon 1- Love that the game gives a link and starts with an immediate reference to Nexomon 1 when you are in the tombs (shows a picture of the crew from Nexomon 1 and says how they were bravest warriors of their generation) sets the scene and time frame of how far in the future the current storyline is- More Nexotraps diversity in Nexomon Extinction compared to Nexomon 1- Improved animations, such as hand throwing animation of Nexotraps- New ‘Capture Change’ breakdown screen where it shows your chances of capturing the wild Nexomon with each subsection and factor- New feeding feature for Nexomon to allow for easier captures- Lots of different Nexomon traps available for each type to improve capture rate- Countdown timer when capturing a Nexomon- Gives Nexomon’s stat information when capturing them as well as description of them- Finally given the option to nickname Nexomon- Nexomon Extinction has critical hits- Better organised storage box system - able to create different groups- No more instant attacked after defeating enemy Nexomon mechanic- There are now held items “cores” and key items- There is now a journal system to show main quest and side quest task progression- A much more in-depth story with plot twists and shock factors- Semi open world exploration available- Nicer environments (dragon island) (underwater city) etc- Better Nexomon designs, more detailed- Unique pathing elements (using Tyrant’s eggs to get rid of fire, jump over gaps, freeze water etc)- More exp required to level up each level - makes it more fun and challenging than Nexomon 1- Fixed overpowered status moves- Status conditions have been fixed and are no longer overpowered- Status conditions no longer automatically heal after each battles - makes the game more challenging- Move accuracy and status accuracy are longer mixed up and can be read separatelyDislikes- No difficulty option to toggle or make the experience more challenging (because of the above reasons)- No EXP granted after each Nexomon defeated in trainer battles - you have to defeat the whole team to get experience- No IV/EV system - lacks diversity- No HM/TM Moves- Rarity System is a bit unstable - you sometimes would find Mega Rares within a few seconds of each other and then Uncommons wouldn’t show for about 10 - 15 minutes of searching- Pre-shaken grass to show where Nexomon are - makes it so you don’t have to go through wild encounters and can just skip every wild battle during the whole gameUnique things to note- No more automatic EXP Share mechanic- Only partial HP & Stamina recover upon levelling up- First turn is based on Speed Stat- There is a rarity system - each Nexomon falls under: Common/Uncommon/Rare/Mega Rare/Special/Legendary rarity brackets- You can get multiple Golden Nexotraps (master ball equivalent to Pokémon)- Legendaries are catchable in the wild
