_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Pokémon, then chances are you'll probably enjoy this. I went into this game initially thinking it was just a watered down Pokémon clone. But as I played, I found myself warming up to the game very quickly. Overall, I had a good time raising my Nexomon and I had an enjoyable time with the game as well. Since this game was clearly inspired by Pokémon though, do be warned that there will be a lot of comparisons to it. Also, for the 6 people who'll maybe read this review and the 2 of you who will care, I didn't play the first Nexomon game. Frankly I wasn't aware that this was a sequel, so take that however you will. I'll start with graphics, then go into gameplay/things I liked and hated, and end off with story, so that way people who read this in a blurb don't immediately get spoiled.As far as graphics are concerned, they're decent. By no means are the graphics reminiscent of Picasso, but it's also not 3rd grade tier art either. The colors are very vibrant, I thought the character art in some instances was cool, not too impressive but still servicable. I did like some of the character and creature art. Deena and Amelie stood out to me as really good. The Scooptor line of Nexomon is really interesting. My favorite Nexomon were probably Rapilux, Rapnux, Voltaic, and Volta. A lot of the other creature designs were pretty "eh", but none of them were really god awful. And for every "Oh, Bulbrit is just a lightbulb" thought that popped into my head, I also thought "Well, Voltorb is literally just a Pokéball so I'll cut them some slack." Some of their names are also wierd, but again, Pokémon also probably had unusual names at the time. So, how's the gameplay? Not to be one of those armchair game designers/developers, but it certainly has its highs and lows when it comes to design decisions. -The Good- One of the things I found pretty great right off the bat is that once you reach the main city and do your first mission, the game really opens up from there. You can go just about anywhere on the world map and run into minimal progress walls. I caught over 100 different Nexomon (there are 381 in total) before I even started the second mission, if that gives you an idea of how open the world is. I definitely liked that aspect about the game! I like the fact that wild Nexomon and trainers scale with you. When I first saw this advertised on the store page, I was concerned that they would scale all the time, meaning levels were essentially not that useful in the grand scheme of things. But, fortunately, they do scale to a point and eventually you can overtake trainers and wild encounters in level. As someone who actually doesn't mind grinding and investing time into a game, that was reassuring to see. I like the fact that trainers want to rematch you as well. I also like the stamina mechanic. Unlike in Pokémon where you can only use a move a certain amount of times, in Nexomon, you can use a move as many times as you like, but this is limited by the mon's stamina and certain moves have different stamina costs. Different moves also have different speeds and crit rates. So there's a strategic element to where you can purposefully use a slow but powerful move to deal massive damage, then use a weak but faster move to try and hurry and finish off your opponnet.  -The Bad, or How I Learned to Huff Sulfur- Unfortunately, there were a lot of things about this game that drove me up a wall as well, or things that I thought they could do better. I'll try to list my groans about the game in order of annoyance. Despite there being more cons than pros, keep in mind I actually really did like this game and enjoyed it, there are just quirks about it that annoy me. The biggest gripe for me was that the Nexodex or the Database or whatever doesn't show where a Nexomon can be found in the world. In the Pokémon games, when you checked the Pokédex, you had an "area" section that lets you get a general idea of where you could find said Pokémon on the world map. Nexomon doesn't have that. You shouldn't have to go to the Steam Guides or Google to look up where you can find certain mons. Speaking of Steam Guides and Google, I had to look up not only the type advantage chart, but also what the status ailments did.  Now, maybe I missed a tutorial or something, but I don't remember any of that stuff being explained. A really underrated thing about the Pokémon games is that they had a Trainer School or something to that effect. This is so dumb 7 year olds (basically me, mentally) could see what status ailments did. Yes, things like Poison were obvious. But you had to be paying a bit more attention to know stuff like Burn reduces your attack by half in Pokémon. In this game I would've never figured out what status ailments like Frail does without looking it up. A lot of the trainers have "Lance Syndrome" and have fully evolved mons. I remember being around the early-ish middle of the game when this was happening. I'm not sure if that's the result of scaling or if that's just what they naturally have, because admittedly I was pretty over-leveled, I was in my early to mid-30s and people were still in their mid 20s in terms of level. Either way, I think trainers having mons in their final evolution before you've even seen the final evolution ruins a bit of the mystery and charm of trying to raise a mon and find out what it looks like. Not that big of a deal though. The lack of encounter variety was also a bit disappointing. For example, and hopefully this will clarify what I mean, in Pokémon you also found mons in tall grass and caves. But, you could also do stuff like headbutt trees and smash rocks. You could also find mons in the sand, in the water, and in even taller grass. In 4th gen you could slather honey on a tree and attract them. If you were really zany, you could use Sweet Scent to attract wild mons...there were a ton of ways to encounter mons! And while these were small bits, they helped flesh out the world and immerse you. In this game it's kind of disappointingly shallow. You only ever find mons in grass or in caves. Another thing that dreadfully needs variety is the evolution method. All of them are level-based in this game. And look, I get it. At this point you're probably just like "damn dude, just play Pokémon", but in my defense, I don't want this game to be just like Pokémon. I do want it to take what Pokémon did well and expand on it further, and this is one of the things that it did well. Different methods of evolution adds an extra layer of character and uniqueness to each mon. Nexomon doesn't have to have Water, Fire, and Thunder stones. Maybe it could have Nexomon evolve in certain locations, maybe the mons could evolve at a certain happiness threshold (which this game doesn't have either. Your Nexomon don't grow more or less friendly with you, there's no friendship) but either way, there needs to be something other than levels.   Finally, I didn't like the fact that animations can't be turned off, at least that I know of. I looked at the options and didn't see a setting. Turning the animations off, would've made level grinding a lot more convenient and expedient. Thankfully, most of the animations are very brief. So let's talk story. It's pretty decent. It's at least on par with the plots of most Pokémon games, though probably a bit better. If anything, it's actually closer to Mystery Dungeon in terms of story structure. Especially in the fact that the guild you're working for turns out to be a bit evil. Well, they're not evil, they just hate renegades who aren't in the guild. And considering you eventually become a renegade...yeah. There's a bit of a twist to where it's revealed you're actually a tyrant yourself and not a human, which I thought was pretty neat. Then you fight the final boss as yourself and the tyrants you revived, which was pretty awesome. The parts leading up to the end does have a "muh friendship" aspect to

_childDocuments_.review: Scratches that sweet sweet pokemon itch from my childhood. The beginning tone is a little off to me - it seems like it's a little embarrassed to come across as cheesy, whilst also ramping up the stakes super early, and in trying to avoid the cheesy stuff so much and escalating the stakes so quickly it kind of rubbed me the wrong way at first. I like the mechanics of the battles, and I have gasped so many times at some of the creature designs - so CUTE! I really, really appreciate the journal section, it is so helpful to keep track of main quests as well as the extra quests. I kind of wish it was a little easier to see at a glance in the storage base what type a 'mon is, and to a lesser extent that the database had a bit more detail. The worlds are beautiful (if a bit challenging to navigate owing to my innately atrocious sense of direction) and the world-building is amazingly robust and satisfying to unravel the more hours you sink into the game. The NPCs who do trades are a great inclusion, and I'm really digging the Shards, Cores, and Whistles and how they affect battles and captures. Speaking of captures: it's well executed and satisfying, imo.It might scratch that pokemon itch, but it is very much its own game, and deserves its regard and respect as such. Nexomon: Extinction stands very well on its own merits alone, and I'm really, really enjoying it!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 6.5/10, it's a decent game, and if you are a fan of the genre you will probably enjoy it. That being said, it has some major flaws which I will detail below.*Now for the long version, I’ll be comparing this game to some of its contemporaries in the genre but you should still get the idea even if you are unfamiliar with them. Let's start with the positives because Nexomon: Extinction (NE) did some things well:- The monster designs and animations were fantastic. As a fan of this genre for over 20 years, it's always nice to see new creature ideas...that aren't just a ring of keys or a pile of garbage that is...- The story didn't take itself too seriously (the fourth wall was more of a fourth sheet of paper), which I personally don't mind. I much prefer an rpg story like this to the naval gazing, pretentious style that is all too common. In spite of the goofy writing style however, the pacing and exposition were excellent, building up to an epic conclusion. -The stamina system is a big improvement over pp. Other new games in the genre (like Temtem) are employing stamina as well and I hope more devs will follow suit.*Now for the negatives, this game really could have been fantastic. I'm hopeful that the devs will make improvements for the sequel:- NE essentially watered down or removed many of the deep customization and strategy elements that are present in other games in the genre. They are no passive abilities, doubles battles, hold items, EVs, or IVs. I wouldn’t mind if these systems were updated or replaced, but instead most of them are just gone, which leads to boring one dimensional combat. Each mon in NE can have 4 cores, which are sort of a hybrid between EVs and hold items, and are an interesting idea. The issue, however, is that this system removes the feeling of having a unique team, and working with their strengths and weaknesses. Instead, you can just catch higher level versions of your team as you level and they will be exactly the same. - The way mons learn new skills makes no sense to me. Every few levels, they keep relearning the same handful of boring skills, with no skill relearner npc. The vast majority of the skills in the game are just minor variations of typing, accuracy, damage, crit, speed, and hax. This is my biggest gripe with the game and just flat out LAZY game design. It is impossible to balance around hax. Of all the things to copy from pokemon, NE picked literally the worst thing about that franchise without even copying any of the interesting support moves. This game does have some support moves, but most of them are unusable, with only a 30% chance to not waste your turn. In fact, NE takes the rng/hax even further, emphasizing luck instead of strategy more than any other game I’ve played. It just isn’t fun. There are also a couple moves that are game breakingly OP (invincibility). My suggestion to the devs is to remove all hax like Temtem. No accuracy, no crit chance, no hax chance. That way you will be forced to come up with moves that are ACTUALLY INTERESTING, and players will get to come up with fun strategies.- The pc moves excruciatingly slowly, and for some god forsaken reason you don’t get running shoes until half way into the game. Beyond that, the battle speed also goes by at a snails pace. I was able to get past this by using a speed hack to play at 3x speed but if it weren’t for that, I honestly would not have had the patience to play.

Some of this stuff may be somewhat changed later in the game but it was not worth playing more to find out, and I wish I had known the majority of this information before I made the purchase.This negative review is mostly for the sense of humor this game has. I could forgive it if it wasn't constant, but it is, and my eyes have rolled back into my head so far that I am having trouble finding them. If you like quippy, meta, self aware, quirky, and memey writing, this game might blow your mind. If you, like me, grit your teeth when a character references the fact that they are in a video game, look elsewhere. The game gives you a companion that has the humor of a social media manager and he never shuts the ♥♥♥♥ up. The point seems to be that the companion talks to characters so you don't have to, as you are a silent protagonist, but instead he just makes jokes constantly about how we are in an RPG and how its so messed up that we are making creatures battle.This is particularly sad to me because I was shocked to find that I liked the world they had set up, something I wasn't expecting to be that great. The world at hand is interesting, but you can't take anything seriously because you will never forget that you are in a video game. The gameplay itself is passable for a Pokemon "clone," it does little to deviate and the lack of double typing dilutes the more interesting features like stamina (which replaces PP from the aforementioned Pokemon). Complaining about a Pokemon inspired game playing like Pokemon may be a bit silly, but I was hoping for something that tried to build on a tired and simple formula. And speaking of formulas, I would really like to see the type match-ups in game and while battling: if having a type chart on my other monitor does the same thing but just takes extra effort, then there is no reason to not have that built in. You could even have match-up discoveries unlock as you see them unfurl in battles. That is all about the battling, however, and the exploration and open-ended nature of the game is somewhat interesting, but not exactly mind blowing. A general positive.I want to give kudos to the visual designers as there are many Nexomon designs I found myself enjoying a lot, and the visual presentation of the game overall is rather good, particularly the UI and the overworld. This just was not enough to keep me on board. All in all, a fine Pokemon type game that doesn't do much I consider special. If you can stomach the jokes and you really just love the "mash flamethrower" type gameplay from the Pokemon franchise, you might enjoy this game more than I.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction feels like a lackluster attempt at recreating the Pokémon formula. While it does deliver a monster-collecting experience, it struggles to stand out. Compared to similar titles like Coromon, Nexomon falls short in almost every aspect—except for puzzles, which it notably lacks. Ironically, this absence is its only advantage over Coromon.The most underwhelming part of the game is its art style, with monsters that fail to leave a lasting impression. Furthermore, the decision to balance the stats of rare and common monsters diminishes the thrill of finding rare ones. While this design choice might aim to encourage players to pick favorites based on personal preference rather than efficiency, it ultimately feels unfulfilling.If you're looking for a great monster-collecting experience, I’d recommend Coromon or Monster Sanctuary over this title. Nexomon: Extinction isn't necessarily bad, but it doesn't feel like a must-play.🔘 MS-DOS graphic🔵 Ugly, but still bearable🔘 Fine, nothing too fancy🔘 Pretty good🔘 Next gen graphic or art🔘 What is the story?🔵 Written by 5 years old child🔘 Something that'll hook you up with the game🔘 You can remember the story after you finished the game for a while🔘 You cannot get it out of your head🔘 You want to delete it after a few minutes🔵 It's not for everyone🔘 Could be bored after a while🔘 Can keep you entertained for hours straight🔘 It's already morning?🔘 Just mute it🔵 Few of them are good🔘 Not the best, but it's good🔘 You get immersed in the game🔘 Sometimes you will need to stop playing the game to hear it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon Extinction is the second game in the Nexomon series and it fixed some issues that I have found with the first game. - You can name your nexomon.- Every nexomon has a codex entry.- Healing is much better balanced with nexomon no longer healing after level up and max healing items healing 300 HP, but most nexomon have less than that for overall health. You do have other ways of recovering health like the crystal rocks that appear on maps that you can smash to instantly recover your nexomon, but at the cost of losing access to that crystal for a while.The world is much more open in this game. You can wander around a fair bit. Although some places are blocked off until you get to a certain point in the story, you are able to go visit various locations and catch the native nexomon from the start, which is quite a boon to get a diverse party right from the getgo.Enemies do level along side with your party's average level, so you are rarely if every going to be totally overlevelled for a specific fight, so fair warning. The new catching mechanic is somewhat contentious for me. I can certainly appreciate the fact that the developers went out of their way to include Playstation and Steam Deck controls for the catching inputs (I use a PS4 controller on PC) as most games default to Xbox controls. I'm not sure I like the actual catching minigame where you need to rapidly hit a bunch of inputs first though. The thing i do like is the fact that you can feed the nexomon to increase their catch rate as well as the game actively displaying various catch rate percentages depending on the state of the nexomon, the nexotrap you are using, the food it ate, as well as any status ailments that would also affect the catch rate.The combat system is a bit more refined. Some combat system thoughts here:- I like the fact that some enemy tamers will switch out their nexomon when at a disadvantage initially, something that other games in the genre rarely do, although I understand why this isn't done a lot as it would be pretty annoying really fast. Here it is done just the right amount to mostly avoid that feeling.- Unlike Nexomon 1 you can't switch your moves out of combat anymore, you need to go to a healing station and speak with the move tutor person. I'm not sure why this was changed as the Quality of Life that Nexomon 1 had where you can freely swap your moves out was great.- Your nexomon will only learn moves of their own type and maybe a normal type attacking move, so a single nexomon isn't going to be able to have move type coverage. A shame really, because I find that pretty fun to play around with in Pokemon.- I personally found most setup moves like giving yourself extra speed to be somewhat useless. Defensive setup moves do work pretty well, but I didn't find a nexomon that was particularly bulky enough to take full advantage of it.The story is a direct continuation from Nexomon 1, but many, many years into the future. I enjoyed it, but found the mid to end game a bit rushed especially with characters offering to teleport you back to X location as if the developers/writers just wanted to hurry up and get to the next scene ASAP. Characters will still very often break the fourth wall and speak to the player directly or reference that they are in a video game in a joking manner, which I found somewhat charming here, but I absolutely hated in other games, so your mileage may vary. It doesn't take itself too seriously. There is a Marvel styled joke towards the end that I facepalmed when I saw the setup for it, but you may find it funny or groan at it.This is a great game and a worthy sequel. There is also a custom mode that unlocks after you finish the game that allows you to setup a subsequent playthrough with various changes like doing a nuzlocke run, randomizing starters and other nexomon, disabling shops, or even just making the game harder by raising opposing nexomon levels. It is a terrific follow up to Nexomon 1. Absolutely recommended to give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this after I had finished the game yesterday.* In short: I will tell you, JUST BUY IT, especially if you're a hard fan of Pokemon* In long: Please scroll down if you want to see more. First of all, I have been a fan of Pokemon for roughly 20 years. And I have to admit, the series have gotten lazy recently.That's when I immediately pick this one, as it is so similar to my fav brand, right at the first glance of my eyes. I want to try something new, something more special something unique.And the more I play, the more potential I see this one has to be an equal rival of Pokemon. Let's look at some aspects of the game:SPOILER AHEAD!* The STORY: the game definitely catches my attention with its dumb, yet somewhat hilarious conversation and scenes. The story begins slowly as you're a tamer (like trainer in Pokemon), then you catch Nexomon, you grow strong, battle with other tamers and villains. But from the middle-late of the game, you realize something darker, a secret that changes everything around you. SPOILER AHEAD! You are a heir of Omnicron - the fallen king of Nexomon, and your mother Lydia had prepared everything for your strength to grow, until then you can surpass the Military equipment that Man had created to stop the war between Tyrants that have been going for centuries to choose for their new King.* The MUSIC: just so you know, I'm writing while still listening to all of the themes having in this game. THEY ARE BREATHTAKING! Every piece of music fits perfectly with the atmosphere and the areas. And I'm talking as a person who has played not only pokemon for 20 years, but also a good amount of any famous RPG games anyone can think of (just look at my Steam profile!)* The GRAPHIC: it's well-designed. It has unique vibe. Personally, I prefer this art style more. The Nexomon is also designed pretty well, some of them pretty did impress me.* The SKILLS: I must say, this one is absolutely the WEAKEST of the series. Throughout my progress, many times I had awaited for the moment the new skill to pop-up, just to feel down immediately as the new skills are rarely better than the old ones. After you train your Nexomon to level 40-45, the new skills after that, seem to be useless, or not worth trying! The PROS of the skill system maybe that each Nexomon has their own unique set of skill moves and skill animation.Overall, to remind you, this is ONLY THEIR 2ND NEXOMON, yet it is already so good. Pokemon has been with us for more than a decade. It is now a monument. Giving this series some time, and I have no doubt that this game will soar high into the sky.

_childDocuments_.review: I had beat this game on switch platform and bought again on Steam for the achievements. After beating Nexomon, I had wished that I first started with the first game and not extinction because it goes great lengths to understand the characters and storyline. Basically Nexomon: Extinction is just that, The Nexomon are all children of Omnicron ultimately and when you abolished it and even its soul remnants they are doomed to die off. You see a world with fragments of old civilization which is essentially the old game.Nexomon: Extinction has a great storyline that'll keep you engaged. Smooth game mechanics, battles don't take all day, a lot of funny puns, etc. There is also alternate color Nexomon to find at high rates, with something like 417 to catch in game. _childDocuments_.review: More than just a clone, this game shows why passion and creativity will always result in better games. More like the original Pokemon games than Pokemon has been probably since Emerald.After clearing the main game, you unlock a Custom Mode that lets you set your own Nuzlocke rules, alongside other challenges or ways to mix up the gameplay. This was added for free by the developers and I challenge Pokemon fans to recount the last time Nintendo/Game Freak did something like that for one of their games despite their fanbases playing with that ruleset and asking for challenges+story for years.Nexomon: Extinction has a good story. It incorporates elements from gameplay and is self-aware about some of its more ridiculous elements, but the overall plot is engaging and better than any Pokemon plotline that's ever been done. It's not revolutionary or anything but hey, I'm here for the gameplay.And speaking of gameplay, Extinction has so many quality of life changes (convenient move respeccing, better move balance for mons, equipment cores) that Pokemon feels hard to go back to after playing this. Looking forward to in-engine randomized Nuzlocke runs for a while to come. A personal thank you to the developers for caring about gameplay and what players actually want instead of only doing what works best for your bottom line.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game.Another monster collection (pokemon-type) game but this one is really colourful and funny (subjective as it does not seem that everyone likes the type of jokes in this game). There is a battle between monsters in this world and humans are caught in a cross fire. Guild of monster tamers is the only thing that can protect them (well, not counting a secret project developed deep in the science lab after analizing tons of anime).There are some scalling issues that some players don't like (when you progress story, all monsters, even those in initial area increase in difficulty) which makes leveling up low level monsters harder later. But there are ways around it. For example, instead of leveling monster from scratch you can just caught it again.I will repeat that the game is really beautiful and I personally like the humor in it, so I recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a person who tends to enjoy Pokemon-type games more than actual Pokemon games, I really love Nexomon Extinction, even more than I love its predecessor.  If you liked the first one, you'll like this one, it's essentially more of the same thing and that's exactly what I wanted out of this game.  It's easily my favorite game in the monster capture/battle genre.  There are so many reasons to love this game.The characters and dialogue are nowhere near perfect and the story isn't groundbreaking, but the game doesn't pretend to be perfect or 100% original.  It knows exactly what it is, a lighthearted game about imprisoning wildlife, making them fight their own kind, and improving their skills by performing the same attacks over and over until they're strong enough not to get crushed by bosses.  It's just a fun time.If you like turn-based RPGs or creature collector games at all, please play this game, it's worth full price and you'll enjoy it.  And go buy the first one too, it's a very similar game and it's just as fun.

Single. Time. I find some new area, I'd have so much more fun with the game.This despite how unimpactful the actual collecting feels, it's more of a chore than a fun experience to find new Nexomon, because 99% of them are the same apart from art and element.And initially it feels like you get a shotgun blast of Nexomon straight to your face, takes out a lot of fun when there's 50 to get in the very first area, making it a fulltime job if you want to try out even half of them. (And when you do take the time, there's no unique feel to any of them really)If they felt useful in any way whatsoever or unique in more ways than the sprite, that shotgun blast would feel more like "I can choose what I want!", rather than "I can collect for collecting's sake and spend hours checking if there are any other rares here"And the items, feels the exact same, nothing really impactful.I'm sure getting a 99 stack of each stackable bonus-item has a noticeable difference sometime, but it feels empty, pointless.Reward me for exploration in more ways than handing me a cookie saying "Good boy, find the next pointless chest" - Pokemon rewarded you with TMs, HMs, evolution items, things that made an impact on your team, not ONLY potions and "Hey, 3% more gold gain, grats"Not even the "secret safes" feels very rewarding, an item I can't use and probably have to collect all in the set to even find out what it does - Probably rewarding sometime 20h down the road when having found all?Only reward in those is the extra money to buy more pokeballs to collect more useless Nexomon.On the plus side the art is absolutely great, the story feels ok to follow, the dialogue has some good humour making it worth reading through. The note on wild Nexomon for how rare they are is a great addition to these games, and love that the difficulty is a little bit more than facerolling through - Elements and different type Nexomon being important for your team is a really good part of the gameplay. I do both like and dislike that the elemental weaknesses aren't what nearly all games do with it, it's a nice touch while also frustrating to re-learn certain "obvious" weaknesses that are switched around.I'm likely to give it another try at some point and see if the 11h mark was too early to make this evaluation, but so far I can't recommend it. _childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a pokemon style game, but while it tries to emulate the original pokemon formula as much as possible, it adds many improvements to make the game more enjoyable.I have not played any pokemon games past diamond (4th generation) but those I did play, I played a lot. While I can’t say whether the current generation of pokemon is faithful to those older games, I can say that Nexomon definitely is, and it brings some much needed improvements as well. I have little desire to reenter the world of Pokemon because I think it is starting to be crushed under the weight of its own backlog. I think pokemon is due for a complete overhaul, but I kind of doubt it will happen. Nexomon kept the simple battle system, the simple RPG mechanics, even things like Mons being limited to 4 moves and trainers/tamers being limited to 6 Mons, a lot of the other details have been changed. I think Nexomon is the sort of overhaul Pokemon needs.We have all new creatures to collect, of course, but if you threw pictures of Nexomon and Pokemon together and presented them to someone who knows neither, they would not be able to tell them apart. They kept that cute, anime monster, aesthetic. I don’t like all of the Nexomon designs (I especially hate the ones that look too human, like Puggard, Cadeto, and Volpressor) but about 80% of them are either fine or good. There is almost 400 Nexomon to collect now, and they are ALL present in the game, which is nice. I hate how we have just accepted that in Pokemon they get released in two versions, neither of which has all of the pokemon. And apparently Sword and Shield will now be the first version of Pokemon that even with both copies, not all the pokemon from previous generations will be included. Another improvement, no contrived evolutions like trading, happiness, or stones, just leveling. We now have 9 types that are well balanced, instead of the 18 types Pokemon has, and all Nexomon are just 1 type.Generally Nexomon is simpler, more streamlined… and I will say better. They thought about how to improve the core gameplay of Pokemon, and I think they succeeded.But not everything is perfect. I actually dislike the art design of the game. The 3D-ish chibi people of the world, I think look kind of ugly, even if their anime splash art counterparts are good. In simplifying things and making the Nexomon all relevant, there isn’t actually too much difference between any of the Nexomon. Status effects, while powerful, don’t see much use because of their low proc rate, pushing you to use just damaging moves. The music is fine, but some songs I found kind of grating. It can get grindy at times. Story wise the game is also a bit of a rollercoaster. I think it really flubs its introduction, as you thrown straight into world ending, time stopping, nonsense without taking any time to introduce the world. There are also a TON of 4th wall breaking jokes while at the same time this sense of hopelessness in the world and characters. While the game gets better as you go along, I didn’t know AT ALL what sort of tone the game was trying to set at the beginning. And while it gets better, the tone never quite gets… good. Which is a pity, because the writing is actually quite good. There are genuinely funny moments and genuinely epic moments, and the story is much grander than any pokemon title I’ve played. A for effort, but C in execution. The bottom line is, if you want a pokemon style game, or a simple monster taming RPG, then this is for you.EDIT: After talking with Pokemon fans, I realize that Pokemon has a lot more depth than Nexomon at the higher levels of play. If your goal is not just to collect all pokemon and beat the game, but rather to master the mechanics and be able to beat other human players, Pokemon delivers a lot more than Necomon.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction may at first seem like yet another  Pokemon spin-off. BUT, after playing it for quite some time, it is so much more than that!I still have so much left to complete - and I'm so eager to continue the story - but I really wanted to review this game because it really deserves more recognition.You start in a world that at first feels like an old-school Pokemon game. It even has that challenge that newer Pokemon games lack! But, as the plot picks up - and it does so very quickly - you soon realize that  I won't leave any spoilers, but the adventure and characters are really fun! You can see for yourself that the art style is great, but there's so much more to appreciate in the game as well!There are 381 different Nexomon to tame (catch). There are unique types, moves, and evolutions to each Nexomon, much like in Pokemon. The designs of the Nexomon are actually, for the most part, very interesting. Some great cool and cute ones to match different trainer's preferences!For those shiny hunters out there, you're in luck!!  I still haven't found one, but my sister's first wild encounter was a cosmic!! (Still so jealous btw, if you're reading this!)I know I keep comparing it to Pokemon, but I can't help it. I'm a huge Pokemon fan, it's what I know!! But, I enjoy this game so much on its own. I've grown up playing Pokemon, learning all the things that go on in that universe. But as I jump into the Nexomon universe for the first time, it feels fun, fresh, and exciting!! It is definitely worth playing and trying out! It has a growing fan-base for a reason!I've already sunk 12 hours into the story and just going around the grass looking for new Nexomon! Also, there's a ton of side quests to gain some extra coin or cool items! I plan to attempt to 100% the game, or at very least catch all the Nexomon! I currently only have around 60 lol!Walkthrough series:  Do yourself a favour, and get this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Having never played the first Nexomon game, I went into this game with no previous impressions or allegiance. The steam reviews show that over 90% of the people who have played the game enjoyed it, so when my friend offered me a free key from Humble Bundle I figured I would give it a shot. Nexomon, as a creature collector, boasts having over 400 unique monsters to tame. This, however, I believe to be an incredibly devious deception. Having played the game through to the end and spent a multitude of hours completing the database (pokedex), the majority of monsters are functionally identical. There are attacks that are indistinct from one another that simply exist in each of the different Nexomon types. Meaning that by the time your monster has learned all of its moves, it will be unlikely to be any different from another one. Alongside the move-pools being shallow and uninteresting, individual Nexomon do not have unique abilities or traits that set them apart from each other - even the base stats that they possess are indistinct; the ranges from one to the other hardly make one more compelling from the last. The only exception to this rule is the 'rarity' of the Nexomon, with common monsters often having strictly worse stats (making them pointless to carry for long).The one thing that Nexomon does that is unique is the Core system; each monster can have up to four 'cores' equipped at any given time. This would be interesting if it offered anything beyond base stat modifications. The cores increase stats like attack damage, monster health and defense. These are so incredibly boring. The only cores that I found compelling were the Bonus Experience and Experience Share, which are almost entirely mandatory because the rate at which the player receives experience is abysmal; the player receives the same amount of experience from any monster, no matter the evolution stage or difficulty. Gaining experience is an incredibly painful aspect of this game, as it takes a great deal of effort to level up (without the full set of fully upgraded cores). Another major complaint that I have, in my pursuit to complete the database (pokedex) I realized that there is no way to know where specific monsters spawn... the database does not show where they exist; it does not even record where in the world you've seen them.Nexomon Extinction is very clearly a mobile game at heart; the graphics make it look like it was an early Flash player game, there is no mouse support (and keyboard keys cannot be rebound), and certain item systems in game (bonus experience, bonus gold, shop discount items, etc.) feel like they come right out of a microtransaction shop - these are not compelling items for a player to find.The story of the game drags on, but never takes itself seriously enough for the player to become invested. The player's main companion, a talking cat, acts as the protagonists voice. Throughout the game there are countless failed attempts at humour which are mostly at the expense of the player's sense of immersion; the NPCs are constantly referencing the fact that you're playing a video game and breaking the fourth wall. It is a tired and overused trope throughout the entirety of the story.  Having no previous experience with Nexomon, I had no idea what to expect with the monsters themselves. I figured I would go in blind and play with 'the rule of cool'; choosing monsters that I thought looked interesting. Despite there being over 400 monsters, so few of the designs feel original. Outside of similar designs like Mimi and Mimorus (psychic-typed humanoid mime monsters, comparable to the likes of Mr. Mime), there are some designs that are actually just established pokemon; shameless copies. When I encountered Enercer (identical to Vikavolt) and Blublub (besides its horrendous name, it is identical to Solosis) I had to look twice, I could not believe how shameless these were. Nexomon: Extinction is a $26 (CAD) game, yet there is hardly anything here to justify its price. This game released on Steam in 2020 and is unlikely to be getting any meaningful updates to correct the many glaring issues with the game. Upon looking further into it, the studio is already working to release the next installment of the franchise, which all but confirms that this game is dead in the water. I cannot recommend this game. There are few, if any, redeeming features. The price is too high for what it is, especially considering that the game is free on mobile. Stay far away from this title.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long-time fan of Pokemon, I was a bit skeptical of whether or not this game would live up to that series' legacy... and I haven't been disappointed. In fact, Nexomon: Extinction has so far exceeded my expectations - it is not a mere clone but a fresh take on the genre with its own identity and ideas to explore. To me, it is simultaneously new and nostalgic, reminiscent of the first time I played Pokemon as a child but incorporating elements from RPGs and darker stories that I've enjoyed as an adult. Pros: + Environments are unique and colorful, art design in general is great+ Worldbuilding in general is just very well done, each city/town has a lot of depth and NPCs have a lot to say+ Most Nexomon designs are very appealing and creative, there are a lot of mons (and you can actually catch 'em all)+ Dialogue is fun and self-aware+ CHALLENGING. The latest patch has decreased the amount of grinding required but the difficulty is still very much alive+ Story is engaging. Going into why might be a bit spoiler-y, but it keeps hitting all the right notes for me+ The music is just outstanding. I particularly love the capital city theme+ The devs have been great so far at fixing bugs and addressing community concerns Cons:- You have to grind in this game or the bosses will utterly demolish you. The game offers some solutions to help make the grind smoother with the most recent patch though- In my experience, mons of the same type tend to play similarly because stats don't differ too drastically between them and there isn't a great variety of moves. This really lessens the personal touch of each mon, but means that even Common mons are viable- There are tons of cat-like Nexomon but I haven't found a single horse-like Nexomon?? What's up with that??? Overall, I highly recommend this game to anyone whose felt let down by recent Pokemon games (particularly if you enjoyed the Genius Sonority games) or anyone who wants more RPG elements and sarcasm in their monster catching games. Newcomers to the monster catching genre might want to prepare themselves for a more challenging experience, but I think it would still be rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the original Nexomon and enjoyed it alot. It was fun, fast paced game with good story and some good mechanics that made the game reasonably fluent even for a collector I am, catching and training all monsters altogether.  (With so many monsters to catch I worried game would be too grindy for me, but I was pleasantly surprised).I was looking forward for Nexomon: Extinction, only to be very badly disappointed. Story looks nice, but open world idea does not work so well with this type of game in my opinion. PC controls are true nightmare. Original Nexomon controls WERE tedious, but nowhere near those. Everything got worse and less playable. The grind is real. Level scaling and absence of all-party exp share makes the game almost unplayable for a collector and multi trainer. I am basically forced to chose between forming a party of favourites and stick to it (not my preferable play style) or put hours and hours into the game. (As tedious as controls are it's not worth the bother to use cores.)I know this often happens with sequels of succesful games. First game is good and devs try to put lots of new ideas and improvements into the sequel. Sadly, those good ideas often prevail over common sense and it's just what happened in this case. I am still playing the game but I think it's very possible I will get tired of the grind soon and stop playing. Pity - I really did enjoy the style of the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon Extinction is what one might call a "side-line" of the classic Pokémon JRPG-style monster catcher. Which is to say, it has its own direction and flow, while still feeling in-line with what you already know and love. There's a lot of Quality of Life improvements over Pokémon, and it'll be too long to list them here, but know that there are some nice takes this game has over what you might have come to expect in this genre.I enjoyed the story, the world-building and the overall feel of the game. I liked the humour too. The graphics are vibrant, the music is good, and the combat is what you'd expect, with a slight twist in that "stamina" is required to use moves. I also liked the catching mechanics; it tells you your capture chances as well as offering ways of increasing said chances (like feeding a nexomon their favourite treat for example).There's a nice focus on exploration and adventure in this game too which is awesome, I enjoyed going around and finding all sorts of areas and loot during my journey, doing side quests and catching nexomon as I went. Speaking of, the nexomon themselves are unique: from the cute to the monstrous - you get some awesome, as well as some bland - but well, with over 400 Nexomon, this is to be expected.Overall, a solid game and especially if it's on sale and you're a fan of this style of game give it a go!

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through the first one and enjoying it so thoroughly, I was a little worried about this one. Especially with the world leveling. HOWEVER I will be the first to say they improved nearly everything that was great about the first one. +The art style, the nexomon themselves, are all very well designed and illustrated.+The backgrounds and scenery feel more alive and painterly. +The fast travel system is greatly improved. +Challenging but very doable. +Not only special, rare, and mega rare nexomon evolve now. Most have at least one evolution no matter the rank. +The quest system give you a ton more to do, special incentives, etc. +The story is better than the last, and much more engrossing.-Some negatives are that the beginning is pretty damn hard. It's a little difficult to get through, but once you do it's a much smoother experience. -Sometimes the level scaling feels a little oppressive. Even as you grow it feels like fighting against a never ending tide. -You have to level all the nexomon you want in your team at the same time. If you don't you'll quickly regret your choices. Try and raised a balanced team early if you want to succeed.-While breaking the fourth wall can be hilarious, it also kind of takes you out of the experience sometimes.-Feeding nexomon can be a little tedious. You never know what food they want until after they face you.  It adds some annoyance to catching the little buggers, as you have to feed them if you want a chance at a catch.Over all this is a wonderful game and in my opinion a step in the right direction! I love the nexomon, the catch system, and the overall direction. I sincerely hope to see more in the future, this is a great monster catching game any fan of the genera should enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Like pokemon, but unhinged.I prefer this game's story over pokemon and all of the others in the genre, by a long shot. The writing is especially funny if you're familiar with these type of catch-em-all games. I really appreciate that character motivations make sense and no one is evil just because. I was expecting the usual shallow story to push your character forward but was pleasantly surprised.That said, the combat in this game is pretty simple. There's no IV/EV, nature or passives. Equipments are kind of bare bones. This isn't an issue for me, I was never big on min/maxing my pokemons so this suits me just fine. There's also no variation in stats from nexomon to nexomon, so there's no breeding and there's not really a point to ever catch more than one of each type. The designs and evolutions for the nexomons are pretty cool, I like most of them. There was a few derpy looking ones, but most of them are very well made.Finally, the custom mode is worth mentioning, it allows actual nuzlocke runs, new game+, etc, and has a lot of customisation. It adds a lot of longevity to the game imo.Looking forward to the sequels!TL:DR cool little game, definitely worth the money if you're looking for a casual experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally bought this game so I could dive into it and make fun of it for being a lame Pokemon rip off. But what started as a couple of hours one night, sending screenshots to my friends making fun of the game.... Eventually turned into wanting to get a little deeper, find more secrets, learn more about the story, grind to level and evolve my mon, etc.What really kept me engaged was the story and the characters. The story actually has heft to it and the characters have a semblance of substance. Pokemon games, for me, have gotten too samey... too flat, they take themselves too seriously, characters and the world feel like cardboard cutouts and nothing really matters. And where Pokemon lacks in those departments, Nexomon: Extinction has in spades. The game actually gives you a REASON to play it out, story-wise. Is it God of War level story? No, but for this genre of game, it more than surpassed my expectations. The characters you meet along the way... guess what? They actually have a purpose and reason to show up multiple times. Characters actually have real motivations for what they are doing. As other reviews have mentioned, the writing is VERY "meta" and joke heavy... and early on it turned me off, but the deeper I got, the more I came to appreciate it. There were multiple 4th wall breaking moments that made me chuckle out loud. And to be honest, the story itself, at it's core... is pretty dark and serious. When they say Extinction, they mean... Extinction. That light-hearted, jokey dialogue really brings a tonal balance to the overall game which, again, I really came to appreciate and enjoy.The map, the art style, the monster designs... All really top notch. It's all just really good, it's hard to even expand on these areas. Just very very SOLID in every way.  Kind of a small thing, but something in these types of games that really annoys me is when evolutions don't "make sense". Like you will have a starter / base monster and it evolves into something completely unrecognizable or just flat out stupid. That isn't an issue with Nexomon: Extinction. And as silly as the dialogue is sometimes, it seems like they took their monster creations very seriously -- which is GOOD. You aren't running around catching literal trash bags or ice cream cones. THANK YOU DEVS. Content wise, I felt I more than got my money's worth. Plenty of side quests... I enjoyed the adequate but not over-the-top resource grinding / collection aspect of the game. The mechanic for creating cores and using cores was really well done. I much prefer that to Pokemon held items. Loved the vault and key hunting. Wish there were even more quests / side activities like this in the game. Perhaps maybe the best mechanic / feature in this game is the ability to re-fight trainers... trainers get stronger, their Mon get stronger, and they have cool new dialogue options as you get stronger and keep beating them which is great. Truly one of the better features in this game and I hope the devs keep building on this and making it even better. It truly makes "grinding" levels and evolutions enjoyable. I forgot what they are called, but in many areas of the game, they provide these "healing rocks" , which fully heal your party and respawn after X amount of time passes. The game itself actually makes fun of the fact that devs were kind of bullied into adding these because players thought the game was too hard... But to be honest, I liked them. It makes grinding / leveling just that much nicer. Spending half the game walking to towns to heal my Mon isn't fun to me. So I don't care if it makes the game "too easy" I see it as a really nice quality of life improvement on the genre.For some quasi negatives.... Nexomon and their evolutionary lines are locked to certain locations, as you level up and progress through the game those wild Nexomon also level up and you begin seeing their evolved forms in the wild more often. This is a cool feature, however, if you miss some of the base forms early on... It's really kind of a pain to go back and try completing the equivalent of your Pokedex because the base forms just aren't as common to find / catch. Maybe it's in the game and I missed it, but we could really use a breeding / day care center. It doesn't even need to be complex. Put two of the same Mon in the daycare, you get a base form back... And added bonus of slowly leveling those mons in the daycare. Simple fix to an otherwise cool system.Also the battle system just feels a tad one dimensional. It isn't BAD, but I feel like there is an aspect missing here. Moves between mons are VERY VERY similar if not identical (depending on type) and the move pool just feels really limited. We might just need a bigger variety of moves, we might need more types, perhaps dual typing... I'm not 100% sure the fix here. But it does feel like the system is missing just one more layer of depth / complexity. The only other thing I would look at improving kinda goes with the battling. But I felt like often times.... moves, stamina, Mon and move type.... just didn't really mean anything. And what I mean by that is, as long as your mons stay at or above the level of the enemy mons... You're gonna be fine. If you do some grinding, you can have one lead mon really carry you. Doesn't matter the type, their weaknesses, nothing. As long as the level is higher, you're mostly gonna be fine. Now, I understand it's that way in most games like this but it feels even more relevant here. If this complaint is true of all monster catching games, it's relevant x10 for Nexomon. Again... I don't know how to fix this exactly, but the formula just needs tweaking and balancing. All those factors of a Mon need to matter more and be weighted beyond... Higher level = More Power = Win.All in all.... Really great game. If  you like the monster catching adventure genre, pick this up. As I mentioned at the start of this review, I bought this game for the memes. But I ended up staying for a funny, meaningful, and truly enjoyable experience. I really look forward to whatever comes next in this franchise. You've all won me over. Thank You.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great sequel! Mostly great, some flaws like any game. Overall, I'd recommend it - just don't play it directly after finishing the first nexomon or it'll drive you up a wall. There's a lot of improvements - you can refight trainers, better menus, more types of nexomon with more move types, coco is a massive improvement over atlas, story is interesting, etc.But there are some flaws - they went full Oblivion (everything levels with you, so you never feel any stronger since everyone/every wild nexomon is within 5-8 levels of you), battles are so much slower (pro - makes non-damage moves actually mean something but agonizing after the first game's quick fights), leveling is very slow. Also! If you have epilepsy or flashing light sensitivity, this game hates you. I don't have a medical problem but this will still give me a headache after a while. And it's not avoidable - every trainer fight starts with flashing lights. And constant shaking screens. And constant explosion sound effects. I dearly wish there was a way to toggle off the shaking/flashing.The biggest negative for me was honestly the change in the artwork - backgrounds are detailed and gorgeous. But some of the character and almost all of the nexomon artwork has massively degraded. They must have gotten a different artist?? The sprites are fuzzy, and even the ones that have good designs are still stylistically so much more simple and oftentimes drawn weird/poorly as well. I'll admit, style is a thing and some of this can be chalked up to personal taste. But the low quality animations, sprites, and even cutscenes artwork is very disappointing for a game revolving entirely around collecting monsters (aka looking at artwork) that you think look cool. Hopefully it'll swing back to great artwork by the sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a decent game with a good story, interesting creature designs, and a massive roster of different creatures. They even added in a bunch of really cool extra features that can be unlocked after beating the game once that hopefully will become a staple in the series (and that more games should have, honestly), such as a built in randomizer and nuzlocke mode.Unfortunately... they got rid of the biggest draw for the series (for me) which was the the fact that creatures swapping in could attack the same turn. This made the game much more challenging than other monster taming style games, which generally are designed so that 6 year old children wearing a blindfold can beat them without issue.  Creatures also never get any kind of elemental based moves other than their own type and status effects are all over the place, and always low% chances to even apply the status (including moves that only apply a status effect).  As a result, battles just feel like a rock-paper-scissors match.  Switch to a Nexomon with a type advantage, click the move with the biggest number, rinse/repeat until the battle is over.  No strategy or thinking required.This game also lacks the most mandatory thing for a monster taming game to be good: multiplayer. There is no trading, which isn't a really big deal, but it also means there is no PvP battle system for the game. As a result there's no real meaning to playing after you finish the story a single time. "Catch all the legendary Nexomon!"... why? And do what with them? "Train your members in the box up to make a new team!"... and do what with it? The game is already over, there are no fights left to beat, just chores to check off the game's list that I skipped because they're all just boring fetch quests where the rewards don't match the resources I have to give up to complete them. Without multiplayer, a monster taming game has no life.TLDR:Good game with fun writing and a large creature roster, but unfortunate mechanic changes from the first game and a continued total lack of multiplayer make this only worth buying on sale and not worth the $20 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: Great pokemon clone. Quality of life features GREATLY improved from the first nexomon title.Pros:- Addition of shards. I like that they can be used for cores, nexotraps, or some extra coin so the player has agency in what to use them for.- Improved encounter rates for rare nexomon.- Addition of tamer (trainer) rematches. Tamer rematches are infinite(!) and on a cooldown.- Wild nexomon and tamer rematches scale with you. NPC dialogue also changes with the story this time and it’s cool to see them react to your different feats.- LOTS of cameos from the first title. I like seeing my old friends (and enemies).- Addition of stackable key items. Provides a good incentive to actually explore the land and dungeons.- Fast travel is available MUCH earlier in the game than in the first title. Thank god.- Addition of specialty nexotraps. I like that they can be crafted with shards or bought outright, so you have two options for acquiring them based on what currently works better for you.- Nexomon designs are great. There are some middle evolutions that just look like a midpoint between the first and third that have no unique features, but this doesn’t really bother me.- Stamina battle system is the same as the first title and still works great.- Character portraits look cleaner and generally more appealing.Mixed:- Core system. It’s neat, but it’s also a pain to have to switch the EXP share ones into the party every single time you change your party. Maybe some sort of loadout system would've been helpful here?- Addition of ghost and psychic types. Ghost is ok but psychic is basically useless. It does, however, open the door for some very cool nexomon designs.Cons:- A few encounter rates, EVEN WITH LURING, are abysmal. If you want to catch every single nexomon you will have to sink extra tens of hours into this.- Still too many 4th wall breaks. It’s funny the first time, not the 20th. A lot of the “game budget too small” jokes don’t land because the game looks and works perfectly fine. Your companion this game is more annoying than Atlas in the first title.- Can't get rid of cores. It's annoying to scroll through all of your obsolete cores. You should be able to sell them and/or destroy them to recoup half(?) of the shards back.

_childDocuments_.review: Great monster gathering game. Here what it has:+ Great story+ Lot of jokes are really good, including 4th wall breaking and reading your thoughts+ And I mean it, lot of truly good jokes and situations+ Lot of nexomon to catch+ There is no shortage for different types, you could easily get ghost/psy/fire types nexomons from beginning+ Nexomon stats are always the same. Doesn't matter if you raised nexomon from level 1 or got it at level 80. _childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good, for what it's worth.TLDR; Get this game if you played the first one or are really into Pokemon-like games. Otherwise, don't.I played the first game on another platform, so I kind of had to get this one too. Extinction does build upon the original game quite a bit, in terms of lore, but you won't really ever feel lost if you didn't play the original. Most of the story building from the previous game is basically trivial. Although, it did feel kind of cool to understand every aspect about the past of the story, so you should play the original if you're into that. Otherwise, you can play this one without doing so.As for the gameplay, it's honestly okay. I thoroughly enjoyed myself for the entire game, but there were a few things that bothered me. Firstly, the game constantly makes the monsters you encounter be at or slightly higher than your current highest leveled Nexomon's level. This was really annoying sometimes because it felt like there was no good reason to level up other than to beat your opponents, which brings me to my next point. The type-system in this game is somewhat frivolous. The only thing that really matters is your level, as well as the general strength of your Nexomon's moveset. This actually made it kind of tedious to beat this certain part of the game, keep in mind I'm using the word 'tedious' and not 'difficult', because, in terms of difficulty, this game has none. You are essentially constantly guided into where you need to go and what you need to do. Whenever that wasn't the case, it would instead just be tedious and frustrating instead of fun.Also, don't be fooled by rarities in this game. Those all mean nothing. What I mean by that is that the legendary ones are literally stronger than the commons by a hair. And if I'm wrong about this....well, it doesn't matter, because it certainly feels that way.I know I just trashed all over this game for the most part, but I enjoyed it. The character designs are great, for the most part and the story is also pretty good. For $20, it's worth it. Although, I'd only recommend it if you've played the first game, or are really itching for a Pokemonesque experience.

Edited/tldr: I would recommend you only buy this game while it is on sale/discount. Story less then half way thru feels super rushed and certain expected features just fall off/are ignored and forgotten about, or not utilized as well as they could have been. Hoping to see improvement as I am relatively close to completing the story now and am saddened by the parts that fell short of what the game was laying the ground work to expect. Truly love this game so far as a creature collector and story teller. Love most of the creatures, huge variety for a single game and keeps most areas feeling fresh. There is a level scale, but it follows the story, so you can stop in an area and become over powered if you want, you can keep fighting trainers over and over every few minutes so it goes super fast too. Especially considering the context. I use the word "homework" intentionally. Pokemon was a  amazing idea back when I was in grade school. Decades later, all it's become is a worn-out blueprint. _childDocuments_.review: Difficulty scaling in this game is completely illogical. There is 'dynamic difficulty' scaling in this game that basically renders all nexomon you catch early completely useless. Once you catch a nexomon, they immediately begin to get out-scaled just by virtue of your main party leveling up. This means there is no point to catching any nexomon early in the game and there is almost no point in leveling your own party--you just have to catch new nexomon as you go along. I suspect this is to incentivize changing up your team often, but in practicality you just never get to keep your nexomon except for your starter. Everything else will get outleveled after an hour, so you just need to catch new nexomon to replace the ones in your party that haven't kept up.

_childDocuments_.review: It should be no surprise that you're being sent out into the world at a young age, all on your own. What was surprising was having a legendary--I mean, a dragon--attack out of nowhere.If you want to see Nexomon: Extinction in action for yourself, watch my video. A nice art style, self-aware humor, a focus on action, and a sense of freedom to explore in the direction you want to go combine to make this a distinct experience from its Pokemon clone roots. You'll be plunged into epic scale plot right from the start and RPG tropes will make sure you don't have a clear sense of what's going on, but perhaps someday you'll destroy the world. Having a loyal companion alongside you to deliver wit instead of exposition and to say the things that you might say as a player will be something you either love or hate. And you don't have to worry which of the 9 starters you choose: I stumbled across one of the others in the wild very early on. And that's something that bears repeating: while the plot pushes you in a specific direction, the world leaves you with several dead-ends open to explore first. You have the feeling of freedom despite the plot's direction.The battle system has its pros and cons. You capture chance is revealed before you throw a Nexotrap. There's also a weird button combination prompt that isn't quite clear on which button to start with (answer: upper-left) or what it adds to capturing. Moves have individual priority, decreasing the importance of levels. Accuracy claims to be par for the course, but of course you'll wonder if it's lying to you. One of my Nexomon evaded three or four attacks in a row. It happens, of course, but it always makes you give it the side eye. The most bizarre part is that you're forced to fight the Level 40-some odd Dragon right off the bat, and somehow your Nexomon is able to survive a single hit.All in all, if you're sick of the direction Pokemon has gone in in recent years, Nexomon is worth checking out. It has a different soul to it, being back in 2D will make you feel right at home.

_childDocuments_.review: A TLDR I recommend grabbing this if its on sale or if youre desperate for a new monster collector. Engaging text and quests often quite funny.The world and story is great but perhaps at a cost to the gameplay.Everything you do will be scaled. Your highest lvl is 50? Wild mons are gonna be nearly 50. This is for wild, all trainers, and maybe bosses? So lots of healing is needed to traverse the world. It semi-deals with it in the form of healing gems found around the map that heal your team. Type advantage only seems to hinder you. What I mean by this is switching into a mon thats "weak" to yours feels completely worthless. You switch in and take an "uneffective" move that does over half your hp. Then go on to do one hit (sometimes even two!) then heal from bag/move and rinse and repeat till the battles over. Status effects are worthless to you and incredibly OP on all enemies.The UI doesnt explain anything, it may say that your move will put them to sleep but fails to say for how long. This goes for almost all ailments. Most of the time your status moves will only effect them for a turn. This does depend any maybe Im horribly unlucky but the only thing Ive gotten consistently more than one turn of is sleep or para. Meanwhile, when an enemy hits you with a status its 5 TURNS. 5 WHOLE TURNS ARE YOU KIDDING ME. Demotivated for 5 turns? Gotta swap or just use your bag for 5 turns. Sleeping? If you dont have an anti sleep have fun waiting and watching your mon die. Frozen? Eat a bag of REDACTED. You 100% need to rely on bag items to the point where it feels less like my team vs theirs and more-so my spam heals and anti-status items vs their team.Its so bad that Im 90% sure you cant even hit bosses with most status', when spamming a 30% freeze move (over 10 times) I didnt get a single ONE TURN freeze. These mixed with the fact that most mons only learn their type and a normal move makes the combat feel like a clunky and really unbalanced game of rock paper scissors. This paired with the emphasis of NEEDING items to succeed really lowers it on my list of monster collectors. All in all it is a fun couple hours but needing to constantly grind makes it feel like this singleplayer game doesnt respect your time at all.Endgame consists of gathering all Tyrants/Greater Dragons/ and Omnicron Children. There are "shinys" in the form of Cosmics aswell.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a creature collector/tamer rpg. They really polished their game sense the first game. You play as an  orphan getting their first nexomon, but quick are attacked by a dragon nexomon. You are secretly tasked to revive a powerful nexomon egg behind your guild's back to "save" the world. The story really subverted my expectations, and turned out x10 better. Same with the combat, they greatly improved on it and added ghost and psychic types. They also fixed and added different status effects, too. And you still get to pick from one of every element for your starter. They did add a weird mini-typing game when you try the capture a nexomon, but it's not that bad. The designs are awesome as well. They did another 300ish different nexomon for this game,  all look super unique and I found myself saying "ooooo I like that one" all the time. This game reminded me so much of the early pokemon games, back when they were a bit harder and didn't handhold you. I love this game alot more than I thought I would. I would suggest you play the first game before this one cause of lore reasons and it's also good. And I give this a 9.5/10.Starter: BehildaFinal Team: Noocidal, Acegon, Yarnesty, Couplet, Sirnymfa

You can find it  3 on Astats    No  No  You can see the achievement for catching all the Nexomon as grindy but it is also a very normal achievement in this type of game  No  No  No  No difficulty option  No  If you’re thinking about getting this awesome game, let me start with a piece of personal advice to start with the first Nexomon game in this series. The main reason I highly suggest starting with the first one is that the story is the best part of both Nexomon games. There are a lot of puns and 4th wall-breaking jokes but that doesn’t get in the way of an in-depth story.  This is a monster collecting game in the style of Pokémon. A lot of people will compare it to Pokémon and it does have a lot of similarities, but in my opinion, this game isn’t a clone as it adds a few twists in comparison to Pokémon.  As I've already pointed out, Nexomon has an amazing story, which I just haven’t seen in the Pokémon games that I have played over the years. This game has a mechanism that it increases the catch chance by a lot if you first feed the Nexomon you are attempting to catch and after you have thrown the trap, you'll have an optional minigame in which you have to push a few buttons in order in 5 seconds. Each button you have correctly hit increases the chances of catching the Nexomon.  Another difference is that the Nexomons that roam in the wild get higher in level. That means that when you first encounter them, they are around level 5 but if you go back to earlier maps later on in the story, those Nexomons are just a few levels lower than your highest Nexomon.   I would highly suggest to first play the game for its story and catch what you can but don’t go out of your way to find them all yet. Most Nexomon have 3 tiers and at certain points of the story, the Nexomon from that tier can be found on all the maps in the wild (the earlier tiers of Nexomon will stay available on those maps too).  You’ll get a few tools that will increase the chance to catch them and you'll get the option to buy the best food which every Nexomon likes instead of having to have the right food type for the full effect.   The developer is still actively worked on the game. It did release with some small bugs and the rating to find mega rare Nexomon was very low but the developer has listened to the players and improved the game a lot in the past few weeks since its release. For example; there are now ways to share experience between non-fighting Nexomons; this was highly requested. There have also been new items added to the game to restore a bit of health or stamina after each fight.   Most of the achievements are for beating the game and catching all the Nexomons. There are a few others for selling ores and have gathered X amount of money during the game but those are not missable and not that hard to achieve.  I've really enjoyed this game a lot and so, I highly suggest getting it, if you like monster collecting games.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this because I wanted a new monster catching game, figured I'd just play it little bits here and there. You can go almost anywhere you want in the world and every encounter will be around your own level, allowing for a wide variety of mons to catch whenever you want- A custom mode once you beat the game that lets you basically adjust every single aspect of the game. Though despite that, the campaign is still a lot of fun and more than worth the price tag of this game- It's a console port and they didn't seem to care much about keyboard and mouse. _childDocuments_.review: I have invested 20 hours in it in a span of 4 days, i only do that if the game is really fun, so there we go.It is a very well done pokemon clone, after a few minutes of gameplay, the game lets you free, this is the very first difference with Pokemon, you can actually explore and go to diferent places every time, it has many side quests, which of course you can do or ignore them completely. There are less elements in Nexomon than there is in Pokemon, and there are not mixed element (ex: grass/poison) so it simplifies your strategy, this ia a downside for me, it doesn't have double battles either, so it ends up being a bit simplistic. Every fight (wild nexomon and trainers) are scaled up to your team (around your highest level in party), this is a double edged sword, the challenge will keep up throughout the game, it won't allow you to have a beast and 5 punching bags that buys you time to heal the beast, but it kills that feeling of having an op party. Battling is fast, menus are designed to use a few clicks to perform an action (ex: A opens combat, Y opens your Nexomon party) and animations are very fast, i really liked this because otherwise it would get tedious after a few battles (we all have skipped changing our Pokemon to a better type in a battle due to being a long process), it also has an energy system, your combat moves will drain that energy (there are potions to refill it) so you need to use more than one in each battle. Trainers are not as dumb as they are in Pokemon, they usually have a lot of Nexomons, with various types and they will try to counter your Nexomon. It has a "core" system that lets you buff your nexomon, you need to craft them by mining ores and refining them, each core has 3 tier, ex: atk +5%, +8%, +10%, you can stack them, so you could add +40% atk in a Nexomon, there are more buffs (atk,def,hp,exp gained, exp shared and so on). Since the very beginning you will be able to catch all types as well, this leads us to the catching system, which i think it is way better than Pokemon. It has a few bars (feeding, tireness, states, Nexotrap, other), each bar fills a total % of catching rate, ex: feeding a nexomon will increase it by x% depending if it likes the food or not, it caps at 30%, getting it to low HP will add another % and so on.I think the art is pretty, and the music is fantastic but i have noticed a few moments in which the music didn't fit the mood of the game, but i think this is a very tiny detail. i like Nexomon's art as well, but sometimes they feel a bit generic or a straight up copy of a Pokemon design.It doesn't have the gym formula we all know either, you will fight bosses, which personally i enjoyed more than fighting a gym. It doesn't have any kind of online, devs have said that it may be implemented in the future, but no promises, so take this with a grain of salt. Also, 300+ Nexomons to catch.
