_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a fun and engaging delve into the Pokemon/Monster Catching genre. If the game looks appealing, I can strongly recommend it for anyone that likes casually playing monster catching games. That being said, there are a few shortcomings it has in comparison to Pokemon I feel.Pros:-The story is very well thought out and has some nice twists and turns here and there. A lot of the pokemon games' stories have gone stale because they always use the same formula of X team of bad guys wants to harness the power of some legendary pokemon to take over the entire world etc. In this game's story, not everyone is who they seem at first glance.-The writing is also very well done. Most of the dialogue is rather engaging, and the devs have littered the game with self-aware jokes that break the fourth wall all the time. I get a good laugh just about every 10 minutes of dialogue I read.-Almost all Nexomon have three stage evolutions, but if they don't their final stage evolution will generally be just as viable as any other third stage evolution. You can therefore make teams of just about any of the nexomon that you want.-Permanent Progression items. In Nexomon Extinction, you can collect certain key items that permanently increase things such as catch rates, money earned, EXP earned, and the effectiveness of all food items. I feel like this is done flawlessly throughout the game and it really incentivizes the player to explore every nook and cranny of the world to get all those sweet bonuses.Neutrals:-The music is quite decent, but nothing to write home about.-The graphics are rather nice but more on the cartoon-ish side. Some people may be repelled by the art style, but it doesn't bother me personally.-The nexomon designs themselves aren't great but they aren't bad either. A few of the evolutions do seem to just be bigger versions of their pre-evos though, which is never a good thing.Cons:-The combat system is quite generic, and, although the devs have stated they want to make all moves equally viable, some are just downright useless and some moves are god tier. This con can be discounted by the engaging storyline and progression though.-The nexomon. There's nothing inherently flawed about the systems Nexomon Extinction uses to flesh out each nexomon in its own right, but nexomon feel much less unique apart from each other due to some of the differences between Pokemon. Nexomon have no ability, cannot have held items (there are cores which I'll cover in a bit), and can't have more than one typing. Nexomon don't have special/physical attack/defense split, but this is more of a preference than an advantage or disadvantage.-The core system. In Nexomon Extinction, instead of held items, nexomon can have up to four "cores" equipped at a time that will provide your nexomon with various stat bonuses. Admittedly, it isn't a terrible system, but I feel that much more could have been done with it. All of the cores provide generic bonuses like attack, defense, health, exp, etc, but as far as I know, there are no cores that have unique effects that would make it much more fun to play around with. The core system isn't terrible, but it could have been much more fulfilling.Final Rating: 8 / 10Overall the game is quite fun in spite of a few of the flaws I feel it has. If you feel like taking some time out of your day to play a monster catcher where you don't have to do much thinking and can just relax, this is the perfect game for it. In that sense, it might be a better buy on Nintendo Switch, but is quite nice either way. You can easily get over 50 hours of gameplay with the 381 Nexomon to find and collect and the overarching story and post-game.Suggestions:-Add an option to disable battle animations to make leveling/grinding a bit easier.-Add two or three permanent progression items for the pickax that give you an extra elemental shard per rock broken.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful pokemon style game with a lot of love in it. The visuals looks great, as does the music and the gameplay. There are a ton of nexomon to collect with over 300 of them to grab including training them and evolving them. The nexomon themselves have some really cool designs and are very cute as well. Nine different starters to choose from, i myself chose the fire type. Because it is inspired by pokemon it obviously plays like it, though it is really enjoyable. It has an interesting adventurous story with great characters and the gameplay is really fun as well. Capturing the nexomon is also quite unique as there is an added element to it. After tossing your trap, a quick time event pops up where it is required to press a series of buttons within a short period of time. Though it does have controller support, the mainly keyboard and mouse controls are excellent to play with. It is basically just w,a,s,d for movement; i,j,k,l for the different actions when fighting; and q and e together for capturing so it does have an easy control scheme to play with. Plenty of areas and biomes to go through as well as an cool story and lore to explore so there is quite a lot of content to get through. Some great humour and meta dialogue is had as well like one time a character was questioning the fantasy of dragon but they were called out by a talking cat. It is definitely a great rpg and can recommend it to those who want to scratch that pokemon itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I've really wanted to like this game, but I can't. Perhaps my expectations are too high after seeing some of the designs for the Nexomon and the world's visuals, it had me hoping this would be a charming little game with a story that was at least coherent...... it was not.Here's a list of the pros and cons if you don't want to read about my experience with the first hour of the game, that rant contains spoilers but it goes into more depth about my problems with this game.Pros:- Great looking visuals- More open-ended exploring- Wide variety of Nexomon- You get to choose between starters of every type, this is probably the best positive- Lots of choices in starting character avatarsCons:- The dialogue- Despite being made in Unity, it looks and feels like an RPG Maker game, with a lot of common tropes in RPG Maker games being used here (Glowing spots for items and very out-of-place chests everywhere.)- Non-configurable controls, or at least I couldn't find any in-game- The dialogue- Very easy to lose track of what you're doing- Animations look weird- Weaknesses are confusing- The dialogue- Almost all of your 'friends' hate you- Pulls a Sonic Boom and spoils later scenes at the beginning- Inconsistent theming- The dialogue- Your best friend is a cat person. Are they a Nexomon? Are they half human? Who is the mother and who is the father? Is he a tamer? Why doesn't he have a Nexomon? Did he just forget to catch one? Is he aware of his reality? Why does he know what an RPG is? Does he cough furballs? I have no answers.Now the next section of this contains spoilers, but understand that the game spoils you on this within the first five minutes of you starting the game by pulling a Sonic Boom, so... legal spoilers??? You start off great with you're character plummeting to their death because an airship they were riding died (Which made choosing my character's avatar difficult, the screen wouldn't stop shaking violently), and then it has a hard cut to some people you aren't supposed to know or care about yet fighting a dragon who is apparently you, and you're the cause of the world ending via a sort of "Third Impact"... What an opening! I've never felt this confused within the first minute of a game! :DSo when the game actually starts at the beginning, I thought "Okay, the intro was bad, but maybe the meat of the game will make this a little better, it can't get worse." And hoo-boy, it not only got worse, it got annoyingly bad. I like to think I have a high tolerance for cheezy dialogue considering I can watch movies like Food Fight and The Room in one sitting and survive, but this game tests my limits by constantly switching between being serious, and pulling the "calling out your own tropes" every other second something happens on the screen. Going into a forest? "HAHA, this is like those RPG games!! Everyhting will go wrong! XD" Doing the capture tutorial? "HAHA, you and I both want to skip this tutorial! We could've just had a skip tutorial option, but we love this joke! XD" Breathing? "WOW, you're such a failure, how are you so STUPID?! Go die in a hole you absolute failure!" Oh yeah, did I mention that the game hates your character despite the fact that you didn't even do anything?! Because it seems like almost everyone wants to take shots at you at every dialogue choice!So yeah, definitely not my favorite game. This whole review may seem like a joke, but so does Nexomon: Extinction, it's made like a parody on games and yet none of it is funny. It might get better later on, but I had more fun in the hour it took me to write this review than in the first hour of the game, so take that as you will.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I recommend this game for anyone who likes playing Pokemon games for just the main story world stuff, or people who aren't really into the complex battle related stuff of Pokemon.The story is surprisingly interesting. There are good twists, the main steps in the plot made sense and the world was suitably interesting to work with without feeling too much of a drag at any point. My only problem with the story writing would be that it feels like there are too many 4th break references, but thats honestly just a personal taste.Gameplay is a lot simpler than Pokemon. Theres the standard set of Health/Stamina/Attack/Defence/Speed and the range of Elements that the Nexomon are categorised in, each with weaknesses and strengths in regards to attacking/being attacked. But thats basically it. There doesnt appear to be hidden stat values like EV/IV and you can't really modify a Nexomon's stats apart from using the in-game swapping buff core system. This isn't really a good/bad thing, just something to keep in mind.There have been some feedback about having a EXP Share in the game and at time of playing they had added it in. While it takes some effort to get, if you get enough it actually works more efficiently/effectively than it does in the Pokemon games.One big thing of note is the world of Nexomon itself. It scales up depending on how many fights you have done (i think?) as well as your progress in the main story. Its also free roaming when you get to an early point in the game, albeit with some blocked off areas that need story progress. This means that its nearly impossible to get an absurdly powerful Nexomon to just sweep through story progression with, but even I managed to get a decent team that was at least 10 levels ahead of what the NPC's had at times. The free roaming was an interesting choice, but it does hurt the story a bit when you get to places you've already wandered around in and your expected to look surprised.Overall while this game might struggle to have a non-Pokemon comparison it honestly does itself justice. I played this having never played the first Nexomon, so maybe one day I'll give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, there are some missing quality of life features and the variety of moves isn't very good, but it's a fun enough game if you're looking for something like traditional Pokemon but with a different feel. In long, I'll go over some of the things that stand out to me:Nexomon almost never have more than one type of elemental attack. If you have a Plant type, it'll know Plant (Grass) moves and Physical (Normal) moves and that's it. The lack of coverage makes the battles switch-heavy. You'll constantly be switching your Nexomon to match up well into theirs, and for the most part, types that are effective against something also resist that type which makes the switch safer. This isn't really a bad thing and promotes using your whole team in each battle, though you feel punished for duplicating types on your team sometimes. Physical types usually have an elemental attack, but don't resist anything so they generally just feel inferior.However, because switching happens so much, it's hard to justify using moves that buff yourself, or debuff the opponent. The pure status moves are also generally very weak. For example, making the enemy use 25% more stamina (PP), reflecting 20% damage, reducing the enemy attack and defense by 15%, a move learned by Mineral (Rock) types that nullifies Mineral damage, and so on. Ones that apply statuses are also quite inaccurate, like a 30% chance to sleep or a 50% chance to curse. Others have odd decisions, such as a very fast move that increases crit rate but lowers defense, which means you go first and get hit with your lowered defense before your next action. I find very few of the non-attacking moves appealing.Some attacking moves are also hardly different at all. My Lunabelle leveled up and had the chance to learn Drill. It has 100 Power, 100% Accuracy, 44 Speed, 5% crit rate, and costs 15 Stamina. She already knew Rocknite Burst, which has 110 Power, 95% Accuracy, 44 Speed, 8% crit rate, and costs 15 Stamina. There are many such cases through the game. Many moves also have a very low chance to apply a status, like 10~20%, which adds a lot of unpredictable randomness, which can be seen as good or bad. Statuses seem to tick down even if the Nexomon isn't on the field, so you can switch out for some of them to get rid of it.The statuses aren't explained in game as far as I can tell, and Stunned doesn't have an icon, so you don't know when your opponent is stunned and can't move. Combine that lack of icon with the low chance of applying it and it's troublesome.Grinding on wild mobs is very not lucrative. It's much better to grind through rematch trainer battles. You can get the ability to run away from wild mobs with 100% chance early on by visiting the Drake Isles and then never have to bother with something you don't want to catch. These are good things for me.The level curve is rather sharp at times. At one point, the enemy levels go from around 18 to around 28 over the course of around three battles. The game levels up as you progress it, so the wild mobs and rematches will match your current progress.There are also some places where it doesn't heal your party despite having multiple battles in a row, so you have to run back to town between battles or be well-stocked on healing items. Escape Ropes are something I miss a lot. There are fast travel waypoints, but I haven't yet found a way to go from anywhere back to the town, which would make a lot of things more convenient.The in-game "Pokedex" doesn't tell you where to capture the Nexomon, so you'll have to look online if you're searching for something specific, and then their locations will be communicated in things like "South-east of the Frozen Tundra waypoint" and you'll have to compare what you're seeing in the grass to what they say should be there to confirm you're in the right place. The filters on their online Nexopedia don't work so you're better off using fan sites like Nexopad if you want to see information on them.Also you can't set settings on the main menu, so if you lower the volume in the settings of your save file a lot, the menu is going to hurt your ears each time you launch the game. Maybe lower the game's volume on your computer's volume mixer instead.All that aside, it's pretty enjoyable and has most of the things you'd expect from a Pokemon game. Metroidvania elements to get new stuff in old areas (like HMs), shinies, 1v1 battles with type matchups, catching a team, evolving them, and so on. But, it does feel distinct from Pokemon. There are no IVs or EVs, and Nexomon don't have genders so I doubt there is breeding, and all battles have been 1v1.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say, I grew up with Pokémon. But I'm sure a lot of you are already familiar with that series. Anyway, nostalgia was the reason I was immediately interested in checking out Nexomon: Extinction. The important question here is: Is it just another Pokémon clone? Or is it actually very different? To be honest, whilst I wouldn't mind a game that plays out like the Pokémon series, I went into the game expecting a generic monster training game without any substance regardless. However, I couldn't be more wrong. Nexomon: Extinction turned out to be such a wonderful ride I never wanted to get off.Whilst Nexomon: Extinction is technically the second game in the Nexomon series, both games are not related to each other at all. The story is independent, although there are references available throughout the game about the previous entry. However, as I didn't get to play the first game yet, this review will be solely based on my experience with Nexomon: Extinction.Nexomon: Extinction opens with introducing the main character who grew up in an orphanage. The protagonist is about to begin their journey and have to select their first Nexomon. However, as the journey advances, it's evident that there is something terribly wrong. Tyrant Nexomon are becoming a threat to humans, and monsters, as they start to go rampage. The main character joins a guild and tries help with the fight, however, there might be more into it than it seems at first glance. During the long journey, the main character will discover a lot of secrets along the way.Yes, yes, and yes! This quote perfectly describes my experience with Nexomon: Extinction. The story seemed generic, at first, with the main character obtaining a Nexomon, starting to collect various other ones, all while having the main objective of eliminating the Tyrants. Well, admittedly, the player usually fights against the main villain but I guess it's more or less the same anyway.I'll keep this short, as I'm positive everyone knows how monster training games work. Nexomon: Extinction implements turn-based combats where the player can either fight against other tamers or random Nexomon. In addition to that, it's possible to catch wild Nexomon with so-called Nexomon traps, as well as giving them snacks, and complete a small mini-game of pressing specific buttons in the right order, to increase the chance for being successful. There are different types of Nexomon available such as water, fire, psycho, etc., as well as different rarity types which made it more challenging if the player wants to obtain every single Nexomon.I would strongly advise to level up the whole party instead of single Nexomon as Nexomon: Extinction implements an unusual system of level scaling so other tamers, and wild Nexomon, are catching up to the player. This feature depends on the player's three highest Nexomons and might become a problem later on when the player has to go through multiple battles without being able to heal in between. I feel quite mixed about this feature as it adds more challenge to the playthrough, however, I found it slightly annoying as I just wanted to experience the story at some point. Regardless, it's not impossible to beat the game, so it didn't bother me a lot.Graphic-wise, Nexomon: Extinction is beautiful. The environment reminds me of the Pokémon series with being able to find wild Nexomon in the grass or caves. Anyway, each city was so different from each other and had a completely different theme — Although I ended up loving each design. Fortunately, the Nexomon itself have a great design too and there are over 300 for the player to catch. I found the legendary ones especially memorable, although it's evident that they're more special. To top it off, when the player gets into a battle the environment doesn't only change depending on which location they're fighting but is also animated with leaves or wind moving around.The cutscenes itself work like a typical visual novel where each character has their own sprite and facial expressions. In the actual game, the expressions don't change, however, there are bubbles appearing above the characters that indicate what they are feeling — And it works out well. Something that really stood out here is that Nexomon: Extinction actually implements CGs for special scenes. Unfortunately, there is no way to look them up in a gallery, but as the character's design is selectable at the beginning of the game, the CGs are slightly altered as well.I expected Nexomon: Extinction to be a clone of the Pokémon series, however, it's much more than that. To my surprise, this game managed to catch me off guard with its well-executed plot and excellent comedic character writing. As a result, I ended up being more interested in experiencing the story than to hunt for Nexomon. Sure, a lot of things are very similar to Pokémon, however, Nexomon: Extinction does its own thing and adds its own charm, along the way, and managed to stand out, delivering an unforgettable experience to me. That being said, I can highly recommend Nexomon: Extinction to all fans of Pokémon, as well as newcomers who are looking for a game with a memorable story.

_childDocuments_.review: Barely passable as a creature collecting game, nothing noteworthy to justify a playthrough. The major thing i was missing here is a good sense of progress. You don't get that from levels, those scale anyways. Most areas are accessible from very early on, so you don't get anything out of travel and exploration either (there is not even a map, what gives?). The main storyline exists, but is nothing to write home about.I disliked the art style quite a bit. I'm not entirely sure if that's only due to preexisting mobile game trauma, or there is something inherently not good about it, but i'll settle on the latter for now. Overly bright colors, stiff animation. A lot of generic elements randomly mixed together. The creature designs themselves have anything from aweful to it's-just-a-pokemon to actually great, but too few of those last ones. The legendaries in particular are rather underwhelming, throwing more stuff on top usually doesn't improve anything. In terms of gameplay there isn't enough to distinguish creatures from each other.Again, the level scaling - at the point where anything wild and tamer owned is just the same level as your team anyways, one has to ask, why even have levels. I'd rather someone do away with the thing entirely and innovate, instead of cludge together something based an established system that usually was included because it worked better than other things. Being able to access a new area and defeat new foes because you became powerful enough for it is something central to the RPG experience. I appreciate the difficulty from not simply being able to outlevel challenges, but that is very little gain from something undermining mechanics to this degree.Lastly, the meta jokes. Why. It's not a good fit for this genre and extremely immersion breaking, just to save a few minutes spent coming up with good character writing instead, some of which - extra tragically - actually exists. Not every game has to be portal in order to be good.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best monster catching game I have ever played!In case you only read the first line I want to stress that point more than any other. I tried to keep this review spoiler free. Just in case this a spoiler warning. I have had SO MUCH FUN playing this game and I want to make sure people wont miss out on this experience. Nexomon is as far from being “Just another Pokemon clone” as you can get. I will include some information for those who are undecided about Nexomon Extinction.Now there are some similarities to other monster catching games but that is sticking to the genre. You need locations to heal your Nexomon. You need people to battle and strengthen your team. But the Nexomon team have included many unique elements to their game that I feel truly sets it apart from other games.Firstly the game revolves around a huge Immersive storyline. The story is a continuation from Nexomon One so while it's possible to enjoy Nexomon Extinction as a standalone game I would recommend starting with Nexomon One. The game begins similaar to most others. You are a young person ready to head off into the world and catch your first Nexomon. You're thrown into a world that has seen much hardship. Whole cities are in ruin. Through the story you can affect change and create a brighter future. You are ready to join the Guild of Tamers. The Guild are a global organisation who are tasked with helping out the population by maintaining peace. Each member of the Guild is ranked according to their accomplishments.  This is represented by two factors. Your Guild rank and Reputation level. Once you get your first Nexomon that is where any similarity to other games ends. The games storyline literally lands in your lap with a giant explosion. From here on you will find yourself hooked by the ever changing story elements and engaged until the very last battle, including the HUGE TWIST which I did not see coming. In addition to the main story there are currently over 500 side quests available. So you will find yourself with plenty to do as you can see from my time spent on the game.Reputation is another unique game feature. Reputation is a persistent measure of your progress and ability as a tamer. Your reputation will increase as you perform deeds for others, complete missions set by the guild and catch unique Nexomon. This affects the world around you too. As you improve your reputation you will notice that interactions reflect your higher standing. Along with this you will find the interactions with many characters, chief among them Coco your friend and companion show you a development team that really cares about the game they have created and they don’t take themselves too seriously.The grinding in this game is more than just earning EXP. There is a lot more effort involved in Nexomon Extinction but the harder something is to achieve the better it feels when you do. So in addition to grinding for EXP you can farm shards. These have multiple uses, chief among them is being combined to form Cores. Each Nexomon can have up to four equipped which provide a boost in battle. These include EXP gained, gold gained and attack power among others. The first two add that extra depth to grinding as I often found myself equipping gold cores to grind for gold one minute and EXP cores another minute. Then you may find yourself hunting for shards to build cores to increase your Nexomon’s abilities in battle.The game contains 381 different Nexomon, all of which can be caught in a single playthrough. I like almost all of the Nexomon designs including Legendary Nexomon however I do understand that this is all a matter of taste. You will need to explore every corner of the world to catch them all too. Within a single area different patches of grass will spawn different Nexomon.The game presents you with a bright, colourful and vibrant world. The graphics are still 2D but this is technically only the second game in the series. Players of Nexomon will note that there are graphical improvements. The world feels much more alive. The game doesn’t have a gym system. In Nexomon Extinction things are different. As the story unfolds you will learn who are going to be your most powerful enemies. There are more boss battles than I can count and a persistent all powerful threat, a final boss that your journey eventually leads to.This game is far more open world than any other game of its type. Almost from the first time you leave your home you are free to explore most of the world around you and there is certainly plenty to explore. I almost did not want to include anything negative but it isn’t fair to present a biased opinion. Without giving too much away the final battle has a section where it feels choreographed. The fight goes a specific way regardless of what you have done in the lead up to it. It does feel like you can lose this battle  but it just feels like the game is holding your hand and telling you which buttons to press. I would have preferred to fight with the team I had chosen and developed over the game.Another area for improvement is the move sets of certain Nexomon were quite limited. For example each type has one strongest attack move. But not all Nexomon are able to learn it. This is fine in the early game but towards the late game Nexomon will have stronger moves and it may leave you at an unnecessary disadvantage. I'm not saying that all Nexomon should have the same moves but they should have the option to have the strongest move of their type.While there are lots of fantastic looking Legendary Nexomon almost all of them are not available for you until after the main story. Now while I understand I would actually have preferred the chance to catch them sooner. When you play through the storyline there is one part where catching Legendary Nexomon would line up with current events.The game uses a dynamic system that governs the strength of encounters. As you progress along the story Nexomon and Tamers become stronger. This can feel like the progress has not amounted to much. Fortunately the system was revamped soon after launch and improved. The fact that Tamers get stronger over time is actually more realistic. Facing the same tamer multiple times and them having the same level Nexomon all the time would make no sense.To sum up how I feel about this game: Good Points•	A deep Immersive storyline that will keep you entertained for hours.•	A beautiful vibrant open world to explore.•	Character interactions that change dynamically according to reputation and achievements.•	A monster catching game doing its own thing and standing out.•	Numerous side quests to give you plenty to do.•	Added depth to characters development beyond simple EXP Gain.•	381 unique and mostly well designed Nexomon to tame and train.•	Lots of fun and humour woven into character interactions.•	Plenty of boss battles.•	Every Tamer can be fought again. This makes level grinding far easier.•	Fantastic sound design. High octane during Epic battles, calm during forest walks•	A game with a development team who really care about the quality of their game and the opinions of those who play and support it.Areas for Improvement•	The final battle feels in places choreographed and preset.•	Certain Nexomon lack a comprehensive moveset.•	The dynamic encounters can make progress feel less effective as enemies get stronger with you. But you can level up faster than others do with effort.I honestly cannot recommend this game enough. This is a fantastic monster catching game and much more than a clone of anything. I can safely say that you will have a hell of a time playing this game. The fantastic storyline is a fun ride from start to finish. Please give these guys a try. You will not be disappointed. You can tell that I really mean it too with almost 400 hours of play time. A new update is coming that will make this game better than it already is. I absolutely love NEXOMON EXTINCTION!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a less kiddy approach to pokemon with alot of QOL changes as well as alot of little bits and bobs to chase then look no further.- Art Style is adorable but is appropriately creepy on the proper mons.- Story is way better than expected.  Not Oscar material, but I've been interested and did not predict where it would go.  Definitely a more mature/grim world but counterbalanced by constant humor.  I want to see where it ends up!- Humor is generally quite good, game knows when to mock itself and the genre.  4th wall breaks are definitely a thing.- Combat is harder than standard pokemon and there are "full heal" mechanics scattered throughout the world to keep fights a threat without making you constantly go heal.   - Catching minigame is an improvement on pokemon.  I know my chances, how to improve them, and it's more than just "beat on the mob until it's low and use a higher ball"- Alot of passive items to find and collect that enhance your progression or QOL.- Elemental strengths/weaknesses matter but it's not utter suicide to fight into your weakness.  Bonus damage is only +25%, reduced damage only -35%.  This goes both ways, just because you elementally counter something doesn't mean it can't chunk you.- "core system" lets you customize your mon stats to a degree and also solve the leveling problem as some cores copy a % of exp from any defeat and if you explore/quest you get some free pretty early.- Tons of unique critters, I'm still finding a some new ones 40+ hours in.Only con is that while it does a good job of weighting accuracy vs damage vs speed and etc I feel like status effects are generally balanced to be a bit weak and the overall move library could use more variety.  Each element gets template moves and variety outside of that exists,  but im not sure how viable alot of the other stuff is.

_childDocuments_.review: A gem of a monster tamer RPG. Nexomon: Extinction is an excellent game and a fantastic follow-up to the original Nexomon. The massive step forward in pretty much all aspects from gameplay to story is very impressive.Let's get this out of the way now: It's very obvious that yes, Nexomon: Extinction is not the first game to ever attempt this genre. Just like Nexomon 1, the inspiration taken from Pokemon and similar games is obvious, and for some people that carries with it a certain expectation of similarity. It's best to let those expectations go because despite appearances, this game is very much its own thing.For one, Nexomon: Extinction has an excellent sense of self-aware humor. It knows when to crack a joke, and when to take itself seriously. I was so entertained by the characters and world that I felt a bit empty when the credits rolled. To me, that's the sign of a really well made world in a video game.The gameplay is a little bit less refined than I'd like, but I can appreciate it for what it is. Battles are very straight forward and your go-to strategy will probably always be to use a buff if you have one, then spam your strongest attack until you run out of stamina. Rinse and repeat. In the next game, I'd like to see a more involved battle system with more nuance and harder decisions.As a whole, this game is very impressive and definitely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid 9/10.Nexomon is quite possibly my favourite game in the monster-catching genre. Some may argue that the combat system is too simplistic, but as someone who plays games to wind down and relax, I find myself quite thankful for it. However the fact that the level of the tamers and monsters scale to your party level can get quite annoying as it means you will constantly have to backtrack and heal up. The graphics and art style are absolutely stunning! I am not much of a fan of the pixel art style, so this is a huge plus for me. The Nexomon themselves are well-designed and really nice to look at. The story is alright, and the character development is... eh.Coco, the cat companion is annoying but in an endearing sort of way, and I absolutely love him. This may be controversial, but I also do like how the game breaks the fourth wall pretty frequently. The sense of humour in this game may not be for everyone, but it definitely made me laugh a lot.All in all, I would definitely recommend this title to anyone looking for a fun game in the monster-catching genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Your enjoyment of this game will depend on how easily you unlearn the bad habits picked up in . No roadblocks! They're gone! At least mostly. Hit the ground running in any direction to build up a full team in the early game. Wild encounters and battles scale with story progress (with small wiggle room of an extra few levels to keep up with a slightly over-levelled party). No more endless steamroll, no more pointless loading screens to birds eternally at level 2! If you railroad the story, enemy levels will overtake you. But don't just sit there and train in the same spot like some traumatic recreation of Victory Road. Nexomon are similar levels everywhere - go explore! Find some vaults, go to locations the story doesn't take you, level as you go. A single over-levelled starter isn't going to cut it. Defense grows slower than attack, so lower levelled nexomon can still take chunks out of you. Enemy tamers have diverse parties too, and they'll switch between them constantly. It's rare to leave a battle without a few scratches and maybe a lost limb. Battles aren't usually hard, but are always punishing. Get used to buying items. There are also rocks that will heal your party, but the game doesn't tell you about them. They're a secret. There's a story! It's quite good, in an anime way, with a mostly funny sidekick and decent writing aimed at teenage+ gamers.  is a fresh bite of Pokemon Gen 2/3 nostalgia. The monsters are generally quite good, and all are usable this time, with stripped down mechanics (no IV/EV, hidden powers, abilities, minigames, safari), single-types (of which there are 9) and equal exp progression. The world is nice, though becomes a little soft on my screen, and quite dark in the details: with parts Pokemon, Twitch chat and Attack on Titan. It is, all in all, very well put together and I've enjoyed playing it immensely. I wonder, with how long it took me to really get my head around the strengths/weaknesses of each type and how to win battles consistently, how accessible Pokemon is to newcomers these days. Kids must go through the thing in a constant state of mild confusion without quite knowing why things work/don't now that there are so many combinations of moves/ stats/ abilities. Although that's much the same as I experienced AoE2 etc. back in the day and I played that as much as I could without getting caught transgressing my 30minutes/day.Small gripes: often a lack of weight/vastness/awe/wonder in key moments. This is not a game that wants to take itself too seriously, and I'm glad it doesn't, but it's stuck at "cute" until it finds deeper chords to strike.

_childDocuments_.review: As a result of being a life long Pokemon player, I have extremely low standards.N:E is a pretty good game, with monster designs leagues above the usual pokemon clones. In contrast to Pokemon evolving from its JRPG roots into the monolith that it is today, N:E takes the reverse approach and go back to the tried-and-true design ethos of the 90s neo-fantasy combat and world building.Pros:* Decently engaging story* Great number of monster designs* Sleek & mostly practical UINeutral:* Very tongue-in-cheek writing, may not appeal to everyone* No dual-typing as far as I can tell. Have to think more as to whether this is a good thing.* Level scaling is very controversial, on one hand it makes progression feels a little pointless at times, on the other it does help with the mindless X spamming that comes with its predecessorsCons:* Very simplified stat system* Rather grindy in placesOverall, very recommended if you're into this type of game.

_childDocuments_.review: To begin, I would certainly recommend this game for anyone looking for a decent monster tamer. It has good fundamentals and overall is rather enjoyable up until the end where it becomes a tedious slog.The Good-The narrator / cat person is really funny and is worth buying the game for his dialog alone-The game is relatively challenging compared to Pokemon-You can't just overpower this game by spamming one monster and one move you will need a diverse and well balanced party. Not being effective is a big deal.The Bad-The story isn't very fleshed our nor is the climate change angle factored in as well as it could be. We never see nexomon migrations fleeing changing climate or anything of that manner.-The characters outside the cat are incredibly boring and we barely interact with them. The two friends of the MC are two dimensional when compared to the rivals of the pokemon game.-The art in cutscenes is bad-The game levels with you so all zones are at your level at all times. This makes it difficult to level up to an appropriate place to beat one of the Tyrants (nexomon's equivalent of pokemon gyms). The gameplay loop ends up being, do missions until you have enough money to buy items so you can face tank your way through the PVE events.-The leveling curve is so annoying that it becomes more efficient to just go and catch fresh leveled nexomon at a certain point to fill the type hole that has developed in your team.-Never felt the need to use any of the behind the scenes crafting systems you can just buy potions and ignore most challenges until the final few boss fights. ConclusionAll in all its worthy the money, don't go in looking for a great story though.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently I can't recommend the game in this state. The devs are clearly not focusing on the most basic functionalities that should be implemented ASAP!! _childDocuments_.review: "Train hard to become the greatestDynamic difficulty will see the world around you get more challenging as you progress, as even defeated trainers come back stronger than before and ready to battle again!"This feature of the game is likely different than what you would think.I was enjoying this game until I realized that the world levels with you. The sense of progression from grinding your Nexomon is lost because of this, and it feels like there is no point to leveling your team up. Sure there are a lot of ways to level your team all at once, but I feel creating a world scaling system like this was a huge mistake. I enjoy the story, the writing, the characters, and the world, but I cannot recommend it purely due to this scaling mechanic. I may just finish the game because I want to experience the rest of the story, but it won't be nearly as enjoyable. If I had known about the mechanic from the beginning, I would not have made the purchase and would not have gifted it to others.If you enjoy the experience of leveling up your team and feeling your efforts paying off because of it, do not get this game. If you're just curious of the story, I say go ahead. The writing also includes Nexomon's recognizable wall-breaking humor.

_childDocuments_.review: No... just no. 1. The humor. Oh god, the humor. I have never seen worse. Fourth wall breaking isn't always funny. Jokes about how the developer was too lazy to change sprites or is too poor to do something arent funny. Jokes about how something doesnt make sense arent funny. It just takes me out of the game experience and I wanted to vomit each time a character made another "joke". There are exceptions, but they are exactly that, not the rule.2. The story. One of the more enjoyable parts of this game. Unfortunately no meaningful way to influence it. Some good scenes and genuinely good ideas, but that's all. At one point you meet a spooky~ character who has potential and he vanishes after... one battle.3. German localization. I don't know what convinced me to play this game in my mother tongue. In germany we would say "Welcher Teufel hat mich denn da geritten?" - It's ♥♥♥♥. Like... One Nexomon was spelled wrong and appearently I was the only person to google that specific monster, because google had literally _Zero_ search results under that name. And then there is "Kabsel"... Who did this translation of "capsule"? A fiver year old?4. Difficulty and Combat System. If you thought Pokemon games were easy in the story mode, think again. Just level your first Nexomon to ♥♥♥♥ and kill everything with your strongest attack. It seems like there are so, so many useless attacks and abilities. Some are waaaay to underpowered.5. The logic. If you thought the antagonist of Black/White made lowkey sense, don't even play this one. She has a point, you know? Funny that some guild tamers are able to capture me, when I'm pretty sure I could have taken all of them without breaking into a sweat. How are there characters displayed as powerful as ♥♥♥♥ when they are suddenly downgraded for story convenience?6. The Nexomon. Some interesting designs. SOME (Couplet, Duh, Lunabelle, Muh). The others are forgettable at best, and ridicolous at worst (Caninui, Lamparos, Ponic, Mallark, Hydrip, Lovinu...). If you think a garbage bag or an icecream cone are idiotic, don't play this game. Where do they get their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clothes? (Poyal, Chowser, Volprofessor) Not everything has to be a dragon or some weird bastard-T-Rex you know? Don't expect me to get hyped over a walking hydrant. Some have way too much ♥♥♥♥ going on, some not enough. 7. Legendaries. Yes, let us catch all the interesting and powerful Nexomon (almost all of them dragons btw) in the post game, great idea. And let us grind for all of them, even greater idea! I have all required tributes but I will never touch this game again and all except four or five will remain uncaught.8. The quests and the grind: Stupid. One small tip: Buy everything at least ten times so you dont have to walk as much. Grind shards for like five hours and you are good to go. And even then I would have to revisit every area like ten times. Annoying as ♥♥♥♥. I couldn't take it any more. And don't think you can go around and just buy the shards or, dare I even say, cheat your way around the grind, no, no. For some reason the option to buy shards doesn't exist and although I bought enough items for my next ten playthroughs I can sit on my money and do nothing with it. The developer thought he was clever with multiple anti-cheat systems ... in a solo-player game. Let that sink in. If they focussed on making the gameplay more enjoyable, maybe this game would even be fun! Oh, by the way: One tip: Challenge every trainer twice as soon as you can if you want the achievement, because if you find out afterwards, good luck finding the exact trainers you're missing!The bottom line is that this game is a simple copy of the Pokemon games with the rare good idea, some good moments, an interesting world, but way simpler, less polished and with far less FUN. I wouldn't even recommend on sale. I just want my 24 hours back.BUT if you're looking for a game for your 5-year old brother or sibling, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: The story is really great. I can't remember a single story line from any pokemon game, but Nexomon is very memorable, and with many unpredictable twists. Other reviews mentioned the music and it's true that it's really good - becomes light and playful when the story is having fun, becomes dark and foreboding when the story is serious, and becomes powerful and exhilarating when in a big battle. It made me actually notice the music in a game! The humor is appreciated, and the vast number of Mons is great. Will probably play through again to try some of the others. Creature design is really cool, and the overall art style of the environments is bright and vibrant. The one area that could be improved is the battle system, which isn't bad, just very simple and lacking depth. This is well made up for by the rest of the game. This game made me a Nexomon fan. Can't wait to see what they do with Nexomon 3.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one of the better Pokemon clones out there, and I definitely 100% recommend it.I'll skip the pros and just write the cons, since there's already a ton of people already covering that stuff.Cons:1. All the Nexomons feel really samey with their stats, there's not really any that have stats WILDLY different than anyone else, like there's none that have way more health than another, or any built like a glass cannon (except maybe dragons). I get that the devs probably intended that as a way to allow players to just pick what they think looks cool, but it makes it more boring in my opinion.2. No traits on any Nexomons. Same as con #1, all of them are just stats+moves+type, no traits to help make them feel different from each other. Also I was really expecting the thief mice to have something like Pickup.3. RNG-heavier than Pokemon, annoyingly. Too many moves come with statuses that have awfully low status rates, and even the non-damaging status moves usually have a 70% chance to work. Heck, I've got almost six hours into the game and I've literally never seen the grass starter's poison move actually poison anything.4. The not-Pokedex isn't great. There's no faster way to scroll through it, there's no location function, none of the sorting tabs are labeled, and I wish there was a way to sort by stats.5. Yuck, level scaling. I don't know if it's tied to the story progression or if they're really scaling automatically, though.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has good graphics, good designs and a nice premise but it lacks a soul and that is mostly because of the weak writing.The constant use of meta humor really throws you off and breaks the immersion. The character Coco, who is your companion, makes a lot of these jokes and is really annoying. A small little meta joke in a interaction with a NPC or an item, I can accept but really? So many meta jokes at the start of the game? During events that are so important for the story? I couldn't really feel the impact of any scene or feel like I was in a different world because the game itself reminded constantly that it was a game and that there are cliches used in this genre. If pointing out cliches was enough to make something funny, tvtropes would be the best comedy work of all times. I also really lamented not seeing little texts in the objects around the world to give you some additional knowledge about how people live their day-to-day lives and to give the game a bit more charm. You can only interact with itens that directly affect the gameplay, which is a bit of a shame. I would love to have more pieces of lore for me to discover by interacting with the enviroment.  I played for a hour and watched my boyfriend playing for two hours and I could never overcome my boredom, although I wish I did since I won't be asking for a refund. My boyfriend did like the game, although he cares much less about writing in games than I do. Maybe if your favorite thing about Pokemon is seeing cool monsters and making them duel, this game will work for you. My favorite part was the cozy and immersive universe and charming characters and these elements are absent from this game so I can't recommend it.

It's a very well made game, it's got a kicker good soundtrack, attractive settings and atmosphere, monster designs and animations are unique and fun, and the story is intriguing, though I have yet to finish it yet due to the grind involved. After a while it gets tiring. After every story advancing event, the whole world gets stronger. Wild nexomons and trainers all scale in difficulty based on your story progress, and in order to keep up you have to spend literal hours grinding every nexomon up to a competitive level before and after you advance the story in any way. You could also just catch wild Nexomons that are already leveled up competitively, but that kind of ruins the fun of having a "team" if you're always replacing everyone in your lineup.I wouldn't say it's a good Pokemon alternative. It's a decent enough game on it's own, if you can survive the grinding. But I don't think it really compares to pokemon at all. It has none of the sense of adventure that old pokemon games give you, no element of exploration, no massive dungeons that take hours to find your way through. It's really just "go here, talk to these people, go here, fight this boss, grind your party, repeat". If you're looking for a pokemon clone, prepare to be underwhelmed, as no game has ever come close to be honest, and trust me I've looked for years for another game like that. But on it's own, Nexomon Extinction is an above average, well-put-together game with a good story and lots of monsters to catch.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got 8 hours playtime right now and I must say that I am thoroughly impressed so far. Most people would assume this is a Pokemon rip-off but it's much more than that and so far I am enjoying it more than any Pokemon game I've played. It has a lot of similarities to Pokemon but also has a lot of it's own features. It also has a much more vibrant world filled with charm and much better written characters. The characters and vibe have a nice sense of humour too. It doesn't take itself too seriously which is nice for a game of this style. The game actually has a story which seems thought out and well written, so far there are plenty of mysteries that I am looking forward to discovering and seeing where the adventure takes me and my character. _childDocuments_.review: This game beats pokemon in most of it's aspects.Pros:Better story than all pokemon saga combined.Capturing pokemon now has several % you can play around (enemy HP, food you give to the target, type of pokeball, passive item %, status effects) so you can min-max better than using always raticate and praying to RNG.You can play vs the same trainer an infinite amount of time. The pokemons of that trainer will rise in level as the story progresses.Instead of getting atributes based on who you fight, all pokemon of the same race(?) get the same base stats and you can modify them through objects (it kills the replayability and the breeding, in case you liked exploiting sexually and ditto and praying to RNG gods).You have "share xp" items from the very beginning and it cuts the grind by a lot.The prices of the items make sense. A food is 1/3 the price of a pokeball, and it improves the chance of capturing a pokemon like if you where using a type-pokeball (x3 the price of a pokeball)You can get objects to disengage from combat with a success rate of 100%.You can get another object where you dont engage with wild pokemons (get ♥♥♥♥ zubats), which can be disable any time.All starters are available to capture. No nintendo-link ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.All evolutions are straight forward, no need to get a moon stone and fight in a day with full moon under the moonlight in the moon forest under the mt moon in the route 4 on a wensday.You can have several safes up at the same time (up to 4)Cons:Some pokemon seems inspired in that 4chan meme of "pick two words, cut them in half, thats your pokemon name, draw something related".You have dragons ingame, but they are not "dragon type", they are just harder to catch.There are no double types (bird with plant and water types are just a big cognitive dissonance for me).Less replayability because no breeding,  less grind (because all savage pokemon rise in level and are captured easily no matter the level) and no hidden stats (you use slots for power-ups).The skills pokemon learn are kind of straight forward, so you won't get crazy combos atm (no rare space and ♥♥♥♥ like that) so you will end up with the strongest type attack of you pokemon, the smallest attack of the type of your pokemon, the strongest normal attack and a 4th utility skill. The skills that don't fit in those categories are easily forgetable. Afaik you can only use your pokemon type attacks and normal attacks. You cannot learn a "plant" attack on your charizard to counter water enemies for example.You can change "pokemon trainer" for any other random RPG fantasy character, and the story still would work.Better than any of the pokemons released since 1998.

_childDocuments_.review: The good: This game has a charming atmosphere, solid worldbuilding, and takes the pokemon formula into uncharted territory. For the most part, the world is very grim dark, with humanity on the brink of extinction. This is offset by the goofy characters, which are pretty solid overall.The Bad: If you're looking for even a modicum of strategic depth, this ain't it chief. This game is 100% dependent on your creature's levels, and that's all that matters. Even the typing advantages and disadvantages don't amount to much. All in all, you just use you're strongest attack over and over until the enemy dies.Overall: I'd give this a 7/10. If you've ever played Siralim or Monster Sanctuary, this game's not comparable in depth. The extraneous factors are better, however. If I didn't like the genre, I wouldn't reccommend this, but if you like monster catching games, go ham.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the good stuff. It's not perfect, but going toe-to-toe with a franchise like Pokemon is hard, and it's impressive to see something pull that off on what I'm assuming is the rpgmaker engine.But I'm getting ahead of myself.What is Nexomon? It's a *long* narrative-driven pokemonlike.Balance-wise, it's at the Red/Blue/Yellow level. Everything is mono type, but there's STAB bonuses and some interesting moves and you don't automatically get a free switch when you KO an opposing monster. There's also a universal stamina meter instead of PP, and big moves take a lot, but you can skip turns to recover it. There's a definite metagame here, even if it's not *super* complicated.Nexomon is also very convenience oriented. You can free-roam a *lot* more than in pokemon. The safari zone is open right from the jump. There's no HMs---just items that your trainer holds. There's no EVs and IVs or other hidden build information (that I'm aware of, at least.) When you approach a patch of grass, you can see where the encounters are in it. You can tell your capture chance based on a monster's status, HP, and other factors. Capturing involves some button inputs, rather than just watching an orb wiggle. You can also find tons of collectible items that boost your overall capture chance and encounter odds for certain elements and rarities, which is a really welcome addition to the formula.In terms of the individual monsters, a lot of them look a little we-have-pokemon-at-home, but there's *tons* of them, and some have fantastic visual design. The concepts get pretty inventive, too. There's bower birds and fire hydrants and ice cream sundaes. It's neat.As for complaints, I can really only muster up a few.The internal logic to the elemental weaknesses in Nexomon feels a little hard to wrap my head around sometimes. Sure, water beats fire. But plant beats...lightning? And psychic seems like it genuinely rolls a dice to decide what it cares about.The writing is also *very* fourth wall breaking. This keeps the mood light, but it's kind of a shame, because the actual plot is genuinely engaging. There's decent worldbuilding and character writing and a few solid twists, but the game tries very hard to keep reminding you that it's just a game. You don't get to really sink in and enjoy the setting.So overall: if you like monster-catching games and you don't need them to be too complex, definitely give this a try. I'd love to see more in this series, but even as a standalone Nexomon: Extinction is great.

_childDocuments_.review: Interested in seeing some gameplay? see below!TL:DR: Nexomon Extinction is charming. The catching system in this game is top notch, cute graphics and a very anime-styled story make for a fun experience. My main problem is the amount of exposition and cutscenes throughout the game. 8/10I know what your first question is: Is this better than Pokemon? Well I think it's very different to Pokemon and therefore it's hard to compare, but it does have a nice 2D Pokemon style feeling which the newer games may be missing.Nexomon Extinction is a great addition to the pet-battling genre of games, it takes the world built up in the first game, adds a bunch of cool new Nexomon and throws players into a new story experience. The game begins by offering you a whopping NINE different starters to choose from, this is an awesome change from other games like this, you are also able to catch all of these Nexomon later, which means you don't have to worry about starter FOMO! There is so much story and exposition at the start of this, it rivals Pokemon Sun and Moon in the annoying amount of cutscenes, it took about 10-15 minutes to reach the first battle of the game, which was also part of the story . The huge assortment of different Nexomon you can catch and battle is a treat, there's a huge array of different options, whether you're into cute animals or edgy dragons, there's something for everyone.The battle system is great, there are 9 different Nexomon typings and an array of different moves and status conditions to try out, the stamina bar is an interesting addition to this genre, forcing you to make complex decisions about how you want to manage the resource. The catching system is much more complex and interesting than others in the genre, there are 5 different ways of increasing your catch chance, and a Bop-it! style minigame in the end. Graphics: 10/10Absolutely adorable pets and chibi style characters make the game a charming experience.Audio: 7/10The audio is nice and chill, easy to listen to while playing.Gameplay: 8/10The gameplay is fun and interesting. There are some major differences to other games of the genre which allow this game to stand on its own.Overall: 8/10This game is extremely charming and the battles are loads of fun. The story can be silly but is still more engaging than certain other weapon based games released in the past year.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun and charming monster collecting game with an enjoyable story. Journeying across the continent and the many habitats we are provided numerous opportunities to fight and discover these unique Nexomon. This game is unafraid to break the fourth wall, and while this may be disconnecting, does offer moments of levity, self-awareness, and express the love the developers have for their product.A massive positive for this game was its inclusion of the Custom Save, allowing us to take on many fun challenges like Nuzlocke or Randomizer with full game support.Though I will list what I found negative please understand that I have greatly enjoyed this game and don't feel any of the issues listed should deter others from playing it. The game is great regardless of my percieved issues, I intend to keep playing and enjoying myself, and I'm looking forward to what VEWO may create in the future.-Straightforward: While there are plenty of side missions/stories to entertain ourselves the game is very direct with its story. It may have benefitted from more time/opportunities to interact with and learn of the world and the people we ally with.-Endgame: This is an arguable issue as the Custom Save system serves as an infinite option for replay-ability. However, the game, outside of collecting the Boss Nexomon, lacks significant challenges or activities after you beat the main story. A tourney system, new area, or Post-Game story could've aided this.-Level Scaling: This is an issue I'm conflicted on. While I love that we can train anywhere and see more Nexomon as the enemies progress in difficulty to the story, it makes it significantly harder to search for specific Nexomon when we're now faced with all the evolutions of an area. Perhaps having determined locations (and an indicator of them in the Nexopedia) for wild Nexomon would've solved the search issue. And instead of only adding evolutions, that can reach the 3rd/Final form, introducing new enemies locked at lower levels would've made it more rewarding to return to these areas.-NPC's: In relation to my first point on story, we just don't get enough time to get to know the people around us. Ross gets humorous moments, but he and Nora don't get enough time to develop as Friends/Rivals for the MC, this is a shame as I'd have loved to work with/fight against them more often to learn more about them. Coco is a dear and constant companion, but it may have been nicer to have a chance to stop and talk to him, or see him fighting with his own Nexomon. Finally we don't get to see many other Tamers, save sparse moments with the Gold ranked, and it would've been great to work alongside or see/hear how others were faring in shared/different missions.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't listen to the review that complains about level scaling!  There are cores that work like Exp Shares and give 25% of the exp gained without having to battle.  You can equip 4 of them per Nexomon and they don't reduce the experience any of them gain from battle.  So basically, your entire team can be gaining 100% of the experience per fight.I almost didn't buy the game because of that one review, but I'm glad that I just bought it anyway.  It's a really fun game with a beautiful art style, tons of Nexomon to collect, a good story, and lots of things to do.  Highly recommended for fans of monster catching games like Pokemon.Edit:  I completed the game and I can say that having only one Nexomon leveled up is a really bad idea.  Plenty of fights have enemies of multiple types and you'd be at a huge disadvantage in terms of type weaknesses and resistances with only one Nexomon.  I didn't have any trouble beating the game though, because I leveled up a team with more than one type of Nexomon to counter whatever was thrown at me.  Anyway, it was a really enjoyable experience and I recommend the game even more now.

I was just wondering if there was ever a pokemon game released on PC and stumbled on this alternative. And I have to say: it was perfect.I used to play a lot of pokemon back in the day and tried again with different new ones, but really didn't like them.Now this game hits every note in my book when it comes to gameplay, story, visuals - oh my god the visuals. I mean, what fun is a game where there is no challenge?When it comes to the story, it's quite interesting as well. It is sort of tragic and humorous at the same time. Especially since there is a lot based upon different things that are just part of every top style rpg game that this game makes fun off through it's characters.When it comes to interactions with different characters, i was amazed as well. There are a LOT of people just wandering or standing around in the city and EVERY single one has their own lines. I never saw a repeat. NEVER. They also change based on what currently happened in the region. So the dialogues were never skip worthy.Now the visual. Oh my good lord. "Purrfect" is all I can say. The style is consistent appart from two small scenes and it is beautiful with lots and lots of little details. The shaders look great, the different weather conditions and the difference between outdoor and indoor scenes is also very well done.PS:Also, for now, I haven't encountered any bugs while playing for about 35 hours.Just finished the main quest (that's the 35h) and there is still more to do. I'm amazed.

detailed_description: An aunt and uncle take their middle-school niece and her boyfriend on an overnight camping trip in WIDE OCEAN BIG JACKET Take part in a classic camping trip: Roast hot dogs on the fire, go birdwatching, tell ghost stories, grab a beverage from the cooler and do cartwheels on the beach. WOBJ is a short story game including 20 chapters, 4 playable characters, 10,000 words of dialog and 8 explorable areas, all rendered in a beautiful 2D/3D art style. \ Playtime: 60-90 minutes (like watching a good movie with friends or curling up to read a book) \ Made in 2019 by Turnfollow \\ CW: Includes a scene in which an adult and a tween have a (platonic) conversation about sex and consent. Also a scene depicting older teenagers verbally assaulting tweens.

short_description: A Camping Story starring: Uncle Brad, Aunt Cloanne, Mord (and Ben)

_childDocuments_.review: Brad and Cloanne take their niece and her new boyfriend on their first camping adventure. Mord and Ben are quite reluctant to begin with. They’re not quite sure what to expect but it’s been a long time since Mord spent time with her Auntie, especially as a blossoming adult, and she is keen for them to get to know her new partner.Brad and Cloanne are quite comfortable in the outdoor environment but less familiar with teenage angst and problems. It seems like everyone will be learning new things on this adventure.Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a short and linear narrative adventure revolving around life in the wilderness, relationships and growing up.If you liked the video and found it useful, I'd appreciate it if you could subscribe to my You Tube channel so that I could make more.👍This was a lovely way to spend ninety minutes of my evening, and the time just flew by. There was something mesmerizing about this game, with its abundance of charm and witty moments. The characters were very likable and the writing was engaging, light-hearted and entertaining.Events are never farcical, they’re just things that could easily happen on a camping trick, but they’re wonderfully presented and uplifting. The relationships between the four are cleverly constructed. Conversations flow between the characters effortlessly and we get to see a range of different topics discussed and evaluated. It’s all kept brief and punchy but it’s testament to the excellent writing that the short exchanges between characters leave such a memorable impression.I think this is partly down to the ambiance of the game. The graphics are striking in their simplicity, with bold colours and loosely drawn environments, and the music is so jaunty and spirited that it invokes happiness. It really is a feel-good game and you can’t help chuckle and smile whilst their adventure pans out.There isn’t much game play. Initiating conversations drives the story forward but this is quite linear and we have no choice who to speak to, just when we would like to start. You’ll find yourself bouncing between dialogue exchanges quite quickly. Sentences are very short but conversations still seem meaningful and often very witty. These short interchanges keep the pace high which holds your attention. At moments you will control each character and sometimes more than one at the same time. Everyone seems to get their moment and viewer’s attention. Moving around the environments is restricted but you will have the opportunity to complete very basic tasks as the game instructs, like lighting a fire, setting up a tent etc. None of these tasks are taxing in the slightest but it is a nice way to get involved rather than just watch events unfold.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played Firewatch, then WOBJ will feel like a familiar but fresh take on walking around the woods and campgrounds. A little slow to start story/action-wise. You will love the characters, though, especially Mord. Some very poignant and unexpected moments in the game that make the most of the limited mechanics. Definitely recommend and it'll only take about 60 - 90 minutes depending on how long you want to linger...
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Wide Ocean Big Jacket is outstanding. I had a grin on my face for almost the entirety of my playtime. Although the events of the game could easily be described as mundane, they are presented with so much charm and character. The game could easily translate into an excellent film; however, the player would then not be so involved in the comedic timing.The text overlays corresponding to various actions often made me laugh, and Mord (the teenage girl) is so refreshingly exuberant about EVERYTHING - it's one of the things I've lost a bit as I've gotten older, and I would like to get back in touch with that part of myself. Although there aren't any real "bombshell" life-changing moments for the characters in the game, I certainly found myself thinking about why and how we develop traditions and about the various "milestones" of life.If you don't require a particularly high stimulation threshold and need your games to be challenging above all, you should absolutely play Wide Ocean Big Jacket. It will make your day.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit that I first thought Wide Ocean Big Jacket was a bit too twee for its own good. I liked the writing and characters, but it all felt very slight. Not that the game or its plot became more weighty, but I came to see its light touch and its decision not to introduce major stakes or conflict as an asset. There are exchanges that are beautifully sweet without ever becoming sentimental, and there's a conversation towards the end that is handled wonderfully well. (Chances are you'll know it when you get there.) The juxtaposition between the kids and the grownups is done very nicely without making either seem phony or twee. If you like walking sims, indie comics and the tone of, say, Night in the Woods, this one is well worth checking out.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: First played this in 2019 and loved it, and I was recently reminiscing about it with a friend so of course I had to play it again, and it truly continues to be one of my favorite games. It's the perfect length and pace to play in a single sitting and the characters and their dynamics with each other are so compelling that it's hard to put down after I finished it. Like, it really is exactly as long as it needs to be, but at the same time I would love to spend more time with these characters. Or at least Mord. Mord will forever be my spirit animal.Also, they even included a chapter select if you want to go back to any of the scenes! I hadn't expected it since the game isn't super long, but it's really nice to have the option since there are some parts where you have different (minor) choices you can pick between.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome little game. Original art style and good story. It can be finished in a bit over an hour, but it's a very enjoyable experience. Basically you just go on a camping trip, and you follow these 4 characters over the span of a few days. There are some gameplay elements, like getting wood for a fire and things like that, but I guess it would best be called a walking simulator. There are not many genuine choices in the game, you basically just follow a linear story. But it was lots of fun. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: If you love travelling, then Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a small charming trip you can take part in without a doubt.I personally, being used to travel a lot, miss travelling while studying at university. With all the fun and all the small shades of family relationships, this game is what brought me to that unique atmosphere back again. And yeah, this was the feeling.I was a part of every of them, a bit of Mord, and a bit of Ben, and, of course, a bit of Brad and Cloanne. There were those two old men, the staff of this lovely camping, and their own pleasant story. There were lots of mean teens, but they weren't so mean in fact. When you travel, everything changes.There were birds singing, and there was the strong wind. Then, the sun was shining, and then it went down the sea horizon. I felt sand under my feet while standing by the seaside at night. I heard squeaking of the trees walking down the woods. I heard noises of burning wood sitting by the campfire. It's kind of a walking sim I should probably warn, and there are no achievements as well, but you'll dive into it in no time realising you don't need them at all. After all, you'll surely never notice it's time to head back home. With grin on your face and a bit of regret in your heart you'll realise that you'd like to stay for a little bit more. No long reviews, it's something you'd rather try for yourself than hear or read about it. If you are ford of traveling – it doesn't matter what you like more, sea or mountains, hitchhiking or hiking, as well as it doesn't matter if you prefer to hit the road alone or with a company of friends – this is the game just for you.And remember, if you see a random bush in the forest–
