_childDocuments_.review: As the car hums past different scenery everyone fidgets slightly. The young girl and boy in the back seats look around, bored probably, as the car zooms along towards a destination unknown to the player. Steering the bright red convertible, a brunette woman in shades shifts her gaze slightly, accompanied by a man that lets his arms hang outside the car every now and then. This is the beginning of a quiet little camping trip. From the store page alone the expectations for Wide Ocean Big Jacket should be set: it’s a short camping trip about a niece, her new boyfriend, her aunt and her uncle. But this simple premise houses lots of simple, slice of life moments that add up to something more. The feelings it’s able to portray with bold colors and sparse lines of dialogue is impressive. The design of the game, from just the menu alone, speaks volumes in terms of the artistic approach of the game. The story isn’t necessarily led by 1 of the 4 in particular and even the setting itself is an important part of how the narrative feels. Mord, a wild, headstrong girl is easily quotable in her silly dialogue but also in the way she is thrusting herself into the role of growing up; she is trying so hard to find out what love and relationships mean and even approaches “the talk” with her aunt in such an honest way  Seeing lines as sincere as this is quite a treat.[/caption] Mord's timid, bespectacled, sesquipedalian boyfriend  gets to have his own touching moments as he discusses his family life. Then there’s Cloanne and Brad who are trying to entertain and protect their precocious niece while deciding where their own relationship should go.  The stylized cinematography, eye-catching color choices, family centric themes, and off kilter comedy are probably familiar. The title card introduction and jangly pop and strings of the soundtrack alone would make it easy to jump to Wes Anderson, but there is more just beneath the bright surface of WOBJ. At times it feels like WOBJ is only a hair away from sliding into an early Noah Baumbach-esque tragicomic breakdown. The dialogue, told with intertitle cards featuring a cartoon rendition of the speaker, manages to be silly and serious at different times. The little details of Wide Ocean Big Jacket also stand out.The color palette is striking, but there is also the sound design. The sound of the road, the ocean waves lapping against the shore, or the zipper of a tent, these sounds seem to pop. When characters speak they each get their own little chime, which just adds onto the charm.This is a very cinematic game with a strong sense of art style. Outside of film influences it is easy to find WOBJ’s kinfolk in games like , though this game foregoes the lack of dialogue. A low poly style with careful color choice is shared among them, but WOBJ opts for a more lighthearted look as it isn’t dealing with murder and mystery like Virgina. They all make interesting animation cuts between interaction or dialogue: for example a character might sit happily with a bottle in his hand, but after another character makes fun of him, the scene changes to him slouching and sad. These jump cuts don’t quite match the erraticism of Goddard, but they do give the game a good sense of pace and playfulness. This humor bleeds into the bold title font that prompts the player, such as when Mord tries to go to the bathroom. As a walking simulator, there are only some moments of interaction. You make a few choices that result in slightly different dialogue playing, there is a small quest to pee in a bush that you can opt out of (you coward),and you can wander around freely in a scene, though these scenes are contained quite closely. There is a nice serene moment of watching the moon on the beach or birdwatching with optional commentary through button prompt. It’s all minimal with no lose condition. WOBJ is meant to be played in full. The brief time the player spends on the camping trip is not meant to linger: the pivot of the camera as characters exchange banter or tell a ghost story all feel special. Wide Ocean Big Jacket doesn’t waste a moment of its short playtime. If there is one criticism I have, it’s that you cannot replay dialogue or go back. This certainly fits the movement of speaking and life, but some lines deserve a second look. Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a short slice of life that is full of charm and heart. It feels like a movie I could easily share with friends or family to chat about. Some of the moments in the game are completely relatable, and a few parts feel quirky and entertaining. It’s wholesome, sweet, and playful. On nearly every front Wide Ocean Big Jacket feels like a special little game that I want to keep talking about, even long after the tents are all packed up.

_childDocuments_.review: Takes the player on a camping trip, with a continually shifting first or third person perspective between four characters. There is no pretence of player agency through false choices (e.g. Telltale) or busywork (e.g. Firewatch), and yet through storytelling is more than a static film like Virginia. Wide Ocean Big Jacket is part of a class of recent games in which a cast of characters mostly just hang out (e.g. Night in the Woods, Mutazione, Wheels of Aurelia) and have conversations. The subject matter touches on a number of issues, but it isn’t really "about" any of them, because such issues are a part of life, which this game aptly shows.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, it was pretty good! I feel like I'm missing some extra scenes, like maybe there are some hidden bits I missed, but I don't feel like digging around for a guide. _childDocuments_.review: Loved the subjects discussed throughout the game, whether it's with more of a funny ha-ha approach or a serious approach. _childDocuments_.review: This is a game that has no real beginning, and no definable ending. It is a snapshot of a time where four very different people's lives briefly cross over, maybe for the only time. A camping trip where this quartet coexist, not easily, but slowly, peacefully. A microcosm of life where there are still problems, obstacles, awkward moments, arguments and mistakes, but there are more moments of calm, introspection and gentle, still awkward humour. It is a story that proves that even if you think the age you're at now is the most important turning point of your life, you are wrong, there will always be another one later. A demonstration that to live is to always be moving, to always be hesitating, to always um and ah, to never be sure but to confidently press forward anyway sometimes because maybe just maybe it'll be worth it. It's a reminder that sometimes it's okay to ramble, and okay to not make sense in the moment, that maybe some things don't need to be drafted, because maybe there'll be someone out there just as confused and scared and weird as you who'll understand and love every second of you. But maybe there won't be for now, and that's okay too, because eventually, the camping trip ends, and we carry on with the next big change, the next great adventure. This game is only an hour long and is barely interactive, but the fact that it made me sit and stew in my brain for this long should be proof enough it's worth playing. I highly recommend this beautifully and painfully real slice of the nonsense that is life.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A short little story about camping and relationships.Very touching, very sweet.A strange mix of a cinematic walking Simulator and a Visual novel.But there are no puzzles to solve and the dialoguen isnt branching. In the whole game there are very few meaningfull choices to make.Still, its a game and could only be told this way as a game.You dont have much say in what you do at what time, but the few mechanics that are there, develop like in a "big" game.The game has fun with em, is cheeky and uses them to make you participate in the relationships between the characters.This way it captures the feeling of a small family trip perfecty and brought a smile to my face many times.Pro Tip: Read the dialogue out loud and give each character a distinct voice. You´ll have a blast!
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Chill camping adventure.If you like indie movies, chill stories about coming of age, and relaxed walking simulators, this'll be a treat for you. The game isn't action-packed or super tense, there's no ominous threats or political intrigue, it's just a bunch of people hanging out camping together. While there's a few mature conversations and swearing, the game never makes itself offensive or crude for the sake of it. Characters seem authentic and act like real human beings, the writing is consistently high quality, and the ending is satisfying despite the lack of major conflicts or trials the characters encounter.The graphics are a bit on the simpler side, but the minimalist models and 2D sprites give the game a big indie feel, which only adds to the experience of playing out an indie film. All speech is handled with white text on black backgrounds, hiding the world during conversations. The glimpses we see of character reactions and posing outside of conversations provides a lot of characterization for the family, despite the minimal animation and abrupt transitions. If you can't stand a game without amazing graphics, you'll want to avoid this one. My only concern is the game's price, due to the length of the content. You can see everything in about 1-2 hours, especially if you do the optional story with the park rangers. The Chapter select is available from the beginning, and there's no achievements to worry about missing. I'd recommend this game if you're trying to introduce someone new to video games, or to show someone what an 'art' game is like. A wonderful, authentic, brief experience in the lives of a few cool people.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: This story is a bit like camping: enjoy it for what it is, but don't expect too much. It's a slice of life, in big and little ways.Getting to know the characters was funnest for me, and I definitely wanted to know what they'd all be up to in ten years time.The artwork was, er... I guess I'll just say "enough". Except for one bit, which was stunning. You'll know it when you get there.If you haven't bought this yet and are undecided, wait for it to be on offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: When I was a kid, I had a small white blanket covered in blue elephants. I'd wear the blanket when my mother would read to my sister and I in the evenings after supper.Today I was able to spend about an hour under that small, elephant-covered blanket which is buried somewhere in my parents' attic.  made me feel safe. Like I was a child again in my parents' living room - rain tinkling on the windows with dishes in the sink. Now in my mid-20s, I connected with everyone in this little escape, surprisingly. From the adults responsible for making a camping trip possible, to the kids which made it special.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little thing with comfortable music and suitable graphics. Uncomplicated and unpretentious, rather a meditative experience. Like someone already said: included a wide ocean and a big jacket, can't complain, 10/10.(The full price might be a bit too much but then again, that depends on one's income. _childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very short game and it's really cute! I enjoyed the dialogue a lot, as it really gave the characters personality. I didn't even know if I would like this, but I'm glad I gave it a chance. I'm not sure if replaying it will get you any different scenes but tbh I'd just replay it because it was enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Idk man it's cute. It feels like one of those shoegaze indie films that you're not really allowed to get mad at because they don't have a budget and anything they do is in the face of a studio system that's designed to stamp them out. That sounds like a cirtique and it's not. Yes it is a little janky but that's still part of the charm. It's a two day snapshot into the lives of the characters at a certain point, and a good emotionally resonant snapshot at that. But giving any more would kind of defeat the purpose, and it does plenty with the time it's given.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: There is a lot in this, at least when it comes to feelings and atmosphere. The writing is absolutely lovely. Great, believable characters. Covering some of the big life (and relationship) questions you'll encounter on your way to the big sleep, and giving them room for you to ponder over and/or reminisce. Mechanically there isn't much to it, which is perfectly fine for what it does, an the things that are there feel well implemented. The visuals also mix very well with the mood the story goes for and allow for some really good scene transitions. Overall fairly well polished, although I never quite understood what the B button is for (is it just a quick turn? If so, why?)Had a great trip, will visit again (still have to do the bonus story).Full recommendation! Even more so after a year of mostly staying at home
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Like a giant cup of a fizzy tropical drink on a hot day. One of those unique hour-long journeys that provides numerous laughs, melancholic reflection, and a big dose of nostalgia captured in different stages of our youth across four wonderful characters - all represented in basic black & white dialogue format x PS1-level polygons. A true whirlwind sneak attack that sticks with you.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: This was absolutely delightful. The trailer and the prologue led me to believe that the progression would be tied to some  object hunting around the environment, but it really isn't and that's for the best. The writing is excellent and unlike most other visual novel games out there the visuals strike a perfect balance of abstraction (for both the scenery and characters). No anime/DeviantArt-esque characters here, but  instead some very elegant use of shapes and silhouettes leaving plenty of room for imagination. There is a lot of care given to all the mechanics too : the text is easy to speed up, the sound design is never intrusive, and even the control scheme for the walking/exploration sequences is streamlined to perfection (only one stick).The authors did an incredible job distilling the experience down to only what really matters. If this is on your wishlist to maybe buy later, buy it now.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Really pleasant 1,5h of your time. At the beginning there are few boring dialogues, but give it a time and it becomes soooo pleasant and entertaining. Very short story, but gives you a lot of fun. If the original price is too high for you for a 1,5h gameplay, then wait for a discount, cause then it's worth every dollar.

_childDocuments_.review: I already reviewed this game on their itch page but here it goes on Steam!This game really hit home for me. I was not expecting it to be this good, but man what an awesome ride. Absolutely loved getting know each character. They felt so real and fun to be around. The combination of great dialogue and simple gameplay really made me feel at home in every scene. And to top it all off, the music is AMAZING. Seriously, I love love love the soundtrack in this game. Thanks for the awesome game guys, this is a true gem and deserves more attention in the indie game community. It's been a while since a game put a real smile on my face and made me wish the story never ended <3
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: The way that the allure of camping was captured in this game inspired me to try it out for the first time in my adult life. That's a true feat.The dialog is funny and sweet without being heavy handed.Clocking in at a little over an hour (if you take your time), it's worth every penny for the magical experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Easily one of the best games I've played all year, condensed into a perfect ~50 minute package. Fantastic characters, genuinely funny writing, and a great  make WOBJ an unmissable experience. I have to admit that, while packing up the campsite at the end of the game, I was a little disappointed to see the end rapidly approaching. But as the credits rolled, and I was left with a view of the campsite where I've spent the last hour, I'm delighted that the folks at Turnfollow had the confidence to leave it as-is. The short run-time ensures that the peaks stand out, and don't get lost in a swirl of filler.Definitely give this game a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Perfect vignette game. The game's characters are well developed and interesting. Nothing really happens, but the experiences are meaningful for the characters in a way that rings true. Broad themes are clear without being heavy handed. The controls are simple with occasional changes that make sense as part of the experience.  Art is simple--in that it is without much detail--but this works well with both the general feeling of the experience as well as increasing the chances of the player experiencing an empathetic connection. Music was nice too. Overall, the game does a great job capturing the feeling of a moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A very cute, very simple, short game about a witty kid who goes camping with her "boyfriend", her uncle and his wife. There are a few events of note and some minor drama but it's just a feel-good, kinda funny little short story type experience. The art is lovely and the music complements the game very well. I've finished the game so it's an hour long. Up to you what that hour is worth I suppose
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Wide Ocean Big Jacket has a lot in common with that wave of awkward coming of age indie films that became popular 10-12 years ago. Although it only provides a surface level view, the game serves as an excellent looking glass for both the warmer and murkier parts of growing up. It's a super quick play through, but the feeling the game creates is well worth the cost of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A short and sweet treat. Reminiscent of Adamgryu's : a charmingly low-fi way to experience the natural world while broaching deeper themes of relationships, family and the self-discovery of youth.I loved Mord, Ben, Aunt Clo and Uncle Brad, and I wouldn't mind a future check-in. Maybe another camping trip in a few years?Remarkable writing and narrative design to so quickly make these weirdos feel like old friends: Turnfollow did the work to get me interested in their lives within the first 15 minutes.Highly recommended! You'll finish in about an hour, which leaves the rest of the day to plan a camping trip and buy your own Glowbones.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A snug, chill, thoughtful camping getaway for an hour or so. Not a hero's journey, but it has a very satisfying beginning, middle and end to it. I hope I won't forget about Wide Ocean Big Jacket and will continue to remember its warmth whenever I go out camping or whatever. Great dialogue and characters, spot-on music.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It's unique in that your experience might even be better the less games you've played, making it a perfect title to gift to a non-gamer who may be perhaps less objective-oriented. That said, I still had a really fun time. Not much here for replay value, and mercifully unsullied by achievements, but easily a title that raises the storytelling bar in its earnest simplicity. (Worth noting is that the free demo is a separate adventure, so give that a spin if you're on the fence or just enjoyed the main game. )
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those narrative games that I'll probably only play once, yet remember fondly for a long time. The wonderful art, snappy, high quality writing and light interactivity, with just enough freedom to explore before being funnelled back onto the story path adds up to a chill camping experience with some interesting people.Once you've played the main game, play the demo available here on Steam too - it's like a bonus chapter with a slice of the world from a different perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A incredibly poignant narrative experience that reflects the beauty of nature as much as that of human relationships. I spent an hour with Ben, Mord, Clo, BJ, and Glowbones, and I lived more of a story than I have in many more expensive or well-known games - a story that I couldn't personally relate to (not a negative) but could appreciate tenfold. I highly recommend narrative/single-player fans spend the small amount for this game. It's simple, yet entirely effective and had me smiling, laughing, and admiring the wonderful quirks of life. I wish I could spend more time with these characters. An hour well spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a fully narrative-driven slice-of-life story about a camping trip.  There's pretty much no gameplay to speak of other than walking around and chatting, but the writing is very good and the experience is quick, charming, funny and heartfelt.That said, most people will see "hour-long charming narrative-driven story" and immediately know if that game is for them or not.  If you're questioning it, then it probably is for you, because sometimes these games are pretty low effort and crappy, and this is not one of those low effort crappy ones.  This is good stuff.  Play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful little 30 minute movie about 4 people and there lives.  The kids are adorable and the adults have some troubles.  I think the walking sim friends will like this very much, but the friends who like shooting games won't like it so much.  I personally enjoyed it very much although I was hoping for a little more interactivity, even a mini-game where you cook the hotdogs. Glowbones is awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review:
Take part in a classic camping trip: Roast hot dogs on the fire, go birdwatching, tell ghost stories, grab a beverage from the cooler and do cartwheels on the beach.

WOBJ is a short story game including 20 chapters, 4 playable characters, 10,000 words of dialog and 8 explorable areas, all rendered in a beautiful 2D/3D art style.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

name: Stonefly
detailed_description: Also from Flight School Studio About the Game Discover the Unexpected World of Stonefly Stonefly is an action-adventure RPG in which you pilot a tiny robot mech in a magical forest. Hop along rocks and leafy canopies while you upgrade your rig with an arsenal of air and wind abilities. Follow the journey of Annika Stonefly as she attempts to recover a stolen family heirloom, strategically battling bugs and critters across an epic story. A New Way to Move The mechs in Stonefly are unlike any machine you’ve piloted before. Flip what you know about games and spend most of your time gliding instead of walking. This allows you to traverse a variety of terrain and avoid the dangerous bugs that crawl around below you. Harness the Wind Invent abilities that empower you in unique king-of-the-hill style combat centered on using wind to push bugs out of the arena. Each bug has its own behavior and requires a different strategy to defeat. The more efficient you are at dealing with bugs, the faster you will gather precious minerals used to upgrade your mech. Vibes & Visuals Stonefly is set to a backdrop of beautiful colors and the techno-nature music of Natureboy Flako. Forge relationships with memorable characters from the Acorn Corps, a band of castaway mech pilots. Adventure through leafy autumn canopies, prickly briars, and misty marshes.

_childDocuments_.review: A tough one to swallow for me, who was so excited to get to Stonefly. The premise of mechs-in-a-bug's-world is too good to resist, and the gorgeous earth-tone colors and chunky, tranquil environments are the sort of world you can't help but want to explore.But the game is bad.Tethered to a clunky sense of movement (are we always flying? ground traversal so useless? attacks launch into the air but also I'm already flying..?), the game's combat is an absolute chore, one whose frustration can be eased by the game's generous invincibility option, for an extremely casual blast through the story. Platforming can also be a guessing game, where the (beautiful!) environments don't always lead you (unless you use your handy point-me-towards-the-goal tracking flies), which makes the prospect of naturally roaming the environment a wonky, just-missed-that-branch crapshoot. The moments of Stonefly I enjoyed were slowly crawling along the foliage, rather than scavenging alongside bugs. And heaven forbid I need to scavenge.The idea of upgrading your bug-mech is a tantalizing one, but the drudgery of resource-gathering is just that. Not to mention story beats are tied to grinding out materials for either A. An upgrade you don't need, but the game insists you purchase or B. An arbitrary "group project" your ragtag squad of scroungers are set on.Maybe the effort to help the team out would be worthwhile if there were some sense of personality to ANY of the characters in the game, though the thrust of the story (your pa's bug-mech is stolen! go get it!) is limp, and the lack of any voice acting or Banjolike grunts and effects to imbue some life to dialogue makes for a total snoozefest of a story, with developments that I didn't make much sense given the characters and, frankly, ones I simply didn't care about.At the risk of droning on TOO long, there are a slew of UI obstructions, combat mechanics, and other downers to Stonefly that further soiled the experience for me, but death by a thousand cuts isn't on the menu today...It's a shame, because the idea is a unique one, and the presentation is really something to marvel at (when the game isn't sliding models across the surface or BUGGING out with frequent [but relatively harmless] visual/geometric hiccups), with an original soundtrack that, occasionally, reminded me of the terrific Disasterpiece score for Hyper Light Drifter. I wanted so badly for this to be good, and I don't take particular pleasure in writing such a scathing review (sorry, devs!) but Stonefly is a game whose potential was tremendous. Instead it's squashed under a rock.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: First impressions are good, the art and music combines creating a soothing experience.Charming characters and a story that invites you to unveil it.As far as I've seen, the game is packed with a good mix of great mechanics, and it looks like more will be unlocked throughout the game.Eager to continue and see what it holds!Edit: I've already finished the game and it was a great experience! Although I've found the grind kind of intense sometimes, in the end i've enjoyed a lot every moment of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Very unique style of graphicsControls are very solid. (Button combos might be a little strange at first but I got used to them and enjoyed them.)Interesting combat style that focuses on pushing enemies off the edge of what ever you are fighting on.Areas were larger than I expected them to be and I found myself exploring a lot.Cons:Abilities were useful but most were not needed at all.Upgrades weren't as impactful as I would like them to be.Dialog is odd due to zero sound, would have been nice to at least have "Banjo-Kazooie" noises. Especially when dialog is happening while moving around the world because reading a little box of text at the bottom left of the screen while doing light platforming is not good.Story is nothing special.Overall:If you are looking for a nice chill experience where you explore an interesting stylized world, gather materials to upgrade your ship and battle some bugs in a king of the hill style combat then this is an easy game to recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: It was hard to give Stonefly a positive review. While it bewilders with a beautiful big bug world, painted in a pleasing, detailed style, the combat makes me want to choke.You can already see the best aspects of the game on screenshots and videos, music is on par and makes for a great addition to your adventures within the world. I also liked the freedom given to you with all your moves - gliding, dashing, blinking, jumping and more. It’s when the game forces you to engage in fights it becomes unbearable to continue playing.I wanna share some info on why you may not want to play this, since battles are an unavoidable part of the game. I’ll go in order of discovery:First off, you’ll meet tiny bugs that bite. They are literally too small to notice in the heat of battle, and yet their attack will absolutely push you off the arena without trouble. Enemy attacks in this game are absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You cannot recover from even one. And the problem isn’t the health, you can repair yourself with ease. The problem is your mental health after having to deal with hundreds of annoying critters and their giant friends.Next, you’ll see that every arena is covered with a border. Fly out, fall below, fly too high - you will receive damage. Considering every single attack will push you off in one way or another, this is literally unavoidable.And every time you touch this border, you are respawned in the center of the arena. No attempts to steer or get rid of enertia will save you, so you might as well always prepare to appear in the center after getting hit. Soon you will start meeting larger baddies. And these have lots of hp. Not only that, but you can only attack them while they are attacking you. This window of weakness is miniscule and you’ll surely need multiple runs to stun even one. And the deeper in you’ll go, the more faulty mechanics and tedious enemies you'll find.I am also disappointed and a bit confused about the controls. The gamepad has so many buttons, yet for some essential tools you will need to press a button combination. For some reason, which I fail to understand, blink and dash are two different abilities bound to different ways of pressing one button.Even with all that, game's not very hard, just tedious and annoying. I didn’t notice any death penalty either. This did make me drop the game though, as combat is basically the biggest part of the game besides exploration and it managed to stop me from having fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: Here are a few of them:* Invisible walls and drop-offs EVERYWHERE, including the middle of limbs/platforms.* No local maps* Unable to speed up or manually advance the _excruciatingly_ slow text* Frustrating combat* Okay, so everything is dead and gone. I can finally leave this area. OOP no, "Returning to encounter" for some more annoying combat. WTF?* Seems semi-open, and I wanna go collect me some stuff for upgrades but 1) Can't figure out where to get some items, and 2) the game will only show me its linear path.Did someone made it so intensely annoying on purpose, so it would take longer?
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love Stonefly so much. There are so many things I could say about it, but I'm going to try and keep it short and sweet.The art is awesome! I loved the design of most everything; the way everything looks hand-drawn, the characters, the enemies, and the mech designs are all great. Unfortunately, an interesting art style and game design do not make a game good on their own.Stonefly was incredibly frustrating to play around the halfway point. The enemy encounters were way too overwhelming to be fun and I found myself forced to turn on invincibility and reduce the knock back just to stop myself from uninstalling the game out of anger and frustration. Some enemies just get too annoying with the number of them they throw at you in the late game. Navigation was tedious and at times difficult. With a mostly fixed camera, it was hard to see where I could go or where I could land to jump and continue on with movement.The story is also slightly lacking. It was hard to follow at times because it' exclusively text-only with no voice effects. It's not a bad story by any means and the ending is heart warming to say the least.Overall, I'd say buy this game on sale if you really want it. I started of this game enjoying it, but as I played I became more and more frustrated almost to the point of putting it down forever.TL;DR 6/10: Pretty environments, bad movement and combat design.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: Save your money or wait for a sale. While there's a lot to like here, this game desperately needs polish. First off, combat is stunted to a frustrating degree. These encounters can best be described as a glorified "king of the hill", where your objective is to stun and push off bugs from leaves using your mech abilities. The abilities initially provided to you are weak - very weak - and upgrades to these abilities don't feel like significant improvements during combat either. The gust and dash abilities in particular made me scratch my head; I felt like I was abusing the system by wavedashing gust when the ability should've just been stronger in the first place. The downtime for the dash ability makes it not particularly useful for movement. The abilities provided also don't feel substantial enough to take on large hordes of bugs; it's very fun being stunlocked by multiple enemies shooting sap before being knocked 50 feet off a platform by a tiny beetle, where afterwards I'm forced to watch a several minute long cutscene when I die. Perhaps a long-range weapon or multiple options for quick maneuverability would have been welcome. Speaking of maneuverability, traversing the world is a confusing and buggy (heh) mess. Your mech cannot jump particularly high, which makes jumping across closed gaped, tiered platforms mildly infuriating. The world, while aesthetically beautiful, is mostly empty. Aside from small landmarks (which serve no purpose apart from being quick travel locations or pit stops to upgrade your mech), exploration primarily consists of jumping from branch to branch, gap to gap, and fighting hordes of bugs. Upgrading abilities often times requires a shop or trader for parts, which makes your "camp" essentially useless if a trader isn't occupying it with you. Progression is obstructed by these mechanics that sometimes the effort to upgrade isn't worth it until absolutely needed. The story of this game is serviceable but is hindered by abrupt scene transitions and awkward dialogue with odd pacing. There would be moments where a conversation would be taking place and the game would just throw me into the level a second after. This aspect of Stonefly especially suffers from the game's lack of sound design. Scripted cutscenes would nearly be silent if music wasn't constantly playing in the background. Dialogue boxes cannot be progressed by the user, which make for bad experiences by slow and fast readers alike. These issues made me feel like something was missing from what should have been emotionally-compelling moments. I could go on, but to me Stonefly feels like a game that's almost out of early-access. I'm not sure if any these gameplay elements will be addressed in the future, but I'd recommend holding off until the price tag is lowered.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: I'm torn on Stonefly. The concept is honestly , but it just becomes frustrating in combat, as many others have said. I do recommend it, but not completely, this lands just above a maybe to me. Sorry this review is long, but I think it's important to go into details on my complaints. Maybe a better player will find these things less frustrating, who knows.Steam says I've played 9.7 hours at the point I'm writing this review, and I've just completed the story, and gone around collecting a few more visual upgrades. I took my time and fully upgraded everything and made sure to collect many resources. But for £15.49, I have no complaints at ~10 hours playtime. I played entirely with a controller.So first the good:- it's really beautiful, both in art style and graphics, the designs of the mechs, bugs and environments are . No other word for it. I LOVE being in this world.- Music is nice, sometimes gets a bit repetitive, but it's good- the controls feel tight and snappy, the mech feels good to control and usually does what I want it to do.- Nice gameplay loop of explore, fight and gather materials, then upgrade and fight harder enemies- Cool mini raids on a giant bug with lots of enemies to rush around and gather as many resources as possible. This adds some variety to the grindy sections. It's still a little annoying, but better than just wandering for ages.- The story is nice, pretty basic but it's a nice little taleThe bad:- can be a little grindy at some points- I felt like the characters could have voices, maybe not fully voiced, but some gibberish option might be nice- exploration is often unclear- the combat.These final two, these are the big issues with the game. Firstly, the exploration, many objects look like you can land on them, but you can't, causing you to fall through the world. This is annoying, but once I got used to it and started to recognise the games slightly subtle visual language, it started to happen less. Often, things you can't land on are slightly darker or more washed out. OK, so I'll follow the path by the little tracking flies that I have, great. The only issue there is that now I'm not exploring and I only found two or three customisation pieces throughout the whole game. When I finished and started going back to explore previous locations more, I immediately started getting stuck, missing jumps endlessly, looking for things I can land on... It just becomes a bit frustrating. I beeping radar or something to help find objects might be nice. It's honestly not that fun reloading into areas over and over again trying to find the one branch you've not seen that takes you to a secret item.But the combat, oh, I have two serious issues with the combat. It's conceptually really cool, you hit bugs from above in the air with little bombs, as you're fast when gliding, then land and blow (with wind) them off the branches/leaves/logs into the void. First issue with this is that the enemies hit boxes are seemingly tiny, the small enemies in particular are impossible to hit reliably. You have a move to group them up when they're stunned, then I go to blow them all off the edge, only half do. So many times I cluster a group of medium sized enemies together and go to blow them off the edge, two out of three go, the other doesn't and then attacks me. You can power up the blow move to send things further, which you'll need to do as some of the arenas are a bit bigger. But they're stunned for only a short period of time, so you stun a few enemies, as you'll have no chance to blow just one off with others attacking you, get in position, then as you're charging up they'll already be exiting stun. Sometimes the enemies get stuck on small bushes, rocks, dips in the ground, anything, and don't fly off the edge. It's honestly maddening. This is my first issue with the combat, it doesn't feel good to blow enemies off the edge, they either get stuck on things, you miss because you have to be impossibly precise, or you don't have time to do it as you want to.Secondly, the damage system of the mech is AWFUL. If you get pinged out of bounds your health goes to zero, if it happens again, systems start shutting down, leaving you with less abilities. This is again great in theory, but so, so, so many times enemies ping you out of bounds seemingly at random. They regularly hit you to clearly within gliding distance, but nope, you 'die' disappear and reappear in the arena with zero health. Sometimes they hit you up in the air (to heights you can get to by yourself) and it kills you. As these happen so often I found myself in busier encounters getting completely swamped, unfairly flung off the stage, zero health, flung off again, wings disabled, good luck escaping now you can't fly, flung off again, legs damaged. There I am, hobbling around the arena, unable to jump or glide desperately waiting for my repair cooldown so that I can start trying again. It feels like a bad design decision to make your health go to zero. Half or a quarter? Ok, it's a challenge. As it is now it just feels stupid.Combining these two issues; an imprecise combat, and a weird damage system, then makes the game extremely frustrating to play at times. Most frustrating though, it when it all works perfectly and you see what it could be. This game is beautiful, unique and thoroughly fun when it goes well, it is SO close to being amazing. I hope Flight School Studio do a little bit of fixing. I'm still looking forward to whatever they make next. This review is mostly a big complaint, but I really wouldn't have stuck with the game for ~10 hours if I didn't think it was good.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: Almost there, but not quite. This game has a lot going to it, in particular when it comes to aesthetics and general handling of the player controlled insect mecha. From the start you'll notice this studio's striking art style which while tending towards the beige still pleases the eye. Characters are colourful and lively and the mecha and enemy designs are quite good in conserving the insect aesthetics while going to their own place. Gameplay is fast and fluid even if I think that some enemies can have way too much impact for how small and hard to see they are. It's rough when a 2 inch bug jawslams you outta the stage three times in a row because you can barely see it, much less its attack charge animation. But yeah, in all flying around feels awesome and combat is decent enough that coupled with a good upgrade system I could see myself going through this game.But man, the maps and guidance system could use some work. By pressing down on the Dpad you will get some flying sparkly things that tell you where to go (think monster hunter world). But alas these are quite falible and in a mere hour playing I found myself going somewhere the mayflies just couldnt guide me out of. This is part the flies fault and part the environments which sometimes let you go places you clearly should not, leading to an endless respawn bug. Also movement is quite janky and sometimes you fall off places you shouldn't, fail to land where you should, etc. This is helped by a dot under your character that signals where you're over but still happens enough to frustrate me. In all finding your way from combat to combat is way too infuriating in this game and for that reason I cannot recommend the purchase.If this is fixed or very much improved upon further patches I will reconsider my vote and refund. As of now I can unfortunately not recommend the game despite my best efforts to like it. I swear this is my kind of game, but then again I also didn't like their character based pinball game which also sounds like my kind of game.

Wish there were more variety of enemies and more boss fights. ◽Quite a few loose ends in the story and character backstories.◽Had to do a bit of grinding for materials for certain upgrades, personally i don't mind it all too much, but it can be an issues for some. _childDocuments_.review: Allow me to start this review with a warning. Stonefly has some big flaws but despite this fact I consider it deserves a positive review. Let's start with what is, in my opinion, the biggest one.It is refreshing when developers try to think outside the box and offer some element, in this case combat, with a new twist. That is  the goal of this team but they have failed, combat in Stonefly is a mess. The main point of combat is to blow enemies away from the platform you are fighting on, the mech you pilot has this function from the start. As the game progresses new types of enemies bring new skills like spitting projectiles or stick to the mech and cause constant damage. Consequently, these new enemies can be countered by your obtainable new features for the mech but the execution is plainly terrible. The explanations of how to use them is too brief and the execution pressing different buttons at the correct time makes you dread when some enemies show up, especially flying ones. The other big flaw is not as important but repeating some levels to get access to a 'bonus mining section' gets boring really fast, this prerequisite should not be present in the game, the only thing it achieves is making the game longer artificially.On the other hand, there are many positive aspects in Stonefly. For starters, the main character is very well crafted, once the initial stage ends you have a connection to her. The artistic style is fresh and captivating, the artists really nailed the tone of every area and the characters. Moving on, the plot is not as amazing as the art style but it is solid throughout the game.All in all, Stonefly is a good game with some unfortunate decisions, especially on the combat side, but the exploration, characters and story are worth a try if you are keen on the art style of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Stonefly

_childDocuments_.review: Just... awesome. One of the most gorgeous games I've ever played, really smart UX to make the perspective work super smoothly, incredibly unique world and gameplay, cute, heartfelt story, fantastic (procedural?) animation that really makes you feel like a bug on a leaf... I literally couldn't tear away from it for almost 6 hours straight. My only complaints are minor. Sometimes it feels like there are TOO many abilities you can use at once by the time you reach the end of the game, upgrading to get them is mostly linear, and juggling them all during gameplay can get a bit tedious. I love the aesthetic customization, but it feels like there would have been room for some ability customization, too (for example, equipping dash OR teleport as opposed to being stuck with both at once, and the inputs being a pretty narrow distinction between them). Additionally, sometimes it felt that enemies would unfairly shoot me all the way off the arena, causing me to respawn on the platform with low health: making the health upgrades feel meaningless, because general passive damage isn't much of a problem: ring-outs are (which is in line with how you have to combat enemies, just felt a bit at odds with the health bar system.)Regardless, I absolutely love this game and am shocked it isn't getting more attention! If you're on the fence, get it: it's innovative as heck.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of bugs.The good bugs: - The artstyle is very cute, simple yet giving everything character- The rig handles very intuitively most of the time, both traversal and combat are fun and don't get boring over the course of the game- The plot is uncomplicated and not too long (took me about 8 hours to finish the story getting all upgrades and cosmetic parts and exploring all locations), it isn't overloading you with lore about the world, but it is engaging and it does a good job of guiding you from location to location- There's just enough resource management to motivate you to explore the maps in their entirety, but not to the point of having to grind for anything- The soundtrack is great, adds a lot to the immersionThe bad bugs:- The maps have quite a lot of holes that weren't supposed to be there, especially at the edges. It a game all about exploring every corner this starts to get rather annoying, especially because sometimes the rig fails to "die" and respawn when falling into a hole, forcing you to return to camp- Sometimes the camera gets in the way of the traversal, obscuring the view with bits of scenery- Occasionally there's some jank in the movement, causing you to momentarily get stuck in terrain (it's fairly easy to get moving again, but still)- On Linux/Steam Deck video segments in upgrade descriprions do not load, and on Proton versions 6 and up hovering the cursor over an upgrade descriprion can cause the game to freeze up (fixed by switching to Proton 5.10-6)Overall it's a great concept with very decent execution, definitely worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: Big feet can't fit in shoes.Stonefly is a rather short game. I made it 9 hours in, with about a half hour of time accumulated from time spent paused, but the game was running.I have yet to complete it, but I'm VERY CLOSE to being done. I've got to unlock only two more parts, otherwise all the abilities are maxed out.The enemies consist of a handful of body types, and a few variants there in either taking more hits (denoted as dots) and/or just in that they hit with a different type of damage. There is acid good, flame goo, and some kind of purple stuff. There are two main flying type enemies, spiders that can hit you mid air with a jump up then wide range sawblade spin, units that stay on the ground and fire very accurate shots, and ones that have more defense and lob big burst shots, and ones that just ram you.There are only 3 main areas. I will admit, the maps are HUGE. But there are only 3. You have checkpoints for places within those big maps. Some checkpoint areas are only accessible during the point in the story they matter and I'm not yet aware if completing the story-line will allow to access those spots again in the event anything was missed.The customization is limited, because the game is short and there are not that many parts, in the event you were seeking deep customization. You can change the core, the legs, and the antenna (or have no antenna at all). Changing cores does not seem to affect anything. You get one core that is good at being in cold weather, but legit there is only one part of the map where it matters and because you unlock something else with the core that is what helps against cold, you legit do not seem to need that core at all to survive the weather in that one area. Legs are the same issue. One claims that it supports slide functions, but I have not once seen the ability to roll across the ground with its wheels. Antenna also don't do anything. So legit all the parts are just for aesthetic appeal as far as I can tell.Nobody mentioned that this game makes use of your failures at the start. Legit, you need to get hit and die a few times to unlock research and there is no penalty for death. You keep your resources, which are the only things that matter, thus only if you don't realize this and try to be cautious and get into that mindset that your failures mean anything will you be self inflicting pain on yourself that you don't need to.Short on resources? Well, some checkpoints allow you to head to camp, and then back to the checkpoint, which resets the map so you can break the rocks and mine the minerals where you previously exhausted them.Want to do it faster? There are 3 titan bugs with a lot of resources laid out on their backs. All you need to do is ignore your deaths and keep mining their backs, which means the most annoying part of it is going to be chasing the blue fireflies around to get tracking to 100%.As you progress to areas, Clara offers the next level of tools and refined resources, and the levels spawn the corresponding materials.As others have stated though, this game is buggy. Several times my HUD for health and damage just disappeared and I seemed invincible until I got knocked hard, fell off the map or into water, and respawned to find my hud and health bars returned. There are encounters that should have fight spheres on them, but do not spawn them. Sometimes, due to this, enemies get stuck and end up safe on platforms that should have been out of bounds and removed them. Sometimes enemies just don't seem to stop spawning in, as if when I pushed them off  they fell back onto the platform instead of being removed. Add in the times that the fixed camera becomes an issue with scenery obscuring visibility of enemies on the map, and it's a good thing death means nothing in this game.Stonefly feels pretty shallow overall, in the importance of combat, in the dialog/story, in the limited customization, in the fact that customization doesn't seem to mean anything to gameplay, in enemy variety, in your variety of attacks (a lot of abilities seem pointless due to death meaning nothing, and their key binds are annoying to perform, and their affects have little significance -aside from the big air sphere, which is the only really important one, because the flies are terrible enemies that latch onto you cheaply).I did not agree that the music was an issue. Frankly its chill and drone enough for me to not worry about it, and I didn't find any tones too much. Then again, I lowered music volume to 80%, so sound FXs would not be drowned out.I agree that the colors tend to blend in too much. Part of this seems to be the theme of being one with nature, among nature, and bugs do tend to blend in. They also would use the bushes to hide in and fire from, or suddenly charge out at you from them. I can't entirely hate on it. Even though in one part we are active at night and one very dark enemy blends into the shadows and can get the drop on you. Death means nothing, so it doesn't matter.And I'm kinda OK with the death meaning nothing, but what kills me is that customization means nothing. This is legit Fisher Price Mecha action. Yeah, it's a very chill game because death means nothing, but I'd have felt better if some functions were specifically tied to the parts and I'd have had to do research to unlock the body of a part, then research to unlock the hidden potential or to level that potential up. The snow stuff should be for the snow stuff. It'd have been cool if one set of legs allowed to skim over water, but to sacrifice the legs can only perform lvl 1 jump. If another would allow the use of only lvl 4 armor, but provided the skill to draw enemies in. But nah, all customization is just aesthetics.This really feels like they kit a point where they were debating going EA, but decided to just release a short game, where you are just there for the ride. I'm sorry, but the ride is very shallow and frankly after I beat it, I don't think I'm going to care to replay it, because it's a one and done kind of trip. There is no point to go back, even if there were an achievement to unlock I JUST DON'T CARE ENOUGH. This journey ends I'll consider that the conclusion and I'll move onto something else that hopefully makes me fell like my time is worth something. But everything is so repetitious and bland to me. I'd never have paid the full price, and I'm kinda bothered that I paid what I did on discount. I'd hope they would take the feedback and improve on and consider a sequel, or maybe just re-haul this game with maybe a mode that changes things so things have more meaning and fix the glaring bugs and issues with boundaries and obscured views, etc.This fell flat on the expectations that were alluded to. 9/25/21Edit: 10/7/21 - I finally decided to polish off the last part. I called the ending. It felt like someone pushed off their homework until the very day before it was due. I legit felt nothing for these characters up to this point and it was the most development I've seen in them thus far.The 3rd stage map is a hot mess on the camera and just the layout in general. I still have an place on the 1st map region that is a question mark and no idea how to discover it, along with 3 parts to unlock.I'm done. I have closure to the story. I'm moving on.

_childDocuments_.review: Stonefly is a fun little game with a lot of original ideas. I don't think I've ever played anything quite like it.You pilot a mech that looks like a small bug. You have to navigate through larger than life environments like a log in a swamp, or a large tree, as if you yourself with the size of the big. These exploration bits are where the game does well- the art and audio design is fantastic.Occasionally the game will shift into combat arenas, where you need to defeat enemy bugs. You'll stun the bugs by dropping small bombs on them and once stunned they can be blown off the side of the arena. This combat system takes some getting used to, and has some quirks to it, but the combat is generally forgiving enough that I quickly forgot about most of my "oh come on!" moments.  You're constantly unlocking new upgrades and abilities to play with too, so the combat stays fresh despite some repetitive enemy types by the final areas. If the occasional moment of frustration is enough to turn you off of the combat this might not be the game for you, but I feel a bit more forgiving considering I don't even really have another game to compare the combat system to.The one major downfall in the game is that- despite it's relatively short length- it can be fairly grindy. Multiple times in the story you'll need to collect a large amount of materials to progress forward. If you explore and fight enemies enough you'll typically have enough materials on hand to upgrade your mech, but the resource sink segments of the story really drag down the pacing and probably could have been reduced significantly. Stonefly is a very inventive game, and I think that's where your level of enjoyment will fall with it. It has some game design growing pains trying to make it's unique style work, but I think the positives far outweigh the negatives.

Anybody remember Cryo Interactive games in the 90s? It's that sort of deal. So, there's still some appeal here, but not for anybody who just wants to have a fun time with an interesting-looking game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; gameplay is a novel platformer with extremely tight controls and a satisfying gameplay loop. The story is simple but has a potent landing that does a fantastic job embracing the gameplay systems. The visuals are very pretty and customisation options are a wonderful touch.  Much like their previous game, Creature in the Well, Stonefly focuses primarily on a solid and novel core gameplay loop with tight controls and interesting enemies/interactions. I also really enjoyed that game. The mechanics are a little unusual to pick up at first given how different the main movements and camera perspective are from other games. But by a few hours in, I found myself using all the abilities pretty much on-cooldown dipping and weaving between bugs and satisfyingly flushing them off with full control of my rig.  Unlike Creature in the Well, the plot and character arcs this time around is a lot more obvious and wonderfully presented with surprisingly little dialogue given how potent the story lands. It's one of the best games in recent memory that has done such a great job blending the final message of the story with the major mechanics and systems in the game. So if you like getting really familiar with uncommon control schemes in a game that'll take you roughly 6 hours to beat, I do give this a recommend. : I wish there was a way to pause the narrative text during gameplay. The game seemed confused about whether it wanted the player to explore or not; where there would be many parts of the map that let you venture out without any reward or acknowledgement but still expected you to find secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Mech platformer-action at A Bug's Life scale. It's fun - I enjoyed upgrading my machine, and riding titanic beetles covered in resources through the forest to harvest more materials. I enjoyed the combat to, for awhile at least. Non-lethal but not quite non-violent, it's about knocking bugs the size of your microscopic mech off balance and blasting them off the sides of the arena with a burst of wind. It's at its best when it's new and fresh and towards the end when you have a whole array of abilities to manipulate positioning, but flags a little in the middle. The story is perfectly serviceable, a few weird snafus aside (contractions are good to use and it sounds weird when no one does!). It looks good, too, in gameplay and story sequences, from the minutiae of how mechs move to how characters emote (better even than some AAA games I've seen, the stylized look goes a long way even if the main character's bare feet are distractingly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ enormous)

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game but i can`t deny it has its fair share of problems  and i wish someday we can get a sequel that improves upon them, i give stonefly a 7/10let`s start getting the positives out of the way:-Visuals: the art style in this game is fantastic, every area you explore, enemies you find and characters you meet are stunning, everything is colourful and the designs are great-Soundtrack:  the music and sound design are great, there is one problem tho there isn`t much variety the music during the chill exploration is the same as the music when you are in the middle of a super intense batlle filled with enemies which made the fights feel kinda weird  what could be better:-Worldbuilding and story: Story is MEH, nothing you haven´t seen before a coming of age tale about a girl trying to get to know herself in a quest to bring back her father´s stolen rig (the name of the mechs), The setting for this game tho had so much potential, riding cool ass looking bug mechs around the treetops, meeting a fun cast of characters and exploring the world was good, but could have been so much better, other than the ocasional cutscene or the camp used as a world hub, you´l never see another rig or character existing in this world, it feels empty and lifeless, you do find all kind of bugs to fight but even then they only pop up when you break open a mining area that attracts them. There are few bits of lore about the world during some character interactions but again, it could have been much better developed.-Gameplay: The core of the game is really good, explore the semi open world, fight baddies and complete some linear missions, player progressions feels good u´ll get a bunch of upgrades during your playthrough that will add to your arsenal during battles, the controls (with a gamepad) are a bit confusing and difficult to pick up, but i did get used to them after a while. Battles are a bit weird aswell, you suposedly need a different strategy for each kind of enemy, but the game throws so many enemies at you that just keep sending you flying away that you´ll usually just spam the base attack and hope for the bestThe worst part about gameplay is traversing the world, movement feels great but you will fall to your death countless times in this game, there is no way to tell if a branch in the distance is actually somewhere you can or can´t go there were dozens of times when i would get to a branch just to go trough it and fall to oblivion-Customization: there are a few options to customise your rig and you can freely change its colours, it is a good system, i just wish there were more options -Camera: You play with a fixed camera that frames you really well most of the times, but there are also a lot of instances where u wont be able to see anything because there is a leaf or  a weird bit of geometry obstructing your viewWhat is missing:Voice acting: this game desperately NEEDS voice acting, i missed half the dialogue because it silently pops up at the corner of your screen while you travel

_childDocuments_.review: Bugs? Mechs? Hell. Yes. Stonefly is a wonderful little game that gives a chill adventure and an experience that left me smiling with the evident charm throughout. Though it has it's rough edges the developers at Flight School Studio clearly put a lot of heart into it, and I sincerely wish them the best with whatever they do going forward. Visuals: Much like with their previous title; Creature In the Well, Stonefly has an incredibly unique artstyle that on top of being eye-candy really helps lend to the overall moods of environments you see throughout the game. Much of my time spent in Stonefly outside of the gameplay was just gliding around to take in the setting. Additionally, character designs (and mech designs) all have little quirks that create all sorts of charming little flares that I can't help but smile at whenever I see. Color schemes as a whole are pleasant and nothing ever grates on the eyes. Even with the chaos that can happen with the amount of bugs you'll sometimes fight on screen the visuals manage to not appear so overwhelming as to clutter the player.Audio: While your taste may vary this soundtrack is incredible. Ever since starting to play it, it has been my go-to music backing me up whenever I find myself working. Natureboy Flako knocked this out of the park, and the soundtrack has a mixture of really nice and chill sounds for exploration paired with higher bpm tracks that pick up digetically as you encounter greater swarms. Additionally the game's overall sound effects give nice feedback for whatever you're doing and jingles such as those when successfully knocking an enemy away or performing certain abilities sounded nice on top of easily communicating necessary information in the clutter of combat. Gameplay: Admittedly when first starting Stonefly's gameplay and combat is a bit weird and hard to figure out at first. Given when you start you both lack the later upgrades and knowledge of the games mechanics things are around their hardest towards the beginning until you reach the end game content. However once you get over this first hump the overall feeling of progression was quite satisfying as you felt notable improvement at each step. While some abilities are significantly more useful than others, the way you are gradually introduced to them while you better learn the game leads to a feeling of working to master that I heavily enjoy. The overall style at play is really unique and inventive in a way that really isn't like any other kind of game I've played before.Story: I've not got much to say other than it's short but sweet. The biggest issue with the story mainly comes down to it being presented in a way that makes it feel like you don't have all the pieces while Annika does, though this is mainly in regards to backstory and her relations with the Acorn Corps rather than the main events.Glitches/Bugs:Outside of the bugs you'd expect to see, Stonefly has a few issues that while not overbearing by any means are worth noting. For one, there's a degree of camera clipping issues that occurs by either going towards the outer bounds of the game or when simply flying low enough that your view is sometimes blocked by a hanging branch or leaf which occurs enough to sometimes hinder navigation and even interfere in combat. Additionally there are occasional instances of model clipping, certain functions not displaying (at one point I could not exit to camp as the button would not display until exiting and re-entering the game), and crashing (though there's a good chance this is due to the PC I've been playing on as of reviewing the game, since it isn't a stranger to crashing even on programs that aren't that demanding) and occasionally certain event triggers not working properly. While these could likely be solved in the future, as of review this is what I've encountered.Again, even with all of it's rough edges I really recommend playing this game. It's a great experience and I really want the devs to get the support they need for whatever they choose to do next, this is the kind of creativity that I really want to see more of in the industry.

_childDocuments_.review: Stonefly is a game about a girl's journey of "redemption" after she becomes responsible for the theft of her father's rig. A rig, in the game, seems to be a machine that imitates the jumping movement of a grasshopper, as the whole story is set in a miniature world where humans are bug-sized. It makes you wonder about what would be the most preferred way of travel in such a dimension, maybe the grasshoppers are the ideal choice.The game does a great job of bringing out in the player a sense of joy and wonder, an almost childish amazement with a bugs' world. As a child, everybody has fantasized about being the size of an ant and live for a while in a garden. Maybe "Grounded" does a better job of fulfilling that fantasy, but here we have a more whole story told in a similarly oriented setting, with the obvious difference of being in an isometric third-person view. The game takes some care in building a world to traverse rather than survive in and tells a story in a sweet short manner using its environment fully.I found a couple of weak points to be almost deal-breaking for me.The game's core mechanic is to shoot at different types of bugs while avoiding their attacks. Depending on the enemy it will have to be hit one or several times before it is flipped over, and it has to be pushed out of the way to fall and finally be defeated. This gameplay is very varied with several different effects that can be used on the bugs, like a whirlwind that raises them to the air to be pushed easier, or a decoy pearl that attracts the attention of all of them. These effects will have to be applied to some enemies so they can be defeated. This variety in the gameplay makes the game attractive in its action, but this positive side is often obstructed by the terrain that battles happen in. Jumping from place to place can sometimes be tedious when the design of the playing field is not well thought out to offer a smooth experience to the player. Even out of battle, the rig can get stuck in unexpected places, sometimes it's not clear where it will land after a jump, or often the player cannot distinguish how high the rig is sliding through the air because of the monotone use of the colors throughout the game. These will eventually be the issues that bring the movement and combat experience down a level, accentuated by a slight repetitiveness and tediousness of the combat mechanic.Leaving that more technical issue aside, I believe the game suffers the most from the lack of voicing of the characters. It's a good story that unfortunately had to be told through text balloons over character's heads and not much more. I don't need to explain what the lack of voices of characters does to a game, but let's just say nothing in the entire story was transmitted with the emotion obviously expressed in the writing. Voicing the characters would have made Stonefly an easy recommendation of a game.One last detail to mention. I couldn't unsee the weird design of the main character's arms. Why are they much wider the closer to the hands they get? Why aren't the rest of the characters like that (except her father I think)? Maybe if it was a more consistent design choice through the characters it wouldn't have been so weird.
