_childDocuments_.review: Hello Awaken Realms. It is now time for a review.First, let's state this review goes for the Conquest mode. I did'nt want to play the campaign until I get to play the board game. Cuz reasons.Now I have to compare Conquest with two greatly beloved games: Slay the Spire and Darkest dungeon.Darkest dungeon similarities are easier and so let's just say in DD a great deal of your performance is based upon the interactions you do with the objects you find. I know this is a very early version, but locations found during exploration lack this depth. Some of them actually benefit you more if you choose the right dialog options, but once you know the right ones, the fun is over.Adding context to those encounters, based on the character you picked, the deck arquitecture, the options you choosed with prior encounters, etc... I'm not a big fan of probabilities but perhaps mild randomens could also add some spice to it (Fountain of health already does, for example), but making best-performant options  for one encounter cut even better performant options on possible future encounters could be something real nice. Or just pivot arounf everything I said. Something. But left as it is, encounters turn dull and mechanical after 3-4 playthrougths, if not sooner.Now, Slay the spire. That game really breaks your mind. And there are MANY (if not most) things they do better. Again, That's an already polished game and this is very early acces, not to say Conquest is a spin-off from the campaign... but delivering perfect abalance on Conquest I think would translate on a much more polished experience on campaign mode.So, talking about broken mechanics? I played 5 runs. First brawler. Easy to understand. Straightforward. The kind of deck you build your first runs to get to know the game. Then a berseker "High risk-high reward" says the description. Ok. That sounds fun and hard to master. I die without opportunity to use the rune more than once with little effect. I should learn.Then I try the Guardian. And beat all the bosses. Even the final boss. He does not touch me so I finish with full health the game. WTF??The guardian is OP. Broken. Lets summarize it in a few reasons:- The only rune which makes a turn fully invested in defense profitable, as you charge your "ultimate".- This rune makes easier and more powerfull the use of 3-cost cards and support cards as "All in" due to the fact you will have a turn with +4 energy + 3 draw every 2-3-4 turns. Also, you can keep the key card required for combo until you charge your rune high enough.- If you draw more blocks than required for a turn, you can keep it, reducing drastically bad draws which make you eat damage.- If you level up and get "Natural blocker", which gives you 1 free block per turn, last reasoning gets doble true.- If you get a perk that carries your rune charges between combats, once you have your foe at 1 hit, you can max your charges then rush next combat turn 1. All combats. Cuz you recharge by defending.- You can even get a perk to heal 10% each time you activate your rune. So basically you get infinite sustain if you are patient.So, guardian rune idea is great but... insanely broken.Now, about the berseker... 4 and 5 runs going for it. Totally unable to use it, even going for high armor, taunting weak attack enemies and stunning one hitters and promoting enemy multihits... there is virtually no way you get more health by lifestealing 25% one turn than what you loose by getting hit 4 times... not unitl you get a very decent 50% armor damage redution or so, and that is not until late game.Some other thoughs...- "Final strike" should not increase DMG when defeating totems. I raised such card with guardian up to 600% DMG by defeating totems until it basically one hitted most weak enemies.- Probably (IMO) part of the problem with balancing is getting hit consumes too much health, so blocking almost everything is vital, but then with the rigth deck of blocks and stunnings there is a point in which is possible to block ALL attacks except very specific combats/situations.All in all, a very promising combat experience but with tons of rebalancing ahead.Keep the good work! Eagerly awaiting the board game :)

_childDocuments_.review: 6 hours in and I don't really have much of a desire to play any longer.In one word, this game is meh. Adequately designed. The setting, art, and voice acting are very well done, but the gameplay just isn't interesting. It seems like it's replaying the same few levels with the same few enemies over and over with the hope that you'll get a unique interaction and progress the story along. Everything except the core gameplay loop is executed extremely well, though. It runs well, looks nice, UI is solid, etc.I picked the pathfinder, finished a run easily, and since then I haven't had much motivation to keep going. I'm fighting the exact same enemies as before, in the same places, with a weaker deck. Even if I complete multiple runs I'll still need to keep searching for interactions until I get them all. The combat is mostly building up combos and unleashing them. You just delay until you get strong enough to win. Every fight drags on even when it's clear you will win, you can't just crush them as every combo takes ages.In Slay the Spire, after you beat the game, that was it. You actually progressed and the gameplay and story prrogressed with you. You didn't have to do the same thing over and over hoping for a random interaction to spawn so you could progress. Not so much in this game. It feels like padding. I would like to see where the plot goes, but it's become too tedious to continue. Maybe I'll return in a few months.Other things:The wyrdness mechanic is cool, although it seems to only affect you in fights so you can safely walk around with the candles out and light one before you start a fight. This game didn't really need to be 3d. It doesn't really add much. The music is good, especially the boss music with the chanting.

_childDocuments_.review: An addictive roguelite deckbuilder with lots of voiced content and paths you walk around like an RPG. Basically, imagine Slay the Spire by way of Diablo. You might well ask, "There are so many roguelike deckbuilders, why would I want this one?" Well, Tainted Grail adds a bit more storytelling RPG flair to the standard formula. Most events are narrated, lots of voiced NPCs, and it lends the game more of a different character. Not inherently a better one -- indeed, some deckbuilding purists will certainly prefer the streamlined speed of pure gaming in Slay the Spire and Monster Train -- but for those looking for a game that's more of a story you're playing through rather than just pure cardplay, this does hit a sweet spot, like Griftlands.Tainted Grail also leans more roguelite than like, which is to say, you can earn various currencies towards upgrades that persist between runs. Even your quests persist between runs -- I started a quest with a Summoner, and had another three runs with different characters before finally finishing the quest with my Berserker. There's a nice balance here between the usual tuning of the deck (and passive skills), and the fact that bosses behave very differently from each other, which means a setup that can crush one boss might get crushed by another, so you need to adapt, be lucky, or have a deck strong enough that it doesn't matter.In short, it's an interesting and enjoyable take on the roguelite deckbuilder genre, and if the idea of having dark fantasy encounters narrated to you like a storybook sounds appealing rather than appalling, Tainted Grail is definitely worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: The short answer is, this is a great game with a lot of potential but this is the type of game where, if you're like me, you can quickly burn out. I enjoyed my 10ish hours and I am interested to play more when more content/rebalance hits but there are some significant issues which will only somewhat be addressed over time. The game itself has good bones. (I will compare it to Slay the Spire as its commonly considered the definitive game for the genre) There are runes for swappable/collectable buffs (no equivalent), items for small intermittent aids to play (potions), passives (relics from StS), and the tried and true mechanic of collecting cards after battles (from level up this time instead of from each win). I’ll list some aspects of the game, generally spoiler free, in which is my assessment at the current stage of the game.Runes – MediocreThese seem a lot cooler than they actually are. You start with one weapon and one armor slot and can theoretically unlock up to 3 slots of each. Each rune type has two effects, one of which will take effect at a time based on the slot you place it in. You can combine multiple runes of the same type to make stronger runes. At first it seems like there are a lot of possible builds which would utilize different runes and that's exciting. What it ends up boiling down to, however, is that there are a handful of runes that are crazy strong and the rest tend to be very weak by comparison. You're going to find a ton of runes over the course of a run and because the pool of rune types is small, I never had any trouble gathering the ones I wanted. There will be variance in the Mythical tier as you will generally only find 1-2 in a run and a couple of them can massively overpower a build/playstyle. There is a random encounter mechanic which allows you to open more slots which is very useful (so you can pack in more of the same runes) and because it often weighted against removing cards from your deck, I don't have multiple slots often. Usable items – Good enoughThese are about as good as potions in StS. Diverse effects, upgradeable through an unlockable NPC. Due to the general imbalance in the game, I didn’t use these very often outside of the early game of a run. They don’t add a ton to the game but I’m glad they’re there. It is nice when special events interact with your inventory, it helps add a little more connection between your character and world around him.Passives – Good-GreatThese are half the game. There a lot of very interesting passives they are the exciting part of leveling up. They often define your build and play style. The big difference between StS relics and here is there seem to be a lot less passives overall but the generally have more of an impact. The mechanic of constantly being able to pick them out of a smaller pool means you will be going for a lot of the same ones playing a character multiple time. It’s still enjoyable but the once you know the whole pool it can feel a little shallow. Deckbuilding – Good enoughThis are not, in my opinion, where the game shines which is weird to say in a deckbuilding game. There are some neat cards but through the over prevalence of card removal mechanics (through an unlockable npc in town, frequently an option during special events and 2 after killing the each of the first 3 bosses) you don’t have much of a reason to use most of them. You assemble an engine which draws out your deck every turn, with virtually every class, and create a combination of broken effects to generate massive damage, negate enemy attacks, stack hoards of debuffs, etc. There are quest cards which you have to do various things to unlock in their useful forms. There are a small number of powerful ones, slightly more/less depending on your build/class, and the rest aren’t worth the space in your deck. This concept of cards not being worth the space is a constant issue and kills what should be a more dynamic experience. There should always be overpowered and underpowered cards, that keeps things interesting and it is a lot of fun figuring out the best choice in the available options. The dynamic that while many cards are mediocre, your starting deck is always trash should make you wonder if you add in a mediocre card since most of your other cards are worse? In here, the answer is usually no. You only add in cards which fit in your specific, drawable each turn engine and you skip everything else. Sometimes you have the handful of cards you need during the first area and will not even look at the options the rest of the game. For this aspect to take off, we need more cards, a little rebalancing on a few and mainly a reduction in card removal/incentive to take more cards. Balance – PoorMainly for the reasons stated in Deckbuilding, you can readily assemble an engine that breaks the game fairly quickly in most runs. Each class I’ve played has a definitive way to play and you will build towards this repetitively when you figure it out. Other than the starting class, which is just a dull trashy mess. One of the big issues here is the power level of several prominent mechanics. The first and most often abused is stun. 90% of the games enemies/bosses can be stunned, which negates their turn. Using duplication or multiple copies of stun cards with a raw your deck each round engine, you can keep most important enemies, or even large groups, chain stunned. Sometimes you will stack stun 4-5 times in a single turn to keep them locked long into their deaths. This is a mechanic that tends to trivialize content and will aid any given class until it gets massive damage combos rolling. The next silly set of cards are the enemy damage reduction 50% cards. If you hit your opponents with two of these, instead of adding more turns to the effect, they stack and reduce your opponents damage to 1 point. This is as good as a stun, works on everything in the game and in the case of summoner classes comes with the added effect of greatly amplifying your damage. Lastly, armor is quite easy to stack and cap at 75% with runes or cards. I really only bothered with the beserker because he likes to get hit, but realistically the cap should be more fluid, with diminishing returns or with smaller buff values so stacking more of it is difficult. Graphics/Story – ExcellentThis piece blows StS out of the water. The story progresses very slowly, but encounters/dialogue are interesting and so far the writing is consistently good quality. The theme is good and the writing ties in nicely with the graphics. My only gripe here would be that the story is really only experienced by the hardcore players that are going to go on hundreds of runs. After my 10+ hours, all but two of which were wins, I’m still left feeling like not enough has happened but I can’t experience more without slogging through another full playthrough with the same strategies. Conclusion:I think this game is worth playing, even in its current form. This game sets itself apart from many other games well. It is nothing groundbreaking with most of its’ deckbuilding/cardplay elements, but the theme, writing, graphics, and handful of unique mechanics which I won’t spoil carry it through. I think it has the potential to become a fantastic game when they add more content and address some of the issues present. I think the difficulty is too high to just mess around and you will be required to utilize the variety of broken mechanics to win.  If you aren’t the kind of person who figures these out themselves or is willing to check online for guides, I think your longevity will be limited without switching to easy mode (I haven’t tested it, so I won’t comment there). That said, 20$ is a very reasonable price for what’s here and you should know well within the return window whether or not it’s going to be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Thanks to its excellent soundtrack, effective drip-feed storylines, occasionally oppressive darkness, and frequent delightful jankiness, this game scratches an itch that previously only something like the original Diablo and the even more idiosyncratic Wooden Ocean have been able to reach. Oh, and it hits all the right one-more-fight deckbuilding spots for me, too.I still have a lot of souls to save and a 'true' final boss to defeat, but even if I bounce off the end game (my Acolyte run went nowhere fast), I've had 20 real fun hours with Tainted Grail: Conquest so far and could see myself doing it all over again a year or two down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail is a card game roguelike title similar to Slay the Spire. _childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail: Conquest is a turn-based deck building game that is set in a dark fantasy world that's tangentially based on the Arthurian Legends.  Honestly, it probably works in its favor that it just loosely mentions Arthur and Merlin and then does its own thing.  There's a lot of baggage associated with those legends, most of it is pretty cliche at this point and Malory's 'original' version of the story is a pretty rough read.  That said, the story is just okay, it's good enough to keep you motivated, but it's not the main draw of the game.It's a rogue-like game, you have a central village and you have 3 areas to explore off of this hub where you fight three bosses.  After you beat these three bosses a path opens up to a final boss and, if you're victorious, you get to unlock a new difficulty level and start all over again.  The enemy variety was pretty good and the enemies were unique enough in terms of tactics and gimmicks that they didn't feel like reskins of each other.  Each run takes about 2-3 hours to complete.  There are some side quests that persist between runs, and you'll have to complete all the side quests to see the true ending.  It took me about 30 hours to do this, so a fair amount of time for a rogue-like.The game offers you 9 classes to play with.  You'll only have one to start, but the others unlock as you progress.  The classes are divided into 3 groups of 3.  Each group has a set of 96 cards to build their deck from and each class has an unique ultimate ability and a pool of 41 passive abilities that they acquire as they level up.  Every time you level up, you get to select one of 3 randomly selected cards (you could also choose not to take any cards), and every even level you also get to select one of 3 randomly selected passive abilities.  At levels 10 and 20 you get to pick special evolutions of your ultimate ability instead of the usual passives.  While I enjoyed playing the game, ultimately I found the high amount of randomness in your deck and character progression was a bit of a drawback.  There is a certain joy to be found in making the most of what you have at hand, however, the three runs I lost, I lost because I did not have anything to work with.  Sometimes the RNG gives you an embarrassment of riches that lets you plough through the content, other times it gives you cards with no synergy and passives that work against each other.  You don't really build your character as much as hope a pathway to victory emerges and try to steer your character in that direction.Despite this I enjoyed the game.  It lasted just long enough that it didn't overstay its welcome.  You can also see from the screen shots and videos that the production values are very good for this type of game.  I'd give it a 7 out 10.

_childDocuments_.review: I purchased this game a while back and finally decided to give it a whirl. Next thing I know 4 hours had blasted past. It's a wonderful deckbuiler with character classes that offer really unique ways of playing (each one has custom cards, passives, and an in-battle quirk or ability). Also, the art is solid and the story is surprisingly well done. I've enjoyed the voice acting and the world has me intrigued. I honestly didn't expect to fall into this one so deeply, but I adore this game and look forward to its future developments. A surprising gem here, please consider this game if you like the genre but are looking for some refreshing twists both in terms of narrative and mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game. If you're a fan of Slay the Spire (in which I have hundreds of hours played) you'll probably enjoy this. It's similar in Act progression yet on a 3D set. You'll probably trounce the early game but much like StS there's Ascension-like levels to work up through. You only start with one class but there's a few base classes to learn (fighter, summoner, archer types). You unlock them and their alternate variations just like unlocks in StS, basically, and each plays differently enough, for a total of 9 classes. Appearance skins unlock once you've unlocked all the classes and can be changed at will any time you're in the village hub before and between Acts once you've met a certain npc. The rogue-lite hub is fun to build up. The hub, characters and story elements along the way are something StS doesn't have and brings... "life"... to the game. The graphics are some of the best I've seen in Unity and shows the developers know what's up. The atmosphere is dark and dreary just how I like and enemy design, both art and gameplay, is detailed and fitting. As of Aug.19, 2021 there's new game modes. I've only run into a few minor bugs and sometimes it feels like the UI was crammed in but I've not found anything to be broken. Glad my friend told me to check this out. I'll now be keeping an eye on their upcoming game, TG: The Fall of Avalon, as well.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Judgement -> An overthinker's dream. Turn based strategy lover here - So what does this game offer that's different? (to keep those of us that usually find a trick to beat the AI in these types of games) 1) It feels like a turn based dark souls. You die, you come back a bit stronger, wiser but your enemies also scale with you lol - Do not think they are the same everytime... Imagine playing dark souls, when you go back to earlier levels and you are buff....Enemies are all in the same place and do the same things, same combinations...Not here.2) For a couple of fights you think you are unbeatable, this feeling happens quite a lot! The enemy combinations are excellent and will tear your "unbeatable deck" apart (in a pinhead voice) IF you don't think ahead. The bosses also create havoc and you must pay attention. One boss took me 2 hours because my strategy was slow and steady....3) Every turn is a puzzleTo succeed you have to plan ahead by many turns. (but it's also fun just to go crazy and die a few runs in row just to explore etc)4) Card combos and different characters. Being honest, my 18 hours so far have all been with the default character. I like to push it until I find that limit then move to the next. The cards really start popping later in the game once you learn to count. Yes count.ie you have 10 perks that are on different counters - 3 hits for one to activate, 4 hits to make this enemy vulnerable, 2 turns before max damage, you ultimate counter is 4 hits from 300%, you deck draw has 10 cards left and you are waiting for a certain card or combo.....BOOOOOOOOOOM 1000 damage. Oops, I forgot about the other 2 enemies, uh oh! This game will make us overthinkers greedy.What is different to slay the spire? You have a base camp that you populate and upgrade. It is really tactical and not just for show! If you're like me and want to get the perfect strategy or die the least amount of times, this is a great addition to the genre. The story and creatures are so f'kin dark it's pure evil++++, I love it. The people you meet, the little stories are completely new - none of this "omg there's a girl who needs rescue, omg I found her, yay happy ending" .... It's all so dark that you actually start appreciating any good news for you or the people lolWhat else?EXPLORATION. Since you have a map and you move around it with your character, other stuff can happen in between fights. Be careful, plan ahead. Yes you can kill everyone and loop back before you fight the boss. What would I like to see in a follow up? Fights in Tight spaces style of play - Where you have decks but also move around a map, so location matters too

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one for the MAYBE PILE at this point in early access. This game is almost completed, but still, a lot is lacking imo. The game is still entertaining and definitely difficult, and the base card battles are enjoyable. Though ultimately  I refunded this game, but may keep an eye on it once it releases in case there are any major class overhauls.  Going by the most recent update (0.99) it appears that the devs are more interested in the graphics and voice overs than actual game play. The fighter class cards are similar to StS, but unique enough to be different and interesting. The summoner classes are all different variants of the same thing, and imo a total letdown. They all summon the same monsters but with different restrictions. The walking around part of this game should be removed and replaced with a isometric view, and be mouse driven. Besides pretending that you're playing The Witcher between card battles, there is no point in wasd'ing around. There's absolutely no point. It's a gimmick as the battles are completely static and cards are played using the mouse. The graphics are not bad at all, but again, there's not really a point to them.TL;DR: If you love all card battler's go for it, if not, then there are better games out there.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: This is a very good roguelike deckbuilder with lots of amazing extra's like good graphics, nice stories and almost full voice acted.Is it the best deckbuilder ever? No, but its definitely in my top 5 (out of +/- 50 played).Every time it gets slow or boring, you unlock a better hero and try again.After you complete the normal story, there is an endgame boss.After beating him, you can keep beating him at higher difficulty.This is pretty grindy, so I'm not sure how many times I'm gonne do that.Overall, 8/10 as a deckbuilder and 9/10 for the experience. 8,5/10 total, would recommend at the normal price. Definitely give it a go if it gets on sale.Edit: So I noticed after completing the full thing that I was only halfway in most sidequests, so I started playing all different heroes 1 by one, ticking off sidesquests while doing so (thats how this game works).This was pretty enjoyable, and before I know it I'm 30 hours in and completed the game on most heroes. So a little more grinding and in 46h total I got all the achievements in the game. I only got 1 sidequests left, and that the one (spoiler alert) that only triggers in the dark. Thats a little annoying, because it takes ages for it to trigger. Overall tha game was good fun, I make it a 8,7/10 overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This game grew on me. At first I was a bit iffy and didn't like the wyrd candle system, but after a while I've really grown to like it. The RPG aspect of this game is also really fun. All quests carry on even if you fail a run.There are 9 playable classes (sort of). Each class has 3 sub classes that share cards, but their passives, abilities and play styles differ vastly. You have a main hub base that you find and upgrade vendors over time. The map system is exactly like Slay the Spire, but you travel between fights in 3rd person.Once you unlock them, I highly recommend new players try the Sentinel or Summoner, Good classes for beginners.The Berserker is my favourite class. The fun of dancing on low hp while dealing tonnes of damage is quite enjoyable.tldr; if you enjoy RPG's and games like Slay the Spire or Griftlands you will most likely enjoy this as it's a mix of both genres with decent graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: + dark atmosphere+ music+ different characters and different styles of playing them+ good combat system- unbalanced difficulty, some classes are extremely strong- opponents and their abilities is not very differentTainted Grail is a roguelike deckbuilding turn-based game in the dark world of Arthur legend. The player in the skin of one of the 9 classes discovers the mysteries of the world covered by the strange fog, solves the problems of its inhabitants, whom he recruits to his settlement to help him in various endless cycles of transitions.The characters are from 3 different factions, where each has its own set of types of combat cards, but each of the 3 classes within the faction uses them a differently and has a different ultimate ability and skills that he gains through levels. In addition to basic cards, combat runes are used to modify character abilities and other various items. Using random encounters on a relatively small map, the player develops the story and improves his parameters. To conquer one map, it is necessary to kill its guard. The game has nice graphics with well-designed monsters, the combat system is good, it offers a lot of variants, but over time it will start to repeat itself as with all games of this style. The sound music page is good, it supports the dark tuning of the game.The difficulty is a bit unbalanced, some late unlocked classes and factions are much easier to play than others and one transition, which consists of 3 guards and one final boss, can be passed quite easily.For lovers of deck building games such as Slay the Spire or Monster Train, it can be recommended, for cheap money, it's fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly well-made deckbuilding roguelite that takes a lot of different inspirations and wraps them up into a wholly unique and very enjoyable package. So far, I've only played three of the nine classes, each of which has been completely different in playstyle. Gameplay wise, I'd say fans of Slay the Spire or Monster Train will find a lot to like here, but the narrative and progression elements make the game welcoming for newcomers to roguelites. Difficulty here is solid so far - you'll likely not win immediately, but the buffs you get from progression make later runs slightly easier and create a good difficulty curve. Really solid pickup for fans of roguelites, especially with the easy to swallow price.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this over a year ago during early access. Only now that the final version has been released do I feel the need to post this. The  final version of the game is filled with an enormous number of bugs. It should never have been given approval to go gold in this state. In less than 29 minutes worth of play in the final version it crashed twice before completing the most basic part of the tutorial. A third attempt to play got part way through the first battle with the one unlocked character you're given at the beginning, then I got a black screen that I was unable to get out of. I tried Alt-Tab, the Windows key, and Control-Alt-Delete to bring up the task manager. Nothing worked. I had to result in using the Reset button on the computer, which resulted in a message that the C: drive was corrupted and needed to be scanned and repaired. After an additional reboot it seems that Windows has successfully recovered from that, but it has lead me to deleting this program from my system.I can NOT recommend this game to anybody. You're in danger of losing your data if you install it, based on my experience with it. My hardware goes well beyond the published requirements to run it so that's not a possible problem. Maybe in another year the devs will have worked out the bugs but I won't be trying it again for some time.

The narration is on point, with each voice actor nailing the gravity of the situation and the essence of their character.The different classes are fun to experiment with and keep each loop fresh.The deck building feels easy and intuitive, allowing for plenty of experimenting.I recommend you give this a try if you like dark, gritty RPGs, a different take on the Arthurian Legend and are not afraid of having terrible runs in-between incredible runs where you feel like a force of nature.

_childDocuments_.review: Get soul arrow class. Shoot them twice, do same amount of damage as other classes but feel better cause hit them twice. Get doggo buddy. Bite them. Good boy, never go into runs without him. (make sure once you have him unlocked, at the start of your run go to the resting fire and summon him, otherwise you will not have him in your run until you go back to the village and summon him)Game has a great dark theme about it, classes are pretty unique overall, difficulty is there for the masochists out there, and an easy mode for the casual gamers just looking to have fun. Hope feels all but gone and as usual everyones problems are yours to solve. I adore the art in this game and honestly the voice acting is quite good. It's easy to get a little frustrated when you are doing well and get one shotted with full armor, several blocks, and full hp but it happens. At the start enemies hit hard, but as you progress and get familiar with the class mechanics, they still do. There are a few ways to get some healing in but do you best to take each fight slowly because getting that precious life force back doesn't come often. Get ready to fall down, get up, and fall back down. You can't always win but you can lose every time. Currency of all forms can be hard to come by and build up for story related missions or upgrades, which sucks but it's just part of the griiiiiiiiind. Solid 8 for me.My only real complaints are not being able to carry over your improved deck into new runs and trash passives. Biggest pro in the game is petting the dog.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: It was fairly buggy in the past, at times which has been its only real downside. It's essentially a card game but I actually think it's a better 3D-Slay the Spire (if you enjoyed that, you should enjoy this), and unlike STS you actually make tangible progress between playthroughs using ingame items to level up your HP/Defence/Quantity or Quality of acquired runes (so it's not just run after run based on RNG). So if you have a bad run, you can work towards the next one being easier! (You have to 'find' NPCs to bring back to town who have separate currencies to upgrade your deck/self/map.)The music is also pretty damn good (it was what first intrigued me to the game and builds a convincingly gritty and mysterious world. Think Arthurian and Norse/Celtic themes. The sound design and visuals are very cohesive. Danheim!)Came for the music, stayed for the playstyles and the engrossing ministories/narration. One or two cheesy character voices like the ghost lol but otherwise captivating.The classes are quite varied with totally different moves and styles (one is "take as much damage as possible to become stronger"; another "avoid getting hit and you do more damage"; "get stronger the more hits you land". There are 3 summoner style classes, again all with slightly different mechanics (one of which can turn into a lich as their special lol) I was surprised how much fun I was having between even 4 different roles, and selecting which new cards would best suit the approach.You might really struggle one run and soon after upping your def/HP enjoy thrashing an enemy. You can up the difficulty to get more/better loot but beyond a certain point, even with max stats it can become hellishly difficult!Intrigued to see what comes next for the series, as the story starts off and is kind of left open ended at the end of the game (even if you break the loop).

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually pretty good even in its current Early Access state, I am curious to see how it improves over time. This is a sort of Slay-the-Spire like deck builder game but also an RPG. Instead of having a map where you choose your next encounter you  play a character on the field and can move around to the events/encounters directly which is pretty cool, though I feel it controls a little awkward at times, and a sore sight on the eyes at other times due to the fog. I think there could be some polish graphics and performance wise.That said, the gameplay is pretty good. There's a handful of classes available already. I tried our a warrior class and a summoner and they played really differently. Summoner uses cards to summon monsters and can't deal any direct damage. Can use the cards to buff/activate his summons instead or add more summons to the field. The more warrior focused classes on the other hands can be about building up damage combos or status effects and so on. Instead of relics, there are perks chosen upon milestone level ups and runestones you can find and upgrade throughout the run.There is also overall progression in the form of the starting area. This sort of home base is permanent and any NPCs you locate on the runs and move there will remain there on new runs. You can then purchase upgrades for these NPCs that will last throughout the next runs too. For example the first NPC can heal you and you can upgrade him to heal for more quality and quantity.The game does seem a bit easy early on, I never really felt like I was in danger except maybe the final encounter but I was able to scale with the encounter and do fine.  However, the game does have "corruption" similar to Slay the Spire's ascension levels. I have not tried these out to a high level yet so it could get quite a bit harder. I think the game is decent. Personally, something feels a little off and thus I put it off for now in favor of other card games and RPGs. I think it just needs a bit more polishing all around. But it's a good game and I'm willing to pick it up again when it fully releases to check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: All hero deckbuilding games ultimately fall back on comparison to the original hero deckbuilder: Slay The Spire. It's impossible to ignore because Slay The Spire did it first and, arguably, is still doing it best. Each new challenger touts its own USP and Tainted Grail's is that it has a story set to a gritty, Arthurian backdrop, which, honestly, is pretty damn good. The environments ooze murkiness, with corruption having twisted all the land's inhabitants. Everyone you meet is eccentric and warped in some way, and they all have a story to tell with voice acting galore in every interaction. The village segment carries some serious Diablo 1 vibes, even containing a guitar strum in the opening soundtrack that sounds almost a direct copy of the one used in the Diablo village theme. All in all, the ambience of the game really captures the "weird Arthur" theme that it's aiming for, and if you’ve been looking for a more story-focused, thematic deckbuilding experience then Tainted Grail has you covered.However, mechanically I feel like the jury's a bit out so far. I'm not deep enough into the game to know if it has the creative deckbuilding staying power compared to Slay The Spire. My reason for this concern is best explained by comparison.In Slay The Spire you're given a basic class template that can go in any number of directions during a run. Each class has its own mechanics and keywords that it plays off of, but the path you end up down depends on which combinations you build into courtesy of the RNG. One game you'll play a thousand armour Ironclad that tanks every hit and smacks back in giant one shot wallops that stomp the enemies flat. In another, you might play a HP-loss focused Ironclad that juggles HP sacrifice to fuel a series of quick and powerful attacks. Each game with the same character will feel vastly different, and your strategy and approach for handling each fight will need to adjust depending on how you’ve built in a given run.By comparison, Tainted Grail tries to load more upfront elements into each character to predefine your build strategy. The current nine characters belong to one of three factions (fighters, archers, mages), and characters in the same faction share the same pool of cards that they'll draft from as they level up. Straight off the bat this means the variety of having nine heroes to play is really a falsehood because, with the exception of their starting differences, there're really only three separate "classes" of character to play. However, to do the system some justice, each character focuses on different aspects of the class card pool, so they will play out meaningfully differently to each other by valuing cards in the shared card pool higher or lower relative to another hero in the same faction. Same-faction characters use the same starter deck (with one or two differences) and are distinguished by each having their own ultimate ability (which is charged up in its own unique way), their own passive ability, and a specific starter card that will always be in your hand each round. These three changes doesn't seem like much of an addition, but they really guide the build strategy of each character.For instance, in the melee class, the Wyldhunter gets a strong, single target attack as their ultimate, which is charged every time they make an attack, and their passive stacks a vulnerability effect on enemies that are hit multiple times in the same turn. This means you're heavily incentivised to take card effects that let you make multiple attacks in a single action because that's how to make the most of those starting abilities. Comparatively, the Pathfinder (also in the melee faction) has a passive that gives them stacking bonus damage for every round they don’t take a hit. Furthermore, their ultimate lets them draw a larger number of cards and gives them additional actions to have big attack turns to make use of the stacked damage they’ve received over turns of blocking, thus they value defensive cards much higher than the multi attack cards a Wyldhunter wants.The result of this design is that you have to play to your hero’s basic synergies regardless of what comes up in the drafting options; ignoring the innate abilities of the hero to try and build something different is inevitably hamstringing yourself. Admittedly, how you implement a build that plays off of those innate abilities will play out a little differently each time, but you’re locking yourself into a style of play at the character selection screen. By comparison, in Slay The Spire you’re handed a much blanker slate and given the freedom to build into whatever comes your way, figuring out a specialisation on the fly.All this said, I don’t know if this is necessarily a bad thing. Tainted Grail is trying to go for theme, so giving each hero its own vibe means you know what you’re building for and perhaps have a greater immersion in the build design process. However, I suspect that repeat playing a character might feel more stale than the myriad possibilities and unknowns you can get from a Slay The Spire run.Back on the positive, there’s no shortage of complexity in Tainted Grail’s tactical card play during fights, which makes it very engaging and, I suspect, holds a sizeable skill ceiling for players to finesse. For instance, each hero’s ultimate can theoretically be activated every turn, but they get stronger if you choose to hold off and allow more charges to accumulate. Knowing when to hold and when to fire are key decisions that don’t always have clear answers to them.Another less fun area of complexity comes from damage calculation. For some heroes this is no issue whatsoever, but classes like the Necromancer and the archer faction heroes would really benefit from a combat calculator to do some of the work for you because there can be a lot to keep track of and its easy to overlook something that ends up hurting you a lot.Overall, I like Tainted Grail. I worry that it doesn’t really have the strength of deckbuilding possibilities that defines the genre, but Tainted Grail is trying to sell you a story as well. When a company splits its resources in this way then the result can be a half-baked product in both areas. Developer Klei tried this with Griftlands and ended up with merely okay RPG mechanics and okay deckbuilding, but I think that Tainted Grail has got decent enough deckbuilding and excellent world-building that justifies the division of resources in its production. Is it the strongest game in its genre? For sure no, but it’s a decent enough entry if you want to take a different hero deckbuilder out for a spin.Edited for Steam Awards task.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked "Slay the Spire" you will love Tainted Grail. And if you didn't like "Slay the Spire", or don't know it at all, chances are you will love Tainted Grail, too!Seriously, I follow this game since the first days in early access and now that it's finished I'm amazed at what the devs turned it into. A lot of love (and work!) went into this project and it shows. For a first title of a small indie studio this is impressive!The 3D world you move around in freely and the RPG part are a breath of fresh air in the deckbuilder/roguelite genre. The game grips you from the very first line of the story. Writing and voice acting are stellar, soundtrack is fantastic and the new graphics are gorgeous. Yes, graphics and animations are still not AAA material but as it turns out, that's not needed for a dark, dense atmosphere! Tainted Grail pulls you into this creepy re-imagination of the Arthurian legend and you probably won't want to leave anytime soon.Be aware there is a learning curve though and if you're not used to rogue-like games the difficulty might discourage you. But every run you get resources and points to unlock more stuff that will help you in future runs. Dying is part of the process! But as your understanding of the game mechanics grows and you unlock more cards you discover new strategies even for fights that before seemed impossible to win. Be aware: The gameplay loop is addictive - in the best possible way!The game explains the basics, but leaves you to discover much of the game on your own - this can be a downside for some. As a new player I know I'd like more handholding. To be fair, for the card game part there is a ton of tooltips so you get all the information you need. And for the rest you can always ask on the very friendly discord server or consult the wiki so this shouldn't be much of a problem.Devs are quick to fix bugs and really listen to feedback of the community. If you're still reading this, I recommend you buy this game immediately! Check your hardware specs though, because from the reviews I take that if you want to experience TG in its full glory it seems you will need more GPU power than you might expect (runs smooth on my RX480).

_childDocuments_.review: Updated=It's finally here! Full release! Well, of the roguelite deckbuilder mode anyway, the main board game campaign is still later this year. The game is much more polished now, though jank ability interactions can still happen occasionally. The biggest strength of this game imo, is how lore and character heavy it is. The other games in this genre(StS, Monster Train, etc) technically have plots, but that really is not their focus. Tainted Grail has npcs you get to know, and the game does a good job of entwining their storylines with each other in a way that makes them very engaging. Yes many of their plot lines are fetch quests at heart, but I genuinely wanted to see where each characters little side story would go. Combat has been expanded a lot since early access also. The third class group has been released and they are really strong. I don't think all 3 class groups are equally strong but it's possible I'm just really bad at playing mages. There's many more abilities added to the pool and there are interesting decisions in every run. There are enough enemy varieties that target a specific playstyle that you have to think and not always just formula min-max. Upgrades that carry over between runs do sometimes feel overly grindy, but I suppose it would be boring if you just got them all too fast as some of them are extremely powerful.Overall Tainted Grail is up there among the greats of the genre and well worth the price of entry. I look forward to the campaign and hope they continue supporting the game.Original=Watched a review of the board game and thought it was something I wanted to play. The plot is basically King Arthur and the Knights went off and never returned, so now you play as a C-tier warrior setting off to see what happened to them. Sadly the game wasn't in stores so it was unlikely for me to get a copy and when I heard there was going to be a digital implementation it perked my interest. My brother gifted it to me so hey I got to give it a shot. As of this writing the campaign is not done and the only mode is this roguelike deckbuilder mode. It's decent enough, but I feel it gates some stuff a bit too much behind villages unlocks. The first few runs were pretty brutal before scrimping enough to unlock some stuff. It's got a few classes with their own mechanics that focus on varying playstyles but the cards you can add to your deck are shared(I actually like this, it makes you think of the possibilities when you see a new card of what the other classes can do with it). The mode is competent but I don't think right now it has anything right now that would make me recommend it over the many games in the genre. But I am excited for the stuff they are continuing to add , optimization hopefully and the campaign eventually. I would say wait awhile for more updates or the campaign before buying it. Or just get it if you really like the theme or setting.

_childDocuments_.review: After the success of games like Slay the Spire, which were able to create a new approach to card games where you control your character(s) directly using the cards you draw. Normally this kind of games have one thing in common: they start out very slowly and get progressively more exciting the more cards you gather, both inside runs and in between them, simply due to the fact that more powerful cards give you access to often crazy combos. In this regard, Tainted Grail: Conquest follows the games that came before it, adding a dark atmosphere and tons of content to the mix. Will it be able to succeed?Tainted Grail follows the legends of Arthur, although re-imagined in a dark way: an incredibly powerful force called the Wyrdness has overcome the lands, killing and corrupting everything it touches. Weird and dangerous creatures started roaming these lands, while lost souls seek shelter from the darkness. Powerful ancient way stones could be able to keep this corruption at bay, but they are few, scattered and dying, as the druids that could have helped in restoring them were killed. The future is not looking good and the present is getting grimmer: heroes must rise against this dark force.Luckily, Tainted Grail: Conquest provides a great diversity of classes: whereas in this kind of games you get three of four classes, this title provides you with 9, each one with completely different playstyles and cards. These classes are divided into three different factions: the Children Of Morrigan focuses on melee fighters with direct approaches, the Moonring faction can instead use magic and bend the Wyrdness to their favour by summoning a number of different creatures. Last but not least, the Watchers of Tuathan focus on ranged fighting, shooting arrows at their enemies and making thoughtful preparations to empower them. The best aspect of these classes is, again, how much they play differently even inside a faction: taking the Moonring classes (they are my favourites, hands down), they are all able to summon the same creatures, but while the Summoner uses its energy to improve them and make them as big as possible, the Blood Mage uses instead its HP and the Necromancer doesn’t really improve them, sacrificing them instead to gain energy for its lich form.This doesn’t mean that all classes are made equal though, as balancing isn’t always perfect. Balancing 9 different classes in a card game can quickly become a very daunting task as more cards are added to the game and personally I found the game to be way easier with some classes: starting with the Wyrdhunter, the only available class in the beginning, I found the game to be very hard and was barely able to defeat the first boss, whereas in my first run with the Summoner I was able to steamroll through packs of enemies, losing my fight against the third boss only because of a misplay.Outside combat you will get a chance to explore the tainted land and to speak with the lost souls that inhabit it. At the start of each run, you will find yourself in the village, a place spared from the Wyrdness thanks to the presence of a grim statue overlooking the center of the place: here you will find a lot of empty buildings, that will eventually return to life when you will find and save different characters that you will find in the Wyrdness. These characters will help you during your runs and represent, along with the earning of new cards, the rogue-lite aspect of the game. Besides providing new items and cards, you will also be able to have interesting conversations with them from time to time.When not in the village, you will venture into the Wyrdness to find and slay four different guardians: the Wyrdness is not a safe place and you will be provided with Wyrd candles to help you in your journey: these make for an interesting gameplay mechanic where you can light a candle (that will burn over time) and cast away the Wyrdness from around you. The utility in doing this is that the Wyrdness makes encounters more dangerous, so these effectively act as difficulty-lowering candles, lowering the dangerousness of the enemies the brighter the candle is burning. Speaking of exploration, into the Wyrdness you will not only find monsters to fight, but also different NPCs to interact with: they will sometimes sell interesting items, stats boost or cards… while sometimes they will just have an interesting story to tell.Tainted Grail’s setting is truly fascinating, similarly to Darkest Dungeon’s: wandering a land filled with corrupting energy and horrible creatures ready to devour you certainly has its… charm we could say. Most of the creatures during combats resemble very well the corrupting power of the Wyrdness by showing monster of horror resembling tortured souls, tentacle-like creatures and totems to dark gods. Venturing in the Wyrdness feels dangerous, especially when you don’t have a Wyrdcandle lit, but the world outside combat does also feel a little bit dead, with you exploring what effectively are maps made out of corridors where enemies are sitting still waiting for you. Exploration is still enjoyable, don’t get me wrong, but overall it would have been a better experience if the whole thing felt more alive.Tainted Grail is a really well built deckbuilding roguelite game with a few unpolished edges. Overall, it offers a really great experience for players that appreciated games like Slay the Spire or Monster Train, featuring a lot of different classes and in general a lot of content. The dark setting is either love or hate, so follow your taste in this regard and, if you suits you, give Tainted Grail a go, you won’t be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: How did this get above 90% positive reviews?Alright, given I did not buy this for the story. Which might be cool, I do not know. But one thing is sure, no matter how good it might be, to unlock more characters, you need to get through the same story, again and again *Cough cough* that ****** suck. Right, that is not why I bought it, I bought it for the tags "roguelike/roguelite deckbuilder," right after patch 1.1 Shattered reality came about.On paper this 1.1 Shattered reality, looked really good. Still do, great graphics, love the atmosphere, animations, even the sounds, but what really matters for a game with above named tags, is the meta game, combat, a synergistic item/card system, and a feeling of accomplishment when beating a big bad boss. On that, it fails. 1. You can't unlock new characters through these new two endless modes!? 2. No paths to take. Funny enough the story mode, do actually kind of have paths to take like you would see in other deckbuilders, but the endless modes do not. But why not? 3. The options you do get "rewards" after each combat, is as pointless as they are plain. 3 choices, between armor, max health and attack. At this point, you might as well just level me up automatically or maybe just find some more intriguing synergistic systems with items and gear, instead of a stat pat booster. Same goes for the card choices, where you very often see the same 1-2 cards come up in a row out of 3 choices. 4. The power levels of the endless modes are either way to easy, or hard. The chill mode "endless power," is rather chill except from the first legendary fight, where you more then likely will die 9/10 times. But the 1 time, where you do get lucky with the limited choices you have from cards, and chose the right stats to go along with it, you will get past it ... and as the name suggest, go on an endless boring run. Yes, The endless boring run. I mean sure, I like the idea, but you will never get that feeling of accomplishment when 2 hitting big bad bosses. Or on the other hand, in endless misery, get beaten 99/100 times before you get to a boss. 5. The only positive I'll take from this game, is that all of the above is something that CAN be fixed giving the developers enough time, but since the game got +90% positive reviews, and possibly a fan base that like everything I seem to hate, I doubt it will happen. I'll crawl back to Slay the Spire, Monster Train, Poker Quest & Griftlands ... that do, deserve their tags.

_childDocuments_.review: tl,dr Now that you got the message, we can go a little deeper:Tainted Grail: Conquest is a little gem and a surprise but with a few flaws. The first impression is striking because it has fully 3D graphics and high production value. Every character is fully voiced (shout-out to voice acting team because they did a hell of job). The grimdark tone of the setting is a nice change of pace from big daddy Slay the Spire and similar games who go for a more comic-bookish, stylized approach.In my opinion the 3D overworld doesn't really add much and  The overall roguelite progression is a bit grindy, but I understand the reason, in TG:C the permanent upgrades are really really powerful and if they made it easier you could crush the game before even exploring the whopping nine classes you can play with. Also the class you start with is possibly the most boring one of them all, so this and the general  of the 3D map can make the first few hours a little bit rough.I might repeat myself but the game really clicked for me when I started exploring the various classes, they all feel unique and they feel broken in their very own way once you get deep in the deckbuilding and start figuring out possible archetypes. 20 hours in, I just finished the game with 2 of the 9 classes and I am just on the second of the 10+ (!) difficulty settings you can unlock. I can easily see myself sinking a hundred hours into Tainted Grail: Conquest without really getting bored. This amount of variety and content makes it stand out and a really easy recommend if you are a fan of roguelites and deckbuilders.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a tough time with this one. It has great reviews, cool voice-acting and a story. I should love this game. I am just so absolutely bored. It's not the repetition of content that's the problem. It's the quality of content being repeated that's the issue here. I've killed the 3rd boss. According to the achievements, only 38% of players have gotten that far.. clearly I'm not the only one who's bored..In the description in the top-right of the store page the devs defined this (as of this review) as a roguelike. It's not. It's a rogueLITE. They're not the same thing, A roguelike means you carry nothing over into your future runs, you just try to do better or hope for better rng. Roguelite, is a 'light' version with 'elements' of a roguelike except you have have unlockables for future runs, and carry some items/skills over into future runs so it gets easier the more you play. That's this. How this is mislabeled by its own creator is beyond me. I mean, do you know the difference? Do you know what you even made here...?Well anyway, with that out of the way, why am I bored by this game? With many rogue-type games you repeat content, a lot. I get that. But this is slooooow, very, very limited, content. It's the exact same enemies time, and time again with very, very little variation. Yes it's dressed up very nice, but it's same few, boring enemies, over, and over and over. RNG of new runs doesn't change the enemies, just where they are. So you still face the same ones, all over again.I'm at almost 12 hours with some classes unlocked, and I honestly don't care about the other (unlockable) classes, because no matter what class I am, it's the exact same enemies, fight after fight, that I'm already bored to tears with. At 10 hours in, I struggled to click the play button. Finally after a few days away I made myself play just now, for an hour and was just not enjoying it. Yes, re-read that, I had to 'force' myself to play this. Maybe others are more easily amused. Maybe I'm missing the 'excitement' of such a slow paced game. Maybe it's just me. What little action there is gets interrupted by something quest-related 2 out of every 3 fights, and many times is pointless until you randomly run into the 2nd half of it's quest, then back to the 1st part again in another future, random run. Repeating content is fine, that's the heart of a rogue-type game, but when it's the same slow, boring content for 10+ hours, it doesn't hold my interest, no matter how well dressed it is, no matter how well voiced it is.. And by the way, yes it still has some optimization issues. When I play this game, and only this game, on a mid-level rig, all the fans on my gfx card kick on and it vibrates - I mean, dayum.  Obviously I am in the minority, but this game is just going to sit until I see more content updates, which, you might be interested to know, it had just before I bought it. I can't even imagine how it was before... holy cow.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, this one deserves a review.I've played quite a few deckbuilder games in my time, and it's always a pleasant surprise when I find one that manages to engage me with new, interesting and varied mechanics. Tainted Grail is such a one.The forty hours playtime are across the last four or five days or so, and given the retail price of this game that makes it an absolute banger. Tainted Grail is a fascinating take on the deckbuilder genre, with a full blown macabre gothic Arthurian-Legend-Gone-Wrong-Police-Called storyline attached to it. You travel through increasingly difficult areas of an insidious forest filled with deformed, demonic bad guys, building up your character to get them ready to face each area's final boss.The first great aspect of Tainted Grail is the story and characters. As you explore these areas, you will meet a variety of messed up, fully voiced individuals who can trade things with you, give you quests to complete, fight you or even join your settlement and provide permanent legacy bonuses that persist even when your run ends. This is certainly a deckbuilder with all the juicy meta-progression elements one could hope for to keep replayability at max, and it's all implemented in a logical yet thematic way. The voice acting quality varies but is generally between C to A tier, nothing hammy, nothing lifeless.The second great aspect is the nine different character classes you can unlock and choose from when you start a new run. Given that the core gameplay loop is Draw Cards/Play Cards/Kill Stuff, the playstyle variety between each and every class is almost poetic. I nearly started typing an entire paragraph spoiling the classes here, but I'll hold off in the hope that you'll want to discover them for yourself. Suffice to say that not only is each class's deck different, but the WAY you play that deck is also completely different, and this makes experimenting with each one a total joy.The third great aspect is the Candle mechanic. Similar to Darkest Dungeon, you have a limited supply of candles that you light as you explore the monster areas. When you encounter monsters, you will receive bonus cards into your hand every other round or so. When you receive one of these bonus cards, you can either play it for an immediate effect, or leave it in your hand and receive an alternative effect at the start of your next turn. Sometimes the choice will be obvious, but occasionally this will prove a fascinating tactical dilemma. In addition, the effect of these cards is dependent on your candlelight level. At maximum light, their effects can change the course of the entire battle in your favour, but at low levels, these cards will actually punish you in battle if you DON'T play them (such as increasing the cost of your other cards etc). In the early game, this presents a crunchy issue of resource management - do you risk heading into the next fight with low light because you're saving the last candle for the boss? What if you don't make it that far?In addition addition, your candlelight burns down the longer you spend in battles. So if you think you're really clever spending 100 rounds lifestealing off the last mob you've caught in a damage loop, think again. You cannot afford to dilly dally, either on the world hub or in battles. Time is against you, and I love it.Sadly no game is perfect, and Tainted Grail does have a couple of flaws. First one is some UI issues - occasionally cards lag out when you click on them, and sometimes animations of selecting cards is alarming slow, making me believe I've accidentally clicked on the wrong one while skimming through my hand at the bottom of the screen.The other slight gripe I have with this game is the obfuscation of key information which can result in a run ending. Sometimes mechanics just don't work the way you might assume they would, and while the tooltips are generally very good, they sometimes don't tell you the whole story. Here are some things I found out "when it was too late":- Armour is capped at 75- Minions with Taunt multiply damage taken from AOE affecting allies- Duplicating the effect of a card that flips does not activate the same flipped side twice- "Lose 5% Max health" does not mean permanent max health- Enemies can trigger each others' damage procsThese circumstances are annoying, particularly when they don't kill you outright, but rather render your deck build impotent in some way, but in the case of Tainted Grail, the prospect of Game Over was simply an exciting opportunity to try another class, another build.Love it. Still playing it. Go get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, but not a great "rogue-lite" to be honest. Too slow and tedious for that imho.You get to pick out of 9 classes (eventually after unlocking), 3 melee, 3 ranged and 3 mages. Each archetype shares a common play type, but each class uses their shared cards differently, has a different ultimate ability and has different passives that you get when you level up. That's quite interesting.The battles themselves are strategic and interesting, often requiring quite a bit of finesse. The story and lore is also interesting ... at first at least, but towards the end it gets bogged down. I can't bring myself to go on however many more runs fighting the same battles over and over again to complete the final quest ... and get, what? Nothing, because the world obviously has to go on, I think. Voice acting ranges from great (narrator/death) to rather terrible, but that's fine. Tainted Grail is too meandering to be a good rogue-lite, where you can jump in and play a run in 30 to 60 minutes tops. No, a typical run takes anything from 2 to 3 hours. That's just too long. The upgrades in-between suffer from a similar issue then. I at least don't FEEL like playing more of this game, because I think I've basically seen it all. Yes, there are more cards to unlock and maybe some different builds of course ... and higher difficulty modes. But are they worth it after almost 30 hours? Not sure.In this case there is maybe too much. Games like Slay the Spire or Monster Train offer more motivation in that regard imho, because they offer more RNG, but shorter play times for each run. They also offer a better presentation. Nevertheless TG is a good game, especially for its bargain price!It's just not a game I think I'll continue playing to "the end" ("final boss" is a joke).I'm not even sure how to finish the final quest, as what is on the map and what isn't is predetermined in a run. So, you might waste another 3 hours to get nowhere. Upgrading isn't fun anymore either. So yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun deckbuilder, albeit still a very obvious work in progress. The world, mini side-stories, and voice acting are fantastic and the clear shining point of the game. Enemy designs and battle themes are also stellar, even if the quality of the actual enemy battles can be inconsistent. The card-based combat revolves around the typical 3-energy "Slay the Spire" style, and is passable but not particularly innovative. My main issues with the combat are the balance and huge amount of meta-progression. I won my first run pretty easily, and have fully beaten six of the nine runs I've played, with lots of passive abilities seeming very obviously overtuned. There are nine different classes (from 3 class archetypes), and they have interesting and unique differences. While the individual classes keep combat fresh, enemy variety is pretty poor and the final boss (and unlockable, "true" final boss) are very underwhelming.The main hub of the game includes a number of unlockable vendors that have tons of meta-progressing abilities bought with persistent currencies, ranging from things like more health potions to straight up flat damage and max health upgrades. I played for about 12 hours, and was nowhere near to unlocking most of these upgrades, and am not really sure what the point of including such grindy upgrades is in the first place. Overall, if you enjoy the deckbuilding genre I would definitely recommend checking this game out. It's enjoyable, and has a larger emphasis on presentation and story than its contemporaries, but can't quite compete with the top dogs of the genre like Slay the Spire and Monster Train.

_childDocuments_.review: ✔ 9 classes sharing 3 separate decks. Each class is quite different from others and plays differently. On the other hand your class strongly defines how you are going to play, so there are more or less about 9 builds✔ meaningful choices in new cards and passives happen every combat on average ✔ it is possible to make your build completely ineffective by getting wrong cards/runes❔ many different permanent progression currencies - it's interesting that there are so many, but some are very easy to get and others ridiculously hard and grindy. As an example there is one, which improves mechanics of injectable runes, including major drop rates increases, but first you need to drop A LOT of them to get the related currency from combining them. The only thing that makes the system work is another currency, which you get for discovering new content, which can be exchanged to other currencies. I think that 80% of my currency came from that source and that was enough for the game to become too easy. Nevertheless reaching 100% unlocks would be a major grind❔ stories and setting - nothing amazing, but matches very well with the roguelite gameplay✘ in terms of difficulty it starts strong, but becomes easy and then very easy as both your understanding of the mechanics and perma-progression increases. E.g. there is a light mechanic, which forces you to use and manage torches, which are extremely difficult to come by at the beginning. In my last run I had more than enough of them at the last boss to go through the game again without any drops while liberally using them. All of it because of permanent upgrades✘ legendary cards have charges, after which they are gone. This results in making you weaker as long as you hold on to them. It's the old problem of keeping the best consumables for an entire RPG and never using them, but worse✘ NPCs you find have a tendency to disappear after talking to them. Sometimes. So you never know if leaving the dialogue to check your stats/equipment is an option. Will choosing quest progression make them disappear? Probably, who knows?Overall it's good experience when discovering how the classes work, but the game becomes far too easy and repetitive over time. So my advice is to play each class once, defeat the bosses and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Slay the Spire with a pinch of Darkest Dungeon served with a dark fantasy setting based on Arthurian lore. There a ton of classes and each one I've unlocked thus far is mechanically interesting, adds a ton of variety, and provide a great incentive to continue playing and unlock more content. The art and music is great, and this game absolutely worth $20 if you like rogue-lite/deck builders.High points thus far- Your "Wyrdcandle", (very similar mechanically to how torches work in darkest dungeon), can add different cards to your hand each turn and add an incredibly interesting risk/reward mechanic. They have two effects that occur either when played or when they aren't played; typically buffing enemies the turn they're played and then providing you a significant buff afterward. Similarly the boss encounters are well designed and also provide their own unique risk/reward cards depending on your actions in the fight. Drawing one of these cards can completely change the course of the fight and the strategy you're using to deal with it. Very cool. There are layers on layers of mechanics, but everything is well explained and the tool tips are designed very well. You may have to take your time and read over effects/crunch numbers when several cards and buffs are all interacting during a turn but you never feel that you're missing information. This game can be very punishing, but rewards you significantly for utilizing your classes mechanics to their full effectiveness. A bad hand can definitely ruin your day, but if you pay attention and play carefully you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail is hands down the best deck-building rogue-like I have ever played. The world is dark and gritty, the stories are amusing and offer a nice side progression, but most importantly the core game play has been polished to something nearing perfection. (Unsurprisingly for a game that just came out, some bugs exist, but the devs are Extremely Active in the discord, responding to our bug reports.)The game has different classes and variants within those classes, each with their own decks, passives, and ultimates, and this provides a framework for exponential options that each feel stylistically compelling.My one and only real criticism isn't actually with the game itself, but rather the marketing. It is touted as having 9 different classes when in fact is actually has 3, each with 3 archetypes. As you play through the game and unlock something that, mechanically, seems quite similar to something that you already unlocked (and even shares the same starting cards) this can feel like a bit of a letdown as you find less options than what you were expecting to find.Speaking to the game's progression, it has been handled very intelligently in a way that adds to the experience without feeling like you are engaged in a grind.Not only do you unlock new characters and cards, but you also rescue NPCs who then work in your village and can each be upgraded with their respective resources. When I initially realized the large number of different resources I was worried, but they are implemented in a completely streamlined manner that requires no managing on your part. The resources are garnered passively through standard gameplay, and can be used to increase the potency and quality of life of your subsequent runs.Lastly, there are cosmetics that automatically unlock, and I am a real sucker for playing dressup. The character customization aspect, while still somewhat sparse, again feels stylistically compelling and reinforces the world that you are entering into.Over the course of about two weeks I have spent 55 hours playing this game, so I can definitely say that I heartily recommend it and am looking forward to further expansions.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game! I'm on lvl6 difficulty so not late game but beyond early game now. Beaten it with one of each of the main classes.The aesthetics are superior to any deck builder I've ever played. The grim diabloesque style works really well here. The progression system is a lot more engaging here than in other similar games since you're slowly building you village. Also, there is actual voice acting which makes the game feel more involved. Overall look and feel of the game is top notch!Gameplay itself is also fantastic! The classes feel varied enough to make it interesting and among the 3 mains classes are 3 subclasses each with their own nuances. I've played my fair share of card games, rogue-likes, and deckbuilders and I'd say in terms of fun I rank this one pretty high. I definately prefer it to Griftlands which is actually the game which got me into this genre. This game isn't without its faults though. One thing I dislike is that a typical run in this game takes over 2 hours. As a rogue-like I don't want my runs to take that long, especially in later difficulties where I suspect you will die a lot. Also, there seem to be far too many cards that are utterly useless or simply worse versions of other cards. This results in a lot of skips for card selection which means my deck feels almost the same at the end as it was in the beginning of my run. Also, my decks seem to always end up the exact same every run. Another aspect I don't really like is how the damage dealt is in a min-max range. Part of the appeal of card games is the precision of planning a deck and executing a specific plan per turn. This can be very difficult to do if you don't know if you're going to be able to finish off an enemy or not. It just adds a layer of RNG that doesn't play into the game well and the devs didn't really implement into the game in a meaningful way. Overall I really enjoy the game and appreciate what the devs made here. You can really feel the production value and the art style and progression system are fantastic. From a deck-building gameplay purist perspective, I will say there are some redundancies that make it less fun than something like slay the spire but still way better than something like the negotiation rounds of Griftlands (bleh). In the end, if you like deck-builders, you should definitely try it out! If you never tried any deckbuilders before, this should serve to be a great segway into them since it has the feel of traditional rpg. 8/10 from me!
