_childDocuments_.review: I've bought the game to have my own opinion about it. It costs about 17€ but I've spent 3,30€ on discount and I somehow still feel robbed. I'm not gonna make comparisons with Hollow Knight since it wouldn't be fair, but I have to say this title is as hollow as fried air. From the top of my head (gonna edit with other points while going for the other ending):Avoiding focusing on the plain issues with the main menu (new commands that get overwritten by the default ones as one replays the game; some options that lack sfx; simply uncomfy to navigate in; video settings that just sets the window size), there is no content whatsoever: uninteresting rooms (you cannot be serious to goodness to make the player walk a linear map TO MAKE THEM GO BACK JUST TO HAVE A BUNCH OF MORE ENEMIES THERE. This is NOT level design, let alone a metroidvania!), broken enemies, no story (let's be real: nothing transpires in the playthrough: there is no pathos in the bosses you defeat, they have no personality, many just have the same sprite), unclear and broken mechanics (istg it just praises tanking, it asks no wits from the players. also, losing life for just moving and double jumping is such a bs when you're just going for the other room, im serious), no replayability, ... there is nothing one would enjoy playing it, let alone to justify the prize (the first playthrough can take at most 2 hours. AT MOST, for 17€).Forgot to say it but: another thing, however minor, is how, for instance, when one defeats a boss, you are stuck in place for up to 3/4 seconds with no animation that hints you're stuck (so ig that's a bug).There are other things that, however minor, show the game was not tested and, hence, nobody cared to get the best game for a better experience like:1. how tf can room transitions last so little? And the up-down transitions are so short one can just go back to the previous room because the player has to move to the ledge.2. Also, when the game is in background, somehow it still registers the inputs (I play with the keyboard and even when editing this review I hear the game sfx doing things while I'm just tiping here).3. Also there are no i-frames after getting hit.4. The dark swords' attack (basically hk's greatslash) lags the game so much when hitting an enemy.5. When falling down, the camera cannot keep up with the player's fall acceleration. This means that the majority of times a player can fall onto an enemy or an environmental hazard and keep going down and down, getting more and more damage.6. enemies can clip in the environmental walls and floors. it's especially frequent in the last bossfight (bad ending) and some enemies such as "the airplane" ones and the "jump to pierce" ones (who played the game knows which i mean)7. very very minor but: the enemies that crawl around the platforms just straightly shift when they get to a surface of a different angle. there is no smooth animation for it. while its very very minor, its still an eyesore8. the "melt n spikes" enemies can melt and slide in midair9. checkpoints literally in screen trasitions? like, come on!10. about transitions: some, everytime single time, they play a noise, like a "locking/closing door" sfx11. ambience music changes between area transition very  clearly12. the credit music doesnt even last for the whole credit scene, The only ups may be the artstyle (that is still not justified lore-wise, has nothing interesting gameplay-wise and at times makes the navigation really confusing, since one can't tell what's in background and in foreground and what can be broken due to no consistency in the room level design) and the bossfight song (which is seriously the only think I enjoyed, even if it doesn't fit with action scenes at all).I've yet to do the good ending but I did the bad ending and  This just tells me that Gleamlight tries to be alternative for the sake of being alternative, without the effort of being it.When I have the will to check the true ending, I'm gonna update the review.But one thing I have to say regardless is: developers please, , get your game tested before release and after major and even minor changes, please please please.P.S.: ah yea and credits are unskippable, why? also i cannot believe so many people were involved in the localization like dude, what was there to localize? the achievements and the main menu? so much written content /s

_childDocuments_.review: Gleamlight is a silent game. No one talks to you, the game itself does not tell you anything. But learning the mechanics comes with easy after exploring a bit and there is great forgiveness with the death system. And neither does "delete".While the music was beautiful maybe more tracks could have helped the game, but honestly, after finding the ending and the True Ending, I am left with satisfaction.This is not a rip off. Gleamlight is its own game, its own story, and definitely its own mechanics. I will definitely revisit it in the future to get the rest of the achievements.Thank you so much for creating this experience!

_childDocuments_.review: It looks like a metroidvania, it plays like a metroidvania, it WANTS to be a metroidvania… but it is not a metroidvania.It is a strange game. From the fact that you gain new abilities from defeating bosses to the dungeon-style levels where you have to find the glorified red button (over and over again) to open doors, it seems to me that the devs had a metroidvania in mind but didn’t understand the key elements that make these games fun; exploration, progression and new abilities. The combat is the cardinal sin; surely one of the blandest, most boring button-smashing games you can find, your character doesn’t do anything but monotonously swing his sword; there’s no combos, no jump and smash attack, no shield to defend yourself, no ranged attack and not even a health bar!Truly, it feels unfinished. The art is good, the name is catchy and some of the movement abilities you gain later on (by the point everyone NOT achievement-hunting has already stopped playing the damn game) are kind of fun, but its repetitive nature and uninspired combat don’t do it justice.I guess I’ll go for the achievements and forget about ever playing the game. Too bad.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I recommend this gameI'm not sure why this game has mostly negative reviews. I think it's a pretty good game, and I would definitely recommend it to other players.I found Gleamlight because of a YouTube video that was saying NOT to call many games (Gleamlight included) Hollow Knight ripoffs, and I decided to take a look at Gleamlight because the art style caught my eye.The art style is beautiful, and I love the stained glass theme that the developers used. I like when the enemies die, they shatter into pieces.Also the use of color to indicate health is a great touch, and I love the fact that it was added so a UI wouldn't be needed. Without a UI in the way, you as the player are able to better immerse yourself into the story and the combatThe combat is great most of the time. The life steal mechanic makes bosses a nice challenge, and adds a nice way to remove item drops. I do find some enemies particularly annoying to fight, but that is most likely just a lack of skill on my part.Also, I can tell this game is meant to be played through more than once. If you play through the game one and only one time, you will miss out on a fair amount of what Gleamlight has to offer.

_childDocuments_.review: Sad to add to the not recommending list, but it really isn't fun to play. It's beautiful, albeit lacking in variety in both enemy and area design. It's not even a Metroidvania as you'd anticipate seeing it, it's very linear and they reuse the majority of it for the various endings. There's only a few areas added to these subsequent playthroughs and sometimes that's nothing, one of the required things to do is run through the game backwards for another ending/boss. It had some neat ideas to deliver the endings, but it just needed more effort. You even unlock a gravity power that shifts the gravity for you but it breaks if you get hit. Instead of that they should've designed it like Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. That level design was stellar when you get to the inverted castle. Nothing in this game requires any effort. Even the jumping is mostly bog standard fluff. There are maybe 2-3 jumps that require any level of "skill" (thought). And that amounts to dropping off a platform, falling below a wall, dashing and then double jumping for required progression. That's the most complex section of platforming in the *entire* game. And on subsequent playthroughs you don't need to do it lol.The subsequent playthroughs also involve reused bosses which are tedious (mostly the flying one). As well as adding really beefy crystals that you have to break to progress each room on the first playthrough they break in 1 hit and it's simple. In the last playthrough (two save deletes later) it takes 3 or 4 hits and it's incredibly annoying. You can use the charged attack as well but it's annoying since it can't be stored properly and loses the charge if you don't use it right away which makes timing so annoying that I barely wanted to use it other than on bosses. You regain HP as you attack and so do enemies so the flying boss is a big tedious battle most of the time as you both chip away at each other while recovering. Just back and forth constantly. Annoying boss. The main questline bosses are all kind of lame tbh.It's very disappointing how shallow of an experience this really is because it could have been a gem. It's just not worth the time and I played through twice on PS4 and PC now. (I bought it on PS thinking it was Unbound for some reason) The time playing after this review will be for the remaining two trading cards and I can't wait to delete this and hopefully forget it.

However, i consider this part of the story. Art style is glassy, christalline and eerie. An entire world made of stained glass, while the enemies pack a punch.There isn't any text in the game. No one talks.A small spoiler for a neat mechanic that might confuse you when it happens:All in all, it's an alright game. If you can, the game can be beaten in an hour or 2. I'd give it a 4/10Hope you'll enjoy the game

_childDocuments_.review:
This is a story of light - of Gleam, in a world of glass stained in darkness.

Welcome to Gleamlight – a 2D action game that will take you through an adventure traversing a beautiful, transient world.

Immerse yourself amid the beautiful stained glass artistry as you navigate without the reliance of any standard game UI, while tracing the world’s mysterious unspoken story.
What will you, as Gleam, sense and feel through your travels across this beautiful, yet fearsome world of glass?

◆A World Made of Glass
The world beautifully unfurls before you with lush trees, boulders of all sizes, and various paraphernalia, all in the form and shape of glass. Prepare to explore this fantastical world where light warms the glass and darkness stains it with bitter cold.

◆A Game Without UI
The game has been designed to immerse players into the world and story without being obstructed by any standard game UI, allowing players to organically enjoy the action and tension of defeating enemies and traversing the world.

◆An Unspoken Story
The story behind what happened in this world, and what is to come is up to you as the player. Discover and piece together the story through your adventure, and save this beautiful, transient world of glass.

name: A Space for the Unbound
detailed_description: High school is ending and the world is ending with it A Space for the Unbound is a slice-of-life adventure game with beautiful pixel art set in the late 90s rural Indonesia that tells a story about overcoming anxiety, depression, and the relationship between a boy and a girl with supernatural powers. Follow two high school sweethearts, Atma and Raya, on a journey of self-discovery at the end of their high school years. When a mysteriously supernatural power is suddenly unleashed threatening their existence, they must explore and investigate their town to uncover hidden secrets, face the end of the world, and perhaps learn more about each other. Set in a small town inspired by 90s era rural Indonesia, A Space for the Unbound presents an endearing story-driven experience with a vibrant environment waiting to be explored. Key Features Throwback to the 90s! Let us take you to Indonesia in the late 90s. Explore rural Indonesia and enjoy its relaxing atmosphere with a hint of supernatural events. Chat and interact with other townfolks and listen to their personal stories. Dive into people's minds Inception-style. Listen to beautiful music composed by Masdito 'Ittou' Bachtiar

_childDocuments_.review: I'd feel wrong to not recommend this because it *really* sticks its ending in a very thoughtful way to re-contextualise its story. However the game does falter in its length and some of its puzzles just being frustrating rather than interesting, especially when its drawing to a conclusion and hurling these at you to yank you back from progressing towards resolution. This is a beautiful story that could have been told in a game half its length with just as much characterisation and a lot less padding and running around aimlessly. Don't be afraid to make shorter games!

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely incredible game. A moving story of incredible depth combined with fantastic artwork, puzzles that were just the right level of challenge for me, and extremely enjoyable gameplay/combat mechanics. An excellent reminder that all *good* fantasy is really just an exploration of what it is to be human and the struggles and triumphs of ordinary life. And that's what this game is---a triumph. I really can't recommend it enough to anyone looking for a game that will affect you and stick with you well afterwards (recognizing of course that not everyone is).

_childDocuments_.review: You can read my other reviews Video review: What at first glance starts out as a touching title that smells like the 90’s, evolves into a story with dark contours mixed with supernatural powers, which addresses the lives of two teenagers with a strong connection, in a city located in Indonesia.A Space for the Unbound produced by Mojiken studios, suddenly appeared on my Twitter timeline and I immediately wanted to understand what it was about. Set on a screen full of pixels, surrounded by a touching soundtrack and small notes in cutscene with anime contours, it tells the story of a boy, named Atma, who like most teenagers, although without major concerns about the subject, is trying to figure out what he wants to do with his future after finishing high school. Raya, his girlfriend, on the other hand, is quite methodical and decides to make a bucket list of activities to do with him. On that list are activities like going to the movies, having a party and inviting all of their friends, among others, which serve as a backdrop for the timeline of the denouement full of mishaps of this adventure.Suddenly Atma finds himself wrapped in a mist that mixes dream with reality and discovers that he has a mysterious supernatural power. With the help of a red book he manages to delve into the minds of people disturbed by traumas in order to help them overcome that less positive moment. This “Spacedive” ability will be one of the most defining mechanics throughout this title. Raya also has powers, albeit quite different. Raya can change reality, transport herself to other places or, for example, levitate objects and even people.All of this sounds very interesting, until it gets to the point where the powers used by Raya begin to affect not only her, but the entire city. The inhabitants begin to behave strangely, certain locations seem to have some kind of glitch alternating between parallel realities and even a rift begins to open in the sky of this peculiar location. Is this real life or just a dream? Atma will be the crucial point in answering all these questions, while trying to keep everything around from collapsing.While the story becomes interesting as time goes by, its gameplay begins to gain somewhat repetitive contours between activities. In the end, the gameplay involves a lot of exploration, going through elements of a visual novel and small moments where it is necessary to click on the right keys at the right times. The main “problem” here is the fact that there are quite a few moments of exploration separated between running from one side of the city to the other where the main objective is the search for the necessary elements to overcome the presented problems. While on paper this is an interesting idea, it is rather tedious to go from screen to screen as an errand boy. There are positive moments during this rush, characters to meet, cats to pet and name, bottle caps to collect, among others, but the feeling of boredom is still very present, especially in Chapter 3 which is by far the slowest in its development.It never becomes a difficult game, there is no learning path or anything like that. Except for small sections that can become somewhat frustrating largely because of the collision area that the character presents in moments of finger dexterity, such as when there are objects falling from the sky. The controls are super responsive, even when it takes a double click to get Atma to start its fastest march.Being a linear story, it is unlikely that you will skim this adventure a second time. It is still possible to miss some secondary objectives. As previously mentioned there is a list of activities with some secondary activities. That said, and for hardcore players, there are also secrets and achievements that are harder to unlock.A Space for the Unbound presents a very interesting teen drama story that somehow manages to warm even the coldest of hearts. The attention to detail of Culture Pop, the construction of an interesting city with engaging characters make this title a winning bet for the kick-off in this year’s Indie games calendar.

_childDocuments_.review: Growing up can be really difficult. Children have very little control over their situation, and many are at the mercy of abusive family or socioeconomic factors outside of their control. I was horribly depressed all throughout elementary school and there really wasn't much I could do except pick up all the pieces and rebuild everything once I was free from domestic violence. Much later my siblings and I struggled to help my mom through a bout of depression and we weren't very successful, but it was very clear my mother's problems stemmed from things early in her life.A Space for the Unbound does a really good job capturing both these angles of depression: a person afflicted with a crippling range of emotions and a confused, caring loved one who just wants to help. It's a tempestuous Bildungsroman, where happy slices of life collide with horrible events building up to a beautiful close, both narratively and pixel art graphically. The final boss battle is probably my favorite in (non-action) adventure game history, and I cried so much that I need time to process things before I finish the epilogue chapter.This can probably be finished in 8 hours, but you'll be playing for around 12 if you're trying to complete all achievements. I actually missed petting four of the animals, so I cheated and edited the save file. Work smarter not harder ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: Exceptional. Having previously played and enjoyed games published by Toge Productions such as Coffee Talk, When The Past Was Around and to a lesser extent She and The Light Bearer, I knew beforehand this game was going to go for the feels factor so my expectations were quite high and thus wanted to wait for full release and not dive into the prologue demo. Oh did it deliver!The gorgeous pixel art was a standout of the game and instantly drew my attention, the love and care that went into creating the scenes throughout is truly sublime. The music was fantastic which I expected since I loved the music in When The Past Was Around and Masdito Bachtiar knocked it out of the park once again, rarely do games make me search them up on Spotify/YouTube to listen outside of the game. Especially with the Arcade mini-game song, now that is a JAM. Made it 1000% more bearable going for that high-score achievement haha!The story was a highlight, it was enjoyable and definitely tries to tug at your heartstrings but it did suffer pacing from the puzzles the game threw at you, albeit easy they did make you do a fair bit of them and there was some sidetracking having to be done which can be a slog, other than that it was good. The characters, although I didn't connect with them as much as I did with the characters in Coffee Talk, were not bad either, there were some dialogue moments between them that were a bit iffy at times but I am going to chalk that up to them translating from Indonesian to English and honestly at the end of the day it doesn't detract from the narrative as a whole being great.The game has a few points of no return which they explicitly warn you of, so if you miss a few collectables then you may miss out on some achievements and have to re-do sections of the game (or restart entirely if you didn't save a bunch) as is what happened to me, but my achievement hunting nature isn't going to dampen the monumental praise I have for this game! Mojiken and Toge Productions have created a gem, hopefully they've made the Indonesian Game Dev scene proud as they have in my opinion created an Indie Game of the Year contender for 2023!Also this game has cats. A LOT of cats. So it has my vote already :)
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: The game is a vehicle to tell this beautiful story.The major attractions here are the story, pixel art, and the music which create a enchanting experience. I won't discuss the story because I think you should experience it blind.The game play is pretty simple and only exists to tell the story. Most of the game play is point and click puzzle solving, but they do sneak in a few cool references like street fighter and ace attorney. If you are not a fan of dialogue heavy narratives, then this game isn't for you.I love this game. I think it's charming, well written, and I love the whole experience. I wish more games were like this. They have a demo of the prologue you can try out and see if you enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is more than a game; it's an emotional journey. From the moment I played the demo, I knew it was something special. Now that I've completed it, I'm more certain than ever. I couldn't even describe the extent to which this game resonates with me and how much I can relate do Raya in almost all aspects of her character. I cried nonstop at the end, and I know that I won't forget the experience I had while playing - it was perfect, coming at a time when needed the most, when I needed to feel understood and empowered to overcome a bunch of stuff that was holding me back.I really recommend A Space for the Unbound to everyone who wants to be touched by a great story, incredible characters and beautiful art. _childDocuments_.review: Honest review of the game. Pros:+ The promotional art and pixel art are both top tier level, they're very beautiful!+ The game itself is very cozy and atmospheric.+ The soundtracks weren't bad, but I also don't remember many of them except the 'Chasing Truth' it was very unique since you could hear the gamelan instrument in it+ If you live in Indonesia, you'll find some familiar references here and there! Could even bring some nostalgia to the 90s setting!+ Some supporting characters in this game have bittersweet backstories. Some are very motivational too.+ CATS !!! Cons :- The game has too many irrelevant fetch quests to proceed with the main story and it's eating too much time. (I got bored of this mechanic and stopped the game for a while)- Atma's sprint is very slow... sometimes I run to the very corner of the area only to find nothing, but I just had to check every corner of the map to see if I missed bottle caps or stray cats haha. (sometimes I wish there were teleport points in this game lol)- The map was really confusing, I know it's a 2D side scroll game but I still couldn't get used to it even until the end.- The main story was really confusing at the first 2 chapters.- Got stuck at some puzzles because of stupid reasons... like that one time when I have used the coin string on telephone once and it was gone from my inventory so I thought it was gone for good but turns out I could still use the public telephone again.- The Bahasa language used in this game was quite stiff and bit hard to understand, it also sounded very formal. In the end I switched to English. Overall I'd give this game 7/10, I recommended this game to my college and online friends from another country especially to those who are curious about our culture.

_childDocuments_.review: Got the game code given by Toge Productions and as of this review I am 5 hours in the game and reached the start of Chapter 3! I will try to go into as much details as I can about the game overall and being as vague and spoiler free as I can below.Let’s get into details shall we.GAMEPLAY 5/5 :The game goes as a typical Side scroller exploration game, with some minigames and puzzle solving in between. I would say the game is quite accessible for anyone. Also, the game has Controller support and so far it works really fine, and I always play games like this using a controller because it just feels right. STORY AT MY CURRENT PROGRESS 4/5:I think the storytelling in the game starts slightly slow and maybe confusing and even at this point I am still left with much more questions than answers, and at the current point that I am right now the story is getting good and it piques my interest to keep playing I might edit the review once I get to finish the game soon. VISUAL/GRAPHICS 5/5:I would say the visuals is very stunning what you see in the trailer is literally what you are going to get, I’ve always been a fan of retro styled games. What I think is unique they captured the feeling that you are really in a rural Indonesia. Living in Indonesia myself I feel the visual they did is really represented well, and I got quite immersed in a lot of the stuff they are trying to put into the game. As I see it, a lot of love and care was put into the visuals.TRANSLATION 3.5/5:Now you might be wondering why the translation is 3.5 despite giving most of the other category bigger scores before you get your pitchforks here is what I think. Bear in mind I played the game in English, and my gripe is some of the words they are using, and sentences feels weird in a way that it didn’t feel natural to me. Knowing that Mojiken is a studio based in Indonesia maybe the script is in Indonesian and then translated to English and I felt some of the translation feels a bit Raw and can be refined just a little bit to fit the English language better. TBF at least the message they are trying to convey at least get across to me, and it’s still bearable to play but its just that lingering feeling that it might can be refined better to feel a bit natural.WRITING 5/5: I would say the writing is good and despite the translation issue I think they did such an amazing job of the dialogue and got me really immersed in the characters and story. Even side characters in the world are also interesting in a way so that I got to feel like I am living inside of the story and not just a spectator. Immersion is the keyword here and they got it!OVERALL 4.5/5:The game is a love letter to Indonesia, and a good one at that. There was a lot of love and care throughout this project, and it shows. I think Anyone looking for a game with really interesting story and a interesting cast of characters. This will be the game for you!If you read all that thank you so much! Hope this review actually help you out if you are on the fence in getting the game

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is an adventure game set in rural 1990’s Indonesia. It features a poignant narrative that focuses on mental health, whilst weaving in slice-of-life style gameplay. Despite beginning development in 2015, the developers’ hard work has clearly paid off. With a unique setting, quality story, art and puzzles, this is a memorable title that is sure to tug on players heartstrings.Set in rural 1990’s Indonesia, players follow Atma and Raya. The pair are near their graduation of High School and must start preparing for their futures. The story begins as a cozy adventure, exploring their small town of Loka City. Suddenly, a supernatural force seems to ruin it all, inserting itself into the lovers’ lives and breaking up the tranquil atmosphere.  The two must further explore the deep rooted cause of this phantasmal occurrence and uncover not only its secrets, but also their own. Despite this wholesome beginning, and without spoilers, the narrative deeply explores the harshness of anxiety and depression, slowly delving into the human psyche, whilst simultaneously being a journey of self-discovery and maintaining its slice-of-life atmosphere.A Space for the Unbound’s narrative is a tangled one, but it surprisingly manages to uncoil its many branches. With many aspects to piece together and many timelines, rifts and characters to remember, it would be easy to fall victim to its convolution. However, the narrative is conveyed clearly, often repeating titbits of important information over time to allow players to gain a solid grasp on the many happenings. None of this felt like over-exaggeration, hand-holding or patronising, but rather, it all blended effortlessly, creating a fantastic foundation to tell its poignant story. Overall, the narrative was not at all what I expected, and the game completely changes into what felt like a different game than in the early chapters. The characters are expertly written and over time, I felt empathetic towards them. Their hardship, their past experiences, it all felt vivid and realistic. Given the games’ length, they all experience great development and growth, allowing players to better understand them. This game has an abundance of reading. Similar to a visual novel, but it does feature large chunks of gameplay through puzzles, mini-games and exploration. Atma also has the skill to be able to “spacedive,” meaning he can see the inner thoughts and stresses about characters he meets. These are usually interwoven with puzzles and further complicated by entering different timelines or “rifts.” You can also pet all of the animals in the game. Really, its also for an achievement! Pet every stray cat you come across, even dogs and ducks. What more could you want! There are a total of five chapters, but the difficulty of the puzzles ramps up after chapter 4. I was not necessarily a fan of this, and did need to resort to a guide for some things (that cursed mathematics equation!)Despite the large amount of dialogue, the gameplay is also engaging, and manages to create an enjoyable flow from start to finish through its many mini-games. The most common are quick-time events involving the precise and timed copying of select keys, or pressing a button when the moving cursor in a bar is green. This is how fighting transpires in the game, or the Future Fighter arcade game. At first, I enjoyed this arcade section, but for an achievement/optional side extra in the game, you must reach 1500 and 1700 points. Only gaining 100 points per battle, and with no extra lives, it is a slog to reach 1700 and the window of opportunity is very slim. Admittedly, I tried many times to achieve this, but that high score has still evaded me (one day… one day).Other common mini-games include stealth sections. These are extremely simple and just involve staying still when an exclamation mark pops up. Bounce a ball with precision timing 70 times, answer quizzes or choose to do the extras and fulfil Raya’s bucket list. The mini-games inclusion helps solidify the cozy nature of the game, and accentuates its wholesome atmosphere (but only in early chapters).For the most part, puzzles are decent. Most are inventory-based, involving searching through different timelines to retrieve items for a spacedive of a character in another timeline, etc. Collect evidence to convey in court, match up the cake to the description…. And complete a confusing mathematical equation. OK, the latter was not so great. Yes, maths is not my strong suit. But I have never come across such a solely mathematical puzzle in a game before. You must search the areas to find multiple hints to the equation such as N=1 (none of these examples are the actual formula) to solve multiple disjointed equations such as 14=2x+n or 4-7n=-1. There are MULTIPLE of these and fair to say, I had no idea what I am doing. There was no find x, or explanation. Just these varying formulas scattered everywhere that apparently led to a code. I appreciate the difference and complexity, but without a guide, I would have been stuck for an eternity.Despite there being only five chapters, these chapters are very lengthy with enormous amounts of content to uncover. Some extra content and achievements are locked to specific chapters. I was not aware of this and always thought I could come back to parts of the town to complete them. Unfortunately, you cannot, and there is no chapter select (but there are manual save slots). Furthermore, I had apparently missed two of the cats to pet and it would be nice to see these added in on the map in a Newgame+ or underneath the chapter they were missed in.The hand-drawn soft pixel art is stunning, and reminiscent of anime styles. It perfectly fits in with the 90s setting the game covers and there are many beautiful, pastel backdrops to screenshot in vibrant Loka City. The characters are not voiced, but the backing audio is playful and retro-inspired. It fits well with the themes of the game, and the finale song is sure to create an emotive response.  Approx 10.5 hours Yes Not really.. there are achievements but going back for these without a chapter select (and if you did not manually save each chapter) can be a pain, as it is a linear story and there is no auto text skip.A Space for the Unbound is a unique game. Its chirpy pixel artstyle, cozy mini-games and many cats to pet give the impression it is a flippant game, but this is not an accurate description. It is heavily symbolic and covers a journey of self-discovery and overcoming mental illnesses. A wonderful and eye-opening experience with an abundance of content to explore, well worth its full price tag of $AU30.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is an adventure game with an exceptionally strong narrative and pixel art developed by an Indonesian team. Experience 90's rural Indonesia, as both high school and the world ends while two individuals uncover mysterious powers among themselves and deal with themes such as abuse, bullying, loss, heartbreak, and anxiety about growing up and not knowing who you want to be.Relationships! Trauma! Repairing and/or making peace with them and moving on! You play as Atma, a teenager that has the ability to dive into people and help them make peace with their troubles. Also your girlfriend seems to have her own thing going on; what's up with her? How is she? Why is she? How and Why are you? You remember what happened yesterday, right?Backgrounds range from pretty to jawdroppingly immaculate. From beautiful vistas to dilapidated buildings, it's super apparent a lot of love and personality was put into the art direction in every single area. Loka City is dripping with a sense of homeyness about it. I've never been to Indonesia in my life, and yet the game managed to instill this sense of nostalgia in me for it.The story in this game completely moved in a way that no other game ever has. It had me feeling emotions all over the place, had me shed a tear here and there, and maybe broke me into pieces and reassembled me a few times. I haven't experienced anything as impressive as this in a really, really long time.I'm so unbelievably happy I was able to experience this story during my lifetime, and, if you play it, I hope you feel the same way. This is an incredible masterpiece of a coming-of-age story. play this game. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was fooled by the overwhelmingly positive reviews.  I should have read the few negative ones.The art is serviceable and the sound is OK (I can't remember the music.)How shall I explain the first 30 minutes.It's an story with some interactive element in it.I was so much crushed by the complete void of anything interesting to do that I was gasping for air, drowned in boredom.The character moves incredibly slowly by default, you have to double tap a direction to make him move at an acceptable pace.Most of what he can do is to "speak" to people, pet a cat and do "puzzles" a.k.a interacting with whatever is on screen. (Yes, that one will not tire your brain.)After finishing the prologue, I'm pretty sure I got the gist of what it will be about : a tragedy.  The hints aren't exactly subtle. I've played a bit further because, being impervious to sob stories, I was still hoping for something interesting to do.I had to give up and cut my losses, my time pointlessly wasted.Reading the reviews, I believe people who recommended this like it solely for the obviously depressing story and the feelings it gave them. (The are comments about tears.)  To each his own.  This is absolutely not for me.If you want tears, just watch Grave of the Fireflies : it's a guarantee and you'll not have to mindlessly touch a gamepad to progress the story.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice and well-written game whose premise has been seen before and you can make out in the prologue, but it's still handled very well. A typical adventure game fare of doing things in the right order with specific items, but the story and its pacing is the driving force to completion and the world(s) is(/are) charming that it's a nice escape into modern era Indonesia with very well done music. The art direction itself as well as the subtle detailing within the pixel art with animations and impacts add nice touches of life which can look very simplified even for pixel art at points but enough detail is there to place emphasis on the emotional points of the game that the game shines from.It can take until the second or third chapter for things to start rolling, especially if you're aware of the type of 'game based on depression and anxiety in a cutesy aesthetic' genre of adventure games, but it's a charming and well-written indie title that's worth a playthrough or two.At the point of whether you'd want to play it would come down to how well you like slice-of-life, supernatural vibe-y adventure games before the story can hook you in.

It's all wrapped up in a gorgeous, hand-drawn art style that feels like a cozy hug.But what really shines is the story. It's like a coming-of-age movie, with all the feels. You'll laugh, you'll cry, and you'll root for these characters like they're your best friends.Overall, This game is a beautiful game that's perfect for a rainy day or when you just need a pick-me-up. It's a reminder that, sometimes, the most magical adventures can be found in the simplest of places.

_childDocuments_.review: Good art, good music, great story.The mix of light adventure game puzzles and a bit of timed inputs keeps you engaged while the mystery keeps getting bigger. Sometimes you need to beat up school bullies, sometimes you play ace attorney, sometimes you sneak through someones mind - the variety is great. Supported by fleshed out characters, lots of cats to pet - the gameplay loops here fit together tightly. Exploring the city in every chapter let's you see changes and gives a feeling of knowing the place. The worst thing about the game is maybe the action sequence at the end - the controls and character animations aren't made for an action game.The english translation is well written and the story really brought a tear to my eye in the end... I appreciate most that it's not super obvious what the angle is from the start.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game. The graphical style is enchanting, the story is interesting, the final twist (no spoilers!) is unusual and nice, the foreign (to me) Indonesian culture is fascinating (maybe it would be better to show even more of the culture, Indonesia is definitely underrepresented in games), and the gameplay provides some diversity and does not distract from the story. That's the good things, and I honestly recommend this game (I did finish it, the playtime has been logged incorrectly from my steam deck).On the other hand, this game is so... childish, for lack of a better word. It's probably a design choice, as the game is meant to represent the events from the point of view of a troubled teenager, but still... I feel that the heavy topics that the game touches are not really treated well; the heroine has a lot of serious problems, the whole game is an exposition of these problems... and then suddenly we are shown that all problems have been magically solved, the heroine is recovering, and all is well. I can't articulate it well enough, but I do have a feeling that something is missing in the game's treatment of its own topics.In any case -- great game, please play it and decide for yourself!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Come for the unique 80s Indonesian setting, stay for the feels. And OMG the feels, like WTF am I crying... AGAIN?Hopefully without spoiling the game, let me wholeheartedly recommend Space for the Unbound. This is first and foremost a very well written and poignant story. A story about growing up; there's school, and friendship, and trauma, and fear, and regret, and courage and... everything. Some parts WILL hit hard, especially if you're from SEA and grew up in the 80s. The prolonged narrative tension followed by the catharsis of the ending is *muak* (chef's kiss).Gameplay wise its very chill, mostly RPG puzzles with very lenient timing/reflex based 'combat'. All of this frees up your attention to be immersed in the characters' stories and taking stock of the beautifully crafted environment. This is a 11/10 narrative experience not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: 11.3h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (18 achievements). No. is a sidescroller adventure game about a high school girl and boy in the 90s era. Set in Indonesia, it tries to depict a rural region as closely as possible with some fantasies mixed in it.- Gorgeous art with a lot of new, close-up scenes in each chapter- Various minigames- Some sections are dragged out for too longIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650Games with pixel art are usually depicted as low-budget games with a lot of limited and reused images. Well, the same can't be said for . It will show a fresh cutscene detailing a close-up look at the characters during the story most of the time, sometimes with simple animations that follow. The animation gives so much life to the characters that it even feels odd when there is none.The game always tries to break your perception of a 2D game - it uses a lot of parallax techniques to make the sky look alive or even make it so that the camera seems as if it was distorted to show you a vision from a different angle. I can't imagine how many times my mind was blown away by the artwork shown in the game.The story is not linear. It uses a storytelling type where you are given the facts bit by bit, and you need to reconstruct what really happened from them. A lot of symbolism will be used to tie the story with the in-game one made by one of the characters. Despite the fantasy theme, what the character experienced is not that far from what people might experience in real life, especially in that era.Honestly, describing the story here will just ruin your experience if you haven't played it. Without giving much about it, it's a story of encouragement, telling how you need to keep going even though everything is tough. Some dialogues might be convoluted, but there are a lot of subtle messages given by the time you reach the end. And that's when everything gets emotional. The build-up for it is very long and can be boring to some people though, especially since some sections can be dragged out for too long. Most of the game's gameplay revolves around quests. You'll need to take them and do what they say, traveling between locations to finish it. And then you take the next quest. Some will require you to , a technique to go inside people's minds to solve their problems. This gameplay is usually mixed with a bit of puzzle element where you either need to bring some items or solve some lock combinations based on some hints.You'll travel between places and interact with objects. The sidescroller format works well in this regard since it makes it easier to find items. Some objects might look useless at first, but the ones that are marked in yellow tend to be important, whether it's now or later. The exit of an area blends so well with the environment. Each area is designed just like any other rural village, with some empty spaces at the intersections. I always changed screens by instinct, thinking that I might just move my character a little bit to the north when I did that. Sometimes, I even forgot that it's a sidescroller game. That's just how great the design is.It seems to derive its minigames from some games, albeit simplified. The most noticeable one is the -like gameplay where you need to do an objection to someone's statement. Another one is a rhythm one similar to  where you need to press a bunch of keyboard keys within a certain amount of time, except that this one is to fight other people instead to dance. Those two, the QTE one where you need to press a button when a moving pointer is on the green color, and the stealth sections are the most commonly used, but there are also other smaller minigames for you to play. The game tends to drag out some things, though. The fighting gameplay tends to be reused a lot—you need to do this so many times in the final boss. The boss was easy to beat, but the lengthy fight just tires me out. Moreover, it also tries to prolong some cutscenes to no end. I understand that the cutscenes look great, but I don't want to wait for 5+ minutes just to see a scene of someone floating in the sky. Some cutscenes also tend to be reused—not that I had an issue with it, but it can take quite a long time to finish and is unskippable. All of it just numbs my brain and breaks my immersion at times.I finished the game in 11.3h. The game isn't difficult to beat—the time-based minigame might give issues to some people, but the game is quite forgiving of mistakes. Also, there is no chapter selection, so it can take a long time to redo the game again if you miss any achievements—you can't fast-forward any scenes!With its gorgeous pixel art and animation,  will blow your mind with its presentation. It also touches on some heavy topics about life, with some mysteries mixed in them. It'll try to drag you slowly to the game, to make you in love with its characters. Some parts might look dragged out, but it won't completely detract you from enjoying the story as long as you manage to get through to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a game with good storytelling and whimsical, bittersweet themes, A Space for the Unbound could be appropriate. Gameplay is not particularly original, and there are very few parts that could be qualified as "challenging": It's more of a mellow experience, and the main focus is the story. If you are looking for a more challenging point-and-click adventure, stuff like Machinarium or the Phoenix Wright series might be more up your alley.Still, the storytelling is delicate and touching, and the aesthetics are definitely interesting: Probably designed by/for someone that was young in the nineties, sometimes it plays lightly on nostalgia. It is still somehow has a unique flavor, at least for people like me who are not familiar with Indonesian culture.I enjoyed it enough to play it through a second time. A recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: "Whispers of Remembrance: An Sojourn in 'A Space for the Unbound"In the labyrinth of our minds, memories lie scattered like fractured glass, each piece a reminder of past pain and buried emotions. "A Space for the Unbound" invites players to delve into this inner landscape, confronting their deepest fears and finding solace in the act of self-discovery.The game's narrative serves as a poignant exploration of the human psyche, touching on themes of identity, trauma, and the power of self-acceptance. Through the eyes of its protagonists, players are taken on a journey of introspection and growth, where the facade of mental wellness gives way to the raw, unfiltered truth of their innermost selves.At its core, "A Space for the Unbound" delivers a powerful message about the nature of healing and the importance of confronting one's past. The protagonist's struggle with high school bullying and the subsequent suppression of painful memories resonates deeply with anyone who has grappled with trauma. The game's portrayal of the protagonist's journey towards acceptance is both heartfelt and impactful, reminding players that true healing comes from acknowledging and embracing their pain.But "A Space for the Unbound" is more than just a tale of overcoming adversity; it's also a celebration of life's simple joys and the beauty of human connection. From baking cakes to petting cats, the game's charming moments of nostalgia serve as a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is light to be found.In contrast to other media that may approach bullying from a more realistic or societal perspective, "A Space for the Unbound" offers a unique and deeply personal exploration of the subject matter. Through its blend of introspective storytelling and interactive gameplay mechanics, the game provides players with a space for reflection and self-discovery.In the end, "A Space for the Unbound" is a testament to the resilience of the human spirit and the transformative power of self-acceptance. As players journey through the game's emotional landscape, they are reminded that while the road to healing may be fraught with challenges, it is also filled with moments of beauty, tenderness, and hope. So open the door, embrace your true self, and let the journey begin.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked lovely but unfortunately it ended up being a chore. Walls of text & endless fetch quests are the game here. There is little to nothing of much else. The characters seem lovely and the world is, of course, very beautiful. Unfortunately for me the sweetness was too saccharine. The writing is also very simplistic and has a habit of over-explaining every thought, which leads to needless excessive text and KILLS all pacing. It is very very slow. Ultimately I may one day finish the game and enjoy the ending but as a game, I have to say, I am very disappointed. Lovely art, probably lovely story, nice characters. Poorly paced game with little to no game in. I feel like this game would benefit from being advertised as a visual novel, as it is essentially just a dressed up visual novel. I do not feel bad about buying and supporting the game as there is plenty here to love, it just didn't cast a spell for me and I was left feeling bored and like I was stuck in a loop of one gameplay mechanics that gets more tedious on each return

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★★5/5 "Fun puzzles, mini game, and a real tearjerker story"(+) A Space for the Unbound is a game with beautiful yet heartbreaking story. The game showed us a lot of emotion that all people have. The game thought us about fear, regret, loneliness, envy, jealousy, sadness, and emptiness, but despite all that, the game also thought us about love, bravery, overcoming, moving on, and most importantly, acceptance. At least that's what i learned after playing this game. (+) I really love how the story turns out. The game itself is like roller coaster of emotions and twists.I totally recommend this if you really like story rich game! I literally cried while playing the last two chapters. And i gotta say, this game will become memorable. Especially for Indonesian.(+) I also like how it really captures "pixelated" Indonesia's town in that time (90s) and what culture does people have during that time for example collecting bottle caps, playing arcade games or trading for YOMAN collectibles.(+) Characters in this game is also well written, all of them are loveable and a fantastic addition in the game especially in story.(+) Mini games is really enjoyable(-) However there is still minor cons that i would like to point out. For instance, i really wished that there is chapter select or free roam to collect missing collectibles. I'm aware that in every chapter the game gave us a chance to do so but, looking for collectibles using wikis or walkthrough video is kind of ruining the experience for me especially for the first run. This comes from completionist player like me so, it is just some minor cons that kind of annoy me as a completionist. Because, if you miss 1 collectibles then you have to start over to get extra cutscene.(-) Don't get me wrong, the puzzle in this game is really fun and suits the theme based on a person we solve the puzzle to. However, it's a really fun and games until you meet chapter 4 puzzles. It's a damned algebra and to be honest i force myself to cheat by looking answer online because i can't stand math. Pretty sure the devs wants the puzzle to suits the people we are dealing with (in this case, it's a math teacher so i understand) but, chapter 4 puzzle really spikes the puzzle difficulty if we compared to other puzzles in the game which i considered really easy.

_childDocuments_.review: I am terribly sorry. I really tried to like this game. I thought it would be right up my alley as it is about coming of age themes and has a very serious plot. I don't care whether this is 'casual-like' or 'visual novel-like', seriously. I don't care whether the gameplay is rather 'simple'. However.... playing this feels like you have to do the dishes because your dish washer has died on you. For a friend you thought you were close with, but turns out you were not. Because they celebrated their birthday with 100 strangers. And you were only invited to do the dishes.The dialogues are terribly written. Everything is over-explained. The endless meta jokes and media reflexive comments have started to make me question my sanity. The entire thing feels like it has been written by 80 year old teenagers, because, dear lord, this thing is filled with pedagogical advise ('EAT MORE HEALTHILY!!!' and 'RESPECT YOUR ELDERS MORE!!!!!' or 'DON'T SMOKE!!!!!!!' Frankly, I try to eat healthy, respect the older generation and I don't like smoking at all, but still it was....... ughhhhhhhhhhhhhh.) Now onto the gameplay. The hiding-mechanic is overused. The 'fetch me this'-passages are repetitive and way too long and over-explained. I can understand that you'd include reminders of what to do in a game, since our daily lives are quite busy and sometimes you just leave a game and pick it up after several weeks when you have time to continue, but, seriously, this has been too much. You are given exact directions and are not even allowed to think for 2 seconds, because they basically solve all of the riddles for you. The graphics are nice, though. And I guess the story's kinda OK, too. I'm also loving the fact that this has been made by an Indonesian Indie studio. We need more of these. Overall: I am 100 % certain this has been made with a lot of love. And if you are able to look past the wonky dialogue, constant tutelage, meta-commentary and repetitive gameplay, this game might be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the unboundStories 10/10Puzzles 8/10Visuals 8/10An Indonesian game that tells the story of Atma and Raya's journey, thick with a typical 90's theme and wrapped in friendly conflicts and issues about the mentality of children in their teens, which are still happening today. what's the issue? you could say issues such as domestic violence, bullying, which make children mentally unstable.The conflicts that are given are also good in each chapter, the characterizations of each character can be identified with only one or two conversations.The mechanics in this game are quite simple, but as development continues to grow, even though there are repetitions, they are not monotonous until the end.My message is why this game is recommended:There are many implicit messages in this game, the semiotics of which can be learned from each chapter as an example for us to recognize mindsets in action, recognize deeper relatives, not be selfish in making choices.

_childDocuments_.review: This isint really a game it's more like a side scrolling-ish hyper story driven game with very light fighting mechanics. And honestly I am all about it. I can't really relate to the very dire issues that the characters faced, despite that I had a lot of empathy for the characters. I think Raya's back story is one that almost everyone faces. There was this meme going around in the early 2010s it was like "young people act like spongebob but end up growing up to be squidward" the whole premise behind Raya's character reminded me of that.Honestly looking back on it, its a very depressing story despite it appearing very upbeat and high note for the majority of its run time. Even if it ends on a high note you cant help but question human nature for the lack of benevolence, community, empathy that was required to end up with the story we have here. Hell, id argue that maybe we should return to the rural village life, it seems so nice to live somewhere where everyone knows you and it didn't make me help but wonder if someone who went though Raya turmoil lived in a western society they'd probably be  either beyond broken or dead.Maybe Dr. Theodore Kaczynski was right

_childDocuments_.review: I had a great time playing this game. Honestly, I wasn't expecting the story to be this rich and I just loved the way it approached the very sensitive subject that can be depression.  We embark in what seems to be an innocent game, calm and comfy but the more the story unfolds before you, the more you get this feeling that something is very wrong with the characters and the universe you're in. As of today, this is the game that has best depicted the struggle of depression and what recovering from it feels like among all the games I've played. I found myself really touched by all the characters (heros  and also antagonists). With this game they managed to combine good puzzles, a powerful and dreamy pixel art style, complex characters, a very smooth and interesting gameplay and good story telling... which is why in the end I really recommend this game. _childDocuments_.review: Wow. This game will forever have a special place in my heart. The story and characters were amazing and the ending was so powerful. It made me cry but left me full of hope. As someone who has struggled with depression on and off for my whole life, the themes of self-destruction, isolation, and healing resonated with me. The music was amazing and supported the story in such an enchanting way.There was times in the middle that get a little bit of a slog, but the beautiful art and characters you meet are enough to keep it interesting. The endings of the middle chapters make you forget about any tedium you just experienced and keep you going toward the most inspiring ending. If you are thinking about quitting halfway through the story -- keep going. It's worth it, I promise.I've heard some criticism about this game's gameplay -- I just want to point out that this is basically a point-and-click game (but in such a way that works great with a controller) and this game is about the characters. There are small combat mini games that are worked in in a clever way and puzzles that are mostly easy but I did have to look up a walkthrough a couple times.Play this game. It's worth the full price. It's one of those games I wish I could wipe my memory clean of and experience again.

_childDocuments_.review: You know when you come across something so amazing, so incredible, that you just don't even know what to say about it? Like no words you can ever put on a paper, or speak, will be enough to do the product justice? For me, A Space for the Unbound is one of those games. I know I won’t manage to fully convey why I related to this experience so much, but if my ramblings here are enough to get even one of you to try this out, then it will have been worth it. And on that note, I will start with my strongest argument in favor of the game:  You can also pet a duck and a couple of other animals. I know, I know, you’re already sold and probably buying the game right now, but since I like to write, I’ll just continue my review anyway! You play as Atma, a high school senior in the late 90s rural Indonesia. As such, you get to walk around and interact with many elements from both that time period AND that location, which was an incredible experience. From jokes such as a computer getting disconnected in an internet café because the owner got a phone call to cultural references like Keroncong music,  Exploring the town is a joy, and it’s all thanks to the extreme care put into even the smallest of details.  The store page says that the game “tells a story about overcoming anxiety, depression, and about the relationship between a boy and a girl with supernatural powers”. This is very accurate. Atma and his girlfriend, Raya, are at the center of the story. Most things revolve around them and the powers they have. The store page even lists one of them: the power to dive into people’s minds. And just like in games like Psychonauts, this is a concept that is explored extremely well in this game, with the player constantly diving into minds to advance the plot and help the characters as needed., employing both dramatic bits regarding the supernatural elements and threats, as well as deeply personal ones, such as the aforementioned anxiety, depression and overall uncertainty of life. The story started off good, and it only got better and better. It’s rare for something to get me this emotionally invested to the point of just… feeling empty by the end, but A Space for the Unbound did it. And the positive steam reviews echo this sentiment, with plenty of folks saying they were very emotional or crying. The story does make use of some storytelling clichés that you might not be a fan of, but I’m of the belief that, as long as clichés are used correctly and do not feel like a cheap way out of a situation, then it’s totally fine. It’s hard to be entirely original. And before you ask, yes, this game did use them well., with some well thought out jokes and believable dialogues. As for the  You move Atma in his mostly 2D plane, and you interact with people and objects. When you do, you bring up a context menu to choose your action, such as talk, interact or use an item. There are lots of interactable things throughout the game, and quite a few are just for worldbuilding, which I appreciate. You can also find shiny objects on the ground that work as collectibles for the game. The first one is bottle caps, of which there are 20. The second are YOMAN letters: a bubble gum brand running a promotion in which you have to get letters from wrappers. Last but not least, you have tales, which are pages from a fairy tale that is deeply interconnected with the story. You mostly get these from story events and from completing your bucket list, which you get in chapter 1. Some of the items there are story related, but a few are optional. There’s also a motivation for completing all this past just achievements and trophies, which is that  Or you can just wait until it pops up on youtube. And while not formally a collectible, there are 25 animals you must pet throughout the game if you want to complete all bucket list items. The horror, I know, petting animals. All of these collectibles, and more, can be seen in the game’s excellent menu, which takes the form of a red book. In there, you can also find a map of the city and your inventory. It’s very nifty!  You’ll find yourself eating popcorn with your girlfriend, beating people up in self defense in and out of arcade games, and even taking part in court trials. Some of the minigames, especially the fights, can be tricky at times, but it’s mostly very easy. Plus, if you fail, you just automatically go back to right before you entered the minigame.  None of them are hard either, so don’t worry about that. However, do expect quite a bit of running around or backtracking for items.Normally, I would mind backtracking and running through the town multiple times, but… not here. Why? Partly because of the fact that the map is small, but mostly because of  The game is an absolute JOY to look at! This is legitimately one of the best looking games I have had the pleasure to play recently. I could honestly gush about this for this entire review. But I won’t. …but I could. At times it’s very calming, at times upbeat, at times it urges you to continue to your objective as fast as possible, and at times it’s just… silent. However the background music presents itself, you can be certain of one thing: it will always fit the mood the game is trying to go for. And in fact, the game’s attention to detail extends even to where the soundtrack is employed! For example: as soon as I enter the library, a place in which we are supposed to be silent, the soundtrack stops., such as the puzzle thing I mentioned, the fact you can’t hand in multiple items to NPCs at once, and the stealth sections (the game does have those) which are a bit of a drag. If you’re interested in the title, you should know that the  so I highly recommend checking that out before you make any decisions about your purchase! Again, I can not state this enough: this game was an incredible experience, and unless 2023 is absolutely phenomenal, I can safely say I already found one of my top 10 games of the year. I really did like it that much.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like it, but i can't, in good faith, recommend A Space for the Unbound to anyone. It's a crying shame, because i deeply respect the intention behind the project. I love the whimsical, yet somewhat grounded premise: anyone who likes Makoto Shinkai movies will feel right at home. The intrigue, even though the plot twists are fairly obvious, still creates an unsettling feeling of uncertainty and dread that clashes (in a good way) with cheerful, bright colors of youth. A Space for the Unbound is mainly a point-and-click quest, but the developers still tried to spice the gameplay up a little with mini-games and little one-off mechanics that successfully break up the monotony.And yet... For every memorable, emotional peak A Space for the Unbound presents an hour of pure, unadulterated filler. Almost every "puzzle" is a multi-step fetch quest that requires you to backtrack multiple times with no other reason than to pad the length of the gameplay sections. It also indulges in "gotcha" moments, where the game deliberately fools you into the wrong solution, while the right one, of course, requires you to back track somewhere. Yes, the hometown of our main heroes is not that big, but that's hardly an excuse. Even more so in numerous dream sequences, where you are often times forced to go back and forth between someone's mind and reality to collect key items. Spacedives represent a wonderful opportunity to do something different, but A Space for the Unbound rarely delivers on that front.Most people praise the game for the story, the characters and the fact that it was made in Indonesia -- an under-represented region when it comes to games. But neither of those three have any solid writing to stand on their own. Sure, Atma and Raya can be sweet, but developers never allow their relationship to truly blossom. There's almost no banter, she's not even a constant presence in the story. Raya is important to the world of A Space for the Unbound, but doesn't really feel important to the player. Yes, the game tries really hard to tug at your heartstrings, but more often than not does so in a terribly hamfisted manner. It's supposed to be so profound and melodramatic that, at a certain point, it becomes difficult to take the game seriously.Oh, and speaking of representing the community, A Space for the Unbound doesn't do a good job. The town itself is cute and full of life, there's no argument about that, but all of its inhabintants are either nameless mannequins with a so-so pixel-art, or just item bots. You speak to them once or twice, they give you what you need to advance the plot, and that's it. The fact that the game forces you to run laps around the town on an endless search for items doesn't make it any more charming or cozy. While, on the other hand, the authors only briefly touch on real societal issues, so as not to spoil the whimsy. In short, it's a huge nothingburger of a letdown, despite the fact that the whole setting is clearly supposed to be warm and nostalgic.Yes, you can excuse some of those flaws by the main plot twist, which i will not spoild. But while it does make certain things more clear in hindsight, again, it does not portray the story in a good light. A Space for the Unbound really wants to be a Makoto Shinkai movie by way of Night in the Woods, but falls tragically short wherever you look. However, despite my criticisms, i hope Mojiken will not stop making games. It is very clear that the devs have tremendous passion and some talent on display -- it just needs refinement.

_childDocuments_.review: I might cheat here since this game is from a fellow Indonesian developer (I visited their office years ago) so my review might be positively biased, so I think I'll have two reviews. This is an early review (only 4 hours and 2 chapters deep), so things may change as I discover new things during my playthrough.Cheating review follows.They nailed the nostalgia of 90s Indonesia culture, so many references here and there (I think I knew one of the bridges...). I giggled here and there (obviously I am playing in Bahasa Indonesia), the casual conversations are not too rigid as I expected, so I guess this time they prepared the script also in Bahasa Indonesia and not translating it from English at the last minutes (I plan to replay the whole game in English to see what global players receive this game, so I may be wrong here). Some of the music resembles Indonesian music (I don't regret at all buying all DLC, one of which is digital soundtracks), although so far I haven't found dangdut music (just two chapters in the game). If you are Indonesian, please do support them; buy it on full price (it's even discounted right now), 90/100 ribu apalah artinya 😁Non-cheating review then.The puzzles are just at the right complexity. At least for my 4 hrs playthrough, they are relatively simple (the staple of adventure game): just collect the correct items to solve them. You might have stumbled the items before you need them, so you won't really struggle to collect later. They might be more complex in later chapters, I'll update this once I finished the game.The minigames are simple enough. The stealth minigame is okay, but right when you think this minigame might be too tedious because you'll need to pass the "enemies" undetected again to reach the same location, they removed it so you can finally pass without worrying to do stealth. Game over is non-existant as far as I know, unless for the arcade one (obviously it's no fun if there's no game over). The maps are not too big, so if you fail the minigames (I did failed for my first stealth minigame since I didn't discover the exact mechanic of it), you are not severely punished to retry the whole map. The fighting game resembles another game which was very popular in Indonesia (or probably SEA), but it's approachable (they only ramp up the difficulty at the arcade game, which is optional unless you are aiming to finish the optional quest). I don't know if they introduce other minigames beyond Chapter 3; I'll update my review once I find them.The visual is breathtaking. I love the vibrant color, and the pixel art is not too pixelated. Sometimes simpler is better (yes I am biased again here, since I grew up with bad graphic games, so this is another nostalgic theme they take advantage on this game). Music is great. Characters have their own personality. Storywise, I can't tell too much, but so far I enjoy the story and some plot twists make me craving to play the game more (without spoiling too much: at the end of Chapter 2 I feel sorry for one of the character and starting to wonder if one of the protagonists is actually bad).Overall, a great game to start 2023. I'm halting my other games to finish this game first 😁PS: You can pet the cat and even name them (although there are predetermined and you can't change them afterwards)

_childDocuments_.review: A very unconventional and overall solid narrative game. It plays with some dark subject matter rather lightly - there were a few moments I thought the game was going to go into a more disturbing direction, but it always seemed to come back up quickly  for air, never dwelling on critical or shocking narrative points for very long before pushing the protagonist into the next chapter. It doesn't exactly hide its twists, so you'll likely put together the central mystery before it's revealed. It seems as though instead of focusing on being a specific type of game or genre plot (mystery, dark, or comedy) the authors were more interested in exploring the depth of its central characters feelings.Due to this, the ending may not hit for everyone if these characters don't click for you (they didn't quite for me), but I can imagine there will be a significant segment of people who think this game pushes all the right buttons. Given the overall high quality and thought-provoking nature of the story, I think it's worth the price to find out for yourself if you'll like it.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the To the Moon series, I had a very high expectation of this game when I saw the trailer. And boy, it met my expectations magnificently and beyond!The game did a great job at what it wanted to do: tell you a good story. Its narration is easy to follow and enjoyable. As you follow Atma through his adventure, you can't help but be invested in him and the characters around him. The more the story unfolds, the more you are intrigued. It is one of the stories that you want to keep reading and see through to the end.Accompanying the beautifully woven story are lovely pixel art and soundtrack. Just like the To the Moon series, pixel art doesn't affect the delivery at all. Rather, its simplicity lets you focus more on the story. The beautifully composed soundtrack significantly amplifies your experience and helps with the immersion as you go through the game.The setting, which is Indonesia, might be a little bit foreign to many but fear not! You will get used to it in no time. I am sure that you can relate to many situations that occur in the game. Trust me.But none of this would matter if you can't relate to the characters. As I said above, you will get invested in Atma and the people around him. The characters are well-written and well-thought-out. Each of them has a unique character and is memorable.The only flaw I could say about the game is how it handle its fetch quest in the late game. Having layers of those is nice. But it can break immersion and the continuation of storytelling sometimes.Overall, I can recommend this game to anyone who loves narrative adventure. Its story and characters are well-written. The art and the soundtrack are perfect. It will be one of the games you will never forget.PS. I might be overthinking about this but the reference to the platypus in the game might be a reference to the To the Moon series.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space For The Unbound follows a tale set in 90s Indonesian about two highschool students, named Atma and Raya. ASFTU tells a story about overcoming depression, anxiety, and the connection between people. Gameplay mechanics are pretty straightforward and simple. It's a side scrolling narrative game with (ofc) a lot of dialogues and also few dialogue options. It also offers inventory system and collectibles that you can get throughout the game. There are also side objectives. The story itself is exquisite. Very beautifully written and wholesome. It takes a slow pace through the chapters, but it was a perfect pace. The theme of depression, self-esteem, and bullying is really what makes the story special. I can't say much bcs of spoilers, but it did make me cry. Characters in ASFTU are also memorable and well-written. The music is also wonderful addition to create the game's tone, a very genius composer I'd say. Art in this game is also brilliant with their take of using pixel art-style with amazing world-building. Aside from the narrative side of the game, ATSFU also offers some puzzles that you have to solve to progress the story. It also offers few minigames that you can play, like arcade. There are multiple endings that you can get if you completed certain objectives.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review games often, but I found myself smitten with this game by hour 4.I feel the need to write this now; If you have any interest in mystery slice of life games, play this game. I went into it expecting a fun little experience with charming characters. What I got? A deep dive into the human psyche as Atma's world falls apart around him. A lot of the TWs were things I've dealt with personally, so I was intrigued by how they'd pop up. Every single one hit me hard, and it's a miracle I didn't start crying. I teared up several times near the end, but that's as far as I got.Many of the plot points are very well hinted through out, too a point where I had inklings of what the truth might be the whole way, but the atmosphere and side characters distracted me enough that I was slow to pinpoint every single twist.After both Coffee Talk games and A Space for the Unbound, Toge Productions is quickly becoming a favorite indie developer of mine. Looking forward to whatever comes next from them.
