_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful story-driven game that's just a few small missteps short of being an undisputable masterpiece. The gameplay can be a drag at times and the early chapters are a bit too slow-paced (partly due to said gameplay), but stick with it and you'll find a deep, emotional experience that's sure to leave a lasting impression. Normally when I write a review about a game, I like to start with a brief synopsis of the story; but I think  is one of those games where the less you know going into it, the better. I'd even go so far as to say that the store page gives a little too much away, to say nothing about the trigger warnings in the opening that led me to predict a major plot point a full chapter before it happened. To attempt to explain the story with as little detail as possible, it follows two high school sweethearts, Atma and Raya, who find themselves struggling with their plans for the future and decide to create a bucket list of things they'd like to do together. What starts with such monumental goals as "watch a movie together" and "eat an entire cake" quickly becomes a supernatural journey of self-discovery, diving deep into the psyche of these two characters to uncover secrets that will change the course of their lives forever. I know that's not a very helpful summary, but like I said: the less you know, the better.When it comes to presentation, it does a fantastic job across the board. The story takes place in the late 1990s, in a small rural town somewhere around Surabaya, Indonesia; and to make it feel as authentic as possible, it's filled to the brim with cultural references and even recreations of regional landmarks. The town you explore is one of those tight-knit communities where everyone knows everyone, and over time you'll learn more about the residents and help many of them overcome their insecurities just like Atma and Raya. The pixel art used for the environments is incredibly detailed to make each location feel that much more alive, almost like the town itself could be a character of its own; and it's punctuated by a beautiful soundtrack that gives an almost ethereal quality to it all.In contrast, I'd say the gameplay is the weakest part of the whole experience—not outright bad, but more noticeably flawed. While it does sprinkle in mechanics like stealth segments or QTE combat, most of your playtime is dedicated to increasingly complex fetch quests in a semi-open map almost like a classic point-and-click adventure game, which feels like a fitting choice given the late 90s setting. You'll typically be given an overarching objective (e.g. find the ingredients to make a cake), and each individual task will, for one reason or another, cascade into a multi-step fetch quest of its own. While I wouldn't call these quests hard, they can be tedious by demanding a lot of running around and a lot of backtracking, sometimes for contrived reasons that at times can feel like unneeded filler. I've seen it argued that the gameplay isn't really the point, but it's a barrier standing between you and the story nonetheless, and I can't blame the players that were put off of finishing the game as a result—especially because I was almost one of them.Something I wouldn't normally bother to mention for this kind of game is the achievements, but I should note while I'm still on the topic of gameplay that there's a little bit of story content locked behind the completion of Atma and Raya's bucket list. Some of that list includes collectibles or other interactions that can be missed entirely if you don't find them before moving to the next chapter, and the only way to go back and get them is to either restart the whole game or take advantage of multiple save files. It does not-so-subtly tell you each time you're about to hit a point of no return, so take advantage of that and don't be afraid to pull up a  if you're afraid that you're missing something.While the story is absolutely the game's greatest strength, the early hours have a bit of a pacing problem, at least in my opinion. The prologue and Chapter 1 (of 6) made a good first impression, setting up the supernatural mystery that drives the rest of the story in just a little over an hour. Chapters 2 and 3, by comparison, moved at a frustratingly slow pace, spending a combined 3+ hours dropping crumbs of information in-between lengthy gameplay segments that just raised more questions without answering the ones I already had. It was around this time that I considered dropping the game entirely because completing drawn-out fetch quests for little to no payoff was starting to test my patience—but I kept going, and I'm very glad that I stuck with it.Chapter 4 onward is where the game puts its best foot forward. The story quickly picks up in pace, and it stops dangling question after question over your head to finally start giving you the pieces needed to put the proverbial puzzle together; all while showcasing some of the best visuals and music the game has to offer. You're introduced to a new gameplay mechanic that adds another layer of sorts to the maps you explore; and despite the fact that this can lead to even more convoluted puzzles, the payoff is so much better and faster than earlier chapters that it doesn't feel as annoying to work through as before. The supernatural elements are expanded in both the gameplay and the narrative; but as the world around our two main characters gets more and more fantastical, their deepest traumas are laid bare with an almost uncomfortable realism, exploring the subjects that lie at the core of the story in a much more grounded and mature way than I anticipated. It balances an overwhelming sense of despair with a message of hope, culminating into a story of triumph over adversity that left me with a feeling that I don't know how to properly articulate—all I can say is that I'm glad I got to experience it.In the end, it struck a certain chord with me that I wasn't expecting; and for all my gripes about the pacing and the tedious gameplay during my 8-hour playthrough, the only thought that ran through my head as the credits rolled was "it was worth it."

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a heartfelt story wrapped around gorgeous pixel art, a nice soundtrack, but frustrating gameplay, extremely on the nose hints that ruin surprises, and endless padding. Ultimately this is a "story game", it is the main focus, and as such is the most important thing for this game. Overall, the game tells a beautiful story about inner struggles, depression, anxiety, self reflection, abuse, loss, bullying, and more. The main character's struggles are sure to be relatable, especially if you play this while you're still in school. The main issue I have with the story itself is that every hint is so on the nose, you'll know most twists and turns before they happen, while not really looking out for or thinking about trying to solve the game's story. This section will contain spoilers: The game opens with the South Star Princess dying, yellow (warm colored) flower petals used for magic, and a dark colored cat. One chapter later you hear of the North Star Princess, but you don't know much about her. You then see Raya's light blue (cold colored) flower petals used for magic, and she has a light colored cat. Complete opposites, totally not the North Star Princess. You know Nirmala wrote these stories, so either you are in her story, or Nirmala has a new identity and taken on the role as the North Star Princess. The game reveales both of these are true. Shocker.This goes for a lot of the twists in the story. They're always very clearly explained before they even happen, and the only sense of mystery the game has comes from the game realizing they're being too obvious, so they have a cat tell you very ominously that "You don't know what's happening, fool, I am very mysteryous, nothing is as it seems". Then in the end the cat just gives up and starts explaining that it didn't want to be mysterious after all, they're all just here to help. This part of the narrative just felt and still feels out of place even after completing the game. The hints are so on the nose, that when you launch the game, the first thing you see is a trigger-warning list. "Animal death", I haven't even played the game yet, and my first thought is "The main character's cat will die, ok". This alone ruined any emotional impact this scene would have had otherwise.Other than that, the story itself is mostly fantastic, and handles the heavy topics with grace. The only thing that really took me out of the immersion was that they made the teenage characters censor themselves during fights. A late teenager would not censor themselves and say "You're such a B-!" when they're in a fight. It's not how people would speak, especially not a high school jock who isn't afraid to beat up people he doesn't like. This happens fairly often, so I thought I should bring it up. Writing aside, the game's biggest issue is the padding. Everything you do has padding. I think the developers were scared that just writing a good story wouldn't be enough, so they needed to insert a ridiculous amount of steps to do literally antything in the game, and it's simply not fun. For example, you need to go buy a cake, but you need to run around every part of town to gather each of the ingrediants. Fair enough. Actually, this wasn't enough, the chef is having a mental breakdown, so you need to sabotage her dream-food by pouring oil into it. The steps finding the oil alone is:Leave dream > Find Oil > Can't buy it, so you find a secret password to get free oil > You need your own container > Find container > Actually the container is dirty, find the one place in town you can clean it lol > Get free oil > Finally sabotage the dish. This was one of three foods you have to sabotage before the chef will help you. So to get the cake you need to run around town a minimum of 3 times. Doing this adds nothing to the story, you can barely call it gameplay, and it makes for an incredibly dragged out experience. It's simply not fun to run around the whole town looking for a random button to press, often with no hint. If it was just a few times, sure, but it happens almost every time you need to get anything done. The worst part is that you can't pick up items before you need them. For example that container you need for the oil, I found that ages before I needed it in a quest, but I wasn't allowed to pick it up.Adding these extra steps is something the game does any chance it gets. You need to break into the school? Cool, find a hammer to break wall (we'll skip every step it takes to find the hammer) > Run back to the wall > Break it > Actually you can't break it now, run for 3 whole minutes to the same wall in the past, then break it > Run for 3 minutes to get back > Finally, breaking it in the past made it decay, so it's broken for real now. What did this add? Another 6 minutes of holding left on the control stick? It wasn't a puzzle because the game literally told you to do it. It's just frustrating. I think if you take away this padding, keep the missions and dialogue generally the same, but without all the extra steps that add nothing, you'd probably save 3 or 4 hours of the game, and nothing would be changed otherwise.Something else that is baffeling to me is when the game introduces combat. You have a quest to beat the "Future Fighter" high score. This is the first time you will fight. Funnily enough, this high score is the absolute most difficult fighting you will do in the entire game. Why make the hardest fight the first? Everything after that is easier by a long shot. It is honestly ridiculous. Sure, you can try it once and skip doing the high score, but the high score isn't difficult to begin with, I did it first try, but it's still weird that they choose to make it the first fight the most difficult.This review is getting quite long, so I will end it here. In conclusion, the game features a fantastic story, gorgeous pixel art, nice music, but ultimately fails in the gameplay department. They should have toned down the gameplay and settled for a shorter playstime more focused on the story instead of tedious tasks, and they should be a bit more careful with the hints. Not saying a game can't be "figured out" before everything is revealed, but it should not be figured out without trying to pay attention to the finer details and without giving it much thought. I am glad I played it, I overall enjoyed the story a lot, but I can only hope they learn from their mistakes when their next game comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: Space for the Unbound" is nothing short of a celestial masterpiece that effortlessly transcends the boundaries of conventional gaming. Developed by Mojiken Studio and published by Toge Productions, this visually stunning and emotionally resonant experience takes players on a journey that seamlessly blends nostalgia, wonder, and a touch of the surreal.At its core, "Space for the Unbound" is a captivating narrative-driven adventure set against the backdrop of 90s Indonesia. The game explores themes of love, friendship, and the universal quest for understanding in a poignant and relatable manner. The narrative unfolds with grace, delicately weaving together the lives of its endearing characters, Atma and Raya.One of the standout features of the game is its breathtaking art direction. The hand-drawn visuals are nothing short of breathtaking, immersing players in a world that feels like a living, breathing canvas. Each frame is a work of art, capturing the essence of the 90s with a nostalgic charm that adds a layer of authenticity to the experience. The attention to detail is impeccable, from the vibrant landscapes to the subtle expressions of the characters.The soundtrack deserves special mention, as it complements the emotional beats of the story flawlessly. The music, composed by Masdito "Ittou" Bachtiar, is a melodic journey that enhances the atmosphere, evoking a wide range of emotions. The sound design, coupled with the captivating visuals, creates an immersive synergy that is rarely found in gaming.Gameplay in "Space for the Unbound" is intuitive and engaging. The point-and-click mechanics allow for a seamless exploration of the richly detailed environments, while the puzzles are cleverly integrated into the narrative, serving as a natural progression rather than a forced interruption. The game strikes a perfect balance between interactivity and storytelling, ensuring that players remain engrossed from start to finish.What truly sets this game apart is its ability to resonate on a deep emotional level. The characters are masterfully developed, and their personal stories intertwine with the overarching narrative, creating a tapestry of emotions that stays with players long after the credits roll. The writing is poignant, introspective, and at times, whimsically philosophical, adding layers of depth to an already rich narrative.In conclusion, "Space for the Unbound" is a triumph in storytelling, artistry, and emotional impact. It transcends the boundaries of the medium, offering an experience that is not just a game but a profound journey through the complexities of the human heart. Mojiken Studio has created a timeless piece of art that will undoubtedly be remembered as a landmark achievement in the world of indie gaming. If you're a fan of emotionally charged narratives, breathtaking visuals, and a soul-stirring soundtrack, "Space for the Unbound" is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving this to give a bit of a counter to the other reviews here which I think are a bit more positive than the game deserves.  It's not a bad game, but it really wasn't worth my time.  It may be worth it for other people though.  It starts off strong, but unfortunately ends up losing a lot of it's steam past the prologue/first chapter.One of the bigger issues is just that it's a visual novel trying to justify why it's not a visual novel...even though it would have probably been better had it just stuck with that.  This means for a 10 hour game nearly half of it is essentially fetch quests that may unlock a couple lines of dialogue relevant to the characters and the story which makes it feel like it drag on and by the time you get to the unlocks you kind of don't care anymore.  It also has a really forced combat system I don't really understand why they included as it felt like it took you more out of the story just to add more time to the game without any real challenge.  While I don't think it'd be a great game either way, It'd definitely be a 7/10 for me had they cut out the fluff or at least made it a lot more meaningful.The story is okay, it's nothing we haven't seen many times before.  It was clear what the surprise reveal was early in chapter 1.  It's major problem is being too on the nose, I love surrealism and weirdness but it needs to have a purpose and not beat me over the head.  For example good weirdness might be you dealing with a bull character that does bull-like things that certain types of people would do to that symbolizes a real character and maybe even eventually showing them turn back if you really want to make sure the player gets it, it ends up feeling more meaningful and natural...this game does the full reverse, instead of revealing the bull was a symbol all along at the end of the bull characters arch the person is just a human, acts like a human, and then randomly turns into a bull at the end for only very tenuous symbolism (because they didn't tie the person to the bull persona all along.)  It also tends to be randomly weird without much purpose, there honestly wasn't much reason to dive into people, it was rare that it felt more impact than a gimmick to get you into a puzzle.  In something like Psychonauts it's a bit on the nose with the symbolism inside the persons head, but you do feel like you naturally get to know them  this game you basically enter in and immediately the character monologues about why their there and then you solve a puzzle and a few minutes later you forget about that character entirely.The art suffers from the same problem, I love pixel art and this is passable, but especially in the weirder parts it just feels like they drew random artifacts to seem weird, there's not a lot of cohesiveness to it.  That being said, some of their higher detailed still images had very expressive characters.That all being said, about a third of players complete the game, if you like games like this enough to be in that third I'm sure you'll enjoy it a lot.  I personally feel every story beat was done significantly better in other games.  It ends up being like one of those movies where you don't hate it, but it's just mimicking things that were better and in a week you'll forget everything about it.

And as an Indonesian, this does feel like the 90's atmosphere (even though I don't know much or feel it in real life because 2000-ish so dunno if it counts, heh).It feels more "alive" in some way, I can tell the developers put so much love and care into this game.- The story. Can't say much about this without spoilers, but it does contain lots of nostalgia and relatable stories that slaps you hard in reality. They also added some Easter eggs and a small tribute to Fahmi, which was a really nice touch.- The music. It's just too good. Unbound, Chasing Truth, and Klambi Abang are my favorites.- Cats. _childDocuments_.review: Wow... as a person who had similar family dynamics to Raya, and had that one dear, kind, patient friend who changed the trajectory of my life... I'm blown away. This game hit me HARD towards the end when everything becomes clear. Gameplay, sure, it was fun to collect things, pet animals, figure out puzzles, get achievements. Yes, sometimes the fights do feel a little bit long, but not so much that it feels like I'm wasting my time, and besides, the game makes you forget about the gameplay, because the story is just that engaging. Was it confusing at the beginning? Maybe, but it's very obvious from the beginning that reality and your perception of it is... off, and that mystery is what drives the plot forward. It's weird that some reviewers state this as if it's a detriment to the game when it's literally just... the story/plot that was already established. Like most games of this genre, all becomes clear the more you progress.If you enjoy adventure games and are seeking an emotional, heartfelt story with a little bit of a mystery, play this game. _childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a mix between slice of life and magic, exploration, relatively easy puzzle solving, with a beautiful pixel art style!------You're playing as a high schooler from Indonesia, and his name is Atma. Chapter 0 is such a great opening in my opinion, and straight away you can explore the world and kinda get the premise of the game.The game loop of A Space for the Unbound is, to proceed the story, you have to solve a problem, and to solve the problem you have to explore the "stage" of the chapter.For me as I'm Indonesian myself, A Space for the Unbound is really touching and emotional. It brings a lot of nostalgia, from the street food like Cimol, the set that's so Indonesian every second, the Keroncong music and easter eggs, the plants hanging on the roof in the hallway of your school, everything made me happy.It's really amazing, as a gamer, that you can experience something like this in a video game. A game that's really close to your life, representing it, and feel really relatable.Everything in the game feels real and close to my heart.If you like indie games like Rakuen, Backbone, To the Moon, and Night in the Woods, I feel like you'll enjoy this game a lot!Thank you Mojiken Studio and Toge Productions for making this, and I hope more Indonesian games like this will be produced in the future. A personal one, that spark that kind of feeling whenever you play it.---p.s. You can give nickname to every stray cats you met. Game of the year 2023 lol.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a very, very beautiful game.The pixel art is outstandingly gorgeous, and manages to shine both in countryside landscapes and more surreal environments. The colors are both vibrant and nostalgic, and I particularly liked that the shading was done with pink instead of black. The sound design is also really good, and the music excellent.The story is good, yet not exceptional. It truly kicks in a quite late, and sometimes felt a little """"""easy"""""" if that makes sense, but what was there was done well -especially with the side-characters. The whole supernatural part is very good, if not very present in the early game. Special applause for the dev team who hired a psychology consultant. Real cool!The gameplay however…So much, way too much of this game is just running back and forth to trigger events so Atma can pick the damn things off the ground, or open a door, or a lock. Yes the world is beautiful, but I wish it was more linear or the map clearer because I got lost so often. The last three acts seldom have this problem, but the first three are a slog to go through Overall, this game should accept to be slightly shorter. We would all be better for it.A Space for the Unbound is, before all, unpolished. Still a bit rough, a bit jagged around the edges, but the jankiness almost makes it all the more endearing. It was made with love, for the characters and the obviously real people who inspired them, for the craft, and for Indonesia about which I learned a lot playing this game. If not a perfect time, it was a lovely one.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick:5/5  This game is amazing.  It has a great story with awesome characters.  The art is gorgeous and the music is fantastic.  I had such a good time playing this game, and I am so happy that I did.  Congratulations to the developers.  You have made something special.More:Ever since the demo / prologue for this game came out, a little over 2 years ago, I have been eagerly awaiting its release.  It's here now, and it has far exceeded my expectations.  A Space for the Unbound was well worth the wait.The best thing about this game is the story.  It is very deep and engaging.  Every time a chapter ended, I was left wondering where the story would go next.  There are lots of twists and turns, but the writing is so good that it doesn't seem cliche or over-done.  Lots of heavy and serious topics are touched on during the course of this game.  It is not at all juvenille, and does have some emotional as well as disturbing moments.  However, most of the time the story is a feel-good ride with a decent amount of humor in it as well.The majority of time in the game will be spent reading dialogue.  While characters are not having conversations with each-other, there are mini-games and puzzles.  I find the mini-games to be very fun and the puzzles, though easy enough, are well crafted and varied.  I can honestly say that I was never bored playing this game.  It changes so often that you always feel like there is something new to do and experience.All of the characters that you meet throughout the game have personality and charm.  Even the characters that you hate are crafted in such a way that you love to hate them.  They all have their place, in other words, and you will remember them and probably enjoy seeing most of them from time to time.If you enjoy story driven games such as RPGs then this game might be for you.  I recommend that you play A Space for the Unbound, and I hope that you enjoy it as much as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: The future is terrifying and there is so much in the world that's so wrong. There's so much to do and so much doubt in the human heart, so many ways to hurt that feeling in our beating chest. And yet we find the will to push through because we're looking forward to petting the cats around the neighborhood, or still have to complete your bottle cap collection, or you've still got to see that one movie with a friend. The will to stay alive and to keep living is beautiful and we can find it in even the smallest things around us. It could feel like the sky is falling and the end of the world is coming, but we know how to endure and to move forward. But you don't have to do everything alone. Whether you know it or not, there is always even just one figure in your life - known, or unseen - who is rooting for you in the sidelines. I hope you have someone who gives you the strength to move forward. I hope you have someone who can sit with you and knows when you need to talk, or when you just need someone to listen to you.The one major critique I believe that's worth mentioning is how the Steam description should have been more transparent of the trigger warnings you'll encounter in this game. Namely, . Saying that it's a story of anxiety and depression was not enough to brace me for the true depth of the game's storyline. I've already seen several reviews say that this game is a "slice of life / relaxing game" which I do agree with, but glossing over the rest of these sensitive topics in ASftU feels reckless to other possible players of the game who may not be ready when they picked this game up. I would strongly recommend having these trigger warnings mentioned in the Steam page. Other than that, this game was a brilliant experience. Beautiful art, a moving story, and most of all wonderful characters written in all of their joys, flaws, and complexities. Thank you for creating such a beautiful game. 8/10 :)

_childDocuments_.review: Review A Space for the Unbound.After taking enough rest for a cooldown and thinking about it with a clear head, let's start the review.First, I want to say that I played this game in English. So my criticism may only be valid in the English version.Ok, before that, A Space for the Unbound is a game made by Mojiken and Toge Production, an Indonesian game developer that won an award (I forget what award), this developer previously made games like Coffee Talk. Basically, their biggest selling point is beautiful pixel art and "heavy" stories. In this game, they managed to maintain that and their music scoring is also better than their previous game, Coffee Talk, in my opinion. Also, in terms of gameplay, I have mixed feelings about it.Yeah, maybe from my tone, you already guessed it. Yes, in my opinion, this game is overrated.My biggest criticism is probably from its ineffective dialogue. Maybe it's our culture or the Indonesian language itself that, in my opinion, when translated into English, there are many inefficient uses of dialogue. Maybe the writer didn't check it first, there were many dialogue tags in the script.My second criticism is in the logic of the story. Yep, the story is more focused on emotions than logic, which for me is a drawback. For those who don't understand. Basically, it's like the story prioritizes the emotions of the audience regardless of whether a situation is logical or not. I'll explain it in the spoiler section later.Let's skip the story narration for now. For the gameplay, I think they were too accepting of the criticism of Coffee Talk, which had less gameplay...In this latest game, I think the gameplay is too much. Like when we're watching anime / movie / other media, we just enjoyed 30 seconds, we're immediately served with a mini-game that I find annoying. This game is very puzzle-like and for me who is not used to puzzles. the game can still be enjoyed even though there are some puzzles that I wouldn't be able to answer if I didn't see walkthrough or ask someone.What I mean is that the puzzles aren't boring, but I think they're too overdone. It's like it's just padding to make the game longer. For example, to open a locked library door, we're asked to find three keys from three different people. And it turns out these three people also have additional quests that need to be completed. After collecting the three keys and completing the quest, my reward for all this is just a 30-second cut scene? Just wtf. Luckily, this chapter is short, otherwise, I would have dropped it in chapter 5.This is also exacerbated by the fact that the puzzles are not always intuitive and often require a lot of backtracking and fetching items. It feels like the puzzles were added just to make the game longer, rather than to enhance the story or gameplay experience.Additionally, the characters in the game are not very well developed and their motivations and actions often feel inconsistent and unrealistic. The game also suffers from a lack of direction and clear objectives, leaving the player feeling lost and confused.I want to complain a bit of story so yeah, Spoiler ahead** Spoiler Begin **My problem with the story is 100% pure from Raya. I get that, he wants to be made relatable but it's silly. And in the end, it's not even made into a serious conflict. For a game that is bold in giving warnings about depression, etc., I think this is too tame. The story is too shounen-like but I don't want to criticize it in that aspect because honestly, the writer seems to like playing the shounen cliche like Naruto. It's not wrong, such a story also touches many reviewers and their pixel art target market which I am sure is more mature than me.I've mentioned before that the story only plays with emotional feelings without any logic at all. This makes the story become fail to be dark as the warning should be. For example, I actually relate to Raya's problems. But because I relate to it, I am a bit meh about Raya's illogical actions. For example, if you get scolded by your parents because of your bad grades, you should STUDY, not act like you're depressed. Damn.Even worse, Raya talks to a stranger (by the way, the stranger is a high school student and Raya is still a kid) and gets more depressed when he dies. I understand that she probably has guilty feelings. But why does the narration make it seem like Raya has imaginary friends and is bullied because of that? That just doesn't make any sense in my book. I know indonesia isn't that cruel to any accident survivor. Seriously. Suddenly, there's a boy who likes her but of course he's the one bullying Raya and she's fine with it. And then she hates him when he accidentally killed her favorite cat? Like, wtf cat lovers really doesn't make any sense. Her actions in the illusion world are really prick and freakish, making it "oh no wonder she's bullied". There's no characteristic of Raya that explains why the main character likes her so much.Oh, and one last complaint about the story is the amount of infodump and loredump, which is forced. Imagine, from the beginning to the end, there are so many infodumps to explain the phenomenon of magic, and even then the scenes are only 1-2 times, then forgotten.For the storymaker in Mojiken, I hope they read Kinug*sa's light novel or at least play Mete*r W*rld Act*r. That's the best way to give infodumps according to me. Sorry, not meant to be a promotion.** Spoiler End **Overall, while A Space for the Unbound has beautiful pixel art and a unique setting, the game falls short in terms of story, dialogue, and gameplay. The puzzles feel like a chore, the characters are underdeveloped, and the story lacks logic and direction. While it may appeal to those who enjoy puzzle games, it may not be the best choice for those looking for a well-rounded and engaging gaming experience.Despite that, I still think that the game is worth buying if you like Mojiken's previous works. I'm 100% sure that this game is an improvement from the previous one. I hope this isn't Mojiken's masterpiece because they have the potential to make even better games.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a heavy yet beautiful narrative-driven adventure about overcoming your fears and growing up, set in a rather unique setting of the 90s rural Indonesia. The game contains depictions of abuse, bullying, animal death, anxiety, depression and trauma so it may not be suitable for everyone.You play as Atma, a high school boy who has a very close friend named Raya. They’re both a bit ambivalent about graduating but together they map out a bucket list of things they want to do before the responsabilities of adulthood take over. While starting out on their adventure, Atma discovers a red book that grants him the ability to “space dive” into a person’s subconscious to help them face past trauma and make life-changing decisions. He soon discovers, however, that Raya has a similar but more destructive superpower that can alter reality itself. I’d say the story is one of those that are quite difficult to explain without spoiling it, but I assure you that it is one emotionally heavy story with many twists and interesting characters, one that will definitely make of you an emotioanl wreck by the end.Visually, A Space for the Unbound is a stunningly gorgeous game if you enjoy pixel art. There are some jaw-dropping images to be seen here, especially when the story starts going in very different directions than you initially thought it would. The character design is highly detailed and I loved the added expressiveness at times with emoji comic bubbles. The script is localized wonderfully and helps bring the characters and the emotions of a given scene to life. The soundtrack is catchy and relaxing and sets the mood for every scene and character. There are also vocal tracks that perfectly capture the game’s themes of sadness and loss and I would gladly listen to every one of these again. My only critique is that the music rarely shuts off, as if the game doesn’t trust the player to stay engaged with the world’s natural ambience. I can’t praise the soundtrack enough for the powerful emotion it conveys. It communicates the emotion behind the game’s setting and twists just as much as the story itself does.Most of the game's chapters are spent free roaming a town and the game will ask you if you want to proceed to a “point of no return” of that chapter. Save before this, since there is missable content. You will encounter tricky puzzles, but I don’t find them overly cryptic, since the hint is usually nearby. The game does not have a lose condition but there will be things like quick time events that require some reflexes. You can fail these but you can try again as many times as you need. The gameplay is fairly standard as you walk around Loka City, interact with townsfolk, pick up objects, name and pet every adorable kitty in town. The side-scrolling, story-driven adventure supports both gamepad and keyboard and both are pretty seamless. There are plenty of arcade-like mini-games that I found to be a bit easier on the gamepad.A Space for the Unbound is an intensely rewarding experience that pulls all the right heartstrings. It may not be perfect, but it has an incredibly touching story that will keep you guessing until the very end. It is truly a memorable gaming experience you don’t want to miss. A true masterpiece that every story rich indie game fan should play at least once. 10/10 recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second time playing something by this team and, once again, I am very conflicted as I write this review.Let's take some things out of the way first: The art in this game is astounding, it's honestly, truly beautiful. The story is filled with mysteries that keep you motivated to keep going and figure what the hell is going on and it's set on the 90s in Indonesia, which is definitely something you don't see everyday. It has cats, LOTS of cats (which you can name from a few set of names and also pet!!!) and overall it's something that you start and immediately get absorbed into. But that only last for the first half or so. There are so many characters that don't really matter. Why are they given the time of the day? Atma, our mc, enters the mind of some people to fix some of their trauma, "fix" them and stuff. But it always demands too much time for such a scratch on the mysteries. The gameplay is also not very creative, the fight scenes are a mix of fishing in Stardew Valley and pressing the right keys in the keyboard. If it was minimal that would be okay, but it's there just for the sake of it. What I mean is there is a great story in play, but so many things that feel like they're there just to make you play for a longer amount of time. I played When the past was around by the same team and it made me feel the exactly same (great story; not so great gameplay). The puzzles are better and more intuitive in this one, though, so that's an improvement from the last I played.The characters that aren't Raya, Nirmala, Atma and Lulu are also pretty whatever honestly. Lulu was a great companion for Atma during the game, but there isn't much effort in the other characters. And the whole beating around the bush to explain what was truly happening made me dislike Raya for a great part of the game as well. I feel if the game just focused on Atma/Raya more it could've been so much better! Because it was great at first, but as soon as it became a "where is Raya?" it started going off the trails. If this game was 6 hours long it could've told everything it wanted, but in a better way, I guess.The ending is what made me give this a positive review, however. That was beautiful. A viewer came to me at some point, commenting that Ollie from Hololive had almost dropped this game for the same reasons I was bored with it (I wasn't dropping though because I was already 12 hours on it or so), but that the ending was worth it. And yeah, it was. Made me cry and everything, and the art was great. Also the best OST of the game play next to the end as well. There were still some questions left unanswered but that didn't really bother me, I thought it was okay to leave it up to the player imagination. But if people get discouraged to play because of boring segments and feel like dropping it in the middle... That's just sad, isn't it? And it deals with important themes as well, such a domestic violence. I really wish it wouldn't beat around the bush with boring characters and boring storylines so much. Oh. And the very last scene (1 minute or so) can only be unlocked if you got all the achievements or all the pages of the book or whatever. If you didn't, the very last scene is extremely anticlimatic and makes no sense (the true ending scene isn't that great either honestly). I tried looking for it on youtube but most people that put up a full walkthrough didn't get the scene either... I did find it later though. But yeah. If it hasn't ended with the credits it would've been so much better! Argh! It's a good game that doesn't feel polished enough, I guess. It's a 5.5~6/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece, with it's incredible storytelling and it's compelling pixel art style, visualizing it's objective to portray 90s Indonesian feel accurately, with references to pop culture existing between then and now. Moreover with many puzzles that would surely give your brain some exercise as you drift through it's story. Basically it's a love letter to the Indonesian people as a whole, appreciating the diversity of their cultures greatly.Now, first impression I got of this game from it's title screen already got me hooked for some reason, the summer feel is just too good you know, and that feeling increases drastically as you enter into the world of A Space For The Unbound, with it's colorful pixel art background, and warm color palette of the city of Loka.As you course it's storyline your curiousity increases, it delves into overcoming your fears and your past regrets and failures, building confidence and telling you that yes, you are alone in this world, but there are people that are there for you. The background music setting you straight on what mood and setting the game is going for. With some brought out by beautiful vocals for the character's themes.And the ending... oomph, I'm not going to talk about the spoilers but if you have the most empathetic heart be prepared for it, a punch in the gut that would just have you speechless sitting there staring at the ending title screen after it comes and goes away like the wind.Some cons do exist, but it only causes a slight inconvenience, there will be a math puzzle, though if you can't guides always got you some help ;)There will also be backtracking here (as a lot of these games do) but I assure you, you will be kept hooked onto it for long.I wholeheartedly recommend buying this amazing piece of art created masterfully by Mojiken Studios and Toge Productions.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, that sure made my eyes a little bit wet. My throat a bit tight.My feelings... complicated.Okay, so, this is another one of those "indie games that are about mental health". And it's weird at first but then the whole plot becomes incredibly obvious somehow and then the ending is both gut wrenching and also touching but most importantly happy. Which is an interesting combo.Mechanically, it's a visual novel with a few minigames thrown in to spice up the monotony of reading text boxes. You'll be reading a lot of text boxes, and also running from one text box to the next. There are some clever puzzles in there, though, which made my brain feel big, and that's always a plus in my book. But it made me wish how that combat button press QTE thing was a JRPG combat system. Think about it.But really, the ending makes it all worth it. There's a very mature message there. Yes, it's about mental health, but it doesn't cut corners, and it avoids the common traps you see when people try to turn those themes into game mechanics.So, give it a shot if you like reading, thinking and crying. Oh, and cats. So many cats.

_childDocuments_.review: A project that proves that video games, along with films, painting, music, and so on, are art. But can we call all video games art? Do all video games catch the strings of your pathetic soul like that? Or are video games just a way to pump out money? This is a unique game, an example of real game art, not ♥♥♥♥ from Ubisoft, EA and others. It makes me extremely sad that the culture that I have lived in for so many years, and that has literally created me myself, is now just a fast-growing business. Every time a game like this comes along, I start to believe again. Into yourself, into people, into culture as a whole, and that's wonderful. Art should evoke emotions, real emotions, should make you feel something... to feel the echo of your soul. A space for the Unbound is a game that evoked a huge range of emotions in me, from sadness, worry and mild depression to joy, faith and hope. A game that tells a story as if you're there, as if it's all with you. A game that shows a believable outcome and development of a person, under the pressure of society, family, his inner demons and the struggle with these same demons. This is the merit of many talented people, just like the author of this review, who love games and respect them as art. It pains me to admit that over time such games will clearly lose popularity and lose all status in the world, but as long as they exist, I believe that large companies will have their own little garage geeks who create great worlds and unforgettable stories, worlds that evoke sincere emotions. Thank you for this piece of art, I will never forget it.  I wish peace to all, because we are citizens of the same world.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really special.  It gets a lot of recognition for it's '90's Indonesia setting, and that certainly adds to it's charm, but this is way more than just a game set in Indonesia.   It tells a beautiful, meaningful story with perfect pacing and storytelling.   The characters and the writing are really fantastic, and the music perfectly complements it.  It plays like an old-school point-and-click adventure game, but it completely avoids the weird moon-logic puzzles that sometimes happen in that style of game.  It has a deep narrative that will keep you thinking about it, but it avoids being the common problem of being so convoluted that it's hard to follow or makes no sense.  It has a good number of side-quests and optional content, but it's set up in such a way that if you choose to, you can easily do it all without resorting to using a guide or spending hours completing collections.  It's rich in symbolism and touches on many important topics including bullying, anxiety, depression, abuse, trauma, and loss.  The game is very emotional and can make players cry at points, but I wouldn't call it a sad game - it's uplifting and bittersweet.  Combine all that with it's simple pleasures: a cute art style, catchy music, unique cultural references, petting and naming all the stray cats in town - it's just an all around wonderful and special game.

_childDocuments_.review: is one of those masterpieces that are very difficult to describe in words; they have to be personally experienced, ardently felt and actively lived. One of its characters mentions at some point in the game, “As a writer, I want to be able to move my readers with the things I create. Change them”;  is the embodiment of this quote: it’s a deeply emotional work of art that will move you and change you.Atma and Raya are two high-school sweethearts who one day decide to make a bucket list of fun things they want to accomplish in the near future. While this acts like a premise for the story, it’s in fact just a way to guide the player step by step into various circumstances that will slowly reveal the actual core of the game: Raya is a young girl having the superpower of altering the reality, while Atma possesses a book that allows him to dive into people’s hearts / minds and help them overcome their inner troubles. Strange incidents start to happen around them as Raya keeps misusing her powers to change little things to their advantage in an attempt to facilitate the completion of the bucket list. Soon enough the line between reality and fantasy is completely abolished and the player is transported into a series of unpredictable events as the world around the two main characters starts to destabilize. The story remains enveloped in mystery right until the end, keeping the player wondering what the actual meaning of all these incidents could be, but at the same time revealing new layers with every chapter. is a gripping tale about reconnecting with your true nature and finding the will to overcome all the obstacles that life throws at you. It deals with sensitive topics like emotional traumas caused by school bullying, depression, social anxiety, domestic violence and to some extent suicidal thoughts.As far as the gameplay goes,  takes the shape of a sidescroller point & click adventure. As Atma, you will explore the streets of the small Loka City, enter buildings or interact with the people you encounter. The linear gameplay and the fact that the game always makes it obvious what the player is expected to do allows them to deeply immerse themselves in the story. Unlike in other point & click games, where you just roam around without knowing where to go, talking to everyone just because you can, collecting every object you can find just because you can pick it up and because it will probably be used in a puzzle,  tightly guides the player through its wonderful story, leaving very little space for mindless experimentation and time-wasting conversation. You will pick up objects only at the right moment when they’re needed, all dialogues are on point and Atma’s inventory is filtered and populated with the only 2-3 items that you can and  to use when interacting with a character. In addition to that, all puzzles are clear and straightforward, usually encountered in the form of fetch-quests, but there are also a couple of light math riddles. Some of the dialogues have multiple choices, and in some cases these are mutually exclusive, other times not. The mutually-exclusive ones do not affect the outcome of the story in any way, and only provide a few alternative dialogue lines.From time to time, Atma will have to use a fighting mechanic which involves reproducing a sequence of keys in a limited amount of time in a QTE style (attack), followed by stopping a moving cursor at a precise location (block / defend). The minigame is designed so that it is accessible for pretty much everyone (there’s enough time to complete it in a rather relaxed mode), even though throughout the game its difficulty increases (you get longer sequences and tighter times of reaction). In case you fail to complete a sequence three times, you will be able to give it a new try starting from the current stage. While the game keeps the difficulty rather casual, for two specific achievements you will need to survive through 17 of these stages without failing, and beyond the first 10 of them you’ll be required to have extremely quick reaction times.In  you will encounter lots of cats, in fact, more than 25 of them. You can name and pet them all, which is obviously optional for completing the game but necessary for a certain achievement. While these sadly aren’t tracked, the other type of collectibles (the 20 bottle caps) are all listed in your inventory. Apart from a couple of cases they are all easily spottable in the environment through a spark that indicates their location. Unfortunately, the collectibles are missable in the sense that you won’t be able to go back to a previous chapter and pick them up in case you didn’t do so the first time. Aside from these, there are a few other missable achievements awarded for interacting with certain items in the world or doing specific actions at the right moment. One playthrough is enough for 100% completion, but due to the fact that you can’t replay previous chapters, using a guide will likely be needed.The game excels not only through the captivating story that it conveys, but also through the stunning (and very detailed) pixel art style, and an equally impressive soundtrack. In all these aspects, the developers included lots of Indonesian cultural and lifestyle references, which give the game a lot of flavor. Voice-acting is not present, yet this doesn’t diminish the warm experience that  provides.Do I recommend the game? Absolutely - I love  for its charm, for its fantastic story with a good character build-up, for its lively art and great presentation. It’s a one-of-a-kind game that deserves every penny for the 12-15 hours of joy that it offers.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to review this game in a way that truly makes it justice, without any spoilers, and I'd rather not do that.It's a game about escapism, friendship, regrets, loss, and so much more. The story is pretty out there, but it delivers an interesting narrative, that feels like a breath of fresh air among the stale and lifeless backdrop of modern mainstream gaming.The soundtrack is quite enjoyable. It's nostalgic, sweet and relaxing, and goes well with the game's setting.Pretty much everything about the game brims with nostalgia. The nice pixel art visuals, the 90s small town setting.Most of the pixel art is great, even though it's a bit simplistic at times and it's lacking in detail, and there are some scenes where it's clear that they didn't put as much effort, compared to other ones.Unfortunately, the game has its fair share of drawbacks.The action consists of some rudimentary mini-games; mostly basic quick time events. There are a lot of them, and they are rather repetitive and tedious.Most puzzles are easy, logical, but some, are tedious, requiring quite a bit of trial and error.There are too many errands with a ton of back and forth. For example, in order to get a simple cake, you have to jump through so many hoops, it's ridiculous; the worst part is that these errands are bland and simplistic in nature (basically, bad fetch quests), and most do not tie into the world or the story almost at all, just being isolated and contained. Would have been great if you would get more insight into the world, characters, lore, through these errands.While for the most part, the writing is pretty good, it has its gutter moments, with some of the dialog feeling forced and unnatural (will not go into details, to avoid spoilers).You can remap most keys, except for the movement keys, for some reason. Interestingly enough, in the 1st demo, you were able to move using WASD as well as the arrow keys. In the 2nd demo and the full game, you can only use the arrow keys. It's not that big of a deal, since you can use AutoHotKey to remap any keys however you want, but still, it would have been nice to have the option to be able to remap all keys.It has some wasted potential. With a bit more polish to its writing, characters, lore, and mechanics, the game could have been a brilliant masterpiece.Even so, despite all of these gripes, the game is enjoyable and well worth playing, ultimately delivering a unique and memorable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Mojiken's New Game: Hype High, Delivery...Not So MuchOkay, Mojiken fans, gather 'round. Let's talk about their latest release, shall we? I jumped on this bandwagon the week it dropped (i think), fueled by Mojiken magic from past games. I was hyped, picture me bouncing off the walls like a caffeinated chihuahua. The art? Gorgeous. The music? Banging. The whole vibe? Perfection personified. I was ready to devour this game whole.And devour I did...the first few minutes, anyway. But then, I hit a snag. It wasn't the gameplay (though let's be honest, it wasn't exactly groundbreaking). It was the dialogue. Oh, the dialogue. Longwinded monologues that felt like reading Tolstoy after chugging five espressos. The structure? Wonky in both English and Bahasa, like a sentence got lost in Google Translate and returned wearing clown shoes.Look, I tried. I switched languages like a frantic tourist, hoping one would click. I pushed through, fueled by my initial excitement and a desperate hope for redemption. But alas, the dialogue was a dragon I couldn't slay. It just kept droning on, sucking the joy out of the game like a Dementor with a thesaurus.So, I tapped out right around the time Atma woke up in the school and started chatting with Raya. Dialogue coma, I tell you. Maybe someday, when the Baldur's Gate itch is scratched, the Valorant dailies are done, and Skyrim's frozen wastes have lost their allure, and the lure of taming cute yet deadly beasties in Palworld has faded, I'll give this Mojiken gem another go. Who knows, maybe with fresh eyes and a pot of strong tea, I'll unlock the secrets of its wordy world. Until then, it slumbers on my backlog shelf, a beautiful mystery waiting to be unraveled. And mark my words, if that day ever comes and the game redeems itself in my eyes, I promise I'll be back to rewrite this review with a chorus of praise. Until then, consider this a placeholder, a testament to my ever-growing backlog and the ever-present hope that hidden gems still await discovery.

_childDocuments_.review: Finished it today.... Oh man... Such a sweet and paradoxical world. It's like a nonlinear puzzle about one's self, conflict, identity and recovery. I am at a lost of words right now. It is so beautiful, I can't even talk. Still crying. It is a story packed with everything for anyone. It has sensible issues, it has courage to face one's fears, it has action (fighting scenes, fighting for loved ones), it has good and satirical humour, it belongs on those unique shelves for great games. PROS:- Story is fabulous;- Character change at the end;- Wonderful art style and graphics;- Music fits every part of the story;- Book for inventory and map;- Collecting coins, letters and pages;- Petting cats and giving them names.CONS: (I must say sorry for this!)- The one thing that really drives me crazy are save points. The save point in this game is bad. When you save and load, it makes you start from the beginning of the checkpoint chapter, rather than the very minute you have saved the game. And this is frustrating because back in 1990s you could save on the spot in a SNES emulated game, but not in this 2023 game. This is bad! - A quick tip: The kid with the ball (letter M) needs to offer a quick tutorial for how to juggle the ball (i.e. press X when ball is on the leg - or something like that);- I cannot think of other issues right now.Forgive my rage for the save point. Because of my 1990s knowledge of games, I'm comparing mechanics of the past with mechanics of the present. You devs of the present have yet to please me. Well, some games like True Fear: Forsaken Souls, Guilty Gear, Legacy of Kain, God of War: Ragnarok, etc. have a special place in my heart. And I think I'm not alone in this statement. What I want to say is that A Space For The Unbound has become right now one of my favorites. It turned out a gem of a game, a must play for sensible hearts. In this light, I must thank my friend for giving this game for my birthday. Thank you, friend!

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound caught me by complete surprise. Especially because I didn't think it deserved the hype even half way through the game. I was wrong, and I highly recommend this experience. Even the price of 20 Dollars is worth it.Reviews for ASftU are Overwhelmingly Positive on Steam, which - along with its promise of a good story -prompted me to purchase this game. I had never bought anything by Mojiken before and from the looks of the trailer and screenshots, it seemed to pay homage to classic arcade style games and point and click gameplay, which it does.Now, being perfectly clear. I don't think Space Unbound is a great game, or at least, does not have great gameplay. It is a good game, but not great. The puzzles are a bit too easy at times, the pacing is off at various points, and the back tracking didn't really settle me in the atmosphere like it seems to for others.The options in the main menu seemed a bit limited to me as well. No chapter jumps after completion, no artwork unlocked for finding hidden achievements... Little things like this would improve the game a bit in my opinion.Half way through I thought, "Yeah this is a good game. But a masterpiece? No, I don't see that."...I was wrong. I finished the second half.Despite my nitpicking of gameplay and my doubts, I can confirm A Space for the Unbound tells a beautiful, masterful story. It is obvious the creators were careful in their research of depicting the emotions of the depressed, the anxious and anger, that comes from someone suffering. What's even more impressive is that anyone can relate, to some level, what these characters are going through, and how they feel.I was very impressed. And that ending, that incredibly moving, gosh darn ending had me re-watching on youtube many times.Well worth everything, the hours and money spent.Is A Space for the Unbound a great game? No. But I don't believe it could be told correctly in another form of media either.Does A Space for the Unbound tell one of the most beautiful, down to earth stories about depression that I have ever played? Yes. And it is done masterfully.I look forward to your next game Mojiken. We need more video games like these. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This gorgeously animated adventure game follows Atma, a young Indonesian man coming to the end of his school career and preparing to jump into the next stage of his life before he and his girlfriend Reya gain magical powers and odd things start happening around their unassuming little town. This is the first step in a gripping plot that zigzags around every corner and lets its mystery simmer before bubbling up to some eye-opening revelations. The gameplay here is a simple graphic adventure fair, where you walk around the Indonesian village solving puzzles and talking to the locals to progress your way. Atma holds a magic book that allows him to “space dive” into the hearts and minds of the residents of his town and solve their internal conflicts. This predictably leads to a series of heartfelt vignettes of those characters’ lives to serve the greater plot between Atma and his girlfriend. My biggest issue with A Space for the Unbound is how much of the moment-to-moment gameplay can feel like a basic fetch quest to pad out some of the lengths but of course, the focus of this type of game is the characters and story, which A Space for the Unbound nails.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a deeply personal experience for me, as someone with clinical depression and anti-social tendencies. Some moments felt like a mirror. It's not a pleasant feeling to be so vulnerable from seeing myself in video games, especially the ugly parts of me, but that's what makes this game special and dear in my heart. Really, some scenes felt like a memory, something I've been through in my darkest days.I love how the developer portrayed depression, very respectful and realistic. It doesn't glorifies nor vilifies mental illness at all. This game also highlights trauma, struggles, family issues, coping mechanisms and everything else humankind experience in an honest and bare way. Gosh, I even almost cried again while writing this review. I do admit, this game hits too close to home because I'm Indonesian too. Now, to other aspects of this game.I LOVE every single detail the developer had made for world-building, visually or through script. The close-knit neighborhood, food stalls, pop culture references, the shops, school, EVERYTHING screams Indonesia in a genuine, nostalgic way. Like c'mon. Warnet. Tambal ban. School as haunted site. The abandoned train cart as secret base. The freaking toko kelontong and batu akik. The story is interesting and not too predictable. Dramatic, but doesn't make me cringe. The ending made me feel like, "damn, someone actually experience this too, just like me." Don't let the fantasy aspect of this game fool you, even the "side stories" could be found in day-to-day life of Indonesian people. The visual and sound style is very gorgeous, it fits the narrative perfectly. I was actually speechless in some scenes from how beautiful everything felt. The 16-bit art and color palette made it so freaking nostalgic. The visual effects, transition, every trinkets and small sound effects. I love it so much. The art director and artists behind the visuals really experimented with lots of perspectives and lighting effects, too.The characters are perfectly flawed in their own ways. Some of them are likable, some are not, depends on your culture, views and morality. They felt real, even down to the minor characters. From visuals to the way they talk, and how they interact with each other. Literally, I could imagine them as part of my own life as Indonesian. I don't want to go too deep in this aspect because I might spoil it too much.P.s : the way CATS dominated this game made it 100000x more awesome. The game mechanics is not the main focus of this game, but it was quite fun and frustating at times. My favorite part is how one of the game mechanics referenced my favorite game, **e Attorney. Like, at this point, this game felt like it was made for me.I could probably talk about this game for hours and hours. But all in all, I just want to give my highest gratitude to Mojiken and Toge Productions for bringing this game to life. This game and all of you inspired me to pursue my passion more from now on,I finished this game in about 10 hours total with 2 achievements left, about to replay it in English because my first run was in Indonesian to get all achievements. See ya!

_childDocuments_.review: Masterfully done narrative and engaging puzzles. This game, along with classics like "To the moon" reminds me once again that often times, we don't need to embellish pixel-styled games with innovative graphics just to create a wonderful experience--having a good story and well designed mechanics is more than enough. The people from Mojiken have hit all of the marks with this amazing side-scrolling adventure. The music, the art, and the story all merges into this engaging game that expertly tackles depression, grief, and social relations. I think what I enjoyed the most was the exposure they gave to Indonesian culture and how it was presented. If you're someone who enjoys puzzles, figuring things out, and also appreciates a well-done narrative, this game is for you. I'm definitely a fan of the developers and will be anticipating more games from them!

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully crafted tale from start to finish. Story is very engaging and intriguing and I believe inspired by Shinkai's movies (such as Your Name and Suzume). The pixel art style is top-notch and very clearly realized with a variety of environments from bleak and sad to bright and beautiful (and everything in between).There is also a clear and delicately handled message about mental health so some story beats can be triggering for some, but I think it worth hearing if you've ever had troubles of your own. Perhaps the biggest gripe most people will likely have is that the "puzzles" require a lot of backtracking and "fetch quests". That said, some certainly tickled the brain more than others and I had a fair bit of fun with. Other mechanics are clearly inspired from other games such as classic fighting games and even Ace Attorney. The spacedive mechanic is also pretty unique and feels reminiscent of Inception (one of my personal fav movies). Run time is pretty decent for the price point at about 8-10 hours. It's absolutely worth picking up.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a beautiful story about loss; the way we cope with it,  and self acceptance; the journey we take to feel at one with ourselves. The game takes us through this journey, and the steps we encounter along the way.The graphic style is beautifully rendered, really making a good effort of making you feel in Indonesia. The characters are believable and make you feel part of the story.Gameplay sets you on a 2D adventure, with puzzles, collectibles, and some fight encounters.The music was beautiful, helping set the scene. The puzzles were on the whole well realised, with the solutions in the environment to be found. The fight scenes revolved around a sequence of QTEs. Although infrequent, I would say these were the weaker elements of the game.Exploration takes you across the map, however there are occasions where you are restricted on where you can go, due to story beats. It can also take a bit of time to work out where each section leads, but gets easier over time.Overall, a lovely story to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for The Unbound is an adventure, point-clicked puzzle with a great storyline. You play as Atma, a high school student who goes on a adventure with his girlfriend, Raya. Both tend to complete their wish list to achieve what they call their goals in life.The game has great pixel art, colorful and cute. I think people will judge this game as a normal puzzle game but it's not. The puzzle on this game are quite complicated but fun. When you solve it, it's makes you feel like completing something big, that's what I say. The mechanic of the gameplay is great. Here you can dive into people mind and help them from inside their heart. There are lot things to do in this game, such as collecting bottle can, peting a cat and even more. Overall it's great experience.Perhaps the downside of this game, for me, is how it doesn't tell you what to do sooner or later. Like there are some items that you can't get if you miss one item in a certain chapter. When you don't complete any collectibles, the game doesn't feel 100% complete. You can therefore go back and play it again, but it's a linear game, so playing it again or creating a new save file can be tedious and a waste of time. I know it's only for perfectionists but for me keeping every linear 100% complete is important.The game is more than 10 hours of gameplay, it's quite short, but worth your money. Give it a try if you want to experience a great story, and for fellow Indonesians, you have to play this game. Trust me it's worth it.

Raya is indeed one of my favorites, her abilities just simply said frightening yet awesome! - Nothing, i don't think i can find anything bad on this game.- One day please kindly consider to re-release this game in 3d-styled / anime format. _childDocuments_.review: Dislcaimer: I played this on my Steam Deck offline, so it says I've only played it for like two hours despite the fact that I'm in the final section of the game.Actual review: I bought this game on a whim based on the fact that it had such positive reviews and knowing absolutely nothing about it. It was a great decision.This is a charming indie game that's part old-school pixel art RPG, part old school point and click adventure, and part something else uniquely its own.It has a bit of everything. Engaging characters, a good story, humor, drama, magic (or at least superpowers), teenage angst, mental health issues, Inception-style dreamwalking, and a ton of cats you can pet and name. Oh, and ambiance. So much ambiance.I was wondering why I felt so attached to these characters and why the setting felt so familiar given that I'm not remotely Indonesian, when I found out that the main story is supposed to be set during the '90's. That was it. What I felt was familiarity and nostalgia because I'm roughly the same age as Atma and Raya and what I was recognizing was the very authentic feeling of what it was like to be a teenager in a small town in those long gone days of the late 20th century before the internet was everywhere and cellphones were even a thing. I don't think I had ever felt like that except when reading a good book or watching a good movie, but never while playing a video game. What an unexpected and interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Content Warnings for A Space for the Unbound as provided by Mojiken Studio: abuse, depression, suicide, trauma, animal death, flashing lightsTackling coming of age and the YA register in a way that games frequently struggle to meet, Space for the Unbound is a 2D adventure game taking flavors from life sims, JRPGs, and Shenmue-style "♥♥♥♥ around and talk to people" puzzle routing. 90s Indonesia depicted in lush pixel art gives a nostalgic sense of place to this Mamoru Hosoda-y fantasy-realism piece. While sometimes a bit verbose or hung up on challenge based sideshows, A Space for the Unbound nails a sense of scale and gravity in its handling of teens on the fringe of their own life where something like the Life is Strange franchise constantly seems to struggle with.This game conducts itself without a huge dependence on melodrama to synthesize character beats with its fantasy elements. While it can be heavy-handed in writing or slightly off with timing or duration, the vital scenes and lock-and-key puzzle moments are meticulous and conservative. The palette and approach to line and weight in the animation give so much life to every second and the frequency at which the team at Mojiken knows when to let that speak is enlightening. I think some of the ways in which abuse are depicted and resolved is a little too simple, but the game doesn't claim at any point to be interested in making larger claims about the subjects. This is an incredibly charming game that delivers on everything it promise in its most gorgeous stills.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10, would cry againLoved the characters.  Good story, fantastic ending.  I know virtually nothing about Indonesia, but the game world felt very fleshed out.I do not recommend trying to get all achievements on the first run.  It started to drag at the middle for me because of this.  I started enjoying it again when I let go of 100%ing the bucket list + achievements.The writers deserve an award for how hard some of those lines + scenes hit.  It's the kind of stuff that makes you stop and sit back for a moment.WHAT GAMEPLAY TO EXPECT (since the store page does not articulate it well):Where you can go and what you can do is tied to where you are in the story-line (chapters), which is pretty linear.  There is some side-content, but it's either tied to the bucket list or just achievements (though it does add to the  immersion as well).  Gameplay revolves around exploring (interacting with objects/animals/people) and minigames.  Minigames range from "stealth" (sneaking past people) to problem solving "puzzles" and even combat (mainly a back-and-forth cycle of quick-time events).  I don't usually like this kind of stuff but they pull it off perfectly and it avoids having to implement yet another RPG level/skill system, thus keeping it simpler and story-focused!

_childDocuments_.review: Inspired by the works of Makoto Shinkai (), A Space for the Unbound tells the story of two high school students with seemingly supernatural powers in Loka City, a town based on Surabaya, East Java. What could possibly happen?The  involves you exploring Loka City. Most of the chapters are spent free roaming the town, solving puzzles, and petting cats (and other animals). There will be quick time events to do certain things like fighting or doing certain puzzles and minigames. You can fail these, but you can retry as much as you want. Near the end of a chapter, the game will ask you if you want to proceed to a “point of no return” of that chapter. The  looks better than I expected. The characters are expressive, and the backgrounds in particular look gorgeous too, parts of the game is basically wallpaper material.The  is the best part, and quite difficult to explain without spoiling it. Go experience it and try not to get spoiled!Also, so many cats to pet.

_childDocuments_.review: An abstract anime-adjacent adventure game featuring themes of anxiety and finding one's place.  Heavily character driven with playful adventure game mechanics.  ASFTU has a bit of a slow start, but that's forgiven by the immense amount of character building required to tell this story.  Where the actual meat of the game exists is during Act 2 where you're whimsically "space-diving" into people's hearts to attempt to repair emotional issues, such as mental anguish, anxiety, depression, overwhelming feelings etc.  The game lost my attention a bit in Act 3 where it tries to tie up all the story elements in an extended walk and talk session.  The themes towards the end fell flat with me and my own personal experiences, but I can see how it might resonate more with other people.  My attention seemed to drift as the extremely heavy dialogue driven third act seemed to drone on.  Expect your typical JRPG trope where every character needs to comment on every little thing with plenty of "..." speech bubbles throughout conversation.  Overall though, ASFTU bravely tackles complex themes and emotions that are typically unaddressed in video games or interactive media.

_childDocuments_.review: The most beautifully heartbreaking game I have EVER played!A Space for the Unbound was the best 10 hours I've spent gaming this year.Some of the puzzles in the main story became unpredictably tougher and chaotic towards the end of Chapter 4, which maybe fun for some players, but slowed down the story progress in that segment. Still, nothing that can't be enjoyable.This game is a walk down memory lane for anyone who has struggled with trauma, pain and forgiveness, and it handles these issues with such careful detail, that even those who haven't seen such trouble will be able to understand the lives of their peers who's struggles they may have failed to understand.As someone who is learning to write for story-rich video games, this is one I will always remember, and come back to. Nothing is more important in a story game, over and above the story. And in such a game, because it is interactive, and choices matter, a powerful and well researched story hits home much harder than anything else.Thank you, Mojiken and Toge. This game is truly a treasure.

_childDocuments_.review: The plus:+++ Beautiful combination of pixel art and color, thus maikng a super comfy atmosphere (mostly).+++ VERY good soundtracks of different genre.++ So many references to the 90s Indonesian (pop) culture.+ Cool mini games.+ Sensible pricing for its length.The minus:- The (Bahasa Indonesia) dialogues seem bit too stiff and do not flow from time to time.- Moderate amount of backtracking.- Certain "mechanics" can be unbearable to do, especially towards the end where you have to avoid the falling debris.The middle of the road:* The plot is actually very ordinary but the devs present it in such an amazing way so it kinda cancels each other out.* The sidequests are hit and miss, be it the puzzle or the story, but I can understand they're there to flesh out the side characters even if it's just a little bit, and it works.Overall it's a good game to play when you need to take a break from your high-octane games.Just go in, enjoy the atmosphere, and immerse yourself. Totally recommended.
