_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo and felt this game is a charming one with some potential. However I see the storytelling being very problematic when the plot in the demo so far established a somewhat serious undertone: establishing rapport with an anxious young girl who faces domestic violence from her father. The plot of the demo ended with a huge cliffhanger where the protagonist faces mortal danger… yet all these are forgotten when the main chapter starts. There’s a girlfriend who is basically a new character, and no attempt to address what happened in the demo is made. Essentially, the game starts telling a new story without resolving the existing plot. Even more egregious is the undertone change from serious to flippant, and then arbitrary superpower was introduced, and the game lost me when it started to demand me doing random chores to please the girlfriend.I want to like this game. The art style is gorgeous and the animation is stylish. However the story seems to be a train wreck that sapped every ounce of my desire to keep going. A lesson to be learned: Nostalgia isn’t a panacea, because it’s not material to those who can’t be nostalgic to the backdrop of the game’s settings.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game with a fair price.It starts with a mystery but the story is actually predictable, you know what's going on half way and the rest is about sticking to the plan and being a hero sacrifice for the princess.A Space for the Unbound is made with beautiful pixel arts, using a fairy tale throughout the story to help player to understand what really happens. It also jumps between time and space, using a magic wand to look into the NPC's mind (mini games) to understand, and eventually to change the reactions so to pass certain events.The warm color in the game made it feels relaxing, however, the stories are dark with school bullying, family issues, self-doubt, antisocial revenge, conspiracy on power etc, due to the wideness of the problems the game tried to display, I personally think that this game has reached at a certain point but failed to give a throughout idea of how to face and deal with it. However, I take it as an important game, besides developers giving players a general idea that "you don't need to care about everyone's idea of you" and "learn to forgive yourself and accept your imperfections", sort of positive and right thinking while you are treated unfairly.I finished this game in 6 hours but it feels long. On one hand traveling back and forth trying to save a lost soul, and dealing with multiple issues while seeing the world crumbling down is tiring. On the other hand, all the battles are all about pressing simple keys they are repetitive and tedious and make me sleepy. Good thing is the ending is well made, the art elevates the entire story, however the bitterness is in the air.Honestly I don't feel much for the characters but I think there are quite a few players who do. I hope they find answers.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m conflicted.  I don’t quite know how to feel after finishing A Space for the Unbound.  I sure knew what I would be getting myself into when approaching Mojiken’s (of Banyu Lintar Angin and When the Past was Around fame) newest narrative piece, but I’ll be honest, by the time I was done I was concerned.  There’s a lot of things I found wrong and a lot of things that I didn’t like.  But like Atma’s and Raya’s journey: We see something in its worst, but must bear through the experiences to see the light at the end of the tunnel.  And let me tell you, A Space for the Unbound, despite all its flaws, is worth playing.I don’t want to delve too hard into the plot because the less you know about it the more interesting everything later becomes.  For Atma, a high school student with an aspiration to become a writer, and Raya, his better half with supernatural talents and personality, their lives become a topsy-turvy road to self-discovery and self-understanding baked into a point-and-click style based in a slice-of-life 1990s Indonesia.You’ll rummage around your small rural town in a 2D side scroll, taking in the sights with Mojiken’s beautiful pixel art.  Each section of the town is bursting with color, lovingly handcrafted with a real passion to show off the best qualities of a tightly knit community.  When we start getting into the meat and potatoes of the story, the double shots of beauty continue with a vast range of different areas, each providing an incredible amount of emotion that really sucks you into each frame.  These moments start off fast and furious, as a beautiful intro scene after a tense moment of mystery ties our shoes extra tight for the long road ahead.  From here, you get to learn about the hustle and bustle of the town around you: populated schoolyards and cramped storefronts to internet cafes and multi-theater megaplexes. The town is about 10 or so areas, which you’ll get used to quickly as the main story does not deviate too far from here.The art department really flexes their muscles in conjunction with Unbound’s main plot mechanic: The Spacedive.  Spacediving, done from reading through a mysterious red book that doubles as your Map/Inventory/etc. Hub, allows you to delve into the minds of townsfolk and use intellect and puzzle-solving to help solve internal struggles within the person.  Spacediving puzzles are usually small 1-2 step processes to complete and none are ever too difficult to complete.  The design of gathering items for objectives by fiddling with people’s heads is a very interesting, albeit exploitative mechanic (one the game fully realizes at a certain point).  Need chocolate for a cake but the general store is sold out?  Get the kid who’s hounding it to like veggies more ala a puzzle literally tipping the scales of obsessing to a healthier alternative.  Trying to get someone to stop making fake apocalypse necklaces?  Make him love his kid more!  I’m not kidding.Spacediving is leaned on a lot to move the story throughout its 11-13hr runtime, which becomes a lingering problem as the game progresses.  With Spacediving being used to gather items, a lot of time is spent solely in fetch-quest loops for the majority of the game.  You’ll be provided a list of what items you need, run around town at a brisk-not-fast pace, find the item but realize it’s blocked by something or someone.  You’ll then Spacedive to complete a character-specific puzzle that lasts roughly 2-3 minutes to get the item.  You’ll repeat this process a couple more times to gather the group of items you need to complete the main objective.  And then you’ll do it again.  And again.  And again.  The core gameplay loop is this and it stretches the game to the point of snapping.What makes this even more aggravating is that there’s some good plot development squeezed in between forced filler.  You’ll get 30-40 minutes of some focused character development and tantalizing crumbs to future prospects of current actions, the chapter will end, and then you’ll do the fetch-quest loop for another 2 hours before you can get back into it.  It’s like the game forces you to complete every side-quest in order to play the main mission.  And while the fetch-quests serve their purpose in providing context and buildup to the task at hand, there’s just too much of it that it deflates the tension of each chapter’s cliffhanger with such a long cooldown period.Unbound, funny enough, does have side quests to do as well.  These side quests are tied to the main plotline of the game.  Side quests like collecting certain items require a keen eye around random spots of the town, completing off-beat fetch-quests around random interactions from citizens, and naming cats that are placed randomly around the town.  These things are missable in specific chapters, so you can see the molasses-like speed this game takes when you’re expected to talk to every person in every part of town while looking for every sparkle on the ground and finding every cat while going through the fetch-quests above just to get a morsel of the main plot, and then doing it again for the 4 of the 6 chapters.  I was about halfway through the game when I started to just lose interest, which I guess I only have myself to blame when I realized all of the above is tied to a secret ending and if you miss anything you don’t get the epilogue and you just have to play the whole game over again and not miss anything.  Tall ask.But, after all this: why am I recommending A Space for the Unbound?  Because if you get past the first 4 chapters and get to the leaner, more focused final 2 chapters: you’ll be rewarded with some of the most heart-wrenching, tear-inducing, spirit-lifting writing you’ll get this year.  I cannot express how well the story pays off in the final act, I sat speechless for the last few hours as questions were answered and ends were tied.  It made everything I’ve talked about worth every moment of it, and the impeccable writing, the vibrant art filled with an ungodly amount of personality, and the musical score to tie it all in…dude I can’t even explain it.  It’s so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good.  It fires on all cylinders and slams it home so well that it almost makes me feel bad about how much I did not enjoy the rest of the game.So here I am.  I’m conflicted.  I don’t quite know how to feel after finishing A Space for the Unbound.  The first half of the game is a disastrous case of doing-too-much to keep you in your seat: repetitive objectives, an overabundance of similar puzzles, and missable items that can ruin the full experience of the story if not found.  But the final third puts together a narrative tour de force of emotion and the quality of the writing, tempo, and atmosphere is something that should be celebrated at year’s end.  I fully endorse taking the time to experience this story, just know the long road ahead will be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I didn't expect this game to successfully hook myself for hours because there are many interesting things that can be found and done in the world. Even though at first I played this game for fun and curiosity about indie and pixel art genre games.In terms of story line, this game can be said to be very good and the development of each character can be felt. The story in this game can be said to be simple, but there are still twists that adorn the story line in the game. Apart from the story line, the quests and side quests that are given are quite diverse, starting from finding someone, solving puzzles, completing mini quizzes, even solving math problems. Personally, the level of difficulty in solving puzzles in this game is still relatively easy and challenging, but this goes back to the people who play it. The world scale of this game is wide but not too big and the world is filled with a variety of interesting content so it's worth exploring further. In terms of visuals, I think it's already very good as a pixel art game. The details given are felt so it's easy to distinguish each character in the game because each has its own characteristics.Personally, the weakness in this game is the map system, which sometimes makes me dizzy when I'm reading the map, especially at the start of the game. Therefore, for me, I prefer to memorizing every location while the map is not too big so it's easy to memorize.For those of you who are curious and interested in this game, it's really worth trying.

_childDocuments_.review: This game caught my attention when I saw its trailer some time ago, and I was captivated by its anime-esque art and character design, as well as the supernatural aspects that were shown. Adding to that, I also got really curious about how they would show Indonesian culture, something I haven’t experienced at all before and kinda looked forward to. A Space for the Unbound is a fantastic adventure set in the late 90s in rural Indonesia, wrapped in a magical and mysterious atmosphere, where our protagonist will be able to dive deep into the heart of people and their feelings, in order to help them with their problems and worries; this is all thanks to an enigmatic and curious red book, which grants him such abilities, and alongside them, a really important duty that he’ll come to know little by little.The  begins by presenting a tale about a princess and her faithful feline companion, which is told through its author, Nirmala; she’s a young cartoonist who, together with the main character, is working on a very emotional and peculiar fantasy book. However, she is unable to come up with a good ending, as she is burdened by doubts, insecurities and fear. It is here that we will learn about the special ability of our protagonist, Atma, who will be able to get into people's hearts thanks to the aforementioned red book; and, using this power, we will try to help our friend with her negative thoughts. One thing will lead to another, and we will then be able to wander around the town a bit. However, in the middle of our errand, a torrential rain begins, and after some somewhat dangerous events, the prologue will culminate. I don't want to comment much about it, since I think it's better not to ruin this part of the story by telling it; besides, it's possible to play it totally free since it has its own demo.Leaving aside the prologue, the story will introduce us to a new character: Raya, Atma's girlfriend, and the story will take a course around their school time, where we can see a bit of the typical student concerns, such as the future and the careers that could follow; something quite realistic and with which many can relate. But these kinds of things are a bit overwhelming and boring for a teenager, so Raya comes up with a list of "things to do'' before graduating; and after filling the list with goals to complete, they plan their next days accordingly. From here on, we will enjoy an adventure both pleasant and tense, with plot twists and more mystical or mysterious moments, such as the constant mention of an enigmatic comet, or the magical abilities that Raya also seems to possess. I found the plot very interesting and fun to follow, especially for the different scenes presented throughout our quest to complete the to-do list, and for the interactions between the protagonists and the different characters that are presented along the way. There are several twists and surprises that I'm obviously not going to tell, but it's a story that goes beyond what it seems at first.As far as the  aspect is concerned, A Place for the Unbound is presented to us in a pixel art style that is very pretty and pleasing to the eye. Both the landscapes in the distance, as well as the nearest buildings or pastures of the rural town, look very elaborate and detailed, and feel very in harmony with each other, thus creating a perfect setting. The characters feature fairly large sprites, designed in a somewhat anime style that I liked a lot, and they are also shown in a more detailed way when the perspective is changed to scenes with larger art. I want to add that simple animations such as lip movements or different facial expressions are something that is very appreciated, at least for people like me who are fans of these details. Without a doubt, one of the most charming aspects of the title. Another thing I found interesting was that Atma's red book is our menu that connects the different interfaces of the game, such as the mission log, the inventory and the map. I must say that I really liked the creativity and implementation of this detail.The  is also very nice and immersive, featuring several different and captivating tracks as expected. Tense, lively, calm tunes; few melodies are lacking, and none of them seemed repetitive or overwhelming to me, quite the opposite, as they aroused various emotions in me as the story progressed, and that’s one of the reasons why I play games. At a certain point there is a violinist, the first of several artists that we will be able to meet, and she will play one of the compositions that I liked the most in the game. The songs with vocals were also phenomenal, I would like to add. The music was a great accompaniment throughout the adventure, and I greatly appreciate the work and love that the developers put into this section. Moving on to the , the game is a 2D adventure game, where we will move from left to right through the town while interacting with the environment, be it talking to the different inhabitants of the town, petting cats scattered everywhere, or activating objects. Following the story and exploring around, we will find different puzzles and mini-games to deal with, highlighting two systems especially: the combat, and the "Spacedive". The combat is turn-based, and quite simple, since all we have to do is defend and attack, but I still found it entertaining. When defending, we are presented with a red and green bar in which a cursor moves, and we have to press the interact button at the right time (hitting on the green part) to successfully take cover. On the other hand, in the attack, you have to follow a pattern of keys between the directional and other buttons to hit our enemy, which reminded me a bit of rhythm games, but only for its appearance. It's a nice addition and gives a little more action to some scenes.As for the "Spacedive", it's the main mechanic and obviously a key part of the story, as it's the name of our ability to dive into people's souls, so to say. There will be various situations or mini-games depending on the individual we are trying to help with their afflictions, and it really is like every person is their own world; so we will have to look for different ways to find the solutions to their problems. I thought it was very neat and creative, a perfect touch in the setting. Expanding a little more on the mini-games, we can find a great variety of them, such as moments where we must use stealth, remember patterns or numbers, and answer some trivia of both the game universe and the real world, among others. I quite enjoyed most of them, although some made me wrack my brains (like a certain part where I had to decipher a mathematical formula, asking for help from my friends in Discord because I'm horrible with numbers), but I especially liked how they were implemented in the different points of the game.In , I want to say that I thought the game was excellent. It exceeded all my expectations, and left me very satisfied. Although I must say that the ending gave me mixed feelings, as it is bittersweet but touching (in my opinion). I really enjoyed the game a lot, accompanying Raya and Atma in their adventure, and gradually unveiling the themes it was addressing, such as bullying, depression, and the courage to accept oneself. The incredible soundtrack, the beautiful art and the cool scenes gave me a very nice and unforgettable experience; it is a game that I consider to be highly emotional in many aspects, and I would like to recommend it to anyone looking for emotiveness, and that wish to enjoy a fantastic story that has its roots firmly rooted in reality.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Gorgeous narrative-driven game with great story and a strong message. Can be a bit repetitive but the game's beautiful pixel art and its simple and linear gameplay override that. As an Indonesian myself, I am generally skeptical about Indonesian-made video games which depict the country. But ASFTU, despite the mouthful title, is in my opinion objectively a fantastic game. It does not "force" its Indonesian-ness to the player; rather, the game uses it simply as a backdrop to a much stronger narrative. The game is  about Indonesia, it is simply  in Indonesia (huge difference!). I really respect the devs' decision to do it this way, as it makes the game relatable to worldwide audience instead of only catering to over zealous Indonesians (#adaindonesiacoy anyone?).The main theme of the game carries a strong message about mental health and it was delivered in a very beautiful manner. The allegorical representation of mental states in the form of fantastical elements in the game is spot on. It may have several plot holes (I won't state them to spare you the spoilers. ASFTU is best played cold, neither knowing nor expecting anything from it), but who cares? The overarching message is much more important than the petty details.Gameplay is very simple. While you can control the main character using multiple buttons, most of the interactions will remind players of old school point-and-click adventures, akin to the Monkey Island series. It does get a bit more variation as the game goes, with the Ace Attorney-style court gameplay and the obviously Street Fighter II inspired battle sessions. They remain simple, but they get the game running smoothly enough. Some mechanics like the stealth scenes can be a bit repetitive and even annoying, but never to the point of you yelling at your monitor.Graphics can only be described by one word: gorgeous. Makoto Shinkai and Ghibli-level gorgeous. Sure, not everyone may like the old school pixel art style, but I guess it was a creative choice which, for me personally who grew up with pixellated PS1 RPGs, paid off immensely. And I suppose ASFTU's intended market is exactly my profile: millenials growing up during the 90s. I always consider that Ghibli's strength is in its attention to detail, and ASFTU definitely shines on this one. Cigarette ads, postal boxes, Javanese blangkon, the details in the game is fascinating. Music is an achievement of its own. I do not think it is the best video game music I have had, but it's still a strong and memorable soundtrack. More than anything, it fits the scenes and themes of the game nicely. Slipping some traditional instrument and musical styles to some of its music is well appreciated. The theme songs also resonate to me as strongly "Indonesian indie music", with all the best meanings that come with the term.Overall, if you like gorgeous pixel art and narrative-driven games with a great and tear-jerking story, ASFTU is definitely for you. It just so happens that the story happens in Indonesia during the 90s; for some people that is reason enough to grab this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Just to make things clear from the start, this is a good game but I do not see myself recommending it due to the experience I had with it (and it involves personal tastes).Positive things I can say for sure about the game : - The artstyle is gorgeous : the pixel art is impressive, full of details and very colorful. The game is full of beautiful scenes (cutscenes or in gamepay) - The music is nice : varied and which match with the scenes > even if the ones used at the beginning become a bit repetitive after some time- Some nice game mechanics However, it felt like a pain finishing the game due to its own pace. A Space for the Unbound has the same issue you can find within some narrative games : a lot of fillers.- The story, even if things get cleared up at the end, feels confusing for 3/4 of the game- You have a lot of long dialogues from which you get low to no information from- Some phases feel dragged off with a lot of unnecessary walking / talking / finding things- - Some gameplay phases also feel dragged off due to the repetition of the same thing over and over again - Some cutscenes / sequences are very slow and force you to watch each detail unraveling instead of getting to the conclusion I wanted to finish the game to have a complete view of it since this was very promising. I was a bit disappointed considering the high hopes I had for this game and due to the very nice feedback it had. It still is a good work from the dev team and for sure is a good sign of interesting games to come :)

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, this one got me.The gameplay is your standard "logic puzzle mind dive" affair, nothing terrible but somewhat bland. Objectives necessary to complete the bucket list are very easily missable... There was one objective that I missed by one (1) interaction and it was quite frustrating. The combat is super-bland but I can't see any other way they could have done it without ruining the game's vibe.But that's where my complaints end. This game - no, this story - is an obvious labor of love of those who put it together, and while it is set in Indonesia, you can make the connection of being a high school student pressured by your family and peers regardless of where you are in the world. The expectations that society puts on children and teenagers are very real, even in the 2020s. The characters' struggles with their life choices and finding their identities are also very real.Structurally, the narrative is "formulaic" but engaging throughout most of the game's run until the very end, when it grabs you by the arm and never lets you go. It's equal parts optimistic and sad, and if you have a shred of emotion in your psyche, you will absolutely feel it.The art direction is fantastic as well, deliberately limiting color palettes and making spritework just crunchy enough. Again, a labor of love here.I put A Space for the Unbound alongside other short, cozy story-based games I love like Gris, OneShot, and OPUS Echo of Starsong. Will I play it again myself? Probably not, at least for a while. But I am very glad I played it at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Hm, no, but quite a soulful adventure.The mechanics are simple - walk left or right (or inside houses) and interact with hotspots using a dial with the available options - examine, talk, interact, use with an object from the inventory. You move rather slow (running is possible) and you can't jump, this is not a platformer. You carry a book with you that contains your current objectives, a map, your inventory and your collectibles.The story is taking place in Indonesia and shows a little of the life there, which is always interesting for me as a Westener. You play a young boy, still going to high school, who awakes from a dream and is now doing what kids do in this age, like skipping school to meet with his girlfriend Raya. You pet every cat you find (kicking them is not even possible), talk to everyone, collect various items either to use in puzzles later or just as collectibles. Collectibles are often at remote edges, but they flash so they are easier to spot. You flirt with other girls, build a cat shelter, meet a bully... but somehow you sense that it is not all as beautiful and perfect as it looks. When humans turn into cat zombies and you begin to spacedive into other people's mind, the story becomes a bit... darker.The game works fine with controller, the puzzles are not too difficult (also due to the limited interface - there are not THAT many options to try out).Wholesome, slow adventure, that is a BIT more doleful than it looks at first sight. With lots of cats. And you might weep.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say this is probably one of the best psychological adventure game I've ever played. The part that always amazes me is the story. This is not just a good game with good story; this is A STORY that portrayed beautifully into a game.There are more than just story. It was so sad that I'm in tears, but I'm also relieved that I was able to finish the story. It was heartwarming even if it was very hard and we had to go through many traumatic events. It's just like in real life where we always have to move on, no matter how hard it is or how painful it's gonna get. I could relate to the psychological side of the story that basically told us that even if everything is a mess, we could always be brave, sort out our minds, and move on. I could say for sure that the story is the best part of this game.I really love the fact that this game is not just a simple 2D sidescroller. It has a lot of cool mechanics that make this game unique in its own way.The first thing I'd like to mention is The Rift. I like how they implement a time-travel mechanic into a rift that could be opened by a Magic Wand. It allowed us to travel through dimensions and timelines. I remember playing a game that had this advanced time-travel mechanic just like this. It's called The Silent Age and it was a very good game. Since then, I can never get enough of this amazing mechanic that actually has influence on what would happen in the future if we change the past. This is one of the best time-travel mechanic I encountered in a game, and this game has managed to implement it perfectly.Spacedive is also a great mechanic. I like how they portrayed the inside of people's mind in the spacedive world. It looked so random but it's actually a great representation of how the thoughts conflicting in their own heads. It subtly explained the depression and the desperation that the people experienced through the stories and mission we should accomplish as the player that go through their minds.There are more interesting mechanics in the game, but The Rift and Spacedive definitely are unique in the game and I really like those.I'm not an art person. I can't draw, I can't sing, I can't play music. However, I can say for sure that this pixel-art with calming music is a perfect combination that blends sweetly with the story. I really LOVE the environment in the game! The setting of this game is in a city called Loka. Loka City is a very beautiful small town with neatly lined local houses; stalls; shops that always stock all the necessities; bridge; beautiful trees and flowers; a community center with a mosque, internet cafe, arcade, etc. For those of you who live in Indonesia, this Loka City is set to be located in Indonesia. So it was a very familiar environment that brings us to nostalgia. I also recommend to play in Indonesian Language if you speak that language, it feels much more authentic.Cats are always the winner. The fact that they chose to put cats in this game is such a great decision. It's a perfect addition to the game! Animals are always the best, cats especially. They also put dog, rooster, hen, rat, goose, duck, and finally the legend Kebo Bule and Barong. We can pet them, name them, and they also played a big part in the game.I love puzzles. Puzzles are always one of the best elements in a game. I always like to solve a puzzle. Unfortunately, no matter how much I like puzzles, this is a bit tiring for me. There are no multiple ways to solve the puzzle, which means most puzzles only has a single solution. And this becomes tiring because completing an objective takes a long time and needs to go through so many steps. Those are actually good puzzles. But one chapter for one puzzle? I ended up got tired that I almost didn't want to do the objectives anymore. There's this objective that needs to be done in a very long way and took a surprisingly very long steps: the single objective in Chapter 2. The rest is still fine, I guess. But this puzzle in Chapter 2 took too long to solve, because it went to another objective, and onto the other objectives, again and again to the point it became tiring.Nevertheless, I still like how the story turned out, and it blends well with the objectives and puzzles. So, I guess this will only be a small criticism for this game. I still like it though, don't get me wrong. But yeah, that Chapter 2 puzzle is something else for me.This game is a masterpiece, I could say for sure. I encountered a crucial bug that wouldn't let me finish this game because I really couldn't progress. However, the Dev Team contacted me and give a really helpful solution to install a beta patch in order to fix the bug. I sincerely appreciate the Dev Team for responding to me and actually give a proper solution. Apart from that bug (and maybe the puzzles I mentioned), this is a very good game. The story is told beautifully. It has a perfect execution of how a story-rich adventure game should be. And the cats! Those are the great "addition" which made the game flawless.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like South Korea has been very effectively exporting music, telly shows and more to a wider global audience for some years now, Southeast Asia is on a roll when it comes to . I'd go out and wager that  and others will continue to spearhead this for years to come. 's non-linearly told story puts you in control of a high school student who collaborates with his girlfriend on a bucket list of things to do before graduation, and then  and it's into figuring out what's going on: is the world ending, are there parallel universes, who is the real villain, and other questions that come up in your typical young-adult-with-superpowers story. At the same time, you get to meet plenty of town inhabitants and help them solve various problems.The developers manage not only to convey the distinct culture, architecture, lifestyle of Indonesia in the age before ubiquitous cellphones, but also to always keep the experience and character relationships perfectly relatable for a global audience. Expect to find mentions of various dishes of the local cuisine, though usually without explanation as to what they actually are or how they taste.The gameplay itself consists of walking (or usually running) through game screens with the arrow keys and interacting with everything around. Getting to all the right places in town will have you memorize the layout (or frequently consult the ingame map). There's a timed action system used frequently, which for the majority of the game is not too difficult. Objectives usually just amount to doing the right thing in the right place, with occasional puzzles to clue together from nearby items.As you would expect, as you interact with the world and the characters, you learn the various NPCs backstories and their worries (that you might help address). Especially the central more fleshed out ones will remain vivid in your mind. The game's themes include family, friendship, bullying, forgiveness, self-discovery. From time to time, there is this unfortunate game design antipattern that I call the "", heavily used in Odyssey and Valhalla so they can pretend they qualify as RPGs: in a conversation you get to pick between two or very rarely three mutually exclusive options that result in maybe two or three lines of dialogue without any other further impact or relevance, and there is no way to access the lines hidden behind the choice you did not take (beyond reloading the latest save and perhaps replaying a few minutes of the game).Depending on your pace and completionism levels, I'd estimate 8–12 hours to finish the game. While you cannot alter how the story unfolds, the bucket list mechanic essentially amounts to missable Steam Achievements. At the time of writing, only about a seventh of the users who finished the story also did everything else (to reach the "true ending"). For that, you truly must play with a guide at hand to know where to find collectibles (cats to pet, and name!, as well as bottle caps of Indonesian drinks) and when to go look for some other NPCs. At least one of these achievements is also frustratingly difficult: in the town's arcade, the previously mentioned timed action system has you execute fighting game combos with very tight timing. Theoretically you could write them down or memorize them ahead of time, but neither is a pleasant idea. The arcade machine is only accessible in the first third or so of the game, and successfully braving this challenge will make most of the other upcoming timed input sequences feel like a walk in the park. There is another slightly frustrating achievement where you must press the interact button with the right rhythm 70 times, and if you exceed 50 but don't reach 70 you have to reload your latest save. (I used  and additionally  and using those avoided what I would consider excessive story spoilers.)I think even the song interludes you get from time to time are missable, so only a fraction of players (again judging by achievement stats) have even reached them.Personally, I wasn't a particular fan of where the overall story went about halfway through the game (from chapter 4 on), but as I don't think my complaints will be shared by too many readers, I won't hold it against the game.I would recommend the game to people who enjoy touching storytelling and don't mind QTE-like action & dodging sequences. Pretty much every time you interact with a cat (or other animal) in town, you get a little speech bubble with a heart emoticon, so if you find that sort of thing heartwarming, go and press that buy button.However,  does not attempt to be /. If you want to solve truly complex puzzles, abhor any real-time keyboarding challenges, expect laugh-out-loud comedy, or want either a branching story or otherwise non-linear gameplay, you won't find these here.

_childDocuments_.review: A poignant narrative unfolded as I immersed myself in the story of a young girl grappling with autism and depression, bringing me to tears multiple times. Up until Chapter 5, I had rated it an eight, but the depth of emotion and revelation in that chapter elevated it to a solid ten in my book. Beyond the psychological aspects, the game masterfully depicted how we often shy away from confronting our true selves, succumbing to the fear of meeting our own expectations. The journey of redemption, discovering one's true essence, and finding solid ground resonated profoundly with me. Life isn't always a smooth sail, and this game beautifully conveyed that it's alright to stumble along the way. The imagery of sitting together on the roof, gazing at the stars as the world seemingly crumbles, was a powerful metaphor for cherishing our emotions and memories. I'm sincerely grateful for the experience of playing such a remarkable game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn to A Space For The Unbound by its lovely pixel art, and after playing the demo, I waited with bathed breath for half a year for its release. I bought the game immediately when it came out, then proceeded to forget about it for the next couple of months, until I finally pulled myself together to play itIt's a masterpiece, it's emotional and honest, exploring many themes, that a lot of people can relate to, to some extent for better or for worse. The story is very linear, but the game still gives you enough freedom to explore at your own will, where the game nails the vibe of the setting and the atmosphere. The gameplay is mainly dialogue and fetch quests running back and forth, but the story and the art, as well as the soundtrack work well to make sure this doesn't feel like a chore, and in my case, I found it extremely satisfying.My one criticism, is that if you miss a collectible, there's a high chance that you won't be able to get it later after you've advanced the story too much, this might be okay for people who don't mind replaying chapters or even the entire game, but for me it was frustrating, and more than once resulted in me going back and skipping through stuff that I'd previously spent 2 hours playing through.Going back to the story itself, yes, it did make me cry towards the end. It's bittersweet, relieving, painful and joyous. I highly recommend this game, and if you decide to play it, do so with no prior knowledge.

The puzzle design has issue where all the puzzles are either over-engineered or just tedious, most of them just being a series of "get these three things to make this one thing". _childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a thumbs up, I really wish I could. Not only because of the fact that it's an indie game where obvious effort and love was put into it, but also the music and atmosphere are really beautiful and moving. And you don't often see Indonesia as a location for video games, so representation is really great as you learn more about different cultures and realities of life that aren't always Eurocentric or Western-oriented. However, as the game progressed, I found several things to be visibly annoying until they completely detracted from the gaming experience and I just wanted it to come to an end merely for the sake of finishing it. Overall, it felt like a complete chore to me and my completionist maniac mind had to get it done with.Although the prologue and the first chapter were more than promising, the fetch-quests-esque features of the game got on my nerves very quickly. You are transported from one place to the next with forced routes for a lot of the time, the dialogues are not really profound, the game mechanics are exhausting and tedious after a while and even the story, which is actually quite profound and emotional, was not really innovative or earth-shattering to me. It doesn't have to be, but I couldn't really empathize with the characters, especially the protagonist Atma. He seems a bit passive and pseudo-heroic in everything and I couldn't really come to terms with this narrative. The game is artificially drawn out and the gameplay quickly becomes repetitive and boring. The worst thing for me was the fact that the game often doesn't even take my manual save into account and simply transports me to where it was automatically saved for the last time. I constantly had to intuitively assess when I could leave the game for good to avoid having to replay certain events and dialogues that had already taken place. I often don't have the attention span to play games for that long at a time, especially when I get bored with the gameplay and am forced to continue until the next chapter or checkpoint (neither of which I can predict). The game had nice aspects and features, but unfortunately it wasn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Memories are like, a million shards of shattered glass lying unanimated in the bottomless pit that we call inner space. You pick one up, it slices your finger and reminds you why you never recalled it in the first place. So you drown it out and make up a facade of remedial mental wellness. "Facade". I like that word. At some point, the facade no longer exists as an abstract mental blockage, but becomes a definitive reality, the reality that doesn't seem quite right from the outside eyes but does it matter if it's significant to its creator? Well yes, actually. As someone who suffered from high school bullying in high frequency and taught myself to block out bad memories to the point that the majority of my past is missing from my head, I don't think I've ever experienced any media with a "your defense mechanism isn't effective if you don't actively fight back the anguish" message as poignant as A Space for the Unbound. It comes in the form of coming to terms with your identities, reshaping your perspective to those around you, making amend to the rage monster inside, seeing grief as the companion to bring you to the next journey, and Street Fighter-style input sequence and QTE blocking even. The air you breathe is the sadness you bear. Dealing with turmoils is a fight in motion, and fighting yourself is the biggest challenge that any individual can see yourself to overcome.Bake a cake, pet some cats, roleplay as Phoenix Wright, getting lost in the wind of hometown nostalgia. Anguish existentialism is inevitable and messy, but nobody promises you the answer, you have to look for it. What also is inevitable is by the time the storm is over and the sky is clear, the hand that let you go is no longer a faint memory cutting deep in your skin, but rather the glass shard that shows you the future ahead.While I appreciate Lost Judgment's more realist and societal approach to bullying as subject matter, I give my utmost appreciation to A Space for the Unbound, for giving us not just a space, but mercy and tenderness to who we are. Open the door, fill your bucket list, be somewhat troublesome (or not), and maybe the next day will shine brighter than the last.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe this game in one word, it's marvelous.The story is absolutely astounding, the music is great, the characters are great, and although the gameplay is standard, it's nothing bad by no means. Make sure to go into this fully blind if you're set on buying it, it's one of those games where experiencing everything blind makes it even more enjoyable. The best aspect of the game is definitely the story, which I don't want to give away in the slightest as it's that good. The only piece of advice I will give is to make sure you complete all of the Bucket List, and the best way to do that is by checking/exploring every area in each chapter. Talk to every NPC, pet every cat (Dead serious), and check the ground, all furniture, and all objects to gain bottle caps. If you're able to get everything checked, trust me it'll be worth it. The game is formatted in five core chapters with a prologue at the start and an epilogue at the end, and from my play time the game's about eight to maybe ten hours long, so not super long. Overall it's a very solid 8/10, which to me means it's great. Highly recommend! I hope this game gets more attention and for the development team to keep making high quality gems like this.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most emotional stories I've ever experienced in a game. While the mechanics could occasionally be tedious, it was never difficult and messing up wasn't punishing.If you are looking for a profound emotional story in a beautiful package, look no further than A Space for the Unbound.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound opens with a fairytale, one about friendship, loss, and self-acceptance that quickly frames a big-brother relationship between small town teenager Atma and budding storyteller Nirmala. Soon, Atma is thrust out of his routine and into a dream-induced series of surreal breaks in reality, forcing him to find the truth about the many people in his quaint waterfront city and his supposed girlfriend Raya. A Space for the Unbound spares no time creating a suspenseful mystery adventure, but paces its 11 hour runtime with surprisingly emotional and complex beats that tell a larger narrative that culminates in one of the more subtle powerhouses of 2023.Mainly, A Space for the Unbound takes the form of a traditional point and click adventure game, running around the small, but dense town in order to pick up various items and clues to progress your investigation into the truth behind strange events. Apart from the standard dialogue and item interactions, Atma can use an ability called Spacedive, which allows him to inhabit the subconscious mind of its target and change their heart not unlike the Persona series. In contrast to the charming tight-knit community of the town, Spacedives present a more raw and unhinged interpretation of the psyche of your neighbors and enemies. Many of the game's most inventive ideas are explored within the depths of the mind and Atma as a vessel for change transforms him into an engaging protagonist, especially as he begins to consider if changing the desires of those around him is manipulative and wrong. The entire game wrestles with difficult moral dillemmas and despite a seemingly singular ending, the game give you the shadow of choice and agency.One of the most staggering elements of A Space for the Unbound is in its presentation; a gorgeous rendition of 1980s Indonesia portrayed in a variety of pixel art setpieces and sonic landscapes. The soundtrack is an absolute standout, with incredible range from catchy earworms to heart-wrenching supporting pieces to the game's heavier moments. The dialogue is a masterclass in realistic conversation, while not losing some goofy and downright hilarious beats of writing (a standout is a quiz-obsessed trio of fellow students). The only exception to the game's flawless exterior is a lack of voice acting, which in my opinion could have been the setup to one of the most incredible performances in games.A Space for the Unbound is not a game I really want to talk much about in premise. It's much more worth taking it all in on blind faith and discovering the charm on your own terms. Whether you fall in love with the charming cast or just like one of the many side activities like collecting bottle caps or petting every cat, there is a lot to love with this game, and it's something you need to check off your bucket list.

_childDocuments_.review: Ho boy. I can see why the reviews are "Overwhelmingly Positive." That was an experience. Beautiful game, and heart-wrenching and honestly, a good representation of what it's representing. Not many games managed to make me feel as much as this did, like a rarity. And maybe a few things hit home a bit. The writing is wonderful, the characters memorable, the artstyle beautiful, the music fantastic, the gameplay delivers what it needs to, the puzzles make you think but are logical and make sense without you resorting to the "try all the combinations and see if it works" method like in some classic adventure games, The game made me do algebra, so I should mark it down a point, exposing me for my poor maths skills! It has a battle system, which does its job but is not one of the game's focuses because it's more of an adventure/mystery game, but interesting enough to be engaging but never draws itself out. There are some Life is Strange vibes, in that I think if people liked it for its story, they'll probably like this, but these guys definitely did their own thing here, but I think if I were to compare it to another game, this is the closest I can think of. The game can hit on some very depressing themes, but it is well paced out with more relaxed and warming moments. And I quite like the setting, 90's Indonesia. I know it's an Indonesia studio, but hey, I like seeing more of the world represented in video games.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished a space for the unbound yesterday, and my heart still feels heavy. I found myself relating to Raya on some way. I shed tears multiple times, and each moment touched my heart in unexpected ways. The endgame in particular was the peak of emotion for me. As the story progressed to its climax, my tears poured uncontrollably, capturing emotions that i can't quite explainThere's something about it that struck me. Maybe it because of the plot or just simply because it was set in Indonesia. It felt eerily familiar as if it reflected some of my own experiences.Accepting things as they are has always been one of the hardest things for me. I often find myself trapped in a situation where I still yearning for the past, unable to fully embrace the present because I can't let go of what once was. There's a comfort in the past, in the memories that I simply refuse to let go—that those moments were gone. I realize now that it's this refusal—this stupidity to accept that leaving me stuck in a state of limboIn hindsight, my ignorance was the root of this mess. Instead of accepting that the past cannot be changed, I clung to the pleasant recollections of what once was and made a valiant effort to bring them back. Though deep down, I knew it was simply impossible to make things "go back to how they used to be" to mend things and this denial of reality only led to more pain and suffering because I'm just struggling to accept that some things are out of control and that's completely okay.I remember reading this quote somewhere, It sounds like "healing come when you allow it to happen". Perhaps, I was so profoundly wounded and could not see a way out, I wrote off this thought as naive at the time. I know it may sound stupid but there was a part of me that refuse to heal—that I don't mind feel this way for god knows how long. Perhaps I was afraid of what's coming on would entail, of having to let go of the old pain's comfort.However, I've been making an effort lately to be more accepting of the idea. I've been trying to accept that the past is the past and clinging to it would only hinder my growth. I've come to understand that it's simply not just unhealthy but also unfair to myself to keep living in the shadow of what once was.From this game, I've learned that no matter how much we cherish the past, It reminds me that I eventually have to let it go. The difficulty of clinging to memories we hold dear and the significance of moving on are both captured beautifully in the game. I have to let go of what once was and just can't linger there anymore. No matter uncertain the future may seem, I have to welcome the present and the future. For what's past is pastI could go on and on about this game but I'm afraid to say too much because I don't want to spoil the story to you who haven't played it yet. With all of its nuances and intricacies, best experienced firsthand. It's more than just a game, it's a journey of self discovery, acceptance, and ultimately, healing. I'll remember this story for a very long time because for the lack of better term, beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review:
A Space For The Unbound is a slice-of-life adventure game with beautiful pixel art set in the late 90s rural Indonesia that tells a story about overcoming anxiety, depression, and the relationship between a boy and a girl with supernatural powers.

Follow two high school sweethearts, Atma and Raya, on a journey of self-discovery at the end of their high school years. When a mysteriously supernatural power is suddenly unleashed threatening their existence, they must explore and investigate their town to uncover hidden secrets, face the end of the world, and perhaps learn more about each other.

name: Starship Troopers: Terran Command
detailed_description: The population of the harsh desert planet Kwalasha needs our help. Their peaceful lives, working in the mining industry, have been disturbed by a threat that they cannot face alone: the Arachnids. Under Colonel Hawthorne’s command, the Mobile Infantry will take back control of the planet and smash everything that has more than two legs. Enlist in this exciting military campaign, meet inspiring characters, visit amazing locations and do your part in the heroic war against the Bug! The Arachnids may have virtually limitless numbers, but they lack the thorough tactical training that the Mobile Infantry enjoys. Position your units in advantageous choke points or on higher elevations. Be wary, however, that battle mechanics such as True Line of Sight and True Line of Fire may limit your field of fire and allow the treacherous Bugs to lay in ambush. Optimize your army by choosing from a wide range of specialized unit types, each with its own strengths, weaknesses and set of unlockable elite abilities. Rifle Troopers can use their shotgun ability to hold back large numbers of Arachnids, M11 Marauders bipeds can unleash a withering mortar barrage and the Fleet Liaison can call down dropships with reinforcements or direct an airstrike to wipe out whole swaths of enemies. The Bug infestation is rooted in elaborate underground hives. These present a unique challenge that demands a delicate balance between aggression and defense. Beware of the numerous tunnel openings, from which hordes of Arachnids can emerge. To eradicate the Bug problem for good, their nests must be eradicated!

_childDocuments_.review: Short game, has a few bugs. The narrative and tone of the game is hilarious, with the dialogue depicting incompetent leadership throwing away the lives of their subordinates for little to no tactic advantage. Just like in real life.In all seriousness, the world of Starship Troopers really has no 2nd thoughts about throwing wave after wave of humans at a problem. The game play shows this, where even with perfect positioning, sometimes the only solution to a problem is to throw bodies upon bodies at it until nothing is left. Huge fan of the movie, the 12-15 hour campaign and scenario list leaves a bit to be desired. This is not an RTS like Starcraft, there are no resources to manage besides drop ship count and the amount of units allotted to you during your respective mission. It is difficult, but not impossible for your position to be regularly overrun, and the AI is pretty consistent on trying to take your bases and outposts from you. Overall, the AI isn't bad at all, and there is a huge difficulty spike starting from about mission 10 or so onward. Gameplay can be extremely hectic until you secure solid footing to make a concerted push against the objective. The hive system is pretty fantastic, and often capturing these enemy spawning nodes is a more difficult task than whatever the primary objective is, especially as the enemy unit list & hive release count ramps up the longer you take to complete an objective. Overall, I highly recommend this title- its short and sweet, not perfect, but it scratches that RTS itch like few others.P.s.The missions that will give you the most trouble are those in tunnels and mines, rather than in the overworld. Limited resources with units that are generally disposable can lead to frustration, take that into account before you buy, otherwise I highly recommend it for anyone who enjoys the universe of Starship Troopers and RTS lovers in general.

_childDocuments_.review: People complain in the forums that all of the good reviews are nostalgia bait stating a flimsy quote with >1 hour in the game. I'll start with the bad first -The story is not incredible. Most maps are linear, not allowing the player to expand out. The maps that aren't linear makes the player have problems with stray hordes of bugs coming upon their outposts and bringing them down. This feels more like a distraction from the objective if anything. Most turrets will be too weak to hold down a base and too much investment in one base will mean too little investment in the other. Sometimes you can clear out nearby hives to prevent attacks permanently, but bug spawners will be hidden out in the desert area where you can hardly see anything. This means if you want to lock down a base you'll have to spend a good amount of time scouring the surrounding area.If the tactical officer's buff is a passive aura, it is hard to tell whether it is on or not.Placing your units under "attack and move" will make the units clump together, and they will often block each other from firing. This usually leads to their death if you're not paying attention.One mission where you're supposed to be defending a half-built massive wall doesn't feel as fun as it should. The chokepoints should be more chokey and clear. There's not a lot of room for tactical planning, and the bugs come too fast to do any planning. Doubling that there is no tactical pause makes that level extra unfun.Scorpion bugs have too much health, or at least for rocket troops. On normal it takes ~3 rockets just to kill one. Maybe make it to where it just takes 2?I found on some levels I would just spam the most powerful unit I had to break up an area, no matter how much diversity I had in my back lines it didn't help.Plasma troopers are exceptionally weak. They feel good at first, but are outshined by MK2s and far outshined by powered armor troops. It doesn't feel like they fill a niche.There is no survival / defense mode.Fleet lia / radio operators often contend for the same spot, making the radio operators obsolete for the most part.Many people complain about the lack of multiplayer, and I'll complain for the lack of a skirmish mode.Waiting on dropships to come down to replace your troops is a pain in the back.You can't play as the bugs. :(The good? Well, to compensate for the bare bones story the gameplay was wonderful for me. On most of the levels it actually matters what your troop composition is. Rockets are useful for weakening bigger enemies and snipers are useful for spitters. Riflemen / Mk2s / Powered Armor troops all fill the same category, but are different enough to be enjoyable. I enjoyed defending bases with engineer turrets. Fleet lias helps act as a medic and the tact officer with his abilities can be potent. The marauders are just mechs for military porn.Despite the scorpion bugs, I've never felt that the difficulty was too harsh on me as there was always a way to get past a hard spot.The game looks good and runs great, I can see myself playing it again in the future. Especially if there are more updates.Linear parts of the game kept me interested, and I felt like I wanted to take time exploring areas in them to find little bits here and there.The tutorial is interesting.Most bugs feel balanced, and the bug composition/variety is enough to keep the gameplay interesting to force you to change your tactics.Fort Meru is fun :)This isn't a "spam RTS" where you just click to get as many units as fast as possible and then rush your opponent with them. By forcing the player to position their troops to have line of sight, the game avoid that.Overall -I feel like a lot of people are expecting too much too early, and with most games that are released like this sometimes it's hard to see the merits of the gameplay at current hand and it's easy to complain, as we want more. Furthermore, I can't think of many good RTS-es like this that have come out recently.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a helluva lot of fun, but unfortunately the game eventually reaches a point where it's not the bugs you're expecting that start screwing you over. The AI tends to prioritize your units when it comes to blocked sightlines and being unable to shoot in directions, but the arachnids have no problem attacking your troopers through solid walls, hiding behind a glitchy lamp post that somehow your troopers can't shoot around, or your troopers just straight up ignoring certain enemies, despite actively being killed by them. The worst contenders are the Spitterbugs, your troopers naturally shoot the nearest enemy, but you can order them to shoot specific enemies. This is important when it comes to ranged bugs that are capable of wiping out your squads or specialist teams fairly quickly. Sadly, your troopers will sometimes just aim at the enemy you order them to shoot, before resuming attacking the nearest unit of warriors while slowly being killed by the spitterbug's acid. At that point it feels more like you're fighting your own troopers' lack of intelligence than the arachnids themselves.I will say, I have sunk 17 hours into this game despite the few glitches I've encountered, with most of them just requiring me to pay extra attention to some of my more particularly stubborn troopers, or adjust positions to better hit an enemy hiding behind a seemingly invisible wall. The characters and troopers themselves all have their own unique but enjoyable quirks, and I think this is the only game where the enemy actively killing the civilians that my army is supposed to be protecting causes me to breathe a sigh of relief that it's just a bunch of unarmed civilians being mauled by horrible space bugs, and not my troopers for once.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun in the sense that it follows the Starship trooper story line. It's a decent game, it'll entertain you for a few days but I do have several issues with it that I hope are addressed later on. 1.  Scenarios and campaign are great but there should have been some sort of infinite wave defense mode where you can upgrade your base and strive to survive as long as possible. 2. Base building doesn't exist, its more unlocking than actually building. Feels like this and the defense mode game-play was a major missed opportunity. Imagine how fun it would have been to be able to dig the hole you die in, in a mode where you're certain to die eventually. This would have probably allowed for multiplayer too, you and a homie could be dying together.3. Units leveling up and getting "promoted" doesn't improve the unit in the same way many other RTS's do it. Your unit doesn't gain increased fire rate, or accuracy, or any of the things that should be involved with units leveling and being promoted. They just unlock abilities that should have already been available.  For example, your rifle units either can be promoted to use a bundle grenade or use a shotgun... nobody should need a promotion in order to throw a "bundle" of grenades (this is also kind of pointless since there is already a normal grenade ability and throwing one or the other results in around a 30 sec cool down for both). Unit promotions should involve some sort of more direct improvement4. The unit pool is also limited. Sure their is around 10 (probably off by 1-3 more) "unique" units, but most of what can be considered line infantry is just a rifle trooper with a fancier gun or a power suit. So already a third or fourth of the "unique" units are just variants of normal troopers. The only vehicle unit is a mech, could have added a tank or APC of some sort. They could have at least let me play as the bugs or something. In short, this game could have, and should be more. It's very lacking, which makes the game feel repetitive after the fourth mission. If your manage to make your way through all the missions and scenarios, theirs nothing left, no replay-ability. For $20 you could have Red Alert 3 or for $30 more you could have Age of empires 3. Hopefully more updates will come along that can address some of these issues at least. Update: Finished the entire campaign. Read somewhere that horde mode and another mode are planned. This also apparently was done a very small team, with this fact and what is expected, i'm going to say get it. Support the devs for more content. Although there are things lacking, they weren't slacking and just randomly gluing things together, I enjoyed the game even during the repetitive missions. Only saddened that there wasn't more. Also please fix the weird jittering with unit badges when zooming out.

_childDocuments_.review: Huge SST fan here. I've read the book. I've watched the OVA, the movie, the CGI kids show from 2000, all the sequels. There are fun elements from each of them in the game. Bravo! I loved it.Also a huge RTS fan here. The game itself is a fun RTS. Each skirmish in the game is almost like a puzzle one must figure out with the correct combination of units in the correct spot at the correct time. Brilliant.Here's what I encountered and what I would recommend that could improve the game:I select a gun turret. I hit 'J' to demolish it. Awesome, that's a good way to quickly get rid of them- oh wait now I have to use my mouse and drag it over to click "Yes". Another hotkey would be good to streamline that, perhaps 'J' again?Engies should be able to repair any structure that's damageable like doors.Entering a bug hive is janky with multiple units. They go one at a time, but the problem is that its unclear how long they will take. Even after the hive is clear, they still go in costing me time and resources on the battlefield. Its messy and unclear; especially when my clearing has failed and now they are all going to die.A lot of secondary objectives can be ignored without penalty or loss of reward. Specifically that "Ambush the column of Arachnids" in that canyon. Yeah, or I could just wait and have my troopers live without consequences.Some clickable units or structures have no face tile in the corner. I also wish the face tiles were bigger so I can enjoy the artwork.For the story, the propaganda vignettes are brilliant, but might I suggest a sort of a simple Starcraft 1 briefing room, just to help build up that story and flush out these characters. There have been many times when the game will stop just for these dialogues. It just slows things down.  A briefing room intro will help give you room to help us as players empathize with our troopers.I love that each unit has a unique voice. Go further with that! Another fun thing you could do is from War/Starcraft; the units could say more wild things as you keep clicking on them. "Rock and roll!"I wish I could preposition my troopers, a la C&C 3 TWs. By holding down the right click, I could choose a simple formation and its depth and direction. Its a mechanic that made things more reliable.Great game! I want more though! This is my wish list: More campaigns, survival mode, co-op, and a playable Arachnid faction and campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: The game concept is definitely a good one  - I never got to watch all the movies except the first one, but loved the first movie enough to give this game a go; and since I do love my Sci-Fi RTS games, I wasn't going to pass this one up.However; unlike other Sci-Fi RTS games, this was unfortunately a disappointment to me.The gameplay got a little too repetitive and I am absolutely HATING how restricted the Base-building/army construction is. Other RTS games I've played usually do one or two missions where it's letting you learn the ropes of the game, but you still have so much more creative freedom in those games. It's only when you start getting later into the game that there is a little more freedom when it comes to Units and Army Building, but outside that, there isn't much else.Starship Troopers Terran Command I just found forced/guided you along certain paths rather than let you create your own way of doing things; taking away a lot of that creative freedom that makes RTS games - in my opinion - amazing.On top of that:- I feel the voicelines do need a little... "work" you could say; some of the voicelines are SUPER overused to the point that I swear every second word used is "APE".- The game is BUGGY - and I sadly do not say this as a Pun. I've had to reset to last saves many times because either my troops kept walking into large terrain formations that glitched them out and got them all killed, or because missions failed to actually progress when an objective was completed.- Going off the lack of creative freedom; I felt the game was a massive Tutorial. It keeps telling you what to do to complete the objective rather than letting you work it out yourself - completely throwing out a good chunk of that "strategy" side of things. Other restricting features were how resources were earned/given - it felt so much like a time-burner just trying to get more Supplies/War Support.I do intend to finish the game at some point; just sadly it isn't the RTS for me - I like having creative freedom with my RTS games when it comes to Base Building, methods on tackling objectives without the games assistance, and army building, and sadly I don't feel that Creativity is there.

Its more of that, with more units, special abilities when units get to top rank and new enemies. I haven't completed it yet so perhaps it will change my perspective as I get further in. _childDocuments_.review: First off, if you haven't, go watch the 1997 film Starship Troopers. It'll provide context and give you an understanding of the universe in where this game takes place. I greatly enjoyed this game as it brought an IP that I thoroughly enjoyed into a video game that I had a chance to play as the other video games made weren't as known or never really took off. My hope is that this spearheads more games and content in the Starship Trooper franchise, similar to how Aliens Fireteam Elite is. For now, there's on a Single-Player campaign and 2 scenario missions. But more content is suppose to be added at a later time.  Pros:+Pretty good story+Combat requires positioning of soldiers which can lead to both fun and stressful situations+Every unit type originates from the movies from the Riflemen from SST 1 to Power armored Infantry from SST Invasion/Traitor of Mars.+Propaganda introductions to each mission is hilarious to watch+Enjoyable and overall memorable mission experience+You're doing your partCons-Scorpion Bugs-Soldiers sometimes don't move when you order them to target a specific target if that target is behind cover, EX being  a hill side. -Scorpion Bugs-Tanker Bugs need a buff, they don't feel like a threat-No Bug Campaign or Skirmish mode or horde mode. -Unit resupply doors in missions where you have a limited amount of troopers isn't explained-Scorpion bug are beyond annoying-Snipers are more or less useless beyond limited trooper missions-Harder difficulties can feel unfair and seem like they require more luck than skill-Trooper firing animations aren't the best-Not much repeatability. Yet. Overall I personally rate this 7.5/10. The game is genuinely fun and had me rethink my strategies and approaches to different situations. If they add additional content, then for sure I can see this game being more popular.

_childDocuments_.review: Would you like to know more?To start off, it's a solid RTS in the Starship Troopers world, it captures that feel of being in the federation by having it somewhat showcase the game in the "FedNet" - A tv show/channel - then during gameplay you feel like a you're commanding your units around like in any other RTS like C&C etc.There's times where I'm stopping to rethink or combat a incoming bug horde attack, keep a certain VIP unit alive, or just plan my move to counter a bug type that I've been alerted to.On that, there's a soft lack of UI tips and tutorial, in game it's just "move unit here", "attack this", "move here" that's the tutorial. On one hand, this was rather bland and basic, and I had to just work out how to set up a firing line myself (left click and drag in the direction you want troops to face)  along with what the red/orange/green crosshair above your units mean. (it's whether they have line of fire on a bug, red is no line of fire, orange is half of them can shoot, green everyone shoots, no-one quits) - The other hand this made me go "Oh, neat, that's how I do that"  - This could be a issue to some people of course.Next good point, they've captured horde amounts well. - You'll watch masses of bugs rush to your defensive outpost, your troops on the walls and blasting away. Then after the horde, you get an objective to send troops to collect something or clear out a bug nest a distance outside the base and there'll be a time limit before the next horde comes.  - Which personally I found a really cool way to do this.The "issues" so far is there's no camera rotation, which at times I wish I could do, but it's not a requirement.Next, base building isn't really a thing, yes you'll find "outposts" that you'll need to capture by having troops stand by them for a while, then you can pick upgrades based on what "resources" you have, and that'll allow you to request different troops. But the problem is; it didn't explain the "resources" at all.One mission, I saw I had 10 "supplies" for troops (each troop costs a different amount of supplies), I had three bases captured and was pushing to a big bug nest, where I started loosing units. I wasn't aware of a Tanker bug removing my other bases (FYI you don't permanently lose them), then I saw I had a no supplies and only three units alive.I had no idea how to proceed, I couldn't reclaim my bases because I was heavily outnumbered and there was a Tanker. It wasn't till I restarted the mission that I saw the "supplies" scattered around the map, I had presumed they was for "war support" - (Base building resource) which I didn't need, but nope, supplies for troops.Game didn't explain that either.But all in all, it's a solid RTS, that I believe on higher difficulties would require more tactical thinking and gameplay (I'm on normal and have only lost one and restarted twice because of errors on my part)Whether it'll be a repeat game I'll play is questionable, the single player is fun so far, and there's challenges as well. It depends whether the Dev's expand on the game to provide more and better replay ability

_childDocuments_.review: Insanely good game and a very good RTS take on a classic movie universe. There are mechanics in the game that are revolutionary for an RTS (for example you can't shoot through your units, you actually have to make an effective firing line). There is a unit for just about every scenario, and I found myself using different goups of units in different scenarios and environments. Additionally, this is a very fine looking game, and comes with very few bugs (no pun intended; there are actually a lot of "Bugs" :P). Before we get confused I'll list a few of the more notable issues I've noticed: - Some minor pathfinding issues in which units would get stuck on nothing. More often then not repeating the move order fixes the issue.  - Sometimes hives constantly spawn bugs even when they're not threatened, which ultimately results in me confronting literally hundreds of bugs when I finally decide to clear out a hive. I am not sure if this is a mechanic to dissuade people who take their time (like me) but it can make some missions extremely difficult if those hives are not dealt with quickly. - There were a few issues with troopers moving into hives that were already cleared, and I didn't explicitly order them into those tunnels. - Not really a bug, but sometimes units can shoot through hills.  - Sometimes unit icons get really big, or sometimes they stay hanging over an area that the unit is not at. Other times, the icons move on their own but then pop back into the right spot. - Some issues with select/de-selecting units, but nothing bad.Besides that, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of the series and looking for a good RTS to sink some 15-20 hours into. I'm excited to see if anything else is done with this game, it's really good!

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing how such a small thing can have such a negative effect.It's the voice-acting, you see. It's absolutely terrible, and it brings down the whole game. It's just so dull and amateur, and when the other elements of the game are also struggling to achieve mediocrity, having such a weight dragging it down is the last thing the game needs.Because, as I said, the rest of the game really isn't that good either. Visually, it's not that exciting, and it's map and mission design are far too linear and, frankly, the whole thing is a bit boring. The game also utilizes the movie license, which - while entertaining enough on film - just doesn't seem a good fit for a video game. But limited as the game is, the combat is satisfying and it's fun to gun down hundreds of giant bugs. Or it would be if the voice-acting just didn't disrupt the sense of immersion by how horrid it is.Maybe I should give the game another chance, except this time play it with the speech disabled. Perhaps I'd have more fun that way. But, honestly, it just doesn't seem worth the effort.

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely great single player RTS that nails the movie setting completely. No unit, mission or propaganda video feels out of place. Excellent atmosphere and tension building, especially with the underground missions.On brutal it can be definitely challenging at times (First playthough in my case), but with some good micro managing, unit placement (Line of sight/fire is a excellent mechanic btw) and broad unit selection it can be done. Balancing is excellent, some missions can be made easier by destroying bug sources before you trigger a certain milestone.Some things are annoying: Wayfinding can be iffy at times. Attack move doesn't allow to align units like normal move does. Alignment can be critical, so this one can break it at times on brutal. But those are only minor complaints. Aligment could even be intentional to increase the micro management workload.I'd have bought this at full price, had I known how good it is.
