_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps the best game I have played all year. The clear love of history, attention to detail and historical accuracy really makes this a must buy for any history nerd. The storytelling is magnificent, with complex moral quandaries and difficult choices, and few right answers that really makes you think about your decision making. The dialogue system is extremely fun and witty and Obsidian manages to thread the needle on making Andreas both his own distinct character beyond a blank slate for the player, while also giving the player the ability to make their own unique version of Andreas, the background and education selections are a stroke of genius in this regard, giving Andreas different worldviews to pull off, every Andreas believes they are doing the right thing by trying to solve the mystery and attempting to save the day, yet an Andreas who spent his years in Switzerland reading books and studying imperial law and an Andreas who spent time travelling through Italy studying the Occult and getting into fights will have completely different understandings of why what they are doing is right.  Pentiment is a game of deep meaning, elegant storytelling, complex themes and thoughtful characters in a package that I believe is the best story certainly of any game this year at least.The art style of the game is exquisite and really manages to capture and evoke the imagery and style of early modern woodcuts, early print and medieval manuscript artistry. The dialogue bubbles themselves, with each character having a unique font based on their social class and Andreas' perception of them is fantastic at giving characters a sense of identity without any VO, and the sound of quill on vellum parchment is like ASMR (tho this may be a turnoff for some). If all this can't convince you of Obsidian's attention to detail then this should, they have period accurate pigs! yes that's right proper long snouted tusked trotters take the stage, none of that modern short-snouted ♥♥♥♥♥. Now that is proper attention to detail.Always been wondering whether that knowledge of banned french religious books, obscure latin sayings, or complex medieval bavarian inheritance laws would ever come in handy? Then Pentiment is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: If you love a good story, especially historical fiction, you will probably love this medieval murder mystery. The game consists mostly of running around and talking to the people of Tassing, coaxing their secrets out and choosing who to suspect and who to believe, interspersed with a few minigames. Time passes with certain activites, and you have to decide what to spend your time on, which investigations to pursue. The game has a bit of a slow start, but the tension ratchets up once the murder has been committed. From there you will be continually surprised by how much deeper and more complex the story becomes.Replay-value is high as your choices will create very different outcomes for the town.Also, you can pet all the cats and dogs. 10/10 would scritch again.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely art style and fun Reformation era historical immersion, but the mystery/investigation portion is comparatively lacking. I see the Disco Elysium similarities that get mentioned in some reviews, but Disco is far superior regarding character development, interaction, and most notably for me, length of story. Pentiment is *short* for a narrative driven game. Part of this is due to the forced-march style of game time, which purposefully puts pressure on you to rush to conclusions on potential suspects before you have to state your case. I enjoyed this element as it gave the investigations urgency, but I think it comes at a cost to getting to know and appreciate all the characters. Yeah, you could play it multiple times to capture all the dialogue, but I don't think the overarching story really justifies that unless you're actively achievement hunting. My biggest issue though with the length is the lack of quantity of mysteries. The game has 3 acts, and it seems as though it would've benefited to have twice that many, or to make the mysteries included way deeper. As it is I would call Pentiment a "visual novella" and that it doesn't quite stand with the other mainstays in the mystery game genre. There are other nitpicks. The game holds your hand through all the side activities - there was one particularly bad example where I was trying to solve a puzzle relevant to my suspect, and the game pointed to the correct answer every step of the way.  Also, "choices matter" is a little inaccurate; it's more like "choices are interesting" - the story is primarily on a railroad, with your choices affecting your seat on the train. This wasn't really a problem for me, as I enjoy mystery games which are practically always railroaded, but I think it's fair to point out. Dialogue checks feel arbitrary - don't feel bad if you miss the majority of these, as unlike Disco you're not going to be able to brute force many skill checks, it's almost entirely up to previous dialogue choices with few exceptions. I spent a lot of time here on the negatives, but that's because I agree with most of the positive reviews. I'd give it an 8 out of 10, and would hope that if Obsidian returns for some more delicious historical drama, they focus on the actual mystery portion next time.

_childDocuments_.review: Just an insanely well-written game. I don't even want to talk about the story too much because it should just be experienced first hand. _childDocuments_.review: This is both a smart and captivating game set in a historical context, yet explains the setting well enough to be understandable without a degree in history. It is oozing with 16th century atmosphere and, despite being 2D, is one of the most immersive games I have ever played.This certainly deserves more recognition for how uniquely authentic it is.Not only does the story offer a very unique take on investigations in a way that integrates beautifully into a video game, it also lets you get to know a few dozen characters both through the main story and optional dialogues and scenes.This really impressed and touched me on multiple levels, you can feel the amount of passion.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment takes palace in 1500's Bavaria in 3 Acts spanning 30 years.It is Art imitating Life imitating Art, visually gorgeous and narratively beautiful.The story unfolds over time through dialog the protagonist has with people that inhabit the small fictional town of Tassing.It all begins with a murder, which you task yourself to disprove, that your friend and mentor committed. Along the way you chose your backstory and interest and meet fully realized characters with rich personalities and unique motivations. Tassing is full of interesting people who will live, die and change over the story's arc and numerous playthroughs. Many of these people you will have a hand in influencing and for some you may even hold their life in your hands. All your choices will matter at least a little, some small choice will have big consequences and some that seem big will turn out not to mean much at all, dialog options will present themselves based on your chosen background and conversations previously made - so pay close attention to the person you want to be and the impression you want to leave.Comparisons with Disco Elysium are inevitable and apt but start at "beautiful art style" and end at "story rich experience beyond main plot". Pentiment is rarely sad or self-flagellating and never crowded with exposition. Where Harry avoid his responsibilities in favor of self-indulgent wallowing in his depression, Andreas avoids confronting his responsibilities and self-doubt by indulging in a murder mystery. Events in Pentiment unfold naturally, conversations are organic and lunchtime is always relative. Chose Pentiment if you're interested in experiencing a rich branching story that you are encouraged to re-experience with vastly divergent outcomes.

The inner Latin geek in me is so happy. Delightful highlights include listening to sound of scribbling as they talk with their speech bubbles. Music/soundtrack compliments the entire gaming experience.Love how your choices do matter and the way you choose your character's background gets reflected within their interactions with other characters as well as how they solve the mysteries in-game. Such a worthy purchase for this price point. Can't wait to finish the rest of this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I asked for a Refund after an hour of gameplay and here is why:  (Obviously, I am a tiny minority for a good reason)On the surface:This game had everything for me - absolutely stunning art, an artist as the protagonist (I am a huge Art History Fan especially for the Renaissance period), narrative driven, point and click,  etc. "There was absolutely no way I wouldn't enjoy a game tailored specifically to my own taste" I thought. Even when I was reading the dialogue I was so excited to find familiar references and to learn even more details for my favorite period. So what on Earth happened? After an hour:I was bored and stressed at the same time! How and why?!? 3 reasons why you might like/dislike this game:1. The Dialogue - there was a LOT of it! That's a great thing, but apperantly not for me. There is SO MUCH you can do in this game, so many characters you can interact with just in the span of an hour. Right away you are bombarded with information, with numerous mini quests, locations, and choices, and the more characters you encounter the more choices and information you are presented with. I only just woke up and I am already being told about what other characters I haven't even met with yet expect from me. My "book" was full with names of monks, nuns, nobles, peasents... and by the time I meet them  and pick something irrelevant as a reply I am ALERTED that they will remember my answer... Wha? I haven't even gotten to work yet, and this shepherd boy hates me for asking him to help his mother! Obviously, the game is doing a good  job at sucking you into the world... too good in my case. 2.  The Choices - so many! Great for most players, and a bit annoying for me. I love games where you can decide what to say, whether to be polite, direct or rude, etc. But...here it seemed a bit excessive. I had to make a choice after every couple of sentences I utter. (And when I picked something randomly they... REMEMBERED my answer! Everyone hates me... ;_;) Even dinner is stressful! I was already having an issue promissing to join certain characters for dinner, when a noble man forced me to agree to eat with him instead without me having the option to pick another date. I couldn't even go back and ask my peasant friends to reschedule. Basically, I was doomed to offend someone (and make everyone hate me... EVEN MORE). 3.  And then I checked how long it takes to finish this game - 15 HOURS! At least! By the end, I was sure I'll be burned at the stake! I was in panic mode! I managed to get an advance to my salary so I can help my landlady, but at the same time I was pretty certain the monks .... WILL REMEMBER THAT!  Every tiny choice I made seemed to have a negative impact! If I was so stressed now, after only an hour, imagine the mess I will be after 15 hours! 4. And finally, my biggest reason why I abandoned Pentiment: I was just bored. Point and click, dialogue-driven games are my thing. But there was too much information (you can't even be selective about), too many choices (that apperantly don't matter so much, but you have to make them every few seconds regardless) and both of these factors resulted in a long game I didn't want to invest 15 hours to complete. Maybe, I would've enjoyed it better, if I was given more time in the beginning to enjoy the world-building and get properly acquainted with the characters directly (instead of hearing about them in the dialogues), before I get to make any important dinner plans. And of course, this review is a bit ridiculous, right? This game is stunning, creative, highly immersive, one of the best looking games I've ever seen! Not to mention educational in a fun, visual way, with one of the most thorough dialogue systems. This game will be enjoyed by many, and I am one of the ultra-sensitive, over-thinking few who couldn't :)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A story-based point and click with a wonderful art style, engaging mystery, and interesting themes of narratives of history and purpose in one's life. If you like visual novels or story-heavy games in general and don't mind a lack of gameplay, then I strongly recommend. Its also appealing to those who know or want to know more about the Protestant Reformation, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Renaissance more generally.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a genuine joy to play. It is a shorter game in terms of length, but the story is possibly one of my favourites. It succeeds in immersing you in the story, giving you both an insight into the characters and (in traditional game review fashion) makes you FEEL like you're in a stressful race against time to solve the murder of Tassing. Sure, some of the skills and mechanics are much more useful and fleshed out than others, and sometimes you only have the illusion of choice, but I feel the overall delivery and atmosphere of the game outweighs any shortcomings.As someone who studies history and considers themselves a medievalist, this game is an utter treat. I wish with all my heart that the town of Tassing was real, because you'd definitely feel it was real as you play. The game nails all of the subtlest historical details, even small artistic things that the vast majority of players would not even appreciate, which is a testament to the commitment to the story and setting. Even the simple act of having a meal immerses you in the world of Tassing and the lives of its residents. There is also an incredibly helpful and easy to access glossary to help you understand various places, people and concepts of the setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The sheer level of research, passion, and attention to detail in this game is brilliant. Pentiment practically oozez love and care from every mechanic, every asset, and every line of dialogue. The cast is large and varied, and even though the dialogue system is barebones compared to something like, say, Disco Elysium, it serves its purpose in allowing you to really immerse yourself in the village of Tassing, and allowing you to feel like you're a part of this little community. It's a real emotional journey, following these people over the course of 25 years, feeling the tumult of change in their lives as the Medieval period is gradually overtaken by the ideas of the Renaissance. The themes of legacy, guilt, and coping with change are woven into the story in a way that feels purposeful and natural.The advice I'd give to people playing Pentiment for the first time is much the same as the advice I'd give to someone playing Disco Elysium for the first time. Your goal in playing Pentiment should not be to win, or to maximise the efficiency of every interaction. It should not be to solve the mystery as quick as possible or to calculate your actions to always get the best outcomes. Although the mystery in Pentiment is well written and is fun to follow, and has a pretty solid resolution, it was not the high point of the game for me. Pentiment's real strength is in its characters and setting. Just engage with people, explore, and immerse yourself in this slice of 16th century life. The rest will follow.It's worth noting that, for a game set in a christian town in the 1500s, the commitment to showcasing marginalised and minority histories in Europe is really exceptional. This game is proof that being historically accurate and being diverse are not mutually exclusive, and in fact go hand-in-hand. Working women, Jewish people, queer people, and people of colour have always existed in Europe to some extent, and this game takes pains to highlight their experiences. I know this won't matter to many people, and that's fine, but as a queer person and a Jewish person, i can't really stress how refreshing it is to see my own identity reflected in a medium that so often ignores and sidelines minority perspectives.I would also be remiss to not talk about the level of research that went into the game. I am not a medieval scholar, so I'm not in a position to comment on the accuracy of small details, but the amount of care that went into depicting the everyday lives of peasants and of monks, as well as the wider political and social climate of the period is very very clear. Pentiment does not only use it's setting as an aesthetically interesting backdrop for it's story, but rather has baked it integrally into every aspect of its story and themes. Even small aspects of the UI - the glossary function made to look like an illuminated manuscript, the different typefaces used to reflect the backrounds and social caste of various characters, the measuring of time by the hours of prayer eventually changing to hours of the clock as Tassing is pulled into the modern era - go a long way towards making the player feel like they're really living through this story. And the tiny details of the dialogue boxes - the moment where the ink settles into the page, the times when characters make typos which they scratch out and correct, the way the ink splatters when a character is especially upset or emotional - I mean, they didn't have to do that. They aren't at all relevant to the plot and nobody would have noticed if they weren't there. But they did it anyways, because, for once, an AA studio decided to not cut corners, not prioritise scale over quality, and commit to putting thought, attention, and love into every detail of a game.This is the second steam review I've ever written, and was typed out in a frenzy after finishing the game. I'm not really a video game guy, so take some of this with a grain of salt. But like. ♥♥♥♥, guys. Go play Pentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like history, you need to play this game. That's really it. If you are like me, and usually more drawn to historic strategy games, give this game a try. It might upend your perspective and your idea on what history actually is and how it's written. Pentiment is an insanely "historically accurate" game (loaded term, I know) but playing this you actually learn a lot about the early reformation era in Bavaria (and Europe), the codex is neatly woven into the game to give you new things to appreciate. You also learn about peasant and religious customs during the game. Initially I wasn't too hot on the idea that there is no voice acting, but the way the game uses font and literacy to convey information makes up for it. The dialogues are also fairly short and straight forward compared to Disco Elysium for example.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is rad.It's a lot of things. It's a cool send up to medieval art, a more accurate look into a time period that a lot of media is content to handwave as being devoid of color and populated with caricatures, and it's also a fun mystery at its core.Some people might call how Pentiment plays a walking simulator, which I don't think is a fair comparison. Pentiment always has enough going on that if you try to sleepwalk your way through it you're gonna miss a lot of stuff. Not only are you looking for leads and clues but if you don't pay attention to time passing while you're off doing things you'll miss out on stuff. there's also occasional minigames that break up the flow of regular gameplay.Similarly, some might also want to make a comparison to Disco Elysium, which also doesn't really work. While there are important choices you make that determine character traits, there are only a few of them and you can only choose a few at the start and then you're locked in, whereas in Disco there are many more skills that you develop over time while making a build. It's enough that if you're the type to really get into games like this, then you might want to do a second playthrough soon after to see what changes.The historical details helped suck me into the story, it was nice to see the people in the story act like regular people instead of Monty Python extras who only say "MI'LORD" and wallow in their misery. Instead there's a cast of characters that range all up and down the social ladder and essentially no one is a braindead idiot. People have thoughts and opinions, and that helps flesh out the time and place the game takes place in, a fictional town in Bavaria during the Reformation, this backdrop gives more context to the story and makes some characters motivations make sense. Even the food is period accurate, with different people eating different meals depending on their station.The art style of the game is one of the definite highlights, showing off illuminated manuscripts, those weird pictures that show up in the margins of books like knights fighting snails and cats with jetpacks, and comparatively more modern stuff like printed woodcut art, it all really highlights how the time the game takes place in is an inbetween period where art is becoming a thing for everyone and not just the church and the rich. Even the fonts and how text is presented get in on it, with styles differentiating between characters depending on their position and how educated they are, sometimes even changing on the fly when new information about a character is revealed.It being a mystery, I'm not going to get into the details, beyond that you play an artist working on Illuminated scripts at an abbey while also finishing their masterpiece on the side so they can start their own workshop. Soon after a terrible crime is committed and the game is afoot.I'll admit that Pentiment seems to be a game with niche appeal, but if you like games with a lot of reading I'd gladly recommend it, and if you're not sure if its you're thing but you're up for taking a risk I say go for it, nothing about this game seems lazy or poorly thought out, Pentiment was made by people who care.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: "Pentiment" Noun. An underlying image in a painting, especially one that has become visible when the top layer of paint has turned transparent with age, providing evidence of revision by the artist. This is a beautiful game about art, history, truth and perspective. This is broadly classified as an "adventure" game but there are no tedious inventory puzzles. Most of the gameplay will involve making dialogue choices that may have unforeseen narrative consequences. If you have a perfectionist's streak, or a desire to always find that "golden path" through a game narrative where you get to save Mary Jane AND the bus full of children, this game will frustrate you. But don't let that frustration stop you from playing! Lean into that feeling and keep playing, ideally without a guide. Follow the story where it leads and draw your own lesson from it. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're still reading, I'll try to explain what I love about this title.First off, it isn't easy to try to explain this, simply because it is so uniquely its own thing. This isn't an isometric RPG in the vein of Pillars of Eternity, or even Fallout: New Vegas's first/third person perspective on post-apocalypse americana, but there  meaningful, tactile role-playing decisions to make here, both in terms of who your instantiation of the protagonist becomes, and how he conducts himself through the game.This isn't exactly a classic adventure game, though it certainly borrows elements and mechanics from that genre.If I had to sum it up, it'd be a period-authentic role-playing adventure murder mystery, rendered as if it was an illuminated manuscript.I keep hearing this described as niche, but honestly I do  understand that. Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous is niche, it has a pile of DMV-grade fiddly mechanics around character builds. Command: Modern Operations is a niche game, it's the best simulation you can get of modern naval warfare shy of getting a security clearance. Europa Universalis is a niche game, running that game feels like getting a double major in history and economics with a minor in political science, each achievement feels like a doctoral thesis in the making.This game? This game is approachable enough that I struggle to think of anyone I would  recommend this to. You find the fun immediately, and the fun will stay with you until the end.It is  beautiful. Every single element was crafted with beauty, meticulous care, and dedication to the craft.It's oozing with gravitas and verisimilitude. The characters feel vibrant and real, the place becomes as familiar as a lifelong home, and the story keeps you guessing until very nearly the end. It's embarrassingly well written,  well-researched.It's jam-packed with impactful, meaningful choices, reactivity to virtually all of those choices, and a deadly-serious story that will percolate in the back of your mind both in between sessions and, I'm certain, long after the credits roll.Get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed playing this so much! _childDocuments_.review: This here has been a master class in story telling on a whole new level. While it may not be for everyone, it's hard to deny the love and care that has been given to this title.When I first picked up this game, I wasn't sure if the art design was going to gel with me. However, very early on I was impressed at how the whole renaissance imagery tied everythingtogether. The overall art style really fits and oozes charm along with the music.The main attraction is the story that is driven by a hell of a lot of dialogue choice. Which pretty much encompasses and swallows the gameplay. No real puzzles or traditional gameplay to speak of, just a vast selection of responses throughout conversation (very much in the similar vein as Disco Elysium). But, my gosh, there is some real impact to everything you choose! Some of the smallest comments can circle back to have a big influence on how your character's relationship will be affected. _childDocuments_.review: Giving this a tentative recommendation. I like the game but I can't help but think that it's commitment to aesthetic takes away from some of just joy of playing the game. This is a story which I would love to re-play and take different paths, be friendly with different people, follow different leads... but man I really don't want to deal with all the tedium of navigating this village.The first time you move from one area to another and the game zooms out to turn the page of a book it's really cute and fun but when you go from your house to outside your house to the town commons to the church to the meadow to the lower abbey to the abbey to the church to the courtyard and finally into the scriptorium and that animation plays every single time it very quickly gets old. That's a sequence of events that will take place many many times in this game and as much as I enjoyed the world and the story I can't bring myself to deal with it more.on the other hand I never grew tired of watching the creative way that speach bubbles are populated with text and never changed the setting to make them instant because I found those animations to be much more interesting to watch even if they probably wasted more of my time. I think maybe the page turn animation could have stayed for going in and out of buildings but it really is just too prevalent in the game in my opinion.The story itself is fun and intriguing. Early on I wanted to push the RP elements to their limit and see what I could do but it quickly became clear that wasn't the point (and that's fine). I liked solving the murders and making my recommendations as to who was responsible and felt invested in the outcomes of each of these situations. The characters all seem natural and authentic and react generally in natural and authentic way.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Finished Pentiment! Will never be the same thanks for that.Okay in all seriousness I don't think this was the most life changing thing I've experienced - in the way that certain works (mainly books) have literally changed my views on life itself. Possibly because I've already seen Andrei Rublev and if there was ever a piece of media about religion and loss and generations that was going to completely fry your brain, that was it.That being said I really enjoyed Pentiment. Like, first game in years I've finished the entire way enjoyed. It really moved me, and I really was drawn into the story, into playing and learning as much as possible. I certainly did not play this game as fast as I could have, hell I even regret some options I didn't take that I wanted to experience (next time maybe)? I really liked the direction of the story. I liked the way we see Mahler watch everything crumble. I really loved the transition into Act III, all these familiar characters and pieces of information that could only make sense to the player and not to the character of Magdalene. I also loved the sense of living through something that this game had. Terrible things happen. People die. Buildings crumble. It seems like the end of the world and then... it isn't. A new season comes. Babies are born. Children grow up. Humans keep living and living and living even when the world seems on a knife's edge. And I absolutely adore media that portrays this. Really more than I care to admit. I love the story of humanity surviving. Because of choices and because we have to. It's a compulsion in all of us, to survive, and, more importantly, to live.I do think this game would have done better were it set a little earlier? I do think that Tassing does not ultimately feel like part of the 16th century, though some of this is of course aesthetic. The style is more medieval than Renaissance to me, and though I do appreciate and understand why Tassing should feel out of time and like a backwater - I mean like, it is and that is a clear theme in the story - I still think a little earlier might have been better? But of course you're constrained by historical events and when the Reformation started so I get it. Maybe I'm just too big of a fan of the 14th and 15th centuries in terms of art. My loves forever and always. Overall I really did like Pentiment though and would give it like... 4.5/5 stars. Again, really rare I complete a video game so in my book this is like Hall of Fame level video game stuff. Shoutout to Obsidian. I may not leave the historical realm for Disco Elysium, but I do love what you did here.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Granted, this game is not for those who abhor slow burns, detailed explanations that seem to go nowhere (but they would later on), meandering experiences, lengthy dialogues, intrigue and mystery. The world of Andreas takes a few hours to set up, and by the time I got there, I was invested in the few characters that I have met so far. This is a game for long weekends, rainy days, and quiet contemplation. It does not want you to rush it. It wants you to take in the beauty of the illuminated pages where the story takes place. Don't get this game because of the hype. Get this game because you want to play it.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games ever made. Plot, sound design, visuals - it all works together perfectly to create an engaging world with a fantastic atmosphere. What is particularly relevant, choices made along the way do matter. A lot is influenced by player choices. This comes at a cost, however, as you can only do a limited number of things in a given day. You will, therefore, miss A LOT. Replayability is another quality of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Prepare for pain. The choices you make matter in this one in unexpected ways. Consequence, action, reaction, flail as you might for an answer, you will inevitably be carried by events. However, don't fool yourself into thinking this is a mystery that you can solve: in two of the three mystery scenarios, you lack the required information to unravel the whole thing and the time to do so- this is the point. You must act with imperfect information and live with the consequences. The game is a wonderful mystery in the style of Night in the Woods, with a wonderfully depicted Illuminated and woodblock artstyle. Few games do as much work to invest in a particular historical moment, and Pentiment goes above and beyond to place the story in a historical moment while not spending its entire run time catching you up on the intricacies of Imperial Law, Botany, the Catholic Catechism. Students of history will be rewarded for knowing what's happening (and punished, hindsight hurts). The writing style is tight in structure, and characters move and change naturalistically with the decades that pass over the story. A few notes: as mentioned earlier, this isn't the sort of game where you can solve the mystery and make it ok in the first act, or even the second. Don't play assuming you can look up a guide and save the innocent and destroy the guilty; one of the points of this story is that truth is a point of view. Additionally, it is not possible to complete every side quest in one play through, and the game is as much about time management as anything else. Finally, with so many leads and interactions, it can be hard to feel that you have exhausted all of your options before you move on to a scene: unless you are compelled, I strongly recommend not hitting every location possible in one playthrough. Simply do your best and don't turn the experience into a chore on top of an emotional one.Strong showing from Obsidian's writing team again with this story; I am eager to see what comes next. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely masterful in every way, every piece of writing feels impactful and interesting, including the writing itself. I've never seen a game put so much incredible attention to detail in the literal text you read before and it's a sight to behold. The story and characters are so well written, I always want to hear what everyone has to say. and the art is astoundingly beautiful, I wish this art style was utilised in more pieces of media.An amazing game I believe everyone should experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a woman who has religious trauma, this was a very healing game for me. To play this game is to be transported into the world of the 1500s when Christianity ruled with an iron fist and to see the remnants of pagan rituals and Roman influences in Europe before they were completely eradicated. You see the community struggle with accepting their Lord and Savior versus the "old ways" and how this affects individuals motivations and actions. It is a well constructed game, well written, and is definitely replayable since there are many decisions you can make that affect NPCs lives. If you were ever loved learning about the reformation and Martin Luther, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a current grad history student it is refreshing to see game devs merging genuine care for history and a engaging video game. Pentiment is a adventure/RPG type of game with dialogue choices that can affect the story. Set in a fictional town in the Bavarian alps around the early 16th century, you play as Andres as he interacts with a diverse and interesting group of people while real historical events affect the characters.Gameplay wise, it is very simple as you move your character around talking to various people with small minigames here and there. However, this is where the game shines as each character you interact with are full of personality. I got so invested into the characters as I laughed and cried with all of them. Once I made it to the end, it felt like saying goodbye to good friends you have spent many years with.What prompted me to write a review was just the attention to detail the creators had with making this time period as immersive as possible. Using the schedule of the feudal peasants to track your time, different food items depending on who you eat with, and the soundtrack done with musical instruments from that time period is some of the ways this game takes in back in time. One giant help was at any time you can pause the game and sometimes the game will define people, places, events, or books/documents that can be unfamiliar to some people but it doesn't break the immersion with long exposition. Overall, this was a fantastic game and definitely worth your time for fans of history and rich narratives.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've had the pleasure of experiencing. The story, characters, and sounds, had me hooked from start to finish. Every time I went into someone's house where the pot was boiling, I wanted to eat some bread and stew!I find it very difficult to actually complete games, because I get bored easily. I have completed one run, and will be going back for the achievements after a bit. The story is so good, and some character customization should make for fresh dialog the next time through. So replaying shouldn't be tedious or boring.You don't want to pass this one up.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Very chill and pretty game if you are into medieval artstyles. Don't expect a thrilling game filled with explosions and mass murder, this is a slow paced, point and click book-like game, pretty old school. If you like to immerse yourself in a good narrative experience, this game is made for you. The story is good and strongly reminds me of In The Name of the Rose by Umberto Eco. Expect a mystery that spans many years with several compelling twists. I heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes a mature setting with a slow murder mystery and branching choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A thrilling and cozy point-and-click game, right up my alley. Not only did I finish it within one day, I also had to force myself from not Googling details because I was so invested in the story and making the right choices. Even though there's a nice wrap up in the end, I can't help but want to play it a 2nd time. Both due to the character trait customization but also the potential dialogues and choices I didn't make in the first run.I only have a couple of cons (spoiler free) If you're not a fan of reading, this might not be the game for you. I thought the story would be much shorter and contain voice acting, but I did not really mind that it was missing. The second con would be that the story sometimes does not take the conversations you've already had into consideration. There were mulriple times in the story where I had already received information, but characters proceeded to act shocked after talking and referencing to things they had already talked about.(Example, there's a part where a couple of people are plotting something, I talk to them about it and they tell me what they're up to. I talk to them again and the other one gets annoyed at the other "never keeping their mouth shut" when they were the one who just told me 5 min ago.) This doesn't happen too often, but noticed it enough to be worth a remark. Other than that, I hope you enjoy it as much as I did :)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game but at most times it felt like a chore. There are around 100 characters and they all have a lot to say but most of it is completely irrelevant to the story and boring. There are just a few choices to make and running around in the world to find clues was tedious and felt quite random - you had to visit each and every part of the map and stumble over parts of the story you would've missed otherwise.--> Go here, talk to x (listen to super long dialogue that is barely connected to anything), go back & fetch Y............for hours!When there is no gameplay the story has to be entertaining but unfortunately it only had a few interesting twists.A bit of streamlining would've worked wonders for this game.  I wonder why a lot of people like it so much - I tried my best and put a lot of time into it.

_childDocuments_.review: I know what you're thinking--what could be more uninteresting than historical fiction in Bavaria during the roots of the Reformation?The problem with that prejudice is that may end up preventing you from playing one of the most brilliantly crafted narrative experiences ever created. The passion, attention to detail, and love oozes from every pixel in this game. It is nothing short of perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I've never written a review on steam in my many years, but this game made me wanna recommend it. If you are down to spend some time reading and engrossing yourself into a rich narrative story - the pay off is well worth it. I was hooked the whole time. You get to know all the characters in the world, their relationships, and you have meaningful choices throughout the game. It lets you feel smart - without ruining the mysteries along the way. _childDocuments_.review: There's so much to like about this game, but I just can't recommend it. It starts out slow and then picks up once the murder mystery story starts. But then a little over halfway through, the pacing grinds to a crawl (from an already slow baseline), and the story veers off into seemingly irrelevant territory and explicit historical investigation.That decision is what really turned me off from the game in the end. _childDocuments_.review: When a lot of the big game developers are more focused on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out GAAS games and games that are broken on release, it's easy to feel jaded with gaming. And then something like Pentiment comes along to remind me why it is I love games in the first place. Pentiment at first glance seems like a ridiculously niche game, where it is a narrative driven murder mystery set in early Reformation era Bavaria, and yet it still manages to pull off being a really enjoyable game. The art style is fantastic, the story and dialogue is well written and engaging and it does a great job of pulling you into the setting. In fact I think the setting is what I loved most about this game. The game is set entirely in a small Bavarian village and its neighbouring monastery with the timespan of the game being 25 years, with several years separating each act. So you get to see some characters go from child to adult,  some who unfortunately pass away in the intervening years between acts and the effect of your decisions on the lives of the village residents. It's a great way of making you feel more invested in the choices you make and how you speak to other characters.I also enjoyed the ambiguity of the murder investigations. You'll never be able to investigate every suspect and piece of evidence thoroughly enough within the limited time so your forced to deduce who the most likely person is based on the limited information you have instead of the game serving up the the actual guilty person on a silver platter.I do highly recommend giving this game a try. It might be too niche for everyones tastes, but for those who think they would enjoy it, it's an absolute gem of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished Pentiment, I wholeheartedly recommend it, if you like stories.  It's by no means any type of action game, much more of a point-and-click (with cool art style), but is primarily about relationships and interaction.   There's a lot of "what is truth, what is the past, how do you know these things, how sure are you of your deductions".  Twice I thought the game was over, and it wasn't (there are 3 Acts).   The style of text used for character's writing is an important artistic point, and ties to the character's life/experience/personality.    While it's fictional, it's very much a period piece and really drops you into it - to the point when it was over, I had to check to make sure it wasn't based on real events (pieces of it are borrowed from real events/people, though).  And pretty emotional; you really feel like these are real characters/people, not cardboard cutouts you often see in games.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is one of the best pieces of historical fiction I've encountered in years. There are some period pieces that aim for a historical "feel" without engaging with the material realities, concerns, values, and ideas that people experienced in their time and place. There are others that deal in willful and playful anachronism (often for purposes of comedy or escapism). Pentiment is neither of these. Don't get me wrong, I am fond of willful anachronism, but this is a story that means it when it tells you when and where it takes place and who its characters are. I played Pentiment a lot in the last semester of my M.A., which focused on 16th and 17th century European literature and culture. There were things that came up in the game I knew well and things I didn't. German-language history and literature isn't my expertise—though I once had to read a lot about guild regulations for craftspeople in Nuremberg that I was excited to see reflected in references to what awaits Andreas after Act I! I especially enjoyed the glossary mechanic for this reason, as a terminally-curious former graduate student. But the precise historical elements that first drew me to early modernity as an area of study are the beating heart of the game. Throughout the time period covered by the three acts, and throughout the real-life 1500s and their neighboring centuries, people in Bavaria and elsewhere experienced changes in culture, religion, politics, and technology at a rapid pace that feels familiar to players in the 21st century. They are destabilized and often afraid, but also excited by the potential of a world that can shift so rapidly. Revolution can come knocking at your door any minute, but in the meantime, you still need to do the chores.This is the function of historical fiction at its best. This game tells a story meant to be received in the present through the realities, not just the trappings or tropes, of what we understand to be true about the past. We sympathize with these characters not because the lives they lead or the things they believe are identical to our own, but because we understand what is at stake for them. The characters tell us what they are willing to live, kill, and die for, and why. These don't have to be the same things we live, kill, and die for (though some of them are), but they are recognizable, on a level deeply, conscientiously woven into the story, as reactions to the world by people as rational, scared, kind, cruel, loving, selfish, intelligent, fallible, and complex as anyone playing the game. I value a work that is genuinely interested in telling a story about the past, even—and especially—when it is also a story about the present.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this up on a whim because I wanted to play something different than the usual action-driven games I'm usually into. After 36 hours of play time which includes starting, stopping, and trying different decisions (as well as completing all the achievements) I had a pleasant time. Pentiment is a quaint little text-heavy, point & click, that is reminiscent of old Sierra games like Kings Quest, etc... But without the odd, sometimes unsolvable puzzles. For the most part, Pentiment holds your hand as you explore the fictional village of Tassing located in Bavaria in the mid-16th century. Icons direct you to interact with people, things, animals, books, or items to progress the story (or just explore). The story itself centers around a murder at the local abbey and you will turn Tassing upside down looking for clues in an attempt to solve this medieval "who done it" mystery. More things happen of course but I feel even a little hint of things would be spoiler territory so I'll avoid saying anything else other than it is cryptic and interesting.The big selling point are the decisions you make and how the rest of the game plays out. Decisions made in Act 1 can carry over into Act 2 and 3. You can play as a pious by-the-rules Catholic or a rebellious scientific-oriented ruffian based on various backgrounds and areas of expertise you choose. Now this is by no means a robust selection you have to choose from but still whatever you choose will influence conversations down the road. Art style is beautiful and pays homage to medieval woodcuttings, murals, and paintings of that time. Also the the history injected into the story is insightful and gives you a glimpse into how peasants, nobility, and the Church interacted with each other. It points out that no matter at what level of society you were, everyone was fallible. This is a good game if you enjoy reading and immersion into a story with quite a few twists and turns that will always leave you guessing. I think by the end of my foray I was ready to jump back into something a little more adrenaline-inducing though as my eyes got tired of reading text and I found myself rushing through dialogue. But for what Pentinent is, it's fine. Not the ultimate in point & click 2D role-playing but certainly not the worst either. The game mechanics are simple and the learning curve is elementary. The story is great and if you're looking for some downtime and a little peace and quiet, then this game might be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A great, charming, one-of-a-kind game. Worth playing if you are at all interested in it, even if just for the beautiful art style. It has some issues, like the speech checks, lack of dialogue at times, and some questionable writing in places, but the good parts make it more than worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be put off by the simplistic look of it, Pentiment is one of the best RPGs out there, in one of the best-constructed and most well-researched historical settings of any game, period. _childDocuments_.review: What a game. "Pentiment" is the folklore game I've always wanted to play. It's the medieval-ish/Renaissance game I've always wanted to play. It's the murder mystery game I've always wanted to play. It scratches so many aesthetic itches that it's hard to know where to begin the praise, but I think I'll start with the deep appreciation of folklore that this game embodies. In essence, this game's message is that the stories we tell matter, and the people who tell them matter as well. The battle between story and storyteller(s) is thick in "Pentiment," and the historical discourse that influenced these positions on stories and how they dispersed is well-researched, cited and able to be referenced immediately in an illustrated glossary, fun to interact with through an easy-to-use UI, and versatile in its artistic rendering. In fact, EVERYTHING you learn about this game is backed up by research that is readily available. "Pentiment" wants players to know that reading is not only essential to their success in the game but also, as emphasized by its diverse cast of characters in different classes, an incredible privilege to be able to accomplish at one's leisure. The characters are beautifully fleshed-out, believable, and diverse in their representations of early modern classes and class warfare. I loved every single one of them and fostered connections with them more than I have compared to other games. The time you spend with people is imperative for not only peace of mind and communal relations, but also communication and cultural knowledge. It's great that something like this can represent that in a video game. Choices matter, and it's harder to accuse someone after sharing a meal with them and speaking with their families. Religious and political discourse/gameplay are also at the core of "Pentiment," and the representation of faith, class, and their conflicts is well thought-out, detailed, and also fun to engage in as a character who themselves embodies a different class and sex (and thus access to opportunities) during gameplay. Secular players might find the many references and thick religious lore a hard slog, but this game demands attention to detail and provides an in-depth (and, again, cited!) look into the world it has beautifully, meticulously recreated. The liberties this game takes with sex, sexuality, and gendered oppression and its politics are also great. I love that both women and men in this game can be proponents of or critics against misogyny, religious persecution, classism, national matters, and more. It makes the game--and the immersion into these characters' lives--more than just a simple point-and-click WASD run. It makes it a real narrative that uplifts the stories and struggles it references while creating a massively successful gamer experience for a contemporary audience.Lovers of folk horror will enjoy this game, as it fits nicely into each of Scovell's Folk Horror Chain's links: Landscape, Isolation, Skewed Morality/Systems of Belief, and quite a few Happenings. I definitely recommend this game for a long rainy day for players who crave stunningly beautiful visuals, immersive storytelling, diverse characters with believable motivations and backgrounds, and good old fashioned HISTORY LESSONS!

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, I was completely engrossed until the ending. If you are someone who appreciates exceptionally good storytelling with rich worlds (yes I am aware this is historical which is why I avoided "world building") and memorable characters (I would die for Brother Piero!) the likes of Disco Elysium, Norco, Pillars of the Earth, etc., this game should be an immediate purchase. This comment on its storytelling of course is itself amusing given its themes (you'll see what I mean if you get it). Presentation is incredible with innovations that other point-and-click adventures, especially those with larger casts of characters, should take some inspiration from. Only negatives I'd mention are a few minor bugs (portraits of the wrong villagers in the main reference books) and one slightly less believable character action. A character does something major that I felt wasn't completely earned, though I know there was textual support for it. This may have been because I chose a background that maybe gave the character weaker motivations for said action than the other ones. That being said, other things I thought were issues were beautifully resolved in the end--and I cried, a lot! Anyway, if you're still here reading this, buy this game! If you are someone who doesn't appreciate or care for subtext, and prefers a straight-forward face-value story, then this might not be for you (again this comment is amusing given the game's themes!) though I think the face-reading of the story I personally still find very interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: - It's very likely the game's artstyle drew you to it. It's certainly what piqued my interest. I'm happy to report that it does indeed look amazing, with the highly stylized artstyle reflecting the medieval paintings and illuminated manuscripts produced in Bavaria during the 1500s- I was also pleasantly surprised by the game's text boxes, which feels like a weird thing to say. There's all sorts of neat little touches. If you're talking to a monk or nun, their speech bubbles will be written in a old-timey gothic script. If you're talking to a printer, the text will plop down on the bubble with a satisfying "clunk" of an old printing press. The text bubbles of people speaking other languages will autotranslate if you have a skill that helps you speak that language. In all, a really cool approach to dialogue- The music is excellent and similarly of its time. The vocal tracks are especially nice and were a little unexpected- You play as a Flemish artist named Andreas who is living in Bavaria while he works on his masterpiece that will allow him to become a master artist. A mystery erupts suddenly after a local baron visits the town. You'll interview people, play a few minigames and puzzles, and use your best judgement to solve both this mystery and the two others that crop up later in the game- I'm being intentionally vague in describing the plot. The story is extremely compelling and well-written, so I don't want to spoil anything. It's definitely one worth experiencing- The writing is also incredibly good, which helps breathe life into the several townsfolk and tourists you'll encounter. Each character feels unique and interesting. Most of them have pasts and relationships that really flesh them out and make Tassing feel much more lifelike. This level of immersion is really impressive when you take a step back and realize that the screen looks like a painting- It's not all serious, though. The game does have a rich sense of humor. Beyond the occasional situational humor and wry dialogue, you'll also play a few pranks and even be given the chance to headbutt an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doctor if you choose the right options- I'm happy that this is an adventure game where narrative choices actually have an impact on the story. Depending on whether or not you piss off the church in the first chapter, the second chapter can have a very different feel to it. Remember that justice was a little more bloody in medieval times, so whomever you implicate as the perpetrators of the various mysteries you solve will face dire consequences- Beyond the typical walking and talking you'd expect in an adventure game, there's not much gameplay. Not that it's necessary in a game like this, but you won't even be managing an inventory- Given the narrative focus and the ability to converse with your own mind when faced with certain dialogue choices, I've seen some reviewers compare the game to Disco Elysium. While there are some superficial similarities and they'll largely appeal to the same audience, you'll be doing Pentiment a disservice if you go into it expecting the same experience. Disco Elysium is such a unique (and in my opinion, better) game that it's not fair judge Pentiment against that sort of masterpiece- I understand that it's difficult (or maybe even impossible) to implement a chapter select in a game where choices matter, but I still really wish there was a chapter select. I want to go back for the achievements I missed. Quick tip for achievement fiends: when it comes time to accuse someone of a crime, be sure to quit to the menu after the achievement pops. You'll be able to make the choice again to collect the other missable ones- Although the game is gorgeous on a larger display, it really shines as a Steam Deck title. It's fully verified and runs perfectly. The frequent autosaves and exploration/narrative focus make it an easy game to pick up and put down whenever you're interested in delving a little deeper into Tassing's mysteries- Depending on how thorough you are on each day of the game's story, you'll wind up with a wide range of completion times. It's probably possible to beat this game in as little as 12 hours if you don't do much exploration, but what's the fun in that? There's a lot of good dialogue to read, history to learn, and subplots to unearth. If you're a fan of narrative-focused games and like your choices to have an actual story impact, this is well worth full price. It's really hard to complain about a game with dollar-per-hour value that spins a tale this good. If you like the art style and enjoy a good mystery, this is easy to recommend
