_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a fantastic interactive visual novel. Everything about it oozes passion and creativity. The story is extremely page-turning.One of my favorite aspects about it is that there are a lot of "persuasion checks" in the game that aren't blatantly shown to you, and you'll probably see "THIS WILL BE REMEMBERED" a lot of times when you won't expect it. The game essentially demands that you think carefully about the characters you speak with - consider their motivations, personalities, beliefs, and so on. From what I understand, the differing pathways don't have a large effect on where the story ultimately leads, but it still made the game feel like a much more interactive, organic experience than most narrative driven games.If you're a fan of this type of thing, you will not want to miss this game!8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Me: *has never played detective games, is not into detective games in general, gets bored and depressed by history and has a hate/love relationship (mostly hate) with religions* "The art style in this game is very pretty. Imma try it for two hours and request a refund if it sucks."Also me, 28 hours and two subsequent playthroughs later: "WHY IS THERE NO MORE FAN ART OF THIS MASTERPIECE? WHY IS THERE NO STEAM SHOWCASE ITEMS? WHY AM I THE ONLY ONE IN MY FRIEND CIRCLE WHO HAS PLAYED THIS?" *pterodactyl screech*
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I have ever played a video game that has moved me as much as Pentiment has. It really made me think about the world around me, my morals, the value of life, plus way too much else. I was hooked by this game's intriguing characters and writing, everything in this game feels so well realized. Thank you, Josh Sawyer and crew for the best book I have ever played.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I got hooked on the plot so much! I loved the characters and exploring their psychology and I think that is the strongest aspect of the game. It felt like I was reading a good book. Not all dialogue is gold but there are some great and even profound bits in there. Some contemporary themes shine through without being on the nose. Gameplay is almost all reading, with very few simple puzzles (quite literally) spread out so you have to be aware of that. Some would probably not even call it gameplay, but the choices and actions definitely have far reaching consequences.The sound aspect is very bare bones with repetitive step sounds and almost no music except for a few key moments. It gives the game a contemplative mood so for me it was not a big deal (the lack of music might even be the best artistic choice). And when the music is seldom there it can be quite haunting and beautiful.On the negative there were a few minor bugs (eg. dialogue looped on itself), sometimes navigating to the stairs was weird and the extra character backstory didn't allow for much role playing as I hoped, because the extra dialogue choices didn't matter quite that much. Overall however it didn't impact my experience greatly, I quickly got invested in the characters I was playing and the demons that haunt them.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished this game. It took me eight hours to completely finish the story. Sometimes I forgot what I had to do so I just ended up running around and talking to everyone until I found the person I actually had to talk to in order to proceed with the story. If you are more focused than I was, I think you could finish it quicker. (also I only got 17 out of 41 achievements just so you know)These are some of the many pros:- beautiful illustration- you can pick the heritage of your character (I dont think it influences the story but it was still a fun feature)- often you will be given multiple options for what you can say in a convo (sometimes it influences how the npcs will treat you, often times it doesnt matter)- even tough there are about 30 npcs you quickly get to know their dynamics and mindset- The soundtracks are complete bangers- I might be wrong but I felt like this game rlly gave me a good look into the 16th century (How the ppl lived, their struggles and the role that christianity played in their daily lives)- I LOVED the minigames, unfortunately there werent many and they didnt take very long or were hard to complete BUT they were still very enjoyable.Cons:- It is a game where you have to walk A LOT, as mentioned before, the map isnt very big, but in the end you walk from person to person and thats basically the game (which isnt super bad but I just wanted to mention it)- The main focus of the game is basically a conflict between the farmers and the church (so if christianity triggers you, this might not be the game for you)- I NEED MORE MINIGAMES!Conclusion:Personally I really enjoyed this game. The main focus is on the story, and even tho I liked how relaxing the game was, towards the end I started skipping the dialogues cause I just wanted to know who the murderer was. I am new to steam and I only have 5 games, but evertime I opened steam I wanted to play pentiment. You dont have to be super focused or remember the controls, so oftentimes I would get something to eat and explore the village of Tassing. If that sounds good to you then I would 100% recommend this game to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully told story with a unique visual style, wonderful music, and an excellent cast of characters. Knew it would be a favorite within the first 10 minutes or so & am replaying it for the third time. It definitely encourages multiple play-throughs by having constraints on how long you have to investigate and having lots of dialogue and actions influenced by the character backgrounds you choose. I have had vastly different experiences every time and I continue to be delighted by the level of attention to historical detail and to the care with which the cast is written. Would absolutely recommend to anyone with an interest in medieval history, especially wrt art and religion.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game has great moments and for Act 1 and mostly Act 2 and that kept me engaged mostly, but Act 3 just lost all that momentum quite quickly in my opinion. I also went in thinking that the Reformation would play centre stage and the conflict between the villagers and the Abbey would be more gradual and influenced by your actions but it unfolds mostly the same, regardless of your actions. Game has great art direction unquestionably and you can interact and have long conversations with most people in the game, making it quite immersive and you end up remembering a lot of names. Wish Steam had a recommend setting in the middle because I actually recommend it if you like reading and murder mysteries, I just went in under the impression of greater theological and political commentary and felt a bit disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Truly an amazing game dealing with various themes of truth, mythology, religion and much more. Leaving us deep thoughts and questions about the intent of information and how that affects the medieval community as a whole in its past, present and future.Wonderful buy. Obsidian Entertainment put their whole bussy into this work of art. Probably with many REVISIONS up till launch as well ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: If you like reading, an engrossing historical setting, and tough choices to continually consider this is the game for it. The animation and art are perfect for what the game intends to portray. My advice though: think carefully about every decision you make, from who you speak to to how you present things. Time is limited and every choice has consequences. How you say things impacts your odds of success with later dialog.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be a difficult review for me to write because I don't think a game has ever resonated with me as much as this one did.This is a beautifully slow-paced, text-heavy RPG, with rich dialogue trees and choices spread out amongst a cast of extraordinarily well-written characters. I often find myself struggling to care to for characters in games. Not here; in Pentiment, I found a whole town of people that mattered to me.The love behind this game is obviously felt right from the time you press the New Game option. Every scene is a history lover's dream, and the care the creators took to represent what life was like in this era of history and in this part of the world is beautifully clear to see.The art style is equally as incredible. With smart and creative usage of its setting, Pentiment intricately weaves the late-medieval-into-Renaissance era art styles and early printing works into the story and characters itself, and looks absolutely gorgeous while doing so.Clever plot twists, a well-paced and refreshingly creative story and an engaging examination of both the good and the bad that religion brings with it top off the already supreme amount on offer here. It has been a long time since a piece of art has moved me like this one did, and I am sad to leave the town of Tassing behind. I think the only thing that surpasses the developers' love for what they have made is my love for their game. I am grateful that I was able to play this game. It's an experience I won't ever forget.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: After finishing my first play through, I immediately started a second. There is a limit on how many things your character can accomplish as the acts proceed, which was frustrating at first, being that I wanted to do everything. Now I'm realising that it really adds to the re-playability, and that makes it totally worth it. I can see going through this game at least 3 times, the story is captivating, the art style is appealing, the choices you make have the most interesting impacts on the story and character development, and it's a joy to play. Excellent value for the cost, highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with a great story, a fascinating world and great attention to historical detail. Not only does it take the history and culture of the timeperiod serouisly, the historical detail blends all through the gameplay and presentation. In the end the player even becomes something of a historian him/herself and has to face all the difficulties accompanying such a profession.I highly, highly recommend this game to anyone with a interest in history!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really love Pentiment, but this is not a game I can recommend to everyone. It's mainly driven by it's fantastic narrative, artstyle, characters, and nothing else. Don't expect any challenging gameplay and instead very long stretches of dialogue . Any form of challenge are the occasional speech checks and trying to get enough evidence to prove a person guilty , but there's no fail state. You aren't punished for choosing the wrong person because the game doesn't give you a wrong suspect, and you aren't punished for failing skill checks because the story keeps chugging along smoothly. The knowledge (otherwise builds) you can form your characters around also don't do much and only gives them different smart statements to say. This may sound really negative, but remember I like this game. I like it a lot actually! It has an incredibly beautiful art style with a wide selection of colors, detailing, strokes, and they try to replicate the ancient drawings we see in biblical pictures. Audio designs is really good as well and I like for each character they have different fonts and writing styles, because it shows how that person possibly wrote and their knowledge in English. You get well acquainted with the main cast as the world of Pentiment takes place in a small religious village. The story is the main selling point. Obsidian Entertainment have always had genius writers exploring deep themes and this is another exception. Main theme for Pentiment being, "Should we preserve the past?" Should we keep, maintain, and teach what has come before despite all the bad things that come with it? Hoping that future generations can learn from it and pass their lessons down to the next? Hope that the scriptures and works of artists will be appreciated, and much like said work they too will be remembered. Pentiment is a huge departure from what Obsidian usually makes, RPG with build diversity and complexity, but that doesn't mean straying off to different genres is bad. In fact, they did a really good job a something new. Everything that Pentiment does well helps outweigh the flaws and makes it a true work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Andreas (You), is a journeyman/craftsman who has come to the Bavarian town of Tassing towards the end of his WanderJahre. The introduction of Andreas and the game mechanics come in a dream. With the representation of his conscious in 3 man figures along with a fourth being a mediator for Andreas in his dreams. After this dream, the game starts you off by talking with towns folk and giving you decisions that will affect the rest of the game in only the first few minutes. Such as choosing where you originally studied for your WanderJahre, your educational background and even certain personality traits. The game has many interesting characters to interact with and even rival against. The game really makes you feel as if you were back at a tense moment in both German, European and Human History with the game foreshadowing the decline of the abbey system and the rise of Martin Luther and the German Peasants Revolt of 1525. The game developers really took the time to to understand this era of history, how the people interacted and the mix of religious elements that were quite present in many European towns and peasant's lives. The writing that is in Pentiment is fantastic. I always love a dialogue driven game where it both limits you to some degree but gives choices that wouldn't seem out of place with the characters you are interacting with. I even like how you can go deeper into some dialogue choices with your conscious and make an inform decision. I feel that the developers who chose the name of this game really made it almost have a double meaning. Pentiment is a term used in art to describe the presence of underlying layers or changes that have been made to a painting. This term is often used in the context of restoration or conservation, as it refers to the visible evidence of changes that have occurred during the painting process. You are the artist and the setting which you are in is the painting. The RPG elements and the background of Andreas as an artist make it feel that you are both the outsider looking in and main witness of the events of the world around you. I highly recommend people getting this game. If you are interested in mystery, historical presentation, RPG development or even just liking the Early Modern Period of history (like me lol), I definitely would say this is a must buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Not the detective game I hoped it to be - you do some clue gathering but almost no deduction at all, only some speculation on what you think was the most likely scenario. But rather unexpectedly the game made me really care about what kind of relationships I build with other characters and I think even Telltale/DONTNOD games pale in comparison in regards to that. It felt important to me what other characters think of me in the long term and I think that's a very rare thing to achieve in a game. So overall I think the game's strongest suit is the feeling of community you establish with other characters. And it's a strong period piece as well too - the game is very commited to an era it's portraying.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly dense narrative game. For the first time in any game or movie with medieval theme, I actually felt inside a medieval setting, with believable characters, plot, background, everything. You can see everyone and how they fit together, not just the NPC that's going to give you the next quest.The game is also super pretty, very unique style, and well done. There are some very poetic/visual scenes that are nice to watch as well.The only con is that sometimes it is a bit slow, due to all the realistic dialogue, it's not exciting all the time.Still, I want to see more games inspired by this.4.4/5 ☆
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A story of an artist in a small village in the Bavarian alps, at the border between the Medieval and the Renaissance eras, that turns into a Brother Cadfael style murder mystery, but with constant musings about art, love, faith, history, power, grief as you talk to the peasants, burghers, and monks and sisters of the monastery in your attempt to solve the murder(s). Takes a lot of inspiration from Name of the Rose, or Disco Elysium if we are talking about gaming, but is its own thing. If this sounds appealing to you, you should get this rare gem of a game.Word of warning - at times it is a very slow, almost sedate game. No action, no serotonin drip feed of XP or loot rewards here. There were honestly one or two moments where I had to force myself to continue, but I am so happy I did. Like a good book, the rewards are worth the effort. As well as learning and caring about the characters, you will learn a lot about history, both secular and religious. This is is not a linear "walking simulator" (though I have nothing against those types of games), the choices you make as you explore and talk can have huge consequences over time in this branching narrative. The ending honestly almost moved me to tears, and this is one of those games I will remember the rest of my life.The art and sound design deserves a lot of praise too. The "quill scraping on paper" sound as speech bubbles appear just keeps sending shivers of pleasure down my spine.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure I'd like it, despite the pedigree of the developers and the unique artyle the base gameplay didn't seem like my cup of tea. But Josh Sawyer has definitely done it. It's not a game for everyone, but it's a grounded game about people with all the heart the developers could muster. It's thought provoking, real, and gorgeous. If you like stories where the stakes are local, and the storytelling is the prime focus, you'll like this game. More of this please!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a special type of game that really stood out to me. Josh Sawyer, creative director of Fallout: New Vegas, one my favourite games of all time, brings to life another masterpiece  that I can easily call art, which is also the main theme of the game: art and its lasting impact on people and on history. The story is written wonderfully, the soundtrack by Alkemie is amazing and the artstyle is one of a kind.As many have said, after playing it you'll grow as a person. Extremely recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game, very pretty. Bit heavy on the reading and clicking, but interesting story, characters and  development. Love how the choices you make alter the story and people's lives, for better or worse and not always like you intend to. Just let the story flow, don't think too hard on your choices to get the 'best' outcome, but try to live it like a human being. It's fascinating. Did wish for a little family tree in the game though, haha.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's been some time since I was last so utterly engrossed and DEEPLY touched by a game. Obsidian did an astounding job in re-creating the life and struggles of people in the 16th century, telling a mystery of human psychology, and above all — visualizing the weight of time. You will find the graphics and the "performance" of text in this game so vivid that they blend perfectly with the story and reward a patient mind with one of the most well-orchestrated experiences unique to video games.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game!  Much more of an explore-and-chat game than a point and click, with a lot of threads to think about and recall from earlier hours of play.  My hours are mostly due to just exploring, looking at different locations in different seasons and times of day.  A real joy to play.  Subject matter might not be for everyone, but everything is done just so well.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a visual novel, the fact that tag isn't there is the main reason I can't recommend this game. It tries to be VERY historically accurate but fails in key places like dialogue, character, setting, and fictional history. Even the fonts they chose are not period accurate. I can see why people like this, its different and is a very well made visual novel compared to most of the trash out there, but its just so dull and repetitive. Puzzles are non existent or EXTREMELY easy to solve. I can only recommend this if this if you've never played a visual novel and would like to experience a decent one (albeit with a very, very dull plot) or if you are very very very very bored and in general dissatisfied with your life and have no interests or hobbies. In the second case I would just advise gym/physical activity and its better for you, certainly more fun, and definitely more engaging
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is a delightful game by one of my favorite developers. A lot of attention was given to the historic context and setting in the story line. It's not a flashy open world AAA game, and that is clearly not the goal the writers had in mind. If you are interested in medieval history or art, and don't mind walking through some rainy villages and abbeys in search of the truth, then you will likely enjoy this game. Lots of wonderful games were released in the year 2022 and this is one of them. For me, it has been a great way to calm my nerves after finishing Elden Ring!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing story about depicting a time rarely seen in this way in games and other art forms. It's a grand fictional piece that builds upon a historically accurate world and small town. The art style is unique and beautiful, the characters are endearing and having finished it I loved and will keep in mind Tassing when thinking about what life might have been like during the Renaissance.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment left me speechless. From its visuals to its setting, themes and narrative, Pentiment brings to life a moment in history in a way that no other game has ever even come close to accomplish. Obsidian really outdid themselves this time and that's saying something, it might even be their best game yet. I won't say anything else about Pentiment because words can't do it justice. It is a perfect example of someone's vision executed with perfection. If you enjoy point and click adventures with strong focus on the narrative, history, art or even if you are spiritual or just enjoy a damn good story with the cast of characters you'll grow very attached to.. give Pentiment a try. It might surprise you just how great it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautiful game-- in story, visual style, and music. After a few hours, I was hooked on this in-depth (and historically accurate) portrayal of the town and time period. The game had great pacing of immersing the player in the vibe and everyday stories of a group of people we rarely hear about in this time period, while still maintaining an intriguing mystery.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a game, it's quite toned-down and grounded in its approach to the (fictional) history it depicts, but it never feels boring or inconsequential. The visual direction really fits with what the game is going for thematically, and looks much better than the small store page screenshots might make you think. The story is engaging and actually allows you to fail in certain ways if you're not paying attention, which is rare for story-driven games. All in all, it's about as good as one would expect from a game director like Josh Sawyer.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: After I finish this game i felt immediately empty: the exact same feeling when you finish an amazing book.I love everything of Pentiment.The artwork, the dialogue, the story, the amazing writing, and the characters.The characters are real, with their joy, sadness, pain, hopes, dreams. their 1500 lives.I think Andreas, Otto, Caspar, Magdalene, Brother Piero, Claus, Sister Gertrude and Tassing people, 'll have a special place in my heart.Thank you so much.Yeah, i cry a little :')
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: If you like narrative games, if you like Obsidian games, if you like Josh Sawyer games, I believe this game will enjoyable for you. With a beautiful graphic look, a deep dialogue system, and tons of choice that will impact the world as you go through the game, the game is just a joy to play. There is also tons of depth in terms of the history that you can learn. Obsidian's glossary system is put to great use here. You can remember characters, or ideas, terms, etc. as links are integrated directly into the dialogue. Things to know: It's not voice acted, so prepare to do some reading. I would play it for a couple hours at a time as anti-programming to the other more action games I am playing. It was perfect for that! There are secrets to discover inside the world. The map isn't overwhelming but feels very "lived" in for a point and click narrative adventure. Trust yourself. Go along for the ride. There are no wrong answers, just the adventure set before you to explore and enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment might be the next modern classic, after Disco Elysium. It's hard to not wholeheartedly recommend this game, even though it is definitely not for everyone. Pentiment is slow. Pentiment is quiet. Pentiment is visually simple. Pentiment is part of the evolution of text-based gaming and interactive fiction. Here are some thoughts I had while playing (most art is best experienced as blindly as possible, so proceed with caution):- Interesting lack of music, making the few moments where music does occur quite effective, even though it is often simple Gregorian chant or historically accurate folk music.- I praise the lack of an Exp. system, or just a lack of useless collectibles, ‘numbers going up’, the constantly being rewarded for everything you do, the ‘game-y’ stuff. It’s more ethical and respectful. The story, the people in it, and your decision-making is what matters here, and we know that. The player doesn’t need to constantly be given a small dopamine-kick to keep him/her engaged, it invites us, forces us to seek deeper ways of engaging with the game. Very brave of Obsidian. - The red line indicating that a short footnote-like explanation is available is a clever mechanic, informing the player, helping us better understand the history and culture without having us read long in-game books that could break the pace.- The time advancing when pursuing leads is brilliant. Everything you do becomes so much more weighty and important. Thinking carefully through all your options gets rewarded, you don’t have the usual luxury of doing whatever you want, when you want. This makes the meticulous completionist mindset impossible, which greatly helps push the player into a way more fitting mindset of weighing your options carefully and engaging with the world and its people more deeply. You’re not just going through a list of people to talk to, you never know when certain options will become unavailable.I have some minor gripes with the minigames and the 'This will be remembered' when certain dialogue options are chosen (why does this need to be explicit?), but both never really spoiled the experience for me, and I doubt it will for other people.Pentiment is the result of an artist being given the time and resources to fulfill a passion project he has been itching to realize since the 90's. It has an integrity I rarely find in other games, a strong artistic backbone that is impossible to remain unnoticed while playing, and one of the first pieces of heavily researched historical fiction in the history of video games. It might do it at a slower pace than it's predecessors, but Pentiment propels interactive writing forward, just like Disco Elysium and Planescape Torment did, and should absolutely not be overlooked. Play it in chunks of an hour or so, over a long period of time, and with a relaxed but engaged mind. Give it some time to warm up.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Your choices do not matter at all. This is not an RPG. The main draw of the story is the murder mystery, but the mystery is impossible to officially solve in-game in the sense that no matter how you choose to conduct the investigation, whether you succeed or fail any dialogue checks, whoever you accuse is innocent. This is because the game doesn't let you accuse, suspect, or even investigate the real killer. Even more baffling, there is concrete evidence for other people being the killer, and its never explained why that evidence was there if they weren't the killer. Its a really cheap bait and switch because I guess they thought it would be a good "twist" or whatever if it looked like it was 99% obvious one person was the killer but they ended up not being one anyway. One thing I did appreciate is that its possible to figure out who the killer is before the reveal, even if there is no concrete evidence behind it and its more of a process of elimination (also a couple of really obvious hints in act 3). Still, there are a ton of holes an unexplained issues with the killer being who they are. I just don't see the point in a murder mystery game that's this linear and railroaded. Obsidian are known for having so many branching paths in their games so I don't think it would have been impossible to do. Of course, the story as-is is constructed in such a way that it doesn't work at all if the player is ever allowed to suspect and accuse the real killer. But still...without interactivity actually mattering, it just boils down to a VN with lots of tedious puzzles and slice of life that serve no purpose. They should have written the story in such a way as to accommodate choices better, rather than write a linear story and then try to shoehorn choices into it so they can take advantage of their reputation for making excellent RPGs.  Which is a shame, because if you look at it as a pure VN, the story is actually quite good. The dialogue is well written, the characters are complex, etc. This is definitely the level of writing we've come to expect from Obsidian. Which is why I would rather have had the game just commit to openly being a full VN. If you're a big history nerd, like VNs, and aren't put off by the lack of choices mattering, you might want to check this out. For everyone else, I would say not.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: So, while it's not long, this game does require a little bit of patience - to be honest, my one complaint is that, if I opened and the autosave had been at a point before when I had exited, trying to get through dialogue I'd done before could be a mite tedious. And in truth, it is a story as a game (albeit one whose details you can affect; heck the trailer I'm now watching shows me a couple of scenes I didn't even realize were possible). However, if that second sentence isn't a turn-off to you, and you're into history, I would highly recommend this. I would also recommend players look up what "pentiment" means, and keep that in mind throughout . . . it really will give you a deeper appreciation of this game's narrative and visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I will say this - if you want a meaningful, historical and very intricate game, not only a fantastic story, but a real thinker, then this is for you. Due to the Name of the Rose being one of my favourite novels, and a passion for history, I fell in love with this game from the get-go. The graphics can be likened to the pages of an old script, with illustrations that are just beautiful. The sounds and ambience of the game are to die for, and I always think highly of a game that really takes the choices you make, in speech and action, into account. Sometimes it's satisfying enough just to explore when you can, in order to appreciate the work and sincerity that has gone into this game. I absolutely loved it. Beautifully made.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Very Mild spoilers hidden.I fell in love with this town of people, their individual lives all layering into a tight nit community. Particularly young Ursula  and young Paul  . Each and every person had their own opinions, beliefs and most importantly lives and history. Learning about them, helping them and simply sharing a meal helped me feel so close to the incredible range and cast of characters and people within. I think this is helped pulled off by the games timeframe, it was, in my view a masterstroke to make the game take place over a period of years, with gaps between each act. Seeing your actions change the town for better and worse made every little decision, even just talking to people, feel tangibly meaningful. Watching as history happens around you, history you only vaguely remember hearing about, It gives you or at least makes you feel something of an enlightening perspective. Learning about history and then using that knowledge as you went, it made me want to look deeper into areas of history I previously did not care for, specifically as an example after playing I wanted to learn about the Jewish history of Prague, and that in turn led me to learning about various other topics such as the Thirty Years War.I believe this should be the future of larger game studios, They can continue making their blockbuster games, open world online games filled with as many buzzwords and mechanics so they appeal to as many people as possible. Because I actually also enjoy those games, but they should ALL set aside resources for smaller internal teams to make games such as this, I think the fact this came out of Obsidian and was spear headed by an incredible team will give other developers and publishers pause to consider this method as an option. Truly I want to see this industry grow healthily and I believe this fantastic game could be that spark. if only internally at Xbox. I want to thank each and every person who worked on making this game, It ment alot to me in my short time with it. Im sure it means alot more to each and every one of you. I know i wasnt able to verbalise everything i wanted to say about this game, But I hope what I was able to say gets across my feelings for this game. Thank you.Oh, and to anyone with even the slightest consideration to playing this, do it. Trust me, its entirely worth it and then some, I rarely buy games not on sale, but this was an exception I do not regret in the slightest.

_childDocuments_.review: This might just be the most compelling, well-written game since Disco Elysium. I longed for something to fill the void that game left, and I think Pentiment just about delivered it. I'll be perfectly honest: There were times when the game tested my patience, because Pentiment is very dense with detail and is certainly just as interested in portraying the mundanity of these characters' lives as it is in the EXTREMELY INTRIGUING murder mystery. The third act in particular took some time to pick up, but once it does... I am so happy I stuck with it. The ending is a real winner. Rarely does a game move me to such a profound degree. You just don't expect it when you first boot up the game, but this is a true tearjerker, let me tell you. One of my favorite aspects about the game is how it handles time. The *finiteness* of it, and the *passing* of it. You can't experience everything in one playthrough, never know everything, and thus you can never truly trust the incredibly difficult choices you HAVE to make. And the choices have such deep consequences for everything in the lovely town you get to know, and the genius of it is that you return to this town at three different points in time so that you get to see exactly how these choices impact the people living there. And don't get me started on these characters! They're a great cast of lovable and hatable and ambivalent folks. Excellent writing is backed up by great artwork, sparse but effective music and boatloads of interesting, well-researched teachings about life in the 1500's. I learned a lot of stuff, and the game compelled me to learn even more. I LOVED this game, I WHOLEHEARTEDLY recommend it, and now I must search for a way to fill the void again...

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is easily one of my favorite games of 2022. This is truly an excellent game and an easy recommendation to people that enjoy investigation/story games and an ESPECIALLY easy recommendation to people with an interest in the Medieval/early Renaissance periods. Here's a spoiler-free summary of the strengths and weaknesses of Pentiment:Setting: The game is admittedly very dry most of the time but I loved it. Pentiment's setting (a 16th century town in the Bavarian Alps) is both extremely refreshing and its main strength. It is beyond obvious that there are people at Obsidian with a great love for this place and time in history and the attention to detail is excellent. You can really sense the history nerd enthusiasm throughout the entire experience and it is infectious.Writing/Characterization: There are a lot of characters in the game and they do an excellent job representing various facets of life in the setting and stand out as simultaneously memorable and mundane. The peasants and townspeople might be predictably God-fearing, but that does not mean that they don't have their own hopes, dreams, opinions, and temperaments. The player character, Andreas, is both distinct and relatable while allowing room for player-side role play. The player is given the opportunity many, many times to choose between being a devout Christian or a cynic, an optimist or a pessimist, a people pleaser or a rude narcissist, and more.Visuals: The art style of the game flawlessly channels the janky Medieval European art feel while also managing to still look good in its own right. The bizarrely illustrated animals both in the town and in the margins of the pages of your journal are all delightful. Even Andreas' slightly strange walking animation feels intentional and thought out.Investigation: Pentiment has a decent chance of scratching your detective game itch but the actual investigation aspect of the game is not particularly strong. Andreas' "detective work" boils down to walking around and clicking on various things/talking to various people and occasionally making decisions about where to spend his time (ex: spend a few hours following someone, have supper with one family instead of another, etc.). The player's actual capacity to "solve" anything hinges on making conclusions with incomplete information (which may be more or less incomplete based on thoroughness). This might be unsatisfying for some people but it is also a distinct and interesting departure from other similar games.Choices: It cannot be denied that your choices matter and make a difference. A handful of your choices will dramatically affect various aspects of the story. However, it is clear that Pentiment does not allow much genuine deviation from the main plot and the player's choices primarily end up serving to flavor the experience rather than actually alter it. In this sense the only "failure" you could experience is not exploring thoroughly enough to feel satisfied. The complexity of the branching paths is generally high but there were a few times where dialogue triggered before it should have or was not changed when it should have been. This was rare enough where it is easily forgivable.Bugs: I'm not sure how prevalent these bugs were for others, but there were two somewhat severe bugs that impacted my experience. First, clicking "Continue" upon opening the game completely failed to function until the game was restarted every single time. Second, each time the game transitioned to the next part after something that could be interpreted as an ending it sent me back to the main menu. Both times I genuinely thought the game had ended and the only thing that kept me from stopping there was going to Google to satisfy my mild confusion. Playing through the climactic section again was enough to trigger the transition to the next part of the game each time but this bug very nearly caused me to miss 3/4 of the game. These bugs didn't affect my enjoyment of Pentiment but they are scary nonetheless.Overall: Pentiment is a hugely refreshing experience that channels inspiration from an underrepresented setting. The developers' enthusiasm is plain to see and greatly enhances the enjoyment. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment overall is a decent murder mystery that is held back by it’s lack of your decisions having any real impact.  This game throws a lot of decisions at the player, some good ideas some bad.  The best part are the numerous decisions you get to make creating you character that makes your character feel unique and gives different conversation topics to discuss.  You can be an occultist or a theologist or even a lawyer.  All choices can lead to very different conversation topics.  The problem is these choices have very little impact.  There is a similar system in Scarlet Hollow, but that game handles it far better where creating your character leads to radically different outcomes in the game.  I would be fine if these choices didn’t massively change the story, but in a murder mystery I would want these choices to affect what evidence your character can obtain to help them solve the murder.  There are points where it seems like the game is trying to do that…but almost always you are going to get the same evidence one way or the other.  It ends up being just more flavor text in dialogue with characters.  Meanwhile in Scarlet Hollow it both radically changes outcomes in the game and gives you completely new insights into the mystery that you would not otherwise obtain making multiple playthroughs meaningful.  You don’t really have that here.  The game also seems to have conversations topics that should cause different events to occur in the game, but these too are illusions.  You really have very little impact on the story, the same story beats will happen.  Which is a shame, this game is not particularly long, it’s about 15hrs.  It’s a good length, but with a game of that length it would be nice if your decisions could affect the story.  It would have been spectacular if different people were murdered based on your decisions or your decisions perhaps caused people to not be murdered. The game does have some decisions that I guess “matter” but not in a good way.  Basically, your time in a day is limited.  So you have to choose what clues you want to search for by interrogating the correct people.   The game is divided into 3 Acts…only Acts 1 and 2 are murder mysteries.  A time limit is given to find the clues to solve the murder in each Act.  I assume maybe if you made like a perfect outline there is probably a way to get all clues within each act…but it sure seems like that is not possible.  I feel this is a problematic game design, because while I like the idea you could get the wrong clues and fail to correctly solve the murder…the initial evidence you get gives you no real concept of where to begin your investigation and further even if you suspect a particular individual there is no indication who in the town you should talk to in order to gather additional information on that suspect.  The game has no save options so even if you know who you want to gather information on you might accidently interrogate someone who has nothing to say about that person.  This happened a lot to me.  Still I probably would prefer this design to a game that just spells it out for you.  The fact the game literally lets you gather the wrong clues and come to the wrong conclusions and it doesn’t cause the game to end is fantastic.It’s just disappointing that choices are not better handled in this game, because I think overall the murder mystery ranks in the top tier of murder mysteries.  It’s well thought out and crafted, so I wish it was in a better game.  I do love the art style, which I didn’t think I would, but the illuminated manuscript theme is great.  However, the choice to have no background music in this game is a colossal blunder.   Having no voice acting is fine…but no music…it’s a baffling decision.  Music is basically key to conveying emotions, especially when the characters have no voice of their own.  I can’t even imagine playing games like Night in the Woods without music, the soundtrack of that game is what brings the whole game together.  The other issue is the sound effects they have are not enjoyable.  I literally had to turn of dialogue sound because the writing sound effect anytime someone talks is unbearable.  I am also disappointed that the game has this 3 act structure but each act has it’s only contained murder mystery.  I feel telling one mystery over 3 acts would have been a better use of their skill and time to make a more complex mystery.  The rest is going to be spoilers Look if you are a fan of murder mysteries this is a must play game it’s that simple.  I would say it’s flawed, but I would love to see an even more ambitious murder mystery told by this developer instead of these shorter vignette style mysteries.   I still think this falls far below masterpieces like Elsinore, Scarlet Hollow, or Disco Elysium in terms of your ability to affect the story with your choices, but it’s still a good game.  #Worth $15

_childDocuments_.review: I spent most of my youth playing mindless games that required lots of time and grinding...to get better gear and other nonsense.As im reaching 40 years old....I have to say Pentiment blew me away completely....it's not just a game...it's an experience.So all those time consuming games were alright i guess..as I matured they helped me appreciate the finer things in life.And Pentiment is one of the  finer things in life indeed.It's one of those games I will remember forever and definitely as some time passes by I will give it another playthrough.Watching gameplay videos of Pentiment doesn't do it justice...the atmosphere is just mind-blowing.Do yourself a favour and treat yourself to this masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: I am on the hunt for story-rich games with RPG elements and lots of style. Pentiment game checked all of those boxes! I'd recommend trying it if you enjoyed Disco Elysium, Roadwarden, Spiritfarer, or Kingdom Come: Deliverance. The game is text-heavy, but it's well-written with interesting and diverse characters. Your goal is to unravel the mysteries of a small Bavarian town in the 16th century. Political intrigue and character development abound. I cried a few times throughout the game.The RPG elements include making frequent dialogue choices that impact the story and customizing your character through four different background features (each with a range of options). I'd recommend selecting the following backgrounds: Italy / Bookworm / Medicine / Latinist / Orator on the first play through to maximize what you can glean from the characters and world. On my next play through, I plan to run the main character as a hot-headed, know-it-all occultist. I'm excited to see how it changes the gameplay!

Sometimes, you might have 10 choices about who you wanted to share a meal with, but then get railroaded into a dialogue where you didn't seem to get any choice at all. It was all cleverly done, but ultimately unsatisfying.It reminded me somewhat of Kingdom Come Deliverance, where many of the same themes were explored. KCD is an amazing and immersive game, so it was hard to stay excited about the plot in Pentiment. You could make Henry who you wanted him to be with the reputation earned by your choices. Andreas is much more limited and sometimes acts in ways you have no control over. Then you have to answer for his choices, which frustrated me. It's probably not fair for me to compare the games, but I was expecting a bit more from Pentiment based on the glowing reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: It's amazing. I don't normally write reviews for games, but oh my god was this game good. It's definitely for a certain niche, but if you fall within it you'll love this game. Pentiment isn't so much a game as it is a narrative experience; you experience a particularly intriguing artist's life split between 3 parts over several decades. There isn't much "gameplay" here, even if there is a good deal of player agency. You almost must have a good understanding of the Early Modern Period along with the Late Middle Ages if you're to enjoy and appreciate this game to it's fullest, though I'm confident you could still enjoy it without such. _childDocuments_.review: Less of a game, more of a pseudo-interactive movie. There are a few problems that may boil down to personal preferences, especially considering the overwhelmingly positive reviews for this title at the time of writing. First, there is the lack of agency. There is very little impact your decisions have on the main character's surroundings. Most of the interactive parts of the game are choosing what order you'd like to view things that don't matter. "Do I run right to look at this flower first, and then left to look at the book? Or book first, then flower?" That's what it felt like for every minute of gameplay.Second, I could find no hook, no tether, no reason to care about any of the people or things happening in the story - because Andreas, the main character, is so unrelatable. University drop-out artist busybody, but otherwise blank slate? Ah, but you can choose what region of the continent you're somewhat familiar with and what subject matter you dabbled in before dropping out. Again, this has basically no impact on the story, and it does nothing to make Andreas any less unpleasant to play as.Third, the plot is weak and predictable. It's obvious half an hour into the game who the primary villain is, and the other various 'culprits' can't even be determined with accuracy. I assume the latter was a deliberate, artsy decision by the writers to subvert our expectations or something. It's juvenile and insulting. It's the equivalent of an creative arts student filming their final project upside down just to be different. Or shaking the camera the entire time to make it feel 'real'. Actually, you're just visually attacking your audience. This is the same, but with the story. And worst of all, it's not like there's anything else to the game. There is no gameplay, there is no role playing, there is no strategy. It's literally just a short story told in a creative manner. But that 'creative manner' is monotonous, and that 'story' is a stale, a-historical dose of nihilistic garbage, wrapped in pretty colors to make you think it  be meaningful.

_childDocuments_.review: is a murder mystery narrative game set in the 16th century in a small alpine village in Bavaria. Taking place right around the birth of Protestantism, the proliferation of books thanks to the advent of the printing press and a growing wave of peasant revolts,  uses a renaissance art style that’s heavily evocative of the masterpieces of the era and shows how seismic political events can have drastic effects on the lives of ordinary working people, many of whom already have enough to deal with. The world in  is reeling from having many of its core beliefs and structures questioned in a way it’s not comfortable with (much like ours today).You play as Andreas, an artist coming to the end of his wandering period who has been working in one of the few remaining scriptoria in a local monastery while developing his art on the side. His world is turned on its head when a visiting nobleman, one of the monasteries' chief patrons, is murdered and his dear friend and mentor, an elderly monk named Piero, is accused of the crime. Adamant to clear his friend's name, Andreas is given only a few short days to investigate by the Abbot, who fears the crime may lead to the dissolution of the Abbey and wants a swift resolution before the arrival of the archdeacon.One of the core themes in  is change and how it’s resisted. Virtually every character is in the midst of a massive change in one form or another. The Church is reeling from the fallout of Martin Luther’s ninety-five theses and the level of questioning it’s provoking. The Scriptorium is dealing with the forced obsolescence from the rise of the printing press and the village is dealing with the increasingly punitive demands placed upon them by the local abbey. This extends to the characters themselves; Andreas is resisting a change due to his wishes of founding an art studio but the laws state he must marry to do so. So, he delays as much as he can, first by taking as long as he can with his art, then by throwing himself into the search for clues about the murder.Thus begins an investigation into the townsfolk and their lives. 's main strength is the deep characterisation of the locals, each one feels like a real person with their own hopes, dreams and fears. There’s a strong current of empathy running through the narrative. By focusing on the minutiae of everyday life,  fleshes out the locals in ways you don’t see in many other investigative games. You delve into their lives not by interrogating them, but by sitting down and eating with them or helping them with tasks. This means you’re not only uncovering information and motives but also forging connections and relationships which will shape how the game plays out in the future.As the game takes place over 25 years, who you accuse and what you discover becomes more rooted as the characters age and change. It also means that thanks to the wonderful writing, you’ll end up becoming more and more invested in their lives. The truly awesome art style lends so much to this. Despite its medieval manuscript styling, it’s stunningly realistic and helps showcase the depth of research done by the developers. If you were a fan of the historically perfect art of , then you’re in for a treat. The whole framing of the visuals as an illustrated book, like the book of Kells, is an inspired choice. The picture zooms out to read the glossary entries, showing the rest of the page, and it combines well with the pages turning to show scene changes.Another fantastic artistic choice is the clever use of fonts. Different social strata have their dialogue written out in their own font, with the local peasantry having their words scratched out in sharp handwriting to the nobles' gothic script, this gives more depth to the characters and further defines their place in the world and how they are seen by others. I particularly loved the printer’s text being stamped out like a printing press. To give even more life to the script, there are even spelling mistakes dotted around which, after a second, are hurriedly rubbed out and corrected. It’s a brilliant trick that gives the impression that you’re reading a living text, one that’s being written right in front of you as the events unfold. Speaking of reading the text, you’ll be reading an awful lot of it. If there is one demerit with , is that it’s not in a rush to tell you the story. The meticulous detail in every aspect of the history and setting takes a considerable amount of time to convey and it won’t be to everyone’s tastes. There will be some gripes about having signed up for a murder mystery only to be repeatedly drawn into several philosophical debates about everything from the role of the church to the nature of man.  is a wonderfully authentic glimpse into the past, with beautiful music, excellent writing and some eye-watering artwork. Its glacial pace, reams of text and lack of a voice cast may put some off, but this game is a rare thing: intricately detailed and a lot of fun to play. If you’re a fan of dense, layered narratives then you’ve found your heaven in .

_childDocuments_.review: Like a fine wine, Pentiment takes time to fully appreciate. The time spent doing so is absolutely worth it. Pentiment's narrative, historical setting, relaxing ambience and infinite dialogue options guarantee that the tasteful gamer will return indefinitely. You will explore the same locations, speak to the same characters...but you will consistently have different questions, forming different conclusions. With only a limited amount of time for each section of the story, be prepared for unanswered questions, a whole lot of "what ifs"...and an interest in the religiopolitical state of 16th century Bavaria! This, however, is the icing on the cake.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic story told in a very organic way. No, you won't get to solve everything perfectly, because there simply isn't enough time to be exhaustive. But fear not, you'll have more than enough time to get to know the town, abbey, and all the inhabitants therein and come to develop emotional bonds with them. If you care about narrative and storytelling, I can't recommend this enough (unless perhaps you've yet to play Disco Elysium, maybe do that first if it's more your bag?)

It looks beautiful, has some great funny moments, and will make you feel the worst you've ever felt in your life. My only real complaint is that since you can't skip previously read text you have to read a lot of stuff over and over to see all the content.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent adventure game (or RPG without most of the mechanics, as you will). It is a lot of fun to follow the chronicles of the main character and it is presented beautifully.You also have a fair bit of agency in this game which makes it feel like much more than your average adventure game. I thoroughly recommend it if you are looking for a slow burn of a game, best played leading up to Christmas.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I probably complete only about 10 percent of all games I start, as I don't have much patience for boredom, sloppiness, poorly crafted worlds, etc. When I finished Pentiment, my mouth was hanging open in appreciation for this love poem to a small village in the medieval Bavarian Holy Roman Empire. The pace of Pentiment is often slow just as village life was slow and routine, but the payoff is more than worth it. I spent 84 hours according to Steam, probably more than many will, but the game is best role-played in small chunks. Pentiment is not for everyone. People who don't like to read much in their games may wish to pass on this one. People who require action combat in their games will be sorely disappointed. People who enjoyed "The Name of the Rose" by Umberto Eco will probably love this game. Pentiment is a video version of a choose your own adventure story. There are some very easy puzzles to solve here and there, but otherwise the game consists of reading dialogue and making choices. And the choices have real consequences - in some cases life or death consequences. A wide variety of subject matter is touched on, including the meaning of faith,. mental illness, the push-pull between societal expectations and one's dreams, the importance of art and literature, heresy, and I could go on and on. But experience it yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Cool adventure game that makes full use of its setting in 16th century Bavaria.  The characters are memorable, and the plot is intriguing.  Art and sounds are phenomenal, and there are little touches that elevate the game.  For example, the font used when a character is talking is based on their work, education level, etc.  Priests and nuns have a Gothic font, the well educated use a cursive-style font, the peasants have a simpler script, and book printers have a block print.    The major negative to the game is that all the decisions you make don't have a huge impact on the plot of the game.  Each Act ends in pretty much the same way, with some actions seemingly railroaded for the sake of the plot, not how you developed the character.  That being said, all the choices you made can impact many minor things throughout the story, and the ending does a good job of highlighting those results.It's a game more about the journey than the destination, but it's a great journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Blew my mind! Very involved thinking, complete with historic notes and extensive glossary. I was intimidated at first but referencing rich historic data with magnificent illustrations was a journey worth taking. I loved how the layers from pre-pagan to pagan to Christianity is peppered throughout and debated in the game. Customizing character development throughout this journey was fun and sometimes dramatic! Surprises at every turn, too! The music is superb, at times haunting and also timely. A few glitches though -- sometimes dialogue boxes appeared upside down AND backwards, then would flip upward and be from left to right. Just putting that out there for updates in case it was not intentional (did not seem so and would happen randomly with characters). I will be replaying this game the entire way through after really absorbing the experience next few days (took 20 hours this time as I made extra pit stops to explore and deliberately deeply at times or to marvel at the rich scenery and enjoy sounds like the waterfall in the forest or a monk singing in the church). Highly recommend for history lovers and people who like a slower paced game with lots to ponder. I'm not even religious but maybe spiritual. It is a game for mystery lovers, intellectuals as well as those who appreciate sumptuous settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: An illuminated text come to life and filled with murder and intrigue? Sign me up! This game is captivating in story and brings nods to history and and art into a compelling narrative. This is a great game to wind down with and enjoy on a rainy afternoon. I am only half way through at time of writing this but cant wait to see what else the producers put out next.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One should not use lightly the word masterpiece and I surely don't. However, this is one of the cases I feel compelled of defining as such a videogame.Everything shines. The writing of course, the interface, the graphic style, the story pace, music and sounds.If you're even remotely interested in investigation games with a deep historical background, unique athmosphere, etc... do yourself a favour and play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is an RPG where you assume the role of a medieval artist through their years in an alpine little village. And there is a murder mystery. And intrigue! But that is not what matters, because what matters is living in the era, through the slow pace storytelling. The art direction is unique, the sound design is smart.There isn't constant music in the background, but when there is, you feel it in your very soul.All and all, Pentiment is an one of a kind experience, that builds steady through the first Acts, and in the 3rd Act, it hits through the roof. Play it for all the above reasons (and also if you don't mind reading a lot of text)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click story that is less about making the "right" choices and more about taking a step back and seeing how narratives weave together to transform into "fact," regardless on if they are true.Less a murder mystery and more the chronicle of a town through time and back again. A story about how people and places change and, sometimes, how they don't This is the kind of narrative game that leaves you thinking about it long after you shut it off and now that I've finished it, I suspect I'll carry it with me longer yet. Tl;dr: If you want to settle into a story, but want something a little more interactive than a book, do yourself a favor and pick this up.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game ages ago with the intent of playing it immediately. Life got crazy and I forgot about it. I had the flu recently and that allowed me to get the chance to actually sit down and play this amazing game.I did not read any reviews before touching the game, keep in mind.It is a time based game, and I wish I spent more time at the beginning exploring, because honestly I thought this game was going to be over in 5 hours TOPS.The replayability of this game is amazing, with almost every choice leading you down a different path. I'm not sure if the end result would ultimately be different, but the stories and the lives of the characters surely have to be effected.This game made me cry and I really was not expecting to fall in love with the characters. 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with a moving story. _childDocuments_.review: My law degree did nothing but piss people off, just like in real life.In all seriousness, if you are at all a fan of any or all of Early Modern Bavarian History, art, theology, frogges, Disco Elysium, and choices with consequences that hit you like a bullet from a flintlock blunderbuss, play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment. The game was great all the way long until Act III. As a player, you can make a lot of decisions. You can make a “huge” impact on the game world. Yes, u can play it differently in another playthrough.  Yes, the lore of the game is interesting, it's interesting to read all the dialogs (until Act III as for me). BUT: sadly, the main scenario is childish, linear, and quite simple. So, “Why negative review?”, until Act III, the same characters as u saw before but 18 years older, and you can catch yourself thinking about why u can now do such things and explore that u couldn't before, after all, the concept of the “Act” still the same – “Find out the traitor, and explore the real history of a town.”. ”Nah, I have already done that before, maybe something new?” — the first question that pops out in my mind. It's okay if you do this as a character from Act I and II, but in Act III you're playing as a different person. Why should I do the same things? In conclusion, the game is great, with good lore, interesting minor characters, their interactions, and some situations you're supposed to be in, but every hour gameplay gets easier, and the plot gets more boring. Also, as a “detective” in game, you can't  charge a suspect that really is an imposter (it's pretty easy to figure out who it is actually).

_childDocuments_.review: I struggle with where to begin when writing this review. Rarely, if ever, has a piece of media touched me as deeply as Pentiment has. I finished my first play-through mere moments ago, and I'm completely in awe of the masterwork of both visual and narrative storytelling displayed by the creators of this game. Successfully portraying the game in the style of illuminated manuscripts must have been difficult beyond measure, but the time, effort, and dedication spent doing so absolutely paid off. I was completely immersed in the art, finding myself speechless at the amount of love and attention that was given to every moment of the game. A particular detail that never failed to make me smile was the text; specifically, how the black letters were written in order, with the colored ink filled in afterwards. The choice of having stylized fonts represent the station of the speaker was inspired. I'm also incredibly impressed by the fluidity of the character's movements; both in larger actions, as well as things like a face turning away from the viewer.On a personal note, I'm extremely grateful for the depiction of "smaller" figures, historically given less attention than the aristocracy. In particular, the portrayal of queer relationships were incredibly meaningful to me. So often, homosexuality is treated like a recent phenomenon, but we've always been here, we've just had to hide - however, that didn't stop them from having fulfilling lives and relationships. The same goes for neurodivergent people - Brother Volkbert is an excellent example of how autistic individuals would thrive in the order and quiet of monastic life. The inclusion of the Sommerfields, Vácslav, and Brother Sebhat also added much needed dimension to flesh out the world of the game and address the prejudices of the time, while still respecting them as individuals.This game intersects at so many of my special interests: illuminated manuscripts, 15th and 16th century monasteries, Reformation Europe, and the daily lives of those present. Honestly, it matches up so perfectly that I had accepted that it could never live up to my standards. I've never been more happy to be wrong. As I watched the credits, I found myself truly absorbing every name that passed by, thanking every individual who clearly held so much love and dedication for a time period so often overlooked. Every last person involved in this game's creation has my gratitude and admiration. Thank you for everything.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could recommend Pentiment.While the game's artstyle and setting are something refreshing, the writing and "choices matter" gameplay are not. Going into this game practically blind (having only read a few Steam reviews), I expected to get a deep, story-rich game where you could truly immerse yourself in a setting not often portrayed in games.Unfortunately, all I received was railroading, unexplained mechanics, misplaced minigames and the bitter feeling of my time being utterly wasted. After playing the first two acts, I felt disatisfied with the way my "choices" were being handled. There is always a sense of being rushed along due to time limits. Things that absolutely should have been dialogue options in key moments were completely lacking, most likely because an arbitrary checkpoint was not reached in a satisfactory manner. There is a system in place for persuasion, which the game only informs you of once one actually occurs. Up until that point, there is no indication that whatever is being "remembered" by characters will be used in a persuasion check.In hindsight, most of my time played was spent running around the town to see if any new dialogue popped up after having a conversation or receiving a semi-confession from someone. For a large majority of the time, absolutely nothing changed. There is no real way to shape your character, to make your choices have impact, or to feel like you've actually done something good for a change. After completing about a quarter of act 2, I just stopped talking to people that should've had something useful to say, because it became clear that I was being railroaded into a narrowing path that the writers carefully set out. After act 2 ended, I just didn't see any reason to continue playing the game at all. I tried to care about act 3, but I really just couldn't.As other reviewers have said; take away the artstyle and setting, and you just have a mediocre Telltale-like story.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who enjoy narrative-heavy and "choices matter" games, Pentiment is wonderful. The atmosphere, the art style, the writing, everything were engaging to me. It really cements how much weight your actions have, and I quite love that.TL;DR - Wonderful plot-heavy and point-and-click game, best for those who love narratives and don't mind stepping into a portal of the far past of 16th century Europe.

_childDocuments_.review: This type of experience is why I love video games.I should start off by saying that I’m not a history buff. I was initially worried that I would miss out on a lot of what was going on. However, don’t let that worry you. Pentiment is engaging from start to finish even if you are rusty on Middle Ages history! If I had to sum up the game in a short sentence it would be ‘It’s like Disco Elysium but in the Middle Ages’.The game starts in 1518 where you must solve the murder of a dead aristocrat. The prime suspect is your friend and mentor, and the person who found the body. You play as Andreas Maler, a journeyman artist. Convinced that your friend is innocent you decide to investigate the murder yourself. The problem is, there are too suspects and not enough time to investigate all possible leads. This is Pentiment’s unique selling point. Time moves forward in this game so there is not enough time to investigate every lead and find all the evidence. Some questions will be left unanswered. There are of course consequences to your actions, with multiple times where you will find yourself agonising over the choices you made. That’s what is brilliant about Pentiment, you will always find yourself wondering what would have happened of we had chosen option B instead of option A, much like you might do in real life. The game never tells you if you have found the right culprit! It is quite possible the suspect you have gathered all the evidence against is innocent and you will never know but is still executed for crime. This of course means you will nee multiple play through’s find get the whole picture of what is going on in the game world.The writing is high quality, interesting, engaging and paint each character in a unique light as you would accept from an Obsidian game. The artwork is also fantastic. It is a mixture of late medieval manuscripts, early print, and woodcuts. There really isn’t another game that looks quite like it. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of narrative driven games. That is what the game is first and foremost, a narrative adventure!Game rating: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend mainly because it definitely tries to push a VERY negative view on the world of middle ages before the Renaissance. Feminism absent but dearly wanted. Martin Luther a background hero who's only issue with the Catholic church were the indulgences (false, he disagrees on many other aspects).Church doctrine bad, monks&priests hypocrisies & greedy & evil - basically the only apparent "good" ones are the ones you do not talk too much to. Let me tell you about some of the characters of the monks and nuns at the monastery without spoiling who is who  : the thief, the one that is "simple", the slut who has an abortion - provided to her by a fellow nun, of course, the gays (yes, two monks), the depressed feminist, the occult enthusiast, the bootlicker, the would-be dictator, the one(s) with big anger issues, the monk-nun couple, the pushover and quite a few that would rather not to be there at all, but they've got no choice. Yeah ... hardly anyone is there because of his devotion to God.Again, without diving into spoilers, the ultimate fate of the monastery and the revelation at the end makes it VERY clear onto the developers views on religion. Let me spoil you this much : it ain't a favorable one.So I would NOT recommend this game for anyone who does not hate, or at least dislikes, the middle ages period and the catholic church.As is the case with a lot of "historical" fiction written these days, it is nothing like a story being told by someone actually living in those times.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game with a fun and engaging story. Unlike some people, I didn't find it very replayable though. At first I did, but upon my second playthrough I realized that my expectations were a big bigger than the game's scope. I figured my choices would make huge differences and it would be almost a totally different game based on a few key choices (eg. in Witcher 2 siding with Iorvath or Roach in Act 1 kind of differences). That said, it's definitely a good game, and definitely worth a buy (I bought it on a good sale and don't feel bad about that), but don't expect as much replay value as I did. You'll get different outcomes based on your choices (dialog and such) but you *won't* get a different world to play in as I believed.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for gameplay or a meaningful "choices matter" experience, you might want to cool your jets. Otherwise, this interactive novel is amazing at what it does. Developers clearly care about the historical context of their game, from art style to social interactions. It oozes character. Yes, it's guilty of superimposing modern values on another society... but there is a valiant effort to make us understand that a 16th Century Alpine people don't share our values system, and that we should maybe be ok with that - just like Tassing's inhabitants are ambivalent . I heavily dislike oniric detours in games, and this is no exception, but it is kept to a minimum, so as not to be unbearable. So, if you like historical visual novels, throw yourself at this. If you're looking for the Next Great Detective Game, maybe look elsewhere; this isn't it.

_childDocuments_.review: Art is about showing the truth of life, showing what you see, not hiding anything away. Treat this game as art -- a showing of Art instead of being a work of art. I've imagined how to narrate in an a-phonetic language (means pure writing -- the plan of an idea on Derrida's critique on phonocentrism) back in my day studying linguistics and prowling philosophy at the university. Now this game is exactly what I could have imagined, perhaps even better. Medieval writing fonts and styles are the core of the storytelling, and it offers me perhaps the best reading experience of all visual novels I've come across. Now, I am not planning on giving too much aesthetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pretending to be a Socrates of a sort, but I am honest enough to tell you that it makes me cry out of joy when I did this hermeneutic work: I routed a thread with the concept of art (not the question of 'what is artwork', but 'art is doing what') through the game. I intend not spoil anything here, so this is all I have to say: It is a honest 'just showing', and it faithfully finishes the task. My sincere appreciation, Andreas (or, Obsidian Entertainment.)

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I just finished this game and what a ride it has been. It has all been exceptionally developed by Obsidian, not in the least through the unique art style they used.While Act 3 was a bit slow in the beginning, the rest of the game is full of interesting characters surprising side-stories and not in the least a fantastic overarching main story-line to bite your teeth in for 15-18 hours or so.Recommended!
