_childDocuments_.review: God, where do I even start? Pentiment is one of the most compelling gaming experiences I've ever had. I could talk for hours about it, all the little things I loved, my feelings about the narrative and style, but this review is going to be long enough as it is, and as we all know Steam users prefer the same memes over actual reviews so I'll try and keep it brief. I adore Pentiment, even though I have substantial problems with the narrative, specifically in Act 3, which I can't really talk about without major spoilers, but a lot of threads are left open, plot points that don't make much sense in restrospect, and decisions that don't make sense in context of the characters making them. Even so, I adore this game, its dedication to its own identity, the way the narrative weaves between whole decades, and most certainly, the art style and sound design.Penitment's most obvious characteristic is its completely unique art style, matching the art style of actual medieval paintings, and sound design that is superb and complementary, creating such a vibrant but also pensive ambience that you just soak in, every second. I wanted more, I couldn't have enough of this style, this small town in the middle ages, in the mountains of Bavaria, and the people you meet. I want more games like this, that commit instead of trying to please everyone, even though I'm aware we are probably not going to get them. The game's narrative and dialogue may not be as crazy and complex as something like Disco Elysium, but as the subject matter is history, it's perfect, the dialogue slowly scratching across the screen, the font influenced by each character's class and vocation and education. The dialogue system was pure ASMR, I never got tired of seeing the letters realistically soak and blotch, filled in with soft sounds of a pen sailing across parchment. The narrative is narrow, but focused, offering certain freedom, but the broad story remains similar, even though there are key spots in the story that can go very differently each time. Again, the first two acts were perfect, but the third act is where my problems started, which I can't really go into, but if you play the game you will know yourself. Even so, Pentiment arrives at a satisfying, emotional conclusion, even if I was unsatisfied and confused at points. Either way, Pentiment is a unique experience, and if you care in the slightest about history and storytelling, then I have to recommend this game, I could go on for hours, like how Pentiment means painting over something, or covering up, similar to the root word "kafara" in arabic, or how it's themes of history align perfectly with the characters, or how I can't get tired of the art style and sound, but you have to experience it yourself. With the flaws and all, I will never forget this game, and revisit it for years to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I applaud Josh Sawyer and the team for creating such an idiosyncratic game in today's market - it is extremely rare to have any kind of modern media that goes so deep into 16th century Holy Roman Empire history and the sociopolitical structure of serfdom. And the efforts made here are clear to see, from the very unique art style based upon sources such as the Nuremberg Chronicles as well as beautiful fonts and music that harken back to the era. All of those things are fascinating and superlative, including the minutiae of the lore behind the game: remnants of Roman civilization long forgotten, the conflict between the church and the peasantry, etc. However, as a game which ostensibly gives you options to role play as and choose your own character to solve different issues, this aspect is unfortunately is quite flawed. It becomes very clear that many of the backgrounds and traits are not weighed equally or at least made to be interesting - for example, medicine ends up to be really negligible or even negative as a trait in the game compared to others. Worse is that, regardless of any of your choices, you are shoehorned into particular ending in Act 2 and 3. Even if the actions of the character you went with doesn't exhibit any of those traits, your Andreas will end up the same, and that is honestly quite disappointing. I also feel that Act 3 is quite rushed and is the weakest, especially in terms of persuasion mechanic. Worse is that it feels like your Act 3 protagonist has a lot of knowledge that the person isn't supposed to have, but you as the player knows because of you saw what happened in the prior two Acts.  In an Obsidian interview I watched, the team highlighted the potential of deep characterization in such kind of role playing, but also why it is so important to them that the game spans 25 years of history to show how much has changed. But unfortunately, I find that these two goals end up being in conflict with one another, and the team has instead tried to place importance on things which ultimately takes certain choice and empowerment away from the player. Yes, it is good to see how much of the society changes due to the printing press and the Lutheran movement etc., but I'm not sure about the very dictated storyline that we are forced to funnel into, including the "surprise" of Act 3 which just doesn't align with the way I played my character in previous acts at all. As a game that seems to require or encourage multiple playthroughs, the game also makes it very, very tedious to replay the game - from the very slow and repeated animation (those flipping pages in your journal are pretty but are just a waste of time) to unskippable cutscenes (how many of those darm clocks in Act 3 do I need to watch???) to the very awkward navigation around town. Would have been much better if we could just fast travel as otherwise I would need to go through multiple empty screens every time I want to check out something quickly at the convent or at the saw mill, for example. The game also does a poor job of giving you context when you "speak" with someone - for example, talking to Father Thomas can actually raise a few different subject matters. I wanted to talk to him about something, but not about something else - but to my horror it was about what I did NOT want to talk about. True, the game smartly skirts it by making the conversation benign, but I would have preferred if I had a list of topics to choose from, a la Gabriel Knight, for example. This would give me, the player, more control of what is said and what is not said. And let's not get into some of those tedious minigames (cookies)....I may have talked at length about my dissatisfaction of the game, but to be honest its merits are pretty clear when you watch the trailer - its unique time period and subject matter, its gorgeous artstyle and its choice-based gameplay. I just wish that a lot of the issues could have been fixed or foreseen, as it is clear this is a flawed game despite all of its merits. I was left somewhat frustrated when I finished Act 3, due to it robbing me of many choices I have previously made, and the "plot twist" I felt was not super well-earned. Despite my issues with the storytelling here (something I notice in many Obsidian titles as of late, from Pillars 2 to the disappointing The Outer Worlds), I still think the game is very worth playing, though I still am looking for a role-playing game with the same depth and possibilities as Disco Elysium and Roadwarden. All those fancy visuals are great, but give me real role-playing and tangible and impactful choices, please. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a fantastic game. If you are like I was and enjoy some Obsidian classics but don't think this one is your style, I'd recommend giving it a chance. This is a rare game that gets better progressively as it goes and has a terrific ending. There are some great emotional moments that even with the 2D art style hit me harder than any game I've played in several years. Honestly. This is possible because the writing is top tier, and the scope of the game allows you to become really invested in the town and its residents. The overall mystery is intriguing and each act masterfully inserts the player character into the events and lives of the townsfolk. I love that the game exists and you can tell it is created by masters of the medium. I only wish more labors of love like this were around. I played the game 100% through on steam deck so can confirm it plays perfectly there and it's a great game for the device.

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece of Art and History. Pentiment emerges as a video game that is as much a work of art as it is a historical odyssey. The game’s art style is a breathtaking homage to the storybook illustrations of the Late Medieval period, offering a visual feast that is both unique and captivating.As you traverse through the Bavarian countryside, the game feels like a walk through history, akin to strolling through the pages of a book or the halls of a museum. It’s a narrative-driven journey that is rich in detail and steeped in the cultural, social, and political nuances of the era.The minimalist gameplay allows the story to shine, drawing players into a complex and enthralling detective thriller. With every decision and dialogue, you shape the path of Andreas Maler, an artist caught in a web of intrigue, making for a super interesting look into the past.Pentiment is an interactive experience that educates and entertains, leaving a lasting impression with its artistic brilliance and historical depth.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves talking to every single character as much as possible and learning everything that I can about the world I'm in, this game is amazing for that. There are so many people to talk to and so many paths to choose that will completely alter how you play the game. I love the mystery aspect and all of the developments that are made in the story. Also I like that there are consequences for what you say/do not say to certain people which change certain things you are able to do. I also love the art style and the way this game uses fonts to differentiate what kind of person you are talking to. Overall I'm probably not even half way done with this game and I can't stop playing it!! I highly recommend checking it out
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game provokes your thoughts on the lives of people under the pressure of authority that had way more power than they do today. You'll witness that it's very rare that people have any choices in their lives and their lives are easily ruined at the whim of powerful people without consequence. There is no hope that justice is served any fairly.Christianity is woven into everything in their daily lives in the period where science is only for academics. God knows how climate will change and how it'll affect on farmers. A new-born child dies but it is how God tests your faith. Both townsfolk and clerics claim the god is with themselves and accuse each other of not being faithful. Although they are religious, and also because of it, they are susceptible to manipulation. Their lack of literacy makes it even more dreadful.Their life is simple and primitive and there is no such things as human rights or freedom of choice, yet their struggles are oddly relevant today.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

Excellent story, memorable characters, and meaningful choices, all wrapped in a perfect thematic bow. Nothing but praise for the meat of the game.Pentiment is held back by its gameplay. An entire game about walking around talking to people is all well and good, but Pentiment encourages searching the entire map whenever the in-game time changes, which is mind-numbingly tedious. While this is optional, I kept finding really interesting and/or useful stuff when I searched, so I felt obligated to keep doing it. The map is quite small, so it's not *that* much of a hassle, but it took up too much of my playtime not to mention it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is ridiculous. We have a game set in the 1500s with TWO gay couples, feminism and probably more I have yet to uncover. I'm surprised there isn't a smug atheist lecturing me about how foolish the peasants are for believing in religion. This is the most progressive set of peasants I've ever encountered. More open minded than people are today. It's such a joke to me, that you make a game set in the 1500s and fill it with political correctness. It completely destroys any kind of immersion that they were going for. I'm not recommending it for those reason. I love human rights, I love the LGBTQ and I am telling you that trans rights are human rights. But I will not sit here and pretend that the 1500s were some anomaly where humans were suddenly progressive and then reverted back for the next 500 years. What a joke.

_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I love this game, the concept, and the setting, but I am so tired of developers being inconsiderate of players' time and patience. Why not have a proper manual save system? "Because we don't want that." Uh, okay. Bravo. So dialogue that can accidentally be unintentionally triggered when selecting the highlighted information caption is perfectly okay, and it's also perfectly okay to expect players to replay the entire game to make a single different choice?Do developers even *want* people to play their games any more?This is a big reason why I find games increasingly insipid and tedious, and play them less and less.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A charming, thoughtful, visually-striking and well-researched game with a cast of characters I was excited to learn more about as the story progressed. It is also one of precious few games of its type to deal with its subject matter, doing so with incredible detail. Though it is a historical game, one needn't know anything going in -- all manner of allusions, ideas and era-specific terms are explained to the player through helpful tooltips. All in all, a worthwhile experience and one of the better games I've played in 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully written, well-researched game. Lots of games utilize player choices these days,  but Pentiment is one of the first one that i've played that really tries to come to grips with how messy choices are and how they and their consequences can weigh on the human spirit.  Best approached like a good novel, moreso than a game. The only negative for me was that there were a few times toward the end where the "game" aspect, like having to walk around and advance dialog boxes, started to feel like it was dragging down the whole experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with an amazing art style and writing. It's basically a mix of a point-and-click adventure and  a RPG. If you're a history nerd, you're gonna love this game thanks to its historical accuracy and a plethora of interesting historical facts thrown at you. The world you get to explore is also quite small, which helps the immersion, since you really get to know all the areas and their inhabitants. The only potential negative is how text-heavy the game is. While I enjoyed it, there were times I wished the game would go on a bit faster. It's niche game, but a gem nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely little adventure! Josh Sawyer's passion project hugely differs from anything else Obsidian has ever done, but I'm charmed. Just play it if you enjoy story/adventure games, 'tis not an RPG. Gorgeous art and great music takes this 20 hour journey to quite some heights. Not an epic game to remember an age, but a gem to enjoy like a great glass of wine. 9/10 one minus point for no voice acting and less music than I'd have liked =)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful and and very refreshing tale about things both small and large. The storytelling is nuanced and choices are always shades of gray. Pentiment gives a unique insight into life during the 16th century in a way that has never been so relatable. The characters in the story have depth and complexity, and even the ones you end up despising will still have a side you understand - what their motives are or how their views shaped who they have become. Also, in the 16th century religion was omnipresent, and as a non-Christian it showed me interesting perspectives into how and why different people believe, and how varied their interpretations of faith can be.Truly a great story and a great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most beautiful games I've played. Like, ever. Fantastic exploration of late medieval culture with its full richness, interesting plot, colourful characters and a lot of humour. The music completes the atmosphere perfectly. Overall 10/10 experience.Pro tip - do go to the library at night. You will witness something very fun
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Yet again, Obsidian knocks it out of the park with their dialogue, choices, characters, art, just the complete package. I haven't been unable to put a game down like this in a really long time, I haven't finished a game in a few days like this in a really long time. This game literally had me dreaming in fresco-style art, with choices in fancy fonts. Beautiful game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment presents a rich and fascinating view of life in the 16th century. The art is beautiful, and there are a great many little touches placed throughout the game that sell the immersion. The story it tells is interesting, and puts a lot of nuance into each struggle. It is unafraid to let you make the incorrect choices (and somehow I made a lot of incorrect choices), but it does still hold you to an on-rails overarching plot and you will never miss the most important pieces.My only major complaint with the game is that of the bugs. As you are presented with a staggering number of choices throughout the game, it is inevitable that there will be a slip-up somewhere. But in Pentiment, characters often reference events which never happened and discoveries that were never made. It was rather frustrating every time I encountered one of these, especially when it spoiled something.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I was certain at a certain point that the credits were about to roll and everything would be deliberately vague and I'd have to replay it a dozen times to know what was going on, because the game had covered almost exactly the length and scope of several similar games I'd played before... But then I got an achievement for completing Act One and knew it was going to be good. And it was.I'm still going to have to replay it again and make drastically different choices, but it's like 12 hours long so at least I can come back in a few years and be totally fresh :P
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game with a beautiful story. Tassing and Kiersau felt alive, the narrative was dense but well-paced and twisty, I learned a lot about how life worked back then and reinforced in my head that the people of the time weren't the Hollywood caricatures we think they are now.It's a lot of reading and people might say you can't make meaningful choices, but your choices absolutely have an impact and the ability to think about how your character would respond to things or behave absolutely helped immerse me into the story in a way only video games can.I loved this game and it will stick with me for a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It seems no matter the genre, Obsidian pulls through. This has been one of the best point-and-click adventures as well as a phenomenal whodunit type game I have ever played or seen, but it's not for everyone mind you. And that's a good thing. This story follows the small village of Tassing in Bavaria during the Renaissance Era and is quite lengthy in text, your're essentially going to be reading a moving book with the potentiality of it even being a small history lesson of that time era if you press tab or click on names and words to be given a brief description of what they are (which was helpful since I don't know my stuff). If you like well written interpersonal relationships where characters feel real and with enthralling storytelling having you guessing the whole way through, making dialogue decisions that actually hold weight and will subtly change what people say or do, then this is a game for you. It truly is one of a kind and will hold a place in my memory for a long time to come.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I hesitate to call games perfect but I think that Pentiment is perfect for what it wants to be.  It wants to be an intriguing visual novel set in rural Germany in the early 1500s and it is exactly that.  The game executes on all levels from visual design to dialogue to decision trees.  It's a really special game and I cannot recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I can impress on you how amazing this game is. TL;DR if you don't flinch at abstract metaphors and enjoy reading, this game is a must.From visually astounding presentation, to a nuanced portrayal of the people, place, and conflicts of an era, this game is one of the most powerful, interesting experiences I have ever had. It is a masterpiece of design.One example is that the art style is lovely, yes. But the way Pentiment frames (and breaks frames) is a work of art in itself. Your conversation with Sister Illuminata at the start of the game is an excellent example of this: that scene belongs in a museum. And you have it on your desktop for $20.Another design triumph is the use of font to indicate affiliation. Not only does each social circle have their own style, a character's font will change as you learn about them. Each font has unique use of size, effects, and changes that add much-needed inflection to unvoiced text.Characters are simultaneously independent, motivated actors in the world and deeply rooted in their environment. Villagers may, for example, grow to become better fathers in lieu of their own stilted experiences. They will die for, or against, the institutions that define their world. Most importantly for the game's faction-choosing system of endings, each character gets a fully-fleshed priority. This bias leaves you torn over every choice you have. Heaven help you when you meet the friends of the person you sentenced to death in the end of Act 1.My final heap of praise is on the game's robust and accessible explanations. Recognizing that players might not have Ph.Ds in European history, Alchemy, Christianity, nor any other subject, this game understands that knowing how to find information is as valuable as the information, itself. The codex is not an encyclopedic essay lengthier than the entire game's dialogue (*cough Mass Effect cough*). No, it's a Kindle-style dictionary HUD. Just hover over a highlighted word for a concise explanation. This accessibility option mitigates the worst part of the game: heavy background knowledge.That being said, this game is not for everyone. It has no combat. The challenge is in choice and social pressure. The amount of text rivals that of a novel. It is abstract, unusual, and requires pondering and tolerance. To several of my friends, this game is an esoteric, alienatingly pompous work. To me, this game is one of the most beautiful things ever made. You know which side of the fence you're on.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: For Ossidian lovers: it's an Obsidian game.For video games' lovers: it's a graphic adventure by Obsidian (even if you only remotely like graphic adventures, I recommend to give it a try).For philosophers: you can discuss Luther, Aquinas or Aristotle, while selecting your forte when you studied trivium and quadrivium at university.For artists: it's an amazing work of art by itself, a medieval codex through which you can play.For historians: they have black pigs, let's start there.For latinists: a mediavalist found fake Latin in the game and Obsidian fixed it.This game is pure love and care for the craft in every single aspect of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare to play a game that feels like such a genuine labour of love on the part of the developers. There's so much to enjoy here. I adore the art style and the feel you're playing through a medieval text. I love the little definitions you get when you click on certain words and the sheer level of detail there. There's an interesting cast of characters whose lives I'm invested in enough, that I'm already planning a replay to undo some of my 'mistakes'. The soundtrack is gorgeous too. It feels like a game where care was taken to make it enjoyable to play and engaging. I'd thoroughly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Good literary style game that plays around with fonts and typology. Very historically focused on the period and the context of it, so much so that theres a bibliography in the credits.Ive seen comparisons made to Disco Elysium. I can see how oblivion took a lot of inspiration from that game, but that game is kind of on another level. If you come in expecting what you got out of Disco Elysium you will almost certainly be disappointing. However if you want a piece of interactive historical fiction with decent characters and even better mysteries, this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most unique games I've ever played. Take night in the woods and medieval Bavaria, mix them together and sprinkle in a whole lot of lovely character writing and you get this game.My choices felt like they had genuine consequence. The decisions I made throughout shaped the story quite dramatically. I'm very tempted to go back and play again to see how differently the story would unravel. I also felt like I learn a lot about a period of history I had almost 0 knowledge of. It feels like you're participating in peasant life in ways I'd never thought about before and through this I got a proper gauge of the sort of life and politics of the time. It really pays off. I loved every minute of it from start to end and I wish there were more narrative driven RPGs like this. Definitely recommend to anyone and everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I usually don't care much for point & click type games, but I love medieval history, so I gave this one a shot and boy am I happy I did so. Most of the time I even forget the game is a side scrolling, page-turning point & click type of game. I just feel so immersed all the time! The setting, the characters, the story and the hot nuns. It's all just so perfect. I've been hooked since I started playing and I just want to replay and make different choices right after I'm finished. I give this 69/69 - God bless the devs and designers.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics are nice and the historical settings is interesting.But the story moves at a glacial pace and some of the dialogue is incredibly  boring.Does'nt help that the map is pretty big and traversal is incredibly slow. Why does this game not have fast travel? I gave up in the third act. I can't bring myself to finish the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. I'm currently doing a PhD in medieval history, and this just ticked so many boxes for things that I already loved, but even without that, the game made me cry several times from how emotionally resonant it was. I wasn't spoiled for the game at all which made it an incredible playing experience. I strongly recommend also going in spoiler-free. The game pulled the rug out from under me several times, and always to great narrative effect. The structure is very different from anything I'd ever played before, so it was somewhat confusing at first, but I honestly cannot praise the game enough despite, and perhaps even especially because of, those choices in terms of structure and narrative flow. That said, I do wish the game gave us the option to save mid-scene. I realize this goes against the spirit of the game, but even so!! The sheer amount of times that I wasn't sure about a choice, picked one, and then closed the game just so I could redo that scene was insane. One recommendation for people going in blind: Be thorough. There are only a few events that cause time to pass and there are a lot of things that you can learn throughout the story that will not make time pass at all while really helping you along the way. Go talk to everyone that you can whenever possible, you'll learn a lot!! :D
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game with high expectations after reading some very favorable reviews. Let's make things clear first: this is not a bad product, but it is more of a visual novel than a game. I enjoyed the story and finished all of it, but I will not do so again. The impact of your choices on the world are quite small. I came to play this, because I thought my actions would have more of an influence on the world around me. The only impact seems to be minor alterations to the story and one of the end sequences subtly shows the consequences, but this is only played once and goes by pretty fast, so it can be difficult to understand exactly what is going on. It would have been better if this part would be a part of your save file so you could study it again.The gameplay is pretty basic in the style of point and click adventures, but towards the end of the game it was frustrating how the game forced you to interact with every single character before you could move on. At one point I had enough and just wanted to finish the game as I did not feel that all of these interactions were particularly meaningful. However, I could not and conversations in this games go by rather slowly. The game world is amazing though and clearly a lot of research has been done to portray this world. It comes across as a believable world and it is not difficult to immerse oneself into something with this attention to detail.If you are fine with that the game is linear and you are looking for a great gameworld with a good story go ahead and buy this. But, if you were looking for something that gives you more opportunity to interact with and change what happens in the world around you and with a high level of replayability, I would probably skip on this one. I have mixed feelings about Pentiment, while good, it does not live up to the hype.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I do sometimes wonder how this game exists, especially from a studio like Obsidian, and especially after they were acquired by Microsoft. It's so niche (like ridiculously niche), such a simple, yet elegant and tasteful artstyle and direction. No voice acting, just reading. I would recommend this little gem even if you have no knowledge of the Holy Roman Empire (I barely do), as the game gives you little tidbits of information to help you along! It's a super fun, interactive history lesson, with super fun, often hilarious dialogue, interesting characters, and rather unique setting. I definitely do have some gripes about some of the "choices" and impacts, as well as the final few hours of the game, but overall, I would suggest giving this one a spin, especially if you're a fan of something dialogue based, historical, and simple point and click action :)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I couldn't finish it.  Acts 1 and 2 were brilliant and very engaging.  Act 3 is a laboriously slow and boring "narrative wrap-up".  I sought out spoilers and learned that murders you investigate have no official solutions.  The ending is only tangentially related, always the same, and there is no way to discover it before it's revealed to you.The artwork is beautiful and fantastically immersive.  I'm not sorry that I bought it and had that experience, but I was expecting a choices-matter game.  This software doesn't fit either of those descriptions.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- The story is engaging all throughout the game. There is no real low-point and no boring section.- A lot of effort went into making the dialog special. Not only do your choices impact some interactions, but there are also other details hidden within the dialog. And different fonts for different characters, which sometimes even change, is one of the most brilliant mechanics I've seen yet.- In the German version, the dialog also seems very time appropriate with the family names being gendered, everyone talking in polite form, and the untranslated city names fitting in perfectly.- Art style, music and sounds are all good and work well with the "being an artist" theme.Neutral:- I like to talk to all the people so I can get to know them and see what they are up to, but only if I can decide who to talk to and when. Unfortunately, there are a few times where the story only progresses after talking to everyone, which can take a while.- The concept of the story is only interesting because of the unusual setting. Otherwise, solving a murder mystery or being in a dilemma of aligning with either of two conflicting parties would be rather uninspired.Negatives:- There is a "hint" system for the dialog, which shows more info about people or keywords. The idea is good, but it shows completely wrong or unrelated info way too often. It could mess up your understanding of the dialog a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: "Church denied by Thomas MoreMontezuma is no moreCurse this German Peasants’ WarI can't take it anymore!We did not start the firet'was always burning as the world was turningWe did not start the fireBut when we are gone, it shall still burn on and on and on..."I think what few people realise is that humans, from our earliest civilisations to our current neighbourhoods have forgotten that even when times change, when technology changes, that people through history were well and truly *people*.What we see in history books are collectives, generalisations on how a people lived, what they all believed and what they all thought. In Pentiment, this idea will fade into a new perspective -- it's roughly 20 hours of experiencing the tragedies, banter, gossip, politics and drama of a humble town through the eyes of an outsider, alienated and withdrawn by changing times and great expectations.The writing and choices in this game feel on-par with other roleplaying greats; Disco Elysium, Planescape: Torment, Fallout New Vegas (Of which shares the same lead director as Pentiment!} And honestly it takes a path that seems closest to the human experience. In the first hours of the game you'll likely come across a really interesting conversation between our main character and a well-read nun, discussing the roles of women in the stories of their time, which would be among the first of the game's many illuminating moments. From the spread of print, the real-time splintering of Christianity and how history is re-contextualised to fit narratives are all focal points here among many others, but the theme connecting them is the beauty in doing. The only thing you'll be punished for in this game is doing nothing at all, and the game points it out, even in the face of hard decisions you make.It's a game so unapologetically human, equally funny as it is tragic, as heartwarming as it is bittersweet, mysterious yet enlightening. There's a lot of quirkiness and joy in this game, but also frustrations and loss. It was such a different time, yet you'd have a hard time not believing the goings-on of the game's setting. We need more historical fiction like this!Human, it's human. I keep saying it but there's no better way to say it. This game is human to the damn core, from the literal layers of our history to the joy in getting together to gossip. It genuinely nails all these emotions through masterful writing and characterisation, with a beautiful style and soundtrack to match. I wholeheartedly recommend.TL;DR: An indulgent exploration of humanity in changing tumultuous times. Very well written, you may cry, you will laugh, get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: $20 for a 20-30 hour experience is a good deal. Probably one of the best stories out of any game I've played in 2022. If you're okay with having to read a bunch and like medieval setting then this game might just be for you. For some it may be difficult to keep track of everyone, who they are/what they do/etc., but the game has a compendium full of character descriptions along with a portrait. Since this is a decision making game it does have some replay value, you won't experience every unique scene in a single playthrough as there is also a bit of a time constraint with certain sections. 10/10(it also got me into calligraphy)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable game. Choices matter and it managed to give me a feeling like I was doing everything wrong at times - but in a good way. While I thought the story was going to lead me somewhere predictable, I found myself instead surprised and at a few points genuinely shocked. I love the style and the setting. I'd say it's pretty replayable as well, since there's different events and dialogue options depending on what sort of character you play. Highly recommend if you like point and clicks and/or mysteries.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic narrative game and a rare gem.Something between a point&click adventure and an RPG.Most of the time, you walk in a familiar environment and talk with people.What is done right:- Presenting history - It's set in early modern Bavaria, in times of Martin Luter, the Peasant War and changes in society, religion, and culture. The game is accessible but doesn't avoid talking about hardcore history. Sometimes it simplifies late medieval/early renaissance reality to popular contemporary taste. And yet, such a large, beautiful and complex game with such fidelity and love for history is a rare bird.- Being a detective - Pentiment is like The Name of the Rose by Umberto Eco. The protagonist talks with witnesses, investigate clues and finds secret passages and occult notes. The time is running out, so it's impossible to explore everything.- Telling the story of a small settlement - The story is set in a small city/village in the Holy Roman Empire and a nearby abbey. Over time you learn the name of each NPC. In 25 years, some people die, and some people grow up. Observing how society changes and what happens to the villagers and monks is the best part of the game.- Visual style - Andreas, the protagonist, is an artisan illustrator. Illuminated manuscripts inspired the visuals.- Writing - The game is very well-written and mature. The writing subtly explains all hardcore late medieval stuff but doesn't dumb it down too much.- Choices and consequences - many minor choices and consequences influence the course of the story. Major ones are also present, but they are not always as significant as I would wish.- Enchanting details - The game is full of tiny bewitching and cute details. Pay attention to little children!Cons:- The mechanics of conducting the investigation may disappoint you because you will not find a satisfactory solution, and the game will sometimes guide you on autopilot.- The game tells you about human meanness and sin, but it's rarely poignant and moving to the bone. More frequently, it's a feel-good story. Sometimes you regret your choices, but simultaneously, you're disappointed that the game didn't allow you to do it right.Overall:Great, full of charm game for patient folks and history lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant. A rich immersive village with characters beautiful realised, gripping murder mystery storytelling that flips expectations and toys with player motivation, inter-generational family and politics, a high commitment to historic authenticity, storytelling that is brave and expert enough to sidebar into deep meditation on (for example) the oft-overlooked lives of women in the period without losing any sense of pace.One of the best games I have ever played.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Like playing through the Name of the Rose, maybe with a splash of One Hundred Years of Solitude. Stellar job in research of late medieval history, it's symbolism and philosophy, unparalleled in video games. Just for that it's a S-tier game, probably usable even as learning material in schools, with the right commentary. Now for the game part. Obviously the scope of information, necessary for the player to acknowledge and process, is vast, but the in-game glossary, always present does pretty good job in help - as well as the colour schemes for each family or group of people. I very much like the way the time flows in the game - pressuring the player into choices, but also describing the daily lives and rythms, making the player experience both the cyclical and linear flows of time.  The game's story starts to slow down in the third part, but that does not make it weak in my opinion. Strong replayabilitym and I can only recommend to anyone interested in history.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this is one of the best games I've played in years. The characters are great. Writing keeps drawing you in. None of that is ruined by what I write after this. I will vaguely mention characters and events, so if you want to go in totally blind just read this TLDR: In some spots the writers didn't adjust the story in accordance with your actions, which feels very odd considering how many things do change based on one small choice.Long explanation. In chapter one as the trailer spoils, the main incident the story revolves around is a murder. If in chapter one you discover enough evidence pointing to the murderer and tell your information to the investigator, it often results in the person being executed.  In my play through I didn't understand how little time I actually had to investigate and chose the wrong things to look into.  I suddenly had to make a choice, let things end for the suspect they have or implicate someone else.  I chose someone who, in my opinion, was the most "merciful" choice.  I greatly avoided mentioning absolutely anything about another suspect who had a motive because they had been through enough.In the second chapter multiple people I implicated, but didn't have enough information to prove them the murderer, had very strong reactions to you telling on them.  The only one who acted normal, was the one I avoided implicating in the murder.In the third chapter, the person I avoided implicating mentions being traumatized by being accused of the crime.  I was so confused, it felt like I fell into an alternate story line.  There's more moments like this but this was the most jarring since I specifically protected the person and it was never mentioned until far later in the story.Theoretically you could explain some discrepancies by the fact that other people must have presented evidence, but it still seemed odd.  Occasionally it feels like they were trying to avoid making extra scenes to show the small changes or that the whole point is that you don't matter as much in the scheme of things as you think.It was still a fantastic game and I hope to see more point and clicks with such good historic backgrounds and choices.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. But Pentiment is not for everyone.However, the fact that you are reading reviews and are possibly interested, it probably means that you're the audience it's meant for. Pentiment is a narrative adventure, so it's all about the story here. There is a few mini games and puzzles to solve, but if you think this is a point and click game with complex riddles and whatnot you are wrong. Pentiment's gameplay mostly revolves around running from place to place and talking to various characters in town. Pentiment works like a storybook really, with three acts that each have a set number of days. Time is a very important part of Pentiment, as you will want to pursue many leads about the murders, yet will only have time for one or two of them. The day passes every time you go through an important story beat and there are only set number of hours. It is up to you to decide which leads are most promising and how you will use your time. So use it wisely.While this sounds boring on the surface, Pentiment is able to overcome simple gameplay with the power of writing! The story is where it shines in Pentiment, and while the first hour is slow (setting up characters and exposition), it really picks up the pace from there. All the characters in town are lovable (with a few exceptions, of course), and your dialogue between them are meaningful and authentic. What you say to them will affect your relationship with them and possibly affect future conversations. When needing a hand, some discussions will have persuasion checks which will take into account your friendship. So if you happened to piss them off earlier... they might not be willing to help.There are lots of choices and there will be consequences (good and bad) for each of them. If you're a fan of good mysteries I'd say you will really enjoy the story, as the various leads and suspects you will pursue will have you scratching your head. Many times in the game I felt like I truly didn't know who did it and chose who I felt would have less consequences. The gnawing guilt that you may have accused someone innocent is a core part of the game, and it's executed very well. While the third act dragged (more than I think it should've) the story as a whole is stellar and the ending really makes the less amusing third act worth going through.I completed my game in 17 hours, but I believe you could take more or less depending on your playstyle. I believe Pentiment is meant to be played at a slow pace, as the conversations between the characters is what makes it truly meaningful (and believe me, there are LOADS of characters!). If you're willing to sacrifice gameplay and are here just for the story, I think you'll like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time playing. I cared about the characters, and wanted to learn more about the setting.I enjoyed the way your impactful choices were represented when the time for respective decisions came.I did experience once bug in act 2, and it looks like its been active for a while. I'm unaware if a fan patch exists.I did experience some thoughts that may or may not come up on your play-through.  I think this thing may be pretty common in in whodunit types of stories, though.I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story.

If im not allowed to redo it just dont let me redo it, dont delete my whole game.
