_childDocuments_.review: A truly beautiful game, with a chill, historical atmosphere, calming music and nice storyline that guides us through the history of the Austrian alps from around the 1480s to the 1540s. We witness and experience important historical events from within a small alpine village community. As someone who lived in Innsbruck for two years and who has a PhD in Medieval history, this game is 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game in a LP a while back, just the very beginning  of it, and it went right on my wishlist, while I ignored the rest of the LP because i wanted to experience the story for myself, and I am glad I did, it is definitely a game you should experience first hand to get the full effect. I saw a review when I purchased it that kind of stuck with me, I don't care to dig for it, but basically, they said that they saw an interview that stated there was no canonical murderer, and this spoiled the game for them. Because it  'didn't matter' who you picked. But just let me state after having actually completed the game, if anyone else feels the same way.... the identity of the murderer is not the point. The game is more about the main character, Andreas, and about the town it takes place in, and that includes the doubt brought on by him worrying if he had accused the right person or not. If there was a canonical 'correct' murderer, you could wiki that, and would never be able to experience those doubts yourself alongside Andreas. The game does disguise itself as a murder mystery early on, but his doubts creep in more and more, as well as mysteries around the origin of the town, all leading to a mindbending twist that I won't spoil in the third act. It's a layered story full of metaphor and history, but at it's core, it is about trauma, grief, tragedy, and how people deal with that and rebuild  and evolve after something terrible happens, both as individuals and as a community.I think the game does have some flaws,  some parts can feel a bit on rails, or get a bit repetitive and/or drag in some sections, sometimes it does feel like your choices don't matter as much as they should, sometimes it just becomes a game of looking for all  the hotspots to interact with. But these are minor flaws overall, outweighed by it's positives. The art is beautiful, the story was great and hit me in the feels, and I would definitely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful semi-RPG adventure game that's really more of a visual novel than anything else. I love the writing and the art, and the soundtrack is gorgeous (if limited to a few mostly diegetic songs that show up somewhat infrequently).  You can pet many dogs and cats in this game (and notably feed one cat a little salami, as a treat).  I also don't think I've ever seen another game with a bibliography in the end credits.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging and unique game with a deep knowledge of history and characters that evolve and make you care about them. The art style is unlike any other video game's - and very appropriate for the setting of the game. It's not quite Disco Elysium, but it's a really good CRPG game, as part of what appears to be a renaissance for the genre (see also Citizen Sleeper). One thing I love is you really don't know for sure whether the people you accused were actually guilty - the game is about collecting the evidence and then dealing with the aftermath of what your accusations have down to the lives of the people in this 16th century Bavarian village. That alone gives it plenty of replayability, along with the choices you make and backgrounds you can choose for the protagonist.8.5/10 for normies, 9/10 for history nerds
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I often play games in a way to see everything I can and achieve all the game allows you. You would think then, a game all about being unsure, without enough time and being forced to make choices with things left half done would be my anathema. A game where you always feel like you should have picked the other path. Instead I love Pentiment. It is a story beautifully told and created by a team with incredible passion that shows in every aspect. At the risk of sounding hammy, it's a game about living with your choices and also just living. And it rules.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's only just hit May, but I'm calling it. This is my game of the year. What I thought was going to be fun casual historical fiction sesh gripped me so tightly that I've been dreaming about it. The themes of a corrupted church, community, ancestry and struggle in a time of upheaval in the 16th century was only surpassed by the love and concern the game very expertly made me feel for its characters, only further wonderfully enhanced by the Beaux tapestry style art.If you're a fan of medieval history and slow burn mystery plots and also feel like a good cry, please check it out. It's an absolutely wonderful experience; not just a game, but historical fiction that absolutely deserves a place as literature that I hope we'll be studying in school before long.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I've got to give Pentiment a very weak thumbs-up.I mean, it's barely a game. The gameplay is "walk around and click on everything with an indicator in front of it." It's very close to simply being a visual novel.But... a really interesting one! The time period where the Late Medieval first began to give way to the Renaissance is a fascinating one that gaming has barely acknowledged, and getting to explore that time period and learn about it was fun....if you don't consider that fun, there is no reason to own this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pure narrative and dialogue driven adventure from Obsidian that amazes with it's attention to detail in the setting. Look through a window to the life of a small Bavarian town in the sixteenth century and guide it's history through your actions. Have no misconceptions: This game is 99 % pure dialogue but it's amazingly written and while the first hour or so is a bit slow once the story gets going it will keep you in it's grip to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a narrative adventure game which exudes a clear passion from its creators for the historical facts of how people lived in the time and place in which it is set. This passion is embodied not only in its setting being authentic feeling in its architecture and props, but also in its characters and their layers of motivations.There is so much to love here. The dialogue system really made me think about how what I was saying would come across to the other person rather than just picking options that had a higher numeric stat behind them. The music, though sparse compared to the ambient noises of the town of Tassing, always felt impactful when it kicked in. This game has a more thoughtful and authentic handling of religion and how it affects and is affected by society than any game I've played before.The central plot is well-executed with good foreshadowing where reveals feel earned and the progression generally makes sense, but what I really appreciate is just the feeling of being in this world and getting to spend time with these characters in it, through moments of joy and moments of heartbreak. It's just a series of really strong vibes.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Instant classic. Played this game a few years ago and picked it up again on steam due to the sale. I liked it that much. Andreas Maler and his journey through the years will never get old to me. Many things are similar to Disco Elysium. This game needs a complete edition. You know hearing Father Guy getting snippy in the scriptorium would be 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: My personal GOTY. A masterpiece combining the best parts of a point & click adventure game with the best parts of a detective investigation game all wrapped in an extremely well-researched historical bow.Pros:Story: The story of this game is probably the best I've ever experienced in recent memory (Some have compared this game to Disco Elysium and, in my opinion in terms of story, Pentiment far outstrips even that high bar). The story has a strong central plot and fantastic characters (Every single Character has a clear motivation, and even when they work against your aims it happens in a way that seems natural even a later twist which in the hands of a less competent writer would fall harshly flat manages too feel justified and you can still empathise with the character).  The decision  is genius and makes this one of the best detective games I've ever played. All of this is without even getting into some of the deeper themes the game explores around Memory, Loss and Historical preservation all of which are handled deftly and in a way that never becomes preachy. Art: Fantastic style defines this game. Every single screen looks beautiful and character designs stand out as being A+. Choices: "Do your choices matter?" I think so. The town of Tassing changes with your actions fairly drastically. Accuracy and Atmosphere: The amount of research put into this game is staggering. It portrays Earl modern life life as complex and correctly identifies how complex and often contradictory various sources of authority were in this period (I particularly was happy to see that Religion and the Church's role in Early modern people's lives were not, as so often happens, stereotyped or ridiculed. The author shows a deep respect for the genuine beliefs of the people of this period something very often missing with games like this but also does not shy away from showing some of the faults in these institutions too). I have never played a game with a recommended reading list but after seeing how much the commitment to historical accuracy added to this game I hope to see more games go this route in the future. Writing: "Wait why is writing down here didn't you already talk about the story?" oh no my friend the writing itself is a character in this game with each "Strata" of the village talking with different writing (The Printers dialogue *Kerplunks* onto the screen all at once, the Peasants speak their dialogue slowly and carefully in rough cursive with frequent misspelling e.t.c.) I loved this feature. Particularly how the writing would occasionally change when we learnt more about the person we were speaking to.Neutral:No voice acting: This didn't bother me too much Gameplay: Small mini games make up the majority of the gameplay. These are all fun and thankfully do not go on too long. More mini games most likely would have crowded the game and the true gameplay here is hunting for clues around Tassing which thankfully never got boring. However I can see how some might be disappointed at the limited amount of actual puzzling.Cons: Saving: You only get one save slot. For a first time playthrough this is fine but it does make one hesitant to go back and play again. Ideally a save slot system could open up after you finish your first playthrough.Conclusion:A fantastic game, my GOTY and easily one of my top ten games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Equal parts delightful and unique, Pentiment elevates itself beyond other games in the interactive fiction genre thanks to a masterful level of artistry in both its writing and design. With its story divided into three, Pentiment's first act places you in the shoes of young journeyman artist Andreas Maler, who takes up residence in the Alpine village of Tassing whilst he completes a commission at the nearby Kiersau Abbey at the height of the Renaissance. However, when a murder rocks the community, Andreas is tasked with uncovering the truth so he might spare the life of his friend, the elderly Brother Piero. Act I is undoubtedly the peak of the game; drawing you in with excellent dialogue, bountiful historical knowledge and deep thematic roots that offer excellent meditations on the nature of art and storytelling. Act II sees Andreas return to Kiersau some years after, where he is once again faced with another murder, and it's hard to not to feel like it's a bit of a rehash, particularly when faced with a noticeable decline in the quality of writing during the middle section of the game as opposed to the beginning. It does choose to focus on more dramatic elements as well as further introspection into Andreas' character, but it also fails to make any particularly insightful commentary through its writing. Thankfully things pick up again in Act III, where you now take on the role of Magdalene, a young woman who works at her father's printing shop in Tassing. When her father is mysteriously attacked, Magdalene is tasked with recounting the history of Tassing and Kiersau in a mural for the town hall, which leads to her uncovering the last few threads of the game's overarching mystery as she learns the truth behind the town and the abbey. While the reveal of the game's antagonist and their motivations felt rather underwhelming, Act III does offer strong thematic commentary on family, duty, consequence and regret that all ties together to make it a largely satisfying conclusion anyway. Altogether the story is well paced and wrought with humour, emotion and sincerity, and although it makes some not-so-subtle strides to remain in line with certain modern-day attitudes, it's undoubtedly an engrossing and masterfully crafted narrative. It's a good job that this is the case, because Pentiment is by and large a whole load of walking about, clicking through dialogue and making choices, nevertheless with the odd little minigame here and there to break up the monotony. You're also placed on a strict timeline to achieve your goals, particularly in the first two acts, and while I can see how it would incentivise replayability, it was also a little frustrating to be forced into choosing some parts of the game at the cost of accessing others. Nevertheless, there's plenty to do and seemingly a number of ways things can play out in the story, not to mention you have a solid degree of control in how Andreas and Magdalene behave thanks to a wide array of dialogue options. Interesting enough, it seems for the most part the "truth" of a lot of what happens in the game rests in the players hands, and although it felt like a strange choice at first, it actually complemented the outcome of the story fairly well. Now, I can't go any further without raising the best aspect of the game - Pentiment is a joy to behold from top to bottom thanks to its absolutely resplendent art direction. The entire experience is framed from start to end as pages in an illuminated manuscript, providing it with an absolutely beautiful hand drawn artstyle with animation that compliments it, and it does so much to elevate the game with its authentic and unique aesthetic. Great audio design also helps bring the game to life, and although I wish it was used more frequently, it employs a fantastic medieval-like soundtrack too. The game is rammed with accessibility features too, best of all being the vast glossary of historical vocabulary you can consult mid-dialogue, helping clear up any confusion whilst also allowing the writers to avoid dumbing down their scripts. In truth, I think a large part of why I enjoyed this game so much is just due to the sheer reverence for art that permeates every aspect of it's development from top to bottom. Art is really what encompasses Pentiment in its entirety; from its design to its thematic elements, every single piece of this game comes together and exudes an unrivalled level of artistic energy that also leaves a wide berth for you to contemplate your own thoughts on its subject matter. As someone who doesn't usually consider this kind of game, I was absolutely blown away even with some minor issues here and there, and if you have any sort of inclination towards art and storytelling I can't recommend it enough.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is an old school LucasArts style graphic adventure game with the premise of a murder mystery set in 16th century Bavaria. As a big fan of Josh Sawyer (Fallout New Vegas) and Disco Elysium, I'm definitely enjoying this one. I will say though, that 6 hours in, it is a much slower burn, and much drier than DE.Sidebar: after 150 hours into Xenoblade 3, this is a very welcome change up from the monotony of banging out hundreds of jrpg side quests.In summation, Pentiment makes an excellent pre-bed, cozy feeling game to settle in for the night, much like curling up with a good book. I recommend it to fans of DE for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: BEST ON DECK: 6 - 7 hours battery, 60 FPS, No Setting Changes NeededPentiment is a unique text-heavy, choose-your-own-adventure that sets you into 16th century Europe. As Andreas Maler, you are caught up in a series of murders that span over 25 years. You are responsible for conducting your own investigation and decide the fate of the communities you encounter, but beware, every decision you make brings you closer and closer to the center of a devious underlying conspiracy.As a quick aside, I want to say I love this game's aesthetics. It is gorgeous and fits the game perfectly. This was definitely a major draw I had to buy the game, but the story is quite fantastic too. Takes a little bit to get into if you aren't a fan of the Medieval speech patterns and wording, but if you can get into it, there's a fantastic game here.As a text-centric, it doesn't take much to run, which is true on the Steam Deck as well! Running with no forced compatibility, you can easily hit 60 FPS with no issues at all! Without any changes, you will be getting around 6 - 7 hours of battery and temps below 60c. This game fits perfectly on the Steam Deck and easily fits into our Best on Deck category.Part of the aesthetic for the game has you "reading" Andreas's story from a 3D book. Since the book is rendered in 3D, the game tends to draw more battery during these scenes. In the opening, this spiked to 12W, but when using the glossary when playing the game, I never saw it go over 10W. I would comfortably say leaving TDP off is still okay though as the actual gameplay rarely goes over 7W drain.The game has a wealth of accessibility options along with it. This includes easier to read fonts, how fast dialog will appear, and the essential text size! For the Deck, the larger size is perfect and while the regular size is readable, the larger is just so much easier on the eyes. With the accessibility features it offers, Pentiment will be a game anyone can enjoy.At Pentiment's main menu, you are prompted to log into Xbox. Since this is an Obsidian game, a developer owned by Microsoft, there is Xbox integration. Unfortunately, trying to log in locked my controls after a couple seconds and I had to restart to bring them back. I attempted to launch with Proton GE and Experimental, but nothing fixed this. Not being able to log in didn't impact gameplay at all though, so I don't see this as a huge let down.Pentiment is a very narrative-driven game where the choices you make matter and can greatly influence the outcome of the game. On top of that, the artstyle is such a wonderful addition to the game that I can't rave about it enough. On the Steam Deck, it runs flawlessly and feels like it was made just for this device. Pentiment is a game well-deserving to be part of our Best on Deck category!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The art is gorgeous, the dialogue options hilarious, your choices actually matter a lot and the mystery is very interesting. I loved how religion was portrayed in this game: accurate to the time period. The story has many layers, from the surface murder mystery, all the way to how history echos through the ages and how we are all affected by it. 10/10 would recommend a thousand times to those who like to read and dig into a story.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I am not normally one for video games on multiple fronts—not the right equipment, coordination, even most financial constraints limit me. However, Pentiment proved itself a wild exception. Easy to follow and learn, one struggles to put the game down once enamored with everything offered. An interesting art style, riveting plots with urgency that leaves you wondering about the alternatives, and packed with history, I found myself grabbing for whatever crumbs the game could drop. I found myself relating to Andreas as well; an unexpected turn, really. The characters were so filled with nuance that you can't help but love or hate them as if you were in Tassing yourself.If someone had little patience, then perhaps I can understand why the length may be offputting or could discourage a second playthrough. However, I look forward to playing multiple times more.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: No voice acting, but if you don't mind a bit of reading and if you like narrative RPGs this is a game you shouldn't miss. A pretty unique setting and interesting characters make for a really fun role-playing experience. While I saw a few typos, the writing is engaging and really well presented in my opinion.The game doesn't give you many options to save and try out different dialogue paths though, which may be a negative for those that really want to explore every path. Despite this potential shortcoming, if you can embrace the mentality of making decisions and living with the consequences you'll be in for a treat.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: To sum it up, I'd say Pentiment is an above average adventure time and I'd recommend it to any adventure games fans. The unique art style feels fresh and is captivating, even though it won't impress you anymore on the latter half of the game. It doesn't help that the whole game takes place in the same town/abbey complex. My main issues with the game were: - Lots of backtracking around the same places, talking to the same people or their relatives about similiar subjects. Due to the nature of the gameplay, it encourages the player to keep doing "full scans from top to bottom" of the town/abbery every day in search of any missing clues that might have appeared overnight. It gets boring really fast.- Most choices you make in the game, backgrounds you chose, etc are mostly there for flavor. You might get this or that character killed but in the end the main plotline is very railroaded. Talk about illusion of choice... - Third and final act felt a bit unnecessary and dragged on for too long. Felt more like a 5 hour epilogue told from a new character's point of view. The story climax, at least in my opinion, also felt a bit underwhelming. What I enjoyed:- Some of the characters are fleshed out and actually interesting to interact with, their personal stories progressing nicely through the decades of the game's timespan. - Somewhat unique artstyle inspired on medieval art, reminds me of those bardcore music videos that were popular on YT recently.- Feels polished. DIdn't experience a single crash or bug during the whole gameplay. Didn't need to fight the UI too.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastically ambitious game! One of the best representations of medieval life in a game. Story-wise it's much more engaging at first and doesn't quite manage to fulfil it's promise in the later half of the game, but the characters are all excellent throughout, and just hanging out with them is a joy in itself. Overall pretty great! 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best (maybe THE beste) narrative adventure I have ever played. I knew nothing about the game but still bought it and it was amazing. It is very slow paced but historically very accurate and also very emotional. You get to know the characters really well in such a short time period and this is what makes this game so amazing. Even though I already knew a lot about the Middle Ages, especially of Austria and Germany, I still learned a lot about religion and the general structure of the society during these times.If you like narrative games, definitely give this one a try!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Went into it thinking it would be more of a detective style game, but it's more of a visual novel in many ways. There's a sense of mystery, but not a lot of puzzle solving. Much of the game is interacting with other characters and learning to know the fictional town of Tassing and its history - having an interest in renaissance and medieval history helps a lot, but it's all very well written.Throughout the game you have to make a lot of choices which advance time and locks out other options, while having only autosave and one save slot - this means there's replayability, but might frustrate you if you're a frequent save-reload type person. I'm a bit of a reload-type person myself, but found it very rewarding in the end due to how the story is written.Graphics are very good, though I wish they went all the way with the style and worked with distorted scale on the backgrounds like in the old manuscripts. Only a few parts in the game truly look and feel like the style of the time, which feels a bit of a shame when they already nailed the character designs.The biggest downside in the game is the backtracking. Tassing isn't a big town, but you have to run everywhere, and because you only have a few limited choices before advancing time you'll run around like a maniac to find all of them before deciding what to go for. A fast-travel system would've been very helpful.Another issue I had was with the dialogues. Occasionally Andreas will reflect on something in a separate speech bubble, but it will pop up after all the other text and is easily skipped. Things in the dialogues also frequently don't show up in your journal, so some things you just have to keep in memory - quite annoying with notes and books you find and can never read again.All in all it's a very good game, but you need some patience with the slower parts and accept it's more story than puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: where to start?  highly recommended, it's a piece of art.  The designs are gorgeous and beautifully curated.  The attention to detail for the historical fidelity is incredible, and the plot, well, it made me question and taught me something ... in short, thanks to the creators of this work.  essential if you love the genre but also a must try for those who usually don't care, fantastic!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game because of its comparisons to Disco Elysium and while they have many similarities, Pentiment carves out a space for itself.Choices don't matter too much in terms of the overall ending, but rather they force you to slow down and pick and choose who you interact with, what stories you hear, and what trajectories characters take over the course of the game. The beauty lies in its characters, art style and its realistic worldbuilding- I loved how much I learned about Medieval Europe, and that's coming from someone who generally doesn't care about that time period.Overall, I think Pentiment is a beautiful story about the passage of time and the resilience of humans, and I would definitely recommend playing through it if you want to experience it first-hand :)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with interesting plot and characters. Choices in the game mostly affect the dialog. but, considering the options and combinations of traits that main character can have, it would be somewhat replayable. Overall, Idea of the story is great and I thank Josh Sawyer and everybody who worked on this game for this amazing experience. I recommend this game to everyone who are not afraid of big amount of text and wants to experience something new.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts on this game:- basically "The Name of the Rose" by Umberto Eco as a videogame. - This is one of the best stories I have ever experienced in a videogame. It is at times dramatic, serious, sad, pensive, or genuinely funny. The ending is a little anticlimactic (although I did not expect several plot twists) but what videogame ending isn't. Your decisions matter and incentivize replays (although I hardly do that). - It looks beautiful and has a very unique artstyle. Who wouldn't want to walk around in a medieval mural?! The different fonts the dialogue is written in are amazing and give you additional info on the persons you talk to. - The setting is, for what I know about the period it is set in, as authentic as a game can be. If you are interested in calligraphy or (the history of) letterpress you NEED to play this game. - The game isn't afraid to adress controversial topics like diversity, feminism or racism and still manages to stay authentic and historically accurate. If you like storytelling, point and click adventures, dialogue and light RPG mechanics play it. Seriously.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so clearly made with a lot of sincere love and interest in the subjects it tackles. Choices felt decently meaningful in a world where many supposed branching story lines all lead to the exact same result, although theres no way to completely alter the ending. I have a few teeny complaints, such as  but overall such an amazing game that tells such an interesting and moving story, while also being a really interesting history lesson - I know more about Catholicism now than after a year at Catholic school. I also know everyone is excited about the art in this game, as well as the use of font, and rightfully so, but the sound design is INCREDIBLE. So immersive and wonderful for setting the world of the game. I cried and laughed and had a wonderful time. My only other qualm is  Also, this is not an issue for me but be prepared to be somewhat confused about small details if you're not a European history buff/know a lot about Catholicism. The game provides lots of context but sometimes it can still be a bit confusing. Nothing that is actually necessary to play the game is unclear though. Proof that passion makes good art.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good and accessible to anyone. Both the gameplay and the plot is not difficult to understand, basically it's point-and-click Scooby Doo but solo and you piece the evidence together to make one (or four) comprehensible conclusion. There are times where everything clicked in your mind but Andreas, our protagonist, are still clueless. Maybe it's how things were back in the day.I believe the artstyle is what draws people in the first place, and it's doing its job vehemently. The BGMs are very neat. They're not always there, but when they are, you know something is going down. Sound effects are really good, possibly the second best thing after the artstyle. The sound of wind, footsteps, and the "This will be remembered" are all very nice. Sometimes the writing sound can be overbearing but I heard the devs added the option to turn it down so there you go. I don't know much about medieval history and Christianity in middle ages, but having a mystery religion thrown in once in a while is nice.Aside from the douche doctor, the bad things I can say about this game is the lack of voice acting. That and you need to run back and forth around the town to find information every new timeslot, it's very tiring fast. It reminds of me Persona 3 on PS2 but without the battles.Overall this is a nice break from barrages of AAA action shooter games we get these days. I hope Obsidian and other devs can churn out more simpler games with good story like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: So amazing. Gameplay wise it's very good. No action but much choices and different ways.    it's not a million miles from Disco Elysium (minus the crazy and the ...... ending). But the big selling point is the visual style. This game is a work of art.  There is nothing like it. For your medieval needs, when KCD is just a bit too massive for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible narrative-based game with well done characters and a very moving story about art, faith and the truth. I loved seeing how the town evolved over time and I'm curious if things will work out the same way on a second playthrough. Your choices really do feel like they matter and little incidental things can end up having big ripples later in time, causing some townsfolk to have happy or sad lives.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is choose-your-own-adventure/detective game set inside of a medieval tapestry. The uniqueness of that idea alone warrants a purchase, but the idea is also well executed, the game looks great and has some replayability because of the many decisions and character backgrounds there are to choose from. Suffers from slight pacing issues towards the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click adventure game where you can see the love and care being literally scrawled onto the page, Gothic letter by Gothic letter.  The world building is omnipresent because its a world that was and is, and accessibly parceled out to you in a journal you will soon come to call your own. Dive into an anti-smoking gun mystery, where guns abound and the smoke is everywhere. Clinging, coughing, fuming, heralding the coming of an inferno. You will ask yourself: is this right? Am I right? Can I repent?
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I know that I am a comparatively short way into this game compared to other reviewers, but I already know I'm going to end up playing through it over and over. The art is outrageously beautiful, the sound design is fantastic with haunting era-appropriate music, the story and the way your choices affect it is phenomenal. Even though this is not /my/ specific era of historical expertise, I know enough to deeply love and appreciate the care and accuracy of both text and art, and I implore you to read some of the other reviews that confirm how incredibly specific and accurate some many elements of this game are to the era it draws on. I grew up on the Brother Cadfael mysteries, and this reminds me very much of those, but with such a broader scope of the world events surrounding the era...cannot recommend highly enough if you love learning about history, solving mysteries, debating theology, or just petting cats.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: really, really good writing (has a lot of slice of life interspersed throughout the main conflicts, which is both really well executed and fleshes out the personalities of the characters and enhances the overarching plot). Also the game looks really good. To me, a lot of illuminated manuscripts look weird due to the proportions, lack of perspective and color choices. The art style of the game is able to perfectly find a middle ground, where it has the usage of those 3 features (like comics and manga of today), while still also having the look of an illumination. highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I loved this game. I have an interest in this period of history so I appreciated the attention to detail.Likes- Art style full of character- Enthralling mystery with plenty of twists and turns- Captures the feeling of being thereDislikes- Characters in the journal are often named differently from what they're referred to in game, so it's difficult to keep track of who the many people are.- Clicking on the thought bubbles instead of the dialogue options often results in misclicks.- Fiddly journal.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game has everything in a unique package: an interesting story that pulls you in from the first moment, well written and charismatic characters and excellent music. The puzzles and mini games are fun and give the world depth. Game mechanics work well and as they are simple there is plenty of room to admire the beautiful graphics.Pentiment was an experience and I will surely return to the game again.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Unusual reflections about art and being an artist, served in the truly unique atmosphere of emerging modernity and socio-cultural and religious changes.  Oh, and of course all this is just a background for a mystery and intrigue, a little in the vein of "The Name of the Rose".Really a labor of love and passion, a true gem and a wonderful story!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game comes off as an historical fictional game, but it is more of a game *about* history. It's a game about how each of our cultural, religious, familial, and personal histories shape us as individuals. It ruminates on how we cling to our history, how we depend on it, or how we bitterly reject it, but also how we can live with it and one day accept it and move forward. It is very moving. It is a game that will make you want to talk with your grandfather about how it was when he grew up. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely phenomenal-- game of the year, for sure.If you love intense TTRPGs and intricate narrative games and game books, this game is for you.If you love medieval history, if you love exceptional writing, if you love amazing characters, this game is for you.If you love RPGs and Choose Your Own games with a lot of replayability, this game is for you.THIS GAME IS FOR YOU. TRUST ME.

_childDocuments_.review: *After pushing through the first chapter, I became hooked. The story and art outshines the few negatives I have. The original review is below for posterity. I do recommend this game now, especially on sale.*Pentiment is on the edge of being great. +Great setting if you like European history + if you want to learn some. +Great art + again, an appreciation of history supports appreciation of the art, but even without that, it is an appealing art style. +The music is sparse but again historically appropriate and wonderfully applied.What in my opinion makes this a negative to recommend is an how gameplay is confined by its --logic and execution.The gameplay is quite simple - just a path with choices - however what is available doesn't always make sense. Sometimes you can enter a place immediately - sometimes you can see that it is there, but cannot be entered - sometimes the option and map point isn't even there. Additionally, the people that can be interacted with changes in strange ways. For example, I understood who I was working with and who had worked together. I wanted to speak to two characters (Aedoc and Guy) who worked with another key character (Piero) - but, without reason, they just said hello.I showed up to work on the day after a key event (I was even told to) but I could *not* actually do the work nor given a reason why not.I understand that the idea might be to discover this all on your own - however the character has obviously been in this town for some time at the beginning of the game and knows where everything is (not to mention who most people are). yet I had to basically check every random room to simply get to work on the first day! (and knowing what cloister, loquiarium or scriptorium are doesn't help). + To the game's defence, it doesn't have a strict 'time passing' mechanism - so for the most part you can choose when time will advance. Yet - during that sometimes (too often) consisted of running around after checking things logically, until finally going room by room to see if what I could interact with had changed.Finally, I had a very strange conversation with a key character (Cecilia) - which blamed my character for offending everyone even though I was careful to be on their side. Again, the logic didn't make sense and I found my character apologising for doing something I did not witness (or at least acknowledge) in gameplay or story. Again, the experience felt fragmented, as if I had missed parts when I was actually rather involved and did not flow well into what otherwise is an intriguing scenario. This leads to a disjointed "point and click on everything" experience which this game *almost* gets away with - but I found myself frustrated at points. The logic led me somewhere, but the game did not (nor explain why not).This game's greatness is too burdened by the pace and logic of the gameplay.Solution would be simple. Add more in context text explaining why certain things are interactable or not - especially as the player character *would* have some knowledge of *why*. They do this in part (i "love" the dictionary feature) but too often what *can* be done to advance the story often does not make sense. Allowing *everything* and *everyone* to be interacted with, but if they are "cut off" somehow, at least give an explicit reason.

_childDocuments_.review: My game of the year, and likely a top 2-3 game of all time for me. While excelling on its own merits as a whodunit, "choices matter" goose chase, Pentiment made me fall in love with a people and a town and a time (so much so that I've been drawn to reading about 16th century Europe in my own time). The art style is excellent, the writing superb, and the attention to historic details is delightful. A must purchase for fans of story heavy adventures or mysteries.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I surely am not a 16th century Lieutenant Columbo, but I love this game. The art style, the attention to historical detail, the way it pulls you into this small late medieval/early renaissance village and its happenings, how lovingly it describes its population and how you learn much about them by sharing a meal with them (with period accurate fares). There's so much to like and immerse yourself here that I many times forgot I was on the clock to solve a murder and as a result had to (almost) wing it when the time came to solve the "case" - much to the detriment of innocents, I fear. As I said, I am no 16th century Columbo, more like 16th century Inspector Clouseau...What an excellent game and a unique experience. A masterwork, indeed. Two thumbs up!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is 2022's finest interactive narrative, a 16th-century detective tale that uses the vehicle of historical mystery to talk about art, faith, class struggle, and land. It is particularly concerned with history as it is made in the day-to-day - the building of people upon the foundations laid by past generations, the passing down of knowledge and lore across eons, what makes a place a place, and so on. Even something as mundane as sharing a simple meal with someone is given plenty of historical significance. Pentiment's finest achievement is in using the popular choose-your-own-adventure/"actions have consequences" gaming conventions as a metaphor for how history itself is made. We explore Tassing at several different points in its existence, allowing the player to track how various decisions they made in gameplay have been canonized by the townsfolk as part of Tassing's history, just as the town's buildings incorporated that which was left behind by its previous inhabitants. The scope and scale of human experience, even in a place as seemingly insignificant as a small peasant settlement, is staggering. Pentiment uses its narrative labyrinth, along with a delightful art style and surprising emotional depth, to remind us of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this by clearing something up I've been seeing too much in these early reviews:  is  Obsidian's take on  (shout-out to the guy who said it was medieval , even though I wouldn't say this is half as difficult or mind-bending).  is Obsidian's take on Ubisoft's . You will not be decking out your detective in the finest gear, min-maxing your favorite traits for the funny dialogue options, and asking strangers if they are (in fact) a member of the homosexual underground. You will be walking from conversation to conversation in a wonderfully realized moving historical artwork, occasionally seeing a special dialogue option but mostly clicking around, wandering through familiar paths in the terrain or choosing between various naturalized (but still deeply referential and historical) dialogue bubbles. You could call it a visual novel with some added religious and historical pizzazz. I would call it a nerd game, but the kind of nerd game for nerds  (and little time for things as complex as level-up screens and deep, engaging combat loops, or long-winded real-time strategy). This game has a bibliography. You will be able to tell. It's also full of lovely little details (like the little errors in the wonderfully specific dialogue boxes that let me go "Oh, I remember the wild days of Middle English too!"). It's a deep dive into the ancient winding world of religion and politics, a less player-oriented Obsidian tale with a lot to give if you can bear a game that speaks a lot more than it moves.In short, this one's for the boys (the boys being all the people with degrees in history and literature).

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to recommend this game. Due to the major flaws, it houses. Story: The story falls apart once you realize that most of your choices affect very little of the narrative. In the first two acts, it feels like you have a chance to do SOMETHING, but once you hit act 3 everything falls apart to a very unearned conclusion.The pacing is horrendous, especially in act 3. The entire conclusion is not earned and feels very cheap. I almost quit the game from act 3 alone. Now, this doesn't mean this is poorly written, a lot of the story is written very well and many moments captured me. Sadly the pacing problem and lack of actual control over the narrative hurts it in the end. Gameplay: It lacks severely in terms of actual gameplay. Most of what you will do is press E or MOUSE 1 to progress the story and continue the conversation.  Sometimes you get to do a very simple puzzle to break the monotony. But it still feels like a railroading novel with the most insignificant choices. It is extremely hard for me to call this a GAME because there almost isn't any actual game.  You can't catch the murderer. You can't stop the killings. You can't stop the revolt. And you can't change the ending. All this amounts to a very slow-moving story that has great parts. But too many boring parts that ruin it in the end. I want to support this type of experimental game. But as I pointed out. This is more of a book with small interactions, and choices don't seem to matter.  If I wanted to read for hours I'll read a book. Disco Elysium had way more dialogue and written parts in it. Yet it gave you CONTROL over the story, it lets you play. Instead of just moving from one part of the map to the other and reading dialogue after dialogue; It gave you options that affected the entire story. It even let you control your character, you don't have to be Harried. You can be rockstar James or something else.   If you wish to support Obsidian BUY IT. But if you want a medieval investigation where your choices matter. This isn't it.  4/10 lacks an insane amount of gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if the developers will see that, but I want to say thank you. This game has brought me back in time, in an intelligent way. Never taking me for a fool, I have followed characters that lived in a world full of doubts, God and social problems, and I think that the gamee has tried it's best to capture the complexity of the period. But while doing that, he made me read the stories of characters and a town that I have grown to love, I have even cried several times by the end of the game. The story in itself and the gameplay are stressfull (you will never be able to do everything to find the whole truth), but they are well written and are included in a beautiful game. Thank youu very much for this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Creative, brilliant blend of mystery, history and pure ingenuity. In this game you will analyze medieval documents, spread and collect rumours at dining tables, and make hard decisions during particularly trying times.For anyone passionate about history, languages, books, typography, and art, there will be something here for you. From the miniscule details like the printer using a printed typeface in his dialogue boxes while peasants are using messy scripts, to the work-in-progress artwork affected by the player's decisions, Pentiment shows great care in its craft.The story itself manages to tie together the struggles of the people of a small Bavarian town which survived through many layers of history: pre-classical, Roman, Christian, Reformist. All are present throughout the vibrant cast of characters that the player meets throughout their journey.Throughout its 3 acts, Pentiment builds up anticipation through clever use of mystery, puzzles, and mini-games up to satisfying conclusion that left me thinking and eager to see another way that things could have unfolded.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: From the storytelling to the visual, this game is really  worth playing. Many hours of wandering around beautiful medieval art (even more if you like to explore and/or have a FOMO like me), beautiful music, and meeting a plethora of interesting characters. You'll have emotional moments, funny bits, unexpected events, tension, and a lot of mysteries to solve with Pentiment.This was a very pleasant discovery.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine. The comparisons to Disco Elysium are kind of strange - these games have nothing in common tonally or in any way really, other than being story based. I don't think enjoying one would mean you'd enjoy the other, unless you just like story games.The story is enjoyable enough, but ultimately your choices don't really matter, the story plays out largely the same way. When I realised that, investigating and making sure I made the 'right' choices became less interesting. But I still enjoyed seeing how the story would end. The characters are interesting and I was curious to talk to everyone as much as possible.The historical tone of the game is kind of strange. Obviously there's a lot of historical references to books, people etc, but it's all quite...shallow. I am only slightly familiar with Medieval history, but I didn't feel like I really learned anything new. All the little "footnotes" you can read don't really provide much. And a lot of the conversations feel way too modern, in the sense that I doubt people would have dared to discuss such topics so openly without fear of getting in serious trouble. Sometimes it almost felt too soapbox-y. That took me out of the story sometimes.Overall, it was an allright game, I did feel emotionally invested and I don't regret playing it. I think the game expects you to do a couple playthroughs, but because of the lack of meaningful choices I am not interested in going through the game again. Worth it on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't been this impressed with a point and click "choices matter" game since TellTale's The Walking Dead. Between the art style, the depth of choice, the historical accuracy, the soundtrack, and the story itself, Pentiment is a wild ride from start to finish that I only wish I could experience for the first time again. You may think you're just getting a murder mystery, but in reality Pentiment is about so much more, and the scope of our actions and the consequences we must deal with only become wider. You feel how even small decisions we make can drastically affect history. The choices the game lays before you are genuinely tough at times, and grey area is abundant. At no point in my entire playthrough did I ever once feel like the game gave me a clear-cut "this is objectively right or wrong" decision. The twists and turns of the story are genuinely fascinating, and at no point did I ever feel the game was subverting my expectations for its own sake. The entire adventure is EXTREMELY well designed. The characters feel and act like real people and are easy to recognize and tell apart. Even the title is utter perfection, and references the very nature of the plot. In short, I enjoyed almost literally every minute of this experience. Once or twice I got frustrated because I simply was not sure how to further the story. But the map is small enough that the answer is never particularly far away. The only negative thing I can honestly say is that though the first and second acts are utterly amazing and thrilling, the third act is where some small cracks start to show. A little too much back and forth. Not as many persuasion checks. A few too many cutscenes. An annoying character. A little bit of the illusion of choice. I've heard complaints that it goes on a touch too long, but I never felt that way. I was too busy digging into Tassing's history, intrigued by literally everything I saw, to notice. Cannot recommend this game enough. Nothing is perfect but Pentiment comes about as close as one could hope. I was completely enthralled from start to finish and am already planning a second playthrough. Not bad for $20!

_childDocuments_.review: A three-act story, the first two acts are incredibly enjoyable. However, the story ends flat in a catatonic/boring third act that is difficult to get through. I am surprised to see the reviews are "Overwhelmingly Positive" when 1/3 of the story is anything but. _childDocuments_.review: I have a master's degree in history - and I'm totally blown away by the entertaining way the game manages to depict the transition from the Middle Ages to the early modern era over several generations. The plot of the game itself is exciting and full of characters that I will remember. I will miss Tassing and its inhabitants now that I have solved the murder case.

_childDocuments_.review: There are so many things I enjoy about Pentiment, I hardly even know where to start. The graphic design is absolutely stunning  - I have a deep background in art, including illumination, calligraphy, and stained glass, and there are parts of this game that feel like I've stepped into a Book of Hours. It's probably the most "intelligent" game I've ever played, and I'm grateful that Obsidian took a chance on a quiet murder mystery rather than action-packed shooter.It almost reminds me of the old text-based dungeon crawlers that we used to play on our clunky old 8-bit "home computers" back in the 70s and 80s.   Oops, I think I might have just outed myself as an old fart;

_childDocuments_.review: As the credits to Pentiment rolled, I leaned back in my chair and contemplated how exactly I would write a review for it. The game left me awestruck, and throughout my life where I have finished hundreds, maybe even thousands of games—that happens rarely. I didn't really expect anything different from the likes of Josh Sawyer and Obsidian though, they have consistently proven that they are top tier storytellers, but even more so than their other fantastic games, Pentiment stands as grand achievement not only in video games, but literature as a whole. And when I say literature, I mean it. Only Planescape and Disco Elysium match the levels of seer words in this game. There is a LOT of reading, so be warned. If you are the type of person to skip through dialogue as fast possible in order to get to the action, this will most likely not be the game for you. It's slow paced, deliberate, and is filled to the brim with 16th century history that will make you actually LEARN STUFF. However, if you are like me and you enjoy curling up with a novel and a cup of tea every night before bed, or if you are willing to try something new and escape from most modern garbage AAA releases, Pentiment will leave you satisfied with it's excellent mystery, it's fully fleshed out characters—I love Andreas dearly—and it's choice based dialogue that actually has an effect on the world, story, and ending. I urge anyone to at least try the game out, not only because it is easily worth it's asking price, but so other developers will take notes from what has been done here. The renaissance of single player narrative lead RPGS is upon us, and I couldn't be happier about it.Edit: Also you should read The Name of the Rose.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It took a bit for me to get into, I'll be honest. Everything about this world is dripping with historical detail that I couldn't hope to fully comprehend. But when the ball got rolling, I cared deeply for this little town and its inhabitants, its rich history and how that relates to the ongoing string of crimes. This was a truly wonderful experience, and I feel wiser for having played it.A criticism I've heard is that your choices don't matter, so I hope anyone going into this game understands one thing: yes, there is a linear narrative at play that will not be derailed despite your actions. However, all decisions, from the choices of the main character's background and personality to the simple conversations with townsfolk to the big accusations at various climactic points, allow each player to slightly influence how the town looks in future acts, discover secrets that they otherwise wouldn't have, and above all else, immerse themselves in and engage with the game in a way that feels completely personal. That type of player freedom speaks to me far more than adding several different story routes that exist only for the sake of replay value, and in that way I think this game's choices matter just fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good game. Style, writing, story - everything is really top notch. It's sort of brutally honest portrayal of the time period with all it's cruelty and hypocrisy is pretty interesting. STORYThe pacing and the story overall is pretty good - though I find that act 3 is the one that drags on and felt largely like repeating/re-learning stuff from acts 1 and 2 that made the game quite boring in a way. No new information was given - only walking around and hearing stuff we already knew,interspersed with a sprinkle of new information and consequences of the past (not even past choices, just the past in general)A lot of good characters - and I use the term 'good' to mean 'characters that sometimes are so unlikable that you will rejoice when they meet their demise' not in the sense they are wholesome. Plenty of absolutely awful tragedies portrayed, all wrapped in a very pretty bow of fantastic stylised art.UI I adore the graphic side of the menus, the stupid little filler animal pictures on the corners when you peek at the lexicon etc. The actual journal/map is clunky and i found the animations playing whenever you change between map and journal a bit tedious to watch every time. The UX/UI aspect of this game is definitely not the best on this.OPTIONSI forgot to add this when I first wrote the review: The OPTIONS are absolutely top notch! Ability to get rid of the fancy fonts in particular was a godsend (I have issues reading very fancy fonts, so the option is very welcome) Also the choice of size of font and the ability to skip animations for the text are great as well.MUSICAnother thing I did find jarring is the lack of music - I actually thought the game was broken on Deck for a while. But no, the same thing happens on pc. It's kind of sparse on the music which sometimes makes scenes awkward (there's a particular scene in 2nd act where people are dancing and clapping and it is REALLY awkward with no music whatsoever) I think they were trying to go for impact and tension with it, but I think at least a little bit of background droning would go a long way than just stark silence (preferences here probably vary).CHOICES?What this game is NOT good at is the 'choices matter' part. I don't feel like they actually do matter at all that much (at least the 'large' events - they seem to stay the same). Or rather, the way it  matters is very minor (some characters won't be around, some might remember what you did in the past, but the overall plot is set on rails I believe) It also seems that, fortunately, the game has kind of only one ending.Big spoiler head (No names or anything, but it does explain how the game handles 'choices'.) Is that a bad/terrible thing? No, I still enjoyed it quite a bit. Overall I'd give it a 7/10. It's a solid game with a pretty good story. Some flaws and pacing issues do occur, but they don't ruin the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, but not without some hiccups. The pacing could be better and there are occasional continuity issues (i.e. some character talks to you as if it's your first interaction even though you've spoken already). I am personally not a fan of the telltale-style "they will remember that" dialogue choices as a plot mechanic, but they don't really get in the way too much. Loved the historical setting and context and the amount of world building done with fairly minimal material. The story is pretty interesting and has some nifty twists too.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I probably shouldn't have binged this game mercilessly in the two days since it's release. Do I regret it? No. After finishing the game what struck me most was how much it lived up to it's name. We are left viewing history and folklore like a hastily covered up painting, where pagan myths are covered up and adopted into Roman myths which are adopted into the christian faith, where the disenfranchised and outsiders are forgotten under the weight of history. This game lives up to the promises of gaming as an art form, it could not have been made as anything else. The more I write this, the more pretentious it sounds so I am going to stop now.Any downsides? Some may find it tedious, particularly after a certain section of the game. I don't know if it has much replayability. And while it is probably the most polished obsidian game I've ever played it is not without it's bugs. Finally while it is intelligent, the constant stream of tragedy harms it's emotional impact.Overall if you have an interest in history, or art, or literature, or just off-kilter games this is a must play. I honestly think that this game and it's approach to history will be studied and praised for a very long time.John
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The game is gorgeous, features strong writing, and does some really interesting things with fonts. The problem is there's just too much wandering around from location to location to find if anyone has anything to say, absolutely murdering the pacing. It's a visual novel which adds a movement mechanic that serves to do little but pad the runtime.The game features a murder mystery set over decades, which suggest important choice & consequence, and while both are present, consequence ultimately end up feeling shallow. Rather than consequence being an outcome you are interested to see, it's treated more as something for self-reflection, and I was left wondering why they chose the murder mystery format of all things. When it's focused instead on examining the period of history it's set in it's a much better game.The third act also didn't land. Over decades you build up social connections and learn the social dynamics, then this is thrown away and you have to do it all over again at a time when it feels like the story should be racing towards its conclusion.An interesting effort to be sure, but one for me that overstayed its welcome and didn't deliver on its promise. While the subject matter is refreshing, the implementation feels like a lesser work of the type of game Telltale excelled at.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the game of 2022 for me and quite unlike anything I've played before. The visual style and music are wonderful and we definitely need more historical games like this. I came to grow very fond of our protagonists Andreas Maler and Magdalene Druckeryn and if there's sequel in the works, I'd buy it in a heartbeat.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great passion project of a game. The little details add so much, and you can tell Josh Sawyer and his team put lots of love into it. Hannah Kennedys art style creates a wonderful personality for the game, and especially the "written" dialogue that describes each characters personality is one of my favorite parts. I'm just so glad games like this, where the team just gets the freedom to create the game they want to make, are still being made. It's definitely a niche title, but thats what makes it even better.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely wondrous game that isn't for everyone. Just to explain what this game is about it's closest to a choose your own adventure with elements of education (You learn a lot about 16th century Europe during protestant reformation & the catholic church trying to stay dominant during that time), murder mystery, philosophical discussions especially about its main theme of how history is remembered which if you're familiar with games like Planescape Torment you'll love your ideas being challenged if you don't mind the game being text heavy & a strong case of a walking simulator that can be engrossing. I know the game is commonly described as the medieval Disco Elysium but I think it more appropriate to what I said above since the only RPG mechanic there is a speech success mechanic depending on choices you make. The artstyle is closest to a holy combination of Monty Python & old medieval art books. I will never forget  which I beg of you to play blind. Having a parent pass away recently  that filled a hole in my heart.I was also pondering thoughts on how to write this review since so many ideas were presented like how we educate the future, possible consequence(s) of erasing harmful parts of history , How grief is handled which I personally appreciated, the beautiful parts of humanity showcasing how destructive & innocent we are in 3 acts, Having a new appreciation on religion especially learning how each of them worked (I loved learning the  & also a rarity to showcase Jewish history) & the love of art despite the chaos surrounding us every day.I don't know how else to say that I'm glad this game was made and I'm grateful for Obsidian for making this despite it not being the norm in today's market especially with how it deals with faith. There might be some prudes that'll be up in arms about how religion is displayed honestly with the amount of swearing it has which is strange to be outraged at considering the other historical subject matter which you're not spared from the details. The only part of the game I was a bit confused about which might require another playthrough was the Overall I strongly recommend this game whether you buy it full price or on sale. If you also want some more reading material Sawyer shared his  for creating this gem.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if Disco Elysium wasn't made by communists, took itself seriously, and concerned itself with murder mysteries in Bavaria during the protestant reformation rather than post-communist alt-modernity, and framed itself as an old monastic text complete with gothic script and illustrations, and you'll imagine something close to this game.A solid 12-16 hour story, great game to beat in a weekend or a week, and thanks to the relative wealth of choice in the background and personality of your character, as well as the variety of far-reaching consequences to the choices made over the course of those hours, a great game to return to.Warning: You might actually learn some real world history by playing this game and might end up getting a masters degree in the class conflicts of the 16th century. Gamer discretion is advised.
