_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment isn't a game. It's a masterpiece. I started playing Pentiment early on a frigid Christmas Eve with the intention of playing it for a couple of hours and became so engrossed I played it for 11 hours straight. I could not bring myself to stop. It's now daylight outside.Everything from the presentation, artwork, story, characters, dialogue, and the soundtrack are so polished, so honed to narrative perfection, that you forget you're playing a game. Instead it feels like you're taking part in an interactive stage play / murder mystery co-written by Umberto Eco and Henrik Ibsen.Graphically the game is gorgeous and told through lush, beautifully animated scenes inspired by the artwork in medieval illuminated manuscripts. However, unlike Terry Gilliam's cutouts in , Pentiment's characters are given high quality animations that avoids feeling 'cartoony'. Character design in particular is excellent, telegraphing information about characters at a glance, yet despite no spoken dialogue in the game they emote their feelings naturally. By the end of the game you will find yourself caring for a lot of Pentiment's characters.Pentiment's story is about solving a murder but at its heart is a deeply human story about the clash between past and present, progress and tradition, faith and science, power and politics, and uncomfortable truths and necessary lies. Throughout the game you'll be tasked to navigate all these things and more as you explore the game's mystery. While there are tons of games out there that claim 'choices matter' more often than not I find these choices superficial or simply offer up slightly different outcomes. Pentiment avoids this trap. At the start of the game you are given a handful of choices for your character's background which, given the opportunity, leads to different dialogue as the story develops. What feels different this time is that the dialogue choices feel weighty and your outcomes will vary greatly depending on what you chose; an artist with a medical background or botanical background will see the world differently than one who went with a theological or legal background.It also does this without abstract stats or skill boxes; it all comes down to your initial choices and how you interact with characters. My only quibble (besides a lack of fast travel) is, despite earning a character's respect through saying the right things, pivotal dialogues can still fail because of a dice roll, even when the roll was weighed heavily in my favor. This, combined with the fact there is no way to create a checkpoint (the game continuously autosaves), it means these failures are permanent until your next playthrough. This can lead to some frustration even if it heightens the consequences of your actions.Nevertheless, after eleven hours I'm still not done with the story. I *think* I may be in the final act, I'm not sure, and even then I haven't even scratched the surface of the mystery. Pentiment is the type of game that requires multiple playthroughs in order to see everything it has to offer. I'm already looking forward to my second playthrough.So should you get Pentiment? Yes. Pentiment has something for everyone.If you have an interest in late medieval / early Renaissance history or art history get Pentiment; even if you don't, Pentiment gives you easy to understand info blurbs that you can bring up mid-dialogue.If you love a good mystery or love losing yourself in a good book Pentiment is for you.If you like morally complex stories that avoid simple black-and-white characters then Pentiment is for you. Every character has their agenda but none of them are purely good or evil but driven by internally consistent motivations.Pentiment is a triumph of narrative and artistic design and, despite his already-lofty resume, Josh Sawyer's magnum opus.Now if you'll excuse me... I need to get some sleep.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: God (forgive my momentary blasphemy), this game is something else.It's just incredible.The art is so beautiful, the music is incredible and the characters and the story is just so human.Almost every choice you make matters, and when you make some of the most important ones you might not be aware just how important that one choice was until much later on.This game is one of a kind.If you love a mystery, it's for you.If you love slice of life, it's for you.If you love history, it's for you.If you love drama, it's for you.And if you just love a damn good game, then by God, it's for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Very good, but I'd rather this be a visual novel or animation than a game. Being a game it has to justify the medium, and Pentiment does not do that very well. Most of the things "game"-y felt like arbitrary filler rather than contribute to the concept. Pentiment is a murder mystery and as such the player may or may not interact with all sources of evidence to come to any sound conclusion - but this too this hardly works in the game's favor as all it achieves is poor pacing.The writing in Pentiment is REALLY good. It is probably one of the strongest literary pieces I've seen expressed outside books, being up there with games like Disco Elysium. It is also rather pretentious, as most literary work is - but not to jarring degrees. Occasionally the game will expose you to rather disconnected historical tangents just to "impress" (especially the first dialogue scene with the Baron is quite painful), but most of the time it flows rather naturally. I would say the game is most enjoyable for those at least vaguely familiar with the late roman empire as it will frequently refer to prominent historic events. Characters are believable and act naturally, as opposed to caricatural and quirky. The role of the protagonist is a bit bland (another historical novel with a journeyman artist in the lead) but allows for a good medium to express "intended" dialogue through. The game clearly expects a more progressive mind to take the center stage here as a juxtaposition, which will most likely succeed considering I don't think anyone born in the early 16th century would play this game. You don't agree, but you want to understand.Worth playing if you're in the mood to read a book. As a game Pentiment achieves rather poor, at times even obnoxious pacing.More reviews at .
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Games as art. Games about art. Pentiment is both.In little time, you will fall in love with the artbook Bavarians and their trials and tribulations. Through death, betrayal, and misery, and using the backdrop of the 16th century (war, famine, religious turmoil!) Pentiment is a game about community, about humans, about family, about purpose.A can't miss game for 2022. Josh Sawyer do a remake of Darklands next, please.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is such an excellent game with gorgeous, thoroughly researched art and historical details. I can hardly put into words how much I love this game.The characters are written excellently and thoughtfully. Almost every choice matters, and you can play several times over and still have plenty of avenues left to explore.I thoroughly recommend it for anyone with an interest in medieval history, particularly that which pertains to religion, art, literacy and publishing. However, if you're looking for a detective/murder mystery game that will test your wits as I was when I first bought it, be warned - you will never find out for certain if your deductions are correct.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It breaks my heart that this gem didnt even got nominated for best visual style.But still I hope you devs know you did something amazing with this game! I'm not completely finished yet but it amazes me how the story progresses not only in itself but every character you meet and the whole village and the church it's so intriguing and exciting to see what consequences you get from the decisions you make. I know it's more a niche-game but I hope more people will play this and see how fantastic it is. Worth every penny!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I'm very torn whether to recommend this game or not. The art and fonts are fantastic and the historical roots exceptionally recreated, the story is quite solid and it reminds me a lot of The Name of the Rose. Sure I could have done with a couple hundreds less reminders that women were discriminated in the Reinassence, but this was merely a bit annoying and not the reason I'm dubious.The issue is that there is no game here. It looks like a graphic adventure on the first run but you realize by its end that it's actually a visual novel and that the only point of picking culprit is to change the story of what happens in the next phase. The investigations are pointless because there is no true culprit, nothing to dig further down that might shed some light on the whos and whys; you can collect achievements, see different dialogues and maybe a bit more of the background, but nothing you do actually matter in the end, it's only illusory.So, is this a good story? Yes, I still think it's a game that deserves to be played just for the feeling. But it's a sham and a severe disappointment from a studio like Obsidian.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the most interesting games I have ever played.  Starts off a little slow, but once you get to meet/know all the people in town, it hooks you!  The story was very interesting and unique in how everything was linked throughout the 3 time periods.  I plan on playing through again and making different choices.  I highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is an art work of a game. The history and story are beautiful. Its cast of characters are so fun to meet and learn about, and potentially have executed for crimes they may or may not have committed. If you like murder mysteries, medieval/renaissance/early-modern history, I think you'll love this game. Its attention to detail is just incredible.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Among the best games i have played this year, a completly unique experience and clearly a passion project for the dev team.Its full of character and attention to the details, from the way the dialogue text is written to the whole medieval aesthetic its amazing.The game consists of 3 acts that depicts the life of Andreas Maler and the ipact he had on the world around him. In those 3 acts you try to solve the mysteries of a town while on a tight schedule and even tho i am not that much of fun of time based mechanics that force you to chose actions and miss content i think it works great in this case and adds suspense to the game. Even tho the game is quite long it doesnt drag on especialy on the first 2 acts and will keep you interested the whole way through.My only complain is that i think the third act is kinda long,since it doesnt have a time mechanic it allows you to explore everything, and i wish it was a bit smaller(even tho i do enjoy what it offers) and instead we had another chapter between the first and second act depicting Andreas travels. But its a small complain and to be honest not really a complain more like a wish. Because even tho the third act is less intense than the rest, its still lovely.Overall this is a great game and i am glad that microsoft gave them the green light to make it. I wish more developers took risks like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: the rumors are true: if you love Disco Elysium, other narrative games, or just get worked up by the beauty of human connection like a big baby, you need to play Pentiment. I don't even know where to begin with this game. The art style is a labor of love, from beautiful landscape pieces and custom fonts to just delightful character designs. Re: said characters, Pentiment puts 'choices matter' under a whole new lens with them, exploring the ripples your decisions make in both the short and long (long, LONG) term on their lives. I say this as someone who struggles with actually replaying her replayable games, but the sheer volume of stories I missed in my first run made me genuinely excited to start up a new file to discover them all.And oh, my god, the writing. This is a game you need to experience with no distractions and full focusing energy--when you let yourself get fully immersed in its storytelling, your heart will break and rebuild more times than that stupid monk clock can spin. If you're not especially sentimental about the human condition (valid), maybe that isn't the ultimate selling point for you, but Pentiment more than delivers elsewhere in the mysteries and minigames you solve interacting with its world (I accidentally predicted the ending, but if you had a stable childhood this probably won't be an issue). Yes, it's got some challenges--there's a few bugs that occasionally skip (thankfully non-essential) material, the dialogue checks have some pretty involved requirements--but Pentiment weaves a beautiful narrative that illustrates meaningful ideas: the pursuit of life's passions, the subjectivity of history, the consequences of a kind heart, and most importantly, petting every little beast you find.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is ultimately a game about doubt, in my opinion mostly doubting yourself. It has a great storyline and extra points for the great research on medieval life and presenting it very "objectively". Characters are fun and goes to show you that you don't necessarily need a "larger than life" anything to make an enjoyable story. What if I actually care about whose pig got killed in the forest from a village full of people that probably never went further than the next village over in their lives? The animations are fun along with the soundtrack. Would praise the lord and drink with these people, 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing point-and-click style story game. The characters are realistic and the dialogue is riveting, but if you are familiar with Obsidian this may not be a surprise to you. The choices matter narrative and the captivating historical backdrop make this game hard to put down, you always want to see what story is waiting for you around the next corner. When the game ends it really feels like saying goodbye to a people and town that you have come to love and cherish. Most choices you make are time locked so you have to make some tough decisions on what direction you want to go in. It took me about 13 hours to complete so it goes by quick, but Obsidian manages to pack in a dense narrative dripping with intrigue and mystery with a satisfying conclusion.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A bit of a spoiler, but you solve two mysteries (one per each of the first two acts) in this game and there are no "correct"/canon solutions; whatever you choose is right (maybe, we never really know for sure). I hate this aspect of the game. It annoys the hell out of me. When I solve a mystery, I like it to be actually solved, with a correct answer/solution. So don't play this game if you want to be right at solving the mystery or "win" in that way--you literally cannot do that, at least not in the traditional sense.Otherwise, cool art, cool concept, decent game play (even if it was 95% running back and forth talking to people and dialogue was boring or slow sometimes). Excellent use of religious syncretism as a theme and plot device (which is also a bit of a spoiler, but for anyone who is familiar with Roman mythology, you'll *immediately* know something is up if you look at St. Satia's shrine at the beginning of Act I, because you'll be like "gurl, whatchu doin' here, when did you change your name??"). Anyways, lots of cool layers about history, religion, myth, and the cultural stories we tell ourselves about our past.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game gives an interesting insight into the every day lives of common people and the clergy under rule of the Holy Roman Empire. I found the stories it tells about the characters very well written and engaging. The art style is also incredibly well done.I would definitely recommend this to anyone who thinks they would enjoy a enthralling, historical murder mystery... as long as you are no stranger to a bit of reading!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Charming art, plus an interesting and complex story. It has good replayability due to the various possible decisions at important (albeit, at sometimes seemingly unimportant) points in the storyline.Be prepared to read a lot as there are no spoken dialogs, but it's absolutely worth it. The game really has some Name of the Rose vibes. If you like investigations and connecting the dots based on spoken or seen evidence than you'll like this game.

_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A bit disappointed really. It's a nice game, but it doesn't feel like you can actually make a difference in it, no matter what you do. I guess I did some things in wrong order, because sometimes the dialog worked as if I didn't already know something - although I already had discovered it. Stuff like that. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Very refreshing take on storytelling. It’s an intriguing mystery to unfold where choices really do seem to matter, but in such a way that you’re never quite sure if you could have changed the outcome, which really lends to the time period and overall theme of the narrative. It’s a poignant and well-realized insight into the times and how history can be told through art, what really determines ‘truth,’ how religion both protected and undermined communities, and how peoples across centuries are more connected than they probably realized. Such a great game. I briefly felt there was a slump in the beginning of the second half of the narrative (no spoilers), but that was soon corrected—much to my surprise. Great twists, immersive score, interesting characters…I could go on! 10/10 Superb!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is an incredible game that delivers a singularly human experience as it delves into how we shape history through culture, oral tradition, and what is finally written down. The sound design is minimalistic but exactly what it needs to be, and the art is as luscious and well thought-out as one would expect a game touting the influence of renaissance-era illuminated manuscripts would have. It offers a thoroughly well-researched window into life during the early 16th century, from duties to dress to social life and even to the food! Tassing might not be real, but having visited Bavaria throughout my life, it feels incredibly real to me. If you have the opportunity to go to Bavaria, Fussen and the surrounding area are likely to give you a feel for what you see in game. Overall, the writing is great, and you really get the feeling that you're part of an older culture. My only complaint is how they chose to tie things together in the end (I would have liked a little more player involvement there) but that's hardly the end of the world. If you're a fan of history, illuminated manuscripts, period whodunnits, oral traditions, unreliable narratives, roleplaying games, and point and click adventures, then this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyed (enjoying) this game a great deal. I'm not sure if this will appeal to younger gamers, but for those with a few more years on the clock -  a good deal of thought has been put into this tale.  In short it's a bit like being the lead character in a cross between "The name of the rose" and "It's a wonderful life".Not sure if all the characters' stories marry with the choices you make, but that's a reflection on how well the game is put together. You lose sight of it being a game of many characters, rather than just your own story. Can't wait to complete Act 2 and 3.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: During my lifetime I've played my fair share of videogames, counting in hundreds, literally. When I'm saying the best game, I don't mean it in some objective sense, taking count of various factors. For me, such game is the one that left the biggest impact. Probably, that goes to Night in the Woods, although my second playthrough 6 years after the first one haven't felt that unparalleled in quality as much as I remembered.Now, I've played Pentiment like 3 months ago, maybe more. But the experience lingers. There is something disturbing about this game. Like the hardships of people are portrayed in such a believable way. Death feels visceral, present. The ongoing murder spree with the sprinkles of magic realism elements create a sense of deep-rooted horror, but in unsettling way rather than scary.The strong impression persists. I oftentimes ponder about the game. But it's not just the excellent story, brilliant dialogue, original artstyle. The best quality for me is how real playing the game feels. A lot of the game is unstated to player. In chapter 2, the game portrays the most authentic depiction of depression I've ever seen in a videogame, yet not once does the game says this verbatim. Other specks of life you notice once you contemplate the game. The crone who wishes to die. Marin, having some strong obvious personal issues you never find more about. The blacksmith, unable to find a wife, decade after decade. Brother Piero, showing genuine paternal care to Andreas, whom Andreas weeps over his beravement. The genius of this game lies in the unspoken. The more closely you observe, the more you see Pentiment as a manifestation of human predicament, a collage of intricacies this experince of life entails. It's so much more than a murder mystery game.If I were to guess a recent game that will reach a cult status down the line, I would vote Pentiment. It's the second time I'm playing this game, and unlike many emotionally strong unique games that had lost some of its spark when I played them for the second time, Pentiment just confirmed my suspicion that it's an outstanding experience that will stand a testament of time.For starters, the games I consider the best are behemoths like Planescape Torment, The Longest Journey, Night in the Woods, Panzer Dragoon Saga, The Last of Us II. I've fallen in love with some of those two decades after their release. Pentiment is on an equal footing in my opinion and it's genius will keep resurfacing in years to come. I'm so glad this game exists.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot, it pains me, but no, I can't. _childDocuments_.review: One of the best and unique games to kick 2023 off!With the first Act done I can wholeheartedly recommend Pentiment. While being developed by Obsidian is a definite green light, the game itself is carved to be a unique masterpiece in a style like I have not seen in games before. A beautiful amalgamation of art, history, storytelling and impeccable writing with an intriguing mystery to solve and world altering decisions to be made.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you to the devs at Obsidian for taking me on this journey! I very much loved the music. Given the rarity of its appearances, I felt it created a nice illusion of how enchanting music must have been over the ages. I met a lot of wonderful and interesting people, but above all, meeting the Son of  was an absolute delight.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Remember learning about Martin Luther and his Twelve Theses in history class? Vaguely? Well Pentiment is set in the 16th century during the time of Martin Luther. That time period is a lot more interesting than history class makes it out to be.In Pentiment, you play as Andreas, an artist working at the local scriptorium. You make images for religious texts. After you finish your current project, you plan to go to Nuremburg to marry a woman you've never met. Unfortunately, things fall soon fall a part after someone is murdered. Your friend is the prime suspect, and you're forced to find the true culprit otherwise he'll be executed. However, as you investigate you soon realize that things are much much more complicated than they seem. Everyone is hiding secrets. No one can be trusted.It's clear the game's creators did their research (there is a bibliography at the end after all), and there are lots of historical and religious references to Lutheranism, the Holy Roman Empire, and Christian and Roman figures. All of this was overwhelming at first. The game does underline the name of places, characters, and important religious figures in red in the dialogue bubble. Clicking on that sends you to a glossary that shows the person's face or explains the place or religious figure. That helped a lot and ended up being quite educational. Something else I like is that choices do matter. When I first saw the notification that the person would remember that I rolled my eyes a bit. There's been plenty of games where you're led to believe your choices matter, but in the end they don't or they are only superficial. Well, I ended up being surprised when a character refused to tell me something. All the actions the game labels important affect your success in persuading other characters to help you or reveal information. The game tells you what choices helped or hindered you in persuading the characters. I appreciated that, as I could see how my choices added up, and it helped alter future decision making. The story and ending were unexpected but I enjoyed them both. The art style is also very fitting.While the game isn't a walking simulator, most of the gameplay consists of talking to characters, interrupted by the occasional mini-game or puzzle. If you're the type of person to skip past cutscenes or dialogue, this is not the game for you. If you like choose-your-own-adventure, story rich games with complex characters, give Pentiment a try. You'll see how interesting history can be.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really love history and also mystery games, and this is an amazing combo of both. The amount of detail that went into this game is incredible, from the art style to the historical setting. The characters truly feel like real people. Amazing game 10/10 would recommend it for people who love stories about how things change over time and also solving murders
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I love being able to kill people I don't like because an entire town decided my word was final as to who was the murderer :DBut if that's not particularly appealing to you there are numerous aspects of the game that I absolutely adore. The art and atmosphere (as well as the historically accurate details put in) make me very happy. The different fonts and small style changes dispersed through the various different people and their education levels is such a nice detail. Personally, my favorite part of the font thing is that all the printing press people have that printing press style thing when you first meet them. My favorite sequences have to be the ones where I am placed within the pages of the book with Sister Illuminata and that one guy, forgot his name. It's incredibly well done to give a perspective into how less widely portrayed perspectives did exist, even if history might be blind to them. It's also nice to play as Magdalene in the third act and live through her experiences as well.Those aren't all my thoughts, I have so many, but the gist is that the story is amazing the characters are amazing the art is spectacular and I couldn't ask for more. I pirated this game at first because I wasn't sure I would like it, but I absolutely adore it and glad I bought it legally, I love supporting such projects and hope more history heavy games will be released in the future; if you're also a fan of these types of games you should too!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept. Some minor frustrations in execution - namely making the player feel obliged to repeatedly check every available location and character whenever anything happens or time passes,  they miss something. This is sometimes rewarded, but often only succeeds in feeling like a chore.Overall I'd score this a 4/5, but your enjoyment will depend heavily on your personal interest in the subject matter / setting and level of patience (or lack of).
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The character desing, the backgrounds, the dialogs, the menues! Every asset is a piece of art and an accurate design. Nerd time: You have a book where you can check real facts about regions, local folklor, etc while the characters mention them and omg characters speaking in italian, french, german... I don't want to spoil more details. You definitely have to play this game if you're a medieval/renaissance culture fan. I don´t feel like finish it, I'm in love with this game and want to live forever as Andreas Maler c:
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I'm in the middle of Act II and really enjoying the detailed narrative the game has built. The characters are interesting and there are surprising plot twists. Navigation could be a bit simpler to avoid having to spend as much time finding where the character I need to talk to wandered off next or which characters might have new things to say, since it does take a lot of time to go from one end of the map to the other. However, I guess this is also part of the exploratory side of the game. I also wish I could interact with more background elements. A lot of things seem like they could have more to say, but options are rather limited.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful and captivating. Clearly an effort of love and someone's passion for history and art. If you have any patience for dialogue heavy games and minor puzzle solving, buy it, and if you love those things, why are you even bothering to finish reading this review when you could be playing it already?Incredible.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A work of art!Incredibly immersive, beautiful and historical art style;I felt frustrated, angry, sad, happy and everything in between, much like the characters in the story.It's one of those games I'm sad I only get to experience in full once - I'd like to play again and choose different things, but ultimately I've seen how the Christmas beer is made :)10/10, loved every minute of it!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent murder mystery with in depth characters over the span on a lifetime in game. Your choices affect the ending because as characters die or are sent away everything is warped to your tune. Worth the money I paid, One caveat however, if you do not enjoy broken sword style games this may not be for you. A solid 8/10 with repeatability, try and avoid spoilers and enjoy :D
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely delightful, choice-driven experience. I think the game has it's fair share of issues, particularly in terms of maintaining momentum from a nigh-perfect first act, but it's a nonetheless incredible experience from start to finish. I'm reluctant to say "especially for a Double AA game" as I feel that may undermine the sheer level of thought and care that went into the world and narrative design, but it should be noted just so one is aware some constraints (particularly in terms of total play time, if that matters for you - one playthrough ran me about 13 hours) will exist. I particularly want to applaud the autosave system, which restricts the save scumming that often hurts the impact of choice driven games. Don't want to go further into any details, as it's worth exploring for yourself to make your own opinion!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Really great game, more so than being a murder mystery, i'd say its a history mystery! saying more would be spoiling it, but the small touches, attention to detail, and visual style kept me hooked. Alot of blood sweat and tears obviously went into this game, the playtime is about 12-14 hours about, but i liked running around so my hours were higher. due to character 'perks' (more so just choosing your characters history) and the decisions you make, this game has replayability though i seed some time to think after the ending of Act III, the final act, before i try another. your first playthrough could look much different than say your second or your third. Theres alot of reading, but the way that the letters flow like theyre being writ or print, combined with the impressive emotion of 2d characters makes a fair bit easier to stomach, helps if you like history! Actually reallly helps if you like history, as the history part, living in and learning about is a large chunk of this game's meat, with a murder mystery that keeps you eagerly speed-reading dialogue to find out whodunnit. History in this game was also really cool and it wrapped so many things together and considered many different points of view, leaving no voice unheard.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent story game, very interesting with compelling plot points and a great narrative. The artwork is beautiful, and they do a great job of obfuscating the ultimate truth throughout the story without just making the plot twists utterly ridiculous and out of nowhere. If you pay VERY close attention, you can yourself get a pretty good theory about what's going on.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I could have played another 20 hours and never gotten bored of it. It was lovely to see the care and attention put into not only the art but also the research side of things. Lovely also to have a tale not about knights and battles but the concerns of the common people and their lives. I'll certainly be playing it again to see what achievements I might have missed the first time around, and I'd be thrilled to see a sequel in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the best writing, some most well written and believable characters, and such a compelling story revolving around this small, Bavarian village. It didn't entirely grip me at the start, but the further I explored and investigated as Andreas Maler- and the more I learned about him and his own life, I became deeply invested and wanted to see this tale through to it's end.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: if this game looks like something you might be interested in: go for it! I absolutely recommend it! If you take your time to really delve into the game world and get to know all the characters and locations and their history, the game will absolutely reward you.One caveat however: Even though this might look like a detective game, that's not really what the developers were going for. This game is more about choices and character development than solving an actual mystery. So if you're like me and try and find the perfect solution to every problem, you might become a bit frustrated. So my suggestion is: make your choices and then just live with the consequences - as difficult and as heart-wrenching as that may be sometimes. :D
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A true labor of love in our gloom, capitalistic times of soulless corporate clones instead of gaming masterpieces! Outstanding visuals, animations, style, and sound. A great way to study history similar to Kingdom Come Deliverance in that regard if not in genre. And also at a very low price! Buy it, rate it, share it, discuss it. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Good story and interesting setting. Having the right expectations is essential to enjoy Pentiment though, because it is not a traditional RPG, it is a visual novel. It is also not a typical murder plot, this element is not the center of the story. The only thing I didn't like is that a couple of plot twists are too tropey and cliché and felt more like stuff from soap operas.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: WOW. I'm going to think about this game for a long, long time. First off, the art style is decade appropriate and you can tell a LOT of love went into researching 1500s religious art, imagery, symbolism, and caligraphy. Secondly, its incredibly heartfelt... the decisions you make are tough and often ambiguous, and it feels real when consequences come around. Genuinely a heartfelt meditation on faith, loss, suffering, accountability... really incredible game.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is maybe the second or third review of anything I've ever bothered to post but I felt absolutely compelled after finishing my first playthrough of this work of art.I cannot sing the praises of this story enough. It holds up well on classic murder mystery fronts, all of the individual story strands are extremely moving, the art is unique and phenomenal, the score underlines the emotional moments exquisitely, all coming together to create an incredible moving experience. Don't go into it expecting to play an action game or anything like that, because that isn't what this is. It's even quite light on standard point-and-click game staples -- there's no inventory or anything like that, pretty much the entire course of the story is decided by character interactions and simple choices, but between all of the little details and obvious love that went into the design (like the little quirks and differences in how dialogue is "written" on to the screen) and all of the absolute spot-on writing and elements mentioned above, Pentiment will make you feel things and be so happy you did. And then don't get me started on the dedication to historical accuracy on top of all that.An absolutely beautiful story.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic experience more than a game.  At the core, it is a achingly beautiful story of humanity and community against a detective/exploration of late medieval rural Europe.  If the last sentence grabs your interest, this game is certainly for you; if not, I would give this a miss.  This is a gem that is text-driven and exploratory with very limited interaction and truly focused on a niche concept that will either excite and deliver on the premise alone, or drive you to look further rather quickly.With that said; I thoroughly recommend this title for most gamers to simply experience.  It is slow, methodical and in the end, quite linear - but there is more character and depth in this work of art than in any other game I've enjoyed over the past decade.  The animation of the expressions, the medieval art that permeates the journey and especially the scrawl and sound of text throughout lends an air of authenticity to the world and for me, becomes the focus.  The mystery that threads the plot together is rarely the central focus of the protagonist; rather the emotional engagement with each character takes your focus.  Where the game strays to reference historical events and personalities of the era, there is a lovely function where you lean out from the action similar to looking at a world map in RPG style games-only here we are treated to more artistic representations of key characters and concepts to keep up with the meandrous plot.For those on the fence; it is worth your time - plot driven, heavily texted and resplendent with characters you generally come to enjoy and worry about; even to the point of multiple play-throughs to see precisely what relationships can change or flourish to affect the world.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, but it's not for everyone (that's ok!), but I have some issues with it.Issue 1: No manual savingI know the point of the game is that it's smaller and by design, it is supposed to be replayed, but it sucks not having manual saving. I've accidentally picked wrong dialog choices and sometimes have no way to reset to that point. It is impossible to know how reacting to certain events might impact future interactions. I get that this is the point, but when I try to be polite to or reassure someone, and it ends up making me fail a persuasion attempt, I can't help but get upset. Issue 2: PacingAct 1 has the best pacing of the game, honestly. You pick your character build, have a clear goal, and a murder happens. There's several suspects and many pieces of evidence. It's early enough in the game where you can reset and explore a 2nd option or a different path. However, Act 2 takes a while to get going, but the investigation part feels very limited. Act 3 seemed like it dragged on too long. I loved seeing how the town builds and changes, but Act 3 had me hoping it was going to end soon, honestly.The game is too long to be a "pick up and play" kind of game. It took me numerous hours to finish the game. While I'd love to replay with a different path, pick a different suspect, and do different choices, it's going to be several hours of a commitment that I am not sure I want to make very often. If the game was a bit shorter in certain parts, or we had manual saving, I would feel more eager to explore every path/choice. Issue 3:Weird logic statesThis game was designed for game pass, and to be cheaper on platforms. It's only 20 bucks. I know they didn't have as much time, but I did find some bugs in the game that impacted immersion.As an example:I had a law background for my character and after helping a widow, she had me examine a letter about her home. She was told she would lose the house because she is a woman and cannot inherit from her dead husband. She will be homeless by act 2 if we do not intervene. If you have the law background, you can point flaws and tell her how to save her house. When you interact with a legal authority later, you can tell him about this and he will intervene on her behalf to make it right. When you start Act 2, she will be happier and still in her home. Despire this, I had some characters mention how she lost her home. One NPC expressed concern about a daughter not marrying and suffering the same fate as the widow I just helped.Another point this happened was that I missed the autopsy of a murder suspect, but I could tell an NPC an aspect of it that I wouldn't be able to know. I was able to tell him that the assumed murder weapon wasn't the real murder weapon and I could say that I was at the autopsy when I wasn't. The game allows you to lie in the game, but it's always prefaced with the [lie] tag. This is rare, but it happens. Logic and branching paths is always hard to handle and it can spiral out of control. I do this for a living and it can be a nightmare making sure all paths make sense. Issue 4: Lack of changes on outcomeYou can make a lot of changes in individual people's lives, but a lot of things don't seem to have a choice. Regardless of what you do, certain events happen. The ending is ultimately the same, key events happen regardless of what you do. It was a fun journey, and whole characters might be missing from the game if you do different things, but you can't do much to the core narrative. I wish the game allowed you to shape certan events in favor of the other party and cause a ripple effect.Still a wonderful game. I'd say 8.5/10 or so.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is essentially a video game version of The Name of the Rose. If that sounds as exciting to you as it did to me, then I 100% guarantee that you will love this game. Take that book and add in lovingly crafted artwork and a branching narrative with RPG character building elements, and you've got Pentiment. This game probably has an extremely niche appeal. A very historically accurate, narrative-focused, RPG, murder mystery? Who would play that? Me. As soon as I saw the announcement for this game, I immediately felt that it had been made specifically to appeal to me and other people with similar interests (i.e. huge history nerds who also like role playing narratives). Its probably not for everyone, but for the people who will find it appealing, its an amazing experience. Its almost kind of a misnomer to call it an "RPG" in the modern sense of the term, because there's no combat. The RPG elements, like the whole rest of of the game, are entirely dialogue/narrative focused.  You are playing a pre-made character, technically, but you still have the agency to control how he behaves, as well as his backstory, etc. I would say that its a role playing experience in the purest sense of the term: you're role playing a person who doesn't have fantastic, superhuman abilities, who can only do things that a normal person could, and who will face realistic consequences appropriate to the historical setting of the game. If you're the kind of person who, when playing an RPG, always tries to talk your way out of every situation, and attempts to take the time to find every bit of information available before making a decision, you will appreciate this approach. Its one of the best games I've played in years.

_childDocuments_.review: I am very interested in European History (mainly medieval). One things that I always found frustrating was finding games that seemed to dedicate itself to proper accuracy of the time period. Most games for that period are macro-strategy games, or stylised settings. Real history has interesting things to say and I want more games that explore that. When I saw this game in the Steam store I was immediately drawn by its unique art style and premise. While it's not medieval in setting (more like Renaissance and reformation), I could tell that it had something to say about the philosophy of the people who lived in the time.The game, without a doubt, is stunning. The visuals are just inspiring--anytime I was presented a new scene I took my time in soaking in every figure, colour, and detail. The characters are wonderful, they are all unique, and as the story takes place across decades, it is wonderful to see how they grow and develop. The story is phenomenal. A simple premise sends you on a journey through theological exploration and history of the region. How it evolved.This game is a journey. There is a lot of reading, but take your time with it--take in every word. Learn the terms/people the game gives you. I feel by the end of the game you will be more enriched.

_childDocuments_.review: The most complimentary description I can give Pentiment is: imagine "Disco Elysium" — which Pentiment director Josh Sawyer said was inspirational to him in a "broad sense" — but with even *fewer* RPG elements, e.g. a game not only lacking combat, but stripped of character stats and even an inventory system. Pentiment is a narrative game that is driven entirely by dialogue, reading (there's no voice acting), and point-and-click movement. Despite the lack of a traditional game loop and features, it completely hooked me, such is the amount of loving detail put into its world-building and writing. I'll admit that I went into this game blind, and bounced hard after the first 15 minutes. I like narrative games, but Pentiment felt a little too basic even for me. I almost refunded the game. But after playing for another 15 minutes, and seeing a couple of beautifully illustrated cutscenes, I was a total convert, and I binged the game for 15 hours over the long weekend. I had no interest in or even awareness of 16th-century Bavaria, yet became totally invested in the seemingly-mundane lives and lifestyles of the town and abbey central to the game's mysteries.It's hard to describe the game's few shortcomings without implicitly spoiling the story's overall scope, but I think virtually all of Pentiment's flaws come down to whether you agree with its creators' philosophy behind their design choices. Even knowing how it ended, I was ready to jump into a new playthrough to see how a different "build" and different choices would impact the town and people for whom Pentiment built in me such a strong attachment. At $20 — $15 during the holiday sale — Pentiment feels like the quriky creation of an obsessed artist, a game so well-crafted but so niche that it ends up causing its developer to go out of business. If you don't hate the idea of a slower-paced game that's 80% reading, I can't imagine you not enjoying Pentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece of storytelling, art, and gameplay. Despite being billed as a medieval story, the gameplay takes place at the post-Medieval end of the Early Modern Period in Germany during the rule of the Holy Roman Empire. To put it into better context— during the period of years that the game spans, the Renaissance ended in Italy, Henry VIII made himself the head of the English Church, and Copernicus theorized that the Earth revolved around the Sun. Of course many aspects of Medieval life were still around by this point, but to simply call it the Medieval period is quite misleading.The setting of the game is a fictional village called Tassing that is inspired by real-world locations but allows the developers to tell their own story which fits into actual history based on what was going on at the time (I won't spoil anything) but gives creative license with the details. The game is immersive, using different writing and printing styles for the speech of different characters based on class and profession, as well as multiple languages (all of which the game translates). The folk native to Germany speak in English (though their language is Early New High German, think the German equivalent of King James Bible English) though written materials you find in game are in ENHG (among other languages like Latin) but they are translated for you by your character.The story centers around a series of murders, but it is more than that. This is the story of a village and its people over a period of change and unrest. Your actions might just influence how things unfold, for good or ill. Fans of the Murder Mystery genre should know, however, that while this game features murder mystery investigation in a good portion of the gameplay, the gameplay does not exclusively involve solving murders. Overall, you will be talking to various people throughout the village, looking for clues, doing tasks associated with daily life in the Early Modern Period (centered around the Benedictine canonical hours from Matins to Compline). One thing to note, if the game warns you a task will take some time to complete, do that task last as it will usually end the day or at least advance the clock by a lot. Also, keep in mind you will not have time to do all tasks especially in the earlier parts of the game so some avenues of the story may go unexplored.Gameplay is simple. There is nothing in the game that requires a knowledge of an advanced control scheme, and no quick time events or other similar abrupt shifts in game play. The game is more or less point and click, and you do get to customize your character by choosing elements of their studies which gives you new options during dialog (such as knowing a particular language). As far as I know there are no right or wrong choices that end the game early, the game will simply progress and you will have to live with the outcome of your choices.The only thing that could be considered a downside in my opinion is the shift in pace and direction at the beginning of the third act (I won't go into spoilers). The pace ramps up from the beginning of the game up to a climactic second act finish and then abruptly slows down until the last third or so of the third act. It almost feels like a different game set in the same setting for a while. The game is still fun at this point, don't get me wrong, but the game had me missing the gameplay that had lead up to that point for a few hours of game time. It does eventually ramp back up by the end and in my opinion it is definitely worth it.I'm hoping we'll get another game in this style from Obsidian, perhaps set in another part of Europe or in a different time period.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews on Steam, but when I do, it is because a game a true masterpiece that has moved me so profoundly that I must implore others to experience it for themselves. Pentiment is no exception. This is truly one of the best games I have ever played, and certainly the best I have played in a while...maybe since Outer Wilds. If you choose to read nothing further, know that if you have even a middling interest in this game, it is worth it and you will not regret it.When I first saw it pop up in the Steam store, I immediately knew that I had stumbled upon something that had the makings of an experience unlike any before. Simply put, it was entirely "my brand." A murder mystery spanning 25 years in a small Bavarian town during the early sixteenth century? Hooked immediately. Character conversations about the philosophy of the time regarding, well, philosophy, art, music, law, medicine, sociopolitical structure, and, of course, a massive helping of theology? A dream come true. Gameplay centered around character development and choices, wherein even the most mundane conversation can have fully realized implications seen in later acts? Life Is Strange, hold your own beer. These factors alone would have had me, uh, selling my daughter to the local convent to play this game, but they had to take it one. step. further. by feeding the senses with historically-informed aesthetics and design. Be still my heart. I adored seeing the different scripts that appeared in speech bubbles, depending on the social status and education-level of the characters (and the paired sounds of a scratching quill or letterpress blocks). The amount of detail put into the ever-changing character and world designs to the manuscripts of our journals is as incredible as it is beautiful. Time and time again, I found myself running around to all the locations at all seasons and times of day to see how the landscape would change. The music, although heard sparsely throughout the game, are all (excepting four pieces) adaptions or improvisations of real compositions contemporary to or predating the setting of the game, including work by Sister Hildegard von Bingen herself, performed largely (with creative liberty) faithfully to the style of the time and with medieval instruments. (Truthfully, I wish the game had featured the soundtrack more prominently, though I suppose hearing only the general din of the environment, save those dramatic moments, was more immersive.)All that is to say, the loving detail put into every other aspect of the game is not lost on the story, which was moving in its superficial simplicity. I came to love and care for the plight of all of the characters, even the more disagreeable ones (save a discreet few who deserve what they got!). As my playtime suggests, I ran around constantly exhausting every possible conversation opportunity I had. No interaction felt too small or insignificant, even if not significant to the grander plot, for me not to pursue every opportunity I had to interact with the residents of Kiersau and Tassing. Watching their lives unfold, helping to shape the course of things as best I could, and feeling the changes and losses alongside them is an experience I doubt I will be able to replicate. Nothing hit me in the gut as hard as the shift from Act 1 to Act 2 though, even as I watched in HORROR at the conclusion of Act 2. A genuine masterpiece of storytelling that will stick with me for a long, long time.

_childDocuments_.review: Here is the selling point for me:you will usually have three-five responses available, but you can only pick one of them. Picking a response often locks you out of all other responses. This is game-changing because it makes you critically think about how other characters will respond and how you are impacting the story and ending. In this game, what you don't say is just as important (if not more) as what you do say.If you love Holy Roman Empire history (especially around the 15/1600s), this will be your jam.But even if you don't, the humanity present in these people shows how similar these people, and indeed people throughout history, are to us today. With murder mysteries, juicy hot goss, and religious oppression, there are plenty of themes, ideas, and philosophies to dive into and explore in this stunningly hand-drawn world. One of the best point and clicks out there.

_childDocuments_.review: You can read other reviews Video review: There are choices that are quite difficult to make, but what if those choices play such an important role in a narrative that goes hand in hand with our character's personality? Pentiment is much more than a simple click of a mouse button.Andreas Maler, played by the player who will be in charge of deciphering the mysteries that this title will bring to the table, is a traveling artist and a dreamer, advised by imaginary entities during his sleep. Each of them is interpreted by his opinion. Between Saints, Priests and even the philosopher Socrates, opinions differ among them in an attempt to discuss ideas and shape an opinion about the changes that Andreas will be facing, due to the choices he made at a certain point in history. In fact, the adventure begins inside a dream of Andreas, who after waking up learns that court jesters are intractable.The narrative begins with little action, in fact, there are no moments of action at all, but even so, it is a title recommended for anyone looking for a captivating story and accurate historical events. Tassing, is the fictional town in the countryside of the Holy Roman Empire, which serves as a backdrop and which at first glance appears peaceful with modest but super friendly people. Andreas's task until then was to work on his great masterpiece, this being an artist with studies in the field and beyond, but also to enter into the routine of working on the manuscripts of the local abbey. However, he quickly realizes that things are not as peaceful as they appear to be, and suddenly finds himself wrapped in a panoply of mysteries that involve even the death of one of his elements.The history and background of Andreas are completely outlined by the player as he advances in time, being able to choose the areas of study that most interest him and even the types of language that fascinate him the most. These choices will have a direct impact on the story and the possible lines of text available at certain times. My Andreas dabbles in Italian studies and a little Greek, fascinated by books, occult magic, and astronomy. It is important to approach all moments with the greatest possible attention since these can lead to a positive or negative outcome in the activity between characters and with this the possibility of acquiring more knowledge about the subject addressed.Not being a Point and Click in its essence, Pentiment's adventure goes through a narrative divided into 3 acts that involve investigation and the player's attention to places that may go unnoticed. In trying to solve the murder mysteries, it is important to be convinced of the decisions taken, since time weighs on all small actions. The simple act of having lunch with a character implies wasting time that can be used to explore another part of the story in more depth, which ultimately can impact the number of evidence for the outcome of the case. And yes, it's easy to get lost in these small actions because without paying much attention, the next moment, you're already in contact with a character that doesn't add anything to the main point. Everything is very vivid and there is a lot to discover. The map can also help with these momentary distractions since the possibilities are more than many. This is not a Sherlock Holmes where the story has only one ending, Pentiment kinda forces you to pick a culprit with the information that you gathered and subsequently live with it.The direct consequences of the player's choices are what make this experience so impactful. Everything rotates and adapts according to the different branches of choice, and ultimately if you are on the side of the village population or hand in hand with the abbey.Pentiment's graphics pull the graphic aspect of the engravings in a book and make everything quite charming. All its characters and surroundings are quite peculiar and specific to the era, or this one is not set in the year 1518. The menu itself is a book that opens between the map, the different characters, the objectives, and clues. That helps the player not to feel lost about what the next step to take. Another super interesting aspect is the possibility of having specific letter fonts for each character, which although some are a little difficult to decipher, manages to convey the personality of the individual approached since there is no voice acting of any kind. Could it be that if there was voice acting this would be a title that could attract more people? Or, on the other hand, would it throw down any kind of depth that can you can drink from all the reading? Pentiment is a breath of fresh air from the studios of Obsidian Entertainment. Slow at certain points, but pertinent and interesting at just the right points to grab the player even in those moments.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One day this game caught my eye, once I started playing, on my TV, my girlfriend (that usually does'nt play games) watched me for a while and as I, she was also amazed by the story, characters, art and setting. We caught ourselves discussing (even arguing) the different choices and intrigues of the game. Amount of depth and details is astonishing, The art is not only part of the story but it's contained in almost every part of the gameplay. The theme seeps out of every aspect of the game, such as your journal is a beautifly animated book, containg hand drawn maps and information you need. The speech bubbles changes typography based on context in a clever way, and with subtle animations can conviene lot of little nuances. The detective side of things is really well made. Until the last moment I did'nt know who was responsible for the events in Tassing. However the reveal felt a little bit underwhelming. One of the interesting design choices is the time limit on your investigation. You have limited time (as in number of leads you can follow) to solve the mysteries, so you have to prioritise and investigate only the leads, that seems promising. That enhances the stress of having to make a judgment from the limited evidence you have. It would be nice to have multiple save slots, or just the ability when you finish the game, review some of you choices and some other leads to follow. One of the issues I had wit the games are the conversation checks. They felt really punishing and you had to be incredibly precise with your answers to persuade someone. Sometimes a one innocent funny remark can fail the pesuasion check.It's a text heavy narrative almost action-less game, so it's not for everbody. Target audience is definetly the point-and-click type of players, however some of them may be bored by lack of challenging puzzles. But if you like narrative games just cover yoursef with a blanket on a rainy day, and get lost in the atmosphere of Tassing and its mysteries.

_childDocuments_.review: A work of art, literally and figuratively. Breaks the mould for conventional murder-mystery games and already has me eager to run a second play-through to try out new skills and conversation options. A game for those who enjoy a good plot, steady progress and lashings of intrigue. The art style is something else ;)

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 Very Good.This is basically an art piece for the modern era. A modern take on an adventure game, set during the renaissance in a backwater village, where the religious class faces future upheaval that is coming in the form of reforms.You play as Andreas Maler, an artist who is plying his trade at the local monastery for the time being. He gets pulled into a murder investigation, and away we go. There's no great gameplay mechanics here in terms of investigation, you basically chase up the clues/suspects, and throw up some prayers as you try your best to find some form of evidence against the accused.The issue is, in these days criminal investigations were basically 'he said/she said,' there's no room for legal eagle's, or blood splatter analysis, this is a time period where you say hail Mary and hope for the best.At times, you will feel powerless, such is the nature of the time period.The murder investigations and the story as a whole are quite well written. It is a snapshot of life in the old ages, with some liberties taken (and that's fine), so that we can enjoy a well crafted storyline. The art style is superb, you may see in the screenshots, that dialogue is written like penstrokes, or printed text, and that's because in the intro, it is established that you're writing a book of these events. So, as you write, you stylise the text depending on the person's education or background, so the clergy often write their dialogue in Gothic font.For those with dyslexia or vision issues, there is a prompt to turn these off, so you can get a more cleaner read.Other than this, there's little else to say about the game. You can shape Andreas' choices and backgrounds, which does help with the investigation, having knowledge of languages or logic, can help you solve puzzles in different ways for example, but his overall character remains more or less the same, he is still his own person after all.Really, you come to this game for a story, an investigation into a murder mystery, and the wonderful art, cast and location. It's a wonderful artistic type of game, and to top it all off, at £15 is beyond reasonable, it's almost a steal.So, yes, fully recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One thing I've noticed about Obsidian is that they always put out amazing RPG's that feel a tad unfinished (KOTOR 2, Fallout NV, Tyranny, Outer Worlds, etc). This game is less advanced mechanically than their usual games but is better for it. Pentiment feels like a fully-realized work of art that never misses a beat. The story and characters are fleshed out and engaging, the world is littered with historical details that I probably mostly missed, and even at full price the game is only $20 which is an absolute steal. 9.5/10 highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: What I immediately loved is that the game offers plenty of secrets right away. I'm a sucker for these, despite being crap at sniffing them out. Alwa's Legacy is colorful, lively, easy to pick up, the controls are intuitive, and the hitboxes are generous. The plot is primitive, almost non-existent, but I can't say that I care about this aspect when it comes to platformers like this one. All in all, it deserves the title of "baby's first metroidvania", and not in some derogatory sense.I also love me a bit of sequence-breaking. Still not sure if most of them were intentional or exploits. Which is a good thing! It takes ingenuity to turn a bug into a feature. I immediately started jumping off my own green blocks after casting them in the air. The secret is to cast them while you're moving up... I think. It's finicky. Then I skipped the first boss's last phase by hitting him whenever possible, pretty sure one can one-phase him with a bit of practice. I adore these shenanigans! And while the sequences break, the game doesn't. At least not on my watch.The setting is a bit on the bland side, but it's also very traditional, familiar even. I like the way everything looks, it's a pretty game. To me, the problem lies in the map design. There are slightly too many empty screens with nothing interesting on them, too many boring dead ends. Traversing the world isn't particularly exciting due to how basic the movement is. It gets a much better flow after you get an air dash, but it happens ~5 hours in, which is slightly too late. I get it that they wanted to make the world feel bigger, but I disagree with the price they paid.Maybe metroidvanias are not my thing? Then again, I adore The Messenger. Although, it's easy to explain: its world was fun to breeze through and had more character to it. Besides, there you could also kill enemies on the go, slash and run at the same time. Alwa's combat is a slog in comparison. But maybe it isn't a fair comparison? Killing stuff doesn't play as big of a role here. At their worst, enemies can be a minor nuisance. On the bright side, the checkpoints are plentiful and you may spend a special "tear" thingie to add a warp function to any of them and teleport at your leisure. It solves many problems, but not all of them.I don't appreciate the obscurity around which Alwa's exploration seems to be designed. I immediately turned on the map markers, but they only work for plot items that are required for progress, nothing else. For some reason, breakable walls, secret nooks, water, and all kinds of optional treasures don't get shown on your map. So, I get a new ability that makes the world my oyster... but I'll be a monkey's uncle if I remember where everything is by that moment! Who do you think I am, game? Crazy... memory... man?.. See!? I can't even make a simple pop-culture reference - I completely forgot each and every character that had incredible memory as their distinctive feature.Due to my memory being trash as a result of numerous concussions and all kinds of intoxications in the past, exploration would've been utter hell for me if not for the 100% Map by Demajen (find it in the guides on Steam). I didn't use it on a whim, it was a necessity. I feel like with all that vagueness, the devs tried to achieve the very first Zelda's sense of wonder, the joy of discovery, or something.Commendable, but desperately outdated. What was an amusing revelation for a lone player once is only a few clicks away these days. Leave the past alone, don't cripple your game's design. Personally, I don't want for modern CRPGs to borrow too much from early Ultima games, no way! See what you can do with all the modern features, learn from The Messenger.The progression system is simple and elegant - you collect orbs and invest them into your three spells. You also get special abilities and a couple of staff upgrades as you go. I don't think it needs further explanation. I have some questions though! Some of the spell upgrades don't make much sense. For example, "drop through a bubble to change your color"? What? "Combine a block and a bubble to create a green bubble"? Eh?You want to know why? To drop through a green bubble and talk to an NPC for a crappy reward. So, you dedicated two upgrades to making a Zelda reference, I see. Lastly, crouching is used so sparingly that it may have been cut out from the game completely. If you don't have a good use for a feature - don't have it.Unlike the overworld, the dungeons are the highlight of the game. This is where my soul found its rest in between the "torturous" exploration. Very reminiscent of Zelda, they aren't too big and offer a great deal of gimmicky puzzle-solving fun. The dungeons have it all! Water puzzles, gravity puzzles, button puzzles, fat puzzles, smelly puzzles, bloody puzzles, come on in puzzle lovers... wait, wrong medium.Naturally, a few puzzles involve busywork, but most of them reward quickness and wit, as they should. And all the bosses at the end of each dungeon are incredibly easy but satisfying. The aforementioned sequence-breaking could also be of use here, but I haven't found a way to do the dungeons out of order, sadly. Yet what matters the most, beating the dungeons and the bosses felt real good, I was enjoying myself.I wanted to praise the game for its mild difficulty curve... but then, near the end, it introduced a ludicrous amount of instadeath spikes, as if trying to compensate for their absence before that moment. I don't consider it the best way to ramp up the difficulty, frankly speaking. The number of instadeath I re-lived during the final hours was quite staggering.I think I know what they went for: the last dungeon should've been the place where everything comes together, where you perfect all the things you've learned along the way, etc. But it ended up feeling like a separate game to me. They definitely messed up the curve I was about to compliment... and you know what? I still will. The spike isn't that detrimental to the experience, the game stays very forgiving. It wasn't a bad 'separate game' is what I'm saying.The more I thought of the game while not playing it, the more disappointed I got. But wondrously enough, when I actually launched it, most of my beefs somehow seized to matter. If this review seems overly critical to you, it's because I made notes when something took me out of the game, but I completely forgot writing them when I was selflessly enjoying myself, which, in fact, constituted the bulk of my time spent in Alwa. Considering the discounts they give, it's a bang for your buck.Yes, all the negative stuff I mentioned above exists. And the good stuff is too basic to write about. But despite some weak spots and occasional inconveniences, it's an extremely warm, comfortable game, a chill time-waster. Connoisseurs of the genre wouldn't even flinch while reading about the flaws I mentioned. They were there from the days of yore, people are used to that stuff. After a year or so, I probably wouldn't remember the game at all, but if someone reminds me of it, I wouldn't spit and make faces, I'd recall the good times.My curator

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? As long as you enjoy jumping and exploring, yes. Defeat an evil sorcerer in a world full of enemies, a few bosses, some secrets and with many platforms. One of the better Metroidvanias, you find a rather big world to explore and it is up to you which direction you take. Genre-typical, all rooms are reset when you re-enter them. One of the first things you receive is a map that helps you navigate the levels. Your magic abilities are quite limited at first, but you soon learn new spells, like summoning stone blocks or bubbles that allow you to reach higher platforms.The game continues the story of Alwa's Awakening. You awake at a portal, not knowing where you are or how to get home in a land where evil creatures roam around freely. Just the town seems to be still free of enemies. Your nemesis from the first game tries to kill you, but just manages to make you loose your weapon which falls into the first dungeon. Reclaim your magic staff and begin to explore the land to finally show him who is the stronger sorcerer! You will soon meet a few inhabitants that might help you, like a smithy or a crazy wizard.I got stuck rather early on in the game when I had to push a switch under a floor panel in a tiny alcove. You can duck, but not crawl. You can summon a stone block, but not push it (far). I really despaired, until I was told that I just had to allow an enemy to push my stone block which then would trigger the floor plate switch. At that time I also discovered that you can cast a stone block high in the air and jump against it. Not sure if this is a legit way to reach higher platforms, but it made exploring a bit easier.Saving can be done at bowls spread thoughout the country, and if you use one of the rare tears you can also upgrade the dish to a teleportation point to traverse the country faster. When you die after loosing your 3 health points, you respawn at the last save point and your death count rises by one. Don't ask me how high mine already is.Gamepad support is fine, the chiptune soundtrack fits perfectly and the gameplay is cool, as long as you like the retro design.Great Metroidvania in 16-bit look. Lots of things to explore, lots of jumps to be made, lots of creeps to kill (again and again).

_childDocuments_.review: I thought Alwa's Awakening was just okay.  It was a decent enough game with some good ideas that was hindered by some clunky execution.  It was the type of game where I came away thinking it was close to being quite good but didn't make its way there.  I was looking forward to seeing the devs take a second crack at it and I have to say Alwa's Legacy feels much more polished and is legit good.In a lot of ways, Legacy is more of the same but better.  You get access to your primary skills much earlier, which means you have a lot freedom in how you want to progress.  There's clear sequence break opportunities that rely on the player understanding how to best make use of the player's primary actions and allows you tackle areas and collect upgrades in a free-form manner.  I had a lot of fun filling out a huge chunk of the map before completing my first dungeon. Warping is also much better integrated here than in Awakening, where it felt there the warp points were placed in a manner that made them feel not as useful as they should.  In Legacy, there's a mechanic that allows you make save points warpable by using a finite item.  There's a decent bit of the finite item spread throughout the game but they're scattered around enough to require some light resource management of the player's behalf, making you give a bit of thought on when to make a permanent warp point.Dungeons are a bit of a mixed bag.  They're fine, but are a bit gimmicky on the whole.  It is cool that the dungeons were designed in such a way that you can play through them with very disparate traversal abilities depending on when you do them. Bosses are okay, nothing great nor irritating.  Overall game difficulty is probably a bit on the easy side.  Outside of the beginning of the game, there's not much talking and I'm thankful for that.  I've read enough witty video-game writing to last me a while and it was nice that once the intro bits (which featured more talking than I cared for) wrapped up, you're basically playing the game uninterrupted with the occasional short npc dialogue.  Previous story knowledge is not particularly necessary.In short, did you like Alwa's Awakening?  If so, buy this.  Did you think AA was okay but could be better?  Alwa's Legacy is basically that.  Do you like metroidvania's that have a real sense of freedom to them instead of having the metrodvania elements feeling tacked on?  Alwa's Legacy gives you legit exploration.  It's good and I recommend it.
