_childDocuments_.review: Happy Game is a disturbingly unique title that embodies the usual Amanita Design visual style and perfectly mixes it together with some really horrific designs. All of the puzzles are intriguing and it's great that you can choose to go back to each of them from the level selected at any time. All that being said, Happy Game is brought down slightly by its short length and little replayability. Not to mention many of the puzzles simply lack complexity and I think the game would have benefited from some more complex puzzle designs. Overall, Happy Game is an adventure that I definitely think any fans of the horror genre should experience once. Just don't expect Happy Game to stick around too long and take your time with it so you can get everything out of its well-crafted world & designs.Link to Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review: While not a "bad" game Happy Game definitely isn't an experience I would recommend.While the game has some great visual ideas it fails to deliver in almost every way.The game mostly consists of finding what to interact with and moving to the right while watching stuff happen.The "puzzle" are either very simple or straight up bad.For example : the rabbit puzzle forces you to fail it once or twice to understand what you're supposed to do. Forcing the player through a failstate removes all the tension of the scene and just makes the puzzles a chore.However, the first "level" is pretty cool and interesting, it's a shame that the rest of the game cannot reach this level of quality.The game also LOVES to take control away from the player and remove all kind of interaction while you just watch things happen, almost half of the game is just you watching scripted events while you cannot do anything. There's almost no use of the medium past the first level and it's a damn shame.The sound design is simply annoying, the main character is making weird noises all the time and it quickly became very very irritating.Now, what about the horror elements?Well, the first 15 minutes are pretty cool.But after that the game gets pretty repetitive, you'll see the same creepy/smiley faces all the time and the creepiness of these visuals quickly wears off.The game never tries to surprise the player by breaking its rules or showing some different stuff. What you see in the trailer is almost 100% of the game, no joke.A lot of people seem to complain about the fact that the game is ~1hour long, I personally don't care as long as the experience is interesting and fullfiling but it clearly isn't the case here.The gameplay elements are so underwhelming that it could easily have been a cool short animation movie, not a video game.Maybe get it on sale if you want to try for yourself but don't expect too mucH.

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow manages to be simultaneously exactly what you expected based on the trailer and still utterly surreal. You are purchasing an interactive art experience more than a game. The puzzles are quite simple and it's really more about experiencing the grim Happy visuals and sounds for two hours or so.  If the trailer appeals to you, the game will. If not, it won't.Will also note the game lacks proper superultrawide (32:9) support. Note this isn't being picky or demanding because of exactly how it lacks it. The game supports ultrawide (22:9) by adding black letterboxes to either side of the screen but those letterboxes only extend to ultrawide widths. Past that, the game renders elements you shouldn't be able to see "off screen", including stuff that should never render at all because it'd never be in-camera. It's like watching a theater performance with the backstage visible past the curtains but worse, because you see rendered game, then black bars, then MORE rendered game with occasional missing elements/artifacts. Game has no graphics settings so can't play not-fullscreen, can't adjust resolution to fit.Easiest fix would be to extend the letterboxes further left/right so they cover up any width of monitor.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun little gem! This isn't an expensive game anyway, but if you're buying this in a sale for under €4 as right now, it's a steal. You don't get a lot of hours out of it - it took me about 5 hours to finish and get all achievements - but its clever art style and sound design totally make up for this. In that respect, it's similar to other Amanita Design games, which I have a soft spot for anyway.The puzzles had me scratching my head occasionally, but nothing was too hard to crack - like true nightmares, they often defy logic and boil down to trial & error, but this goes hand in hand with the game's premise. The gruesome or scary bits are nothing to freak out over, I could happily laugh about them, but they are well implemented and simply fun.TL;DR: I had tons of fun with this title, and to me, that's what matters.

_childDocuments_.review: Happy Game is not a happy game. The goal of the game is to keep the child happy in the midst of having nightmares spurned on by a demon smiley face. To do this, you are confronted with atmospheric horror, visually stunning puzzles and challenges that, while not terribly difficult to figure out, are still pleasing and rewarding to complete nonetheless.  If you're an achievement hunter don't worry, you're able to load individual levels in the event you happen to miss one. There are no jump scares, so if you're the type of person who prefers games with thriller elements like that, or looking for a game that's kind of atmospheric thriller-esque, this would not be it. Having said that, the twisted simple atmospheric visual horror that uses elements we all readily recognize from childhood somehow comes out as more disturbing and, if you have a morbid sense of humor, then *way more fun and rewarding* than other games which work harder to *actually* scare you.  If you catch this game on a discount, def give it a chance, it's absolutely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: As soon as I opened the game, I was greeted with a wonderful melancholic melody that captured me and drew me in like a warm sweater on a cold, rainy day. I instantly bought the ost, and I highly recommend if you like synthy, melodic type music. Hats off to Czech alternative band DVA for making an absolute banger of a soundtrack. Happy Game is a simple 2D point and click sidescroller with a story that is anything but simple. Grab, pull, twist and spin terrifying nightmarish objects, from decapitated bunnies to corrupt smiley faces as you venture through a child's living nightmare. All he wants is his comfort toys, question is, does he ever get them back?

The main objective is obtaining objects such as toys and a pet dog to make this kid happy again. There isn't a real punishment if you do fail on something; no bad endings. _childDocuments_.review: It's a game of remarkable set pieces nestled within irritatingly stop-start rhythms. It does not feel cohesive in the way that, say, Machinarium does, but the visuals and audio are both really ambitious and sometimes transfixing. Plus, it's just interesting to see Amanita's vibrant animism turned on its head so everything is buzzing with malevolent energy like in a Thomas Ligotti story! _childDocuments_.review: I have liked every Amanita Design game that I've played (and most of them I  like), but Happy Game was kind of a chore for me to get through. If you haven't played any of the other games by the studio I would highly recommend them in general, but would recommend trying one of their others first before this one. If you've already played and enjoyed their other games then I think this one might be worth considering, but I personally didn't enjoy it much.Most of the puzzles consist of first figuring out what interactions are possible and then figuring out how exactly to use those interactions to solve some obstacle. The second part of that, the puzzles themselves, are adequate, but not great. The first part of that, however, did not appeal to me and was more often a source of frustration rather than satisfaction. It often wasn't obvious what could be interacted with, but at least there weren't ever many choices. It also wasn't obvious, however, whether a click or a click and drag or something else was having a good or bad or any effect. I have played and enjoyed many games with this kind of gameplay (notably many by Amanita Design themselves) and so I'm not sure what it was about Happy Game that felt so off to me. Maybe I wasn't enjoying the actual story experience and that predisposed me towards being less patient than I normally would be? Whatever the reason, even though I usually like this kind of puzzle design it wasn't really working for me in this particular game. I often found myself thinking things like: "Was I supposed to have to do that so many times, or was I just not doing it correctly before? Is there a difference between clicking and dragging? Is anything different happening? Is that animation that just played supposed to indicate positive or negative reinforcement?"Finally, the art and story and presentation: It felt to me like it was just trying way too hard to be edgy or disturbing, but it didn't work for me. I was aware going in that Happy Game would not, in fact, be a happy game, and there are many games (and movies, books, etc.) that I love that could be described as "dark", but this game just didn't work for me. I am sad to give a negative review to a studio whose art I otherwise think is amazing, and it seems like my opinion may be in the minority based on the current Steam rating of "Very Positive", but the vibe of this game, for me, felt like something an angsty middle schooler might make, trying to think of how shocking they could make things that were usually happy like smiley faces and bunnies. I didn't feel any of the heavy emotions or dread or unease that I usually associate with something going for this vibe; instead I more often found myself rolling my eyes and wondering why the game was trying so hard to be edgy or disturbing simply for the sake of being edgy and disturbing. For how over-the-top the game was I think they maybe could have added a bit more humor to just fully embrace it (there were a few places that did this and so maybe that was the intent throughout and I just didn't pick up on it). The screenshots on the Steam store page give a reasonable idea of what the game is like art-wise, so I guess you can judge for yourself whether it appeals to you or not.

_childDocuments_.review: Happy Game is NOT a happy game... it is a wonderfully weird game of pure madness and nightmare fuel! Fair warning when I say weird, I mean it, this is one bizarre game and I have played some weird games. That being said however, I feel that this game should not be overlooked. Happy Game has little story apart from a little boy trapped in nightmares trying to navigate his way through them in the most simplistic manner possible, i.e. getting to his ball, his stuffed bunny and his dog. In his way stands some of the strangest twisted creations that evoke feelings of Jhonen Vasquez, Salvador Dali, and almost Chronenburg-esque creatures and landscapes. The game is very simplistic (but not in a bad way) with an easy point and click UI, and the puzzles being well thought out.Final thoughts, Happy Game is a wonderfully disturbing puzzle game that is probably unlike a lot of other games you have played. The gameplay and puzzles are on par with most other games of this style; however, the true draw of this title is the over the top almost hallucinatory visuals and disturbing imagery. I would highly recommend to any horror fan, or any fan of surrealistic or horror artwork. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Length <1hr 30minHappy Game feels like the perfect psychedelic nightmare of pure happiness, a 2D point and click puzzle game which sees the player dive into a dream world made up of warped images of happiness.The visuals of Happy Game and the animations really make the game stand out, levels look different from each other while monsters have this perfect mix of happiness and monstrousness. Everything feels alive in the game, with small animations for almost everything when the player interacts with them. While a lot of really creative scenes which allow for iconic and memorable puzzles, as well as some really creepy visuals.While the puzzles do possess similarities it is the visuals which make the puzzles all feel different. Puzzles are basically: interact with an item and place it in the correct location, set up a level to prepare for an event (usually run away from a large monster), or interact with the screen in correct order. While the basics are the same, the visuals make the puzzles feel different with one moment you are organising all of the toy parts, and the next moment you're trying to rip the heart out of a monster. Succeeding a puzzle always feels rewarding, with a horrific end or a great stand out moment of progressing.Happy Game is really worth the play, the puzzles at times may seem a bit obtuse, just keep an eye on the screen and what changes when you interact with an item. _childDocuments_.review: From someone who grew up on Amanita Design games, this is just as great as all of them, if not better. I feel like there are two different types of Amanita Design games. There are the ones like Machinarium or Samorost, and ones like Botanicula, Chuchell, or Happy Game. The ones like Happy Games, almost always have their sound design done by DVA, a czech, ex-couple band, who make sure that the sound design is always extraordinary. (Fun-fact, I actually know them personally through my father.) The sound effects are very similar to Botanicula. There are so many easter-eggs to Botanicula, and other Aminata Design games, that it almost seems like they're set in the same world...? But really. If you want to really get your mind blown, you should watch the music video of DVA's song 'Mulatu'. It is the exact same concept as this game, and I couldn't believe the sheer amount of conspiracy-theory-material. Game Theory should really make a video about the whole story of these game. Anyways, 10/10 game, amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game. The first thing I immediately noticed was the great art style. The game's style is one of the best I have seen. It's creepy and intimidating. They make scenes with bright colors and a positive atmosphere feel terrifying. The game doesn't use major jump scares to scare you, it actually makes you feel nervous with the creatures in the game. The second thing I liked was the soundtrack. The music matches the environment and adds another level of immersion. I must add that while listening to the music, . Some people might not think that's a big deal, but I never get goosebumps from anything auditory. The third thing I enjoyed was the actual gameplay. The game doesn't have anything too groundbreaking, mainly just clicking and dragging to interact with stuff, but it's full of puzzles that require some brainpower to solve. Some of them I thought were very clever. My only complaint would be that I wish there was more content in the game.Overall,  is a good game. The style and soundtrack combine with the gameplay to produce a great final product.

_childDocuments_.review: This game really is amazing.  The horror aspect of it is really well done.  It's one of the few games that influences the players emotions intensely, in my opinion.  It captures dread, disturbance, and isolation really well, among others.  The art is also beautiful and the style is consistent, which is really hard to do, so kudos!  Another part I enjoyed was the relatability of it, even for someone who doesn't experience such vivid nightmares.  I'm sure most people have or have had dogs, and I can say that the third nightmare definitely hit me in my heart.  The same goes for the toys as well.  Most people have some kind of childhood toy.  I'm not sure if it was intentional or not, but it made it a lot easier to relay a sense of unease to the player.  This was all just a really long way of saying I love this game, though.  Really good job!
_childDocuments_.name: Happy Game

_childDocuments_.review: Amanita Design continues to impress, just an year after the ambitious Creaks, with this smaller but nonetheless enthralling short experience. Unlike their previous games, this is the developer going into uncharted territory which is surreal psychological horror much like Fran Bow or Coraline. They once again show why they're the masters of pointing and clicking. Each interaction with an object is coupled with bespoke, memorable animations that can range from being cute and silly to the nightmarish and brutal. There is a playfulness to their games and just the action-reaction loop can be satisfying in of itself that you can't just get from simply watching an animated film. There are plenty of horrifying and surprising twists to the narrative that I won't spoil but these are a couple of hours you won't forget.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful experience, and a true piece of art, but falls a little short in game-play. It's a great experience don't get me wrong, and the soundtrack is really catchy; Happy Rabbits in particular was an instant add to my work playlist, and hearing it for the first time made solving the puzzles a pretty entertaining time. Like I mentioned prior, the game-play runs quick, and the puzzles are pretty good. The game itself takes less than two hours to beat, and could even be 100%'d in under that time if I had to guess (There aren't  many achievements). The puzzles as well were only mildly challenging, though not at all dull. The main mechanic of using your cursor to pull on objects was done quite well, so there's never a boring moment. I also wouldn't say that the game is too much of a "horror" title. While the imagery is absolutely psychedelic, and certainly disturbing, I hadn't personally been spooked much during my play-though. If you're a stickler for replayability (or sensitive to flashing imagery), you'd be best off just watching a YT video of the game as there's no end-game content as far as I can tell. Overall, I'd recommend the game to anyone looking to experience a sweet, albeit bizarre, adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game by Amanita Design. The game's strong point is its puzzles which were very unique and for the most part enjoyable to complete. The game's art style was also pretty interesting and while it might not be everyone's thing I personally found it enjoyable although I wish it was more scary than cute. My main complaint with the game is its story. There are no words so the entire story is conveyed through sparsely placed backflashes and whatever is happening on the screen which would be fine if it was done well, but its honestly not. This lack of story presence made going through the game feel very lackluster and just being interested in what kind of crazy thing would happen next carried me though rather than any kind of story element. After finishing the game I just kind of found myself asking "So, what was the point?" and "What did it all mean?". Even if you piece together the bits of story there are still just so many parts about the ending that do not make any sense whatsoever that the ending just feels very dissatisfying and confusing. The game is also very short (around 2 hours) but you can tell a lot of work and care from the devs went into it so its up to you to decide if the price is worth it. If you enjoy puzzle games and creepy things you will enjoy this game but if you are looking for something that still has puzzles but a much greater story element I would say play through Amanita Design's "Samorost" games (Samorost 3 in particular) instead. Overall "Happy Game" is a decent game but due to the lack of story and any kind of explanation the ending is very dissatisfying and not very impactful, and for that reason I cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: A short game, less than 2 hours long, but intense. Quite an experience, a unique one; certainly a nightmare that you wouldn't like to have. The puzzles are entertaining and very ingenious, but the way to solve most of them is the same idea, therefore they become easy to solve. The art and music is just amazing, which is clearly what stands out about this game, which was stated early on when the Teaser Trailer came out. The art is astonashing, in its unique way and style; every character, monster, scene is wonderfully designed. The game is dynamic, constantly the environments and monsters change, they are not what they appear, they change drastically, so you wonder what will be next, what horrors you will have to face. You are amazed by these while having at the same time a scared face. And the music, just a few tracks, but beautiful (ironically some tracks are). Good work from DVA there. (SPOILER) I wanted to catch the ball and the puppy as much as the boy wanted, so that I could hear that beautiful, hypnotic and somehow optimistic melody. But the melody is always interrupted by the nightmare that is hidden behind that cruel ilusion, and at the same time it is the innocent desire of the child to reach what he wants. You constantly go from an apparently idyllic, calm world - a Happy Game - to the terrifying, impetuous and psychedelic reality of the nightmare, with touches of humor that is sometimes cruel and absurd. Great game, wonderfully done. Again, a unique experience. A terrible nightmare. Great work from Amanita Design :)

name: The Unfinished Swan
detailed_description: From the creators of What Remains of Edith Finch. Explore a mysterious all-white landscape by splatting paint to reveal the world around you in The Unfinished Swan. As Monroe, a 10-year-old orphan, you'll follow a swan that's stepped out of an unfinished painting and wandered off into a surreal, storybook-inspired kingdom. Each chapter brings surprises, new ways to explore the world, a host of bizarre (and sometimes dangerous) creatures, and encounters with the eccentric king who built this empire.
about_the_game: From the creators of What Remains of Edith Finch. Explore a mysterious all-white landscape by splatting paint to reveal the world around you in The Unfinished Swan. As Monroe, a 10-year-old orphan, you'll follow a swan that's stepped out of an unfinished painting and wandered off into a surreal, storybook-inspired kingdom. Each chapter brings surprises, new ways to explore the world, a host of bizarre (and sometimes dangerous) creatures, and encounters with the eccentric king who built this empire.
short_description: From the creators of What Remains of Edith Finch. Enter the surreal world of The Unfinished Swan and explore a mysterious, hidden kingdom by splatting paint to reveal the world around you.

_childDocuments_.review: I jumped at this title when I heard it was by Giant Sparrow. Edith Finch was a brilliant game and I was eager to see what else this team had accomplished.Initially, I did not know what to make of Unfinished Swan. You start in a white world and start shooting random splotches of black ink. I was not impressed.  Then, I realized that an environment was beginning to take shape around me. A bench, a path, a dock, a fish jumping, a garden, a doorway.  Soon, I was hooked.Unfinished Swan is a journey through a storybook with a king, a castle, a dark forest, etc. While each chapter has it's own feel, all require you to modify the environment as you go. This may be accomplished by shooting paint balls to reveal details, building blocks to create a path, growing vines to bridge gaps, etc. As you move through the chapters, there are balloons to 'liberate' and story pages to uncover. There is no inventory and the puzzle element is figuring out how to navigate through one environment to the next.The art is unique and different chapters have different styles. The sound track is fairly minimal and I played with my headphones off for most of the game. The exception to this is the narrator who does a wonderful job of reading the story, as it unfolds.I truly enjoyed this game. It had some challenges in terms of jumping and finding balloons in difficult locations (balloon gathering is optional). Overall, it is just a really interesting game to explore. It feels like a child's fairy tale but has layers of complexity.If you are a thoughtful gamer who wants to experience something different and intriguing, I highly recommend The Unfinished Swan. It is absolutely nothing like Edith Finch but it is a very well done game that stands on its own.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Unfinished Swan shows a desperate finding for something that remains unfinished. _childDocuments_.review: I would just barely recommend this game. I had hoped this game would deliver some of the magical realism of What Remains of Edith Finch, which I consider to be one of the best games I've ever played. But where Edith Finch wins out is in the narrative and the characters: there's a richness and darkness there that captivates you, even when the gameplay is repetitive or simple. It feels like you're building and living the story as it happens.Not so in The Unfinished Swan. Although you are building the world (quite literally) through a series of artistic decisions (paintballs, platforms, vines), the magic exists only in the gameplay, not in the story. Yes, there's a little storybook tale about unfinished paintings and magic kingdoms, and maybe it's all meant to be a metaphor about the unfinished stories and art we leave behind on this earth, but it never really came together for me. It felt, dare I say, unfinished? (I'm positive I'm not the only person to make that joke, but let me have this one.)However, the environments were interesting and varied, and it was a delight to reveal and shape them with paint splatters and other artistic techniques at your disposal. The mechanism for creating/revealing/illuminating the world changed from section to section, which helped keep things fresh and created a minor puzzle-solving element that was interesting enough.The downsides, however, were that: It could be I'm the wrong audience, but I think this came could have benefited from being longer with a better storyline, or shorter, left to a proof of concept. I was enthralled at the beginning, but it quickly lost its luster for me. Still, I respect what the game was trying to do, and it did some of those things well. Get it on super sale, and keep your expectations low: it's a light, charming, somewhat repetitive puzzle platformer with a decent gameplay mechanism. That's all.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a beautiful and creative game that implements an unique spin on the "throw paint" puzzle game genre.  The levels are well designed with new mechanics introduced in each chapter and hidden collectibles (balloons) throughout. These balloons can be used to unlock toys which can help you find collectibles and give you an upgraded ability.  The game can be finished between 2-3 hours and features a relaxing soundtrack. _childDocuments_.review: I was delighted to see this lovely little game get a release on Steam, it's one of my very favourite PS3 games.This is a short (~2 hour) long light platforming adventure game. Not quite a walking simulator, fairly close to the vein of the developer Giant Sparrows' other game What Remains of Edith Finch, though shorter. It takes obvious visual inspiration from the Little Prince. Many people know this as the "paint splat" game -- and yes, the first mechanic in the game is that the world is completely blank and you map it out by firing blobs of paint that splash, revealing surfaces -- but actually the game is much more than that. Each section of the game offers new mechanics, and at only 2 hours it's not going to overstay its welcome.The story is a sweet meditation on, frankly, pretty relatable things: an absent parent, a feeling of inheriting the family shame, a sense of "great men" who keep trying to start things and never finish them.One special note: there's an achievement for doing what amounts to playing the first segment of the game blindfolded. I sincerely recommend spending some time thinking through the right way to do this and trying to do it. It's a very fun exercise that few other games can deliver, enabled by the unique mechanic I mentioned above.If you're looking for challenging puzzles or a lengthy game, don't bother, but if this is the sort of genre you like, I think this is an excellent example. It's also quite family friendly!

_childDocuments_.review: Let me just start by saying that I adore What Remains of Edith Finch. It is one of my favorite games of all time because of how it blended gameplay and storytelling so seamlessly. So, when I found out the developers behind Edith Finch had a previous game I knew nothing about come to steam, I bought it within minutes of finding out. I LOVE the concept of this game. Painting your surrounding to reveal what comes ahead and using the paint to solve puzzles is a really novel concept. The storytelling is more story-like than Edith Finch; both literally and metaphorically, which is either a good or bad thing depending on your preference. Sadly, I wasn't able to finish the game. I played it for about an hour before I realized I had a pretty bad headache and was feeling quite nauseous. I realized that I became motion sick from playing the game. After quickly looking it up online, I found out I wasn't the only one who got motion sick playing this game. This isn't a negative review but I want to be honest and say I can't recommend this game (as of writing this review) because of the fact that I got motion sick playing. I honestly don't know what did it, because my favorite genre is the FPS. I wasn't originally going to post this review, but after seeing other people online say the game gave them motion sickness, and seeing how one of the other reviews on here said the game made them dizzy after 20 minutes of playing, I decided to post this review. TL;DR: It's a good game that is super creative, but I got motion sick playing it. Go try it out for yourself before writing this game off after reading this review.EDIT: I slept on it and finished the second half of the game. I loved the second half and it was super creative in how it handled its mechanics. I am still going to leave this review as "not recommended." I wouldn't say the motion sickness killed the experience for me, but it did slightly negatively affect it. As for what may have caused the motion sickness, I asked a friend  and he said that "if the brain doesn't have reference points it dies" on discord, which I guess makes sense. Again go play the game because it is really that good and hopefully you won't have the same problem that I did play it!EDIT 2: I am awarding this game for the Steam Awards for Best Narrative. _childDocuments_.review: Aspiring developers of walking simulators need to take note of . Its first and most memorable mechanic is throwing paint around to reveal an otherwise pure white world, and it does what many in that genre fail to do despite the name: it makes walking engaging. To be clear,  is not itself a walking simulator. It just aims for many of the same goals. There are puzzles, but they’re all fairly easy, so the emphasis is on the environment and the experience. It was a wise choice, because the environment is a joy to explore and the experience is terrific. The narrative is that of a charming and mildly poignant children’s storybook – it won’t set the world on fire, but it opens the door for a variety of inventive mechanics, from directing the growth of climbable vines to constructing life-size blueprints. The only significant fault I have is the standard one for short, artsy indie games: missed potential. Particularly, having established that its mechanics can be used for puzzles, it’s disappointing that the game only does so a few times for each. Still, what’s present is more important than what’s not, and what’s present is a lovely, memorable journey.

Mouse support, on the other hand, is iffy in the menu system.Basic game  mechanic of finding your way with splats of paint is cute, but gets lost in later levels with what feels like grafted-on concepts to get the industry-standard four-hour minimum. Also, some of that later game play calls for quick reactions and moves that the early play doesn't need. _childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a first-person exploration and traversal game developed by Giant Sparrow, the same developer that created What Remains of Edith Finch. The Unfinished Swan is not new, having released in 2012 on PlayStation 3 and then on PC in 2020, but I only now got around to playing it.You play as Monroe, a newly orphaned boy, inheriting from his mother a single painting depicting an unfinished swan. One night the swan leaps out of the painting. Monroe follows it, embarking on a magical journey through a surreal, dream-like world.The Unfinished Swan ‘s world is initially wholly white. However, Monroe can hurl paint drops onto it, revealing details like walls and furniture. The game’s world is a blank canvas that only solidifies when painted. For example, what was formless white is suddenly a black frog that leaps into a nearby pond.As the game progresses, it introduces new mechanics, such as the physics-defying, AntiChamber-like puzzles; buttons and levers to activate ladders and bridges; or hurling water to encourage the growth of climbable vines. You can also find hidden balloons that unlock upgrades and additional material.The game slowly reveals a fairytale-like story through narration, about or from the world’s prodigious but eccentric king, and storyboards, complete with child-friendly line art. The music is also ethereal, consisting of glockenspiels and light strings, reminiscent of Tchaikovsky’s Dance of the Sugar Plum Fairy.Thematically, The Unfinished Swan views grief and impermanence through a child’s imagination. The normally mischievous act of splattering paint allows Monroe to find certainty, meaning and agency where there is none. The shared act of painting links Monroe with his mother. Metaphors have power.The Unfinished Swan is also moving because, by seeing the world through Monroe’s eyes, we can experience things both superficially, as he does, and with an adult’s experience and context. Implication and inference also have power.Despite its age, The Unfinished Swan still holds its own as novel and thought-provoking. It is short, taking under four hours to complete, and wraps up its story positively but with restraint. Those looking for something contemplative and unusual will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This was made in 2012, and at the time was probably pretty groundbreaking. I think we've come a long way in narrative-driven games since then. In fact, this very studio has created works that far surpass Unfinished Swan.Gameplay wise there are things to like and the opening section has real impact, but the mechanics and controls soon become clunky. A feature introduced in the late game is pretty cool, but again the implementation quickly gets stale. There's also a critical flaw in the way the collectible subquest works: it requires very careful replaying, but the game is not fun to replay. In fact, I'm annoyed because the frequent use of 'no return' design specifically means I couldn't go back to explore the few areas that I think I missed. The chapter system doesn't really alleviate this.Story-wise... it doesn't quite land. Hard to explain why. Although there is a part where it becomes unexpectedly threatening, which was effective, and it has an undeniably brilliant voice actor right at the end. But fundamentally it feels overwritten and too aware of itself, with a conclusion that wants to be poignant but can't decide how to go about achieving it. It reads a lot like an American trying to emulate Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, and... not succeeding.Look, I don't  playing this game, exactly. It was fine. It might be worth grabbing if you're curious - in the same way you might, for sake of an actor or director, watch an old film that hasn't aged very well. But eight years after release, I can't really recommend the average person picking it up. Go buy Edith Finch instead.

_childDocuments_.review: the unfinished swan is a first person story focused indie game from 2012 with a very neat aesthetic and clever remixes of mechanics from other games that were popular at the time in much more lo-fi settings without resorting to the common violent verbs of most games. it is kind of a struggle to say much more then that at the time i'm writing this because this is a 2020 port of a game from 2012 being played in 2022 and......it's good. it's a good game! but it's not a game that you will lay awake and think about for hours at a time, replaying events and reliving the emotions you were feelings and thinking about how the design of those moments work. the unfinished swan is strongest in it's first two acts, aside from the comically rapid pace that it delivers the 2012 Indie Game Trauma to you before shoving it aside (seriously i hit new game and within 10 seconds im an orphan with a dead mom) for the rest of the narrative. and the narrative is fine! the game is fine! but it's rarely more then that. i really enjoyed the 2nd act with the power to cover a city in ivy and the way it made me think about the spaces i was navigating, but after that it never reaches that high again. however, i want to restate that the game is still good! it's like the indie game version of a subway sandwich. i don't know. i liked it! though it should be mentioned that the pc port's controls and the way the camera works never felt quite right on mouse and keyboard, and while they do give you settings to dial it in to your comfort, it never feels responsive enough. other then that, the game is fine! it's fine. as far as a studio's first game goes, you can do a hell of a lot worse! it's fine! it's good! it's fine. it's. fine.

The latter was unfortunately my case. ______________________________________________________________Let me start off by saying that I don’t think this is a bad game. _childDocuments_.review: What a delightful experience.The Unfinished Swan is a first person, puzzle-walking simulator hybrid, where objects only take shape after you splash them with a glob of black paint. The ink only provides a rudimentary outline for the game world, and it is up to the player to navigate their way through this weird monochromatic world. This however is just the first chapter and subsequent ones switch up things quite a bit. They have their moments, but none are as interesting as the first thirty minutes of this game.Because the game is so very short - two, maybe three hours long - no one stage lasts long enough to wear out its conceptual welcome. As soon as a puzzle concept becomes tedious, Swan switches things up, sometimes really dramatically.Worth picking up. Too bad its brilliant concept wasn't pushed further.

_childDocuments_.review: Elegantly surreal minimalist game with an equally nice flowing fable-like storyline and a fairy tale ending. Definitely recommended for someone who wants a game that thinks a little bit "outside the box" without leaving you in the middle of a trail of stupidly hard unsolvable puzzles.The game starts with this bleached out white screen/canvas and a small circle cursor. It took me a while to realise I could "paintball" the canvas and reveal the surrounding scenery. I found by paintballing minimally just enough scenery was just enough to see where I was going. However, that meant there were "gaps" between paintballed scenic detail, and bleached out white canvas and, therefore, attempting to moving between the two areas initially made me feel like I was going to fall through the "gaps," which was mildly nauseating - but not to the extent that it made the game devastatingly unplayable.You could go full bore and just paintball every bleached out white bit but that would have the opposite effect of just creating a dark abyss with an equal lack of detail. So you reconcile the way to make progress in this game is to paintball just enough to gain a contrast between the white and the black.Then, in the detail, all this stuff like abandoned carts, boxes, statues, gates, and the like starts appearing. But next you are left with the expectation that you are supposed to interact with these elements and achieve something with it - not in this game. In this game, these elements are merely "3D paintings" and you really are just groping around looking for an unexpected exit to the next level, like corridors, stepping stones and stairs. There are also "clue" golden webbed footprints that indicate the direction the escaped swan may have moved towards. However, because a swan has wings, then some of these footprints appear in inaccessible places, meaning you need to go round a detour in order to trace where the swan may have ventured.Just when you think you have mastered the paintballing in black, then the next chapter starts with a slightly different twist on the paintball feature and scenery interactions. The resultant collection of chapter twists and "paintball" features gives the game a compellingly intricate yet minimalist sense of finesse. Very enjoyable without being disappointingly short.The only issue I had with the game was the auto save feature which only saved at the end of each section. I just wished there were more save points available!9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a captivating blend of art, philosophy, and unique mechanics that creates an experience like no other. The game takes you on a surreal journey through a mysterious, blank world where you, as a young boy named Monroe, must navigate using splashes of paint to reveal your surroundings. This simple yet ingenious mechanic immediately sets the tone, inviting you to explore an evolving landscape that transitions from a puzzle-based adventure to platforming, and even survival elements.One thing to note is that some players have reported experiencing motion sickness while playing, likely due to the game's unique visual style and movement. Personally, I didn’t have any issues, but I usually don’t get motion sick, so keep that in mind if you’re prone to it. The story itself is a bit abstract and might leave you scratching your head, but I think I got the gist of it by the end. Despite the confusion, the narrative has a dreamlike quality that fits well with the game’s aesthetic.The gameplay is straightforward and enjoyable, starting with puzzles that evolve into more complex mechanics, like creating your own platforms in mid-air, surviving dark areas filled with dangers, and even escaping a flood. Each chapter introduces a new twist, keeping the experience fresh and engaging.I managed to complete the game in under four hours, including all the achievements. Most of the achievements are pretty easy to get, like collecting all the balloons and finding the hidden stories, though there’s one called "Minimalist" that I found frustratingly difficult (I literally screamed while doing it cuz it was so frustrating)! But overall, the achievements are accessible and add a little extra challenge for completionists.I initially played The Unfinished Swan because I was curious about its connection/or if there is a connection to What Remains of Edith Finch, another masterpiece by the same developer. The connection isn’t explicitly clear, but it does add an intriguing layer of depth to the experience...or so I think lmao?Overall, The Unfinished Swan is a short, unique, thoughtful game that’s well worth your time, especially if you appreciate games that blur the line between art and gameplay. Despite a few minor frustrations, I highly recommend it for anyone looking for something different and meaningful.

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is Cafe Sparrow's first game. They would later go on to release What Remains of Edith Finch, one of my favorite games of all time, so I was super excited to play this game and see where they started from. The game is good, I don't think there's much denying that, but in my opinion it's nowhere near the masterpiece level that so many people have thrown its way. While the gameplay is unique and it tells a touching story, neither aspect is developed enough to reach the levels of What Remains of Edith Finch, or other similar games. For a first game from a studio with so few people, it's a very unique game worth experiencing.  The game's story takes place like an old story book as you learn that you are a young orphan who's mother has recently passed away. He's only allowed to take one of her paintings with him and he picks her favorite painting, an unfinished swan. He travels into the painting and this is where the game begins. You learn about a king with the power to create things with his magic paintbrush and travel through his kingdom, learning about his life, and how his kingdom came to be. While it certainly had it's moments (especially in the final chapter) it often times just didn't feel like it was moving along in a meaningful way, or offered very much to the game. This isn't necessarily a bad thing as every game doesn't need a super deep and emotional story, and there were certainly themes that were developed throughout the game but I felt like the developers could've pushed deeper into said themes and it would've created a much more thought provoking experience. I only bring this up because due to the massive number of reviews saying the story brought them to tears, or changed their outlook on life as a whole, I was expecting something on the levels of What Remains of Edith Finch, or Before Your Eyes. Instead it's a story that only scratches the surface of what it could have potentially been. As you travel through the king's kingdom you must solve puzzles by affecting the environment around you. Each chapter has a different unique mechanic. These help to keep the gameplay varied but unfortunately  everything moves so slowly. Your walking pace is pretty slow and there's no sprint option. The worst offender of the slowness are the puzzles dealing with the vines. These vines must be splashed with water in order to grow them so you can reach new areas. Often times the area you need to reach will be quite far away and you'll have to spend a few minutes just sitting there throwing water at these vines in order to get them to grow. There's no worse feeling in a game then knowing exactly what needs to be done abut being forced to sit and do nothing. Simply making the areas smaller, or making the vines grow faster would've easily fixed this but ultimately it's not a major issue. The puzzles are never challenging. Many of them require 0 thinking and this isn't a bad thing, just don't come in expecting a challenging game. The Unfinished Swan is much more focused on the story and overall experience than difficult puzzles. Throughout the game there's balloons that are hidden. If you find enough of them you can buy "toys" that give you new abilities more or less such as a rapid fire option, which is MUCH needed since you will be clicking the mouse button to automatically fire every single ball, which you're doing essentially nonstop. This should've been a default feature as within 10 minutes of starting the game my finger was getting sore.  The Unfinished Swan is a game worth experiencing if you're into shorter story focused experiences. It's definitely not a "walking simulator" as it has quite a lot of interactivity with the environment. It never gets crazy in depth with any aspect of  the game, but they're all developed enough to create a pleasant game with a couple memorable moments in it. While $15 may be a bit too much for it, if you can get it on sale and are interested in, it's worth a play through. For more reviews follow my

First some background.I really enjoyed what remains of edith finch and got this game since it was made by the same team, if you expect a similar experience you will be disappointed. I took my time in this game and i still finished it in under 90 minutes, even so some core mechanics of the game managed to become tedious in that short time.This game is a gimmick with a story that relies heavily on a few core mechanics, but, given only this I would still recommend it on sale, now for the real travesties which resulted in my negative overall impression.1. The game does not support 3440x1440 resolution, but only 2560x1080... why? It would be so easy to include this option if you would have gone through the effort of porting it properly. 2. The game sometimes had occasional framedrops, which is not an issue in itself, might be due to my hardware, the real issue is that the mouse sensitivity is in some way bound to the FPS. This means that a lower FPS will increase your sensitivity?? Was this tested at all before you released the port?? _childDocuments_.review: I've also played this on PS3, PS Vita and PS4. It was great to revisit this gem. It has a lot of neat ideas, the overall use of them remains relatively simple. But I don't think it needs to be overly complex with puzzles to be fun. I'd say it's an "artsy" type game, but the gameplay is more traditionally structured than most of what you'd expect from that label. But it's different. The game starts with you in pitch white, with only black paintballs to find your way through (with a sparse gold to give you direction  and unchanging land markers). Then you move to a shaded area where it's easier to navigate, but the black is still required. Then eventually you start to grow vines to climb around and to help see with blue/water balls which temporarily outline the enviornments that offer no visability on their own. And then into the darkness where light is your guide and the surprisingly intuitive and neat 'building' sections.Despite having played through the game multiple times always forget just how much variety is in the experience. They packed a lot of ideas into the game with such simple mechanics. It's quite neat what they accomplished.The art design is awesome, the book illustrates are adorable and the voice acting/narration brings it all together to fit the storybook aesthetic/theme perfectly. It all just works as such a complete package.  The PC version changed up the main menu look which is interesting. Each option is more of a 'picture' in a frame rather than just a list like it was before. And the "toys" (upgrades basically) are shown in the book rather than a list. Not sure why those things were changed, but it's something I noticed looking at a balloon guide (can't seem to remember where they all are despite having done all the trophies three times)If you like different types of games, kind of in the vein of Journey, Flower, Abzu, and the like then you owe it to yourself to play this. It's right up there in quality. It just has a more structured design with a more straight forward narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: This honestly feels like a tech demo with an ok story attached to it. The throwing paintball gimmick is cute, but it gets VERY tedious and repetitive with the amount the game wants you to toss out. You'll spend half the game spamming the button just to see where you're going.And on that note, the game is really hard on the eyes. A lot of the game is bright white and you have to paint your surrounding, but you can only paint it pitch black. The pitch white hurts visually, and the high contrast doesn't help. Later levels do away with this, but a few areas instead go into the pitch black surrounding where you can't see anything which isn't enjoyable either as you try to guess where to go next.There's a vine growing mechanic for a few levels which is also cute, but also confusing. It's not always clear where the game wants you to go, and growing the vines is slow and tedious as you need to spam click and wait a long time. You're left spamming the paint button and waiting for the vine to grow in 5 different directions until you finally see where to go next. It could have been really charming is it was a little quicker and clear as to where the vines were going. The game also seems to lock key elements as unlockable for no reason. If you paint the surrounding all black, you can't see. But the ability to clear thrown paint is not a default ability, instead requiring a few collectables to unlock. Why? Other than a bit of padding on a tech-demo, there's no reason for this.All in all there's something here that could be turned into a cute 3h game. But currently its 3h of tedious gameplay and a few moments that made me go "oh huh nice" for about a minute or two. The story is serviceable, but its not amazing by any means. Even as a storybook tale for children it's not that good. For the $5 I spent on it, it was an OK 5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent proof-of-concept that doesn't find its "voice" until the very final stage. _childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a masterfully crafted example of what games and the industry I think currently lacks. Even though the game isn't very long and it comes up short on the content department. It's deceptively simple and straightforward until the last leg of the journey when all the loose strings form a gorgeous bow. Gameplay mechanics are given to you without much explanation but, they don't need any. Within about 10 seconds or so of playing around with any new skill you'll instantly become an expert. My appreciation for the lack of explanation is such a high light for me since most games tend to hold your hand. On top of that, you have these incredibly interwoven levels that are so enjoyable it's almost like playing a Disney movie. I hope this game doesn't fly under the radar for too much longer it's such a wonderful little gem. Highly original, all-ages friendly, and so easy to pick up and understand. Unfortunately, I do think that $15 maybe a bit steep for about a 2 hr run time. However, I do think it's worth your time and money since there is some replay value in some of the extras you can obtain. I'll happily give this game an 85/100 for how much enjoyment I got out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a very good casual puzzle game, okay then the story. Monroe despite just being 10 years old has already gone through a lot of heartache having lost his mother and forced to live in an orphanage the only thing he has to remember her is an one of her unfinished paintings a swan, but one night the swan in her mother's painting is gone and a mysterious door appears, after going through it Monroe is in a weird fantasy world where only his creativity will be able to get him out.Okay let’s get into the likes, the gameplay is really good I really like how the paint concept is used from revealing the world in the first level, making vines grow in order to climb them and even making platforms it was quite a good concept.The puzzles are very good basically there environmental puzzles basically using your paint to reveal something or create vines to climb or create platforms it can be a bit challenging while not being frustratingThe graphic is really good it has a great use of color as each color really pops and is quite vibrant and the great designs of the world has a sort of painting like look to it, it all just as a fairy tale/painting look feel to it all.The levels are really good nicely diverse with plenty of interesting locations that really take the whole canvas/painting look to its maximum, honestly just makes you want to stop and stare at it all sometimes. The story is really good very heartfelt that has a storybook quality to it, especially when you find there little storybook pages that tells you about the king of this land and overall helps with the main story, I also found the themes of the game like responsibility creativity and leaving a legacy to be quite well told. The music is absolutely beautiful with each track being a joy to listen too.Okay let’s get into the dislikes, now in the story I told you that there are these little storybook pages that tells you about the king of this land and while it is quite good there is a problem with it, after collecting all of them it doesn't unlock bonus content that allows you to listen to all of them without having to go through the whole game. Also is this right here is not a dislike more of a warning, I don’t know if this is just me, but as I was playing the game I started getting kind of nauseous I don't know if it was the game itself or something else I just want to warn you in case if it was the game.Okay now that I told you this The Unfinished Swan is a very good casual puzzle game, with very good gameplay, really good graphic and a really good story. Now do I recommend this game? Absolutely but I would suggest if you start feeling queasy to take a break now and again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: I initially gave this game a negative review after it ate my save in a crash a little over an hour into it. I since went back to bumrush through the progress I had lost in order to see the end of the game, and honestly? I stand by the negative review.Thing is: this game is mostly known for the fascinating gimmick of starting off in a world that is . Not just white, not just untextured, but so devoid of any features you can't make out  what so ever until you initially pull the trigger on your paint gun and get your first frame of reference for the world. A really,  cool gimmick, but naturally not one substantive enough to carry a whole game by itself, and so is dropped after only 40 minutes of gameplay. The game then continues with other, far less interesting gimmicks for another 3 chapters which feel very generic in comparison. The story is also barebones and clunkily told, so you really wouldn't be missing much had you put down the game after the first chapter.If you want a game that does something similar, but actually commits to it for the entire game and has a more interesting and well told story to boot, I would recommend checking out Scanner Sombre. Very similar, but instead of starting you out in a completely white world with a bucket of black paint, you start out in a completely black cave with a LiDAR scanner and VR headset (also playable in VR)

_childDocuments_.review: Creative, lightweight and surprisingly pleasant despite the audacious premise, the only downside is how short it is. [18/20⭐, 4h🏅, 1/5💡] The Unfinished Swan follows a boy exploring (and messing with) his father’s attempts to create something to be remembered by. Although technically a shooter, it plays as a creative and “artistic” exploration game, with each chapter exploring a different mechanics. You can see some of the ideas that were later perfected by the team in , although not as impressive or ambitious. The boy is in a quest to find out more about his father after his mother’s death - the titular swan being an unfinished painting left her. The plot is told as a fairytale as the kid interprets his father’s story, so despite the gloomy premise it’s cute and whimsical, without taking itself too seriously.  The game is all about the experience - it starts in a literally all white room where you have to shoot paint to fathom some details. It’s so preposterous that it shouldn’t work, but it does, and the best moments are when you look back at all the mess you made throughout the level. The soundtrack is top-notch and fitting for the ambience of each chapter. The voice acting is a bit exaggerated, but it makes sense as the story being read to a child. The gameplay is simple, it’s essentially a shooter where the projectiles have a different effect in the environment depending on the chapter. Progress is mostly through exploration, although there are some straightforward puzzle and action sequences. You can die, but you’ll just respawn in the last position. The game auto-saves after each level, but the level progress is not saved. It took me 4h to complete the game, which is rather short but understandable for a game where each chapter plays as a unique experience. There is a single progress slot, but you can revisit previous chapters from the menu. Achievements are mostly straightforward, and related to finding hidden collectibles (and a slightly tricky one for minimal shots).

_childDocuments_.review: Gameplay: Think Splatoon with puzzle elements. Until it decides to change the rules.Lots of things annoyed me about this game. After one day of playing it, I had repetitive strain injury. For 85% of the game you are doing the exact same thing and it gets pretty tedious.It's one of those games that changes the rules to suit itself. You're prevented from doing things you should be able to do, purely because the game needs that to be the case at the time.No autosave, which is a MFer when you're trying to clear/fully explore a level. The game will tell you it's saving, but if you die, you'll go back further than that point. I don't know that I've ever had a game mislead me about a save point before.This didn't feel fully realised as a concept, or in practice. It felt like the story was abandoned halfway though. I don't feel like I learned anything about the characters. All in all, bum.I could only recommend it for a couple of quid.

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Hard miss, which is unfortunate given how much I liked their previous game.The white on black in the first level hurts my eyes. Turn down the brightness?Now it's even harder to make out where everything is from lack of contrast.The mechanics are just spamming paint everywhere which hurts my hand - I was expecting something a bit more relaxing. This would entirely be a non-issue if holding down the mouse just shot paint in bursts rather than forcing you to spam-click.The first puzzle is just unintuitive guesswork. I have no idea if I'm skipping missable collectables since you're lacking depth / blind as a bat for aesthetics: form over function. You need to shoot paint to see ceilings, floors, walls, etc, but if there's too much paint you then have the opposite problem where it blends together and since you need to shoot paint to move objects - but physics is wonky since objects collide with terrain - there's paint EVERYWHERE and you can't unpaint something so there's a definitive threshold of clarity vs time you'll pass real quick.What little of the art I saw in the introduction sequence was nice, the narration is really nice, I felt a spark of childhood magic again for a bit there, but ♥♥♥♥ if it isn't just a frustrating mix of visual clutter and RSI.

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Play as Monroe, a young boy recently orphaned and left with a paintbrush and single painting of a swan his mother never finished. In his first night in the orphanage, before going to bed, the swan leaves the frame and goes through a magical door that mysteriously appeared. Enter a white kingdom, splatter paint to find your way and follow the swan. Not only is this game massively disappointing, it inspires headaches and motion sickness. The puzzles are barely that, the story is 1-3+hours long, unremarkable, the ending was inadequate, and the only reason I can think of why this game has so many positive reviews is because it’s a side story of a character in What remains of Edith Finch, Milton Finch. There is an open ending and aside from showing you what happened to Milton you learn absolutely nothing about the character you play as or interesting story elements that were shown in gameplay. If the puzzles were better, I could give this a positive review, but they are so mind-numbingly easy you can complete them without realizing they were supposed to be an obstacle. In one notable example, you are shown this huge and elaborate maze, and I was actually excited to see and explore it to find more story text, but once you enter it, you teleport to the finish line, and you move on to the next chapter. I wish I refunded this game then.

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: A very beautiful and philosophical tale about providence and broadening your horizons. This game makes me feel in a way that we are very much limited by our own perspectives, and that all we need to see is that there are so many unexplored possibilities all around us that we haven't even considered. I'm just a few mini chapters into the game, and I plan on continuing, but what I've come to realize from my short play-through is the important meaning of remaining open to possibilities. There will be, for example, a room you're in and unless you've explored it with the paint balls, you have no idea that that room has a chandelier, a stairway, and a balloon in it. If you remain narrow-minded, and focused on getting from point A to point B in a short amount of time, you'll miss the forest for the ink-splattered trees.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful little game with a simple, but very unique and interesting game mechanic: Painting the environment as you go -- in different ways.The first five minutes were kind of uninteresting, until I stopped and looked back at the trail of paint I had left behind which created a very beautiful outline of the level. This made me smile, and gave me a feeling of joy that I rarely get from games.The game does not try to overstay its welcome, and I would say the playtime of about 1.5-3 hours is a good length, since I don't think the idea could have been stretched much further. It is not difficult (although there was a puzzle or two that became a little bit frustrating to complete), and if you like short, relaxing games that are different from the rest, this is definitely one to try out.

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The unfinished swan is a game that tries to fill the same niche as something like journey, flower or abzu. But where those games shine with wonderful experiences, heartfelt stories or memorable sequences, the unfinished swan falls flat with a core premise that sounds interesting on paper, but in practice is more tedious than fun. Giving the world color as the only mechanic starts to feel bleak faster than you'd think. And even though each level tries to spice things up a bit, the gameplay isn't engaging enough to not just have it be a walking sim. The thing though with walking sims is that they have brilliant stories to tell, experiences that stick with you for a lifetime. The unfinished swan's plot is predictable and nonsensical and the payoff isn't worth sitting through the rather short runtime. The visuals are nice in the later levels but there's a lack of memorable setpieces that leave you in awe. Things like journey's slide level or finding the shark in abzu, there's none of that here. So in the end, the unfinished swan is a rather pale experience that whilst not overstaying its welcome, doesn't offer enough to make it worthwile at full price. The game regularly goes on a very steep sale though, and for that price and time investment its alright but nothing special.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I enjoyed playing this and will enjoy the second playthrough. If you're considering this game, definitely take the time to explore the first part of the game a bit. It's beautiful and deserves that exploration anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Really pretty art styleCool premiseCollectables !! I love hunting for collectablesCons:Motion sickness, somehow, don't know how they managed that onePure white graphics put me into actual shock, pitch black graphics had me squinting like I'm 70 years oldWithout spoiling the story too much, I found the ending unsatisfying and (ironically) unfinished. Character that is objectively a not good person is let entirely off the hook for no reason and the main character is just kinda,, given a thumbs up and a dangling thread of an ending to their story. Maybe that's the point, but I personally found it to be lame. Tl;Dr: I kept missing a single balloon on the last level and it would crash every other time I played it a quarter of the way in. On the third crash I looked at my reflection in the black boot up screen and went "well, at least I'm almost done with the game" and then realised that maybe instead of continuing to push on I should just go to bed, so I booted up a guide, was done in a minute, uninstalled the game, and had a pretty mid night of sleep.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: I generally enjoy exploration games which are somewhat arty, but this game just didn't do it for me.The story is childish and dull, those reviewers who describe this game as 'captivating literature' need to get a grip, I'm afraid.The (single) gameplay mechanic is strange and sometimes unintuitive. The per-level mechanics (vines, lights, block-building) are a little random and don't build on each other.It starts very intriguingly (the first 10 minutes are cool), but after that the game feels like a collection of arty demos which have been stuck together.The one thing I would say is that this game is oddly pretty. The vines in particular are very nice to look at and play with.This might be something for you if you enjoy arty childlike adventures where the gameplay mechanics don't matter to you... but for me it's a no.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a few Annapurna games, and they are gorgeous and thoughtful. I have really enjoyed my experiences with them, but they are also short. They tell interesting stories, but then it's over.The Unfinished Swan is another like this. I do enjoy it, and I do recommend it, but not at full price. I completed the game in 2-3 hours. Spent some additional time trying to get all the balloons, but it became too tedious to go for 100% completion, and there's no other real reason to keep playing. Keep that in mind for yourself when deciding to buy or not. With that out of the way, the game looks great and is a very neat, novel puzzle experience, and I did have fun with my time in it.I think the first chapter was the most challenging with regard to the puzzles, and the later chapters overall didn't add a lot of new mechanics (some,. but the experience was actually easier). With the exception of the final chapter, there's no urgent drive to solve quickly, so you can just enjoy the experience. After starting the game that way, the final areas, which introduced a "timer" mechanic, were a little jarring.There are a few little easter eggs to find, and some of the balloons are really tricky, even with the end game toy, but still not worth more than 1-2 playthroughs.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: It is just super boring to be honest. The gameplay is pedestrian -- it is more of a walking simulator than the puzzle game I was expecting from the information on the steam page. The game basically consists of you spamming the "throw paintball-thing" button hundreds or even thousands of times. It is just really repetitive. There is a story accompanying the constant walking & throwing, but I don't much care for it. Seems exceedingly generic about a sad boy who learns to see the world in color -- the game is a visual metaphor for this as the world starts out black & white and gradually increases to a more colorful canvass. TLDR -- I would avoid this one. If you want a puzzle game, there are a myriad of other puzzle games out there with more in depth mechanics or fun factor. If you want a walking simulator, just play What Remains of Edith Finch by the same studio ironically. The Unfinished Swan is just a perverse amalgamation of the two genres that just doesn't work.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: It's not apparent from the Steam release; but this game was made for the console market back in 2012 when artistic games were rarer and held to a low standard accordingly. One of Annapurna's weaker games.The visuals are not compelling (bordering on ugly); the puzzle mechanics are limited in range (and trivial); the story is uninteresting (and  short). I expect to forget this game within days of finishing it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing, confusing, inspiring. Got chills at the end. Tbh I got kinda bored at around 65% of the game which made me abandon it for a year. Feels good to finish it tho.7/10, nothing would've changed in me if I hadn't played it, but still I'm just happy that I was able to finish a game that I was looking for since 2012 when I was a kid.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel...nothing. While the main gimmick is neat, the game itself just fills me with absolute apathy. I don't hate it, but I also don't want to keep playing it. _childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: A properly artistic game with an immersive world and beautiful soundtrack. That being said it was also disappointing to see so many opportunities wasted. I felt like so much more could have been done with the color mechanics and the levels. The game felt a little short, almost as if it ended right when it was getting on a roll. Some of the achievements are fairly frustrating as well, such as having to go through a level completely blind. All that it requires is a lot of time investment to "map out" a path during a proper playthrough and them mimic it going in blind. It's nothing but a time waster. Regardless, I this is a pleasant litle game and its potential ties to "What remains of Edith Finch" makes it a good storytelling experience.

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a pleasant game that takes a decent weekend to beat. It is made by the company that made What Remains of Edith Finch. The game is very unique using a paint brush in order to paint your level. It makes each person’s playthrough unique. Each person will paint the level in as much detail as they want. Each level was unique, playing off a certain gimmick. The first had a completely white canvas that you filled in, the second was more defined with more platforming and the 3rd level had a more dark color palette. The music and graphics were both pleasant. The story was simple, but told a good story about leaving a legacy. Overall the game was fun and pleasant, but nothing about it completely blew me away 6/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: It's funny this game plays with visual themes of light and dark because it sits squarely in the shadow of What Remains of Edith Finch. That's a tough game to follow up and It's difficult to not form expectations for this game if you've played Edith Finch. This is a perfectly good experience in isolation. I didn't mind it. It certainly felt like the right length and it kept the gameplay mostly fresh throughout. my one major criticism is forcing the player to look at things. Not good. Bad game dev! Bad!!! I really hate that!!! it makes my eyes feel weird and I don't like it!!! I will see your game!!! All I'm doing is seeing your game!!! If the gameplay is looking around and shooting paint, don't take over 50% of it because you really want me to see what this chapter is called!!!!! it's only annoying!!!! I'll see it!!!!! I promise!!!!I completed this game in one sitting and I actually did feel like I had my time wasted so I'm not going to recommend it. It felt like it didn't really have anything meaningful to say and I certainly don't remember anything past the king's terrible English accent and the first level with the paint throwing. I'm glad I got it on sale or I'd refund it but honestly it felt more like a waste of time than a waste of money. I'm not gonna refund because I do want to support this dev but this is not a good game imo.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: So everyone seems to have failed to mention something rather important about this "game".It is a children's book. Not it is inspired by a children's book. Not it has childlike whimsy. It is an Ages-3-and-Down children's book, but first-person.And while that does mean I'm about 30 years too late to fit into the target audience, I doubt I would have liked it even as a kid. It is two hours of "fun" stretched out to four via slow pacing, glitches, and softlocks that force you to replay entire levels (of which there are four, with no checkpoints unless you unlock them).And yeah, I've only played a half hour, but the entire game is only about four hours. It also allows you to skip to any chapter if you find enough hidden balloons so I can assure you that the end of the game is no better than the beginning.Just buy a funducation game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: Terribly bad game design that would make you so much motion sickness.There is a white screen, the only way you can see the world is throwing a black water ball that splatter the world, but if you too much throw the ball you could hardly see the world  because the screen was just changed black from white, so you need to control how much ball you need to throw. You have no idea how long your ball is going, like sometimes your ball hit a wall immediately after you throwing or it goes down into a hole after a second, those unexpected result made me so much uncomfortable and feel sick.I quit after 5 minutes playing because of motion sickness so maybe in the later game the situation will be changed, but I gave up with no regret. As I've requested the refund already, you could understand if your brain would be ok with the game then request the refund if not. The dev should've focus on making a story telling walking simulator instead of this, and I would rather play What Remains of Edith Finch again.
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed opinions, but for the sake of posting I'm giving a thumbs down. Note: This review is preliminary as I have yet to finish the story.I don't consider myself motion sick, but games with liminal space triggers something in me that makes me want to throw up. Unfortunately The Unfinished Swan is one. The very first chapter is by far the worst, splatting colors in a monotonous pure white environment while your head is on a swan's neck by pivoting everywhere is NOT helping. As for the story and exploration, I didn't expect this game to pass the impossibly high bar that is What Remains of Edith Finch, but even with a lowered expectation the story it failed. Cutscenes are few and far in between, revealing barely any story before forcing you on another trek in a monotonous world. However, exploration and level design is very unique and something I have not seen elsewhere, which I like. When I play more of this game I will update this review as I see fit.
