name: Suzerain
detailed_description: Dive into Suzerain with the Expanded Edition Purchase the Kingdom of Rizia DLC! Embark on a royal journey in Suzerain's first DLC. Embrace the crown as King Romus Toras, and lead the Golden Kingdom to a new era. Reclaim lost territories through diplomacy or force. Engage with noble houses and oversee the resources of Rizia. How will you reign? About the Game Embark on a thrilling story as President Anton Rayne, steering Sordland through a pivotal time. Confront potential border conflicts, deep-seated corruption, and economic turmoil while navigating complex political dynamics in Anton's first term. As the leader, your choices will shape Sordland's destiny. Gripping Story : Traverse a 900K-word branching political saga packed with deep and layered conversations. Choices with Impact : Make critical decisions on security, economy, welfare, and diplomacy. Your values will be tested beyond the confines of your office. Your Legacy : Drive Sordland towards one of 9 unique major endings and more than 25 sub-endings. What will your legacy be? Grand Cast : Engage with a diverse cast of more than 50 characters, each with unique personalities and ideologies. Duty vs. Personal Values : Witness how your presidential decisions influence the country but also your family and relationships. Stay Informed : Keep tabs on the state of affairs through country or interactable city tokens, policies, situations, news and reports. See the impact and result of your actions. Discover the Suzerain Universe : Read about newly introduced nations, codex articles about history, and feel the pulse of the world events. Emerging from the vestiges of a traditionalist regime and wrestling with a challenging transition to economic liberalization amidst a recession, the populace of Sordland craves democratic reform. Economic uncertainty casts a long shadow as the political landscape transmutes, with rival superpowers casting keen, watchful eyes on the unfolding scene. Stepping into this maelstrom, you, as President Rayne, must forge effective policies alongside your Cabinet and influential figures. Balance the precarious scales of politics by retaining loyal allies, gauging your values against political necessities, and steeling yourself against potential adversaries. Remember, each character in this narrative carries unique ambitions, fueling the complexity of the political landscape. As the drama unfolds, the delicate equilibrium between your duty to the nation and commitments to your family will be put to the test - a balancing act that challenges the essence of leadership. Can you hold the reins of presidency successfully while being a good parent? Best of luck, President Rayne - Sordland awaits your leadership.

_childDocuments_.review: A narrative-driven political simulator with rich lore, fleshed out characters, and impactful decision making. This niche title has unexpectedly become my new favorite in its genre!I'd recommend Suzerain to anyone that wishes games like Civ or Tropico had more focus on story and wonky political decision-making, as opposed to city sim elements or positioning your units on a board.A moderate degree of political literacy and a willingness to read is required to properly enjoy this game - but if it sounds like it's up your alley, it'll most likely be very up your alley!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I dont think I've ever left a review for a game before, but I couldn't not for this one. It is without a doubt one of the most immersive and enjoyable story driven games I have played in a very long time. I found myself genuinely caring for and despising characters. I'm not sure I have ever finished a game and started again straight away. Despite it being incredible, there is one issue I have - it isnt particularly interesting to replay. Yes with lots of different endings there is plenty of content I haven't seem, but it all rests on the same decisions. Things that I think could help this would be:Make some Random events that pop up rather than be so scripted - perhaps triggered by the state of the economy or tension in the countryI would also have liked to have had side quests developing relationships with each of the characters. Yes this happens through the main story, but it would have been a nice touch for each of the characters to have their own arc with no real baring on the main story. Still, these wants of mine are the difference between a fantastic game and an incredible game - I cannot recommend it highly enough
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Since my first days of Steam I never saw a game like this. Calling this a simulation would be an understatement. I can proudly say that it was one of the best, if not the best, experience I've ever had in a game. I hope that there are always development studios that love a game as much as you have seen here.It's always the quality that counts. Nothing more nothing less . . .
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: First playthrough, I successfully:-Drove Sordland into a great depression-Collapsed the value of the Sordish Ren-Had half of my cabinet resign on me. -Bolstered military, education, police, and health spending to levels never before seen-Empowered Sordish feminists-Collaborated with media moguls and was found out-Was betrayed by the Judicial System-Was the first Sordish president to be impeached, convicted, and sentenced to life in prison-But I sent my son to a nice collage, at leastOverall, a fantastic game, and I  make all of these mistakes again. This cannot be prevented.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece of a game. Suzerain helped me understand how the political system works, how diplomacy has its flaws, and explored the philosophies of capitalism and communism so well. I wasn't able to be the best president but I pushed for human rights which was good enough. Certainly not going to get into politics thanks to this game. But damn, I was in for a ride. Keep in mind that Suzerain is heavily text based. I'm not much of a reader but the amount of decision making involved in this game is huge, making it feel less like a novel.10/10 highly recommend. Super educational game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm hooked. Being a leader of a country in turmoil is like trying to balance a glass triangle at its point on your pinky finger in one hand, while feeding an angry wild lion with the other hand while balancing on a unicycle at the edge of the tallest skyscraper. While not wearing pants. But it's one hell of a ride. Buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Has the appearance of great depth at first, but is largely based around pre-scripted events. Some of the more complex and interesting game paths, such as constitutional reform, can lock out extremely late in the game for very silly reasons (ordering a salad, not thinking several thousand words earlier to hold back one personal wealth). The only real way to play without guides is to hammer your head fruitlessly through the same unbelievably long dialogue sequences to work out how the designers WANT various events to turn out, and then doing them again...and again...and again. Play through it once, enjoy crashing out and leave it there.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, should buy even when not on sale.It is an interactable novel about a president in a young and unstable democratic nation. The first time you play is the absolute best, storywise. But it has a lot of replayability. Don't expect it to be easy, it won't cater to your wishes and desires. Every little decision you make matter for the endgame. You will break your head trying to find out what you need to do to win. But all the lore, flavor, and possible outcomes make this game amazing. I absolutely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I played in a while. Given the setting and CYOA mechanics it was surprisngly engaging and kept me glued to my sit for two days straight.I tried to play fair, but in politics, as we all know, it doesn't really work. Really itching for a second go at it, but I feel like it's one of those things that better left lingering.

_childDocuments_.review: Take one half Crusader Kings and one half Disco Elysium. This game is full of tense political machinations and decisions that will follow you for your entire presidency. No victory is easy or comes without a cost, and it does a great job of showing just how your choices impact Sordland. Just an incredible game. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there were more political choose-your-own-adventure games like Suzerain that has this much depth of political content and world-building lore and history. This game is a unique gem and there are no others like it that I can compare it to. Centrists and the uninformed of real-world history and political theory - beware.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game simply because the ending is so completely broken that it destroyed the entire experience for me and erased the desire I had to replay it.On my first run through I:- Fixed the economy and ended the recession- Kept the  country out of war- Saved the country from a polio outbreak, also provided free medication nationwide- squashed extremist violence - kept a balanced budget- expanded the national education system- completed several major projects And what did I get for these achievements? Impeachment and life in prison....sentenced to thunderous applause...This is simply broken and ruined the entire experience of the game. I get that there should only be limited positive endings but this just made no sense and didnt match my accomplishments. I was planning another play through the entire time but this ending simply took the wind out of my sails and I cant bring myself to try again.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much recommend this. Now, just so people don't go in expecting the wrong thing. This isn't a game like Democracy where you got full control of what to launch and where. Better compare it with a Choose Your Own Adventure story, with a whole load of detail. The mood is best compared with the game Hidden Agenda.  It doesn't shy from reminding you that there is a price to pay for doing some right things, but it's not too grimdark, and it shows you the consequences of your action, good AND bad.  And it doesn't do it in dry numbers, but in newspaper stories and reports, bite sized bits that tell you how you're affecting the lives of people.It's way more personal than most nationsim games as well. Your president is a character in the world, with a wife and kids, and those things affect you as well. I found myself caring about all those folks.Bit of a content warning though, depending on how the game goes, it might contain a suicide. Nothing graphic, but it is discussed.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is well thought out and designed.  The authors clearly know their history.  The story is realistic and conveys the sense that you really are the individual at the head of this country.  While it is largely a chose your own adventure, it has nice layers to it that makes the story feel alive and dynamic.  The writing does an excellent job of making your decisions feel like part of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has a passable portion of knowledge in political science ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°), I appreciate the attention to detail the devs have put into making this game feels true to life. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stellar writing and worldbuilding. Being a politician is difficult. Despite my best intentions, I have had playthroughs where I plunged my country into a deep economic and political crisis, after which I was convicted by a military tribunal. I have had others where I died trying to protect my family after losing a war I had initiated myself, riding the high of hubris and overzealous advisers. On other hands, I have presided over booming economies and happy, healthy and educated citizens. It sure brought a smile to my face.A Morgna wes core!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I've almost completed a few runs of Suzerain now, and it's definitely worth purchasing. It's very replayable and a single playthrough can take a good amount of time. There are a few things that in replaying I find a little confusing or annoying, but overall the game stands up despite of this.The worldbuilding is very detailed and clearly is meant to be similar to the politics of the real-world, with you as the president engaging in issues from constitutional reform to economics to whether or not to progress women's rights in Sordland, your home country. There are some breaks from the politics with time spent with your family, which I found refreshing and interesting in my first playthrough (it feels a little more tedious in replays, but is still good stuff). On the one hand, I appreciate the very detailed country with many cities and political groups and figures - but on the other, there were moments where I struggled to remember the importance of a given town or couldn't see a good reason as to why investing in one city over another would be more beneficial. Often there are a lot of details available about things that aren't neccessarily helpful as a player unless you have a great understanding of economics/social systems (for instance, you can have an advisor give you the numbers run-down of how many hospital beds per citizen there are or tell you about the current GDP), but in a few cases there strangely isn't enough detail available to make choices that you really understand the impact of. To me, it feels like there is a great focus on details that are interesting but not always choice-altering, and not enough on some of the strategies that actually could influence your decisions. That all said, I do enjoy the amount of effort that clearly went into considering all the details of the world, and it makes the country feel real and the decisions have weight.One major critique for me is the lack of ability to go back to a certain point of the story and continue playing. Although I appreciate the finality in choices-matter games, for a game with a length like Suzerain's it feels tedious to start completely over from scratch just to see how different choices late or mid game could alter things. I think the finality of choices is good for the first playthrough, but I would love "checkpoints" in the story where players can go back (maybe to a certain turn or chapter) and continue the story from there. This could be something that only unlocks after completing a full playthrough.All in all, though, this game is very interesting and complex and I appreciate that the choices often have a number of measurable impacts on the world rather than one clear result. This encourages players to test different strategies in the game to see how the world changes, even if those strategies don't align with their real-world political values. I would love to see more of this world, perhaps a sequel could be based in a different country of the world with a far different political climate!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Not only is this one of the best political games I have ever played, but possibly one of the best games I have ever played in general.It is also very realistic, trying to balance budgets and economy, family and career, foreign and internal politics.It has been a long time since I was last this immersed in a video game. I didnt just live through someone, I was that someone and what I did mattered and had an effect.It is truly saddening that in the end I failed my nation.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: * Great is really impressive, depth and storytelling sometimes is over the roof.Cons: * Speed of animation is painful (especially when replaying game) and no auto-skip of dialogues that you already saw (on consecutive runs) * Unfortunately it has quite a big flaw, not enough feedback. You signed trade deals, you invest into infrastructure, you got reports that all is improving at pace. Suddenly there is unrest everywhere and your adviser that 6 months ago told you that unemployment dropped from 16 to 12, says that currently it stands at 24%. I have no idea what happened and why but nothing could be done. Game is based around meeting that are scheduled by NPC's so you are only allowed to passively watch everything fall apart. * At times you can make accidental decision (like accepting bribe) only because you went to some meeting and game didn't allow you to refuse an offer. This spoils quite a bit of immersion. * Some characters just disappear in the late game * Typical issue for game branching narrative: inconsistencies, dialog lines that not follow your earlier decisions, or choices that have no outcome whatsoever * Lack of epilogue fallout style is a big letdown * As with many games (especially those with branching storylines), early to mid game is superb, top-notched, mid to late game has increasing number of errors, mistakes and becomes shallow

_childDocuments_.review: This is a text based game. So, if reading isn't your thing, keep clear. You play the 5th president of a fictional republic stuck between a Capitalist West, a Communist East, and a Monarchy to the North. You need to tread the line between these foreign powers while governing your own internal polices like Healthcare, Education, Policing, and Military. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, but recognize that the "action" is all text based dialogue - and a lot of it. _childDocuments_.review: I'm stealing this entire review word-for-word from Hexaboo, because they have said everything I wanted to say and with more skill with words. "Suzerain is a fairly good and fun game, but I don't think its current rating on Steam (93%) accurately reflects its quality, for the shallow experience the game delivers past a certain point, so here's a fat thumbs-down.The basic premise is excellent, the game uses dialogue choices to guide you through your life prior to your election, and beautifully throws you into a quasi-realistic world of the 1950's, to lead a country with a detailed geography, and people with extensive bios, opinions and allegiances. There is so much to explore in addition to the story, and the story itself captivates you with difficult choices interspersed with all the boring appearances, functions, and official dinner parties that you have to live through for that authentic head-of-state experience. The game does not let up, and you will easily spend the next 10 hours aching to see what the next decision brings, what the newspapers write about you, and whether the economy finally gets back on track.But once you go beyond just the story and the basic world building, you can really feel the game was made by a bunch of first-world libby millennials who don't know better, and clearly had no intention of changing that. The whole 1950's world of the game is an incredibly hammy projection of the modern mainstream in politics and economics, like having a whole party of neoliberals, second biggest in the parliament no less, even though their economic policies were a very marginal academic idea post-WWII, and never got to any power until the 80's. Sure they're everywhere now, but what the game dismisses as 'old, outdated Sollism' was the very successful and burgeoning capitalist mainstream in the first world that made rich boomers rich boomers. The social liberalism of the liberal bourgeois party in the game is also fairly anachronistic: they wouldn't give a crap about any downtrodden or minorities, certainly not in the 1950's.The policies that make you a dang commie in the game are the typical watered-down and anachronistic 21-century third-way social-democrat ideas like 'let's not privatise schools, pretty please!' or 'let's choose the state-owned enterprise over privatised ones to build stuff just this once, despite obvious government failure, obviously!' The phrase about 'guaranteed minimum income' as this bold socialist thing in the end really reveals the lack of research in creating the universe of the game (it's neither bold, nor socialist, nor period-appropriate).There was no attempt to break out of the usual moulds, and give the player a good deal of freedom to weave their own credible story, and offer them an exciting slice of almost-real history. That all in addition that there is no player agency in a pure game-mechanics sense. You are the head of what looks like a reactive branch of the government, rather than the executive. I know there are limitations in terms of what you can have in an interactive-novel game like this, but having virtually no influence on the composition of your cabinet, and no active control setting policies in the country really ruin the idea of you being at the top of executive power.All in all, don't expect any kind of management gameplay in Suzerain (Democracy is a decent, if limited, option for that). It is an interactive novel, and will deliver enough good story for one playthrough. However, the game is way too shallow and repetitive, and doesn't offer enough player decisions and agency amid all the text fluff for any replay value."
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Remarkable game. Unlike most politics simulations I've played, this one does not give you the metrics associated with your decisions ; you have to try and discern which trigger led to which result later in the game, but apart from economic decisions, which are calculable, the game won't give you exact or immediate information about them, just like in real life.This makes the game appear unforgiving at first, which it is if your goal is to achieve a perfect presidential term ; but then again, achieving a perfect first term is extremely hard in real life too. The game makes sense when you approach it as a simulation of writing a page of history. In the end it does not matter so much if you "win". You can have a run that's extremely difficult, in which you end up assassinated or imprisoned, but which result is a turning point in the history of your fictional country.One must not be afraid to start over multiple times to explore all the options or find out how to achieve the desired reforms or results, and to not be helped by the game while doing so, in order to appreciate it.All I can say is that I truly hope to see more installments of this format, either as a sequel or in a different setting.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! It is nearly perfect in its immersion, but there is one thing I heavily noticed: Its heavy-handed approach to Feminism. It goes so far as to completely disrupt the logic of the game world.The beginning status quo of the game indicates a strongly paternalistic society in which women are not allowed to study what they want, in which they earn less for the same work in the same position and in which they don't get to have careers at all.But your starting cabinet is distributed evenly with regards to sex. And there are many female leaders of oligarchic / capitalistic structures who would be very rich and influential in everything. At the same time, we are always reminded that women are oppressed in this game and lack rights and representation. This is where the quota-based writing approaches its limits. It hinders any meaningful change within the game by basically making up an issue which has already been solved. There are many female leaders to interact with here who were in that position for more than 10 years and more. Many trailblazers and "first female to ..." are seen here which would be impossible in the state which the game describes. This completely breaks the immersion. They inhabit strong positions of power while the game pretends otherwise. It would have been far more impactful to really showcase such a society with the player being able to tangibly change things, by, for example, appointing a woman to the cabinet and doing these first steps.Apart from that I can wholly recommend the game for everyone who would like to try their approach to survive an everchanging political landscape with many, many conflicts which point back to our times and our recent global history. Great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best narrative games I've ever played. Every choice is agonisingly multifaceted and consequential. Compared to something like Democracy, the human nature of individuals lends itself to better understanding how politics plays out in the real world. I'd highly recommend this to anyone interested in politics regardless of affiliation. Or just those interested in narrative, choice-and-consequence-based games who don't mind the generally more serious and sometimes depressing tone of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I continue to be astounded at the amount of content in this game. Every choice you make seems to have meaning, and is reflected both in little news snippets as well as actual effects on the game. I'm only nearing the end of my first playthrough, but it looks like you can choose to be any kind of leader you want, from a tyrranical despot to a corrupt free-market capitalist, to a bleeding heart activist for oppressed minorities. Characters in your cabinet all have their own personalities and agendas, and your interactions with them - even though they're portrayed only in text form - seem very real. Of course, this doesn't stop the game creators from injecting some humor in the game - I won't spoil any of the jokes or references, but I had a couple good chuckles when I stumbled upon them. All in all, I highly recommend Suzerain given how much content it has for its low price.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this review is a "I recommend it, but I wanted more." It is also long, but I hope you will read the entirety. I clocked in a solid and relatively non-stop 11.5 hours, but I wanted at least twenty. Mild spoilers will be listed at the very end of this review that talk about this. This time decision is completely unrelated to the price, as it is well worth this amount, I simply wanted to play more.Suzerain has you take the role of a newly-elected leader of a not quite mediterranean/balkan/baltic/who knows country. All you need to know is that there is the not-United States, the not-USSR, and you border many countries of differing opinion about you, your country, and there are questions of all political flavors and even ethnic issues. It is an *extremely* well developed simulator, with the simulation understanding my decisions and giving me feedback that was not meter-involved besides a bar showing "economy". Your advisers give you advice, cannot be trusted completely but are not out necessarily to backstab you in comical or immersion-breaking fashion like many other games. There is also not a hard-coded ridiculous "it was me all along!" reveal of one of your cabinet members, every single one of them seems human to the extent that I was feeling certain feelings for characters that were quite literally a static image and text. This is without a doubt the best political game I have EVER played, and without a doubt the most realistic one I have ever seen. In my playthrough I chose to embrace capitalism and the west, as well as support these goals, which for many games would mean that the Republic of Lespia, the westophiles and capitalists of the regions, would be my best friends. However, in Suzerain, probably because of a previous deal with the Republic of Wehlen thec leader of Lespia was not a fan of me, for spoilerish reasons. He demanded too much, deals broke down, and I refused. The fact that Suzerain has one event influence another, yet still allows something to happen, blew me away. Usually Visual Novel and Political type games like this are extremely railroaded, with true choices masked around dozens of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones that are easy to identify, but not so with Suzerain. Every decision felt like it mattered, and even though I "won" I regretted many decisions I made along the way, like a real leader, but stood by my decisions. This is a masterful game about tough decisions for a fledgling country that will have you love every minute. A Morgna Her Coren!*Spoiler Parts Below*-  Very Mild spoilers about one of the potential game ends (wow theres a way to win), and the aftermath.There are elections in the game, which should be obvious, and your game "ends" if you win your re-election. As I was clicking through and reading the dialogue presented talking about my re-election, I thought to myself, "man, I really hate early access games. They would have stopped the game right here and I would have to wait a half year to play more."And then the game ended. This is my only gripe. I wanted more. I wanted to keep going and fulfill the promises of my first term. I wanted to shepherd my people through the hinted at war/dispute between two powers you'll see about. I also wanted to see if the nation that most threatened mine would be crazy enough to pull the trigger, since I had massively reformed the army with brand new equipment and an unnamed higher power had completely reformed and modernized our air force. In fact, I could see the issues being linked, since the two powers butting heads could very easily drag me into their struggle, which could drag said unnamed higher power into the conflict. If the developers manage to read this, then first thank you for this masterpiece. And second, give me more.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I have pushed into chapter one, thus far, but I am pleasantly surprised. _childDocuments_.review: This was an absolute treat.From the screenshots, it might look like a Civ / empire building strategy type game, but it's absolutely not. You're the president of a small country in a fictional version set around the 1930s, in a place similar to eastern Europe. It's entirely story driven - you could call it a visual novel, but it's also a political simulator. The gameplay revolves around making decisions on how you lead the nation, interact with the public, and try to balance your family life. There seems to be a lot of flexibility in the different paths you can take, and the writing and choices are really well presented.There have been so many moments that have been really difficult to decide on, even if I know what I'd like to do morally. It's really well written, and plays great on the deck

Clearly the writers are playing it very politically correct not to be caught up in this cancel culture of late. they should have stick to real facts. very disappointing. for the gameplay itself, 0 repeatability.

_childDocuments_.review: The rapid switch from naive idealism going into office to panicked realpolitik as you're trying to just keep things together is amazing. Everybody has an agenda, and it's not necessarily aligned with yours. Mostly, this is a game of figuring out who's going to support what you're trying to do and who's going to oppose it, and how you can work with the cards you're dealt to turn out with a majority.Or at least, that's how my game played. I tried to legitimately make the country a better place, while respecting democracy, fighting corruption, and working with my enemies rather than suppressing them. Ultimately, I got a 'good' ending, but I did have to do some things (or maybe, just allow some things to happen) to get what I wanted. It was so easy to forget what I'd done, until that interview towards the end started dredging up my past decisions...If you've got the patience and are going to try and meaningfully engage with the themes and setting of the story, you'll enjoy this. But be warned, there's no real 'gameplay' to be had here beyond simple budget balancing. Think of it as a visual novel, and you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has got a great premise and its design is refreshingly different. The plot is compelling and the back story extensive. Decisions are never easy. You have to choose very well what you want to do since you're lacking resources all the time. Unfortunately the outcome of your decisions is often erratic. I seemed to be doing well at the end of the penultimate chapter. The economy apparently stopped contracting. Unemployment was down,  inflation was very low, the budget deficit had disappeared and apparently I increased my party’s standing in the polls by 20%.Two turns later with the only event being a failed commemoration attendance of the Bludish massacre involving the damn construction everything suddenly fell apart with no warning and in my opinion no logic.Unemployment was suddenly back from 10% to 16%. The GDP had apparently contracted by 60% (200 billion per year) during my tenure ( the only mention of it ever during my term stated GDP contracted 2% in my second last year and I had ostensibly stopped the recession) but I somehow managed to reduce government debt by 60% (also more than 200 billion total) which seems impossible under these circumstances.The health minister resigned because of a badly raging polio outbreak. I had procured a vaccination but chose not to distribute it widely because the situation was still under control. Eventually the minister resigned because of a severe pandemic but less than 10.000 people died in 4 years and I was never warned of it being raging badly or given the option to start emergency vaccinations. An announced mandatory vaccination law apparantly never made it back on the agenda despite the crisis.The economic minister resigned as well because the economy took an illogical turn for the worse after being in good shape two turns before.I could go on….The last act destroyed my positive experience of this game entirely and I now wish I had not wasted more than  10 hours on this unbalanced  work in progress.Edit: I gave this another try and went through a second playthrough. I actually did enjoy my first playthrough as well but was bummed out by the erratic result of my choices in the end.In my second playthrough I chose a different playstyle. Since there are many different decisions to be made this playthrough led to many interessting new developments. Overall I had a good time and this leads me to change my review into a thumbs up in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most exciting and intriguing role-playing stategy games I've ever played. No one can be trusted, nor should you be quick to judge everyone. Not every enemy is truly your enemy and the same goes for every friend. You have to consider facts, emotions, logic, and context when you interact with characters in this game.All of these aspects are fully in effect in the DLC, which is a great upgrade compared to the base story.Overall I hope this game gets more funding so that we can have more DLCs with a vaster and more in-depth story, expanding the world of "Suzerain".PS: " I would love to play a superpower ;) "

_childDocuments_.review: I got really absorbed into this game, reading every minor report about the cities in my country and what the newspapers had to say. If you like visual novels, but also like Paradox games - congrats, you've just found a game worth 7-10 hours of your time. You've got pretty good agency over what happens in your country, although one criticism may be that it slightly over exaggerates how fast development programs (economy, health, education, security) can actually pan out, so that everything can happen over the course of your presidency. Theoretically, there are probably 4 or so ideological paths you can carry out, but I don't know if I'll end up going back to complete them.Be warned - every decision you make is permanent (Until you start a new game). _childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic concept. I absolutely am enthralled with the idea of this game; an rpg with management and policy choices that synergizes with itself across genres beautifully. The rpg elements immerse you in the consequences of your actions and the attempts to sway you--the personalities and the dramas--while the management side shows you the macro effects and trade offs between choices.  I dearly hope this becomes a mainstay of the genre, and that others will expand upon it. I would write a list of pros and cons, but others have sketched them out rather well. I will say, a significant problems is a lack of ability to save and make different choices or explore how they play out. I understand the choice and trade-off, but there's simply no defending the inability to do so in a game rich with both dialogue options and choices. As with others, I've misclicked more than once, or typed a number while writing in my notes that triggered a decision accidentally. One thing no one has really mentioned is the inability to make policies freely, which I consider vital. You can only choose policies at set moments in the game, but then the dynamic changes and you're left unable to do anything to respond. For example, the threat of an invasion might make you reconsider increasing military funding, but your defense minister will just complain about the lack throughout, such that even if you change your mind you actually can't change it in the game. What I really want from this type of game, is a true crossing of genres between management and rpg, where  you freely can initiate policies (even if they get voted down later) so that the immersion of your defense minister lambasting you for not doing anything about the budget feels more real. Instead, I felt I was simply tied up by a game mechanic. It would greatly enrich this game if they gave that option, not only for the normal reasons, but because the dialogues with your ministers are so enthralling. Your visit to the school where you see the rampant propaganda and inequality might move you to shift funds from something else, but unfortunately it becomes a moot point that just makes you feel bad about a thing you had no idea existed until now. Such a simple change would greatly improve the game, and moreover make it more a revolutionary entry into a new kind of genre. It seems they might have over emphasized the rpg side of this, in the end, when the infrastructure for the management side is all there, right down to the number of seats you have in the Legislature. The writing is inspiring though, I really can't say enough about it as it makes the whole thing come to life. Those moments when you're sitting at the table with your family, or bantering with your mentor about life are such beautiful touches. The outrage expressed by your ministers, the banter between speeches and after, it's all glorious. I would in any case highly recommend this game, though you should be prepared for a good amount of reading as that is the main mechanic of the game. Trust me when I say that doesn't sound as bad as it might though. They really put it together nicely and everything feels so real for such a relatively simple game. I really hope this publisher, or others, will expand upon this and make it into a proper management/rpg blend with more of a focus on the freedom to do things on your own rather than sticking to the sequential order of things the game forces you into. It gives it a stronger rpg feel, but personally I would prefer more management, and then dealing with the rpg consequences and such as a result of actions I took wholly on my own initiative. I applaud the creator's creativity though, I never thought of something like this and they've done it pretty well at the first stab with a low budget. Here's to hoping now they double down.8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The game relies heavily on text o deliver it's narrative while obscuring what your decisions actually mean. A politically centrist approach is discouraged. There is very little good choices in the game with most choices causing you to lose something either support, money or the economic/social power. Lots of negative reinforcement here. If the game actually was more transparent about your decisions instead of obscuring them to make the game more narrative focused it would be more playable. Right now it feels like make choice get bad result, reload make choice get bad result. Down the road bad result hits you again.  repeat ad nosium.Weird decisions like not having saves in 10+ hour single player game (Checkpoint system is lacking), lack of information and the not being able to backtrack choices really hurt this game. The game is also very dark and after a while wears on you. The strange thing is that it feels like outcomes are outside of the player control. Again with the lack of transparency on choices. If I had a clearer Idea of what did what I wouldn't feel so sour on the game. Feedback is important. You can make tough games as long as the player can see what they are doing wrong. Forcing the player to use guides outside the game to play your political sim where only right wing or left wing extremist choices are the only valid ones is a hard not recommend for me and for the most part I like political game. At the very least the game doesn't force a specific ideology down your throat. Dialogue is well written and since the game is 99% text dialogue that is important. The last 1% of gameplay is overhead map navigation...rivitting. As it stands though it feels more like a choose your own adventure or visual novel (without CGs) that you play once. Even with the extra choices I can see the long winded dialogues getting very boring if you were trying to go for achievements or be a completionist.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, the developers make a great job but I have to say No because the game needs major improvements. 1. Dialogues are pretty cumbersome. On the second or third run, it gets ridiculously annoying to get through these dialogues over again. I assume, developers didn’t want players to enjoy exploring different scenarios; from which I conclude this is the game is to play two-three times which brings to other conclusion that the price should be $5 tops 2. Dialogues are full of meaningless response choices. It’s basically white noise that doesn’t affect the outcome. I understand, developers wanted to create a special game atmosphere but providing with three or four greeting responses at the beginning of every dialog (that doesn’t affect anything) is too much. Or the driver character that doesn’t affect anything but waste time. I’d suggest a straight-to-the-point dialogues option or something like that.3. At some point it gets pretty boring reading long dialogues. I’d suggest liming choices to a few where you actually can make meaningful choices. I’d also extend the game story and the complexity with different outcomes. Like similar to other text based games, such as "Crisis in the Kremlin". I’d also mark choices with the corresponding colors. For example, red – confrontation/demand/threat, gray – neutrality/consideration/information/deception, green – agreement/reasoning/compromise, etc4. There is no way to save the game. Only one autosave file. Why? It’s frustrating to read forums where people ask what folders/files they have to copy on their computers to go back a few steps. Forced Iron-man is unnecessary. Copying save files every time before next steps is inconvenient, people won't play this game for long. If devs want make this game a successful product and create dlcs they need to ensure that it's engaging and comfortable to play5. Undeveloped dashboard. You can’t actually see the main indicators like inflation, GDP, unemployment, etc. It’s buried in exhausting two or three dialogues during the game. There is no way you can see how your choices actually affect the economy, political processes, main political powers, support of the parliament, business-public-army-police opinion, etc. Every choice is tied to dialogues that you have to wait to pop-up. Newspapers alone are not helpful.6. 99% of dialogues are linear. It doesn’t matter what choices you made before and how they affected the game, the same/all dialogues will pop-up as scheduled. So, no random events/dialogues tied with previously made decisions.7. There are no advisories/notes/recommendations/consequences on choices or how to improve certain things (see “country overview” dashboard). You have to guess or read forums. So, for example, how the heck to improve “Lorren Rust Belt”? Ah, hello, any suggestions? Like build the road and keep surplus or something. Same for the main indicators (see 5.)8. Including Notepad for notes is a desperate attempt to help players to keep track of this mess. 9. I’d not even suggest, but it would be nice to have some kind of simple dubbed (with actual sound like in "This is the Police" game) animation/pictures for main events like speeches or key-dialogues. This would bring another level of interaction to the game.I hope the developers can improve this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a misery simulator, nobody sane would want to be in Anton Rayne's shoes.There is a big hope in the beginning, you promised reasonable goals, there is enough budget and you seem to have excellent team to do the job. But then...The strive to make every important person happy while trying to get the country to modern democratic (in my case, be a dictator if you want) state without ancient nonsense turns out to be utopia.No saves, an ironman mode if you will, but it can be very frustrating. Game reminds me a lot of 80 Days around the world which I like but it's so easy to not being fast for 5 seconds and you miss the whole game, brutal autosaves. .It would be awesome if game was narrated it would make for smoother and enjoyable first run and add personality to each character. But obviously it's load of text and it would be costly nightmare to do a good full covered quality narration of this scale.There is still some work to be done, most of the decisions are well discussed with others, but some are done with short tooltip and there is no discussion or confirmation about them. All the laws passed by the assembly you can veto or sign are never discussed before they land on your table, only news mention it. This adds to the frustration of no easy reload and resulting to annoying save scumming.I had 2 unhealthy gaming days of this doing two runs, I wish I would have taken breaks and split up the game, but the story and 'what will happen next' thing is too strong, damn it. _childDocuments_.review: The most realistic political ruler simulator I've ever played, and I've played a lot (too many).  This game captures what it's like being a singular person in a position of power, relying on no shortage of assistants and cabinet members and party mates and family members and business owners to get anything done.Gripping.  Practically educational for understanding how power works.  And an ACTUAL "Your choices matter" game, for once, because your choices could result in a war, or a famine, or a plague, or a revolution.Memorable characters, surprisingly effective soundtrack - considering how restrained it is - and a plethora of information that never bombards you.Can't wait for the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played through the game twice, and I can recommend it to anyone interested in an engaging political strategy game. The price point is currently perfect for this game right now, as it is basically the cost of going out to the movies. Suzerain is very well thought out, the story thread is believable, and I found most of the political mechanics work as they would in a hypothetical nation of the 1950s. There is a smaller, personal story line that follows your domestic life, which adds a bit of unexpected depth to your President. The game mechanics are simple, and nicely designed, making it more visually stimulating than some past games about political strategy.Now, a couple of caveats. No matter what your politics are, this game is biased toward a neo-liberal ideology. For those who do not know what that is, it is basically a belief in very basic democracy reliant on corporate "donations" to fund political parties, with nearly unregulated free market capitalism, no public health care, few social services, and only cursory investment in public education. In an economic crisis, they would recommend austerity.I have heard of people winning as a communist leader, but it sounds like it was a very particular kind of path they had to take. A balanced game politically would have several win paths that could be taken, be it full-on fascism, capitalist democracy, social democracy, or full-on communism. I would also add here that it seems highly biased toward militarism, as there is an immediate threat of incursion upon starting the game. If you choose not to fund the military enough, you may very likely lose.The budget in this game is broken. In real governments, when the economy is booming the government actually takes in more revenue through higher income taxes, through more trade, and production - especially in countries that have some nationalized industry. As it stands now, the only way the budget is affected is if you pass legislation that costs or will merit you budget points, and getting a +1 or +2 is exceedingly rare. This seems like the developer wanted to make the game "more challenging", but it just forces you to run the country in debt constantly. This is an annoyance, and I think there should be some effect on the budget if you have the economy either maxed out, or in a shambles. I had a fully maxed out economy, but my budget was at -8 for a while, which had people complaining that we were in a debt crisis. How was that a crisis? We were in debt to ourselves. It just made no sense, and as I said, where was all of my wonderful revenue from my hot economy to ease the debt?One final critique: The player is very beholden to the story. You tend to be a very passive and reactive entity in the game as president. There are times when you are given decisions to make, but they are still "given". Maybe this is unfair, but in a second version, some consideration to this fact might be given. How can the player be the main actor in the game play? Even though there are a few problems with Suzerain, it is still a strong game, and is fun to play.  It is pretty complex, and I appreciate the thought that went into it. The developers did  some amazing work threading all of these paths together into a cohesive game.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is truly an immersive political "visual novel". Although the world is fictional, it has many connections to our world and as result it is very believable and immersive. Set during a "cold war" between capitalist West and communist East, the game places you in the shoes of Anton Rayne, newly elected president of Sordland. You will be presented with various choices during your term ranging from how to deal with deep recession to how to respond to multiple differing internal and external threats preparing to take advantage of the weakened Sordland. You must be vary of many factions and persons trying to influence your decisions. Do not however underestimate your opposition, as they are ready to end your presidential term prematurely given the chance if you force them no other choice.There are many ways to play the game. You can basically choose yourself what kind of a character Anton Rayne is depending on the choices and answers you make. You can be right-wing or left-wing, authoritarian or libertarian, progressive or conservative, corrupt or idealistic and anything between. I felt that choices I made truly mattered and changed how the game progressed, as there are so many different ways to react to and solve those problems. I have only played one game so far, but I can confirm that that path worked well and felt very immersive all the way from the beginning to the very end.I consider this probably to be my favourite political simulation game of all time. Only con would be the length as I managed to get through the game in ten and a half hours, but as they say, quality over quantity. I am very eager to one day try a different path for Rayne and Sordland.I will end this review with a lengthy summary of my game for those of you who might find it interesting. There will be spoilers.*Spoilers*In my playthrough Anton Rayne took as his utmost goal to continue free market reforms of the last president as a means to lead Sordland out of the deep recession that was forcing this once fine nation to a path of certain new civil war. Investment programs, privatization initiatives and free trade deals are examples of the measures taken to revitalize the economy. Rayne was not a puppet to the local oligarchs however, as along with the market reforms he also adopted many pro-employee programs to help them during these difficult times. Minimum wage laws and relief coupon bills were passed through the Great Assembly with the support of the president, even though the mighty corporations were against these reforms. As a result, after his four-year term the economy of Sordland had recovered. GDP almost had almost doubled, and unemployment dropped by staggering circa 12 percent.Second goal of Rayne administration, probably at least as important for the stability of Sordland, was to reform the old constitution. It had made republic of Sordland to something of a presidential dictatorship. With skillful diplomacy the Rayne administration managed to pass the constitutional reforms both in the legislative Great Assembly and in the upper Court. Sordland was on the path of democracy. New constitution included reforms like lowered election threshold, clear division of power and curtailed presidential powers. It was not perfect, as compromises had to be made, but result was acceptable by all standards.During his term Rayne also managed to lead Sordland to join the alliance of western capitalist democracies, ATO (equivalent to our NATO), raised living standards of all citizens, showed diplomatic excellency avoiding conflicts abroad and helped the dire situation of women and Bludish minorities in Sordland. His personal life felt the stress of the presidency too, but in the end his family always stayed by his side. As his term came to an end, Rayne had yet again managed to get his divided party to unite for his reelection by defeating his nationalist conservative opponent within the party. Rayne had finally gained the upper hand, or at least so he thought, only to lose it all in the upcoming elections. The people of Sordland had decided, that they wanted even more liberal reforms in the future. Major opposition party had won the elections for the first time in the history of Sordland. Although a loss and a vote of non-confidence for his party and rulership, Anton Rayne felt relief for the first time in all of these years of turbulence. Finally, the Morning had come for Sordland and her people.

_childDocuments_.review: A very well written game with a polished UI. The world building is very good and the game immerses you into its world, the characters all have different personalities, goals, and relationship to you based on your decisions, the world feels alive. Going from crisis to another crisis always keeps you on the edge and the game prevents you from feeling too secure at least that was my experience in my first playthrough as a reformist-centrist president. The game is also very replayable since you can always go down a different path. The only part of the game I felt could've been improved more could be epilogue, the way your re-election works doesn't make sense like you can pursue stuff like constitutional reforms, women's rights, bludish rights, workers' rights, healthcare, education, etc hard but they don't seem to be able to offset a stagnant economy, loss of your conservative base, and corruption allegations and you will come in third. The game doesn't make the factors playing into your re-election clear for instance in one of the reports it said almost 54% of women in the country supported me due to my women's rights legislation, so that would be almost 27% of the electorate, add to that additional liberal support, rural support, and bludish support, I don't see why USP would come third since the game tells you that they won a big majority last time despite getting like 40% of the vote.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished a run through the game, which took nine hours! I am very impressed by this title.It takes the visual novel format and offers a fantasy amount of options and directions which appear to matter to the progression of the story. There are one a few occasions where I was frustrated by the lack of an obvious solution/answer, in almost every situation a diversity of options are presented for how to progress.The story is good, the setting/world amazing and the characters likeable.For anyone interested in politics, cold war, american or eastern european, this game through it's fantasy setting manages to fit all of them into one nation, with you at the helm. I completely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I greatly enjoyed this game. It has a great story and intricate world building.In real life, Sordland would be a country in Eastern Europe or Balkans. The fact that its developers are Turkish certainly influences this. Beware some negative reviews, this is not a game where you easily impose American ideals and standards only to be loved by everyone. A lot of politics is compromise and you cannot please everyone. Sordland is a complicated land with ethnic and religious strife as well as history of civil war and authoritarian regimes. The country is at a crossroad between the old ways of Nationalism, Communism, or Capitalism. Sordland isn't a superpower but a nation trying to survive as the world slowly gets divided in a Cold War between the world's two big superpowers. What part it does or does not play in this conflict is entirely based on your actions and decisions.I ended my first playthrough as a Centrist Reformer who changed the constitution, improved rights of citizens and women, and joined NATO (I mean, ATO). My Anton Rayne did not fix the economy but resigned at the end of his term happy to spend time with his family, knowing that he brought real change to the country. I look forward to seeing how playing a die-hard Communist or corrupt Nationalist changes these decisions, outcomes, and story within game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be honest. This game is one of the best games I have ever played. It is a game where every choice matters, from in office, to your own family. With over 350k words in this story, the ways you can play this game is endless. Each of it's endings shocks you to the very core and it changes your stance on politics. Politics is where you are lied to and forced to make difficult decisions where someone will be mad with each choice. Suzerain IS Politics. This game has taught me so much about how the real world works and I think the point of this game is to change how you think on how the world works. No such thing is just White or Black. It's all gray. Every choice you take has a good and a bad. Every Ideology has a good and bad. Communism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Capitalism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Reformism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Authoritarianism is neither good or bad. It's grey. This game is a MUST PLAY if you are up for a challenge. My only complaint is that not enough people know it. -MJ

_childDocuments_.review: "Children will die because of this decision.  How does this administration sleep at night?"A great question posed by the Sordish newspaper "Radical".  The truth is, by this point late in my first term as President of Sordland, my long-term predecessor Tarquin Soll has appeared in my dreams.  Or should I say nightmares?  I'm not really sure.  But it a testament to the strength of the political world-building in  that Soll has infiltrated my subconscious, something that Dostoevsky achieved with  but few if any video games have.It also speaks to why [i/]Suzerain[/i] is my new favorite political simulator.  Most that I have achieved are high-level economic simulators that let you set essentially whatever policy you want, and see how it affects things at a statistical level.   (and presumably its sequel) is in this category, and is immensely unsatisfying, especially given its title.   does a little better by leaning into the "trends and forces" theory of history and making it so you generally have to bend to the demands of the populace or face unrest, but the trends pretty much move in one direction during its time period.   has multiple political parties and lobbying to pass legislation, but the situation remains high-level.  In , however, you are confronted both with the human impacts of your policies, as well as the impact of Sordland's legistlative body, the Grand National Assembly, and the Sordish Supreme Court.  Think Chief Justice Hawker is going to approve everything you do?  I wouldn't be so sure!The newspaper system is a thing of genius, as given the different viewpoints they advocate, it's almost impossible to satisfy all of their audiences at once.  And that points at what makes the game so compelling in general - you aren't going to make everyone happy.  Did George H.W. Bush make everyone happy?  Did Bill Clinton?  No.  Neither will you.  Your advisors will disagree.  Some of your policy choices will backfire.  The economy will fail to revive, or you will fall into a debt trap, or you might wind up angering your next-door neighbors in Rumburg, or perhaps all three.  And it's not just national policy, you've got a family to tend to - or ignore - at home, too.Which leads to the next point - the character building is on point.  In a remarkably short period of time considering how large the cast of characters is, the game builds the characters into people you know and care about.  You'll be amazed by some of their actions, reacting as you might to gossip about one of your old friends, and likely come to favor and grudgingly put up with others - and the ones that you favor and begrudge may be different than mine.I recommend playing your first playthrough as you would if you really were made president - favor your policies, make compromises, or don't - and see how it goes.  I've enjoyed a great high point driving on the newly-opened H-3 Highway from Lachavalen to Arvory, and a great low point... well, it's more like a  of moderate low points from a policy level, and one major disappointment in another character that I won't spoil for you.  I thought I'd be doing pretty well by Year 4 of my presidency, and instead I can point to some policy improvements that ought to pay off over the long term, a lot of things that haven't panned out so well, and a likely upcoming election loss if I can't find a rabbit to pull out of a hat somewhere.  Perhaps by trying to make everyone at least moderately happy, I've instead made everyone unhappy.Which leads to a final point - it's difficult.  So many games make it easy to fix things and make things so they seem to be going well, and  prefers to take the approach of "reality is difficult, and a game about it should be too".  It's a weighty game, despite occasional moments of levity.  If you want to govern a utopia, go play .  By playing  , you'll instead have some understanding of why Jimmy Carter said he couldn't have handled the stresses of being President at age 80.  You'll understand why all but the most stratospheric of presidents have a mixed legacy.  And you'll likely both want to become more civically engaged, and really not want to have the stresses and responsibilities of the highest offices at the same time.Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys reading and discussing public policy or politics.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a US congressional staffer and I have never played anything like Suzerain. It's a masterpiece. For one, this game made me significantly more thankful to live in the United States. For all of our problems, bribing politicians is not the cost of doing business and our neighbors are not say, warmongering monarchies. Differences with the American political system aside, there is no game on the market that captures political decision making so well. In essence, a great bulk of governing is being in a room with many different people giving differing opinions and having to make sense of why people are saying the things that they are.  That is also in essence, the core gameplay loop of Suzerain and thanks to excellent writing and characters, it succeeds in making this an engaging yet authentic experience. My only major complaint is the way legislation was handled. Bills from the assembly being sent to my desk often seemed to be presented at random and there was no discussions with any of my advisers prior to deciding whether to veto them. Considering the large impacts many of these bills have on the country, this was a surprising oversight in an otherwise excellent experience. Despite that flaw, as someone who participates in the political process on a daily basis, this game is the real deal. I bought the game on a lark so I know little about the background of the developers but a huge congrats to the team on a job well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is not a strategy game, but you'll manage a country. It's not a simu, but you'll end up having to decide major investments and chose an excluding path that will get you celebrated as a hero or direct to jail. It's not (only) a textual RPG, but you'll be playing the president of a country trying to enter the modern era, and also manage your relations with your family.Get ready to read a lot, a whooole lot of very well written stories, interlaced with lots of very well written wikis.And this is the main point : the world Suzerain takes place in is the main character of the game, and it absolutely rocks. Discover a 1950's alternative earth, with complex political issues, racial tensions, economical challenges, betrayal, suspicion, fake smiles and crooked diplomacy, greed, communication wars, ancestral feuds and game changing alliances, war, conspiracies and so on. The whole political part feels really solid, and lets you decide how you handle it : you're in charge of the fate of Sordland, and you can make a paradise from it, or give Sordlanders and the world the nuclear hell you think they deserve, it's up to you. Chose a political path, lie, cheat, stay true, betray or get betrayed, jump into the free market mutation or stick to planned economy, charm the Assembly or the oligarchs, please the generals or get a secret police, ban unions or sign treaties, launch infrastructure modernization or close borders, start a war, build peace, whatever, but don't forget : you're not alone coveting power.The whole game is pretty much linear, but the choices you make really make every run unique, and it's a good 50 hours or more run.If you feel like being president, enjoy challenges, political shenanigans, or just a very well written textual adventure, do not hesitate longer : Suzerain feels like playing a modern era Crusader Kings without the boring strategical map troop movements. Stick to the stories behind the curtains of power and leave the rest. The only blades in the game are the one you're gonna stab in your friends' and allies' back, or the ones they're gonna stick into yours. The whole feeling is pretty casual in the mechanical aspects of the game, but the story goes deep into the subject, and lets you go through a rollercoaster of emotions, which I think is the point of a good narrative medium.If you're bored with political games being too kind, not complex enough or afraid to face the harsh realities of the modern world, you're gonna enjoy Suzerain. A lot. And play it again, to see if a worse solution to a problem is not even funnier to play. It's not your usual strategic simulator and a system you will understand then dominate. It's more like riding a donkey on steroids with a bee nest sticked to its tail : enjoy the ride while it lasts, but in the end, you're gonna fall. And if you ever compare the before/after pics of presidents, you get why Torpor games did a tremendous job.Welcome the Dark Soulest Roguelike Political Simulator ever. Have fun. Be nasty. Your opponents are gonna be worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Unreal.  The amount of thought and care that went into this game is clear.  I played all seven hours at the time of writing in one complete playthrough.  This game is for those who want real, thought provoking content, as long as you don't mind text-based interactions.  I am already thinking about what I'm going to do in my next playthrough.  However, I don't know if I'll be returning to it all that quickly.  That's no slight to the game at all, it's merely that I don't think I can approach it with a fresh perspective until I finish thinking about everything that was brought up during my first run.  There may be political sims with more depth, or more choice options, or more characters, or more length...but I challenge you to find one that is more emotionally inviting and rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was worth every penny. The choices are vast, and the plot full of intrigue. Everyone around you is an enemy to Sordland - you are its lone savior. Left wing, right wing, centrist, liberal, conservative, - it doesn't matter where you stand, everyone will stab you in the back. Your only friend is the humble motorcade driver: Serge. He is the only one to appreciate you. Reward him well.In all seriousness, this game is amazing. If you enjoy text based adventure games, visual novels, political intrigue/politics in general, then this game is a must. It puts to shame games like "Democracy" which focus too heavily on the numbers side of things or "Tropico" which focuses too much on micromanaging. This is a story - it's your story. Your alliances. Your friends. Your enemies. Your backroom deals. Your politics. Your dreams. Your mistakes. Don't let the ironman save system dissuade you (there are no save files except "current"), this game is about finishing what you started, dealing with your mistakes, and realizing you won't be able to make the perfect choice. You're only human, President Rayne. A Morgna wes core!

_childDocuments_.review: Fake game with bogus choices. Between random options with random outcomes it constantly fails to inform the player of their progress. 1) People, who want a story with random unpredictable outcomes they had little agency in, may enjoy this. 2) People who like a sense that they contributed to the particular story that is being told will be disappointed. 3) What the software does is present a choice of undesirable options, unlikely outcomes, then sticks a tag to the player and pretends it was them.4) Some positive reception comes from players who replay this to figure out the different routes and play with meta-knowledge. Like in Groundhog Day. Totally breaks immersion in the first place. But also, the developments are gated by multiple event choices, so figuring out how to "unlock" them is difficult, and will lead to heavy railroading and boring repetition.5) Without common sense able to help much, players could methodically grind all the permutations to see what they do:But at that stage we are trying to wring out reward and content of a software that refuses to give it the normal way.6) Developers seem too young or inexperienced to see that all parts of this story are told from the rear end, and it's not working. If you are a peasant dreaming to be president, play this to see how other peasants failed in their imagination.

_childDocuments_.review: The best game available on the market  if you want a game which allows you to shape the country  you rule.  Suzerain gives you  freedom in choosing between different economic models, democracy or dictatorship, diplomacy or warmongering. The best part of this game is a broad cast of characters ,which are going to support or oppose you depending on your objectives, which make the game feel much more engaging than similar country-ruling games. Beware that if you try to do much at once you are likely to fail, as resources aren't limited and if you aren't careful you might end ruling a country in multiple crisis. I recommend starting cautiously and trying to achieve specific objectives and sacrificing others. Despite being a story driven the game has a high replayability value as you can see by the hours on some reviews and it is well worth the price especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Brilliant political simulator and story, perfect for anyone who enjoys games like the Campaign Trail or the old do it yourself adventures. 7.5/10Pros:-Extremely well thought out beginning that introduces you to the setting without an exposition dump.-Vibrant cast of characters who you can end up being allied with or completely opposed to depending on your actions.-Decent amount of freedom in choices-You will be punished for your actions and almost everything that goes wrong will be because of your choices, nothing ever comes out of the blue giving you a great sense of control.-Very fun to replay, either to go down a completely different path or fine tune the one you took before.-Very entertaining end screen.-The occasional extremely fun moments with dialogue, though these are less common than I'd like.-Can be quite difficult and punishing.-Decision making is very empowering, unlike any game I've ever played before.Cons:-Ending feels rushed, sometimes unsatisfying.-Dialogue sometimes feels clunky and lacks the character and wit that make games like Baldur's Gate and Pathologic so fun. You'll often find yourself skim through swathes of dialogue to get the gist of what people are saying. Definetly the biggest pitfall in the game.-Especially towards the end you don't get satisfying conclusions to storylines you might have been interested in. Who won the election after you're impeached? What happened to Frens Ricter? Did siding with the West ultimately tip the balance of power in the continent? These are all questions that, if answered, would go a long way to demonstrating how much of an effect your actions have.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a difficult game at times, as the choice you make really do leave an impact on how the story and narrative will unfold as you get later on into a play-through. There's also a steep curve in terms of knowing what decisions to make, and how they will affect your administration, depending on your administrations political leanings. What I especially appreciate about this game, is that unlike many other Diplomacy / Politically charged games available on STEAM, this one doesn't punish you for unfairly for having inherent conservative ideals when you play, if you play according to said ideals. It reacts in a fair and balanced manner, which is refreshing.Overall, it's the best of this sort of game I've played thus far, and I'm hopeful for an eventual successor.

_childDocuments_.review: Great political simulator. I have just finished my first run, and oh boy was it a wild ride. The game starts off with you taking the reigns as leader of a nation in economic and political turmoil.  I managed to make an amazing economic recovery by introducing some privatization and aligning myself with the capitalist nation of Arcasia. I even joined ATO (this game's version of NATO) to essentially neutralize the threat of my northern neighbor Rumberg who clearly was looking for a reason to invade me with their much more powerful military (which I also defunded to help the economic recovery). I managed to successfully reform the constitution through compromises, though it didn't go as far as I would've liked. I tried to be nice to everyone if they were nice to me. At my peak, it really seemed as though most people liked me, and I was massively popular among the general population for leading such an economic recovery and introducing reforms. I seemed all but guaranteed to win a second term in office to take my reforms further.Everything was going very well until it wasn't. Soon after I resumed playing today, I was informed that impeachment inquiries were being made about my dealings with the leading media company. Way back at the beginning of the game, I had decided to collaborate with the owner of the media company for both of our benefit. It was the only real corrupt decision I made all game, and I had mostly forgotten about it since I didn't even really need the help much. It was going well, until I made a fateful decision to create an anti-corruption police force. I guess I thought I could prevent them from looking into my dealings and instead they would bring down all the other corrupt officials, but looking back that was very foolish of me. Sure enough, while they were investigating the owner of the media company I cooperated with, they discovered the meeting I had with him at the beginning of my term. It wasn't long before they found out the content of that meeting. My Chief Strategist turned on me and spilled all the beans, probably because he was mad I didn't make him my Vice President after my previous one resigned. Upon this news breaking, most of my cabinet resigned and were disgusted with me since I gave the appearance that I was a pro-reform and democracy politician while also collaborating with a billionaire oligarch to rig the media in my favor. I was convicted of treason (by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court who I had sparred with many times before) and sentenced to life in prison, which I served for about 20 years before dying. If you are looking for a game where you get to make many choices and most of those choices truly matter, look no further than Suzerain. I can't wait to try again with a different plan to see what other results I can get.

_childDocuments_.review: Just completed my first play through at 14 hours in length.  It's been quite a ride to be honest.  The narrative driven experience is very well created.  Choices taken really do matter.  It's a reading marathon so if you are not up for lots of reading then this might not be for you.  I highly recommend this game though as it has kept me entertained for the entire duration of that 14 hours.  I'm already planning another run through with some different choices - I'm not going to spoil things for anyone by listing them here.  For such a low price this is a great game.  Thoroughly enjoyed it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an outstanding political simulator that gives you an incredible amount of room to make each and every playthrough different. You can't savescum, meaning you have to live with your choices. I just finished my first playthrough, and I can't wait to start another one.
