_childDocuments_.review: So I originally bought the game on GOG and joined the Suzerain discord server to help with testing and got a free copy.The game is so good, I honestly would haven't minded buying it twice. This game is a text RPG with a visual novel flair, your choices matter and one choice can harshly affect your ability to do things later on depending on how your characters react to you.This game gives you alot of room to maneuver politically and while it can come off with a bit of Western bias - you are perfectly free to succeed if you choose to go with a socialist economy and the like. This is a perfect game for any one person who loves political intrigue, a flair of rogue-like with it's iron-man save system and realistic character development.Certain endings are WAY harder than others (winning war vs Rumburg alone took me 15 playthroughs of testing) and replaying the game can come off as tedious sometimes, but if you're invested, it's easy to get past them just by space-barring every conversation that doesn't require your input for the country. All in all, I'd pay $60 for this game if they expanded it more and included DLC for a 2nd term.This is a great way for Torpor to get themselves world-wide acclaim as a game development company and I look forward with hunger and anticipation of their next product, Suzerain-related or not.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game, because it really tries and it does some things really well.But in the end I wouldn’t recommend it.The game tries to be a very realistic simulation, and a text based life and politics simulation. And to some degree it does that very well. The problem with the game is there’s no real way of getting feedback on your decisions. On my first play through I spend a long time, as most people would, trying to build support for certain government reforms. The game and the actors in it told me we would pass these reforms, everyone I talked to said they would support them, compromises were made and everything was looking great. Then the day of the vote comes and the No, but failure. Now that’s disappointing, but the problem for me is that I have no idea why the vote failed. Everything the game was telling me was saying otherwise. So maybe the NPCs were lying to me?In a way this realism is interesting, and maybe what some are after, but for me it makes for frustrating gameplay. I have no feedback on my decisions, and I have no idea what went wrong or when. Furthermore there is a forced autosave after every important event, so you can not go back and try things another way.The only way to try again is to, well, replay the last 12h. I don’t really feel motivated to do that.I generally like hard games, but for me I need to understand WHY I failed at something. Otherwise it becomes a frustrating trial and error, and combine that with no save system and you’re looking at either rolling with the punches and guessing at what you could do different on the next play through, or giving up.So on the whole, interesting game, but quite frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say about the game? Well to be honest the writing is great. Like extraordinary great. It will literally make you laugh and cry and the story is really relatable and not some politically-biased crap. There main problems about the game is that it's not really accessible. For a text-based game it's not acceptable to offer just support for one language. Having your game translated in at least a few languages greatly boosts sales and is really not impossible to finance even for smaller studios. Secondly I wish the game would support Steam remote play but that's probably not on the priority list. Another problem about accessibility is the lack of responsiveness from the gameplay itself. It's pretty hard to plan ahead when you have a hard time finding out how your decisions affected the country. There is a country overview and there are newspapers and reports but it's not easy to see the difference between what is fluff and what is a key result of your policies. Or take the budget for example. It's very hard to find out what budget you could spend if you have no idea how much money you will make back over the future. It would be much better if there are funds added to your budget each turn so you could plan. On the top of that the economic development will jump up and down immensely for no obvious reason. So the only system that really displays how you are doing is as reliable as an old rusty teaspoon.I wish I could rate this game neutral, but to reflect how torn I am I will give a thumbs down over my private account and a thumbs up over my curator page

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good political sim/visual novel. It is text-heavy (of course), and I think it's really well-written. I love how detailed the world of the game is, with many wiki-style entries for important places, ideologies, historical events, political groups and people. You can see how much love and effort went into this game.Highly recommended if you like politics and story-heavy games with meaningful choices. _childDocuments_.review: Without power, you can't make change.I loved this little game.  I found myself furiously reading line after line of text, thinking about the various political interests and constituencies that would either love or hate the directions I took  (and/or the way I communicated them), determining whether I needed to reach out for new political allies or protect my flank and shore up my base, and, most thrillingly, occasionally finding myself compromising on my own ideals (the way a great game will) to generate more power with which I could then pursue the policies I felt strongly about.I'm a political science grad and an attorney, and this game is very good on two levels.  First, it scores points for realism, in the sense that you're immediately confronted with the fact that you cannot get everything you want without angering damn near everybody.  You can't get rights and equality without prosperity, you can't get prosperity without security, and you can't get security without power. Therefore, power = rights?  This is heady political stuff.  And so I found myself trying to garner more and more power and partnering with very questionable political players at the risk of being considered a tyrant in order to enact the reform and humanitarian policies I set out to achieve.  The plight of being a leader forced to make compromise (with others and with yourself) is what this game brings to dazzling light.Second, it's a fun game to play.  I found the adaptive nature of the game and the cause-effect to be intuitive and sensible (even though the political realities could be frustrating).  The ambient music is nice, and the level of detail is perfect - unlike Mass Effect or Skyrim that have tomes upon tomes of background literature, the people who wrote the memos got the  that the reading is manageable and not so overwhelming that you skip it entirely.The only critique I will give is length of the game.  Admittedly, the game summary says it's about "your first term," and I missed that before playing - I was fairly disappointed when the game ended after being reelected (yay!  hint: be a centrist).  I realize that the game can't be a repository for decades of subsequent political developments, personalities, events, and consequences, but at the same  terms of additional gameplay, we're only talking about more text bubbles and map updates, right?  Doesn't seem too much to ask for another term, so that you can gun for reelection AND have another go at governing.  I digress, as I plan on going back as a nationalist dictator with a penchant for violence.  Also, is it possible to get into an extra-marital affair?  Let's find out.-Scooter

_childDocuments_.review: I was very optimistic towards this game given its glowing reviews and my love of choose-your-own-adventure games.  Unfortunately, the writing is inconsistent and largely dull, the characters are uninteresting, and the "choice" system is terrible.  Most of the "choices" you make (dialog options) do not matter in the slightest; often, these are variations on the same response or wildly different statements that go largely ignored.  As a result, it is often difficult to tell when the game is actually asking you to make a choice.  Sometimes, all the dialog options in a conversation are ignored and the only choice that matters is the last one (when an advisor asks what stance you'd like to take) while other times, seemingly probing dialog options very early in a conversation will lock you into a stance you didn't want to take.I really wanted to like this game and was hoping it would scratch that choose-your-own-adventure game itch, but ultimately, I couldn't bring myself to keep reading/playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is probably one of the more enjoyable political simulations that I've ever experienced. It is very different to the other games in the field such as Democracy and is far more story oriented. At times I felt as though I was very involved as President Rayne and making the decisions that would take Sordland forward but it is not without flaws. The writing is quite hokey at times with a clear SJW bent which does feel contrived given the mountain of other problems facing the country. Furthermore it does feel that your choices are binary in places and it's as simple as A or B. However there are some decisions that may have you second guessing and the consequences of your actions are not necessarily immediately clear. The codex of characters, organisations and regions is really well done and helps to immerse you in the story more, and the feeling of a world is something really missing from other games in the genre.Pros+ Immersive world+ Good soundtrack+ The weight in decision making+ ReplayabilityCons- The writing falls off a bit and at times feels forced- Abrupt and unsatisfying ending (there are multiple endings)Overall I can confidently recommend Suzerain for political nerds such as myself. If you like political sims with story this is for you. It's more akin to a visual novel than a sim but it is highly enjoyable while it lasts.

_childDocuments_.review: The best game I've played in a while - hands down. Work, life busyness and changing interests mean I don't play videogames anymore however this game changed that. Sinking a good amount of time (32+ hours) over the past week after work, I can heartily recommended this text-based choose-your-own-adventure game to anyone interested in strategy, resource management, politics (duh!), corporate decision-making, and roleplaying and immersion. This game sits at a unique intersection between all these things and does it with no competition. I'm immersed, submerged in rivalling political advice and suspicions of intrigue, and my girlfriend jokes I'm addicted. I also co-govern the country with her when she comes round. Suzerain rewards sound decision-making and attention to detail. It doesn't spoon feed you - you remember a detail from an hour ago? A suspicious gap on a potential political hire's resume? Factor them in your decisions and avert disaster. Good outcomes from your choices are seriously satisfying, and bad decisions leave you winded - it’s that well-designed. I have never felt so much suspense playing a videogame (or while watching a movie or reading a book) ever. I held my breath up to an important vote that could make or break my administration, I wondered if I had done enough, and... I'll stop it there. The story is well-crafted and well-written. Final comment: I work in the public sector, I like politics, and I like strategy. With that in mind, I seriously recommend this choice, Mr President.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really cool concept and pretty well executed as well. Also I really got into the story at first. However I feel as though you are set up to fail and in the end that just ruined it for me. You can no doubt min-max your way through the game by failing a few times first and knowing all the events and triggers. But that ruins the whole point of a story based game to me.I think the developers idea is that you are supposed to side with one of the few ideological groups in the game and not actually exercise your own judgement at all. Either you're capitalist, commie or a facist but oddly enough not a centrist as most decisions are without any nuance to them. So best way to play seems to be to pick one of the factions and go all in on them. And I'm sure you'll win...I'll give an example of lack of nuance: You can either choose to limit migration or leave it unregulated. It's a black and white decision that will piss off one of your two neighbors regardless of which way you go. Why can't I just regulate it on one border and leave the other one open? The leadup to that decision even said 'it's a nuanced decision' and then I'm given a binary option. A more options would even make sense in the story context as one border has some Taliban like terrorists on it and other has some actual civilized people.. FML.One other weird situation I had was when I asked my Gestapo to assassinate someone. Only for them to somehow poison the persons dog instead. My chief came back and literally said "The dog drank the poison instead." Like what in the name of..?! Did you pour it into the dogs water bowl and expect the assassination target to get down on all fours and lap it up from there? I can't even..So high marks for concept and technical implementation. But at its ultimate goal of being an actually fun game / engaging story I feel it falls short of. As such not really recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has solid writing that gives an authentic view into how complex and messy modern republican democracies are and how you must push your agenda while doing a political balancing act to actually stay in power. There is also a planned extension where you play as a monarchy, which will add an extra dimension to the game.The game is an RPG with a central narrative and different endings determined by certain choices during the story. It's not a grand strategy sandbox where you can freely choose to rule as a Dictator or communist leader and choose your own fate from there. Imagine Democracy 4 dynamics with a sprinkle of Disco Elysium world building, and a small splash of Tropico. If you're in the mood for a political visual novel with decent replay value, give it a try.In terms of specific complaints of the game (Minor spoilers ahead):-Be aware decision-making and the consequences are more scripted than it appears on the surface, in order to fit the narrative. Also there's a lot of dialogue to skip through when replaying. Remember, it's more of a visual novel than a sandbox.-It needs more romance options. Politicians can be scandalous and you should be able to romance at least one other person besides your wife, then have it become a scandal with consequences. You can accept blackmail, successfully cover it up, or have it leak to the public and be shamed, etc. The game is basically set up for a good scandal, but devs decided another character does the cheating, not you. Your task is to do damage control instead.-I find it odd the conservative faction are against privatization during a recession. Typically, wanting state control/big government is something the nationalists would want but not necessarily conservatives. The conservatives prioritizing fundamentalism over fiscal conservatism and not being flexible about it is just odd, but understandable somewhat given the world building (Sollism).
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's been said that a good game is a "series of interesting decisions".Essentially a "Choose Your Own Adventure" type game, Suzerain is a game where the central mechanic is making interesting decisions. In addition to the interesting decisions Suzerain is populated with interesting and believable characters, competing factions with competing interests in a believable setting of rival nations. Indeed, it is the interesting characters and setting that make the decisions feel consequential and the gives the game an impetus that I've encountered in few other games. I'm not at all a fan of "novel" type games, but this hooked me early and has kept me hooked to the extent that I have been at it for ten hours and will definitely finish it. There are no "walls of text". All of the information is presented in the form of punchy conversations between the player and the many characters in the game. There is also a comprehensive codex, but I found that I used it more as an aid to inform and remind and didn't feel the need to cram loads of lore to get into the setting.Unlike many of these type of political simulation games it *doesn't* make you feel like no decision is a good one, and nor does it distill politics down to a series of numbers that players must balance or push. Every decision has consequences and no decision will appease every constituent. Sometimes consequences are unintended, but all of them can be reasonably predicted by paying attention and immersing yourself in the lore of the setting, which is essentially a fictional analogue of 50's Cold War Europe.I don't know whether I played it towards the developer's political biases, but I felt like I was making progress for the betterment of the country and society. That said, there are some agonizing decisions and some you'll definitely that wish you could take back. But rather than regretting these decisions, or making you feel like you have messed up the game, they become part of your story, and ones that make the game more believable. As of writing I haven't completed the game, but I'm deep into chapter 4 of 4, and there is definitely a feeling of things "coming to a head".And then, just as I thought I couldn't be happier with the game (which really is great) in Chapter IV the developers drop in a Toto reference just because they could. The sheer audacity of it makes the game worth playing all by itself and has to be experienced to be believed.It's brilliant!A great game. Decisions keep coming at you at a pace that makes you want to keep playing to see how things turn out. Give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Very simply, there is another review around that states "I did what I would have done and it worked out." I am here to say, I did what I would have done and  and during the next playthrough I . On the third try, . Lastly, I know from accidental spoilers that you can , etc., etc., etc...The fact that my game was different than the other review, and from the other games I had played, is what you're looking for in a good review for Suzerain. The game is intricate, enjoyable, and replayable. You definitely feel like the leader of a struggling nation. Your allies feel like allies, your enemies feel like enemies, and both can become the other as you understand (and exploit) their desires and weaknesses to help you secure a future for your country. The creator put a lot of thought into the personalities and paths you can discover, and you can easily get at least 4-5 solid playthroughs before even considering the Rizia DLC. The price is worth it. You should buy it. That said, there are two flaws in the game:1) The map is beautiful, and the icons are nice, but it doesn't really change in the way that a usual map-based grand strategy game does. If you're into beautiful maps, you'll love it. Just don't expect to paint it. The game is beyond that simple objective anyway.2) The entire game is dialogue-driven. You can make the dialogue go faster by clicking through the narrative, but be careful not to accidentally click a confirmed response by your character, because there is no going back. For this, you need to engage with much of the same dialogue during subsequent playthroughs, and so replayability suffers a bit. However, I think it would hurt the game to offer simple, dialogue-skipping options such as (Stay Sollist) or (Push Reforms) or (Be Moderate). The feeling of being an actual person among actual people is unique, and I'm personally okay with this singular issue with replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: After my first play though I must say that the game was interesting up to the end. Addictive, Specially if you find interactive stories appealing. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a game replete with... if not flaws, then 'even better if' moments; minor limitations that prevent it from receiving an assignation of 'excellent'. In many ways, it's reminiscent of the 'choose your own adventure books' - it's a political storytelling exercise rather than a simulator, and, as such, player agency is reactive, not proactive; you will get to make choices in response to events or as a result of the urging of your advisers, but you do not have the freedom to chart your own course in quite the way I might have liked (say, by taking the initiative on foreign policy *before* things start happening, or allocating more than a budget of '+1' to a particular branch of government). Its world is incredibly detailed - perhaps too detailed, or else in need of a narrator, as the sheer amount of text can be a little overwhelming at times. And yet. I can honestly say it gripped me like an electromagnet. With every decision, be it seemingly inconsequential or blatantly world-changing, I found myself second- and third-guessing every tough call I had to make. It's the first game in years where I found myself completely caught by the 'one more click' mentality, and then I'm there at four in the morning after losing my re-election campaign, wondering what I did wrong - or if I actually *did* anything wrong. After losing and seeing my Anton Rayne live out the rest of his life in epilogue, making wine and reconnecting with his son, the game asked me if I had any regrets. I can't honestly say that I would have done anything differently, so perhaps my honest progressive reformer was only meant for one term? At any rate, 'losing' didn't give me any sense of dissatisfaction.I can already tell that this is a game I'll be revisiting many times, in spite of its limitations. 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game very much, yet the tedious conversations that have little to no impact on your relationships combined with the puzzling responses from the NPCs, and, frankly, weird responses that don't match the situation are deeply frustrating. Coupled with the general lack of depth, the result is a game that is rather wearisome to play. Resource management - such as it is - functions at the macro-level and isn't particularly interesting because once you've made a decision, you're unable to make any further adjustments. The political component lacks nuance and the NPCs behave like caricatures. There's no ability to truly adapt to changing circumstances and the game moves inexorably forward in what is essentially an unenjoyable choose-your-own-adventure. If you're looking for something thoughtful, enjoyable, and nuanced with a high degree of replayability, this is not the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: As a devoted fan of political simulators  text-based/visual-novel style games, I had my eye on this for some time before it released. I can honestly say that it far surpassed any of my expectations. It was extremely engaging and I often found myself forgetting that the world that Sordland inhabits exists only within the game itself.Playing through the story felt like watching a prestige television drama, and I often found myself emotionally exhausted after playing through major story events. The characters (including the man you control) were believably human and each had realistic strengths, flaws, goals, and ideals. If you, like me, strive to reform the government and resist the machinations of the "old guard," you will often find yourself frustrated by setbacks—unmotivated or unwilling politicians, reactionary elements in Sordland, even internal and external threats from Sordland's neighboring countries. Of course, this makes it so much more rewarding when you manage to succeed.This is not to say that that is the only way to play the game. Though I have no experience doing so, you can increase Sordland's national defenses and become isolationist, ramp up the military and become a warmonger, or devote yourself to working closely with allies resembling either the United States or the USSR at the height of the Cold War.The visuals are simple but crisp (the game map is represented by an actual political map) and the soundtrack is amazing: intense at the right moments, relaxed when it needs to be. With the recent overhaul, the UI has become even more informative and intuitive while retaining everything that originally drew me to it. The mechanics are also simple to learn, allowing the focus of the game to remain on the story.Overall, my only regret after playing this game is that I will never again be able to experience it for the first time. Luckily, the Rizia DLC will be releasing soon! I  recommend this game, especially if you share my interests; 10/10 is not enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a deeply rewarding and deceptively challenging text-based game. I've felt sorrow and unconstrained joy at various points during my three playthroughs. Overall, it's a good "third world Central-Asian/Eastern European sim" game. The more I've played it, the worse my outcome seems to be. I almost fixed the economy until I enacted two new taxes. I almost got the constitution modified until I botched a Supreme Court Justice interview. I've seen friends become enemies and colleagues become adversaries. I've seen social progress stonewalled and international tension boil over. This game frustrates and engages me. As a whole, definitely worth a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: In a word: obsessive. A game you start playing and then look at your watch and realise you've been playing for 3 hours non-stop. Not just a "one more turn" game, but one that is incredibly compelling as all your choices are taken into account. You take over the presidency of Sordland, a politically and economically troubled, socialist republic - it's future now in your hands. Will it be dictatorship, democracy, planned economy, crony capitalism or your best effort in between? The game allows you to pick your path.The basic nature of the game is that of a Choose Your Own Adventure, but with so much detail on its characters, history and geography. The quality of the writing is high, yet there are inklings that the creators were leaning more towards liberalism than conservatism and you don't get to argue much in favour of how things may have been better pre-revolution. My one criticism is that the game doesn't have much nostalgia for the old times. The second President of Sordland is the political figure that most conservatives rally behind - a corrupt, tyrannical monster. I hope the upcoming Kingdom DLC goes some way to allowing greater freedom in this respect (I'd love to play as a monarch in a modern setting). Still, it would have been nice to have been able to invite the old monarchy back from exile, if only to be able to serve as private citizens - and show conservatives could be something other than racists in one group, and scheming backstabbers in the other.I recommend you act precisely as you want to during your first playthrough - don't try to game the system, don't read guides or spoilers, and don't feel too upset about how the game reacts to your choices. I fled the country after my first playthrough - but I left with some satisfaction that my family were safe, and still loyal to me - and that I had laid the groundwork for future success. I wanted to go for a "perfect" run for my second playthrough, which I have just completed. Sordland has emerged as one of the biggest economies in the world, the envy of its neighbours. I am now waiting for Update 2.0 before I give this a third playthrough - where I intend to run an authoritarian regime and set myself up as a dictator for life. I can't wait.

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of things this game could improve upon, but for what it was - it was an incredibly gripping playthrough and I was very sad when it came to an end because I wanted to keep playing forever. The positives: - World building. You become incredibly invested in what happens. - Realism. You can't make everyone happy but you can navigate their disapproval the best you can.- Introspection. Do you sacrifice your in game economy for your real life morals or do you do something bad to be able to hopefully do more good down the line with your increased funding? The negatives: - Lack of saves. When you make a mistake or if you experience unexpected consequences out of no where, you just wasted 5+ hours of your life because you can't go back to an earlier save or roll back a decision. In some games it makes sense, but for a game where very little will change on your replay ....... I have no desire to sit and read through everything again to try to find a new ending. - Questionable logistics of certain events. For the game to constantly say you've done an amazing job and you've fixed the economy and managed to improve the lives of all of your citizens and increase Sordland's international standing, and then let you lose your bid for reelection felt ... off? It left me wondering how you could actually win the reelection when it didn't inform me of mistakes I made to fail. Overall: amazing game, worth every second spent on it, but would massively benefit from a guide, more meters to gauge your citizens' approval, party approval, etc, so you know what you need to work on, and a better save system.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a phenomenal game. I haven’t seen anything like this ever, it swept me off my feet. I couldn’t recommend it more.The first time I saw Suzerain I thought It was some kind of political sim, or just a plain old grand strategy game. But to my surprise it was part of the “choose your own adventure” genre and the only gameplay was making decisions in text form. Nevertheless I was instantly hooked on. The game has an ingame codex about everything of interest, it works more or less like the dialogue system in Morrowind. In the first 10 or so hours I did nothing else but to read most of the codex. The attention to detail on everything was breathtaking. It had detailed histories of most of countries, it explained the alternate ideologies and even had information on every single company of interest, not to mention all the expansive biographies of relevant, and not so relevant characters to the main story. But that in itself is not the thing they did the best, as they say the devil is in the details – they made it in parallel to our reality. Meaning you can contemplate on real issues, their ramifications and ultimately discover your own personal views on the various matters. The more I read, the more I questioned everything I knew and believed. If that was not enough to immerse myself in the world of Suzerain I was met with a diverse cast of characters. Which ranged from an alcoholic best friend to a power hungry judiciary. As the storyline is concerned it was nothing short of perfect. It had high intensity drama, as well unexpected plot twists and most surprisingly quite a lot of real life references. I was so enthralled at some parts that I felt like it was real, to be frank I even shed a couple of tears. The game is extraordinary but not without flaws. The one thing that enraged me is that the decision making can feel static at some moments. I am specifically talking about taking some dialogue option which seemingly doesn’t have an impact to the story, but to the contrary it has. This can be an issue as it dictates relationships and further events, but I don’t think it’s something that can’t be fixed.This game is a must for everyone who has the time to play through it. Its price is adequate, for it has about 26 unique endings which gives it a lot of replayability value, but for the sake of saving money I will recommend waiting for Suzerain to be on sale. But at the end of the day it's not only a game, but also a medium for understanding the real problems of the day. Not only does it address real issues but makes YOU make the real hard hitting decisions. Will you be different, as you think you’ll be or will you understand that this is a thankless job.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of review I have completed two playthroughs. Summary: A solid and enjoyable text-based political RPG that will keep you engaged and guessing. Definitely worth a go at this price point.I was looking for a political RPG style game as I wanted to try something new. Suzerain is a great place to try and immerse yourself in this type of game especially for less experienced players in this genre. From the get-go the writing pulls you in and is intriguing. The story very quickly chucks you into chaos which requires you to make a string of critical choices which impact a number of events over the course of the game. It is all a balancing act and this adds a lot of replay value. My two main criticisms of this game are related to the feeling that the game seems rushed near the end. So first is pacing, which is actually well paced until you get to the final 1.5 acts. Events move along far too quickly during these sections of the act, some critical decisions that you make here either seem to have little no impact whilst other decisions have too great of an impact or are not given enough time to have an impact. The final act in particular seems to move way to quickly and I am sure it was rushed. The second problem I have alluded to in the previous section which is about consistency and sometimes the lack of depth in some of the decision making processes. If memory serves me well than there is not an instance where you ever initiate any actions. Rather as President you only seem to react and accept outcomes. For example, during the alliance talks there is really no room to negotiate even though you are there precisely for that reason, to negotiate. You are there just to please you opposite number. PROS: - Greatly written narrative that is engaging and intriguing. - Lots of critical decisions to make which is greatly adds to the immersion. - Clean UI that is easy to follow and study info. - Replayability CONS: - Although a great narrative is being told the story doesn't really belong to you. Perhaps this was intended by the developers.- Limited game modes. I think Suzerain can benefit from a 'Free Mode' or 'Marathon Mode' in the post-game. If you want to play as a full blown dictator, go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent choose-your-own-adventure political novel about leading your minor power country through turbulent times. The writing is well crafted, and aside from a few anachronistic terms that have been created in the recent past (personal stimulus checks, the deep state), you could easily be fooled that you're looking at a 1960s snapshot. Make no mistake though, just because it's a choose-your-own-adventure doesn't mean that it's easy to make it through. Your actions and dialogues have consequences, many of which can take a long time to be felt. Characters have personality and agendas, which can and do conflict with whatever you decide to do. You need to not only read the text, but also catch subtext and read between the lines if you wish to be anything close to successful. Your economic decisions also take time to fully develop, and can have especially nasty surprises. Do not think that the only effect of your policies is what is written on the page, or you will run into trouble.My personal favorite character is Lileas Graf, as though I disagree with her on ideologically, I can still find common ground with and sympathize with her a lot in other areas, even with a communist Rayne. She is no strawman Sollist (conservative, roughly speaking), and I respect her for that, even though she tends to be my antagonist.The game's slow burn pace does hurt it in subsequent playthroughs, as it takes awhile to go through the opening stages again, and the rude economic surprises are not nearly so welcome when you're trying to go through alternate endings and have to slog through hours of work to test something new. Your budget in particular is hugely influential, and a screwup here WILL turn your run into a slow motion crash no matter what. From what I can tell it is nearly impossible to make it through Rayne's term blind without a deficit, unless you purposefully keep a huge surplus or read a guide. The trial and error it would take to unravel the economic game on your own would take hours, so if you want the best endings possible, either grab a guide or prepare to trial things for a looong time. Still, if you like reading a book's worth of material on Cold War politics, you should definitely pick up this game and give it a run or two. There are entire aspects of the plot that go untouched in certain routes, so you definitely get additional content out of trying another path. As to the plot itself, I'll say this: Everyone has an ideal that they want to make reality, Everyone. How much are you willing to bend in order to make real change? And what happens if you compromise without an agenda of your own? Well, good luck Mr. Rayne. You'll need it. A morgna wes core, Vectern sis da!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game that finally scratched my itch for a political simulator. It's a narrative choose your own adventure kind of game, but I found the choices and their outcomes compelling and enjoyed turning Sordland into a communist state, an seeing the different challenges and problems that emerge, even if I got overthrown by a military coup in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Started a welfare state with the best education/healthcare/equal rights system in the continent, avoided WW-III, drove the country to a depression owing to long-term economic plans that'll take fruition in the next term; got impeached by Old Guard purist conservatives for using connections to get my dumb-ass son to University since he failed his exams. 10/10 will rot in jail again Eff Luci   en.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very detailed and at the same time, well written. It seems to have captured the immediacy of your decisions in the backdrop of a well-written story and world that is both believable and complex with the range of decisions that have to be made over different ideological terrains. I'm barely an hour into it and I'm completely hooked. The music isn't bad, the graphics and interface are simple clean and well organized. For 14 dollars CAD this game is great value.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best interactive novels and political simulators out there. This game doesn't preach whether communism/capitalism is good or bad, but instead, it puts you in the shoes of a president so you can make your own decisions and see its consequences.10/10 would recommendIf you like political fiction and interactive novels, this will be the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, lots of choices that very much influence the path you put your country on, i only got one ending so far with a 16 hour first playthrough. I recommend this game for anyone who likes visual novels, enjoys political sims, or for someone just looking for something new and fresh to play. I look forward to seeing more from the devs, A Morgana Ves core,  Vectern sis da!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent choose-your-own-adventure style look into becoming the president of a fictional yet familiar nation and trying to guide it and yourself to success through whatever means you choose. Will you push through your reforms through back room deals or try to stay true to your convictions?Held my interest throughout - and I am eager for more like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic political choice based game. Really enjoyed the story and character development. Lucian is the GOAT. Started riots, went to war, had a Great Depression, betrayed the people, betrayed foreigners, supported foreigners, accepted bribes then nationalized said business --- obviously you shouldn't give me any modicum of power.Waiting for Suzerain 2 --- I want my second term and world domination ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin? This is, in all honesty, one of the best games I have ever played. It is a political simulator rpg that masterfully grasps the functioning of a presidency, a country and a world. Where other political simulators are often limited in their scope, Suzerain succeeds in highlighting every factor that matters. The press their reactions, the backroom politics, the international ramifications of a certain decision, ... - it's all there.Every decision - no matter how small - has an impact and shapes the game environment around you. I have found this game to be a true blast to play, and it has become one of my favourite games of all time. There's no doubt that I'll be replaying many times to try out different paths, as there are so many to choose from. I'd like to really commend Torpor games for this masterpiece, and I wouldn't mind seeing some more additions or similar games to this being released: it's a very refreshing experience.To all those who generally like political sims, decision- and strategy-based games: pick this game up. It's truly worth it. If you don't, you might be disappointed, though I'd still reccomend simply trying it out: you never know! 10/10, will play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: VERY good political simulator. Amazing lore, story, and characters. Decisions you make *heavily* impact you later down the line, and since you can't save, you have to deal with the unforeseen consequences of your decisions. The game also offers a ton of replay ability, as one playthrough you can be a full-on communist revolutionary reforming the constitution, and the next you can be an ultra-capitalist declaring a state of emergency and undermining basic human rights. The sheer amount of options is insane, and this game is fantastic.I demand a second term.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: What a great game where you constantly wonder if you are making the right decision. In the end, I really felt like, as a player, I really made an impact on this fictional world. Trying not to be too hot headed or not act at all. Thinking about larger consequences and managing personal relationships in the game. I sense the game is rather challenging and one wrong move (and an unforgiving save system - which I love) can make you reel. You should not ignore the news reports or the city updates - it is a good brief for what lays ahead. In terms of replayability - I am sure it has some - but the story I formed as a player felt great and some tough choices early on meant that in the end they paid off.Great game for a strategic thinker.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent, if quite difficult, game.  It's a bit more "choose your own adventure" than political simulator, but it does a good job of showing a republic on the tipping point in the Cold War.  I do wish there was more chances to reverse a decision after you've come to it, or to negotiate deals with other powers.  But the game is a vital and interesting story set in a (fake version) of an area of the world and time in history that is not sufficiently covered today.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game recommended and at first it does look like an exciting political simulation. Unfortunately the dialogues are very long winded and it's a LOT of reading. The world building is great with all the detail, but I very much prefer a more condensed experience. I enjoyed playing it for 2 hours, but I'm going to request a refund, because I don't see myself playing this for much longer. While I'm curious how the story will unfold, this is just too much on the reading and not enough on the strategic decision making side. TL;DR: This is unfortunately more a visual novel than a strategy game.I wish I could give a neutral review, as this is certainly an entertaining game IF that genre is your taste.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a hard game to recommend. The story is rich and engrossing, but there is so little information to help guide your decision making. You think you are turning the economy around only to find out the growth graph is meaningless. It points practically straight up for dozen turns in a row, you still end up in a depression. You make a series of decisions and there is no feedback on what those decisions influenced. Very confusing interactive novel, but still a great story.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A well-written and intriguing experience if you enjoy political thrillers. The main caveat is that a blind run will most likely end in failure, as the game does not give you enough information to succeed without foreknowledge. I guess the idea is to replay it until, with enough experience (trial and error), you get an ending that satisfies you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: this game is amazing. i just have some recommendations that i think would make the game way better.-remove or fix authority. you never have enough authority to complete anything worthwhile, i say just overhaul authority and make the amount of authority gained based more on the happiness of your citizens,  and military might.-add more in detail war gameplay, as well as more options to control troops and station them beforehand.-more industry, and military industry options, like bombers, agriculture and things like that through decrees.- make the industries cost less to build. they should really only take around 0.5 energy per turn per each one,  1 energy per turn is just too costly to get anything done, because they eat up so much power, and you usually go into a deficit as soon as the game starts so it doesnt really give you any chance to build stuff, especially when you only have 2 options to increase power output in the early turns.- more diplomacy options, like more accessibility into trade, and actual dialogue with other continents other then Merkopa.( and i want to be able to promote monarchist revolution as Rizia with graces help across those continents, and some options to become a colonial superpower by colonization, or with diplomacy by promising them that they wont struggle as much as they have been by themselves if they were just under your direct rule)might add more recommendations later if i think of anyalso any developers seeing this, these features these are just suggestions so feel free to use them

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't felt the need to review a game in years, but this game has made me do it. Suzerain is a great experience filled with intrigue, serious decision making and tense moments. I cheered at successes, felt my heart sink as my goals became filled with road bumps only to cheer yet again when I over came them. The game looks simple, and it is, with a simple but appealing map to look at with newspapers and discussion to show the workings behind the map, you will be looking at this screen for the vast majority of the game.However, that's not a bad thing as I think the writing overall is superb, I genuinely felt connections to the characters, my friendly driver Serge, my Cabinet and my Wife. And that's what this game is to me, I feel like a president, I feel like I have the power to change the nature of the country, of these character's lives who I either loved or despised (Not for bad writing, but for their corruption, bigotry etc). This immersion made each choice I made serious, I thought through things hard, especially with no ability to save manually meaning once I've made my choice, I've made it (At least outside of conversation, you can reload if you miss-click in those) which further made me more invested as I thought over ever little thing that could go wrong in the future.Overall, I think the game is really well written and takes serious thought from the player to do. I have only done the democratic reformer route, and even then I saw so many opportunities to shift my decision to more controlling or less... wholesome decisions. The game is gripping, fascinating and while simple, very immersive to me. I give it a great rating and while £12 seems like a lot for a text based game, I can assure you there's possibility of replayability with different paths, choices and endings, some bad, some good but all interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best entries I have seen into the underexplored genre of narrative/strategy hybrid games.The presentation is excellent, the characters are likeable, the world is interesting and generally believable, the arc of the game is logical and the choices feel consequential.There were only a few instances where dialogue seemed to forget past decisions, and they were largely inconsequential. As that's always a major difficulty with games of this sort, I think that's quite good. I should note that your experience with games of this sort is heavily dependent on your individual playthrough. I have only completed one playthrough, so while for me the game worked very well, I can't say how well the game adapts to different choices.That all being said, I do have some concerns about the flow of certain events, such as , and the . It also feels, at least in my playthrough, that the . In general the last chapter of the game felt a bit weaker than the earlier parts.Additionally, there were a few instances that may have been bugs, as the budget seemed to change without explanation a few times and it was never clear exactly how the economic situation bar was supposed to work.Even with those issues, it's an excellent game. I look forward to another playthrough, and I'd be very interested to see the developers explore the concept further in another game.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain. What can I say about this game other than that it is fantastic? This game has got to be one of, if not the best political strategy/sim games that I have played. Suzerain allows you to lead the Republic of Sordland (a nation in the middle of an economic crisis) under the Rayne administration in whatever way that you would like. Do you want to transform your country into a totalitarian Oceania-esque police state? Maybe you'd like to see your nation transformed from an authoritarian democracy into a worker's republic and align yourselves with the communists? Or perhaps you'd even like to make Sordland a neo-liberal stronghold and an economic superpower? In Suzerain, you can do just that! It is also presented in a believable way, with in-depth things like discussions of policy with your ministers, to managing foreign relations and considering other countries views on your domestic policies. The thing is, though, that you are not free from the consequences of your decisions and ambitions. Yes, you can transform Sordland into a socialist utopia, but do so carefully, as you could easily upset the conservative wing of your party and the general staff, risking a coup. Not only that, but all of your decisions on economics have significant and heavy impacts; you will notice if your policies are successfully implemented or have failed.The lore and story of this game is amazing, too, with histories of the various continents and countries all written out, to even something as seemingly small as the histories of individual companies and corporations. Pair this with a well-told story and memorable characters (like, all of them), all with complete backstories, and you have a believable and extremely immersive world that will involve you almost instantly; you'll feel like you are living in East Merkopa.I should also mention that the soundtrack for this game is lovely, and really adds to the relief and tension of some portions of the game.However, something that I have noticed with Suzerain is that some concepts are left rather vague, like the passage of time and the economy. Timespans between turns can range from a day or two up to months. This can make it rather hard to understand where you are in your presidential term. As well, the economic health of your country is simplified to a bar graph of projected economic growth or shrinkage, but you do not get precise values for important economic factors like unemployment, inflation, and GDP from this, and you only learn these at specific meetings with your minister of economy- it isn't readily accessible information apart from that. These don't impact the overall quality of the game too much, though, and are just things I've noticed to keep in mind.In the end, if you haven't played Suzerain before, go ahead and pick it up, even if you aren't a very big fan of text-based games! It is just amazing, and definitely worth the asking price considering the quality!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Had it less than a week and already played 2 full games (first game honest good leader, second game corrupt murderous leader - both fun to play). I will start a new game for a 3rd time and go for the anti-oligarch, not corrupt route (I don't want to be impeached this time). I just wish the game didn't end after the first term. I'd have loved the game to continue for a 2nd term in office for another 4 years. Overall I'd score this 9/10. Excellent game with lots of depth.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm loving this game, its the sort of political simulator that I've wanted for a few years, with everything that's going on in the world. Although it's essentially a text-only game, the added portraits and map really bring the game to life and help create a truly living, breathing world in your imagination.You make decisions at every point and there are so many people to talk with and side with or against.... it really is a very very interesting and in-depth game that covers so many political aspects.Talking to your key strategist, heads of economy, agriculture, education, military, along with shady media and corporate barons in the shadows.... The game really tells a fantastic story that will stick with you for a long time.With apparently 9 different endings, I am sure that once I have completed my first run through in my preferred political style, it could be fun to play with different ideologies.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really like that I have to click through the same conversations to replay the game. Sure you'd get new conversations eventually with different decisions but I'd have to slow down my clicking through the scenes I've already been through if I don't want to accidentally skip the new ones. Plus you won't see the results of the new playthough until 8 hours after starting the new game. It's just tedious clicking through. I like Democracy 3 better as it's just a top down political simulator that I can tinker with and see the results immediately. No faffing about with the same endless dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a very complex, intriguing political simulator with a wealth of different outcomes and player choice. 9/10 for me.The biggest thing I want to commend the devs for is their fair and pragmatic approach to the different political philosophies that exist in the game's lore as well as their real life counterparts. As a very politically involved person, I am always interested in finding a political sim that actually offers some levels of broad political depth and intelligence, and not just "freedom and liberty vs tyrannical 'radicals'" liberal slop. Suzerain offers that intelligent depth in its politics, and I am most pleased to finally play a politically oriented game that does not portray socialist governments as cartoonish prison cities with egotistical dictators. Do you have a radical plan for Sordland? Awesome! you could definitely achieve your goals, but you have to play it smart. This game takes place over the course of a single 4 year term. Know your limits, how to spend, who to ally with, and how to compromise. Whether you aim to bring the next socialist revolution, maintain the status quo, or go full gamer mode on women and  minorities (if you're some kind of psychopath), there is most likely a path for you. highly recommend for anyone that likes visual novel/style games and politics.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: After having played a bit of the 2.0 update, I can say that most of my issues with timewasters have been resolved. The game now lets you save your state (heh) and even Ironman mode has some pretty liberal autosaves that you can revert back to. Great improvements.Interesting world and narrative, if a bit derivative of Cold War era nations and ideologies. There's other reviews you can read if you want to know about the plot and worldbuilding. Good for one or two playthroughs if you get it on sale. I can't recommend however a game that doesn't respect your time.Your first playthrough will end in failure, most likely. Maybe in your second one you learned to avoid the mistakes you made the first time around and clutched a better outcome. Or maybe you used a walkthrough - I didn't but it's okay either way. So now you want to start exploring some of the zanier political paths, like a being a secret police wielding dictator or a communist. That requires a lot of trial and error and the game discourages experimentation due to its boneheaded insistence on making every run an Ironman run. There will come a point in the later chapters where an opaque choice you made earlier will ruin your entire run. This means restarting and sitting through the intro quote, prologue and initial chapters - which atmospheric at first, are now frustratingly slow text crawls and transitions and scenes you've read before. It's not an exaggeration to say this portion can take up to 2 hours or more before you catch up to where you were before the restart. And then you'll most likely have to do it again. A worryingly large amount of reviewers have 40+ hours in the game. Some even have more than 100. This is too much for a CYOA game. The game doesn't have 40 hours of fresh content. It has a maximum of 20 hours of fresh, original writing - the rest is just nuisance. And you'll have to put up with a lot of nuisance to get to the good bits. Is it worth it? In my opinion, no.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is at it's core a choose your own adventure book, where you're making decisions and set things will happen because of your choices. And yet... it's more. It's so captivating! It's got a lovely map, showing off the various towns, where you'll see news reports from your actions. It's got characters that all have their own personalities and goals (that you don't know). It's got tough decisions. Well done to the devs on this. I've very much enjoyed it so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Having completed my first playthrough, I believe I'm ready to review.Suzerain is very much like a 'Choose Your Own Adventure' novel. Except that it's about x20 more complex.You play as the leader of a small country. In what appears to be a fictionalized version of north-eastern Europe.The entire game is based around making decisions. However, that's pretty much all you do. It's like if you took away all of the gameplay from 'Fallout: New Vegas' but left only the dialog choice sequences. That might sound bad, but it's actually quite enjoyable.This is a game for people that have a deep understanding of politics, or people that want to. There are a number of factions. Nationalists, conservatives, socialists, communists, oligarchs, and an ethnic minority hellbent on terrorism. It's not as simple as picking a side, however. As you'll need multi-partisan support to accomplish anything.The number of branching paths is staggering. With every decision having a ripple effect.For instance, I made some deals with the democrats to get a bill passed. However, this angered the conservatives. 18 months later, and the most conservative member of my cabinet resigns. That character then went on to challenge me in the primaries. And I was defeated!I would like to give more examples, but I can't. It would ruin the game. Because the only thing you do is read, make decisions, and deal with the results.I have only two significant complaints about the game.First, there's actually a little  story. It took me around 15 hours to complete the game for the first time. (It'll probably take you a lot less time. I read slower than most people.) As such, I'm reluctant to continue my second playthrough. It may be months (or even years) before I'm ready to go again.This is compounded by allowing only one save file. Which auto-saves. I want to see the results of alternative actions, but not if it's going to take 15 hours to get through.Second, the game's writers have a clear bias. The democratic socialists are presented as people just trying to make the world a better place. They are compassionate and honest. The conservative nationalists are resistant to any changes at all. They are paranoid, racist, fearful, angry, hate-filled, xenophobic, religious, traitorous, and irrational.If that seems a bit one-sided? That's because it is. That said, it's a fictional version of real life. So, I feel like I can let it slide.This is a game for people that listen to talk radio, read a lot of world news, are politically active, vote, or care about the future. You also gotta love the slow burn. It's definitely not for everyone.{SPOILER!}Result screen for my first playthrough:

If you make well thought out choices, you can lead your country out of a recession. It basically took me two playthroughs to get what I call the "perfect" ending. I would love to see another game from these guys, really was a good time. It is basically a graphic novel, if you don't like to read then this may not be for you. Either way, great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. Lovely music, the writing is great as well. Definitely a commentary on Turkish Coup history as well. But there is a bias towards a certain take on the history and that definitely is felt through out the game. Soll feels like an analogue to Kenan Evren but they are again picking at Ataturk as well indicating some uber-ethostate or blind personality cult narrative which is one isn't correct, two is in bad taste when the guy spent his entire life to implement a multiparty democracy regardless of ethnic background. There isn't enough perspective to include how much religious cults were threatening democracy and how more American-liberal (PFJP) crowd worked to install them into the bureaucracy. The communist-conservative divide is very simplified in this narrative. More so again USP (analogue to CHP) didn't install the 10% barrier to make sure they were the ruling party, it was there to keep the islamists out essentially not "Bluish" people. I am just disappointed that with so much love given to the production narrative falls so short as a commentary on the history, it feels more like an European history student reading about Turkish history to write the plot about oppression vs freedom and less like actual Turkish speaking people conveying a context in a clever way. Otherwise it is a very successful production, if you acknowledge the clear bias and philosophical faults.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me of Yes, Your Grace which I enjoyed immensely. Suzerain's gameplay is centered around a decision-making chain that unlocks a richly written story of your own making, and while giving you a quasi-resource management role, you are mostly there as page-turner-in-chief, waiting for the results of your last decision to unfold. The characters are well articulated and their personalities are developed, although delving into them is part of a structured narrative as opposed to something the player has agency in. The sequence of events is more or less the same through playthroughs, which while repetitive from game to game is not necessarily bad. I rarely found myself skipping dialogue on the 2nd playthrough that I'd already read in the first. I would recommend it highly to anyone who enjoys watching a thrilling story of political intrigue and personal decision-making unfold without knowing where it will end.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, this game takes a long time. Roughly 10 hours a playthrough. Lots of reading, not much you can do in the way of strategizing because of the unpredictable nature in which the game unfolds. This alone would be fine, but the nature of the game prevents you from having save states, which means so much as a tiny misclick forces you to replay hours worth of game time or get a bad ending, possibly the same ending you already spent 10 hours to achieve. Secondly, there are multiple things that can ruin a playthrough that the game doesn't give a lot of indication as to how much leeway you have before one of these unfortunate events occur. For example, if you want to liberally reform Sordland, you need to be aware that the more liberal the policies you implement, the higher likelihood there is for a coup. So how liberal can you be? Well that's anyone's guess.Thirdly, for a game where you're the president, you have surprisingly little control over a lot of your circumstances. I know that that is part of the beauty of many good games, I've played games were my character had little control over his circumstances, but not in the same way this game does. EVERYTHING happens by event, and there is no real consistent thing you can do yourself to improve your situation until a favorable event happens. Out of money? You're going to have to wait and hope an event happens when you can tax something (though doing this tends to hurt your economy). Low on popularity? Wait for events and see if there is something you can do to increase it, though the game only tells you once a turn (and turns are like an hour long) if your popularity is low, and even then only when it is really low and very hard to reverse and the notice itself is pretty easy to miss. Ended a state of emergency too early? Too bad. The game doesn't tell you, or even advises you, on when to end a state of emergency, it just has you redo the last few hours of the game again, which brings me to the last point I'll bring up in this review (though I could go on for MUCH longer)Th game has very, very, very little replay value, even though events therein will compel you to go through wide swaths of the story again. This wouldn't be too terrible of a deal if you had save states and didn't have to restart from the bare bones beginning. The dialogue doesn't change much, and the events that were disappointing to begin with are required to be reread with all the gleam and brilliance of asphalt, and you need to interact with everyone you hate again. Diplomacy is about not getting everything you want, but diplomacy in this game is incredibly narrow-scoped as to how you can negotiate. For example, one character, Gloria Tory, is somewhat necessary to get your reforms passed. I got one set of reforms passed on one playthrough after much negotiation, then on another playthrough, trying to pre-empt many things she would disagree with, simply didn't put those points on the bill and made it the exact same bill I passed in the previous playthrough after negotiation. Guess what? In spite of it being the EXACT same bill she passed in the previous playthrough, she refused in the next one because of how stupidly negotiation works in this game.Overall, I think the game had some interesting concepts that I enjoyed at first, but I wouldn't recommend it to anyone unless you are really fond of repetitive visual novels that give you bad endings quite frequently for being a good person and send you to the very beginning instead of to a save point to fix your mistake. If you like that sort of thing and have unlimited time, this game is for you. If you prefer games where there is more to do than read and hope for the best until you've wasted enough of your life to attempt a planned playthrough, then I would recommend literally almost any other game.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has a great premise and a captivating story. That said, the games presentation (and marketing) contradict the game play experience. Make no mistake, Suzerain is little more than a novel with limited RPG elements and a frustrating strategy game interface.Suzerain  a strategy game and neither is it a political simulation. There is essentially one story, one plot you are following. There is no variation. Every time you play it, you're faced with the same series of events, the same faces, the same actors, the same political situations, and despite radically different attempts, the majority of your choices will land you in the same spot. Suzerain taunts the player with a veneer of choice.Your choices in Suzerain have very little impact on what actually happens. The majority of major events are boiled down into a few main outcomes, and depending on certain choices made before the game starts, you will almost inevitably find yourself there.In regards to the writing, the story initially drew me in, but upon additional playthroughs (something which encouraged by multiple different paths and over 80 Steam achievements). The fictional world of the game is neither charming or interesting. The nations, regions, and people are charactures of real ones, but the charactures are grating and at times offensive — if its meant to be satire, it's not good satire. The overwhelming number of characters hamfisted into the story (combined with their obnoxious names) leaves you utterly confused as to who is doing what, where, and why. Don't get me started on how you also have to learn not fictional region names, but also numerous fictional city names. Constantly zooming in and out of the map from the dialogue screen is physically sickening.This leads me an irking issue with the game in general. The lore of the game and core mechanics seem to have been written by someone who is both heavily biased and largely ignorant (or just didn't care). You can't challenge a free market economy. It's obnoxious. Your advisors, those around, everyone urges you to constantly pursue capitalism. The game has already decided the outcome of your choices. If you choose one route, it will not allow you to succeed. Keep in mind, I say this as a staunch capitalist. If I'm given a choice, allow that choice to be viable.Which leads to one of the biggest gripes with the game: choice. In a game which gives the facade of agency, most of your choices have no impact. You will choose to click many options. The game assaults you with a nauseating amount of choices. Do you say "let's begin" or do you say, "Welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining us." This choice or some variation of it make up the majority of the interactions you will have in this game.Again, remember, the developer wants you to *play this multiple times*.The indicators in the top left of the screen are next to useless. And, honestly, most of your decisions which affect the indicators too. Even if you're doing amazing with the economy, it will reflect in the red until suddenly, the economy is great and everyone loves you. Have you ushered in peace and stability by focusing funding on the military and police? You will still see repeated dialogues and confrontations about how there is "No Stability or order in Sordland." The consequences from decisions are often unclear or irrelevant to the actual decision. Often times, your decisions have no discernible affect in the outcome. The number of significant events which just cease to ever be mentioned again or have any impact on reality.I want to like this game. If you had asked me after my first play through, I'd have told you I loved it. But multiple play throughs later and I can't recommend this game.  If you want an okay political with a little bit of choose your own adventure thrown in, maybe. But, honestly, don't expect much more depth than "Reigns" from a game three times its price.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is very well made, it has extremely good narrative, deep conflicts and it is extremely engaging. Highly recomend it. Politics is a very controversial topic, by it's own nature and I went into this game expecting it to have not be able to represent consquences of decisions properly. And yes, there are tons of moments in this game that the choices offered are all bad decisions and you need to chose the least bad one.A good example is how the game handles the economy. There is only one oportunity in the entire game to reduce taxes and this results in a small boost to the economy. The rest of the economic decisions are either the president himself negociating trades, the government spending money to build stuff, or the government giving money to random people. And every time you do one of these ridiculous things, you get some sort of economy point. Health and education also follow similar paths, it is a simple: The more goverenment throws money at something, the better it gets.Even if you start the game chosing to follow a market economy, almost all the options available in the game are from the comunist dictator playbook. And if you choose to not do the crazy comunist stuff, the game punishes you heavily.I suggest reading material from the Chicago or Austrian schools of economics, so that they are not forgotten in the next game. I've finished the game with a ton of money in the treasury, nothing good to spend on, and no option to not take it in the first place.The part where I was impeached and arrested for fake reasons was very realistic though.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I have pros and cons. After a couple of full playthroughs my recommendation is to play it. I really enjoyed the game, the first play through was extremely fun and interesting and I've not played anything like this before so was pleasantly surprised.Most of the game is pretty much reading dialogue, it's basically a book/story you're going through but your decisions and the things you say matter and change the outcomes of certain things and the entire story in general. You have a cabinet of ministers you converse with about many topics and make decisions on which direction to take the country, there is even a home life where you will spend time with the family and your interactions matter there aswell.You are given opportunities at certain times to invest in projects but this is not like sim city or anything, those opportunities only come at specific times in the storyline.Now here are my gripes with it. This game seems to be heavily biased to a narrative of globalisation. Basically you must follow what the devs expect you to do in order to succeed otherwise you're destined to fail at every turn. You need to be in favour of ideologies like open immigration, free market, capitalism etc and even changing politics to let more political parties in despite the fact they have ties to militant groups. It gave me Northern Ireland vibes. A lot of the stories/narratives I recognised from the real world.Technical issues do plague the game, several instances I noticed my past decision were not remembered and future dialogue didn't add up. I made a decree for example to allow protests to continue yet the police and news were acting as though I'd not done so. The economy date never reflected what the cabinet or news was saying, I had the economy in a really positive state and a budget surplus and yet the cabinet and news kept saying the economy is so bad we're heading for a depression then after the chapter changed it for some reason wiped out my economy and budget for literally no reason. Speaking of the budget, I made some sacrifices in one playthough to give myself a better budget surplus to put into projects to improve the economy and infrastructure yet the game never gave me any opportunities to spend it. I just kept getting the cabinet and news telling me the economy is crap and everything else is crap etc but not a single chance came up to spend my budget surplus and I ended up reaching endgame with a surplus inspent. Made no logical sense.My final gripe is the fact you WILL LOSE this game. It is designed so you never make it past one term. It will do whatever it takes to finish you off. Don't even think about going to war with the country to the north who IS coming for you, even if your military is top notch and your general tell you you're way more advanced because the game uses it as an excuse for an endgame conclusion and the enemy WILL beat you immediately.All in all, it's an interesting and fun game to play but don't expect to be happy with how things work out in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: A well made story-driven political RPG. Mostly using a mix of the visual novel style with simple GUI elements you lead the politically tumultuous country of Sordland. _childDocuments_.review: Overall, it's a good game. I enjoyed it a lot. However...From what I understand, we can only rule the country for only 4 years, namely for a presidential term. Then I read the description part again and noticed what it says: As President Rayne, lead Sordland into ruin or repair during "your first term..."
