_childDocuments_.review: Sincerely, knowing that on the official Discord account there was a counting of positive rewiev, I was tempted to do some lil' trolling and publish a negative one and give Letanomics dude an aneurysm, but I simply can't. Truth is, this game is what I craved for years. Suzerain really has the ability to capture you in its world while being able to feel important in it.Every choice I made, from what place you are born to your first term ends had as tangible, great impact as small, interreletional one. Small pieces of dialogue reflect every subtle decision you made along your journey throught your precidency, making it lifeful and real.Next thing, the characters. They are the main element of your journey. While on the outside governance seems more numbers and actions, on the inside there's the real part of it: relations, alliances, compromise and a silver tongue are necessary to fulfill the objective to have an efficient cabinet. Sometimes is really too efficient, unreal in a certain sense, and the possibility of a reshuffle, while surely tedious to implement for the necessity of new characters and the respective dialogues, could be nice.at the end, you will realise that every character, excluding only a few of them, is a piece of ♥♥♥♥ on his own. They will be just corrupt, or powerhungry, or maybe being actually good but acting in very, very wrong ways. You will conflit with them, and you might be tempted to oppose them simply on spite, but remember: they aren't just people, they represent a group more vast that you might think, the voters.obviously, not only the home front, but even external affairs need your intervention. During the game you will have the possibility to meet the leader of various countries, making decision that will resonate in History. In a world consumed by the strife of the gargantuan political presences of Arcasia and United Contana and their respective ideologies, would you pick a side or decide to remain neutral, isolating yourself or paving the path for your country to be more than a piece in the great chessboard of Merkopa?Good Ol' Ideologies, the things that drive the world, the people and their leaders (most of the timef or this ones). the game offers you the possibility to pave your own path, be as a reedemed nationalist or a die-hard communist. as I said before, remember the people you govern: your path will influence their opinion of you based on a consistent historical viewpoint of Sordland (the country's name). being able to balance everything will be crucial to gain the favour of your fellow politicians and citizens. some choices are more difficult than others, but it will be your job to figure out something. Fortunatelly, the game offers an extensive and detailed codex about the main characters, countries and historical events: using it is highly suggested.Last but not least. achievments. it feels strange to read it, they aren't the main part of the game, so why in this review?I want to say that I was deeply impressed by how easy it was for me to get achievment, even some rare ones, by simply playing the way I wanted to. In most of the games they are just some crazy s**t, a challenge that require specific, unnatural choices in a gameplay sense, but in this case I was able to get a lot of them. these choice is very courageus and the most correct that I ever seen. Achievments, in substance, became a way to track your choices, leaving an indefinitly lasting mark. Sometimes, I look at some of my ones, being able to remember why I receive it, what I did and how much was that playthrough exciting. That's something that everygame should strive for.I absolutely DON'T recommend this game to everyone. Only a small fraction of all the gamers would like this tipe of game, which sometimes seem difficult even for me for its wall of unskippable text: but if you are a part of it, You will love it. I consider it another courageous choice by Torpor Games, not every developer house have this specific, yet surely passion-oriented playerbase.Good game!

_childDocuments_.review: For reference, the time at review is how long it took me to finish one playthrough.Can't recommend this game enough. It is short, but that relatively small amount of gameplay is absolutely packed  with content. It's a dense game for politics nerds with excellent replayability. It's a lot like  a more narrative-packed and fleshed-out version of the prologue for Tyranny (another excellent game). It feels like you have meaningful control over the country, although there are certainly surprises you have to contend with. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is essentially a text-based, narrative-focused RPG with some very light grand strategy mechanics. You play as the newly elected president of Sordland, a fictional country in a 1950's inspired setting, which is grappling with political instability, an economic crisis, and a potential invasion from a powerful neighbor. You are free to decide your character's political beliefs and goals, but you will likely have to make unwelcome compromises in order to achieve them.Overall, I really enjoyed Suzerain. It's very well-written and features a cast of unique and interesting characters. The game constantly asks you to make difficult decisions where you will upset someone important no matter what you do, and thus forces you to really think about your actions. I also love the soundtrack and art, which do a great job of immersing you in the story.However, I will mention a couple of negative points. First of all, I would have liked the mechanics to have had more depth and transparency. It's often unclear what the effects of a particular choice actually entail, and you often have to guess about something that you really should be able to know, which can make the game extremely punishing for first-time players. Being able to see more detailed information about your economy, popularity, etc. would alleviate this, along with more ways to mechanically interact with your country between dialogues. Second, the later sections of the game feel a bit rushed and could've done with more content fleshing out what's going on.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I greatly enjoyed this visual novel/government simulator. The story is intriguing and the writing is well-done. The world-building is excellent and there are in-depth pages on each character, organization, and government system. Choices do matter and manifest in consequences that ripple throughout the entire game (many not seen until much, much later).Where this game falls flat is replayability. Unlike other reviewers, I would argue that this game definitely warrants multiple playthroughs. I have done two (at the time of writing this review) and will likely do one more to try decisions on the opposite end of the political and economic spectrums. A massive failing of this game is to not have discrete save files where one can pick up and replay at points in the campaign on one's choosing. I really wish I could go back to certain points in the campaign and choose an alternate path without having to replay from the beginning. There are multiple game-ending choices, resulting in bad endings, that can really deflate the feeling of a playthrough. For gamers without a lot of spare time, the lack of a save system really makes this game a hard one to recommend without this caveat.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The premiere president simulator / visual novel. I don't even really like most visual novels that much, but this game really has a LOT of choice involved and is impeccably reactive to your choices, so you don't just feel "along for the ride" on a linear story. Far from it. You be the president you want to be! Or at least... you can try. And maybe fail. Spectacularly, even. But hey, that's politics.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game about politics. And you have to really like politics to enjoy this game.It's a game that on the surface encourages you to play multiple times, but in practice does just about everything in it's power to discourage you from wanting to do that. There is no button to skip dialogue, there's no way to see if you've chosen something in a previous playthrough, there's little indication of what outcome your decisions actually have, little indication of what actually matters, and a pretty lousy save system.This might not be readily apparent, but some time into the game you're going to be confronted by a vote. And if you didn't play the political game perfectly, you're going to lose that vote and everyone is going to spend a good long while dumping all over you and you're terrible decisions. And then you're going to want to reload to try some other variables, and then you're going to be really annoyed at how much you need to replay.Oh, and you can only get achievements from playing in torpor/ironman mode, so I guess the intended experience for a non-perfect run is to just sit in your failure until the game deigns to end.It's a good game, but for someone else. I hate it.But the game part of this is only just a fraction of what it has to offer. The real meat of it is in the world and the story unfolding... but since both of this is told through the medium of "game", you're going to have to avail yourself to the veritable wikipedia of information about the characters, places, religions, ethnicities, political stances, economic models, etc. ad nauseam to feel like you're making informed decisions and engaging with the story. And if you can get into the swing of things, it can be really engaging. But there's going to be a vote. And there's a good chance you'll lose that vote. And then the story will focus on dumping all over your decisions, everyone will tell you everything you did was pointless, and if you're anything like me you'll realize that the story hasn't been entertaining enough to overlook the frustration of constant pointless reports and frustrating gameplay before the failstate, and it's unlikely to become any better after.It's a story that's best enjoyed with a walkthrough on hand, or with a lover's patience.It's a good story, but for someone else. I hate it.If there was an option to reccomend the game with an asterisk, I'd choose that. But as it is? I'd either recommend a book for people who came for a story, or a game for the people who came for gameplay. This is just an uncomfortable, ungainly mix of both.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's an elegant text-based political simulator. Probably, the best of the kind. Lucid writing, intriguing narrative with engaging dilemmas. Good visuals and music help a lot too.  Theme and gameplay work together to make navigating the minutiae of endless dialogs ridiculously fun.  I made several runs in search of political harmony in Sordland, learning to accept my inner unapologetic centrism, and it was rewarding despite unvoidable the repetition of some parts. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo over the summer and came back for the full release this month.Pros: I like the writing, and the experience of statecraft is immersive. The various people you meet all have distinct personalities, and they represent an impressive array of conflicting interests you have to placate. Real-world issues (the Cold War, for instance, or stateless minorities seeking representation) are enciphered behind a surprisingly thorough fictional world. Your decisions have complex knock-on effects that, while not always what you want, are narratively satisfying.Cons: For being a game that consists entirely of a desktop map with text boxes laid over it, Suzerain is surprisingly resource-hungry. The current build (1.0.4, I think) eats several gigs of RAM. There are infrequent but distracting typos. Revisiting the full game, I found myself forced to replay the story again from the beginning, going through all the same beats. This is going to make replay value low unless I make drastically different choices in subsequent runs.Of note: The game is driven so completely by text and value-balancing that it's almost a statecraft dating sim. I don't mind this at all, but I could see it being an unpleasant surprise if you don't know that's what you're getting.Verdict: Worth it if you're interested in exploring a small but well-crafted world through a whole lot of reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of games that try to challenge your ideals, whatever they may be, but few actually succeed in doing so. This is game absolutely blew my expectations out of the water in that regard.There were many times I had to put the game down to think about the choice before me. The country's need weighed against what I thought was right and I admit that a number of the choices weighed heavily on me for the rest of the game.I liked that the game isn’t bias against one ideology or the other either. There are clear advantages and disadvantages in going left or right or taking authoritarian or democratic approaches, not just nationally but as you act on the international stage also.The entirely text based story might put some off, but I’d say this is a must play for anyone who likes well written stories or is interested in politics.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Well, what a great game! I enjoyed every part of it and wished it never see an end. It was a great journey. If you are looking for a sandbox experience with politics, this is not a game for you. But if you are looking for a politics game with a pretty decent narrative, this is just the game for you! And by the way, I must admit as a Turkish citizen that, the main narrative of the game was pretty similar to those of Turkish one. If you liked the story behind the game, maybe you should take a look at Turkish history and politics!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text based adventure about the president of a young, struggling republic. The stereotype of a political game is that they are vehicles for poorly disguised propaganda, so I'm glad this one actually manages to represent the subject matter in a mature and fairly realistic manner. Particularly the fact that, just like in real life, it's impossible to please everyone.The story is also generally well written and it can change a whole lot depending on the player's choices, although I think some events may be semi-random. Apart from that, there's not much else about the gameplay as it's a text adventure after all, the player is limited to picking dialogue choices and ticking boxes every once in a while.On the topic of limitations, one would think a game with so many possible story paths would have a lot of replay value, but sadly I believe this isn't the case because of the mandatory ironman mode. I think that's fine and a completely valid design choice for the first playthrough, but it's annoying to be made to repeat the entire first chapters every time. It doesn't help that some actions have dumb consequences, such as a tax on imported sumptuary goods instantly shrinking the economy of a developing nation by 20% or how refusing to ban a violent organization doesn't have any negative repercussions for public order. Overall, Suzerain has my full endorsement for the first playthrough, but I'm somewhat disappointed by the lackluster replay experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps one of the most intellectually satisfying games I have ever played. Every decision seems connected and the consequences matter. My only real issue is that it only lets you play your first term. Hopefully this is something that gets expanded later but either way its satisfying with a solid amount of replayability.

_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I just started playing this game, and it has captured every bit of my attention. I've honestly been ACHING for a game lately that grabs me and keeps me hooked, and after a few purchases- I can safely say this is hands down the winner. The story is so freaking rich, even the smallest choices already seem to matter, and I can't wait to see how everything plays out in the long run. Seriously, guys, buy this game and support the devs. They made something amazing here.Edit: I just need to edit my review, because- holy damn. The more I play, the more blown away I am. Every character you interact with has a distinct personality. In a lot of games, we see a "copy-paste" personality of a person. You know who the bad guy is, who the hero is, etc. We look at a personality and think to ourselves, "Oh, they're just like the guy from [Insert game here]. You get nothing like that in this game. In Suzerain, you have to truly pay attention to the dialogue- simply put, because you truly do not know the real motivations for the key players you come across. From the smaller characters to the larger ones, each undoubtedly has some kind of agenda; but it's difficult to truly see what that agenda is. What makes this so great is that every dialogue choice, every word, action, etc. is a careful one. I'm finding myself looking at my options for a good few minutes before finally choosing, because I don't know if I'll be blasted for it later by the guy who controls a large media corporation that is angry because I shot down a business deal, or if the public will be angry because I let a questionable group of individuals attend a funeral.The more I play this game, the more intricate (and, frankly, political) it begins to feel. I might have to edit this review further, honestly. Simply because this game just continues to rise to the top of one of the most impressive and amazing games I've ever played.[Here's hoping the devs can see this, because this part is for them]: You guys have done a tremendous thing here. I can't wait to see what kinds of updates (if any) may be added to the game, or an expansion of some kind. Regardless, thank you for something remarkable.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game, really well written. The game constantly gives you different solutions for the problems of the country, and as far as I saw, nearly all your choices matter. In some games like Democracy series, its best to stick to a single plan like free market economy, or liberalism, but this game kinda puts you in a more realistic situations like modern politics, where you have to make populist decisions, or make decisions as lobbying efforts.Character portraits, the map, overall graphics are very nice as well, it really adds to the story.One small disappointment I had was the ending. By the time story came to a close, I was super invested into the story. Around that part was where the story reached its climax as well, but it ended really fast, and it was kinda buggy.Despite that though its an amazing game, with very successful story. Try it!

_childDocuments_.review: Well written political choose your own adventure. Lots of difficult decisions to make and I found myself glued to the game. Blitzed through it in a few days.However, I think the endings can be a bit lame. It feels like some paths will set you on a negative ending no matter how skilled your decision making is. And given the strange decision not to include an option to reload saves, I personally feel replay value is limited despite the large number of possibilities/endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm normally not a fan of visual novels and was on the fence about trying this game for a long time, but I'm glad I finally picked it up.The writing is great. I was really invested in the story and the characters by the end. Decisions are often genuinely difficult and impactful. There are many different ways to play, each with very different endings. That being said, I didn't have the patience to sit through a second play-through. The game doesn't lend itself to quick replays - you can't load from different saves or fast-forward through dialogue - so it feels like a slog sitting through mostly the same conversations again.Getting a good ending is hard. The game sets you up for failure, starting you off in an economic recession and relentlessly attacking you with crisis after crisis. For me, this was part of the game's appeal, as it forces you to make tough choices and compromise on your ideals. Honestly, I'm impressed with the level of nuance you're able to bring to your play style. However, I felt some of the hidden mechanics are confusing. It's hard to gauge how big the effect of a decision is on the economy, and I was surprised that the country plunged into even deeper recession despite heavy government spending to stimulate the economy. On one occasion, I presented a proposal to my opponent that gave almost everything he wanted from the start, he still required convincing to agree to it, for no discernable reason.Overall, though, I heartily recommend Suzerain for anyone who has even just a passing interesting in political drama.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This (for being a text based game) is one of the most immersive games I've ever played. You actually FEEL the burden of power and with every decision you make you're never not sure about if I've you're doing the right think.Visuals are very nice and the games is neatly presented. There are plenty of different situations and choices. As the story is quite linear, replay value is maybe focused on having different results by the end of the game and roleplaying, but all in all is a truly great game.I sincerely hope seeing this studio develop another similar game, if possible with more free decisions - in Suzerain all of theme came when game tolds you, you can't for instance talk to anyone as an own initiative.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I managed to "win" my third game. There seem to be some inconsistencies between the "simulation" part (economy, approval, etc.) and the narrative, the game can shower you with negative reports on one turn while your ministers tell you how well things are going in the country, also some choices may have hard to predict *immediate* consequences that made me resort to some save scumming. (I don't mind hard choices having some unforseen consequences further down the road)Nevertheless I enjoyed playing choose-your-own political adventure. I felt the pressure from the diverging interests of the various characters and factions, and the weight of the troubled history of Sordland. The game's world, and the situations presented to the player, are more or less directly inspired by things that happened in our world's past, I like that I could draw parallels between Sordland and several real-world countries.Not one of the best games of all times, but still an interesting and enjoyable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not often leave reviews,however this game is a very good one.One of the best political games on steam.If you are interested in games like Democracy 4 and Yes,Your Grace,this game is a must buy.There are up to 20 sub-endings in this game,meaning that you can play it many times and overall,the game is very customisable .Besides,I am hyped for the new DLC involving the Kingdom of Rizia .Interested in seeing where this goes.

_childDocuments_.review: Unique immersive story-rich game. After finishing Suzerain looked for any other games like it but couldn't find any. There are sort of similar games but none really like it and that match the polish, craft and focus of Suzerain, its very detailed world, background, range of characters and personalities, and interaction of choice and consequence. The choices and consequences reminds of games like The Witcher or Alpha Protocol where results of decisions made can be felt through much later in the game that has a big impact.Worth multiple play-through to not only see other outcomes but fun to be a different character completely with the choices you make and how you interact and treat other characters. Music is nice that fits different scenes well and ramps up during important points to further the the immersion.On first play-through some mechanics like the economy bar may not be clear to understand at first how they function. How big its impacts is along with the passage of time, through each turn which greatly affect your ratings and how the story can massively change direction. There were one or two interactions I felt I was only asking questions to advisers to learn more about a topic before of an actual choice I wanted to make but instead the conversation took me down the path I did not want and to a decision I did not intend to choose. Towards the final chapter as everything came to a head thought the game ended a little too quickly and could have been fleshed out a bit more but was still a fantastic experience.Nice presentation, style, music, story, characters, decisions and immersion.Cannot underestimate that I think there isn't any other game like it. Built a unique story and character rich game world and turn based style visual novel with choices and consequences gameplay.Update for 2.0 release. Great to see more fleshed out detail expanded for the game world with nice UI and presentation changes.

_childDocuments_.review: Take this review with a grain of salt. If you enjoy text-based simulators that makes you feel immersed in its world, this game might be for you! This is more for me to vent and explain my exasperation with this game.As I am writing this, I am still gripped with the feeling that I should love this game. The text-based decisions and storytelling, a cast of characters that often feel fleshed out with clear motivations, and the atmosphere of the world building (one that mirrors the cold war atmosphere of our world) has at times made me feel as though I am in the shoes President Rayne as he attempts to pull Sordland from the brink of crisis. Yet at the same time, every attempt at the main campaign (successful or not) has left me frustrated and wishing I hadn't bothered. This game is walls of text leading to political/social/economic/interpersonal decisions that have major implications with little to no feedback as to how those decisions will affect your play through. The only indicator of economic growth? A single line on the top bar that either goes up or down. I had my economic minister tell me all the great things my economic plan had wrought and that we were making strides to tackling the recession. In the next breath he tells me that Sordland has entered a depression cycle due to "The Debt Crisis" and we have failed to address the people's economic concerns. Following this conversation, the economic bar graph shows a super green upwards trajectory despite the depression. What frustrates me more, you cannot find a solid explanation or consistent reasoning for when events like this trigger. I can only assume that My VP tells me we are going to sweep the elections with a 20% gain for the party despite lowering the threshold to 3% for new parties! We are headed for re-election! The result: I lose the election as the USP comes in third...The next turn. After navigating a diplomatic mission spanning the entire campaign to avoid going to war. And spending money on all ministries except for military to address welfare and corruptions concerns. There were no indications that I had suddenly lost this support at any point.2.0 added additional content for Bergia, leads to a greater story line regarding the Bluds. However, This game PUNISHES you for not knowing the sequence of events ahead of time. You are forced to use guides in order to get an optimal outcome, and even then the guides are not fool-proof. There is a lack of consistency on top of the lack of transparency as to which events or bills or decisions affect the big picture. It gets especially frustrating when you have go back through the text trees every time you restart.This could be because I am just not patient enough for the game, or that I am obstinate in my play style, however I can't help but feel baffled by how this game is structured. What's more, 3.0 came with the release of the Kingdom of Rizia DLC that looks intriguing on its own with unique mechanics and I was initially excited to transfer my Rayne campaign over after purchasing. I am glad I decided to wait until I played this game again to remind me what I did not enjoy about it the first few times around.Also, Despite all the additions to the game after 2.0, Kind of a let down, and even moreso when you consider there is a more in-depth war mechanic in the Rizia DLCRegardless, I encourage you to look at what others think. Many others enjoy this game, so I must be missing something!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I have to commend the developers of Suzerain. I haven't had such a fun and unique experience in such an original and in-depth world in years.I'll admit, Suzerain will not be everyone's cup of tea. If you're looking for an action-packed triple A title with next-gen graphics this game is not for you. If, however, you're a foreign policy / economics / political junkie who doesn't mind reading through mountains of lengthy text, considering your options, and thinking about the unintended consequences of your actions then you will love Suzerain.Suzerain sees you taking control as the president of a fledgling democracy (?) and attempting to guide it to greatness. You'll deal with economic recession, political assassination, foreign border incursions, human rights abuses, nuclear deterrence, trade negotiations, backroom deals, espionage, bribery, media manipulation and more, all while attempting to stave off internal rebellion within your party as you seek reelection.The choice is yours and the ramifications are real. Will you relinquish power and enact democratic reforms or will you succumb to your lust for autocracy? Will you embrace capitalism and deregulate industry, or will the state gobble up commerce and provide for the people? Will you engage with the superpowers on the biggest stage, or will you stand alone as a rogue-state?It is impossible to keep everyone happy. You will make enemies. The choices you make will have unintended consequences and as basic economics teaches us, every policy you enact will have winners and losers. The losers will want retribution and will not sit idly by if you govern in a manner in which they disapprove. They will eventually come after you.Suzerain is not perfect, however. Flaws exist which hopefully will be improved upon if Torpor games chooses to continue the Suzerain experience with either sequels or expansions. I genuinely hope they do. (Torpor, if you're listening, please take my money!)For instance: while your actions definitely have consequences, it still feels like your choices are somewhat constrained by text based yes/no, up/down, left/right options. As a fan of the Democracy series, I'd like to see some more nuance in my decision making with sliders and pie charts, perhaps, that provide a broader extent of numerical-based resource allocation options. This happens only once in the game to my knowledge but not, as you might imagine, when determining the federal budget. Bewilderingly, your potential budgetary decisions for key departments are merely decrease, maintain, or increase.This manifests itself in a somewhat simplistic view of economics and budgeting; if you engage in deficit spending your budget may go down to -5 while if you cut spending your budget may go up to +5. Meanwhile your economic growth is indicated by a red-to-green bar that occasionally grows and shrinks in response to your decisions. It'd be nice to see more complex implementation of budgets and economics in future iterations of the game.Further, access to important information is mixed at best. While the UI includes a very helpful codex and wonderfully in-depth encyclopedia it's almost impossible to figure out at a moment's notice things like GDP, unemployment, quality of life, support from voters and/or polling numbers, and so on. Several times it might feel like you're making decisions in the dark considering this is very much a text-based storytelling game and seems to avoid hard numbers like the plague. More numbers and fewer words would go a long way in fleshing out economic decisions in particular.Finally, and this is just the cherry-on-top of my wish list, it would be nice to have more options regarding your campaign. So much of your time is spent governing but it would be nice if the game actually introduced a few elements from the campaign trail in the final chapter. Maybe you've been a great president with an incredible list of accomplishments but run a terrible campaign and can't communicate an effective message to the voters. Would be neat to see.In any case, playing this game has been overwhelmingly entertaining as the multiple playstyles offer almost unlimited endings. No two games will be played the same and it's impossible to "win." Ultimately you'll have to sacrifice part of your agenda to keep allies and your side if you want to win reelection.Highly recommended and these developers deserve to be supported financially. I genuinely and truly hope this is only the beginning of Suzerain universe and we see more to come in the future.A morgna wes core! Vectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: I was honestly super enjoying this game! I played through the first three chapters, and though I had a rocky start, my economy bar was nearly at full, and my social reforms were being gradually passed. But then, seemingly arbitrarily, upon the start of chapter four, my economy crashed? I do not understand. The game itself seems to be confused, with the newspapers running stories simultaneously critisizing and praising my economic policy, and with Symon reporting almost nothing but positives in my economy report, and then telling me that we were in the sordish great depression. I have no idea why this happened? Everything seemed fine, and then a single loading screen killed my country. Which is shame, because before this I was super invested! All of my decisions felt like they had consequences, and nothing else felt surprising or arbitrary. The game is well written, the graphics are wonderful, the music is so perfect that it's honestly a shame to shut the game down just because it pauses the music. But this one thing is a huge dent in my enjoyment. Overall I do still reccomend the game, I am just complaining I guess.

_childDocuments_.review: "Political simulator" isn't quite an accurate descriptor for this game.It is a decision maker where there is a LOT of text that the decisions seem to have little to no impact, and then a few MAJOR decisions, which are clearly black and white.Played enough to realize it isn't a "game" but more of a "choose your own adventure" novel. Which is great if that's what you are looking for, but based on the one photo of the split of who was in the government, I thought it would have some game mechanics other than choice based outcomes.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a worthy spiritual successor to the game Hidden Agenda from 1982. Suzerain does a fantastic job of making me care about my choices and the characters they affect by making the effects obvious, but not predictable. I highly recommend anyone who has ever scratched their heads at the apparent incompetence of real world politicians to give this game a try.The one drawback is the lack of spell checking of the text that is the essential driver of the action of this game. Hire someone to go through the text and correct blatant mistakes like "From henceforth" and using "two" instead of "to".I still wouldn't want anyone to miss out on this game. Buy it now!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a unique experience, that first playthrough is something I have never experienced before, because I did everything I thought was right and failed in my goals. This is such a well crafted experience, because it differs from other games like Democracy and other 'government sim' games. You inherit a country in crisis, many factions are already against you and your allies, internal and external are few and far between. Want to go into this challenge of a political maze with good intentions, ideas or even morals? You will not last. This game is the part of politics about facing reality and compromising to achieve goals, or becoming what you hate in order to avoid resistance. Greatly looking forward to the DLC!

_childDocuments_.review: I find this to be a fantastic game in the way it manages to create engagement and stakes behind almost every decision. There are some minor improvement points. The game's economics - though technically simplistic - are troublesome as it takes time to understand how much "points" you might have to spend and roughly what can cost points and what cannot. The story is also deterministic as far as I can understand; taking the same actions in 2 different games will yield the same results. With the number of choices available this still leaves room for replayability, but you might end up having to replay the early chapters because you fail to understand the scope of the budget. However, in my opinion the game more than makes up for this with its engaging characters and how every decision is a conversation which someone will react to. So many situations that feel tense just because a decision might turn out to have a big impact (politically, personally or economically).
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The best political game I've come across. It somehow feels like a tabletop RPG. Very addictive, intriguing, and well-made. Punishing and oppressive for the most part, yet that's not a bad thing. It has been years since I enjoyed a game this much; reminds me of childhoood fun. I hope the team behind it continues to bring forth quality games, in which case I'll undoubtedly keep supporting their work. If you're at all into geopolitics and/or have strong ideological principles, this is a must. However, I can imagine anyone looking for casual fun will enjoy this, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great visual novel with many endings, it encourages replayability with the many outcomes and special dialogues but it really feels like a chore for each consecutive replay just because you have to go through the same starting dialogues in the first hour. Developers please, add a fast forward conversation or save point so we can skip the intro and starting turns to find the different endings. It'll make the experience for us more enjoyable. We don't want to see the same intro for 10 times just to get the ending we want. It's a great political story that parody real cold war history, great one the first run but the time it takes to get to the good part may be a drag in any future play.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has many hidden mechanics and is extremely unforgiving. This is Murphy's Law the gaming simulator. Some people will enjoy the long and complex narratives, I found them interesting the first couple of times. The long drawn story with only small variations becomes a time drain by the third play through.Combine the unforgiving nature of the game with the time commitment needed to play it, and you eventually get frustration. Not something I am looking for in my gaming experiences. Some will enjoy this game. Make sure you have patience for long dialogues, difficult politics, and a game world built to be against you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an incredible game about Cold War politics. You play as the newly-elected President of a country struggling to emerge from under the shadow of a military dictatorship, poised halfway between the capitalist west and communist east, standing on the precipice of an economic depression, with potential enemies and friends on all sides, and no clear mandate from the people other than "fix it".What makes Suzerain so great is that it's concerned not just with what your policy decisions are but what your relationships are to all the other power players in the government. You might have a brilliant plan for pulling your economy out of the recession, but can you get everyone else on board? Can you reform away the constitutional relics of the dictatorship without getting yourself deposed like the last guy? Every character in the game has a detailed history, as do you, and that history matters as much as your choices in the present when it comes time to convince or threaten them onto your side.Furthermore, despite its depth, the game is short enough to engage in multiple playthroughs to try different approaches, and the game will reward you by unraveling new secrets and playing out new confrontations in completely different situations each time. You get a lot of game for your money!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

The game has all you need from freedom movements to epidemics to riots and even, war. I recommend that everyone gives this game a try.To add a personal perspective I was touched to see how much of this country felt like mine. I hope every Sord, em I mean Turk can play this game and look at their countries politics in a better light.

_childDocuments_.review: Very glad I decided to pull the trigger on this. Story has been super engaging and I'm very invested. Has tons of levers you need to maintain and consider to get your policies through, leading to a number of touch decisions.. will likely do another run pushing for new agenda + try out the DLC after i complete my current game. The game is primarily reading and keeping tabs on world events that come up in conversation / the news, but the writing and feeling of making large, impactful decisions makes this game seem so much more,
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a gorgeously detailed political simulation that lays bare the truth of what government really is: a conveyor belt of shadowy Machiavellian characters desperately trying to push their own agenda by whatever means are necessary behind the curtain of 'democracy', and the politicians who either bend to their pressure or face the inevitable consequences.A lovingly descriptive world is brought vibrantly to life, within which you can spend hours gorging on detail and generally immersing yourself in the history of this fictional universe. Ultimately you will be left despairing in the face of the truth: true revolution through parliamentary politics is an impossible dream, but the journey to that realisation is beautiful enough that it is definitely a road worth travelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I was quite pleased with how this game turned out, after having anticipated it eagerly for some time. As a political simulator it understands the importance of telling a narrative. The game's idea of letting you be the presiden does not just amount to giving you a bunch of buttons and sliders to control everything from the tax rate to the cost of health care. Instead it situates you in a larger historical context (in an alternate history) where all the issues that come before you are the results of a multitude of forces both within your nation and without that shape the politics of the day. And these issues that you make decisions over have consequences in turn, shaping the present and future reality of your presidency and country. The gameplay is inextricably tied together with the narrative, where the events that unfold affect what gameplay choices you are presented with and what choices you make impact what will happen next in the story.In short the game is a story-driven simulator game with heavy emphasis on choice & consequence. The kind of game we could use more of, in my opinion. The political vision the game presents tries to cast a very wide net, giving you glimpses and interactions with a large number of topics and issues (which history nerds will recognize from many different places), and more often than not letting you as the player express sympathy or opposition to them. Quite a fun game to play, if you accept that the game revolves around a lot of text, and that you must live with your mistakes as there are no reloads.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever left a review on Steam before. Suzerain is unlike any other game I've played. Its story is rich and engrossing. I found myself hooked to every line and scenario in ways I typically experience in novels I love. The choices are sometimes clear-cut, but more often than not it is brutally challenging to pick a path or discern the best option. Every action has consequences, and those consequences certainly are not always apparent. There are wide-spread ripple effects that can impact your run in ways you may not have considered.The characters, world, and scenarios are thoroughly fleshed-out. You can (and I did) spend hours reading through the codex entries. The game intrinsically rewards you for doing so, too, as the added context from the codex can greatly increase your ability to make informed decisions. I am excited to try more runs of this game. At some point it is less about winning or losing (though maybe I'm biased, happening to "win" on my first run-through), but about exploring this world and the wide range of options it holds within.I have only a few constructive criticisms:* I would have loved a zoomed-out map view where I could see the entire region without scrolling.* A read-only view of the world for context would have additionally been neat* There were a few typos (I think I counted four total that I noticed) in some of the dialogue. Understandable given the immense amount of writing in the game, in hindsight I wish I'd taken note of them.* There were times, especially when voting on bills or programs, where I felt I didn't have the ability to discuss with advisers beforehand for context and strategy.* I wold love if the end-screen detailed the most important journal bullet-points of the runThese points pale in comparison to how engaging and fun this game is though. Absolutely worth the $15, you will get more out of this in time and enjoyment than from many modern $60 AAA games.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing narrative driven political journey that puts you in the position of being 4th president of Sordland, Anton Rayne, a new leader to a country with a turmoil filled past that has left long lasting impacts on the culture and state of the nation. You must save the country from a recession, address the concerns of a lingering military threat from the nation of Rumburg, deal with the Oligarchs whom dominate the private sector, enact or oppose democratic reforms, determine the budgetary priorities of your administration, deal with scandals, and make constant hard decisions that will ultimately decide the future of the Sordland. This narrative does all it can to draw you into the story behind Sordland, the current climate of the world geopolitically and most importantly the life of Anton Rayne whom you play in this story. Your decisions shape Sordland, will you enact Democratic Reforms, will you make the Soll Dictatorship look like a walk in the park, or will you succumb to the many temptations by Oligarchs and attractive women looking to take advantage of your presidency for their own agendas. What will you do? I will tell you what I did, I bought this game and highly recommend it. It is one of, if not the best political sim available. The game is an absolute masterpiece when it comes to making hard decisions in which you feel the impact of every decision,  in addition to creating a realistic political narrative with amazing world building to back it up. It would be a mistake to let this gem slip by without even giving it a try. And this narrative presents enough choices to give you the ability to replay this and see dramatically different results for both your character's ending and the impact of your decisions on the world. I know I certainly plan on replaying the story to see what different routes I can bring Sordland down. Hopefully you will too!(P.S. I have been following this game for quite a long time and I can say for a fact I was not disappointed and the team who worked on this did an amazing job and deserve all the love and support they get for this massive achievement)

_childDocuments_.review: 8 hours for a single play through and i'm already planning a few more to see how much difference the choices make.But the game itself is beautiful for what it is, I got everything i hoped for after playing the demo.Always being on the brink of collapse and having to allocate the non-existing budget to try and save something, every decision felt heavy and always kept me wondering if I did the right thing.Sadly i'm not as good of a writer as the game creators, so the review is lackluster, but to sum up, be sure to try it out if you're not afraid of reading, a lot, and like the idea of managing a country and internal politics.For sure my top 5 game this year. so far I've:Still have plans for additional runs.There are some minor issues with flavor texts/comments triggering without you completing required actions but probably the main issue for me personally is the lack of a "skip text you already saw" setting which would increase the replay speed a ten fold, as despite a lot of branching possibilities the main issues and the main story path is the same.

_childDocuments_.review: This should be quite an interesting experience between a political sim and a choose your own adventure game. But it’s really not. You can do a perfect job and suddenly without any explanation something tanks in the passing of chapters. I’ve once reached full economy growth going on a full economy state (capitalism, free market and so) but at the start of chapter 4 everything tanks without any explanation. In the same game I calmed all the internal problems (with the most troublesome racial group and the farmers) but suddenly there is unrest everywhere and when you try to understand who is provoking it the games answers on “don’t know, someone is pissed”. This is not even remotely fun, the game is rigged to be one way or you lose, is worse than a choose your own adventure, it’s basically a railroaded experience triggered to fail if you don’t play as the devs wanted.After three playtroughs and after seeing some guides, cause i really wanted answers, is pretty clear that every nationalist, capitalist, liberalist or generally on the right side is a game over, winning by nationalism or supporting a free western market is basically impossibile without a guide, meanwhile if you join the not-soviet or go for full communist choices the streets are paved.This is horrifying agenda, the game punishes you on doing all the right things just cause the devs wanted you to follow only one way, theirs.Avoid it at every cost, if you want a political sim there is better, if you want a cyoa game, there is better.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Its pretty good. Its basically a multi choice story where your actions will have immeidate or long term consequences in your running of a country. it shows (in an exaggerated way that makes gameplay more fun) how politicians have to juggle who they want to please and who they want to piss off in order to get the things they want implemented or removed done. You will not be able to keep everyone happy, and you will not be able to solve every issue at once. Expected things will happen in unexpected ways.The one thing that may turn most people off from this game is the amount of reading you have to do. _childDocuments_.review: An absolutely captivating game that I just happened to buy on sale and wish I  had discovered earlier. An absolute gift to those interested in the blending of politics, ideology, strategics, consequential relationships, geopolitics, quality writing and decision making games. Bought and played on the 2.0 update onwards.I could not put this one down, even after my first disastrous run cut short by the ramifications of my rash decisions. Immediately followed up by a second equally captivating playthrough and many more to come I am sure.You will need to read a lot (this will be a dealbreaker for some), and you should invest time in game to learn the hand crafted world with the in game codex and map, but you will be rewarded with an immersive and compelling story, driven by changing set of events depending upon your choices. UI is simple and intuitive, map and characters have good art style and font is nice and readable throughout the game. (important since mostly text driven). I experienced no performance issues in 25 hours over multiple long sessions. I will be buying the DLC and have high hopes for the continued quality of the game with the addition of another playable country. My ONLY selfish wish is that we got to play out a second term, to see our past efforts in motion and new challenges to face, though I do recognise the gargantuan effort that would be required to push forward a story with already so many consequential decisions made and multitudes of alternate paths. Thanks Torpor games, it's a 10/10 in my book. Also EU4 comet sense reference 11/10
