_childDocuments_.review: Plays more like a visual novel than a political game, but there is plenty of political science going on in the background. An impossible amount of lore building out this fictional universe, enough to make it feel real and lived in. The occasional typo, sometimes dry writing or sometime limited options does not dim the fact that it's a fantastic political story with believable characters and twists big and small. Appropriately, for a game about politics, probably the game with characters who have lied to me (both big and small lies) more than any other.I first played the game when it had come out recently. Playing it again now that the free update is out and an already complete game has even more meat on it. As a bonus, it works great with a controller - my second playthrough is on the Steam Deck, and apart from some small text and options that fall off the bottom of the screen, it's been a smooth experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Brothers and sisters, I've never reviewed a game on Steam ever and I felt compelled to here. This game is phenomenal. I felt genuinely invested in the country I was running, and felt personal connections to the team I worked with to implement changes. I found myself frustrated when they argued, emboldened when things worked well, and chastened when, despite my best efforts to provide for the people, I still drove the economy into a historic depression and retired. A nice touch were the newspaper headlines and clippings that support or tear into you from every political perspective, to the point where I started begrudging a few papers as rags and others as frustrating when, despite me being aligned with them, they still ripped apart my reforms for not being "good enough." I'm excited to start my next playthrough in an attempt to navigate the waters better.An utterly brilliantly designed and well written game. I cannot wait to play the DLC and whatever else these developers come up with.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets so many things right and even perfect that its almost impossible to not recommend this game.I will start off by saying its NOT a Political Management game like the Democracy series. This is a linear story whose outcome you massively influence. Imagine a text based Tell Tale game but your decisions actually makes a difference. The first thing you will notice is the extremely detailed lore of the fictional country. Every historical event, landmark, politician, city, political party is extremely detailed and contains lots of information. Take any politician  you will get to know so much about them, their background, their actions, their motivations that you can connect to them and understand why a particular person is the way that they are. You are pulled into this fictional world where every person has a story, every country has a history, every political party has a motive and you feel like a real person making real decisions. I cannot stress how well this is done in this game. Bravo!Secondly, This is not just a game where you manage some budget slider and click a few check boxes. This is a extremely deep simulation where you are given a situation, like which major infrastructure project to invest, whether to take a bribe, be capitalistic or socialist, be traditional or reformer, which country to ally with and a myriad of other choices that directly effect both short term and long term outcomes. I finished the game and went to see the achievements and realised there could have been dozens of other outcomes. This makes replaying the game at least a few times worth itThe political structure is extremely detailed and realistic. You can implement changes to the political structure and see how it actually works and effects your country like Amending constitution, removing the president's power to veto, separate The judiciary with legislation etc. If you love politics and its structure, this is a treatThere are no vague choices. Every choice is distinct and leads to different outcome. Almost no two option for a situation was the same or would have led to similar outcomes. Makes it easy for you to make decisions because you know what it would lead to and how varied it would be. This game pushes you to take a distinctive stance and gives you all the background and motivation to not just be a Centrist, something that's very difficult to implement since being a centrist is always easy. You will always have a sense of what you want to do and what stance to take and your hesitation will come from the political ramifications of those choices, not from the feeling of "Eh, both sounds equally good"There are some issues in the game though. Flow of time is very difficult to comprehend. There is a rudimentary turn based system but time also flows during the turn. Its difficult to grasp how much time has passed between two actions. So sometimes an action you take will show its fruit 1 turn later while some will show right away.The budgeting system is extremely simple consisting whole numbers. You spend somewhere, you get a -1 to that number and you get an income, you get a +1. Its a linear game so this is expected, but I really wish there was more freedom. I cannot change the budget of something unless the story wants me to, or abolish a law right away. The story progresses linearly and you only can make changes in that flow. That's what the game is, but I just wish there was more freedomThis game has been a treat for a political nerd like me. I was pulled into a believe able political struggle of a fictional country and I enjoyed every second of it. I highly recommend this game to anyone who has any slight interest in Politics
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is actually a really good game, whether it is a first play through or numerous plays to see each ideological pathways. It is very immersive and shows a brutal, realistic depiction of a leader thrown in a political arena of backroom deals and intrigue. You would have to make gut wrenching sacrifices in decisions to not do what's right but to do what is necessary to achieve goals.HOWEVER,I cannot fathom the lack of saving features, and I would like to stress as a person with wants and needs, I cannot restart an hour and thirty minutes worth of game play each time I forget one step to be successful. I understand that the developers desire to nail this, "your decisions are important" but options should still be available. Permanent ironman just ruins multiple playthroughs especially when this game has a standard script that you would repeat over and over again. Therefore, while I did enjoy the game, this would be a neutral review (as steam does not have that), and I look forward to Torpor's future endeavours.UPDATE: Iron man can now be disabled- the game is great!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely sure how realistic this game is but it certainly -feels- realistic in how it challenges you to navigate the political sphere. There are no clear cut paths to victory if you can call any ending a victory as you juggle the many demands of factions within your nation.Gameplay: It's one of those games where you click through dialogue options to progress the story in a direction you'd like it to go. You're expected to read the in-game Newspaper alongside various dossiers to get a good understanding of the world around you. Doing so will allow you to make better/informed decisions when it comes to dealing with faction interests.I wish the game had a better method of showing you the potential effect of some dialogue options because sometimes the text responses aren't as clear what the intent behind it is and then next thing you know you've pissed off religious sector.Overall, it's an entertaining game with enough twists and turns in the story that it will suck hours out of your life if you enjoy reading and exploring the politics of running a country. It showcases why no one is truly all powerful. No king rules alone and you have to keep your supporters happy if you intend to stay in power... Which is easier said than done when you're trying to juggle the fact that there are other countries in the world that are bigger/badder than you are and willing to mess with you for their own needs/interests.One thing I wish the game allowed you to do more of is break the mold and gain more influence to mess with  other countries more. But then it'd likely be a different type of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an interesting experience; a (mostly text-based) mix of a RPG and a political simulation where you step into the shoes of the newly elected president of a democratic country on the verge of crisis. You must face challenges such as economic recession, political intrigue both foreign and domestic, as well as scandals and plots.This is a game which I find myself returning to every now and then to see where my different decisions will take me. I give it a 5/5 rating!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A great game from a great team! I loved playing this game as it is very authentic and you feel the exact environment as if you are really President Rayne! It is a solid story, and its very human. The good thing about this game is although it looks like you have limited options, you really decide the flow of the story. Thus, you may play it a few more times than you would expect. I congratulate the developers of this game! It is clear that they consist a diverse set of people and they are not leaning one way or another from a political perspective.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I really love it since this involves politics and real life simulation of it, and not just dots and lines. I do hope tho that the game is further developed. Like, I would love for the President to have more personal-life options, have an affair maybe? with a guy? or with a non-binary? However, the most needed development of all, I want this to be more than just one term. And, why can't we dwell into more social issues? Also, how does the economy work? Somehow, on my second play, I got the economy development to the max, without knowing what exactly caused it. Was it just because that I gave the tax cuts? the game dev really needs more research into the 1950s economic.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a truth about the world: Everyone has their own ideas on how things should run, and when you're in charge of a nation, that's going to cause headaches and rob you of sleep.Enter Suzerain, a game about precisely that. In short, Suzerain is a political sim/visual novel. Instead of giving you a country to do with as you will, you will follow a relatively linear plot, but with a lot of freedom to steer it. As Anton Rayne, newly elected president of Sordland, you couldn't have wished for a messier start. After a couple decades of coups, civil war, and stagnation that culminated in a catastrophic recession and societal collapse, you've got your work cut out for you. No matter what you promised to get elected, whether reform, or to uphold the legacy of the past leaders, you will need to contend with people who wouldn't like anything more than your head served on a single platter, and that's before you face the fact that the nation is in shambles, a lot of problems need fixing, and you don't have the resources to tackle them all.The characters you meet all have personalities, ideals, dreams, and agendas (though some are more fleshed out than others). Understanding them is crucial to winning their support, or at least getting them not to oppose you directly. Sordland is a troubled nation in an unstable region of the world, the world itself is locked in a Cold War-esque era of ideological tension that's threatening to turn hot. Guiding a nation to reform or to reclaiming some sort of a past glory in such an environment is no easy task as vultures circle. The game doesn't shy away from difficult topics and does a brilliant job in relaying a second truth about the world: People have reasons for their ideas and agendas, and those reasons are rarely as simple as "Oh, they're just naive/misguided/bigoted fools". This, especially in today's world, is going to make the game extremely niche, and not only because of its very specific genre mix, and I do need to congratulate the developers for making something this daring. You will be forced into decisions. Some of them will be easy, some of them will not. How easy or hard they are will depend on what kind of President Rayne you want to play, but nothing is free, no good deed goes unpunished, and no ideal exists in a vacuum.Want to get of a corrupt Chief Justice? You may want to pass legislation that allows you or the Assembly to remove judges from service, but what kind of precedent does it set, and is that the right way if your problem is limited to that one judge who puts personal gain above duty? Maybe you recognize the fact that the office of President holds too much power, and wish to address that for the good of the nation, but how does that help if your own proposal, if it passes, can get you booted before you manage to accomplish any significant constitutional reform because some vengeful rival decided to use it against you and then install someone unscrupulous?Suzerain does well to realistically simulate the politics of the real world - as in, even if you don't opt for campaigns based on guile and deception, but value honesty and transparency instead, it's still going to be a tangled mess, and you will not accomplish anything with just ideals and charisma, because, in the end, no man rules alone, and Anton Rayne is no exception. Every decision you make will affect the nation, and the region. Sometimes even something as innocuous as phrasing your proposals may make someone support or oppose you. Or what you order for lunch when meeting them. Do not take power lightly, for it is not a toy. Suzerain may not appeal to a wide public. It's slow, it deals with topics that people can be uncomfortable with, and it really pushes the message hard, that the world is complicated, people are complicated, that sometimes doing something good will involve a painful concession somewhere else, but you'll still be expected to figure it out and deliver on what you promised to deliver, no matter how bad your hand may be.So, good luck, Mr. President. You will have a hard time. Your choices will have consequences. And you will question if you're doing the right thing, even if it looked brilliant on paper.And, with the 2.0 update, you'll have even more content, lore, character development, and headaches. Give it a whirl, it's worth it!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a lot of fun so far. Finally made it to Chapter II and I'm satisfied with the decisions the game allows me to make. My initial plan was to align myself behind the old guard and oligarchs to try and hang on to my presidental powers and I've been able to do that successfully so far. The game even allowed me to target the head of the reformers, which I had wanted to do but didn't know if it would allow me to do. They've put a lot of thought into the game and I can't wait to finish this run because I'd like to attempt another after.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Holy crap...this game is incredibly addictive.  While only 4 hours into it, I can't speak to the replayablity but its so far a lot of what I want in a political sim game.  The narrative is great and the writing is immersive.  Love what they've done with the Codex, giving you little details you don't really need like how the Maroon Palace was built or the backgrounds of characters.     All I can say is I hope the devs add more to this or make another game of similar quality- 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, I would like to point out that this game is a purely text-based game, with only a map design to at least visualize a little what's going on. This game is 100% about decision-making with almost no "chance outcomes" (apart form maybe one or two situations).Also there is a fully automatized auto-save, meaning that if you botched something up, there's no way back. Either restart or try to get something interesting out of this run nevertheless. (well apart from within the very same scene, where a reload before it ends will let you replay it in full, but enough spoilers)All this doesn't scare you off?  Great, this game is for you. Because in what it does, it really does well imo. You have several paths you can stray down and for all of them, the game provides you with the proper means, but for many, you need to make your choices very carefully.As you will have taken from the basic description already, the game puts you in the situation of a freshly elected president of some fictious country with a certain negihborhood. And you can lead it in many different ways, all depending on your decisions. There are many main endings with many, many subendings which really gives this game a high replayablity. I keep coming back to it, just to try a slightly different approach, or even something completely new. Also to see which achievements I can still get along the way, even in a bothced up game!What I also like is that the game totally doesn't fail to be clearly cynical about politics in all. While you explore the different paths, you will learn more and more about what is going on in the background, what agendas certain people have, who orchestrated certain events, etc. etc.So, in what the game does, really thumbs up from here - great job!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: one of the best games I've played. the level and quality of content in this game is absolutely amazing. I love every aspect of it, the newspapers, the economy, the military etc. I love how this game has managed to make me think like '' hmm if I assassinate this guy instead of that one, will their political party fall apart?  or should I just arrest them both.''  Torpor, Great Job! but please when will there be new content and what will it be? I'm dying from suspense! I can't stop myself from wondering what it will be? will it be your second term as president, will it leading a different nation like Rumburg or Lespia? Please tell us!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game manages to scratch an itch in my brain that no other game i played so far has been able to. I love the political simulation, the weighing of what you want to do with what you have to do to fix this utterly broken mess of a country.Its astounding how much joy one can get from finally managing to reduce an election threshhold by 7%.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps one of my favourite games I have had the pleasure of playing through in the past 4 years. Suzerain combines many aspects of games that I like to enjoy away from the competitive sphere. Suzerain is  a game in which every single choice you make affects an intricate web of geopolitical moves, and one wrong move can send the entire house of cards crashing down. Both the base game and the downloadable "Rizia" content pack provide interesting ways to govern over your own country, from touching upon the precise delicacies of a very corrupt democracy akin to the Russian Federation or any of the other post-Soviet states, or the absolutism of a kingdom in a world not fit for those ideals anymore, a kingdom focused on the export of its natural resources not dissimilar to the Gulf states or the developing nations of Sub-Saharan Africa, while keeping balance between noble houses that feels torn from Italy during the Middle Ages. As far as the decisions you make in this game, almost every single thing you choose will come back to bite you in the ass hours, or even days later depending on your playstyle, which if you don't take notes using the in-game notepad or a physical notepad, you may end up forgetting who bribed you to align a certain way- be it oligarchs or leaders of nations (oligarchs). I certainly have ended up doing this many-a-time, and then have to salvage the situation. Which only adds to the fun, as no leader is perfect, and it makes for a great challenge to come up with solutions on the fly, and can make your situation even worse if you are not careful.At the time of writing, I have not finished the Rizian story, but going off of experience with the Sords, this playthrough is bound to be fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is the ultimate CYOA Political Sim, and it was really a lot of fun. At first the game is overwhelming with everything going on, all the people and countries that are important; but the game does a good job introducing the characters and gameplay in the first chapter. I wish some of the choices were more explicitly clear on what your response was choosing, because I definitely contradicted my policies without realizing it. Also, there appears to be a bug after starting a new game and customizing the character, everything is inaccessible (menu, conversation, etc), forcing a restart of the game. I mistook this for the game being unplayable at first occurrence, but I liked the prologue so much that I reinstalled and was able to play fine after that. But on my second playthrough I experienced the same bug. After closing the game and opening again, no issues. Anyways, back to the game, you really feel the consequences or benefits of your decisions throughout the entire game. From the policies you campaign on in the beginning, to every bill that crosses your desk, to what department needs funding; everything ends up mattering. I really, really enjoyed the storyline and all the vastly different directions you can take the president. I ended up as a Centrist on my first game. I thought I would play this through once and be done, but there were so many regrets I had; I just had to start playing again. First playthrough took ~25 hours reading through all the text (massive amounts). I am certainly skimming through quicker on the second round. Definitely recommend to anyone interested in political sims, CYOA, and who like reading!8.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I've never written a steam review before but my excellent experience with Suzerain has prompted me to sing the praises of a game that I've thoroughly enjoyed. Suzerain is a nuanced and engaging political and economic simulator set in a fictional vaguely eastern European nation called Sordland in the 1950s. You play Anton Rayne, the newly elected 4th President of a troubled country facing several seemingly insurmountable challenges: a deep recession, a flawed and fractured political landscape, and looming international crises. On its own these challenges make for interesting player choices. Do you privatize certain industries to bring market forces to your country or do you maintain state control in order to prevent people from being exploited by businesses? Its all up to you. But are you ready to accept the consequences? Your decisions will impact the lives of many and not always for the better.In the political arena, your nation must come to terms with the complicated legacy of its living, but retired, larger-than-life founder, who casts a long shadow over your Sordland's constitution, your presidency, and fellow countrymen. However, not all struggles you face will be a result of his decisions for Sordland's customs and ideas around ethnicity, nationality, gender, and ideology are deeper and more pervasive.To top it off, you must balance your personal relationships with all the important figures in Sordland. From business people, to prominent elected leaders, and members of your own cabinet, you will make choices that inspire, disappoint, and frustrate many who you will need to rely on to fix your country. Meanwhile at home you struggle to balance the needs of your family with the demands of your job as president.While all the above pieces are enough on its own to make a worthwhile experience the thing that elevates Suzerain above other similar strategy and simulator titles for me is the writing. Torpor Games have been able to create deep nuanced characters, each with their own motives and realistic reactions to the world and your choices. Some are petty, others professional. Negotiating with someone to ideological, another leader might be more compromising. For President Anton Rayne, the player character, the writing is particularly strong and flows in a way that makes the path you walk realistic while keeping the characterization strong. Is Anton good at hiding his worries and frustrations? Does he value his principles above making a material difference for his country? Does he believe that his compromises are worth it. Is he a power hungry raging misogynist? You are given a wide range of ways to respond to the world and your own choices that forge an interesting and believable character. The dialogue is witty, the world filled with deep lore, and the humor of the game shines through when you need a chuckle. Multiple times during my playthroughs I found myself in shock, disturbed, humored, saddened, and deeply touched. To me, the writing matches any decent novel and has impacted me in a similar way.If I had one personal frustration with the game which was the save feature. Torpor clearly want your decisions to matter so after almost any choice your save updates to make you live with the consequences. As a design choice it works well and works to resist your impulse to save scum and simply enjoy the result of your decisions, good or bad. This feature is probably one of the best in the game but after one or two playthroughs I found myself wishing to experiment to see what different choices in the dialogue would do. However, the autosave feature does, in my view, limit that kind of experimentation as you might have to restart a save or create multiple save files in order to conveniently accomplish this. Nevertheless, the auto save feature does help make the game what it is and is better for it. However, maybe Torpor's future titles could explore a chapter save feature, but my gripe here is minor and did not severely impact my enjoyment of this excellent game.I am certainly looking forward to whatever is next in the world that Suzerain has created. It has become one of my favorite games this year and I've recommended it to many of my friends who also have found enjoyment in the story, characters, and choices that Suzerain offers. Suzerain is clearly a labor of love and that dedication shines through. In an era where many studios cannot seem to write compelling stories Suzerain stands above. For anyone who is a fan of strategy games, rich stories, choose your own adventures, and simple gameplay. Suzerain might just be for you.A Morgna wes core. Vectern sis da!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game thinking it would be something similar to the Sorcery! series by Inkle. However, I found mixes of intrigue, strategy, and especially moral dilemmas that I was not expecting. The replayability is quite strong, but the repeated dialogue can get quite annoying since it takes up time just going through trying to get to a point where you can diverge your story. Other than that, this game is exceptional, and just one trip through this game's story (10-15 hours for me) is worth the price. I highly recommend this to anyone who is interested in games centered around story, branching dialogue, and politics.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a choose-your-own-adventure game with the backdrop of you becoming the president of a fictional country on the verge of collapse after a major political upheaval. Did you promise the people freedom & liberty or order & security? Did you promise to help expand civil rights to the minorities of one of your provinces or did you promise to sell shares of the state-run company to an oligarch to help secure your reform package (and finances)? Do you even care about your promises? The game does have quite a bit of replayablility due to there being three fairly different story lines you can go down (status quo, left, right) with each of those options having some variations on what your Left or Right looks like in this universe. Like are you a Social Democrat (very difficult) or Communist-type, an Authoritarian Democrat or a Nationalist Autocrat or even a puppet of a bigger badder country who knows that now would be the time to take land they believe is their's.If any of those things sounded interesting to you then I would recommend trying this out. Be warned, you'll probably lose a couple of times.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the best of its kind in the niche genre of political simulations and text-driven games.It achieves something that I've never seen in the dozens of political games so far, and I never realized we missed; which is that the practice of politics and power is social. Every decision happens in a meeting room, talking to and convincing people who all have their own agenda, and will try to convince you to go in their direction. Most political games are going with the dashboard/spreadsheet click-on-buttons type of management, which is never how real life will be.To realize the complexity of this social political decision making, means that the game is essentially a visual novel with a linear progress, but where choices do matter. The game is actually pretty hard, but fair, because it does give you all the information you need to understand what your choices will imply... if you pay attention.Anyway, it's a great game. it's very clear to me that the people behind this game are history and political nerds, in a good way. They even managed to make a game that doesn't feel partisian at all (whereas in many political sims, you can feel where the mechanics want you to go...).
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's not often that I feel the emotion that a developer puts into their world, and yet I cried and laughed and felt the excitement and optimism from the people of Sordland. I highly recommend this to anyone who wants to try something a little different. My only cons are the intro takes up a lot of time and REALLY want both the train and highway projects together!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I do like this game but after some time it becomes painfully obvious that the endings are very poorly designed. Despite all the freedom the player is given throughout a playthrough, not adhering to specific conditions results in always getting certain bad endings. Rather than having endings that fit the player's choices, the player ends up forced to change choices in order to get specific endings (or, rather, not get them).Despite the wide breadth of things that the player can undertake, the nature of the game funneling you into certain endings if you actually do some of the things severely limits your choices in the end. "Mistakes" made early on - and I use the word "mistake" very liberally here - result in failstates showing up hours later.Not only does this idiotic design go against the rest of the game, it's made a million times worse with the whole "one auto-save only" thing and how one playthrough typically takes at least 6 hours. It's not uncommon to play for 2-3 hours only to realise that the game is screwing you over with one of its nonsensical failstates yet again, meaning that your current playthrough is worthless.The endings themselves are also severely lacking. Follow-ups on what happens to individual characters and factions would have gone a very long way.It's a real pity because there is a huge amount of potential here, and the game does feel like something magical on your first playthrough, but the bad ending system and barebones endings just ruin the entire experience. Once the magic wears off and the veil comes down, it becomes very clear that the game just does not respect your time, and that most of what you do doesn't actually matter.Extremely disappointing.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A not-so-bad game for killing time. The game is basically based on your choices, and there is no load/save feature so you cannot undo your mistakes. In that sense, it's realistic. It also could be a bit repetitive since most of the time you do everything right and one thing wrong (which costs you a loss). To come until that decision which you want to change, you need to replay the entire scenario until that point, since there is no load/save feature. It's a fun game for a few rounds, but then it gets repetitive and boring due to this repetitiveness.The scenario is basically the cold-war era country trying to thrive in the middle of a messy geolocation. Your neighbors are problematic, you have also major domestic problems. The scenario walks you through these and lets you follow your own approach to these problems. The country you're playing resembles cold-era period Turkey a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Wow what a hidden gem, heard about this after Rob Zacny  from Waypoint Radio recommended it. If you like actual choice with consequences this is a game where your decisions matter, really they're ALL that matters. It sort of felt like playing a season of "House of Cards." My favorite part of the game is the interpersonal relationships that you develop and how each character has their own agenda, people will lie to you, steal from you, take advantage of you, just like real life! And it's up to you to parse out who is telling telling the truth and who has interests other than their own in mind. There's multiple different endings.. but ... they don't all happen at the end ;)  The game can go multiple different ways, and there's some pretty wild outcomes. It takes a lot to hook on me on a game these days but I couldn't stop playing this, looking forward to starting another playthrough to see some of the other outcomes you can achieve.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Hello! I just finished my (first) playthrough, and it ENDED really badly, but up until that point, despite not QUITE winning, I constantly felt like I was JUST ABOUT to turn this country around! I bought it in a sale but got 16 hours play out of a playthrough, with SOME inclination to replay and fix things (but I'll need a break, it's all too fresh).Some excellent twists, some foreshadowed some not. I love the in-depth discussions!In fact, my main gripe is that 2-3 of what I considered to be the biggest political decisions (that I don't wish to spoil) are suddenly presented as personal choices WITHOUT speaking to my Cabinet? Which I found odd, and I hope that changes later. Another change I wish they would show - you see the state of your economy in the corner, but I wish you could also see that line as it evolves. Yes, it's going up now, but how far down did it sink first?If you plan on playing, I advise:Be OK with the veto. I was operating under the belief that my party / the majority wanted every policy to hit my desk, so said "yes" more than I should have. Don't get too overdrawn. I spent most of the game below -4, which I saw as government funds rather than country funds, but unfortunately it was also apparently hitting the whole country's economy. If you like:PoliticsText-based AdventuresTricky DecisionsGet this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game has both great components and poor sections. Hopefully the following will help you determine if it's for you. The first playthrough is a tour de force of tense decisionmaking, the decline from idealism into cold practicality, and dealing with the shortcomings of others. When it's over, it's not always clear what decisions led to the ending, It's a solid 6-8 hour experience, and if I wrote the review then, or if you only want that one playthrough, I'd recommend it.The following playthroughs are the problem. The text-heavy gameplay means either re-reading the same text once again (there's really less variety than it first appears) or just mashing the space bar until a choice pops up or you see new text. This glacially slow gameplay loop combined with an ironman style seve system means that the number of different endings is immaterial unless you're interested in reading the same story again and again with a handful of changes. I've played this through two and a quarter times, and I won't return.If you're in for one playthrough, I really strongly recommend it. I played until the sun came up that first run. The graphics are fitting, the sound is reaonable, and the decisions feel like real decisions. It's a solid story, and it's great that first playthrough. If you're willing to just spam space, manually back up your saves every turn, or just min-max ruthlessly or follow a guide, you'll know better than me if you want it.If you want a pure governance sim with replayability, it's probably too opaque and slow.Again, if you're keen on getting one amazing playthrough, treat this like a recommend, but I don't see this as replayable, and the ends are simply frustrating. A game with multiple endings, mostly hidden metrics and mechanics, and a slow game tempo, combined with ironman saves, is simply not something I can recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is handsdown the best political drama ever portrayed in a game. Taking heavy inspiration from the Cold War politics of our own world, while still putting a unique and captivating twist on its own setting, the game focuses around the life of a turbulent country's president, as they(you) navigate their way through a web of interesting political dilemmas. What separates this game from the rest that attempt this kind of story, is that Suzerain takes a much more human approach to politics. Rather than being a faceless entity that controls a nation, only looking at perfect statistics and percentage sliders, you roleplay as a living person with their own unique background and worldviews.I can honestly say this is one of my favourite games of all time, and would recommend it to everyone who comes across it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A great game for those with a passion for politics.The game is detailed, and you have a great deal of power as President of Sordland - power to define the direction of your economy, the budgets of each of your sections of government, the state of the constitution and more. But all of your actions have consequences, and you sometimes feel these consequences long after making the decisions. And many actions will accumulate over time, leading to one of the several possible endings.I thoroughly enjoyed Suzerain until the end, where I was struck with confusion as to the ending I received - but after some clarification, I believe I understand why it happened. However, it still left me feeling bitter, because I don't believe it was the ending I deserved and it still arose as something of a surprise. But it's not enough to sour the entire game.If you love politics, you should love this game. Keep in mind that if you're not a keen reader, you probably won't enjoy this game so much.4/5.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE BEST political game to date. The amount of detail that has gone into this game is astonishing. Every single decision you make will influence your country's success or decline. Hours upon hours worth of quality story telling and decision making. There are a multitude of complex issues that need resolving. Such as stimulating your economy to dealing with difficult foreign policy. If you are a fan of political games, this is a MUST HAVE.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Great political adventure. Lots of options to go through a wide range of political perspectives and very interesting character dynamics dependent on your choices. Your choices also feel as if they actually matter which some games choose-your-own-adventures fail to accomplish. The game is also quite difficult, but it is representative to how politics of a country are inherently complicated issues.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare for a game to be so realistic and well written that its choices help you explore your own personal character and morals. I feel like I just finished a gigantic therapy session, where this game was a Freudian fever dream letting me explore my own values and goals. How far would I go to defend my goals? What are my goals? Do I keep my promises? How do I approach conflict? How much do I crave power? Who do I choose to stand beside when times get rough? I feel more human somehow for playing through this. But I don't think I can play it again. I got a good ending (2nd term), my head hurts, and I was on edge the entire time. Thank you for creating this work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game to anybody who likes stories in games. I don't think I've ever felt as emotional in a game as when, in my first playthrough, I failed to pass my constitution through the Assembly. The world is incredibly rich and believable, and the variety of branches in the game's story are staggering. For its price point this game is an exquisite and very grown-up gem that I don't think I'll ever forget.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s an interesting game that gives a firsthand look at how complicated it is to run a country, especially one this broken. At first, I was delighted with the decision making and chess style politics, but the ending is usually the same and straight out ridiculous. Unless you’re completely militaristic and kissing up to your bald general, you’re going to get coup by the military. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a game almost a visual novel in which we play the role of Anton Rayne, who has just been elected president of Sordland, a country modeled on post-Atatürk's Turkey. Sordland is in a difficult situation. He is threatened by, among others, a polio epidemic, war with Rumburg, the Blud rebellion and economic recession. The interior of the country itself is not prepared for sudden changes either. There are fascists in parliament, Soll's conservative influence still remains in the hearts of many politicians. Oligarchs control the country economically, and propaganda education destroys subsequent generations. Put in this situation, Rayne can decide to become a reformer, a sollist, a dictator, a commie, a capitalist, a nationalist, or whatever his heart desires. But he will never be able to fulfill all his goals, because despite becoming president, it turns out that his control over the country is far from perfect. Anton will often have to wonder what is more important: democracy or security, workers' rights or the state's economy, rapid reforms or influence and re-election, and finally politics or his own family.Apart from the great lore and characters, this is the first game since Beholder 1 that presented me with really difficult choices with far-reaching consequences. There are so many choices and they influence each other so much that even though the game does not contain random elements, you often never know exactly what to expect, almost as if you were playing a roguelike. I highly recommend it to anyone as long as they're able to withstand reading a lot of text.

_childDocuments_.review: For the given price tag, it's a really nice game. You can dive into a realistic-feeling role of decision-making under realistic-feeling political circumstances, and the game compels you to do your best and weigh in earnest your wording and your decisions, so you get a solid couple of hours of convincing immersion into a story. The game shows its limits when you about mid-game begin to realize that your freedom of influencing the overall situation is in fact very narrow.As other reviewers have already pointed out, you have neither real alternatives in choosing your path (you can't go radically communist or fascist, neither in the prelude nor in the game itself), nor are you sufficiently informed to prefer a better decision over a worse, so the game feels rigged (a) for centrism and (b) for failure. I managed to make only one term as president before succumbing to economic depression and political intrigue. For example, nobody told me in advance that promoting women's lib would heavily drain my budget.As you neither get a clue where exactly you could make alternative decisions to avoid the last outcome nor can go back to an older savegame to change your path at a specific point nor have an incentive to start again from the beginning, the game doesn't offer you any replay value. It's mainly interactive story telling of a political drama. For this I give this game a thumbs-up, but only because it didn't cost me more than a paperback novel from the station bookstall.

_childDocuments_.review: ===You should read this b4 buying===Unfortunately there is a character limit, so I can't flesh out my points as well as they deserve to be. Oh well. There are two main problems, the story problem, and the game mechanics problem. =====Story=====The second half of your play through, about 6 hours in, you become a wet rag, and stop doing anything. It's like your character gets a lobotomy and just sits there. Then someone takes you over, coup, invasion, superpower, whatever. Everyone seems to be experiencing this problem, no matter the play style. The threat, whatever it is, is hinted at well in advance, but the game never gives you any options to do anything about it. You gotta understand, the whole game is scripted like those "Walking Dead" comic-book looking games. You basically just choose from responses. You can't do anything that isn't a pre-written event, offered to you at a specific time. Like, idk, missions. The game presents you missions, you go do them. The choice is in how, chosen from among the pre-written responses. So if the game never specifically offers you a way to solve a problem, it CAN NOT be solved. You will run into this. No matter your choices, you will not succeed. I am curious whether this was intended, or just the result of the dev team not being able to tighten up the exponentially branching possibilities. I can totally forgive the later, but it's got to be fixed. pronto dude.====Mechanics====What I cannot forgive is the entire other half of the game. The Economic system. It is absolutely abysmal. Literally retarded.I originally wrote a longer review, so I'll just post whatever fits from the economic part here now. Feel free to read until you get bored. TLDR: don't waste your time! Go outside! Pet a dog!Alright here's what fit:"It's really tempting to get into some economic theory here, and I feel like the game is literally designed to encourage that conversation because you are designing an economy in the Cold War...but I'm not going to. I'm not going to say that National Debt is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ issue. I'm not going to say that historically recessions and depressions have been created, not stumbled into because of 'UnEmPlOyMeNt'. I'm not going to say that economic development comes from actual work, not capital....there, I didn't say any of those things ;)I'm just going to talk about the things we can all agree on. The basic math. First of all, there is no budget, and it isn't accounted for periodically. You use these things called Budget Points (ok sure), you have so many when you start from the decisions of the last administration (yeah), and you allocate them to projects you like (great). Problem is, there is no financial cycle. You see, the world runs on schedules. Periodically, Governments replenish their BUDGETS. Even if you treat a Government like a household (don't!), there's income and expenditures. Money comes in, and it goes out. Every year you get more money, and then you spend it. Very simple.The game doesn't do that. Budget Points don't get replenished every year! You NEVER get a Budget Renewal! These budget points...they can be allocated for a 6-month-long construction project, and you will continue to have a suppressed budget total for 4 years! It's infrastructure! It costs a lot to build, but once it's built it basically just sits there, making you money!Imagine you leave college, you've got 40k in the bank (somehow...) and you move to a new city to start a new job. You should buy a car, so you can get to work. You are making 80k a year at your new job. Good for you. So you buy a real nice 40k car, and then someone tells you, "ok, we'll take that 40k in your bank, and another 40k every single year until the end of time. You make 40k now. Same job, but only 40k, permanently.". It's like, what? No, I continue to make 80k a year, and make a one time payment of 40k. When I get paid again at the end of the year, and for all the years to come, I still get 80k!Not in this game!There are a number of choices that heavily factor in on your playthrough here. Because of this dumbass decision, for instance: you can send checks to 'the people' to alleviate their suffering when you get elected. Stimulus checks. [-1 Budget]. So...are we just doing that permanently now? Did we just implement UBI? 'Cause you are NEVER getting that Budget Point back. When the new year comes...the money doesn't get replenished. So that must mean every Sordish citizen is getting a phat check every month, continuously, for the whole 4 year term, right? Ok. So why does the game tell me people are starving in the streets (yeah, just casually thrown in some report is that 'people are dying of starvation'...like, how is that not a bigger thing?) if I'm literally sending them food money every month? Why do my farmers complain to me that their industry and regions are failing because they can't sell all their crops? Am I not giving starving people money? Will starving people not usually buy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ food if they are starving to death and have money?! It's a simple government subsidy to the farm industry (except hungry people are actually getting food....imagine lol).Why is unemployment a 'serious' issue if everyone is on UBI? Unemployment didn't go up when I sent the checks out, so apparently no one quit their jobs, so apparently we are producing the same amount of goods/services....so...why are these problems still around? Alternatively, where did my money go!?You build a highway, and that money is taken from your total cap. So, does it cost as much to maintain the highway every year after it's built as it does to build it in the first place? Cause that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nutz. You fund the construction off 'hundreds of schools and hospitals' across the country, and your budget is permanently decreased. Does it cost as much to staff these places as it took to build the giant buildings?!  You increase the budget of the police to bring national stability to rioting streets...so what now there's just hundreds of SWAT guys with riot shields walking around everywhere? Is that just how we roll now? Cause they stopped protesting like, 2 years ago.....You see what I'm getting at?Here's another very simple thing that got totally screwed up: You can increase taxes on luxuries by like, 10%, from 25 up to 35%. [+1 Budget Point]. Ok,  You can make enough money from that, immediately, that you can fund a huge construction company to build a national highway [-1 Budget Point] that goes half-way across the flipping country? HOW MANY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LUXURIES ARE THEY BUYING HERE?!? That's a LOT of money, apparently, from a very small, niche tax. We're talking tens of millions of dollars. So, is the luxury market in the country on the scale of hundreds of million of dollars? My GOVERNMENT'S BUDGET never went above 2 Budget Points, but the luxury market is the equivalent of 10 Budget Points? ARE YOU TELLING ME PEOPLE ARE SPENDING MORE ON CAVIAR AND YACHTS THAN MY ENTIRE GOVERNMENT IS SPENDING on the ENTIRE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ COUNTRY?!?!Scale aside, the basic accounting skills are still absent. Is it a one-time thing, or a permanent revenue increase? Cause I didn't change the law back after 6 months....so this is a new revenue stream, right?....(You might argue that people stopped buying luxuries when the prices spiked, so I got a little money in the short term, and them killed the industry, but that makes no sense. The price spike is immediate and pronounced, so would be the response. You don't go buy an overpriced diamond bracelet for your gold-digger, see the 10% increase and say, "Gee golly, that's too expensive!...tomorrow. But today it's fine.") So I should be getting a brand new shiny budget point every year, right? So four times over my term?BTW why wasn't this an option at the start of my term? Why am I only being given the option in the last 5 yards of my Superbowl game?Look, this is really important. This game is ABOUT managing a co-"

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: the game is decent in production quality, but poor in game-play with fundamental flaws in it's design pillars.It seems the developers, by design, decided that the game should be inherently difficult. Choices are inherently manufactured and artificial - that is to say, the game is designing these decisions to be intentionally binary, and intentionally convoluted. You will find few, if any, decisions in the game that are purely advantageous, just as you will find few, if any, decisions that are purely disadvantageous. The designers probably felt that this would be interesting game-play, with a constant tug-of-war over resources and advantages, leading to complex decisions and difficult decision-making.But that never really pans out. And I think the problem here is the nature of the decision making process. For one, a game this interested in the give-and-take nature of these decisions should provide detailed information about the effects of your policies. But it doesn't. The game hides away the effects of everything you do. There are some tabs that allow you to generally guess at the progress you're making, but they're far from helpful.Secondly, the decisions themselves are entirely linear. In fact, I don't know why the developers wasted time in developing this nifty map interface, when you don't really ever need it. In fact, if the game were structured like a visual novel, it could have probably sufficed. And there's an inherent problem when some elements of your game are entirely useless.That aside, the structure of the game is entirely linear. That is, each decision happens in exactly the same order. Sure, some decisions only come online when certain events/criteria are met. However, one playthrough as a free-market proponent will look exactly like the last. Although, as I said before, each choice has its own advantages and disadvantages, there are still  choices. So if you want to accomplish anything, your choices are actually rather limited.As for linearity, this is especially telling because nothing is extra. In fact, there are no side events. Each event is directly linked to the main plot. . This is no TellTale game, and that much is pretty obvious.The final issue I have is an inherent flaw in the design strategy. The game is intentionally forcing you to make tough decisions. That, I can respect. However, it completely eliminates creativity.  You just sit there and take your lumps cause you're a passive puppet. Even in real life, they call it the bully pulpit for a reason. You don't have to just sit there, there are things any leader can do. Organizations are unnecessarily limited in their scope, situations are unnecessarily contrived, and the golden ticket of outside-the-box thinking is stupidly limited. In that sense, the game is more of a clicking simulator.There are lots more design flaws, but the last thing I'll mention is the economy meter, which plays a big role in the game. It's far too oversimplified and far too whimsical. It rises and drops seemingly at random. Negative effects that should take months or years ding you instantly. And positive effects perk up only a little, then randomly start decreasing for seemingly no reason. And also, cause it's a linear game, you only have a limited number of options to deal with it. I actually had a government surplus at one point, and my council said we should spend more to jump-start the economy. Done deal, I thought. But no. It seems that by that point, I had passed all the events for investing in the economy. So at that point, I had money, but apparently nothing to spend it on for at least two chapters.And it's this type of contrived design that irritates people. Difficulty for difficulty's sake isn't an achievement. Making a difficult, but fair, game is rewarding. Dark Souls is tough as nails, but if you study each enemy, get good, and practice, you'll win. It's fundamentally a fair game. You make a fair game by giving players information, opportunities, and appreciating the decisions that they make. If someone makes all the right dialogue choices, you should reward them by giving them very unique choices. It might make the game easier if they have those additional options, but they earned it. Give it to them. This game is certainly no Dark Souls. And it isn't really worth buying. Do yourself a favor, and move along.

_childDocuments_.review: I see what the devs were going for here, but I think the execution was fumbled. I played for just over an hour and made maybe... 4-5 decisions that seemed to matter? The rest was reading and/or clicking through reams of flavour text, and choosing between options that didn't really matter. For example, the game loves to give you 4 different ways to say hello to someone, and 5 different ways to say goodbye. This is stupid and waste of the player's time. Just skip to the meat of the decision. Similarly, most of the dialogue options are flavourful, but don't meaningfully affect the game, or at least not any way that I could see.The quality of writing is good, but there's just too much of it. It got frustrating fast trying to find interesting decisions, when the game prefers to vomit exposition, newspaper reports and briefings at you. I had zero motivation to read all of this when there wasn't any chance to actually apply it to anything. As Sid Meier said, a videogame is a series of interesting decisions. I was presented with lots of decisions during my playtime, but none of them were interesting because none of them were meaningful... or if they were meaningful, this was hidden from the player.I do not understand the praise this game gets and the fact that there aren't more haters. I went in expecting a strategy game, and instead I got a visual novel wearing the skin of Hearts of Iron... colour me disappointed. I want my 61 minutes back.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:Honestly, I can definitely say this is one of my overall favorite Steam games even past some significant flaws. The game has a very in depth story within both Sordland and the Suzerain universe. Sordland is under new government formation after a raging civil war between the socialists and nationalists, you choose your own background of how you grew up and how your career went leading up to your presidency which semi affects the game-play during your first term. The game does great at having immersive value with extensive history, some well written characters, and a wide arrange of choices to make as you see fit. It also does well as allowing a wide range of decisions to be made whilst not limiting you to only that path, for example you can become a sort of dictator but still be appeasing to minorities or go for a communist route whilst still making some capitalist decisions. You make all these decisions whilst also trying to appease your Assembly   which is mostly consisting of USP (your party) with still extensive influence from the parties founder who you might not agree with. Existing in both a party and a country with much Stalin-like influence is a great aspect to your term as you try to make decisions that may or may not stray from his influence which inevitably upsets one base or the other. There are also in-country factions to interact with which have can have significant political or national influence based on your decisions. In both these factions and your party are some very well written characters who are not super predictable and some even being hard to read or having alternate motives with my personal favorites being Kibenar, Lucian, Tory, Alphonso, Soll, Morgna, Graf, and Holl.Negatives: I can say I love this game but cannot simply overlook its significant flaws simply because of my own bias. To start of is economic systems. It is very hard to precisely know how well the economy is doing other than very infrequent updates from your ministers and a very confusing bar at the top of your screen. With there being 2 economic routes of free-market or a state-run economy, it adds a nice tweak that you are in charge of the economic direction but it is damn hard to actually run these economies since you can never fully know how well the economy is doing and your economic status only tends to matter for very few occasions like avoiding trade war, budget changes for ministries, and avoiding the great Sordish depression. Building off this point, there are not many points where you economy actually makes money even if the economy is doing well, most of your funds will come through either extensive trade with few select nations, massive privatization of state run services, or by not spending money on half the things your nations needs. I find it pointless that my minister reports that the consumer market is enthusiastic or the L-1 Rail is doing very well for the economy if i am not going to see any slight increases to my budget. It is just a bit frustrating when you cannot sign half the bills you need or fund the ministries you want without allowing private sector and the Oligarchs to run the country behind you. Speaking on the limited trade ability is the few nations you are allowed to interact with, on the map you see in the store pictures, you only can directly interact with Wehlen, Lespia, Agnolia, Valgsland, Rizia (hardly), and obviously Rumberg and you can only trade with some depending on your economic and political directions which makes sense but is disappointing when the trade selection is only 4 countries rather than the 20+ nations on the square map provided. I understand that this is all within a singular 4 year term but it would be nice to be able to simply interact with some other nations like Kyrute, Agard, etc like how you speak with ATO or CSP. Nevertheless, I am just expressive because I really enjoy the game as evident in my hours spent staring at dialogue and would like to see a bit more practicality in these creative ideas inserted into the game. It is still absolutely worth the money and has really good replay-ability to try out the different runs to do (dictator, reformist, communist, capitalist, etc.) and run the country how you see fit. Just remember, the Old Guard are not your friends

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an amazingly engaging political simulation game with a high degree of replayability. Choices do matter and there are a lot of different outcomes based on those choices. The lore of the world is pretty well designed, clearly drawing on early Cold War geopolitics and certain countries are rather clearly stand ins for real world countries. However the focus on Sordland, the country you are President of, creates a deep and engaging world with its own history. The game lets you play as anything from a Democratic Capitalist to a Military Authoritarian, to a Nationalizing Communist and pretty much anything else on the political spectrum (the game shows you where your character ends up on the political spectrum compared with other characters in the game after each play through). Other characters are also on the political spectrum and this influences their goals and agendas. Put simply I recommend this game to anyone with an interest in geopolitics.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for April 2022, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 3rd, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A visual novel mixed with a country simulator. Suzerain takes a bit to start. The first half-hour has you playing the backstory of your character in a visual novel style while making choices to define your character. Do you stand against tyranny or avoid conflict? Do you want to become a lawyer, economist, or history professor? Each of these helps define your character.Then one day you become president and the real game begins. You’re in charge of a vast country and now need to bring the country out of the current recession, fulfill promises made to the populace, and navigate the waters of the presidency. This is done through a lot of visual novel style discussions complete with the player asking questions, and choosing different answers depending on the situation. These answers should likely change the course of the country or the game, but I didn’t have enough time to see this. There are nine different endings and even more sub endings so it’s very likely what you do will matter throughout the game. Pick this up if you like the idea of a visual novel that’s focused on running a country, rather than trying to date random waifus. It’s a unique take and the writing is well done, but it’s also a lot of writing. It is an interesting concept though and I’m curious as to how far it will take the story. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who's a big fan of visual novel games where decisions you make greatly impact the story (think Ace Attorney, Nonary Games), I was greatly drawn to Suzerain. It's a game where reading is a big component (gasp) but it's incredibly well written and so easy to get drawn in. I found it surprisingly cosy - I would play it at night to unwind but got to bed in the wee hours as I got so immersed in Anton's (the protagonist's) story. You have a lot of scope to build Sordland the way that YOU want it and you'd be surprised at how your convictions change over the course of the game. The fact that there are multiple different endings for this game (having just finished my first run-through) excites me to continue. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an extremely in-depth and engaging political simulator with an amazing story and deep lore. In it, you play as the president of Sordland, a fictional stand-in for many Eastern European and South American nations during the cold war. You will find yourself dealing with a nation that, for the past three decades, has experienced revolution, coups, civil wars, and economic upheaval. Internally, you will face an economic recession, an aging infrastructure, a corrupt establishment, political extremists, and separatists. Externally, you will be faced with superpowers vying for influence over you and neighbors who threaten war. To say it can be stressful at times is an understatement.There are multiple paths to take and various solutions to choose from.If you are fine with a lot of reading (the game is almost like a visual novel), I can't recommend this enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphically there's not much going on, everything you do revolves around staring at a map or clicking through dialogue boxes.But that's OK, because the story and world are quite immersive. Every choice seems to matter a lot, and you're not encouraged to save scum. Characters try to convince you to side with them, and there are compelling arguments and reasons to take most paths. Ultimately your resources are limited and you can't please everyone, so you have to decide what's most important: your principles? The economy? The welfare of your people? These sorts of choices will greatly shape how you experience the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is, overall, a good game, even if it is not without serious flaws.First of all, it must be recognized that this game is original, both in its concept and in its universe.I would like to see more games with this concept : not a political/strategy/management simulation game where you manage everything in an abstract way, but rather where you directly incarnate the leader on a daily basis, with his personal problems, power relations that are embodied by personal relationships, etc., and which therefore has aspects which are very typical of a "visual novel."This kind of game is very rare: I only know of "Long Live the Queen" and "Yes, Your Grace" which are close to it, with a very different approach than Suzerain, RPG-oriented for the first, and very simple strategy for the second. Suzerain is trying to be a realistic political simulation, with difficult relations with the different political forces in the country, with the National Assembly, an economic recession that must be faced, etc.In terms of general quality, I would say that Suzerain is a better game than "Yes, Your Grace," but not as good a game as "Long Live the Queen," although this is still a very relative assessment given that these games have different approaches.The universe of the game is also very interesting, reminding me to some extent of Disco Elysium.It's a totally alternative world to ours, but also very close to what it might have been in the 1950s/1960s, with a cold war pitting a capitalist bloc against a socialist bloc, in a region quite similar to our Middle East. The player becomes president of a country that seems to be more or less an alternative Syria. It is not, however, a copy-paste of our world, since the socialist bloc still seems less authoritarian than ours (the equivalent of the USSR looks like the one that might have existed if it had not been led by Stalin but by Lenin, and the larger socialist neighboring country is more inclined to promote self-rule, resembling communist Yugoslavia in some ways), and the region still has some important differences with the Middle East. In short, it is quite interesting to be president of a country in this universe.This game is a lot of fun. But although it has a concept and a universe that I like very much, I must also admit that it also has some serious flaws.A list of the flaws :1/ If the narrative structure of the game gives the player many possibilities (+++), which is excellent, it still leads to some inconsistencies (--), even if I'm hopeful that patches will correct them. 2/ The characters lack charisma. (It's a point on which "Long Live the Queen" surpasses Suzerain by far.)I didn't get attached to any of the characters in the game, except maybe the protagonist’s wife, and to a certain extent his son (his very young daughter, on the other hand, appears to be totally transparent, which contrasts very negatively with the character of Cedani in Yes, Your Grace, who has a similar but very interesting profile).But for the rest, the player essentially spends their time with boring politicians and bosses, which is, in the end, quite realistic, but not really exciting. The person who is supposed to be our best friend is really annoying, the ministers are only characterized by their political positions (which are far too different to belong to the same government, giving the impression of a sort of national unity government ranging from ultra-nationalists to free-market maniacs to socialists…), etc. Finally, only the other Heads of State have an interesting personality.3/ Some of the biases regarding the consequences of your policies are questionable. In itself this is not necessarily a problem. It is necessary to stand a position and it would have been impossible to satisfy everyone. While some biases seem desirable (for example, gender equality is good!), others, especially those concerning the economy, seem really strange. I will explain the problems I have with the game’s economy in detail in the spoiler section.4/ Oh, and I almost forgot: you can't manually save! You only have checkpoints and can only load the last one! It's a deliberate choice from the developpers to deepen realism, but it's really a poor choice. It lowers the replayability a lot, and we're old enough to know how to have fun, seriously !In conclusion, I would say that this game is worth buying because it remains a very nice political simulation, but keep in mind that you will not necessarily agree with all its biases and flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text adventure game combined with a political sim. Things arent obvious like a democracy game, you make choices about yourself, family, and attend meeting with your cabinet and meet up with various interests from local leadership, to media moguls, and nefarious oligarchies. There is a ton of lore you have to sift through and you have to choose your decisions very carefully and even what you say in front of certain people. This is one of those games ill probably do a run once every six months so that i can come back to it with curiosity again
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: **There is a key component if you will like Suzerain. If you enjoy reading or if you don't.** Without question if you're somebody who has a low attention span or doesn't enjoy reading, even when the context is intellectually stimulating and shaped by your own decisions **IF YOU DO NOT ENJOY READING** you will not enjoy Suzerain. **IF YOU ENJOY READING** and engrossing narratives that have almost endless possibilities and consequences with the task of being thrust into the president of a country with a unique approach of love and care put into their game. The game is not voiced acted instead filled with branching text and dialogue, with numerous options and paths. Suzerain rewards those who pay attention to the narrative and punishes those who don't use critical-thinking when coming to a decision.   - this is done though in such a way that you're not sure as the player if you resolved each conflict the correct way, and finding that out in the future is what makes Suzerain such a compelling unique journey.The game is a agonizing balance of push and pull and decision making. Who should you trust? Should you make allies? What are your policies? Do you have religious ideals? What is  the focus of your administration? That will be up to you, and Suzerain does allow you to do that - I rarely felt constricted in what I hoped would be a option in my choices related to decision making, I often regretted the way I resolved some conflicts due to the unforeseen consequences and outcomes, but that is something I'm eager to tackle in another play-through of the game, that I can confirm changes drastically depending on the paths you take as President. I'm currently nearing 20 hours and haven't completed an initial run yet. It is a VERY challenging game if you're somebody who must have the game play out like a perfectionist - but I stress to not look anything up online, and live by your decisions as that is a major strength in this game - and makes the replayability all the more fun, as I am very eager to play another run of the game that will be DRASTICALLY different than my first thanks to the freedom of Suzerain. Like I noted, if you enjoy reading, choose your own adventure games/books, and complex narratives and politics and potential scandals, all wrapped up in your own quest for world domination or peace or whatever other direction you might take as a world leader then Suzerain Is the game for you.I often pondered if I wished to purchase the game, and was concerned about the occasional negative review. Some mentioning bad translation. The translation of the game is perfectly fine and in 20 hours I noticed only one poor translation as follows:  "are you ok?" Was replaced with "are you fine?" I stress there is little to no other translation mishaps and anyone saying otherwise is being beyond critical as that is the most minor of details to complain about and somebody who already was put off by this genre. Give the game a try if you can, as you will enjoy it if you identify with my above points. If you've been on the fence about buying it I highly suggest to go ahead as the price more than justified the return with hours of gameplay and replayability, and if it is ever discounted on sale there is even more reason for you to purchase and give it a try. Suzerain, a game I should have tried a long time ago as I enjoy it very much and look forward to continuing to play, and play again multiple times after my initial completion. I applaud the developers as I enjoy this genre very much and hope to play other games like this. I regret not trying it sooner. 10/10 from me. (YOU MUST LIKE READING AND THIS TYPE OF GENRE HOWEVER!)

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game - exactly what I was looking for. I always wanted to play a political game where I could form domestic policies, engage in high-stakes geopolitics, and contend with various domestic factions/cabals. I have found other games like Crusader Kings, total war, etc... and simulators too intense from a micro/resource management angle. This game takes the best parts of those and streamline it so you are dealing with domestic and international issues the macro level. The fact that there is a strong narrative angle to this game takes it to another level. It's possible to do well in this game without outside help, but be prepared to make sacrifices and accept that you will have to disappoint a lot of people (including yourself) to stand a chance at achieving what is most important. Blood will be on your hands -it's up to you to decide how much and for what.

Furthermore, the game provides you with a codex full of information on the characters, organisations, alliances, nations, political parties and more. This game is one of a kind.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought on a whim and spent about a week playing it off and on. The game is a text-based political management/sim that takes place in an alternate reality to our own, mirroring aspects of our real-world Cold War era. I sought to bring change to the country of Sordland and was surprised by how much the game truly let me do. There's a lot of flexibility and your choices will lead to multiple different outcomes, and can sometimes be reversed entirely. If you have a passing interest in politics, this game is a great way to introduce you to the "behind the scenes" aspects. I found it engaging from the start and when my democratic constitutional reforms passed with huge support, I actually felt pride. As the game came to an end with so many victories and better opportunities behind President Rayne, I was excited by the prospects of a second term, but unfortunately, that didn't happen. All in all; buy this game if you are interested in politics, want to experience a different type of story, or want to destroy a Queen Elizabeth stand-in.
