Won't recommend it to those peeps who quickly got bored reading, this is a text adventure game, but you might get interested in the storyline. Every choice you make counts as there's no saving button, every choice also has different outcomes. No matter how many playthroughs you go, it will always be a different outcome. You can't satisfy everyone. From internal to external politics, everyone will screw you, so choose carefully.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly such a hidden gem and incredibly unique - you will struggle to find any game that scratches quite the same itch. That being said a fictional political simulator RPG is not for everyone.The story is great and the intricate web of decisions and outcomes makes for many thrilling play-throughs. Having completed the game 4-5 times and had several other attempts go south I can say I am still experiencing new twists and different options even now. It's the perfect game to come back to every six months for a little weekend escape.You will grow to love and hate many of the characters, from Serge the friendly driver to Mr. Tusk the evil billionaire oligarch. Half the joy of the game is in finding all of the different interactions with these characters - it's quite fun to go from cozying up to a character in one play-through to "mysteriously disappearing" them in another.Seriously, try the game. It's clearly a labor of love from the studio and one that is STILL getting updates years after launch.A Morgna wes core, vectern sis da! Glory to Sordland!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: When I became President of Sordland, I was an idealistic reformer determined to solve the tough problems I faced, who would not bow to corruption. The economy was in recession, my party was divided, the constitution was broken, extremist groups threatened internal peace, and our aggressive neighbor's next target seemed to be us. I had some successes, too. A cautious free market policy saw the economy slowly recover, trade increased with our neighbors, and a diplomatic foreign policy averted war when we joined an alliance. At home, the constitution was reformed for a better democracy after a tough fight, women's rights saw a breakthrough, and I acknowledged minority grievances.It then all went wrong. A debt crisis broke out and the economy plunged into a huge depression. We lost control and every day I read new reports of protests and fighting between different groups. I threw my best friend to the wolves for a major scandal who then killed himself, then my driver friend died saving my life. My party would be crushed at the next election and I had decided to retire when worse came. The military overthrew me in a coup and I went to jail, not the first president to be crushed by Sordland's broken system, but not the last after my failure.My second try, I pursued similar policies but won re-election in a landslide. The economy was booming and we had joined an alliance with the West. Women's rights were secured, a new constitution was passed with 90% of the vote and the minority Blud group came peacefully into the wider community with new rights. I had a loving family and the country as a whole was pursuing the Sordan Dream thanks to my leadership. Some would say I had certain financial irregularities, that I was too close to oligarchs, that I bribed opponents. That I may have averted the Rumsberg danger, but at the cost of tying us to a greater danger of a cold war that could go hot at any second. They claim that I neglected healthcare, education, workers rights. Some say that the strange affair where my VP chose to resign was hushed up. My vaunted anti-corruption campaign may have taken down one minister, but many more in the shadows were left free from justice. But you shouldn't listen to the critics. Just look at the totally free press- they all freely chose to sing my praises. After all, everything I've done has been for the greater good. Right?Suzerain is a good game and a pleasant surprise. Most strategy games have the player as some detached observer who can pursue the rational course, but here you're stuck in the middle of a lovingly detailed country that reminds me of 1950s era Turkey (and some other countries too, this is their own unique creation), a much more realistic version of politics than usually given. But there is also downsides to this approach compared to say Paradox. While the political situation makes everything from a nationalist dictator to a Communist dictator plausible and everything in between, close to the same things will keep on happening. With no save slots and lots of not needed small dialogues, I ended up skimming through my 2nd run. I wouldn't count on replaying the game too many times. There is a certain fog of war, which makes sense, but some of the economy and security matters are rather opaque- I'm still annoyed by the way my debt crisis broke out. Bills should have a little discussion before choosing to sign, as it makes no sense that I don't know anything about the political consequences until after I decide. Despite these complaints, I still enjoyed the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played for a crazy amount of time yet, but so far I've made it through a lot of the game without noticing any typos or errors, which is surprising due to there being a LOT of text in this game. There is a robust codex and information keyword system that lest you double check what's being discussed at any time, and a personal favorite feature, multiple news sources that have different takes on your political actions, so if you take some actions a paper related to a group that would disagree with that action might say that you're stupid or hopeless, while another while commend you as sane and always making the right decisions

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: HELL YES!!! Got addicted and played for 16 hours on my first day.Apart from the occasional typo or questionable grammar in the dialogues/ descriptions, this game is just amazing. Firstly the immersion is very high, it really felt like you ARE Anton, because of the extensive backstory. In game there are multiple references to real life events/ conflicts, such as looming invasion, I really felt for Ukraine, or the discussion whether to prioritize industry and the centers or agriculture and the periphery. The main screen (map) and other controls are very intuitive, although I wish you could read the same status report twice, always knowing whats going on is a bit draining. The in-game Wiki (Codex) is also very detailed and expansive, I just can't remember everything I read. That's what your Notes are for. however, I found mine to become very chaotic after one chapter and so I stopped using them completely, wanting to advance the story more rather than keep track of my books. The dialogue includes many funny references, even some meme references. I am very glad to have played this game, it really made my day. Literally. I couldn't let go of it, and so I finished my 1st playthrough in one 16 hour sitting. If that doesn't tell you how good it is, nothing will.

_childDocuments_.review: Many thanks to Torpor Games for making this amazing game. Despite its many shortcomings, it is still, by far, one of the best political simulation games.However, I would like to address the issue of language support. Being a visual novel type of game, supporting only English is a very big challenge for many non-native English speakers, especially considering the huge amount of text in the game.I am from China. There are a lot of people in China who have provided Chinese localisation for this game for free. However, due to the specificity of the game, there are still parts of the Chineseisation that are incomplete as well as using translation software (e.g. deepl, chatgpt, etc.). This makes it difficult to experience this excellent game, but there are still many players in China who love this game.We hope that the production team will bring us an official Chinese version and expand the game's content in subsequent releases, two countries are still too little for us!!!! And hopefully some of the unreasonable game mechanics can be changed!At last, thank you Torpor Games for all your work! We hope to see more of your work!Translated by deepl.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a well written world and story. I got immersed and quite invested. I haven't played a game before where you're the leader of a country and that means you're a physical entity in the world, signing papers and holding meetings, as opposed to an omniscient overseer, who somehow magically controls every component of their country. Anyone with an interest in history or politics should consider it.You'll have to persuade (or bribe) people to get reforms pushed. Most people aren't on your side. You will make hard choices. You cannot afford to do everything, or even most of the things you want to do. The game benefits from there being multiple paths to take. There's many endings, and so far I've found two. .Complaint: The game's systems, especially the economic system, are horrendously opaque. On your first playthrough, you won't know how much you should spend or save, because it doesn't tell you how many spending decisions there will be in the future or whether you gain more budget over time (you don't - debt happened). You won't be told regularly enough how things are going. You won't know whether you're on track to meet your goals or not. Advisors will not tell you of the implications of your decisions (which is called advising), only insist you make them. You can think you're doing well the whole game (everyone loves you, growing economy, peace on the streets) and then have everyone decide they'd like you to resign anyway, and also the economy explodes. God forbid the game give you enough information to plan ahead or make good decisions. Even so, play the game blind, at least for your first run. It's a story game first and foremost. Play as if you're the president and make the decisions you'd make in his shoes. You can look up guides for specific runs/endings afterwards. If you want to do well (spoilers): .If you're looking for a game that's actually about simulating a country/economy, let this one pass you by. It should be thought of as a multiple-endings story about politics rather than a real country-running game. If that interests you, grab Suzerain and dive in.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a good game. For approximately 80%. But the end dissapointed me so much that I just can't give it thumb up.I dislike games that demand you to lose again, again and again untill finally the stars align (or you use walkthrough) and you finally do something you should be able to do on your first walkthrough - not fail. Unfortunately, this is exactly that type of game. Even worse there are literally no "legal" ways (as far as I know) to change something or go back few steps. The game has 1, an ONLY ONE, save file which gets replaced on every checkpoint. Why? What was the reason behind it? To make the game "hardcore"? Well, congratulations, you did it I guess. But would it be so horrible to make it an optional feature (like Crusader Kings 3 with it's optional "Iron Mode", for example)? The reason because it's such a problem for me is this: I've spent 14 hours according to Steam to finish the game I was having fun, honestly despite the game problems (I'll get to them later) untill the end where you  and that destroyed me. My country was prospering, well-fare, military, law and justice, economy, everything was excellent, but I lost and got the bad ending. I cannot change anything, cannot fix anything, I just lost the game and 14 hours because I didn't perfectly follow a guide. . So yeah, as much as I liked most of the game the ending ruined everything for me.Good.-Interesting although not new concept.-Visual design is nice, especially liked portraits.-Visual character customisation, not much, but still nice.-Freedom in choices.-A pointless, but still nice roleplay. Hypothetical example: you meet with your minister, you can say "Hello", nod your head to him or shake his hand. All three choices don't give you anything, they just advance the dialogue, but, at least for me, they allow to "get into role" of my character so to speak. Developers easily could've removed these micro-choices without losing anything, but they still decided to add them and that's nice.-Hyperlinks in game text and glossary. That was very helpful.-Game actually makes you think and shows very realistically (compared to other games) how politics work.-Low price.Bad.-Too difficult without any ability for "casual" playing.-Game expects replayability, but doesn't give any tools for that.-No tutorial, at all.-In order to get good outcomes from events it's not enough to just don't make obviously bad choices, you have to either strictly follow a guide or restart the game a lot of times. I honestly doubt that many people will get "good" ending on their first try without outside help. And dependind on how late in the game you'll ♥♥♥♥ up it's more than 10 hours of replaying.-Sometimes the game restricts you too much and choices are arbitrary. For example you can improve the army and have to choose which branch: land, air or naval. Why the hell can't I improve all of them? I have enough funds. Improve equipment or hire more people? Why not both?! Made the wrong choice? -I felt the family and personal life of MC wasn't developed enough.-Music is forgetable and I personally found it slightly annoying, so I quickly decied to mute it and turned on mine.The game has potential and if there will ever be a second part I hope that it will be better.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really didn't want to like this game as much as I did.This game is kind of a Central/Eastern Europe simulator. Analogues of both the major capitalist and communist powers of the early Cold War appear. The practical political questions that face you mirror those facing small powers during the early Cold War. You can choose to focus on healthcare, infrastructure, the economy, law enforcement, or military spending, but given your limited resources, each choice has drawbacks and successes, such as they are, come dear. Just as the early Cold War saw small states forced into the umbrella alliances of NATO or the Warsaw Pact, in Suzerain, you can choose to align yourself with capitalist or communist mutual security treaty organizations. Each choice will both enhance and restrict your options diplomatically.  The game does a fine job of slowly ramping up tensions overseas and each foreign policy decision feels like it has real stakes: do I recognize this island as a possession of a neighbor and gain an alliance? Do I stand by and watch as crimes against humanity are committed, and win favorable trade terms? Domestically, you face an embittered ethnic minority and a tradition of political violence that threatens to erupt into full blown civil war. Your constitution is creaky and the people generally demand reform. Even within your own party, those loyal to your nation's controversial former leader, Soll, and those eager to see Sordland break free from his shadow, squabble. The intraparty tensions have real consequences for your own agenda. Will you cut a deal with the Old Guard, or establish a new police force to root them out? Will you ally with the reformers and risk emboldening the opposition, or will you close ranks with the Old Guard and embrace Sollism? Even the class divisions of Sordland can be exploited. You can choose to cut a dirty deal with the Oligarchs, earning their support for your efforts, or you can try and break their power forever as a champion of the people; each choice brings unexpected consequences. Your own family and friends form a huge part of the game's content. Your wife's desire to see the liberalization of Sordland and legitimization of the rights of women might prove an asset- or an embarrassment. Your son's choice to join the military or attend university is more political than it would appear at first glance. Even your chauffeur has opinions and demands you have to consider and balance. One thing I want to highlight about this game that I think is exceptionally rare:  Characters have consistent motivations and qualities that inform their decisions and how they react to your own choices. Human frailties and flaws are telegraphed early on; sometimes these frailties lead to bad ends. The dialogue has a few moments of well-chosen humor (although I don't know if I'll ever be able to forgive the Toto reference), but generally the serious tone of the game is maintained throughout. This gives real gravity to every text option you click. I'll never forget the tense meeting with a Supreme Court justice as I sought to earn her support for reforming the Constitution. Depending on how I handled it, she might secure the votes I needed to win. It was a delicate balancing act and I chewed through my fingernails wondering how far I could push her before risking losing her. Ultimately... well, you should find out for yourself. The game excels in these moments. It's because of the writing. It's exceptional and believable.Overall, I am delighted with this game. P.S. While I normally deplore the bloated DLC-heavy state of game design nowadays, I want nothing more than to have one, or god willing, two more terms as the Sordish president. I like this game so much I'd pay full price for a "sequel" depicting Sordish society in the mid-to-late Cold War.

_childDocuments_.review: The most immersive political game there is.This plays more like a visual novel with gameplay elements. The DLC adds more gameplay to it (Moving units on a simple map) Gameplay is typically only choices of A, B, C or D. The consequences of these choices stack and at the end of the game, you may have destroyed your entire country because you didn't appease the right people. Getting a "good" ending is almost impossible without a guide on your first playthrough. It's beautiful in its simplicity.  If you are considering buying, get it with the 'Kingdom of Rizia' DLC. Don't buy this if you expect a strategy game like Hearts of Iron or EU4. It is a slow-burning visual novel. A wonderful novel at that.

I ended up spending the rest of my life in a prison cell.

You always have several ways to handle problems and opportunities and your choices can have completely game-changing effects. Results in good replay value too. Well worth your time and money.My only petpeeves would be the soundtrack (its good music but way too repetitive) and that you're sometimes not entirely sure what a decision actually means because of some strange writing.(Bought for 8.11€)

_childDocuments_.review: 11/10 Legendary video game almost one of a kind. It can be a little difficult to learn. But the feeling when finally everything goes as you envisioned is amazing.Also just to be clear this is not a grand strategy game like hoi4 or EU4 or anything else from paradox.This is a narrative game masking as a political simulator.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Apart from being entertaining, it really makes you think about a lot of things (basically, making choices in complicated situations where each option has advantages and disadvantages). This genre (narrative RPG about politics) deserves so much more games and attention from developers in general.What is true is that your choices take time to take effect. The game is quite slow. But that's actually how politics really works. So, I don't think that's a bad point.At the end, you could be frustrated not to be able to go further, as if you had just finished a book and wanted to read the sequel, but this sequel didn't exist. This is proof that the game is very well written.

_childDocuments_.review: 28 hours on a text based game, this is probably the most i have played, at least in the past 20 years. Very strong political game, if you do not mind reading. 100% this is not for the "regular" gamer, this is a thinkers game, each decision (or at least most of them), play a role in the future and there is a wide variety of approaches to take in each scenario. I recommend this game for patient gamer's who like games such as "Democracy". If you played that, this has a similar feel, just in this one there is way more roleplaying and less policy making.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to upvote this game so bad.I really do.It is genuinely an amazing game, it is extremely complex and has a very well-thought story. I love playing it.However, it's mechanics, being hard to define and having impacts on the player hours ahead of making them, makes the ingame frustrating and annoying. I cannot play this game without a guide anymore just because I'm afraid if I do one wrong thing, I'll destroy the run and accidentally crash the economy.It isn't fun to play when you feel like everything you do can destroy your progress at any time.That being said- if you like that, get the game. It's genuinely a great game with some of the best writing and choices I've ever seen. It hurts me to press that 'no' button. But I just can't enjoy it without a guide.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game! Very realistic and authentic political athmosphere and it doesn't feel like just another game that gives you the same results no matter what you click. Of course the main events and the endings are scripted but there are many ways the game can go and not like the same things happen no matter what decision you made before. And not only the countless decisions you are confronted with but also the nouances in between seem to matter in what direction the game develops. Very refreshing and innovative and a must for everyone with an interest in politics and/or history. The only thing that I found a little bothering is that you can't manually save and go back to any random point in time where you might wanna try a different approach without going through the entire story again from the very beginning, but at the same time this made every decision even more challenging because there is no going back - just like in real life. Please, Torpor Games, give us an extension to the game that allowes us to lead Sordland in a 2nd term after getting re-elected. I would pay the same price as for this version.

_childDocuments_.review: Can it be frustrating? It can. But unfortunately, that is the price of entry to this masterpiece of a game, where every decision feels loaded with consequence, and where simplistic video game ideas of morality and psychology are set aside for a much more nuanced and sophisticated understanding of politics and politicians than I've ever experienced in a video game; perhaps more than I ever expected to experience.The choices are rarely simple, and most of the characterizations are well-drawn, with more than one layer: reminded me of the TV show Borgen in that way. And while the dialogue OCCASIONALLY creaks in translation, it's generally quite strong, with small but crucial nuances differentiating many of your options.But of course the great thing is that there is no one right way to play. Yes you'll be frustrated when you are coup'd, or your constitution doesn't pass, but while I stumbled into a successful socialist government my first time through, it was equally fun to play as an inept nationalist or corporate stooge, even when I "lost."Really can't say enough good things. But I'm also aware it's a very smart game that asks its players a lot of questions, and that's not for everyone. But if you've read this far, you surely know of yourself whether you're the kind of person that will like this game. For me, it is one of my hundred favorite video games ever made.

Rich in history and the characters are all fleshed out with very believable motivations.But Sordland is a state deep in turmoil and getting anything done is actually (probably realistically) extremely difficult. The game is brutally difficult and you should not expect to survive on your first playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting roleplay as a leader and political intrigue. Also educational in terms of socio-economics and statesmanship. It's neat to feel a partial connection to what a statesman has to grapple with. All this with having a very simple dialogue driven mechanic; it ain't Civ or Anno.Cons: Sometimes the dialogue interactions can get a bit boring or run a little too long. I think it could do with 1 or two other simple mechanics or balances to keep it interesting.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: If this game seems like it might be up your alley, it will be. And well worth the price.The game models a wide variety of intriguing issues, and a President Rayne that properly consults his Codex and the advice of his Cabinet will be able to navigate the intense diplomatic, economic, historical, and political crises facing Sordland through his first term...maybe. Lots of replay value for those interested in seeing alternative paths through the political chaos.Be nice to Serge.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: You play as the young leader of a nation, recovering from civil war and despotism.The world is fictional, but has parallels to mid 20th century Europe. Capitalists and Monarchists to the West; Communists to the East.You are stuck in the middle, trying to steer your nation towards prosperity. This is a very detailed RPG game, you can shape your character and your nation is many different ways. You have to deal with complex and interesting characters, with their own motives and ambitions. The dialogue is well written and highly engaging.The world you are in has a lot of depth, there is a lot of information to take in. If you want to read about the events, of the 7th century you can. Every character has a very detailed biography, there is backstory to pretty much everything within the game. The world is deep and believable. I have not finished my first play through, I believe the game is repayable. There are many different paths to go down and choices to make, that would make every play through different. Highly recommend this game

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Well-written. All the characters are memorable and their actions and motivations feel realistic.- Unlike a lot of political sim games, there isn't one "right" ideology that produces an unambiguous win condition. I've had fun playing runs that were super capitalist or super communist, democratic vs. authoritarian, etc. Each have their own challenges and tradeoffs.- The sound design and artwork is fantastic.Cons:- There are many hidden mechanics. E.g. the game tracks public opinion but this isn't visible to you in the UI. That may have been a deliberate design choice, but it made subsequent playthroughs less fun/easy to experiment with because I didn't know which choices were relevant to the game mechanics vs. pure roleplaying.- Limiting you to a single auto-save slot makes subsequent playthroughs less fun because you can't jump to a particular branching decision to see what would've happened if you made a new choice. I honestly would've liked something like the save system in Detroit: Become Human, but again, it seems like the game made a deliberate artistic/design choice to discourage this kind of metagaming.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best in its genre, Suzerain is a political intrigue sim that offers true freedom in rule from being a communist to being anarcho-capitalist and all of the baggage that comes with that, an international community that reacts to your every decision and a wide cabinet of ministers you need to keep happy.While each decision on their own hold little weight, the depth provided by your overall decision style is unmatched, it really feels like you're building out a politician, rather than assigning yourself into a box. I recommend this game if you want a 'choices REALLY matter' narrative sim.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, but don't buy it until they add some sort of save system. The lore is interesting, the complexity is phenomenal, and I think it is a fantastic example of a political simulator.That being said, the forced Ironman aspect of the game severely diminishes the replayability of Suzerain. The game loves its writing, rightfully so, but I get sick of dealing with dialogue that does not have many options over, and over and over again. Given the fact that there are 3 main paths to go (Constitutional Democratic Reformer, Autocratic Putinist-Erdoganist Constitutionalism, and State of Emergency enthusiast), and the fact that the margin of error is soooooooooooooooo small, that one small dialogue choice results in failure (i hate salad), there is nothing but pure frustration after 4 hours of slogging through monotonous lore and background. And guess what? You're stuck with that failed result, because the game told you that you were going to win just to lose and give no explanation. I get it, the game is a political sim, and politics is a tense, merciless world. But I'm playing a video game. I just want to PLAY THE GAME. I get so mad at this game, BECAUSE I love it. I  to see what happens. I  to get all of the achievements. I  to explore all of my options, even the ones where I fail. But if i want to do anything, I have to slog through an hour of dialogue that I've already read and I already know.I've seen some comparisons to Dark Souls-style difficulty, but I disagree because in Dark Souls, YOU DON'T HAVE TO RESTART THE GAME BECAUSE YOU ACCIDENTALLY ROLLED OF A CLIFF AT THE LAST BOSS.The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante did it best: the option for ironman, and save points every chapter.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a political simulation game that puts you in the role of President Rayne. Who is tasked with rebuilding his country after a bloody civil war, a twenty year dictatorship and the country recovering from an economic depression. How you tackle the challenges of the state? That is entirely up to you.Suzerain system and story is a refreshing take on story building and economic management. Democratic or Authoritarian? Capitalist or Communist? Isolationist or Trade Bloc? There is no correct options and this is what makes Suzerain shine. You can attempt to play as a Democratic reformer or a dictator and win if you play your cards right.However in the game of presidential thrones, you win or die.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an underrated gem. How is it nobody is talking about this game, I myself came upon it when searching steam and was immediatly struck by its description and screenshots.Suzerain is all about your choices, you take the role of a newly elected president on a country that is facing tough times, people want to move on from its dark past but some members of the assembly and government want the country old values to remain. It is a clever war of attrition that you battle throughout the entire game, trying to please everyone whilst making changes.The game is very hard to get a good ending, at least it felt like it on my first run, I completly botched everything during the last part of my term and had to go into exile or risk prison just because I tried to stand up to the Old Guard.The storytelling and replay value of this game is beyond amazing and you are doing yourself a disservice for not trying it out. Also, amazing soundtrack devs, I never tired of this game's tracks and it helped build momentum in tense situations and calmness when it was appropriate.Hope we get some dlc for this masterpiece, I will be replaying it countless times!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text-based adventure that sees you leading a fictional, failing Eastern European country a few decades after a civil war. You are faced with difficult situations in which you must make tough choices about how to lead the country. It's interesting, but I can't recommend it at full price for two reasons.First, the game has little practical replayability in my opinion. The game does not let you reload an earlier save, so if you want to change anything you have to play the whole game again from the beginning, and a playthrough takes about 10 hours, unless you just skip all the text (which defeats the purpose). Even skipping through the text it takes over 4 hours to try for a new ending. That's too long. While I appreciate the ironman gameplay, I think it should be optional, at least after the first playthrough, so that people who want to experiment with alternate endings don't have to spend such a long time going through the same stuff repeatedly.Second, the game bundles decisions together in a way that annoys me. For example, there is the question of whether you want to reform the education system. I was playing as a Sordish traditionalist who was making reforms to improve the country without losing its core values. The existing, traditional education system has two facets: 1) it teaches students patriotism - to love their country, to want to serve it, and to revere its founders as great men, and 2) it guides boys and girls down different paths, where girls are generally prohibited from taking advanced math or science classes and are always funneled into homemaking (unless their parents can afford a private education). The minister of education wants to abolish both of these facets. There is no way to say "let's improve girls' education, but keep the patriotism". If you want to improve girls' education, you must also abolish the patriotism. Let me choose!For another example, a big issue in the game is women's rights. Men are legally allowed to beat their wives. Women's primary place in society is the raising of children. Etc. The minister of education - plus your own wife - want to push through a women's rights bill, but some of their proposed policies are destructive, and, if the game was implemented realistically, would foster poverty and homelessness among many poorer Sords (including poorer women), while primarily benefiting well-off women who already have many opportunities. Others would harm families and set the country on a path towards long-term demographic implosion. But there's no way to pick and choose. You can't say "let's protect women from domestic violence and give talented girls equal access to education but not try to push all women into the workplace". It's all or nothing. Either you pass policies that would ruin the nation, or you support men beating their wives. C'mon! Let me choose!Overall, I enjoyed my first playthrough and I want to try again making a different decision or two, but I can't justify spending so many hours to try the game a second time.

_childDocuments_.review: This an amazingly immersive game with lot of politics, relationships and presents the real struggle and inability of fixing problems in a country as its leader. It has great characters which you get to interact with across the entire game which makes you truly care or despise them. Thanks to the atmosphere every time you have to talk and make a decision holds so much wait. I fell in love with this game, finishing my first playthrough in the three days I owned it. However it isn't perfect. For one dealing with the economy and people in the game is much too vague on the whole and doesn't properly represent your choices. I made trade deals and built railways and agriculture yet the economy just sat there and I only made money off of random tax laws. I changed the constitution and helped people from all sides and yet by late game only one group in the entire country supported me. The biggest complaint of all is something that happens with alot of game like this, FINAL TURN FAVOURITISM.  By that I mean every single decision you made is completely undone by one or two in the late game. Perhaps it depends on what path you go down but this happened to me and I HATED it. It felt like my 15 hours of leading this country, learning these characters and making these tough calls were undone by no fault of my own. And yes I am very sour about this cause I was grinning my ass of throughout this entire game and I was in near tears by the end. The variety of choices in the game is staggering and I highly recommend it for the writing, choices, world building and atmosphere alone. Those points I just made against it probably only apply to certain paths, I guess I'll have to find out when I replay it.  A Morgna wes core. Vectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: I am blown away by Suzerain... every chat matters, every decision more, with relationships and tensions captured beautifully - from world leaders to narky teenage sons... The game starts with a series of life choices that form your backstory, and how you are seen by everyone when you take office. From there it's an epic struggle to turn a country around. The country has suffered a long serving Junta, and then a first elected president whose term ended in the tatters of a failure to deliver reform.  Billionaires, border tensions, bigots, racial tensions, unlikely allies, goose bumps, unintended consequences, scandals, negotiations, pandemics, speeches, gender politics, awkwards moments, dread, compromise, heart warming moments, pandemics, people you totally despise yet have to work with, a genuine feeling of a fear for your own life and small talk with your friendly driver... it has it all.I'm closing in on the end of my first term, and it's been a rich story with incredibly well crafted characters. So much has happened, and the world is so deeply imagined that I find myself rather beguiled and engrossed in what will happen next. In truth I bought it suspecting I would play it for half an hour, think 'meh', before getting a refund. It's now my best game of 2020, and I've played a frig of a lot of great this year in lock down.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: My biggest issue with the game is that there seems to be a huge disconnect between the decisions you make and the events that unfold.After struggling to revive the economy because of the lack of information provided as to the effects policies would have or the overall state of the economy (represented by a single line), I managed to turn things around. These were the economic results of my term:- Inflation: 2% (down from 10%)- Debt: 310 billion SR (down from 427 billion SR)- Unemployment: 5% (down from 16%)- GDP: 513 billion SR (up from 310 billion SR)I simultaneously enacted policies that gave more rights to workers and increased wages, while investing heavily on education, leading to improved standards of living. I fought against the oppression of minorities and brokered a peace deal with my warmongering neighbor, avoiding a war.Despite all this there were widespread riots which sprung out of nowhere calling for my resignation, I lost my party's primary elections and finally suffered a military coup.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A beautifully written and thought out political game that should get massive credit for making a choose your own adventure story into a pretty legitimate strategy game. You play as the newly elected president of a country modeled after a small, as of yet, unaligned Eastern European (called Eastern Merkopa) nation during the early decades of the Cold War.Pros:-Great writing and historical fantasy setting that feels real (and dangerous)-Meaningful decisions and riveting drama-Really awesome codex containing all of the history and characters relevant to the game, complete with clickable links that keep you going from article to article as you get immersed in the history of Eastern Merkopa-I suffered a coup at the end of my term so I don't know if the game can continue with being reelected, but a single play through was quite long (for me approx 8 hours)Cons: -There is a lot of information packed into little reports which you can click on around the map. They don't seem to drive the game forward however, so clicking around the map appears to be largely perfunctory. Your main task is just to click on story driving events, which are usually at the capitol on the map, so basically you are just clicking the map to open dialog boxes that go through the story. Ultimately the player needs something to do in between dialog boxes, but I wonder if there is a better way to handle that.-After my first play through, I didn't feel a strong urge to play again because I didn't want to play through dialog that is unlikely to change even if I changed some of the choices I made. For me, the big damning choice was neglecting the military, which turned on me and led to a coup. However, I didn't feel super compelled to play the game again because only a few choices would have been different. Long story short, I think replayability on this is going to largely be based on the amount of time since your last play through. Once the dialog is fresh again, I'll come back and try new things. I think it would be better if there were save points automatically made at major decision points in the game, so the player can go back and make a different choice without having to go through a lot of the same dialog preceding the decision.Wishlist:-Sandbox mode-Random map / procedural generation of story and events-This game in other regions and settingsConclusion:A really wonderful indie game that is worth checking out if not just for the experience of your first single play through of the game. Looking forward to more games like this and expansion on the concept from this developer and others.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most brilliant games I have ever played in the political sim/text-based RPG category. The writing is engaging and elaborate. It continuously paints vivid atmospheric images with grace.I found myself hooked and immersed in the game after starting and couldn't really stop thinking about it until I finished my first play through. It does a great job of investing you in your character and their journey. Congrats to the awesome devs for crafting this work of art. I can't wait to play your other games or expansions for Suzerain. A second term expansion would be awesome especially for players who got re-elected, you can't help but feel left wanting to continue the movement you started for a bit longer before the game ends.

_childDocuments_.review: I've done about 3 playthroughs so far. One as a nationalist dictator (basically Franco/Mussolini), one as a Communist autocrat (basically Lenin/Stalin) and one as a moderate capitalist reformer (closest to my real views).This game is very fun! I love the writing. I like how every decision has weight and consequence, especially if you try for the Dictator route, since one mistake when negotiating with politicians or planning your reforms can ruin your entire run and force you to start over. All the real-world parallels (e.g. ATO and Arcasia being NATO and the USA) are easy enough to understand while still being unique in a way that adds to the depth of the Suzerain world's story. The world-building is superb with your own nation (Sordland) and all your neighbours having unique national histories, beliefs, structures, and approaches to political matters. The characters you meet in the game are also very well-written and have distinct agendas and personalities, making them all believeable individuals as if they were real politicians. Some of them appear to be nods to historic personalities and if you know your history, it'll be very easy for you to connect the dots and figure out who's being parodied. Some of them you will grow to dislike (screw you Tarquin Soll you meddling dinosaur), some you will use and abuse, and some you will come to adore (Sure thing Serge, I'll pay for your kids to go to university you wonderful man)  I also enjoyed the realism in how if you push too far in any direction without appropriate measures and safeguards, you'll either get ousted in a coup, betrayed by your ministers, impeached by the Supreme Court (Damn you Hawker!), or lose the second term election. You can also get assassinated or killed in a war, but no spoilers! So in truth, unless you're going for the absolutist dictator approach where it's a case of "screw everyone except me", you have to make deals, compromises, and maybe take/offer a bribe or two. It's a brilliant allegory and reminds me of the saying: "politics is the art of compromise." The big thing at the start is fixing your economy, then trying to pass constitutional reforms if you want to be a pro-democracy reformist or a dictator in the making. Otherwise, you can try to stop the reforms if you want to maintain the status quo (hail Soll) From there, many other things can potentially unfold including a refugee crisis, genocide, trade deals, diplomatic posturing, and even a war can break out in the late game if you don't handle a certain situation smartly (or if you want the war and deliberately push for it!) Hell, you even have family life to contend with: a son, a daughter, and a wife you may not always see eye-to-eye to...The game has many branching paths that you can go down, depending on your character's ideology, past actions, recent decisions, and so forth. These mean each run will be different if you don't pick the same choices every single time, so the game provides a lot of variety for you to explore, depending on what kind of President you want Anton Rayne to be. I've played 3 runs and I'm nowhere near bored of Suzerain and I imagine I'll keep playing for a long time just to explore all the possibilities. Do you like political games with a lot of machavellian scheming, meticulous planning, and tenacity spanning? Then this is a game for you.A morgna wes coreVectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: Such an enriching experience - yet apparently no great political experience required! I am thoroughly enjoying feelings of great responsibility and influence, and am desperate to do the right thing for my people. It's such a relief to play a political game with simplified economics and numbers, one which passes some judgement on your moral compass, and shows you the repercussions of decisions real leaders make, and why sometimes it is hard to avoid some pitfalls. Whether this is all an illusion and the system behind it all is no more elaborate than say reigns, i cannot say, nor do i especially care. It's fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Almost over the whole distance this was an extremely immersive experience. The game is unique and there is an admirable script, immersion is achieved by text only, etc.Ok, storyline... despite best efforts i got into a war with "Rumburg".- Unlikely, that "Rumburg's" blatant aggression would go unsanctioned in the exposed international scenario.- Unlikely, that the ratio of displayed forces and what is told about equipment would suffice for more than some, not too intense, war of attrition for "Rumburg".And I don't  like that the overall achievements of the playthrough were not debriefed.Would've been fine if one could take the narrative seriously up to the end. - I didn't manage to do so.In a way it was a rewarding experience, nevertheless.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mostly based on text and interactions with other characters via dialog options. You first decide on details of who Anton Rayne (you) is, most of it is flavour, but some decision do in fact impact later gameplay (E.g. your starting personal wealth).Gameplay centers on Rayne's interaction with important members of political establishment which want different things from you; the Old Guard want's to preserve the status quo while reformers want to... well reform. So you must pick and chose who Rayne will align with depending on what you want to do.There are a few quite significant events that don't use dialog for player input, But in general game is about a nation and Anton Rayne. So it's not like games from paradox's where you have a full Reign over your nation with dynamic borders. Map is Suzerain is very static.Once your term in office is over (or ends abruptly) we get information of what happened to Anton after which the game ends. Overall the game has detailed lore and despite the fact that most actions rely on degree options it feels like the choices do in fact matter, However many endings there might be, it might be a bit tedious to read all the flavour text (like inauguration ball) especially when you can't save and reload (beyond check points anyway)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The mandatory ironman mode is not a good idea.  I understand what they tried to pull off with this challenge, but you can end up losing hours upon hours of work from a decision that you don't fully know the ramifications of.  I'm sure that appeals to some people, but for others like me, I do not have a huge amount of time to dedicate to replaying a game.  The whole experience now is ruined and leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A modern day Hidden AgendaThis game is very similar to the 1988 game Hidden Agenda and that's a compliment considering the legacy of that game.Suzerain is interesting as it has an immersive story line, and full interactive map with a decked out codex.I get the frustrations that some people might have but this isn't like Democracy 4 or Lawgivers where it's simply a simulation. Suzerain is more comparable to games such as For the People and Lapse: A Forgotten Future where the story line is the main focus while the mechanics are just an added bonus.Do I recommend this game? Yes! The replay value is pretty large and I hope they expand the game in the near future.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Probably, the greatest story game i ever played. This fictional world is just wow................... not to mention the insane outcomes you can do as president rayne. I wish we had dlc for this, but the devs thanfully are making more content for this universe, which i overwhelmingly support and i wish em the best for the future.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is brilliant on all levels: realism, immersion, plot. It's very well written and believable. However, my centrist-reformer path led leads to two extremely weird outcomes:1) I could not figure out why the constitutional reform did not pass. I secured support from both wings of my party and from the biggest opposition party. There's was no realistic explanation why the voting failed, even though everyone promised their support. I then found out that letting my wife abort the speech of the mayor on some local event pissed off conservatives and that tipped the balance. XD. 2) In the late game, the internal rebellion breaks. At this point of the game, my economy was doing great, I had a balanced budget, low unemployment, low inflation, secured international position with alliances with 2 democratic countries (Agnolia, Lespia) and democratic superpower (Arcania), I also mitigated the Bludish problem by giving them autonomy. But the rebellion is scripted and it has to break out. It was hillarious when I read reports, often from the same town, one report saying that the economic situation is fantastic, new business opening, new opportunities etc. etc. and the other reports saying that agry mob occupies public buildings, militias clashing with police and people hate me :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really addictive with so so many different outcomes, depending on what you want to do.It somewhat reflects the day-to-day business of a President: endless paperwork, signing documents, meetings with the cabinet and countless other decisions to make. The game makes me feel like a real leader with all the mixed feelings after any controversial decision.If someone asks me about this game, then I would say it's recommended to give it a try. They will not regret the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: To be neutral, yes. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played in my life. It is a visual novel. A choose your own adventure game about political power in a richly defined and immersive universe. This game takes a lot of reading. The main way you play the game is through reading through dialogue with your ministers, reading status reports from around the country and ratifying legislation. There is even an extensive codex filled with background information about every nation, person, corporation, branch of government etc. This is a very nerdy game. You will get the most out of it if you take your time and get to know the world that you shall be playing in and, most importantly, the country that you shall be leading.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to be a peace loving socialist? You can do that.Do you want to be a militia-focused warlord? You can do that.Do you want to be a pro-education feminist capitalist? You can do that.Do you want to be an overtly racist anti-immigration womaniser? You can do that.Do you want to be part Shark, part Tornado? You... well, actually you can't do that. I never said the game was perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A fun little game that puts you in the shoes of a newly elected President struggling to help your nation navigate an economic downturn, civil unrest, Cold War-era politics, troublesome ministers, greedy billionaires, and external threats from neighbouring countries.Took the radical centrist route of providing decent public services whilst allowing (most)* people to get on with their lives and (*shocked pikachu face*) we had an economic boom, improved civil rights, reduced infant mortality, strong trade, military alliances, and I got re-elected despite being kicked out of my own party...*Sorry, not sorry, communists.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great text-driven / choices matter political story. I admit I got way too invested. My first run ended in disaster -- I compromised on my ideals a little, but not enough I guess. Overall I find this game quite hard if you're not looking at a guide online, which is not a bad thing. Really helps illuminate the tough choices that the leaders of developing economies had to make in the Cold War when sandwiched between the US and the USSR. Perhaps the same thing will occur in the future with the US and China. Either you give up control of your economy and culture and free your people to the enormous influence of the West, or you retain control (and perhaps cultural independence) through corruption and abuse of human rights.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: 100% have to recommend this game. The storytelling is unreal and every choice you make really has a huge impact on the future. There were moments in the game where I felt great sorrow for characters involved. There are points where you are soaring high, and the future looks positive. However the idealism will fade, and managing the conflicting powers, making deals with the Old Guard or the Opposition in order to push your agenda through the Assembly. and various scandals will wear on you. At the time of this review, I've only done one playthrough, and attempted to transform the nation with an idealistic and progressive agenda. However it resulted in furthering the economic downturn and a particular dealing I made led to my impeachment, of which I was sentenced to life in prison, my family left with nothing. 10/10 can't wait for the second playthrough.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain plays like an interactive story—where decisions influence the outcome and change relationships in meaningful ways. It is really well crafted and the devs did a great job of making every choice feel consequential. I enjoyed it quite a bit and would definitely recommend it. I will say that I don't personally see much replayability. There are 9 different endings, but because the major events/decisions are scripted, you end up basically playing the same game and choosing different dialogue options/decisions for the sake of unlocking the different endings. I have no doubt the different decisions create a totally different vibe as the story progresses but for me I don't have much interest in playing again and forcing myself to make decisions I wouldn't normally make just for the sake of unlocking outcomes. This isn't a critique of the game—I enjoyed it very much—just something to be aware of if you are a player like me that generally enjoys playing "naturally" and not making decisions just for achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, it's one of the best political sims I've played.  I want a sequel.  A friend gave me this game and I cannot praise it highly enough.  I love the setting, the hair styles, and the attention to details.  i love the music of the game--this is rare for me. Another great feature is the consequences of your choices--in this game your choices DO have SIGNIFICANT consequences.  Even something simple can have major implications down the line.  Sometimes I get tired of games that pretend to offer you choices but don't in reality. This is NOT one of those games.  In a very real sense you set your own fate.I love the wit of some of the dialog choices.  You can be snarky, kind, or downright rude.  You can choose to do something you object to, or not do something you object to.    The consequences of your choices make sense.It does have a "permanent save" feature--there is no load option outside of the main menu.There are enough branching paths that there is a TON of replay value--you cannot possibly get all of the achievements on one playthrough.  That being said, an option here to skip dialogue you've already seen would be very useful.9/10(I don't care for some of the language choices--this deducts 1 point.  If there was an option to remove the swearing/foul language that ever so often crops up, that would be nice.)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I can't remember how this was suggested to me, but it was as if Paper Please got a more substantive sequel with a different kind of politics. Games like this in general are based on all sorts of glib economic assumptions that I wish weren't being made, but that being said...it's a fun diversion and with the multiple outcomes -- and the ability to edit files -- it's got a bit more replayability than you'd anticipate. It's less "simulator" and more text-sim with better graphics, but it's fun and affordable. I can recommend it for sure. I beat it for the first time within a few hours [choosing early retirement], but I'm god with the speed and will surely return to it and try some of the other outcomes over time.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A really excellent narrative-led political management/simulation/visual novel game. It is an incredibly interesting game that puts you in the seat of a president leading a broken nation with an absolute ton of decisions to make in how you rule, what policies you put forward, and how you respond to the many threats that rise up to meet you.Frankly, if you're interested by any of that, don't read anything else, get it, play it for the first time, and make the choices you think are best. Once you're done, come back around, read the memes and reviews, and realize just how different everyone's experiences are.Some people claim that story results are often similar (and I will admit there are a lot of things that produce *similar* results) but I think a large part of that is that they are make the same or similar choices across playthroughs without realizing that it's producing the same results in the context of the rest of their game.Some people said they constantly faced threats from the military, or that their economy was always crashing even though they made gains, but the key is that these people didn't love Sordland . My first playthrough, liberal progressive with some free market leanings, supported highly democratic government reforms, invested in the development of our rural areas, boosted education and police spending with a focus on rooting out corruption, and  we got caught making a backdoor deal to influence the media but who wouldn't take the offer from a media mogul billionaire to just subtly suggest that maybe my rule isn't so bad. We're running for re-election after all. And , maybe my vice president drowned himself after a sex scandal because I threw him under the bus but frankly his philandering, gross expenditures, and lack of decorum were on him. And , maybe, just , a conservative cabinet member left my cabinet specifically to run a re-election campaign against me because I didn't go far enough in some places, despite the fact I boosted her ministry's funding, but in the end I beat her ass and won that re-election and let me tell you, my second term would have been glorious (but the game does limit you to the lengths of your single term, which I think does make sense because most of the interesting stuff is in regards to tensions rising in that one term).And then my second term was selling my soul for power by becoming a fascist dictator and eliminating all dissent. I died in my palatial office with a gun in my hand when Rumburg invaded because we  ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up our defense strategy, especially when we pissed everybody else off so much that we didn't even have allies. But, hey, if we had won that war, I'd be a .This game is great. Yeah, there are complaints, but I find it really interesting to play it through and find out more about what the differences are from all the choices you make. I'm excited to play the DLC at some point, and I hope the devs keep working on games like this and more.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: If you like political dramas with turn based decision making it is quite good. Downside is that its more of a read and choose game and it has no real  time game play in it. Its read and choose your path. It is engaging and gives a good feel for competing interests. Its not Tropico but few things are. Worth the money and your involvement.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I am so pleased I took a risk on this game and played it. I was hooked until I finished. They story kept me on the edge of my seat and had many twists and turns. I was particularly impressed with decisions having ramifications throughout the story, it gave them real meaning and made me regret some of my choices. I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Really liked this game. It becomes very hard to find very well written political games these days, and Suzerain is great at it. One suggestion could be about the volume of texts and possible decision making opportunities. Some of the content is too long and it is tiring to read all that text; that could be reduced. In addition, it would be great to see more opportunities to actually make decisions (investment decisions, etc.).
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Exactly what I am looking for in a political sim visual novel. Which is that your choices actually matter. Want to make a free market capitalist democracy? Go ahead. Want to make fascist dictatorship? Just be sure to rub elbows with the old guards? Want to make a highly progressive socialist democracy? Your wife will love you for it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game with lots of twists and layers. It does an excellent job of giving you the uncertainty of whether or not your policies will have the intended effect or be viewed in the way you're intending. Balancing different factions and ideologies, trying to figure out where people's loyalties are, and if outcomes are due to incompetence, greed, or maliciousness meant that by the end of my run I was looking forward to retiring.My biggest complaint is the feeling of being railroaded. Many times there were pieces of legislation that I was fine with 90% of the content for but was forced to veto because that last 10% could be crucial. Being able to indicate which sections I found problematic so they'd be kicked back to the assembly would have been a huge improvement. Even if only 30% came back again in an amended form it would have felt better. I also didn't feel like I was given options to telegraph which parts of the potential legislation I had issues with ahead of time. There were conversations before the legislation was voted on but many times (especially late in the campaign) this only gave me options like, Full support, Full Rejection, or waffle. I wanted to be able to indicate which parts I couldn't support as well as which I could. I wanted to have options for a staggered approach to legislation (We can do part A and B now, but part C I can support in a year). Options where I could counter offer or have more granular options. Specific instances were the EPA % (30 or 40% would have been nice), Women's Protection Package (when your core is traditionalists), BFP amnesty (limit to certain types of crimes), or the departmental budget (+/-3 is punishing as hell when most other decisions cap out at +/- 2). Being able to adjust the budget in 1 unit increments and then have a corresponding number of picks we could use would feel more natural.I'd also really appreciate an economic status graph. I couldn't tell if the growth indicator was giving me information on where I was (aka things are bad but improving) or just giving me information on how the amount of growth (very negative growth but now there is a bit of growth, you could be anywhere overall for economic health). The details seem like they could be buried in a menu someplace but it would be convenient if you could click on the indicator and then be taken someplace to get more context.Despite those two issues it was still a fun experience and I had fun trying to get my constitutional reforms through the assembly and supreme court.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a phenomenal game. It adds an interesting story and character development to a solid political simulation. It is very re-playable and has multiple endings which is always fun to explore. It is the most entertaining political game I have played to date. I would highly recommend this game to political junkies and fans of text-based narrative games.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is the first game that I played that made me ACTUALLY care about the decisions I made. The writing is thoughtful and interesting, the characters seem real and all have their own priorities and biases. The story is amazing, the choices you make impact the country and the people around you. You have the choice to be a Stalinist, Democratic Socialist or on the other side, neo-liberal or even a fascist. If you are looking for a political choose your own adventure, this is the game for you. Keep in mind though, this game has very heavy reading. So if that's a problem, this game may not be for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a strategy game, and it's not entirely a simulator. This is a story-first game that throws you into the leadership of a convincing and troubled nation facing threats from within and without. You get to choose your responses to events and your policy agenda, but you'll find yourself largely at the mercy of a drama manager that will try to run you aground fairly effectively.Personally, I enjoyed this game a great deal and appreciate it's nuanced and mature story presentation.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Have been playing this game and thoroughly enjoying it other than some minor gripes about some of the inconsistencies like how girls are so oppressed they are forced to study knitting and home crafts but have also simultaneously reached the highest echelons of power from the cabinet room, the head of the Central Bank to the Supreme Court. Every step of the way it seems I have had some influence on how the story develops by the decision I make which have included offering and taking bribes. Now for some crazy reason I am at one of the  most critical points of the entire game where I can achieve the central goal to change the constitution and the only options I am given when offered a deal is to reject it!Like WTF? Why would the developers make it so obvious to steer the story in a single direction after allowing players such freedom of choice throughout the rest of the game?Has ruined the vibe and left me feeling ripped off!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game, very well structured, generally engaging, truly political. Set in a fictional yet familiar world, this is clearly intended to be a 1950s central bloc country simluation/roleplaying game. For the most part, it plays that tune very well - and the world is convincing and easy to get sucked into. One major criticism arose from my first playthrough: There are two topics which this 2020 development team clearly misrepresented about a country such as this in the 1950s. Attitudes to gender roles and female leaders in general are simply unrealistic. This topic plays heavily into the game in ways that are too inflexible to truly capture the past. Consider it a re-imagining or censored version of the past. The other topic which is glossed over in the same way, predictably, is immigration. Ethnic strife is still, to this very day, perceived very differently in the centre-east than the west - and international attitudes towards this area didn't form in the way the game presents it until the early 2000s.It's a shame that inevitably some historical revisionism seeps into games like this - but I suppose it is literally a fake historical world anyway. The game remains very enjoyable, and a true credit to its developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really immersive and well-polished. It has the same limitations as any heavily narrative-based game - that is, you're stuck on the paths that the developer mapped out - but it made me weep for the plight of my country, and that's something that only the best-written games can do. If this team makes another game, I'll buy it immediately.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after watching a video on YouTube about it. I liked the prospect of an intimate political simulator but i find myself disappointed in playing the game. The story and the choices and absolutely 10/10. It is very well written. I only experienced immersion breaking a couple of times but they really did ripe me out of the game world. Just a couple of weird word selection and repetition. or where gold is referred to have a "quality", Gold has purity not quality. There is also a couple for scenarios in-game where you're agency is robbed from you. There is a nation in game that i would equate to an i world Iraq under Saddam. Without spoiling the game i made his situation untenable and i had broad support throughout the diplomatic community, assurance rather. BUT STILL I LOST THE VOTE. Literally every named voter was on my side and i lost. This isn't player choice this is railroading to tell a story. Here im talking about the Rizia DLC. But there is situations in the main story where this happens as-well. I'm just disappointed. This happens well into the story too and at this point i don't care to finish it. I don't feel like the choices i make in-game will actually amount to anything. In a game that revolves around choices this isn't what i expected.If yer into a Point and click adventure, more power to ya. The game is on sale as of time of writing. If, like me, you were looking for an intimate political simulator your up $hitcreek without a paddle.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to recommend this game, but I just can't.Great idea, poor execution. Choices are arbitrary and the clues meaningless.When I paid great attention to details and made a very solid and consistent run, balancing everything, I ended up with a failed government and lost elections.But when I tried a wild run, where I went all bonkers, I ended up being called a 'centrist' and was re-elected despite the fact I ruined the constitution and fought a war against my neighbor.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. Who does not like reading, do not buy it. But I have to say the story is exciting and the authors did great work. I played two careers and never succeed. it is a really tough game that seems to reflect political reality very well. Every decision can be important and you have to be careful and think about some decisions a long time. I really wonder if there is a way to win in this game and to succeed as a president. Right now it seems impossible to me. But this is why I like this game. i am going to try it another time with a total different and maybe complete crazy plan and see what is going to happen :D
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished the game, I have to say it is the best political game I've played. The depth of information about the different institutions, individuals, and states is incredible. The game really illustrates how difficult it is to stay pure in politics. Even though I tried my best to revolutionize and reform the country I failed miserably (got impeached and died in jail) due to unscrupulous backroom deals that later caught up with me (and which I didn't conceal too well). Either way the game is extremely well made and I definitely recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to feel like you're having a real impact in this game, you're more of a passenger along for a story. There is a lot of dialogue fluff, but no concrete information on possible outcomes of the choices you're presented with. Sometimes you need to argue until you get to a decisive "what is your decision?" text, other times a seemingly offhand response or a followup question will close off an entire story branch with no warning. You get no real feedback from your decisions, you usually just get informed of the consequences some time down the track, no opportunity to correct course in the meantime. There are also numerous inconsistencies (possibly bugs?) I've encountered. Having a binary decision presented to me to allow or disallow something, but the only button available is the allow button. Reports from my cities that their economy is doing great, they're steadily recovering from the recession, that unemployment is down by 15%, that entire regions are experiencing unprecedented economic growth, the line for the "growth" metric trending positive, and yet in the same turn my economic minister solemnly telling me that our unemployment is out of control, our economic reforms have all failed for reasons that are never explained, and that we're on the verge of a depression. It's hard to not feel like you're being railroaded down a particular narrative path. The developers arrogance of making the dialogue so damn tedious to sit through, then not allowing you to save at will is what really kills this game for me. Replayability is zero, there's no way I'm sitting through hours of fluff doled out one slow sentence at a time to change a decision I made in the first half of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a visual novel or as the developers call it a "text-based RPG" and a political country simulator. Its a ficttive eouropenish in the 1950.The story is really well written with good characters and a fleshed out world. You can also have different runs with a lot of different ideologies, you can really define your own Anton Rayne.I really like this game and hoping from more good games from the developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As President Rayne, lead Sordland into ruin or repair during your first term in this text-based role-playing game. Navigate a political drama driven by conversations with your cabinet members and other significant figures. Beware or embrace corruption; shirk or uphold ideals. How will you lead?
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

name: Monster Truck Championship
detailed_description: A true Monster Truck simulation! From Las Vegas to Orlando, go head-to-head against experienced drivers in drag races and freestyle competitions! But before you can pull off doughnuts, wheelies and bicycles, you must first tune your truck to perfection. These machines are spectacular and impressive yet highly technical to drive. The game faithfully reproduces all the unique demands of mastering these powerful trucks, including independent front and rear wheel management, mass transfer anticipation in bends, and predicting bounces after jumps.   But what's performance without style? Customise your Monster Truck to reflect your style and show it off to your 7 opponents in online mode. 16 different Monster Trucks Over 50 customisable elements 25 arenas 3 different leagues
