_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft... what a game.The first few hours were the most fun, unlocking so many new things to do, and exploring all the recipes. After a while I started doing the same thing over and over, just different combinations of potions. At first it looked like I would never finish those potions, but combine Potion Craft with chatting to friends or waiting for someone, and time passes like nothing. Sometimes I found it a bit unclear what the customers wanted, but there are enough guides out there that will help you out.Towards the Endgame, I started reading the first 3 words of a request and already knew what they wanted. It's also really interesting, that they made so many different requests, depending on whether you got good reputation or a really bad one. I find it a bit sad, that once you got everything of the main story finished, there is nothing else to do. You can keep earning money into to the hundreds of thousands, but you can't really do anything with it. It would've been really cool if you could customise your shop or upgrade/customise the garden. Also you can't do anything with the 25+ leftover levels you gained.A little tip; Make sure to sort your Recipe Book and don't put every single recipe you find in there. Once you got it all sorted you can really start making money like hell.Overall I found the game was really fun, and I can recommend it to everyone as a good past-timer.

_childDocuments_.review: Stylistically beautiful, mechanically interesting. Potion Craft provides a solid foundation in mechanics but falls short in a few aspects that lead me to not recommend this game in its current state. Map exploration is one of the core mechanics that let players discover new potions, refine existing ones to higher quality, and collect experience orbs to level alchemy. While it encourages players to experiment, the limited daily resources is a serious hindrance that punishes inefficient use of ingredients and mistakes like excessive stirring, grinding, and diluting.Finite resources also cause needless tedium where you feel obligated to haggle each customer as to "not leave money on the table". Especially as the ramp up in demand for the highest quality potion comes quickly after a few days, expectations for optimal resource management creates a level of unnecessary stress.Limited potion recipes detracts from the feeling of progression as it fails to strike a balance between the cost and quality of life. Buying new tabs to prevent the need to reproduce high quality potions creates a strain on your money that could otherwise be used on ingredients that are already sorely needed for exploration and experience.As it is early access, there are features that have yet to be added that may alleviate some of these issues. However in it's current state, the game needs to decide whether to lean into being a punishing resource management focus or a relaxing sandbox take. Potion Craft definitely has the potential to rectify these problems with some simple balance changes and more generous exploration mechanics, and I hope to see them addressed in future patches.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - The gameplay is solid and the art direction is amazing, but the moment to moment gameplay has little variation and there is no meaningful progression after map exploration. Updates are very slow (on the scale of years, not months). Expect  less than 10 hours of gameplay, 20 if you push it. Fills the niche of a calm, relaxing, vibey game, but ultimately feels like unfulfilled potential to me. --------------------------------------------------So, had I written this when I first purchased this game in early access, around 2 years ago, I would have been singing this games praises. However, in the time since, we have only really had 1 meaningful update. The "1.0 release" didn't really add much after that. Since then, they have committed to the "garden update". This is baffling to me, since the garden is so minimal and far from the core gameplay, calling it a tertiary system feels generous. After a year, the garden update has still not released. Given this track record, I recommend you go into this expecting that the game never receives a single update.So, is the current content in the game worth the price? Well, the game is very well made for what it currently is. The gameplay revolves around adding different alchemical ingredients to your potion to build a path through a potion map towards your desired effect. There is a lot of satisfaction from exploring different combinations of ingredients. Discovering new potions, refining old recipes, all good stuff. Add on to this the economic challenge of maintaining a stock of ingredients without running out of money, and you have a compelling gameplay loop.However, where the game really shines is the aesthetic. The sound effects and visuals are spectacular. The sound effects of the mortar and pestle are top quality: grinding weeds, mashing mushrooms, crunching gems, it is pure bliss. The art is beautiful, I love the faded yellow background and how it sets off all the colours. And the music, oh, it is just pure vibes. This just elevates the elegant gameplay to an obscene level.Where the game suffers is longevity. Since you can only explore the map once, the game gives you the alchemy machine to extend the gameplay. Each alchemy recipe requires a list of highly specialised potions which are supposed to be challenging to make. However, as the potions got more and more complex, I ended up finding them quite tedious. It was the same thing as making the regular potions, just with more steps. And for all this, the rewards are salts that are never economical to use due to how many herbs they require to make. Yay.Moreover, once you figure out how to make money efficiently, the act of exploring itself begins to feel tedious. Who cares if you burn a million herbs revealing the map, you're rich. Optimising potions doesn't matter either, since you can afford the extra 50% material cost. I guess this means you can use salts without worrying about the cost, but you can't save salt recipes like potion recipes. Instead, you need to save the constituent potions and combine them in alchemy machine, every time. This can result in just flicking through menus for up to 2-3 minutes for the higher salts, once again, just feeling tedious.Beyond that, all the tertiary systems are lackluster. The garden is essentially a pity mechanic to stop you from running out of herbs completely. The haggling system is a glorified quicktime event that gives you free money. The merchant quests are just regular potion requests. The karma system is entirely superficial and just changes your customers from villagers and knights to murderers and warlocks. I suppose the karma system is kinda neat, but again, not much change in gameplay.The thing that hurts the most is, I can see the devs vision for this game, and it's beautiful. More than 2 maps, each with their own mechanical twist. Different ingredient types with their own quirks and niches. A variety of alchemical recipes serving as milestones to mark your mastery of the system. Character questlines and charming stories from a creative cast of NPCs. A customizable shop you can add your own personal flair to. And it's just probably too much for this dev team to handle. I'm sure the war in Ukraine impacted this dev team, as I'm pretty sure they have at least some people from Russia, and for that, they have my sympathy. However, this sluggish pace of updates started way before that, all the way back in Early Access. There are so many features were promised then that just never made it to full release, and they are nowhere in sight. I doubt we'll ever see many of them.If I could give this game a mixed recommendation, I would. Because I really do like it. The fact I got 70 hours out of it is amazing. But a lot of that was just replaying the same content over and over, sustaining myself purely off the chill vibes. And the vibes are great, don't get me wrong, but if you're on the fence, probably skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft takes place in a magical fantasy land where a single-salary income can support a two-story household, a garden, and a pastime activity on top. During the day you do customer service for the local townsfolk in order to fund research into the alchemy field; in between jobs you tend to your garden, as well as trade ingredients with the local vendors - both of which you must do proactively if you wish to meet the demands of your customers.The gameplay loop consists of attending to the queue in front of your shop while doing various chores to maintain your stock of plants and minerals. Your objective is to sift through the rambling and smalltalk to figure out what the customer wants, devising an elegant solution to a problem that may or may not have been within your field of expertise to begin with. If this is not the most accurate depiction of customer service out there, I don't know what is.Jokes aside, figuring out what each customer wants breathes life into the game by giving each a distinct personality, making you feel like you're actually talking to them. Going out back to make a unique item for them ends up being an incredibly satisfying experience, mostly due to the clever implementation of the potion-making system, as well as the UI that helps do so more intuitively - both of which I will go on to describe now.First, a base solution for the potion is chosen - the map which the player will chart a path through to get to any one desired effect. These effects have a predetermined location, however the map is initially shrouded in fog-of-war, and obstacles block your path - so discovering where the effects are and getting to them, play a big part in making a potion. The marker must travel to the effect and sit on top of it to be applied to that brew.Getting to these effects is done by adding ingredients to the solution. The ingredients are categorized based on the direction they take you in, and the pinwheel UI can help limit the choice to any one direction. Hovering over an ingredient shows you the path it allows you to travel even before adding it to the mixture. Ingredients are also colored based on their element, and are categorized by type - herbs, shrooms, and minerals.The idea is to chart a path towards an effect in the most optimal way possible, without hitting obstacles, without wasting materials, and with as much precision as you can. This is because potion strength varies based on how accurate you were in your assessment of the potion marker trajectory. If you were able to fit the potion snugly within the effect's confines, you will make the potion strong, netting you extra pay and reputation with your customer-base.Part of what makes potion-crafting feel so natural is the act of physically manipulating the tools you have at your disposal. It is possible to add raw ingredients to the concoction, however, if you want to extend the path an ingredient will go, you have to grind it to a fine paste with the mortar and pestle first. You can also add more base solution with the teeming ladle, in order to move the marker closer to the center of the map at no cost.To make a chosen effect stick, you fan the flame under the cauldron with the bellows, and you mix the concoction inside the cauldron with a mixing spoon to move the marker along its designated path. I do wish there were more tools to manipulate ingredients, perhaps a chopping board or a grater? However the act of physically moving tools to reach your intended goal is what made the gameplay loop so immersive and involved to me.You can save the potion recipe with all its ingredients in your recipe book, personalized bookmarks and everything. I do wish the customers asked for (or at least appreciated) the effort put into customizing each bottle and writing its labeling, as if you were a pharmacist directing patients on how and when to use medicine. However, that part of potion-making remains optional, despite the personalized label icons and bottle shapes. Saving recipes is done to prevent tedium and repetition during consecutive play, though you may save a recipe before having an optimal ingredient, forcing you to redo it. Or, you may run out of a saved ingredient completely, having to chart a new path altogether. Still, I appreciate the amount of customization and freedom you are given with the recipe book and the recipes in it, it's certainly a nice optional feature in the game.The vendor encounters inside the customer queue are what enables you to purchase new ingredients, and are the main source of new ones in the game. The garden eventually becomes unable to support customer demand, and cannot grow the large variety of plants needed for full recipe optimization. This is something the devs intend to address with an update, however the implementation of this garden remains lacking as of writing this review.One vendor in particular is the source of new recipe book pages, and, more importantly - blueprints for alchemy station parts. If I had to voice a complaint about the game, it'd be that alchemy is made extremely repetitive in the later parts of it - with each rock requiring a combination of multiple specialized potions, and each subsequent rock requiring its predecessor, one you already use to craft the alternative powdered recipe.If you don't save the recipes for each potion, you quickly find yourself repeating hours of work just to get to the last progression point you've reached. This is because making rocks is the real goal of the game - with the last rock created the game can be considered complete. I also wish there were more uses for these rocks; as it stands, there is one alternative recipe for each rock aiding in potion-crafting, and that’s about it.Another complaint I'd like to voice is the way the reputation system interacts with your customers during the day. You see, the more people you help, the more customers you receive per day - which actually doesn't matter, since the passage of time has no bearing on your resources or character. However, customer demands are split into good and bad asks, and helping each customer nets you either virtue or infamy, never both.If you have lots of virtue, you attract customers with good intentions - those that ask for health, courage, growth and improvement - and vice versa - with infamy, those looking to hurt, sow fear, steal, or manipulate. I can appreciate the variety of asks put on offer here, but helping all people will eventually only attract one type, and you may end up in a situation where you only help good or bad-intent customers, without the variety the earlygame offers.Before I wrap up, I want to mention how much I appreciate the game's presentation, namely its use of vibrant colors and whimsical depictions of plants and stars. It's very endearing, and gives the game this fairy tale look that's been done extremely well on the artist's part. The sound played as you pick up each ingredient and grind it to a paste, then throw it into the cauldron, is also very calming and soothing for this type of game, almost ASMR-tier.To me, Potion Craft is the ideal busywork title, including just the right amount of interactivity I'd have wanted to see from my simulator. Each task has an involved process of steps: evaluate the board, select the right ingredients, grind them to the right degree, throw them into the cauldron, mix everything and bottle it, then finally serve it to yet another satisfied customer.There's a real sense of progression with each saved recipe, each earned sack of coins, each spread rumor about the little shop you've opened to advance humanity's knowledge of the occult. It is also open-ended, meaning there’s room for the devs to add more content after the final rock has been created. I genuinely have high hopes for this game, that it will continue to improve and be built upon with each new consequent update.

_childDocuments_.review: The game loop and progression system is tiring more than interesting. The shoppe barely evolves, the herb garden doesn't change all that much. Really just the item count and variability, which is just enough to make you want to, but not always, attempt to explore a new part of the potion map. The map is very unforgiving with how you can create paths and explore. More often then not, I feel like my efforts were wasted in exploration as i never felt rewarded for my time. The new potion i learned was weighed down with the sheer number of ingredients i wasted just trying to find it. And now i gotta do it again to make a legit recipe for it.A possible progression improvement could be instilled on map navigation and traversal with a learning/logic branch on the leveling tree. Your alchemist could make ingredient group inferences to help you streamline/strengthen your path to new or stronger recipes. "This ingredient goes into fire > it will also go into explosions > will it also go into light creation? This ingredient goes into healing > will it help me make a better growth potion too?" A way to improve the "fast travel" mechanic as it were. This seams more streamlined then the hundreds of ingredients i have to constantly scroll through. I played my 9 hours over a weekend, and i think that might be it for a while. I may return later, but i've had my fill as of right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a refreshingly inventive game that transforms the process of potion-making into an art form. With its medieval-inspired, hand-drawn art style, the game invites players into a beautifully crafted world where alchemy feels as mystical and intriguing as you’d imagine. The visuals are a perfect match for the theme—earthy, detailed, and with a sense of warmth that makes the whole experience feel inviting.One of the game’s strongest points is its originality. Instead of simply mixing ingredients in a traditional inventory, Potion Craft uses a creative system where players grind, stir, and even adjust the heat of their potions, all within a delightful crafting interface. Each action you take affects the potion’s outcome, requiring experimentation and a bit of intuition, which makes every successful potion feel like a personal achievement. The creativity extends to customers' unique requests, encouraging players to experiment with new combinations and potion effects.The game’s balance between relaxation and challenge is another highlight. On one hand, it’s soothing to grind ingredients, explore the alchemy map, and create potions at your own pace. But on the other, the intricate recipes and demanding customer requests can be genuinely challenging—and even a little frustrating! This balance adds depth to the gameplay, keeping it from becoming repetitive while still providing moments of zen.Overall, Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a wonderfully creative, visually charming, and engaging game. It’s ideal for anyone who loves experimenting and enjoys games with a mix of relaxation and challenge. Whether you’re looking for a calm, meditative experience or a brain-teasing puzzle, Potion Craft has something for you. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game during Early Access, and while I have enjoyed it (enough to play for 73 hours). I feel as though it is not updated enough to combat the repetitiveness of the game play. The last major update was in December of 2022 and it is now 8 months later. I love seeing the dev logs on what they are currently working on, but having no timeline on when those updates would be implemented causes me to lose interest quite completely. There are many times I forget that this game is even in my steam library because there are barely any updates. The game itself is nice but not amazing. It has a good and unique art style, and they have added more unique challenges, but the availability of magic pages for your recipe book allow you to easily save the recipes for any of those challenges so they no longer require any work. In fact, when I originally started playing, I had the recipes saved for every potion (weak, regular, strong, and the unique ones for the stones and salts); it caused the game to just be series of repetitive clicks (practically a money making simulator). The last major update had quite nice improvements on haggling, and customer base. They also added merchants asking for potions to bring more materials. They added a new potion base, new ingredients, and did a lot of maintenance on the reputation system. I enjoyed the updates, but for as long as the updates took to implement, I was underwhelmed and disappointed. The next major update looks promising, but with no real deadline in place for when that update will come out, I am not optimistic that the game will illicit any different emotions than the last update. I would personally prefer much smaller, more frequent updates over one massive and disappointing update once a year.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is excellent for 5-7 hours; and not after.In a few words, ingredient RNG is hell.Randomly scarce ingredients due to the merchant not selling them requires you reinvent the wheel by remaking old potions a LOT. I found myself with a huge surplus of money (Like $25,000); but the merchants never having the basic ingredients for me to buy! I wish I could spend one day a week to leave the Potion Store, and go to the Herb store instead!!I hit a wall around Moon Salt (40%ish through the Philosophers Stone crafting tree), where making progress becomes multiplicative. You need to keep remaking the precursor reagents of the stone; which was fresh hell because I hadnt saved the reagent recipes, since I thought they were one offs.Critiques and comments:1. Please please, for the love of all that holy, allow us to at least request specific ingredients from the Herb/Mushroom Seller for next time....2. Spending one day a week to go buy/procure select ingredients would be godsend.3. Make it clearer we need to remake the reagents a dozen times.4. Some way to upgrade the Enchanted Garden5. There's a "Shop" which implies you can upgrade the Cauldron, Spoon, Ladle, etc; but no one sells these?--------------------------For new players; here are some tips:1. Buy way more Crafting Recipe pages than you think you need.2. SAVE THE REAGENT RECIPES!!! You need to remake the beginning reagents at least a dozen times.3. Buy all of the Sale Ingredients every time they appear.4. Pray the basic ingredients are available.

_childDocuments_.review: An extremely satisfying game with a lot of promise. I originally played the game for the first time almost a year ago and stopped playing due to reading one of the dev-logs that stated how the game will be vastly reworked and saves from earlier versions will be incompatible. Despite being slower than a slug that was given a tier 3 slowness potion, the update finally arrived, and it delivered a LOT.What I don't like/things that should be reworked:-Certain potions are far to costly to make(that is, if you wish to make them tier 3, which you should, to get a greater price). I'm looking at the potions on the water-map that need a certain ingredient to give it some much needed chutzpah, so to say, to perfect them to tier 3. The ingredient for it is very costly to make and depletes Far to soon, not to mention it only goes in a certain direction, which is really debilitating if you need it to go in the other direction a little bit, and instead it makes almost a full circle, making you waste even more of the precious moon salt(not to be confused with moon sugar)-Some npcs have requirements that are literally impossible. For example, there was one person that wanted a fear potion and it HAD to be made from one ingredient, otherwise even if you give them the potion they want, they'll just leave...what you need to know is that the fear potion is on at the north-west side of the map(if i recall correctly) and is LITERALLY impossible to get to using one ingredient because of in-game obstacles-In a way, npcs are too randomized. Now obviously this isn't a huge problem, its merely immersion-breaking, though for some its obviously a big problem, understandibly so. Certain npcs that walk into the store will sometimes ask for potions that cost more than a thousand gold(with or without negotiations)...like, you mean to tell me you can buy yourself a potion like that but not normal clothes instead of rags? Seems a little suspicious.BUGS:Literally haven't experienced any so far, not when i played it a year ago, not now. The game seems to start up somewhat slowly and close with a bit of a hiccup, though that could be related to my computer.What I like:A lot of unique ingredients were added and some reworked, giving you even more ways to create potions, the majority of which are really cool looking, have cool names(poopshroom, hehe), or create awesome pathways, though I will say, there are ingredients that I look at and i'm like: how in the bloody hell am i supposed to do anything with you???I love the fact that there's a recipe book and that you dont have to recreate every potion, and that you can even position your recipes/bookmarks within the book.There's a lot of things you can customize about your potions. You can change its name, the shape of the bottle, the shape of the label, the symbol of the potion that appears, its a lot of fun. I can only hope this level of customization will continue and expand in other ways, such as decorating/re-designing the mortar and pestle, the cauldron, the shop etc etc.there's a wider variety of random npcs which is nice, gives the world you're in even more depth. I wish you could interact with them more, so you could immerse yourself into it even more, but maybe we'll get it one day.The music is just good enough for you to not have to look up RPG Playlists on youtube(some may beg do differ, of course), though I do wish there were a lot more.the sounds are eargasm level, especially when you crush rocks.a new 'map'(oil-based) was added with a unique and good(but really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying) obstacle which is awesome, and the map's necessity is explained through exploring and finding out that certain potions are much easier to make here(tier 3 variants anyway).The base map(water-based) was reworked and made just a little more challenging.As mentioned above, some npcs may have requirements(fully randomized, as far as im aware). Some are secondary, meaning you can do them but dont have to(doing so gets you more money than usual, so its almost always worth it), while some are mandatory to fulfill or the customer will turn away, even if you have the correct potion available. It's a VERY good addition, though as I have said, it needs balancing.VERDICTThis game is TONS of FUN. it has so much potential to be the ultimate chill game that it's getting disgusting. I do hope there will be more customization to make the game feel even more cozy/homely, maybe even the ability to have pet(s)?Gameplay-wise its almost at the perfect balance of fun+challenging, though due to being able to wear out/experience a lot of things in the game it can get REPETITIVE to some.If you ever considered buying it, then, considering the price of the game, you ought to go for it, whether its on sale or not, I highly doubt you will be disappointed to a degree that you regret the purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love the way they managed to make a virtual thing feel more real. Like I don’t just click the screen to grind the herbs and things, I have to hold the pestle and grind it into the mortar for a little bit (I can even do a downward stabby motion as if I’m pounding the absolute hell out of the ingredient if I want to be silly) til it’s ground down. It actually makes a difference how much I grind it too! And with the stirring function, it’s the same too, I can technically over stir something. Stirring is how you advance your piece in the map and you have to make it land on certain markers to make different potions so you can end up moving it past the mark if you’re not watching what you’re doing like I did at the start of playing it. It's such a wonderful little game, but be sure to keep an eye on the time in real life otherwise you might end up playing until 4AM like I did last night lol

_childDocuments_.review: Grab your vials, alembic and crucible because you're in for a treat with this little wonder!Do you remember when gaming was fun? Do you recall when games bore challenges and rewards? Do you reminisce the days of high school chemistry? Then I welcome you traveller, to Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator.Step into the literal parchment of this story... you, a lowly beginner alchemist plant your roots in the local town to become the next Master of concoctions! Starting off humbly with a garden of mystical ingredients and little knowledge of the paths ahead, you must discover ways to brew potions as efficiently and creatively as possible.This 'puzzle' game will have you hooked for hours.To support your newly opened Alchemist's shop, you must spend your days picking and buying ingredients and utilising them to make specific potions for the various customers that enter. Do a good job and they pay well... But are you good and kind? Or slightly cunning and a teeny bit eeeeevil?When you create potions you can choose a righteous path to support the town and the various denizens that populate its winding alleys by selling them for a good reason. Or you can choose to support the wicked, and fuel their desires to wreak havoc on the local population. Either way, your decisions matter and will dictate how your reputation can attract certain customers.Haggling for the best deal? Great for the coffers, but hindering on the reviews. It'll take you longer to build a positive reputation if you keep bleeding their purses dry! But with shiny coin comes more ingredients, special crystals and alchemical equipment to advance further into the world of potion crafting.If I were you... I would transmute the very essence of your bank balance into Potion Craft and set yourself on a gorgeously crafted journey, hooked by a repetitive but stunningly designed soundtrack that will have you humming in your sleep. Seriously though... how have they created a looping soundtrack that you can't get sick of?!Genuinely relax, enjoy the game, and find the best way to create your potions and remember fellow alchemist... with practice, comes mastery.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: I'd just like to preface by saying that this game is by no means bad - in fact, it is quite good. The artstyle is very pleasing, the sound design is crisp, and the UI is very clean and manageable. For the hour I played, I enjoyed it quite a bit. While Potion Craft is therapeutic, I couldn't help but feel as though it got rather boring quickly. Personally, I wish the actual "alchemy" process was more involved, instead of just clicking and dragging, being that it is the main gameplay loop. There is a little too much breathing room for a process that should feel far more honed. As much as I appreciate that you are given time to explore and experiment with different potions, the experimenting process is somewhat dulled by the fact that you can see clearly what exactly will and wont work ahead of time, rather than actually discovering that the potion is useless, volatile, or any other undesirable characteristic. I do wish there was a lot more visual feedback for tinkering with potions, and I'm of the belief that it could use some heavy improvements or even a complete redesign. My final complaint for the game is that while graphically it's sound, there is too little color for a game about alchemy, where in real life, the color of a chemical is largely important. The amount of tan/light brown that is plastered everywhere is disconnecting and makes the game feel somewhat gloomy and spiritless.All in all, the game seems promising, but I would not recommend it in it's current state for anybody looking to sink more than a couple hours into it. Hopefully the developers are willing and able to give it the attention it needs to properly fill the niche alchemy/potion making genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Seems simple but is surprisingly addictive. There's a lot more going on than just making and selling potions. You can spend time perfecting a recipe to use a wide range of ingredients in their most efficient usage, rather than just one ingredient that you soon run out of. You can sell potions to dubious customers when you need coin, and reject their business when you need reputation. You can experiment to gain experience and unlock new effects or better paths for more difficult potions. Top it all off with some lovely music, sound effects, and pleasant art style and you have yourself a winner. My only criticism is that I want more, and I consider that a win.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a gift bought for me by a friend who thought I'd enjoy the game. My friend was right. _childDocuments_.review: Very fun and relaxing game.Outside of the unique visual style, the biggest strength of the game is how tactile it feels. You feel the difference between grinding herbs or crystals and pouring water into the caldron.On the other hand, it doesn't offer a sand box. Meaning, you can't grind both things at the same time, for example. It works more like a puzzle game. And as many puzzle games, once you figure out the rules, the game becomes less interesting.The recipe book in particular, trivialize the mechanical aspect of the game and makes it a series of repetitive chores. Fortunately, the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and it is very short and sweet. Because of that, the negative aspects don't hinder the good and relaxing experience.All left now is waiting for the garden and skills update.

_childDocuments_.review: I love supporting certain games in early access that I can see have active development, and plans to take flight into a 1.0 version. This seemed like one of those games to me because I bought this earlier on in its development before we had the steam achievements, and whenever there was a giant label below the main room that said something like “we will implement this feature soon,” or something. And they did. Which I love this because even something as simple as this shows follow through. These smaller observations out of the way, let’s see about reviewing Potion Craft.✅ - I bought this game in early access because it's an interesting concept before I saw dozens of games that released that were related to potion making. (Here I'm not looking at release dates necessarily, but for me this seemed like an original idea and a distinct simulator game). Over the course of the early access and release, there have been noticeable quality of game improvements that have been excellent. (For example, the haggle mechanic. You used to have to hit the skill checks and then inevitably -- hopefully if you got the max amount -- you would have to hit a final skill check on the left or right. This isn't the case anymore. When you've maxed out, you've maxed out. I think this is a great improvement and doesn't force you to have to try and manage hitting a bunch of skill checks to hopefully get near the max.)This is one simple observation that I’m making regarding the game that is a quality of life improvement, but the collective of all the changes that have been made about this game are important. It’s what makes the game better in general. ✅ -- despite the varying, sharp shades of brown that color the entirety of the game, and that might normally seem as an eye sore, the art style is distinct. Not to mention that there are plenty of other colors with the patrons, the UI in the potion making screen, the greenery, etc. But there is a shade of sepia over almost everything. Despite all this, I like how it is. There are some hints of realism while maintaining a somewhat cartoonish style of the patrons visiting the potion shop that you have. This is a noticeable positive for me. ✅ to what I would imagine Medieval times would be. I don't know if the music is actually accurate, but again, the point is not to be accurate to what exactly Medieval times was, it’s more just “does this seem pretty original and interesting,” and it seems original to me. It becomes more of a background feature, too, after a while, and I am inclined to turn it down because it loops, but it is enjoyable nonetheless. ➖  -- This is mostly an observation of the game as this is mostly stating the game in general, and it doesn't have to be a lot of things. Really the thing here is that whenever you buy this game, you are buying a game where you craft potions. This is the primary thing you are doing. This isn't a game like  where you are able to get gear that you later sell in a shop and buy upgrades and such. No. You are making potions, you are selling potions, you are upgrading your workstation. That is mostly it. I enjoy this, though. For $15? Absolutely.❌ - I can't quite place this idea, but whenever I play the first game that a developer publishes (not makes, mind you. I realize game developers make a lot of games before they publish their first game, etc.) I feel as though it happens that the game catches this distinct quality of "Okay, let's make this thing, get it out there, so that we can understand how this works as far as developing, marketing, patching, listening to feedback, etc. goes, and then we'll either make a new game that we actually want to make (For this I think of "An Airport for Alines Currently Run by Dogs" being published first by Strange Scaffold and then they make "Space Warlord Organ Trading SImulator")  or improve upon this existing product  (like Hopoo games and the Risk of Rain series.)" I know that's not succinct, but I'm hoping someone understands that thought. More importantly, here, the game does one thing -- make potions. I get how this could be frustrating to some, but whenever the core gameplay mechanic is presented to you almost instantly, and there's an expectation of this very particular gameplay loop netting you hundreds of hours of gameplay, maybe a readjustment of expectations is necessary. Whenever there’s a game out there that shows gradual improvement over time, is a game that is the first game a developer publishes, continues to support development after the game is released actively, and is a decent game, I want to give it credit where it is due. With original artwork, original music, a core gameplay mechanic that seems to have enough polish to function well, and much more, I can absolutely recommend this game for people who want a game that doesn’t try to do too much, and you just want to make some potions for people.Strong 6 to a light 7 out of 10. ✅✅✅➖➖

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently (Early Oct 2021) in early access, but here's what I have to say about the game as it is right now:First off - what's currently here is really, really good. The gameplay captures the "part science, part art form, part guesswork" vibe that all fantasy alchemy should aspire to incredibly well, and the tactile interactions of crushing up ingredients and brewing potions is completely knocked out of the park. Everything looks and feels really great. It's very clear that the developers wanted to get the "feel" right before diving into the "big picture" features like progression and such, and their work has definitely paid off, because it really is just a pleasure to interact with the game even in its current state.Here's the Early Access asterisk to this review: This game definitely feels like an early access game in a lot of ways. There are several buttons plainly labelled "this feature isn't available yet", a handful of mechanics (eg Reputation) have no real impact at the moment, and there isn't a lot of weight to the currently-available progression. The missing planned features means that the main thing you get right now is the "core gameplay loop" of making simple potions to satisfy customers every day and unlocking a small handful of advanced recipes to tinker with. This is very enjoyable on its own, but it gets a little repetitive without an impactful progression system to build toward. You definitely get the sense that a lot of the vision for the game hasn't been completely realized just yet, but the fact that the core of it is *so* good just makes me really excited to see what's coming. Overall, I do really like what's here, and I can absolutely see the amazing potential this game has going forward. I'm glad I bought it! I think anyone who just likes the idea of being a fantasy alchemist brewing up potions will have a lot of fun with it even as it is right now. Definitely worth picking up or keeping an eye on.You can get an overview of planned features in-game by clicking on "About Early Access" in the menu, and I'm really, really looking forward to all of it - especially stuff like having more control over gardening and growing ingredients.

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a nice aesthetic and vibe, but once you realise what this game actually is, the 'fantasy' of brewing potions is obliterated and what's left behind is a fairly uninteresting mini-game that you'd likely see as an afterthought in a full-fledged RPG.Basically, the way this game functions is that customers request potions with specific criteria, with a little bit of personal interpretation to figure out what they want most. For example, they could request a healing potion, a frost resistance potion, poisons, etc. There's also an alignment system, but it doesn't seem to alter gameplay in any real way, just what potions you're crafting and what flavour of NPCs you talk to.The problem is that crafting any potion is no different to any other. To craft a potion, you're given a map, and the ingredients you use determine your course on the map. What this means is that you're not crafting potions in a way you might cook or produce something in real life, but rather you're rolling along a flat space in directions determined by whatever ingredient you're using. It's not a potion crafting game, it's a map-navigation game.I'm not a game developer so I can't tell you what a truly immersive potion crafting game should look like, but Potion Craft loses any immersion/fantasy when you progress into more complex stages and you're randomly throwing mountains of ingredients into the cauldron to explore an uninteresting map interface to discover new potion qualities. This is what I mean when I say crafting one potion is identical to crafting any other - you're simply using ingredients to draw out a path to whatever quality you're looking for.Another let down is that potions for me, as an RPG addict, are synonymous with usability. They're made to be used! But the game blue-balls you with a total inability to use anything you craft. I feel like there could be a whole extra half of the game attached to this that requires you to use potions to find and acquire ingredients. They've teased the ability to use growth potions to increase the yield of your garden (which is the only source of ingredients aside from merchants), but you can't use healing potions, because you don't have a use for them, you can't use charm potions to barter with NPCs or Merchants, you can't do ANYTHING with them, whereas to me it seems like you could multiply game options with the use of potions. Again, this is why I say there's no difference in crafting potions, because you can't use any and the method of crafting isn't unique. Once you have a number of recipes recorded, then there's even less gameplay/decision making involved. It's like working as a cashier, but also not being allowed to shop at the store you work at. You don't care what the customers buy, because you have no interaction with the products you're selling.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is worth playing, but don't expect to play it very long until they expand on the gameplay loop. It is about experiencing what a nice crafting system could be. What would essentially be a simple side-minigame in another MMORPG, has been purified to it's concentrated form and expanded into a full game in here. Unfortunately, for now I find the game "finished" at around mid-game. Everything later than that seems like a more tedious repetition of the the exact same routines. I feel it lacks on a story-wise and the puzzle-wise front. Nevertheless, developers are constantly working on it and posting devlogs, so we will see how it goes. IIRC I bought it on sale, and for that I am grateful -- the game earned for itself. If I had bought it at it's regular price, however, I could have been underwhelmed and disappointed. This game works as a prototype or art form, but to be a fully-fledged, 100% completable casual title it needs some serious core gameloop improvements. Nonetheless, I am happy that I experienced this piece, thus I recommend trying it out... but at the same time -- maybe wait for a sale, or for some major patch first.Pros:- Unique and simple mechanics which are fun to play and mesh well together- Beautiful art and meticulously crafted details shine brightly in this game- Calm and serene atmosphere without any pressure of time and without inducing a fear of missing out- Mechanics are generally intuitive, assigning one of 8 attributes corresponding to the ingredient gives this game another layer of depth- UI and UX are very good, it is just a pleasure to interact with this gameA room for improvement:- For a game that you most probably spend long time playing during one session, the diversity and amount of music is very lacking. At times it even makes me dizzy listening to the same music on a loop, which forces me to either close the game or mute it. For example dwarf fortress has 18 or so, minecraft has 2(3?) albums while this game, for now, has only 2 very similar tracks.- It has (a bad type of) grind at times, and from what I have heard and experienced already, the it's even more severe mid-to-late game. Several repetitive in-game days often pass by without much progress and doing essentially the same thing over and over, crafting the same potions but varying the ingredients from time to time, only to wait for a specific merchant to bring you a new part for the alchemical or none of the ingredients you lack the most. I Definitely didn't reach end-game. Maybe I tapped onto the front doors of the mid-game, but for now it gets quite repetitive. I have not unlocked the new alchemical map -- I got tired of doing the same thing over and over.- It feels claustrophobic at times as well. Seeing the fields outside the windows makes you want to go outside and explore the world. Seeing the bedroom makes you want to interact with it, but it's essentially a whole screen added for the sake of one and only interaction - the bed to skip a day.- There is a purely cosmetic mechanic of the reputation that has no real gameplay impact, but it has a yet untapped potential.- There are several places where you can progress, but they feel a bit disconnected. The Alchemist's path feels a to be of little importance and not very impactful. I Breezed though 4 pages (almost half of the book) in one (6h?) sitting almost without noticing it. Talents are a bit weirdly distributed in time: you can reach level 28 and learn >50% of all the talent levels in the first sitting. I guess final levels are the hardest to get, but if not, You may be wondering layer "what now?". I see they have plans for new talents so I'm looking for that and maybe some more improvements on that system.- Haggling is something that you almost always want to do, so there should maybe be some balancing on that matter. - Performance: for a game that moves around a bunch of sprites, it has a surprisingly high impact on the my machine. From the simplicity of the machanics and graphics I assumed this game could be played on a toaster. but it felt a bit sluggish at times and ventilators start working considerably louder. I also don't understand the very long load time, somehow? It uses 2.2 GB when in background (on Linux Proton), 85 vt-threads and 20% processing power of a 6 core processor? How?- There seems to be a lot of content (look at all those potion stickers!), but it's quite inaccessible due to the grind. I find maps to be a bit too big, the trips of potions too long and the lack of different starting points tedious. Maybe if there was some way to move the potions larger distances it would be better. For example some kind of pressure mechanic - when brewing under pressure, the whole map would shrink (or the ingredient path would expand) allowing for travelling bigger distances quicker?- Alchemical machine is underwhelming. After using it you are left with "...was that it?"My ideas for growth:- It would be nice if the potions crafted in the game had some more uses. A good example is the upcoming feature of the wild growth potion for plants. Crafting a potion of fire or a potion of cold is essentially the same thing but using different ingredients. It would be nice seeing some real impact those things have on the world around us. Libido/love potion could affect bees which would in turn pollinate flowers, or increase a chance of random plants growing. A Potion of strength could be used to break a broken door for the inaccessible part of the house (or the city, read below). A slowness potion could be used to increase the accuracy of using tools, while a speed potion would amplify the effects of paths or something- If the alchemical machine was more interactive, it could give another dimension to the game. Twisting corks to mix potions in right proportions, pouring out the sludge or sediment from vials, heating and keeping mixtures at good temperature for a certain amount of time, adjusting angles of tubes, lighting up flames and adjusting their height and strength, connecting the tubes, releasing or increasing the pressure and whatnot are some of the examples I would think about adding if I were a part of the team. Maybe instead of buying whole sets of alchemical machines we would buy flasks and components which we would later combine and place on our own? Managing space and using available tools?- There is an untapped potential of discovering the world's lore while progressing through the game and feeling like a part of the a living universe. Merchants could bring books or tell tales. We could buy paintings of distant lands or explanations of the origin of plants etc.- There is a place for a story about the mystery of the alchemical cottage and it's previous owner, which we would progressively unravel. Rooms we could unlock, repairs we could make, notes and bits of knowledge from him etc.- It would be very nice to see some more locations. A city or a village, a cave, a forest, a tavern, a castle and whatnot could be added. Different shops in the city to make use of the earned money and use the potions to interact with NPCs in there. See them walk around and do their things. Haggle for tools with villagers, use strength potion to break the doors of a closed abandoned shop, use potion of nightvision to access a cave, Combine it with the reputation mechanic to make some locations more accessible or restricted than others, for example bad reputation would prevent you from interacting with rightful shop owners but would in turn give you access to the backalley and black market, where you could buy some exclusive forbidden items. With good reputation you could buy certified exclusive goods from good merchants etc.Ultimately this game is constantly growing, and planned features will probably resolve some of the issues mentioned above, so I'm only looking forward to it! The above critique doesn't impact my positive reception of this game, and I still highly recommend playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is decent fun for a good run. I've played it for 37 hours at the time of review, and I've been reasonably entertained for most of those hours. Pluses: - Unique game mechanic - and that counts for a lot for me. Depicting the process of inventing and brewing alchemical potions as a journey around a hazard-lined map is an interesting one, and it allows you to come to a variety of solutions using the materials you have on hand. - Pleasantly off-the-clock. Take as long as you like to fulfill a customer request, brew a tricky potion, or discover a new alchemical element. - Cozy in a relaxed, tinker-around-with-this way. Minuses: - It recognizes that you need some sort of save points on the map, but the mechanic is clunky and you often can't save exactly where you want to be - at least, I couldn't see a way to save a position that wasn't a completed potion. - After a while, it does get a bit same-y, especially given the lack of non-potion save points. I began to groan when I saw a long-distance brew, and that told me that I was nearing the end of my enjoyment of the game. - The tabs system for your potion book is handy, but it gets crowded and harder to use as you brew more potions. Some sort of organization system would be helpful, like second book or whatever.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game for the price, relaxing but weirdly engaging at the same time.I started to feel that "Zen" level of concentration that comes from other activities like playing an instrument, working with tools... or practicing an actual trade, which is what I felt like I'd learned by the time I finished playing. The game recreates that realistic vibe through the physical experience of using your lab instruments. You can stir rapidly or slowly, but with the movement of the mouse and the animation onscreen it's easy to forget that you're not actually stirring. You can pulverize ingredients methodically or even violently with your mortar and pestle, but again, the translation of mouse movement into onscreen action gives a sensation like you're actually working in your own laboratory.Things start out simply enough, and the mechanical underpinnings of the game stay pretty much the same, but challenge and complexity continue as you progress through the game. This comes from a few different factors. Initially, there's a scarcity of effective ingredients to work with. As you progress further, your toolbox gets bigger but your objectives on the alchemy map get more and more difficult to reach. And as all of those pieces finally fall into place, the game generates new novelty through the sometimes-exacting specifications put forward by your customers - combinations of effects, including/excluding certain ingredients, limiting the number/type you can use, etc.By the time I got to the VERY end of the game and picked up the last couple of achievements, I kinda just wanted it to be done with... But, then again, there are so many games in my library that I never 100% finish because I feel like it's not worth attaining for the level of effort involved. This was within reach, so I went for it, and I certainly enjoyed all of the hours I put into the game short of maybe the last 2-3 that I did just for the sake of being a completionist. Maybe there's some room for improvement in the gameplay loop all the way toward the end of the game? Either way, I'm not too concerned.Maybe my only other complaint is that Potion Craft has ONE single music track on a perpetual loop - listening to a 2-minute loop for 30 hours can be tough to manage in large doses. But they've mentioned that that's something they're already working on, so by the time you pick up the game and get to the 10-hour mark maybe your head won't be ready to explode and you won't need to take a day to cool off.Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game, and I plan to revisit it once they add some of the new features they've hinted at. But that's not to say that Potion Craft doesn't already feel complete in its current state. It was fun, it will be the next time I pick it up, and I feel perfectly fine recommending it at the full price listed.On a side note... If you like dark humor, feel free to start catering to some of the more questionable people who visit your establishment and asking you to do questionable things. I got a good laugh out of some of the ridiculous explanations customers gave me for a bunch of their potion requests.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for around 40 hours, from the beta launch to version 1.0 . This game has a lot to offer, both in gameplay and visuals, but is a little bit rough around the edges in a few ways that over time become more grind than actual engaging gameplay. The core mechanic in Potion Craft is, as the title would suggest, crafting potions. You use ingredients that lead you in different directions on the alchemy map in order to discover and create potions with new effects. The other portions of the game are spent selling the potions you've learned to make, improving new recipes, and seeking out ingredients both familiar and new to you.Recently, the game moved into version 1.0. I feel that 1.0 may not have been advertised entirely accurately, as I myself thought a lot more content would be coming to the game. I was both excited and disappointed by the content that was added in version 1.0 after launching it for the first time. There are some places where the game feels fresh and exciting, and some where it's the same, excruciatingly similar slog to the beta.Here's the good, the bad, and the ugly of it all:+This game has a really calm and relaxing atmosphere+It will challenge you, but has an obvious endgame where you have a recipe for every potion and every part of greater recipes+It feels gratifying for one of the visiting merchants to ask you for a potion to help them find you more ingredients+Getting over the hump of not having enough ingredients gives some real satisfaction for an hour or two+The new haggling system mixes things up and makes you consider whether a tiny health potion is worth haggling for, whether because of the skill it takes, or the time it takes.+For what it offers, I feel that this game is fairly priced. It doesn't feel like the developers are trying to squeeze money out of anybody, and you simply get exactly what you pay for. Much better than paying $15 for an indie game that can be completed in an hour.-Hearing the same music over and over again gets a little grating after a while. Sure, you could mute it and play your own or watch a video on the side, but I feel that doing so really takes away from the atmosphere of the game.-Merchants feel as though they need more depth, though this has been improved on slightly already. I think it would add a lot to the game to have more ways to interact with them, even something as simple as showing off your salts or created stones to the sorcerer in exchange for some advice.-Not being able to save large recipes that use a dozen different potions is a large obstacle. Though it's not the end of the world to click through the recipe book and cook up one of each potion in order to craft something, doing it once for each tier of stone gets tiring quickly.--People often ask for things that seem entirely impossible. For example, a potion effect in the corner of the map that clearly needs more than one ingredient, they will ask to be made with only one ingredient. Even worse is that these stipulations are often required in order to make the sale at all, forcing you to turn a customer away and lose reputation.--The last three or so hours of 100% completing this game are a complete slog. Beyond having every possible recipe written down, there is really no end-game content beyond grinding out the last stones and achievements. There is nothing to keep you on your toes besides occasionally whipping up a weaker version of a potion you already have a recipe for.--The new haggling system often feels unresponsive in that sometimes the hits feel completely off, or I have to click the mouse twice in order to get it to register. --Once you've completed every achievement, or even just completed everything the game has to offer, there's no fanfare, nor any point in playing for even five minutes longer. I don't think that the gameplay loop is exciting enough to warrant further play, as it's just repeating the same three actions over, and over, and over again.Overall, I think this is a really nifty little game that will sometimes challenge you to think outside of the box. What it feels like it needs above all else is some more work done to pad out the content that does exist in order to create a gratifying endgame and achievement hunt.

_childDocuments_.review: 29.1h (100% achievement, finished the game) No (the game might be grindy depending on your playstyle). Yes (1 achievement). No. is a management game that combines potion-making and shop management. You will craft potions based on customer demands and sell them. The potion-making mechanic allows you to be creative, whether it's to make a potion based on the available ingredients or find a way to make the same potion with fewer costs for more profit.- A lot of potion varieties to craft- Freedom in creating the potions however you like- The end game can be problematic to some people; potion-making becomes exhausting to do while shop management becomes repetitive- Buyable ingredients rely too much on RNG early gameIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 did a good job to depict the medieval setting. The brown color is used as the majority of the game's visuals, with characters and objects that look like drawing from the same era. The relaxing music that accompanies it also helps to promote the medieval theme, making it feel as if you are there.The only "story" that you'll get from the game is the cutscene when you start a new game. The rest of the dialogues will be coming from your customers to tell you what potion they want to buy.The game title describes the gameplay perfectly. You are a potion maker in the medieval era, and it's your job to make potions based on your customer's demands. However, they won't say which potions they would like to buy right away; instead, they will tell you about their issue, and you need to suggest which potion they should buy by presenting it in front of them. Some requests have more than one solution, and although some are easy to figure out, others can be vaguer, making it hard to understand what they really want.Customers differ based on your reputation. Serving good people will increase your reputation and attract more good people while serving the bad ones will decrease it and attract more bad people. Both sides of customers have different sets of requests: good people will ask for something that can help them do their daily jobs, and bad people will tend to look for ways to kill others. To be honest, I found the bad customers' requests to be more straightforward, although sometimes I appreciate it more than the more obscure requests from the good customers."All roads lead to Rome" is the perfect idiom for potion-making in . It is done in a map-like interface where you need to move a flask to the flask symbol(s) on the map. Each symbol will give a different effect, with a higher quality if you manage to bring the flask closer to the symbol. Ingredients are used to move the flask - each ingredient has a different pathway, and you need to decide which ingredient to use based on your stock and strategy. You can get more profit if you manage to make a potion with fewer and/or cheaper ingredients, although those adjustments aren't mandatory.Ingredients are limited, especially in the early game. Random ingredients might spawn in your garden every day, but it's usually not enough. You need to purchase more from the NPCs that are coming to your shop every day to fulfill your needs. However, their selection is randomized. It's easy to overuse a certain ingredient early game, making you unable to make a potion from the recipe that you have saved. It takes time to make a potion and redoing it for some potions every few in-game days just because you run out of ingredients is exhausting.Speaking of exhausting, the same can also be said in the end game. Although the game is fun, the last 10h feels more like a chore. You are forced to make a potion with effects that are located very far from the map, ruining the experience. It was fun to make a perfect potion for each type, but having to spend your time making a potion with multiple effects that can take a very long time to finish is not. It's easy to get burned out from making each potion because of it.I finished the game in 28.4h and continued playing for one achievement for 0.7h. The game isn't hard to finish - it takes some time to get used to the potion-making mechanic, but it only takes endurance to finish it once you know what to do. Yes, the game is overstaying its welcome. It becomes a chore to finish once you have finished making all of the potion types. I lost motivation in continuing because I felt that should be everything that the game has to offer, but it forced me to continue playing by giving tasks to mix potions with different effects that can take a long time to finish as a finale. It took hours to get them all after a lot of complaining.Serving the customers becomes some sort of relief later on, but it also turns out to be repetitive. You need to listen to what they want, make a potion with a single click, sell it to them, and repeat it all over again. Some customers might ask for a custom request, but with the potion-making being exhausting as it is, I find it easier to either give them what I have or reject them, even if I had to take a hit in popularity that affect the number of incoming customers. Having too many recipes is a nightmare since there is no paging option. My experience with  is a bit mixed. I thought the game would be like  at first, but it ends up focusing more on the potion-making rather than the shop mechanic. Although I enjoyed the game at the beginning, the end game ends up as a chore, ruining my experience. The game becomes manageable once I tried to play it in short bursts, although the exhaustion is still there. I could recommend buying it because I enjoyed 90% of the game, but please keep in mind that the last stretch of the game won't be as pleasant. I would even suggest stopping playing the game altogether after it reaches that point unless you care about the achievement or still enjoyed the game - there won't be an ending or anything waiting for you after you finished everything.

_childDocuments_.review: WOW, I am so disappointed in this game. As a fan of dorky little sim games, I had been looking forward to this one for a while. I waited for a sale (bless you Steam, or I would have lost even more money on this game) and only paid $8.99 for this but it still feels like an L. I'm not entirely sure what the developers of this game were thinking... You have this wonderful idea for a potion crafting and selling game and, instead of focusing completely on the actual crafting part of potions, you tied "crafting" (I use the term loosely here) to a map and exploring said map? And TRUST ME, I hear you when you say "Well wait, crafting but based on map exploration sounds kind of neat!"; I was with you there buddy, trust me, but let me try to explain through a VERY long winded review. Buckle in.Now let me nip this in the bud right quick: the map is just that, a map. A paper map. A pirate's map. X marks the spot and all. It's cute and it fits with the style of the game, but you yourself do not explore it, and all movement on this map is tied completely to the loose term of "crafting" I'll be using throughout this review. You put your ingredients into the cauldron, be it crushed or not, and then stir to make the potion bottle move across the map. That's the gameplay loop. There are also whirlpools you can choose to move with (they will move you a small distance away) and skeletons/bones(?) on the map that will basically instantly kill you. The crafting happens when you find a bottle on the map and "craft" your potion in that spot. It does not matter the ingredients you put in it to get you there, so long as you got there.This itself is baffling to me. You created a crafting game where the gameplay loop is move around a map? And perhaps I could see /some/ merit in it if you had to use specific ingredients to even craft the potion when you got to it on the map, maybe? But you don't even need to do that, just any old ingredient that will get you from point A to point B will do. And then there's the stuff on the map. Jeez bro, what is with this? Was the map too easy to navigate so the devs had to quickly slap some stuff ontop of it that would diversify the experience and drag out the runtime? Navigating the map already takes ample resources to get from A to B; any you'd like, yes, but ample of them. They all have designated move patters associated with them - one item always goes to the left in a silly squiggly way, while another item will always go right in a silly squiggly way and so on - so you already need to use your resources sparingly and in an optimal pattern to get where you need to go on the completely fogged/hidden map. That's well and fine, and could be a fun way to do things: use an item associated with "wind" that goes in the direction of potions all associated with wind and discover new "wind"esk potions. But... then they slapped these skeletons or bones or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they are onto the map and... they just fail your potion almost instantly whenever your giant potion bottle even slightly touches it? And so what that does is it fails your potion and sends you all the way back to the starting point of the map. All your resources used and all your time wasted. And sure, there's a dilute option that moves your potion a little bit, but all it does is move it back to the start point, so in most situations it isn't helping you. If anything, why not make the dilute move you slightly away from the closest skeleton or fail state or whatever it is? It makes the map extremely hard to navigate because, remember, we only have a few set navigation patters to choose from. It also makes it so, when I need to go around a skeleton, I have to use ingredients that I feel would NEVER be in the potion I am attempting to craft (aka so it will move me in a completely different direction on the map). The whole thing feels counter intuitive and, if that weren't bad enough, they throw more at you on this map! Remember the whirlpools I mentioned earlier? (It's okay if you don't, it's been a minute.) Well they have this neat little ability where they can teleport you to another part of the map nearby. Love that! Makes navigating those skeletons a lot easier right? They're probably designed in a way to help the player, as a mechanic, go in the right direction with less resources. WRONG. It's like I said, the map was designed to be counter intuitive. The whirlpools almost always made me feel like a fool for using them. On the perfect path to a potion and want to see where this'll take you? Assuming it'll be closer to the potion? IDIOT xD! BEGONE INTO THE SKELETON PILE! ..... Like... why? Thanks for the gut punch niceplay. :\ Speaking of counter intuitive, what's with that tutorial? I'm sorry but LOL what the actual ♥♥♥♥ was that tutorial? You teach the player what a mortar and pestle does and then don't teach us about: the whirlpools, the skeletons, the diluting, the auto-craft feature, the reputation system, haggling, the gifting mechanic, whatever was in the basement idk I refuse to play more to find out, etc. And listen, that's not to say that I didn't appreciate them telling me that crushing the ingredients makes them more potent, but you had a whole text box for what I just said in 7 words and then no tutorial for that entire list I just typed up. Why? You already built the UI for the tutorial boxes and everything, all you had to do was type like 10 more things. I'm about to do a whole lot more typing than those tutorials would have taken and I'm doing it for free just to ♥♥♥♥ atop your game so like... I think it would have been worth your while.Meanwhile, the real tutorial of the game is given to you via the quest log. Read what to do, do it, book crosses it out, you get progress toward a perk. It works, but it's just so poorly delivered. The perks are very bland by the way. No idea why that's even in the game. Pressure to have it like other game do? Idk it's boring and useless.It's like... I want to give this game more credit cause I love the art, music, overall concept, good chunk of the writing, and some of the smaller concepts within the game but.. it's just so hidden by a bunch of annoyances that I can't excuse. For example: Love having a reputation system, but not only did it take me at least an hour to even realize it was there (because again, no tutorial, never pointed it out) once I did finally figure out it was there and how to make it go up or down I not only didn't understand what the point to having a better reputation was but I didn't understand what was making some sales increase my reputation while some decreased it. For example: I had a pretty bad reputation by the time I noticed it was a thing. I fulfilled all requests that came in and chalked up all the extremely bad requests as just quirky writing and moved on, but found out that wasn't the case and started trying to improve my score and reject people with negative requests. I thought the game might be less black and white about things and I fulfilled some requests that I told myself were "morally grey" and should be allowed. The game did not agree. Okay, that's fine. I will only give the most goodest and neutralest of patrons my beautiful potions. "NAY!" said the game, very loudly into my reputation meter, "-6 YOU FIEND!" The ♥♥♥♥?! The dude had an almost identical request to one that gave me a positive score like 3 customers ago. I don't get it. I just don't.idk I'm running out of characters and at the end of the day, it's just a game that disappointed me. I just don't want someone that was expecting what I was expecting to waste their money and be sad afterwards. This was 1 of 4 purchases I gave myself for the Steam Winter Sale and I feel a bit cheated with all these lame, overused systems in a potentially cool game. Don't get it if you liked my review, get Recettear or We. The Revolution. If you hated the review uh... why you still here? Go play the thing.That's it. Bye.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying while I was given a free copy, I played the demo well beforehand and knew that this was going to be a day one purchase for me provided the price point was not outrageous (I was pleasantly surprised to see it was quite reasonable). Anyway, on to my thoughts:Potion Craft is an incredibly unique and relaxing potion creating/selling simulation game. The potion creation method and exploration allows for a multitude of ingredient options (some more efficient than others) to create and eventually sell your concoctions. The characters, situations, and moral dilemmas from the various encounters keep the overall lighthearted gameplay interesting.The artstyle and music is quaint, the audio effects (although sparse) are satisfying, and the UI is simple but fit the setting well.While there are many other features and content that could be added and some aspects could be nitpicked, I am very excited to see what comes of the early access phase but don’t let that label fool you, it is a perfectly competent and entertaining game as is.I recommend giving Potion Craft a try; I had personally never played anything like it previously and I’m glad I was able to have the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a 20-30+ hour relaxing medieval sim with in which you craft and invent a multitude of potions, dabble in chemistry, and slowly work toward making your Magnum Opus, the Philosophers Stone. Running your day-to-day life is peaceful, there are no time constraints, no micromanagement, and the day ends when you want it to. Taking care of the shop is pretty simple, customers come in, ask if you have or can make something, and depending on what you give them to solve their issue, you get reputation points that affect what kind of customers that show up. As expected, having a negative reputation gives you creepy necromancers, murderous assassins, and terrible people in general, while a positive reputation will give you normal working citizens looking for something to help their backyard garden grow, nobles looking for some amusement, town guards, and other friendly wizards. Actual potion making is pretty fun, interacting with your tools to grind down your ingredients, stir and heat up your cauldron, inventing, discovering, and bottling something useful. Eventually, you will have a plethora of book tabs and saved recipes in your notebook, something for any situation. With book tabs, you can automatically make any potion you’ve made before, provided you have the exact same ingredients you used in the initial making of said potion. You have two Alchemy Maps, in which your potion is either water or oil based, which changes how and what can be made, and as you gain experience, you get points to put into useful traits and learning skills. To overall highlight my positive experience, despite coming out of early access and hitting the market with a positive impact, there are still frequent updates with a major one coming out in the near future. At the time of this review it hasn’t been released yet, but a garden expansion + more interaction with it has been planned, new talents and skills to pick up, more ingredients and salts to create, shop customization, more merchants and customer variations, more maps and even more potions. The developers are also a frequent sight in the community itself, showing off the development processes and running art festivals. The community, while I’ve only lurked, is very positive and I hope to see more of the above in the future.
