_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game! Potion Craft makes you feel like a real alchemist; from the game mechanics to the art style, using a wide variety of ingredients and equipment. _childDocuments_.review: You’re a novice alchemist and you have finally found somewhere to settle down after travelling around. You have found an old abandoned house which seemed to have had an alchemist live there prior to your arrival. It’s got a garden ideal for growing herbs and other ingredients, along with alchemy equipment in the basement. It’s been a while since anyone has lived there and the alchemy equipment is in need of being fixed up but after some hard work, you’ll have your very own Potion Shop up and running. For now, though while the alchemy equipment is out of use, you have your trusty Cauldron, Mortar and Pestle, Bellows and Water Ladle. Using these basic tools will allow you to make your potions, you have a couple ingredients to begin with. You can just put the ingredients straight into the cauldron; however, you’ll get better mileage out of your ingredients if you crush them in your mortar and pestle. You will get twice the benefits out of crushing your ingredients than if you just dropped them straight into your cauldron. Using the Water Ladle will allow you to add water to your potions, it will move your potion bottle back towards the centre of the potion map where you started.  To make potions you will have to put the ingredients into the cauldron. This will then lay a dotted line with an “X” this way and that on the potion map, the map is almost completely covered in a Fog of War. As you potion bottle moves around the map it will reveal more of the map along with open books and potion bottles with a Question Mark on them. You will need to add ingredients until laying a path to one of the bottles with a question mark on it. Stirring the cauldron will move your bottle along the dotted line laid down by your ingredients. Next you will use the bellows to heat the potion up in the cauldron after a few blows of the bellows a puff of smoke will appear from the cauldron. This is to let you know that the potion is completed, revealing what the mystery potion is. Finishing the potion will have it put into your inventory allowing you to sell it to a customer.  You can create a mixture of potions so instead of finishing a potion upon reaching a potion you can carry on to another potion bottle. This allows you to mix two or more types of potions into one potion, such as you could have a health potion mixed one that restores mana. You can save a recipe in your book of potions, although you only have enough space for five potions. You can use these saved potions to create them with a push of a button should a customer want one. This will save you from having to add ingredients and is handy for those potions of more complexity. On the map you will move over some books, collecting these will unlock Talents which you can use towards four categories. The categories are Alchemy Map (Visibility Radius), Alchemical Practice, Trading and Haggling. They have levels ranging from six to ten levels depending on the category and they cost from one to three Talents to unlock. In your little place you’ll find the front area is your shop, here every day customers will come and tell you their problems and you’ll have to get the right potion for them. If you offer them the wrong potion twice then they’ll leave your shop not very happy. However, if you give them what they want then they’ll be as happy as Larry. The happier customers the more your popularity will grow. While you can sell your wares for a price you can also try to haggle for a better price, this will also go for passing merchants which will visit you in hoping that you buy some of their ingredients. You will find items and mushrooms which you may not have access to, which can lead to need potions. The backroom is where you’ll prepare all your potions, out back is your garden, here you’ll have some herbs, mushrooms etcetera grow each day. You can collect these items and use them to prepare potions for your customer's needs. In the basement is your Alchemy Machine however, it’s seen better days and is currently unusable. You can repair the machine if you find a merchant selling the parts you need to bring it back to its former glory days. The final room in your place is the upstairs attic, here is where you sleep at night after a hard day's work. Once you have done everything you can in a day going to bed will reset the day, allow need ingredients to grow and be ready to make more potions for the customers knocking at your door. You’re not going to be able to keep everyone happy, there are going to be plenty of people who you’re unable to sort a potion out for. This could be because you don’t have the required ingredients or knowledge of the potion a customer wants. You will have to uncover the potion map as much as possible revealing all the potions. However, scattered around the potion map in between the potions and the books are piles of Skulls. You don’t want to have your bottle move over these skulls as your potion bottle will empty the longer time you spend moving over them. If you empty your potion bottle crossing the skulls then the potion will fail and you’ll have lost all the ingredients you had in your cauldron. There are goals to complete as you progress, these goals can be found in you’re the Alchemist’s Path book. Currently there are Seven Chapters with varying amount goals to complete. Completing all goals in a chapter will open the next chapter and you will also gain a reward of some sort upon completing a chapter.  The game is still in Early Access currently so there will be some problems along the way, news things being added to the game and even possibly some things removed. So, bear in mind that it is in Early Access and things can change. There’s more to come in future updates with new potions, maps, upgrading your garden and more. The game is easy to play and learn, it will take some grinding to fill the coffers, uncover some of the potions, fix the alchemy machine and you will upset some folks by not fulfilling their requirements but your reputation will grow as will your shop. The game is a little bit copy paste what you did the day before for the upcoming day so far. I haven’t been able to get the alchemy machine up and running yet, I’m a bit short of the old pennies when the merchants come a calling. In the settings there’s option for Window Mode (Borderless or Windowed), Limit and Show FPS, Language (English, German, French, Polish, Chinese, Korean and Russian). Positives  + Nice artwork + Easy and relaxing to play + Active developers Negatives  - Repetitive - No achievements - No cards currently Become the latest buzz around town, with folks from near and far visiting your shop for potions to cure ailments, poisons to rid vermin or even a potion to make paint glow in the dark in Potion Craft. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cute little game. The concept is simple - use your resources at hand to make potions to solve the townsfolk's needs. The mechanism an interesting one - your ingredients plot out a course on a map, and you can grind them to their full course or limit their effect. One by one you add them, to reach a desired effect. The closer you get to the point on the map, the stronger the potion. If you make the perfect potion, you can save the recipe for the next townsfolk who needs it. If you don't have the right ingredients on hand for the next time, you can try plotting another course using different ingredients.  It really does feel like you're a master at your craft, grinding just so, stirring just so, diluting just so, knowing which plants can be used as a substitute when you don't have what you need.To be honest, most of the goals in the game are self motivated. Personally, my primary motivation is creating the most economical recipes. There are mechanism to level up, and there are goals, but most of them you meet during the course of play by customer requests. It seems like the developers are working on more features, which I look forward to.Overall, this is a fun little casual game, especially for those of us with a perfectionist streak. If you were hoping for more from Pottermore's potions game, this game will scratch that itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I am very excited to see its full release! I have completed all current goals (as of 6/20/2022) within 30 hours. In its current state, I wish there was more ingredients that take you Northeast, as there is one (maybe two, depending on if you count the red mushroom) that takes you that direction. A skill tree would be preferable to what we have now, as there is no way to make it your own. With only 4 categories for your skill points to go into, it feels very limited. I would also like something to do with the extra skill points after you bought everything you could, like maybe a way to trade them for cash (maybe the value could fluctuate each day?) or perhaps a way to trade them directly for rare ingredients or other things like that. A way to separate regular ingredients from the crystals would be nice, as i found myself having to dig through every ingredient to find the crystal I needed. _childDocuments_.review: In Potion Craft you play as an alchemist setting up shop. Customers begin to arrive with a range of different needs and you have to brew something to match their requests. Despite the simplicity of the concept, Potion Craft does well to make the experience engaging and fun. Harvesting and selecting ingredients, crushing them, stirring the cauldron, discovering new effects, placing potions on the scales, haggling etc. means you're involved in every step of the way and the game never becomes boring.The dialogue of the customers is varied enough so as to not get repetitive and the progression system ("The Alchemist's Path") provides a good balance between being challenging and flowing with natural discovery of the game's mechanics. The game offers a high degree of customisation, allowing you to give unique names, symbols, labels and bottle shapes to all of your creations which is a nice touch. Recipes can also be saved and quickly brewed using a recipe book, which is ideal for when you don't feel like manually brewing a potion (although I usually find myself doing so anyways because I enjoy it).Potion Craft's style is incredible. The music, sound effects, dialogue, and visuals all do an excellent job at creating a magical and old-timey atmosphere. The world of Potion Craft has a real charm and charisma to it - it's easy to get lost there.I also have to mention the tactility of the game; the experience of Potion Craft feels very hands-on. The herbs in the mortar and pestle provide just the right amount of resistance and the potion bottles have a certain weight to them that feels very realistic. It's clear that the game has been crafted with huge attention to detail.The game runs smoothly and I've never encountered any bugs.Despite being an early access game, Potion Craft provides a satisfying experience with a decent amount of content. Almost twenty hours in, I'm still discovering new recipes! With that being said, the game is lacking some features (such as shop upgrades and alternative potion bases) which will likely come in a future update. I'm usually wary about buying early access games but I've been really impressed with what Potion Craft has to offer so far and am excited to see where it goes upon full-release.

_childDocuments_.review: (all the chapters or main objectives) / achievements:   30hr +   from 10hr onwards   1500+   1400+---------------------------------The main goals in game are to create legendary substances and their respective "consumables".There are 5 Tiers of legendary substances and each need all the preceding tier ingredients to make, and you will need to make 2 substances of each tiers to complete the objectives.i.e. You have just made a Tier 4 substance, and your next objectives will be making a Tier 4 consumable plus a Tier 5 substance.So you will need to use your Tier 4 substance + 12 potions to make the Tier 4 consumable,and another Tier 4 substance as an ingredient (making it from Tier 1 to Tier 4 again), + another 12 potions to make a Tier 5 substance. This situation happens in every tiers throughout the game, from Tier 1 to 5.You will be serving 1400+ customers, so you may not want to brew the potions from map every time.And for the ingredient potions of legendary recipes, many of them requires you to travel back and forth the map, corners to corners, or 5 different spots on map.So you will not want to do them twice for any recipes, but save the path of recipes so you can one click it when you need to make them again if needed.The game becomes a resource management issue, you just need to replenish the ingredients, buying all the discounted goods from merchants everytime, and one click the recipes to serve customers until reaching the final reputation required.For the reputation system, there are no endings for the good or evil side, no stories or hidden missions to complete, just different types of customers you will encounter.Consumable are so tedious to make, and you may not want to use them on fulfilling the customer additional needs, but just saving them to make legendary recipes. Therefore making the consumables are merely just objectives to complete the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Charming and engaging game play loop of making and selling potions to make enough money to buy ingredients and gear to experiment with new potions. The mechanics really made me feel like a medieval alchemist, experimenting is fun, failures frustrating and successes rewarding both mechanically and emotionally.  Obviously the rest isn't there yet, but developers, if you're reading this, you HAVE TO make the vendors more accessible. Whatever RNG formula that decides when they show up would spread them out so far sometimes as to be down right game breaking. If the dwarf doesn't show up for 20 days that's fine, he just sells 'shortcuts', but if the wizard or herbalist don't show up for 20 days the game is in a total stale mate. Maybe make a 'go to town' option, or put a shorter cap on the spread like if they haven't shown up in 5 days they pop in guaranteed?Other than that I'm looking forward to future content. There's a morality gauge that doesn't do anything yet, maybe make some potions stronger/weaker or easier/harder to craft based on morality? I'd love to see a story element added via recurring characters like the herbalist and the brewer and the fisherman etc. And upgrades for the shop and especially the garden. I wish it kept track of how much I was spending to make potions, the profit margin was always just a guess, so a ledger element would be cool. Also the music is great but a bit thin, it gets repetitive quick.Final verdict: Cute and fun mini-game that in it's current state didn't really feel worth the sticker price but shows a lot of potential. Maybe buy, for sure follow.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is a great relaxing game.  As many have said, it can get a bit grindy and boring when you hit a lull in progression.  Some of the negative comments have been about the lack of specific resources available for harvest/purchase when needed.  I think the reason for that discouragement is the misconception about the game's genre.  At it's heart, Potion Craft is a puzzle game more than anything else.  Figuring out how to reach specific potion effects without the ideal ingredients is part of the fun early in the game.  Later in the game, you may have better ingredients, but not the ones you have used in saved recipes.  That forces you to revisit some of the easier potions to try for better efficiency.  This game is definitely not for everybody, but I think it's definitely worth a look for people who like puzzle games.  I wholeheartedly agree that it needs some more exploration and maybe more world interactivity.  Upcoming updates with Talents 2.0 and Garden 2.0 look perfect for that.  I'd love to see some actual adventuring to gather ingredients, meet customers that become regulars, etc.  That might taint the allure of this game's simple relaxation, however.Look up some videos on gameplay before you buy, but don't go too deep.  The exploration and discovery is a good chunk of the fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is a game where you play as an aspiring alchemist who runs a shop in a medieval town. You have to mix ingredients, brew potions, haggle with customers, and manage your finances. Sounds fun, right? Well, not so much when you have to deal with the most annoying and demanding customers ever. They want potions for everything: love, health, beauty, strength, invisibility, you name it. And they’re never satisfied with the price or the quality. They’ll complain, bargain, threaten, and even try to rob you. And don’t get me started on the ingredients. You have to gather them from the forest, the swamp, the mountains, and other dangerous places. You have to dodge traps, monsters, bandits, and angry villagers. You have to spend hours grinding them, boiling them, stirring them, and hoping they don’t explode in your face. And you have to do all this while keeping track of your recipes, your inventory, your reputation, and your competitors. It’s exhausting!Potion Craft is a game that will test your patience, your creativity, and your sanity. It’s also a game that will make you laugh, cry, and rage quit. It’s a game that will make you feel like a real alchemist, for better or for worse. Would recommend to anyone who likes a challenge, repetitive gameplay, and a good sense of humor.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is a really chill alchemy simulator. While you are still running a shop at the end of the day, profits are easy to come by as you have no operating costs beyond the ingredients, which you get free batches of every day. So you build up a list of recipes and dole out potions to everyone knocking on your door. Then someone asks for something new it's time to get to experimenting. The potion making is pretty unique - alchemy effects are spread out on a map, and every ingredient follows a certain path. You have a variety of tools and methods to make slight alterations as you add one ingredient after another, charting a course into the unknown and finally settling on a potion effect you can add to your mixture. Taking a direct route and landing right on the effect gives you the highest selling potion for the fewest ingredients, netting you big profits, so it pays to keep manually making the potion until you've mastered it. Then it goes in the recipe book where, provided the ingredients are available, you can recreate  the potion with a single click. With some savvy trading for more ingredients with merchants you can have a stockpile of everything you need to cover all your clients' needs. But all that money has to go somewhere, right? And that's where the game introduces a sort of back-room tinkering aspect. When the shop shuts for the day and there's no more clients, you might decide to brew something truly outrageous just to explore the map and complete challenges, like getting 5 effects in a single potion or finding stuff people haven't even asked for yet. These expensive experiments soak up a ton of ingredients and often then results aren't really useful in the shop. But they work into a narrative relate to every alchemist's dream - making the philosopher's stone. Unfortunately, this is where the game can become a little bit of a grind. At times your quest will be locked behind tasks that require specific merchants to come along. Maybe they turn up but you don't have the money to buy what you need, maybe you've got the money saved but you're waiting for days, just filling the same orders for the potions you had recipes for long ago. When you spend more time in the haggling minigame than brewing new and interesting potions, it can start to feel like the game has slowed to a crawl. I do like what's here, I love the challenges and I think it's worth playing, but I'd almost want the economy to be even easier because the fun here isn't actually the mundane business of running a shop. It's the late night experiments to create something weird and wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft has a nice idea at its heart, of a geeky potion-crafting and -selling simulation. Its art is endearingly old-fashioned, and the central conceit of the alchemy map is original and interesting. Also a shout-out to the pleasant and helpful community.But then the game spoils it all by adding a twitch clicker game at its heart in the essential haggling mini-game. You have to do this in order to make enough money, but if you're not an FPS twitch fiend—if, god forbid, you're just an older gamer looking for a nice relaxing potion-making game—you're going to crash and burn, losing all your money.This haggling mechanic, so central to the game, fatally undermines everything else the game is trying to achieve. There isn't even a mod on Nexus to guarantee haggling success—I know, I looked, because I really wanted to be able to rescue the game. As such, with deep regret I cannot recommend Potion Craft to anyone who isn't a whiz at manic twitch clicker games.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is an alchemy simulation game that sets you off as an novice Alchemist opening up shop in a town that's left void of an Alchemist.The town's folks will come to you with their requests for potions and you would have to decipher what type of potions they need based on their plight.The game is split up into “rooms” in your shophouse. There’s the shop where you would do your selling to customers, there’s your laboratory where you would make your potions, enchanted garden where your ingredients are grown and the basement where your alchemy machine is at.What might capture the player's attention is the art style and animation that simply oozes with it's own unique-ness.Visually it has its own style, from the static sprites to the animations. Pick up an ingredient and you'll see some leaves falling off. When you pound the ingredients down with the pestle where it changes form from leaves and turn into a broken down mush. The way the potion boils in the cauldron with bubbles spewing out, something about those little details that make it visually appealing, akin to Banner Saga’s animations during the dialogue scenes.Before you can start brewing you would have to visit the Enchanted Garden for ingredients in order to make your potions. Ingredients spawn at the start of the day and seem to be random on what spawns. Shifting over to the laboratory, you add ingredients into the cauldron or pestle and mortar to mix, there is a recipe map in the background that acts as a preview to how far you’ll get with that ingredient in order to reach its “destination” potion that can be discovered on the same map itself. You can either add the ingredients straight into the cauldron or pound the ingredients down (this can double its “distance” on the map) to your desired range in order to avoid traps that would make the potion fail or in order to land directly on the potion “destination” to get a stronger mix. The flexibility of potion making is what I appreciate. You can use different concoctions in order to reach the same destination.Once the potion has been made you can save the recipe so you can simply make the potion without going through the same process which can get tedious with long playthroughs. The shop floor is where customers buy the potions. You can either sell it straight to them or haggle with them through a minigame that can result in you making a more tidy profit. From the foundations that are in place, I’m enjoying what niceplay games have made so far. It can either be a Zen potion crafting simulator or one where you try to milk the customers as much as possible in order to bring up that gold count. This is one to look out for if you’re into this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: This non-recommendation is to inform the developers that I don't think some of their ideas for increased difficulty are realistic or fair to the player. Adding conditions like "I only want a potion with 1 type of ingredient" is not just unrealistic, it's unfathomable that anyone other than a mage or alchemist would come with such a request, and realistically, they probably wouldn't make such an utterly ludicrous stipulation either. The requests to avoid or include a specific ingredient are much more realistic and understandable. Any limits on the number of ingredients are just silly. How is a bloody peasant supposed to KNOW what's in the love potion you just offered them? How are they supposed to KNOW you didn't just give them a health potion? The game uses some direct logic that defies the reality that most of your customers wouldn't be able to discern the effects of your potion until they actually take it.And the hits to reputation are silly as well. If I refuse service to some idiot who comes in and DEMANDS a potion with only 1 ingredient AND multiple effects and refuses anything that doesn't meet those IMPOSSIBLE criteria, why should I get penalized for telling that customer to go somewhere else? And at higher rep levels, the hits should be LESS, not more. Because your reputation is STRONGER, the complaints of a single person should mean LESS. Here's the simple logic, as your reputation increases, more of the populace will have been your customers and also had good experiences, thus the effect of a dissatisfied customer's complaint will be dismissed by the greater balance of good experiences. This effect would naturally increase as your reputation level increases and customers beyond your town also carry word further.It might make more sense if these complications were tempered against your trading skill, which at this point doesn't help you much except to acquire gold a bit faster. It would also make some sense that you could haggle a customer down on their requirements, like instead of 1 ingredient, you could haggle for 2, or 3 depending on your skill.And why is everyone demanding poopshroom when it hasn't even been offered for sale and I've literally never even acquired it? Why are customers demanding impossible criteria that my only option is to refuse? Just for more artificial difficulty?

_childDocuments_.review: If this game was a potion, I'd say that it has a very well-developed base, with many innovative properties ripe for expanding upon, has a pleasant smell and an appealing texture. But the rest of the potion was made by taking that wonderful base and pouring water. More, more, more water. More water. Endless deluge of the clear liquid, enough to fill the entire cauldron, flood the lab floor, and ruin your downstairs neighbour's ceiling. In the end, the aquatic ordeal leaves the potion completely devoid of anything it could've been, and you end up pouring it down the drain.It starts out . There isn't much of a plot, you're just a young alchemist who stumbled upon an abandoned workshop (biggest wish fulfillment of 2023) and decided to reopen it. People ask you for potions, so that's what you get them. The brewing system is ingenious: adding ingredients moves your "potion marker" on the effects map, and in order to get a particular effect, you have to reach its designated point, and heat the potion up to a boil.At first, the map is pure joy to explore. You're constantly finding new effects, collecting experience books, finding out how the map itself works, and unlocking milestones that make you move forward in the "Path of the Alchemist", which unlocks new NPCs, new ingredients, new merchants.But then... you slowly start noticing the unmistakable flavour of . Everybody wants a healing potion. Sure, I can brew you a healing potion. Oh, what's this? I'm out of a critical ingredient! But I can replace it with something else that "moves right", I'll just save both recipes so I won't have to do it again. Oh, but in order to get more exotic effects you have to move further into the map. And it's just so slow. So many ingredients just so you can explore the map. The same path, over and over again. Take the ingredient, smash it into pulp, put it in the cauldron, repeat. And again. And again.Note that many actions are achieved by the "pumping power of the mouse" so to speak. So to crush an object in the mortar, you literally have to crush it by holding it with the mouse cursor. Same for stirring, same for pouring water, same for using the bellows. Not only this becomes extremely tedious later on, it also makes crafting tier 3 potions an exercise in ridiculous mouse precision (it's not about the recipe, it's about making the potion marker be  in the right place. Hint: doing it is not fun).Eventually, a new option shows up: you get an alchemy machine that's supposed to be able to craft legendary recipes. Wow, a gameplay change! Exciting! Until it turns out that those recipes still need lots of "normal" potions to be made, and often these potions require a weird combination of properties that will have you make your potion take a very long trip across the alchemy map...And that's what this really boils down to. Everything is just so shallow and tedious. There is a reputation system, but it's pretty much a bare minimum. There is some dialogue with unique NPCs (including a discount Geraldo del Riviero), but it's quite rare, and incredibly short. There is a barter system with a nice dressing of difficulty levels and topics of conversation, but in practice it's just a QTE, and not a fun one.Like I said: there's a solid base, but it ends up drowning in an industrial amount of water. There's more to complain about, such as the annoying way the game provides you with ingredients (they're working on this part at least), but I think I've said enough.To wrap things up - some statistics. This is a game with 17k reviews at the time of writing, indicating a very successful, well-known indie game. And yet, the achievements paint a quite rapid dropoff rate. Some 50% of players have completed the first chapter, only 25% completed the third, 11% the fifth (I gave up right before that)... and only 0.9% have beaten chapter 10, the final one. Part of it is probably because a lot of people are drawn in by the unique art style without considering what kind of game it is, but I think a lot of people simply find the game gets very boring very fast. That's what happened to me at least, and I have an inkling I wasn't the only one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a fun, chill little game! The customer requests get a little repetitive (I mean, I had 3 people in one day complaining of a toothache - BRUSH. YOUR. TEETH. AND. GO. TO. THE. DENTIST. PEOPLE!!), but it's still fun. I always love the potion making mechanics in other games, so this is a neat little way of running my own apothecary! _childDocuments_.review: Falls off by midgame. Basically game is completed by that point, but it lies to you asying that you also need lvl 15 of popularity. Exploring the map, perfecting recepies, progressing and getting new tools and getting new interactions with customers are all fun and cool, first 10 hours are a good neat game. But then you realize that your already lvled all the percs, explored all the map, have all the tools, made all the recepies you could ever need and aren't getting any new customers. _childDocuments_.review: I'm surprised this game has so many positive reviews. I lasted about 3 hrs of gameplay. The mechanics of having to grind the herbs and stir the pot quickly becomes tedious, especially once you've discovered all of the nearby spells and are trying to travel further on the map. Spending a lot of ingredients and time to travel only to have the potion fail is a frustrating feeling.I kept playing for a bit to see if they would add a feature that automated the grinding and stirring, but it doesn't look like that happens. I think the game would greatly improve if it recognized doing those slow manual actions is novel in the beginning, but needs to be automated as the player advances.I achieved developing the first crystal, and when I saw the recipe for the second crystal my reaction was "nope, no way," haha. It would take way too much time. If I saw this as more of an idle game where I was multitasking (listening to a podcast while I played, i.e.) and slowly working through the goals, perhaps I wouldn't mind so much?The whirlpools while discovering potions are a cool idea, but rarely seem to help out with travel - they don't go far and usually send me back the way I came... awesome..However, the game does have great aesthetic and graphics, it is a neat idea, and it is satisfying problem solving and achieving a lvl 3 potion. It seems the developers are still actively working on this game, hopefully there will be updates for the better.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed my time with this game. It has a fun, unique art style, I just love the concept of running a potion shop, exploring the potion map to find new types is fun at first, and learning about new mechanics like crystals and void salt early on. That's my main issue with the game: all the evolutions of then game are early on. At first the gameplay is fun because it's a new system, and the fact that the game iterates on it early by giving you new plants for different traversal, things like moon salt that change up your strategy, learning how to effectively use water and whirlpools, new goals by having a bunch of routes to go for new potions as well as the alchemy machine giving more interesting goals than new customers, the shopkeepers asking for more complicated potions to improve their shops. However, you get through a lot of the truly new stuff decently early on, and you start to realize how repetetive a lot of the game is. There's a lot of plants but they barely differ in mechanical use. just different directions. The skill tree has very little depth and is really just linear upgrades in 3 categories. Having a low reputation  makes it so you find more dubious customers, but that really doesn't change the game much. New alchemy machine creations require different combinations of effects, but obtaining each effect is pretty much the same. Haggling is decently fun, but it functions the exact same way as a simple timing minigame every single time. You get into a pattern of waking up, picking your garden, buying as much as you can from shops and selling to customers what you can, seeing if you can make any new alchemy machine progress, going to sleep, and repeating. Picking your garden takes 3 seconds, and the npcs aren't particularly interesting. You start to get a lot of repeating requests down to the reason they need it, and it feels rare to find one you have to think about or that has multiple options. It's frustrating to make a potion that should help, but the customer doesn't see it. For example, I had a customer wanting to burn a place down. Of course what they really wanted was a fire potion, but I had an explosive potion on me that should work just about as well realistically, but they would only accept fire. The game just becomes so monotonous eventually where now I just play for like an hour every few months.TL;DR: It's a cute concept for a game that starts pretty strong, but becomes monotonous very quickly
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: A little interesting but there's nothing really here. At best this is on par with a free flash game. The basic game play loop is fine but that's it. Wake up, throw plants in a pot, sell it, go to sleep. There's a hint of some progression with unlocking more potion effects but doesn't go anywhere.I normally wouldn't leave a review as there's really nothing to comment on, but the devs seem to be a little dodgy with their updates. They know this game isn't that interesting and keep posting how they're going to add all this new content, that one day this game would actually be worth something.This next update will make this game worth it, buy now. We fully released the game, buy now. We about to increase the cost, buy now. Hype hype fomo hypeI have played through this game twice with a long gap in between and have seen no substantial changes. If there's a good discount and you have nothing else to do then maybe give it a go, but don't fall for any of the announcements claiming they're going to add something new. If this changes I'll try to update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: ETA after a year and a half:No meaningful updates since launch. For months and months on end, they kept promising new shiny things while not actually delivering any new content. At 1.0 "release" the game still wasn't actually finished, which can be proven by how many additional (and crucial) features they promised right after the "release"... Or by how many existing features are visibly broken even as of now, with e.g. buttons and UI sections that literally don't do anything, but still made it to "release". This would be tolerable if it was left in this state for a month or two. Not 18.And look, this is not some programming rocket science. It's a cute grindy 2D game with simple mechanics. All the foundations are already there. So how the ♥♥♥♥ do you manage to not finish something this simple for so long, with the absurd amount of cash you already have? Five people should be able to finish off all the promised features in three months. And I'm a dev by trade, I'm not just making this up.At this point I consider this game a scam, a half-baked cash grab that was only "released" because they wanted an additional cash influx after their EA money proved insufficient for finishing production. And see, it worked. They already got incredibly rich off this game. So they don't even have a material reason to actually finish it at this point.Right now I don't expect anything good from this team, and personally, I'll surely never buy anything from them ever again. If you still want to spend your money on Potion Craft, well, I can only say I'm sorry you got successfully lied to.-----Original review:A very pretty and very gripping, but ultimately boring grind. A super nice experience on the surface, but as of 1.0 release, it seriously lacks content.- No plot or story of any kind. NPCs are absurdly dull. Despite the "reputation" system being in place, there's no story-driven decision-making in giving specific kinds of potions to specific people (which was so well done this year in "Strange Horticulture").- No variety. Only two maps are not enough. The sequence of all tasks is exactly the same after ~10h. The "soundtrack" is one single repetitive piece looped over and over (!!!). There's no equipment upgrades or variations. Why can't I switch my "wooden spoon" with some "golden spoon" that would work differently?- No challenge. After ~15h you're rolling in money and ingredients and can do literally whatever you want. The customers with very particular demands are still fun, because they give you fun puzzles to solve (and all of them seem solvable so far, which is a huge plus). But to *get the fun customers to come* you need to grind through hundreds of boring ones. I'd love some "hard mode" that only gives you the most demanding customers and is actually punishing in some interesting way if you don't manage to serve them (e.g. limits your potion-making abilities). Also there's no achievements for those fun challenges, even though they would be perfect for that.I'm happy to wait a year or two to see if this gets any meaningful updates, but for now I can't really recommend it over many better games.

_childDocuments_.review: Started strong with an extremely disappointing follow up. Feels like it should still be in early access.The base idea of adding ingredients to move around the map is fun and carries the game for a while, but you'll keep doing pretty much the same thing for the rest of the game. I was expecting new alchemy equipment but that never shows up and making potions uses the same gear from start to end. The only change you'll see is that new ingredients become available with different paths and the potion effects you're going for will be further away. Sometimes this means more complex paths to get there, most often it just means it takes longer to make the potion.It feels like the first quarter of the game was carefully developed, then the rest was padded out with filler to have sufficient content to call the game finished. Everything outside the potion crafting is very barebones too, which makes the game feel even more unfinished.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game on the surface, I had a good time delving into the atmosphere of the game and the interesting system for discovering new potions.The issue I have with this game is how quickly the alchemy minigame begins to take up the majority of your gameplay time. This would be fine if the minigame was more engaging. Unfortunately you eventually realise it's really just a matter of moving in a certain direction on a map. Putting an ingredient just allows you to move in a certain direction, that's it. There's no sense of combining specific ingredients, they all just move you in a certain direction, so the uniqueness of each ingredient feels a bit lessened. Then you also hit the issue of having to make incredibly convoluted "potions" to reach far away spots on the map. That's where to me it's no longer a game about alchemy and more of a game about moving through tight spaces with clunky controls. That minigame is pretty cool in concept, but it quickly lost its charm. I would have liked less focus on travelling through the map and more focus on using specific ingredients to get certain effects.  There's a lot of things that could have been done with the minigame itself too, like having more than one kind of obstacle, letting you go through certain areas if you have certain kinds of ingredients for instance. Or at least making it easier to reach the more complex potions. Or just less focus on spending a ton of playtime on that minigame and more focus placed on interacting with npcs or building your lab in various ways.I also just have no interest in going for the philosopher's stone. Doing this game of cautiously going around the whole map just to make a specific potion that is a fraction of what you need for one step of the game's completion feels like pointless tedium to add more play time to the game. They got everything right, except their core gameplay. Please understand I'm here to play a game about alchemy, not spend hours slowly moving around on a map. I wanted to love this game but I don't think I would ever go back to it after a few hours of playtime. But hey, at least it was a fun time while the charm lasted. Despite my complaints, I would say it is worth the price since it's such a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to exactly 2 (two) types of people. People like me who sincerely enjoy repeating the same task over and over again, not expecting anything to change, but slowly chipping away at clear, if not slow, forward progression. And people who watched the trailer or gameplay, heard the sound that the mortar & pestle make when used, and felt their brain light up with serotonin.To be absolutely clear, this game can get repetitive very easily, and frustrating at times.Repetitive in that you're continuously putting the same puzzle pieces in different positions and fine-tuning delicate actions all the time, but also in that after a while... The game just runs out of unique dialogue. Granted, this doesn't happen early, but it does happen eventually. Also, the actual final challenge of the game isn't a puzzle, it's resource-management and logistics. Chaos from even the simplest source can ruin the process and grind all progress to a halt, much like what I imagine a person in the potion-making business would say about potion making. But, y'know, less fun.Frustrating, in that you absolutely cannot auto-pilot this game. Each action has to be deliberate and thought through, and if you try to take shortcuts it will just re-balance the price and availability of the ingredients in the shop to make sure you don't get any more of that one ingredient that's really good for that type of potion, or that other one that basically just makes the potion for you.If either of those sound like a horrible time, and not a "Pshaw, I'll get over that" moment, I rescind my recommendation.However, on the topic of things that could be easily patched after I post this review, the slated updates do promise a way to plant and harvest more of specific ingredients, so that might solve a big issue right there. They could also patch in twice the dialogue, seems probable. But these updates have by now taken seemingly almost an entire year to come to fruition. I'm just saying, if you're looking forward to swift updates and relevant, clear and concise (and most importantly public) communication about those updates, Satisfactory is on this very same store, with a different type of optimization challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some engaging elements, it's a fun concept, but it doesn't really seem to go anywhere with that. The worst thing is that as more dialogue was added it seems to have gotten more confusing to new players. I had recommended this game to people in the past, but from the time I recommended it to the time they played it, the game changed in some subtle but significant ways where it asks players to make a leap in logic and that leap is multi-directional so they might end up all over the map and still not find what they where looking for. In some ways that is fun when the game does it well because it helps you explore segments of the map and be adventurous, in others it feels like it's wasting your game resources and real-life time. And when you are reminded of the fact you are playing a game and spending a portion of your life on it and you just want to make it to the fun part... weeell that's not a good thing. On top of that, this game has made a lot of promises and I have seen others mention this as well. Where its been a long time and they keep promoting and collaborating with other games while never really adding those features. I think a lot of people feel wronged by this and it's understandable. So while you can have a bit of fun with this game it is hard to recommend it as it might be frustrating and you might be buying it thinking that you want to see all the flashy new things they say they will add and because it seems as if they are actively working on it. But as it has been years, it's hard to believe in that. And the full game release is barely different than its early access version.

It doesn't even feel like an early access game, so I can't wait to see what they will add in the future! I loved streaming this game, it was super cozy and I had fun roleplaying an alchemist! So thank you for making this charming and lovely game!

_childDocuments_.review: Far too much of a grind. Much of the game's mechanics just aren't synergistic. I've had enough gold in my playthrough since the end of the first month to clear out the inventory of every merchant that comes by -- even the marked-up items -- and yet, despite also having some pretty optimal recipes for each strong-quality effect, using the most efficient ingredients and using an oil base when necessary, I am often bottlenecked by the scarcity of ingredients, so I can't progress the chapter and have to just wait and hope I get lucky enough for the right merchant to drop by next run. I can see how that variability of ingredients could be fun and push you to approach potions creatively, but serving the same requests a dozen times before you can log off the game is such a drag, you just get pissed off when a patron gives you some oddball request, even with substantial gold yield; and when they don't give you that much gold, it feels like the game is insulting you. This game makes me audibly groan, but I've sunk so much time into it, I feel like I have to see it through. And I'm doubly insulted when I sail around the whole water map over and over again to make an ingredient in the alchemical machine, only to see that the "save recipe" button isn't an option. And I ask to myself, "Should I make more than one of this ingredient? No, they would give me that option if I need more than one for the playthrough, right? And I only have so much of each ingredient," only to unlock the next recipe and see that I need to make that previous ingredient again, right after I deleted the recipes for the previous one to make space.The gameplay loop is fun but far too shallow for how much it overstays its welcome. This game does not respect your time.Seven hours later into the game. I figured out I can make multiple recipes for a single effect. I've decided to brute force the special ingredients by buying a whole bunch of magic paper, more than can even fit on the recipe book screen. I just made five albedo and all the necessary recipes for the philosopher's stone...and the game just crashed on me. Just rebooted the game, and all my recipes are gone. Hours of work, down the drain, because I didn't want to go to bed and have to deal with more customers before being allowed to save. I think I'm going to commit Minecraft.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great and I understand that it's still in early access and there's very much a possibility things will be fixed, but there are few issues I have with the game so far. The tutorial was unfortunately lacking. Maybe I missed some information, but I had no idea adding water to the potion would help me not die from hitting the bones during the crafting phase. I learned it from a YouTube video. My other main complaint is the lack of journal/recipe space. I am not able to save very many recipes and instead I have to write them down on my own notebooks. It's a minor thing but still incredibly frustrating. I should be able to save all my potions as I do them in order to keep the game actually running smoothly. When it comes to buying the new set for the basement, it's a bit frustrating try to save up enough to buy it when I have to constantly buy new pages, crystals, and herbs for when I run out. It wouldn't be that big of an issue if I wasn't constantly struggling to make the potions needs for the customers. It's a bit frustrating handling the customers. It's hard to find new potions without possibly wasting a ton of herbs and supplies. I understand you can get more from the garden after a new day, but in order to move on to the next day, you have to help the customers or just flat out deny them and ruin your chances of advancing through the game. Other than that this game is great. It's a fun experience and quickly becomes addicting. I hope to see a few more changes as time goes on. The game is still fully playable with the listed complaints, it's just frustrating at times. I'd definitely highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique Artstyle with cute little animations. One of the very +Points at this Early-Access StageMedievial Tavern Song which fits the Alchemist-Themed Game. Nothing mind-blowing but definitly goes strong with the Atmosphere.No Story. All the costumers telling little Storys but overall it's more an gamplay-driven GameMaking your own Potions with Ingridients is a very fresh and unique Idea and you should give it a try! But after a couple of hours you will notice that it is an Early-Access Game. There needs to be Upgrades for the Shop, more Characterdevelepmont. (Things the Creator already put in their Stagemap).But after fascinating 5 Hours I'm kind of tired.Yes - you should play Potion Craft if you like the Alchemist-Themed Style of the game. I will sure come back when there is more Content to explore. You maybe could wait a couple month for a sale where also put in more content in the game.           : Played 4 Hours        :  None          :  11€ on sale   :  Easy-Peasy (EARLY ACCESS If you like that sort of Review, check out my Profile for more! Recommending every game over 60
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: If you like the game from the beginning then it doesn't really get boring even if you complete most of the objectives concerning crafting - the combined requests, and later requirements for potion effects and ingredients keep things fresh and interesting. If you get bored of selling one group of potions, you can spend two in-game days and completely flip your reputation level to get a new kind of clientele. After a while, when you gather a sizable stash of ingredients, you're able to experiment quite a lot with the most optimal routes to specific effects. Things like a book where you can save recipes to which you can buy pages is a very cool addition too. Developers have shown that they're planning on adding more mechanics to things like the garden which I would say is the most basic (but still cool) element of the game.It's certainly not a game for *everyone* but it's a great game for those for whom it is.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Love:The simplicity of the game to get started but the other options like the recipe book with notes, skill points, tasks to complete, and customizing your potion display are all awesome. With the strategy involved in who you sell to and other possibilities of what's to come, makes me excited to 'tune in' on this game. This is a very relaxing game to me. The animations are not overdone (no worry about fps). Discovering the map with different ingredients is a very interesting idea. For me the game has not crashed or lagged once, again lending to my sense of relaxation.Not as much love:Like others, the music can get a bit monotonous although its fitting for the game experience. Would love to see more variety. I'd like the 'option' of having the a different color scheme to the game; I DO think the current scheme may lend itself to the calming effect it has on me so not totally sure about this. Limited interactions with patrons. I'm not sure if there are more plans for this.I'd love to see an option of a way to trade/share/interact with fellow game players somehow. I think that would be an interesting concept.I've not spent a ton of time with the game yet so I know there is more than what I've experienced, but bottom line is that this game is addicting, relaxing, well thought out, and worth every penny (and more) of what I've spent.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: The game is already as deep, if not deeper than I was hoping. The puzzle of how to get the potion made with minimum and least rare ingredients, along side trying to figure out what the new equipment is for and bartering with customers' requests makes this a game I would recommend. I am, however, eagerly awaiting some of the features that are not fully in as an early access game. The manual is a real contender, I want to hear the lore and figure out some things about the game. I am not sure if you can choose what to plant in the garden at any point, but I'm hoping so!
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Only 1 hour in, but ill be playing more of this game.  Very polished for an early access game, and more content than I expected.  I really like the flexibility of creation that is the main potion crafting mini-game.  The amount of careful and precise mouse movements to get a tier 3 potion!  So exciting when you get it right!  Easily worth $13 bucks.  I am excited to see where this game goes through early access, the "coming soon" sections are tantalizing.  Great job devs, have not seen a uniquely styled game such as this in a while.  Everyone else, buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked fun enough in the trailers, but nothing can really do the gameplay justice.It's oddly satisfying how many unexpected variances there are to making the same potions, the customers don't feel repetitive and even feel like each one has a bit of an adventure to it too.I'm VERY excited to see how this game continues to develop and grow, especially already seeing how the developers care about the feedback they get and are very passionate about their game.This is a definite recommended game, hours can easily fly into this game and it's VERY relaxing too. Not built to pressure the player but rather to ease you into hours of relaxation and brewing.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Very chill game about crafting the strongest potions; aside from customizing funny labels and potion names there's not much of a point to experimenting with once you develop/search online for the most efficient recipe for the tier 3 potion of each effect. That said it's still extremely satisfying to find out the right amount of grinding for each ingredient or using different ingredients evenly so one ingredient doesn't run dry while others pile up. The game is apparently still in early access but I honestly don't know what could be added everything is so polished; haven't even encountered a single bug or glitch. There's already a fully fleshed out "endgame" with the alchemy machine and if you hard-lined the game you could *maybe* finish in 10 hours so its not lacking in content.The game is already well worth the $15 price tag (which has been discounted for the past month as of writing) and if any more gets added the devs will need to up that number because it feels a little unfair. 9/10 easiest recommend of a storefront sim ever
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft seems so simple--almost simplistic--when you first see it. You have a map of alchemical effects and you use the paths provided by ingredients to move your potion bottle to the effect you want. That simple formula is somehow extremely engaging. It has sucked me in and held my attention more than many more complex and dynamic-seeming games. I think the game design craft is the real magic here. It's worth a look.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: i think a lot of determined effort went into this game, and it shows. However, this game is extremely limited in what it offers players. First of all, the core gameplay mechanic of manipulating the herbs to advance around a potion map is very 2 dimensional, in that it very much stops being engaging within a very short time span. The game actively encourages you to not waste plants to explore the map, because you have limited funds and limited plants, so going too far too quickly can lead to customers leaving unsatisfied. Furthermore, once the player gets a hold of the very basic mechanics that are crushing the plants and then adding them to the pot, the game is entirely learned and will not progress. I spent about 68 minutes with this game, and I went from mildly interested in this brewing mechanic to entirely done with it in record time, because it went from "oh thats cool" to "okay now I have done this about 50 times and nothing new is to be learned or mastered about this". Whomever they hired to do the art style for this game is a master artist though, well done on that, the game looks beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review:
Potion Craft is an alchemist simulator where you physically interact with your tools and ingredients to brew potions. You're in full control of the whole shop: invent new recipes, attract customers and experiment to your heart's content. Just remember: the whole town is counting on you. 

Every day customers will come to your store looking for solutions to their problems. You will face consequences depending on what you decide to sell them. Attract guilds, befriend notable figures (or feud with them), gain riches and influence - and one day, you may even decide the fate of the whole town.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

name: YesterMorrow
detailed_description: What is YesterMorrow? YesterMorrow is a single-player time travelling 2D platformer, mixing action sequences with puzzle elements, all wrapped up in an engaging story about our young hero, Yui, who must save her family and to change the fate of a world that has been plunged into endless night. This can only be done by journeying into the past and repairing the mysterious Clocktower controlling the cycle of time. Setting Her world - destroyed. Her family - kidnapped. Join our heroine Yui in a desperate attempt to save everything she loved. Learn how to use Everlight, embark on a journey through four islands (Forest, Desert, Ice and Clockwork island) and use time travel to overcome obstacles and access hidden locations. Free your family from the clutches of Shadows! Find out what really happened to the Sun and whether it can be reversed. Features Learn how to wield Everlight, unlock six special abilities and use them to cleanse your world from Shadows. Explore a vast world of YesterMorrow spanning four different islands (Forest, Desert, Ice, Clockwork). Encounter dozens of creatures and defeat challenging bosses. Use the environment to your advantage and solve puzzles in different ways. Traverse the world in two different timelines. Enjoy the serene calmness of the past and battle your way through the corrupted world of the future. Discover the rich lore as you interact with the world and its inhabitants. And don’t forget to pet all animals! Locate hidden areas and collect power-ups and lore entries. Supported using public funding by Slovak Arts Council

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous pixel-art, but... that's about all i can say about that game. Story starts simple and doesn't really grab attention too much, platforming feels really floaty and not enjoyable, physics on moving blocks and puzzles feels way off, cutscenes are slow and non-skippable... Didn't finish, because puzzle-platforming started to feel like a chore. That's a no from me.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, sir, I would agree to that question. It's a cute platformer made in Slovakia that requires fast reflexes, but offers a fair level design and very tight controls to overcome any challenge... after some training. You play a young girl named Yui that tries to save her village from a terrible fate of endless night. Years after the invasion by the Shadows who now corrupt their world, she finds a way to travel back and forth in time, which might give her a chance to save the future. Platforming, killing enemies, learning special abilities, finding secret rooms, petting cute animals just waiting to be caressed... all the usual stuff, including some really great bosses. Apart from that, there is a lot to see, some puzzles (involving time travel) to solve, people to talk to and did I mention... cute animals to pet. Ultrawidescreen is not supported, a controller recommended. Saving is possible at save points spread throughout the levels. The game feels very polished, but it really lacks cloud saves. Fantastic action platformer with an emphasis on platforming. Run, jump, and roll to save your family (and world).
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: "YesterMorrow" is a decent platformer. It's a tad bit hard to my taste, and some segments are, in my humble opinion, too long to replay in case of a failure, also some mechanics could be more polished (talking to NPCs requires you to stand a few steps away from them, the cutscenes can neither be skipped nor fast-forwarded). This game is a great pick if you're into platformers.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 5/10, poor controls and limited options but a cute and passable experience overall. Very pretty game with a standard but fun plot. Cannot rate it positively as the keyboard controls, which do not seem to be changeable, were horrible to get used to and made the platforming annoying. It may be a better experience with a controller but with the dialogue and cut scenes going by at a snail's pace I don't feel like giving it another chance.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: YesterMorrow is a cute platformer, very simple yet you have to pay attention to the environment if you're going for the 100 %.   Sounstrack is amazing, sceneries are amazing and it has a calming atmosphere overall, except for when there is a boss and the music changes to a hype type of music.The development team is amazing, they streamed the game a few times and it was really nice to see the developing team do a speedrun of a game they created.Oh, and Yester has the CUTEST collectibles ever,: you have to find and pet cats and dogs all over the map
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent platformer. It's lengthy, has great controls, excellent level design, and it's fairly challenging too. It can be frustrating at times but I enjoyed myself and enjoyed it from start to finish. The time travel stuff isn't as interesting as it could have been, though, and the controls can be a bit finicky at times, but it's nothing major. Easy to recommend this one.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Pixel art is great, everything else feels slightly unfinished and early access.-Movement and physics just feel slightly clunky-Dialogue and cutscenes are unskippable, slower than they need to be, and pretty uninteresting.-The music loops very awkwardly and doesn't always feel like it fits the game, the OST is also incredibly short which would explain that a bit. Pretty sure in 1 hour I only heard the same 3 tracks loop.-Certain sound effects are either completely missing or extremely quiet, the whole mix of the game is a bit weird.-Level design feels unecessarily large, filled with mostly nothing or straight paths and basic jumping-Enemy's feel like they are placed very randomly and collision feels strange.-Game direction is completely missing sometimes, no idea where to go or what to do, easy to get lost.I gave it an hour and felt like I had enough. Pretty early on I felt like something was off with the game and after an hour it didn't seem to improve, so I'm gonna say pass on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing platformer with beautiful pixel art. The gameplay is smooth and feels great. My ONLY two complaints of this game is lack of keybind settings (can be fixed with steam overlay) and NOT BEING ABLE TO SKIP THE CUTSCENES OR AT LEAST THE DIALOGUE OF IT! The cutscenes are painfully slow. Past that cutscene complaint, this game is solid.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Actually really nice game. Less combat more puzzle, speed/timing and precision focused with growing difficulty of the levels. I wish there would be some kind of hints/names of the portals or marker on map where you are, because levels are huge and you can get lost pretty easy. There is also no option to "teleport/travel" to location you want, so you have to remember every level. Controls on PC can be frustrating sometimes, there is no option to change the keybindings, also I got troubles to throw the bomb up, w+arrow up, wasnt throwing up very often. Do not listen to bad reviews with only 1-1,5 hours playtime. The game starts be more challenging after 2-3 hours.Overall nice game, would play it again for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Great puzzle platformer with beautiful pixelart style, good story (simple but good)It would be good if cutscenes could be skipped. After playing demo not that long ago it was somehow irritating.Its hard to find spots where its possible to talk with npcs.While I played there were some bugs, probably will be better with some updates (stuck at worm boss where it froze after being defeated, next 4 times one of traps didn't worked, only after 5 tries it worked as supposed to)
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game had potential to be a decent platformer however there's 2 things that breaks this game:- Plenty of bugs. Leading to softlocks because of how the save system works, because the whole game is one persistent world more or less. So if you get to a savepoint and do something and die then anything prior to said death gets saved regardless and does not reset which can lead to plenty of softlocks.The first boss can lead to a softlock, I saw it slowly happen because you have 2 ways to kill it, but one of said options just bugged out and went away. But I quickly understood what would happen if it continued further so I just quickly killed it with the last option available. The second one which ended my run is when you get to the hub island which leads to everywhere else. The moment you save on said island and then teleport and happen to quit afterwards leads to a permanent softlock because the teleport items you use get stuck on the other side which you can no longer collect/visit because the save takes you back to the main hub.This could have been avoided by just having said items be a permanent addition, but I guess they tried to be fancy where it didn't matter and only made things worse.It's also running on some unstable Unity version and being abandonware more or less doesn't help either. - Floaty platforming mechanics, from rubberbanding to snapshotting due to said floaty mechanics. This does not belong in a game like this.It's like this game had zero QA which really shows on the 2nd boss and everything else I just mentioned.Avoid!
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game is ok but not great. I'm on the borderline of a thumbs up or down, but the complaints feel significant and there's no shortage of Metroidvanias that do better.Pros:* Generally does all the Metroidvania stuff competently. Controls are ok, and while the powers aren't super unique they at least have their own spin on it.* Generally good platforming challenges.* The optional challenge rooms are clearly labeled as such.* It uses the dual-worlds gimmick well.* Not much backtracking (so far). Generally always clear where you should go next.Neutral:* Pacing is a bit slow, but that's because it's going for a more cinematic feel.* The story's nothing special, but they did put some effort into the setting and included a bunch of lore bits.Cons:* Combat... is weird? Your attacks don't kill most enemies, they just force dark spirits out of possessed enemies. The freed animals are just as aggressive and don't even change their attack pattern, and the freed spirit is itself sometimes quite dangerous (mostly because your first attack is awkward to hit them with). So there's not much point to attacking. And in the Past (aka half the game) the enemies aren't even possessed. Enemy design isn't very great anyways.* In some places it has a bit of a problem with things that can hurt you looking similar to the scenery. Also, the dark barriers that block your path in many places are only partly destroyed when you attack them once; they leave a little bit at the top and bottom which still hurts unless you attack them again. It's hard to see, unintuitive, and even when you remember it just slows things down.* As far as I can tell, there's no proper map. The "map pieces" just give you lore dumps. No map in a Metroidvania is a big problem, and kills any desire for completionism. At many times I had vague if any idea where I was relative to places I'd been before, though it was still clear where to go to advance. In any case it's very linear and your path only occasionally loops back on itself.

The sountrack gets really annoying after it repeats itself all the time. Especially when you are totally mad finding the way. The so called map is totally wrong, it is just a picture and you basically have no clue where to go to meet the goal.Overall not great not terrible. 5/10I would not recommed this game.

name: Hohokum
detailed_description: Take on the role of a curious flying kite-like being and travel to colorful, curious worlds waiting to be discovered. Interact with characters and environments to uncover secrets or simply roam at your own pace and be amused at the surprises that unfold. While there are goals and activities, at its heart, Hohokum is a playground - a place to wander about and get lost in. - An Expansive and Playful Universe with loads of eclectic characters and toys to interact with, like a gigantic playground. - Stylized Gameplay Encounters – From diving with sea creatures to soaring with kites, each world has custom goals, activities, interactions and secrets to uncover -- no two places look the same! - Captivating Original Artwork – Brought to life from the imaginative artist Richard Hogg, the world of Hohokum is surreal, youthful, and full of color and fun. - Entrancing Original Soundtrack – Hohokum features music from various talented artists in collaboration with Ghostly International Records.
