_childDocuments_.review: I can say without much hesitation that this is easily my favorite of the party packs. All of the games are some of Jackbox's best, and visually the game really pops.Can't speak much to how it works for streaming since I only play with groups of friends, but I'd recommend this to literally anyone interested. For more specifics on the games included:Quiplash is always solid, and this iteration is no exception. Being able to add custom sets of prompts adds so much potential, and the base prompts are solid as ever. Thriplash is a really nice addition too, and the claymation of the background looks cool as hell, if a bit trippy. The Devils and the Details is a really charming game that has players working together while at the same time trying to do things to raise their own personal score. Personally I think it's a lot more fun with less players, since communication is key, and with a full group it's hard to coordinate, but it's pretty fun either way.Champ'd up is easily my favorite. The concept of creating characters to pit against each other is so charming and has lead to a ton of chaotic rounds. Being able to tag in previous drawings during the second round adds an extra layer of strategy to it as well.Talking Points is a really cool concept done extremely well. You have to give a presentation on a topic you choose out of one's players submitted, but the slides how images are controlled by another player. Whether or not you like this game is pretty dependent on how good you are at improvising, but irregardless it gets a lot of laughs. And Blather Round, which is a really solid charades-like game where you have to describe something via a jumble of words the game provides you. My only issue with this is that the game crashes 90% of the time when I try to play it. This only happens with this game, and I'm not sure if it's an issue in general, or just on my end. Irregardless, it's fun enough that it's been worth the risk.Overall, this pack is very worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Best Jackbox pack in years, and arguably the best ever!Most packs have one or two great games, one or two okay games, and one or two duds. #6 was extremely weak, with most games being merely okay and several being pretty bad - I maintain that #6 is the single weakest release of the entire series. #5 was also a little lacking, though its best games were pretty great, which balanced out the other not-so-great ones.As such, Jackbox 7 had a lot riding on it. It needed to be a return to form in order to keep the faith of the fans. Man, did it ever deliver. Three out of five games are all-time Jackbox top ten contenders, the fourth is really good with the right crowd, and the fifth isn't great but certainly nowhere near as bad as Word Spud, Zeeple Dome, or Joke Boat. Here's my breakdown:Blather 'Round: One of those games that seems so simple you can't imagine how it could be any good before you try it, but then once you get into it your whole group doesn't want to stop playing! Because of its guessing-game nature it's the only game in the pack limited to six players instead of eight.Talking Points: This is SUCH a weird game, but if you're playing with the right crowd it can be my-stomach-hurts-and-I-can't-breathe hilarious. It's most similar to Patently Stupid and has a similar setup, with fill-in-the-blank lecture prompts instead of problems. Encourages and rewards good team play, which is nice. I recommend this one with a smaller group, though it plays up to eight.Quiplash 3: It's more Quiplash, which is good or bad news depending on how much you like Quiplash. I love it, so it's great news for me! As usual, it plays best with a big crowd, preferably the full contingent of eight. One warning: the claymation visuals can be overwhelming for people with visual sensitivities, but you can turn it off in the options.Champ'd Up: This pack's obligatory drawing game, and it's a classic. A lot of groups will think this is the best game in the pack (for my money it's Blather 'Round, but your mileage may vary). Weirdly similar to Bracketeering in structure, with a mix of guided and blind prompts generating weird drawings of gladiators who then do battle for bizarre titles. Really great fun, even if you suck at drawing, and the drawing tools are unusually advanced. Again, recommended for a big crowd - best with six-plus, though it's still fun with four.The Devils and the Details: The dud of this pack isn't really a dud at all, it's just not my style of game. It's a mostly-cooperative crisis management game like Bomb Inc, Space Team, and Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes. I've been playing over Discord, and I suspect this one will work better in person, and I'd recommend a smaller group - with the full eight it would just be a nightmare to play with everyone talking over each other. Doesn't give any room for creativity, either - the comedy all comes from the game's writers. It's perfectly fine, but easily the weakest in the set.I honestly think this might be the best overall Jackbox party pack ever. I will concede that some other packs have better games, but they also have some rubbish ones pulling the average down. The games in #7 range from fine to excellent, giving it the best average. At the very least, it's the best pack since the excellent duo #3 and #4. if you've enjoyed Jackbox in the past but were disappointed by packs #5 or #6, grab this one. It's amazing!

_childDocuments_.review: (At the time of writing this, we have managed to squeeze out 21 hours of playtime)I dont often write reviews, but when I do (on any site, really), it's because I have enough to voice/share about it that I feel like I'm doing a disservice if I wasn't being transparent about it.  So, grab a seat (if you didn't bring your own), and allow me to indulge you about my thoughts on this particular Jackbox Party Pack.I'm actually in love with every game on this pack, which is saying something, because this breaks the mold and trend that the other packs share.  I could name at least one "unpopular" game on every other Jackbox Party Pack from 1-6 where I, as the host, would wish in the deep recesses of my consciousness that the gaming group would steer us away from playing.  JPP7, in many of our opinions, seems to an even distribution of requests and interests piqued.  I will say that some of our non-artistic friends may initially lean away from ,  they quickly learn that, like in  of JPP3, artistic skill does not translate to points or fun.  They realized it's more about the real estate of your imagination, creativity, and sense of humor, rather than who has drawing experience or the best tools at hand.  JPP7 is the example of a product that was sculpted with (1) the lessons the developers have learned throughout the years of creating all these packs, and (2) the voices of their customers -- nay, fans and content creators -- when it came to mitigating the impact that Chaotic Evil forces would try to impose onto streamed and publicized games.(click the spoilers if you want the TL;DR descriptions of each game)The five games are:  * Quiplash 3 * The Devils and the Details * Champ'd Up * Talking Points * Blather 'Round SYNOPSES, REVIEWS, AND RATINGS OF EACH GAMESame format as Quiplash and Quiplash2, with an exception to their Final Rounds, Round 3.   (If you had been under a rock and have no idea what Quiplash is, then I'll simply describe it as a freestyle Cards Against Humanity where the Card Czar is more of a Democracy where points are awarded based on how many people voted for their favorite answer between a contention of two).The final round in this particular pack is called "Thriplash", where players will be provided with three prompt lines (of up to 45 characters max, per line) where they could design an answer card that will be revealed one line at a time from top to bottom.  The claymation artwork on this game is not only present on the game itself, but also animated on the devices that are logged into Jackbox.tv.  There are endless waves of commentary in our games where people feel "satisfied" or "intrigued" by background and foreground art.  The timing between transitions is a major improvement, as well -- Quiplash3's rhythm between scene wipes, moving from prompt to prompt, and presenting the Thriplash makes downtime feel like a thing of the past.If  had ruined your friendships, guilds, or gaming groups, then get them back together with .  For those who have no idea what this  game or are new to Jackbox Party Packs:   is a very straightforward team-building game with a minor element of competition present within the scoreboard and "Selfish Tasks."  Your contestants become a demonic family unit that has to deal with earthly chores, else they be banished back to the underworld by Satan.  Imagine if , escape rooms, and browser-based mini-games all had a baby born of polygamy -- that's basically this game.  You will eventually learn that using  will net you all higher scores, individually and as a team.  The game is very beginner-friendly and easy to pick up, but it will be up to your team as a whole to learn how to master (if you want to optimize scores, of course), and this is what gives it a very high replayable factor.  I imagine that even after you achieve all "A" ratings on their extensive list of episodes, the game will naturally maintain its charm to those who enjoy cooperative play.I gotta say, the first thing most people mention during their first playthrough of this is the /soundtrack.  Beautiful jobs, Devs! The best way to describe this game to another Jackbox player is to ask them to imagine that a , where, in this new version, players have more control on what images and mottos are assembled together, and instead of an Asian-inspired dojo-theme, it has an MMA/boxing scene.For those who tire in my comparisons to games they've never played before: this game will prompt players to illustrate/draw a character that would be pitted against another player's character, with the catch that in each pairing, there will be one person who has no idea what the original prompt was that inspired their opponent.  Imagine freestyle Pictionary and democratic Cards Against Humanity as the parents of this game.The drawing interface and tools on this game are AMAZING improvements to the drawing interfaces from any of the Jackbox Party Packs, including Drawful2.  The outline/pen tool is anchored as a separate layer than the highlighter/marker tool, where the latter is the bottom layer.  What that means is that when you want to fill/color in your drawing, the marker will  override or hide your beautiful work, and thus you don't need to worry as much as before when it came to perspective illustration.  Do your outline, color the character in with the marker, and done!  (And yes, an Undo button is provided!)So this is a unique game of its own, but it's practically like  mixed with giving a Powerpoint Presentation.  The only people who won't be able to participate effectively are text-only players, as this game requires a presenter who can improvise to an audience (there is no stand-in host like in  or .  I think this game is a great exercise for becoming better at public speaking, especially if you're playing with supportive and constructive friends.  Out of the two times we've played this with very different groups, at least one person is laughing to the point of nearly losing their breath.  There is also a Free Play mode to go beyond the boundaries of the vanilla game.This word association game is the odd one out, being that it requires 2-6 players; kind of a bummer that it can't hold up to 8 people.  However, do not underestimate the entertainment value that fans of the classic board game  and trivia-heads would get out of this.  With a limited set of clues and very restricted communication (in fact, the password holder shouldn't talk or text at all), players try to get the rest of the contestants to guess their "Person, Place, or Thing."  Like in , the password holder may start using anything the guessers submitted to help guide them towards the more accurate answers.  Our group is in love with this game, and it is one of the most requested games in our game nights; the pacing of the game is pretty fast, with satisfying cadences of

_childDocuments_.review: Stuck at home? Hate seeing your friends on a 480p call in Zoom? Need a game to satisfy all those inside jokes your friends make? Jackbox Party Pack 7 has got you covered. An amazing sequel which holds up to the name of the Jackbox series. It is one of the best packs which I can for absolute sure recommend to anyone. The Jackbox Party Pack 7 has five amazing games which do their part in making the whole crowd laugh.Let's start with the game we all know and love!Quiplash 3. You might think there isn't anything new we can add to the Quiplash series, but let me just say, that's what we think when Fibbage 3 came out in JPP4. Quiplash 3 follows the same as Quiplash and Quiplash 2, write a funny or witty answer to a prompt and players vote on their favourite answer. The answer with the most votes win. So what's different? The final round! Usually in Quiplash 2, we would either fill out a comic, acronym or etc. In Quiplash 3, you instead follow 'Thriplash', you fill out three separate answers to a prompt. A prompt may be 'Three Things I Should Not Have Brought To School', the answers appear in order, the first, second and third. This is what makes Quiplash 3 the best among the Quiplash series, you could write a funny punchline at the third option or try writing something dirty and suggestive in the three options you get. It is definitely the game that made my friends abandon Quiplash 2 for this version.The Devils & the Details. What can I say about this game? It's innovative, cooperative and fun. You play as a family of devils trying to do mundane human tasks. Each task gives points to the family score. You must achieve a certain amount of family score to finish the day BUT WAIT, THERE'S MORE, there are individual scores for each member. You can decide to do a family task earning points for yourself and the family OR try doing selfish tasks which only award points to you and not the family score. Usually these tasks are available a few times, other family members have to stop you if they want to ensure you do not get a high individual score. Every task is a simple one, just follow the instructions, other tasks are more complicated and require multiple players to complete. I do not wish to spoil much of this game but definitely check it out if you're buying the pack. My friends and I had a lot of fun, as we chaotically shout and yell at each other trying to complete tasks. Unfortunately if you are stuck in lockdown, unable to physically play with your friends, I would NOT recommend this game, as it is much more fun if you're playing next to each other, rather than online. It just isn't the same.Champ'd Up. An amazing drawing game that can get you laughing at either the ridiculous references your friends make or how terrible your drawing skills are. Champ'd Up is what I would call one of the better drawing games (besides Patently Stupid). I always hated the drawing games unless it was wacky or fun. For example, TeeKO was quite mundane and could get boring after a few games but with Champ'd Up, you never know what category you are going to get. Simply put, players must draw a 'superhero' according to the category they are given, which can range from 'Hero of Cyberpunk' to 'Hero of [Player] Dreams' and it is quite amazing to see how much your friends suck at drawing. Then after players draw their first hero, they are prompted to draw an 'underdog' to compete against another player's hero, except they can only see the drawing but not the category. Because of this, I feel Champ'd Up is really strong in the party pack, it has fun and wacky ideas with lots of replayability, always ensuring we get a glimpse of terrible drawings and sometimes (honestly my friends are terrible at drawing) you get drawings that should just be framed at an art museum. Played this multiple times and honestly we always came back for a second session, this rarely happens as we usually want to play TMP2 or Quiplash 3. STAY AWAY IF YOU ARE NOT GOING TO DRAW ANYTHING, honestly the amount of times I've seen people not draw anything is ridiculous, the fun part is drawing whatever! Be creative and try to play along! P.S. This has such an amazing soundtrack, go listen to it.Talking Points. The nightmare of every introvert, presenting without any preparation or script! Talking Points is one of the most unique and interesting games, you get a topic to speak about (usually a prompt filled out by another player), then when it is your turn to speak, you will be paired up with another player, that player will choose the slides and text for you while you try your best to present to the other players on your topic. Points are awarded based on how many upvotes players give to your speech, players may give upvotes and downvotes throughout the whole speech. The player in charge of your slides will get a cut of the points earned. It is a good game to get people in a party-ish mood, I've played this several times with my flatmates and they have always seem to get a kick out of it when we present something outlandish and ridiculous, sometimes even offensive! The fun is just watching your friends try to justify their extremely controversial topic in a speech. The drawbacks obviously is that you have to talk! Any friends that are not going to talk or give any effort, tell them to stay away from this game.Blather Round. The ridiculous guessing game that justifies the existence of your friends who know too much about movies/books/films/geography/etc. Blather Round is a game where you have to give clues to other players in the forms of sentences (formed by the game itself, you pick them) of the answer you are given, it can range from a story to a place to a thing. There are not limits to how many guesses people can make, so guess away! The player can also pick other player's guesses as part of their sentences to give more clues! You are usually given three options to pick from and if you don't know any of the three options, you can refresh and can three new options. There is an easy option to pick from but you obtain less points. There are two rounds and they play out the same. The game definitely has strong suits, with your friends trying to outguess each other while furiously typing away. There are many drawbacks however, there is a strong sense around Western culture, so any players that are currently looking into this from a different culture needs to have strong knowledge in Western movies and people, there are some options are not oriented based on culture but it still is a factor to take into account. Additionally, what is disappointing is sometimes if you refresh, you might not even know all six of the answers and are forced to pick an easy option, it's not a big deal but it is something you should note when you are playing this game. Other than that, this is also a solid game in the party pack, my friends had tons of fun with Blather Round, even going for second sessions similar to Talking Points and Champ'd Up. It can be a hit or miss depending on your group of friends but do take my word that all five games are worth a try at least ONCE.All five games are solid, meaning they are fun in each of their own way and are not dull. It's not like the other packs, where one game falls short compared to the rest. I strongly recommend all five games on this pack over JPP6 but just SLIGHTLY. Consider JPP6 and read my review on both before making a choice. My recommendation currently: JPP7JPP6JPP5JPP3 (Only if you are considering NOT getting 7)JPP4JPP2JPP1

_childDocuments_.review: My friends and I have been playing packs 3-6 all the time for our game nights and we tried this pack out on release. In my personal opinion, like with a lot of Jackbox games, these games are more fun if you don't worry so much about the scores. Quiplash 3 - Quiplash has always been a classic and having another one is even better! Our games felt a little more smoother and faster-paced than previous ones, and the change to round 3 really pushes our creativity more than just making up acronyms or tv show names.Devils and the Details - Oooo boy, this game got us very rowdy. The idea of working together as a team in addition to boosting a personal score really tests who your friends are. It's pretty chaotic if you're playing this online with friends since screaming over each other in call to help with tasks, but that's just another fun element that encourages coordination.Champ'd Up - My artist friends thrived here. Plenty of drawing to do and it's funny to see how players interpret prompts in different ways for their champs.Talking Points - Our Patently Stupid games have prepared us for this moment. Obviously the outcome of this game depends on how your friends can handle impromptu presentations (hello, stage fright!) and try to make them as serious or as hilarious as they want.Blather 'Round - I was personally skeptical about a game that seemed like another Heads Up, Taboo, etc. However, jumping right into it made us realize how crazy this game can get. Some of my friends had a little trouble with this game as English is a second language, but overall this game is a simple and quick way to get the Jackbox Party rolling. If only it could have more than 6 players.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best packs in the series. Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a must have for groups of friends, whether it be in physical parties or streamed online. Quiplash, arguably the most iconic game in the series, makes a come back in this entry. The final round Thriplash isn't as strong as the other final rounds of the previous 2, but it is still an insanely good time. The Devils and the Details is a chaotic game where players must cooperate with each other but can betray each other to rank #1 devil. While this may not be everyone's cup of tea it is a well made game. Champ'd Up is another hilarious drawing game in which characters must draw opponents to battle each in funny categories. It's a great time no matter the drawing skills of the group. Talking Points is an improv game in which players must give presentations on topics without knowing what's on the slide. It's great to see everyone panicking trying to make connections. Another A+ game in the series. Finally, Blather 'Round is a word guessing game similar to Pictionary but with words. While it is the weakest game in the pack there is still fun to be had with it. Overall Jackbox Party Pack 7 is one of the best packs in the series, a great choice for a party game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down the best Jackbox Party pack yet!Quick rundown of the games, not how to play, just what I liked/disliked about them.Talking Points: One of my new favourites, as long as everyone is prepared to laugh along and not take it too seriously, this game is awesome, one of my new favourites. Love the intro theme too. 9/10Quiplash 3: Quiplash is basically a staple of the party packs at this point. Nothing too special or new, but a solid game non the less. I love the art style for this new one, I do wish that the final round could switch more often like it did with quiplash 2, but that's just my opinion. Always a good one for new party pack players. 7/10Blather Round: This one might be the hardest of the new games to figure out how to play, but its a pretty good game once you get the hang of it. Only problem is if you choose even a slightly hard character/story/object then it can take a while to get it or not get at all. It's probably my least played game, but still a good one 7/10Champ/d Up: A lovely combination of TKO and Drawful, two of my favourite games. With most of these drawing games it can get pretty lengthy but the guessing element keeps the game entertaining, and the fact that you can bring back old fighters is the cherry on top of this game. 8.5/10Overall this is one of the best if not the best party pack. It doesn't have too many hard to learn games. I'm gonna play this a lot with friends and family. My favourite game has to be a tie between Talking Points and The Devils and the Details. Definitly recommend this game to anyone looking to get a Jackbox Party Pack. Remember this is all just my opinion :)Overall the pack is a 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: Worth it for Quiplash 3 alone, but Quiplash 3 definitely isn't perfect and the other games are still worth a look atQuiplash 3: Amazing. Thriplash has soured so many games because someone will sweep the leaderboard with "♥♥♥♥ piss ♥♥♥", or will sweep because nobody voted for "♥♥♥♥ piss ♥♥♥", and if nobody put The Three Dreaded Words then everyone will say "my Thriplash sucked and I lose off of this." No one likes Thriplash, no one likes the profanity-free version, and I hate Smitty's smug voice.The Devil and the Details: Pass. No one quite knows how this plays and nobody was ever a fan. Game is a mess. Champ'd Up: Decent. Given how specific the premises are, rarely did someone's "response" drawing (where you can't see the prompt) ever beat the original drawing. People had fun drawing stupid things to dumb titles, and every once in a while you'd get a drawing that really went above and beyond, but like... not really? TKO is better in my opinion, but I like this one.Talking Points: Pass? Completely dependent on how creative your friend's group is, because nothing is lamer than someone saying someone stuttering their way through, or just staying dead quiet. Definitely a game we had to "warm up" to before playing, and after warming up we'd just play another game. Really depends on if you have friends that can do a lot with a little and can talk for minutes on end, and like... most people don't think that's very fun, and if you do then not everyone in the party does too. Also, the scoring system is completely arbitrary, each presentation taking several minutes can mean this game can drag on with a full party of 8, and the real winner is whoever gets the most laughs.Blather 'Round: Decent. Basically 20 questions, but as a group. I thought it was lame, but some of my friends legitimately enjoy it and want to play it every time we open Jackbox. _childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend or not recommend this game in essence. The game to me is more of the same of the last party packs. People say this is the more definitive party pack that has come out in a long time and I would disagree. This game has games that are failures just as much as other Jackbox Party games. Peoples tastes will change and will have different things they hold dear and other things they despise. For me Devil and the Details and Talking Points was the worst of the pack.I will go through the games and tell you what I thought of each of them. Nothing much to be said with this, Its just more of Quiplash and that's essentially it. However, they tried to make the prompts more robust which I thought only made it harder to come up with funny things, I had to truly stretch my creative mind to make the game funny. And the Final round of making 3 answers to the prompt was very lackluster for a final round. At this point, they need to just make Quiplash a bigger stand a lone game and stop trying to use it to lure people in.Good game, but its a co-op experience just like Bomb Corp (Jackbox 2) but more chaotic. However, the same problem arises with both where after you play it a couple times, there is no need to ever play it again. The replay value is very low. I hear a lot of people love this one. I find this one absolutely a miss for me. This is essentially the most drunk game you'll find on a Jackbox game. I personally think that you have to have a highly dull or tame sense of humor to find this fun. It's absurd, but it's jackbox absurd so it's filled with PG to PG-13 internet meme humor which is not funny to blurt out to me. I would even say this is one of the worse jackbox games in all the packs down there with Earwax and I know I'm in the minority there. This is essentially a more robust version of TkO'd. I think its almost safe to say that this is just an objectively better game than TKO'd. One of the few jackbox games that made me want to run it back after playing it once. One of the better drawing games in all of Jackbox. This was a game that was more along the lines of a true party game. It is essentially password, taboo, monikers, timesup! etc. But instead of you describing who the Person, Item, Thing is that you chose. You have to use premade prompts to describe what or who it is. Which can result in a lot of frustration in friends or a lot of cheering in getting the guess correct. In conclusion the game is just another jackbox game. There will be games friends don't like and other games friends will love. I can tell they put more love into the artstyle and aesthetics of the whole game. But the mechanics of the games are more or less the same thing as all Jackbox games. Prompt reading, fill in the blank, and drawing with 3 rounds for each game. But because of this, I have to give a thumbs down for me personally because I already have a way to play Quiplash without this game and Blather Rounds is already a game that has 100's of different names (that everyone has access too). So owning this game and paying the $26-$30 price tag is not worth it only to essentially play Champ'd Up.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely underrated.So when my friends wanted me to play this game I thought it's just another one of those thousands survival hams. Oh boy, how wrong I was.It starts off normally making you fight small creatures and lower human enemies. You craft basic tools and cook meat. All equipment has different Tier so you go through the different stages like wood, stone, iron, steel and so on. Difference in this game is that you not only invest points into your character attributes when you level up but also into "feats". Meaning you have to learn and plan what you are going to craft and the most important point: You can't learn everything on your own. Solo play must be extremely hard. I experienced the game on my dedicated server with 2 friends and we could split the feats so everyone was specialized in one feats "tree".After you start to explore while improving gear and building your base the game suddenly takes a turn.There are rare NPC encounters with actual great voice acting that tell you about the lore. The map barrier is lore based and makes it feel more natural. The world in general is not generated but static and is extremely well designed. The soundtrack in certain areas contributes to a deep immersion.

_childDocuments_.review: While my review for this game as a whole is going to be negative, I'm saying that I would recommend it at the end of the day because it's a popular party game set, and despite my thoughts on how it's designed, it does have a lot of general appeal.With that in mind though, I just don't really care for a lot of Jackbox games. I'm an artist and I like doing the drawing ones, but besides from that a lot of the games, especially the ones that have some type of competitive goal, don't really feel like they're well-balanced to give people a fair chance to win, especially if they didn't do well early on.This isn't as big of a deal in the games with a more standardized system of who did the best, but especially in the more subjective games like Talking Points, Quiplash and Champ'd Up (as well as several from other packs that I won't be talking about because they aren't part of this specific product), it feels like the act of actually *winning* the game is based on so many factors entirely outside your control that it may as well be luck-based. For example, the two big factors in the Talking Points system are the engagement and the final awards at the end. The engagement system doesn't really work well because it relies entirely on people remembering to engage on their device, and if someone forgets to do that, it can tank your score regardless of how well you did. The awards system isn't much better since there's no guarantee that people will use it to actually reward people who did well- most of the time in my experience they just give it a funny name and hand it to a person for le epic troll. Because of this, the actual main part of the game has very little affect on the final results, because the systems used to measure how well you did are both inconsistent and subjective, based on factors that you as a player cannot control, making victory feel hollow and defeat feel unfair.For this game specifically, I'd recommend just having it so that the players rank all the speeches from best to worst in the end instead. That way the factors of who wins feel like they actually relate to the speeches themselves, rather than just the trophies in the end and who spammed the clicker when.Champd Up is also an issue for some similar reasons. How it works is that one person draws a character who is the "Champion of X" and another person draws what they think could beat that character in a fight without knowing the title. While there is an underdog bonus to compensate the second person, usually the first person ends up winning because the second person's drawing doesn't fit the theme- something they couldn't do anything about because they didn't know what it was. So, the first round just feels entirely based on whether or not the second person got lucky and drew something that fit the theme AND worked well against the first drawing. The second round feels a bit more interesting, with a secret second category thats revealed after the first voting where you can swap your character out for another, but usually the end result just winds up being the same as the first vote and that person wins out. Because of the way these are designed, it feels like most of the actual decision of who wins is based mostly on getting lucky with prompt compatibility, and it ends with the same issues as Talking Points.Quiplash is a bit better in this regard, because it doesn't feel like it's necessarily luck based- but the entire game's premise is based on "who's the most funny" where comedy is basically inherently subjective, so there's not really any way to do well there either and the end result also feels out of your hands.I haven't really played a lot of Blather Round, so I'll skip that and move onto Devil in the Details. Devil in the Details is a very controversial addition to Jackbox- people either love it or they hate it, and at least for me personally I hate it. The entire premise is really interesting and seems fun, with the players being a cast of demons living mortal life on the surface while trying to fulfill a quota of goals set by their overlords down below- it seems like a really fun idea for a high-stakes team cooperation game, but then you get to the individual competition part. Here, they advertise that family members can take on selfish tasks in order to get a lot of individual points while slightly hurting the team score, and whoever has the highest individual score wins the individual division. This seems fine and dandy, though it makes the game a lot more toxic, but then you realize that a lot of the selfish tasks require you to spend a lot of time doing them, and that stopping someone from doing a selfish task takes much less time by comparison- so if someone just so happens to get to you doing a selfish task early on, you fail it and get behind on points. Since stopping someone from doing a selfish task takes so little time, and it's also openly advertised that you're doing one to everyone else in the game, you have a very high chance of being entirely out of the running if you get stopped from doing selfish tasks- not helped by the fact that stopping someone from doing a selfish task gets you points, so I'm just kind of left wondering why anyone would go for selfish tasks in the first place, and makes me personally feel betrayed by the game encouraging you to do them on several occasions. It's genuinely frustrating and I don't like it.Overall, the games in Jackbox feel very poorly designed in ways that punish people for trying to win them, and that issue can deter anyone who has any interest in the competitive element, because the game makes it not really *feel* like a competitive game with a level of skill involved despite its insistence on making the games competitive. If you play these party games with winning in mind, you are not going to have fun, and unless you're someone who genuinely believes they can put any care about the end result of the competition at the door, you're going to feel burnt out by it very quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Solid pack with only one total dud, worth it for sure and also a good starting pack with a lot of variety.Quiplash 3: Take Quiplash 2, remove the absolute mess that was The Last Lash, replace it with a much more entertaining final round, and make using safety quips actual sort of viable. Great game and a good start to the pack.The Devils and the Details: The dud. It's basically just Among Us tasks for 15 minutes with the tiniest bit of social deduction (which just boils down to "check the main screen to see if someone is doing a selfish task occasionally"). Try it once just to see the jokes, then move on.Champ'd Up: Drawing game with a cool twist of "first person gets the prompt, second person only gets the name and drawing of what the other person made". Not super dependent on drawing skills and has given a lot of good laughs to me and my friends.Talking Points: Give a presentation based on a user generated prompt. I really like it, although it does require a bit of willingness to speak to play, really open to creativity and low stress if your group enjoys it though.Blather 'Round: This one is... odd. I really like it, but you have to be wiling to think outside the box and go with some really oddball guesses and clues in order to go places. Still worth at least a few plays unless you or your group hate it.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick overview over every game before I give my overall take on the pack itself:Quiplash 3 is, in my opinion, the best Quiplash that has been released as of July 2024. The biggest problem with the first two games (including the original and XL as one) is the final round: both games reveal all jokes at once, which hinders the presentation and makes the jokes less funny. This edition fixes that problem, and since Quiplash is a proven formula and popular party game already, its inclusion makes the pack a safe buy if you do not already have a pack with a Quiplash installment.Champ'd Up is among the best drawing games that Jackbox has released. It is somewhat similar to Tee K.O. in design, but is slightly different in concept, designing "champions" of certain categories rather than designing T-shirts. I won't go much further into it, but as someone that is not good at drawing whatsoever, I have had TONS of fun with this one and it may be my personal favorite Jackbox game period.Devils and the Details is an interesting game with a much different approach than anything Jackbox has done in the past, perhaps aside from Push the Button. I have heard everything from very positive to very negative opinions on the game. Personally, I'm somewhere in the middle, but have enjoyed playing it. It is definitely worth a few tries.Talking Points is among the best presentation games in the Jackbox series. While many are not comfortable with standing up in front of people, if you have a group of friends that know each other well or are willing to have an audience, this game will give some of the best and funniest memories in the whole series.Blather 'Round is very solid. It may take some time to understand for some players, but I find the game to be very underappreciated. Most of the other games in this party pack are very high-energy (which makes sense, because it is called a "party pack"). While that is not a criticism of those games, Blather 'Round is not a game that takes a lot of energy or effort and instead has a lot more of a general appeal. It is similar to Charades or Heads Up! in a sense, and although it isn't a "wild party" vibe, it is a very welcome addition in this pack.Possibly the best pack purely by value. None of these games feel like misses to me, and chances are, most people will REALLY like at least 3 out of the 5 games in this pack: it has a Quiplash adaptation, potentially the best of two kinds of games (drawing in Champ'd Up and presentation with Talking Points), an interesting idea in Devils and the Details, and a nice wind-down game in Blather 'Round.If you are a series veteran, I strongly recommend adding this to your collection solely for Talking Points and Champ'd Up. If you are new to the series, I think that this is one of the best packs to begin with (that and Party Pack 3, which is also critically acclaimed).

_childDocuments_.review: Hilarious installment that is worth it for just one game alone. I really like the Jackbox series. Just as Knowledge is Power, it is a party game with lots of fun, silly animations and a high replay value. Unlike Knowledge is Power however, Jackbox is a little bit more versatile. Instead of being bound to your PlayStation and your smartphone, you can now use your phone or your pc/laptop to connect to jackbox.tv, and play. The connection and overall stability of the game is also a lot better.There are many Party Packs for the Jackbox games. Each pack offers a set of minigames that you can complete with your company of friends or family. Most of them revolve around choosing the funniest answer, predict who might have answered a certain question in a certain way, or, in general, just who made the most ridiculous drawing. Throughout the mini games, players score points, the player with the most points wins. Easy and simple. Of all the Jackbox Party Packs, the seventh installment came as a very pleasant surprise. However, this is only because of one masterpiece of a minigame. To start off, you got Quiplash, a game in which you describe a word or situation with three words. These are then displayed beneath each other and two players fight for the most lolz and get the points.After this, you got Blather ‘Round, a pop culture guessing game. You just guess answers and try to guess which player might be right. Simple, a little boring but fun enough. Another very disappoint game is Talking Points. You get a series of pictures and need to comment on it. A little lazy in my opinion. Then you got The Devils and the Details, a game in which you need to do chores as fast as possible to earn points. Personally, I thought this one was a little chaotic, too complicated and overall, not that much fun.When reading this, one could question why I would even play or recommend this game, but then came Champ’d Up, the best game in this whole pack. In this game, you draw your own unique hero, name it, and let it battle against another player. You win the fight by receives the most upvotes from other players. This process repeats until a winner remains. The animations and art style of The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is colorful, jolly and silly. My biggest compliment here, is that all animations and slides within the games, are really fast, keeping the pace of the game at a very healthy levels.The silly sounds, the jolly music in the background, enhances the experience and lets you have a good time with the game. With the right company, I can get aches in my stomach from laughing and I think that The Jackbox Party Packs are the best party games out there by far.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 was great, but only because of one game. Champ’d Up was hilarious and I would startup this Pack any time to play it again.Definitely recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: (Edited after playing Blather 'Round)For context, I've played most (but not all) games from packs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 as well as a little Drawful 2 and Fibbage XL with friends and family. I don't have all of those games on my Steam account, though. Anyways, time to review this pack. Keep in mind that this is all just my opinion.Champ'd Up - 9/10I've never been a super big fan of T.K.O. I think I'm in the minority there, though. Champ'd Up, however, in my opinion, is a big improvement (since my packs 4 and 6 reviews, I've played pack 10 and I honestly still like Champ'd Up more than both T.K.O. installations). It's creative and has well-thought-out mechanics. My main complaints with T.K.O. are that its pacing is a bit poor and it falls apart if you metagame. Champ'd Up not only solves both of those problems, but it adds new mechanics and ideas. Swapping out champions is smart, and the whole underdog idea is clever and funny. This might honestly take the cake for my favorite drawing game.Blather 'Round - 8/10Solid game. It's a very simple concept but it's well executed. There's a lot of fun strategy here, like giving the speaker words to use as hints instead of them being guesses, if that makes sense. It's a very simple and easy to learn game from my experience, but the more I play the more I enjoy it. Some prompts can be very difficult depending on your group and who knows about them, which weighs down this game a bit, but I still think it's a fun and engaging game.Devils and the Details- 6/10I think my opinion of this game has changed a lot from when I first played to now. At first, I really liked it, but the more I play, the more my opinion of it sours. I think the mechanics are cool and nice ideas in theory, but in practice, most of them are useless. Selfish tasks, for example, are really creative, but almost never worth it. They're too easy to cancel, and it's basically free points for the player who stops you. Of course, this is just from my experience, so take that with a grain of salt. The team tasks often don't give enough points to justify them, too, from my experience. It's alright as a game, and works well in both small and big groups, but the more I play, the more I feel like most of the cool and interesting mechanics don't mean much in practice.Quiplash 3 - 8/10I can't speak to the quality of any Quiplash games before 2, but I think this is an improvement for sure. Quiplash 2's main weakness is the final round. It isn't bad, per se, but it feels like it could be better in my opinion. Quiplash 3's addition of Thriplash as the final round is good and well executed, keeping the humor of earlier rounds and ending the game well. As for the visual changes, I personally like the animation style. It's nice, and the addition of motion sickness mode is cool, too. It still has the problems that all Quiplash games have in that it requires a lot of wit and humor, so if you aren't playing with funny people, it's really hard to be humorous. It takes a lot of effort to be funny here, at times. When it's funny, it's hilarious, though, but some people (including myself) struggle with coming up with funny things on the spot. It's a Jackbox classic, and the 3rd installation doesn't disapoint.Talking Points - 8/10This game is simple, but well-executed. It's funny and has a lot of room for creativity. It encourages spontaneity and doesn't require as much wit as Quiplash while still being hilarious. It's a great game and very well made. It is definitely an improvement over Patently Stupid. It's better than Junktopia, too, despite Junktopia being in pack 9. However, the voting system is what holds it back for me. In groups where no one metagames, it works fine, but if you're playing strategically, then it sort of falls apart. That's a minor complaint, of course, and most groups will do just fine with this. Overall, it's a nice game, though.Again, keep in mind that this is just my opinion and if you disagree, that's perfectly fine. Everyone has a right to enjoy or not enjoy certain games. Hopefully this review is helpful.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is the laugh-inducing lifeline your gatherings have been waiting for. It's a virtual circus of comedy, an assortment of mini-games that'll make your game nights unforgettable with side-splitting humor."Quiplash 3" is the game where your quick wit takes the stage. You'll craft the funniest responses to quirky prompts, and your friends will judge your comedic prowess. It's like stand-up comedy where the audience is the star, and it's a barrel of laughs."The Devils and the Details" puts your group in the shoes of a suburban family of devils. You'll be juggling chores and trying to maintain a low-key demon lifestyle, all while dealing with the absurdity of everyday life. It's like The Sims on a caffeine high, and the hilarity is endless."Champ'd Up" is the game of absurd artistry. You'll create larger-than-life champions and pit them against each other in epic battles. It's like a comic book convention where your imagination runs wild, and the results will have you giggling uncontrollably."Talking Points" is all about making up speeches on the spot, and you'll be given the most bizarre slides to accompany your oratory. It's like a PowerPoint presentation gone hilariously wrong, and you'll be amazed at your friends' public speaking skills—or lack thereof."Blather 'Round" is the ultimate guessing game where you'll be using limited words to describe elaborate phrases. It's like charades for wordsmiths, and you'll find out just how bizarre your explanations can get.As with previous packs, all you need is a smartphone or tablet to join the fun, making it inclusive for everyone. It's the ultimate level playing field where everyone can be a stand-up comedian, a suburban demon, an artist, an impromptu speaker, and a word wizard.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 will reveal just how creative and zany your friends can be, which can be both entertaining and a bit unnerving. You'll question your friendships, laugh till it hurts, and wonder if you've stumbled upon a group of comedic geniuses.So, if you're ready for a night of rapid-fire humor, domestic demon chaos, artistic battles, spontaneous speeches, and language riddles, The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is your ticket to comedic euphoria. Gather your crew, embrace the absurd, and get ready for an unforgettable evening of pure digital hilarity.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: The games in The Jackbox Party Pack 7 are really good, and I highly recommend picking this up as your first Jackbox Party Pack.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a great pack of party games, and I have thoughts with each game. is my favorite game in this entire pack. A presentation game where you have to present impromptu, while another player assigns you text and image slides. Usually I don't vibe well with presenting in public, but I oddly find myself having fun presenting in this game. Especially considering how really in this game points don't really matter, what matters in this game is making the most insane, funny, and sometimes absurd presentations. Though I will say, it does bug me that this game does have a scoring system, and at the end you are asked to give out awards, which could heavily affect a player's score (such as if one player made an outstanding presentation, but never received any awards). There's also the Free Play mode, and I'm not sure if this was entirely done as an afterthought, none of the charm present in the original game is here, especially jarring without any music at all. Despite this, I really like Talking Points, and it is a go-to game if you getting Pack 7. is also a good time as well. It has taken me months to get warmed to this game, and as of now I do prefer this over my classic-favorite Quiplash 2. The art style, visual presentation, the final round Thrip-Lash where you get to put out three separate responses. Heck, most of the time we played this game, we never really listed three items and used it to add suspense to each response. I'd say Thrip-Lash is a better final round than whatever Quiplash 2 pulled out, but I feel that XL had a better final round overall. While Quiplash 3 is the same game as the other two before, I think it stands out just enough to be a great game to play. is a surprise to behold. You and up to five other players play a game of charades, only that you have to enter fill-in-the-blank statements and everyone has to guess what that prompt is. People say this is the weakest entry (more on that later), but I like Blather 'Round actually. The fun is that each guess will always have a text-to-speech voice replying, and what the presenter types out can be funny as heck. For instance, we had several users (me included) spamming the word "bread" to another player, tho in all fairness, it was supposedly to get things moving along as we were playing a modded Blather 'Round and wanted to get the custom prompts. Then there's the fact that there were instances where I immediately typed the answer in just seconds in and it just made for a very enjoyable experience. Besides that tho, you really need a group of people willing to comb their way into guessing each topic as quick as possible. Because if they aren't guessing well or the presenter creates vague responses, no one will be able to have fun. But I do like Blather 'Round. is a fun concept for a Jackbox game. You do the basic household tasks to get your devilish family working in a human society, but you can also unleash devilish tasks that if taken, you earn your own selfish points but also raise a bar that if raised too much will cause a family emergency. There's also challenge tasks that also give a lot of points, tho it's necessary to nab them as quickly as possible in order not to miss out on scoring points. This game is enjoyable to play, but I prefer (for the most part) to play Jackbox games on a browser, and I had issues completing tasks as a result because my browser cannot easily drag or rotate something that a phone could easily do. For instance, anything related to swiping or rotating is hands down the more annoying thing to do, but it gets used to once you figure out what to do. I do enjoy chaos too, with everyone talking over each other, tho it can be difficult for many and I'm sure that it is impossible to do teamwork tasks if everyone is unable to hear each other. Especially if they're muted. This game is really fun, I love the sitcom aspect and that theme song (nobody skips the intro please), but I think it's a game that asks more for what it's doing. But it's good for what it's worth.Honestly the game lineup here has been fantastic and outstanding...except for one. I'm not listing it for mental health sake, but just so you know, if I'm feeling a bit stressed or pressured to make something funny that fits a prompt and as a way to counter someone else, I'm not having fun, and I would love to not play a game that does this to me ever again. I can enjoy the Quiplash series because I know what I'm typing, but not with this one game. So besides this minor hiccup, I'd say this Pack is outstanding and if you want to host a Jackbox game night, please consider buying The Jackbox Party Pack 7.

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the best of the Party Packs. If not, then it's one of the top three. You got:Quiplash 3: The game where you and your friends write funny things. It's okay if you draw it badly, as long as that and the name are appealing. Blather Round: A game of text prompt "charades" where you are limited by the clues given and by what the audience gives you. Having the text-to-speech read the frantic guesses is the best parts. After a round, people start typing in dirty words. Talking Points - just an insane business presentation where someone picks the images and you read or pick out the words. My friends and I would play this more but it reminds us of our actual day jobs too much. Devil's in the Details - one of those games where you work together to achieve a common goal. Since you can't write about dirty stuff it wasn't that appealing to me or my friends. Does contain Devils, which we all liked, however.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 has to be one of the greatest and one of the most fun party packs in my opinion. This is one of the BEST Jackbox Party Packs in the series and the best for beginners. This party pack has 5 new exciting games such as a Threequel from a previous Party Pack, a drawing game, a presentation game, etc. This has some of the best games in the whole series.Quiplash 3: An amazing game returns! Quiplash 2 was a pretty average sequel to the original Quiplash. However, I always feel like the sequel had lacked something special about it despite it always being fun to play with friends. Quiplash 3 had made Quiplash so much more fun and so unique about it such as the clay like style and the new 3rd round that had made it more enjoyable compared to all 8 answers being in one round that made it feel not enjoyable. This new round had made it feel more fun and in general a great game. Definitely the best Quiplash and one of the games that you should play with your friends as you can make a bunch of funny prompts to laugh at with everyone else.The Devils And The Details: A very unique concept for a game but I have some mixed feelings on this game. I would say this would have A LOT of potential as a game and could've been an amazing game. I LOVE the characters and the theme of this game entirely and it is so creative with all the tasks. However, the way the game worked was very complicated at first and requires a big amount of teamwork in order to get points. This could be a fun game but some of the mechanics are very annoying and some tasks can be very tedious. Champ'd Up: This game is AMAZING. Everything about this game is pure S-tier and it is such a fun game to play with your friends. If your into art then this is one of the most creative games for you to play. I do think Tee-K.O is still a more fun option but this game comes in a very CLOSE second. Playing this with my friends was a huge blast and I have a lot of fun laughing with my friends over the creations we make.Talking Points: This has to be one of the most funniest games to ever exist in the Jackbox series. The point of this game is to present to other people including an assistant who chooses images to present in front of your friends. This game is such a funny and wild experience to play and it is honestly one of my favorite games to play as you can get a lot of laughs out of it. This is recommended to anyone who is either into improv or just willing to display a funny presentation and make your friends laugh. Talking Points: Freeplay is a very messy mode for this game and seems really rushed and unfinished but its so funny how you can just add whatever you want. In general though, this game is one of the best games for this party pack.Blather 'Round: The final game of this party pack. This game is basically charades. I do think this is a very underrated game and I think its decent. Although the prompts you get is a bit hard to guess and describing the thing itself has limitations, it can be fun to play if you are just chilling with your friends as it isn't too crazy of a game. I think one of the silly things about this game is the text to speech and how it can completely interrupts the host from talking. If you just want to play something that is calm and fun, then this game is for you.To conclude, this party pack has to be an excellent pack to play with your friends and laugh together. Although there are some nitpicks I do have on some games, its still a blast and is a great experience for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have the money, and love Jackbox, please buy this pack, behind (unpopular) Party Pack 8, this is the one I always find myself and my friends going to.QUIPLASH 3: As somebody who always hates it when party packs reuses old games, I LOVE QUIPLASH 3, the art style is 100% my favorite of the current 3 quiplashes.  But besides the artwork, usually jackbox will reuse there old games and change everything that made them fun to make them look like a "new game".  What I like about this is that it doesn't change to much, while the changes that were made make the game more fun, the thriplash addition was defo necessary and causes for more laughs!THE DEVILS AND THE DETAILS: By far my favorite game in this pack! This game has "episodes" you can play, and there are a ton, making the replayable of this game insane, where you can play this more than once and have a totally different experience.   Besides that, the sheer chaos it causes makes this something me and my friends go back to all the time.TALKING POINTS:  So much fun! The amount of BS that you have to make up ON THE SPOT can cause for so many laughs and actually makes me involved with what is going on.  I will say if you want to play jackbox with random strangers, for this pack this would be the game you should play.  The laughs come from what you say on the spot, in Quiplash and Champ'd up, its usually only fun with friends making jokes at each otherCHAMP'D UP: I'm never a fan of jackbox drawing games, I wont lie, and this is no exception.  For somebody who usually hates drawing games, this ranks 3rd out of all of them for me (behind Tee K.O and Drawful Animate) I have two major issues with this game which makes it not my favorite in this pack unlike other people.  1. I think this game is a little bit to much like Tee K.O, where you name and make character that "battles" against another where whoever gets the most votes wins, and personally I think Tee K.O. does this better.  2.  I hate how in the second round you can switch fighters in the middle of it after you can tell you are losing.  I've had multiple experiences where I am winning in the second round then a fighter gets switched out for something like a pe**s and it wins automatically even though its not on theme.  I think this game is overrated, HOWEVER, like I said I am not a drawing game person, so I would say when you buy this pack this is a game you should try, however, I don't think this is a game worth spending the $30 on solely to play that game alone.BLATHER ROUND:  Everybody universally agrees that this is the worst game in the pack, and its not even that bad which should tell you how good this pack is.  I think its a fun game, and a good concept, it makes up for the fact there is no trivia game in this pack for us trivia lovers like myself.  I just think when you play Blather Round, don't go in expecting as many laughs as you would get from the previous 4, sometimes the way words are formed can cause some laughs, however its just simply not as funny as the other 4, however I would say behind the Devil and the Details this is the 2nd most challenging game to win.CONCLUSION: I think this is a great pack, the only people I would say not to buy this are people who play jackbox for solely the trivia because you will get none of that here.  This is the pack you would 100% get the most laughs from with friends, even strangers, if you have the money, and want to buy a pack, I would recommend buying this oneRANKING OF GAMES:1. Devil and the Details2. Quiplash 33. Talking Points4. Champ'd Up5. Blather Round

_childDocuments_.review: A Party Pack full of Jackbox Goodness.Jackbox Party Pack 7 is the 7th entry in the Jackbox Party Pack series and currently at the time of this review is the one I've used the most during game sessions. Featuring 5 unique party games this easily has to be one of the best packs you could get as your first pack and with it being so recent you have a ton of polish and production valve given within each game that's it's just a enjoyable experience.The first game is Quiplash 3. The third entry in the very popular Quiplash series, where quirky prompts get responded by whatever you think is funny, crude, or both! This game has become the best game to warm up especially with a group who aren't familiar with Jackbox as it's simple to pick up and generally very fun. The major difference between the previous entry mainly boils down to new prompts, a very distinct claymation art style, and a new final round. Overall another great Quiplash entry.Next up is Devils and the Details, which is sort of a hybrid mix of both management and Wario Ware. Here all the players are in a family of Devils and have to complete human tasks together while at the same time competing to get the most points with the help of devilish tasks. I feel this game is best with larger groups as you have have a handful of people working together while someone else is secretly breaking the rules and then someone notices and calls them out. It's quite chaotic and might be confusing at first but the payoff is spectaular. Huge props to the sitcom theming, theme song, and character designs.Up next is the obligatory drawing game Champ'd Up! This game is quite similar to other head 2 head drawing games but with brawl-esque theme, having you design champions for a category. The catch is that your challengers get no context for your prompt and simply have to go off of their competitor, making the standoff being quite wild and hilarious. I personally love this game as it has caused the creation of a few designs I would later go and recycle for my own art. Overall, a fantastic drawing game and another game I often bring up to play.Now here comes Talking Points. This game is the embodiment of fears of presenting a presentation with absolutely no prep. As this game has you make a presentation with a randomly choosen prompt while a partner creates the slides from random images and it's up to you to make a convincing enough presentation. It's honestly a pretty good concept only if everyone's on the same page and willing to actually present cause I could see a lot of shy people not being too fond of this game. At least the trophy mechanic is quite entertaining.Lastly, there's Blather Round. While it's a simple guessing game, the use of making jargon/broken english sentences to make the people guess what your prompt is along with a TTS voice is just very fun. This game does have a lower player limit than the others I would agree on that as even with 4 players it's still a lot of fun trying to guess through the broken nonsense of words. Also love the theming and narrator for this game.Overall, Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a phenomenal bundle of games with each game having some sort of merit and appeal. I mean if Talking Points in my opinion is your worst of the of the bunch you've made a damn well Party Pack. Easily some of my favorites are in this pack and there's Quiplash 3 so it's very good starting place for those looking to get into the Party Pack Series.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: For those of you not familiar with Jackbox, it's a fantastic set of games (that's streamable!) that are played using your phone or any browser capable device to drive what are essentially Gameshows. Of all the Jackbox Packs, the 7th is one of the strongest ones:- Quiplash and its sequels are always fun. The carnivalesque tune and swirling claymation vortex will haunt your dreams. It's competitive response where players face off 1v1 to give the best (read: worst) response to a prompt. Ending on a Thriplash (a 3-response prompt) makes for a fun an discrete ending.- Champ'd up is the drawing version of Superflight where you draw the Champion of X. Here we discovered that the Champion of THE PURGE is clearly "A GIRLSCOUT DEATH CULT"- Talking Points is an improv game where you hold a Ted Talk... and someone else drives your slides. Best served with alcohol, nothing like breaking your fear of public speaking but giving a completely improvised nonsense talk to your friends.- Blather Round is verbal charades meets Mad Libs. You're given a "thing" and you have to describe it prompt with fill in the blanks and pool of words. Phrases like "He is the Soft Big not Nice", "So much burning!" are used to describe pop culture and everyday objects. Gotta use your thinkin' meats to put yourself in the presenters brain, and try to see their angle as well as assess the clues.I'd say a a little pricey for $30 but I've more than gotten my moneys worth. 7 is definitely worth full price. No brainer at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Jackbox games are great to get a few friends on and have a laugh. You will need some voice communication, however, to enjoy this to its fullestChamp'd upThe drawing game of the pack, pitting your drawings against each other. relatively easy to pick up and play. When I play this with friends, we tend to gravitate towards this one.The Devils and the DetailsDespite being a blast of a game, it outright requires communication between players in order to play. if you want to play online with strangers i would advise against this game, however with a group of people sat together or over a voice call it can workBlather 'rounda more relaxed game in the pack, it is generally overlooked being the weakest game in the pack, due mostly to all the other games being overly good. _childDocuments_.review: Planes: Fire & Rescue (also known as Planes 2) is a 2014 American 3D computer-animated comedy-adventure film produced by Disneytoon Studios and released by Walt Disney Pictures.[4] It is a sequel to the 2013 film Planes, a spin-off of Pixar's Cars franchise. Dane Cook, Stacy Keach, Brad Garrett, Teri Hatcher, Danny Mann, and Cedric the Entertainer reprised their roles of the voices of Dusty Crophopper, Skipper, Chug, Dottie, Sparky, and Leadbottom, respectively. New cast members included Hal Holbrook, Julie Bowen, Ed Harris, Regina King, Wes Studi, Patrick Warburton, and Dale Dye. In this film, Dusty Crophopper is assigned to become a wildland firefighting plane, after he learns that his engine's gearbox is damaged.Planes: Fire & Rescue premiered at the El Capitan Theatre in Los Angeles on July 15, 2014 and was theatrically released on July 18, 2014 in the Disney Digital 3D and RealD 3D formats. The film received mixed reviews from critics, with many calling it an improvement over the predecesssor, and grossed $147 million worldwide on a $50 million budget.[2]Since winning the Wings Around the Globe race, Dusty Crophopper had a successful career as a racer. Unfortunately, his engine's gearbox becomes damaged because Dusty routinely operates the engine beyond its design limits. With that particular model of gearbox now out of production and none available anywhere, Dusty's mechanic Dottie fits a warning light to his control panel to ensure that he doesn't damage his gearbox any further.No longer able to race and faced with the possibility of returning to his old job as a crop-duster, Dusty goes on a defiant flight and tests his limits. In doing so, Dusty exceeds his limits and makes a forced landing at Propwash Junction airport, causing a fire. The residents put out the fire with some difficulty, but the accident leads government inspector Ryker to condemn the airport for inadequate firefighting personnel. Aggrieved at his carelessness, Dusty offers to undergo training to be certified as a firefighter to meet the necessary regulations to reopen the airport.To that end, Dusty travels to Piston Peak National Park, where he meets a fire and rescue crew under the command of a helicopter named Blade Ranger. The leader of an efficient unit, Blade is initially unimpressed by the small newcomer and Dusty's training proves to be a difficult challenge.Maru, the team's mechanic, replaces Dusty's original undercarriage with two pontoons fitted with retractable undercarriage wheels for his new role as a single engine air tanker firefighter. During training, Dusty learns that Blade was formerly an actor who played a police helicopter on the TV series CHoPs. Later, Dusty is devastated by a call from his friends at Propwash Junction, telling him that all attempts at finding a replacement gearbox have failed, and his racing career is officially over.Lightning in a thunderstorm over a forest near Piston Peak starts several spot fires which unite into a serious forest fire. The team fights it and seems to have extinguished it; but later, during the grand reopening of the park's lodge, visiting VIPs fly too low and create air eddies that blow embers about. This creates a larger fire, forcing the need to evacuate the lodge.A depressed Dusty's education in the midst of the large fire falters, much to Blade's frustration. Things come to a head when Dusty makes a forced landing in a river while trying to reload his tanks against orders and is swept through the rapids with Blade trying to extract him. Eventually, the pair make it to land, and Dusty confesses his physical disability. Blade advises Dusty not to give up. They shelter in an abandoned mine while the fire passes. The situation is complicated because Blade was gravely burned from protecting Dusty in the fire and is grounded for repairs. While Blade is recovering, Dusty learns from Maru that Blade's co-star Nick Lopez from CHoPs was killed during a stunt gone wrong on set that Blade was helpless to stop. Afterwards, he decided to become a firefighter to save lives for real.When the wildfire threatens the lodge, the national park's superintendent Cad Spinner selfishly diverts the entire water supply to the roof sprinklers to prevent the lodge from burning. This prevents the firefighters from making fire retardant for their firefighting duties. With only their pre-existing tank loads, the firefighters manage to help the evacuees escape the fire.Dusty is alerted that two elderly campers named Harvey and Winnie that he met earlier are trapped on a burning bridge deep in the fire zone. He races to the scene and pushes his engine to the maximum to climb vertically up a waterfall to refill his water tanks to drop water to save the campers, as the only other surface water nearby is the river in Augerin Canyon, too shallow, twisty, and rocky for him to scoop from. Simultaneously, Blade shows up and assists Harvey and Winnie by hooking up Winnie, preventing her from falling. Dusty successfully drops water and extinguishes the bridge fire, allowing the campers to escape just before the bridge collapses; but his gearbox fails completely, his engine stalls, and he crashes.Unconscious, Dusty is airlifted back to base where he wakes up five days later to find that park ranger Jammer is now in charge of the park, to much delight. Maru tells him that not only has his structure been fully repaired but he has built a superior, custom-refurbished gearbox for his engine that allows Dusty full performance once again. Impressed at Dusty's skill and heroism, Blade certifies him as a firefighter. Propwash Junction is reopened with Dusty assuming his duty as a firefighter, celebrated with an aerial show with his new colleagues from Piston Peak.During the mid-credits scene, the audience learns Cad Spinner has been demoted and reassigned to park ranger duty in Death Valley National Park.

_childDocuments_.review: We've played all of the Jackbox games and this one always is a big hit. Playing as an audience member isn't fun, I accept that feature is just for streaming and playing it in huge groups.Quiplash is fun, it's a good standbyBlather Round is excellent, one of our favorite games. Partially because the narrator reads out everything you write and we're immature buffoons at heart. Regardless, it's one we always make time to play. The only problem is it's limited to 6 people and it should really allow for 8-10. You'll quickly run out spots when playing with other couples.Champ'd Up is good but Tee-KO from another Jackbox game is more fun. We haven't tried it since the latest update -- I think they added some new features. There wasn't really enough to do and making terrible T-shirts is more entertaining in our group*Update* Devils in the Details - this one is very fun, it is tricky to play virtually because you have to talk over each other. Very chaotic and fun. The minigames feel much like the super simple Among Us style puzzles with required interaction between players. It's a weird game and we had a great time shouting over each other. Talking Points - we had a good time with this one but it has some flaws. When the presenting helper gets the right images and the presenter finds something to run with it is very fun. It's frustrating when the helper gets stuck with images that the presenter can't use -- nonsense images can definitely add to it, but the helper doesn't get enough controls for finding photos for slides.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a pretty great pack and also came out at a time when pretty much everyone was stuck in a bad year but this pack definitely redeemed a lot of things and helped with the stay-at-home atmosphere of the time. This is also the pack I recommend people to start off with to get a feel for Jackbox along with Party Pack 3.Quiplash 3 of course expands Quiplash even further and is always a great time. Definitely one of my go-tos although I would've preferred more variety with the Final Round but it's still a solid addition to the series.Blather Round is another one of my go-tos even though I definitely have gotten too good at it. XD Would definitely be down for more Blather Round content for that reason. It's basically charades but in the form of constructing sentences for people to guess a variety of things. Definitely a quick one to do with people.Champ'd Up is one of my favorite drawing games and in many respects, I do actually prefer it over Tee K.O. which I do find a bit too involved at times but this a sharply-paced version of it where drawings face other to see what fits the prompt best and it is a lot of fun.The Devils and the Details is a co-op game in the vein of games like Overcooked matching that level of chaos but with a humorous family of devils theme that satirizes sitcoms. And players can also be selfish to try to get more points.Talking Points is a great presentation game that does make it mandatory for people to either be in the same room to vocally present or on VC. It's definitely a gem that makes fun of TED talks and is best with the right group of people. I have been in a couple games of it where only the streamer presents for everyone but imo, that misses the point entirely and is not nearly as fun. I'd rather just vote for people on their own merits when they are presenting themselves instead.So overall, this whole pack is a winner and honestly a great one to start with if you are new to Jackbox.

_childDocuments_.review: This game happened to be the very first Jackbox pack I've ever played in a Discord VC, and my gosh, I haven't laughed so hard in ages. It took me a while before I actually bought it myself, and I don't regret it one bit. All five games are a blast to play in a group, whether it's on the couch or through a voice call. Quiplash 3 is simple yet hilarious, The Devils and the Details is charmingly stressful, Champ'd Up is incredibly competitive, Talking Points is stupidly endearing, and Blather Round is just plain fun. I cannot understate it enough, these games are stupid amounts of fun for everyone, especially with the family friendly filter that I use very often with close mutuals and of course, my family. If you haven't played Jackbox before, I HIGHLY recommend starting with this one. It's fun, chaotic, and will have your laughing 'till your lungs fall out. Be on the lookout if this game is on sale through Jackbox's official site, these packs go on sale almost all the time.
