_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This game is perfect. Do yourself a favor and buy it. This is one of the most beautiful games I have ever played. The story is well written with soft world building that really allows you to make the story yourself. There are elements of Nordic mythology, particularly Finnish mythology. The puzzles can really stump you but they're not impossible. The developers put a lot of time into the artwork of the game. It is incredible at times. I completed the game and didn't encounter a single bug. This game deserves to be played, the developers have truly made something special here. I only have one complaint: there really is no support for colorblindness. I know that the colors in this game would really be hard to have accessibility for colorblindness/color deficiency, so it really isn't that big of a deal. I had a really tough time with chapter 7 because of this. Overall, I recommend this game to everyone, no matter what your preferred genre of games are.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very cute game but it has a lot of flaws as well.I feel like a lot of people, me included, are starved for animal related games, so we tend to look past a lot of issues. This game is one of them. It's a neat game for sure, the animations are nice, the world looks beautiful and you follow a sort of wholesome story throughout the game while solving puzzles and collecting spirits. But the game also feels very lifeless a lot of the time, with a huge map that may look beautiful but is vastly empty. Parts of the game often suffer from confusing design making it hard to tell where you have to go next, I often got stuck thinking I broke the game or missed something, just to look up on youtube where to go and learned that the way forward was just hidden behind some badly lit path that was hard to see. The game is sadly also very clunky with the fox controlling a bit awkward, especially when running/jumping around platforms. For the price the game is asking, it honestly just lacks too much content. 90% of the time is spent walking around a massive empty map, solving a few puzzles here and there. Often you're even slowed down by the game itself, forcing you to slow walk. You can beat the game in 2-4 hours and in the end you didn't really do all that much. If you can see past that, it's still a beautiful game with a cute story. I enjoyed it, but it really only is something for animal fans and you also should get this on sale probably.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to play this game mostly because the art work and aesthetics caught my eye and I have to say I was thoroughly surprised by how much I have enjoyed it. I fell in love with my foxy almost instantly and even shed a tear on at least one occasion as a result of me creating an emotional bond with (yet another) video game character. I have to say, I still don't fully understand the full meaning behind the game or the ending of it. I felt like it ended far too abruptly with little in the way of explanation however there is a strong chance that I may have missed or misread some of the background and lore from the etchings found throughout the game. Nether-the-less, an absolutely gorgeous game with challenges that were not 'too' challenging. Would consider going back and playing another play-through at some point in the future. Developer should be proud of what they have achieved. Certainly recommend giving this game a go.

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game for anyone who is seeking an incredibly casual gaming experience. Overall, it's a calm, story-driven, exploration game but I warn you, if you need some excitement in your gameplay - turn back now. This game feels like a slog to get through by the end of it. The controls need tightening, the story (a key feature of games like this) feels barely there, the puzzles aren't very challenging, the music didn't seem to align with the events happening within the game, invisible walls are present everywhere and don't allow for any creative freedom, it still uses save points instead of allowing you to freely save, and the biggest issue is there is no reason to feel compelled by this little fox, his spiritual friend, or the journey that they are embarking on. There was never any tension or adversaries which didn't give me to feel any compassion toward him or the spirits he was helping along the way. There are some pluses for the visuals and the music score itself (even if the timing with moments in the game weren't great) was beautiful. I could easily see me jamming out to this soundtrack. But overall, I struggled on if I'd recommend this game or not. It had some redeeming qualities and was enjoyable for a bit, but over time it became stale and a slog to get through. However, there are people who enjoy slow-paced games like this - so if you did, kudos to you. And if you have loved ones who you're introducing to gaming or little ones that you want to hand them a controller but not give them anything difficult/scary to play, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: How many words does a good story need? In some cases not a single word at all. Spirit of the North is a fantastic example of purely visual storytelling. And it's a really beautiful story. I don't want to spoiler too much, so lets say: You're a fox on a big adventure. You explore the nature, ancient ruins and you solve puzzles. The puzzles aren't too hard so they should never be in the way of progressing the story.And the art is just beautiful. The graphics, the soundtrack ... it's a very fairytale like experience. Great to relax and enjoy a few hours in a fantastic world of nordic mythology. There is no combat, no danger of dying and no time limit. If you just want to take your time to explore a beautiful story (and you like foxes) check this game out.

_childDocuments_.review: 'Spirit of the North' is one of those delightful little games that pops up every now and then. It doesn't need any narration to tell the story. It's all done with the music and scenery.About the music, it fits the setting so well. Many times it took me back to feeling like a kid again, watching some fantasy movie on a winter night and feeling a little bit of that magic touching you.The scenery is also fantastic. I've been cursing myself in the last few hours of gameplay for not taking more screenshots. Many locations are simply beautiful.The gameplay itself lilts along as lightfooted as the fox is, introducing new mechanics in a simple way that never confuses or leaves you stuck, but can still provoke some puzzle solving intuition at parts. Highly recommend playing with a gamepad.Overall a fine 9/10. Only marked down for some awkwardness in the menus setting game resolution and the fact I managed to softlock the game in such an easy way in chapter 5 (hint, once you've gotten the spirit form ability, do NOT go through that door again).

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game.  The sense of freedom that the fox gives one running through the open spaces is simply liberating.  I wanted to explore every nook and cranny the environment could offer.You play as a fox, accompanied by a spirit guide (or wisp), wandering a beautiful landscape.  Progress through the eight chapters by interacting with the environment, opening locked or blocked gates or getting past walls by solving minor puzzles or using the fox’s magical abilities.The goal is to find and stop the source of the disease that has destroyed the long-dead human civilisation that once flourished there, their ruined buildings still infested by choking red vegetation and spores. On his journey, the fox can also seek out and find 28 shaman skeletons scattered throughout the chapters to set their spirits free (not essential to finish the game). Chapters and even parts of chapters can be replayed from the menu, which makes it easier to go back and find any missed shamans or their staffs.It is a relaxing game.  Explore.  Discover.  Reflect.  No hurry, no shooting, no killing.  Great, relaxing soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game because it looked beautiful, and it doesn't disappoint in that department. It's good for "getting away" and doing some exploring, which is particularly nice given the situation in the world right now. The music is relaxing and there are some details that are endearing: like the fox curling up when you pause. As others have mentioned, the jump mechanics could be better, which can lead to momentary frustration when you have to re-do some steps. If you like Journey, Ori, etc. this will probably appeal to you. The graphics are better than the mechanics, and at times the lack of instruction will force you to wander for a bit until you figure out what you're supposed to be doing. I found myself getting more frustrated as the combination of janky mechanics and lack of direction compounded as the game got harder. Someone asked me if I liked this game, and I do like the game, but at the end of it all, I can't give a straight answer. I think I will like re-playing this game. The puzzle challenges in the game weren't the star, figuring out where to go and what to do next where the real challenges. If you buy, stay patient and take in the views. I often found that I had wandered far, far away from the task at hand so don't be afraid to restart a level just to get back to the beginning and try again. If you're wandering for too long, you probably just missed a turn/stone that was closer to the path that you realized. It really is a beautiful game, and for that reason I will play it again if I just want to chill out and get away for a bit.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this and Bramble in a bundle. Bramble was excellent. This was boring and the platforming was not fun. I ended up following a walkthrough so I could find all the shamans as I thought that was the best part of the game. In fact, that should have been the purpose of the game instead of just mainly walking a fox around a level. The problem is that the shamans can be easily overlooked. Luckily enough you can go back to certain parts of the chapters and find the shamans you missed. The ending is a major letdown. Most chapters have long stretches of just walking along. I guess you are supposed to enjoy the scenery and the music but for me it was just plain boring. I clocked in 7 hours of playtime but at least half of that was just walking....and walking....and walking.The controls are passible and there is no chance of death. You do getting injured at certain times which make you walk extremely slow. Which again does nothing but stretch out those areas. I guess I would rate it a 5 out of 10. In the end, I would have rather played something else. I was hoping for some emotional attachment to the fox but that never came. I cared more for the poor shaman souls.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: While some of the jumps and moves required by puzzles can be a bit tricky (especially if you're trying to achieve them on a slow or old machine), this is a thoroughly charming and beautiful game - particularly for someone who is new to games, like me. It doesn't lead you by the hand at all times, so sometimes you can feel a little bit lost as to where you need to go next. However this really makes for an immersive experience. A haunting musical score and beautiful graphics make for a heartwarming Nordic-themed tale, which manages to convey a magical story without the need for words or oral explanation. Very pleased that I chose this to be the first game I have ever finished. The final scene had me in tears!
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

If I wanted to play on a gameboy screen, I would buy a worthless gameboy. Hello... This is PC. I dont know if this is a ported game or whatever, but there is zero excuse for not adapting it to PC if you are going to port it over. If it wasnt a port then shame on you to no end. _childDocuments_.review: This is the best fox walking simulator I’ve played so far! It absolutely nails the mood. Gorgeous, wide-open landscapes bring a true sense of adventure. A small, yet compelling story is told only using pictures and environmental details. Minor platforming and environmental puzzles are sprinkled in to help encourage you to pay attention to your surroundings. The soundtrack is touching and perfect, despite most of it being only a half-hour looping playlist (Music sorta reminds me of Halo). And probably most important of all, the fox is adorable! There are so many little details and animations and mannerisms. In my 16 hours of play, I never got bored spending time with this little guy.Unfortunately, the game is plagued with all kinds of… very interesting problems. I was able to forgive most of them because it got the fundamentals so right, and that should really say something about its quality, but unfortunately I can’t give this anywhere near a perfect score. Here's a small sampling of them!  There isn't enough room for a comprehensive list of complaints, so you'll just have to find the rest of the game's quirks and problems on your own...In the end, still an absolute must-play for a fox fan. If the trailers and screenshots look beautiful to you, go play it! Just remember, it’s first and foremost a walking sim – it requires a lot of patience. If you’ve got no patience, this genre isn’t for you. Go into it with the mentality to chill out and meditate to some gorgeous visuals, and enjoy being an adventurous wild fox for a few hours!7.5 / 10!(5 hours is a good estimate for a casual playthrough, and about 12 for full completion. I resorted to a guide for 3 shamans, and for the Kindred Spirits achievement.)
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this, I really do, but oh my God not being able to do anything with the camera angles is driving me up the wall.  I need to be able to see where I'm going!  I need to know that there's a rock in front of me before I bonk into it!  The tech here is really undercutting the gameplay and the scenery.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: The game is basically walking simulator with minor platforming and screenshot mode. You are a fox that meets a fox spirit who local people used to worship before it went to sleep (I think? It's explained through pictograms like in Hob so you have to assume most stuff) and some sort of plague in form of red plants started and wiped the population. You're running across chapters through linear areas and try to find a way to progress utilizing the spirit abilities. That's literally it, that's the entire game.However the screenshot mode is there for a reason as handcrafted (although not perfect in some spots) environment is extremely pretty. Music is from the "background noise" category though as it repeats similar theme over and over but modified to current situation.Not much else to be said here, it's a pretty good game to relax to.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fox lover buy.There are other reviewers who have written much better than I could hope to. All I can say is this was my first time playing this sort of game, and I was very pleased with it. One of the more relaxing games I played and to be honest I'm kind of one of those players that has to go see everything, and talk to everyone. _childDocuments_.review: Got this for free on a fanatical sale.  Played about an hour and a half one evening.  It's ok,  The graphics and music are top notch, the problem that had me lose interest is the gameplay.  Or lack there of.  I am fine with "walking simulators" if the story is intriguing or engaging.  Here with the story being totally non verbal it is really hard to care about anything.  I compare it to Abzu.  What abzu did so well is it was a. short. and b. had great visual story telling.  This might be short people say like 3ish hours, I still found it wearing my patience thin.  Might be fine for an evening on a deep sale if you like non narrative experiences. _childDocuments_.review: ***EDIT***Turns out when you use the correct keys for movement (WSAD) and NOT the arrow keys, it isn't so twitchy and frustrating. There's still areas that require a lot of coordination and alacrity in movement to accomplish but not seemingly impossible if you are a bit older and have slower reflexes. Would actually quite recommend. It is a shortish game, but the price tag is pretty low, so I would say very worth it. I apologize for my earlier rant.***ORIGINAL REVIEW CONTENT***I just wanted a nice, relaxing game to play. Run around, explore, figure out some puzzles, take some dead guys their sticks. At first, this was perfect, and then I hit the twitch parts. For someone who has the reflexes of an inebriated sloth, trying to accomplish things where I have to be able to press five different keys on the keyboard at about the same time really ruins any experience. I can get games that are difficult and challenging by nature. Games that have that competitive feel to them, even if you're only playing single player. This game doesn't have any of that and still has the stupid gotcha junk. I even recommended this game to my kid when I first started playing it because it looked peaceful and fun. The landscapes are beautiful, and the music is soothing. It seemed to have everything. If I had only played about an hour more, I probably would have realized my mistake, but instead we're both just annoyed and frustrated. I won't say I wasted the money on the first purchase because the game is what it was advertised to be, minus the twitchy puzzles. Unfortunately, in order for my kid to play, I also purchased a second copy, that was definitely money  short, if you're looking for something peaceful and relaxing, this ain't it. If you're looking for something high impact and competitive, this ain't it either. I really don't know what the target audience is here.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game with a lovely true ending. Although it lacks a variety of content even for a short game, the content that is there is well done. Examples: Though the soundtrack is short and so repeats a number of times, that doesn't distract from the tone it sets. There's few complex animations such as climbing, but the regular movement looks quite natural. The puzzles are very simple and get reused, but the beautiful scenery still made them feel worthwhile.Really the only problems with it I had were twofold:First, in some areas it's hard to tell what you're expected to do. If you miss a small thing and get lost you can even end up having to backtrack a ways. (Player advice: If you're following something and lose track of it, keep moving forward and it'll find you after a while.)Second, the second-to-last chapter has a gigantic map but is very easy to get lost on. Which makes it a bit-hard to get the true ending if you don't know to look for it. It also makes the achievement to find a bunch of spots in this chapter, which can be well-hidden, very tough. (Player advice: You'll have to complete another achievement throughout the earlier portion of the game before this one becomes possible to complete, too.)P.S. It is weird that the foxes bark like dogs. Yes they can do so but almost never actually do. Would be like having wolves bark or feral cats meowing. Also, even if it's just a texture change, it's nice to have the choice between tom fox and vixen skins.

_childDocuments_.review: is a captivating adventure game taking place in a fictional world that's highly inspired by the Icelandic landscape. You play as a spirit fox, a unique creature capable of interacting with the spirit world, as you journey to the top of a tall mountain to stop the spread of a disease that's plaguing the land.The narrative may be short, and the lack of dialogue and objective markers might be a detriment to some, but to me, I found the story to be heartfelt and beautifully told. There's plenty of room for speculation as to its meaning, and there's a great deal of world building for you to interpret. Despite its overall haziness, it's compelling and holds your attention.Likewise, the gameplay is just as engaging. Unlocking new spiritual abilities as I progressed was enough to keep the gameplay loop refreshing, and the presence of puzzles makes it challenging. It's pretty difficult to get lost and confused, but there are some areas that make you think a bit.My favourite aspect of  was the level design. As you can easily tell from the screenshots, the game looks gorgeous. Each environment you travel to has an incredibly high attention to detail; they are practically begging you to explore them. The abundance of invisible walls is slightly disappointing, but it doesn't put too big a hamper on the levels overall.All in all,  is an easy recommendation from me. I really enjoyed my time with it. If you liked games such as Abzu or Journey, then this one will be especially right at home for you. If you wish to see a more detailed review, be sure to check out my video review: Thanks for Reading!
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: While at times the mechanics can feel slightly repetitive and the lack of direction could leave me feeling frustrated with where I am supposed to be going (especially at a point near the end where the environment in a specific chapter looks exactly the same throughout), this game made me feel moved by the time the credits rolled. Through its subtle storytelling, amazing visuals and beautiful soundtrack, I can wholeheartedly say that I had a great time playing Spirit of the North.Would highly recommend that you check it out if you are looking for something to scratch that itch that games like Journey and Ico leave behind.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: You play as a fox. That's what got me to play Spirit of the North (SOTN). It's nice to play as a non-human protagonist for a change.Spirit of the North has zero dialogue and zero combat elements. Even so, it succeeds with its simple (and ambiguous) premise of a fox moving across gorgeous scenery, guided by its companion fox spirit. You will find yourself stopping often to take in the environment around you (as well as use the handy Photo Mode to take screenshots). The final end credits scene in particular is jaw dropping; more games should have interactive end credits parts!SOTN succeeds in terms of visual spectacle and relaxed gameplay. Its metaphysical themes also offer much room for open interpretation.This game is a great play for those looking for a calm walking sim to wind down the day with. The sleepy and slow pace of the tracks add to the casual ambience of the game. It's a great listen for the first few times. After that, the tracks feel tiresome and repetitive. I wish the devs had added more tracks as well as more variety to the soundtrack.Spirit of the North is a great game to play on ultrawide monitors at max resolution. There may be occasional stutters and FPS drops in some game areas--this is particularly the case in "red zones."As a walking sim, this game is great for doing a meditation session or a mindfulness exercise. I enjoyed the immersive flow of being a fox in this natural world interwoven with metaphysical elements. I recommend ignoring the urge to hunt for collectibles as that distracts from the mindful aspects of this game.Sadly, I cannot recommend this game for Fox Truthers. SOTN allows your fox to bark using a specific mapped key. But there is zero lore that tells you what the fox is saying.SOTN is a short, sweet and fun game to 100%. None of the achievements are too frustrating to get. The grind for collectibles is mild. Video guides may be needed for one semi-tedious achievement.They're Good Foxes Brent, 12/10

There is a nice little bit of puzzle solving, but nothing too difficult that will take you out of the experience.In the end, the journey and story being told were the best parts for me.Also, I absolutely love foxes, which added to the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: First, foxes don't dog bark. They squeak, yip, and scream. However, if you reach THIS level of nit-pick, you know this is a great game.The atmosphere is captivating, and the environment is equally as stunning. I went slowly, because I wanted time to take in everything, explore every corner, and see all the sights. I wanted to exemplify curiosity, as befitting of a fox. On that note, I enjoyed the simplicity of being a ordinary fox exploring the world, instead of some Chosen One superhero pursuing a world-ending super villain. The simplicity of being an ordinary fox exploring the world made for a very calming experience.More importantly, you are encouraged to explore. In fact, you WILL miss important stuff if you don't investigate every corner. There are even a couple times you get a key later on, but then need to backtrack to find what that gives you the ability to unlock.As for the story, you are not told anything. You only get bits and pieces here and there, and only the ending puts those bits and pieces into context. Some things, I totally called it, and other things, I did not see coming. Without spoiling anything, the ending is very personal, and I am glad it ended the way it did.If you want calm, relaxation, curiosity, and exploration, absolutely give this a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely beautiful and the music was wonderful. An absolute treat to play and the ending had tears welling up in my eyes Q-Q It was so beautiful and precious T~T I did not expect to get punched in the heart like that but oh my goodness. So glad I finally played this, it's been in my backlog for ages. Highly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: I personally found this game very enjoyable. I enjoyed exploring, finding secrets and doing the (not difficult) puzzles. It has an interesting non-verbal story and the scenery is beautiful. I found myself taking lots of screenshots along the way.- The story/tale- The scenery and art- Ability to explore, - - Completing all the achievements. - The fox sounds like a dog, but it isn't a big deal- Gameplay can be quite slow, very slow in some cases (on the positive side, it allows you to enjoy the experience, but on the other, it will drive impatient people crazy)- Puzzles are quite easy- You are mostly searching around to find things- Music is very nice and relaxing. However, there is only a handful of different music and they are played depending on the mood of the map you are in. ((Edit: added this last point)

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is beautiful, and a true spectacle of design, bit, I wouldn't recommend playing this game without a guide. Without a guide, this game is somewhat of a confusing and aggravating mess. It is possible to get soft locked at certain points in the game if you do a puzzle in the wrong order. Despite the game being a platformer of sorts, you are completely unable to strafe (move midair after a jump), meaning you lose control of your character immediately after jumping. The platforming can be a bit clunky, the puzzles a bit confusing, and the movement rather annoying, but beyond those somewhat minor issues the game is absolutely beautiful, and a great playthrough experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: This game had a lot of potential don't get me wrong. The game is beautiful, the music is nice too.Unfortunately, it would be the only good things I would point about that game. A lot of reviews just says that it's a good looking game but they ignore the major defaults of that game. The controls are really clumsy so the platforming in this game (there is a lot of platforming) is pretty frustrating. You have a limited amount of actions you can do because this is a really chill game but some of them can only be performed under certain circumstances. Of course it is normal, some things aren't meant to be done whenever you want. The problem I have with these actions is that 9 out of 10 times it won't work because you're too close from it or you're not facing it properly. Sometimes it will work even though you're far from it or not even facing it and on a few occasions, you won't even receive the power from it because you can't get close enough in order to get it.Another problem is how they handled the camera. First of all, the camera is entirely manual, so it won't slowly reajust when you go somewhere you aren't facing which isn't that much of a deal. The main problem is that when you unlock a new area, you're camera shows you what you unlocked (pretty normal for any games) but i found the amount of time it's in a locked state way too long just to show that a wall went down. And while the camera is locked, you can't move you just have to watch. It didn't show the new path just a few times which made me wander around looking for the next area.Speaking of which, the game doesn't clearly tells you what to do. The tiny spirit following you will show you once what to do but most of the time your camera isn't facing it so you'll have to find on your own.The last issue I had with the game was the menu system. This is a chill game so you'd assume that you can leave whenever you want but the game doesn't save unless you reach a save point, reseting your progression in that area on your next playthrough. The settings layout is not optimal but it's fine because you don't have to go there often.Now please remember, this game isn't awful on it's own, it shows a lot of potential and i'm sure that the studio behind will be able to publish a great game in the future but i cannot recommend this game a the moment.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: Spirit of the North is a fantastic experience. It’s pretty light on plot but rich in environment and setting, with well thought out gameplay and simple mechanics. The main protagonist is an adorable fox and it’s absolutely delightful to romp around in the wilderness with him/her. The music is beautiful, the atmosphere is gorgeous and makes you want to explore every part of every location. _childDocuments_.review: The game was beautiful, atmospheric, and a bit of an emotional journey as you make it through each chapter, emphasis on "a bit". The idea behind the game is not a bad one; I was attracted to play this game because playing as a fox blessed with spiritual divinity in order to free the world from darkness sounded like an experience I would have liked. I was disappointed to see that, mechanically, this is just a puzzle solving game, but lacking in cleverness as the solution to each puzzle is quite obvious. Despite how gorgeous this game is to look at, I found myself quite bored, and I wish this game offered a little more than a visually stunning experience. More difficult puzzles to solve, better interaction with more spirits and animals so that the story is told actively rather that retrospectively, and perhaps some suspense would've been nice. You, the fox, are literally the only living thing throughout the game, and nothing else moves except doors and platforms. That means that there is no risk, there is nothing that threatens you, there is no "game over" aspect.But the question is: did the developers deliver the experience they wanted players to have? I think they did, mostly. I believe the intended vision behind this game was to make a relaxing, atmospheric work of art that envelopes you with intrigue, much like a painting can do. If that was their primary objective, then they succeeded. However, it is obvious that they wanted this to be a puzzle game too, but that did not turn out so well. I think the decision to make Spirit of the North a puzzle game was a bad choice. Making this game a terrifying action thriller would have portrayed the awfulness of the dark better, made the atmospheres pay off with greater emotions, and made our role as the hero that much more real. The light and beautiful, as well as dark and awful tones, are already present in the game, so an action thriller would've been a great complimentary piece to the primary objective. I would also suggest adding a wholesome, heart warming romance between the two foxes to try to build a stronger bond between them.Moving on to the rating.How well was the developer's vision executed?6/10 : Again, I think the focus here was the art, and they did an absolutely fantastic job, but the rest of the game needed work.How well did it meet my expectations?2/10 : It exceeded what I expected in terms of visual majesty, but none of my other hopes I had when purchasing this game saw the light of day. Simply put, this isn't what I was expecting, and the parts I did expect were lacking, save for the visuals.Expectations aside, did I enjoy this game for what it is?3/10 : I can't say that I hate this game, I did like the scenery and the subtle feelings of discovery, especially the wonder I felt near the end, but to say that I enjoyed this game is a stretch. If all you want is to explore a beautiful environment, you can surf Deviant Art and Fur Affinity as much as you want for free without puzzles to solve and get more out of it than Spirit of the North. But if you're looking for a stimulating puzzle game, or a decent fantasy adventure, I wouldn't bother.Overall Rating?4/10 : A mediocre game I didn't particularly enjoy, but if this is the kind of game you are looking for, then you will be delighted, but expect some degree of disappointment regardless.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to give a short review of this game. However, I honestly do not feel good to just give a simple thumbs up or down. First, I did enjoy this game. But I feel like this game has a lot of unused potential. It is by no means a bad game. But I think it is only 30% of what it could have been. To explain this I should probably start with what I expected. I recently played Gris and expected a somewhat similar game. A "walking simulator" that shows me a beautiful world and tells me a nice story. Certainly not as artistic but with its own distinct style. A few little puzzles and a few movement sections on top. Love that kind of game. Now to what I experienced.Too many of the areas just felt unnecessarily empty. It felt like nothing was happening. There was no puzzle to solve, no obstacle to overcome, no mystery to uncover, no emotion that you were supposed to experience. Just press forward and wait.Also... Invisible walls. This game has an insulting amount of them placed in sometimes the most ridiculous places blocking me from making jumps that were completely irrelevant while it was incredibly easy to access areas I was not supposed to be in. I softlocked myself 2 times simply by playing the game and got annoyed because I could not jump over objects that were otherwise easily jumpable. Furthermore, since the fox was presumably a Skyrim horse in his last life sequence breaking in this game is ridiculously easy. You will automatically do this when playing casually. However, all in all this is an indie game. If you know about these issues and you know what to expect this can still be a decent game. The music is amazing and although it sometimes feels empty, the game does look really good. Somewhat repetitive after some time but the good kind of repetitive. The story is easy to follow and I genuinely liked the experience of playing a fox. I think the biggest issue I have with this game really is that I feel like there is so much unused potential. To me this game is an amazing concept that has to be polished to make it a brilliant game. It has all the right elements. If only the developers would have been brave enough to use them.TLDR: Typical indie problems but I suggest buying this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Spirit of the North is a visually stunning game with a sound track that creates waves of emotion. You control a fox, journeying through a magical northern landscape, accompanied by a spirit fox/entity. Along the way, you have the option of 'waking' the dead by matching corpses with staffs. You recharge your spirit energy by finding blue flowers and then light towers and destroy darkness to create a path to the Spirit World. As you progress, you earn additional abilities and new fox 'skins.' Puzzles are about finding things and activating spirit stones in the proper order to open new areas. At this point, I am deep into Chapter 5 (with 70% achievements) but I have enough hours invested that I think I can fairly assess the game. While you learn a bit of regional history from the stone carvings, there is no real story up to this point.  I don't know if more will be revealed when/if I make it to the Spirit World towards the end of the game.I find it interesting that the game is described by others as 'short' and a 'walking simulator.' For those with strong platforming skills, that makes sense. For those (like me) with less-than-stellar platforming skills, it is a long game and it is a challenge. Some of the landscapes are very complicated, with complex jumps required.  If you choose the option of finding the staffs to wake the dead, you will be doing a LOT of searching  every corner and it is easy to get lost. There are rock towers, cliffs, waters that rise and fall, and multi-level paths that twist and turn. Did I say there was a LOT of jumping required?  Much of my time in-game went as follows: Jump, miss, backtrack to jump point, jump, miss, rinse, repeat. The good news is that you don't fall to your death when you miss. You just end up somewhere 'below' and have to navigate back which may require even more jumping. I alternated between keyboard/mouse and a controller. I'm not sure I could have gotten this far without having both options.My only complaint is that the game has an automatic save at the end of each chapter and several check points during each chapter. This means that I have played longer sessions than planned in order to get to a save point and not have to repeat sections that were hard for me. You can also 'pause' the game and let your fox curl up and sleep until you come back.For me, the game is definitely worth the effort and frustration. I often take a break so I can come back with a fresh pair of hands for the next difficult jump. Several times I have resorted to a guide (posted on the Steam Community page) when I had not idea how to proceed. The guide is also a good resource if you are looking for staffs/corpses because some are WAY off the beaten path.I would recommend this to those who love to explore a beautiful world, don't mind the lack of narrative, and are willing to take on quite a bit of jumping. Having an affinity for foxes is also a plus! One added note: I own Lost Ember which I have not played to completion. I find Spirit of the North more compelling but, in many ways, very similar.An added note after completing the game... what an ending! Definitely worth the hard work to get there and have some tissues handy if you are prone to being emotional!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a thumbs-sideways review; I'm ultimately recommending it, but with some serious caveats.Spirit of the North is a third-person (well, third-fox) exploration/puzzle platformer game, where a fox explores a series of breath-taking northern vistas seeking to unlock the mysteries therein and defeat some sort of evil, red fungus for............reasons?!?!Positives:*Graphics*  The landscapes and ruins look bloody fantastic, just by turns lovely and awe-inspiring.*Gameplay*  New elements are added periodically which switch things up and keep the game from becoming too bland, too soon.Negatives:*Storyline*  You may have gathered from my opening statements that there isn't a lot of compelling writing going on, and that is unfortunately to the game's detriment.  You see, the entire "story" is conveyed only through visual story-telling (on screen cut-scenes, glyphs and carvings, etc.) which leaves  much unsaid and unexplained.  You never really know what is going on, e.g. what is that red fungus, why is it taking over, what the heck is actually going on?!?!?  Yes there's sort of a story-line, but it is so thin and ill-explained so as to be positively diaphanous in thickness.  And that hurts the game a lot, turning it into a series of pretty ruins and landscapes that you explore for no real good reason (defeat the evil influence of a corrupting force of........what, mycology, pure evil, WHAT?!?! ).  The glyphs and carvings don't do nearly as good a job of explaining the mythos of the game as the designers might have thought, resulting in a pretty game, all but devoid of narrative heft.So...........the game looks great and plays well, but you find yourself not truly knowing why you're doing what you're doing, except in such a vague, gossamer thin fashion as to render the story bereft of dramatic meaning and gravitas.I'm still going to recommend it, but I did find the game more than a bit dissatisfying, despite the eye-candy.YMMV.....heck, I'm sure someone out there has written a novel based on the compelling naratives they discovered within the game....

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this a "meh" rating. The game is gorgeous, though the fox model, imo, needs some TLC. The music is great, however in some areas it's a little intense for what the game is. I think it would be better with a Breath of the Wild type music.As for gameplay, I was a little annoyed that I couldn't sprint at the beginning of the game. You get it after maybe 10 minutes of playing, depending how long you want to explore and appreciate the environment. With that said, control and movement is just not good, plain and simple. In a big open field it's no problem, but if you are need to might tight and precise movements, it can be a little annoying. Next, swimming and water & forced animations. Holy cow is water annoying. Sure, you swim slower than you sprint, which makes sense, but half the time after getting out of the water you are forced to stop and watch a short animation of the fox shaking the water off. Pretty obnoxious after the 20th time. Lastly, possible spoiler, so ignore this part if you want, but each time you activate something with your spirit ability, you gotta go find another flower patch to reacquire your spirit ability. I understand why that mechanic is implemented into the game as it affects the puzzles, but needing to run over, activate the animation, and wait for it to complete so you can regain the spirit ability is annoying. Sure, it's only 3ish seconds, but that time adds upThe game, at least for the first two chapters is extremely linear, and this is coming from a guy that grew up on the Legend of Zelda. I believe there is a chapter select option at the main screen, but I did not investigate it. The reason the linearity is a problem for me is because I am an completionist, or at the very least a collector. I like to collect as much as I can, within reason of enjoyability. In the trailer and pictures above, you can see monk type NPCs that can be awoken with staves. If you miss a monk, there is a decent chance you cannot go back to get them, then you gotta start the chapter all over. That's a big oof for meLike I said, I wish I could give this game a "meh" rating. Definitely not worth the $20, imo. I bought it 70% off for $5.99, which would be a great price imo, but the linearity, mediocre controls, and forced animations make it less enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: There are no enemies, health bars, timers, inventory, map, or compass. All you have is peaceful music and a vast, beautifully-rendered world to explore.And, infuriatingly, somewhere out there is the one thing you've got to find that will let you into the next section.Giving this game a thumbs-down was a hard call for me to make. I'm a fan of foxes, and I love exploration games. And I did feel drawn into it enough to play this one through to the ending (about six hours). The world really is gorgeous, the puzzles are short and simple, and I liked the mystical mood it set.The problem is that the world is divided up into sections, and you can't leave the current section until you unlock whatever's blocking you from moving onward. Maybe there's a fallen monolith somewhere that you need to magic, or maybe you need to find a staff and bring it back to its (long-deceased) owner, or maybe you need to step on a pressure plate to change the water level. The problem with the beautiful scenery is that much of it is the same color and texture of gray, and there are so many boulders and ruins and narrow corridors that it's easy to get turned around and find yourself going the wrong way. So I found myself spending many minutes running back and forth across the same area, trying to figure out what I had missed or where I was supposed to go or what I was supposed to do next.The main character, a fox, handles like a truck - it really could have used more fluid animations. It is accompanied by a blue glowing sprite which flits annoyingly between the fox and the player too often, especially when I'm trying to maneuver the point-of-view to have a better look at where I'm going. I spent most of the game carrying around a staff (in the fox's mouth) because I couldn't find the frozen corpses to deliver them to. Holding down the Shift key changes the fox's gait from a trot to a sprint ... for five or six seconds, after which it has to catch its breath; I'd think a wild animal should have more stamina than that. (I did notice that holding down the Shift key and just letting it up for an instant every few seconds let me maintain a near-constant sprint. Bug?)My biggest disappointment with this game was the lack of story. Why is the fox exploring these ruins? Did he really die at the beginning of the game? What's the spirit all about, and what's going on at the end? What's with all the red diseased-looking stuff? Nothing's answered (though the very end of the game offers a little bit of material that's up to the player's interpretation). If the game's creators had worked a bit of plot into the game, given us a way to identify with the main character and relate to whatever's happening here, I think it would have been much stronger.But, as it is, "Spirit of the North" is a relaxing few hours if you enjoy exploring and puzzle-solving and dreamy music, and if you have patience to spare.

_childDocuments_.review: At its current state I'm sorry to say that I cannot recommend it.It feels like a 0.8v game, where a lot of things are decent but a lot of others need some more attention. The horrible obstacles hitbox and the weird jumping where you jump sideways if you have wall in front of you. And ANNOYING invisible walls really close to the player at some points. The game's mechanic is pretty repetitive having to do the same thing over and over again in different scenarios, and exploration is not reeeeeally rewarding, as there are only a few interesting things beside the skull guys.I can feel the game has potential, it was just not used to its best YET, and feels like an early access game.

_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy relaxing but also emotional games like Journey or ABZU, then Spirit of the North is an easy recommendation. You control a fox deity and solve puzzles while tracking through often beautiful and vast landscapes. The music is great and it does give that emotional punch when needed. For an indie game, the graphics are also superb.Keep in mind that the game is not as polished as the cult classics mentioned above. Sometimes the animations glitch out, and once I even managed to do a sequence break that didn't allow me to finish an area - prompting a checkpoint reload. But nevertheless, even though Spirit of the North doesn't quite reach the heights of Journey or ABZU, it is a solid recommendation for the fans of this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but if you are looking for a calm, relaxing game with a gorgous world to explore, this may be for you.A walking simulator taking place in a beautiful, nordic world. You play an ordinary fox who is sent on a quest by a ghost fox. Follow the ghost through the amazing scenery, through caves, along slippy slopes, discover ancient secrets, solve riddles by taking items in your mouth and carrying them to the right place. The game is along the line of the fantastic Lost Ember, a rather similar game, so if you enjoyed that you might also like Spirit of the North. The focus lies on exploration, running, jumping, sliding, swimming, howling, exploring little labyrinths, discovering stuff. There is no talking, the story is told through environmental storytelling and little cutscenes. Your magic fox friend shows you old wallpaintings that explain what happened to the world and why there are everywhere human skeletons. The game saves during its chapters. Controller works fine, ultrawidescreen is not supported.Chilly exploration game. No fights.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: I've only got 2 hours in so far and it's a bit different from the stuff I usually play, but I'll strongly recommend it at this point. The landscape visuals are beautiful, the music is great, and I like how there's no tutorial and you just kind of have to figure it out. The fox is also frickin' adorable.  It doggy-paddles in the water, shakes itself dry, AND you can wag it's tail (that does seem to have a mechanical use in dark areas).  I'll admit I teared up a little at the end of the prologue after it had been whimsically following the spirit fox and sliding around on ice and playing in the hot springs. Based on the store page thumbnails, it might get a little darker later on, but I'm enjoying it as an atypical game so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very pleasant and beautiful game! 4/5 stars!First, of course, the game is beautiful. The fox is super cute and the lighting effects in particular are very nice. It's extremely atmospheric, and has decent variety of environments while still feeling cohesive. The soundtrack is really lovely and fits the aesthetic well, though there are some awkward transitions at times. The story is simple enough, but it has enough character and uniqueness that I found it engaging. It's not a particularly dark game (and no combat/violence/gore besides skeletons), but there are some darker elements and a general sense of melancholy that I enjoyed and found interesting.Gameplay-wise, they do a really good job of making things intuitive without using dialogue, text, etc. (not perfect, but really good IMO). Most of the game is quite forgiving, so it's easy to trial-and-error things a time or two until you figure it out, but for the most part I caught on quickly. The puzzles are slightly challenging at times, and they're varied enough that they don't get repetitive. There is one "collectible" that is (for the most part) not necessary to complete the game, but that I think actually adds something thematically. Most are pretty simple to get, but there are a few that you do have to hunt a bit for (I was able to find them all within two playthroughs without looking at a guide). Collecting them gives you different skins for your fox character, which is a fun addition. It took me 8.5 or so hours to complete the game with all achievements (I did use a guide for the Kindred Spirits achievement).I only have a few complaints:1. The platforming is *very* frustrating at certain points. It's unclear exactly where you can and can't jump (particularly when climbing/jumping up ledges), and the fox is a little floaty at times. Sometimes you just aren't supposed to be able to go somewhere, but it takes a handful of attempts to realize that it's not just the controls being annoying. This doesn't happen often, but I did find myself quite irritated a handful of times.2. There are a few brief areas where the walking gets a little tedious. The opening chapter, for example, has a lot of empty caves with not that much to look at, and you haven't unlocked the ability to run or dash yet. This gets better as the game goes on.3. There are a couple parts where the player has to follow the spirit fox, and the player character's walk speed is faster than the spirit fox's. This is a nitpick, but I don't understand why game devs do this lol.Well worth the price overall, and a fun little game if you like chill, atmospheric stuff!
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: I do recommend the game... BUT... there is a but, a big one... Actually there are several.ProsYou are a fox. (Well... kind of)Music is gorgeous.Stunning visuals.It's incredibly relaxing (Until you get stuck)Fox skins can be unlocked, and they are gorgeous. <3It's cheap.ConsJumping...: The jump mechanic is very janky and not very intuitive, and the geysers are painful to time correctly. Fox... or is it?: While the fox is gorgeous, it has issues... That bark is a dog bark... I have never in my life ever heard a fox sound like that... Same goes for the panting noise it makes when its out of breath, and since you need to bark as frequently as you do, it keeps taking you out of the immersion...The camera: While the camera is just fine, it's easy to control and all... But whenever you are to progress and the camera just locks on a location, it's sometimes helpful to show you where to go next, but often times it just janks your attention away from the things you were doing, and since you need to explore everything to truly see each individual area anyway, then it's just intrusive.Story...? It starts off strong, then it disappears into weird corners of the world, and you need to go not just searching, but spend way more time than I am personally comfortable, on double checking the areas you go through, and as there are a lot of check points, you can't go back to the part you missed out on if you accidentally progress... Oh yes, you can go back through the chapter mechanic in the main menu, but all the puzzles need to be done again, and you start at the very start of the area of each part in the chapters... It's painful, it's janky... and annoying.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: A very pleasant experience with great scenery and a nice story. A common mistake of the story/puzzle genre is creating a labyrinth that leaves you wandering around for hours frustrated and wondering what to do. This game avoids all of that and the feeling of not knowing where to go, or what to do, next never lasted long. The game leads you forward without the need for any maps or quest markers. Its a relief that the game doesn't directly tell you what to do or how to play but it is easy to understand regardless without any tutorial.The story is simple enough to understand without having to actually read anything at all, and the atmosphere always seemed to match the music and the part of the story they were telling with each chapter.Great game.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: Truly truly an amazing package of graphics, map design and music that outweighs everything I write below and makes this a positive review.However, be mindful that you won't be getting the best feeling of controls for a game that requires such an amount of action. Despite good overall map design, there isn't a clear difference in looks between walkable paths and unwalkable ones which have invisible walls right above it. There are also a few design flaws and glitches that are irreversible when triggered and may cause you to restart the entire chapter/section.The following user-defined tags about this game may not be accurate:Fox - Yeah it's a fox / two foxes but it barks / they bark.Puzzle - I wouldn't really call it a puzzle game as the logic behind the same mechanisms in different places isn't consistent (e.g. sometimes your spirit form can't dash even when charged and you have to charge it another time, also some shamans unlock necessary paths for progression but others don't). There is also a huge lack of guidance so be ready for a lot of wandering around the entire map section (which can sometimes be really big!) searching for stuff.Relaxing - Yes but not all the time. Don't buy this game if you aren't comfortable with black and red plague infected plants. (But if you are, killing them and purifying places can be quite satisfying.) Also you can't expect yourself to be relaxed if you're stuck in this section for like half an hour because the game doesn't give you any clues.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: Let's just rip this band aid off first: yes, the bark is super annoying, that's not how a fox should sound. Even though they can bark, it's much higher pitched that the game portrayed it. That's not how foxes be!With that aside, the game itself was very good. First of all, you play as a cute fox! And not just that, a cute magical fox with a spirit wisp friend! Love that. I also love the other visuals in the entire game. The naturescape is grand and beautiful, the ruins are intricate, and the plague is visceral while not unnatural or grotesque. In terms of gameplay, the puzzles are fun, if fairly simple at times, and there was a lot of running around. Having the wisp was really nice touch, though sometimes it did take quite a bit for it to kick in. Having some fun other mechanics in there, like all the shaman with the staves you have to find, and the secret murals means there's value in a replay.I'd say 8-8.5/10, it was quite fun to play as a magical fox running around a ruined world.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: I love games that involve puzzles and this one does not disappoint. The puzzles are at times difficult, especially when having to use the abilities you acquire later on in the game. I love the idea of this game, and the fox is adorable. The only thing I don't really like is that you can't save in the middle of a chapter, unless you hit a checkpoint. But overall I've really enjoyed playing it so far and may consider playing a second time to find all the hidden achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece like no other. Truly a spectacular game. I love foxes and the animations of the fox are spot on, and the effects were just gorgeous. It looks so good you just run around without a care in the world. The soundtrack is also awesome and fits the mood perfectly. The only small complains I have is that one chapter had this extremely annoying, bright red coloring that really hurt my eyes. And that chapter was pretty long too. Might want to tone that down just a little bit. The rest of the chapters with that red stuff were fine, it was just that one chapter that had this annoying effect.Also, the game wasn't always too clear what you needed to do next in order to advance and I think I cheated a couple of times to get forward. Don't think things were supposed to work the way I did them. But that's nitpicking.Overall the game left extremely good taste in my mouth and the final chapter was just amazing! The rewards you get along the way are also a super nice bonus! If you love foxes like I do, then this game is a must. It's beautiful, peaceful, relaxing, and just pure joy to play. 9,5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Zero Spoilers Review:You control a little fox running around a Celtic style landscape, in 3rd person view.Really easy controls. Nice 2016-ish graphics, very good for an indie game.Simple atmospheric music.Lots of puzzles to solve. No combat at all. Just physics, tagging, maze and searching puzzles.You can do everything at your own pace. No time challenges.Genuinely very relaxing.NEGS:Short game! Can rush through it in only 2-3 hours if you want.Fixed save points.Movement can be annoyingly slow at times.VALUE:I paid about £3 in Xmas sale. That's OK for such a short game.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being a bit buggy with the physics sometimes, this game was a BEAUTIFUL experience with stunning landscapes to explore, good OST and chill vibes. It truly gives that sense of melancholy and longing for something that has been lost long ago and also makes you realize the insignificance of man against the vastness of the world.Regarding the level design, I think it's a bit flawed since sometimes the environment/narrative doesn't communicate well enough what the game expects you to do. _childDocuments_.review: I love little games like this, and this one was really lovely.It's one of those that drops you into a world of abandoned ruins, and your goal is to solve the puzzles to open the way to progress to the end.I love the visuals of this, and the fox is so adorable and magical.I did get stuck once or twice on the puzzles, as I don't have a very logical mind despite how much I do love puzzle games. But asking my partner to have a look through another set of eyes generally got me through.There's never much straight story telling in games like this. There's no dialogue or written text and developments are shown visually through the characters actions and movements. It's sweet and beautiful, and I always like those.(I'm writing this months after playing and finishing, so I may have forgotten a little or got some small details wrong, but I felt it deserved some expressed appreciation)

_childDocuments_.review: I have very mixed feelings about this game and I'm not sure whether to recommend it or not (after finishing writing this actually, with how heated some of the issues make me, I don't recommend it). It is very similar to games I love such as Ori and Kena Bridge of Spirits, but in comparison to both it falls flat. I like the world, I generally enjoy playing games where the main character is trying to fix the world by ridding it from evil and freeing spirits (especially when a game is visually nice to look at which this is). But in playing it all the way through (which took about 9 hours for me over a few days), there were a couple key points of frustration that took away my enjoyment of the game and made me not want to play it again (and reluctant to get part two when that comes out soon). My main issues with the game are outlined below:1) Frustrating jumping. You have to be super specific and it's very punishing when you're not. Trust me, it's not a skill issue it's a game issue because it's very inconsistent which makes it super frustrating. I enjoy challenging platformers and other games (again, like Kena) that have complicated movements, large maps, and sometimes difficult combat/puzzles. In addition, which might need to be it's own section, I ran into many bugs and glitches that were maddening. Two mainly stick out to me but I'll only explain 1. They're both either in chapter 4 or 5. Doesn't contain spoilers:                 -The worst one for me that almost just made me quit halfway through, was a point where you need to stand on a button which activates another pedestal that you're supposed to jump on in spirit mode to go up. The issue is, the pedestal starts moving the instant you stand on the button, giving you no time to a) go into spirit mode and b) work with the horrible jumping to actually get up on the pedestal. Seriously, this was almost impossible to the point where I was second guessing if I was even supposed to go up there because it just would not work. Again, serious design issue that could be addressed by giving the player like an extra second before the pedestal begins moving up.2) Where are we even going? As previously mentioned, I enjoy games with very large or open world maps (Kena, Hunter Call of the Wild, etc). But if you have a huge map, you need to make it very clear what the main character is supposed to do, where they should go, and what sections are off limits to the character or not. This game made it so challenging to determine if an area could be a hidden area or just impossible to get to and was inconsistent that I was always second guessing if I was going the right way. Can I jump on the little bricks on the side of the wall or not? Can I walk on the castle rampart walls or not? Do I need to? Especially when there are hidden shamans you're supposed to be helping, it needs to be more obvious how one might get to those areas otherwise a completionist like myself is just running around like an idiot (dealing with the horrible jumping), and still not finding the staffs or shamans without looking thorough walkthroughs (which takes away all the fun). And then, when I do watch a walkthrough, it only shows me that I was doing the right thing and going the right way the whole time but somehow just wasn't able to actually get there. Annoying to say the least. Chapter 7 is a prime example of not giving enough direction where I ran around forever not quite sure what I was supposed to do and afraid I was missing possible collectibles or important things. 3) Last rant, I promise. Most games where you can find additional hidden collectibles at the end after you beat the game allow you to keep all the skills you learned which usually assist you in getting to previously inaccessible areas or solve additional puzzles. This one time locks you in whatever skills you had learned on that level AND makes you play the entire level over again - horrible puzzles and all that were hard to get through the first time - AND doesn't make it clear which shamans you found already or which ones are new ones meaning you could easily go through all of it and still miss them and not know which ones are which and have to do it all again. This makes a completionist like myself who generally wants to get all collectibles and all achievements extremely frustrated and I'm choosing not to do it because I don't want to deal with the gameplay. I would much rather play through Kena again which didn't have any of these issues.

_childDocuments_.review: This Review Has Spoilers!This is my personal review from my recent experience of Spirit Of The North.This is a very lovely, and stunning game to play on the PC. There are a few pros and cons about the experience I had.Pros: The graphics are stunning, landscapes are beautiful. The main character (The fox) Is equally as beautiful, as long as you keep the camera far enough away. He still looks good, just the way the fur is looks a bit outta place.The story was wonderful to experience, the puzzles were interesting and fun.Is a bit short.. But sometimes short is a good thing.Music is soothing, calm and relaxing.. cut out on me once, but never did after that.My chat and I had tons of fun playing, watching and talking about this game.Cons: The main con I have to point out..  I feel left out of parts of the story, mostly the how and why. From what I gathered, the female spirit lost her mate/partner, somehow, and this lead to the end of humanity in the whole area?.. Okay. So you and this female spirit join together ontop of a mountain to stop this red chaotic energy spilling out causing more bad red things.. Cool.. But supposedly before the humans were taking care of the foxes on the mountain, who is going to look after their bodies now?.... These gaps in the story keep me up at night in deep thought.., sorry about that haha.Controlling the fox in a small space is near impossible, you either jump in place, or move pretty quickly.I forgot that I had the spirit form ability once or twice.I'm pretty sure I glitched though a puzzle once, as the solution online wasn't what I did at all.Needs to be mentioned again, the story keeps me up at night wondering about how and why about particular things :PAll In All I absolutely love this game, My chat loved the game, I've almost completed the whole thing, just have 2 achievements left at this point. I would recommend this game to anyone who needs something calm and chill to play for a little while.
_childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: The music and scenery are lovely.  This was a nice game to play when I wanted a peaceful distraction for a little while. I played it chapter by chapter that way.One thing I had a hard time with was navigation. There were some parts of the game where I felt totally lost and frustrated. The guide had disappeared somewhere and I didn't know where it was. I like exploratory games, but I think it would have improved with a little better guidance on the direction I need to go.Otherwise, this was a lovely play, and I would recommend it to people who like beautiful games and stories that can be interpreted in different ways.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a beautiful game, but for me it feels empty. I missed the narration, it left too many unanswered questions, often I felt frustrated with the puzzles, and it did not compel me to continue. I finished it, but I expected much more, it could have been much more. On the other hand, the atmosphere is amazing, the visual and the music is very good, the fox is very cute, and when the tasks did not cause frustration the game was very relaxing. _childDocuments_.name: Spirit of the North

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly beautiful game that took about 7 hours to complete while taking my time and not rushing through the story. Visuals and music is top notch and the story is all about "show don't tell" and they've pulled it off really well. The puzzles at the start of the game are fairly easy and straightforward, they then increase in difficulty as the game goes on and are just challenging enough to make you think without it getting frustrating or you getting stuck.I played it with a controller and found the controls and abilities quite intuitive. I read some players saying the jump of the fox felt slightly wonky, but I really didn't think about it. Perhaps it is different if you play with keyboard and mouse.Another thing that I appreciated was that while you could play this game as a completionist, looking for and completing all the hidden tasks, it is never required that you have to finish everything in a chapter to progress in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon hearing Spirit of the North described as a mix between Okami and Death Stranding, my curiosity soared. How could a game merge these two seemingly distant worlds? After playing, I can confirm it's not far off, though there's more, or perhaps less, to it, depending on your perspective.Spirit of the North casts you as a fox who forms a connection with a guardian spirit in fox form, protector of the Northern Lights. Together, you embark on a quest to uncover the mysteries of an ancient civilization and combat the encroaching corruption. While it might seem reminiscent of Okami with its mystical fox protagonist, the similarity ends there. Okami is a whimsical and charming adventure, while Spirit of the North takes the slow path, offering minimal hand-holding and requiring patient exploration and puzzle-solving.Spirit of the North may remind you of Death Stranding, at least in terms of its exploration. There's no narrative or dialogue directing your every move. You're left to navigate narrow caves, expansive meadows, and crumbling ruins, searching for answers. The pace is methodical, with seemingly little reward until later in the game.The game's story unfolds through hieroglyphics etched into stone slabs scattered throughout the world. At first, these inscriptions seem like gibberish, but gradually, as you explore the abandoned structures and ruins of the previous civilization, it starts to make sense. The pieces come together at the end, making the aimless wandering feel more purposeful.You'll come across staffs in your journey, which you can reunite with the spirits of ancient shamans from the extinct civilization. This act brings them peace, but whether it unlocks a special ending is uncertain. These moments provide some enjoyable challenges, and you might want to go back and collect them all if you missed any.Spirit of the North includes platforming sections, particularly around the ruins. Unfortunately, these segments can be maddening. The fox's running and jumping controls are decent, but jumping feels somewhat floaty, making precise jumps a challenge. The fox's slow swim speed is irksome, with no option to speed up. Worse, even puddles turn into treacle as the fox slugs through them and shakes off excessively upon exiting. Also, environmental glitches can disrupt your progress, impeding your enjoyment.The game's visuals are a mixed bag, with stunning panoramas but inconsistent textures up close. Textural disparities affect rocks and the fox protagonist, with fur appearing dated when viewed too closely. On the plus side, the game maintains a steady framerate and short loading times. The audio design shines, with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack by Joseph Gifford, although some additional musical pieces would have been welcome to reduce repetition.Spirit of the North is a game that encourages you to slow down and savor the journey. The intentionally slow pace immerses you in the fox's shoes, creating a sense of discovery. It's a long, introspective journey, and while it may not be for everyone, patience yields a unique tale of self-discovery.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice short game, took me about 6 hours to complete along with all achievements and collectibles.Visuals are very nice, especially from chapter 2 onward and the music is nice throughout.Gameplay consists of exploring semi-open environments with some light platforming and puzzle solving. There's just enough new mechanics and abilities scattered throughout the game to keep things interesting and to open up new possibilities on how to solve the various puzzles.Storytelling is almost entirely done through environmental context and short cutscenes. The way almost all environments keep your end goal visible or just out of sight is very nice and gives you a good sense of scale and purpose in what you're doing. The story isn't world-shatteringly incredible but I found it enjoyable while making my way through the game and was interested enough to see what would happen and where I would go next.I got it on sale and don't regret the purchase, if you're interested in short story and exploration focused games, you might like this one.Also there's dedicated bark and tail wiggle buttons.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, my feelings are mixed. It's just a little over 3 hours of gameplay total. It's cute, but also rather empty. Large open world yet annoying hitboxes make navigating awkward at times and there is deceptively little content within said world. The main problem I found was the sheer lack of guidance you would receive. For such an open world, I would have liked far more in the way of prompting in where to go. The puzzles were annoying not because they were hard, but because they were relatively easy, and if you were finding it hard, it was because you had missed something on the map and had to look for it rather than the puzzle itself being challenging. The tone of the map itself changed rather dramatically early on, and I have to admit I wasn't too fond of the fact that the change was permanent. While initially I enjoyed the change of pace, I very quickly found myself missing the original.The final chapter I found rather dull. The final stretch is too open, takes too long, and has basically nothing in it. The visuals, while nice, aren't at the level where they can make up for the lack of content.The worst part is the groundwork is very much there. It feels like this could have been, and still potentially could be, a great game. It just needs more to do. As it stands though, I don't believe the game is worth it at full price, for three hours of largely empty or easy gameplay. If you see it on sale, then I'd say give it a go. It's a nice game in its own right, despite what I've said above.

_childDocuments_.review: Grudgingly yes - If you can put up with janky controls in exchange for a cute, indestructible fox.Story: After the disappearance of the Guardian of the Northern Lights, devout shamans set out across the land in a desperate search to find her. Along their journey, they stacked stones as a beacon to guild the fox home. Hundreds of years later, after many generations of shamans had passed away without success, shamans continued to set out across the land in search of the legendary Spirit Fox. They stacked stones as they went clinging to the hope that doing so would one day guide the fox home and save their people from a deadly plague.The good:- Organic environment, it looks like a vast open environment, but somehow the structures guide you so naturally that you don't get lost- The storyline was quite beautiful- No soft locks- You need to recharge your powers and there is no shortage of "stations" to do so- Fox is indestructible, you can jump of anything- When it works it is pretty greatThe bad:- Janky as hell controls which becomes apparent when you need to do the athletic stuff- Fox needs to be aligned perfectly before making a jump. No changing direction mid-air- Even then he sometimes jumps into random direction, making even simple jumps a pain in the ass

_childDocuments_.review: Spirit of the North is a chill, exploration game where you play a fox journeying forth to heal a corrupted land. This land is clearly inspired by the landscapes of Iceland and Scandinavia in general, and it makes for a beautifully breathtaking game. There were so many moments in the game where I had to stop and just admire the picturesque visuals and the lighting in front of me. It looked so real at times. It also boasts a really relaxing soundtrack that fits well with the theme of the game as well as the sense of exploration. It's definitely worth listening to the soundtrack after finishing. The gameplay compels you to explore these landscapes to find solutions to puzzles, clean the area, and advance to the next area. Along the way, the game uses environmental storytelling to allow you to piece together what happened in the past to warrant your journey. In this, it does succeed. Spirit of the North combines all of these to make a memorable 4-5 hour journey that is sure to engage your emotions by the end.8/10
