_childDocuments_.review: Absolute gem of a game. Despite the looks and what the name might suggests this game is more influenced by the classic transport tycoon games, than any of the many mobile drug tycoon games you might have seen on the app stores. While not as deep as the former(but its getting there) it adds its own mechanics that keep the game fun; juggling between your dirty and laundered money, managing your cartel and their members (which each having different personalities and skills), dealing with authorities and other gangs and factions, gang wars, alliances and assasinations.Managing your economy seems highly polished to me with many means of optimisation and automatisation while your cartel members can also serve as transportation to additionally tweak some processes manually or getting stuff from A to B on a short note.I can kinda get why some reviewers might feel underwhelmed playing the tutorial and the story but I think this comes down to the fact that these modes are very long and in no rush, the game don't just throws you in to deal with everything at once but rather will unlock the game mechanics over time as you progress. Once you are dealing with the full scale of what the game has to offer, you certainly will have a blast (there is also a Survival/Sandbox mode for those who dont want to deal with that). If you are interested in games like this or the theme, this is the game for you.Also the music is just CHEF KISSHighly recommend

_childDocuments_.review: The game is an interesting concept, but some mechanics need a bit of work. You can set pretty simple production lines, but the residences all hoard money for some reason only sending out the excess to the buildings that launder it. There should be an option to decide how you want to distribute your money (like sending more to the buildings and leave more room in the residences). The mechanic of legal goods also might need some revision. As it is, the game assumes that you are selling a mix of legal and illegal goods (using the legal packaging to use the high capacity ports). But for some reason when selling only legal goods, they are still classified as "suspicious" anyway and it forces you to change the type or suffer more "terror." The combat mechanic is also a bit too simple, as is the diplomacy (in my opinion). Other than that, it's a relatively straightforward game, just make sure you use the in-game encyclopedia to learn how to set up your production chains and you should be good.

_childDocuments_.review: Really solid start.  This Early Access is exactly how devs should be using early access.  They've limited a bunch of available options - so for instance, there are buildings and factions and actions unavailable - so that they can focus the Early Access on balance, gameplay and interaction / information design.  Very respectable approach.  The devs are already making updates based on feedback from the community in those areas.  There are areas that need some work for sure but it seems that this is the focus right now - a constrained set of problems to fix.  For instance, there is a bit of a learning curve around how to get a money making empire going that is missing some key information design to let players know where the problems are (mostly around transportation).  Likewise, the Lieutenant's model for loyalty is an interesting mechanism but might be a bit heavy handed currently and needs some additional nuance.  Finally, there isn't really any diplomacy or relationships between the rival gangs or other factions - I hope something like this is coming and it isn't just a paint the map-style game. The art style is awesome, the soundtrack is phenomenal, this game is on the right track.  Buy it now if it is discounted or put it on your wishlist.  This is one that is doing it right!

_childDocuments_.review: A pretty fun game, especially after all the recent updates. If you like the drug war / cartel topic as well as supply chain management and strategic planning - you'd definitely at least spend quite a few fun hours. Also it has a bit of a board game vibe, in a positive sense, with all the character and resource allocations around the map. I always enjoy games where your hard work results into a self-sustainable clockwork of businesses, and you can just take a moment to watch how it all works.While it might look simple on the surface, it's grown to be fairly complex, especially if you want to do things right and not destroy a whole play-through accidentally. It's actually quite a remarkable & motivating feature to know that even if your empire is doing well and growing, a chain of small mistakes can all result in a (realistic) disaster. For example, a seemingly successful empire of mine got into an eventual collapse that started from one of the lieutenants losing loyalty and starting to uncontrollably kidnap people, which made my terror level (how wanted you are) skyrocket, resulting in DEA paralysing a crucial part of the business. And all this happened while most of my thugs were far away fighting a rival gang. And from there it went down like dominoThis is just one story of many that the game can generate, which makes it reasonably replayable. Especially now that they have several campaigns that can go into quite different plot branches. And then there is also a grind element that I always both love and hate - while spending a whole play-through to unlock just one new character or a (optional) building may seem excessive - it does give an extra motivation push that I often lack in other games. So let's summariseWhat I enjoy: + complex production chains+ non-trivial supply chain management+ frequent strategic redistribution of limited resources+ many characters with a story and unlockable abilities+ Rich world with many unique factions (mayors, militarymen, rebels, natives, gangs...)+ Enough diversity in each playthrough and sufficient replay-ability+ Humor and good dialogues / storylinesWhat I enjoy less:- too much micromanagement sometimes (which is avoidable though)- somewhat plain combat system, which could definitely benefit from more non-trivial player involvement rather than just comparing strength numbers of two armies - The map is great but you wouldn't want to restart in the same region too many times. Some sort of procedural maps (even if not as balanced and perfect) would be a great addition. Or at least randomizable soil fertility areas- Diplomacy with rival gangs is also a bit shallow at this point. It's not so fun to just trade resources manually back and forth across the map to improve relationsAll in all, it is totally worth it if you enjoy some of the described aspects. And given how passionately the developers have been listening to feedback and improving the game, I am sure more great improvements are coming!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall while I'd recommend the game, I'd caveat that I'm recommending it as a story driven campaign game.   Not as a sandbox game.  If you're annoyed by how other sandbox games in this genre don't let you run a narco empire or the like, this game is not going to scratch that itch.The various missions they have with plot lines, scripted events, etc are fun.   You get a decent amount of freedom in setting up your drug empire and the plot pacing keeps things fresh.  The scripted events also compensate for the poor AI and some of the repetitive game play aspects.However as a sandbox game, this game is bad.    Poor AI, extremely static maps, limited play styles (you can basically either do optimal path supply chain every time or get into micromanaging terror level and other issues).   No matter what part of the map (and there are only 2 maps) you start on, things are going to devolve into either you doing the standard approach or you fighting the core mechanics of the game.  They have things like map sectors with guerrilla camps and covert airfields, map sectors with international airports where you can bribe customs officials, map sectors with harbors, etc.   But nothing really changes, it's same supply chain, same shipping, and maybe slightly different flavor text in the dialog screens.   You don't change your play style based on the kind of cartel you're running and your partners.  Overall it's just not engaging.Initially when I purchased the game I actually was pretty disappointed in it, I did the tutorial and then jumped into sandbox.   Put the game down after that experience.   I've since come back and played a couple of the campaigns and enjoyed all of them.   At the sale prices it's a reasonable value.

_childDocuments_.review: Cartell Tycoon is a light- to mid-weight economic strategy game in the style of Tropico. Most tycoon games are pretty bad, because they just try to mimic the greatness of true milestones like Railroad Tycoon and just slap on a theme. There have been exceptions of course, and Cartel Tycoon is a decent take on the genre. The cartel theme is nicely implemented, with money-laundering, gang wars and of course, a production chain with plantations, airports, and luxury mansions. The presentation is nicely done and builds on stereotypes known from gangster tales like Scarface or Braking Bad.The story is mostly told by text dialogues - I have not yet played enough to tell you if it's a compeling story or not (I mostly played alpha). While the basic economy and building part of the game is pretty basic stuff, the devs added some nice flavour like the money laundering mechanics: Police will raid your buildings, if you just expand your business without taking care of getting all of that money "cleaned up". Also, you don't just play as a single character: Your capo and his thugs all have special abilities, but might get killed if they expose themselves too much. (Probably also by some story-driven events, which I have yet to see). Then, another character will take over. The player also has some control over who gets into a potential successor position.Best part about this game is the great soundtrack, which gets you into a caribean (middle american?) summer mood.Recommendation: Pick it up on discount, when available.

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Hello Comrades and welcome back to another less than 10 mins review, today I'm taking a look at Cartel Tycoon. Cartel Tycoon is a survival business game inspired by the 80s narco trade.  Can Cartel Tycoon make you feel like el Patron or is it another pretender that'll end up with a colombian necktie? Lets find out//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//I love the feel of the setting, I feel like I'm seeing a map of a Colombia set in the 80s- so kudos to the devs for immediately immersing me. There are a lot of graphical options that can make the map look absolutely stunning, and best of all for an EA game- it runs smoothly. I love the character models but I'd love to hear them voiced (and id make changes to some of the script, Moon Moose hit me up, changing certain words like "si" with "pariente" or "compadre" would make it more realistic to the people speaking) //Gameplay//Alright so gameplay mechanic is simple. You build farms that produce opium or other drugs, you sell them at an airport and you get money. What separates the game? The Dirty/Legal money mechanic. Money laundering is something you'll have to look into as the more money and problems you cause, the more eyes you'll have watching you. At first the DEA will come looking to investigate you, or your acess points i.e where you sell your products from (in which case you'll have to shut down operations until the investigation is over). Having legal money could legitamize your operations, making it harder for any federales to come down on you. You'll make use of warehouses, to store product and even smuggle contraband using workshops to put "illegal items" in cases of say, fruit, coffee or various other packaging. There are also rival gangs who will try to contest spots like airports, docks and cities to take your source of income. You can combat them by sending some of your Lietenents that you recruit. Each character has an attack stat and go up against your opponents attack stat. The winner will be the ones with the higher stat but contesting spots will only lead to a "turf war" that can attract the attention of government agencies so be wary of your terror level.//Price//24,99 USD//How many hours estimated//Currently it is in Early Access and it has a campaign and sandbox mode with multiplayer & survival coming soon. I've only scratched the surface in terms of gameplay and have about 5 hours into the campaign. Survival and Multiplayer intrigue me, and they will most likely warrant a look from me on arrival so at its current state i say give or take 20 hours. //Final Thoughts// I have to say, having lived in Latin America for a few years I'm not too fond of the terror cartels bring, I don't watch Narcos on Netflix nor support any narcocultura- yet I was drawn to this game, but mainly for it's parallels to the Tropico series. Is it Tropico meets Narcos? Yes but if Tropico was stripped of it's charm and depth. Cartel Tycoon isn't bad, you can just tell it's in early access. I like the Money system they have, always having to launder money but the micromanaging of it can be tedious at times. You'll always need a LT of yours to deliver dirty money to certain spots or they wont be functional- wheras Legal money can be access from anywhere? Stuff like that breaks immersion for the player, id love to have the ability to pay my ruffians dirty money, and maybe add a 10% upcharge since it is afterall dirty money.Sandbox mode is hard, even when you set your beginning point at easy- within the first 5 mins of your gameplay a rival gang will attack you rendering a pivotol point of yours useless.  I hate having to hire muscle from the get go especially when their upkeep is 300-450$ (and of course ifyou try to pay em in dirty money, they wont be paid). It is managable if you know exactly what youre doing but even a local operation can seem overwhelming at first especially as you will lose control of buildings if you don't have a LT in place. Say you do take your LT out to help out with operations like balance your warehouses or deliver money and you lose control of the place you had parked them in. Here comes the rival gang wanting to take over, now it's not hard to beat em as they usually range from 8-11 Attack points at first BUT- now your terror level will raise (even if you control the city) and the DEA, Police, Federales will keep a closer eye on you, shutting your Airport or Seaport down for a few days of investigation all while upkeep is still charging you. There definately needs to be some balancing done as the game is not finished yet. Overall Cartel Tycoon  is a neat game with a fun concept, at 24.99 USD though, it's not worth it's price just yet. I'm excited to see what Survival and Multiplayer have to bring. I want the devs to give sandbox mode more options, like rival gangs not attack for certain days. I'd like for our terror level to be able to go down. Perhaps have a setting where one of your LTs that arent protecting a property to take money from the airport or seaport and take it to your safehouse. Maybe the ability to turn off the LT's catchphrases "a donde te gustaria ir" "como estas" that got old QUICK. It's just a lot of nitpicks I have with the game and hopefully the devs listen to their community because in it's core Cartel Tycoon is a good game. It's a pretty game, and the Dirty/Legal money concept is amazing just falls a bit short in execution. I would advise that you hold off for a sale on this or wait till a few updates to pick this up.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say I absolutely love this game. I love economy management games, and this is very nice for that itch ... BUT there are some major bottlenecks and mechanics that are kinda annoying that pop up when you wanna grow.1) Terror/Loyalty System - I like the idea of this, basically knocks you down if you grow too fast. However my big issue with terror there is no way to get rid of it on any real effect manner. You have to go to a mayor and spend loyalty which makes sense, but this leads to the problem of loyalty being very hard to get early game. This forces you to grow very very slow at the beginning which can get boring just waiting to launder money to then buy loyalty to then decrease terror. I think this issue can easily be resolved by increasing the number of building that each city has... which is another complaint.2) Money Laundering bottleneck- I've seen other comments mentioning this and it can get to be a problem but you reach a point where you simply can't launder enough of your "dirty" money so you again just have to sit and wait for your buildings to produce clean money. This I believe can be fixed with increasing the number of buildings that you can have in a city. I will say once I got to around 3 cities each with banks it wasn't too much of an issue.3) This is probably my biggest complaint, I really really REALLY want the developers to add the ability to move resources from one warehouse to another. This would really open up automation, cause another bottleneck is if a warehouse has too many buildings it has to attend to in its radius it can get bogged down. So I can design very neat supply chains that would be effective if this mechanic were added. A side of this would be I would really like if they added money houses, I was reaching a point where all of my residences were full, which also caused smuggling routes to overflow with money (1 border checkpoint, 1 seaport, 2 airfields, had a hotel and 4 Residences). This is partly the money laundering bottleneck but I would really love a dedicated building where you can just store cash, make it to where if the cops seize it, you lose it. All in all, this game was a breath of fresh air, causing me to leap forward in time when I really got invested. I cannot wait to see what the developers add, but if you like any tycoon games, this is a worthy addition to your library.

_childDocuments_.review: Been playing the game for about 15 hours now and got somewhat bored after that. I mostly played the game in sandbox mode with standard difficulty. First of i really enjoyed the concept of the game but i did find the implementation to be lacking. I played in the sandbox starting region marked as having unbeatable difficulty but i eventually ended up having millions of dirty and clean money without expanding to other parts of the map and eventually got bored and realized there is no real reason to expand or start new production chains to further increase my money even though i defeated 2 rival cartels by them essentially commiting suicide by constantly attacking my buildings till their total power went down to 0 and this caused their whole operation to collapse for some reason. Combat is as basic as it can be, basically to win you need to have a greater power rating when either you attack or they attack and this was easily remedied by just hiring lieutenants who has a higher power rating than 0, together with my leader i was essentially able to repel all attacks coming my way with no issues. The game also has mechanics for how much people like you that give you bonuses depending on the rating, let it go to low and your leader dies, it was very easy to just buy a casino and just spam the charity event so you the rating goes up and i used it to buy a favor from the major to lower my terror rating.. The terror meter rises when you commit violent acts or smuggle drugs without packaging or smuggle with a package type that is considered suspicious (i assume this is caused by using a certain kind of packaging for too long but that is very simple to change). And the most tedious part of the game is the constant micromanaging that is needed for keeping your production chains in the working order if a warehouse is too full you generate terror so you constantly need to change your production in order to adapt. This would also be a very trivial thing to do but not if you end up having several production chains to watch over. It become clear that the best thing to do was to just maintain one production chain and then optimizing it as efficiently as possible and then occasionally just change the packaging depending on what package type is deemed suspicious at that smuggling spot. Generally speaking the game does seem to hold a lot of potential but i really cannot recommend it as the game is just very shallow and simple when you understand the mechanics. Improving combat as in having to actually buy weapons for your cartel (or why not armored cars and similar crazy stuff) and also implementing a diplomacy system for the rival cartels would be a big improvement and in general it would be great if there would be more uses for the money you earn because after a certain point i did not find anything to spend my millions on. All in all could be recommended to buy on sale and could keep one busy for an evening or two but not really any more than that.

_childDocuments_.review: So, after 12 hours of playing, I got bored. I already have millions of dirty money and clean money. What to do next? My suggestions for improving the game and creating "infinity":1. Character auto-generation.At some point, I stumbled upon the problem "Ran out of lieutenant characters", the game as a whole becomes unplayable, because. you simply do not have enough strength to attack other cities. How can this even be? Why make each character with a unique face, name and skills? I think you need to seriously think about the system for auto-generating characters so that they cannot run out. Like in "Crusader Kings", where the face, name and skills are generated in any quantity and are always unique.2. The strength of the gang.Now the main force is the lieutenants. Their strength is pumped by "work" in the delivery service (in my case they carried money from one residence to another). I think their "strength" needs to be completely reconsidered. To become strong - you must seriously think about creating your own army. It might be worth adding something like "Sports fields", where you can recruit new fighters (not lieutenants), which would increase the power of a lieutenant.3. Politics.Sooner or later, when you no longer have money problems, you want stability and influence. Here you need to participate in the political life of the country. It would be nice to add political parties to the game. Some parties will clearly be against the cartel, others will be neutral, and still others will support it (for money, of course).4. Journalism.When you bought all the politics, then the journalists will bring you problems. They will write the truth, which greatly spoils the relationship with the political parties that are "in your pocket." Therefore, such journalists must be eliminated. The "silent kill" skill, which is currently not used in any way, would be a good help here.4. Diplomacy.Ability to form alliances with other cartels to eliminate competitors. Of course, diplomacy is not eternal and at the most inopportune moment your friends will leave you.In general, the game is great! But don't stop there!

_childDocuments_.review: Would you like to take control of a drug cartel in Colombia, but fear the dangerous working environment? Don't worry, Cartel Tycoon is perfectly safe!It is inspired by historical events in the 80s, but tells a completely fictional story. If you want to know what really went on back then, watch the popular Netflix series Narcos. Well, at least that one is also based on some actual events, Cartel Tycoon only borrows the basic scenario from reality. Currently, two of the planned four game modes are already implemented: story and sandbox. A survival and a multiplayer mode are to follow in the future. In the story mode, we play a young man looking for a job who calls up a newspaper job ad and is promptly hired as the manager of a drug cartel that is being set up. Just like that. So we get a small hacienda, some dirty money and a few plants to grow. We pull up the necessary infrastructure to grow plants in it. So much for hidden opium fields in the middle of the jungle, the drug lord with style builds high-tech greenhouses on his huge property right next to the main road in the immediate vicinity of the capital! We harvest the plants and smuggle them by various routes to our buyers in the north.The game is essentially an economic simulation. We build farms, warehouses, connecting roads, drug laboratories, an airfield and not to forget our own luxury villa. There we grow opium, cannabis or vegetables and earn more and more money by selling them. We hire staff, research new drugs (or other improvements) and take over hospitals, banks, casinos, churches and the like to launder our dirty money white as a sheet. Other drug cartels are massacred, the local police are bribed, and our own empire is continually expanded. If you enjoy creating perfect circuits of goods, Cartel Tycoon might be fun for you! Unfortunately, you also get shot sometimes, but that probably falls under occupational hazard for a drug lord.Business/building simulation. Running a drug cartel was never easier.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not really a fan of the "fix it in post" method of game development, but I'm also not going to complain that a game that started in a bad state ended up coming around after another year of development. That really is the review I have for Cartel Tycoon. When it launched, it had some good ideas but couldn't really figure out what to do with them. After a major revamping of how gangs, logistics, heat, and combat worked, it has reached that coveted plateau of being basically okay. I hesitate to heap too much praise on it because it's still a fairly simple game, but its mechanics all finally work together.The core premise is drug production. You make them. You sell them. After that, the game avalanches into a fairly robust number of routes to take. You just need to keep making cash and laundering money, so... you could build all the production and do all the sales yourself. Or, you could buy drugs from a rival gang. Sure, it takes a chunk out of the profits, but it also bypasses a lot of logistics and tech restrictions. You could do it to curry favor, keep the heat off your back, or set up recruitment. Will you take a route of terror to power? Better stockpile arms by making nice with local militias and gangs, or give up infrastructure to run them yourself. Hell, combat isn't always the answer: gun smuggling can be quite profitable too! Or maybe you'll just grow vegetables and go broke. It's up to you. It's interesting, a little chaotic, and a bit annoying, but it's not boring. That is how I know the game improved. I went from "Okay, what now?" at launch to "Hrm, could I improve my cocaine throughput with the seaport and reduce operating costs? I should probably source avocados from the local towns, and I'll need a few new workshops for packing."As I said before, I think the game still needs work. In the modern day, it's easy to think games can always get better, so I would like to be clear: my complaints there sum up as balance issues and things that just don't matter. I will avoid hammering them here because you can have plenty of fun before you run into them. Still, what matters is the core loop works now, and the game gives you quite a lot of ways to go about running your drug empire. After winning a game, I felt smugly confident going into the next and had all the same issues running my empire, which is a compliment. I sincerely want to see some more polish, QoL, and mechanics, but as it stands today, I can flip my thumb from down to up and recommend it for what it is, not what I think it ought to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Cartel Tycoon:~~~~~~~~~~~ We all know that one of the richest men of the 1980's was the drug lord, Mr Pablo Escobar. Incredibly, he was mentioned on the Forbes' list of international billionaires from 1987 until 1993 . . . This is mind-blowing (and I am not talking about the product - nose candy - that he was producing in Colombia)! While the D.E.A. and other Cartels chased him, small groups were starting their own operations somewhere else in South America. And you are one of these people who are going to try their luck of becoming the next drug lord in Cartel Tycoon.Cartel Tycoon is a strategy, survival city-builder management developed by Moon Moose and published by tinyBuild on the 19 of March 2021 on the Steam platform. As the game is currently an early access, you can play the Story and the Sandbox Modes. The Survival and Multiplayer are not available now. You can choose to start your empire anywhere within the 10 regions available on the fictional South American map in the Sandbox. Each region will have its own level of difficulty, and some areas will have a point for your exportation, such as an aerodrome, a seaport, or a checkpoint (customs). In this mode, you'll start from scratch and see how far you can develop your cartel. I would strongly recommend playing the Story mode before the Sandbox, as you'll have a bit of an idea of how the game works.  In the story, you'll start from the Amado region which is located down south of the map. You'll start with one residence, an aerodrome, and you'll control the region as you own the main city. From there, you'll have to complete tasks to progress through the game.As you start the story, you'll see that you'll have access to both dirty and legal money. It means you can choose how you want to build your resources (farms, warehouses, etc.) as well as the buildings within each of the cities that you'll use for laundering the dirty money. However, it will be more expensive to purchase buildings in the cities with the dirty money, and you'll need to have one of your lieutenants deliver the money to the city before the building can be erected. The other thing to be aware of is the running costs of your operation. If your farms and all other infrastructures have been built with dirty money, you need to have enough dirty money in your coffers for the running costs. However, you can switch the upkeep costs between dirty and legal money on all your farms, warehouses etc. But you can't swap the upkeep costs for the buildings that you own in the cities. It's easy at first but it will become tricky very quickly. As your cartel grows, control more regions and get access to other means of exporting your products north to the U.S. of A.  Your organisation will not only attract rival gangs but also the D.E.A. Raids and investigations for the D.E.A will become more frequent as the terror gauge which is located on the top left of your screen grows. This gauge has 6 round icons, and each time you reach one, the D.E.A will become more attentive in your dealings, and if it is full, well, you'll be taken down by one of their bullets! Things like attacking a rival gang plantation or infrastructures, having farms, warehouses constantly full of illegal goods, robbing a bank or having to give a cut of your profit by going through the city of a region you don't control will raise the terror gauge. So, be attentive to the buildings that you produce the goods from. If they have a warning icon on them, you'll need to do something about it. If you don't do anything,  the D.E.A. will seize it, and you'll have to wait several days and pay big legal dollars to have it back. Investigations will occur at your exporting points, which are the aerodromes, seaports and checkpoints. Turning off these locations for the time of the investigation will usually do the trick, but your profit will take a bit of a dive. You can counter the terror gauge if you increase the loyalty gauge, which is next to it. How do you do that? Well, it is very simple! You can make donations through some of the buildings you own in the main cities, such as churches and casinos, or you can hold a festival at the Salsa Club. These actions will be painful in terms of money but will raise the loyalty gauge, and then you'll need to talk to the Mayor and ask him to ease the heat with the authority and D.E.A. When you do that, the Loyalty gauge will go back down next to zero. The terror gauge will also go down but only to the value of the Loyalty gauge you use. It is essential to hire more hands on deck as your cartel grows. Bear in mind, your cartel can only have 15 people in total. You can hire lieutenants at your residence and in the cities which are located in the regions you own. You'll need to use these lieutenants to transport dirty money and attack rival gangs' buildings or defend your assets. Each of these lieutenants have combat capacity (power), which is a number. If you attack an enemy structure and their combat capacity is 2 and the lieutenant you send has 4, you'll acquire it. And if it’s vice versa, you'll lose it. Don't freak out as it doesn't happen instantly, and you can send more of your goons if needed. I really enjoy the fact that you can promote your people up the ladder with additional abilities. Don't forget, you'll have to pay your goons with legal money, and you have to keep them happy. Oh, and if a D.E.A. bullet strikes you, one of your two associates can take over and keep the game going (well, with a small part of his predecessor cartel).There are several things that you can't use just now in Cartel Tycoon because it is an early access, but let me tell you, this is coming along very well. I am really excited to see what the next update will unveil. The game provides good graphics and atmosphere. The tutorial is minimal (part of the story), but you can access the game Wikipedia, the book icon on the top left of your screen, which will give you all information you need to know. It's a solid Early Access, and you can play hours on end with the current content.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics+	Great concept+	Plenty of replayability+	Good game Wikipedia+	Very addictive+	Trading cardsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Minimal tutorial-	Take a while to get used to-	No achievements as yetStep into the shoes of a drug lord and run all aspects of an illegal operation in Cartel Tycoon! 7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

But there are many aspects of the game that really need tweaked.

_childDocuments_.review: It's decent. If I wasn't interested in the theme as much, not sure I'd play. The tycoon portion of it is decent, but it's not the best I've played by far. It's easy to find yourself completely buried in poor decisions with no way out without much warning as a new player. For example you can run drugs through a city for distribution and sale without issue, but if you run money through a city in the same way you start getting destroyed with bribes and it raises your "police alert" level very quickly. By the time I realized the money route delivery I had set up was bad, I had lost half my savings to bribes and had now alerted the DEA to myself, which left me getting constantly investigated every couple minutes at all my distribution locations requiring me to just shut them down over and over. With seemingly no way to lower that back down, it soiled my learning experience and initial play through pretty badly. There are other ways you can screw yourself like this without warning as well, which in the end will make you want to just abandon your campaign and start over even hours into it. Let's hope some of these things find improvement. As of now will mark positive, but I hope that's not seen as without issue.The balancing and ease of entry are major issues that I see reflected through a lot of reviews on this. I think it was probably a bad idea to release this without having 15-20 hours of smooth play through availability, but that's neither here nor there at this point.On the positive side of things, the game looks fantastic. In building placement and design it's very smooth. The story had a cool "Narcos" feel to it. The artwork and animation is really solid. In viewing the buildings and research system it would seem the game has a good amount of layers, which we all know without depth in any game of this genre it will fail hard. I hope this has the ability to keep us excited way into a play through, also how different is this going to be each time I play it, because that's going to matter A LOT with how much people like this. These questions are not able to be answered due to the problems trying to get started and get through the tutorial. I am fairly disappointed the opening of the game was not better suited to learn without getting walled in by bad decisions you had no idea you were making.

_childDocuments_.review: Great art, style, intriguing theme, the UI is pretty good and the blend of game genres (A bit of Tropico, a bit of Gangsters, throw in some Tycoon elements and light RPG parts) is fun and interesting!Where things fall apart though is the game balance. It is , like 90s is this game broken? bad. More than half the time you won't know what you could of done differently to get a better result, and the other half if you manage to avert disaster there is something else coming minutes later that effectively ends the game for you anyway.If you get through all that and do manage to be 'successful', you'll find there is very little to do. This is a clear case of the game using a difficulty curve to hide the fact there isn't much content or an endgame. That feels like punishing design.I understand it is early (early) access, and this will be adjusted over time... But it's just not there yet, and even with the dev's aware of this issue, so far all the fixes/additions have felt like they have had little impact on the actual issues. (for instance, the whole paying lieutenants part feels like a hot mess). Worse yet, despite all these balance issues if you look at the forums, , I know it's still April but April fools passed a while ago. . This along with the lackluster updates pushed me to leave a review.I'll keep my eye on this game (and update the review accordingly), I don't regret buying it as I think it has a lot of potential -  but I don't recommend it as of now.

name: Blue Fire
detailed_description: Journey through the desolated kingdom of Penumbra and discover the hidden secrets of this long-forgotten land. Explore mystical temples, where you’ll need to master the art of movement to survive increasingly difficult 3D platforming challenges. During your adventure you’ll slash your way through daunting adversaries, encounter survivors and take on strange quests to collect valuable items. Hardcore Platforming Leap through deadly traps and master movement to navigate gradually demanding platforming challenges. Lost in the Void Far from Penumbra, there is a lost land called The Void. Find Void entrances throughout the world to uncover abstract platforming challenges that require great mastery to gather the valuable rewards hidden inside. Slash Your Way Through Great Adversaries Encounter dangerous enemies with distinct fighting styles and partake in intense combat-platforming boss fights. A Haunting World Travel through the perished world of Penumbra to explore unique areas filled with diverse enemies, sharp 3D platforming challenges, quests, collectibles and more. Encounter Peculiar Survivors A long time has passed since Penumbra fell into darkness, but those that survived the kingdom’s fall will aid your journey to unlock valuable rewards. Collectibles Once a rich and lush kingdom, Penumbra is filled with many collectibles and items to discover, loot, collect, sell, trade and purchase. Upgrades No great warrior can battle the dangers lurking in Penumbra without the proper equipment. Upgrade your swords, collect valuable amulets and unlock new abilities to transform into a fierce fighter.

The Zelda elements are fairly weak, so I wouldn't get it if you are only interested for that. Especially the combat and most bosses are just turn your brain off fights, apart from the final boss and the dlc boss which were pretty good. I played it on normal so maybe it's better on hard, but I feel like hard mode would only make the bosses more fun but the regular enemies more tedious.Overall I feel like it is pretty rough in some areas but the core gameplay of platforming is very well done with interesting challenges, for me it had around 12 hrs of gameplay in it.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well executed adventure/platform game.Main focus of the game is on its platforming, broken up into metroidvania style progression arcs in which you collect more movement technology and progress though the game.The world is beautifully presented with a soothing soundtrack and the route gives you plenty of agency to backtrack to previous areas to pick up secrets and flex on your new abilities.Controls are responsive and tight, which is really critical for the precision platforming needed, particularly in the challenging void sections.The free DLC adds 16 more platforming levels and another boss all of which are dedicated hardcore endgame content which pushes all the mechanics in the game to the limit. Well worth a look, even if you arent a fan of the genre

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like the reviews on this game are quite mixed and I have to say, It's also the case for me. While I really love the game, I will also admit that it falls just short of a masterpiece for many reasons. Would I recommend the game ? Yes. The Plateforming is fun and their is the "trying to find things out by yourself" that is really nice. It's completely worth the 15€ I paid for it. I will probably be playing much more than I already have.The game is graphically nice as the whole, but I find it very offputting. At some point, you're not too sure what you're looking at because of the low amount of texture details and then there are some textures with a really high amount of details (looks like some open source texture from blender). As for the lore, I feel as if there is something missing to really make the player captured and engaged in the game. Moreover, doesn't feel like a finished game at the present moment, it's lacking the last "attention to every detail" shiny varnish.  On a final note, the game isn't graphically demanding and cheap, so opening the game to linux and mac would have been nice, but I do understand that they've used unreal engine to make the game which restricts them in the available systems.  In conclusion, I feel like this is a test run for the developers (ROBI studio). This seems like their first big game and they have proven themself to be more than capable of creating a fine game. It shows a lot of promises and I believe their next game will the real deal.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game after seeing one of Iron Pineapple's videos about soulslike games, but I don't think this could be further from that definition. Aside from the death mechanic where you lose your money and recover them where you died, Blue Fire is a game that mixes elements from platforming games (it reminded me a lot of A Hat in Time, which is high praise from me) and Legend of Zelda-like dungeon exploration (there's a lot of other similarities like small quests, the structure of certain places you visit and the appearance of the main character, which looks like a mix between young Link from OoT and the Knight from Hollow Knight). The platforming is its strongest point, with exploration that demands you mix your moves in the most optimal way, extra missions with progressively higher difficulty called Voids (self-contained maps that put your platforming skills to the test and reward you with extra health points and containing currency to expand your spirit slots, basically passive powerups for attack, platforming, defense and whatnot which you obtain via quests or exploration) and a very, very well done soundtrack (ranging from moody and melancholy to upbeat and mysterious depending on where you are). The recent update also added a lot more content, which I was fortunate enough to play given that I only received the game two days ago and absolutely stormed through it to completion and full achievement hunt. Combat isn't really very demanding, until you hit the midway point in the game. Then you need to pay attention. Some bosses will be very challenging, especially the last one.Definite recommend for me if you're into Zelda or story driven platform games. I really hope the devs add more content because I'd love to have an excuse to dive back into this beautifully crafted world they created.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: My opinion about this game keeps flip-flopping, sometimes i think it is great other times i think it is awful. If you are on the correct path and exploring new areas, interacting with NPCs and scoping out secrets it can be great but if you are lost wandering around it isn't so fun. So when you first play this game the movement will feel a little slippery, almost as if the character wasn't walking but on rollerblades. After an hour or so you get used to the movement and it will feel fast and responsive for the most part. The best part about this game is the platforming, climbing huge structures and navigating tricky terrain is just enjoyable. The combat is okay, for the most part you just want to explore and enemies are annoying you while you do so. The boss fights are pretty fun, you have to dodge attacks until the boss becomes vulnerable and it is your time to strike. The bosses are pretty easy if you do all the quests and voids, I didn't die a single time.It is very easy to get lost in this game, sometimes the game indicates where a path leads to but often it doesn't. Also some areas lead to more than 5 other paths and everything looks kinda similiar which is a problem especially because the game doesn't have a map. Another issue is that not only can you get lost but the game also does a bad job of making obvious where you are supposed to go. I ended up climbing the entire huge tower in the abandoned path before getting a double jump, in hindsight that was not intended however i spent like an hour doing it because I didn't know that.The biggest issue with the game is probably the camera, it is very reminiscent of the Super Mario 64 camera. Often times you simply cannot see what you are doing. In some of the tougher challenges you will die just because you cannot see the platform you are supposed to land on. Especially on levels with moving obstacles you will often just die because it is nearly impossible to judge how far away an object is from you. The game also has a lot of quality of life issues that make you wonder why it is designed that way. If you are doing a puzzle with a timed switch and fail, you have to watch 2 cutscenes to try again instead of hitting the switch again resetting the timer.The only character that you can sell your items for money to is in the city, so to buy everything from the thief vendor later in the game you have to teleport back and forth 2 times, and go through a total of 4 loading zones just to buy everything from him. Why can't i just sell my items directly to the thief, or any other vendor for that matter?Falling in the void often makes you wait multiple seconds before it resets the level and then after it resets the obstacles might be on an entirely different cycle making you wait even more. Also falling the in the void doesn't reset your extra dash or jumps and it doesn't reset some platforms, making you wait even even more.DLC: I only played 4-5 levels of the DLC. Some are fun, others aren't they are mostly hard void levels where the camera really is miserable, i don't think i will clear the DLC as it isn't required for the steam achievements but it is there if you want more.If i'm undecided about a game i usually recommend it but it does have its fair share of issues.

_childDocuments_.review: In all honesty, It's just kinda fine.It basically combines the gameplay and vibe of the late 90's and early-mid 2000's Zelda games with the some of the souls mechanics when it comes to enviroments, collecting of "souls", use of bonfires (in this game "shrines") for healing and upgrading yourself, etc.All of this sounds like a really innovative and interesting combination of genres in theory, but the execution falls short of being anything spectacular in my opinion as it fails to really do anything interesting that other games in these genre's aren't doing to make this game really stand out in any particular way, It's just kinda of a basic mashup that fails at being a really good platformer nor a really good souls-like either.With all of that being said, I don't think it's a bad game by any means, but it's not great either. It's just kind of okay in a way that keeps you playing but will have you probably forget about it once you're finished.May be worth a pick up on sale if you really like platformers

Before all of this, I really enjoy the game but I wouldn't recommend it for the reasons below.The thing that I like in this game is the hardcore platforming because I am a masochist at heart. That is the part that i enjoy in the game, other than that I do not know if it's only me but the combat is not great it's just not satisfying and the hitbox seems off. Lastly, when you got hit it's like the NES Ninja Gaiden, which means that you could get stun lock especially from the final boss.So, if you enjoy a hardcore platforming game I think you will enjoy this but if you are here for the combat or the story or something, I wouldn't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no reservations about full-heartedly recommending this wonderful game, except for the caveat that the combat, while adequate, is far from a major draw, and the void puzzles, regardless of difficulty setting, can be some real head-bashers—as in, they're so hard they'll feel like bashing your head repeatedly against the wall. But for the most part, the latter caveat applies to a select few of the total puzzles, and they are, technically, optional. Also, I can't help but admit that, while tough, they are never exactly "unfair," and gitting good will carry you far.The world as a whole is full of personality, approximating a kind of N64 Zelda-meets-Dark Souls. The story is a mere pretext for the action, and is therefore rather thin, but many adorable characters and an overall charming aesthetic more than make up for any lack of context. The star of the game is its platforming, and it absolutely shines in that department. Jumping, double jumping, charged high-jumping, wall-climbing—and all with nice, tight controls and good responsiveness. Good audio and a great soundtrack are icing on the cake.

_childDocuments_.review: Did I enjoy this game? Well, I guess, yeah. Is it a good game? Uhh, not reallyHow do I explain this... You know, imagine yourself as a young inexperienced game developer, who likes to play games. You play different games, notice cool stuff and think "When I'll make a game, I want this in it! And this! And this!", without really thinking how all these ideas go together, or do you even need them, you just add what sounds cool. Most of the time these projects don't survive past planning stage or tech demo, but this game feels like it's a project like that that went to completion. Just a bunch of cool ideas held together by duct tape without regard of how really these ideas go together. They have . In a exclusively single player game. There are uses for them, to get some random treasures and trinkets, but this feels more like an afterthought, "aaa, what can we use this for?". Or also - this game has corpse run mechanic. I.e. - when you die, you drop all your money and you have to run to the place where you died to pick them up. And I  corpse run mechanic, that's why I've never managed to play Hollow Knight more than couple hours. But here I didn't even know that this game even has corpse run mechanic, simply because on default difficulty it is so easy, that the only time I've died - it was on the final boss, and by then I've already bought everything money could buy in this game - and it's not like it's hard to grind for money in the first place. At least in HK corpse run had a purpose, Blue Fire have zero need for a corpse runBesides weird design chimera, Blue Fire does not avoid common problems of 3D/platformer/metroidvania combo. Platforming in 3D is frustrating, because it is very hard to measure distance and correctly choose direction - I mean, when you try to dash and go about 30° to the right of where you wanted to go. And you really feel how janky it is in voids - challenge areas. And combination of skill-based gameplay and metroidvania gives you "do I not have an ability that is required to proceed, or I just have to jump better?" - and it's inconsistent, sometimes it's the former, and sometimes it's the latter, had this happen to me both ways in the same area. Also a thing to notice is combat. It's there. It has block, it has parry, it has three hit combo, it has combat-performance-improving accessoires, and it has no depth. I dunno, maybe it's just default difficulty, but I've never had to use anything besides attack-attack-attack-dash-to-avoid-damage. Combat is not this game strong point, and I believe that it would be much better if it wasn't here at all. It feels like it was added purely because "all games have combat". Enemies are not really enemies, more like obstacles you after certain point (when you level up your mana to max) just avoid instead of fighting, and they are more like just annoying than engaging. And so are boss fights. It would be much better if instead of doing your regular "dodge attacks, attack yourself until it dies" it was some sort of, I dunno, platforming challenge. Play on the game strengths - even if they are a bit janky, platforming is still more of a focus in this game than combat. Devs should've go all-in on itSo, after all this negativity, why did I still leave a thumbs up review? Well, despite everything, it is still fun. And when Blue Fire does something well - it does it  well. Despite jankiness, I loved platforming, abilities are fun to use and combine to traverse the land, even if they are simply dash, wall run, double jump and spin attack (that you have to charge ahead of time, and then you can use it to raise yourself higher - I really liked how it works). I loved world design, a set of varied interconnected zones full of stuff to explore. I loved exploration, and finding all these treasures everywhere - even if most of them don't do anything besides completion percent. Seeing that chest in main city way higher than you can reach - and then finding where you can wall run, double jump, dash and then spin attack, to find a neat cosmetic item felt really satisfying. I loved sidequests, and NPCs (even though first time seeing every one of them was like "wait, new enemy? Ah, no, it's just NPC"). And while story and lore are far from perfect (and it occasionally drops plot threads), the game tries to create an interesting setting, and I find it admirable.So, in the end, it is a deeply flawed, but, ultimately, pretty fun game, if you can stomach negatives, you will probably enjoy positives

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard. It's hard but it's fair. The platforming challenges are fun and I loved going through and completing them all. _childDocuments_.review: Misses the MarkBlue Fire is an Action Platform that seems to take inspiration from games such as Legend of Zelda with an atmosphere of Hollow Knight with a small, grimm, protagonist that doesn't says much.Let's compare two games a few games for a moment:Blue Fire vs TLOZ: Wind WakerBlue Fire vs Jak and DaxterBlue Fire vs Sphinx and the Cursed Mummy. What does these games have that Blue Fire Lacks?Personality, there is nothing about the characters, enviorment, music or even the bland artstyle that may captivate my attention such as the games I mentioned earlier. _childDocuments_.review: This game is not just Zelda + Dark Souls. This game is more like Zelda + Dark Souls + Mario 64 (platforming). Making something so familiar yet so different. Cell shading style animation and voiceless dialogue filled with grunts and groans brings on major WindWaker vibes. Lock-on fighting system, bonfire shrines and expansive interconnected level design give Dark Souls vibes. And 3 dimensional platforming level design gives off major old school N64 platformer vibes. Giving this game a solidly new, yet uniquely familiar feel and an all around fun and challenging experience. I highly recommend this game to anyone who just wants a good game to lose themselves in for a while. Very fun. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another iffy recommendation.You can tell the creators have a good understanding of the basics. Level design is fun, lore is decent, and the controls are tight.It feels rather unpolished, though. Just a lot of little things that you'll notice that more experienced game devs would have ironed out by now.Like, for instance, when you jump, there is a particle effect that looks like it's meant to be a trail behind the player. Instead, however, it spawns in all at once in a vertical column. This means that when you jump, a pillar of particles appear above your head. Worse, if you just tap jump, and thus don't reach the height of your jump, your character's head won't even reach these particles.It makes jumping look more like you're being beamed up by aliens who lose interest partway through. It's not a big deal, but it shows that someone somewhere didn't know how to make these particles emit from beneath the player as they moved upwards.Another small one I noticed were on these plus-shaped rotating platforms during a void challenge. When you stand on them without input, your character slowly slides across the surface as it moves under them. It's minute, and so not a big deal, but it's again a sign of sloppiness.All these small things don't bog down gameplay, but it makes the game feel more like a college project more than a finished product from a serious development studio.Also, to those drawn to the game for the Soul-Like tag, that is a straight up lie. The game is not anything like Souls. It's incredibly easy, for one. Seriously, none of the bosses are harder then you might expect from a Zelda game.As for atmosphere, it's much closer to Hollow Knight then Souls, in that while trying to be dark and atmospheric, it's in fact fairly light-hearted with colorful characters and a sprinkling of comedy here and there.It's a fun game, just probably reserved for discount purchases only.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic platformer that draws inspiration from so many amazing titles. From Zelda to Mario to Hollow Knight, heck even Dark Souls. The pacing, exploration, difficulty followed by beautiful artstyle and music score. Gameplay and movement evolves constantly but never in a way to overwhelm a player but rather make you feel getting powerful.If there is one platformer to recommend this year, this is the one. This is coming from somebody who is rather bad when it comes to platformers; some of the challenges were incredibly hard but were a joy to get into rythm to complete. This game will punish and reward you in equal measure.

_childDocuments_.review: I gave an unfavorable review a few months ago for this game, because although it was quite beautiful and with good ambiance, its engine was bad and lacked precision. I dropped the game after a few hours, frustrated.Now I must say that upfront: the engine has been improved greatly, making this game actually interesting to play, and sometimes even very pleasing! Some "Voids" (special platform levels) are particularly well designed, and I enjoyed playing through most of them.That being said, that game does not have much for itself apart from that. I wanted to dive into the lore, but the lore is not very interesting, and is told in the most awful manner (i.e. by random characters popping out of nowhere just dumping a huge "legend of Thingy McStuff" in an unskippable cutscene).If you don't mind, I guess you should be fine. If that bugs you, that game might be a bit disappointing.(spoilers ahead)The lore is weirdly too complicated, yet too superficial. There are 5 gods, and the first too temples are the home of 2 gods, the other three dungeons don't have gods, but Lords, that are entities that corrupt the Queen, which is not a god but very powerful, and also one lord needs four flames to be lit, and there is another temple that needs 4 fire thingy holding the ashes of a forgotten warrior...In the meantime: who am I? Why am I here? What happens at the end (there's only a 3 second cutscene)? What is this alphabet that is used like four time throughout the game with no way to decode it (that I know of)? It is just a big mess and I think it is a shame. Sometimes the story seems to be driven by the gameplay in a very un-organic way, and sometimes they are just completely uncorrelated (why are there 6 statues of god in the water temple? Why not 4 or 5? Why are the first too entity in the dungeons are gods but not in the other? Actually I feel like the dev team only had time to implement 2 dungeons and a half; in which case I am sorry to point this out :( ).All and all, each time lore was being delivered to me, I was slightly annoyed, and felt like everything and nothing was explained to me. The last boss (which is........ not very good) felt meaningless, and I did not understand the last "cutscene", and feel like the story isn't finished.Anyway, for its gameplay the game is okay. In term of visuals and aesthetics it's good. But it is still a bit annoying to play, and it did not make feel anything worth.Oh, actually, Mia and Mira are very cute. I liked the composer's sidequest.

_childDocuments_.review: Great Game overall. The platforming sections and the voids were all incredibly fun to do and felt completely fair. _childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty strong platformer, the controls feel tight, the progression feels natural and there are varying degrees of challenge that can be approached using different methods and tools. It's pretty cool how tightly knit this game is. The explorable world is not very big as you are restricted to a gothic castle in the sky. Even with it being small you will spend quite some time in every area if you're the type to explore. There are hidden weapons, quest items, cosmetics and additional powers for you to discover in every area of the game. The game is a platformer with some very light Metroidvania and Souls elements, if those elements and combat have more priority for you than the 3D platforming then this will not be the game for you. Combat with the average enemy gets dull pretty quick as your combos are very limited, . The boss fights don't really bring anything innovative to the table but make excellent use of the game being a platformer. I think my favorite thing about this game is the voids. The voids are optional platforming maps that you can complete for additional souls, these souls can be spent to unlock equipment slots for additional powers such as the triple jump or double gold bonus. Voids can be approached from several different ways, especially when you start to unlock your spirit powers. These bring together the best components of level design that made PS2 era platformers so good. If you love that older era of 3D platforming games like Jak and Daxter, Vexx, or even Spongebob Squarepants The Movie The Videogame, then this is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the love child of Hollow Knight, A Hat in Time, and Zelda (particularly Wind Waker in terms of art style).It's pretty great, and criminally underrated.The problems I have with the game mostly revolve around its lack of support for certain settings, including but not limited to: Lack of support for resolutions above 1080p (it was locked to that resolution for me, and I saw no way of changing it), an inability to switch to a borderless windowed state, and no support for PS4 button layout on controller, or any others besides Xbox.Gameplay wise, besides the mini synopsis I gave in the first sentence, I could mention the fact that there is no map, and little to no direction in the game's quests, but this wasn't a problem for me until I started going for completion, since I tend to explore as much as I can for stuff anyways. There aren't many resources for finding the secrets, so I recommend looking at the Blue Fire Wiki if you are going for completion.Contrary to what you'd be led to believe from the "Soulslike" label, this game is laughably easy. Some platforming sections are pretty challenging, but combat against enemies is a little pathetic on Normal mode. I was considering playing on Hard mode because of this, but I didn't wanna replay the first section of the game again to do it. I didn't die a single time in my entire playthrough.100% yes, you should! Especially if that first sentence piqued your interest.  This game is a pretty hidden gem with a lot of love and care put into it, even if it feels a little unpolished at times. This game does what it needs to incredibly well, and I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Updating my review after 100%ing the game, leaving the original below for posterity:After giving the game a fair shot and playing it all the way through, I'll upgrade my review to "it's ok". Not bad, not mediocre even, not necessarily good or great, but just ok. Maybe not a thumbs down, but if there was a "meh" option between the two, that's where I land on this. A lot of my gripes with the game from my original review still hold true, chief among which is that platforming feels floaty and slippery. This is somewhat lessened as you get more of the movement abilities, but in a game that is (after playing it all the way) first and foremost a platformer, this is a big con. There are "void" platforming puzzles which are cute little platforming challenges that never get -too- difficult, but to me they felt like they were overly punishing to pad the length of what is a relatively short game. Admittedly, as a budget title, the length is not an issue relative to its price. In a way, I wish that they had done a beta or demo and taken some more time to really incorporate some player feedback, polish the gameplay, and maybe if those were all in check, they could have added more to the game itself. The first two dungeons feel somewhat like a Zelda game, but after that it became more of a linear romp with some uninspired reskins of the same enemies you saw in the first 10 minutes of the game. Seriously, I think there are 3 enemy archetypes that are re-used for the entire game, plus a unique one or two that I'm forgetting because they appear so infrequently. There are a lot of clear inspirations here, but they never really lean in to one in particular, and it results in everything feeling half-baked and underdeveloped. So instead of a solid platformer with Zelda-like dungeons, you get a passable platformer with incredibly simple puzzles and mediocre at best combat. The later bosses are way more exciting to fight than the first two and even make good use of the platforming side of the game, however the moment-to-moment gameplay fighting monsters and traversing the world is a chore. There is little to no incentive to fight enemies, which I guess if that's the point then mission accomplished? But in doing this, a LOT of the game's systems become inconsequential. Upgrading your mana feels pointless because the ranged attack is incredibly weak, and dodging is so much more useful than the shield, which has a very tight parry window. In a game where a lot of attacks have little to no wind-up, this makes an already unattractive shield option that much less attractive. There definitely could have been other uses for magic, or at least some way to buff your magic options beyond "here's more MP". The only passive perk that does anything for those magic options is one that "reduces the cost of shielding". Which brings me to another point: cryptic passive descriptions. How much is it reducing the cost by? Does it reduce the cost to channel it, or reduce the cost when it takes hits? Is it by 50%? 25%? 5%? You could ask these questions for all of the passives, as there isn't a single one which gives you any value as to what extent it "improves" your abilities .The pacing of the game is also to its detriment. Your upgrades are mostly front-loaded, but the healing items are actually pretty heavy in the endgame side of the game. You start with 2 heals, can buy 2 more pretty early on, then there is nothing until the last 2 areas which each give you +3? That's not to mention the plot even, which I guess is going for a cryptic Souls-like "learn from the world building" but fails pretty miserably on this front, with a very forgettable plot and a world that doesn't feel at all lived-in the way that something like Hollow Knight does. Those are big shoes to fill, I get it, but as mentioned in my original review, entering in such a saturated genre like this makes it just that much harder to stand out. Being a passable game just unfortunately isn't enough right now, even as a budget title.If you can get it for $5-10 and love platformers, sure. You could buy worse games. But you could also buy way better games, even for that cost. The developers seem to be active in patching their game and I didn't run across any bugs / crashes in my 7 hour playthrough. There's something there, and for a first game it's honestly not bad. If these guys had a bigger budget, more time, and more experience, I think they could really make something special.Original:In a genre like Metroidvanias that is currently saturated with excellent games, anything that enters the market becomes less "is it a good game" and more "why should I play it over [x]?" In my short time with Blue Fire, I can't think of a great answer to that question. The platforming can feel slippery and frustrating, enemies have attacks ranging from "spammable melee with no wind-up" to "hilariously long recovery frames and no tracking" with little to no discernible pattern between them, and the dungeon puzzles so far have already become repetitive 3 hours in. Additionally, a complete lack of any world / area map is a bit of a baffling decision in what's meant to have at least somewhat of a collect-a-thon aspect to it. There tend to be a lot of little frustrating design decisions throughout, such as how you can lock on to pots, which the game loves to do when trying to enter combat. If you're an absolute diehard for early 2000s platformers and Metroidvanias with a remote Zelda influence, sure pick it up on sale, but only if you haven't played the numerous phenomenal entries in those genres. At the time of this review, it's currently in the August Humble Choice and will likely be on deep sales from here on out, which is unfortunately where it feels like this game belongs.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an amalgamation of some cool games. The platforming of A Hat In Time, a death punishment & recovery system similar to Dark Souls (as well as emotes, which now have rudimentary gameplay use), a castle sprawling with vile meat walls from Amnesia: The Dark Descent. _childDocuments_.review: I wanna start with saying that i don't hate this game, and was not sure if I would recommend it or not, but the last boss made me decide.This game is okay. It's not bad in any shape or form.The mos difficult thing about this game is the damn camera angles, adjusting the camera while doing jumping puzzles gets very annoying.The combat is boring to a point where you just skip the mobs, the lock-on doesn't really work and the flying enemies are very hard to hit.Now, I played this game on normal, and it was extremely easy. First time I died was on the last boss. But since the combat is very boring and not flowy at all I really wouldn't wanna try it on a higher difficulty.It is a unique game with some jumping puzzle challenges, and if it wasn't for the camera angle being very annoying and was the main reason I failed jumps, they would be very fun.There are some sidequests, and they are quite boring to do, and many of them involve backtracking to NPCs you may or may not have seen.The boss fights are very tedious, easy and boring. This game combines the challenging platforming of Hollow Knight, backtracking for key progression items like Metroid, dungeon design loosely inspired from Zelda, and aesthetics borrowed from Hollow Knight and Dark Souls. _childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a fun, if a little wonky, 3D platforming metroidvania, that can best be described as a cross between Mario and Zelda wearing the flayed skin of Hollow Knight.In a mysterious floating castle, you awaken as a litle knight in a cloak with two swords and an edgy haircut. Based on a few cryptic hints, you must travel the Land to Seek the Gods and Purify the Corruption to Restore the Kingdom and Banish The Shadow. The story and general vibe is threadbare and deeply derivative. Ain't nobody launching a middling YouTube career off of videos explaining the Lore of this game.In general, everything not tied to gameplay is somewhat lacking. Not bad, but very drab and unimpressive. The environments are pretty dreary and not hugely exciting. Since everything takes place in a castle of sorts, every area feels like one of the dungeons from Ocarina of Time. Imagine if in OoT, to get to the Fire Temple, you had to pass through the Forest Temple and the Water Temple, with no open outdoor areas inbetween, and you'll have a sense of how the world of Blue Fire feels.It's not bad, but with such a flimsy story and cute characters, having everything look and feel like a Dark Souls Playmobil set kind of drags the mood down unnecessarily.Luckily, the gameplay of Blue Fire rules. Platforming is quick and technical, with plenty of aerial control, but not a lot of time to react. It's a geruinely very clever mix of 3D platforming and exploration, that perfectly translates the escalation and expansion of abilities of a 2D Metroidvania into 3D. You start with a jump and a dash, but by the end of the game (provided you explore the world properly, that is), you'll be walljumping, double-dashing, triple-jumping and just generally swoocing through the levels like a ♥♥♥♥♥-up grasshopper. The game really rewards exploration, and just like in a more traditional metroidvania, if a challenge is too hard for you, just try again later when you've bulked up on movement-enhancing upgrades.It's this sense of progression and growth that had me hooked.The game is the perfect length for what it is. I 100% completed it with relative ease in about 12 hours. Any longer and I would've gotten tired. It does the trick and doesn't outstay its welcome.I bought this game on sale and absolutely got my money's worth. I'd love to see a more polished, aesthetically interesting take on this kind of 3D Platformvania some day, but for now, this will do nicely. Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a nice and intersting 3D platformer with cool dark theme of postapocalyptic/magical world. It's set in a huge levitating castle on the middle of a postapocalyptic, completerly destroyed world where there is nothing but dark, dead lands. It not a long game (15-20 hours for 100% completition). Controls in this game are comfortable and easy to learn. Parkour is interesting and gives you lots of possibilities to explore the world. The world of Blue Fire as I said before is a big castle, which is split into 8-10 big areas with lots of secrets to discover and collectibles to find. Besides pretty good main storyline there is lots of side quests to complete. Skill system is pretty good as well. You can buy and find different skills like double/triple jump, sprint, long dash etc. I had a lot of fun just collecting everything possible. Although the game is fairly easy there is some hard challenges and bossfights. But don't buy this game if you are looking for a challenge. It's more about story and fun rather than difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: This is how I sum up this game in two words:SWEATY PALMS!Fun adventurous hack n slash games that feels like a mix of Zelda and souls-type elements. Simple gameplay, high need of exploration from area to area. It's not open world, but the areas are like a giant cage, or tunnel with multiple exits, but some requiring a new ability to reach. You can learn new things to do better things like jump higher or wall-jump (way more abilities, but that's spoiling). There are no armor upgrades, just health upgrades and you finding new swords that are stronger than what you have equipped. I spent 22 hours in the game to get all 22 achievements, but I guess I suck, because many others beat the game in nearly half the time I took. I spent 2-3 hours on some tough platforming challenges that I wanted to complete, because the reward was always worth it. The only downside is no direction on where to go or how to find the next area, unless you explore every place that has a ledge or someplace you can walk on. The game gets better as you find NPCs with upgrades, or spirits to help aid your character. The mobs will respawn in the area if you enter the area that needs a loading screen. There are maybe 8 areas in total (rough estimate), but can take a while to explore every bit of it. This game is definitely worth the cost value and would be a definite recommendation from me.
