_childDocuments_.review: 15h 22m (based on the in-game clock, 100% achievement, finished the main game + Void of Sorrows DLC) No. Yes (11 achievements). No. is a 3D platformer game with action-adventure elements in it. You will have to explore some areas, clear closed-off platformer sections, and defeat bosses. It also tries to incorporate some Metroidvania elements, introducing power-ups that allow you to access new areas and possibly secret items.- Challenging and unique platformer sections- Power-ups to make the platformer sections easier- Widely explorable areas that hide secrets and easter eggs- Enemies can disrupt the platforming sections- Combat relies too much on platforming controls- Dashing to flying enemies tend to not workIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 characters use simplistic models with cell shading techniques. Characters only have glowing eyes as their facial features, with a black body that makes them look like shadows. On the other hand, backgrounds look more realistic with their textures and shadows. Despite the style difference, they look good together, especially since the camera tends to be placed far from the character.I couldn't seem to find anything about the story. The game has a lot of world-building, though. Most dialogues tell about how everything came to be, and the threat that looms over the place. However, it doesn't tell more than that.  You can only make assumptions - there isn't even an ending after you beat the final boss.'s main focus lies in exploration. You will use your platforming skills to explore the areas and finish some quests. These quests are usually in the form of finishing a dungeon and beating the main boss, which again, involves your platforming skills. You can only do basic skills at the beginning, but more techniques like double jump and dash will be available as you progress.What makes  unique from other games is how it does its exploration. You can take the more direct path to exit the area and progress with your quest, but doing a full sweep on each area will net you more items. Some areas will also be inaccessible until you get the right power-up. Most items tend to be useless, though. The only thing that you need to watch out for is the existence of s, a closed-off platformer section that can give you an extra heart if you manage to complete it. Entering a  will teleport you to a closed-off platformer stage that you need to traverse to reach the exit. It's not as easy as it sounds, though - some areas might require several tries to finish due to their difficulty. Luckily, checkpoints are scattered between the areas. It still won't make it easy to beat, especially since some checkpoints are still placed far from each other, but it makes most s manageable. I don't even think I could beat them without dying once.Some s require you to have a certain power-up, but it never tells you that you need it to proceed. It also works the other way around, though. Completing s will be easier once you get more power-ups, which can be easily done as long as you explore everything. To be honest, the  is my favorite part of the game. The power-ups feel like a great excuse to test out your platforming skills and the  seems to take on the challenge by providing worthy stages that you can try. You will have to try the levels over and over again until either your muscle memory hits or you get lucky, and although I kept on saying I hated it, I ended up saying that I loved it once I finished it. I want more.Sadly, the combat feels like an afterthought. I don't like how enemies can stagger you when you get hit, but they can't be staggered in return. Their attack also persists for several seconds after their attacking animation is over. Moreover, they have a lot of HP and attack quickly, making it hard to dodge with a dash. You can always use a shield to deflect the attack, but I found that the shield takes too much mana - you can only recover it from attacking the enemy, but trying to kill an enemy without taking damage with the shield will net you less mana than you had before the fight. Besides, it's faster to just spam the attack button to beat them.The most annoying thing about enemies is how they tend to ruin the platforming sections. Flying enemies will be placed between some platforms and you need to kill them if you don't want to die from falling because they hit you while you jump. There is still a chance that you might fall if you don't manage to land properly after you attacked them, though. This causes an issue in one of the areas where you need to climb a very high tower. A single fall will mean that you need to redo the climb. Bosses feel similar. They might have different attack patterns, but I found half of them to be vulnerable to attack in mid-air. This forces you to fight at that height, which can be hard to execute if you don't have all the extra power-ups that can make you stay in the air longer. Dodging boss attacks also can be problematic, especially if your extra power-ups are in cooldown. I found myself dying from falling more often than I thought in the boss fights.Luckily, bosses can be cheesed. Although potions can take a long time to take effect, you will find yourself killing the enemies before you ran out of potions. I only died ~3 times in the main game, and 2 of them happened because I forgot to use my potions. The DLC boss is different, though. They feel unfair with their HP - I had to change my power-up loadout to the one that gives extra damage before I could beat them.The in-game clock says that I finished the main game in 11h 27m. The DLC content is only accessible post-game, and I finished everything in 15h 22m. There are 2 difficulty modes that you can choose at the beginning, and the regular mode, the one that I chose, felt right for me. It wasn't hard to beat but it still manages to give me some challenges, especially the s.The game manages to balance the exploration and  sections perfectly. To be honest, I was overwhelmed by the number of s in the DLC - I was almost burned out from all the annoying platforming, but the exploration sections in the main game helped to give me some time before I could tackle another one. Moreover, I like how each  looks unique and still manages to test my platforming skills with its difficulty.If you buy  for its action-adventure content, don't. It might have combat, but that's not where the game truly shines. You want to get  for its exploration and platforming sections - the s. It's all about navigating the terrain, overcoming obstacles, and testing your platforming skills.

The game's visual presentation, characterized by a sleek, neon-infused aesthetic set against shadowy backdrops, left an indelible impression on me. The contrast between darkness and vibrant lighting effects created an atmosphere that was not only visually dynamic but also mysteriously alluring.From the outset, the narrative in Blue Fire unfolded in a subtle manner, leaving room for interpretation and discovery. The game's lore was intricately woven into the environment, with cryptic NPCs and atmospheric storytelling inviting me to delve deeper into the secrets of Penumbra. The mysterious ambiance and enigmatic characters fueled my curiosity, encouraging me to explore every corner of this enigmatic world.What truly captivated me in Blue Fire was its gameplay intricacies. The platforming elements demanded precision and timing, and the protagonist's acrobatic abilities, from double jumps to wall runs, added a delightful fluidity to my movements. Navigating the interconnected environments felt like solving an intricate puzzle, with hidden secrets and shortcuts awaiting those willing to explore.Combat in Blue Fire proved to be a thrilling test of skill. The fast-paced encounters, coupled with diverse enemies and their unique attack patterns, kept me engaged and on edge. Mastering an array of weapons and abilities added layers to the combat experience, making every victory over a formidable foe a satisfying achievement. The game's challenging difficulty heightened the intensity, ensuring that each battle required my full attention and strategic thinking.The Void entrances, or dungeons, stood out as a highlight of my journey. These challenging areas seamlessly blended puzzles with combat, showcasing the game's clever level design. The atmosphere within these dungeons, coupled with their intricate layouts, added a sense of accomplishment to my progression through the game.Ariel Contreras-Esquivel's musical score further enriched the experience, adapting seamlessly to the changing environments. The ambient tunes and intense tracks complemented the gameplay, enhancing the emotional impact of key moments. The synergy between visuals and music contributed to the immersive atmosphere that enveloped me throughout my time in Penumbra.However, Blue Fire was not without its challenges. Occasional camera issues and minor technical glitches slightly marred the experience, though these were mere bumps on an otherwise exhilarating journey.In conclusion, Blue Fire became more than a game; it evolved into an immersive adventure that resonated with me on multiple levels. _childDocuments_.review: This game has an amateurish design, but polished finish, feel to it -- everything is very straightforward, with regards to combat, platforming, even the art style is a shallow cover for the same-old, same-old for every platform brawler I can think of.This game has a feel to it, like a resurrection of the PSP-era "Death, Jr." franchise -- the art style is similar, and the gameplay feels simplistic, in the same manner.  A lot of early 3D platformers had a similar feeling, and they are utterly uninspiring today (TBH most of them were bad then, as well).It's a simple 3D platformer with very simple fighting mechanics, and take my review with a grain of salt -- I got tired of it after about 30 minutes, because I just couldn't find anything original, or otherwise appealing, about it.  The controls were pretty responsive, but the level design is such that I got myself stuck, unable to even kill myself, in some places in the first dungeon, just trying to platform from one broken staircase to another.  No charm, "modern" indie game art style (i.e. bland, cartoony, but in a depressing way), no elegance in the dance of combat, and the platforming was simple and occasionally broken -- although I suspect this part, at least, gets better (the first "void" level had some sparks of platforming interest).  Combat moves involve attacks + uncontrolled motion on the part of the player character, which sometimes cause you to fall off the narrow platforms you fight on, to your death, while locked to an opponent, unable to perceive your immediate surroundings accurately.  Since some odd lava blobs are littered randomly around the environment (in the early level, at least), and tiny blobs enter each combat with a larger foe, the combat is really more about avoiding the environment while staying locked on to the main enemy, and jumping in and out to attack without falling to your death, than it is about dealing with the actual challenge of the opponent.  As such, it's not fun, it's just a relief to be done with, so you can get back to platforming.If you're looking for even remotely good brawling, combined with platforming, avoid this one.  If simple platforming is all you care about, and the occasional "environmental don't-fall combat" sounds fun to you... I guess?Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is an interesting but flawed game.As a platformer it has an amazing moveset that you unlock and upgrade as you progress though the game that makes exploration very fun, though general movement can feel very "loose" and sometimes imprecise, but this can be gotten used to. Combat is very floaty and movement based but also feels generally imprecise.The world is fairly well designed with its platforming challenges and with how interconnected the world is. Unfortunately, with no map, it can be very easy to get lost an have no idea where to progress. The voids act as mini platforming segments ranging from pathetically easy to annoyingly unfair for some of the hardest voids. The game is far from perfect, but it is worth at least giving a look for just how fun the moveset is to use once you have everything.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphics – 6/10Sound –7/10Gameplay – 5/10Story – 3/10Replayability – 4/10Overall – Blue Fire is kind of a weird game. It plays like a low budget version of The Legend of Zelda meets Brave Fencer Musashi. One thing this game would greatly benefit from is a map system, I’m confused why they didn’t have a map system with objective markers to make the exploring a bit more intuitive. _childDocuments_.review: This is a definite must play for people who enjoy deep and fluid movement in their platformers. Blue Fire has some of the best movement in any game I have ever played, and the progression of your move set is vary satisfying as the game unfolds through upgrades that you gain in dungeons as well as spirits that you may find while exploring. What the game lacks in story and combat it makes up with a deep atmosphere and rewarding exploration that will make you want to see exactly what the next location holds.

_childDocuments_.review: Objects visuals not matching hitboxes. Really? In a platformer?There is a clear path over a statue to reach a "secret" item, but the hitbox for the statue is a much larger and less detailed chunk than its visuals. Literally trial and error to figure out where the path leads through invisible walls, requiring a jump through unknown obstacles. Every failure is a half minute climb back up, mostly waiting for a damn slow elevator.TL;DR Tedium and frustration combined. Boring, unrewarding, yet broken enough to make you angry.And plenty of other issues. Ledge grabs often fail, wallruns trigger when they shouldnt.Combat is clunky mess. Way too easy by default, yet horribly clunky to offset that. Shield/parry has an unreliable delay, enemy attack hitboxes are way off, and some can just stunlock and kill the player once caught, without any chance of escaping.Targeting an enemy or object turns the simple, short and horizontal dash into a long distance teleport almost, but does it unreliably. Sometimes the normal dash is executed even when locked, sometimes it drops the player close to the enemy, but still just out of attack range. Otherwise, the mechanic is exploitable to bypass certain platforming sections.Backtracking, backtracking. No actual gain, no worth, no challenge. Just remember stuff to get back later when you have the ability to actually reach it. Then you get a pat on the back, and something mostly useless.Killing a normal enemy is sometimes more fun than a boss... Why am I playing it? Well, I don't. Not anymore. Halfway through, no thanks, enough for me. Got plenty of other (better) games.This game might worth its price, but not the time spent on it.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from a few little things here and there, I honestly found this game a lot of fun to play (as of me writing this, I've been playing it for 12 hours straight, with an extra 4 hours coming from the previous day in which I started playing it for the first time lmao), the platforming aspect is always fun to play around with and I believe the gameplay styles it shares with popular games such as The Legend of Zelda and Hollow Knight are executed well here. Combat outside of boss fights however is somewhat repetitive, though personally that didn't take much away from the experience as the environments were fun to explore and look beautiful, even with the game's relatively simple designs. I would definitely recommend that anyone, especially people who love platformers, get this game immediately because I absolutely loved it and intend on doing multiple playthroughs as it was a blast to play. Definitely a game I'd recommend to all my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: Hi internet-stranger!As you can see I have played this game for 14-ish hours, I did everything it asked me to do, I got all the  achievements there are to get and now I sit here, contemplating how to talk about Blue Fire.I will keep this short and simple:Blue Fire...... starts off as Zelda, then turns into a "open world exploration game" without any sense of directing you towards your goals.... is crammed full of instanced jump-and-run skillchecks, that will make your eyes bleed.... has cheap,  cheap difficulty spikes caused entirely by the fact that enemies start out as pushovers, then suddenly stunlock you to death while dealing incredible amounts of damage.... forgets how it wants to be played and rushes you towards an ending once you get to the half-way mark.... only lasts 10-ish hours depending on how dedicated you are to finding everything in this game.... assumes your Galactic Alphabet is very polished, otherwise you are faced with boss monologues which you won't be able to read.... has the same 2 enemy types for the entirety of the game, one being a floating turret, which will kill you, whenever a new rendition appears on the screen.Blue Fire...... may possess the most responsive and natural feeling controls I ever experienced in a 3D Platformer.... also has some really challenging and fun instanced jump-and-run skillchecks (which makes the horrible ones feel worse, tbh).... has really cute character design.... offered me 14 hours of not-being-bored.... will be 100% completed achievementwise from just finishing the main storyline and all sidequests, which are conveniently placed around said main storyline.Blue Fire is a really nice game, it's fun to play, it's responsive, it's a great platformer and has a rather charming look to it.Sadly it has major flaws in the way it is build, it feels rushed, like half of the game hasn't been made and instead you are sent out to do some stupid exploration quest in order to fight bosses that seemed to have belonged into proper dungeons instead.Over and over again you will find yourself biting the dust because of ridiculously stupid reasons, like enemies hitlocking you, stunning you over pits or bosses insisting they have to float over a vet of lava, so you can only fight them in the air, then you slip, get hit by the boss, are hit by the lava and upon respawn you respawn in a void-zone causing even more damage. 1-2-3, dead player!The game is frustrating as hell, despite all the fun you have inbetween, which, all in all, makes Blue Fire even more frustrating and a real disappointment.This could have been a dark and gritty Zelda-like, with an amazing story, fun dungeons and platforming and instead... it's kind of a mess.

_childDocuments_.review: to be fair, i will say the good things about the game as well as the bad.the gameplay is nice and all, its fun and the concept seems great. the graphics are pretty as well.main issue is the constant crashes, every time i crash i end up starting from the beginning of the game with my items still intact, that means i was not losing my saved file or anything but it just decides to throw me at the beginning of the game and i have to run all the way again across 2 maps (with checkpoints unlocked).the keys are sometimes unresponsive and i have sat in an empty place just testing it, 8 out of 10 times the dodge button actually dodges, 8 out of 10 times the shield actually opens when i use it, same with my attacks, i click 3 times sometimes for the attack to come out. i changed the keybinding to only keyboard and the problem was still occurring. _childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is an interesting start. That is the first thing that comes to mind when I think about how I feel about this game. My overall feeling with it once I finished it was contentment, with a feeling of slightly missed opportunity that was filled in by how solid other aspects of the game are.Graphics are simple, soundtrack is good, yadda yadda yadda. You already know the deal.What stands out here is the gameplay. Metroidvania platformers are extremely fun. This is one of those and therefore is extremely fun. Using a limited moveset to get around the map, only to use your expanded moveset later to breeze through it is a defining moment of this game.Combat is alright. Parrying, Arial bounces, dodge. It is all here. The thing is though, you are platforming through the combat it creates this satisfying dodge and weave play style that is very nimble and unique. It is extraordinarily easy though. I played on hard, and the combat was pitiful in most cases. That is not what you are here for though, you are here for the platforming.The platforming in this game is so good that it holds everything else in the game up. While the other aspects may be ok or lacking, the platforming is a proper challenge that will test your patience and willpower. By no means of the word is it undoable or the hardest, but it is a fun challenge. Especially with the DLC this game has.My major complaint with the game is the badge system. It is kinda just tacked on. Sometimes they're borderline useless (Damaging dodge anyone?). Other times they are game breakingly good. The double double jump and double dash in specific. Those trivialize some of the void challenges. They do give way to some fun skips, but they feel like a last second addition that doesn't mesh with the rest of the game most of the time.Voids are the peak of this game. Most if not all are extremely fun bite sized platforming challenges. I love these so much, and they felt so rewarding to playthrough. They made a whole DLC dedicated to challenging voids, and it is 100% the most fun you will have with the game. Sadly, there are no achievements or even a sign that it is there, so I almost missed it. Just make sure you play it. It is extremely fun.Blue Fire is overall a great game. While some aspects are lacking, none are bad, and the platforming more than makes up for any short comings. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a great game beneath obnoxious faults. Jumping and dashing feel precise and easy to control. Gaining more platforming abilities leads to exploration in a way reminiscent of classic Metroidvanias. Combat has a hit-and-run like fluidity to it. BUT, and it's a big but, there are flaws ridden throughout that frustrate the moment to moment gameplay. The most noted issue is a lack of checkpoints within the Void platform challenges. Any challenge above a three star rating, you can expect to be extremely lengthy, and one mistake sends you back all of the way to the beginning. You can be 99% of the way through a challenge, having collected every orb within, and one error means back to the beginning, and these challenges are no joke. I like the challenge. I appreciate what the developers are demanding of players, but these challenges are ruined by a lack of proper checkpoint systems. Then there are various other small issues that need to be addressed. In the open world, while exploring, falling sets your character back on platforms you're not sure of, and there is no time to readjust to the reset. That means, if you jumped away from a platform near a ranged enemy and fall, you are sent right back to that platform with the enemy mid-charge on their ranged attack. This has led to deaths that feel frustrating as I cannot do anything to prepare for the reset before getting hit again. The game does not stop you from selling more Ores than you have room for in your wallet. Without realizing the wallet limit of 2,999 initially, I sold easily 10,000 worth of Ores, losing 7,000 of the value in the process. I could not reset this mistake because of the auto save system. Lastly, I have had numerous bugs and crashes throughout my four hours with then game so far. Even with the auto save feature, you are sent back to the last shrine rested at, meaning I have spent 10 minutes of progress lost multiple times. One major bug I had made my character hurt himself in confusion every time I swung my swords. I was simply trying to hit a lever and my character ended up beating himself to death. This has been a lot of complaints, but I genuinely have had so much fun with the game when not dealing with the aforementioned issues. I am really invested in the moment to moment platforming, branching exploration, and appealing aesthetics (the music is great, varied instruments with a flair of Austin Wintory). This has a classic Zelda vibe with heavy-handed influences in Dark Souls and Hollow Knight, all in a good way. I really think the Devs have something great here, they just need to go back and address these issues that frustrate their otherwise great game. With that in mind, this game sadly sits at around a 6/10 for me right now. I do plan on finishing this game because I find it fun, however I will not be attempting to complete all of the side quests and challenges like I normally would want to do with a game such as this. If the Devs can go back and correct the design frustrations I have and patch up the game to rid it of bugs and crashes, this game could easily jump up to and 8/10 or 9/10. As of now, buy this game if you are craving a challenging 3d Hollow Knight. $20 is not too much for that. Otherwise, wait and see if the Devs make updates to the game over the next few months.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is entertaining, though in parts lacking depth and polish. The reason I don't recommend this game is that Steam Cloud saves don't work, due to the Steam Cloud directory and the actual save data directory being two different folders. It should be easy to fix, and in fact the devs announced that the problem was fixed in patch notes a few months ago, but the problem persists. I hope that some day the problem will be fixed, for real, and I will finally be able to recommend this game, because despite its flaws I had fun playing it. Once I know that future players won't have to relive my frustration at losing their save and having to restart the game, the fact that I lost my save won't affect how willing I am to recommend this game to others.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing first effort for the developers, but not without its issues.  I had a mostly great time 100%ing this game.For major issues, the combat sticks out as the easy target.  To put it bluntly it is not good, but it feels like the devs know it isnt good.  That doesnt make it okay, but I think the devs designed around its flaws pretty well.  Your basic swing comes with a dash forward making controlling it pretty awkward.  Ground fights turn into these weird skating matches with you dashing around the enemy or zooming to a different target.  It doesnt help that enemy variety is lacking all around, both in moves and types.  The dashing makes platforming awkward too, but I dont think this one is actually a fault, just something you have to get used to. Anyways, since grounded combat kinda sucks the devs focused on aerial combat for most of the major fights, which is much more reliable. This means its greatest issue isnt really that big of a deal in retrospect, even if in the moment it can be annoying.  As for the much better side of the game, the platforming, I dont have a ton of complaints.  Some platforming sections were a little rough and as always in these kinds of games making your way through the world in the beginning is a little painful, but by the end, you are insanely mobile.  I was pretty impressed with what the game would let me do with a full mobility build in terms of skipping sections or tackling them my own way.  You have so many options of what you can do mid air that its actually a little hard to keep track of.  But I very much enjoyed mapping out the exact string of jumps and dashes needed as I pushed forward through a tough level.  Doubly so when scouting a level and saying "no way I can make this jump from here" then proceeding to do it.  Something I found neat that I would like to see in other games or expanded on in future titles by Robi Studios is useful emotes.  They basically act as a collectable in this game, as each one will unlock a chest for you nearby.  Right now you just stand on a plate with the picture of an emote, but it would be cool if NPC's could react to you doing different emotes.  Just as an example, doing a threatening emote to a shop keeper could produce different results.  If the shopkeep is a coward maybe he will lower his prices to appease you, but a brave one would raise them in defiance.  When the emote seller told me emotes would be useful my mind raced with ideas, and even though what Blue Fire delivered on was a little middling, I think an expanded system could be really cool. One last note.  Its pretty obvious that this game wears its influences on its sleeve.  This in and of itself is not a bad thing, though if done poorly it can be.  I think this game teeters close to that line, but doesnt cross it.  Yes, it has Hollow Knights charm system, Zelda/Dark Souls' exploration, and 3D Mario/A Hat in Time's movement systems (hell one of the emotes is even a direct reference to hat kid), but I think they mesh together well enough to become something unique.  Nothing exists in a vacuum anyways, and if those are the games you're pulling inspiration from, then I think its no surprise that the game ended up being as good as it is, even if a little rough around the edges.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, I just beat this game 100% and I can safely say that I had a lot of fun. That said, this game IS janky as heck, and often feels like the developers just pilfered a bunch of stuff they liked from other games together into what feels like both a masterpiece and a hot mess. And it takes quite some time before it hits its swing, so patience is a necessity. I would recommend that if you are a fan of A Hat in Time, the 3D Zelda Games, Hollowknight and Dark Souls, and wanted to see what would happen if you smashed them together into a half-baked, shambling, yet strangely charming abomination, then I would say go for it. Otherwise wishlist this game and wait for them to fix some of more egregious bugs. Or lacking that, for it to go on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit - took 12 hours to get 100%. Love the Banana costumeRecommended - this is a fun platformer with a lot of ideas (potentially too many ideas) that keeps you going with swift progression and lots of stuff to collect. Definitely had a great time so far and thinking about completing this 100%It kind of does everything without being a master of anything:- it has a Zelda-like story and structure, but its very straightforwards, - its a bit souls-like with currency and corpse runs but without complex enemies- its a bit metroidvania like with abilities that unlock new areas and secrets via backtracking, but theres not a great deal of variety in abilities (dash, double jump, wall grab, spin boost) and you execute skips early on without much trouble - it has some Mario Galaxy like platforming courses which are the best part of the game, especially if you want to challenge your platforming abilities on those 5-star courses by removing all the handy spirits like long dash, double dash, extra spin height, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially I was reluctant to leave a positive review, as for the somewhat steep price the game offered clean and fun gameplay, but not a lot of content and replay value. However now that I've seen that the devs still update the game and add free content, bugfixes and balancing I can very much say the game is worth it. Gameplay is fun, rebalancing was needed and delivered in some areas, specifically the fire boss was a harsh difficulty spike, but that all got fixed in the recent update. The void update also added a lot of new content, doubling down on the game's strong platforming mechanics, adding another 10 hours of great gameplay. Strongly recommended if you enjoy 3D platformers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked a lot more appealing in the trailer. It's not a bad game, honestly, but there's better things out there.I went with normal mode because it's, "For new players," and didn't expect it to be so easy. I only died once, and it was to the final boss. Up to that point, I hadn't been paying attention to my health at all because whatever damage you take can be mitigated by a healing-on-kill spirit. Nothing did enough damage or ever really stood in my way. Half way through I just started avoiding enemies because I wouldn't gain anything by killing them. Needless to say, the combat isn't by any means challenging and neither are the bosses. The first boss is a joke. It's a plant that shoots a wave around itself that does so little damage you can tank the entire boss without healing yourself. The rest are a bit more creative, but none stand out as especially fun or challenging. The platforming is the highlight of the game. Some of the void missions feel like a joke, but the four and five star ones are especially challenging. The main challenge is really just angling the camera into just the right spot so that you can actually gage the distance between you and the wall, diamonds, spikes, and blades.There's nothing about this game that is punishing or there to make you suffer. It's cute, simple, and kinda boring.As for the lore, there's barely even one. Nothing deep or complex by any means.If you don't like dying, and you want to play a relaxing platformer, Blue Fire is the game for you.Maybe it's more of a thrill on hard mode, but there's nothing about my experience that makes me want to play it again. I got every achievement in one go. Why go back?

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty much Hollow Knight 3D. If that speaks to you, just get it already. If you're that scared ya won't like it, just get it with a discount. It's well worth the money and they're still working on updates/patches!If you really want me to talk about why you should get it: you get total freedom with the movement, which in return gives you the option to skip certain parts of dungeons or reach areas much earlier than you're supposed to. It's a ton of fun and the developers don't mind at all. You've some extra "shrines" ala Breath of the Wild that give you more health. Some of those can be incredible difficult (potentially sadastic), but the movement makes it a ton of fun. The difficult spike is kinda everywhere, but I expect nothing less from a somewhat Metroidvania game.I didn't really bother much with the story, not always in the mood to read a ton. The characters are all very great, I wish that they weren't only useful for 1 quest and that's it, but hey!Looking forward for more!

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a solid game when it comes to it's core fundamentals but one that I honestly found to be pretty easy. Once I booted the game up and started playing it I found that there was some fair challenge when it came to not only the platforming but also the combat. The issue is that as I progressed further on the challenge in both of those categories started to wane. Combat as the game went on felt like it went from trying to be fairly balanced with offense and defense to being able to just unga bunga my way through. Then there's the platforming. Once I got my hands on a set of souls, equippables that give you different perks and abilities most of the platforming challenges fell to the wayside. By the end of the game I had a triple jump that could then use two air dashes that then I could use spin jump for increased height. It's absolutely broken how good some of the spirits in this game are. Now that's not entirely a bad thing since it meant I could stress test the platforming challenges and find new ways to navigate the world. With my two biggest sticking points of the game out of the way the rest of the elements are perfectly fine; Just fine. Story is there but I didn't really care too much for it. Characters are charming if one note. The art style is great and it makes the world feel both bleak and colorful. The ost was serviceable but I couldn't remember a single song from the game. I do recommend the game if you're looking for a 10-12 hour adventure.

If the game did not have these flaws it would probably be an 8 out of 10 and if it had a lot more content (Hollow Knight level content) and a map, it could be closer to 9 or 10.Either way, I enjoyed the game for what it was.

_childDocuments_.review: As many others have said, it is a cross between Hollow Knight and Zelda.  Overall, I really enjoyed this game, good platforming, metroidvania, reasonable sized maps + length of game.  The platforming is very tight and unforgiving, which usually is a good thing.  I however struggled with the character feeling super floaty and hard to control precisely, which was frustrating in a few areas and voids.  The combat is not a huge part of the game, which for me is a plus - you will always be very very squishy, focusing more on dodging and moving, which is fine, as the game gives you tools for it.  Once I obtained the double jump upgrade, the game REALLY opened up and the movement started feeling very nice as opposed to just okay.  Other reviews complain that the game goes from a linear structure to 'open world'  That's not really how it felt to me - once it was less linear, it was more metroidvania -- where can I go now that I can wall ride and double jump?I received this game as a part of my Humble Bundle monthly subscription, it took me around 11 hours to 100%.  While I spent some time lost, I eventually figured everything out, only needing to look up the location of 2 voids that I had missed.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a strange mix up of Zelda in tone, Dark Souls in mechanics, and Journey in appearance...with LOTS of platforming. A strange combination, sure, but one that works in practice.Blue Fire starts off with very little exposition of the world you're dropped into, and while it does manage to explain some of the setting and lore, much is left to your imagination. This might bother some, but the mystery and intrigue behind the world kept me just interested enough to get through the story being told. All in all the story is quite a simple and straightforward one, with some optional humorous and melancholic sidequests peppered throughout.Mechanically, Blue Fire is truly a platformer at heart. Your bread-and-butter arsenal of jumps, dashes and wall runs will carry you through most of this game's challenges. Both level design and combat are designed around platforming, with much of the obstacles in both relying on your ability to successfully navigate the environment to progress. In combat, much of the challenge relies on dodging attacks, as most enemies are quickly vanquished (as are you)! You will be darting in and out of attack ranges to deal damage in almost all situations and this is only complicated by enemies' area of effect attacks which pose additional obstacles to stop your approach. Other enemies will float over dangerous terrain, requiring you to jump towards them and hit them in the air while ensuring you've left a jump or dash to return safely to the ground. At the very least, combat was always demanding, and at worst it became predicable as enemies types and strategies began repeating.With so much demand on precision, it was great that the controls were up to par. There's a lot of finesse to master in Blue Fire and learning the slight difference between a short hop and long jump, or a short vs long dash is an important skill in many of the demanding (but optional) "void trials". These are short to long platforming sections that will really test your abilities. There are multiple of varying difficulties which, when completed, give you an additional heart as well as containing a currency in them that allows you to purchase additional "spirit slots" (which grant you place abilities which amplify your combat, platforming or other benefits). These trials varied from entertaining to downright frustrating as some are very, very long and dying places you at the start, instead placing checkpoints throughout to ensure you didn't need to complete the easier, rote beginning. Thankfully the rest of the game outside these trials is relatively easy. There is a dark souls-esque feature that drops your accumulated experience at the place of your death, which you can then retrieve if you manage to return there the next life, but this was honestly never a problem for me, as most deaths relating to platforming placed the lingering soul at the start of the platforming section rather than on the isolated platform I was trying to reach. Combat as well is rather simple with one button required to attack, a useless ranged fireball (more useful to interrupt opponent's attack), and a shield which counters with good timing (not terribly useful as most combat is aerial). Most platforming required in the main game is rather tame, especially compared to what is present in the void trials.At the end of Blue Fire I was left quite pleased with my 15hr experience. Most of my memories of the game come from the quirky characters you might find in a Zelda game, the lovely (if simple) aesthetics similar to Journey, and the feeling of power I gradually gained by the end of the game with the various weapons, abilities and skills I unlocked. There's plenty to love here and the game never outstayed it's welcome; on the contrary I wished it was a dungeon or two longer! Besides, what other game lets you dress up as a dual wielding banana who can break out to techno music whenever you want?

_childDocuments_.review: Title: A Journey of Light and Shadow - Blue Fire ReviewBlue Fire is a 3D action-adventure platformer developed by Robi Studios and published by Graffiti Games. Set in the mysterious world of Penumbra, players take on the role of a small warrior named Umbra, tasked with uncovering the secrets of the realm and restoring light to the world. With its unique blend of platforming, exploration, and combat,  offeringa thrilling and memorable experience that is both challenging and rewarding.  Umbra, who awakens with no memory of his past or understanding of his purpose. Across his journey, he encounters a variety of characters, each with their own stories that provide glimpses into the world's history. Additionally, faces off against numerous foes, hinting at a much deeper corruption that has taken hold of the realm.One of the game's strongest aspects is its engaging gameplay mechanics. The platforming sections are precise and responsive, with a variety of moves at the player's disposal, such as wall running, double jumping, and dashing. The combat is equally satisfying, utilizing a combination of melee attacks, dodging, and parrying to create intense and strategic encounters with various enemies and bosses.The world of Penumbra is beautifully crafted, boasting a distinct art style that combines elements of darkness and light. The varied environments, from the haunting Void to the lush Greenpath, are rich in detail and atmosphere. This is further enhanced by the memorable and immersive soundtrack, which perfectly complements the game's overall tone.Also offers a wealth of content, with numerous side quests, collectible items, and hidden areas to discover. These optional tasks provide additional challenges and incentives for exploration, rewarding players with useful upgrades and lore-filled tidbits.However, the game is not without its flaws. Some players may experience occasional camera and control issues, particularly during more complex platforming sequences. These can lead to moments of frustration and unintentional deaths, disrupting the motivation to continue...Additionally, the difficulty  can be inconsistent, with some sections presenting substantial difficulty spikes. While many players will appreciate the challenge, others may find it off-putting, especially when coupled with the  control issues.Lastly, the storytelling  is relatively minimal, relying on environmental cues and scattered lore to piece together the narrative. While this approach can be effective , those seeking a more in-depth and coherent story may be disappointed.In conclusion, Blue Fire is an engaging and challenging action-adventure platformer with a beautifully crafted world and memorable soundtrack. Despite some occasional camera and control issues, and a lack of in-depth storytelling, the overall experience is one that fans of the genre should not miss.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire starts with you waking up alone in a container filled with water, not knowing where you are or how you got there. Ok I know what your thinking and yes this sounds very much like the start of Breath of the Wild and... uh... well... I got nothing but moving on...Other then basic tooltips for movement and other controls, the game doesn't outright tell you where to go, which is great because immediately Blue Fire is already setting a precedent that if you want to make progress, the only way to do so reliably is to simply adapt and explore.On the topic of adapting, the first thing I noticed when hoping into Blue Fire is just how good it feels to move in this game. Running, Jumping and Dashing is incredibly fast yet precise all at the same time. This flows equally well into combat situations, which Blue Fire is certainly not shy to introduce you to.Shortly after your first battle experience appears a chest, where you'll find your first permanent upgrade. A shield. Its a simple feature and doesn't come into play much in the rest of the game but it does sets the stage for the rest of your adventure. In just the first 5 or so minutes of the game, Blue Fire has told you that exploration and discovery for the most part is up to you, and that at least for now, your character is incomplete.For those of you who’ve played anything close to resembling a Metroidvania... Alarm bells have already started ringing and you're likely already expecting that there may be sections made inaccessible until you've progressed a bit farther into the game. Within the first 5 or so minutes of gameplay, Blue Fire has already introduced you to the concept of dungeon keys and surprise encounters... and 5 minutes later, Blue Fire introduces the idea of quest, side quest, and a glimpse to the grand narrative of the entire story. All without direct explanations or immersion breaking tooltips. Its a small thing and not really something you'll notice unless you actively look for it... or unless something so directly pointed towards the player is said that it completely ruins any sense of immersion you may have gathered at that point....[/code]Combat takes... a bit of a back step in favor of movement here. Sure it can feel REALLY good at times to hit the perfect parry before delivering swift justice...but that high only last for so long when your fighting the same 3 or 4 recolored enemies over and over again. Not to mention that enemies... Don't really do a lot of damage. Now before we continue with this line of thought... please do take this with a grain of salt as I have committed the unforgivable crime of selecting the... Normal difficulty... So... Just keep that in mind.Very early on, it gets to the point where enemy damage output simply can’t keep up with how much health I have to tank with. This makes combat encounters feel very mundane to say the least. I thought I could fix it by just raising my difficulty but it turns out that once you start the game, there's no changing that...The healing ability. Now having a healing ability on its own is certainly not a bad thing for a game like this to ship with. Dark souls famously has the Estus Flask and no one complains about that so why is Blue Fire any different? Well healing Items like this aren't usually meant to serve as a reset to combat. The Estus Flask will typically works as a walk back for maybe 2 or 3 mistakes before your back where you started. Blue Fire doesn’t work that way... for most of the game, your healing ability i enough to carry you all the way through a dungeon and to the next shrine or previous shrine if you have to backtrack...The times where difficulty does spike up feel random and misplaced compared to the rest of the game. Add the fact that you really dont have to fight the enemies past a certain point as the currency rewarded for defeating them is used only as a way to buy a limited supply of mana upgrades. Once you’ve upgraded that mana bar completely, theres no other reason to even engage with these guys unless your forced to.[/code]I ran into 2 boss battles that I thought were genuinely entertaining. As far as all the other bosses? Well...Throughout the entire game, there's an emphasis put on movement, exploration, and discovery. When ever you find a new permanent upgrade, the game either puts you in a situation where it'd be beneficial to use it or had given you the upgrade after leaving an area where you wish you had it. Yet when it comes to most boss fights... non of that stuff matters.Kind a like now is a perfect time to round out this video.Whilst playing the game there were so many moments where it felt like Robi Studios really wanted me to sit down, take a breath, and ground myself in the experience I was in... Yea that's right... This whole game is a huge vibe check...The whole is greater then the sum of its parts and for that reason, If you’re even a little bit interested in what Blue Fire has to offer then I’d say Its definitely worth picking it up.

Well, Blue Fire's story and mechanics is easily understandable and you get more powerful and better at platform parkour over time. Speaking of parkour, The voids are challenging and fun. _childDocuments_.review: Noticeably lacks in polish, but it's fun for its money. Some might find the lack of checkpoints frustrating, however this is more of a platformer, you'll rarely ever be forced to fight. And there are only a few Void trials that could get on your nerves if you insist on doing them as soon as you can.The combat is very, very simple. The shield, its parry and the magic attack you'll never need, thanks to both your dash and double jump refreshing whenever you hit an enemy mid-air. They don't seem to scale in any way either, so it's mostly mashing the attack button and staying airborne while dodging away whenever an enemy attacks.Platforming is decently fun, but feels like it's restricting itself. You get most upgrades for it at about 25% into the game, but it never makes it complex nor gives you a whole bunch of freedom with it. You make the jumps you were meant to make. Voids are sort of an exception for this, because they (well, actually only a couple) demand something of you, and if you fail you have to restart it from the beginning.There are a whole bunch of collectibles, but they're either 1) useless, 2) quest items, 3) ore for sale or 4) robes that have no gameplay effect. You also find spirits sometimes, which are basically Hollow Knight's charms, but there aren't that many of them. They do have a pretty significant effect on your character, but mostly the movement based ones. They're what makes it fun, I'd say.Bosses are a highlight as far as combat goes, but they aren't very complex either. Closest comparison would be Zelda. The game could've benefited from way simpler combat that didn't feel like you have to spam attacks.Still, pretty good for its price. And you'll probably enjoy it a lot more if you don't feel the need to be a completionist and leave the voids you have trouble with for later. I got 22/22 achievements, and one of the worst parts of the game is probably the UI. Especially when you're trying to quickly go through shops.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like if Mario and Zelda had a baby, who then grew up idolizing Hollow Knight. Platforming is a little floaty, but there are traversal powerups - and so many modifiers for those powerups - that in the right hands this game has as much platforming versatility as any 3D Mario title, and it feels great.There is no map, but there are only a handful of interconnected, visually distinct areas. IMO, no-map was a good choice.The other main point of frustration will likely be the Void zones. They're self-contained platforming challenges, but the aforementioned upgrades significantly modify the level of difficulty, and I think only the first one is actually mandatory. Blue Fire has great gameplay, interesting lore, and plenty of character. It's not the longest game, but they've already added their first  DLC update (which doubled the number of Void zones). I got it with Humble Monthly a while back, but even if I had spent $20 on it today, I'd be very happy with my purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: just play hollow knight. blue fire seems to want to desperately be hollow knight but 3d, but it's just not on that level lol. idk i'd rather play hollow knight than blue fire. hollow knight's more fun in literally every way.in terms of actual review though:The game is inconceivably difficult to navigate. you won't make any progress unless you bash your skull through a wall, because there is no map, and also backtracking is literally a requirement to progress the plot and get to some of the later bosses.platforming challenges can be needlessly unforgiving. the first dungeon has a challenge where you're timed, and if you screw up and fall you have to start over, but you're new to the game so you literally don't have the expertise the game wants and expects you to have, so you're kinda screwed and you have to do it over and over and over and over again until you finally manage to get through it.It does this again just before the second dungeon, but worse because its a giant tower, not a 2-minute task, and you'll get knocked out of the air numerous times by poorly placed enemies that you can't kill because you're out of mana and there's no way to reach them with your swords, and also they freeze you midair so you can't reorient yourself in time to keep from losing massive massive chunks of progress unless you're extremely lucky.There's a void challenge where the hitboxes of the obstacles are too big, it makes trying to get through it feel like scratching my nails on a chalkboard. It doesn't feel like I'm the one screwing up, it feels like the game just hates me in particular for daring trying to complete the stupid thing.Progression is a gigantic drag, I enjoyed it at first but after walking through the world 50 times for an hour or two because I couldn't figure out where the hell the next town was really soured that. You can't have mapless navigation, confusing structures, AND hidden entrances to plot-relevant locations. Actually, scratch that, your plot-relevant locations shouldn't be hidden to begin with, I had to look up how to get to firefall river and I only barely figured out where to find the ice forest areas.It's also sometimes extremely unclear what I need to do to get further in the game. I have no idea how I got as far as I did in the first place, aside from just wandering around and collecting stuff. For a good chunk of my experience I thought the game was JUST stoneheart, the forest boss, the sewers, and whatever the first area is. I was not excited when i was told about the ice area, I was solely "oh there's more places? okay where" and then spent 30 minutes trying to figure out where it was.The combat is boring and a bit unintuitive. Fights aren't fun. Don't buy blue fire hoping for combat, it's just not a combat-centric game, it's a platformer with a sprinkling of badly-designed enemies.Enemies don't receive any kind of knockback, they can still attack even as they're taking damage, meanwhile you, the player, can be knocked back several in-game feet or whatever and you'll have to run back up to it to try n hit it again.Flying enemies are a massive pain and often the only way I can easily reach them is magic, which rarely ever does enough damage to take them out in a reasonable amount of time. Some of them can be reached with your swords, but they might hit you before you get up there and knock you away or, uh, off the stupid ice tower.The bosses' attack patterns have no regard for how the player character is designed; I don't think it's possible to beat the first two hitless, because it's impossible to jump all of their attacks due to how the jumps are timed.Overall it's just not that good a game, which is kind of a shame. The lore is kind of neat, the platforming can be really fun and it's rewarding, but the bad experiences and the terrible balancing really stick out. You can only fail so many times before you want to do something you know you won't fail miserably at and have to start over.You can only deal with so many Paths of Pain before it loses meaning.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire~~~~~~~~ROBI Studios just brought in another of their excellent 3D Action-platformers, Blue Fire. An excellent mix of well-crafted gameplay with amazing audio and visuals. A dark fantasy filled with hack and slash combat and platformer elements with a strong push to explore the game's beautifully crafted world. Initial reaction to the game? A fun hack and slash platformer with stunning visuals, which also comes with a strong storyline. But it’s not all sunshine and sunflowers, Blue Fire also comes with it’s a fair share of issues which we will get to in a bit.Plot: Penumbra is a far-away, desolate kingdom, engulfed in darkness and ravaged by the dark forces.  Penumbra once was a peaceful and prosperous land but now it’s in the grasp of malevolent forces. Just when all hope of light fades, a hero awakens in a laboratory. He finds nothing but death, destruction, and darkness upon breaking free from his comatose slumber. Now our young hero must investigate these dark forces and save the kingdom of Penumbra from their grasp. Gameplay: Right from the get-go Blue Fire pushes players to explore and investigate the world that surrounds our main protagonist. At first, nothing is certain and there are very few clues given in the form of item interactions as to where the story is heading. But as you explore further into the game, you will be greeted with more pieces of the story through the NPCs. And as you explore you will encounter handy stepping stones that will give you more insight into all the neat features of the game. The base movement machines are simple and effective, with WASD to move and the mouse to move the camera. So far so good, but where the game starts to confuse me a bit is with its jump machines. Many people seem to be okay with it ,but tbh I am not a big fan. To perform some simple jumps all you have to do is face the right direction and hit W and jump at the very edge; simple enough. For longer gaps, it’s the same process; just hit Dash with the ALT key. I actually changed main to CNTL Left for convenience, which also works well but I failed quite a few times due to lag/game freeze midair. My main issue is with the difficult jumps, that felt quite unpredictable and difficult indeed with these controls. Even when performing jumps from static object to another static object I failed a lot!! Why? I have no clue. One moment it’s all seamless, and the next I’m constantly failing.  This is mainly due to the lags/freezes that I was facing, which is cool by me as every game faces issues, but these random unpredictable jump fails are weird and kinda hard to explain. Jump machines are really important when it comes to Platformers, so I think these issues should be resolved asap. The good thing is that the difficulty level goes down as you begin to upgrade your main protagonist, boosting his stats. It was mainly getting more jump airtime that helped a lot for a noob like me. Combat: In simple words, I absolutely loved it! Simple left mouse click combat system, which works really well with Blue Fire’s simplistic movement and jump machines. The game also features a decent target locking system, which works really well and surprisingly adds a fun flavor to the game; it’s hard to explain that a basic target locking system makes things more interesting, but it just does. You also get to use abilities (which for the most part work well), and power by collecting mana and being in the fight. Felt a bit underpowered and taxing. The enemy types and bosses you will encounter on your journey are pretty well designed, and they playout really well, with each having their own unique thing, and every time you encounter something new it totally throws you off-guard. The enemy types and the bosses are not too difficult to beat but they can certainly pack a punch if you’re not ready. Blue Fire also does a great job of involving the environment around you, and its platformer elements are put to good use. World design: At some places it’s dark and grim with an appropriate light gradient, and on the others it’s well-lit but appropriately tuned out which fits the game's theme nicely. Other than the Lava and the manner in which the main protagonist interacts with it, I loved every single bit of the game’s world design and detailing. Very well thought out throughout the game. Music and sound effects: Awesome background music selection that goes really well with the theme of the game. Gave my playthrough a great flavor. The same goes for the sound effects, which are very well-designed and thought out (apart from the sound it makes when you interact with the lava; that one is pretty annoying). Positives: + Great Storyline + Good number of quests and side quests + Fun combat system + Void Challenges + Great visuals + Great background music and sound effects + Well thought-out platformer elements + Encourages exploration Negatives: - Quite a few lags/game freezes while jumping- Not a big fan of the jump machine- Certain sound effects could use a retouch - Abnormal loading times - The game often froze while loading A great hack and slash platformer with an incredible storyline and enjoyable combat system.  7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Didn't finish this one...Nice enough graphics, atmospheric world. At first, this platformer is fun, but the longer I played, the more and more stuff enoyed me. _childDocuments_.review: ⚔️ Short & casual clone of the classic 3D «Zelda» (with «A Hat in Time» vibes & small, but unnecessary parasitism on the hideous «Dark Souls» mechanics).• The plot is just nothing special (at all, it's boringly predictable and uninteresting).• Dull design decisions (slow opening doors, constant "locking in a room with spawning enemies" cutscenes, weird checkpoints, completely useless, but hidden items).• The economy is broken, you're always rich, even if don't sell junk (you don't yet know about its uselessness).• The worst thing is the Voids. There is a lot of emphasis on these. The initial ones don't present any difficulties, but the five-star ones — a hardcore nightmare. JUST WHY? «MEAT BOY» SECTION ISN'T FUN, IT'S EXTREMELY LAZY GAME DESIGN! STOP DOING IT!• Also, can you name a game that has been ruined by new free content? The first DLC is terrible. It adds nearly two dozen of new REQUIRED to complete hardcore Voids (just not worth your time). Often see an opinion: "the combat is weak", but it was forgivable, until the DLC boss, where it's shown in all its glory (probably the only place where you can completely die).➤ It's all just sad, because this game still can be fun & interesting sometimes, but it's on the verge of "just okay" games.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished the main campaign and I must say this game is probably one of my favourite games I've played in general, Blue Fire is a game that exudes atmosphere in a way akin to Dark Souls and in fact in a few ways it takes from Dark souls, not in difficulty granted but in certain tones and the healing system, in fact it's a mix of many inspirations, some of which I'm sure I must have missed and that's something I genuinely like to see, a game dev who takes all the good aspects of games while making it, it's own thing, to note as I said Dark souls but also Legend of Zelda and a hat in time of which there's a reference to, in fact possibly two with a certain outfit dood.The gameplay for combat is basic but not on a bad way, you have defend of which can also parry for more damage on your next attacks, obviously your attacks, both ground and aerial, a magic attack which I admit for the cost could use a little more kablam! at least on flying enemies of which I wager it's somewhat intended otherwise melee is vastly superior, as well as a myriad of things you will get that will help you traverse the world in many ways, sometimes in places I don't even think the devs thought we'd go to even dood! XDThe music is nice, great in each area, the area's themselves all looked really nice for the visual style of the game, everything ran super well too that said the windowed mode could use some work, sure you can expand it manually but that's if you can get your mouse cursor in the exact right spot and you need to press the windows key to get out in the first place which is all kinds of awkward dood.The difficulty was odd, as long as you were careful it wasn't hard in battles bar two bosses in the main campaign and I honestly realised the one I was being kind of dumb with even, so possibly just the last boss was difficult and even then as long as you have all the upgrades it's not too hard, in fact the main difficulty at least to start or if you don't explore is traversing the environment which is also ironically one of the most fun parts of the game as it loves to slowly expand how you travel throughout the world and find secrets including...Ducks! seriously! although good luck finding them :p although they are just for fun, nothing to get from them but I digress the main difficulty is moving through the world itself, especially for the challenge stuff dood. There's a whole bunch of outfits ranging from just colour changes to actual outfit changes, some of which are super nice! a bunch of weapons too which only really have a visual change although two may? have elements to them but I never really tested that out myself, enemies although samey to fight had some decent visual designs to them and improved attack patterns and speeds at times too dood.The void quests as you will see quickly into the game are how you get more health among other things if you look for them, this part of the game gameplay wise in particular was the most similar to A hat in time but while again much like everything else making it, it's own thing with it's own visuals and creative ways to traverse the puzzle, some of which may challenge a lot of people if they aren't great at moving using all the game has to offer which I can see personally happening a lot dood.So in short? for the price it is especially right now as I write this review, it's just so much yes I could strain my voicebox saying just yes to it, it took me 14 hours to beat and now I still have the "free" DLC to play through which adds lore and a new boss among other things, does it have some jank?...actually it kind of doesn't :O the devs behind this game really outdid themselves and I seriously hope they do more games of this quality in the future, especially with the generosity and effort of all the costumes and free expansion to the game, may add more after I beat the DLC but that's it for now! thanks for reading dood!Free DLC edit: So now I finally beat the DLC let's talk about it, I think they did a great job of concentrating on the games strengths in the DLC, it's all new voids although in this case with the purpose of progressing the DLC and one set designed for a bonus Tunic and weapon, there's another costume too but I won't spoil the surprise dood~ The difficulty is definitely there, if you haven't gotten all the spirits I highly suggest you do although it is certainly more than possible without them but I feel some are controller throw worthy if you aren't good at these styles of games, you also as in the DLC description have a boss who is a shocker of a boss all things considered along with a lore dump to go with it dood.For free it's a super great DLC, it could be out of some people's skill level but maybe I'm just being too pessimistic? either way it's a great challenge that felt fun and it all worked, there were no glitches, there were no wait why can't I do this even though I should be able to? it was all on me, if I failed I failed and honestly I appreciate that a whole lot as someone who hates losing a lot to something because it wasn't refined enough or just plain broken, especially considering how intricate the level designs were dood.So when I try to do reviews I always try to look at both the good and the bad, keeping bias out as much as I can because no matter how much you like a game there will always be flaws and there are a few minor flaws as I've said with combat difficulty being too easy, if I were to be nit picky lore stuff doesn't always stand out enough to see it but like that's it, the devs really did an outstanding job and the only reason not to like it at least in my eyes is if it's just not your genre of game and if it isn't? that's fine, we all have different tastes after all dood ^-^7

I swear to god each one was prettier than the last and it was incredibly hard to know which one I wanted to keep on, being that they were all so pretty.The game did hold me in though. I played 7h straight and didn't even feel time passing by. It made me want to continue playing constantly and the NPC's are really cool and the dialogue is awesome as well. I loved the side quests and you can get 100% achievement on steam by finishing all the quests, which isn't that hard.On normal the bosses and mobs are quite easy, which I didn't mind because I'm in it more for the journey itself. Overall 8/10, I do recommend giving it a shot if you want something to play but dont know what to play <3
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: You can feel Blue Fire's potential as you're playing it, but it feels like it never saw a playtester's eyes. There are a lot of little quality of life issues that should have been caught and fixed. For a game that requires as much precision platforming as it does, the controls are very slippery. A lot of the games systems feel thrown in at random or hacked together, and the story/quest chains feel pretty messy. Worth it if it's on sale and you have 10 hours to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game immensely, I experienced crashes like some of the other reviews are saying, but it wasn't enough to make me stop playing or softlock me out of the game. I did have some problems with the spirits spawning after I died, so I lost a lot of ore. But overall the game was fun! The platforming felt good, the art style was nice, the later boss fights were challenging, and the spirits made finding them feel worth while. The only problems I would say I had with this game was the lack of any direction when completing quests, I felt that I had to wander around a lot until I ran into something that I could now access this time. A map, or a little guide on where you should go for the quests in the quest log would be a massive improvement. I also think that the ore that you obtain out of chests should have a note that says "can be sold" I stock-piled it because I thought it might be needed for an upgrade system later on. The story felt kind of non existent though, I had no idea why I was doing anything, all I knew was that I had to kill some shadows.The strategy guide that the dev's released was very nicely put together, however I wish I knew it existed before I got stuck on the final boss for an hour. Overall I enjoyed it, however with the rough edges I believe that there just needs to be a bit more polish in this game and then it will be something great! 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little game, it's a shame to see that it doesnt seem to sell that well but i'd recommend it to anyone that likes platformers like hat in time or mario, It goes for a sort of mix between a 3d platformer and zelda and i think it achives this reasonably well. It does come with a significant amount of pet peeves for me. For one the level design isnt that strong, some very tedious sections that feel like time wasters are present and the challenge levels could really use checkpoints halfway though for some of them, the combat also feels very sloppy and unresponisve. In quite a few areas the game feels underutilized, like why have these hundreds of robes if they dont even affect gameplay in any obvious way, or why are some weapons described as if having status effects while they seemingly just deal damage just like all the others. There are quite a few small things like this that dont feel properly thought through and i think with the next project this team will probably have worked some of those things out a bit more. Still, pretty good, deserves more attention.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: My initial impressions of this game on release date were not amazing, decided to save myself the frustration after an hour. Tried this game again after the recent balance update, and had a marginally better time, but definitely not one without problems.The main game is interesting and doesn't hold your hand in where to go, which is either a positive or a negative based on if you're into that stuff. It could have done with a quest log that at least gave you a better nudge instead of having to find specific NPC's.  Boss fights were not memorable or interesting, by the time you get to the 2nd half of the game you can just tank everything and mash attack. This is the game at it's worst. The voids is where the game is at it's best, It's hard enough to not breeze through and easy enough to first try it if you're a god gamer, even on the 5 star difficulty voids (not me.) Reminded me a bit of White Palace in Hollow knight but with a bit less elegance and no depth perception.  100%ed the achievements in about 6 hours so it's not overly long but doesn't outstay it's welcome either. Overall I did enjoy this game and it deserves a chance if you're remotely interested in 3d platforming, the combat and enemy variety isn't there to fully recommend it to anyone else but I'm glad I went back to it. I rate this 7 kebabs out of 10(Edited: my mandatory 1 typo per review fixed)
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire may be a fairly basic experience but it reminded me of some other games I've played and I liked spending time in its world. It's fun and it's blissful to control, although the camera killed me many times. I felt good while playing and at the end of the day that's all that really matters. The Dark Souls references are okay. The menu noises, the death groans, the boss and level design, the atmosphere and NPC/quest design, the lore and map layouts, the shortcuts and macguffin hunting. The combat and other core design elements are borrowed from other titles. It's one of those indie titles that's clearly an amalgamation of the teams favorite game elements thrown into a vaguely nostalgic blender. Doesn't overstay its welcome either. 6.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: A true love letter to the Legend of Zelda, Dark Souls and Hollow Knight, which are some of my personal favorites! It has been great so far, but the game keeps crashing half of the time I enter into a new area. Hopefully the devs can work that problem out so I can continue to explore the mysterious world they created!EDIT: The game only crashed 2 more times through the completion of the game after that, thanks to the devs for working so hard on this! The game was truly a delight and cannot wait to see what they have coming down the pipes next! Definitely recommend this game to anyone who appreciates LoZ or adventure games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: The problem with this being a precision platformer is that there's not a lot of precision to it. You stumble around trying challenges and you don't know whether you've got the skills to tackle them. Some stuff you succeed at feels like you lucked out or found an exploit. And when you get your double-height triple jump, double dash, extended wall run and the extra high spin, it feels like you can just fly around all of the challenges and your only fault was struggling with stuff earlier, rather than knowing where to find the tools to cheese it.Combat is barely there and feels useless. The only thing you get out of fighting enemies are an item that lets you upgrade the magic remote damage spell. The damage that does compared to the melee option is so low, it's really not worth even bothering. Fighting mechanics are very rudimentary and the trailer really does mislead you into thinking it's a substantial element of the game.The world starts out by building expectations, but fizzles out into generic filler pretending to be lore.The only "souls-like" thing about this game is dropping you coins if you die (which is not even a common thing to happen) and having to go back to get them. It's ok, because you actually have a cap on how many you can carry. They're very easy to farm and you don't need them for much anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: If you love platformers, you'll love this game. But I mean, you MUST love platformers. Something as simple as going to a building within the hub world is a jumping puzzle. Everywhere you want or need to go is a jumping puzzle to the point where it almost feels like padding to the game.I'm recommending this because I love the style, the character and the obvious love letter to other games I love. However, I am not a big enough fan of platformers to traverse a world exclusively by jumping puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Part 3D Mario-style collectathon, part Zelda-style action adventure, with just a pinch of cutesy Dark Souls (or Hollow Knight but not bugs, if that's more your speed) for flavor. There are a few places where the game feels a little rough, but overall, Blue Fire comes together super well and is really fun to run around in. The DLC is full of some really tough challenges.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely fun but I could not ignore many things that bugged me, for instance, the many many similarities to hollow knight, such as the almost charm-like system, the mentions of the void, even the swinging of the duel blades matches similarity to the knights nail. I'm not saying stuff wasn't original, like I'm a big fan of the main characters design but that could be recipe for a lawsuit. Secondly there are many glitches and problems with the flow of the character such as there no being any downtime between getting attacked by a creature, it leaves you in a stun and lets every enemy nearby pummel you. Also I'm not 100% sure but in the first area in the room with the boxes you have to climb up to unlock the door for I'm pretty sure I took falling damage? Which shouldn't be something to worry about in a literal platformer. And take into account I only have 31 minutes on the game so far and I'm seeing this all already. This isn't made to harass the game developers because this game genuinely looks nice but you need to fix this stuff if you want an indie game like this off the ground.
