_childDocuments_.review: Ever Forward ReviewEver Forward is a fairly solid puzzle game. It’s a bit rage inducing and its story can be a little confusing, but I enjoyed the experience nonetheless.IntroHello everybody, I’m back for yet another review! In this one, I’m covering an indie puzzle adventure game called Ever Forward by Pathea Games.Unlike many of the games I review on our blog, I actually knew what I was getting into with this game since I played through the prologue (Demo) for the game prior to its release.This game’s puzzles can be quite infuriating though and there’s one particular puzzle early on that made me want to rip my hair out I was so angry. It took me quite some time to finally make it past this point, and it’s the same one that gave me issues in the prologue as well. The other puzzles were a cake-walk compared to this puzzle largely because it required luck and absolute precision to get past, and I’m not exactly the most precise player in the world. Still, I managed to get past it (After a good 50 tries) and I completed the game within a few more hours.I think that about covers our brief introductions, let’s get our thinking caps on and get this review started!Story and SettingTruth be told, I’m not really 100% sure what this game’s story is supposed to be about. Even after playing through it I’m still kinda scratching my head as to what was going on because it’s incredibly vague on the story details. I know the story revolves around a 12 year old girl named Maya and her mother but there’s a lot of underlying details about what is happening that are completely missing. My guess is that there was an ice age that occurred which ended society but I’m not entirely sure if that’s what was going on. From what little information that was available that’s my best guess.The game’s story is also told through brief cutscenes that take the form of memories that Maya is reliving. These memories give you an idea of what happened to Maya and her mother.One thing I’ll admit is that I’m a little mixed on the story overall. A bit more detail as to what was happening in the world outside of Maya’s story would have definitely helped in making me more engaged in the story but alas, I felt a bit disconnected from the story and wound up focusing more on the puzzles rather than what was happening story wise. I still watched the cutscenes of course but I didn’t really find what was happening very interesting.GameplayMuch of your time in Ever Forward is spent solving puzzles in areas I’ve decided to call puzzle realms. They’re separate from the open world section of the game and are linear in nature.I noticed that there were some puzzles that were removed compared to the prologue version that I played. Some new ones were added to take their place as well. Other puzzles were altered a bit to make them more difficult. It was pretty neat seeing how much the beginning of the game changed compared to the prologue for the game. There was also a new beginning cinematic too.Gameplay wise, the game is pretty solid. Some puzzles are definitely harder than others, but they’re all doable. The toughest puzzles were definitely the 5th and the last one. Those required a bit of luck and precision to complete which added to their difficulty quite a bit. The rest weren’t too difficult to figure out, but they did require some outside the box thinking.Graphics and SoundEver Forward’s graphics are quite impressive and I liked the overall feel of everything as well. It has an animated feel to the art but it also has a bit of realism mixed in as well so it’s not completely animated. It looks great regardless though and the open world and the puzzle realm’s differences contrast each other very well.Sound wise, the game’s voice-overs are all in Chinese, since that’s where the devs are based in. The voice acting is quite good too. The game’s music fits the game very well as well and gives each area a very different feel, which enhances the game’s scenery quite a bit.ProsExcellent Artwork/GraphicsGreat MusicGood Voice ActingGreat Puzzle DesignConsThe Story Felt Lacking In Detail As To What Was HappeningSome Puzzles Were Absolutely Rage InducingFinal VerdictOverall, I find myself a little mixed regarding Ever Forward. The story left me wanting, and story is very important to me, but the puzzle design is quite excellent, as is the graphics and audio. That said, I still feel the game is worth experiencing nonetheless, and if you’re a fan of solving puzzles, you’ll like the ones included in Ever Forward. If you’re looking for an in-depth story with your puzzles, you’ll likely be a little disappointed with the game like I was.In the end, I’ve decided to give the game 3.5/5 stars. It’s definitely not a bad game by any means, I just wish the story made a lot more sense than it did.

_childDocuments_.review: had some time in the prologue version, so I whizzed through the intro stuff.Game is good, the graphics are neat looking, there's some flashy RBG displacement effects when you enter new puzzle areas, but it's a neat effect. Game performance is pretty bad, I have to drop my settings to keep a steady 60fpsNvidia 1660 GTX 16 GB Ram it's fine, however; as the game is still pleasant to look at with slightly lower graphics. But the framerate does chug a bit here and there. Luckily, this only seems to be a problem in the " hub world " Your game flow is as follows : You navigate a hub world, not unliek something you would see in Banjo Kazooie, only you can't really jump, or fly.. or do much outside of a brisk jog. But the map is simialr, you will traverse it until you find red infected looking tree roots, and you'll find a building or door or something with a wicked red glow - these spots warp you to the puzzle world, and this is where most of the game is.The puzzles are... not bad, but " puzzle " is cutting it very very finely on the line.Your basic moves are stealth related, each puzzle involves you needing to move a cube from one spot, past a " roundy-bot ( very sensitive Ai robots that detect very slight sounds and movements, and instantly zap you, should you get within range.There is no " stealth button " you automatically walk slower when within range of a roundy bot ( represented by a blue cone of light )so you sometimes activate a floor panel with a cube, sometimes you toss the cubes in a particular way to distract the roundy bot long enough to spawn another cube, and run by it. after you complete some puzzles, you can summon your uh, cube that hovers with you at all times to fly to each puzzle in the area. those sections are pretty janky to control, overall the girl you control has this tank like momentum goin for her, like, if you start running and then stop suddenly, she kinda takes a few steps more than you would expect. And this does kill you in plenty of puzzles, you just gotta be careful.after you complete like, 3 puzzles usually; you get a story cutscene to explain a bit about what's going on in the real world.It's a neat lil story, bit of a slow burner on the pickup.for the price, absolutely worth it- the presentation and writing were good enough imo, they seem apt to add more content ( already with one that should be free, but some weird issue happened with it, idk - if you buy the game in the first week, you get free DLC puzzles, so it's something they can add more onto after your main story has been completed.I mention this, as the game seems a little light on content, just based on the cheevies I've gotten, and how many are left- and the rate I got them at ( they all activated pretty much when i completed a story cutscene ) I can't imagine there's more than 3 hours atm. I could be wrong, as I am not at the end of the game - I'm purely going by the achievements. I'd still recommend it. it might not be as advanced, or artistic as say; Iris.Fall - but it does a good job on it's own being a pure story based experience, with some nice visual presentation and a solid idea for " puzzles " I just don't feel like they're all that puzzling at the moment.If this changes, I'll update my review to reflect it; but I still recommend the game at the moment. cheers
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Really nice aesthetic but that's the only point that initially caught my attention.After playing I can say the subtitles are not properly synced, sometimes missing (I didn't understand the ending for this reason). The story in general may be a bit forced too.And finally, some of the levels felt too convoluted to me. I don't know if it's just me or not because I played other puzzle games such as Monument Valley (recently) and Manifold Garden which mess around with perspective and gravity respectively and I had no need for guides.I'm not sure, maybe give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Straight up loved the first chunk of the game.  interesting narrative, interesting gameplay, puzzles are sick!  I am about halfway through and all of my saves decided to lock to on top of a roundbot.  meaning I am left to start over or stay in an infinte death loop.  Great options.  I think it is great in concept, but not playability.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game for a while and can say for sure that it has amazing visuals, the soothing background music goes along pretty well with the visuals. The gameplay feels pretty good to. Only issue is the difficulty of the puzzles, sometimes it feels too easy but sometimes it feels astronomically difficult, so I guess the difficulty progression can improved. Other than that, it's an overall good game as of now.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: A short but beautiful and fascinating little game.This game revolves around you solving puzzles to unlock memories telling a very emotional story throughout that process. The puzzles weren't that challenging in my opinion, though some of them activated some brain cells and i think that's good because I probably couldn't have felt the story that way if I would've been stuck on a puzzle for hours. The graphics in this game are simple yet expresses the feelings the game wants to give you in a quite beautiful way accompanied by very calming and nice music.I really enjoyed my experience and I recommend this game to anyone who wants to go on a beautiful yet emotional journey.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: short verdict: could be more radical, but is radical enough.interesting game. i kinda didn't like it but it is a cool game. pros: the graphics are really good! interesting story. if you like 3d puzzle games, you'll probably want to play this because it's pretty original and unique.cons: it can be frustrating at times because the controls are kinda clunky and you have to be SUPER precise sometimes. some things aren't explained very well.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Oh my, how can i start this review? This game is simply awesome! The graphics are beautiful, the music is incredible, the backstory is really thrilling...I can't even describe it. But the only thing that made a little unconfortable, was that, by the ending of the game, it becomes really, really hard. So, i admit, i had to watch some videos to pass them through (haha). But that doesn't make the game bad, it only makes it hard. It's a beautiful game, and a wonderful experience.(9/10)
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting mixture of clever puzzling situations. Like you got puzzles but you also got puzzling puzzles. There were moments, I was embaffled by the puzzling situation, stuck if that is a better word. After a night of sleep, bringing your mind to ease, you hit your head because the answer was just there... Don't you dare saying this game is like PORTAL....!!!!Animation is superb and the story which gets unfolded is amazing. A language I don't understand, but luckily it has subtitles. That is a plus. You want to know more about the story, eventhough you got an idea of what is going on. Enduring the puzzles just for more story telling! That is the reward!
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles are fun and engaging, with simple to understand mechanics and sometimes complex solutions.It has a feature that allows you to make your own checkpoints mid puzzle, so you don't have to run through the beginning of a puzzle a hundred times because you keep making a simple mistake, more puzzle games need this feature.If you like puzzles get it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: I had received the beta copy for this game and had ended the game before its release, and I must say it happens to be one of the games of this year that I will not ever be able to forget. I usually play AAA games or competitive shooters, and for the first time I can say, this platformer-puzzle game has blown my mind away. I wrote a detailed review if you want go in-depth about my views here - However I will cover this gist of the review here,The game is platformer-puzzle game based on the story of a girl named Maya, she is lost between her imagination and reality and we need to dive into her world and overcome the fears which are in the form of puzzles. There are many people the claiming the puzzle being too hard, I personally got stuck in only 1 puzzle. But I thought about it for the rest of the night, and next day morning I was able to do it. This game offers the people multiple way of solving a puzzle, which enables you to think it your OWN way. I only used the hint leaf once at the ending of the game which was 100% worth it because it was the smartest puzzle I had ever come across and I was in shock, that the developers can even think this way. Special shoutout to all the people at Pathea Games for being a genius along with being talented. The next thing I want to discuss is the game visuals and HOLY, WHAT WERE YOU THINKING ? They literally wanted to make a game so good that people won't forget, and damn they did so. The low-poly textures, the neon lights, the ambient, the island, the water, the sky, everthing I see in this game, I fall in love with it. And at the last, the story of this game, is so well written, and it truly blows me away that this game has such a good story, mind blowing visuals and the smartest puzzles all together packed in one single game.100% recommended, if you're reading this, it is worth the shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: So, I'll be quick here.3.5 hour playtime.The story is good, though a bit confusing near the end.The gameplay is pretty spot on, puzzles have a good range of difficulty.The hints are a bit annoying as they don't appear near you automatically, they appear in set locations.Graphics are fantastic.It's cute, and fun. At $15 dollars, I would say it's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

_childDocuments_.review: Ever Forward is an adventure puzzle game following the story of a girl named Maya. Maya is lost in a strange world somewhere between reality and imagination. She is alone to confront her despair on her journey of discovery, where she must unlock her memories and confront her fears to unravel the secrets of the world. Players will need to use their observational skills and intelligence to solve multiple puzzles to piece together the mystery of Maya’s past and what dark secrets she has buried. A beautiful world that comes to life through breathtaking graphics, Ever Forward is coming to Switch from Pathea Games, the studio that brought us My Time at Portia.
_childDocuments_.name: Ever Forward

name: NORCO
detailed_description: Buzz About the Game NORCO is a Southern Gothic point & click narrative adventure that immerses the player in the sinking suburbs and verdant industrial swamps of a distorted South Louisiana. Your brother Blake has gone missing in the aftermath of your mother's death. In the hopes of finding him, you must follow a fugitive security android through the refineries, strip malls, and drainage ditches of suburban New Orleans. Immerse yourself in a surreal and uncanny South Louisiana NORCO’s painterly and cinematic pixel art draws the player into its quotidian sci-fi world of disappearing swamplands, labyrinthine oil refineries, and other landscapes inspired by the titular town of Norco, Louisiana and other parts of Greater New Orleans. Sink into the rich field recordings and sound design by fmAura and a driving, post-industrial electronic score from Gewgawly I. Unravel a mystery in a world haunted by the past and threatened by the future What starts as a straightforward search for your missing brother quickly spirals into a multigenerational mystery. The lines between salvation, memory, technology, and nature bleed together into a uniquely compelling, contemplative narrative rooted in Southern literature, pulp fiction, and point & click adventure games both classic and contemporary. Explore alongside sharply drawn characters with deep roots, rich backstories, and complex motives A chaotic bayou pirate, bar-stool private detective, escaped security android, and your stuffed childhood monkey will all offer assistance in an eroding and uncertain world. Solve puzzles, fight your way past corporate security goons, and infiltrate an influencer cult squatting an abandoned mall on the outskirts of New Orleans.

_childDocuments_.review: Although I am ~2 hours deep into the story, I feel compelled to spew good things about this beautifully weird game that oozes mystery mood and the still-warmth of a surreal futuristic Americana.I played the demo during Steam Next Fest and was delightfully shocked with how original and rich the storytelling and world-building are. Between the art, sound design, and music, you can feel the effort and love put into this experience - it's incredibly inspiring and impressive.Don't be scared of too much reading! Reading can be fun, and marvelously strange stories are crucial to the medium. This game is $15 right now, well worth the experience and feeling evoked playing this gem.Support smaller devs and stories/experiences that challenge the form!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a game made by people who did not set out to make a video game. The creators had something to say and eventually found, through an organic process, that a video game was the best way to say it. This is the good stuff - the fiction that's saying something true.I don't want this to sound pretentious or hyperbolic but Norco is the closest thing I've found to literature in a video game. Norco deserves careful pacing and reflection. Set aside some time and play it in a quiet place where you can be immersed and where your imagination will be free to fill in the gaps of it's impressionistic style. No one will experience it the same way. I can imagine coming back to this game much later, when I'm at a different place in my life, and having it impact me in entirely novel ways. More than anything else I hope this game inspires other artists to take up the interactive medium to tell their stories. If any of the devs read this, from a guy who loves video games and also works in the oil business in Louisiana - thank you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A really excellent point and click game about cyberbiological viruses, the progeny of Christ, and the effects of well timed expressions of parental affection. I did it in about 6.5 hours of playtime. Assorted thoughts: The soundtrack rips. Left my screen resting for like 10m outside of Keith's car outside the mall for that ~1m loop.DO NOT pet the cat too much.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Tentative recommendation, though i wish I liked it more.The pixel art is great, the sound design is fantastic, and the music is a great mix of moody jazz and electronic beatsThat being said, everything else feels pretty weak. I've had a hard time caring about what is going on bc I'm constantly pulled between narrators, timelines, and next to nothing makes sense. Some of that you can attribute to a typical 'detective noir' story but I feel like you should at least feel a connection to the characters - but the characters I've encountered so far are at best irritating, at worst a text-spewing nuisance. And for a story full of political intrigue, corporate malfeasance, mystical cults, and religious symbolism.. the writers didn't have a single idea or opinion they wanted to convey. Think the ending of "Lost", where things just wrap up without rhyme or reason.I love New Orleans and the idea of a Southern Gothic Cyberpunk game had my attention from the get-go, its just a shame that it hasn't inspired anything in me since the first act
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you've found your way to this page then you're probably already the target audience. If you've played Disco Elysium, Planescape:Torment, or Kentucky Route Zero, then you're primed for they type of experience this game is going to deliver. Waypoint Radio had an episode dedicated to an interview with the creator you can listed to here:Additionally, it works great on Steam Deck. I completed majority of my playthrough there.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: What the actual **** did I just play? It's uh... it's a game that's for sure! lol Music is good, story is all over the place but not at the same time. I wish there was more in certain points but the story overall has an interesting set of messages and the mystery of it all is interesting. There's a lot of tiny little things you can miss which affects things later which is a bit annoying but it kind of shows you how the games going to roll from the start. There's a lot of weird stuff in here from freaky robots, to gorey scenes and religious whack jobs. The gameplay is mostly point and click type stuff but they throw in retro RPG combat and QTE's as well. Don't worry they're not hard or anything. But there are some resource management bits that can be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you're not following a guide. This game has some IRL relations to the region as well. The oil company in the game is basically Shell oil in the same locale. Look it up if you're bored or watch "That dang dad"'s video on it on youtube. Pretty wild stuff. I'll give it an 8/10 just for it's originality and one or two points got a genuine laugh out of me. I didn't get particularly attached to any of the characters but that's just me more than likely. It's got a good cast overall and some genuinely shocking moments. Play it. Absolutely worth it if you like PAC games, and it's on sale as of this review.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Game consistently required reloading prior saves or quitting and loading it to work because of UI bugs. I think it has something to do with controller controls? but often these issues occurred while trying to save in the first place, or witching between menus (like the phone apps). I also found switching between your mothers story and your story a bit headachy. Think it would've been a lot cooler if you discovered your moms storry while playing as Kay, rather than just experiencing it yourself through interruptions of Kay's journey. Story is good overall. Story is the games strong suit. A classicish point and click in terms of mechanics. Short and simple game. 2.5/5
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is an incredible fever dream of a story. It's tangible, relatable, aching, and compelling; and mutates into a bizarre fantasy. Other reviewers (Hatchet) have done a better job at explaining the shortcomings of the weird (and disappointing) second half. I got a lot of closure from the lore docs in ditch-whit-1, on geographyofrobots's itch.io page, and from episode 112 of the podcast 'Gaming in the Wild' which covers an interview with Geo of Robots.I still enjoyed it, and spent about 7 hours on it (offline, so it doesn't show my time)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This a great point n' click experience with a worthwhile neo-noir, southern gothic, narrative. Equal parts clever and mysterious. The modern slang gets a bit grating, especially when characters undercut serious moments by interjecting "bruh". It feels misplaced, and writing this down now feels like I'm making it up, though I'm dead serious. The humor is fine, it just lacks a true sense of meaning beyond making the writers smile (sometimes). I like the story and I like how much of it is left to the player to fill in, in a satisfying, reading comprehension sort of way. Some game writing fails to trust a player with the information given so that is certainly refreshing. Fun time and felt weird to live in the game's world, in a truly great way. 7/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, especially for the Steam Deck. At the time of writing this review it's listed as "playable" for Steam Deck and not "verified" but it ran flawlessly. A fun point and click narrative driven adventure set in futuristic Louisiana. With any game in this genre the characters and story really have to deliver, and they did. An extremely creative story, memorable characters and fun puzzles, this is a game that shouldn't be missed.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished it. Having trouble putting words together.I went on a road trip around the US last year, and on my way down the west coast was surprised by how many giant factories passed by, puffing smoke into the air. One even had Google reviews, where it became clear that the town residents who worked there posted good reviews, and everyone else wanted the factory gone.Those did not compare to the oil refineries in Louisiana, one of which I had to pull off of the highway to properly behold. Certainly I'd seen images of them, but in real life their scale is hard to believe. And they're so bright, both because of innumerable light bulbs and the infamous refinery flame spouts. Even going through the pictures I took while worried the refinery security was going to attack, the size of these things accurately portrayed in none of them. I'd already played the NORCO demo by this point, and had it in my mind throughout my time in the area. There was even an encounter with an old man working at a convenience store somewhere around 1-2am who asked me if I believed in God with a crazed look in his eye, something I would not know was reality foreshadowing this game until the past week.So my impression here, forming as I type this, is as follows: The surreal imagery and sublime writing in NORCO combine to seem more accurate to my brief experience in the places resembling the real life Norco than any photo or video I've seen.A lot more can be said about this game, but I'm currently trying to untie my thoughts. So maybe later. For now, just know that I'd thoroughly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If William Gibson were from Louisiana, NORCO is probably the kind of thing he would have written. A strong blend of family drama fueled decision making with corporate over-extension crashing into local superstitions that may or may not turn out to be true, and all presented in a powerful and dreamlike way to keep you wondering if what you're experiencing is real or an illusion brought on by digital psychosis or chemicals or your own mind rebelling.NORCO utilizes a slick first person point and click interface for you as Kay to figure out what has happened since you mother's death. Navigate between rooms and locations, interact, join forces and fight with a wide cast of weirdos and freaks, hunt for clues and map the relationships between them in your mind.Beautiful game. If you've read any reviews you've spoiled too much already. If the trailer or free demo didn't intrigue you enough then I'm not going to convince you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just begun maybe about an hour in. Pacing feels nice, not overwhelming although get into reading mode. Enjoying the visuals, narrative, location, fun creative world building with potential to become more challenging the further I go. So far it feels like my choices have held a lot of weight, which feels good! And I don't feel like I'm going to get soft locked or pulverized for missing a small detail, always a +I'd recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this until the ending, which disappointingly left a lot unresolved and unanswered. On balance I still enjoyed it though and would recommend it. I played the demo of this around 2017 (it was completely different) and don't remember much except enjoying it. I'm also from the South and hadn't gone home in a long time and had a lot of other weird parallels with the main character here, so that also colored my playthrough some. The best part of Norco is the high weirdness all co-existing in a single real place. There's a lot of wild stuff going on, but people still have to use the toilet, go out for groceries, and pay the bills. The wild apocalyptic biblical predictions, cyberpunk dystopian eco terrorist body horror, and goofy humor all roll one into the other, blending into something unique and, somehow, plausibly human. The devs have released a kind of lore pack that addresses some of my issues with the ending. An info dump isn't as satisfying as an in-universe explanation but it's something. See it here:
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A stunning achievement. Think Kentucky Route Zero mixed with something like Football Game or Red String Club. It's very much about the slow violence of capitalism, the creeping disease of it, while also being just an interesting southern gothic cyberpunk mystery set in Louisiana. This is a point and click adventure, but it... deviates at interesting times, with interesting thematic consequences. I adore this game, the music, the art style, and just the creativity. The ending is pretty strange but thematically it works. You've never experienced a story quite like this, and certainly not in quite this way, I promise you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I expected a bit more from Norco because it was kinda trending and while I liked the dreary setting and atmosphere, it also felt like stuff was just happening and then the game was over.  Maybe that was the point or maybe I'm big dumb... could be both.  Hard to say.For a point and click adventure, I never had to look up how to solve any of the puzzles and that's a big plus for me (because it makes me feel smart).I liked the aesthetic.Giving it the Thumbs Up because it's still an interesting ride and the price is right.-e- Also, pretty easy to get 100% achievements if you care about that sort of thing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. The story is a little confusing in the first hour but as the game progresses you get the hang what's going on. The art and the soundtrack is fantastic. The story blends sci-fi and religion, it's worth checking out if you're into narrative games involving a lot of reading, it almost feels like reading a sci-fi novel. Voice overs would be great but they're not there at the time of writing this review.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The story is not going to be for everyone. It's very weird and surreal. Even a while after playing I'm still scratching my head about what parts of the story to take literally, and which are more symbolic. But it's definitely a game that stays with you, in a good way.Overall, I'd describe the narrative as a nuanced exploration of a daughter-mother relationship, paralleled with the human and environmental cost of big oil and the gig-economy in southern Louisiana. Even if the story is not for you, I'd still recommend it for how masterfully the game uses the point-and-click genre for storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, with incredible sense of place and atmosphere. Memorable and haunting characters. Doesn't spoon feed you the plot. The puzzles aren't especially complex (and it can spoon feed you the answers sometimes) but it's really about exploration and the journey rather than puzzle solving. Lived up to my high expectations.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I felt like I was part of it all, wandering through every last stretch of the wretched, deteriorating land in Norco, and, having found myself now a stranger to where I was supposed to call home, I was haunted at once by a peculiar sense of nostalgia for a past I never had, and an ever-intensifying curiosity about my own detachment. Truly an experience. The writing is fairly strong: poetic, enigmatic, and, at times, fresh as morning dew.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A short but worthwhile story. If you're a fan of Disco Elysium and Citizen Sleeper and enjoy the likes of Jeff Vandermeer, this may be a game for you. A little bit of environmental sci-fi intrigue, corpo bashing,  supernatural weirdness, and silly dialogue options to cut the tension.Overall, I really liked the story and interactive mechanics. Largely a visual novel with a couple of mini-games sprinkled in, none of which are particularly difficult. Content warnings for substance abuse, religious iconography, and an unavoidable (non-graphic) depiction of suicide
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Truly unique and new settings are few and far between, and the game works hard to create its own vibe. Much of the game is a vessel to deliver details about the world, and it's a fascinating thing to explore. Impeccable character writing keeps it from feeling like a lore dump and allows you to see the world through the characters that inhabit it.The game also avoids many of the unpleasant trappings of the point-and-click genre. It uses inventory items sparingly, never overloading you with a dozen pieces of trash. It's never confusing about where to go or what to do, while still allowing the player agency to take additional steps to influence the world.This is a contender for game of the year
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A unique point-and-click. The writing and the world building are very much the highlights here. It has something to say about our world and its future. I was constantly reminded of Jeff Vandermeer's books (like Annihilation, Borne, and especially Hummingbird Salamander), with a little bit of Disco Elysium's wry humor sprinkled on top.I don't necessarily think it sticks the landing with how specific the ending is (in all its vagueness - I hope you know what I mean once you get to it) but the journey there is well worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Eloquent, humorous yet poignant writing tells an engrossing tale that is brought to life by wonderfully immersive pixel art and sound design. Yutsi/Geography of Robots faithfully captures the mysteries (and truths) of growing up in the deep south, and touches on themes that, despite being science-fiction, felt totally relatable. NORCO easily holds a place among the best point-and-click adventure games I've ever played (and I've been playing them since the early Sierra/Lucas Arts days).
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't ever really feel compelled to write a review for a game, but this is an exception.  Please follow the reviews and know that if you take the time to read and follow the story, it is a great ride.  Around 5 hours for me to finish the game at the price of going to a movie.  This is well worth the money in my opinion.  The sound, graphics and story all work in unison to create an environment that is both believable and unbelievable at the same time.  Geography of Robots creates a world that is grounded in reality as if this could be the near future.  Buy it if you like to experience a great story with not much of a challenge.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really have anything substantial to add to the polygon or uppercut crit reviews, or indeed to any of the steam reviews - I think the Disco Elysium comparisons are reasonable, although I do also think that Disco Elysium was almost boundlessly optimistic while Norco is melancholic to the point of being depressing, despite daft jokes and quirky characters. The art and music are stunning, and the writing is gripping. There's also minimal-to-zero 'moon logic' and pixel hunting, making it quite easy to blitz through to the somewhat abrupt ending in about four hours.But perhaps the most resonant thing that I took away from Norco was the string of wikipedia pages I opened to try and get to grips with what i'd experienced in the game, as well as the IRL Norco, LA, where the developer grew up. "Norco, Louisiana". "Fenceline community". "Shell plant explosion in Norco, Louisiana". "Cancer alley". "Toxics Release inventory". "Sacrifice zone". "Locally unwanted land use". "Transport divide".Things are bad, man, and this game won't help you feel like they're getting much better. Give it a go when you're feeling just a bit too happy.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The first time in a long while I've really loved a game. It's more of an immersive graphic novel. Very well written and enjoyable to read. The art design, music, sound, pixel art, is all really well done, but the story is where it's at. Very immersive and enjoyable world to vibe out in. I really recommend digging into the story and the characters as much as possible. It's not a game for everyone, but if you're looking for a relaxing late night vibe of a game, this is it. Point-and-Clicks have a mindfulness quality built into the genre. The music and story-telling really ad to the immersive quality of this game. I love using the optional CRT monitor emulation mode, but I'm an oldie. It helps me remember how immersive point and clicks felt to me at the time. I do plan on replaying without CRT to really appreciate the pixel art. You can tell this is a game created with a lot of love. It has a quality that AAA titles will never be able to emulate. It's something people want more of IMO. Games created with this much love and attention are rare. It's nostalgia, existential, sci-fi, history, future, cool-characters and... there's just a lot lot to appreciate about it.Apart from the story and the vibe (which is what I'm here for),. the gameplay is simple but it's not a cakewalk. There are larger riddles you must solve, and challenging mini games. You are casually solving a mystery, which is a lot of fun to uncover. It doesn't ever feel repetitive. The mini games always result in something surprising and/or the game itself is unique in some way. There are generally a lot of ways to get hints if you are stuck on any particular puzzle (i.e. talking to other characters). If you're someone who just wants to progress a story as fast as possible to beat a game, this isn't a game for you. You've got to know going in that this game is a total vibe game. You've got to want to read and immerse yourself in it. Take your time with it. The creators did such a good job making a detailed story and setting. The text is so well written, concise, and fun to read, but the game does allow you to take it as deep as you'd like, allowing you to discover characters and stories deeper if you want (you do want) . Anyway I'm rambling but this game is great and I suspect I'll replay it a lot into the future to get the most out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game over a year ago when it first came out. I played it a little back then, but for some reason it took me until now to actually do a full playthrough. I regret waiting so long because this game is amazing. It really blew me away multiple times. It's like an amalgamation of all my favorite things; Blade Runner, Kentucky Route Zero, and Disco Elysium rolled into a stylish point and click adventure game with great writing, great atmosphere, great worldbuilding, and great characters. It had some genuinely funny sections to balance out the surrealist creepy overtones and the noir tragedy undertones. One scene in the final act actually had me tearing up a little. The endings are a little obscure and mostly ambiguous, but I like to think that the one I got leaves a little bit of hope for Kay (who is probably one of my favorite characters in all of gaming). I really loved this game from start to finish, probably one of my all time favorites. Definitely check it out if you're interested in the cyberpunk and/or surrealist genres, or if you just want a game with a very well-written story.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If Disco Elysium is a meditation on lost futures and the value of self destruction, Norco answers with an indictment that we might be inhabiting the end times and should hold on regardless. Every scene and character portrait is a painstaking work of art that works along with the dreamy soundtrack to draw you into the gorgeous, hazy bible belt setting. The point and click gameplay is straightforward (and at times a little overbearing with handholding), with small minigame sections to mix things up somewhat, but rewards interacting with the world and the people in it to uncover another small truth about it. I don't think I've come across anything that quite captures the sense of melancholy and unease that dominates the current moment in the 20s.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The story in this game is extremely enthralling.  Lately when I play a story game, I find myself accelerating to the end.  However with NORCO, the setting and story grabbed and held my attention all the way until the end.It’s intriguing and very well done, so much so that I’d elevate it to (what I would consider) art.  There’s too much time wasting slop being pumped out these days, it’s nice to see creative people putting their skills to work and gaining recognition.We need more quality over quantity, especially in the VN genre.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: How did this get made, much less published? Point-and-click adventure game combining Southern Gothic, cyberpunk, magical realism, and post-[insert socioeconomic concept here]? Yeah, that screams Mainstream Investment Opportunity.Yet, it did get made, and it’s amazing. Lots of comparisons are made to A Night in the Woods and Kentucky Route Zero. They’re valid.  NORCO and the Pennsyltucky Games both combine the struggles and insecurities of the post-American Empire working classes with obscure academic concepts. Whereas A Night in the Woods goes for a cartoonish ironic metaphor and Kentucky Route Zero spins a mystical, aching sadness, NORCO is aggressively psychedelic, hardnosed, and nihilistic.This is not the most punk thing I’ve ever played, but it’s the most accessible punk thing I’ve seen in the interactive space, and that accessibility draws you in for a pretty wild ride. It starts with a future fried hyperlocal take on New Orleans, with its rotting infrastructure and twin income streams of petroleum and gullible tourists. There are tiny stabs at the city’s popular kitsch – vampire novels, voodoo shops, ghost tours, and questionable street food. But these are footnotes compared to the obsession with environmental damage, climate change, hurricanes, flooding, and institutional collapse that underline life in The Big Uneasy these days. The scene is so thoroughly soaked in a hard boiled tincture of Eric Brockovich-meets-Neuromancer verisimilitude and wry humor that the post-humanism, cryptozoology, and psychedelic mysticism come crashing into the frame with surprisingly dramatic force.Is it perfect? Nah! For all its deeply perceptive powers, NORCO fails to invest the player in the main character or the McGuffin of her tepid affection, her brother. The endings – while gorgeously nihilistic – hold little emotional weight as a result. NORCO, literally, loses the plot by the third act. The “Well, that happened” cliché can just be slapped on the experience as neatly as a packing tape on a gaping wound. This feels like the result of trying to cram a large novel’s worth of concepts and characters into a running time the size of a short miniseries. On a mechanical level, NORCO is less impressive. The minigames feel tacked on, formulaic, and immersion breaking – existing solely to avoid the “walking simulator” label. The ending areas suffer extensively from asset reuse, robbing them of uniqueness. But the game rewards those curious enough to try illogical item combinations, poke around in dialogue trees, or click into obscure areas of the map. Like the real New Orleans, there’s a lot to find in the darker corners of NORCO.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I would highly recommend this game to any point-and-click adventure fans! It is something to check out even for those that simply enjoy nice storytelling, well-written characters, and atmospheric games. This game oozes style and atmosphere!It is a techno noir game, that reminded me of Blade Runner, a mystery bigger than life in the style of the Da Vinci Code and a kind of autobiography and reflection on a real town in the United States called Norco. I would even dare to say that Norco is a character on its own.Part of the game is a typical old adventure-style game, part is like a visual novel, and part is like a textual adventure.Pixel art graphic style is suitable and only elevates the game to a higher level. For music and sound, I also only have high praise. The soundtrack is simply as haunting as it is beautiful. All those things just enrich the game.Puzzles in the game are quite well balanced and not obscure at all. For me, game mechanics are hit or miss most of the time. Some mechanics are put in the game just to consume the time as I see it. Mind Map, though nothing new in games, is superbly done and enjoyable. Maybe my favorite mechanic. I liked most puzzles, even though they are easy to figure out and they are generally nothing that special. I'd say solving the puzzles just follows the flow. The game isn't too long and it doesn't overstay its welcome.Story-wise, there are a lot of different topics, but they are masterfully interwoven. There are also quite a lot of moments that, even though the game is mostly serious, had me laughing. Those little moments are best experienced by finding them on your own. A combination of serious topics, with masterfully added quirks and humor, is top-notch!The game has multiple endings and some of the choices do matter. I'd say its creators are big fans of old point-and-click games like, for example, Monkey Island, and I believe some of the puzzles in the game are inspired by it.Don't let this game slip under your radar, especially if you are a fan of the genre.My only problem with the game is that most puzzles are just too simple, but even with that issue, Norco is one of the most enjoyable old-school adventure games in recent times.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, NORCO. My shoes are still caked in swamp mud and my hair smells like cigarettes after playing this game. NORCO is a narrative driven point and click adventure game like no other. It pulls you in with beautiful art and witty dialogue then holds you under until you taste the despair. Settle in and live a life that is not your own. I'm not from Louisiana but I feel like a little piece of it is in me now. If any part of you is curious about this game you should play it. It's a special ride. Thank you for this game and please make more.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Breathtakingly beautiful. Gloomy, depressing, sarcastic in a very dark way. Absolutely love the unique images here. They are raw but with various shades that convey so many emotions, which help build up the atmosphere. And please don't remove the robot-like voices of the characters! Human voices just don't seem right in this game - here nothing is natural and authentic, all half-ruined and altered, if not destroyed completely. The factories and the machines, the cult and the app that drove people to work for nothing, the diseases and explosions, the natural disasters... It's a journey of trying to find something authentic and to make a change, isn't it? It's also about people there, those desperate residents who strive for something exciting and new to change their stagnant life, who used drugs or violence or religious ecstasy to feel something real. Despite the narrative being really appealing, I do feel that there aren't many possibilities to interact with the characters, therefore the players can not bond with them when some events related to them happen (for example, Million.) I mean we have a lot of functional dialogue with characters, and they help us understand what's going on and fill in the blanks, but we don't get to know their own stories and backgrounds, which can give us a break from the scenario and introduce who they are in their own life story, outside of our journey. When I saw Million's face as stars in the sky, I was not moved; when I saved Kay's brother Blake, I didn't feel a thing, for he didn't even say a word to me. There's certainly great potential in the story and the connections between characters, and I do wish there's something more to be found.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a strange, surrealist point and click with an weird ass story, good humor, fantastic pixel art, and great atmosphere. I love its depressing, futuristic take on New Orleans and its suburbs and was captivated by the increasingly surreal events NORCO presents. The puzzles are also fun and many small choices causing certain outcomes make me interested in a second playthrough-- not because they affect the story much, but because of the fun new characters and scenes I might unlock. It's also paced well at 6hrs. Well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended to everyone, but ESPECIALLY if you're from South Louisiana. There is a universality in what it's presenting that will strike true regardless of where you're from: about Home, about industrial sickness, about online, about dysfunction.  But it cannot be overstated how much NORCO is Norco is New Orleans is Louisiana. Within the towering flamestacks and twinkling lights draped in sci-fi spectacle is a living, breathing place that this game captures in such a raw, poignant way that I'm not even sure how to begin to articulate. It feels exactly like the many sleepless nights spent at my grandparents' in the suffocating heat, watching car headlights blink over the overpass from the window, trying not to think about the roaches skulking on the walls.Quite a few published reviews focus mostly on the sci-fi elements. I don't want to downplay them, because they are an integral and well-executed part of the whole package. But to me, the reason I'm never going to forget this game is because of its setting and characters taken straight off of the cushions of my family's couch. Short and beautiful. Worth it for the pixel art alone. Great soundtrack. Compelling story. You're missing out by skipping this one.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome eye candy pixel art and enthralling atmosphere, with a melancholic 'late-stage capitalism dystopia' vibe. However, the game seemed to me to shift tone midway, as though it got lost in what it was trying to say, feeling like it had a great premise without knowing where to take it. Still, a memorable game due to its visuals, mood, and originality.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A southern gothic science fiction adventure game taking place as the protagonist Kay returns to her hometown in a post Civil War US amid worldwide catastrophes in order to find her brother after your mothers death from cancer. New Orleans is an industrial dystopia overseen by the Shield Chemical corporation (a stand in for Shell Oil that is in the real life area) and as you explore more you learn about a mysterious client your mother was working for and the different people that had taken an interest in her. The lead occasionally shifts to the recent past where you play as Kay's mother. Norco has little focus on traditional adventure puzzle solving where you mostly find and combine items and instead will often give you multiple ways to handle a problem, minor turn based QTE and memory based combat, text adventure scenes, driving a boat in a swamp set in an alligator hand puppet's poetry. While Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero dabbled in some similar themes and dealt with stranger and magical elements of an otherwise often serious and more realistic setting, Norco goes further into the strange and leaves with much less concretely answered.Well written characters and story filled with corporate conspiracies, ghost, scamming tech companies selling false hope, cryptids, humor, cults, broken family ties, and sudden violent twists with strong world building, a melancholic dreamlike atmosphere, and some of the best artwork in the genre (or industry in general). The mind-map mechanic is utilized well to fill in character details as you learn more about people and examine your thoughts on them or on the information you have learned, also giving a clearer picture of their face over time.Screenshots:
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco feels like a game tailored for me. Geography of Robots made a smart choice by extracting the 90's adventure game pixel art design while leaving the tedious and unintuitive puzzle design.This game is all about the narrative. Between the dystopian cyberpunk politics and southern gothic tendencies, there's a lot of world building and characters to chew on.The combat is nothing special, but it was never supposed to be the focus. I do wonder about a version of this game that has no combat whatsoever, but it doesn't affect the overall impression. Can't wait to see what else this studio makes next.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Despite all the critical acclaim and hype, the game disappointed for me. It isn't entirely bad, there are worse games but it just seemed to be a bunch of random things mashed together in the end. If you want your games to make sense throughout and have a satisfactory conclusion this isnt't it. It's basically a 4-5 hr long acid trip in the form of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a narrative masterpiece. It's artwork that's decided to use the video game medium as a way to tell a story and a beautiful world.As many people are saying, NORCO isn't a game for everybody. It's primarily point and click, with simple, straightforward puzzles, a point-and-click mode of navigation, and little mini-games for battles and certain travel sequences. I shy away from calling it a game, really - it feels more like an interactive visual novel, than anything else. But there's so much beauty in that.I am a sucker for rich storylines and a pixel art style, and NORCO delivers on both fronts. The art is GORGEOUS. It's like if old paintings were pixilated. Huge praise to the artists and art directors that came together to create such a visual masterpiece. As I made my way around the map, I found myself engrossed in the world. I often came back to different scenes just to marvel at the way the colors and lines blended together and immerse myself in the artwork, which mixes cyberpunk and antique art in both a literal and visual way. I think it takes incredible talent to be able to do something like this.The story is a poignant exploration of nature versus nurture, of technology versus natural forces, of religion and corporate interests and how they corrupt humans and ecosystems alike. The story, without going into much detail, concerns a young woman, Kay, who returns to her hometown of Louisiana in search for her brother after the death of their mother. She finds herself embroiled in various conflicts, whether it be the aftermath of a neo-Christian cult that has sprung up in Norco, the devastation that the oil industry wreaks upon the swamps and bayous of Louisiana, or the strained relationships between Kay and her family members. Alongside this, the player also assumes the viewpoint of Kay's mother in the weeks before her death and her own adventures prior to Kay's return.NORCO is confusing. There is no real resolution to its plot. Many questions are brought up only to be left unanswered. Many loose ends are left behind by the end. More than just a linear plot, NORCO shines because of how it explores various themes and allows its players to draw their own conclusions on topics that may be too complex to resolve with a single stance. I think that's what I love about it, honestly. It's more speculative than anything. If a beautiful pixel art style, thought-provoking storyline, and fantastic cyberpunk Southern Gothic setting are all things that you're into, I highly recommend NORCO, it's one of the most beautiful games of its genre that I've played thus far, and it's left me thinking and feeling things I can't describe.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up in a bayou town not far from Norco. That Leblanc character could be a relative of mine. Now I live a few states away.This game hits so hard, one gut punch after another. The pixel art, writing, and soundtrack are all gorgeous. I've been recommending it to friends and family, even ones that don't play a lot of games.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Hits a little close to home. A reminder that some things run deeper. Norco is surreal - it blends the real and imaginary. This allows the player to see the familiar in a unique and novel light. Don't focus on making explicit sense out of everything - and instead concentrate on what this one makes you feel.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game will make you feel things you havent felt in a long time, and make you look at the world and our very near future in ways that indescribable. If you like true detective season 1, if you appreciate the occult significance of the time we live in and its effects of technology in our society, and if you are at all looking for answers in the bleak hyper real hellscape that is modern life look no further than Norco. This game will haunt your dreams and your nightmares, it will make you look at industrial architecture with melancholic sadness, it will make you reflect on the decisions youve made in your own life to get where you are now. It is as trip and a half without the need for any drug (though I dont doubt it would be worth the trip to try it on certain drugs)If you at all appreciate the significance of the time we live you do yourself a disservice by not playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO contains an incredibly grotesque and industrialised city, with a slew of characters ranging from downtrodden detectives to manic religious icons that spread as you play through the characters Kay, and her mother. While the often whiplash-giving twists can be hard for players to comprehend the full picture of this mystery, the game mechanic of recollecting and gathering makes going through all dialogue rewarding. I squeezed around 10 hours of game time, involving 3 playthroughs to obtain all the achievements as well as absorb as much as I could out of the stunning visuals, and fleshed out characters that exist in this universe. This is a trippy game for sure, but also comes with a contrast of silence if you will - there are often times where outside of all the god-talk and trippy bird quests that you simply explore a perfectly human town, interacting with their daily lives, stuck in a limbo of wanting to do something, but knowing the push-back it comes with. As for gameplay, this isn't the kind of point and click mystery where you might get stuck and search up a walkthrough, I find that it's incredibly well designed and simply by reading the narrative (or the blue highlights) you would be able to figure out everything on your own. The phone mechanic also feels great too. tl;dr, maybe the real journey of NORCO was the garetts we've made along the way!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Best game of 2022 so far for me, and I don't say that lightly. Finished in about 7 and a half hours. but it has a surprising amount of replayability in it--alternate endings, alternate dialogue branches. Details of the story change based on choices you make in the game, and the consequences are delightful and feel impactful. Something as seemingly meaningless where Kay was in a wild party might end up carrying a detail that gets referenced all the way to the end of the game,  The writing honestly makes me jealous as a wannabe creator for just how good it is. Recommend you play with a Louisiana native just to see how many references they catch in the gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you like point and click puzzle games, this is a good one. Not insanely difficult, and it will not leave you in any jams (looking at you, Wadjet Eye) so relatively accessible and genuinely quite surreal and endearing, if not a bit prophetic. Some people say the plot line is not very believable, but I think it explores a lot of the stranger corners of human spirituality and consciousness, especially the desire to believe in something when all hope is lost. Definitely a worthwhile experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is an effective sci-fi dystopia because it is set hardly a generation in the future, with characters dealing with only slightly exaggerated versions of the problems and technological promises of today. The ubiquitous self-checkouts leave people angry and unemployed, false prophets lead wayward incels into a Mars-bound death cult, nature melds with AI to produce nightmarish amalgams that spy and feed information to shadowy organizations - all without ever feeling overwhelmingly bleak. The story is interesting and engaging, but relies heavily on Christian imagery and themes, which may not appeal to some.Beautiful pixel art, soundtrack, and writing, too.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished yet, but from the amazing ost, to the beautiful art, the amazingly written story so far, and above all, the sense of humanity it keeps for the people of Norco as they try to eek out their lives in the shadow of the local oil company is really just hitting every possible note for me.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: really love the game, it's art is gorgeous, the music is fitting.. but the story hits too close to home for me.losing my mother at 13 to cancer and my father at 15 also to cancer, then being in the memories of the main character and mother is just too painful.don't think i can keep playing without tears welling up inside. sooo guess i'm stopping in chapter 1.highly recommend but caution to anyone who's lost someone close to cancer.it's very emotional and heart tugging.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what this is. It's an amazing game, but at the same time, it feels like an LSD trip on salvia. Lots of references to Christianity, very well done but creepy sound design, story which I am not sure how to make sense of.Buy it, play it. Wouldn't call it game of the year, but certainly worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is best enjoyed with your drink of choice and in a quiet room. It's all about the ambiance and letting the game pull you into its universe bit by bit. You don't have to rush it, the "puzzles" aren't terribly hard but you should take your time and talk to everybody. They all have a story to tell you. Between the gorgeous pixel art tableau and the atmospheric music, this game does a better job telling you a good story than most AAA with less.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco was very enjoyable. It draws you in further and further. Usually I don't like "First Person" style adventures and prefer 3rd person style adventures because to me the scenes oftentimes fell too dull and lifeless. This is definitely not the case with Norco. Great pixelart. The scenes are animated just enough so the game feels lifely. Great storytelling. The light arcade action portions were just the right difficulty to not be obtrusive. Only con for me was that I could not scroll back up the conversations and would miss bits of dialogue if there were many dialogue options printed at the end that would immediately kick the unread portions of text out of screen.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: In the bayous of Norco, Louisiana, ghosts linger. Not the types in horror movies that jump up in your face, screaming unabatedly, nor the ones you see on strange found footage that you proceed to show all your friends. These ghosts are vestiges of the past, remnants of a bygone time. A time that won’t come back. Having grown up in Norco, Kay is no stranger to its peculiar inhabitants and rural landscapes. But one day, she’s had enough. She packs her backpack, leaves the only place she’s ever known, and heads for the road. This is how she spends the next five years: aimlessly travelling from state to state, not really achieving anything, her existence reduced to a shadow. But then, her mom dies of sickness. Overcome with a feeling of regret, Kay travels back to her hometown — to Norco. But home is not as imagined. Slowly but steadily, a power conglomerate is taking over the local towns, and the Norco she knew is getting overshadowed by their capitalist ideals and futuristic machinery. Her house, too, is in shambles, the messy kitchen and living room serving as gateways into the past, a trip down memory lane, if you will. Kay describes these events with a certain apathy, like they belong to a different person; the person who vanished when she ran away. Her ghost. Like one character says, she’s a  Plenty of games have tackled the homecoming trope, but none do it quite like Norco. Typically, this return to a former life concerns itself mostly with what has already happened, the details the protagonist already knows about but we don’t. The home Kay returns to, however, is different. It has changed, molded into a gruesome shape by family dramas, disease and perhaps even occult occurrences. And this is only the beginning. Slowly, the strange circumstances around Kay’s family and the happenings in Norco are revealed, and a mystery shapes. Carried forward by sharp, concise writing, Norco shifts into something much different and far stranger, a dazzling piece that maintains a fine balance between uncanny and mundane.  The story is told not only from the perspective of Kay, but also a character in the past. Often, a premise is introduced in the past and then further explored in the present, merging these two viewpoints and making the transitions between them almost seamless. As such, you never feel like an interesting part of the plot gets paused, delayed even, by something else. It’s rather clever. The gameplay also varies, with cascades of different ideas and concepts colliding. An encounter with guards in cutting-edge armor sees the game shift into a turn-based showdown reminiscent of a JRPG, with each round having you either attack with a character or heal them to prepare for the next turn. Then, you attend a puppet show about a hunter travelling the swamps, and you’re transported into a top-down view of the area, able to control the direction of the boat and make a few discoveries along the way. And in perhaps the smartest segment, you undergo a reading of your memory and must decide which recollections to keep and which to forget. Few of these segments are innovative, but together, they lend Norco an ever-bending and unpredictable nature. What’s so impressive about this story is the way it manages to wrap everything up by the end. A seemingly random encounter early on turns out to be related to a major plot point, and every element of surrealism, no matter how weird, carries a deeper meaning. These aspects don’t feel like they were randomly thrown at a board like dart pieces, but rather like intentional decisions made by the storytellers. I was so engaged that I even started taking notes, attempting to grasp the deeper reaches of the symbolism.  The game carries in its juxtaposition of rural America and the supernatural a likeness to the magical Kentucky Route Zero. Just like the ragtag cast travelling the dreamlike roads of Kentucky, the characters of Norco face uncertainties in life. They’re driving down blurry motorways in a car fueled by doubt, suppressed by the changes occurring around them. Some try to fight it by searching for purpose, while others give in to the hopelessness. It puts things into perspective. In a world ruled by the rich and the fortunate, can we — us normal individuals — even hope to change anything? At the entrance to the oil refinery that towers into the skyline, a sign says, “for a greener future.” Feels awfully familiar, doesn’t it? The truth is, as pretentious as it may sound, we live in the world  of Norco. The small get suppressed by the large, faceless corporations control our daily life and opinions through bureaucratic algorithms and overwhelming technology. Bleak when you think about it, isn’t it?And yet, we cling on to life, try to give it meaning. One of the fascinating groups in Norco is a collective of religious zealots all going by the name of Garrett. They wish to transcend this earthly prison, to build a spaceship and reach for the stars. It’s a grand project, one likely to succumb under its own ambition, yet it has a symbolical power. In our own world, too, there are people trying to escape from mundanity. But then again, we all start out reaching for the stars; most of us just give up on that dream. Theoretically, this game is set in the future. People have stopped using traditional ways of measuring time, there’s an android with what seems like real emotions, and even the local gas station, which lies on an empty parking lot in the middle of nowhere, is managed by an automaton. Yet I would often forget that this is purely speculative fiction. It sure doesn’t feel far from our own world, both in its depiction of towering corporations, but also in the technology that, when you think about it, is not too unachievable. That’s an achievement.   This is what Norco means to me. It’s a reflection on the world we live in, a subtle critique of the way conglomerates crush and oppress the small, but also a story about the people we meet along our individual journeys and the things we leave behind. With heavy symbolism and wacky yet ultimately human characters, it’s an extraordinary work of magical realism, and it achieves this with a rare brevity, every line of dialogue flowing into the next, not a single word wasted.To present your ideas is one thing. To do so through delicate hints and the circumstances of your story? That’s art.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after playing it non stop sleeping for the night in-between on PC Gamepass.While I don't come from the area this game takes a lot of its inspiration of, it all felt familiar and identifiable to me. In spite of its melding of cyberpunk aesthetics to its overall background, the game is very much a reflection of what a "normal" life would be these days. Its a very personal tale not just of the central characters but also of the area itself. I wanted to know more of why certain characters became who they are as well as what led to this place becoming what it was. Its writing, artwork, and soundtrack help get all this across and really highlights why interactive media such as video games can have its advantage over purely literary works. Would I feel like books could match the same level of detail? A good author could definitely do so but would my attention be held long enough to do so? I guess i don't have personal confidence in myself these days.Mechanically it's very much a point and click adventure game, though I greatly appreciate its puzzles not being obtuse and are overall very easy to follow. One aspect of the game you could argue doesn't fit in with the rest but I appreciate its inclusion if only for its variety.I also want to give special mention to its artbook included in the special edition of the game. It not only includes the game's beautiful pixel art but reference photography, sketches, newspaper clippings, and narrative information about the game as well as interviews from some of its staff. Absolutely worth looking through after beating the game and part of me is hoping a print version would be released down the road (as well as some poster size prints for some of its artwork so i can throw them up on my wall while giving more of my $ to the developers)It's easily have joined my collection with the likes of Disco Elysium and Va11-Hall-A of games that transport me into a place in time that felt like I've been there this whole time. Play this game
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I came for the visual, ambience, story rich point and click and I stayed all until the end as I loved it.I used a guide to get all achievements which are possible in one play-through (just need couple of save to go back to just  before a choice as there are only couple of mutually exclusive achievements).Very much enjoyed the game and will recommend to any fan (or anyone) of point'n'click who are looking for a story rather than puzzle focus as there is no real puzzle/object to combine.

_childDocuments_.review: Came for the fresh angle of Southern Gothic dark future with The Leftovers flavor, stayed for the Kentucky Route Zero vibe in the Disco Elysium suit. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I'm from around New Orleans, and so rarely do I see mostly-authentic representations of this place. I like text-based games and weird philosophical ♥♥♥♥, so it seemed like it'd be right up my alley. But Norco was sadly underwhelming. I played it from start-to-finish in two sittings, doing a mostly-completionist playthrough. The plot is barely coherent and the ending(s) are disappointing. I'm not opposed to convoluted narratives in games; for example, I'm a huge fan of Kentucky Route Zero, which has similar vibes to Norco as they both stem from the Southern Gothic genre. But Norco's narrative goes beyond convoluted to inexplicable, and not in a good way. Leaves you unsatisfied, and it's hard to glean any deeper meaning even after reflecting on it. It does have some redeeming moments. The artwork can be good, and they nailed the regional character-- it looks just like the Greater New Orleans area. There are some events and dialogue that are quite provoking. However, these redeeming elements still don't make it worth playing. Probably not worth your time or your money.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I purposefully waited a couple of months before writing this review because I wanted to see if any parts of NORCO would stay with me. And I am glad to report that my appreciation of the game has actually increased with time. Although I feel like it is basically impossible to write a review of this game without coming across a little pretentious, here is my attempt;NORCO is essentially a Faulkner book wrapped in a really depressing (in a good way) futuristic setting. It's the classic southern tale where the world seems both stuck in a distant glorious past and also moving steadily towards an unsure future. The art style is the main selling point. Yes, it is pixel art, but not all pixel arts are created equally. NORCO's visuals made me feel nostalgic for a nonexistent past, you know the feeling. This is definitely one of the best uses of pixel art in gaming. There is not a lot in terms of gameplay, but still, there are some really cool moments with engaging game mechanics like a section where you get to traverse a lake. If you can vibe with it (especially with all the southern gothic thing) 10/10 chill experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is totally my type of text-heavy game. The writing throughout is top-notch. The pixel graphics are stunning. The way they capture light in those graphics, whether the flicker of refinery flames or the warmth of a sunset, is just beautiful. Plus, pixel images don’t have large amount of details, so there’s no distracting players’ attention from the text. Perfect balance between immersive storytelling and gorgeous visuals.Some complain that too much info in dialogues and items are unnecessary to push the story line - just boring extra work. But I just love discovering them and piecing together the vibe of that unique place and time in NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: What did I just play.I was worried the lack of animation and a lot of text would bore me, but nope. It's one of the best games I've played, topped only by Disco Elysium, and Lion's Song also comes to mind.The developers have a lot of fun with the incredible art, crafty zoom ins, and minimal movement. As the game progresses, the art is just getting more and more insane. I love it. Gorgeous.The music and sound is so pleasant and moody, and the first second you play in your room feels like everything is a bad dream, the day is beautiful and full of hope. Hahaha. Ha.The arcade fight was cute. I felt I had something to do and was fitting for the game. Easy.But the story and the world are something else. It starts casual. It proceeds to become less and less normal, both weird and realistic. There is a cat you pet that foretells stuff, but you just don't believe it.The way the real world mixes with increasingly futuristic and ludicrous themes is so well written and out there, I can only be jealous of the creativity displayed. I want a developer commentary mode, which is a documentary probably to cover everything in the game.Masterpiece indeed. I don't know why this game isn't more popular. It should!

_childDocuments_.review: I may replay this game, which is unusual for me. Interesting vision of a near future; pessimistic, but nihilistically optimistic and vaguely reactionary. It doesn't bluntly intellectualize much; It instead uses allegory and myth, the supernatural, surreal and day-to-day, supported by a mostly plausible setting, to bring its world to life. This is what makes it so compelling: the marriage of believable and fantastic. It's a short novel that doesn't feel dated, and there's plenty of patterns and mystery to sink your analytical side into. The music was probably the weakest point. Puzzles were fine and fun; combat easy. More days of fuel pirates and cults lie ahead.
