_childDocuments_.review: An engaging story that carried me in a feeling of sci-fi surrealism and unexpected twists.I loved how Norco manages to transmit the characters personalities so well, without actual recorded voice - excellent writing.The pixel Art is wonderful and together with the music and sfx were very successful in portraing the many different environments and moods.The simple yet challenging systems used for the mini-games, get extra credits for being implemented in an adventure point & click - it's refreshing and brings an extra layer of dynamics with that action component.How all of the above fits around a story that bridges history and fiction, reality and prophecy, religion and technology, was  masterful.A work of Art, special and unique, Norco is the result of a lot of good choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much my thing, this felt like the southern gothic lovechild of Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium. I love when games try dare to try weird and out there things without fear of alienating the audience. A mix of visual novel and point and click gameplay elements, its real hook is its writing and visuals. It boasts some of the most moving and evocative writing I’ve read in a videogame probably since playing Disco Elysium last year. It’s hard to wrap my head around how a team gets to write and actually design such an experience. It’s also comprised of beautifully crafted pixel art. There’s a particular frame that instantly became my new desktop wallpaper. And the music, what a surprise. Just a terrific moody score that goes so hard.There’s just so much depth and thematic nuance here, enough to think about for a long time after playing. It oozes creativity and artistry, and a certain kind of weird earnestness and sincerity.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO garnered my interest initially due to its setting of a sci-fi magical realist Louisiana ravaged by capitalism and the unquenchable greed of oil companies. It reminded me of two of my favorite games, Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium, which have become common comparisons to NORCO. NORCO definitely initially feels like it’s trying to follow in the footsteps of those games and their mix of fantastical elements and grounded themes pertaining to our current world, and initially it does a real quality job as the world is an enthralling and resonant one. The game’s graphics and aesthetic are beautiful in their own beaten down, grungy way, and bring the setting to life. The prose is also mostly of similar quality to KRZ and Disco and be quite evocative and got me into the game pretty well. The puzzles are fine; there’s not a lot of them, but they fit with what you’re doing in the narrative so they’re not moon logic-y. The game also has a combat system where you have to match symbols or time your clicks right. Combat in a point and click adventure game usually ain’t the best idea but it’s mostly alright.Unfortunately the game gets more and more nonsensical as it goes along; it loses the thematic strength and character writing it had started off with and the whole final conflict just feels so far removed from the initial one of the protag’s mom investigating the oil company’s shady dealings. Both KRZ and Disco had surreal endings too, but they still reinforced and were grounded in the real world themes both games had been building the whole time and tied into the arcs of the main cast wonderfully. NORCO’s ending feels like the devs just ran out of time and ideas. The ending just also throws a bunch of the combat encounters at you in quick succession too which also makes think it was rushed.  It is actually frustrating because I feel the game was close to being great, they just really needed a second pass on the third act.Overall NORCO is still a quality adventure game worth your time but I really can’t help but feel its “The Kentucky Route Zero we have at home” as it were and it could have been more.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it's definitely a weird game. I don't even know what to say about it.I don't agree with people saying it's similar to Disco Elysium, or that if you love DE you'll love this. DE is probably my favorite game ever and I don't find them similar at all, it's just alot of text in both. However the writing in Disco Elysium is god-like, it's like an impossible standard to compare to. There is nothing like it.The writing in Norco was a bit difficult to follow, I found myself having to read the same thing over and over. It's often too abstract. At times I was like come on say what you want, say it with your chest!Gameplay-wise, I didn't like that you don't see your character, you kinda just click through different locations, like it's almost just static images with a little bit of animation that you interact with. I've never been a fan of games like these. (I know there's probably a word for these sorry, english is not my first language.) I don't know why, but I really really like seeing the character that I'm playing, and being able to move them around and see them interact with the world. Otherwise I sometimes feel like I'm just sitting there clicking through images, I just can't get fully into it.However, despite all this, Norco managed to suck me into the story and I did enjoy my time playing. I don't think it's something I'd want to play through again, but I do recommend giving it a go if you like weird story games (with lots of reading). It's definitely memorable.This game reminded me of Loom for some reason.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An excellently written game overflowing with striking visuals and beautifully surreal audio. The entire mood of NORCO is one that will linger long after you’ve finished the game, like waking from a bizarre dream that you can’t shake. This is a feeling that I chase and so rarely find in games or other media. NORCO requires your attention but that is not difficult to provide. I felt captivated throughout my entire playthrough. I encourage anyone who plays to take their time. Explore everything. Read the books on the shelves. Watch some TV. It all adds up to make this game what it is. Many of the characters are flawed yet endearing, and relatable in their own ways. Even the more ridiculous ones. (We all have a little Garrett inside of us.)

_childDocuments_.review: What an experience. I don't presently have the brain power to write the kind of review I would want to for this game, but I wanted to capture some thoughts while the experience is very fresh in my mind.If you are even remotely a fan of Southern Gothic, you'll enjoy this game. I honestly cannot say that the story or setting remind me of anything else I've ever read, which is refreshing. There is, of course, a heavy dash of magical realism that is handled masterfully. Even if you have no idea what on earth is happening, it's still very coherent. Watching things fall into place at the end, where even the most minute detail of the game was suddenly very important and relevant, was a real treat. I had to put the game down for two months because of moving and my work schedule, but I was able to recall much of what had happened in the previous two acts as I picked up at the start of Act 3. The vibes were immaculate, the music was amazing, and the story was engaging. Is it the best point-and-click game I've played? No, but it is the best one I've played in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a good game with a horrible story. There is:stunning sights with gorgeous pixel artfantastic point and click gameplay with systems that keep the player from being lost, beautiful but also funny writing that doesn't censor its often very inappropriate humorect. ect. It's simply a good point and click adventure!The problem lies with the story. Upon playing the free first act, you should discover 4 deeper themes this game aims to inspect in its (by then) expertly set up story: However, the plot is indicisive about which way to head in. While playing, it feels like you are untangling many different storylines that promise to be involved with one another - while the game is really just stalling -, until the very last chapter, where the game picks (in my opinion) the most uninteresting theme and bends everything towards an inconclusive and nonsensical end. Even the central mistery of the game, , is not related to two thirds of the story. This clearly is a more personal game for Geography of Robots, nonsensical or not- but the story is just disappointing. Even if you try to "untangle the authors personal ties to the real Norco in Lousiana", it will still be devoid of sensical meaning. Maybe that is the underlying conflict this game seeks to portray, but I felt this made the entire story fall flat. TLDR:The many facets of the story, which lead to a wonderful gameplay experience, end up being nothing more than loose ends on a story that struggles to find its deeper themes.

_childDocuments_.review: I am sorry to give this a 'thumb down', as it is obvious that a lot of thought and creativity has gone into this game. Norco is a mix of American Gothic and, perhaps, magical realism, with a bit of cyberpunk thrown in. There are some interesting characters and places to be discovered. As much as I can judge this, having lived in the Deep South but not in Louisiana, these are well chosen. Two features of the game ended up disappointing me. In terms of gameplay, there is not much here for an adventure, in my view. Norco's classic adventure puzzles are for the most part too easy and transparent. At the same time, there is quite a number of action sequences and challenges that require quick reactions; these feel out of place, poorly done, and, at least for me, not enjoyable at all. Then there is the way the game's plot is constructed. Norco's particular brand of magical realism (or perhaps surrealism?) comes with an 'anything goes' kind of storytelling, which makes major plot points quite frequently seem arbitrary and random. For this reason, the game did not manage to hold my attention.There is clearly much to like here, and other players will perhaps be more forgiving than me. Still, neither Norco's gameplay nor its story managed to convince me in the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a point-and-click adventure game developed by Geography of Robots. Set in the futuristic titular town of Norco, Louisiana, it sees you in the role of Kay, who has returned home after years of wandering throughout the US following the death of her mother. When she gets home, she is greeted by the family's AI robot, Millions, to be told that her brother Blake has gone missing. Kay resolves to pick up the pieces that remain of her childhood home and ventures out into her hometown to track down her brother. This is fairly well-worn ground for a story, find your brother, salvage your home. But then Norco goes and tosses you headfirst into a densely layered magical realist sci-fi tale with religious cults, oil companies, conspiracy theories, Aliens, sentient AIs, and space rockets. Make no mistake, this is a Sci-fi game to its core. But one which goes so deep into the genre that it reinvents its tropes even as it fulfils them. Alongside the usual themes of climate change, industrial capitalism, and slavery, Norco uses the traditional sci-fi trappings to delve into intensely human themes such as loss, familial strife, poverty, and regret. The town of Norco is a hollow, soulless place. An area that has been bled dry by the surrounding oil company, Shield, to the point that whatever hasn't been stripped to the bone for a profit has sunk into the industrial swampland that dominates the landscape. It's also, as you'll find when you start exploring, populated by a load of complete weirdos. After all, who else chooses to stay in a town where the land and air are toxic and anything of any worth is immediately taken? And it's here, in this assembly of nutcases that Norco calls a population, that the game world comes to life. Norco has easily one of the most well-fleshed-out casts I've seen in a long time. Every single character has a backstory that makes them seem real and that drives their, at times childish, actions. There's the robot Millions who showed up with your mother one day and won't speak of its past, there's an eco-terrorist called Lucky who you're never quite sure if he has a cause he's fighting for or if he just likes blowing ♥♥♥♥ up. The local PI constantly talks of how well he's doing and how he's one of the few remaining good guys, but his office is so run down that the toilet is next to his desk, and won't tell you about a break-in at your house until you buy him a round and some fries. One of my favourites is a local called Keith who's setting up a boxing-themed news website called "Keith's corner" in what is one of the most hilariously wrongheaded endeavours in gaming history because, you see, Keith is a complete idiot. He's a gloriously stupid character and that's what makes him real. He doesn't have any insight or even anything interesting to say, he just wants to say something to make it seem like he's got a handle on things, when in fact, he's just as clueless as everyone else. That, in a nutshell, is how Norco manages to sell the more fantastical elements of the story. It presents them straight up as matter-of-factly as it can. The characters react to these as though they were mundane, almost trivial things to consider. So when the guy you've been helping on a job-share app finds out that the app is run from a warehouse by a giant eagle with alien machinery for entrails, reacts to this news by shrugging his shoulders and saying "I see a lot of weird stuff on this app" it doesn't break immersion, it reinforces it, because this guy has other ♥♥♥♥ to deal with and needs the money to keeps the lights on and his family fed. This is a result of the short-termism that poverty inflicts on people. That's why no one seems to want to leave Norco even though it's poison. They're all just trying to make it to tomorrow. I also need to point out that the writing is second to none. I'm serious, this may be the best-written game for years. It may even be better than Disco Elysium or Kentucky Route Zero. It's definitely on par with both of those classics. The story is split into two main branches, Kay's search for her brother and Catherine's, Kay's mother, final moments before her death. Telling the story in this two-pronged manner helps keeps everything fresh and always presents you with new backgrounds and interactions. The descriptive text is almost poetic in places and the dialogue is written as authentically as possible given that the writer is actually from the area depicted in the game and it contains some of the funniest scenes I've read in ages. It's a testament to how good the writing and setting is of Norco that it has taken me this long to mention the stunning pixel art. I've been constantly amazed by pixel art in recent years and this is no different. The scenes of complete poverty and desolation are so detailed and perfectly capture the despair that hangs over this town like a thick fog. Each scene brilliantly conveys the brooding atmosphere put forward in the writing and some of the more surreal scenes are striking in their beauty and detail. On top of all this, the soundtrack is excellent. Truly excellent. So good I wound up buying it. In conclusion, will you like Norco? I do think you will. I think it's easily one of the games of the year. Norco is an intelligent, evocative story of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world and its inhabitants. It tackles themes head-on that are rarely even touched upon in gaming. That's not just in terms of its portrayal of a community buckling under capitalism, but also in its compassionate, thoughtful portraits of people on the margins. That, even in the most desolate places, there's always hope and the warmth of human connection to help us find meaning in our lives. As the game itself puts with one of the best lines ever: "Even the synthetic has its time and place"

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER FREEIt's a magnificent game. Stunning visuals, good sound design. intuitive game design and over all incredible writing with a powerful message. Now, that's a lot of adjectives, but this is the not-too-long list of if this game is for you:     - Do you like the idea of a Louisiana-Bayou-Southern Gothic setting? Try NORCO! (Same answer if the Resident Evil game you liked most was RE7, based on setting alone.)     - Are visuals something that you value a lot in a game? Especially in an artistic way? Try NORCO!     - Do you want a story that's meaningful on a personal level, while also relating to bigger and deeper issues in the current world that we live in (with an anti-corporation sentiment on top)? Try NORCO!     - Do you like vaguely poetic and definitely beautiful writing that makes you reflect about it even if you're not playing? Try NORCO!     - Do you want a relatively short game you can play in a few days or a really invested evening and night? Try NORCO!     - Do you like explorations of Americana*? Try NORCO! *For many of these points, if you don't like them it's probably not a game you'll be interested in, but this question is optional. Yes, the game feels deeply US centric to me (in a very emotional way, not necessarily patriotic), but as someone who's never stepped foot into the United States I quite enjoyed it. It's more of an added bonus, I think. I wouldn't recommend it if you have trouble with taking things genuinely: while this game can be funny, it's better if you engage with the topics and the core emotional dystopia right away and get personally involved. Also, there's relatively not that much room for personal choice, as the story is lineal, so mind that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very dear to me. It presents plainly the often contradictory balance we must strike in our lives between industry, the land, familial ties, and just straight up surviving. Nobody comes out clean, but we're lucky to make it through with a few laughs and a few bumps on our heads.I'm from Luling, a community across the river from the actual site of this game. This area, the River Parishes of Southeast Louisiana, very rarely gets any accurate depictions in media. The closest -- at least visually -- is the first season of HBO's True Detective, much of which was shot in Norco, LA, but its setting is more inland. Growing up here, though, nothing is as painfully accurate a depiction of growing up in "Cancer Alley" as you'll find in this game.A lead developer on the game, Yuts, has been my friend for a while. We didn't grow up together, but our lives took similar paths. Watching this game grow from early sidescrolling efforts in JavaScript to a final game with multiple talents involved has been an unparalleled joy. For the first time in any media, I saw myself and my lived experience depicted.The amount of research that went into this game by such a small team is astonishing. Echoes of real world locations and events are depicted, distorted through a dark lens and placed into this timeline to weave an unforgettable narrative. Nearly everything in this game has an actual world counterpart, even if they're partially obfuscated by a warped technological veneer. For a local, this feels like one big Easter Egg (like, Flannelass is straight up an actual well-loved member of the New Orleans DIY music scene), but NORCO never comes off as an in-joke. Broader themes of exploitation of land and human life in the name advancement of industry are clear and should be witnessed. Incels and edgelords from the internet exist everywhere, and the cult of personality surrounding their figureheads is examined here. This game is of its time, but it could be set any time in the past or next 20 years.NORCO is never hateful or accusatory in its tone. It asks no direct questions, and it asks no more of the audience beyond their attention. It's wildly funny at times, especially so if you care to note the distinct identity of residents of the River Parishes. There is no overbearing narrator; everything presented is from afar, like a dream you can't slow down. Encircling the reality of industry and its massive impact on life without explicit condemnation is a feat ... especially since the narrative is primarily grounded in a reunion of the Madère family.Selfish as it may be, this truly feels like a video game that was made just for me. Often I feel that there are too many video games, that as the medium grows and becomes more accessible, we've seen a glut of garbage (クソゲー) and naked attempts to cash in. Games that are trying to "say something" can be limited by the conventions of the medium, expertise of the writers, or external pressure for accessibility. In my view, NORCO doesn't suffer from this: the celebration of Southeast Louisiana as a painful place of beauty that is forced to coexist with industry, that maybe you need to escape from but which you're inextricably tied to is done with a clear voice and I feel it in my bones.God bless the Madères, and God bless Norco.

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what Backbone wanted to become, initially disguised as a classic detective story, at some point turning into something completely radical, but stumbled precisely at the moment of this transition. Here the classic "homecoming" is transformed into some insane mix of Southern Gothic;  dystopianism and Terry Gilliam's distorted absurd images;  political manifestos, none of which are shoved down your throat by the creators; crazy mumbling in your head, as if you are preparing to remove the corpse from the tree in Revachol, but again you will be too lazy to do it. Describing the plot in detail in this case is a useless task, because it is precisely in the ability to convey even the strangest things to the player as accurately and beautifully as possible, the unique way of arranging the plot into a single monolith, that the unbearable charm of this thing lies.The game does not seek to make you comfortable, but this is what immerses you in some strange state of southern relaxation. That relaxation that begins somewhere in a jazz bar with a glass of bourbon, and ends in a mangrove with alligators wandering nearby. Even the genre of the game constantly seems to elude you in the fog of deceptive swamps, whether it's an adventure quest with puzzles, or a visual novel with a non-linear narrative, or something else. And it works. Surprisingly, it really works. Perhaps the point is the attention with which the creators approached the development of both the story and the characters. Every minute you understand that the authors are incredibly fond of the strange universe of their game, investing in its creation the most valuable of themselves, striving to polish even the smallest details that many players will not even get to during the game. And it is precisely this quality that most of all unites this game with Disco Elysium, and not obvious markers, even if the magnitude here is not millions of words.NORCO brings a lot of discoveries, but the most important of them are extremely interesting new creators, whose name must be remembered. Geography of Robots team - my respect to you personally for the excellent work. It's like a breath of fresh air, giving hope that the adventure genre is far from saying its last word and is able to evolve. Bravo.

_childDocuments_.review: If a cinematic point-and-click tech-noir adventure with lots of birds and a sublime score featuring sludge masters Thou is something you would enjoy, welcome to NORCO.NORCO is a debut point-and-click adventure game developed by Geography of Robots and published by Raw Fury (Kathy Rain, Whispers of a Machine). The game follows Kay returning to her hometown of Norco, Louisiana, to check on her younger brother after the death of their mother. The town is an industrial hub and a shadow of an oil refinery that works 24/7, providing the region with jobs but also with pollution and property issues in a near future of environmental and economic downfall.The game introduces several interesting design choices. The main heroine and her brother have smiley faces instead of regular faces in photos and on character icons, while all other characters appear normal. That makes the story a bit more personal, I guess. Another notable thing is the absence of proper voiceovers; they are substituted by artificial ones that only convey the character's voice but not what the character says. Some barking and laughing NPCs were especially amusing! Humor in the game is dark, awkward, and often self-depreciated. For instance, the showgoer's "hotdog adventure" is hilarious, but only if you are willing to listen through the whole thing by requesting the showgoer to continue with the chagrin. Also, renaming Shell to Shield with the slogan "A Greener World Awaits" is pretty comical.Going through the game was compelling because its mood and atmosphere corresponded with my mindset; the experience might be much different for those who maintain a positive outlook. The only thing that I did not like were religious connotations, even if twisted enough to call them blasphemy.NORCO is bird-heavy. You get all kinds of birds in different manners as they shape both the story and the setting. From a casual mention of little wrens nesting nearby to a gruesome scene of a gigantic bald eagle, and from prolific bird calls to epic Mardi Gras bird costumes, Geography of Robots clearly intended to feature birds as much as possible. One way or another, the game also mentions ducks, crows, egrets, pelicans, cardinals, and more.What is your favorite bird-related scene or idea here? Let me know in the comments. I will tell you mine as well.As NORCO is rooted in Louisiana's cultural and industrial landscape, it's only natural to hear the local sludge band Thou in a mix with otherwise somber ambient music by Gewgawly I.Sometimes epic, sometimes jazzy, but always mournful, synthetic tunes with occasional instrumentation shape the principal soundscape. Distorted drone/doom songs by Thou give the necessary heaviness to the most dramatic moments, and the abundance of natural sounds in appropriate areas like swamps contribute immensely to the whole thing.In my taste, the game's audial side is a masterpiece in itself.Even if depressive and tense, NORCO is an outstanding story-driven adventure set in the grim future that will surely grab the attention of those who appreciate its overlapping themes.One warning, though: if you miss your mom or experience difficulties in relations with your older kids, the game might be a bit too heavy on those matters. Tread it lightly!

If you, like me, want an active participation in understandable game mechanics, this game is not for you. _childDocuments_.review: Norco has a charming artstyle and it is very intriguing once you first start the game out. However all that quickly wears out since the game's story is rather pointless, with very poorly written character dialogue and very out of place mechanics. While the game does a good job of immersing you into the world from the start without overexplaining too much, I just found zero reason to care about the it. The characters are all either very bland or they all talk like they are from 2014-5 forums and image boards. BRUH BRUH BRUH. The game does offer some very significant choices they are very few and far between, it's, for the most part, linear without any good puzzles to spice things up. It throws a  couple new mechanics here and there trying to keep up variety but they all fall short. The RPG fights are laughable and the boat sections are tedious. The story as a whole also suffers from a pacing issue, while it was short it felt like it dragged on because it offered no intrigue. For a point and click there just isn't enough interactivity with the environment (while good at the start, this gets a lot worse about halfway through the game), and Kay, being the blank  slate that she is offers no interesting descriptions or thoughts about anything around her. There's even a "mind map" that lets you keep track of characters and everything that has been happening yet there's no flavor. We are supposed to be in a mind of a character and it's basically just a game wiki. There's just nothing interesting there and it all felt like a big waste of time. Neither the journey or the ending felt fulfilling in any way. I love good point and click adventures but this just isn't it. I'm sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed the game in 3 sessions, mostly being utterly sucked by the fascinating story. This is a near-perfect game, for me a strong 9,5/10. Two years have passed and I am still listening to synthwave tracks by Gewgawly I and heavy Thou tracks. You get a crazy, gothic and cyberpunk tragic story with well-written characters and interesting locations. The game is mostly slow-paced, focused on narratives, but it fastens up when needed. _childDocuments_.review: An absolutely wild ride of an adventure game.This game will take you all kinds of places. Lots of them amusing, some of them unpleasant, and most of them unexpected. The gloves are off, and the writers went on a wild goose chase, in which they were riding the goose and dragging you, the player, along with a lasso... and the games is all the better for it. Wild, unpredictable, full of several memorable moments, micro-interactions (clown make-up for those who know), but also with enough of a trackable narrative that it doesn't leave you feeling completely lost with no real sense of what you should be doing.Sometimes the prose goes a bit too heavy and sacks the pacing (especially right at the beginning), the boating mini-games- while being a welcome way to break up how reading intensive the game is- also moves at a snail's pace and hinders the forward momentum quite a bit. But all in all, well worth the purchase, well worth the play, and something that will likely stand out in your memory for years.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I went into with great anticipation. To the game's credit, many of its elements are wonderful. The star of the show is the worldbuilding. NORCO's setting is deeply thought out and lived in. It feels like a real place that one would want to explore. Within the first act of the game, you do explore, and it's here the game shines; the people you meet, the areas you visit, the sounds and music, all engaging. As the story builds, it seems to be weaving a tale that straddles the line between thrilling and emotionally resonant. However.As the game approaches the end, this balance is completely thrown out the window. The people we met vanish, plotlines left either unfulfilled or resolved in a lazy and unfulfilling way. Where we could have an emotional climax we are given a silly and tonally off action climax. While I know the developers avoided this influence, I can't help but think of how Kentucky Route Zero rounded off its story. It, too, was a jarring shift, but one that over time built towards bittersweet resolution, one that allowed us to say goodbye we spent all this time meeting. I think NORCO wants to be A Game of Some Importance, that has Something To Say About Life, in the vein of the aformentioned KRZ, or Disco Elysium, touchstones you see mentioned in other reviews here. Whereas those were games by writers, this feels like a story by game developers, shackled to the idea and tropes of the classic Adventure Game.Having played through to the ending, it threw the earlier parts I really did love into a new light. Characters I thought would end up important were left by the wayside. Mechanics I thought were for throwaway gags ended up being vital parts of the game. To put it bluntly, it infuriated me. There was such promise here, to be thrown away by such a unfufilling ending. I wish I could recommend this game. There's so much love and care in most of its corners. To its credit, I'm only so infuriated by it because it did make me feel things. It was never boring. But, like the rushed ending of the Game of Thrones series, the lack of impact of the ending made me rethink the worth of the rest of the story. I'm sorry.

_childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Welcome back comrades, this is MF Kraven & you are watching less than 10 mins reviews. The Youtube series where I take a look at games i think seem cool & give my thoughts on them in less than 10 mins.Today I take a look at Norco. Norco is a text based point & click adventure game set in a dystopian Louisiana. Visit your childhood home full of trauma to bury your recently deceased mother, but upon arrival fall into the surreal story of your small refinery town that awaits you. But can a point & click game in this day hold up to gaming juggernauts or is it not worth getting? Lets find out//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//Described on their steam page as a Southern Gothic point & click doesn't truly do this game justice. See, Norco has a pseudo nightmare aesthetic that drew me in. I come from a small suburb in Los Angeles where the factories were prominent & the scenery haunts me to this day. To say it is surreal is an understatement, it's filled with scenes that seem oddly familiar.... in a nutshell the ambiance of Norco elevate the artstyle of this game to almost recommend it to you guys based on it alone.//Gameplay//As aforementioned Norco is a Point & Click adventure game, expect to read a lot. There are a few instances of "mini games" or it's condensed fighting mechanic that offers very little other than a remember a pattern, timed clicks and two short boat "adventures".Well half of the genre of point & click relies heavily on the story and while it starts off very innocuous it quickly turns sardonic, religious undertones accompanying strafed relationships in a family- it makes for a story that actually- hit very close to home... Your brother Blake has gone missing in the aftermath of your mother's death. In the hopes of finding him, you must follow a fugitive security android through the refineries, strip malls, and drainage ditches of suburban New Orleans. What comes in the journey to finding him, you'll never guess.//Price// 14.99 USD//How many hours estimated//I finished the story in about 5 hours. And while it does feel tempting to go back and 100% it.. I think one go around on the story is enough for me. I'll elaborate further in my Final Thoughts.//Is it Playable on Steamdeck?//While it is playable on SteamDeck, the combat and minigames are far more tedious on it than on PC. Plus without Steam Cloud- I had started my adventure on SD originally but when i tried it out on my laptop, none of the save data was there. Luckily for me, I was only 20 mins into my adventure so I just opted to play it completely through on my laptop.//Final Thoughts//*deep sigh*Wow what a story, Norco is undoubtedly a tour de force. The story hit way too close to home, no pun intended. I also fled my family home and traveled across the country seeking a new home, my sibling is also a very coddled person with the same kind of tendencies as Kay's brother, my mother also terminally ill... i have a strained relationship with. My childhood home is a mausoleum of nightmares.... but why am I opening up about all this? Simply said, Norco did a number on me. Clicking through Kay's home seeing the unfolded laundry, pills on the counter, overall just unfinished business of her mother gave me a grim look into my future.The journey to finding your brother spirals almost immediately into the whimsy and over-complicated. See the narrative structure is approached in an artistic manner, you have a mind map that can catalogue basically all the information you need from each character you meet or setting you remember. Its divided into three acts however you are switched between the main character Kay and her terminally ill mother. You see the world in two very abstract perspectives and while I can appreciate the effort- the parts with the mother, I could not wait to get em over with. This is where my subjective opinion will drag this a bit, all the characters feel real, they feel gritty, I'm truly disgusted by some of them. The way they talk with such dissonance, malcontent and disrespect... I found myself needing to take brief pauses and realizing I may need to speak to a therapist- I joke but I cant praise the writers of this story for conveying people in ways I've dealt with first hand.But going back to the plot, it's something I can't truly talk about without actually spoiling anything and in my opinion it's a story that should be at least experienced once. There are a few funny interactions here and there and ill say this with no context. Hot Dogs. Santa. Garret. It's a beautiful game with a haunting cyberpunk esque story. There's corporate espionage, terrorism, murder, drugs, & a hillbilly getting his ass kicked.I recommend Norco 100% to anyone who wants to indulge your brain in a little bit of literature. Maybe it can even take some fringe FPS players down a notch... it's a nuanced story for admittedly pretentious people. Still- I say buy it Now.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the hardest parts about writing reviews is talking about your experience with a game – without spoiling that experience for any potential players. And I experienced a lot in ’s  alternate reality Louisiana that I would like to talk about – but unfortunately can’t.  offers a lot of surprises related to its mysteries, so even broadly talking about how much I enjoyed a certain puzzle mechanic for example would ruin the fun for new players. And with a playthrough only lasting between 3.5-5h, even the smallest bit of information might be crucial.So instead, I’ll only be able to broadly talk about what I enjoyed in  so much – and why I would recommend to it to everyone who appreciates a narrative-driven game that is light on actual gameplay, even for a point & click adventure.The best thing about  is, without doubt, its world and characters. It only took a few minutes of playing and I was fully immersed, drawn into the game.  immediately sets itself apart from other dystopia-depicting games by choosing South Louisiana as its setting – and keeping the technical advances of its world on the smaller side. While I love a good sci-fi dystopia, sticking with a more “realistic” future makes the game even more haunting.With dozens of mysteries to offer, you’ll quickly want to see what answers the world of  has to offer. With a literal “mind-map” keeping track of the protagonists’ thoughts from the beginning, which is being expanded upon learning new information, I was quickly invested in unravelling the web of ’s secrets. And there sure were plenty of things I was wondering about, be it the protagonist, some of the characters & their history or the world itself.But not only was  drawing me in with its mysteries, it was the world building itself that really made play through the game in one go. Strange places and even stranger inhabitants made me want to see just what’s next around the corner. Thankfully,  carves out its own identity in the big market of games depicting dystopias by focussing more on the unique aspects of its South Louisiana setting. While common elements of modern dystopia stories are still there, I never felt like they were taking frontstage in a way that made me go “haven’t I seen this before?”.Instead, I was pleasantly surprised by how wonderfully weird  can be at times – one scene especially made me burst out in laughter because it was just that unexpected. Others kept me on the edge of my seat because I just could not predict where things might end up. In the case of gameplay though, thankfully, I was always able to predict what to do next. Point & click adventures have the tendency to keep a player stuck when it’s too unclear what to do next – but  evades this problem by always offering a help function that doesn’t break your immersion: If you’re moving around with a party of multiple characters, for example, you can ask them what might be next. I personally think this is a great way to offer help but still not remind you that you’re just playing a point & click adventure game in the end.That said, I wouldn’t mind if the puzzles were a bit harder to solve. While there are some great & unique ways to solve problems in this game, most of them are also very obvious and don’t require you to take a pause to think. One could argue that this makes the story flow better, as you spend more time reading dialogues than thinking about how to solve a riddle, but then again,  IS a point & click adventure and not “just” a visual novel. Still, this is an extremely subjective topic and I’d definitely rather breeze through a game thanks to easier puzzles than being stuck with too hard ones. Treat  as a point & click adventure with a focus on narrative instead of gameplay and you got it right.While we’re back to talking the narrative, I want to use this opportunity to speak about the characters of . As I mentioned earlier, you can expect a lot of strange personalities – however, they’re also more than just that, more than being strange for the heck of it. Dialogues are the primary literary device in , which explores a lot of topics, from setting-typical ones like the consequences of capitalism to more niche ones, like internet culture & influencers. Thankfully, the dialogues in  are really well-written, so they never come off as forced or unnatural for the characters.As for the story itself, well, as other reviews have already said: The final act of  can be somewhat divisive. Some plot threads or characters are tied up more hurriedly than I wanted them to be while others feel like they haven’t really been wrapped up at all. Without doubt, it can be said that the final act of  moves at a different pace than what came before. If that’s a good thing or bad thing, if lingering questions are a sign of quality or not, that’s something quite subjective.Personally speaking, I think I would’ve preferred a different final act. In fact, I’m still not completely sure what to make of it. It’s highly possible my feelings about it are going to change over the next few games but as I finished – and hours later, as I’m writing this review – I feel more taken aback by the final act than getting a wrap-up as great as the events leading up to it. I would’ve also preferred it if it leaned less into the  side of things than it did.However, and this is the more important part, I’d still recommend playing  regardless. It’s just such a unique game, from its setting & world to some if its puzzles, that it would be a shame if it didn’t get more recognition. Sure, due to its chosen genre and setting, it’s not exactly a game for everyone. But if my and/or other reviews make this game sound interesting enough for you, please, give the game – or its free demo – a try! It’s been too long since I’ve played through such a refreshingly unique dystopian story, that even a weak(er) final act shouldn’t stop you from seeing what  is about.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could give NORCO a neutral rating rather than yes/no recommendation then I would. Normally I would start my reviews with  a synopsis of the story and what you do in the game but I can't do that for NORCO. It's a narrative-driven game but even if I spoiled the story, the spoilers wouldn't make sense without context because the story is so crazy and out there. Even with context it barely makes sense. Instead, I'll provide a summary as best I can.NORCO is a point and click narrative heavy game set in a fictional, possibly futuristic southern US. There are religious, specifically Christian, themes and symbology that run through the story, though it's not overbearing and doesn't dwell on it. It's very hard to review a narrative heavy game while avoiding talking about the story too much but suffice to say this game is largely about reading! Most of the gameplay is reading the story then selecting an option or clicking the right thing on screen, apart from some brief and VERY light turn-based combat that is so infrequent and basic that it's not really worth discussing in more detail.I'm a huge fan of narrative heavy games and I don't mind doing a lot of reading at all. For reference, Disco Elysium is one of my all-time favourite games. I actually picked NORCO up because it looked to be along the same lines, but NORCO doesn't come close to the greatness of Disco Elysium. It's not a bad game but it's quite short and it feels like it just kind of ends. The worldbuilding is lacklustre and so many characters' motivations go unexplained. Events happen but the game rarely tells you . What NORCO has is good but I found myself wanting more and the depth that I was hoping for just wasn't there.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore the art style and story of the game. It is very depressing but also witty and the characters and the dialogues with them are masterfully done. Something else is the sound design. Since the game has no voice acting, only rumbling, the sound of the environment had to be believable and it really is. It captures the atmospehere of the area around New Orleans and it is accompanied by great soundtrack. I played demo of the first act, then I bought the full game and the progress save is possible to be used. That's why the short play time showng.Very big thumbs up and reccomendation. :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: While not super complex or challenging, Norco has fantastic world building and a thought-provoking plot. The art style is great, and the characters are memorable and well written.The game has appropriate levity despite its otherwise serious and oppressive tone. The setting and world building are great and feel grounded, even when the story veers into the surreal. The puzzles aren't very hard, but do well to drive the plot and kept me engaged. The plot and setting left me wanting more, and I would love to see further titles in the universe or lengthened sequels. I would highly recommend Norco if it catches your eye.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't yet played it through, but NORCO is a tour-de-force of storytelling, graphic imagination, pixel art, regional history, left critique, and environmental science fictions. The gameplay is smooth, the puzzles are well-designed, the soundscape is impeccable, and the art is stunning - the use of light and texture belongs in a museum.It's a work of political art that is also deeply local and deeply rooted in a real place with a real history and real wounds. It's rare today to see a video game that is so deeply attached to a specific place and history, and it's very meaningful to see that in NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: I have just finished and immensely enjoyed playing the closest thing to an interactive (and very playable) novel...and I mean that in the most complimentary way I can express this point.  By this I don't mean that the game is typical Interactive Fiction.  Norco looks gorgeous with its unsettling and dark pixel graphics; the music is brooding, understated, and unsettling; its UI is intuitive, using a shadowgate-style corner in the bottom right along with a helpful world map (yet it stays minimalistic, as you are meant to feel as if you are looking through the eyes of the enigmatic and unseen protagonist); the gameplay is varied during the times you are not in adventuring mode, with a trippy combat system, a cellphone UI, and a boat navigation system; the atmosphere is familiar--it takes place in a world we recognize by its American cities, and yet there is always lurking...just underneath...the tinge of the unfamiliar--be it supernatural, alien, psychadelic, or just an uncanny yet unmistakable sense that something is always amiss.  You are meant to always be off-balance no matter which of the game's 2 timelines you are currently playing through.  But make no mistake, this amazing game uses all of its considerable assets to frame the most important parts in this game in expert fashion.  First, we have Norco's environment.  Norco, located in southern Louisiana is already by itself a unique place that this game almost treats as a character in itself.  The mysterious amalgamation of the supernatural, of magic, and of the religious are a natural part that comes with Louisiana's rich history.  Along with that, the enigmatic dialogue, vague suggestions of some unknowable mythos too deep to truly understand, and the existance of impossible beings make you question what is real and what is not.  It also helps enhance the constant sense of paranoia as conflicting stories have you guessing who is your friend and who, perhaps, might be using you for their unknown and yet nefarious ends... and guessing what those ends may even be.  Yet in the midst of all this fantasy, we have a sense of the familiar as well.  We have a home, a cell phone, cryptocurrency...and from the very start, even though we start so far away from Norco, we inexplicably find our way back home.  There is a sense of an unending cycle that is more powerful than your will...that while you may change things from day to day, in the end, the cycle will inevitably repeat itself forever.  Your face (which is not shown) is immaterial...irrelevant...only a trivial curiosity compared to the scale of the issues you wrestle with in this story.  I am aware that this explanation I have written all seems so nebulous as I explain it, but that is where the writing and the dialogue in this game truly shine.  Locals talk like locals and act like they are unique, but familiar identities in this strange land.  And somehow, while local yourself, it is you that is the stranger.  The dialogue (of which there is quite a bit) is all expertly written.  The prose is professional and arrests your attention and grips you firmly.  It is the impotus that keeps you searching and thinking and wondering and attempting to make sense of it all as hard as everything may be to grasp.  However, a VERY helpful tool in this game comes in the form of the mind map in the top left of the screen.  It displays a visual representation of your interactions and how they intertwine as a web, but by clicking each item in the web, you get a very helpful summary of the protagonist's current understanding of the events which have occurred up to the point where you have played.  All of these factors: the beautiful pixel graphics, the music, the ease of movement, the story, the dialogue, the writing, they all come together to create a work that is greater than the sum of its parts.  I have deliberately minimized an explanation of the story and characters, as I feel it is not necessary to get into that in order to know if this is a game you will appreciate.  Also...the most fun I had in this game was in reading through the story while knowing nothing ahead of time and attempting to wrestle with this tale that is so complex and irregular and severe, and mysterious, while in a way also being strangely familiar.  I will summarize: if you don't mind, or even enjoy reading, you will find an incredible adventure that is well worth your time.  If you are not a fan of clicking through text and would rather shootaman, this game isn't for you..but then again if you are reading this far, chances are this is not the type of person you are.10/10  if you read this far, dont think. just buy. thank me later

_childDocuments_.review: A post apocalyptic sci-fi mystery set in a small town rural south Louisiana swamp! What’s not to love? This is the best point and click game that I have every played. The writing is superb. The setting and general mood of the game is right up my alley. The characters are unique and quirky and dreary. The story keeps you guessing and never drags for a second. This high concept sci-fi stuff sometimes can be a drag but this is not the case here. I recommend everyone gives this one a shot even if “reading” games aren’t usually your cup of tea. You may find yourself pleasantly surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this game if you are a Disco Elysium fan who wants a little more of that vibe. Both games have very similar themes, narration, and art direction.I felt overall underwhelmed by what the game seemed to promise; the scope of the story was all at once too grand and not grand enough, and the conclusion ultimately felt unsatisfactory. There were perhaps too many bizarre and absurd elements in the world to make it believable or cohesive, and the half made attempts at social commentary and odd humor didn't aid in that. its fine for what it is, but I can't help but feel that this developer is capable of greater things.

_childDocuments_.review: (I've never written a review on Steam before, but felt compelled to do so for Norco - as even if it only encourages one more person to play it, I would be happy with that!)Norco is a hard game to summarise. To describe it as a point and click adventure would seem to do it a gross disservice, but if you're really looking to force it into a box I guess it would be that?! However, the ambition of the storyline is breathtaking, the characters are genuine and memorable, the dialogue is frequently hilarious, disturbing or both, the artwork is incredibly beautiful even when representing hideous environments, and the mechanics that carry the whole thing along are novel, smoothly integrated and most importantly fun.Discussing too much of the story would spoil the best aspects of the game, but broadly speaking it is about an alternate near future Louisiana community coming to terms with the fallout of the petrochemical industry, both physically and emotionally. Each of the characters, as well as the earth itself, is scarred or displaced by generations of abuse and are grappling - collectively or individually - to understand and transcend this legacy. However, if that sounds too high-brow for you it also features one of the greatest toilet humour sequences I've ever encountered, and has motorbike riding androids... and also a minigame where you can agitate a cat to the extent it blasts into orbit.All in all I cannot recommend Norco highly enough as an experience. I was dubious as to whether the mechanics would be interesting enough to carry me through the storyline, and in the end I'm incredibly thankful that they were because I found the whole experience uniquely thought provoking; profoundly disturbing and beautiful in equal measure. (Afterwards if you are interested, there is a lot of fascinating writing about the colonial history of the parishes of Louisiana and the surrounding Gulf of Mexico, and their direct lineage to the petrochemical corridor and its socio-economic effects; I would seriously recommend checking them out for some greater contextual insight. However this is not at all mandatory to play the game and fall in love with it!)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Once I picked it up I couldn't put it down, wonderful poetic writing and dialogue, great characters, amazing setting, beautiful artwork, had a blast. The perfect combination of seemingly retro mechanics with an extremely contemporary and interesting authorial voice. If you like off-beat adventure/IF games with a great sense of place, you can't go past NORCO.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Was looking forward to this game since I first heard about it and it most definitely met (and exceeded) my expectations. Incredible story, brilliant gameplay. My only complaint is the length, but the depth of lore and spectacular characters that  this game manages to pack into a 5 or 6 hour runtime honestly blows my mind. Buy this if you're even slightly interested,
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Great atmosphere, world state, soundtrack and overall vibe.I had hopes for the Mind Map system to be an extra layer of puzzles and conclusions (akin to recent Sherlock Holmes games) or different interpretations to the events of the story. As it is, Mind Map system only reviews the story elements, which is great too, but I feel the game could have used a bit more difficulty in terms of the puzzles.But then again, the story had me few times laughing manically to the madness of the world, tearing up to the stories of the characters and left me speechless at the end.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: the music, visuals, and atmosphere are top notch - the vibes are all there and i'd recommend solely based on that fact.however, through a more critical lens, the game definitely does feel indie at times with some of the gameplay mechanics which are pretty barebones and rough around the edges, although it's still more than most other point-and-click games have.the writing is decent; it definitely favours a more abstract, surrealist tone to forgo much of the actual explaining that they might have to do otherwise and because of that the plot itself becomes somewhat muddled, especially towards the end. or maybe i'm just spoiled by disco elysium, which, at least with regards to themes and writing, shares some similarities with norco.feeling a strong 7 to a light 8 on this one
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is your typical pont-and click adventure, with items to find, places to visit and decisions to make. There are a couple of turn-based battles. It's the only element of the game I would define simply "average", because the rest is very good.The game mainly revolves around text descriptions and conversations and both are very, VERY well written. For the most part they are not verbose, which usually is a difficult balance to strike. To enjoy the game you still have to like reading, though. I do, but it's not for everyone.The pixel art and the music are well executed and always appropriate for the storytelling, but the best element of the game is the story itself. I'm not going to spoil anything, let's just say that it revolves around a big oil company and a group of fanatics. It's pretty crazy and emotional at the same time.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews for games on Steam. This will be my only one, because it deserves to be written about. NORCO is a game, that despite being a point and click, has changed me. I have never played a game before that has left me with such a strong feeling of being haunted. Literally, when I finished the game this feeling of unease followed me around like a ghost for days afterward. The game left me in deep thought for weeks. As an avid reader, the narration is immaculate. The story is so layered it's impossible to understand the depth of it all with just one play through. Playing it a second time is equally as enthralling, trying to pick up the missing pieces. The love that the entire team has for Louisiana can be seen and felt through the attention to detail in every sense of the word all through the entire game.Every character, all of whom feel are destined to face some sort of tragic, ill-fated doom, garner moments of empathy from the player. It's all tragic with grimy moments of dark humor.The attention to detail in the pixel backgrounds, rich in color, are animated in such a way that gives this game a nice touch. The music is haunting, becoming more and more distorted and sinister as you progress through the game. There's nothing I can say bad about this game.I could go on and on, but I will end by saying if it's a game that deserves to be bought and played it's this one. Amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO has a bunch of unique ideas, but I felt like they failed to follow through on some of the most compelling facets of their story. I still found it to be overall an enjoyable and thought-provoking game, if a bit disappointing in some ways. If you're into unusual, story-driven, word-heavy games, it's probably worth picking up. But if this genre isn't normally your cup of tea then you might want to pass on it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked NORCO, but it is also a game that requires players to have a decent tolerance for religious imagery, unanswered questions, and mysticism. I happen to enjoy that sort of thing, and I also appreciated the cyberpunk aesthetic of the earlier sections and the invocation of current issues, such as medical debt, climate change, or corporate encroachment on small communities. NORCO is also text-heavy and the experience requires a lot of reading, but for me, it had enough interactivity to still be enjoyable as a game. Players who are less fond of reading may want to play something different.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing writing, very far removed from anything else I've ever played/read. If you're someone who is drawn to strange unique things definitely check this out.It is definitely heavy on narrative, gameplay is somewhat light, but honestly even if that doesn't sound appealing to you, you should check it out anyway if the strange story is at all interesting to you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I savored this game and wish it lasted 4 hours longer. The graphics, the ambience, the sharp wit. I will be looping back for achievements.-Too many near-future *-punk narratives go out of their way to utterly debase all humanity. I'm tired of my nose being smothered into the muck of melodramatic robo tropes. Been there, done that. The suburban swamp world of NORCO, with its multi-generational cast and the uncanny familiarity of indigenous techno-Catholicism, glows with heart and soul, even when all the chips are down. Call it NORCOZY. -This is a weird reference but if you're a fan of “iceberg memes” or "rabbit holes" you'll probably like this story? Can't say much without spoilers...-All the chill vibes of retro point-and-click adventures without it being a tiresome pixel hunt. Enough difficulty to make you feel like you're unraveling a mystery worth unraveling - not just auditing a game script-My one critique is I did feel rushed in the final act. I still have questions...A slice of Americana for dessert, with a bittersweet aftertaste

_childDocuments_.review: modern cosmic horror. i had the pleasure of visiting new orleans for a week once, and while i was there all i could think about was the disconnect between the sort of spirituality being advertised to tourists and the possibility of another world beneath all the cracks in the pavement. i wrote down these journals in the style of a lovecraftian protagonist. it was fun! so you can imagine my delight at seeing a game that is not only set in the bayou, but also knows how to construct and make rich a version of it that crosses over into cyberpunk, magical realism, dark comedy, and horror. i've been playing this game off and on for months, and sometimes i'd boot it up for just 30 minutes, read some dialogue, get absolutely lost in the synth soundtrack, and find myself doing something else entirely. i don't want to detract from how visually rich and colorful the art style is, but it really felt like i read a book. specifically, it captures that feeling of a book you can't put down. i'm not generally one to play point-and-clicks with a lot of text, at least until recently. highly recommended for people who want to play call of cthulu in a setting where half of the NPCs call you (female protagonist) "bruh"
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game. Really enjoyed it.  I grew up with old school point and click adventures and this definitely brought me back, but also kept things fresh, engaging and really whacked out (in good way).   Not predictable and really felt like an experience that was great, but was not what I was expecting.  Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's a long, humid night in this game's sci-fi story. It feels dreamlike sometimes, but that sort of surreal horror is the only way to communicate the emotional toll that this very real world takes on people.We can all see it coming, but few people seem to really feel it.This game has a few lightweight QTEs in the combat, but that isn't what the game's about. There are a couple 'grand' puzzles that I believe are designed in a way to make you feel reasonably clever, too, really feel like you pulled it all together. So that's good also.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a game that captures multiple tones successfully while other projects in games, television and film, struggle with just one. I went into this game apprehensively, as I'm truly not the biggest fan of point and click games, but as the story, enveloped in themes of existentialism, class, and religion, unveiled its true self the further I got in, I found myself lost in the journey of Kay and her many party-mates. Though this game definitely isn't for everyone, I truly believe it to be a perfectly crafted Southern-Gothic tale with healthy doses of science fiction, eldritch mysticism, and absurdist hilarity.I hope Geography of Robots continues this formula down the road as this one has become one of my all-time favorites.A narrative experience unlike anything I've played before.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a point and click adventure game. The character Kay comes back home after her mother's passing. This leads her into a story of finding out more about the mysterious network and how her bloodline might be significant. It's an interesting storyline. It also has robots so win! The game does have a lot of text and immersive descriptions in them. I personally  like games like this but I know not everybody wants to read a giant text wall all the  time. There are several humorous characters, as well as some heavier serious themes. There are cats, and not to spoil anything, but one of them has a unique "power". The mapping system is a different one I haven't experienced yet. It actually displays the different direct locations on the map in which you can click. I actually found it incredibly useful compared to most mapping systems. I have no sense of direction so in games like this it's often difficult for me to tell where I have/have not been. This made it super convenient to figure that part out. The puzzles in the game were moderate difficulty. I was able to solve all of them without getting additional help from the internets. I hate puzzles that are over-the-top and with solutions that make no sense. That wasn't the case here. I would say everything could be solved if the texts were well-read. Overall, a lot of positives. Story rich, moderate puzzles, cats, robots, and a nice mapping system. Downside to some people may be the large walls of texts. That depends entirely on preference. Would recommend if you like those aspects of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: one of those games where you are immediately sucked in by the art and atmosphere. a surrealist neo-noir story set against the backdrop of a crumbling cyber gothic version of southern louisiana. very well written storyline with memorable characters and even a funny moments that made me genuinely laugh. the only other time I had this much investment into the story of a game in a similar genre was Kentucky Route Zero, even though that game dragged on spots (albeit one of the best game soundtracks I've ever heard). visual novel / point-and-click adventure type games are very hit and miss for me, but this is one of those experiences where every element of the game all bounce off of each other and create this really potent and memorable experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game from people who understands what a good game supposed to be. Art is never lazy to provide you visual details, music never your carbon-copy cyberpunk synth preset but anything which greatly dive into NORCO's unique setting. And most importantly, this is a different setting and it doesn't try to be something like 'other games'.  Even though, the whole game seems to be pretty basic, it's filled with small details which makes me appreciate and express my huge respect to the developers of this game.Speaking of other games, I've noticed that the dialogue system is inspired from disco elysium and the mind map system inspired from Pathalogic 2. Which is VERY good because those two were the most innovative decisions within 4-5 years. This is a game from people actually understand how to make a game - with amazing vision and creativity.If you like adventure games like gemini rue, technobabylon, promordia, disco elysium and pathalogic, this is a must play game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is an excellent latterday point and click adventure set in a deeply intriguing soft-cyberpunk Louisiana brought to life through a host of fascinating characters and simple yet evocative game design. The core of the experience is the narrative, which aspires to explore lofty themes concerning the relationship between identity, spirituality, and class and their roles in our technologically alienated society. To this end, I think it achieves admirably. Its magical realist bent and prose that interweaves apathy and wistfulness into its dreamy tone definitely reminds me of Kentucky Route Zero, and in many ways it examines a similar cultural cross-section, but Norco definitely has its own messages to impart and its own vibe to convey. The plot is strong, if slightly thin towards its climax, but the game has more than enough to offer in its densest parts to make up for it. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: +loads of varied and inventive puzzle mechanics (day of the tentacle style point-and-click, rhythm action, riddles)+compelling story (sad, funny, sadfunny)+beautiful in sound and vision-no real opportunity to get lost, as NPCs are _constantly_ _repeatedly_ telling you what it is you're meant to be doing in a way that can get a little irritating
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: southern gothic story steeped in christian mythology thru the gameplay of a japanese adventure game. basicly an excuse to talk to louisiana weirdos and go thru this little ode to an area that will be lost thru time and climate change. a nice mix of overly dramatic conversations/prose about what it means to live in the dying gasps of an area intermixed with 30 paragraph stories about guys their toilet experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's deliciously absurd. Reminds me a bit of Kentucky Route Zero, but with some nice silliness, secrets and more interactivity. Finding secret dialogue and extra items feels amazing and the characters are so good.Don't play it if you don't like puzzles or you feel stories need to "make sense". _childDocuments_.review: it really reminds me of disco elysium? In that it's a game with intense social commentary, but that it doesn't take itself too seriously. It's not afraid to be funny and silly with its characters, and as a result, these characters feel incredibly grounded and real. The art is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorgeous. My one gripe with it is that I wish it was longer, and that the ending feels a little disjointed. you should play this game
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game belongs at least adjacent to Disco Elysium in a conversation about excellence in video game writing. A beautiful, horrifying, funny, and deeply poetic game which somehow manages to be acutely a game about the present and the now, despite containing androids, mutants, and visions from God. Feels like a dirge in video game form, and it uses the video game part well, using the interactive medium to make you feel, more than anything else, like a person in a family, a person with history, a person who has come home.If I had to criticize anything, there is a combat system which feels not ancillary per se, it adds a bit of spice to the otherwise-straight-adventure-game gameplay, but it's definitely not interesting. Some of the puzzle design also features a smidge of pixel-hunting and a smidge of moon-logic, but nothing too terrible on either front.Genuinely something special, play this immediately.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game knocked my socks off and made me cry all in one sitting. The art, story, and characters are at the same time deeply grounded in the emotional realities of SE Louisiana and transcendent in the scope of their imagination such that when a friend asked me to not spoil the plot of the game for her I realized that I probably couldn't if I tried. If anyone is reading these reviews and wondering, "okay we get it, so the game nails Louisiana. But how's the cyberpunk?" I want to make it clear as someone who's not from the area but lived there for several years, that the Present in Louisiana, especially in places that white supremacy and capitalism have left behind, like Cancer Alley/Death Alley, Angola prison, or Isle de Jean Charles, is more cyberpunk than many of the futures I've seen imagined for other games. Norco is genius in the ways it's made that clear in this game.This was a 10/10 for me! But I'll admit it's probably not for everyone, especially if you don't want to read much or like to play games that are difficult. I think the most difficult part of this game is working through your own feelings at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing narrative! Southern Gothic is a genre I've never dabbled with, but this game gave me such a wonderful first experience with its aesthetics. I've never thought of the American South this way — it is indeed a suture of industrial capitalism (the olden days of plantation and the newer ages of oil) and evangelical faith (of multiracial origins). And they both rely on the myth of a New World (although in their own narrative, they'd call it *the* New World). The artworks and the music  (including the SEs) did an exceptional job setting the atmosphere. I enjoyed every single second of this game!
