_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a great dystopian sci-fi game about subservience, following orders, and familial relations that recalls Sierra adventure games with its off-the-wall dialogue and zany worldbuilding skills. While feeling sufficiently DIY and home-y, it reaches deep into the well of insanity, foraging for berries of wisdom. Unfortunately, none can be found here in the land of Norco. Utilising an interesting mind-map functionality, it notates player knowledge in a way that can be discovered as you go, which I never revisited in order to remember, however unlocking new nodes felt victorious, and delineated progress very effectively.Balancing humour and grisly violence, it portrays despair but doesn't succumb to all-out bland self-seriousness. There's a gonzo and wacky vibe to a lot of the occurrences, and while the game doesn't quite focus on choices defining your personality, there are dynamic reactions to your dialogue choices that are entertaining to experience.There are underlying themes of NORCO that touch on topics that are running rampant today, although I feel the commentary only runs under the surface, seemingly preferring to let the player draw those parallels themselves, and with great caution.Overall, I enjoyed my time with this game. There are things that could be improved - some of the mechanics feel a bit clunky, and because it's all fairly linear, I got stuck a few times and had to look up a local walkthrough video to find the next part - however, overall, I'd say it's definitely one of the more enjoyable and well-thought-out games in its genre.Recommended. :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a fantastic point & click adventure that ties a personal tragedy to a very specific region in Louisiana. The game explores a bunch of themes over its three acts, including capitalism and its effects on the environment, religion, (blind) faith, generational conflict, gentrification, internet edge lord subculture and so much more. The written dialogue between characters felt realistic, never too dramatic, and most importantly, made me care and root for or against them.The core gameplay is simple, there are a few combat parts sprinkled throughout that are nothing more than trivial, the puzzle solving ranges from finding the right location to progress the plot to using gadgets on your in-game phone. There was only really one time where I hit a wall and got lost but that was because I didn't pay attention to a specific line of dialogue, thankfully you almost always have a sidekick with you that recaps your current objective and gives you hints on what to do.The beautiful pixel art landscapes are accompanied by an evocative synth soundtrack and the ambient sound effects did a fantastic job of getting me immersed in this weird world.If there was one aspect I would criticise NORCO for, it's that the game wraps up at an exhilarating pace. There is what you could call a "point of no return" that didn't become apparent for me after I crossed it. What followed in the last 45 minutes, some reviews I've read might say it's rushed, I can see the intention behind it. Just know that when the credits of this game are rolling, you will still have unanswered questions. But does it invalidate the experience we had? Do we need the answers?Overall, you're in for a fascinating story set in not-so-distant alternate reality swamplands. I know comparisons to Kentucky Route Zero are easy; both games explore the history and cultures of a troubled region in America. But what separates the two is that KRZ had a scope far bigger than its main cast, it paid homage to various forms of folklore and art and served as a vessel for all kinds of ways to tell stories.NORCO focuses more on a very personal and tragic story of a family in disarray and takes as much time as it needs to explore its characters and their connections to the titular town and the area of Greater New Orleans. Yes, both games grew from a recent genre of local narrative games, but I would describe NORCO as the realer sibling of KRZ, even despite how surreal some parts of its plot felt.It's a great game, a great story, and the devs are very cool. I think that about sums it up.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretentious arthouse game where you play between a daughter and a mom who have to solve a mystery that really goes nowhere and is a game about why you shouldn't let hobo's into you life.In the SCARY HYPER FUTURE of Louisiana instead of gambling, jazz bands, people arguing over LSU, over priced drinks and terrible city planning, you instead now have a CYBERPUNK-light future where instead everyone enjoys arthouse puppet shows and having the most absurdly non-human dialog on the planet. Honestly, the problem with NORCO is the story sucks. It's boring, it has probably the worst conclusion I have ever seen in writing where it gives it up every single interesting plot point to instead whimper and die in the most laughable endings you could ever imagine. The puzzles in the game? Not bad. You don't need a guide or anything and they don't feel too tedious, but it's really just a writing problem. The author, a man I can only assume who wears a beret and makes Stephen King look like the brevity king makes this feel like such a slog - But unlike other authors, he has a million interesting openings and then says "AW SCREW IT! IT's TOO HARD TO TIE THIS UP!" and instead Poochy has to return to his home planet.NORCO also has an identity crisis. Does it want to be comedy? Family drama? A horror? A morality tale about capitalism gone wrong via SHADOWRUN style cyberpunk-isms? What about a goofy story about ghost swaps and a noir style hammy detective? Oh, that's not enough? Why not add also in some three stooges style slapstick and fart jokes. Well, it tries to do all of it and fails miserably. This isn't worth buying or playing. It's pretty much a uninteresting hipster game where 99% of the cash you get to these guys will go to overpriced coffee and cloves.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The introduction part may let you think, you will just walk through a strange world - but as soon as the intro is over, you are full in a story, which asks for action (light), puzzle solving skills and mystery ! The story is partly sad,  people, you meet are crazy, hopeless, weird but others are by your side and help you with your task to find out, what had happened here in this town.  Good thrilling story with excellent art style and music.  Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: - Interestingly stylized pixel art that oscillates between scenes of dystopian cyberpunk decay and oddly beautiful--but often creepy--psychedelic scenes- The music is fantastic. The credits song is a banger and worth sticking around for- This game pulls off "weird" well. The narrative is cohesive and complete, just strange- There's imagery and subject matter that some may find disturbing, but those facets of the game lend themselves well to plot's themes. I wouldn't call it tasteful, but it is consistent with the game's world- Like other well-crafted adventure game worlds, the setting feels like another character. You're often given the opportunity to look at the skyline during important moments, and it's worth doing- Despite the dour themes investigating the various catastrophic results of unfettered capitalism, the game is full of humor. If you explore enough, you'll find extended gross-out gags, darkly funny situations, and some incredibly absurd scenes- It's a story-focused point-and-click adventure game. You can imagine the gameplay- The story is a lot to process, so I'm not itching to jump back in anytime soon. Wouldn't mind getting the remaining achievements someday, though- Ran perfectly, no bugs. Won't tax your hardware too badly- Should only take 5-7 hours to beat- . It's a great story. If you're into adventure games, this is one of the best of the year so far
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I tried to lower my expectations when it came to Norco, but when I got to play it, it pulled me right in and I have enjoyed every minute of it. It will tell stories about loss, terminal illnesses, religion, hope, and penetrating sadness with a will to come over it. The presentation is what caught my eyes, the writing and all the details made me played it through 3 times. I would suggest this game to anyone who is mature enough to handle it. Give this game a chance, you won’t regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. What an incredible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ride! It's an incredibly original and captivating story with characters that feel very human, real and sympathetic. Really scratched the itch that Disco Elysium left me with but also definitely captured my sense of nostalgia in a very new way. The CRT filter was a great touch and the pixel art graphics are beautiful in a way that seems to capitalise on a minimalist art style. My only complaint is the length of the gameplay but I will be watching for anything from geography of robots in the future. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I very rarely binge any games, but NORCO made the cut. It could have done without the quicktime event-ish fights, but I didn't mind them. The depth and length were pretty Goldilocks level fit for me (a bit less than nine hours to complete) although I do understand why some feel that the game is intentionally padded with filler to stretch the playtime. Despite the surreal setting and story, the internal logic and puzzles are congruent, which make it a relatively easy solve. With the built-in gameplay aids I doubt anybody would ever get stuck, while allowing everyone to take only as much advantage of them as they feel comfortable with.Characters and locations feel thin at times, even if everything is woven together nicely, but I enjoyed the trippyness and the mystery of the whole so much more that it didn't bother me in the slightest. Being able to just move forward with clear enough pointers allowed me to focus on the text, putting the pieces together, and trying to guess where the story would take me next. 4/5, would probably play through again, even if just for the missed achievements.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: a truly stellar and singular game. the vibe is herculean, brah. memorable writing throughout with meticulous attention to character and voice. though norco never cannibalizes its influences, fans of philip k ♥♥♥♥, twin peaks, true detective, space/police/hero's quest, will find shades of each dancing in the periphery of this modernist paean to home. BUY BUY BUY
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is this type of game that you like or dislike. It doesn't grow on you. It is offering something plain and simple : you just have to be the right target for it. At first glance, we can tag this game as a story-based point'n'click. The gameplay is not taken only from those genres. It takes a bit of everything to deliver many aspects through mini-games. The gamer is thrown into this universe made of pieces cyberpunk/voodoo/religious subjects. This is what makes it so good : it plays perfectly on several sides to avoid redundancy.This is also part of why I really enjoyed NORCO. Mostly, the game doesn't take you by the hand. It doesn't have to as the puzzles are really easy. You have to discover what you want. You have to be a bit invested to really appreciate the story. By the way, its unfolding is at the perfect pace until you get drag into it for good. For sure, the end seems kinda rushed as there are still some loose ends. We own to imagine what we want ! The universe is strong, I am sure it would have been longer if the team really wanted to develop it.To sum up, NORCO is, for me, a good cocktail of gameplays & universes delivered with the right amount, at the right time. The demo sets the tone for an hour of your time which will help you making sure it is a fit for your gaming style.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is so painfully "of the moment", both stylistically, themtalically and ideologically that its undeniably enigmatic and successfully executed atmosphere is robbed of a lot of gravitas by its cloyingly pandering hip-ness. It's a game that feels as if it is becoming dated as you play it and one that will never be called "timeless". It's clearly class-obsessed but is trope-filled, meaning such themes are barely given any of the fair, in-depth thought they deserve outside of surface-level mentions. Probably saddest of all, the much-lauded writing amounts to C-tier work, at best, in the pantheon of amazing PC Game writing. It's perhaps even more hindered out of the gate by all of the hyperbole of so many fawning mainstream reviews, which set up fans of great game writing with inaccurate expectations going in.If you want a game that makes you feel like a train hopping, DIY show-going, roach-filled microwave-owning, salt of the earth "interesting person" who is surrounded by occult magic and mystery in your tragic family, but is under the thumb of big oil and evil industry, buy this game! If you know shallow, mostly gameplay-free poverty porn visual novels when you see them, then you'll see it in NORCO fast and be sorely disappointed in the missed potential of so many possibly interesting ideas that amount to a mish-mash of "vibes and feels". Finally, I like point and click adventures and games with experimental attributes, but when simply pointing and clicking IS the entirety of said adventure in a story that more or less tells itself, with little player input or choice, I consider the experiment unsuccessful.--"Blake is...a lot. An edgelord." -NORCO
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Short experience, but extremely interesting and full of depth and different points of view from which to analyse the events of the convoluted plot. Sometimes it is better to leave some things to personal interpretation. While I might not remember the specific names involved, I certainly will remember what I took from this story.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Even amidst the adventure game renaissance that we've all been so fortunate to live through lately, "NORCO" stands out as one of the best and most original of the pack: a mash-up of sci-fi, surrealism, and suburban Louisiana slice-of-life. Your mileage may vary regarding how many off-the-wall story elements you can take, but it never succumbs to annoying "lol-random" irony or pretentious self-importance. It even manages to be genuinely funny at just the right times! And as one of those people who easily loses track of even a "normal" game's plot, I was able to follow along throughout the end.I only wish I'd realized up-front that the game comes with an "Expert" mode that you can toggle on the settings menu. Although it's definitely an adventure game and not a visual novel, "NORCO" signposts its puzzle solutions quite heavily, especially if you're playing the default (non-expert) mode. Some folks may appreciate this level of hand-holding, especially if you dig the modern emphasis of point-and-clicks towards story over puzzles; but I preferred to turn off the more obvious in-game hints. Even on expert mode, I wouldn't describe "NORCO" as a difficult game, though it has enough puzzles and non-linear exploration to solidly qualify as a classic adventure.A quick word to the action-averse: "NORCO" contains about a half-dozen arcade fight sequences. In typical adventure game fashion, these are quite awkward to play, but they are also nearly impossible to lose. If this sounds like a giant turn-off, be advised that you can disable these sequences on the settings menu.A special shout-out must be made to the incredible pixel art of this game. "NORCO" features dozens of landscapes and street scenes of New Orleans and its run-down, industrial environs, all of which manage to be both moody and loving at the same time. If they ever make a sequel to that wonderful "Art of Point and Click Adventures" coffee table book that came out a few years ago, I'm sure "NORCO" will be prominently included. I only wish the end of the game had included a final piece of art instead of just a wall of text, but this feels like a needlessly petty complaint to make of such an overall incredible experience.Hats off to the "NORCO" team for one of the most unique, engrossing, and even moving adventure games of the modern era.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A reasonably well-made narrative experience. It does nothing special. Doesn't excel in any aspect. It tries to tell a mindblowing kind of story that might amaze some people who's never seen similar one. But if you have, it's all just meh because the presentation is simply mediocre.Another part of the draw might be the American rural culture, specifically that of South Louisiana. But as a non-American, I simply don't feel it.In conclusion, I can see someone enjoying this. But to me, coming here seeking good writing, good art, or deep characters to know, I came away disappointed.(The playing hours is inflated due to me leaving the game open at all time. Not indicative of actual game length.)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Best point-and-click adventure I've played in recent years. Really solid and immersive game. Fully recommended!Shout-out to the text settings panel where you can pick your preferred font, colour, size and speed for the text, which is something so obvious yet so ignored by most of the text-based games out there and I'll never understand why...
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this is one of the best games I've ever played. Gorgeous, alluring, captivating all the way through. The art is stunning, the writing is stellar, and it's an experience I'm still thinking about weeks after playing. It's up there with Kentucky Route Zero, The Last of Us, and Bioshock in being some of the most thought-provoking examples of Americana that expands beyond the realm of video games. So far, it's definitely my game of the year, and it's one you don't want to miss.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Never heard of it, but took a chance and grabbed it during a Steam sale - because it looked interesting. What an awesome find. For me - in most game categories - story is everything, and NORCO did not disappoint. It had;' - classic mystery elements that pulled you forward - appropriate puzzles (challenging, but didn't slow down the story) - family relationships, warmly and honestly realized (both hopeful and sad) - some interesting - and also twisted - characters - well written interactions (albeit sometime obtuse) - lots of humor and funny references - sci-fi tones, including a cool robot - a toy monkey (should have had more screen time) - a very "special" catI have 400+ games, so I intended to occasionally jump in and out of this one. Once I started, I binged for 12 hours over a weekend and finished. I had to know how things would play out. I was not disappointed. Plus, the "Point and Click" style  meant I never had to put down my beer.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: “NORCO” is a game that I thought I’d really like as it is some kind of a mix of an adventure/point-and-click game and a visual novel, two genres I am quite into. I tried the demo and enjoyed it wholeheartedly. Strangely, the longer I played “NORCO” the less I enjoyed it. But let’s begin with the good:-The soundtrack is great. No spectacular songs, just some very good atmospheric synthietracks. Never repetitive or annoying.-The story is intense and overall well told but a bit longwinded.-The gameplay is an interesting mix of different game styles.-Hardly any tiring backtracking.Well, here comes the bad:-About halfway through the game I started to lose interest in the plot as I got tired of reading through those aforementioned longwinded texts. As I stated before I like visual novels, so I am used to reading large quantities of text. I usually enjoy it.-I did not care very much for the pixelated art as it feels forced. What I mean is, the art looks as if some really good and mysteriously dark artwork has been brutalised into pixels. At the start of the game it was tolerable, but somewhere in act 2 I started to wish the devs had chosen a different style.-I think the storytelling really suffers from the jumps back in time when you play as the protagonist’s deceased mother. The first time this happened I got significantly less involved in the story.-There are some extremely annoying mini-games in “NORCO”. Clicking fast on circles, remembering sequencers of symbols and the worst of all: navigating a boat through labyrinthian swamps with incredibly clunky controls. Those mini games are not really difficult, they are simply extremely tedious. So much so, that after 7,7 hours of gameplay, being stuck in swamp somewhere in act 3 I decided to give up. I simply don’t care anymore how the story ends.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a great, short adventure game with very particular and interesting tone and style. The story is interesting and at times was quite surprising to me. The characters are decently written and the key figures are memorable and interesting. At times the game can be *very* funny, but the overall tone is often more serious and filled with a certain sense of enui and "lostness", but this is well done and not overdone. Note that there is a, in my opinion, unfitting and poorly executed combat system, but since a past update these can be skipped (rather, automatically be done). This is not a big minus, because combat is very rare and not important to the game as a whole at all. Play the demo, see if the graphics and tone of the game vibe with you. If they do, you can expect a nice story spiraling towards an endpoint that you probably would not have anticipated going into this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This isn’t your typical point and click adventure. There is hardly any inventory puzzles or any inventory management at all. Not once did I have to combine an item, and throughout the whole game I think I only used a handful of objects. It was a nice change actually not having any silly puzzles involving inventory items, it made the adventure seem a lot more realistic and engaging.Instead, progression is hampered geographically mostly, with locations being unlocked by talking to different characters who reveal destinations which can get added to the map, or by examining objects for clues. There are still plenty of puzzle elements but they’re very logical which makes it so much more fun to solve. I usually get stuck in these types of games and when I look up the solution I always grimace because the solution is stupid or unrealistic.I didn’t get stuck in Norco and I think that is because the puzzles were intuitive and plausible, but at the same time quite imaginative. There are a few interesting gadgets to use in some puzzles and some clever mini games that tie well into the story. I think it hits the right difficulty level between keeping you challenged and engaged without leaving you frustrated and wandering around aimlessly not knowing what to do. The story and character interaction are the main draw of this game and the puzzles entertain but they don’t bog you down and break up the flow of the story. They just add an extra layer of interaction and immersion. Currently, there is no diary or notepad entry system so you will need to take notes on paper in certain situations.I have never been much of a fan of visual novels, nor much of a reader of books. I tend to lack the patience or discipline to read too much text. There is an awful lot of reading in Norco, but it is so well written that I honestly didn’t even think twice about it, and actually thoroughly enjoyed the experience. If you’re visually impaired then the text size, font, and delivery speed can be changed in the settings to hopefully cater for most needs.The dialogue is presented at the left or right of the screen rather than at the bottom. It took me a while to get used to it and I found that I was missing a lot of the visual treats on offer because I couldn’t read the text and view the graphics at the same time with the way it was displayed.I enjoyed playing the different characters, teaming up with them and discussing the case as we progressed. It gave a feeling of comradeship and teamwork and bonded me closer to that character. The mind map feature was original and acted as a useful reference for story arcs and relationship reminders, and it felt quite rewarding unlocking a new node on the map.Norco looked and sounded gorgeous with some beautiful and imaginative locales and a nostalgic sounding synth soundtrack that’s both relaxing and atmospheric.I would have liked more than three save slots, especially with all the achievements, and it would have been useful to include time stamps.The town of Norco has various locales you can visit which you can travel by foot using fast travel or travel by car to places located on your map. Travelling by car costs money but it is worth noting that you will never run out of money as it gets topped up as you get overdrawn. Talking to characters and observing the scene are your main avenues of investigation, Pressing the space bar highlights all things of interest and will reveal either a , a  or an . Selecting the magnifying glass will examine objects or people giving a brief description, possibly revealing a clue or adding a location to your map, the speech bubble initializes a conversation with the character, and an ear symbol means you can listen in to a conversation.You play as Kay mostly and different characters join your party throughout the game who you can interact with and ask their advice in certain situations. A green circle appears next to their face indicating they have important information to share or you can interact with them at any time. You also play as you mother, Catherine, in events leading up to her death.Through conversations, observations, or examinations you might uncover information that is added to the mind map. The mind map is a web of connections which slowly evolves and builds as you play, uncovering truths between characters and revealing events that have a bearing on the story.There are some imaginative puzzle and mini games. You have a mobile phone which has a few different gadgets that is used in certain puzzles, like a voice recorder, and virtual reality. The mini games were really fun and absorbed into the story excellently.There are some rudimentary combat scenes involving QTE and memory sequencing. A decreasing circle intersects another circle when you have to click your mouse to score a hit and you have to remember up to five flashing boxes in sequence and repeat them to kill enemies. It’s very simple and I never died once in battle.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Endless streams of dialogue and descriptive text with almost no dialogue trees are what characterises this visual novel, masked as an adventure game.I loved reading in Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium. Here it's more like reading a book, and not the best one at that. Some ideas are straight out stolen from Kentucky Route Zero, like a dialogue tree about memories of yours, that change through player interactivity. But KRZ used this in a masterful fashion with many choices, which in turn shape the story, here it's rather lackluster with one or two choices. It's used once (maybe twice) and then never again.Four times I encountered this: You walk down a corridor and then get the 'choice' to walk further down and see what is there or walk back. Progressing forward doesn't change anything else, so why pretent like there is interactivity while you as a player are only supposed to read on.The more interesting dialogue is like in old adventure classics, you have several topics and just click on every option to get some information. But those games had something else - puzzles, there are hardly any here. The few puzzle mechanics introduced (of which one or two were pretty good) are hardly used at all and to very little effect. There are some rather boring exploration sequenecs in between that are like taken out of Kentucky Route Zero, just without hardly anything for you to discover.In the XII Games / Wadjeteye game Resonance there was this great idea to use impressions or memories like inventory items. In Disco Elysium you had thoughts you could use to mess around with your stats. Here you have a mind map. But that only serves the purpose to remind you what the plot actually is. This plot is somewhat ok, but mostly also just borrowed from here and there. The graphics and the setting I really enjoyed, but in the end I was pretty bored and angry at this game, that brings nothing new to the table and also can hardly be called a game at all.If you want an adventure game, better go buy Dropsy or any Wadjeteye realease.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've played. Easily ended up being one of my favorite games. From the pixel art style to the music to even the sound of the characters talking, this game is truly a great piece of work. The story was super well written and it wasn't like any other story you might come across in a game. It definitely kept me wanting more and more. I couldn't stop playing. I also really enjoyed how different each character was and the character development. You could easily tell what kind of person they are by how they spoke to you, or rather how their dialogue was written. You have to read everything they say, which I thought was fun. I was invested in this game. I even got a bit attached to Kay (the main character) as the story went on. It even made me cry at the end. This game follows one story line and it's not the kind where your choices affect the outcome, like Life is Strange, but that does not at all affect how good the game is. As soon as I finished the game, I knew I would be playing it again because of how much I enjoyed it and to get the achievements. It was definitely worth playing all over again and the achievements are pretty easy to obtain. I definitely recommend this game if you like reading, pixel art games, and a great story. I will definitely be playing it again!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know where to begin describing my recommendation for this game. Never has the fusion of southern US swamp gothic and a dystopian corporate sci-fi (semi-)cyberpunk settings (with a vaguely mentioned civil war in a crumbling USA in the background) ever crossed my mind. This point-and-click adventure game is as nostalgic as it is fresh, the puzzles are a fair challenge, the story is both tragically earnest and yet humorous (and at times outright bizzare, but in a good way), and the pixel art-style is absolutely gorgeous. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I had been supporting this game through patreon since I came a crossed it on itch.io! I am so glad to be able to see the final product and it is amazing! It was more story heavy then I had anticipated, but the world building was immersive and incredible. Like others, I was always entertained and each time I learned something, it felt so rewarding. I really loved the memory mapping, and thought it was very innovative. I loved the art and the music. The mini games in the game were good too. I liked a lot of the mechanics that the game used. I highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, magical tale of people left in the middle. High-tech dystopia meet religious zealots meet greedy corporations meet the sheer power of nature, and everyone that is left forgotten in their wake. I'm sure you won't find two identical interpretations of it, but isn't that what great stories are about? Emotional, ridiculous, tormented and naive (sometimes all of it at the same time) Norco has some very good writing and is beautifully executed.  If you are remotely into point and click games, and appreciate a good story, go for this one. It won't disappoint!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a point and click that tackles abstract themes about Religion, family and guilt in an even more abstract manner. While being as vague as possible, Norco still delivers a narrative which is tight and keeps you clicking as you uncover layers upon layers of mysteries. A lot of text is like poetry, and sure seems inspired by religious texts. If you enjoy such darker mature themes, you would also enjoy NORCO.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I got off work early and picked this game up on sale, on a whim. I fell in love immediately. I finished the game in one sitting and was absolutely enamored with the world, story, the atmosphere, the characters, all of it. Do yourself a favor and give the game a shot.Also, LeBlanc is the greatest character of all time bruh.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant narrative of a dystopian yet familiar town named Norco. The story is both so absurd yet feels so familiar. The characters feel like real people, even if they are strange, even when they are in bizarre circumstances. The writing itself is also beautiful. I have to give props to the writers too for being able to balance the creepiness and the humor; characters being funny did not retract from the thrill and scare. You constantly get both and it is wild ride. When it's not funny or scary, it's a tearjerker. Please play Norco
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to parse what the game's trying to say. Taking the plot literally is a fool's errand. Trying to unravel what constitutes as metaphors nipping at our ankles becomes indecipherable. I love the cyberpunk-surrealism that sprouts throughout the game. Duck being the most fascinating and unique surrealistic entity. Truly remarkable. Ultimately, a neat point and click, but it lacks substance to hold it together. The story leaves the player unsatisfied. Plot threads are left empty, characters aren't explored, the themes are presented but not capitalized upon. The nostalgia that the house evokes with its music and scenery is excellent. I could never recommend this to someone to play. All it has are vibes, and a few neat puzzles. Ultimately, the story left me annoyed and bored.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, I tricked a guy into eating rotten hot dogs. I run into the same guy later, where he retells a VERY long story of him getting food poisoning. He can’t find a bathroom, so he sneaks into a rented prom limo, takes a s**t inside, gets locked in and driven around, and eventually ends with him running from the cops. Also, you can buy drugs from Santa. Brilliant stuff.I enjoyed Norco because it plays opposite to most point-and-click games. Namely, 1) the puzzles/problems have straight forward solutions and 2) the UI has loads of quality-of-life aspects that make playing quick and easy. This lets you enjoy the main attraction: the unique characters, crazy situations, and dialogue.In reference to point (2) above: you can back out of any dialogue instantly. You fast travel without any animations. Pixel graphics means no load time. Party members nudge you in the right direction. Really helps with the pacing.Unfortunately, the actual plot makes no sense. It asks a lot of mysterious questions, but never provides satisfying answers. It’s still enjoyable because it works like an absurdist comedy. Nothing makes sense, but who cares when you can talk to sentient birds, infiltrate a teenage cult, and gift dismembered heads?

_childDocuments_.review: Holy Crap, what a game!!! Are you looking for a sci-fi environmentalist adventure? Norco is the ticket. _childDocuments_.review: I don't even know what to say about Norco, so I'll try to keep it brief and ask you to watch RagnarRox's take on the game on YouTube.This is a profoundly American story, yet it felt extremely relatable from the start (I've lived my whole life in Buenos Aires, ARG). There are a lot of topics that don't particularly affect me in my personal life (religion, homesickness, estranged family, etc.), but it all still connected on a very visceral level; the storytelling prowess of the Geography of Robots team cannot be overstated. It has some of the most beautiful and creative pixel art I've ever seen, but I feel that the music is what made me fall in love with its aesthetic vision; both are unique and wonderful. The gameplay mechanics were simple and intuitive, and you'll always have elements to guide you in case you get stuck or somehow can't advance.The game is probably not for everyone (its narrative style definitely adventures into some nice and weird places), so I would recommend trying the demo first in case you're not too confident about it; I think it's a very faithful representation of the rest of the game. I noticed several accessibility options in the menu, but didn't feel the need to use any of them, so I don't know how effective they are.Lots of love for the GoR crew and everyone who made this work possible... And Crouton, obviously.

_childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of point & click adventures, possible more than a hundered, small indie games and demos included. It's one of my favorite game genres and Monkey Island was the one that started my passion for gaming.I loved a lot of them because i liked the humor, the story, the characters. Sometimes, but rarely there are games that hit a special spot within me. Kentucky Route Zero, Fran Bow, The Blackwell Series or Night in the Woods for example.NORCO is another one of these special games for me. I'm not sure what exactly it was, but i felt it as soon as i finished watching the intro. Since this won't help you make a decision whether you should buy this or not, here are a few more tangible reasons why i liked this game:The atmosphere, the writing is imho exceptionally good. This game was clearly developed around it's story, not just a story wrapped around a gameplay concept, like many other games. It's not a game about challenging gameplay or tough puzzles. It's really 95% just about creating a virtual world, that's dark and sad, but still so interesting, that you like spending your time in it for hours. Some really funny moments included as well.I know this is probably a very subjective "review", but maybe it helps someone to make a decision. Buy this if you like The Crow, Film Noir, Kentucky Route Zero, Disco Elysium or dark gothic movies/books/games and good books/stories. Don't think you'll be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Life was never easy for you so you left home and decided to explore what the world had to offer, but then your mom died and you decided it was about time to come home just to check on your brother, Blake. When you arrive home you find that something is definitely not right, and your brother is nowhere to be found. There are whispers that your mother’s death, caused by cancer, wasn’t as straight-forward as it first appeared, and that there’s some sort of dark underbelly that is trying to pull you into its depths.In the game, NORCO, you will be playing the role of Kay, the estranged daughter. The only thing that is slightly normal is the robot, Million, a robot that your mother rescued and used as her assistant in whatever strange investigation she was conducting at the end of her life. You will visit different locations all over the city, and a couple outside of the city. In most of these areas you’ll get to interact with the locals and discover how strange and mysterious things have become in your hometown. The game is primarily driven through your dialogue choices, and you will notice that highlighted text in the game will be of the utmost importance, so when you see some, make yourself a note. I can honestly say that it definitely helped keep the game moving when those highlighted text items were part of a solution to a puzzle that stood in my way. You will be retracing your mom’s last days, as well as trying to figure out whatever happened to your mom. If you are not a gamer into doomsday savior vibes, this is probably not for you, but without giving too much away, I wanted to just state that this game has DOOMSDAY VIBES all over the place. There’s a ton of different characters, some you want to strangle, some you feel sorry for, there’s even a couple that you wonder how they are still alive, but overall the characters all have their own personalities, and that helps the gamer get further immersed into the story. The one thing that really made me scratch my head, throughout the game, was the very strange battle mechanic(s). It felt like the developer thought the game needed a bit more spice, or knew that the game needed some battles to the death (which for the record NONE of my characters EVER came close to dying). You may have noticed that I put that ‘s’ in parentheses when I said battle mechanic, and that’s because there were a couple disjointed ones slapped together. Now that being said, and the fact is that this game is very puzzle heavy, the mechanics are puzzles in themselves, so I guess that was the developers approach.This is definitely a game that is not going to be for everyone, but there’s something to it that kept me playing from start to finish. From my understanding there is more than one ending to the game, but once I completed the game for the first time, even though I felt there HAD to be a better ending than the one I had, I did not go back and try again.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a point&click adventure game where you interact with the world and characters by clicking them. There are a few combat areas where you're required to memorize patterns and reproduce them or respond to simple quick-time events. They are rather easy and offer little challenge if you use the right type of character.Compared to other genres where you, the protagonist are the strongest member of the team, here it felt like your partners were.Exploration is done by interacting with the world by clicking and speaking with characters. Exploration is done across the city of NORCO from both Kay's perspective but as well, her mother, Catherine. I normally don't dive into point-and-click adventure games and my biggest problem was the fact that I've had to read quite a bit through dialogues. I'm not the type that enjoys doing it and games usually fell off for me without a narrator/voiceover that helps my ADHD brain to keep focused. I found myself often moving away from my PC doing something else than actually staying hooked and exploring the game willingly, hence why I spend so much time with the game.That shouldn't stop you from trying the game out if you're into adventure games, just be warned that if you're not into these types of games it might not feel as fun. The main thing that attracted me to this game was the visuals. They look like the old-school type of point&click adventure games back in the 90s with a very surreal and interesting touch.Despite its simplicity and art direction as a pixel art, the game tells a lot through the minimalistic look. One of the most interesting parts from this game was the sound effects and music. I think they are done pretty well to keep somewhat an intriguing feeling at times and not feel annoying at all despite it's repetition.I really wish it had a voice-over for those who love to listen to stories than to read them as I am very sure I would have paid more attention to random dialogues and gotten more immersed in the main plot.  The story is a rather strange and fascinating one. You play as Kay, a girl who lost her mother to cancer and returns back home to find that things have taken an unexpected turn. Your brother, Blake is missing and you partner up with some of the strangest characters, yet fascinating individuals in a quest to find your brother and uncover the secrets behind your mother's death and the city you once called home.I found the writing to be well thought out, where characters held somewhat of a good background despite not requiring to know them for a long time. The game can get rather strange at times in what events occur, so be prepared for "WTF?" moments as well as humor sprinkled here and there. The game can be completed in possibly an hour to a maximum 6. It depends on how quickly you wish to go through the plot, how fast of a reader you are, and how much you want to engross yourself in the world. My time spent is partially to repeating from the very beginning a second playthrough to get 100% and as well being away from keyboard.Difficulty wise it's not something I found hard at all. Combat is rather straight forward and people with experience with turn-based strategy might find it extremely easy. The game guides you well enough and it's not difficult to keep track of where you are and where you need to be if you communicate with your companions and other NPCs you meet in the world. NORCO can be a hit or miss for people, depending on how you view and how familiar and how much you like the point&click adventure genre. For some, the game might bring nostalgia and the plot might be considered a Masterpiece, while for others might be an interesting and strange story that forever will confuse you with its plot. I personally feel in the second category, but that might be just me. Please do take my personal opinion of the game rather objectively and consider trying the game out despite me liking it or not as much.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited a long time for this to come out, so when it was finally released I bought it right away. There's always a chance of being disappointed when that happens, so I'm glad to say that wasn't a concern for me at all.NORCO is a point and click adventure game and the way it proceeds feels like it has a lot in common with the old 90's hypertext novels that fell out of fashion. A parallel evolution of the visual novel, it feels like the team learned from mistakes of the past where the puzzles you deal with make complete sense and you're rarely, if ever, scouring the screen for a single pixel that you need to click on to proceed. Combat feels a little tacked on from time to time but is relevant to both the narrative and the overall vibe, so it's never onerous (and the game provides an option to automate it if you feel the need to do so).As far as the theme - NORCO is a southern gothic cyberpunk manifesto. The very definition of high tech and low life where the marginalized and impoverished people of NORCO live under the shadow of a corporate oil behemoth that's poisoning the land and water while even stranger things happen where they can't be easily seen. This is totally unlike games along the lines of Cyberpunk 2077 or Deus Ex where you're a sort of superhero-esque combat figure - you're a drifter who came home to her ♥♥♥♥♥♥ town after her mom dies to help tie up loose ends. You deal with the people around town you grew up with, slowly realizing you don't know what you even look like - and apparently others can see that, too.There are mysteries you don't even know are mysteries when you start playing, mysteries you're never even told you're trying to solve, nested carefully like matryoshka inside each other where you're never sure if you've made it to the last doll. NORCO is a little light on gameplay if you're looking for tight action and a fast pace. But thematically, it's beautiful. The audio is terrific, it's not a farce but it does possess a wry and pointed sense of humor despite the bleak environment, and it's a fantastic example that cyberpunk - perhaps something of a zombie genre, now - still has flashes of life left in it if people care to look for it. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: just an incredibly well-written, atmospheric, experimental, and brutal point & click adventure.not brutal in terms of difficulty with mechanics, but more challenging in terms of its writing and what it has to say. if that sounds pretentious, it's because games rarely have challenging narratives (which I don't have a problem with regarding individual games, but I'd love more games that provide as much food for thought as NORCO does). I'll clarify what I mean, exactly, and will try to be broad and avoid spoilerish chicanery. this game grapples a lot with severing ties with blood relatives--namely parents. are we obligated to forgive our parents if they traumatize us or treat us awful? why can people who were treated TERRIBLY by their parents still feel some ethereal connection to them? it's a very rough topic that speaks to me as someone who has mutually disowned both of my parents. they mean nothing to me, but this has all been relatively recent to me (been about 3 years since I last spoke to either) and I don't even know if either of them is alive still. to be honest with you, I don't really care, they were terrible and violent and cruel and vindictive--and if reading that makes you a little uncomfortable, you now know what to expect from NORCO. it is painfully honest.edit: I find it genuinely, deeply disturbing that someone "found this review funny". nothing I said here was even darkly humorous, and it was 100% earnest. edgelords gonna edgelords, I guess.edit 2: edgelords when they see some stranger discussing how a piece of art spoke to their experiences with parental trauma and then saying that finding this funny is emotionally unintelligent and disturbing: "wow, wouldn't I be so cool and so funny if I said this was funny"

_childDocuments_.review: Every iteration of , from the game’s initial demo to the release of the first act, has clarified its weird, haunting voice that little bit more. That’s an obvious enough observation, but it was a voice that promised more than most. And as each iteration expanded the art’s dimensions, that voice’s potential was amplified. Still, I was uncertain of its reach. Now  has arrived, having deliriously flung open its doors, and my first trip down the rabbit hole is over.Thinking about it some hours later, I’m pretty sure it’s one of the best games ever made – or at least a fresh direction of travel for the medium.When her mother succumbs to a persistent cancer, Kay returns to her hometown of Norco, Louisiana, after an exile’s journey across a collapsed America. Beneath a molten sky abused by smokestacks, the family home is empty except for an android whose face sparkles like stars in a pool. Kay’s brother should be there but he’s vanished, leaving bad vibes in his wake. With some prompting from the android, Kay sets off in search of him, exploring shadows old and new as an arcane mystery quickly devours what’s left of her life.American greats like McCarthy and DeLillo and even Dos Passos percolate in  mystic dystopia, but the language is its own. As a piece of eco-criticism,  is a revelation, crafting a world we both know and do not know. Possibly the last world we’ll ever know if we can’t take apart the dead-end capitalist perdition we’ve all but committed to. , with exceptional clarity and imagination, demands nothing less to avert an apocalypse that connects every one of us.But for the developers, that apocalypse has a personal nexus. Sat on the Mississippi River just west of New Orleans, the Norco of the game is a strange and sinister dreamscape, textured with history and biography. Like a reflection on a beloved memory of home. Only that memory has been contaminated, phosphorescent light blinking on sallow water. Stretched into its own future, memories like these are up for grabs and committed to servers, taking the last piece of home.When I went looking for Norco in the present, I was struck by the hotspots on Google Maps: they were almost all oil companies, as if that passed for an identity. Somewhere in the ley lines connecting this unforgiving industry, the tragedy is very real in a place that’s only ever been owned, cultivated and drilled. The accumulating tragedies become something like a scream in the game, channelled into a statement about the singular tragedy of the failed American system. And as I write that, I want to reach for  –  is that damn good.As a point and click narrative adventure,  is just as exploratory. There are items to gather and people to speak with, but the genre’s hallmarks are kept to a minimum. Instead,  is a layering of experiences, always mindful of perspective – whether that’s Kay’s or her mother Catherine’s, who share the narrative. Perspective informs what players .In one sequence, you’re slinking through a rainy night at the behest of Superduck, a horrifying artificial intelligence that operates like a self-aware Craigslist. Superduck’s mission spins into infiltrating a motley crew of gross white dorks, who have shacked up in a local mall. To gain entry you need to utilise their leader’s mobile app to find digital signposts across town. It’s weird as heck, but also completely believable, and it’s the framework for your back-and-forth between locations and characters.The action unfolds organically, opening nooks and crannies in Kay and Catherine’s respective nights that find the profound nestled in the mundane. Small scenes that indulge anecdote and myth, deepening the flawed, broken, and messy humanity splattered over Norco. Small scenes that don’t ever lapse into whimsy; each one inserts a fresh layer, building towards catharsis. You rarely run into such snapshots in games, making them all the more special here.Creatively, it’s not easy producing something fundamentally about Now – and  really is about Now, in case there’s any question. It’s a problem that pops up in far too much literary fiction – reflexive observations on the present that lack authenticity. But there’s nothing reflexive about . Its understanding of digital languages, and their impact on self and our internal and external landscapes, is behind all the amazing pixel art, the dreamy, eclectic music, and every perfect bit of prose.The game just sort of  what matters , which is what the best science fiction does, right? The water is rising, the institutions of government fraying, and the collective madness building, yet still we retreat into the loveless inhumanity of corporate systems. Even their own creators can’t escape them in , in one of the game’s many quietly devastating moments.Which is all just to say  is a vital piece of videogame art that absolutely everyone should play immediately. Its dreamscapes shift beneath us, bending towards the quasi-religious until you want to cling tight to the few hands left in reach. Because as unrelentingly bleak as it can be,  is still holding out for a better world than the one it sees dead ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of interesting ideas that ultimately don't fit together very well. It's nice to see a game set in Louisiana, and it captures a lot of aspects of that region well, but the sci-fi elements feel half-baked conceptually, the motivations of the characters—villains especially—are a bit cartoony and incoherent. Overall, the worldbuilding just needed to either be more realist, or more surrealist, and the middle point that it chooses just feels a bit cheap and lacking in detail. However, it does have some fun puzzles and characters, hinting towards what the same team would be capable of with more resources and discipline. If the game had an even more broadly simulated and nonlinear world with more choice and consequence, as well as more realistically explained sci-fi elements or no sci-fi elements at all, I'd probably be raving about it, rather than being disappointed but nonetheless intrigued by what could have been. Still, there's nothing else like it on the market, so recommended on those grounds alone.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of indie sleeper I enjoy greatly.  I was googling something else about Norco (the city) and happened to stumble on something that indicated the game dev worked for years and learned how to do pixel art just to get this game realized.  The odd art style lends to the story.     Although it's heavy on dialogue, it's not overly so and the pieces add to the game as you work through the mystery to solve what happened.  This game is a slow burn best enjoyed as a snack.  Don't burn through it in one sitting.  Play in short stints.  Google in between and learn about the real city of Norco that this game is based on; it's eerie that real life has some parallels.  This game has a new take on its approach to point and clicks, and it's worth unveiling it slowly.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game based off the stunning screenshots alone and didn’t really have much expectations. The best parts of Norco are definitely the visuals and the setting. The writing is also a standout for sure, it can be somber and emotional one moment, then sharply funny the next (poor hot dog guy). _childDocuments_.review: Norco is a fresh breath of personal and weird storytelling in a market saturated with open worlds full of chores to do. Norco is not a distraction, it is a story about where we are and how it is awful. It is your friend commiserating with you in the midst of a global pandemic as you stare into the twin barrels of capitalism and climate catastrophe, nodding and saying, "Yeah, maybe we don't make it. Want another beer?"I have never been to Norco or Louisiana, but I suspect anyone who grew up in a suburb or a small town will be able to commiserate with the prose and people of this game. There is one moment in particular, in Act 1, where you're standing in the street and you can hear a dog barking. The sound echoes off the asphalt in a way I heard so many times growing up. It's a sound of summer, of wandering outside 'cause there was nothing else to do, of feeling alone and anxious and wanting to just run away, to find yourself, to find anything other than the mess you are stuck in. Norco's story and presentation will stay with me for a very long time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A spectacular story, rich in sense of place and atmosphere, told with supreme confidence.A game whose story is as interesting as the finest novels, but with the extra stuff a videogame can add sitting richly atop it.A game that picks from genres as it sees fit in totally appropriate amounts - not too point-n-clicky, not too text-adventury, truly just a goldilocks balance.This game has some serious topics at heart, but it somehow manages to be this divine balance of seriousness about them. In that sense, it feels like a game of our time but not a game intent on making you suffer under the weight of issues in our time. Norco is way more subtle than that, and that's what I mean by its confidence. Climate disasters hover in the background without it being shoved in your face, a large corporation controls the happenings of our world, and we are far past the point of being able to question whether the systems that govern us are truly fair, but there's no voice of the author interjecting to tell you it's smart or brilliant for doing so in ways that I think can affect even the most well-respected pieces of media in our time. And in that sense there's a hope in it - that lack of obsession with doom pornography really offers space for Norco to find joy in our/its world.It's interesting that so many people are mentioning Kentucky Route Zero; this feels more like a game about the South from a true voice of the South; it's less neurotically self-considered than KR0 and much more comfortable sitting in the setting naturally. The more you play Kentucky Route Zero the more you realize it's a toybox of its creators' passions, as much art object as story, whereas Norco feels decidedly focused on the story it's telling. And in that sense I think they're quite far away as games.All in all, a serious work of art and a delightful game. The way the story is told in interweaving narratives is also masterfully executed, the pace is perfect - what else to say without sounding overly effusive? The main character is a tiny bit underdeveloped, there could be more there, but the world is so interesting you probably won't think about that much.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not from the American South so I can't personally relate to the setting as much as some folks, but Norco's writing and atmosphere are very good. The pixel art and look is decidedly low tech but provide a unique experience, and the character portraits are very expressive. Gameplay wise, Norco is a simplistic adventure game with simple verbs, item use, and companions that deliver some hints. There are battles but the tactics are very simple, and they're usually a bump in the road more than anything. Buy this game if you like dystopian, surreal narrative games with a heavy helping of social commentary. My only complaint is that the way things wrap up felt abrupt, even as Norco doesn't outstay its welcome. The narrative is more about a creating a feeling than trying to explain itself clearly. Compared to a game like Disco Elysium the characters and plot feel cryptic. On the other hand, Kentucky Route Zero (which I enjoyed for different reasons) is much more highbrow and abstract.  A final note: The soundtrack is very good. I don't think I'd listen to it outside the context of the game, but it sets the tone perfectly.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a very long or challenging game, but the pixel art is gorgeous, the writing/story engaging, the general vibe somewhere between Jeff VanderMeer and bayou gothic, and a decent soundtrack to top it off. It's the kind of game I want to replay right after finishing, knowing the plot's secrets, to see all the hints and foreshadowing I missed on my first run.The only two minor issues I have with the game are 1. the record dialogue function is finicky and tends to disappear as I tried to click it, and 2. having a trigger warning at the start that weighs blasphemy on the same scale as suicide (seriously that's a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥).

_childDocuments_.review: My mom called me today from my childhood home in the Biloxi area, roughly an hour east from nola on the gulf coast, and she told me about her depression, isolation, inability to cope with family being gone or passed. An hour later, I finished Norco. This game is an artistic achievement in atmosphere and allegory for any audience, but being from the area (especially after having fled it in adulthood) makes it personal. Beyond recognizing the I-10 overpass and Metairie and the early-imprinted memory of watching your mother pull up carpet after a flood (Georges, for me), there's a desperate melancholy that comes with knowing your home is being slowly but surely washed away. The experience of going home to visit, seeing the changes that sculpt and disfigure your past, the new developments and the abandoned businesses both, is made physical. A corner of your consciousness set fluttering free to swallow the land. You can bet I sobbed like a baby walking with Kay through that house as the waters claimed it, seeing it as mine in my mind's eye, recounting my memories alongside hers.It's not a long game, not a huge investment of time or energy. It's forgiving for people on a trackpad and it's honest with the choices it gives you, and their consequences. It's dark without reveling in its darkness, sincere in its love of people and place, and as enjoyable as it is gut-wrenching. If you happen to be from the area, whether you're a Blake or a Kay, so much the better. I'm going to call my mom back.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, NORCO is one of those games which one has no qualms about recommending. Something of a detective mystery interactive visual novel with unique characters and a fantastic setting straight out of a modern weird fiction short story.It is simple, succinct and well made. The art direction is depressingly pleasing, the vibe is mysterious, cosmic and dreary. It pulls at some deep emotion which is not quite nostalgia or melancholy but something in between. Well written with a nice soothing soundtrack, I am assuming a few secrets and more than one ending. There is nothing in here I would like to complain about apart from the need for more combat sequences perhaps which were fun button prompts, or  short memory games.One play through took me around 6 hours and for me it was worth it at full price since it is pretty beautifully made with love, it is clear that a lot of effort has been put into it. In short, a visual treat, get it for the story, the art, the writing and the unforgettable interactions.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I've followed the development of Norco for approximately two years and am very proud of what it's become. This is an extremely ambitious project for such a small team and is clearly inspired by intimate and personal life experiences. The grounded descriptions of mundane memories -cockroaches in a microwave, the smell of a grandfather's old pick-up, the bayou and the poverty- contrast strongly with what I can best describe as post-left esoterica: bitterly ironic collapse mysticism, poetic descriptions of intelligence networks and industrial infrastructure, and pockets of flavor text that seem deliberately written in the style of analysts like Deleuze and publications like Tiqqun. Not to mention the blend of paranormal and technological horror.At no point was I sure where the story was headed, and the ending was fittingly surreal and tense. My only complaints are that it left a lot of questions unanswered, which was unsatisfying in a few places; and that Lucky was rewritten from being an insurrectionist android to an elderly oil pirate, but he's still a very rad character.What else? The art is fantastic- this much I expected from everything I'd seen of Geo's work beforehand. The music and atmosphere are at no point bad and contribute well to a tense and heavy atmosphere. The gameplay is largely inoffensive but doesn't shine, either. The writing -the one thing of which I wasn't sure what to expect- turned out to be exceptional, thoughtful but concise enough that it never felt like I was just reading walls of text, poetic and clever and always just a little bit detached and mournful.Norco is absolutely worth the price, you should really find out how good it is for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a game I've been looking forward to for nearly a year, so I jumped on it ASAP on release date. First, a few things that are perfect without compromise: the art, while pixel based, is still gorgeous, capturing an amazing sense of melancholy right away. The sound design and music is just as incredible; they work together to form what I can only describe as some EXTRA thick vibes, of rot, and loneliness, and disrepair. The story is also just as interesting, at least in Acts 1 and 2, and honestly most of Act 3. Characters like Million and Superduck had me interested, immediately, and chomping at the bit to learn more. Really my only criticism has to do with closure on both the story, and many characters. It ended rather abrupt, leaving me with a lot of loose ends and questions. It wasn't bad enough for me to regret playing, but the ending did leave something to be desired.All in all, play Norco. It has a lot to say, and you should listen to it.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved every minute of this game. The visuals alone are breathtakingly beautiful, but the writing is what really drew me in and kept me hooked. I found myself pausing at multiple points throughout just to take in the details and admire the gorgeous pixel art as well as the music and sound design. So many moments really stuck with me, but the song that plays in Dimes outside of Duck’s house is one I lingered on for an especially long time. The ambient sounds of birds and traffic added so much texture to the experience and left me feeling homesick.This game would be impressive regardless, but knowing it was made by such a small handful of artists is remarkable. Norco strikes the perfect balance of being deeply sad, hauntingly surreal, and surprisingly humorous. It’s apparent how much care and attention to detail was poured into this piece of art. As a native Louisianan, I am so grateful for this. While I don’t think someone has to be from or have even visited south Louisiana to enjoy or appreciate the game, I do think having a deep understanding of and relationship to the area makes the experience of the game that much more meaningful. This is the first time I’ve seen my home accurately reflected in all its nuance and am left with feelings of nostalgia, heartbreak, and pride, rather than embarrassment and frustration. Highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for an adventure point and click game, but what I got is probably best described as narrated experience. Gameplay is there mainly to drive the story and presents no challenge. Norco isn't about solving tough puzzles, it's about following the narrative and reminiscing about your own life. Visual style is nice (and great at places), music is OK, plot is present, but it seems a little bit out of focus, as if multiple themes and ideas were tied together in a dream-like sequence, which never really gets to a satisfying resolution (at least the way I got through the game in approximately 8 hours). The best parts of the game IMO are: unique atmosphere, beautiful narration and opportunity to reflect on Norco's many themes, which include but are mot limited to: strained family relations, memory and regret, cancer, environmentalism. P.S. yes, it kind of reminds me of Disco Elysium, but Norco is very much its own thing

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give this a "recommend" because I wouldn't have finished it if it wasn't worth playing. That being said, I do have a fair number of criticisms of the story. Narrative Design: 4/10Tone/Setting: 8/10Plot/Drama: 7/10Story: 4/10Themes: 2/10Character Arcs: 4/10Dialog: 4/10In terms of gameplay, at the end of the day, it's a very conventional and basic point-and-click adventure game with no deviations from the formula other than how some things are presented. They get the structure of that done perfectly, there was never a moment where I was majorly confused as to what to do next, the interactions and critical path were very clear, and a lot of the optional content was easy to engage with, though I know I must have missed some more obscure things. My favorite thing that they did differently was how they log all of the things you've learned in a "mind map," which makes getting exposition about the (very weird) story very easy.What this little adventure game gets perfectly right are TONE and SETTING. The art, sounds, and demeanor of all of the characters come together into a vivid picture of the world that the creators aim to immerse you in. It's grimy and it's weird and it's kind of uncomfortable, but it's also fascinating, and the classic "point and click adventure" formula fits right against the setting incredibly well.What the game does decently is CHARACTER WRITING when it comes to making clear and evocative characters. However, while the dialog is incredibly evocative and does well to make crystal clear characters, what the characters actually SAY is not particularly compelling. The prose and dialog try very hard at a poetic "mystique" contrasted to plain vulgarity, but because there's so much more of a focus on VIBE over SUBSTANCE, you don't really get anything out of any individual line no matter how poetic or funny it might be trying to be. Ultimately I lump "character writing" of this type into "tone and setting," because the characters end up serving as strong pillars of the setting without ever providing compelling arcs or drama in their own right.The story and plot are RIVETING in terms of dramatic beats to get you invested in how absurd the scenario is that is unfolding. However, there is a lot about the setting and events that undermine the story, with the setting presenting a very mundane and dry presentation of MOST aspects of the world (going into so much detail about the nature of the environment, the politics, what it's like to really LIVE in this situation) and then proceeds to have most characters not truly question just how absurd the premise of the plot actually is. Sure, some people say "man, that's crazy!", but that's not really enough when what's happening is so insane. Just calling something crazy is not the same as actually questioning and analyzing it, and this story is NOT interested in characters actually trying to understand the situations that they're experiencing (whether that means understanding the situations literally, personally, or emotionally).The best example of this is when the protagonist meets his mom's friend who is the "originator" of the "Superduck." He literally explains the craziest ♥♥♥♥ imaginable to the protagonist, and she has NO QUESTIONS about ANY of it. The story just acts like people would accept things that they obviously wouldn't, especially given other things they've questioned or not accepted. If stuff like this was happening all over the world all the time, that would be one thing, but there's a clear insinuation that all of this is new, weird, and scary. I can see that the writer is trying to get across a theme of "the world is always weird and scary, why would these salt-of-the-earth people care about some new weird and scary thing," but I just don't feel like the setting is absurd enough to support the absurd story, and this just causes a lot of tonal dissonance. My last major issue is that the story itself is too full of vague poeticism. There are a lot of ideas thrown at the screen, but I'm not convinced they really have any kind of interesting interplay. I'm not left thinking about or considering anything meaningful about what was presented after finishing the game, it all just kind of boils down to nihilistic absurdism with only a veneer of heart. The implications of what it means for your character to "succeed" at the end are immediately undercut with a sense of imminent doom in their future regardless of the outcome of what happened in the story. I am fairly certain I got the "good ending" because of one or two things I collected earlier in the game, but the story is so obsessed with its own nihilistic tone that there can't actually be a "good ending."The real issue with "vibe" versus "substance" here is that none of the themes presented really go anywhere or have anything to do with each other, and the themes, story, and character arcs do not interweave in such a way that they elevate or progress one another. You've got a hodgepodge of themes that go nowhere: corporate greed, religious absurdity, modern technological absurdity, family "trauma", etc. The events that occur don't really resolve any of these themes, the themes don't really have anything to do with each other, and at the end of the game, it just feels kind of like you went on a slow-paced Disneyland ride through someone's bizarre hallucinogen-fueled dreams about their ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up childhood growing up in Louisiana.Obviously that was enough to get me to finish the game, but the writing clearly has literary aspirations that it's unfortunately not living up to.
