_childDocuments_.review: Very good and intriguing game.The gameplay follows a point-and-click style with some enhancements. There is some combat that involves choosing who to fight, each requiring a different type of memory game to see how successful an attack is, this adds some very light turn-based elements, it isn’t used very much at all so it works well here. There are also some segments that involve navigating a boat around, these are less enjoyable but minimal and break up the text well. The point-and-click aspects are done with hotspots that can be clicked in order to get information as well as using an inventory to have objects interact with the world. There is also a light party system that adds some light RPG elements to the game. All the little bits come together to make a pretty effective and engaging point-and-click-style game.The story is the most important part of all of this, the premise is that the player is Kay a girl who left home and has been busy for a while, she comes back following the passing of her mother to find that her brother has also gone missing. Throughout the story, great mysteries will be presented and unraveled as themes of familial trauma are dealt with. The story also deals with the impact of Capitalism on the town and the disastrous climate change it helps bring about. A refinery owns most of the town and area and lackluster safety has caused it to flood many times, people are without jobs and get replaced with machines. Another theme follows AI and its effects and how it can be dangerous. There is also a rather bizarre theme about the elusiveness of cults for young tech individuals that believe everything can be solved with space exploration and get wrapped into things they don’t fully grasp. It features cryptocurrency to help illustrate this point. Southern folklore also plays a role as crazy stories about local legends are told and explored. Characters are given many dimensions and their own flaws and motivations that make sense for them. There are also some comedic moments in the game to break up the bleak and dystopian nature of most of the rest of the game. All of these elements come together to tell a beautiful story with exceptional writing.Despite being pixel graphics each piece has a lot to say. The warmer summer-like colors invoke an almost hellish heat as this Louisana town with a refinery would exist. The pieces have great detail and convey intent incredibly well. It features both realistic depictions and strange creations of Sci-Fi.The soundtrack is very nicely done. A more subtle sound but it works well with what’s presented. Each piece feels somewhat distinct and fitting to the locations they’re found.Norco is an incredible game, it has some amazing writing that tells a fascinating and deep story.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: : I have been interested in this game for a long time now before a publisher was even announced for it. I also played the Act 1 demo, so I kinda knew what I was getting myself into. Also, I'm originally from Greater New Orleans, the very setting of the game, so I definitely had a personal investment in enjoying the game.Okay now the pros and cons.✔ The setting is quite accurate to the real-life Greater New Orleans, with just enough changes to really make it its own setting that stands apart from anything else of its kind.✔ The pixel art is on point, with varying styles and complexity which convey each area and function the art has. From the simpler areas of Norco proper, to the vast panorama of New Orleans, the art has its place.✔ The music is in the same vein, ranging from eerie atmospheric pieces, to thumping, intense sequences.✔ The writing is absolutely top notch here. The writers clearly had experience in the Greater New Orleans area with the more local flair and vernacular, but also don't flood the writing with it. It's still understandable to players not from there. Also the juxtaposition between this informal tone with more sweeping, grandiose prose, sometimes in the same scene, really shows the mystique of the setting and the characters within it.✔ The game eases you into the different mechanics you'll run into during later parts of the game, so nothing feels like it just suddenly happens and throws you out of the immersion.✔ The "mind map" is a wonderful mechanic which helps you keep track of the relationships between characters and story elements, updating them as relevant info is mentioned during the game.✔ The puzzles are engaging but not obtuse, allowing the player to enjoy the a-ha moments of figuring it out without too much of the head banging against the wall of trying to figure it out in the first place.✔ The game is dense, has lots of content, but doesn't overstay its welcome. In my first playthrough on stream, it took me just south of 10 hours to complete. Not bad for a $15.00 purchase!✔ The game offers several font choices, since it's heavily text-based. You have some serifs and sans serifs, but most notably it has OpenDyslexie as a choice. OpenDyslexie is a font specifically designed to mitigate most, if not all, of the difficulties which arise when someone with dyslexia is trying to read text. Its inclusion surprised me and it's what I used for my streaming of the game to ensure that as many viewers would enjoy the experience.❌ There are moments which may trigger seizures in people with epilepsy. There is a warning when you start the game, but there is no way to turn that off.❌ Navigation through locations with multiple rooms or areas can be a little clunky at times. Sometimes there are areas you can click on the scene which move you to another area. Other times, you can only navigate to another area through the minimap on the lower right of the screen.❌ You can't scroll up on the text bar, which does me no favors whenever I forget important details when reading through the otherwise excellent writing. When I get to a point where I have to make a decision based on what I read several paragraphs ago, I can't go back and reference that information.❌ The pacing feels off during the later parts of the game. It feels like there were some loose ends that should have been tied up, but perhaps time constraints got in the way and they had to resolve the main plot points.I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who:• is a fan of the point-and-click adventure genre;• enjoys stories where the mundane and fantastic stand side by side;• loves games with strong writing;• and/or want a fresh take on a near-future, dystopic, slow-moving catastrophe-in-progress setting.The game has its fair share of faults, but for a first outing from developer Geography of Robots, and against all of the bigger things it did right, I think this is a must buy!

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea what genre I'd describe this as, to start with. There's elements of point & click in here, the occasional simple turn-based fight (though never very difficult, it feels more like an expression of mood and maybe a little tongue-in-cheek parody of such things than a real attempt at making combat a part of the experience), there's a few choices you can make...it feels quite varied, but never incoherent or scattershot. The story and world is very intriguing so far, there's a lot of melancholy here, a lot of rot everywhere you turn, and despair at the way Norco's world is going. I was first turned on to this game when looking for recommendations of things that are like Disco Elysium, and in terms of the narrative and how it's delivered, the tone and state of the world, there are similarities...but I also would never want to do this game the disservice of calling it a copycat or trying to imply it's not very much its own thing. I think if you liked Disco Elysium, you'd probably like this, I know I do. I also think it's different enough from that game that if you go in expecting something that uses even a vaguely similar framework for delivering its gameplay and story, you'll be quite surprised and taken aback.It's a little tricky to summarise Norco, but I can confidently say that I love the depth and style of the writing, and I enjoy the way it blends different gameplay and presentational styles to create its own unique voice. Like I said before, there's a lot of melancholy in everything from the writing to the art style, but it is also quite funny at points and it doesn't shy away from revelling in the odd bit of surrealism/whackiness. It's a game where you alternate between playing as a grieving, estranged daughter and her cancer-stricken mother, but it's also a game where you can pet a cat so well that it rockets through the ceiling out of excitement, or pressure a man into telling you the thrilling story of how he broke into a limo so he could relieve his diarrhoea, and it moves between these very different tones with a skillfulness that makes it all feel perfectly consistent.If that sounds good, then you should absolutely give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I was recommended Norco after Disco Elysium, and like Disco Elysium the writing and story are phenomenal. On top of that, the pixel art and soundtrack are pretty dang good too. Norco takes place in Norco Louisiana, which is apparently a real place. It's a small town with an interesting atmosphere after a large oil corporation moved in next door. You'll go about investigating fanatic cults, the oil business, research facilities, what secrets they're keeping from everyone, and how your late mother was wrapped up in all of it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic! The visuals are gorgeous, the soundtrack does a great job of really immersing you into the game, and the story left me speechless for a solid hour after finishing it. The characters are interesting, and the game manages to be both beautiful and unnerving at the same time, in all the right ways!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic dialog, world building, art-style and a generous helping of toilet humour. Story might be a bit too abstract (or is it?) your never quite sure what is real. In that respect it kind of feels like an homage to Kentucky Route Zero. In fact if you liked KRZ then I think you will definitely enjoy this. If your into old school point and click adventure games then I think you will also get something out of it; it will certainly tick the nostalgia box in terms of the graphics and overall feel but don't expect too much (if any) of the traditional point and click puzzles. Game is fully playable with mouse, lots of accessibility options in terms of the fonts and although the scene navigation implementation was a little bit unusual it worked surprisingly well.Overall highly Recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game that's been released this year in terms of writing, in my opinion. Fantastic surrealist play on Louisiana. If you liked Kentucky Route Zero or Disco Elysium, you'll love this. The gameplay is mostly driven by narrative. There are a bunch of "secrets" that might not be possible on your first run, however. I can only hope there are more games like this in our dystopian future.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure: I'd been following the devs of this game for a while on social media and they reached out and gave me a key for it. That being said, I'd have gladly paid for it, so I'll do them a favor back by writing a review. This is one hell of a game. It'd be up there on my list of favorite games even if it didnt feature a twisted, near-future sci-fi version of my home town. I don't think I've ever played a game that resonated more with my sense of dread over the future of this region, country, world, etc. It's being mentioned in the same breath as games like Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium, which is well deserved. It is very different than those games but it shares a little something, a little common adventure game and writing DNA, with both of them. I saw someone describe it as a game made out of Shivers (the stat from DE which is, by and large, the voice of the city the game is set in), which is not entirely true, but not entirely untrue, either. It's a fairly short game, but it's very tightly paced. Shout out to the devs, they did this story, this setting, these characters, justice. ♥♥♥♥ the Garretts.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Set in a technologically advanced near future, Norco is a hauntingly beautiful pixel art depiction of Norco, Louisiana; a town run through by the oil industry, robotics, and mother nature. And while I did like a lot of the humor and general craziness of the game, it's ultimately the somber moments that really stand out, offering some of the best bits of writing in any game this year.I do think the game probably could have used some reworking to better drive home its themes and ideas, but I also kinda don't care. Because those few sobering moments of inevitability will always stand out to me. And whenever I think about Norco, I will see those oil refineries burning a hole through the night sky. I will hear those synths and horns crying out for a better day that won't come. And I will immediately be brought back. And to me, that's more important than worrying about all the details.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fully immersed since I've started playing. I've been attentively going through every bit of text since the writing, accompanied by the ethereal and inebriating soundtrack, really work together in pulling you into this carefully crafted industrialized dystopia. Will keep playing to see what other surprises are waiting for me down the road. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I came across this game during a frenzy for pixel art games, not knowing what to expect. While it has the most stunning pixel art, its real strength is definitely the narrative. From the moment I started playing Norco, it felt nostalgic, with a sense of familiarity and emotion. After my first playthrough, I found myself getting teary-eyed whenever I thought about the game. It stayed with me in the most unexpected way, like a homesickness for a place I've never been to. During my second playthrough, I realized the combat system kinda sucks, but I guess that's why there's an automated combat option. The game is also quite short, but I don't see this as a negative given its long-lasting effect on me.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I love how Norco manages to be pretty weird and grounded at the same time. Its narrative, characters, sound design, visual effects, everything just come together and makes for a truly unique experience.It really shines in the first and second act. Towards the end, it becomes rather linear, which is not bad, but it feels like its world has shrunk a little.I'd say if you're curious about it, it's worth checking it out. Just install the app and do what the duck says.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Great point and click adventure, amazing writing and story.  Get it on sale, it's a short single playthrough at about 6 hours if you're fairly thorough.  The "combat" is easy and there's an option to auto win if you prefer.  The puzzles are good, there was only one that gave me significant trouble, and it's much more about the story and the characters and the world building.

_childDocuments_.review: I keep thinking about this game. I love this game. I love the unashamedly poetic writing that manages to avoid pretension, I love the idea of a slice of life in a magical realist post-cyberpunk deep south -- in fact that might very well be the best setting for a game ever. I love how effortlessly it manages to root itself in reality and society.Be aware that the demo is not fully representative of the whole experience, the full story is a wilder ride than the first act lets on, which is not necessarily a bad thing. It's its own thing, a unique game which deals with mundane and current topics in a way I haven't seen often in video games, and while I've read reviews that state that it will never be as impactful as KRZ, in my particular case I disagree. Yes, its conclusion feels like there wasn't ultimately much to say, but it does so in a way that feels so true to life that I still can't stop thinking about it.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game on GOG, Purchased on Steam for review because the top comment was bothering me so dang much. This is one of my favorite games of 2022, if not THE top contender.NORCO is an absolutely stunning foray into tiny industrial city misery. It is personal, intimate, and not afraid to showcase the absurdist heights of despair. To claim that the game eschews all its themes about family, loss, exploitation and so forth past act 1 is just *blatantly false*. It is an outright refusal to engage with the text & imagery on its own terms. This is an adventure game that proves point-&-click is not dead, and that it doesn't have to resort to uninspired, extensively backtrack based, random-option-roulette puzzles. The design of its UI is simple, interactive, and immaculate. One of the gameplay features is that of an in-character mind map, where you can question certain portions of the world unfolding around you and watch how the intricate web of events and people comes together. The pixel vistas can be gorgeous, immersive, and sometimes deeply unsettling. (Maybe even all the 3 things at once!) I love the TV filter.NORCO It is ALSO a southern gothic filled with magical realism elements; YES, THIS IS A *WEIRD* GAME. That's exactly why it rules! This is an entire school of literature, specially literature about complex, difficult to grasp feelings. More to the point; NORCO is explicitly telling a story about the insanity of late-stage capitalism (REALLY late stage, as the game is set in some near robot-bearing future,) and how that sense of invasive aimlessness and endless exploitation can sometimes feel just like a farce, even more so if you're among the poor. How people of all ages react to a sinking economy and dying earth in the most ridiculous, outlandish ways: conspiracies, cults, apocalyptic religions, aliens, crypto schemes, SpaceX, "That Da Vinci code sh*t."And that leads me to my next point of praise: this game is really funny. Don't get me wrong, we are broadly dealing with a lot of heavy subjects here (The protagonist's mother has just died from cancer, her brother is missing, the oil refinery looms unkillable and all consuming above the skyline) but NORCO understands that Real Human People have awkward and stupid interactions as one of our main paths to communication - and that it's not a bug, but a feature of our species. The people in this game have memorable faces, distinctive speech patterns, riveting dialogue and a LOT of heart. 'Atmospheric' doesn't make a dent in it for me. The humor adds depth to the very real structural decay that surrounds their region, and it hit home Hard for me. These are some of the people I know.I'm reminded of my favorite short story collections, where real events are extrapolated through a narrative voice that balloons the minutia of day to day life into wildly strange encounters with the unknown.The writing is almost effortlessly entertaining. A good bulk of the game is just dialogue, and it never feels like a chore, because our rotating cast of comedians and tragedians keeps each moment alive and counting. The game has 3 acts and a few story-progression minigames sprinkled in the middle for fun's sake. The combat can be turned off as you wish. The pacing in NORCO is tight even as you play in two different timeframes- first as Kay, then as her late mother, alternating between the two to build a larger version of the truth- and in many ways I feel as though the experience hasn't left me after reaching the end.I want to play this game again and see what little intricacies I might have missed the first time around. I also want more people to play this game, desperately; maybe they'll have the same bugs my brain does and have as much of a good time as I did.If you wanted to try NORCO, please do. I can't wait to see what the developers will come up with in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: What a good, weird game!It starts slow and almost mundane but chooses unexpected directions to go from there.The game masterfully conveys a sense of place through writing, art, and music. You don't have a character who can freely explore — instead, you switch between different screens-locations. And yet, you feel like you are there. It all comes together into an open-ended experience. Not all questions are answered, and not all mysteries are resolved. You are encouraged to interpret your thoughts and feelings, and maybe dig some more if you wish.It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing experience. Maybe the only point and click adventure game I've not only enjoyed, but was utterly addicted to from beginning to end. I’ve never been so satisfied with such a short game. The setting is this wonderfully unique take on cyberpunk mixed with Southern American lore. Every single screen is filled with beautifully hand-crafted pixel art, dripping with atmosphere and hypnotic animations; every single area in Norco would make for an amazing desktop background or poster. The writing is sharp from beginning to end and there wasn't a moment in my eight-hour+ playthrough where I wasn't engaged or that I was filled in entirely on what was going on; there were always several mysteries hooking me at once, character's whose motivations I was unsure of and several clever twists that kept me hooked on Norco up until the finale. In Norco, you play as two characters in two timelines - Catherine, a sort of eccentric ex-researcher who’s resorting to a new form of employment via a mysterious corporate phone-app in a desperate bid to secure money for her children before she dies from cancer. Then there's Kay, Catherine's daughter who bailed on the family in pursuit of her own life and is returning home after her mother's death to explore the mystery surrounding her death with the help of her mother’s old droid, Million. Kay is more of a player surrogate and while her story is incredibly interesting, she's far less expressive in my opinion then her mother, Catherine, who really steals the show due to feeling more like a fleshed out character with real struggles you can fully empathize with. Other characters you meet along the way are equally interesting, from a cult of disorganized adolescents who call themselves "Garretts”, a reoccurring character who thinks Catherine is the descendant of Christ named Pawpaw, it would be wrong of me to spoil to many of the details but they're all great and their often ambiguous motives add to the ever growing mystery. It explores several different themes and tones throughout the story, somehow balancing edgy humor, surrealism, religious themes, and just being down right real and depressing sometimes.There was even one segment that was on the brink of horror with one moment that gave me an incredibly good  scare, I never knew what to expect with Norco and that felt wonderful. The setting itself of course steals a lot of the show both from the presentation and the writing. Being based in and inspired by areas from Southern Louisiana, but taking place in a warped dystopian nightmare version of it where corporations rule through a network that's supposedly connected to a “living brain”, there is just tons of backstory and lore fleshing out this very real world. The game does a wonderful job of keeping a lot of the plot points and lore together through a mind palace like mechanic in the game where you can track story beats, characters, and revisit it to work out new plot threads that could help you advance in the case. Though I do feel that this mechanic could have ultimately served more of a purpose, as it’s ultimately there to simply expand on information. There are also several mini games mixed throughout to sprinkle some variety on what you'll be doing throughout the game and these were all well done. Fighting for example occurs several times with each character having their own little mini game during battle. There are a decent number of puzzles and they're all pretty easy to figure out, with important information usually being highlighted. Though the devs thoughtfully included an expert mode you can check on so key info isn’t highlighted, though I doubt it would make it any harder. The really good news is in this point click game there is ZERO-pixel hunting, with the game usually emphasizing you find information. This means that the entirety of the game is spent focusing on Norco's excellent story and exploring its breathtaking locales. Overall, if you couldn’t already tell, I thought this game was amazing from beginning to end and I think you should BUY IT! I rarely think shorter games are worth the experience but this is 6-8 hours of pure bliss depending on your reading time and how much you explore. I really hope we get a definitive version with some of the cut content the dev has mentioned or even a sequel – I NEED more of this world and this writing.

_childDocuments_.review: I would 100% recommend playing Norco. GORGEOUS pixel art, cool music, great writing, fun mechanics and interesting and compelling world building. It made me laugh out loud, confused me, amused me and made me cry (like actual tears streaming down my face sobbing kind of crying, although I have to admit parts of the story hit really close to home). Finished it in one 6 hours sitting because I could not stop playing... do yourself a favour and play this.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to write a really long, detailed review about this one day coming from the same parish Norco itself is in, but I'll save that for the next time I play through it. Even though I'm not much of a writer and it'll probably be a mess. I felt like this game perfectly captured things I've never been able to properly express. There were parts of it that had me sobbing, I felt so seen in understood in a way it was like ripping a nightmare from my brain and putting it on screen in a video game. But that's not to say only people from southeast Louisiana can find something of value in this, I think absolutely anyone can play this and find things that they connect to and relate to.It's a wonderful work of art and I am so glad it was made.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine a life as child, you're morbidly obsessed with a demonic city, illuminated in the night by flaming skyscrapers, dressed in black smoke clouds. It floats on the horizon, across a swamp of cypress tree husks hinting to the natural glory of a landscape ravaged by man in a different chapter. You on look in horror, fascinated, something pulls you there, but it's hell on earth. You now know is a refinery. People work there, live there, and die there, as it poisons and provides.Then someone makes a beautiful, soulful game capturing everything that speaks to you about this place. It's such an incredibly sincere and thoughtful homage to the trauma of living in marginalized spaces like Norco, Louisiana, and it runs much deeper than "big industry" moving in and changing things. Every screen is worthy of living in a frame on a wall, the music will drag you in and envelope you in this tragic world, the narrative will make you cry.

_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I hear a lot of people compare Disco Elysium and NORCO and I see where they're coming from but it is more that the prose can be very evocative or surreal that I believe their comparisons are based on. If you're looking for something akin to Disco Elysium it's not exactly this but it's still good! I put about eight hours in (probably 7 if you rushed your way through it) and I enjoyed them. I'm, personally, from the Mid-South US so there were some references to places that I recognized or have been myself although this is a different timeline than our own. There's an intriguing premise that develops and some opening questions about your past (as well as a later sequence involving 'versioning' at the beginning of the second act that likely impacts the game in a way I will need to go through again to truly figure out) that serve as a way to just let you have a bit of say in how Kay feels about their childhood and parents before it lets you loose. The narrative is fairly consistent with the occasional absurd easter-eggs you can act on that people will continue to remark on and the music has a good feel to it (in addition to the ambient sound design). I also genuinely appreciate any game that allows you to use a key (spacebar, here) and see all the interactive elements rather than having to run your cursor over every pixel. Also worth mentioning is that I never ran into a cheap 'gotcha' death trap or anything. Interacting with things in my environment, exploring never got me punished.There are some things that people who are sensitive toward religious themes (Not sure if Louisiana is technically Bible Belt or not but it's right next to it if not but Christianity is very present) might be unsettled by but they're part of setting and story. There is a warning up front about people sensitive to suicide or depictions thereof but I can say it's pretty brief and nothing you see in any detail and it's clear it's not done for shock value given story elements and plot threads. it is tied to so if you're only sensitive to graphic depiction or morbid attention to it then you are likely fine (I can't speak to how sensitive you are to it, just offer my observations). A particular I feel worth mentioning: They offer multiple (four, I believe) fonts and three degrees of scaling as well as coloration to customize to your preferred taste or readability. Especially worth mentioning is the OpenDyslexic font that allows for easier reading for some of those who deal with dyslexia which I thought was really, really cool to see the devs take the time to do. I don't have it myself but it's just really cool that they went and added that little bit of accessibility for a text-heavy game. Another element people might be conflating with Disco Elysium is the MindMap. Do not expect to have conversations with yourself about your actions. The MindMap occasionally offered a bit of extra detail but it seemed more like it was there to remind you of story elements or possibly let you pick a few details about your memories or thoughts related to particular things. It certainly has a purpose but it is not the 'thought cabinet' you would expect in a comparison to Disco Elysium. I know I have mentioned that title a lot but it's simply because the biggest draw was the mention of the title being so frequent but the early discourse around the game and descriptions of the set-up and what the devs were aiming for is what got me to buy it.I'll stop myself from going into nauseating detail and just say that I enjoyed my time with it, I didn't have any bugs and there is absolutely no 'try this inventory item on everything you see' kind of puzzles and you don't carry a backpack full of inventory items.  I recommend the game to people who are into surreal and/or darker themes and while I feel the ending left me rail-roaded that might be because of choices I made (but I am unsure if you can progress to the end without them) but it's a story and enjoyable. It's got a really good atmosphere and I'm honestly looking forward to seeing what more these devs put out in the coming future. I'm planning on jumping back into this for another playthrough soon to see how much the story changes with different choices me.Buy it! There's a free demo of act one, even, give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is, for lack of a better word, a very weird game. I bought it after I saw a YouTube video talking about the game and I really don't regret buying it: It's an experience I don't think I ever really had with a game before, and even though there are things in the game that didn't really resonate with me, it's going to be an experience I'll remember for a long time.Norco is a point-and-click-game, but one that follows a very fleshed-out story with a broad cast of characters living in a corporate town that is poisoned and deeply marked by the oil refining complex that slowly takes over town and buys out everyone else. The game is a mix of detective mystery, finding items and using them in the right spot, solving riddles, and incredibly creative and experimental game controls. For the most part of Norco, you talk to characters and slowly unravel the mystery of your missing brother, your dead mother, the company that rules your town, a weird cult, and a weird supernatural neural network. Norco is actually a real place in Louisiana, just that the company destroying it in real life is Shell Oil and not Shield Refinement and I really recommend just looking up stuff about the actual town, because it's real-life paralells are quite interesting to look at.The game deals with quite a lot of heavy themes, but has a way of wrapping them in layers of humor and metaphor, that I at first (in all honesty) found a bit off-putting, but later started to warm up to. I think the game was at its best when it was cryptic and dark and poetic, starkly contrasted with comedic moments that made the emotional scenes even better. When I just had finished the game, my impression was that some plot points just didn't fit the story and were out of place, and while I later came to understand that a lot of these beats had a grander meaning later, the game at first still left a rather sour taste in my mouth, as I found the ending way too absurd.What I think I loved most about the game were the absoluetly beautifully written prose texts, story beats, and the game's willingness to occassionally be evry dark and somber. The characters are all very loveable and very distinguishable in how they are written and what I really enjoyed was how no character in this game was only likeable or only unlikable - I think every character had both sympathetic sides and unsympathetic ones and that was really great to experience, because they all felt very human and very grounded, with real troubles and worries, but also with ideals and hopes. I found the story generally really engaging, even though I think initially wasn't prepared for how absurd the game would get at times, because I at first expected this to be a more grounded story I was a bit thrown off when the focus at the end kind of shifted away from the themes I personally found the most resonant to me and really embraced the absurdity of the story coming to a close in a very bizzare way, that takes some interpretation to be understood. Regardless of the story, Norco both had plot points where I was stunned in awe at the scene and the descriptions and at other times had moments where I was laughing my ass off because a scene was so bizarre and entertaining.Norco is a game that often introduces a random mechanic out of the blue and forces you to react, and I really enjoyed that part of the game - Norce didn't just feel like a standard point-and-click game with a narrative on top of it, but like the game developers really thought about how to make each part of the game stand out mechanically, and it works really really well, especially since almost every single one of the game's bizarre mechanics is used again in the last stretch of the game, creating a great finale.There are some really cool moments where you feel really smart for having figured something out - a lot of the passcode riddles in the game are really creative without feeling contrived and at one point, recording something in one act will help you when you're almost at the end of the game and these moments just feel great! But I felt like the game was holding my hand like 80% of the time - important stuff people say always gets highlighted in green and that makes it less fun if you actually had the thought yourself - ESPECIALLY if then a companion repeats the hint another two times, just in case you forgot, and I know that some players need that, but I felt like 50% of the time, riddles were a bit too on the nose. There were very few moments in the game however that I found contrived or illogical, which is almost never the case in point-and-click games and I really liked how logically coherent the game was. There were 2-3 points where I was a bit confused because a thing was either very meta (I don't want to spoil what it is, but near the end of the game you do something really unethical for literally no reason and someone screws up and in turn does something that helps you. But there is NO reason why you would, as a character choose to do that very unethical thing in the first place) or a thing wasn't really logical (at some point you have to use an item to find something hidden, but there is no reason why you would think to use that item in that situation), but those were really the only moments I felt a bit at loss.The music and art of the game were really great and even though I usually am not the type to like pixel art styles, the compositions and imagery often really impressed me. The setting and world are beautifully done, and I had a lot of fun exploring the locations in Norco.Generally I would say, I totally recommend the game if you like experimental, cryptic, mysterious games and are open for plots that are a bit more absurd, too. This game really isn't like Disco Elysium at all, but if you liked Disco Elysium, I think you might enjoy this game too! Also - if you played a lot of old school point-and-click adventure games, I think this game will make you feel really melancholic, but without the game being clunky and incomprehensible. For the price it's being sold for, I think it's totally reasonable to buy Norco!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this game primarily for my appreciation of the art and sound, since both are awesome. I think where I have issues with this game is the story. The story doesn't really know what it wants to be. It starts off great, and sets an emotional somber tone. You feel like this is going to be a deep moving experience. But then, soon the story flips upside down to where it just gets so far out there, you kind of lose interest, and aren't sure how you even ended up there. I don't know if that is some intentional twist they wanted to achieve, but if so it kind of misses the mark. If they had included some interesting puzzles that were a little more in-depth and more interactions in general (along the lines of Maniac Mansion) I think the game would be great despite the lackluster story. For this price though, it's a pretty interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Just wanna say, before I get into my review, I have played and finished this game, though it was on game pass. I bought it on here and played a tiny bit of it so i could be able to write a review and also to support the devs. This is probably one of the best games I have ever played. Like, jesus ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥. The narrative is perfect, like flat out. perfect. From start to finish it grips you into a moody and almost haunting story but is also able to hold such a beauty and light even in its darkest parts. This game's ability to take so much from reality and pour it into an experience like this, it's just outstanding. There was so much love and effort and detail put into this game and each of its interactions, and I can't really think of other games that I have played that have made me feel in the way this has. It has like that effect that people described when playing something like The Last of Us or any other modern game that has a really gripping and emotional narrative. Its characters are more than memorable, and some of the offhand comments and throwaway lines from these characters have become writing that I think about even after reaching end credits. The pixel art of this game is also, just, to die for. And the soundtrack is like the cherry on top to just a really amazing experience. I just love how hauntingly beautiful this game is, and it is an experience that I think will stay with me for the rest of my life. Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game positively surprised me. I went in blind and was amazed at the incredibly touching writing, both humorous and dramatic, sometimes even poetic. The atmosphere and character dynamics while switching between playing each of their perspectives is what makes this game a unique experience. It touches on heavy subjects in a curious way and connects tragedy with absurdity in what i can only call art. It's not very long but packs a punch. Absolutely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get what everyone finds in this game. Disco Elysium left a huge Disco Elysium-shaped hole in my heart that I try to fill sometimes, Norco was often recommended as a similar experience so I tried it. The game starts promising - setting, graphics, narrative all feels nice, and then it just all falls apart.First of all, the plot is irrelevant to the setting. With minor adjustments to characters and MacGuffin, the story could happen in any other place, which really takes away from the surreal atmosphere authors try to build. This together with short storyline of the game never allows you to feel the world around; despite all the interesting ideas behind it, the setting always acts like decorations, not a place. You wish you could explore it more but the game gives you a set tour so you feel like the in-game characters complaining that it was supposed to be fun only to hear in reply that it was fun for the authors to write it.Characters are underexplored. You never really get the obsession of everyone else with MacGuffin especially when the main characters are decidedly not that interested in it so it’s hard to relate with their motivations. Your actions lack effect on both in-game or from meta level. It is okay for Point & Click games to be linear but at least some of the things you do should force reaction from other characters but the game pretty much tells you that whatever you do doesn't matter. This culminates in the ending where, for example, the choice you make about your brother, who is the supposed focus of much of the story, is barely acknowledged.Gameplay is pretty boring, combat is lackluster and the game would do much better if it was removed altogether and replaced with narrative choices. Some puzzles feel like they were created only to pad out the already short gameplay time. Generally, it feels that the game would work better if it played to it storytelling strengths rather than try to fit to gameplay clichés.Overall, the game leaves you wanting for more, for a deeper experience, for a more meaningful social commentary rather than allusions it prefers to make, for a sense of closure in the end. To quote Macbeth, it may not be a tale told by an idiot, but it is full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: this review is hard to write, because i barely have words to describe what norco is and how it feels. this is one of those games that absolutely destroys the concept of games not being art. it's a game that reveres its influences and setting, but not by putting them on a pedestal - it displays all the gritty glory, the dark and the light, all at once, and manages to be faithful and cohesive. it's a game that is both distant and personal - weird and unfamiliar, but in a way that draws you in, makes you feel at home, even while you're surrounded by things that make no sense to you. it is truly a masterpiece and i can't recommend it enough to people who like to really feel things when they play games.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Came into this game because I was looking to scratch that Disco Elysium itch, and this game came up more than anything.But boy, was it something else.I can see why this game is being compared to DE: both fall into that "serious game" niche where, through powerful storytelling, you come out with new ways of looking at the world around you rather than just being like "haha cool that was fun". And to be very fair, if you liked DE, you will probably enjoy this game too, and vice versa.But where as DE deals with ideologies, NORCO is much more grounded in how landscape is lived and transforms those who live within it. It is the critical geography to DE's political philosophy. It is much smaller in scale-- both literally (in terms of game size) and narratively (for its themes and overall story)-- but not necessarily for the worse. Sure, you could argue that in the end, NORCO is every bit as anti-capitalist as DE, perhaps even more so, but while playing it you get the sense that all those talks of big ideologies fade away in the face of the bayou, the refinery, the streets, and the sheer  of it all. And the grandest ironies of them all is that even those who tries to escape the confinement of such materiality ends up being mortally confronted with its brutal, unmistakable reality.So at the end of the day, even though I've just spent this whole review comparing this game to DE, NORCO is its own beast, and all the better for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco deserves all the praise I can give it and more besides. From a long tradition of adventure games comes something that builds upon it and still feels so unbelievably, shockingly new? It's singular. I can't begin to explain it to you without taking away from its wonder. I can't tell you what part of it coheres most in my mind, because they're all fighting each other for the top spot. I'll be thinking about Norco for probably the rest of my life.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is so good, it made me pause my Elden Ring playthrough lolIf you love story – driven games, PLEASE give this one a chance! It tells a very engrossing story that starts out pretty familiar, but by the midpoint takes some unexpected turns going places I didn’t expect it to go. It’s so hard to put down, because the writing makes the game flow seamlessly, from start to finish. Whoever WROTE this game, give this person a raise or something, because the writing is so smooth and natural. It’s poetic without sounding pretentious. Idk how else to describe it, but it just feels right. Overall, the tone of the game is rather dark and bleak, but there are moments of humor and real comradery, which balance it out. Funny situations happen quite often actually and unexpected friendships form from time to time. Somehow looking back at the game I could recall a lot more hilarious interactions than sad ones, so maybe it isn’t as hopeless after all :)I also love that this is a Point & Click adventure that you could actually finish without looking for a guide. You always know what to do and where to go and it’s such a relief after playing Full Throttle and Monkey Island lol. Hey, maybe I’m just too dumb for those games, but NORCO is actually FINISHABLE without pulling your hair out after sitting for hours on one puzzle. I know this review is all over the place, but this is my first one, so that’s that. I really wanted to write it, because this game is SO GOOD and I just wanted to share my feelings! If you are a fan of strong writing, please try it, you won't be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Every moment up to the end of this game had me more and more enraptured. The characters feel like they have depth that you'll always be left wanting to explore more, the world is interesting and funny, the lore marches to its own tune. The art and music is also beautiful. I was mildly disappointed by the ending, but I might just not understand it properly, or maybe the rest of the game was so good I could never be satisfied. Regardless, worth it if you like games like kentucky route zero or disco elyisum, character driven sad and mystic stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Grim and mody visual novel (or slight puzzler). The strong parts clearly are the atmosphere and the writing style. Note there is an expert mode which might render the game actually a game. I missed it, but I would encourage you to give it a try - it's really off-putting easy otherwise.What I'm not sure about is the narration. 1) For me, many of the humorous/playful/cheerful parts didn't really blend with the dark, gritty scenery displayed elsewhere (e.g. the ). Imo in such a gloomy scenery the only humor which doesn't conflict is sarcasm/cynism. 2) I didn't really get the story yet (I'll do some more research on that), so this point might be improper. But my first impression is that the story couldn't decide where it's some kind of fairy-tale, where it's a grim and realistic journey and where it's just a delusion of yours (example: ). Of course, it all could be "just in your head", but you make progress by dealing with such unrealistic events, so it's hard to take them all as just imagined. Or it's really just a fairy-tale where lots of wierd and unrealistic stuff helps you to breeze through dire situations, but then again, that would conflict with the whole build-up of this place, or at least it wouldn't be my cup of tea.Anyway, recommend! Despite all, it's a beautiful, haunting game with an unconventional and interesting story! Maybe it's a bit to convoluted/confusing, but you have to judge that on your own.

_childDocuments_.review: As haunting and seedy as it is twisted and darkly amusing, NORCO is quite simply one of the most impressively conceived and written point-and-click adventure games I've ever played. Its plotting can be dense and intentionally obtuse, but its gameplay design is very smart overall, featuring a superb array of dialogue and lore to chase through exploration, as well as a series of puzzles that engage the mind without descending into moonlogic.This is the kind of game that may demand a couple of playthroughs to fully grasp its storytelling, but enthusiasts of point-and-click adventure games will nonetheless find this to be one deranged hidden gem. Just watch how many times you pet the cat. Mistakes were made.

_childDocuments_.review: "are video games art?"Maybe not all games are art. But NORCO definitely is. Speaking as a native of south Louisiana, this game FEELS like home. The oil refinery down the road, Interstate 10, Airline Highway, and some just entirely unique regional vocabulary from the mouths of characters who feel like the real life people I grew up hanging around. Both a loveletter to the people and a critique of capitalist endeavors. Undercurrent of the grime of things, and a mix-in of modern netizen vibes.  AND THE ART. The art is a gorgeous romanticization of the sunset mood.I could not have had a better time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's weird, dark, sad, and funny, but it also felt really earnest and compassionate. Even toward people the game ridicules. Some real-life people really are caricatures of themselves, and the ones in Norco felt like authentic, outrageous caricatures I have met. Their inclusion felt like it was done in a spirit of familiar, teasing camaraderie, not like an attack or sneer.One of my favorite things is when a piece of media makes me feel like I'm a part of a big, eclectic, intricate, ridiculous global-cultural-temporal tapestry. Norco is an absolutely beautiful experience all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam recommended me this game because I played Disco Elysium, and I have seen people make ample comparisons between the two. I suspect this is because both games primarily take the format of reading long stretches of writing & selecting dialogue responses, because that's where I felt the similarities ended. NORCO is uniquely American in the themes and ideas it asks the player to confront, opening by making the player evaluate what balance they believe should be struck between what they owe themselves and what they owe their communities (to, I would imagine, the tune of a largely individual-oriented answer). It then spends the rest of the game asking if it's wrong for that balance to stay the same when you find out your community is dying.Don't let the backwoods setting mislead you - NORCO is asking players to confront questions that even Silicon Valley wunderkinds are staring down the barrel of every day. I admittedly missed the big-picture applicability of it until a character in the game described themselves as an "internet of internets." That was the moment it hit me: NORCO has so seamlessly and lovingly blended some of our most pressing contemporary ideas (the all-encompassing sprawl of surveillance capitalism, the death throes of the environment under traditional capitalist endeavors, the seeding of a certain type of neo-fascism into American communities and the inability of most to fully articulate it, class war) into its setting that I hadn't been able to recognize them on first pass. This is a part of the country that I didn't grow up anywhere near, and I had to shift my framing of these issues, which I am more familiar with, to be able to see them as the residents of NORCO are seeing them - which, as NORCO shows us, is often as a monster breathing down their dying necks.Steeped in a culture than encourages ruthless self-sufficiency, NORCO makes us ask how far these things have to go to become our problem, even when the problems that are solely ours are building up by the minute, and how we justify the answer being too damn long. This game isn't long or fancy, but it has deeply stuck in my head since I first started getting into the meat of its story. This game is worth playing, and worth re-playing after that.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a captivating adventure game with a disconsolate world. It feeds you a relatable setting and includes a quirky cast of characters. The main protagonist, Kay, is a faceless person that can be entirely different from you, or the same depending on the choices that you make.The gameplay mechanics are designed as an efficient pipeline for immersion: simple and intuitive. NORCO is a point-and-click that leans on simple dialogue trees. The dialogue is effective at keeping your attention and absorbing you into the world, which is precisely what it should serve to do. And yet, despite its simplicity, NORCO has moments of brilliance wherein the beautiful prose stops you from mindlessly scrolling and makes you think about a deeper meaning.What immediately struck me about NORCO is the 90's nostalgia that is reminiscent of other games from my childhood, namely Might & Magic IV: Clouds of Xeen and Might & Magic V: Darkside of Xeen. I can vividly recall the real MT-32 tracks of Xeen within the instrumental soundtrack. It often has a funky, upbeat, and at times melancholy surrealism that compliments the dark, dystopian atmosphere in a near future New Orleans. Each area of the game has a fitting theme with elements of jazz or front-and-center punk distortion. I'm also convinced that Might & Magic and its RPG derivatives played a role in inspiring the party system, in which characters situationally join your group on the sidebar and add their own flare to the mystery, offering you helpful and funny dialogue.Rather than shoehorn an attempt at the profound right in your face (as a modern AAA title would), NORCO presents you with the world as an abject reality: You are a passing traveler with a hand in the direction of your own fate. NORCO's combination of simplicity, prose, and nostalgia render it as a game well worth playing — and one I would recommend to gamers and non-gamers alike.-Ssschah

_childDocuments_.review: I love PAC games, and this one especially because the puzzles are usually pretty straightforward. I only really have used a guide once so far. I really enjoy how much the story feels like it can breath and move without getting broken up by a painful puzzle. Some great PAC games like Grim Fandango are good and all but end up with a lot of wandering around and feeling stuck. Not so with Norco.I also love the story, art, SFX and the unconventional (occasional) combat. Great game

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a short, point and click adventure game.The story is a highlight, managing to capture horror and heartbreak both mundane and fantastic. However, due to its brevity, characters are largely flat and the story overall lacks emotional depth. Though the setting itself is very distinctive with its mix of industry, poverty, and mysticism. The pixel art is gorgeous and at times psychedelic and the game overall has very strong visuals. On a similar note, sound design is also excellent, strongly emphasizing the identity and mood of each location visited in the game. Gameplay is overly simple and easy. Whether its the point-and-click segments that dominate the game's runtime or the rare mini-game based combat encounter, it's almost impossible to lose or get lost.Overall, a solid thumbs-up from me.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: As others have mentioned, it's a game that desperately wants to be the next Kentucky Route Zero, yet it doesn't understand what made that game so powerful. Norco's biggest flaw, as with many fantasies and SCFY stories, is it's a well-developed world without characters (It's one of the reasons those genres are so hard). Instead of letting the story happen naturally and showing growth, it just tells you what happens and what to make of certain aspects of the world and narrative. There isn't the ambiguity and the multilayered depth of KRZ, and exposition and overly explanatory dialogue trees lack the focus of KRZ's innovative approach to players making the script as they go, rather than choices matter twine based design.Its got some great industrial backgrounds, but some interiors are severely lacking, and it has a habit of shoving obvious symbolism in your face to imply its depth. I'm honestly bewildered by the reviews. I was expecting another point-and-click masterpiece and ended up rather disappointed. It's far from bad just don't expect anything revolutionary beyond an interesting concept. I liked features like the mind map, which helps to organically put together narrative information and the mystery of Norco, and I think with another game or writer, the dev could make something great. I don't know, the writing has a very first draft feel and definitely had the potential to be excellent with some more time. Check out Backbone or KRZ if you want some better diselpunkish noir mystery point and clicks.

_childDocuments_.review: Great story, atmosphere and music, slightly marred by a combat system that feels both annoying and unnecessary. Thankfully, fights can be auto-resolved. The rest of the game is a mix of magic realism and Southern Gothic, set in a dystopian near-future New Orleans. The characters are well-defined, the dialogue polished, and the 10 hours of gameplay feel right for the story and the price. Highly recommended, if you don't mind some dark themes.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely enjoyable. NORCO could be best described as a mix of point and click adventure in an RPG set up, where you investigate the strange things that happened around your mom's death and brother's disappearance. There's fun mix ups in what you're doing, including a simple and quick battle system with a focus on little microgames, exploring a swamp via overhead angle, and puzzles revolving around making use of a smartphone. The writing is very strong, going from complex and resonate prose to top tier sh*tposts where a cult member will go on a tangent about bong hits or you can listen to a guy you tricked into eating old hot dogs earlier describe what happened after when he couldn't find a bathroom.It also just looks beautiful from start to end, with lovingly crafted sprite art on every screen, and some really out there imagery alongside the attempts to capture the reality of the actual real oil town of Norco, LA. Good, resonate music, lots of text options for accessibility needs, and a solid seven hour length with some added replay value to mess around with choices and get achievements you missed. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is bizarre and beautiful. I was actually taken aback at how its final sequences shook me, almost to the point of tears. I have such a weakness for stories about families and the distance we put between ourselves and family for all sorts of reasons, intentionally or not. The game’s layering of religion on top of that core conflict, swinging wildly from its maximally absurd and blasphemous grotesque representation to a light touch with how the more grounded characters treat it, made it all hit a little harder for me.Don’t have it in me to unpack those themes or the other heavy topics the game tackles that are very much about that specific space in New Orleans, but they certainly made me feel some type of way! The off-beat humor also certainly made it all go down a little smoother, which its disarming presence reminds me why I was also so taken by Disco Elysium.It also deserves a lot of praise for its music. The synth soundtrack is brooding, melancholic, sinister, and at times surprisingly chipper, setting the mood perfectly for every scene. It does so much to elevate the storytelling, and I hope more people appreciate it as being just as important as the striking pixel art and excellent writing.

_childDocuments_.review: There are certain books and movies that might hold a certain amount of niche indie appeal for the general public but then tend to be pretty well known in whatever specific region they're set in. For example, Cormac McCarthy's novel Suttree might be fairly well regarded by people who know about the author's less popular works, but if you ever go to Knoxville Tennessee it's much more widely known and talked about, specifically because they have a connection to it because of the geographical location in which it's set.Videogames are a medium that doesn't really lend itslef to that in the same way, in my opinion. There's a few games that have New York, Southern California, or even New Orleans as their settings, and yet those games never really take on any special meaning for the people who live in those places, at least not as far as I'm aware.Norco might be the first game that actually manages to hold a specific regional appeal for the place in which it's set. Nothing else like this has ever really been made in the videogame space that focuses so specifically on a particular place and the weird realities that make up that place. As someone who has spent his whole life on the Gulf Coast, this feels very special to me, but I do worry that this game might be too niche, and too regional to ever have any broader appeal.Norco is a traditional point-and-click adventure game with some mild turn based combat, set in a dystopian cyberpunk version of Southern Louisiana.Gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from such a venture. It mostly involves interacting with the environment through clicking, some mild puzzle solving, and a lot of dialogue. There are some (very easy) combat sections mixed in depending on the choices you make which are turn based RPG combat/quicktime events.The main draw of the game is of course, the setting and the story, all complimented beautifully by the exquisite pixel art.Since the setting is the main thing I'm focusing on I just want to say that I think it's very special to see a game come out like this that highlights this particular region of America because I've looked for sci-fi interpretations of Southern Louisiana and the Gulf Coast before and I gotta say they're almost nonexistent. Most of the time if New Orleans or this area gets mentioned in science fiction at all it's usually just as a half-assed warning about global warming and they'll say the whole region is underwater. But there's so much about this particular part of the world that is unique and fascinating that makes it perfect for interpretation in the context of sci-fi but this is the first property I think I've ever seen that attempts to do that.Norco is a real place in Southern Louisiana. West of New Orleans and dominated solely by oil refineries and factories. Industrialization, it's effects on the environment, and the parasitic relationship it has with the people who are harmed by it, but also rely on it for money and community, that's a perfect theme to be explored by the cyberpunk genre, and Norco is a perfect place to set such a story. In addition, the game shows us the region's similarly parasitic relationship with religion, politics, and hints at a much wider world where all of the current problems America has been facing have been magnified tenfold.I absolutely love this game and it's story but I do worry that many gamers won't be able to connect with it since it ties itself so specifically into the nature of this one particular region.The pixelart beautifully renders all of this as well, like I said. I'm always a sucker for good pixel art. Especially when it gives you scenic swampy vistas that you can just sit and stare at for a while to absorb the ambience.The game makes a big deal about it's soundtrack but I wasn't as impressed by it. Although it's good none of the songs in particular really stood out to me, except for maybe the overworld theme, called 'Parish.'Overall I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants to give a forward thinking cyberpunk storyline a shot, and is comfortable with it being light on gameplay, and having obscure references. But although I heartily recommend it, I do worry that the game will end up only having a certain kind of niche, regional appeal to the people who are familiar with the setting it takes place in, the same way only other obscure pieces of media have done so in the past.

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game. I wouldn't spend too much time trying to explain, but I think if you are a point and click fan, or enjoy graphic novels this one is for you. Beautiful visuals, deep writing, amazing music, a variety of different gameplay sequences, intriguing story, morbid jokes, and so much more. Completed it in 6 hours. Highly recommend this experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Poetic, impressionistic, bleak, funny, and intensely absorbing, this is the most engaging adventure game I can think of in years.  Don't let any of the descriptors I mentioned scare you off- Norco is accessible and fun. The stunning graphics bury deep into your psyche's nebulous nostalgia zone, so much that you will find yourself deeply missing Norco, Louisiana when the game is done. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Every living thing wants to survive. We all do. When we are backed into a corner, stuck in a horrible position we've been in all our lives, unable to imagine a world outside of these constraints, we become desperate. Hope always leads to desperation. Its so much, it could push nature itself into investing in cryptocurrency and God into trying to leave earth forever. Norco will kill itself, there is no other option. And there is beauty in that. May be the best point and click ever, who knows, I've only played a handful
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the immersion in the religious southern gothic / sci-fi setting that Norco proposes. One of the best game I played this year.A well written story that was thought-provoking, I enjoyed reading every bits of text that the game was willing to throw at me.The story comes with one of the best pixel art I ever saw, and the OST is also absolutely stunning. I found myself in awe several times just by looking at the scene while being rocked by the mesmerizing ambient tracks. Feeling melancholy, yet a strange calmness.Playing this game also gave me the opportunity to learn about Norco IRL, and knowing what I know now makes me see the game and some of the themes it adresses in a different light.I already was interested by this area, but playing Norco strangely made me long for the Bayou. I'm thankful for this wonderful journey.Oh and there is a random dude with a Eyehategod tattoo, so that's pretty cool.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this was magnificent. The game's very opening, that is, the intro and the exploration of the house and its immediate surroundings, weren't immediately appealing, but things pick up quickly. And once NORCO gets going, the only thing stopping it is the finale.Overall, I'd describe the experience as a cross between Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium in about 3:1 ratio. There's a lot to take in, there are plenty of characters both important and not quite, there are mysteries to consider, and I have to admit that the game's ending managed to blindside me, so I'll be busy digesting it for a while, I feel.So, some initial and mild misgivings about the game's beginning aside, NORCO is a stellar ride.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Apparently, an absolutely insane 6-hour-long point & click adventure game.Graphics are utterly gorgeous, the music is absolutely wonderful. The story is certainly unique and engaging, but Christ is it nuts. Gameplay is simple and relatively on-rails, with some light-medium puzzles and a few minigames to space it all out. Humor is modern and irreverent, and so is the social commentary. The characters are very colorful with wacky, vibrant personas, in a kind of delusional Louisiana at the end-times. I don't really know what to make of this, it's certainly a very polished game, it's certainly a very good game, and for better or worse it's also a really bizarre one.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This was a flipping trip. Holy cow, I enjoyed this way more than I thought I would. It's like reading a good book, and at the end, you're left thinking about everything and just... kinda speechless? The devs were kind enough to provide an 'after-game' lore dump answering some questions that I had that got me even more interested and hooked. But I digress. Overall, this game is great.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Just when I thought Elden Ring would be my game of the year no contest Norco swoops in and knocks me off my feet. This is a story that is scarily close to my personal experience, and my god this story is written with so much poetry and humanity. I cannot recommend this game enough, everyone should play it. Game of the year undoubtedly.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty pixel art and intriguing prologue but fails to produce a coherent story or any payoffs for any of its numerous loose threads that continually pile up all the way to the credits roll. Poorly implemented combat sequences that don't fit the overall concept of the game and UI/journal elements that only serve to create more confusion in an already frazzled narrative. Rather, the 25 spliced together dialogue lines that do not weave together into anything resembling a story. I've got no motivation to put myself through it a second time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is an extremely cool, evocative, idiosyncratic point and click linear adventure game set in an at least somewhat fantasized version of Norco, LA. It has a dreamlike quality without being too fantastical. The dialogue conveys a depth of emotion and quirky humor. The pixelated graphics perfectly tie everything together. The only negative is the "fighting" elements that the game contains are not really interesting or difficult, to the point where I question why they were even included. But you can get through them quickly enough and everything else about the game is amazing, assuming you like this style of game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to describe the game on a mechanical level that makes it sound good, at times the route gameplay and puzzles felt simple and underdevolped, but there were major points were I felt extreme emotions as NORCO revealed and reveled in it's themes. It is such a surreal experience, but every single thing it covers feels poignant and real regardless.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you're wondering whether to buy it, yes, absolutely do to try it out if it looks decently interesting to you. To me, it's a masterpiece of atmosphere, writing, game design, and art. It has impressive worldbuilding, a luring backstory, artwork to mesmerize, and a soundtrack to lock you in... and then there's that ♥♥♥♥♥ Rosie, who I'm guessing to be the digital manifestation of one of the dev's early childhood trauma likely permanently imprinted by what I'm sure is a lovely aunt named Rosie. There's no other way someone can come up with something like Rosie without some serious issues that need to be addressed sooner rather than later. Go see a therapist because I'll need a reference for a good one - I got second-hand trauma from that experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I sincerely wanted to love this game. its story telling and world building was great. however, every moment of "oh whats going to happen next" and "am i finally going to get an explanation of what this is?" ends up being for naught because the game falls flat on its face at the end where you receive a convoluted strange ending, that answers none of the players questions and leaves them with even more than they did before. its a poor feeling to be carried through a game with questions about multiple plot points just to end up having none of them reconciled or even touched on in the end. the game has 3 chapters but feels as though it should have had 4 or 5. I dont know if this game has multiple endings, but the ending i got made me not want to play through again to find out.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It starts strongly, but at least one more act is needed to fully wrap up the story (it ends way sooner than expected), leaving us quite underwhelmed with 3 so-so endings and plenty of underdeveloped characters. It's a general "indie-title plague" so should get used to it by now.Overall what's there works quite well, albeit some tackiness (what's up with the cat?) and overwrought segments that don't go anywhere (flooded house metaphor returns way too often). Music and sound design are a big plus !It's all cute and sad and a bit too short for its own good.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game. Bought it on release primarily due to the fact one of my favorite bands, Thou, did some music for it, with no other expectations. Immediately drawn into the nostalgia of games I grew up playing like Snatcher but with some clear Disco Elysium influences - namely future surrealism and a text system that instantly felt familiar. As far as point and clicks go this is about as easy as it gets. The game pretty much holds your hand from A to B with the exception of the very light RPG elements that occasionally come up. I played this on a Steam Deck which made the battle minigames incredibly hard until my dumbass remembered that the Steam Deck is touch screen at which point the game resumed being a walk in the park.Utter weirdness and originality oozing from this thing while it somehow still manages to be somewhat affecting with a story about grief, trauma, and loss (and a Juggalo sidekick that really put this over the top.) Loved every minute.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Story rich text based adventure, not choose-your-own sadly but with a lot of details and optional dialogues / exploration set-pieces.  The atmosphere, characters and dialogue all work really well together to deliver a fun game. One (-) downside it has is that the game is short. I was able to fully finish it in under 7 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting point and click adventure about family, grief, supernaturality and greed. The story kept me curious enough to finish the game with only two sittings. Pixelart is topnotch, the environmental elements is great, charming sound effects and dialoge is very fluid and sometimes bizarre.The game is pretty simple both gameplaywise and characterwise but its a fun ride if you want to play something that is not as demanding on the player.6.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Add this to your list of "well written" games. Also to your list of "surreal Louisiana cyber-noir" games. Also to your list of "I can't explain why it's good, you just have to play it" games.If you ever lived in Louisiana, you should play this, because there are very few good works of art set in Louisiana."I have anxiety, should I be worried?"
