_childDocuments_.review: This game is intense. It has elements of Hotline Miami, David Lynch movies. The writing is immersive, characters express a lot in the way they speak. The game is often scary. It's not difficult, which didn't make me enjoy it less. I play these kinds of games like a data-miner. I never do what I'm supposed to do, I always leave that for last while exploring every other possible avenue first. And I've found that the game doesn't give you much space to maneuver, but what it does give you is handled with care. I would have finished this in one sitting if it wasn't for the fact that I literally passed out while trying to play through the night. My head propped up against my pillow, with the laptop on a tray, screen aimed at my face. I slept until morning, listening to the background music in Duck's library. This soaked me with the atmosphere of the game. It's so intense, it ended up feeling suffocating. I kept playing because I wanted to get out of this dark tunnel. You keep going deeper into the mystery, you find answers everywhere yet somehow everything becomes less clear. Also, I love how the Quack currency crashed in value by over 100% in a few days time. Nice little detail. I wonder how many people noticed that. There seem to be a few branching paths, nothing major, but I haven't checked. At one point I had to choose between different drugs. At least, it seemed like I had a choice, but my lack of money chose for me. The music is great in this game. And the dialogue noises are really cool. The customization options for the fonts are great. The CRT filter gave me a headache, but it's there if you want it. It's kind of interesting. The people you meet, the whole narrative. It's the story of the world we inherited from boomers. Who grew up in a world where everyone knows everyone, because they haven't left their town. Where I grew up there was a massive brewery, and a sugar factory. So you had the wheat and sugarbeet farmers, the people who worked at the brewery and the factory. It often smelled like yeast or the boiled beets, depending on which way the wind blew. And the people don't really change. At some point in their life they get stuck on repeat, and then they ferment and become stale. They talk about the same things over and over. It's charming in a way. The characters in this game really reminded me of that. All of them obsessed with something, mostly the past.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An oil soaked fever dream which unfolds in a distorted and dystopic future Louisiana. Dense worldbuilding, beautiful pixel art and an understated but evocative soundtrack combine to render a palpably decaying world occupied by: a mall-dwelling cult of micro-influencers, a rogue security robot, and hand-to-mouth gig economy workers carrying out bizarre clandestine tasks in service of a mysterious (and vaguely sinister) phone app.The best point and click games transcend the limitations of the genre because of truly excellent writing and this has that in abundance. Strongly recommended if you're in the mood to soak up some melancholic near-future sci-fi, which occupies a strange metaphysical void somewhere between the work of David Lynch and Charlie Brooker. Despite the dystopic atmosphere, it's also genuinely funny at times, successfully tapping in to the same vein of wry satirical humour as it's influences.It's not going to blow you away with any gameplay innovations, but it's well worth playing through for it's immersive atmosphere and memorable storytelling.“Black as midnight on a moonless night.” - Agent Cooper (Twin Peaks)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Since it's coming up, let's talk about my game of the year. Norco was an early contender when I played it at the beginning on 2022 and it has kept its spot rightfully. I love how down to earth this game is even by cyberpunk standards and I love its music and I love its silly plot and the little vignettes you get into this New Orleans community. It's special in a way I can't describe. Play it if you like point and clicks. Play it regardless. It's that good.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you like narrative driven adventure games with beautiful pixel art, then this is well worth a look. It’s the same price as a cinema ticket and you’ll get a good 5-7 hours of enjoyment here. I’d suggest going in blind. It’s the most intriguing game I’ve played in a while, and not knowing where the story was going made it a lot more fun.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The game equivalent of sitting down in a comfy chair, feet up, it's nice and cool and the rain is pitter pattering on the roof. You feel at ease and at peace, ready to enjoy your book.A game dripping with atmosphere, with dialogue richly written, graphics really showcasing how to use the medium to create an enviornment (even if they're pixel) and music adding the final detail, creating a beautiful, enthralling story that's fun to play and a pleasure to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a dystopic sci-fi adventure game about a nomadic drifter named Kay who comes home after her mother passes to find her missing brother. Taking place in an overindustrialized part of swampside New Orleans, Norco's thematic ties to capitalism, oppression, connection, and loss flourish within a gorgeously bleak color palette of pixel art and a script that should be recognized as one of the medium's best.Norco mainly plays out like a standard point-and-click adventure game. Much of the 6-ish hour runtime is spent hopping between locations, talking to the quirky characters, and finding items and information to move forward. These elements are standard fare and the game mostly swings on the easy side in terms of logic and item usage. There are no out-of-pocket inventory combinations and most instances of a puzzle can be solved with a few seconds of backtracking. I was only stuck at one moment of the game, where the mindmap didn't say there were new options to explore. Speaking of, Kay is able to source her thoughts and progress into the mysteries of Norco with a detective-board-like mindmap. It's not very complex, but it was nice to browse when I came back to the game between sessions or wanted a quick summary after long conversations. Apart from the main plot, Norco has a knack for detail in its literature. Many of its best moments are the descriptions of the world, a land pulled apart by division of inequality and rebellion. The lore here is so rich that the game is most enticing when you can fully sink into the bats*** insanity of it all. There is also a light combat element, which I actually enjoyed. Using basic JRPG mechanics, you perform attacks with the characters in your active party by timing moves, akin to Paper Mario. It was a welcome addition that I actually wish was a little more frequent and had a broader purpose.As I mentioned, the world is unbelievably realized in Norco. Each of the environments is a dark, twisted pixel masterpiece, and the character design and the grimy nature of the aesthetic connects you to Kay's home and her struggles. Norco isn't afraid to push boundaries, and several moments flip the traditional genre style and add in new ideas to the presentation that are clever and surprising. The relationship of the player to their audiovisual experience is played with in subtle, intelligent, and sometimes off-putting ways, but all to serve the story brilliantly. Special mention must go to the music, which is a blend of electronic hellscapes and funky tunes that capture the energy of a land seeped in culture on the precipice of insurmountable change. Many of these tracks I will surely be listening to in the coming weeks.What I wasn't expecting most from Norco was its acceptance of choice. Right from the opening, you can choose elements of Kay's backstory, and you can continue to make foundational choices throughout your playtime. Dialogue doesn't just run you through every option, so conversations feel weighty and real, and several achievements and interactions have binary choices that have alternate options. I'm usually not a fan of having an amorphous approach to character like this, but Norco still manages to contain the setting and tone despite what options you choose for Kay and her family.Norco is going to be one of 2022's best titles. In a year where more than ever, understanding the value of family, our homes, and the growing dissent in corporations, the internet, and humanity at large is at its critical mass, the game handles its lofty perceptions of reality and dials it in for a crafted, enjoyable experience you should not miss.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO, by developer/artist collective/terrifically named Geography of Robots, is a bitter sweet Southern Gothic psychodrama about family, capitalism, religion and everything in between. It’s an absolutely masterful use of the point and click format to explore a multifaceted narrative, with a presentation that perfectly recreates the razor thin line between dream, nightmare and reality.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco has a lot of weird, sometimes goofy, characters and abstract moments. Yet it combines those with a serious story in a cohesive manner. Gameplay-wise it's a point-and-click adventure, which sees you interacting with items, environments and people in order to find out more about the story, about certain characters or to solve puzzles. The weakest part of the game to me was the combat: a series of basic QTE's, though it did not hamper the overall enjoyment at all. The visuals are amazing and they definitely punctuate some of the more impactful moments in the game, while also bringing all of the strange characters to life. Sound-wise there was a good amount of ambient noise, though no spoken dialogue, as the voices were portrayed by indistinct warbling sounds. The music was beautiful, melancholic and it fit the mood of the scene(s). This is a great game if you enjoy a story that makes you think. That makes you want to explore and find out more about everything going on.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, which combines some uncanny psychedelic motives, retro style and ton of gloom and dismay (I'm guessing, drawn from the Louisiana "vibes"). The gameplay is fairly simple, so for the old-school gamers it will be a walk in the park. But beware of some nasty bugs. I got stuck in Act 3 and was able to continue only with a fortunate help of the tech support. Suggestion to the developers: next time don't opt for cheap QA in India and add more polishing to the game before release.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A game that knows what it wants to be, tells its story, and leaves with you with both more questions than answers as well as satisfactorily answering the one's it cares about. Needless to say, I left NORCO wanting to dig even deeper into its fully fledged world but also understood that sometimes the act of trying to answer a question is more worthwhile than actually getting any resolution. Check this one out if you're into cold opens, depressing corporate futures with diesel-punk aesthetics, and characters that feel real-er than they should.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, screw this, I have better things to do with my life than click through this pretentiousness.Today is the second time I have attempted to play through Norco after a bug deleted my previous cloud save, and it's the second time I have bounced off. It's a shame because the setting sounds unique and interesting - a 20 minutes into the future crustpunk Southern gothic jam fest... And it is that, kinda, except the dialog is boring, the characters are flat and the locations are disappointingly dull. Everything is described in these long-winded, meandering snippets of pseudo-poetry that make you feel like you're reading a collage of English Lit essays instead of playing a point and click adventure game.I wasted 20 hours of my life plodding through similarly tedious prose in Disco Elysium, and that game never had any payoff, the characters were as vile at the end as they were at the beginning, and all I got out of it was pretentiousness points that aren't worth anything if you don't hang out in the kinds of circles where people listen to cassette tapes and stroke their chins and talk about antiestablishmentarianism or something. If that sounds like you and your friends group, you might appreciate Norco. If you're a fan of point and click adventures, there are way better ones out there. If you're an indie gamer who liked Kentucky Route Zero, eh, this is not that. I know this sort of stuff appeals to a certain demographic, but it is not me. Buyer beware.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: there is no way i can coherently express how much i adore this game - maybe my cosplay of the protagonist and all of my fanart will do it justice? not sure. just can't put into words how much this game resonated with me. beautiful pixel art. wonderful prose and worldbuilding. surreal, at some points humorous and at other points heart-wrenching. i keep finding myself thinking about it long after i've finished playing it, it's a story clearly written with a lot of love and care.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: True Detective like mystical P&C adventure? Oh my how excited I was to see it and first two acts lived up to my expectations so much! Even with some dull "What-what was I supposed to do to progress?" stuff Narco still hold me tight in it's grip with solid dialogue, intriguing world building and some plot-twists.And... Act 3 just feels like hasted ending. All the plot hooks somehow got solved off screen, the pacing becomes so fast you don't realize the game has already ended. Personally, I think they cut of 2-3 more acts in between. I just wish this hasn't ruined it for me as a whole experience.But this South USA industial theme is strong and worth checking out even just once.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A gem of a game that draws you into its world and holds your attention right until the end credits. What I really appreciate is that some of your decisions actually have consequences beyond just solving a puzzle, and you are rewarded for paying attention to the characters and locations you encounter.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just finished. What an incredible game. Easily just went on my game of the year list already.Exactly the kind of things I love about these kinds of games. Great writing, awesome art, music with great atmosphere, a really strong sense of place and the best kind of weird weird WEIRD. Thanks all for making it, absolutely loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I just don't get it. The writing and narration is more like a series of thoughts where one in no particular way joins with the next to form an understandable, intelligible, and cogent story line or plot except in the most generous interpretations and loosest way. Perhaps this is on purpose to make the game seem trippy and strange but to me it just makes me think, "what the am I watching? Who the hell is Blake? Why are you asking me how I feel about someone I don't know? Why am I clicking on a teddy bear." It just comes off as lazy to me. But hey...maybe I just don't get it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game hits different. The high quality writing, surreal but familiar setting, and gorgeous pixel art make for an engrossing point and click experience that you're best off going into completely blind. If you've heard this compared to Disco Elysium, yes the two narratives do share some themes in common, but they are very different experiences overall.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is a different game. It takes Point & Click games to another level. The script is well written, the characters are well design and the total atmosphere of the game is attractive and make you willing to know more and more. I am a Saudi so that drives me to read more about the New Orleans and it's history with flooding and it reminds me of the tragedy of the Katrina hurricane 2005. The Da Vinci Code is the main layer of the story but the game gives you more regarding the new trend that everyone is looking for the stars to immigrate from planet Earth.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Mad. Just mad.Incredible art style, and really well written - reads like a mixture of True Detective's Rust Cohle's internal thoughts, Disco Elysium, and Stanislaw Lem.Devs crafted this lovingly. Someone asked about the lore on the community forums, so they essentially programmed a little web app where you can get additional info and perhaps some answers to your questions after the game.That being said, the world and happenings throughout this game are very much open to interpretation, and by design. Not everything will be explained by the end of the line.Not unlike a great chef, NORCO's story supplies just a tiny bit too little of the good stuff. If you don't like that about a game... well, this might not be to your taste.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An exceptional game, a must play for fans of story-rich adventures. The dystopian suburban setting is eerily reminiscent the deindustrialized exurbs of today. Themes ranging from automation to abandonment to ecological collapse are dealt with thoughtfully and are woven expertly into an enthralling narrative that is paced well and avoids genre tropes and pitfalls. The characters are fully developed and the relationships among them are realistic and complex. It's easy to get invested in the characters and you'll find yourself raging with them against the despair of powerlessness in the face of monolithic corporate power. Amidst all the anger an elusive motif of justice haunts the story and drives the player forward. An excellent soundtrack combined with striking artwork and compelling writing create a weighty atmosphere that at times can feel almost suffocating. Norco is an excellent game whose narrative maturity is a breath of fresh air; it proves that games can not only be art but vehicles for truly excellent storytelling.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: +While I wouldn't say I'm a known fan of the Southern Gothic genre, and the fringes of world building are muddled (i.e what year is it exactly? What wars are going on?) I do feel that the world building is  cohesive enough to keep me engaged. I did get a few chills as I remembered the summer bible camps I was forced to attend in my teens, of how the surrounding wetlands really felt like alien landscapes that could swallow any and everything.+Mechanically it does a few neat things that won't surprise people who play modern point and clicks, but they're executed well and never overstay their welcome.+The soundtrack is pretty good; it's reminiscent of FTL's atmospheric, almost detached sci-fi with a dash of doom metal. It really captures of the creeping dread of traveling the bayou as you watch sun set into night.=I agree with negative reviews saying the back-end of the game takes a drastic turn in terms of story - though I feel it's less of a writing issue and more that you can really feel where the devs ran out of time and/or money. I don't necessarily think the game would've been better as 10 hour game vs 7~, but I do feel more side content would've fleshed out key characters or better stitched together certain story beats.-I did run into some minor bugs - lingering character portraits, a couple audio glitches and the game soft-locked once, but nothing a reload of a save or just carrying on couldn't fix.The game definitely has it's faults and there are story elements that may feel dated sooner than you'd think, bu it's post-modern genre blending makes it a stand out experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This really resonated with me.I read a lot and play a lot of story driven games, it is something that I take into great account. I can forgive a lot of things if it doesn't get in the way of the story. Norco balances so many things and manages to make them interweave seamlessly.The amount of lore, worldbuilding, characters, and concepts the developers can cram into this 8-10 hour runtime is astonishing. The pixel art and the sound design pair very well together, the characters all have their own texture and feel very unique. It waltzes that character v characterization line all the time and still manages to make everyone feel like they have depth. You feel sympathetic for monsters and empathy for characters you barely get to engage with. Finally, these different strings and notes all create this haunting story of New Orleans as it is sloughing off it's primitive path and being born again in the brackish waters of the future.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Weird. So weird. The best kind of weird. And it gets more weird as it goes on, too. Basically the game feels like True Detective  Season 1 if Rust had schizophrenia. A bonkers mix of cyberpunk, depressed futurism, rusting oil rigs and swamp fever dream. There are a few images toward the end that I'll never get out of my head. Wish we had more games like it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A quirky point-and-click adventure game set in dystopian Louisiana. It's like a combination of the LucasArts games Full Throttle and Beneath a Steel Sky, but with a Faulknerian twist. The game is more cinematic than challenging; there's no hunting for the right pixel to click on, no using ten different items on a thing to see what works, nothing like that. In fact I found the game to be a little *too* easy -- the areas you can explore are small, you never have more than 2 items in your inventory, and your companions and so-called "mind map" are always on standby to tell you *exactly* what you need to do next in order to advance. However the game does contain several mini-game sections that were a refreshing challenge compared to the easy point-and-click main game. The story is completely on-rails; I can only recall three instances where there's more than one way to complete an objective, and even then the "choice" is not about making a moral decision or anything like that, it's just two different ways to accomplish a task and whichever one you happened to try first is the one you go with. If you want your adventure game to present you with moral dilemmas and meaningful choices with far-reaching consequences, Norco might not be the game for you, because it contains nothing like that.The pixel art is gorgeous, and the prose is incredible. And often hilarious -- there were quite a few parts that had me laughing out loud. The story itself is kind of silly, but not every game needs to be a self-serious commentary on societal problems with heroes and villains and epic choices that decide the future of the world. Sometimes a game can just be about poor people in a polluted swamp trying to earn some money so they can pay for their next meal. And the result is still beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic pixel-art dystopian adventure game set in a narrative world that is kind of a cross between True Detective and Blade Runner.  I haven't had a game hit me so hard on so many levels in quite a while.  They art, humor, writing and music are all incredible and come from a very unique voice.  Can not recommend enough.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Artistic aesthetics with gorgeous pixel graphics and nice chromatic palette. Sometimes it looks like a vintage graphic novel.- Well designed, immersive dystopian world with lots of details and post apocalyptic elements. It has solid, surreal, kind of depressing atmosphere. So unique.- Good writing. Descriptions are great, the stories that you read feel alive and the dialogues are always interesting. It has some strong poetic moments too.- Awesome characters with unique appearance and vivid personalities. Some of them are completely crazy and it's hard to forget them afterwards.- It has some interesting, refreshing mechanics for the point and click genre. Having companions and talking to them is great. The mind map with all these thoughts, nodes and lines connecting them is interesting too.- Nice lore. The town has history, characters with rich backgrounds and there is a small small network of human relationships going on.- Cool storytelling with flashbacks, and secrets that gets revealed to you gradually making it even more interesting. The actual story is a little bit over the top for my taste though.- Great music that enhances the dystopian atmosphere.- Inside all this darkness and mystery it has some moments with pretty inspiring sense of humor.- Good design that guides effectively your glaze to the interactive objects inside each screen eliminating pixel hunting. There is a reveal button that helps too.The bad- Despite having some refreshing mechanics its puzzles are pretty straight forward, unchallenging and lack imagination. Also, it tends to guide the player too much making the game easy and linear. You're doing many things mechanically without much though.- The story has great beginning building a mystery that promises rational explanations. Yet, after its middle point it gets over the top with things that look random and excessive like it desperately wants to impress the player. The endings are abrupt and leave many questions unanswered.- The RPG style, turn based battles are shallow and don't fit the point and click style of the game. Even more there is no need for a big final boss battle.- There are only few interactions with objects per screen. Some more comments on scattered things would make it feel more alive and immersive.- Voice over would have made it much more atmospheric, replacing these annoying mumbling sounds.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Early GOTY-contender on the strength of the writing alone.Reading into the history of Norco is like being presented with a disturbingly clarified mindmap of American wounds that remain gaping to this day; slavery, murder, corporate indifference, economic collapse, widening inequality, and reactionary politics. Set in the same district, NORCO is a confronting video game; a confident, biographical and bewildering point-and-click narrative experience that feels more like something you inhale rather than play, with an effective cocktail of magical realism, societal heartbreak, and bummer coolness.From the opening act of the game, it feels appropriate to draw direct comparisons to other luminaries of the ‘video games for wonks’ genre, such as Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero, as you wade deeper and deeper into NORCO’s magical realist miasma of inter-familial trauma, vicious class critique, and gorgeous, kaleidoscopic renderings of a constant Louisiana pre-dawn half-light.The game knows when and how to puncture its darkest moments and depictions with some of the most incisive and word-perfect jokes, relieving it from simply being a slog of desperation. In one moment, a character in a bar can be plied for more information about the whereabouts of your brother, provided you do something to quench his thirst. By the time the conversation is over, your contact is three pints deep, hoeing into some ridiculous ‘loaded fries’ on your dime.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed it thoroughly. I understand why people would complain about the ending because it is pretty jarring, but to me it felt like it was in line with the themes of the rest of the story. If you're a fan of Sci-Fi, philosophy, the bayous, and detective point-n-clicks then I would definitely recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: "...There is something antagonistic about returning home to the American suburbs: the vast swaths of copy-pasted homes; of meticulously manicured lawns; of fences and stone demarcating delineated spaces; of dogs barking in furious animosity when strayed too near. Everyone here is a little king or queen of their empty fiefdom, solitary in their halls and wondering why: when they’ve walled everyone off, an empty loneliness is all that seeps in with the draft.There is a certain melancholy of coming back to a place you thought you left behind. In connections frayed and left behind in disrepair. In things left unfinished and unsaid and undone. In time spent in repeat, comforting in its familiarity, a reminder or refrain of things lost and then rediscovered.It was something I wasn’t prepared to face..."A diary entry on Norco, The Southern Reach Trilogy, Citizen Sleeper and the travels between. On searching for home, and ultimately, a place to rest:
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I am of two minds here (not a spoiler or maybe):the game does an amazing job with having its own style - the music alone is like, very very plus good - and doing the great sci-fi-ish thing of having a world you gets revealed as the story goes on without hitting you over the head with it too much (I'm looking at you, theatrical release of Blade Runner with inner monologue). considering how small the team is, the overall design of the game and atmosphere and etc feels very fleshed out, especially for what it is - a retro throwback to umm POV-based point and clicks (think "Deja Vu" which I played on the NES back in like 1885 or whenever), but with a lot more self awareness in the storytelling - even in minor details such as representing the main character with a shaky neon smiley face.but at the same time, its not for everyone. Point and click games are usually billed as mysteries, and atmospherically (and in the story, I guess) this is a mystery, but the gameplay itself is much more along the lines of an interactive novel or "walking simulator." There aren't a lot of choices, and the puzzles are either bascially handed to you or simply consist of "I need a rock, I will have to go back to the location where I saw a rock" None of that bothered me so much, and most newer retro point and clicks tend to lean this way to avoid the dangerous excesses of the 90s (I'm looking at your Day of the Tentacle, though I will always love you) where puzzles could not be solved by anyone in touch with reality and any rational person today would give up and look it up online. This is all fine.What was a bit more ambivalent for me:a lot of different mechanisms show up in the game both for gameplay and for story purposes. The Mindmap gets a lot of praise, for example, but the other stuff ranges from the obvious (picking up stuff to go into your inventory) to a bit more complex (having a smartphone with some different apps, or combat). These things all make sense as implemented and work well within the story and gameplay, but they are all used VERY sparingly. You pick up items and carry them around, but they definitely go out of their way to avoid the 90s logic here (e.g. I pick up a random piece of dried bread in a bakery in Act One because the game lets me, and in Act Four I use it to pick a lock somehow.) Everything you need to do is given to when you need it, and not much creatively is required. The more complex mechanics, such as involving the phone, seem like they could be used a lot more but instead kind of just fade out: they worked for the story and experience, but in the end a lot of it felt to me like I had gone through a narrative tutorial where I was learning how to play the game, only to have these things never come up again and spend most of the following act simply moving through rooms and reading text. The game felt very short because of this (also it took me less than 5 hours total) but at the same time more.. maybe not immersive so much as .. deliberate. There aren't a lot of answers here, but the path leading up to them (which stops short) is very careful to make you consider where you are going (even if you dont get there)So I liked the game as an experience, its clear the devs were interested more in telling an impressionistic story or painting a portrait or some kind of abstract thing like that rather than making a "game" in the old fashioned "kill the turtle men!" way, so, again, not for everyone, but I would be very excited to see what they did next.8/10 you get to pet the cat (but you shouldn't)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare that I find a game that just *works* as well as NORCO. A perfect mixture of great writing, beautiful pixel art, melancholic tone, and interesting characters. NORCO understands the stultifying anxiety of living in an increasingly impoverished, crumbling country in the grip of ruthless capitalism and fascist paranoia. It also has a minigame that lets you pet a cat so well that it launches itself into orbit. It rarely gets better than this, folks.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A veritable masterpiece. There are few games that can capture distilled American Misery. NORCO is one of them. If you want a window into the american Louisiana experience. How the government let its people die, both past and future tragedies. Haunting, beautiful, we are all a refinery on fire. The soundtrack is amazing Gewgawly I and Thou create a really incredible experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, nice narrative, amazing music and spot on pixel art. The story is not for everyone, it reminded me of old SIERRA adventure games. It started with a young girl reluctanly coming home after her mother's death. Then you have to search for you brother that's nowhere to be found. And from there... anything is posible. Great weird ride. If you're on the fence with this one, give it a try. It won't dissapoint.

_childDocuments_.review: Few games offer up a sense of place like NORCO does, and fewer still are able to make that sense of place so familiar. These people all live in my town, until they don’t. In NORCO the line between reality and absurdity is blurred so often that you begin to question if the line has ever really been there. Of course it hasn’t. NORCO doesn’t offer us a glimpse at a horrible future, like all great science fiction it just rephrases and recontextualizes what is already here. And NORCO is nothing if not great sci-fi.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretentious but lovable little gem. Pixel art, appropriately minimalist ambient music, very well-written dialogues, and a hauntingly melancholic bayou-meets-Blade Runner atmosphere. The ending was downright cretinously incredulous, but, overall, it's very enjoyable for enthusiasts like me who love story-rich, must-read-thousands-of-lines gameplay. Also, the UI is really excellent and makes playing with a controller and reading a breeze.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A story-driven point-and-click game where the search for a missing brother spirals into a bigger mystery. Heavily focused on narration where you follow different characters across swamps, churches and rural parts of Norco. Most of the achievements requires you to find different items and complete certain objectives. Guide is available for how to complete them and the achievements are straight-forward and not particularly difficult.The game tells a good story in a interesting setting. The lack of voice-acting means you do a lot of reading but the artstyle and dialogue create a great experience in this point-and click adventure. Even for someone like myself who isn't particularly interested in these games got hooked and finished the game, which I can strongly recommend for others.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco brings a thrilling experience with a mystery that'll give you lots of goosebumps, complemented by beautiful soundtrack and dark art style that gives off a weird but comfortable feeling of nostalgia and dread. The characters are well written and story keeps you hooked as you solve the mysteries behind a poor, decaying city.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't say I play to many point and click adventure and visual novel but every now and then one of these game does catch my interest and it happen to be Norco. Narrative:Norco is a visually beautiful pixel art southern gothic sci-fi point and click game that I am seriously considering to be Game of The Year for me personally. From the well written narrative that has many humorous moment as well and much darker depressing story that left me feeling sad,depress and honestly just gave this haunted feeling of dread at time; had me captivated from beginning to end. There also many WTF moment that just caught me completely off guard. There is no voice acting in this game which could be seen as a negative but the game is so well written and the use of many natural phrase and dialogue make this game very easy to digest and understand. There is complexity to the writing but it not going to stop you from understanding the core story depicted.Music:The music is good, from electronic to jazz, it not overpowering and give off a very atmospheric and moody feel which set the tone for the game. Visual:Visually stunning pixel art style that has many fluid animated moment such as scene of driving the motorcycle down the highway to watching the bird fly off into the distances. It good, nothing more to say about this. lot of the game location are detailed very well.Gameplay:Point and Click Adventure game for the most part which include travelling to different location, interacting with people and object, multiple dialogue choice that has minor affect on the story.  There also a few QTE moment for some event as well as these short puzzle game which I found to be some of the weaker part of the game for me.Final Thought:Overall it a really good game with a few minor negative that I believe are just not worth mentioning. It a rather short experience with three act that should take about 7-8 hours to complete so hopefully if anyone does pick it up, it doesn't end up in the backlog for to long.. I totally recommend if your fan of game like Disco Elysium, Kentucky Route Zero and even if this is your first time playing a point and click adventuring , it still a game I definitely recommend for first timer of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★"Norco" is a mesmerizing journey into a dystopian world unlike any other, blending captivating storytelling with innovative gameplay features to create an experience that is both immersive and thought-provoking. From the moment you step foot into its hauntingly beautiful landscape, you're drawn into a narrative that is as dark as it is compelling.Set in a near-future version of the Gulf Coast, "Norco" presents a world ravaged by environmental collapse and corporate greed. The landscape is a haunting mix of neon-lit cities and decaying industrial ruins, each corner hiding secrets waiting to be uncovered. The attention to detail in crafting this dystopian setting is breathtaking, with every pixel dripping with atmosphere and history.What sets "Norco" apart is its innovative gameplay features. Rather than relying on traditional mechanics, the game encourages exploration and experimentation, allowing players to uncover the story at their own pace. From hacking into corporate databases to scavenging for resources in the wastelands, every action feels meaningful and impactful.The narrative itself is a masterpiece of storytelling, weaving together themes of identity, power, and resistance in a way that is both poignant and thought-provoking. As you delve deeper into the world of "Norco," you'll encounter a cast of characters who are as complex and flawed as the world they inhabit, each with their own motivations and agendas.Visually, "Norco" is a work of art. The pixel art style is both retro and modern, with its vibrant colors and intricate details bringing the world to life in stunning detail. The soundtrack further enhances the atmosphere, with its haunting melodies and pulsating rhythms perfectly complementing the game's dystopian setting.In conclusion, "Norco" is a triumph of storytelling and game design, offering players a truly immersive and unforgettable experience. Its dystopian setting, innovative gameplay features, and captivating narrative combine to create a game that is both engaging and thought-provoking. If you're a fan of dystopian fiction or innovative indie games, "Norco" is not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretty solid visual novel in the style of old console VNs like SNATCHER or The Silver Case, where there are semi-point and click segments in addition to the walls of text. I've gotten I think a little more than halfway through the game and haven't gotten to any points where I felt outright bored, though there were a few parts that I felt kinda dragged a little. I think my one complaint about this game is that the UI isn't always the best. There's a part halfway through the game or so where you get a voice recorder that you use by clicking a tiny red button underneath text in a dialog window. The problem is that left-clicking is also the "advance the text and/or close the dialog window" button, and a couple of times I wound up accidentally clicking out of dialog that I wanted to read because I saw something that I wanted to record. Actually, there is a second thing. The game is ostensibly a cyberpunk story along the lines of SNATCHER or Policenauts, but it doesn't feel like one for the vast majority of the plot. The setting for the most part is present-day Louisiana, and apart from a couple of things (namely humanoid robots and AIs) it doesn't really feel cyberpunk in the way that the old Kojima VNs did. It also doesn't necessarily get its setting across or do worldbuilding as well as a game like Disco Elysium - NORCO takes place in what is effectively a low grade post-apocalypse, but unless you're reading a bunch of optional material you'd have no idea this is the case. I almost feel like it would have benefitted by taking some inspiration from Policenauts - namely the Saturn version - and having a glossary or something you can access to sort of explain things along better than it does.Even with the writing issues, NORCO is still a solid VN and I'd absolutely recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Interesting story. Stays interesting until the end.-Solid characters.-Fun dialogues and scenes.-While I wouldn't call it's soundtrack a masterpiece, it works really well with the game's setting and themes.-Despite mainly being a point & click game, it introduces a couple of gameplay systems here and there that serve as a breath of fresh air.Cons:-The game can feel a little bit too artistic/abstract for me at times. This is 100% a personal thing, I just tend to prefer a less "abstract" narrative. It's not a problem anyway, in other games like Kentucky Route Zero, it's abstract narrative completely disconnected me from it's story. In Norco, it just got mea little bit  lost in a couple of dialogues, and I just had to re-read some stuff.-It frequently uses modern slang. Words like "memes", "influencer", "brah", "bruh" and the like pop up in most dialogues. I guess this is a personal thing too, I'm just not used to read this kind of language in games (and I don't really find it appealing), so it kind of made me roll my eyes a little bit whenever a character said one of those words.Veredict:-Really fun and interesting experience. A little bit too artsy at times, it's still an amazing game that I would recommend anyone used to playing narrative games.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game. It created an interesting, surreal world filled with characters and themes that I will think about for a long time. Gameplay-wise, it's rather simple. There are some puzzles, but they aren't hard to figure out. Some mini-games switch things up every once in a while, but I could imagine some people being finding them annoying. So while there are puzzles, the emphasis is definitely on narrative. So if you don't enjoy reading, this might not be for you.What really shines is the narrative, the story, the style. The atmosphere this game creates is excellent and really sucks you in.It's a beautiful indie game. A real gem. I was sad when it was over after just a few hours, but happy I got to experience it. I'd love to see more from this world.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice indie game with original storyline, cool artwork and some nice music here and there. I believe it is worth its money much more than may other games do, but read on if you want an honest opinion. Now if we're being realistic, is it as good as the reviews suggest? Probably not. For some reason people are going bonkers in the reviews over exaggerating things, and not only in this game but most games. Dunno it may be an age thing, I may be getting too old for games or maybe new gamers have low standards, dunno.People compare this to Monkey Island (!) and other classic point and click adventures, and this is truly beyond me. This game has much, much room to cover before it can be compared with classic point and click adventures like Monkey Island, Broken Sword, Full Throttle, Grim Fandango, Day of the Tentacle, Runaway, and many other classics I'm forgetting right now, First and foremost it lacks the fun part of those games, being that this game indeed fun at parts, but I wouldn't say the whole experience was fun. The 'riddles' are also too few and too easy which is another disadvantage for me. That being said, it is definitely not a bad game and makes for some very interesting few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I would heartily recommend this game. Point-and-click adventure games are not really my thing, but this one kept me wanting to see it through. That in itself means that it was really good.The writing in this game is truly excellent. The atmosphere built up through the art design, the sound design, and the general rhythm of the game are also really good. It was really quite engrossing at times, and as such I had no trouble finishing this game across the space of 4-5 days. The story was interesting, and the characters seem deeply human. The game hasn't convinced me that I should now dive into a ton of other point-and-click adventure games, but I think that if you are like me and don't ever engage with these games, NORCO is a good candidate to pick as a way to dip your toe into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely one of the most impactful and incredible games I have ever played. I find myself thinking about it pretty often even though I only played through it once. The story is insanely rich and well thought out, I've really never seen anything else like it. I was so absorbed in the plot and invested in the characters and what would happen to them. _childDocuments_.review: What a great game. It reminded me a lot of Thimbleweed park, but the first person perspectives allowed it to create brilliant painterly compositions. I don't think it's all that interested in the often frustrating gameplay of point and click adventures, allowing the story to unfold at a refreshing pace. I was really pleasantly surprised with how funny it is. From the trailer and visuals it seemed to be quite heavy, and while there is a lot to unpack from certain events it's always fun because of the quirky interactions. I don't think I've ever had an opportunity to play a game as a wisecracking, middle-aged cancer patient, but it's nice to see Catherine's story told with so much wit when the world is flooded with so many either depressing or schmaltzy depictions of the same material. A really beautiful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially a bit worried that this would be one of those games that leaned too heavily on the visual novel side of things - with gorgeous graphics but minimal gameplay and overtly complicated writing - a subgenre I'm not that fond of.However, those fears were unfounded. NORCO is actually in many ways more of a traditional first person point and click adventure with puzzles and some minor rpg/action elements, a mix that might sound odd, but works really well with the games story. And the story is definitely unique: equal parts southern gothic and cyberpunk, this tale of broken families and religious fanaticism in a polluted capitalist dystopia is convoluted, but totally engrossing. A big reason the story works is the meticulous production values: The graphics are some of the best pixel art I've seen, the music(by doom metal band Thou) is both ominious and dreamlike, and makes the exploration of desolate malls, underpasses and ghost bayous feel like a perfectly realised world. NORCO is by no means a game for everybody, but it is totally one of a kind, and a must-play for adventure gamers who likes their retro cyberpunk/sci-fi point and clicks with a healthy dose of refreshing twists.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you like point and click adventures and you have a high tolerance for despair, it's definitely worth playing.  Just know going in that it's a huge downer, it does have enough wit to keep it palatable though.It doesn't make the best first impression, I was worried it would be nothing more than purple prose when I first started it, but after experiencing it all, the writing definitely won me over, both the more poetic text and the grounded dialogue were both great.

_childDocuments_.review: Poetry, in words, in images, in world conjured and story told. It's a beautifully written game, evocative in its surreal and meditative aesthetic. It went in directions I did not expect, delving into the esoteric. Thematically, it's in the lineage of Disco Elysium and Night in The Woods as concerned with the intersection of past with present, and futures once imagined, lost and stolen. This is a work of American hauntology.The artwork is beautifully rendered via detailed pixel art. I have never been to Lousiana and New Orleans and I found myself throughly immersed within Norco's depiction of this region. Given the developer's having been raised in the town of Norco, there's a clear personal connection and intimacy that comes across, a sense of place, of belonging and displacement. These are not mutually exclusive. There's a tension throughout. There's a social function in this. Much of the town and region's history is interspersed throughout the game, and the company, Shell, plays a key role, loosely disguised as "Shield." History here is not static. The past exists in the present, running through it like a livewire, shaping and reshaping it. The writing's good enough to pull this off, with poise, poignance and profundity.The writing's also pretty funny at times. While some things don't land as well as others, but one moment in particular had me laughing my ass off. I'm also impressed by the quality of the characters. Some great exchanges between them.If I have any critiques, it's that the combat is basically just a placeholder, but it functioned well enough to lend excitement to the moments where it was deployed.

_childDocuments_.review: If this game piqued your interest, but you're on the fence, I would say dive in.  The game plays like a good book reads.  The characters are real, interesting, and distinct.  The plot is wild in the best way.  The world is so interesting to explore.  I haven't been pulled into a game like this in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a stunning work of art. I'm sitting in my home in South Louisiana, seeing the drainage ditches outside and then it reflected back on the pixel art on my screen. NORCO feels like a conversation with a familiar face. This game touches on topics like disaster capitalism, community exploitation and extraction to approaching religious zealotry with a sense of earnestness. The gameplay is simple and effective, storyline enrapturing and bizarre. I enjoyed the subplots getting different phone cases to the achievements you can get. I encourage anyone to get this game and I'm excited to play through it again.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game walks a tightrope of whimsy, melancholy, humour and complete wank and pulls it off for the most part. Some nice gameplay sequences break up the point and click monotony and the pixel art is incredibly well done. The writing is good for the most part although admittedly it does disappear up its own arse a few times over the journey. At around 6 hours Norco doesn't outstay its welcome and I found the end to be oddly moving.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a year since I played this game and I still think about it from time to time. I see refinery towers on the horizon, neighborhoods falling into neglect, and all powerful algorithms herding humanity about like cattle. Norco isn't about the apocalypse, it's about the present. But what makes it special is that it's also about a really gross hotdog.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is 2022's Night In the Woods/Kentucky Route Zero/Umurangi Generation, and one of the first of a new generation that replace clunky text boxes/speech bubbles with a Disco Elysium-style text scroll. Set in the poisonous shadow of the Shield (Shell by way of Shinra) oil refinery, a young woman returns home to find her brother following her mother's death. Though not as snappy as Disco Elysium, it can be quite funny, such as infiltrating the all-too-believable tiktok influencer cult that's taken over the local mall or a lot of the incidental writing from people trying to live normal lives in an increasingly bizarre world. But ultimately I'd describe it overall as a bit drier and more art-y in the vein of KR0.

_childDocuments_.review: Blade Runner meets Sherlock Holmes meets your childhood(this game makes you remember growing up and your home). NORCO is an extremely near future corporate dystopian mystery point and click game. The graphics are unbelievably beautiful; NORCO is true art. The writing in this game is on par with Stephen King, and that's no hyperbole. As a 38 year old gamer burnout whose tired of all the same ♥♥♥♥, the depth, nostalgia, horror and wonder are extremely novel. This game doesn't hit my dopamine like call of duty, but I don't play call of duty, I play this instead. Why? _childDocuments_.review: I found myself being somewhat overwhelmed by the narrative, largely because there is so much going on in terms of world-building, not to say that it didn't have many good moments, but for me, some of the side objectives were more enjoyable than the actual plot. The game is very artistic in the way it approaches the narrative structure, you could potentially see it as heavy-handed in some aspects, but my criticism of it is largely subjective, and I can see that a lot of work went into making it. I often found myself confused by the details - constantly trying to find some solid ground from which I could attempt to analyze it. I think the writing in this game is generally really good, the problem for me was that sometimes I didn't care for the characters, or maybe the game didn't give me enough of a reason to care. Now I wouldn't say that story does not take itself seriously (well okay maybe aside from those 3 side achievements), but at the same time, there are moments where it undermines its own efforts to be something suspenseful. What I find very interesting is that for a game that should in theory have a lot of tension, it completely ignores it and just chills all the way to the end - I mean, maybe you could interpret it as an artistic choice, that is how I choose to see it, but it has an unusually relaxing atmosphere all things considered.The length of the game really depends on how much you are willing to read, I would say it's closer to 7 hours, but if you skip a lot you will only get 4 to 5. There are all kinds of creative gameplay elements, even a very underdeveloped combat system, but it's still a narrative game, keep in mind that it has a lot of text walls. So the combat system does not have much of a presence, there are only a few fights in the game so it's not even remotely relevant, and while the characters do have some unique attacks (not sure why because they are completely unbalanced), you will generally complete the fights on a first try anyway. The world has decent support for optional achievements, and as I mentioned earlier some of the best dialogue is in those side quests, I had some genuine laughs listening to the limo story and the conversation between Paw and Santa. There are some detective-like elements where you have to connect the thoughts to progress, although the game mostly holds your hand and helps you with the color-coding. It had some moon logic with the puzzles, sometimes I found myself backtracking and clicking everything, but overall, the puzzles were creative and I will take that over something generic - you can also click on the characters and they may point you in the right direction. I thought the exits were a bit confusing, I initially thought all connected areas would have exits on the screen, but sometimes the map itself has the exit which is a bit odd.(+) So the game has a lot going on with world-building and various narrative surprises. I would acknowledge that it has good writing, but personally, I was a bit overwhelmed. There were still moments that I enjoyed, and I will disagree that the ending was not interesting. Among the alternating chapters, I enjoyed Catherine's playthrough a lot more because she was a character, and not just an avatar.(+) The world has various optional objectives, some really funny interactions as well, I would highly recommend doing as much as you can. Good achievement support.  (+) Overall pretty enjoyable artwork and music, lots of locations to visit, good amount of content, and some creative puzzles. (?) I don't really have any objective criticism for the game, it was just a bit too much for me with all of the artistic ideas, on a personal level I don't fully appreciate having random things smashed together without a clear purpose. For example, you gave characters different attacks, one is like 3 times better than the other, and you only have what, some 6ish fights? The second swimming minigame was a bit odd, compared to the rest of the game you didn't put as much effort into its visuals. One thing I think could have been better, I would often return to characters to see if they had something new to say, but you kept many old locations without giving them much to do. So for example I would record ***** ***** ***** from Santa, and I am thinking to myself, surely everyone will comment on these, surely the devs were thinking this far ahead. Just small world-building reactions, not having as many of them made the world feel, smaller.Honestly, very subjective review, it's a very artistic game and it really depends if you appreciate what it does. My interest in the story kept going up and down, I thought the tone in the game was flatlining a lot, even during the moments of suspense and danger. It seems like an intentional choice to make this game very chill, so in that sense, maybe I am just biased, I just think it should have made me worry for the characters more than it did.

_childDocuments_.review: A good mysterious and introspective point'n'click, quite poetic, enthralls you almost immediately. Amateurs of the bizarre and the occult, don't hesitate, this little game is a gem, the music, the graphics, the characters, the writing. It's hilarious and caustic, it's original, it shows the ugly side of many things without trying to shove any opinions down your throat. One playthrough is roughly 6/7 hours, there is some re-playability and many funny achievements. Loved the "phone cases" you get to collect around, my favorite was the Gator one. Loved the fact that it takes place in Louisiana, loved the whole ambiance of the game, so refreshing and modern gothic horror.The only thing I wish I saw more was, as the game progresses, we don't get more stuff to click around, it's mostly "the path forward" or the things you should interact with later, which happens a lot in indie games as the whole development takes so much time and effort, they concentrate on getting the game out. But it also leaves a trail of mystery, you get to think for yourself, it's unexplained, it gives you an adrenaline rush.Overall, Norco is an indie treasure; I bought this game because I enjoy the art of Jesse Jacobi (@pit_of_bones on instagram) and I'm really happy about it, completely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO has a lot of good things going for it. I absolutely loved the beginning of the game, the captivating Southern Gothic vibe, beautiful artwork, captivating characters, an interesting mindmap mechanic, and the fascinating mystery of the protagonist's missing brother.Not only was the presentation stunning, but the themes were absolutely hitting too. NORCO seemed like it was about to really delve into a deep discussion of the socioeconomic consequences of industrial spoliation, automation, and class conflict in this interesting dystopic sci-fi setting around a real-world Louisiana oil town that its creator has a deep personal connection to.However, about halfway through the game, NORCO inexplicably  and almost everyone that you met and everything that you did in the 1st act becomes irrelevant. The change is sudden, and everything interesting that the story's been building up to is dropped. I powered through until the 3rd act, hoping that this was just a slump, that  but the story only dragged from there. That was roughly the point where I gave up and just used a walkthrough to see the conclusion, which was  It's a such a shame because the game could've potentially been so cool, a fusion between Southern Gothic and Sci-Fi is an objectively rad one, and hybrid genres like Weird West and Crime Fantasy have produced great works like Iron Council or Disco Elysium. However, these works are great not because of how they bend convention or shirk common tropes or have excellent world-building, but because they use their odd setting as a vehicle to discuss interesting and poignant themes. NORCO fails to connect its setting and its interesting genre subversions to what it has to say about the world.It's such a shame because you can sense the complex mix of disgust, love, familiarity, resignation, hate, and love that the creator feels for southern Louisiana. You can tell that they have a lot they want to say about it, and for a moment they almost manage to. I wouldn't have written such a long review if the game didn't make me feel *something*. But ultimately the games doesn't manage to cohesively weave everything together and very little of the themes are followed through on. In the end, you're left with the distinct impression that there are two games: an absolutely exceptional first half that hints at real greatness, and an absolutely bewildering second half that squanders that potential. And because of that, I can't really recommend NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: : This game was played to completion on Microsoft PC Game Pass. isn't just a game; it's an experience that defies convention and should leave a profound impact on players willing to immerse themselves in its dark and surreal world. This narrative-driven adventure, developed by Geography of Robots, stands as a testament to the potential of video games as a storytelling medium, pushing boundaries and blurring the lines between reality and fiction.From the moment you step foot into the sun-soaked, yet hauntingly eerie landscapes of , you're entranced by its atmosphere. The game masterfully captures the essence of the American Gulf Coast, where oil refineries and marshlands create a unique backdrop for the unfolding mystery. The visual artistry, blending pixel art with photorealistic imagery, lends the game an uncanny and dreamlike quality that keeps you engaged and curious throughout.The story of  is its ace in the oil (so to speak), weaving together a complex tapestry of personal struggles, corporate greed, and the supernatural. As you navigate the life of a young woman seeking answers about her missing mother, you're drawn into a web of conspiracies that challenge your perception of reality. The writing is masterful, rich with nuance and symbolism, as  it expertly explores themes of environmental degradation, memory, and the human psyche.The characters you encounter in  are multifaceted and deeply human, each contributing to the game's immersive and thought-provoking narrative. The voice acting is exceptional, capturing the emotions and complexities of the characters, and adding an extra layer of authenticity to their interactions.'s gameplay is both innovative and intuitive. As you explore the world, you'll engage in conversations that influence the course of the story, making meaningful choices that affect the outcome. The puzzles, while challenging, are rewarding and seamlessly integrated into the narrative. The game doesn't hold your hand, allowing you to discover solutions and connections on your own, enhancing the feeling of agency and accomplishment.The musical score of  is a mesmerising blend of ambient sounds and haunting melodies. It complements the game's atmosphere perfectly, enhancing the tension and immersion as you delve deeper into the mystery.While  is a triumph on almost all fronts, it's not without a few minor flaws. Some players might find the pacing a bit slow at times, and the surreal narrative could be disorienting for those seeking a more straightforward experience. However, these elements contribute to the game's uniqueness and are part of what makes  such a memorable journey.In conclusion,  is a true gem in the world of indie gaming, pushing the boundaries of storytelling and gameplay. Its captivating narrative, atmospheric visuals, and innovative mechanics create an unforgettable experience that lingers in your mind long after you've put down the controller. If you're a fan of thought-provoking narratives and are ready to embark on a surreal journey,  is an absolute must-play that showcases the artistic potential of video games.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a character narrative that never shows its character. It is a somber societal reflection on the vast American limbo that we find ourselves in today. On paper, we are at such a fast paced and eventful point in human history. Norco explores the role that most of us play in this eventful era, the role of sitting back and watching. Set in Norco, Louisiana, a suburb west of New Orleans, the southern industrial swamplands bleed through every inch of the game. Corporate overexpansion controls every walk of life in this small town, just like it does in every town today. Finding the moments of beauty in this horror is something necessary. Norco manages to reflect this very real, horrifying reality while still being able to feel comforting and providing life-changing, potent moments of existential meaning for us nihilists. Masterful writing, imaginative and unique worldbuilding, breathtaking art direction, and an unspeakably beautiful story.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a game like few others, it's hard to make an area feel so rich with culture like it does. And I really think you should play it.

Also in the second half  My biggest critique of the game is how your mother is written  Also the megacorp plays way less a roll than you think it does overall. _childDocuments_.review: norco was entirely not about what i imagined it would be about, but i was so glad to be surprised. the text style and language reminded me a lot of disco elysium. i enjoyed the mind map mechanic to keep track of the developments you learn. the characters and story were compelling and excellent, i also enjoyed the art style a great deal and found the switchbacks between characters really interesting! my one wish (not even a criticism) is that i wish you had explored the relationship between two characters a little more from one side rather than the other, as it didn't feel as well thought-out. you can clearly tell the care that went into making this game, and the sporadic spots of humor and secrets/alt pathways you can find if you hunt enough feel worthy of your time. i can't say that i've played many games like this and doubt i will find similar titles, but that's completely fine, it was an amazing and unique experience that i will for sure recommend to anyone looking for a great few hours spent on a carefully crafted point and click story game!

_childDocuments_.review: I’m not sure if Norco quite succeeds as an adventure game, but it fascinates me.Much has been said about Norco’s foremost influence, Kentucky Route Zero. These are, after all, both games about ghostly fugitives of the “American Limbo”, whose characters drift through the vast, empty spaces of a dreamy and mythologised American South. But while I consider KR0 to be a perfect example of the genre of magical realism, because it treads carefully between the mundane and magical worlds without falling into either — its mystery or magic, as critic Franz Roh put it, is of a kind that never intrudes upon the real world but rather “hides and palpitates behind it.”Norco, instead, swiftly departs from its beginning wonderful ambiguity into realms of pure sci-fi or psychosis in its final act. As a literalisation of religious and familial or petro trauma, I can get on board with this, it’s like the moment when the mind just breaks and floods; but it’s a intrusion that seems so abrupt and so incongruous with the meditative pacing that came before. There's also a bizarre combat gauntlet in the final stretch — not sure why, because video games, I guess?This game is also a frightening example of petrofiction, and the monopoly of the city's oil refinery, Shield, on the natural landscape and the lives of its residents, feels monstrous. Shield burns whatever will burn, and the fires spread. In protagonist Kay’s dreams these monolithic industrial structures become cathedrals, places of worship; the worship of Oil and its refined products, its shining cities. I would love to see more games explore petroculture.And for fans of the Southern Gothic, there's a lot to dig into; the Christ-haunted landscapes of Flannery O'Connor or Cormac McCarthy are realised in the cinematic style of True Detective. The pixel art is marvellously evocative of not just a state but a state of mind.Ultimately, I think I like Norco as a set of disparate evocative ideas more than as a game itself. For me it never coalesced into a thematic or emotional whole the way KR0 did. I’m not sure Norco had one thing it was trying to say, or a grand thesis statement, but perhaps it doesn’t need to. Sometimes it’s enough to be like Kay or Conway, just passing through.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game for my university's video game reading club, like a book club for games, and honestly? I'm so glad I did. _childDocuments_.review: This game is so clearly a labor of love and vivid proof of the artistic merit of the medium. This is my first time reviewing a game ever, and my first point-and-click adventure, and I could truly not recommend it more. Everything from the pixel art, to the music, to the writing is fantastic. _childDocuments_.review: i finished the game, threw my arms in the air, paced around the house muttering for about twenty minutes, dragged my partner to the PC, watched them play through the entire game in one sitting, they finished the game, threw their arms in the air, paced around the house muttering for about twenty minutes.that was four months ago and there isn't a day that goes by where i don't think about this game at least once, and it's still a regular topic of discussion between us. an absolute masterpiece of storytelling and art.update: it's been nearly a year since i wrote this review. we STILL talk about this game at least once a week. it has become a constant reference point for what interactive storytelling can achieve, if not storytelling in general.
