_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a fantastic game, I wish there was a button to recommend 1000 times.Being from West Monroe, Louisiana I can both attest and deeply relate to the depictions of refineries and entire communities centering around these industrial complexes. These things are not pretty, and to see this sentiment echoed in media, specifically pertaining to Louisiana, is reassuring and comforting. Alongside this potent and accurate representation of the land being depicted, the story is heady, riddled with religious symbolism, and honestly psychedelic at points. The narrative is dramatic and intense, bringing me to tears at several different points with its heartbreaking honesty surrounding the dynamic between the protagonist Kay and her family, and filling me with frustration in reference to industry's impact on surrounding communities. I found the mind map to be a really good tool for recounting details of the narrative, and enjoyed seeing it develop as I uncovered more about the characters and locations in NORCO.Aside from the gripping story told throughout NORCO, the art and mechanics keep the game alive and constantly reinforce the sense of discomfort and regret provided by the narrative. There were several moments where my jaw dropped at the sheer beauty of the scenes, namely the depictions of the bayous and refinery stacks littered throughout the game (oh man @ that introductory train cinematic). The puzzles were fun and thoughtful, and the use of the cellphone as a critical gameplay mechanic was fun and fit well with the narrative. I know I've picked up my phone to make money on DoorDash- it makes complete sense that Catherine would seek money on QuackJob if times were hard. I also enjoyed the boat driving sequences, and found them to be very visually striking as well. The combat feels great, and the major encounters of the game are both humor-riddled and engaging (drone priest rules, baby). Utilizing sweet monkey to do battle was a really fun way to introduce combat mechanics as well, his gaze is powerful. Another important factor of NORCO is just how funny it can be at times. The game strikes a remarkable balance between heavy subjects and lightheartedness, and keeps the player pushing through the occasional emotionally difficult material. Detective LeBlanc is genuinely hilarious- I wish I had his level of confidence.I could write a book on everything I liked from this game, and I can't encourage a purchase of NORCO enough. Personally haven't been this moved by a piece of media in a long time. If you're looking for a game with a thoughtful story, beautiful art, great thematic music and sound, and engaging mechanics, this is the one.LeBlanc for president
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where when I load it up, I just sit for a moment to take in the title screen. It's just one of those games that's immersive from the start and where everything comes together -- graphics, attention to detail, atmosphere, plot, writing, characters, soundtrack, and gameplay. The mind map that helps you keep track of the characters and plot points is incredibly useful, too, and I wish more adventure games had it.I'm no Louisiana native, but the depiction of the setting feels authentic, and I like that it weaves real-world locations and events into its narrative -- Norco is a labour of love by locals, and it shows. It's suspenseful, it's funny, it's gritty, it has so many unexpected twists and turns, and it is endlessly creepy. And the ending. Oh my god, the ending.If you want a game that has a wonderful story and also offers an introduction to the rugged life in a Louisiana refinery town, with a dystopian/futuristic twist, buy this game. If you want something to compare it to, it reminds me partly of Night in the Woods, but also the horror game Last Door, but trust me, it's its own thing. This is the most creative game I've played in years.Edit: oh, and it's one of those games where everything fits together. Things you expect to just be throwaway references to set the mood end up being tied into the plot.Also, I love how there's optional things you can do throughout the game to influence the story, if you're clever enough to think about them.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Not really a game for me. I am a huge fan of point and click adventure games, but this really didn't do much for me. The story was not that interesting, and all the way through it tried to be a lot more "artsy" than I liked I guess... The puzzles were trivial, but that would have been ok if I had fallen more in love with the story. All in all it was more of an interactive story than an actual adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Never thought that a pixel art point-and-click game would manage to capture such rich atmosphere. NORCO isn't just about atmosphere, it's a beautiful looking game rich in story and characters, it is funny, smart, a little eerie, somewhat sad but above all, entertaining. I can confidently say that throughout my ten hour playthrough there was never a dull moment. That alone deserves applause.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to describe NORCO to your friends is like it's "basically Present Day Louisiana, except you have a C3PO sidekick" and "post apocalyptic louisiana, but the apocalypse is just like 3 more years of the current trajectory of what's going on" and "cyber punk southern gothic eco terrorist core" and "really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sad but really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good." This game made me ache for the people of Louisiana, and furiously heartbroken all over again about the struggles that permeate the area. It's a story that ignites frustration and rage in me when I thought my heart had been almost completely scarred over. My mom has cancer right now, and I played this game between weekends of commuting back to my hometown to help her. The guilt, fatigue, feigned and real apathy, obligation, grief, and rage that returning to your hometown under those conditions is captured .... truthfully. Despite (or due to?) the unrelenting bleakness of the setting and story, the game was so cathartic. I felt emotional the entire playthrough and I am still thinking about it weeks later.Also I just want to say mechanically, my favorite thing about this game is the mind map. It really felt like I was remembering things about my hometown and making connections. It was really cool. ok thank you for making this game bye!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Short, sweet and beautiful storytelling. Everything about the game is a beautiful re-imagination of what "find the objects adventure" games can actually be. The actual story is strange in a familiar world, and everything in the UI of in-game world to the dream-like detailed animations and set designs made me want to soak in as much of the universe the designer set out to make.If you like a great story, play NORCO.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Other people have said much better words about this (to which their recommendations are why I played it) but let me be one more to say it's great. Excellent sprite work make the world feel surreal yet genuine. No game writing quite has its finger on the pulse of the current cultural moment quite like trawling your decaying childhood suburb struggling with several vying corporate takeovers amidst dumb image board posters complaining about sjw mods and their favorite hentai
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of very well written reviews, I'm just going to say that I'm glad this masterpiece exists. I always loved the idea of point n click games, but their tone and story we're off putting for my taste way too often.  This is what I always wanted from games of this type - a truly moving and meaningful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Well, it's definitely the weirdest game I have played in a while and even after finishing it I'm not quite sure about some aspects of the story. But for me that is a good thing, your mileage may vary. The setting is a weird amalgamation of blue collar rural Louisiana , Cyberpunk and some good old fashioned mysticism. The writing is stellar and quite honestly the best part of the game. The gameplay mechanics are typical although slightly modernized point and click mechanics. The puzzles are for the most part intuitive and well done.Overall highly recommended but you may want to wait for a sale as I completed it in about 9 hours( but I am slow as ♥♥♥♥ in these games).Edit: Forgot to mention the pixel art. I'm not the biggest fan of pixel art but the art for this game was so evocative that it bears mentioning.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a game of hauntingly beautiful contrasts, where on the backdrop of the titular town of Norco, Louisiana amidst a country in chaos, swampland meets oil refinery, contemporary suburbia meets cyberpunk future, and quiet, beautiful days meet loud, mysterious nights. All these contrasts surround the mystery of a brother gone missing, which on the surface seems simple enough, but deep down involves multi-generational secrets and conspiracies. Are you ready to dive into the bayou and learn more?
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I'd enjoy Norco as a fan of point and click adventure games, as well as narrative-heavy games. Unfortunately the further the game went along, the more it lost me and left me wanting to get to the end so I could move on with my life. The writing just seemed flimsy to me and every part of the world felt utterly forgettable. Same could be said for the puzzles and game systems, if you skip this game you won't be missing anything.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game. It's a cyberpunk bayou adventure game with intense themes of religion and climate collapse all taking place in the greater New Orleans metro. Play time is pretty short, but the writing is absolutely captivating. Puzzles were challenging for me a couple times, but it doesn't suffer from intense Moon Logic like a lot of other adventure games. Highly recommend, but maybe I'm biased since I grew up on the gulf coast.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible. Aesthetically innovative in the way that you can only do if you're telling an authentic story about a region that you know deeply well. You won't find any fetishized plantation homes, appropriated voodoo culture, or romaticized mardi gras aesthetics in Norco. Instead, you'll find religious-trauma-informed surrealism, oil-refinery-dystopian cyberpunk, and hurricane-flooded horror. The mystery is quite compelling, and the mind-map mechanic is such a perfect way to track your findings through this surreal point-and-click adventure. Play if you wish that Night in the Woods leaned harder into the horror elements, if you're aching for media to tell a real story about Louisiana, or if you're a fan of point-and-click adventure or narrative-heavy games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Scores well on style, ambiance, music and conceptual story-telling themes.Scores poorly on narrative cohesion, game-play (barely there, even for a screen/text-heavy based adventure game), bugs (items disappear), and most of all engagement: the narrative fails heavily to live up the promise of its conceptual premise. The characters are shallow, barely sketched out, and flat. The story is not so much a woven completion as it is a few scraggly threads that end frayed and disintegrating. This is clearly a passion-project of someone who wants to capture the vibe of an area they very much care about, but in the format of an adventure game that passion fails to translate.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I'll state that this game is beautiful. The pixel art is great and the subtle low-key effects are clever and add to the immersion. However, it is not something you play for 'entertainment' and all the rave reviews all have the same theme in common -- some deep message they all personally related too. If you are like me though, it really is just a slow, boring game that has a dark message that I have no interest in diving into and take no enjoyment from contemplating. This is more an 'artsy' point-and-click that is beautiful but lacks any real aspect of fun. If you are okay emotionally connecting with messages of abandonment and religion for leisure, than pick this up and enjoy the bizarre but very-written ride. If you want to sit back, have some fun on a cool adventure that features fun puzzles and an engrossing story -- avoid this. Good game but the rave reviews are just hype.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

The story started kinda basic, but quickly started picking up, weird things was happening in the city, somethings off. The game get's weird on you, religious, internet culture it has so much great stuff. But I didn't particularly like all the mini games and puzzles, they took me out of the game. _childDocuments_.review: Yo, my beautiful bastards,Get ready to dive into the sweaty armpit of America, where the spooky magic of the bayou meets the crusty, rusted-out wreckage of industrial hell. I’m talking about the hauntingly badass game, Norco.From the second you fire it up, Norco drags you into a Louisiana that’s like... weirdly real, but also trippy as hell. It nails that Southern Gothic vibe like no other—environmental decay, broke-ass economies, and folks who just won’t quit. It’s all woven together in a story thicker than swamp mud.You play as a character grinding through a world that’s basically Louisiana with its guts hanging out. All that real-world mess—pollution, corporate greed, and people just trying to survive—isn’t just some background scenery. It’s baked into the bones of the game. You feel it in every step of the journey, like the game’s calling out the BS we see in real life, and it’s doing it in a way that hits you in the gut.And let’s talk visuals—pixel art that straight-up slaps. Every soggy swamp, busted-up refinery, and rundown shack feels like it’s alive. The sound? Oh man, the sound wraps you in this sweaty Southern blanket of cicadas and far-off storms, dragging you even deeper into this twisted beauty of a world.The people you meet? All kinds of wild. Some are beat down by life, but damn if they’re not fighting. Others? Well, let’s just say there’s some spooky stuff going on under the surface. The whole cast brings a storytelling punch that you don’t see in many games. It's all depth, no filler.And because I’m a freak like that, I hit up the devs for more juice. Turns out there’s a goldmine of extra lore and backstory you can dig into if you’re feeling obsessed—like me. Trust me, once you start, you’re gonna wanna know everything.Norco ain’t just here for a good time; it’s here to make you think. It’s like a neon sign flashing “wake the hell up” while still keeping you hooked with a killer story. It’s rare, it’s raw, and it’s brilliant.To wrap it up: Norco is a masterclass in storytelling and atmosphere. It’ll take you down a swampy, metaphorical river you didn’t even know you needed to cross. If you like your games with some brains behind the beauty, this one’s calling your name.Stay magnificent, my beautiful bastards.Key Points:Your ever-classy commentator,The Magnificent Bastard

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to encapsulate NORCO as an experience in a short, spoiler-free review. However, I can fully recommend this game to anyone looking for something truly unique and inspired, with an excellent story, beautiful art, and atmosphere.A large part of what I think makes this game so captivating is how it contains bits of normalcy interspersed with sci-fi and surreal elements which is expressed in both its environments and its themes. It remains relatable on a human level while also being completely alien in other aspects. A perfect balance of the benign and the surreal. What is, on one hand, a very interesting depiction of life in an alternate New Orleans and a very personal story, also manages to be something incredibly unusual and captivating. NORCO paints a desolate and at times, very oppressive picture of the future. Moments of warmth are few and far between. However there are some great bits of comedy here and there, which all seems to land pretty well- the game can definitely be very funny.I believe the pixel art speaks for itself in just how well-crafted it is. Each environment has a distinct atmosphere that absolutely adds to the experience. It very much immerses you in it's moody southern landscapes.Most of the gameplay is what you might expect from a point-and-click adventure game. Mostly dialogue with some puzzles here and there- none of which are too difficult but are satisfying to complete and progress. It does take a unique approach with some mechanics and puzzles though, which keeps things feeling fresh and interesting.This game is a thought-provoking experience unlike any other that is undoubtedly worth the time and money. If you're considering it, just buy it and jump in. You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Quality writing, engaging story, and most of all an unmistakable amount of love and care that went into this game. The sheer amount of specific details and quirks that are displayed in every single backdrop and line of dialogue is astounding and fully immerses you in the world of this Southern Louisiana town. This game feels like both a love letter as well as a candid portrayal of a town that's past its prime. Add in the extremely personal familial aspect and this game is guaranteed to tug at your heartstrings. Definitely planning on playing it again and would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys story-rich or point & click adventures

_childDocuments_.review: I was born in Baton Rouge. My dad and his side are from New Orleans, and I remember trips on the weekends. Of course, everything changed with Katrina. Family spread, drifting apart. Playing this game was a reminder of what I loathe and love about Louisiana, or home. I relate so hard to the protagonist Kay. The meandering web of Southern religion justifying the absurd, the lost of family members to cancer, the tangle of family relationships with lies sprinkled in. To me, this game hit hard. I think I cried twice. It was a beautifully crafted game, and I felt giggles of approval of the inside jokes *wink wink* Mr Bart, Esplanade Mall, pointing out bald eagle nests on I-10 (to name a few)But not only was it beautiful, it left me feeling melancholy. I can't be sad because I already know about Cancer Alley, I already know that our world is being held up by a barely functioning swamp, and I know that oil rigs and companies couldn't give a crap about the environment and what they burn down. I loved this game. I didn't want it to end, because then I wouldn't have this version to turn to. I don't think I'll view another sunset from Crescent City Park or The Fly without thinking about y'all. I could go on and on...Obviously I have a lot of feelings about this game. So I'll just leave it with: buy this game, it's wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a truly excellent and highly intriguing point and click game with a surprisingly expansive story after what originally appears to be a simple premise. You primarily play the role of Kay who is returning home for the first time in years after her mother's recent passing and then discovering her brother has gone missing. The narrative then unfolds into a delightfully complex tale of sci-fi mystery and conspiracy. It's certainly one of the most powerful stories I have seen in this genre. The writing is superb, the pixel art looks fantastic and the overall atmosphere is really well crafted. There's also a few interactive elements with combat and moving around the map which adds a nice extra layer to the gameplay. Thankfully you aren't too bogged down in puzzles and pixel-perfect searching like in some similar titles. Sadly there are a couple of frustrating sections in the second half and some users may also find the narrative leaning too far towards crazy within its complexity as the game wears on. The story does make some pretty big shifts but I think most people will be fascinated and hooked especially if you are familiar with point and click games of this nature. Overall, NORCO is a brilliant 6-8 hour experience that will keep you engaged right to the very end. It's also an absolute steal in the sale and you can even play the whole of Act 1 in the free demo!

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is visually beautiful, conceptually dense, and tremendously well-written. More importantly, it has something very few video games do: a narrative voice unburdened by the tropes of the medium that is nonetheless extremely well served by its form. The experience is somewhere between a point-and-click adventure, hypertext fiction, and political-psycho-spiritual manifesto. It's deeply strange and sad, but hopeful enough not to leave you completely grated by the harrowing events of the story. I see the comparisons to Hunter Thompson, KR0, and other well-known examples of hallucinatory road fiction, but this is in a genre and class of its own, particularly with regards to its depictions of terminal capitalism and the complexities of family, place, and belonging. There's also an abundance of hilarious and astute nods to crusty/anarcho-punk/crimethinc aesthetics and subculture, if you came up through those scenes. Even if none of NORCO's specific references resonate, the visual, sonic, and emotional landscapes are irresistibly compelling.I barely ever write reviews, but I can't recommend this enough. For me, it delivers above and beyond all expectation, and I'm genuinely grateful to see something this far off the beaten path of video game narrative supported in finding a wider audience. I hope it sticks with you as profoundly as it's sticking with me.

_childDocuments_.review: An engrossing, cerebral sci-fi point-and-click adventure game set in rural Louisiana.  The game starts off in the small town of Norco, Louisiana as you take on the role of Kay, a runaway who is returning home upon the news of her mother's death.  As you learn more about Norco, its residents and their collective history, the game morphs into a different playing experience altogether and becomes something truly special in the process.The game's strengths lie in its atmosphere, set piece design and honest depiction of Southeast Louisiana and its residents.  It's clear that the developers have a connection with New Orleans and its adjacent rural communities, and it shows in the idiosyncrasies of the game's NPCs and accurate recreation of some of the game's locations.I'd recommend this game for fans of minimalist, atmospheric, story-driven games.  The payoff is rewarding.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some gorgeous writing and visuals, but the ending has left me at a loss. Think if the original Neon Genesis Evangelion was a thriller set in rural Louisiana.The ending just kinda peters out, leaving too many threads unresolved, too many characters dropped without a completed arc, and no catharsis. I feel like the game was just one last, load-bearing scene away from a 10/10, auto-recommend, but instead it sorta leaves you hanging.I'm still recommending this game, because a lot of its ideas and mechanics are incredible and ones I hope to see in future narrative games. Not to mention the incredible pieces of pixel art that made me legit disappointed whenever I only got to spend a few seconds with a cutscene background (might buy the artbook just for that). I also loved the incorporation of rural working class culture, touching on topics of climate collapse, labor exploitation, and late-stage capitalism.Despite my gripes, it's a beautiful experience, and I want to leave this with a huge thank you to the devs for sharing this weird and wonderful little fever dream.

_childDocuments_.review: A really wonderful piece of storytelling :) You can find creativity in unexpected places! The developer has mentioned their work in GIS - which, on the surface, sounds about like the least inspiring thing imaginable. But that would be wrong. There is such a precision about the layout of this game - a lot of thought went into why environments are the way they are, and how those environments affect us. It certainly helps that the developer grew up in these very environments - but NORCO really makes it feel like you're the one who grew up here. And in a point-and-click adventure, that's already a lot!You can feel that same respect in every character, and in every bleak development. The art and music hold up their end, but my favorite part was just how human everybody feels. You can really lose yourself just listening to people talk. I appreciated this dedication to telling, for the most part, a very contained story, allowing for layers on layers of dialogue.There are a ton of instances where it would've been so easy to throw in some repeated line of dialogue and leave it at that. You have to convince a character, for example, to split off from a cultish religious group - you have to go and record other members explicitly defying their faith. You learn that the group is generally anti-technology, and you recorded one kid talking about being on his phone all the time!In the game, though, you do learn that the cult recruits people on a message board. So, I half-expected this character  to get outraged, and half-expected an autogenerated 'That doesn't convince me' you would get from any other line of random dialogue. But the developers actually thought of that! They have a special line for that bit of dialogue! There are so many instances like this where you really feel like you're having a real conversation, and I just love that!Apart from the little things though, it's just a very interesting meditation on identity in the modern day. We find identity, now, in increasingly niche and bizarre places - the game makes the point that in all of its strangeness, the world is still grounded in the same institutions as always. If I have one criticism, I thought the ending was a little too grand. The sheer bleakness isn't the problem - I think that fits pretty well with the game. It's that NORCO, to me, felt like a very personal story about being caught up in things out of your control. There's a little dissonance there, I think, where we are small and malleable, but our protagonist is... ultimately not that.But overall, I loved it. Even if I would call the game pessimistic, there's definitely this thematic out routed in empathy - and, without spoiling anything, how you understand that will impact the game. All in all, it's a wonderfully thought-out story with very human characters that convey a lot of emotion.Also, I really love Million :)

_childDocuments_.review: At first I wasn't sure if I should buy Norco but after completing it I can say I really enjoyed this game.Yes, there's no voice acting and you have to read a lot but it really didn't bother me as I quickly realised that the developers put a lot of heart into Norco.The story is interesting and has a lot of facets, it touches topics like sience fiction, family drama and social criticism in a very believable way.But it also has a funny, humorous side so it keeps a good balance storywise.The game mechanics are good old point and click with some nice additions.You can use maps for faster travel, there´s a fighting mechanic and other more or less unique things in this game.The player also has freedom of choice and can actively forge the story right from the very beginning.Be it in conversations or deciding to progress in a violent or stealthy way within the storyline and choosing different endings.I also have to praise the visual stile of Norco, despite being a pixel art style of game (or maybe because of it)  it really looks nice and has a lot of interesting visual ideas.If you´re a fan of old school style point and click games with a good story and great visuals - go and get Norco.

_childDocuments_.review: When I was young, I wrote a lot of very bad songs that I thought were very deep and meaningful and serious. Mostly they were just shoddy assemblies of genre cliches and tropes. That's the vibe I get from this game. My problem isn't with the concept, to be sure. I really enjoyed Kentucky Route Zero, for instance, a game that Norco desperately wants to be. But this just ain't it. This doesn't feel real or substantial or earned. It feels like a costume being tried on, or a fake accent, or an awkward poem scribbled on the outside of a math notebook. I've read a lot about the "great writing" in Norco and I'm at a loss to understand what I'm missing. What I experienced ultimately has the styling and energy of a Thought Catalog essay, or a bad personal zine written by a teenager in the 1990's.I guess I appreciate the aspirations at work here, but I don't think any of it lands. Obviously, the story and the writing are intended to be the stars of the show, but they're creaking under the weight of pretension. All of the text feels cloying and pandery and a little too eager to be Very Meaningful in a way that the author doesn't seem capable of achieving. And the Crass sticker in the character's childhood bedroom made me groan out loud. Skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: And once again, we walk into the tricky bed of thorns of 'games as art.''Norco' would likely be classified as an adventure game above anything else, but the puzzles are infrequent and generally of low difficulty.  The combat is simplistic and a bit awkward, but it's so rare it hardly matters.  Occasional deviations into different gameplay modes, like driving a boat, can be safely rated as 'serviceable.'  So it's up to the writing, characters, and production to carry the day.  And my goodness, do they ever.Personally, I'd classify this game as a visual novel.  It's those elements that are going to hook you in if you're going to be hooked at all.  'Norco' is a story of delightful contradictions, celebrating both the beautiful and the grotesque; the sacred and the profane.  The setting is... cyberpunk lite, let's call it?  Think 'Blade Runner' shot through the prism of Southern Gothic, where rogues and tramps huddle together for dear life.  Everything in the game seems to be rapidly decaying, from the people to the land itself.  I wasn't surprised at all to find out that the project began as a documentary about the devastation of Hurricane Katrina to Louisiana, given the game's grim tone and focus on environmental destruction.  And as the land falls apart or is shattered by heavy industry, what about the people who live there?  In 'Norco,' they suffer quietly, go mad, look for God, join a cult, or, in the case of our protagonist, they run like hell until circumstances call them back to whatever home they may have left.So, let's get the obvious comparison point out of the way - 'Disco Elysium,' the 800-pound gorilla of modern games-as-art.  The developers don't cite it as an influence, but there's no denying that 'Disco' has made the waters much safer for games like this to swim in.  There are some strong points of similarity between the two games - long strings of gorgeous purple prose, finding beauty in urban decay, a tangible Marxist influence, and so forth.  I can't flat-out say that 'if you liked one, you'll like the other,' as 'Norco' never hits the heights of dark hilarity that 'Disco' does.  (Granted, how many games have?)  But 'Norco' is bleaker by design, where even the "good" ending is pretty macabre.  'Disco' offers the faint hope of redemption and a better world; 'Norco' is basically an hourglass draining out.  Also, a shout-out to 'Kentucky Route Zero' is probably in order here, too, although again there is no stated influence.  This just seems to be a genre of game that is taking shape organically via modern economic circumstance.I'm not going to touch on the story much - it would basically just be spoilers.  Fair warning, though; if you've recently lost a parent or have a sibling you can't quite connect with, this game will hit especially hard.  I literally called my parents after finishing this game the first time to remind them that I loved them.  This world of ours is designed to isolate us; this game shows the consequences.  One of my favorite moments is when a character in poor health tells one of your allies that the best thing he could do for him would be to simply visit more often.  It was perfectly bittersweet.Production-wise, the pixel art is fantastic, full of detail and style.  Nothing hits me quite like gorgeously-depicted ugliness.  One of my favorite little touches is when a character will occasionally emerge from the shadows, but slowly, so it's not so much a jump scare as just... unsettling.  The music holds up its end, too, haunting and eerie exactly when it needs to be.  Everything is very somber, like you're at the wake of human civilization.So should you buy this game?  You kind of already know the answer, don't you?  I mean, it's unlikely you landed here by accident while looking for the hot new looter shooter.  If you want to travel across Louisiana with a rogue's gallery of characters and tons of beautiful florid prose, hop on board.  (There's a free demo available if you're still on the fence.)  I like shooting zombies as much as the next person, but I'm grateful that more and more games like this are emerging, which take the medium into deeper waters and stay with us long after the credits roll.  Escapist fare is fine, and maybe even essential, but perhaps, like the protagonist of this game, we escape too often and for too long, averting our eyes from an admittedly frightening reality that needs to be dealt with.  I pray we're not at 'Norco' yet.  Maybe we are.  In either case, make sure to reach out to everyone that's important to you, and seek out and embrace the remaining beauty in our world.  It can all disappear so quickly.Highest recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Kentucky Route Zero by way of Monkey Island, with a dash of Disco Elysium.---EDIT: Having completed the game, I feel the need to provide a counterpoint to some other reviews which expressed dissatisfaction with the Third Act of the game. While subjective personal experience is certainly important, especially for a game as abstract and interpretive as NORCO, it's also just that -- subjective. I loved the final act of the game. It genuinely brought me to tears. It also made me call my mom.NORCO's greatest strength is its utterly unique Industrial Surrealist / Southern Gothic atmosphere, held together by evocative pixel art, gripping prose, moody soundtrack, and singularly melancholic worldbuilding. NORCO's First Act feels magical in part because you're experiencing all these elements for the first time, and the world is still being constructed around you such that you genuinely don't know what to expect next.From this perspective, it's understandable to feel like the Second and/or Third acts are disappointing, because at some point NORCO becomes more than an abstract tone poem and instead consolidates its setting and characters into a discrete plot. Compared to the infinitude of possible stories that could have branched out after Act One, it's easy to see how some people may find the specific story told to be disappointing compared to What Could Have Been. However, I don't think it's fair to take this as a mark against NORCO -- if anything, it's a testament to the creators that the world they've created is so vibrant and resonant that the specific story they tell seems to pale in comparison.Kentucky Route Zero manages this dynamic in part by remaining abstracted above any singular plot or character arc. Every Act and Intermission feels like an isolated vignette; there's an ensemble cast of perspective characters and no clear protagonist; the ostensible 'goal' of the game (to travel the Zero to deliver a package) falls by the wayside almost immediately and is practically a MacGuffin, a contrivance to motivate the player's continued engagement with KRZ's world. This isn't a complaint about KRZ, which is a phenomenal piece of work that I pretty clearly love, but as an experience it's definitely more "art" than "game".By comparison, NORCO is a much more "traditional" adventure game: you (mostly) play as a single perspective character throughout, the mechanics and presentation of the game remain fairly consistent, and there are fairly clear goals and antagonists (though you have a bit of freedom to decide what matters to your character, which may influence which forces you perceive as antagonistic). The game lays down a lot of cards in Act One and doesn't pick all of them up by the finale, but on the whole I was satisfied with the story it told. The characters and events that set the game's plot into motion are interwoven somewhat densely, and if you're not paying attention throughout it's more likely you'll come away feeling like some plot threads were left hanging. Once again, though, the aesthetic is the star of the show here. If you like the *feel* of NORCO, the plot is really just an excuse to keep hanging around its world.Judging by the liner notes (yes, this is the kind of the game that has liner notes), a lot of disparate people contributed to this game, but it only came together because of the vision and labor of a comparatively small number of people. Frankly, it's a miracle it exists at all, and you should buy it to help ensure there will be more games like it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully written and scored with visuals to match. The game is hilarious and very moving. The developers have woven a world of AI, cybernetics, the occult, sleazy P.I.s, hobo prophets, alligators, cryptids, cats with jet thrusters in they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ asses and a very cute monkey, draped in a veil of southern gothic against a backdrop of the very real ways in which the Shell corporation has destroyed, and is continuing to destroy, lives and communities in coastal Louisiana. Being poor is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ death sentence and Norco makes clear a large factor contributing to that reality. But none of this takes away from a deeply felt family saga; the sci-fi and the occult and the magic-realism, that's all just the trappings of this game. Norco doesn't simply say that capital has gouged our world, destroyed our community and killed our loved ones; it expresses how that feels. There is an undeniable atmosphere to this game's tapestry, its thick and vivid, a sense of longing, aching loss and tiredness. In the end its the little things you remember, the minutiae, small things you wish you could've said, pauses you wish you had acted on, trivial moments which in hindsight you wish you could stretch out for a millennia. And how it feels to lose them, and how it feels to live in the shadow of what took them from you, to have to breath it in every day, as it blots out the sun.

_childDocuments_.review: Beyond its poetry and entrancing pixel-scapes, Norco has a powerful, magical pull that I have felt from the other side (of the planet). I saw so much of myself in its people and I saw so many parallels between Norco, Louisiana and my own hometown. There is universality in places like these - towns ruined by corporate greed, corruption and natural disaster.  After ruin and tragedy, there is poverty, homelessness, gentrification, catastrofitti, hopelessness, list goes on, but there is also people trying to cope and to fight. Norco gets this more than right and this aspect is something I've related to the most. Though it's seemingly sombre and bleak, it's full of heart. Through everything you experience playing this game, you can feel the love the developers have put in it. It's really intimate.There's an odd sense of comfort behind everything Norco tackles and shows, behind the fact that a story like this can exist and be so magical. I'm hoping we'll see more of stories like this in the future. I hope my town will get a similar treatment one day. I'm thankful to have learned about a place like Norco through this game. I'm thankful to have met the wonderful people behind this landmark piece of art. And I'm so excited to see what's next for Geography of Robots.

_childDocuments_.review: It offered me a good amount of confusion and not for a moment I felt the game wasn’t artsy enough or interesting. It’s bold, experimental, interesting. The constant flux of new backgrounds, characters, story threads, small gameplay systems, worldbuilding, and some shocking moments changing the formula kept the game fresh. A Visual Novel that feels like a true adventure game, with fancy visuals, explorable areas, and very smooth “puzzles” that offer no actual challenge, but help with pacing out the moment-by-moment experience.At the same time, something about the game hasn't resonated with me on an emotional level. It’s a “me” problem. I saw the game praised for its anticapitalist, post industrial themes - and because of my interests, those topics are now getting a bit stale for me, no matter their value. I didn’t enjoy the humor, aside from Pawpaw, but it’s definitely crafty. I already had my share of searching for stories about leaving your home and having another look at your difficult family relationships, and this time they just bounced off of me. I didn’t enjoy the religious themes. I didn’t feel so captured by the wetlands as I was playing Kentucky Route Zero, but KRZ had the advantage of being the first game that sold them to me presented in a similar fashion…I think I just played through a masterpiece, but it occurred at the wrong time in my life. Maybe five years ago it would inspire me like no other game, but right now, I can only appreciate it on an intellectual level. And the small shard of intellect I have left tells me I should return to NORCO in 2028, and in the meantime say - if it feels like you’re a part of the target audience for this game, you can trust that it’s as good as people say.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a short point-and-click "mystery" game. Isn't worth getting imo, but see for yourself:=Solid conversation/text system=Has a very cool mechanic of piecing together a "mind map" of every person, thing, and piece of info the protagonist knows so far. Well established; snappy; and the story sometimes plays with your expectations of it.=There is TONS of unexpected comedy. All the dialogue is played straight, but the people you encounter and the things you have to do for some achievements are gold.=The story, even at its highs, is not the most engaging. It'll please you in some cases, and might interest you with its themes about the bleak future and the nature of religion, but other times, it just kinda falls apart. Lots of awkward dialogue throughout, plus a weird choice to incorporate internet slang into the vocabulary of the future.=Has some borrowed RPG elements like a changing party of characters and some turn based-fights, although the latter is practically nonexistant (you even have the option to automate it).=Because the story is so short, the narration and dialogue are very GM-like. Lots of pushy "you  care for  character because of  reason!" Especially getting started in Act 1.=There is no real mystery to actively solve with the puzzle pieces you are given, nor will most of the dialogue choices affect the story; you just sort of passively experience the story and then  it starts to come together.=Some bugs surrounding the conditions to get certain achievements + the saving system being not very polished = a somewhat annoying trip for achievement hunters.=The catherine sections in Act 2 were so unnecessarily finicky.

_childDocuments_.review: Short and Sweet. Not much in the way of actual gameplay. There is no real challenge to the game. All the game's mechanics work towards building the atmosphere of the game and telling more of the story. Having just played Disco Elysium I feel a bit disappointed that the game railroads you through most of the actual mystery. I would have definitely enjoyed a game that challenged me to put the pieces of the puzzle together myself and given me different outcomes based on the work I put into uncovering the story. That being said. This game is awesome and through the art, writing, and music, paints a vibrant tragic world that is fun to get immersed in and explore the characters that inhabit it. The game oozes style and while it may lack in overall challenge or gameplay the absence of said mechanics does help you get right to the heart of the story allowing you to take it all in at once. Would definitely recommend to anyone looking  to explore a unique setting with compelling characters but who might not want the added challenge of more strenuous or complex game play.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A nice story driven point and click game, well made. Nearly two hours in I'm confident to give a positive review.I have to point out though, I thought the "poster art" painting for the game of a few people sitting on the back of a car was really ugly and put me off buying it earlier. The pixel art is much better. Love the CRT Mode.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it at first, the monke was cool and petting the cat until it launched through the ceiling was funny. I can not stand how boring and limiting the "game" part of this is. The writing is good and I can see real effort in the themes and story. As a game it is not fun. I wasted several minutes at a time frustrated at how the only way to progress in the game is to find the ONE valid spot to click to advance the story. There is no journal or log to go back and review what was actually important information to move on. I was sick of it once I got to the "puzzle" of trying to move points on a digital map to remove all the drones from a zone, but you only have 10 moves to do it and then it is reset. It is incredibly limiting and I hate "games" where there is only one possible solution and you're just stuck until you find the one "trick" to solving it. I know I would just be looking up guides constantly if this is how hard it is this early on.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Visually lush and tonally evocative, Norco fails to stick the landing in ways that undermine the rest of the game retroactively. That is, the *plot* of the game resolves well enough — you figure out what happened and why by the end — but the emotional arc is muted almost to the point of nonexistence. There's no epiphany or catharsis, no moment when the disorientation and alienation of the game's terse, poetical style and worldbuilding suddenly coheres into something meaningful or moving. The recent genre touchpoints are Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero, but both of those games were *deeply* invested in the emotional realities of their protagonists, even if the presentation was fractured, elusive, and allegorical. Norco establishes some potent tensions between family, place, and legacy, and then doesn't actually *do* anything with that setup.It's a game well worth playing — the presentation and moment to moment writing are both phenomenal — but it never becomes more than the sum of its parts, unfortunately.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me relate to things I pretty much don't have anything in common with.Every backgrond is a work of art, the soundtrack mesmerizing, the world feels melancholic, yet cozy and nostalgic.All of the main characters (and a few side ones!) are made memorable by how bizarre or surreal they are.The story itself is one of the best works of sci-fi I got the pleasure to experience in a while.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very tentative review with the hope this game can only get better. I have finished the game after 4 hours and have achieved two endings. I'm happy to come back in a few months to play it again after some some minor QoL adjustments, i.e. fixing dodgy click spots, no ability to scroll text, important text highlights before you know things are important and no option to turn them off. The story is a very tantalising offering giving explanations, while consistent often don't have to make sense. If you are a fan of neo-noir style films such as Blade Runner, Donnie Darko or Under the Silver Lake you will get a kick out of this. I still feel like I am missing big chunks of the tale but as I said I am happy to come back.Only major gripe is when it comes to combat or puzzles the game grinds to a halt to shove them in your face. it feels a little disjointed and took me out of it. But hey, small passing issue in an otherwise good game.If you've read all this check out the Demo at least, you'll work out pretty quick if you'll like it or not. Whats to lose?
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a few days since I finished my first run of Norco and I can't stop thinking about it. I couldn't put the game down and played through the whole thing in one sitting. Since then I've been listening to the soundtrack on repeat and trying to wrap my head around what the hell just happened. I don't even think the game itself has the answers I want. But it feels like that's part of it. Mysterious, confusing, metaphorical, strange, otherworldly, darkly funny - "magical realism" done right. This is the kind of fiction that transcends genre or medium and gets at you in a wholly unique way. A must play.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely boring.I couldn't bring myself to care about anything or anyone, and I tried. The game just vomits a lot of names and characters with the presumption that I know them, without giving any context. So all the conversations were meaningless to me.If you call a random number and someone picks up, that conversation would be way more interesting than anything I've seen in this game.Another weird thing is, you make up your backstory as you go, so they'll ask you questions like:Did you get hit on the head? Or did you NOT get hit on the head?Oh gee I don't know! That's a tough one.I personally would not recommend. But you should read the other reviews and make an informed decision.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic pixel art and cinematography enhance this Southern Gothic Cyberpunk mystery, but the real flare is in the writing, which manages to be both poetic, poignant and pretty funny, with a strong dollop of the sensibilities which allowed Disco Elysium to revitalise interest in the Point & Click RPG genre.Highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I've started playing "Norco" and after 1 hour and 45 minutes I reached Act Two.So what is this game about? It plays in some futuristic version of Louisiana, USA, where several floods have changed the world and now an oil refinery named Shield pretty much owns and runs everything. You play as Kay, a young woman who once left her hometown to look for luck at the west coast, only to return home at the news of her mother's death. Your brother, Blake, has always stayed home but now you can't find him. Luckily there's this robotic version of a butler/personal assistant (who reminds me a bit of "Guardians of the Galaxy"'s Nebula, only less grumpy) who helps you look for him.  During your explorations you unlock elements in a mindmap, which works as some kind of notebook to keep track of important information. There's some hints to your mom finding something weird in a lake, but she succumbed to cancer before having a chance to share her findings.  At the end of Act One you get a flashback to two weeks earlier where you suddenly play as Catherine, Kat's mom.If you like reading fiction like me, this is a game for you. It plays like reading a book. There's lots of text, but it's well-written text, it's a story that pays attention to detail. There's not a single generic description of hotspots in this game; everything earns its own paragraph.The game isn't voiced, so you'll have to do your own reading. There are some weird gameplay elements (like QTE's, a version of Simon Says, and having to navigate a little boat through a swamp during one very strange puppet show) but luckily they are far and between. I haven't encountered any puzzles to speak of, other than going to a store to buy a spark plug to fix a motorbike, and finding a stranger to go buy a hotdog from a vendor in exchange for information.Most of the gameplay centers on how you react when talking to other people, but I haven't seen any special consequences following those discussions.4,5 hours into "Norco", I'm still in Act Two, and the game has taken me places I never expected.There were actual battle sequences I had to go through! Man, I haven't done that since my Final Fantasy days so I took a lot of damage, and luckily I had no need of phoenix downs.So for a moment there the game felt a bit like those first person RPG's where you search through a dungeon looking for treasure and fighting monsters. There was this puzzle where you have to move drones through different security sections so you can pass through unseen. Other than that I'm just following the flow, talking to people, and seeing where things lead. I feel like I don't have much handle on the plot and am just tagging along for the ride, with no idea how it's going to end.I finished "Norco" in about 8,5 hours. And boy, did this game keep surprising me! Suppose they ever make an adventure game of season 3 of "Twin Peaks", then it would definitely have the look and feel of this game.Lots of stuff happened, I'm not going to elaborate on them, but finally there were some cool gameplay elements added to what is otherwise a very much narrative driven game. I got a recording app on my phone which I had to use to manipulate NPC's, and it was quite interesting to hunt after the correct voice samples. I had to steer a boat all across Lake Ponchartrain, with an added puzzle element to unlock more of the map but which was actually way too easy but still, it was fun to actually have something more interactive to do in this game.There were some more fight sequences, and then the finale came. Not going to elaborate on that either, except I loaded a saved game to get a second ending which was just as bad, and then I loaded an even earlier saved game to finally get the good ending. I like how you really had to pay attention to the details to realise what to do to get that good ending, because I didn't realise it the first time and it's very easy to move on without having done it at all.I don't think I understand everything that went on in this game. Like I said, "Twin Peaks" season 3. But I'm glad I played this game, which was very different from the games I usually play. I'm glad the demo intrigued me enough; it was all the text that won me over, combined with the gritty visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A gorgeous, brilliantly-written point-and-click fever dream set in Louisiana and New Orleans. I enjoyed the demo and the full game surpassed my expectations. This definitely isn't the sort of game that everyone's going to love, but...if you like David Lynch or enjoyed Disco Elysium or Kentucky Route Zero, this is your kind of game. If you don't like games that require reading, you can skip it.Very highly recommended and would love to see if these devs put out anything in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco. Another standard-bearer of the last ten years of video game renaissance, which reproduces a winning formula now widespread: evocative 2000's graphics, often not instantly appealing, paired with elements of a somewhat forgotten genre reduced to its primary essence, combined with authorial writing (we've seen this blueprint in Disco Elysium, Signalis, even Golden Idol), here taking the form of a goth cyberpunk adventure in rural America.The project began over 10 years ago with a series of sketches in the actual locations of Norco, Louisiana, a town born out of a Shell refinery, of which the developer, then in his twenties, is a native. From those powerful landscapes sprung the idea for a video game.It is said that the a good cyberpunk work is not about the technology but using it as a metaphor for current phenomena and issues, and here Norco is second to none: it includes references from environmentalism to neoliberalism to the pipelines of the alt-right, evangelical preachers, and crypto-millionaires, plus a stateless protagonist with elderly and sick parents with whom our generation can easily identify.The game's formula is that of the visual novel, with a substantial amount of text that characterizes the game world in an almost poetic manner, with clear references to Disco Elysium, even in the interface itself and the attention to typography. This genre is married to the modernized and simplified skeleton of a point-and-click investigative adventure, of which Norco captures more than anything else the flavor, avoiding the typical difficulty and inaccessibility.While I very much appreciate the inclusion of a Pathologic-like "mental map", which in the end feels even a bit superfluous, maybe in a testament to its usefulness, these are not exactly my favorite genres, as i find it a bit difficult to maintain the necessary concentration, but Norco's unique atmosphere and its attention to every detail did not make me regret undertaking this journey.4/5
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco leads the player to underestimate the degree to which its world-building differs from that of simply a realistic dystopian future. It is a story that I would only describe after establishing that it borders on being more than can be described. It is a game with mythical and cosmic inclinations that leave me with a deep sense of misunderstanding and a subconscious terror elicited by its incomprehensible scale of meaning--something like a dream.Also, the cat flew through the roof.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to complete this game fully before giving an honest review. As someone who lived in Southern Louisiana for the first two decades of their life and moved away out west for work, I didn't want to give this game a great review on just nostalgia and an ache for a past life. So I finished the game and I can still solidly give this masterpiece a 10/10. I'm not going to give away plot points as I want everyone to experience this game on their own. The story is rich and inventive with sci-fi and gothic elements that make the moody atmosphere pop. The writing is beautiful as well, as I found myself getting lost in the visual descriptions as you often study your own thoughts in the game. I don't think I can describe how beautiful and creepy the pixel art can be in this game. This game is by no means a horror game but I did jump a couple of time due to one particular character. "Eerie" and "unsettling" are the best words I can use for this game in some instances and its freaking great. The game felt fresh with all of its little surprises.My one complaint? I wish it was longer, but I know the developers worked hard on this beauty.  I loved this game. I may play it again one day to relive the days of riding down Airline Highway and the Bonnet Carre spillway.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Come for the vengeful alligator spirits and shopping mall cultists, stay for the gorgeous pixel art and brilliant writing!NORCO is a point-and-click adventure game set in the cursed bayous and oil refineries that lie outside of New Orleans. Kay returns to her hometown Norco after the death of her mother and disappearance of her brother—throughout the game you switch between Kay's perspective and her mother Catherine's. It's not wrong to describe it as a dystopian sci-fi story, but I think that it might be more appropriate to describe it as a haunted and magical realist parallel universe. It's a game that is both deeply gloomy and funny. It has a strong sense of place, developed largely through the lovingly rendered pixel art environment, but also through the top-notch writing and sound design. The characters and environments you interact with generally feel grounded and real, until the game confronts you with well-crafted moments of rupture and subversion. The game is worth playing for the story alone, but the design of the environment makes it an experience to savor.The game mechanics primarily unfold through dialogue and interacting with items in the environment, although there is also a pretty nifty "mind map" in which you can refresh your memory or further ponder narrative events as they unfold. The only quibble I had with this game was with a few of the mini-games—specifically the boating and QTE-style combat encounters. I found this part of the game experience to be frustrating and it felt like a prolonged distraction from the story and writing elements that drew me in. Part of this is that I was playing the game with a set-up that wasn't particularly well optimized for fine mouse control, so it's possible that these would be less frustrating with a decent mouse. Also, to the developer's credit, I never got a game over in these mini-games (despite feeling like I was close to one every single time).
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Story had me on the edge of my seat, trying to put the pieces together. Beautifully tragic narrative of a mother and daughter, with really funny moments of levity to get you through the pure misery this story can inflict. The prose in the descriptive sections of the game really made me feel like I was in the AU world NORCO is set in. The art direction is gorgeous. This is one of those games I wish I could play again for the first time. Highly recommend for a short, but sweet experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Reading some of the reviews here, I feel like I was playing an entirely different game to everyone here.I went into this game with really high hopes, looking forward to an interesting point and click experience (one of my favourite genres!) - but I got very sick of the writing very quickly. I didn't connect with any of the characters, the worldbuilding was boring. Halfway through the game I was really bored and started skipping through dialogue because I didn't care, and the last 20% I was just trying to check the game off. I should have stopped playing earlier really.There's also a bizarre inclusion of a combat mechanic that really makes the world feel extremely fake. One of the first events you come to is some big guy who's a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and says you can't go into a shop so you just beat the snot out of him. Then shortly after you're trying to break into a facility to retrieve a cardboard box of gubbins that you don't know the contents of, because it was stolen from you. You have to do this by beating up two robots with rifles, who shoot you repeatedly but it's fine I guess? You can just lose the fight where you get shot like 5 times and there's no penalty, which just makes the world feel like there's absolutely no stakesMaybe there's some hidden meaning that I just didn't 'get' that makes this game a beautiful piece of art, but I guess I got too bored to get anything out of it. Really couldn't recommend it at all. If you want something along these lines, the Bithell Circular games are enjoyable text adventures (Subsurface Circular and Quarantine Circular), or Disco Elysium is a fantastic pick, but if you're reading a review for NORCO, you probably already know about it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't dabbled in quite so many adventure games as I should have over the years - I had a brief play with Monkey Island 2 back in the day and enjoyed Discworld on the PS1. However, after playing the fabulous Disco Elysium, which one could argue is more of an adventure game than an RPG, I wanted to carry on with well written story telling and mystery. Norco didn't disappoint - the story was engrossing and touches on some interesting themes, the characters were well rounded and the setting complimented the graphical style - it actually took me back to my Amiga 500 days. Hopefully "Geography of Robots" have more gems like this up their sleeve.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely my favourite point-and-click game ever! The vivid, beautifully-realised world immediately pulls you in: familiar yet uncannily unfamiliar, as the best fictional worlds tend to be. The pixel art is great, the narrative and plot fascinating and bonkers in equal measure, and the characterisation vivid (quite a few really memorable characters). The writing is bleakly funny, both in terms of the overall tone - the merging  of crass consumerism with religious themes is handled with sardonic, yet warm, humour - and in the witty dialogue, which features some brilliant lines!There are no really obtuse puzzles, such as one finds in, say, Thimbleweed Park, which will be  good news for some (it was for me), perhaps not so good for others. It plays beautifully, all the interfaces, systems and mechanics work brilliantly (aside, perhaps, from the few combat-type scenes, but this might just have been me).An excellent game!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a Southern Gothic point & click narrative adventure that immerses the player in the sinking suburbs and verdant industrial swamps of a distorted South Louisiana. Your brother Blake has gone missing in the aftermath of your mother's death. In the hopes of finding him, you must follow a fugitive security android through the refineries, strip malls, and drainage ditches of suburban New Orleans.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

name: Detroit: Become Human
detailed_description: Detroit: Become Human , the award-winning video game production from Quantic Dream , is finally available on Steam! Featuring world-renowned actors including Jesse Williams (Grey’s Anatomy), Clancy Brown (Carnivale), Lance Henriksen (Aliens), Bryan Dechart (True Blood) and Valorie Curry (Twilight). WHAT MAKES US HUMAN? Detroit 2038. Technology has evolved to a point where human like androids are everywhere. They speak, move and behave like human beings, but they are only machines serving humans. Play three distinct androids and see a world at the brink of chaos – perhaps our future - through their eyes. Your very decisions will dramatically alter how the game’s intense, branching narrative plays out. You will face moral dilemmas and decide who lives or dies. With thousands of choices and dozens of possible endings, how will you affect the future of Detroit and humanity’s destiny? PLAY YOUR PART IN A GRIPPING NARRATIVE Enter a world where moral dilemmas and difficult decisions can turn android slaves into world-changing revolutionaries. Discover what it means to be human from the perspective of an outsider – and see the world through the eyes of a machine. THEIR LIVES, YOUR CHOICES Shape an ambitious branching narrative, where your decisions not only determine the fate of the three main characters, but that of the entire city of Detroit. How you control Kara, Connor and Markus can mean life or death – and if one of them pays the ultimate price, the story still continues… COUNTLESS PATHS, COUNTLESS ENDINGS Every decision you make, no matter how minute, affects the outcome of the story. No playthrough will be exactly the same: replay again and again to discover a totally different conclusion. FULLY OPTIMIZED FOR PC Detroit: Become Human is brought to PC with stunning graphics, 4K resolution, 60 fps framerate and full integration of both mouse/keyboard and gamepad controls for the most complete Detroit: Become Human experience to date.

Every choice you make affects the outcome of the game, with one of the most intricately branching narratives ever created.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a brilliant game with a great story. It's not perfect, sometimes it's obvious that the writers want you to feel a certain way about the issues/themes demonstrated and there are a few "huh?" moments. Despite that, I still love it as a high production value, narrative-focused game in an amazing setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human has a great premise, great visuals, great sound, great story and mediocre game play. Quick time events are something quite foreign to PC-gamers and I don't care for them at all, never have, never will. I don't know if this mechanism works better on consoles, but this is archaic game design from 25 years ago when they didn't know any better. From Fallout 3 back then to Cyberpunk 2077 of today we've seen it all evolve over time and somehow the designers of D:BH have been living underneath a rock. I don't get it, all I know is, it's ruining the game for me. I will try to stick with it, but it's frustrating as h3ll. I don't care for time sensitive game play in an RPG. I don't like to be forced to make 5 second decisions that can drastically alter the plot in an unwanted direction or shorten the story because of the death of a main character. I want to enjoy the game on my terms, not on those of the developers. And don't get me started on the lack of save games (replaying a chapter from check points later on after you fell for a beginner's trap does not count). Also, the game does not apply its own concepts it teaches the player on how to disassemble or disable a deviant android without destroying it. This game had so much potential. Do better next time, if there is a next time that is. (Review in progress...)
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I've always watched people play it but for a great game like this you also need to pick up a copy and enjoy this title for yourself because it's definitely a whole new look into the world of human and machines and how dangerously close we have been getting to this world that is right around the corner but i have been enjoying playing this game so far and it's fun having friends help you make decisions or just see what will  happen when you chose this one decision that will alter the rest of the game and i'm only 8 hours in lol
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly the most immersive game I've ever played. If your preference is for shooters or tons of action, this game may drag at parts for you but will still be enjoyable. If, however, you enjoy story-based games that force you to contemplate what it is to be human (or a person), that allow you to connect and feel for the characters, this game is perfect. I don't like to ever say I have a favorite game because often times it depends on my mood, but this game challenges my stance on that. It has moments of intensity, beauty, and tragedy all based on your choices. The replay value is also incredible as you can literally play a second time and feel like you're playing an entirely different game.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: When i get to the Capital Park , the game consistently crashes. I get a Driver error message. Even tho my drivers are up to date. (Rx6600)Looked it up online, and apparently you have to revert you're drivers to 2022 drivers.Yeah no thanksSo if you are using an RX6600 watch out cause the game might not be playable anymore half-way trough
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: There may be some shoddy reviews and i've only played through this once and luckily managed to get the good ending, everyone survived apart from Carl and i though i lost Luther too. I will say this..This game was a absolute dream to play, the story is brilliant and i love the way the three characters intertwine together. There is emotion and loss and happiness and joy. This game had a couple of moments it genuinely made my eyes leak. an absolutely fantastic play i would definitely recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I love games like this. Multiple endings, if you make a mistake you don't have to save and reload you can just play it that way the next time. Love this game. It does make my graphics card work awfully hard though. Beautiful graphics. Great game. 10/10. I haven't beaten it yet. If something changes I'll update.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I freaking loved playing through this. I connected with each character and, with every choice I was presented, I legitimately had to think through how I thought it would play out in terms of character development. Some things I messed up on, some choices I made on accident by fumbling with buttons in the action scenes, but that definitely makes me want to go back and explore the other endings this game has. 10/10 will play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of the most amazing rpg's to have ever come out, in my opinion. There are so many different endings, even involving the most minor decisions you would never think of. Detroit: Become Human, is a perfect and well rounded game, and it makes you fall in love with it and the characters every single time. Would highly recommend playing it!
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. Absolute garbage PC port.Stutters are constant. The game's randomly minimised itself a couple of times. Completely unacceptable for a game that came to steam like a year and a half ago and was on the Epic store months before that. The devs have had tons of time to fix all the performance issues, but they obviously don't give a ♥♥♥♥.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: What makes me to buy this game is I was deeply moved by the story, especially Kara's story. I felt that she is just like a mother who wants to protect her child. The storylines for Connor and Markus are great too, but what makes me decided to purchase this game is Kara's storyline. Overall, the gameplay is good. I like the graphics, character designs etc, soundtracks (especially Kara's main theme and the little one). I like the music that really match with the stories and characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like playing a movie. It is so incredibly written, I was so invested in each of my characters choices, and their personal growth. I cried a lot through out the game, especially when I royally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ things up! I highly recommend going into the game blind, don't look up any guides and don't replay any of the missions until you finish the game, because it all pays off in the end when all of your choices come to fruition. The graphics are gorgeous, the soundtrack is so beautiful and moving...my only complaint is that sometimes the controls can be a little wonky with the camera angles. Overall, 10/10 will play again multiple times because there are so many choices to make. I got it on sale, but if you are really itching to buy this game, it will be worth the $40, imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This game was truly a work of art. The storyline, 10/10. The gameplay, 10/10. The characters, 10/10. The emotional distress, 10/10. The stress, 10/10. The consequences, 10/10. Overall, this game took over my entire life for the entire gameplay. Makes me want to reply it over and over and over and over again.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: While most choice based games result in your choices not mattering at the end, this game breaks the mold. There are countless endings, all of which can be impacted by your decision with each character throughout the game. Truly raises the question of morality and the philosophy of what it means to be human in an engaging way. Would highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could express how amazing this game truly is. It's a literal masterpiece and has captured my attention and emotions. I haven't felt this attached to a game since Red Dead Redemption 2. The massive amount of decisions the game gives you can drastically alter the outcome of each character, the characters future and how they view you personally, and much more. I cannot recommend this game enough. Full price or discounted price, this game is definitely worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just wow! I'm absolutely blown away by this game.What a MASTERPIECE! <3It is so refreshing play a game with an emotional and deep story nowdays, and Detroit does it in an awesome way. Yes, this is a game for everyone that enjoy good characthers and good stories. The gameplay is relatively simplistic - you walk around, interact with people and objects, and make choices. During more intense scenes, you'll participate in quick time events. For me Detroit: Become Human wins out over Telltale's Walking Dead games or Life is Strange due to higher presentation value and a vastly greater array of choices.Here, your choices really do matter, and after each chapter, you get to see how many ways your decisions could have potentially played out. It's a novel way to show to the player how many options they had and greatly increases the replay value. Your choices have an impact on what happens as well as your relationship with other characters. After some types of decisions, you see immediately whether your choice had a positive or negative effect on another character's opinion of you, keeping you on your toes and incentivized to make the best decision possible. It's not so cut and dry though, with decisions often being perceived well by some and not so well by others, again opening the door to more viable gameplay options.This is one of the best games i've played so far and REALLY recommend it.
