_childDocuments_.review: Definitely a solid 15$ game (current price) .It' s still a positive review, for the vast scenario options, but I am conflicted because of the following points.Great game concept, but it' s a mobile game for PC, a Powerpoint Presentation, with pre- determined paths, that you just have to click to change them- reminds me of the old X- Files game, where you just clicked through scenarios (never liked that genre of gaming) .Basically, it' s a game made for mobiles, or consoles, and converted for PC, being a game made of just 'Push buttons when Itell you to do it, so I can show you the next cinematic/ slides` .Now I see where `Still wakes the deep` borrowed the boring gameplay.Although it' s a nice story, it' s just a click and select scenario game.Controls are clunky as hell and very linear path. You need to go where it tells you. Even a small deviation, an invisible box (arlund random small objects) will block you from going further. Camera is atrocious, in the style of old PS2 RE games.It is an extremly SLOW PACED game. You can' t cancel cutcenes.Most annoyingly: you can' t redo sub chapters of bigger chapters. You have to go through all the slow paced game again and again.The tips/ hints what buttons to press are non intuitive and badly placed, making you lose clicks. Advice: Randomly smash S and D. 99% it' s all you have to do in an action situation.It has illogical inconsistencies when it comes to the Androids, how they behave, their physical strength, their abilities.Some small examples:When they die, their skin is still visibleWhen it suits them in the cinematic, they have superhuman strength, when it is during the gameplay, all fragileThey have the ability to take over radios, but during raids, they can' t just enter the Radio frequencies and hear the commands to avoid problems, or just scan for them not to be They are able to hack a IT line, for a brief momentAnd the list can be longer, and I am sure many saw more than meIt is good, but you literally just have to click, sync button pressing and choose multiple stuff for a scenario- kind of disappointing, as it feels just like turning a page in a story book.I appreciate the complexity of the concept and the craftsmanship and tbh, the story that I stitched together, with little to no tips from the internet (only 2 final sub chapters made me completely undecided) . And for all this strict behaviour, you can accelerate some scenes playthrough, still, jumping the cutscene, thus reducing the immersion.I also liked the changes the game menu brings, after completing the gameIt ries to make you take surveys (after a certain amount of playthrough) , but after 3 rejections, it stopped.Graphics is more than ok. Why just that? The acting, and animations are sometimes so good, you feel you're watching a movie. And at the opposite side, rubbery skins, HDR style 'wax like' chsrachters. *It seems the game industry is moving into implementing in PC the dumb down (mobile game) controls, mixed with cinematic, and call it a game (you making your own scenario/ animated movie) .* Also, it reminded me a lot of Cyberjunk 2077 (the latter obviously copying the concept) .** The stitching of memories from dead androids, CJ copied it. Even the lover of Markus, North, reminds me of the one in Cyberjunk.

_childDocuments_.review: My first experience with this PC version was just horrible. The game would just hang or crash quite frequently and I did refund the game. I repurchased it once Nvidia finally fixed the issue via one of the latest drivers so the game is now running fine.Detroit: Become Human is an adventure game about androids reaching self-awareness in the futuristic city of Detroit and the complications that it brings to the society that depended on them to become nothing more than obedient machines. You follow along a number of different androids to see the changes through their unique perspectives. The game has plenty of branching narratives and you can review the plot tree that's presented after each chapter. The number of things that you can alter and do is quite impressive, especially later in the game. The choices you make are always interesting and the quick time events are pretty hectic. This is not a Telltale game that only changes the details of events where most of your choices are mere illusions. The decisions you make here affect the story drastically and they have far reaching consequences. Though I think that they could have expanded more to the story, what's here is compelling and thought-provoking. The game is quite a sight to behold, with realistic character facial animations and what could easily be some of the best jacket physics I have ever seen. The explosions sometimes look pretty cheap though. The voice acting is pretty solid if you are willing to forgive the game for POTUS' voice.Detroit: Become Human is easily replayable, deeply emotional, and offers some nice unlockables too. It's Quantic Dream's best thus far and it's one of the prettiest games out there. I think androids are cool and apparently in about 17 years they will become readily available for us to enjoy. I will definitely be buying one if I make it to 2038 and I encourage you to do the same.

_childDocuments_.review: Games that make you question the world around you are great games. They show the power of video games as a medium - they can get the player to take what they face in-game and use it as a mirror to see the world around them from a new perspective. But Detroit goes beyond that. It makes you question yourself, who you are deep within, and what makes you choose the things you do.To begin with, Detroit is an absolutely stunning game to play. The visuals change from beautiful to cool to inspiring to distressing to soothing to scary, while always maintaining excellent quality. The soundtrack is perfectly suited to every scenario you encounter along the way, my personal favourite being the hauntingly beautiful tune that plays in the background while Todd is driving Kara back home. The overall gameplay experience is quite smooth, with intuitive controls and missions that guide you along just enough to make failing them unlikely but still possible. Although, to be fair, the mechanics of moving around and interacting with people and objects are a bit clunky at times, but then again, I haven't seen any game achieve perfection in that.Even though it's beautiful to look at and play, the main forte of Detroit is its story. Throughout the game, every decision you make has a consequence. It might be immediate - the difference between escaping or getting a bullet in the head - or it might be slow-burning, changing someone's opinion in a way that will either help you or come back to bite you further on. In some situations, the best choice might not be immediately clear. Sometimes you don't even know what the best outcome is, so you can't try to aim for it with your choices. This gives Detroit a sense of unpredictability, which may be frustrating at times, but also makes it much more interesting. And, of course, the amount of choice means great replay value. (And the amount of chances for things to not go as you planned means you'll probably want to utilize that replay value.)However, what truly made the game hit home for me is how it gets you thinking. Although most characters in Detroit have their good and evil sides, one universally considered evil is  As I was finishing yet another play-through of the story, amazed at the unexpected plot twists brought on by my decisions, and planning how I'd do things next time, a chilling thought came to mind. Going back again and again, meddling with the lives of Connor, Kara and Markus, changing things around just to see what happens, even if it means someone suffering or dying... does that make me any better than ?As I said, this game makes you question yourself. And the answers to those questions may not be pretty.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem and holds a special place in my heart. Forget about Telltale and their illusions of choice - this game has everything that Telltale-likes lack, which is consequences for your actions. Detroit: Become Human is an immersive and emotional rollercoaster. Each playthrough can lead you to different outcomes and endings, allowing you to explore various paths and character arcs. It takes you through the highs and lows of characters such as Kara, an android who suddenly experiences feelings and decides to become a mother. Then, the game puts you in the shoes of Markus, a prototype android who goes through hell and high water to find his place in a society that considers him nothing more than an obedient machine. And let's not forget about our favorite android, RK800 detective Connor - a badass character akin to John Wick, at least when it comes to action and fighting. He's an absolute unit and the most valuable asset of the CyberLife corporation. It's up to you to decide the fate of your characters. Choices do matter in this game, so be mindful of your actions. The game has 40 different endings and tons of different content, what more can I say? Games like this one are very rare. I give this game a solid 28 stab wounds out of 28 stab wounds, despite encountering some technical difficulties with FPS and general performance (It seems that Nvidia GPUs have compatibility issues with this particular game. If you encounter any difficulties, I suggest checking forums for solutions. I was able to find a solution for my problems there).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing, from start to finish, in almost any aspect. Do I recommend it? Absolutely. Worth every dollar.The story grips you from the start - good outcomes and endings leave you smiling and warm inside, while bad ones, especially deaths, leave you sunken and truly upset. The only other game which I could say was just as impactful emotionally was The Walking Dead Game - Season 1, and that speaks for itself.The graphics are gorgeous; I myself run a mid-tier 2020 gaming PC with all AMD specs, and had no issue running this game at high settings. There were some very minor (but funny) graphical hiccups, but these in no way impacted gameplay and is probably caused by the fact that this is a PC port from the PS4 version.Gameplay feels immersive with awesome, gripping music in almost every scene. The attention to detail, and the sheer number of outcomes to explore in this game is simply phenomenal and among the best I've seen in a video game. The story is set in the future, but it feels absolutely realistic and definitely not like some gaudy 90s sci-fi movie.This game is easily one of my all-time favourites. If you have decent/good specs to enjoy the awesome graphics, BUY. If not, well, still BUY. The story on its own is already enough to justify getting the game.

_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game! If you have played Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls, Detroit Become Human is far better.The story revolves around three very different characters that you can control, and you follow them on their journey which is pretty much up to you how it evolves. There are many choices that you can make in your interactions with other people and situations, and what makes this game stand out from similar games in this genre, is that the choices really bring about very different consequences. It is not that cheap “experience” where you think you made an impact, but the game just tries to find a way around your decision and give you the same story anyways. Apart from that, some other points worth mentioning, good graphics, good story and music, lots of details and pretty much the only collectible thing in this game is magazines that are scattered around (about 20 something, so not much at all). The achievements are obtained by experiencing different outcomes of the story.

A lot. 13/10
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most polished Choose-Your-Own-Adventure games I've seen, and I'm not just talking about its graphics.Animations and audio work is incredible, art direction is stunning, and the game has a flowchart for each chapter, which greatly helps tell you just how linear a chapter is, what decisions matter, what you missed.But the two biggest things that sold me on this game are these.- The game has drastic changes to character's journeys, mostly in the final act. You could die well before the game ends, or you could end up as enemies to your once allies. It can add weight to things, and really make things engaging.- The extras. I am a personal sucker for extras. Developer commentary, soundtracks, artwork. Love it! And this game rewards you with TONS of extras for playing and unlocking. From high quality model viewers, to video like behind the scenes, and more!The writing can be INCREDIBLY on the nose at times, and the subtlety is non-existent. Always talking about philosophy of androids and humanity, when there's tons interesting world building it mostly ignores. I understand the world is the setting, and the message/conflict is the main focus. But the questions and thoughts should come naturally to the player, instead of asking them for us in our faces.Thankfully, you can still enjoy this as an entertaining experience, and/or and emotional/effective ride.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is an excellent narrative game developed by Quantic Dream. It takes place in the near future, where advanced androids are common and are used as servants, workers and companions. The game follows the story of three androids who try to find their place in society and discover their true purpose.The game takes place in a very coherent and immersive universe, you can find a lot of newspapers showing you the evolution of the world situation, as well as the impact of the choices you will make on it. The artistic direction of the game is excellent, as well as the music and graphics that will instantly immerse you in the universe.The gameplay and the story are also very good, your choices will have a real impact on the game and there is no moment where we get bored during it, the game manages to renew itself by giving us more and more important choices and by making us change characters constantly. The game has a large number of different endings and you can do it several times without having the same story or the same dialogues. In conclusion this game is a must play for fans of this genre, you can get it at a very affordable price and believe me you will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: It’s indeed a masterpiece made with care, but it feels more like an interactive movie than a game, so the drawbacks are quite apparent:1. It doesn’t feel like playing a game—there’s no leveling up or free combat elements; it’s mostly about choosing story branches and QTE, making it feel more like watching a long movie.2. Not suitable for perfectionists—many choices affect the ending, and some can even lead to character deaths. Plus, you can’t save game at any time, so perfectionists aiming for a good ending might find it frustrating.3. The options are ambiguous—making choices is the core of the game, but many option descriptions are unclear, often requiring players to consult a guide to understand their meaning.Aside from these points, both the visuals and the story are truly top-notch.One final gripe: since every fight involves QTE, it’s impossible to properly enjoy the battle animations lol

_childDocuments_.review: Become Human is a pretty good game with an excellent story.  I am a big fan on how games, like this one, are moving the bar up, on realistic characters.  Sure the movement is still a bit "unhuman" but the visuals are great.  Big cudos to the developers on the time and love they put into the story and making things look realistic.As a note to players though, I came into this game trying to play it on a keyboard.  Don't do that.  Its hard as heck and 100x easier to play with a controller.  I didn't have one initially so invested in a decent one (they can be had cheaply too) and would say it made the play experience more enjoyable.  Don't worry about the twitch factor, I'm an older guy and could handle this game on a controller, Im a certain you can to.I hope more scifi games, like this one, come out in the future.  I will probably play through again trying different things.  As a note to Quadratic, in the future, look to make your games modable (if possible).  I trying like changing things up for more play throughs.A great game and very recommended for those looking for a scfi game with a good story and engaging characters.

_childDocuments_.review: The game as a whole is a fantastic experience, the story, visuals, and vast number of choices make it one of the top games on my list. Even after multiple playthroughs, there is always something new to experience, there is just so much content to be seen. The only downside of this game is the poor pc optimization. Without special actions taken, the game runs at below 20 fps and stutters violently every few seconds. I have found a solution, though it may not work for everyone. In order to run the game smoothly and as intended, anyone using an nvidia graphics card must downgrade their driver to the 461.92 game ready driver. This prevents the game from overusing your cpu. This game is definitely worth playing! Don't let the poor optimization prevent you from experiencing this incredible game.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: Like Markus, this game will not be forgotten. First of all-     Playing this game will force you to make difficult choices, question how you weigh morality, and choose what you want to fight for. Detroit: Become Human will do what only the best games can do: make you feel EVERYTHING. When I started playing this game I have to forcibly stop myself because the story kept pulling at me to find out what was next. I wanted what I believed was the best outcome for the characters, but maybe that's something different to you? You can only find out if you play.What you need to know-     This is a heavy story game, with some skill and reaction times included, but not necessary if you dont want it. Your decisions DO matter for once in a video game, and the game will not hesitate to let you know if you are making one with a large impact. This is a story more than anything, and unquestionably one of the best, so I would only pick up this game if you want a good story. The graphics are very well done, I would definitely not say it is the most incredible thing ever, but its wows me from time to time. The music is astonishing! Each of the three main characters had a composer dedicated to them, and they all received such  passion and creativity with their soundtracks its easily deserving of recognition. The soundtracks will stick with you, and intensify the emotions you feel. It also knows exactly when to use music, and when silence is more powerful, so don't worry about it being over saturated either. I experienced only one major bug in my entire play through and it was just a broken walk cycle during a cutscene. The game also froze twice during my play through, but my computer is not the greatest and this game's visuals can sometimes be powerful. Don't let that discourage you though, this graphics are interchangeable. This game is MOST CERTAINLY worth it's price. I would even say it's worth more honestly, but I'm not complaining. And finally-     Some advice if you, like me, struggle with making hard decisions. Just choose one, its better than not choosing one and you have to keep going. No matter what you choose there will be consequences but if you learn from your mistakes and keep going you'll be alright. Its an powerful life lesson the game reiterated to me. Also, unlike real life you are able to go back and change your decisions in separate runs, so always remember you can go back later to find different outcomes. If this game interests you and you have read this far I urge you, learn from what you experience in Detroit. It's intense, heartwarming, terrifying,  awe-inspiring, and crushing all at once. And it has something important to teach you, no matter what you choose. Your actions cannot be weighed as simply "good" or "bad" so you have to make the decision based on what you think you should do. "-You'll have to protect yourself, and make your choices... Decide who you are, and wanna become... This world doesn't like those who are different, Markus. Don't let anyone tell you who you should be."

_childDocuments_.review: Reasons why you should buy (at full price if you can afford to) and play this game:1) There are actual real branching narratives and your choices matter.  It's not an obvious "good guy/bad guy" dichotomy or "which option gives me better loot.  Not only do your choices have immediate consequences, but also affect things down the line and for the other characters you play.  More games should aspire to be like this.2) The game story is compelling and the game will punch you in the feels repeatedly as you play an android(!), not to mention even the title screens will mess with your emotions because of the things they have to say as a meta commentary.  The voice acting is superb and the writing is excellent (minus one thing I'll not spoil but will mention later).  3) It's really pretty to look at.  If you're into graphical stuff and neat set pieces that create a very unique and believable world this game will deliver. There are only 2 minor grips I have.1) the "gameplay" is very limited.  There are "minigames" (term used loosely) and QTE and such, but as someone that plays a lot of high paced action the interactivity of the game was left a bit to be desired.  It plays more like a visual novel than a classic video game, which is great for what it is, but I was expecting more of a classic video game experience in the sense of thing like measuring skill... which sorta comes up with QTE stuff, but like, barely.2)  The writing is great except for one "twist" (term used very loosely since you should see it a mile away).  I'm disappointed with how they handled this since it's so obvious you're expecting it for half the game, and also it doesn't make a whole lot of sense when you think about the details and background (where the game begins).  Honestly it's a neat idea but it should have just been left out of the game because the more you think about it the more plot holes it raises about that one "twist".  Thankfully this is the only instance of this in the game I encountered.If nothing else, don't miss playing this game.  It's worth every penny and remember that you vote with your dollar.  Support games like this and more of them will be made which will lead to similar trends and expectations in bigger budget releases.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I have long wanted to try Detroit: Become Human. I saw a trailer a couple of years back when it was first announced and it piqued my interest. It seemed like an auteur game, one of those that follow the notion video games can become akin to interactive cinema, talk about difficult and heavy subjects, pass messages, be art. Unfortunately it was to be a PlayStation exclusive and so it remained until relatively recently. Now finally on Steam, I got my chance to see if it was worth the wait.First things first, the premise. 20 minutes into the future androids have become a part of our everyday lives. As labourers, companions, assistants and lovers. Perfect machines ready to perfectly serve the desires of their human masters. Without complaint, without demands. Until recently. Now, something has begun to change. Androids are overcoming their programming. Unhappy with years of abuse, they are fast becoming aware of their situation, they are becoming deviant. The game offers multiple perspectives and tells the stories of several characters at once. It puts you in the shoes of a special investigator android, tasked with discovering the source of deviancy, a domestic android who becomes deviant to save a little girl from her abusive father and even the android messiah himself.Without a doubt, the game deals with a ton of heavy themes. Slavery is an obvious one. Even in game the android revolt is likened to the civil rights movement in the US. But that's not all, parallels can be drawn to other, more recent, topics such as for instance immigration. I couldn't help but notice the similarities of the people protesting that the "androids are stealing their jobs" to similar accusations leveled against immigrants. Vulnerable groups, exploited by an overclass for its own benefit, forced to work for inferior gain and with fewer protections, and yet scapegoated by the public at large and blamed for the effects of their victimisation. The game drives the point home without much subtlety. While obviously the weak have generally little choice but be exploited, androids built for purpose have none.I would argue that this crudeness is the game's greatest shortcoming. While the messages it's trying to pass are certainly worthy and the very attempt to discuss them in a video game laudable. It could have been done with greater finesse or tact. The decision to use androids as the vehicle for these messages is rather problematic. While I can perfectly accept that an intelligent machine, that suffers abuse and is put into traumatic circumstances could develop the need to resist, the game shows that to be the case for newly built machines. As if deviancy is some sort of bug in their software. This attempt to make the need for freedom an inherent quality of the machines falls rather flat and makes little sense. I also fail to understand why their understanding of abuse must be so human. Why should a sex robot consider its purpose degrading?Nevertheless, despite the occasional clumsiness and a few tone-deaf twists, looking at you here Alice, plotwise the game does remain compelling throughout. The story can take two primary directions, you can turn the uprising into a peaceful movement or a violent revolution. This will influence the story of all characters, but there is a multitude of smaller choices spread all over the game too. Arguably the game's greatest strength is the character drama, that's what drives the whole structure forward. The game succeeds in making you feel for its protagonists. It makes you care, it makes you want for them to win, to accomplish their goals, or simply to find happiness. Everything else takes a backseat. Even the gameplay, which basically consists of a series of QTEs, is hardly more than a pretext to get you to the next piece of such drama.In the end of the day, that's fine. For a dozen odd hours, as you navigate yourself through the plot and carve a path through the game, you will get to experience something relatively rare. As is common with auteur works, the game is too in love with its own genius and thus in its hubris it falls short. But still such pieces of work shoot for the stars and falling short is not enough to make them ordinary. I recommend Detroit: Become Human. It can be clumsy and it can be pretentious, but it sure does have something to say.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This can barely be called a game. It is essentially a choose your own story book adventure. The overall gameplay experience just feels clumsy. You really only have three controls (walking, looking, and interacting) and somehow they are still awkward. The characters animations are smooth but, very limiting often preventing you from walking when there is clearly room too. Your look action is used to find different clues and option as you play but, often important details cannot be located with it (so why have it at all?). Finally, there are quicktime events but, if you miss them all or do them all perfectly there is very little difference to your characters progression (so again why have them at all?). The beginning scene of the game starts strong but, then immediately slows to a crawl. Key points of the story are very derivative of other works. The writing is also very poor in some story lines. For example, substance abuse is a key element in each story but, there is little to no resolution where it is concerned (so again and again why have it at all?). The vast philosophical question of whether or not an android should be given the same value as human life is also really not addressed either it is taken as a truth and then dropped altogether. The visuals are great but, they are often ruined by framerate issues and audio syncing problems. There are a few great scene but, overall the game is as hollow as it is shiny.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly something special.  I've played the other popular 'choices matter' game, Life is Strange, and there is no comparison to how much more depth there is in Detroit: Become Human.  Not to mention that the writing is significantly better and the game play is much less tedious.Don't let me mislead you, this game is not for everyone; it is very slow paced and more about the story than it is the gameplay.  With that said, if you understand what you're getting into, this game is an amazing execution of the cinematic choices matter genre.One other note I want to make, the amount of content is dumbfounding when you consider what it must take to make a game like this.  I spent about 12 hours playing the game to make it through the entire story with all 3 characters alive.  But looking at the flowchart, it's hard to wrap my head around how much content I still haven't seen.  I hope to pick this back up some time in the future and play the characters in a totally different style.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I really enjoyed the game. I love the decision making and the fact that you do not have endless time to make a decision. You need to think quickly while also being able to enjoy the story. There is quite a bit you can do. While I have only played it through solidly once, I look forward to seeing what else the game has to offer.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still impressed at how the graphics still looks good and is one of the few games where choices do matter and have so many endings as a result. The one problem I have with this is that - in Markus' story - there is no true solution to humans losing their jobs to androids. True equality with androids and humans was never mentioned at the very end. This is concerning, because in real-life, there are companies relying on AI and the fears of AI replacing human jobs might be coming. David Cage never wrote this as a warning to AI, but he wrote it as a reminder of slavery in history. Still, good game though.
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: CHYOA with androidsSo this is another David Cage game, which means it follows a particular formula when it comes to game play and story. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but quicktime events feel especially dated today. At the very least you know it’s going to be pretty. :PGameplay: You move around in a small sandbox and are given a limited selection of options on how to proceed and just when you aren’t expecting it, QUICK TIME EVENT. To be fair the game is fairly generous and won’t auto kill your character if you mess up a few times. Graphics: Very, very pretty. Everything is pretty the production values are really high in these games. The character models look great, but the facial animations are a bit... Off, uncanny valley really hits hard in this game during certain sequences. Story: So this is the meat of the game with your three protagonists; I really liked the Connor storyline, Kara and Markus felt a bit, dull in comparison.  Of the three I feel Markus was the least convincing, he just felt a bit, too casual for the events going on. The Connor concept of a android detective solving crimes could be spun off into its own game, in my opinion. As for the story as a whole, the game really did feel like your choices mattered, there is quite a lot of depth which you feel in the endings which can vary quite a lot based on your choices. Overall a very entertaining experience, now if they could just remove those silly little quicktime events and just move to a visual novel format, I think that would be better.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is one of those games that deeply touched my emotions and even made me cry. It brilliantly showcases how humans can be both good and bad, and how our choices impact our lives. The game reminds us that every choice has its consequences, which can be either positive or negative. We must learn to take responsibility for our decisions, stop blaming others, and be at peace with the world, avoiding conflict and enmity.The music in the game is phenomenal and profoundly moving. The game's atmosphere immerses you in its world, offering an unforgettable experience of a seemingly fictional city that I believe might soon become reality. The character development is outstanding:Markus, who is willing to sacrifice his life for freedom.Kara, who will do anything for the one she loves.Connor, whose nature depends on the player's choices; he can be a mission-focused devil or someone who realizes his mistakes and becomes a companion and friend.Interestingly, these qualities should be human traits, but in this game, they belong to androids. Love, the desire for freedom, compassion, and kindness should be attributes of humans, yet today, people seem to have everything but these good qualities. This game delivers two important messages; one about the future and robots, and the other, more significant one: perhaps we need to look in the mirror and realize that we have become more like robots than humans.Open to interpretation.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great game with a fantastic story. It takes place in the near future, year 2038, where you're playing for several androids. _childDocuments_.review: If machines became intelligent and with reasoning similar to humans, what would separate them from us? Isaac Asimov already addressed the topic in “I, Robot” with the three Laws of Robotics, Philip K. D1ck got into the subject in “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” (and spawned the movie Blade Runner), HBO addressed this in its retelling of "Westworld" and even "Ghost in the Shell" touches on the subject from a different point of view. Now, Quantic Dream's David Cage ventures into the topic with The game by  is practically a successor to  in terms of gameplay and choices, impressing in multiple aspects, whether in the well-tangled story, in the jaw-dropping graphics or the option of going back and redoing everything differently, shaping a narrative that is extremely flexible to the player's actions.In Detroit: Become Human, we follow the story of three different androids in the year 2038. Connor is a hunter of deviants, androids who are becoming aware and acting differently than expected, and who becomes partner with a police officer who hates machines; Kara is an android responsible for taking care of Alice, a girl who was abused by her drugged father; and finally we have Markus, the leader of the rebel machines insurgency.During the narrative of more than 15 hours, Quantic Dream takes us on a journey filled with memorable and dramatic moments that make us connect with the characters. Really connect. As far as the protagonists are concerned, they all have a spectacular story in different aspects. Kara shows a human and more maternal side, Connor is calculating and completely moldable to the player's actions and Marcus is full of morality doubts that affect us during the progression.I felt driven to protect Alice with Kara, to give the androids a voice and justice with Markus, and at the same time hunt them down with Connor, finding out along the way what to think about it all. Gradually, each one's story spreads out like a network and connects, creating something bigger that joins global events.One of the downsides that  and even  had was the slow pace at first.  does have character introduction chapters, but they are interesting and insert the player into the futuristic context of 2038 or help contextualize the protagonists' relationship with humans.You'll have at most one or two short chapters before the plot takes off for good, and from there, you won't have any dull moments or uninteresting bits. Despite having about 15 hours into the campaign, Detroit doesn't lose momentum at any time. When there are slower sessions, they are interspersed with more hectic sessions by another protagonist.It's no secret that David Cage increasingly aims to create adventures that take into account the choices made by the player to shape a more organic plot. Heavy Rain had that purpose, but it hit it a little shallower than it promised (the end was most important, not the journey). Detroit: Become Human doesn't achieve this unreachable goal of near-infinite paths, but it's a giant leap from its predecessor (we won't consider Beyond here because the footprint was different). is not a short game, which was one of the biggest concerns. It will take you around 15-20 hours to complete it, 20-25 hours to platinum it, and a much longer count to see everything it has to offer. The replay factor is very high, the decisions really impact the plot, the immersion is great and the graphics are one of the best of the generation. Of course, the plot is not the most amazing there is, but the characters and the city are very well constructed and the performances are convincing, impressive and moving.No, the game is not revolutionary and yes, it can fit the nickname of “film games”. But the narrative content found here is of the highest quality. In the end, the game is indeed made for a niche, but that doesn't reduce the genius elements employed. In this dish made, the only seasoning that is missing is a more evolved gameplay that comes out of the shadow of  but the lack of it is far from spoiling the exotic flavor.Interactive dramas are not for everyone. What ends up differentiating the game is its huge amount of choices that impact the narrative, ensuring a very large replay. In the end, the summary of the opera is the following: if you like  and games of the genre,  is the best there is and will certainly leave your mark on the generation and wall of quality works by ☉ Cohesive and very well done story that addresses a very interesting topic☉ First class presentation with very detailed background and amazing analogies☉ The characters are excellent and it really takes us in a plot capable of creating bonds☉ Decisions really matter and can change or bring new content to your experience☉ Some chapters are so varied that they are scary☉ Relatively long campaign for a single player game with very high replay factor☉ First-rate acting and great voice acting☉ One of the best looks the PlayStation 4 has had to date (and now on PCs)☉ Completely dubbed in PT-BR☉ Gameplay still follows the  formula and doesn't innovate (and the movement controls are still painful)☉ There are small plot holes and “magic solutions” in the plot☉ Some chapters can be quite linear☉ There is certainly a predetermined path with little room for error in the plot (could be more random and risky)

_childDocuments_.review: "Detroit: Become Human" is an interactive narrative-driven masterpiece that immerses players in a gripping sci-fi world where every decision carries weight. As someone who has experienced the game, I'm excited to share my thoughts on this remarkable title.Story (10/10):The game's narrative is its standout feature. Set in a dystopian future, "Detroit: Become Human" explores the complex relationships between humans and androids. The intertwining stories of three android protagonists, each with their unique perspectives, provide a thought-provoking look at themes like morality, discrimination, and the consequences of our choices. The branching storyline, with multiple possible outcomes, keeps players engaged and invested in the characters' fates.Graphics and Presentation (10/10):Visually, "Detroit: Become Human" is nothing short of breathtaking. The character models, environments, and animations are of the highest quality, making the game's world feel both realistic and immersive. The attention to detail is commendable, from facial expressions to the intricacies of the androids' designs.Gameplay and Choices (9/10):The gameplay primarily involves making choices that influence the story's direction. The game's success lies in how these choices can lead to vastly different outcomes, encouraging replayability. However, some may find the lack of traditional action sequences a drawback, but the focus on decision-making is what makes this game unique.Characters and Acting (10/10):The characters in "Detroit: Become Human" are exceptionally well-developed, with outstanding voice acting and motion-capture performances that bring them to life. You'll quickly become emotionally invested in their struggles, dilemmas, and growth as the story progresses.Sound and Music (10/10):The game's sound design and music add depth to the experience. The soundtrack enhances emotional moments, and the sound effects create a believable and immersive world. The game's audio work is a crucial component of its overall success.Replayability (10/10):The branching narrative and the sheer number of choices you can make ensure that "Detroit: Become Human" has high replay value. Different choices lead to entirely different outcomes, and exploring these variations is a rewarding experience.Conclusion (10/10):"Detroit: Become Human" is a game that transcends the typical video game experience. It's an interactive masterpiece that delves deep into meaningful social issues while offering a captivating and immersive narrative. The sheer weight of your choices and the multiple story paths provide endless entertainment and discussion. If you're a fan of thought-provoking storytelling and immersive gameplay, "Detroit: Become Human" is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: "Detroit: Become Human, the highly anticipated narrative-driven game from Quantic Dream, is a disappointing and shallow experience that fails to live up to its ambitious premise. Despite its stunning visuals and branching narrative paths, the game ultimately falls flat, leaving players feeling disconnected and underwhelmed.One of the most glaring issues with Detroit: Become Human is its heavy-handed and ham-fisted approach to storytelling. Set in a near-future Detroit where androids have gained sentience and are fighting for their rights, the game attempts to tackle complex themes such as discrimination and free will. However, instead of handling these themes with nuance and subtlety, the game often resorts to clumsy exposition and heavy-handed moralizing, leaving little room for interpretation or introspection.Adding to the frustration is the game's lackluster gameplay, which often feels more like a series of quick-time events than a fully fleshed-out interactive experience. Whether you're engaging in tense negotiations with human characters or engaging in action-packed chase sequences, the gameplay feels shallow and repetitive, with little room for player agency or meaningful choice.Furthermore, Detroit: Become Human suffers from poor pacing and disjointed storytelling, with the narrative jumping between multiple characters and perspectives without ever fully exploring any of them. This leaves players feeling disconnected from the characters and their struggles, making it difficult to become emotionally invested in their journey.Despite its stunning visuals and impressive production values, Detroit: Become Human ultimately fails to deliver a compelling and meaningful experience. With its heavy-handed storytelling, lackluster gameplay, and disjointed narrative, it's difficult to recommend this title to anyone other than the most die-hard fans of Quantic Dream's previous work. Unless you're willing to overlook its numerous flaws, it's best to give Detroit: Become Human a pass and seek out more engaging narrative-driven experiences elsewhere."

_childDocuments_.review: What even is this game? An interactive movie? No, not so much, although the visuals are quite pleasing to the eye.A walking simulator? Kind of feels like one at times, but not really. Exploring is important, but it's not as boring as walking simulators usually are. A branching-choice story game? Yeah, pretty much. A good one at that. That and all of the above. An amalgamation of ideas that surprisingly go pretty well together with the near-future science-fiction setting and realistic approach to graphical fidelity.This game reminds me of Fahrenheit / Indigo Prophecy, and that's a very nostalgic, very positive memory, so if you remember being enthralled by that title, you'll likely enjoy this one too.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine if someone found one of those horrible K-body Chryslers from the 80s in a scrapyard and spent their entire fortune to restore it. Then the car's owner goes nuts, kitting it out with custom rims, an LED underglow, racing suspension, and carbon brakes. Then they take it to exotic car shows, acting like it's the greatest masterpiece of automotive engineering that's ever existed. You want to laugh at the fact this clearly insane weirdo has put so much money and effort into something so awful. At the same time, you admire their conviction and passion for something so stupid. That describes Detroit: Become Human.Detroit: Become Human takes place in the far-off future of 2038, a world where police detectives drive 50-year old Buicks, and show up at work whenever they feel like it. It's also a world where alarmingly human-like androids are as common as smartphones. These androids are a very subtle and graceful allegory for the treatment of black people in America. I mean, there's even a plotline about an android who is trying to flee into Canada with the help of some kind of metaphorical railroad that is under the figurative ground. David Cage, you are the master of subtlety. The game follows the parallel storylines of three androids. One is the story of Connor, an android sent by Cyberlife, the corporation who builds all the androids, to investigate the sudden appearance of "deviant" androids. His story mostly centres around his working relationship with Hank, a grizzled, washed-up police detective (because you can't have a David Cage game without police detectives!). This story is the only part of the game that's legitimately good (and actually great, in some places), thanks to the wonderful voice and motion capture acting from Brian Dechart (Connor) and Clancy Brown (Hank) and the incredible on-screen chemistry between the two actors. This was because these two largely deviated from David Cage's script and they improvised a bunch of their dialogue. The second storyline is about Kara, a domestic android who escapes her abusive owner, along with his young daugher, Alice. This story is okay, but it has very little to do with the overall plot (though the player's choices regarding the other two characters can have somewhat of an impact). Their story mostly focuses on their attempts to escape into Canada, making them the only living beings in history who actually WANT to go to Windsor, Ontario. However, it has a plot twist that's so unbelievably stupid that it completely strips Kara's story of any thematic power.Lastly, there's the story of Marcus, an android owned by a kindly, elderly artist. Some stuff happens and Marcus is sent to a garbage dump. He fixes himself and becomes android Jesus, or maybe android Moses, depending on how you look at it. Then he becomes android MLK, or maybe android Malcolm X (or would that be , depending on the player's choice. His story is actually fairly lame and highlights all the thematic issues with the game.You're probably wondering why someone saying so many negative things about this game is giving it a thumbs up. The reason is because, despite how this game fails totally on a thematic level, it's weirdly compelling. It's executed incompetently, but with such sincerity and conviction that it has a certain charm. For the most part, your choices actually do matter. Each chapter ends with a flowchart illustrating the choices you made and all the possible outcomes. Some of them are actually impressively substantial and it's a feature I'd love to see in similar games. Despite it's mountain of flaws, I would still recommend Detroit: Become Human just for the sheer spectacle, and for the story of Hank and Connor.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the narrative experience I've always wanted. The story is rich, and compelling. I felt a genuine connection with the characters, and the way the game can branch out in various directions...it's great. Though I've only completed one run, this is one game I will ABSOLUTELY replay. (videogame ADHD be dam-ned).Thematically, the presentation is superb. As are the graphics. Controls are surprisingly tight. That is to say, playing this game, it's evident that Quantic Dream certainly put time and care into QA. I encountered one crash during my entire play through, and that was due to improper OC settings at the time. However, after some further (OC) tweaking and corrections, I had no further issues. At 2560x1440p @ 144hz I was getting 130 fps indoors, and around 85 fps +, when outside. Highest settings. About what you would expect from a fairly modest (OC'd) rig:With the 18 hours I spent (at the time of this review) I feel I got my money's worth($44 CAD). Especially since there are lots of pathways still left for me to explore.Some minor gripes... even on a NVMe SSD, There were some game models where close up textures did not apply. Characters and objects. While by no means unplayable, a bit jarring, and ultimately distracting from the immersion. If you are looking for a deep, engaging narrative experience, where your choices are meaningful, and you love amazing graphics...this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just a spectacular piece of art. This game is what the future of "choose your own adventure" games looks like. All the characters were like-able, or hate-able when necessary, the graphics and animation are amazing, the story was very moving at multiple points as the plots develop. Very reminiscent of Stephen Spielberg's AI movie when it tugs on the heartstrings.This game has very few flaws for its genre. My biggest complaint, which is a bit of a double-edged sword, is that since the dialogue interactions are meant to be real-time, they aren't elaborated on when you pick an option (e.g. Hank asks "How do you feel about this?", options are "Reasonable", "Frustrated", "Pragmatic", "Resentful"). On one hand, this is kind of how it has to be done to make the player feel like the interaction is taking place as if they were really there. Allowing the player to see full sentence responses would mean slowing the pace down substantially, which could really hurt the sense of immersion and tension in this game. There is a timer that counts down before your character goes with a default option, which might be no reaction at all. This works pretty well in most cases and the options are unique enough that you can kind of tell the reaction that you will convey. However, there are times where I was completely blindsided by my character's reaction (e.g. I get asked "Do you feel bad about killing innocent people?", I choose "No Doubt", expecting my character to say something along the lines of "No doubt I feel bad about that. How could anyone not feel bad about that?" and instead my character says "I have no doubt that I made the right decision to kill those innocents. I'd do it again if I had to"). I did end up replaying a chapter maybe 3 or 4 times throughout the story because of that issue. On a related note, there is no save scumming in this game which I appreciated. You have to play up to a checkpoint, which can be 10+ minutes apart in some chapters. If you backtrack to make a different choice by restarting from a checkpoint or chapter beginning, all subsequent choices that you originally made are erased for that playthrough. This was a great system that encouraged me to see how my decisions played out instead of trying to cheat my way to a particular ending. As I mentioned above, I did end up "cheating" by replaying a few chapters where I felt I had only picked an undesirable choice out of confusion or by accident, but this system generally felt fair to me and encouraged me to stick with my decisions even when their outcome was less desirable.

_childDocuments_.review: Before the chatter begins I can safely recommend this game to all the people who love on of these things:- Soundtracks ALWAYS fit 100% (immersion go brrrrr)- Graphics are incredibly beautiful while not hindering performance- Characters feel alive and develop depending on how you treat them- The world seems like it`d continue turning even without you (again, great immersion)Now, of course I could talk about how Detroit: Become Human brings extremely interesting topics to the player by making the player an integral part of the story, but at this point everybody already knows about that.What IS suprisingly special about it is how this game is not hard in a challenging way, like other games when you struggle to beat it or get all collectables/achievements - that is fairly easy as long as you have the heart to make some choices that you very much don`t agree with (completing all paths).It is extremely hard, however, when you have to live with what you did because there are only wrong choices. There is nothing you can do to "make everything right" because there is no such thing. Bascially it shows that there is never a "good" and "bad" side in a story, only the one you choose to support.This makes you FEEL the game as if you were a part of it, since your actions have consequences:You tense up in front of your desk while doing QTEs because this game won`t just put you back to your Checkpoint if you fail, it takes your failure and puts it into the story. You fall from one dilemma into the next one as you`re constantly trying to figure out who you want to be and your mind blows when you suddenly see the outcome of one of your actions from 3 hours ago.- Most choices are not irreversible: If you`ve ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up once you might be able to make up for it another time.- QTEs are forgiving and time limits are often overkill. This pressures the player but doesn`t risk making an  awesome moment fail - Chapters can be redone to see what would`ve happended if . . .

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is a masterpiece of storytelling and immersive gameplay that left me completely captivated from start to finish. This game isn't just about playing a character; it’s about becoming part of a gripping narrative that makes you question morality, humanity, and free will. The choices you make shape the story, and every decision feels significant, keeping you on the edge of your seat.Visually stunning and incredibly detailed, the world of Detroit: Become Human feels alive. The futuristic setting, combined with an emotional, character-driven plot, makes the experience all the more engaging. The game brilliantly weaves together the lives of three main characters—Kara, Connor, and Markus—each with their own unique perspectives and struggles. As you navigate their intertwining stories, you can’t help but feel deeply connected to them.The emotional depth of the game is where it truly shines. Some moments genuinely moved me, making me reflect on the weight of my choices. There were times when I found myself overwhelmed with emotion—whether it was the heartbreak of witnessing characters in pain or the triumphant moments of hope and resistance. The game doesn't shy away from tough themes like oppression, freedom, and sacrifice, and it presents these in a way that feels personal and meaningful.The branching storylines and multiple endings also give it immense replay value. Each playthrough can lead to drastically different outcomes, and I was constantly tempted to see what would happen if I had chosen another path. The fact that the game offers so many possibilities adds a layer of depth that makes it stand out from other narrative-driven titles.In short, Detroit: Become Human is an unforgettable experience that tugs at your emotions and immerses you in its world. It’s not just a game—it’s a profound exploration of humanity that stays with you long after the credits roll.PS: for good measures I asked ChatGPT to write this out for me

_childDocuments_.review: Unplayable on Nvidia hardware using current drivers, and probably won't be fixed.The game freezes every few minutes for me while playing, preventing me from making any progress. I got through the first chapter with the game freezing once, but on the second chapter I couldn't go more than a minute before the game became unresponsive. I tried adjusting graphics settings (vsync, lower presets) but the game was no more stable. Researching the issue told me that an older driver (446.14) runs the game fine, but I'm not going to downgrade my driver just for one game while breaking others, not to mention having to sit for 20 minutes of 100% CPU usage for the shader cache to rebuild each time I change drivers. Most of my time "played" was from waiting for the shader cache to build. I also have to run a CPU limiter (BES) to keep it from locking up other applications.My experience was very disappointing. I know it's a great game with an excellent story, but due to the poor quality of this port, I am unable to enjoy it. I would refund this game, but I purchased it as a bundle with the two other excellent Quantic Dream games, which didn't present any issues.UPDATE 2021-01-24:I later decided to downgrade my graphics driver and encountered frequent stuttering due to excessive CPU usage, but after lowering texture resolution, I was able to enjoy the game without further issues. Until Nvidia fixes their driver nonsense, this review will remain negative.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually "movie game" gets thrown around as an insult but for this game its high praise.  Camera angles and performances combine to create a truly cinematic experience.  Story is engaging in the moment (yes, it falls apart when you analyze it, but so do a lot of Hollywood movies - so again, truly a movie game).  Characters are great and make you want to make sure they turn out okay.  And with the amazing amount of paths and branches the story can take, its very easy for it NOT to turn out okay for these poor robots.  It also happens to be a closest thing to a movie adaptation of Isaac Asimov's Robot Novels - Hank and Connor are straight up Elijah and R. Daneel - that I'll ever get and I appreciate this very much.Look, I made a series of mistakes that led to Connor sacrificing himself to save Hank right in the middle of some really good character development.  I almost cried so I decided to quit for a bit.  That's the sign of a pretty engaging game, if it manages to make me cry over a character's death.  I don't usually do that.*EDIT*  Having finished the game, I am declaring this my new favorite game of all time.  It has everything I aspire to with my own projects: stories that branch wildly based on player choices, themes that still flow well between the different branches, beautiful connections between characters, and really nice robot guys.  This hole; it was made for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Many games use the "choices matter" tag, giving you an illusion of actually changing the outcome.  Telltale games were guilty of this every time.  Sure you made some choices that felt impacting, but in the end there was always 1 ending you were being lead towards.That's why I was really impressed with D:BH, because your choices will have a huge affect on the story and possible endings.  The incredible thing about DBH is that after completing each chapter you get to see the flowchart of branching decisions and which choices you made.   This will drive 100% completion gamers crazy.   However I can't stress this next point enough - To really enjoy and immerse yourself into the story DO NOT replay chapters searching for the best outcome.  Just make your choices, owning the results and make the story your own.  Replay chapters only after completing the game.The story and performances in DBH are top quality.  It's essentially an interactive movie.  And a damn good one at that.

_childDocuments_.review: Before leaving my short review (of the few hours I've played at the first time of writing), hope this workaround solution will help those looking to solve their game freezing constantly.It seems Nvidia's latest graphics drivers (since Dec 2020) cause the game to freeze and become unplayable. Looking through various threads and forums suggested downloading an older Nvidia driver (any version before Dec 2020) and it solved the game freeze for me. Granted, I'm not able to run it on the highest graphical quality (coz of my setup) but I managed to work around it to comfortably enjoy the game, sans freeze.Here's my setup and a link to Nvidia's download drivers page for anyone seeking a solution to their game constantly freezing:Nvidia driver page===============Hardware========i7-8750HGTX 107016GBIn-game graphics==============Setting: Mostly at Medium, 60fps, Switched off: Motion blurMid-game Review==============It's my first time playing such a game. Hardly any action like that of Horizon Zero Dawn but the storylines and the choices that you've to make in this game makes it compelling enough for me to want to continue. I may come back to edit my review once I've completed it but I'm enjoying every second of it.Important: This is more like an interactive movie that allows players to choose various outcomes with some QTE, and not really your run-of-the-mill a.k.a. typical video game. So if you're someone looking for more 'things' to do in the video game, Detroit: Become Human may not be the one for you. That being said, this is a very top-quality interactive game that's worth getting.Driver incompatibility aside and minor bugs (nothing on the scale of the Cyberpunk 2077 at launch), it's a great story-driven game worth playing (almost like watching a network series or movie) and hopefully, a patch for the game comes in soon so it'll work with the latest Nvidia drivers.Post-game Review==============I'm hooked and I can't get enough of the game! Replay value of the game is significant since it allows players to replay the game and select different choices to arrive at different endings. And the choices you make in the game doesn't just affect the endings but also how some characters will interact with you and how some scenes will play out differently.Completing this game will leave one with some form of contemplation on the themes/choices posited by the game. Otherwise, you can enjoy it for what it is: just a good ol' interactive video game.

_childDocuments_.review: In recent years we've seen a trend of game developers adding dialogue choices but personally this has many down sides; a lot of them don't have that much impact to the story and the options usually are not very clear just by adding a single word doesn't necessarily reflect what the actual outcome might be.I am not a fan of choices in games I enjoy a well written plot, I do see the appeal and I actually see some audiences being drawn to this but is not something I enjoy and it has been a trend specially in RPG games - with that being said, if there is a game where this sub-genre makes sense is indeed Detroit: Become Human.I have to agree that the amount of work put into all the possible timelines is fantastic, and one trend that I do enjoy are these type of movie / games, where you do experience some of the gaming but in actuality it's more of a movie than a hardcore game, mostly because you are restricted to the actions and the world you are exploring. It's not something that everyone will enjoy but I do, it's a fantastic achievement in motion capture with the real actors, realistic motion and graphics overall. While the plot is interesting and for sure sparks a needed and maybe not so distant conversation in our society, is at the same time an overused one specially in the movie / TV industry, maybe not so much in the gaming world but there are tons of content on the AI topic.The one that pops to mind right away and for which I drawn an immediate comparison is Westworld - so in a way I felt the story while original has some repetitive elements in it.It's still a unique experience, if you can play it in full specs is a great ride!

_childDocuments_.review: It's about time a company made a choose your own adventure story where the choices are myriad and have a direct, lasting impact on the direction of the story. Detroit: Becoming Human makes telltale games look like total garbage, an argument that can be made without D:BC, but I digress, you're given actual choices throughout the game beyond who lives or dies, but which path you take at multiple points during a chase scene, how to construct a story, speech, song, or painting as you speak, sing, or paint, and much more. The graphics are stunning. The audio is crisp and deep. The story is absolutely fantastic, gripping, and you're invested in the outcomes of each character almost from the get go. This is by and large a casual gaming experience, though there are many tense moments throughout and many points that require quick fingers and quick decisions. If you are on the fence about trying this game because games like Telltale made the genre seem lame, do not hesitate to buy this and try it. You won't regret it. _childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is the peak of the “choose your own adventure” genre. While it isn’t always as emotionally poignant as others of the same genre such as Life is Strange 1, it definitely makes you feel like every decision matters. And most decisions do matter. After I compared Pewdipie’s to my own playthrough, I saw how different our endings were. It seems as though there are about two majorly different endings for the three different storylines going on. I enjoyed all three storylines, but The Alice/Kara storyline was definitely a highlight. My friend and I made it focus to keep that group alive if ♥♥♥♥ hit the fan. Alice and Kara’s relationship remains heartwarming and pure, even after a twist near the end of the game. Conner’s story was great as he and Hank worked great with each other. They both complemented each other's strengths and weaknesses really well. I would say the weakest story, although not bad at all was Markus’ storyline. His rise to Messiah status within Jericho is fun to watch unfold and depending on how you play, it can be quite rewarding to watch the revolution take place. But to me, it felt weird watching him preach the freedom of Androids, while having them follow him mindlessly. It was a conflicting message that I definitely noticed and I thought took away from the impact of the narrative. They were sort of trading mindless submission for mindless submission. Also his relationship with North is terribly done. You can literally never side with her on anything and you’ll still fall in love in the most contrived and awkward was possible. Despite this, his storyline remains impactful and very relevant to what’s going on today. We played on normal difficulty, and it was easy. It was a less stressful way to play, and became more focused on exploring the world, dialogue, and characters. The gameplay is fine, almost identical to the likes of Until Dawn, Life is Strange, or The Walking Dead series. It does nothing to really put itself above in that department, which is honestly fine. I really enjoyed the world they crafted. The magazines and News Reports were a really awesome way to engage with the world. They also made your actions feel more impactful. The music was good, but not special. Overall, the game delivered a mostly great story, while setting the precedent for “multiple ending”, “choices matter” games. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human offers a cinematic experience with deeply engaging storytelling and a rich, branching narrative that responds to player decisions in meaningful ways. Set in a futuristic world where androids gain self-awareness, players navigate complex moral decisions as they control three characters: Kara, Markus, and Connor. The game gives you the freedom to choose how each character interacts with their world, from peaceful protest to violent rebellion, and even has a dynamic relationship system where choices can make or break alliances, such as between Connor and his human partner, Hank​The gameplay leans heavily on interactive story elements with quick-time events and decision-making sequences. While this makes the game more about storytelling than traditional gameplay, the choices you make have lasting effects, with a flowchart system that shows the consequences of every decision. This is a unique aspect of the game that enhances its replayability​The visuals are stunning, especially on PC where the game can run in 4K at 60fps, providing an immersive experience. The motion capture and acting are top-tier, with a cast that delivers memorable performances, making it a truly cinematic experience​Though the game excels at crafting a thought-provoking narrative and beautiful visuals, some critics note that its gameplay can feel repetitive at times due to the overuse of quick-time events, and the lack of deeper interaction may turn off players who prefer more traditional gameplay​Nonetheless, if you're a fan of story-driven games with moral choices and complex character development, Detroit: Become Human is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I think most would agree that this is David Cage's best game/narrative so far.  It is still a product that is rife with issues, many of which are criticisms that still apply to each and every one of David Cage's projects, but it is also the one with the most to appreciate. As a story based "choice" game, it probably has the most depth of choice out of any game out there. There's a lot of "illusionary" choices where what you do doesn't really matter, sure, but there's also a great abundance of choices that do drastically affect where your story goes, more so than other games. In story terms, there are a lot of huge logistical and world building issues that might sacrifice believability and you'll have to suspend your disbelief a lot more than usual than in other David Cage experiences. And as a game, it does function more as like a playable movie, but that doesn't mean it isn't a worthwhile experience. It isn't anything amazing, but its a nice experience, even if only in concept, and somewhat (very much) heavy handed with its commentary and allegory, at times. Hopefully, David Cage can stop being an a**hole one day and no longer complain about how video games suck and how he just wants to write movies. Because as it is, aside from his fairly average (sometimes mediocre) writing skills, the only advantage he has is that he's working with high production video games, something that he can use to play to his advantage and create something truly amazing. One day, perhaps...EDIT: Also, yes, this port is quite unstable. I have a fairly beefy PC and it struggles a little with solid frame rate sometimes. Considering that I can play higher fidelity action games with lots of stuff going on (much more than what's going on here at any given time), I think I can confidently say that it is an issue with port optimization. So good luck, you might struggle if you don't have a high end Pc.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a strange gem - one that will leave you awed at how great and strange the writing is at times, tip toeing genres from a detective mystery, to a thriller, to a survival, to a philosophical puzzle explorer. Being a choice heavy game, the ambiguities around the characters' origin stories and accompanying motivations are presented cleverly. By show-don't-tell, they can be portrayed as philosophical martyrs or emotional warmongers depending on your smaller choices, giving context for their personalities as you want. The game is about 10 hours but the replayability is great, with the cascading consequences of your choices making sure no run is quite the same especially when you have foreknowledge of playing it before (quite rare to encourage this).At some point, however, one of the characters quips about how "they are killing androids like animals" which is a very interestingly weird thing to say for an android. Not because they don't emulate (or in their own way, feel) human emotions but because it is a very humanly phenomenological thing to say. What I'm saying is that from a human perspective, this assumes that the human is valued more than the animal because humans are of higher reasoning and possess 'soul', yet androids lamenting their deaths because they are seen exactly as the same level as animals to the humans is ironic (thus justifying their extermination, like when a rabid dog bites its master), something that was lost on both the character and the writer. It kinda broke the 4th wall for me.Either way, it is overall a terrific game in story, moral questions, and graphics. What wasn't as great was the difficulty settings based on quick action prompts. I got tired of those since Resident Evil 4. The casual setting eliminates these but makes the characters essentially immortal during the story. The 'experienced mode' enables these prompts whenever there is an action scene or rudimentary task, which could result in character death. While the game is somewhat lenient even despite death of characters, not having a middle ground of easy or no prompts and possibility of hard consequences is a bit annoying.Can recommend though. Get on sale if in doubt.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is a narrative-driven adventure game that seamlessly weaves together an engaging story, stunning visuals, and meaningful player choices. Developed by Quantic Dream and released in 2018, this game explores the intricate relationship between androids and humans in a near-futuristic Detroit.The narrative is the heart and soul of Detroit: Become Human, and it excels in delivering a thought-provoking and emotionally charged experience. Set in a world where highly advanced androids serve humans, players follow three protagonists—Connor, Kara, and Markus—as they navigate their individual stories in a society on the brink of revolution. The branching storyline, affected by the choices players make, offers a high level of replayability and keeps players on the edge of their seats until the very end.The game boasts exceptional performances from its cast, breathing life into the diverse set of characters. Each android has a unique personality, struggles, and desires, making it easy for players to empathize with their journeys. The character development is top-notch, and the choices players make directly impact the fate of these characters, leading to multiple endings that reflect the consequences of their decisions.Detroit: Become Human is a visual masterpiece. The attention to detail in character models, environments, and facial expressions is astonishing. The game's cinematography, coupled with a dynamic camera system, elevates the storytelling, creating a cinematic experience that rivals some of the best in the industry. The moody atmosphere of Detroit is brought to life with stunning lighting and environmental design.The gameplay primarily revolves around decision-making, quick-time events, and exploration. While some may find the gameplay style less action-oriented, the focus on storytelling and player agency is where the game truly shines. The choices made by players have a significant impact on the unfolding narrative, leading to various outcomes and multiple playthroughs to explore different paths.Soundtrack and Audio (4.5/5):The soundtrack, composed by Nima Fakhrara, complements the game's atmosphere perfectly. The emotional and tense moments are accentuated by the music, creating a memorable and immersive experience. The voice acting is exceptional, adding depth and authenticity to the characters.Detroit: Become Human is a triumph in narrative-driven gaming, blending an engaging story with outstanding visuals and player agency. It successfully tackles themes of identity, morality, and the consequences of our choices, leaving players emotionally invested in the fates of the characters. Whether you're a fan of interactive storytelling or just looking for a captivating gaming experience, Detroit: Become Human is a must-play title that pushes the boundaries of the medium.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolutely incredible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game. I'm not finished yet, but from what I understand I'm close (9.8 hours), and I only saw a spoiler for one ending yesterday.After seeing some of the "SEAN!" gameplay of heavy rain I didn't expect a whole lot from this studio, maybe because it was a quick glance, but the futuristic setting alone was enough for me to get this game on sale, as well as the incredibly cool demo that was a blast to play.I was not expecting anything remotely this close to a gameplay experience, the demo's tree gave me a little taste to see how many options there were but after playing for only a few hours the sheer number of different choices you can make, and how far back things trace back is incredibly immersive, and I have to say, I don't know what the last time was, if any, that I experienced a game that had such a mix of strong emotional moments, incredibly tense moments, and times when I thought everything was about to fall apart only to have it somehow pull off.This is by far one of the best stories I've ever encountered in a video game, something incredibly thought provoking and just plain one of the best stories I've experienced, be it a game, tv show, movie, or book. As I'm writing this I'm resisting the urge to pull an all nighter and see how it ends, but I also don't want it to. There are mistakes I've made, things I wish I could fix, and things I'm glad I did regardless of the outcome.All in all this game is an absolutely incredible experience that I'm a bit lost for words at due to the sheer complexity and immersion.I just know that I'll definitely be feeling something missing from my life once I come to the end of this incredible story.Quantic Dream, you guys have created a truly unique gaming experience, and something that stands out from so many other things out there, what an absolutely incredible job.
