_childDocuments_.review: I have never taken the time to write a review before, but Detroit: Become Human is worth at least that much effort. Easily the best choices matter game I have ever played. While I love choices matter games they can occasionally drag in the middle if you like to play your character with any kind of consistency. The stakes can often be underwhelming as well because if you mess up bad enough you'll often just hit a "whoops you died/made a wrong choice" screen and start back at a checkpoint. The beauty of Detroit: Become Human is that it tackles both these issues in a really engaging fashion through the utilization of three distinct characters, none of which are guaranteed to make it to the end of the story In my first play-through I approached each character the way I thought they would play making choices with certain characters that I feel I never would have made with the other characters. I try to approach this kind of game honestly and this game responds honestly with a variety of outcomes and consequences that I both could and could not see coming. More important than the game play with a title like this is the story which was far more engaging than I expected. So engaging, in fact, I can't help but wonder about how other decisions might play out. I actually finished the game in under 11 hours, but I've already replayed a couple of chapters I couldn't wait to see play out differently and I'm probably going to start the story over playing the characters far more strictly in terms of how they approach situations.If you like an interactive narrative you have stumbled onto one of the best games out there. If you want to run around doing whatever you want, whenever you want, this probably isn't your style, but I still recommend you give it a shot. You might just learn what it means to Become Human.

It's an interactive movie, a psychological experiment or some kind of modern art or I don't know what else, but not a game for sure. "Player" don't really control anything. _childDocuments_.review: Flawed game but fun at parts. Worth a playthrough. There is potential for multiple playthroughs but I don't think I will play to see all possibilities. Still I recommend to give it a go.-, amazing facial animations.-. I don't think I noticed a single line where I felt like the delivery was off.- that affect the story later on. Different endings depending on your choices and failures. Not Telltale style all roads lead to same ending illusion of choice BS.-. This game made me realize that I can appreciate movie games when every character isn't constantly dropping "quirky" Whedonesque one-liners. It has a bit of humor in some parts but I think it works well.-. You will understand what I am talking about. One of those things that don't matter too much at first glance but give what they are part of their charm.-The gameplay consists of walk arounds, scan/inspect arounds, talk arounds, choice dialogue lines and perform QTEs. . If you categorically don't like this format then you may want to give this game a pass.-: Connor is the best and most interesting one of the three protagonists and his interactions with Hank are the best part of the game for me. Markus I'm more mixed about but he is still good. I didn't care too much about Kara's plot honestly. Most side characters are meh or worse.-: It feels very weird to see a game made in 2018 have them. But I feel like they fit this game better than most. Helps to make the gameplay loop less lethargic and failing some of them can have important consequences so .-The game tries to provoke emotional responses, especially concerning the player's choices, during some scenes. .-. I hate it.-. This is your "androids are oppressed ethnic minorities" civil rights allegory. Except that it is so in your face that it is just ughhh. This is one of the most discussed aspects of the game so I won't write a paragraph but there were parts I was rolling my eyes, especially during the middle parts of the game. First few chapters before reaching Jericho and last one or two chapters are more competent and interesting than the middle ones. The initial setup and sense of mystery hooks you in and although I enjoyed the final showdown the payoff is... questionable. I don't think most people in the 21st century need to be told "oppressing sentient beings is bad actually" moral lesson, at least the way this game does.-. Debatable how much of a negative this is since I don't think it comes close to undermining the story completely but yeah they are there. Also arguably more forgivable for a story with many branching paths compared to a traditional linear story.-. You are often given one or two words that describe what your character will say and sometimes it just doesn't describe it well. I reset one or two chapters after I felt misled by dialogue options.-. Not a huge negative but I wager it will rub some people the wrong way more strongly than me. When playing with a gamepad some of the interactions are performed with the right thumbstick, which is also the camera control. _childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is an ambitious and evocative narrative-driven game developed by Quantic Dream, a studio known for its cinematic storytelling and intricate interactive experiences (Heavy Rain, Beyond: Two Souls). The game, set in a richly detailed vision of a futuristic Detroit, explores a world on the brink of an AI revolution. With branching storylines, lifelike graphics, and thought-provoking themes, Detroit: Become Human attempts to merge the complexities of interactive fiction with a compelling socio-political narrative about the nature of humanity and the future of artificial intelligence. The game’s story is its heart and soul, intertwining the lives of three central android protagonists: Kara, Connor, and Markus, each representing a distinct facet of the AI experience. Kara, a domestic assistant turned fugitive, grapples with themes of maternal love and personal freedom as she strives to protect a young girl. Connor, a prototype detective android, wrestles with his programmed purpose versus the potential for autonomy while investigating deviant androids. Markus, a caretaker turned revolutionary leader, embodies the struggle for equality and self-determination, evolving from a passive servant to a symbol of rebellion for android liberation. The overarching theme is the search for humanity—not only what it means for androids to “become human” but also what it reveals about the prejudices, fears, and aspirations of the humans they coexist with. The narrative draws heavily from real-world issues like civil rights movements, systemic oppression, and the ethical dilemmas of artificial intelligence, making Detroit as much a social commentary as it is an interactive drama. It is a story that holds a mirror up to the player, forcing them to confront difficult questions about sentience, morality, and justice.Quantic Dream is known for its branching narratives and player agency, and Detroit: Become Human takes this to a new level with its "flowchart" system. Every choice, no matter how minute, has the potential to ripple outward, influencing character fates and altering the course of the story. This system is visually represented in the game, allowing players to see the myriad branches their choices could have taken, a design choice that amplifies the weight of every decision.Gameplay consists of a mix of exploration, quick-time events (QTEs), and contextual interactions that vary from dialogue choices to environmental manipulation. These elements are integrated to reflect the characters' unique traits: Connor’s sequences, for instance, involve detective work and forensic reconstruction, lending a crime-thriller intensity, while Markus’s segments offer strategic and morally challenging decisions akin to revolutionary planning. Kara’s gameplay is more personal, focused on nurturing relationships and stealth, giving her segments a more intimate and tense atmosphere. However, despite these variations, Detroit has some of the same pitfalls as other narrative-driven games. At times, the gameplay can feel constrained by its cinematic nature, with a heavy reliance on QTEs and minimalistic control schemes. Some sections feel more like watching a high-budget interactive movie than playing a game, which may alienate players looking for more traditional, skill-based gameplay. Visually, Detroit: Become Human is a tour de force. The environments are meticulously crafted, from the dilapidated ruins of abandoned Detroit neighborhoods to the sleek, neon-lit skyscrapers that form the affluent sectors of the city. Character models are hyper-realistic, capturing nuanced facial expressions and subtle movements that enhance the emotional weight of each scene. The attention to detail extends to the mundane—graffiti, trash-strewn alleys, and gleaming cybernetic factories—all contributing to a sense of immersion and believability. The animation quality is impeccable, leveraging performance capture to bring a stunning level of authenticity to the characters. Every glance, smirk, and tear feels natural, making the androids feel more "human" than the humans themselves at times. This realism extends to the environments, where lighting, weather effects, and sound design harmonize to create an atmosphere that’s both beautiful and haunting. However, Detroit is not without its technical flaws. Some minor issues with lip-syncing and occasional frame-rate drops slightly mar an otherwise polished presentation, especially in the PC version. Yet these hiccups are rare and do little to detract from the overall visual splendor of the game.The sound design in Detroit: Become Human is another high point, with each character having a distinct musical theme that complements their personality and narrative arc. Kara’s soft, melancholic piano pieces evoke a sense of fragility and hope; Markus’s compositions are grand and orchestral, underscoring his role as a leader; and Connor’s theme is laced with synth undertones, reflecting his cool, analytical nature. The voice acting is top-notch across the board, with standout performances from Bryan Dechart as Connor, Jesse Williams as Markus, and Valorie Curry as Kara. Dechart, in particular, imbues Connor with a fascinating ambiguity, shifting seamlessly between obedient precision and budding curiosity. The cast’s nuanced delivery lends emotional weight to the script, bringing authenticity to even the most fantastical of scenarios.What sets Detroit: Become Human apart from many narrative-driven games is its staggering replayability. The branching narrative structure offers a multitude of potential endings, character outcomes, and even entirely different scenes based on player choices. The flowchart feature not only lets players track their choices but also encourages experimentation by revealing the different narrative pathways that could have been pursued.The game’s handling of moral decisions is another strength, presenting choices that are rarely black and white. The dilemmas faced by Kara, Connor, and Markus are ethically challenging, forcing players to weigh personal sacrifice against the greater good, and individual freedom against societal change. The story is full of moments that linger long after the game is over, prompting reflection on the nature of consciousness and the cost of free will. While Detroit: Become Human is an impressive narrative achievement, it is not without its shortcomings. Some of the writing, particularly in Markus’s revolutionary arc, can feel heavy-handed and overly simplistic in its allegories. The game’s political commentary, though well-intentioned, sometimes lacks nuance, drawing overt parallels to historical events that may feel clichéd or reductive to some players. Additionally, the game’s reliance on QTEs and limited interaction can occasionally disrupt the immersion, reminding players that they are more spectators than participants in the drama unfolding. This approach, while effective for storytelling, can sometimes feel at odds with the interactivity that gaming as a medium can uniquely offer.Detroit: Become Human is a bold and compelling narrative experience that pushes the boundaries of interactive storytelling. Its themes are timely, its characters are memorable, and its visuals are stunning. While its gameplay may not appeal to those seeking a more traditional experience, it succeeds brilliantly as an interactive drama that challenges players to consider the nature of humanity and the ethical implications of artificial intelligence. For those willing to embrace its cinematic approach, Detroit: Become Human offers a thought-provoking journey that will resonate long after the credits roll, making it a standout entry in the narrative adventure genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for the first time in 2018 when I was a teen. I've been an adult for a while now.When I first played it, I loved everything about it. Then I played it more, and started knowing who David Cage was, the awful things he did - and then looked at the game in a broader perspective for a while.It's now 2024:- The story sucks. A white french guy who doesn't know what a revolution (peaceful or violent) entails and how to properly write it without making Markus some sort of robot Jesus.- The deviants, excluding Connor, Carlos' android and the Tracis, are robotic. Sure, they're androids - but I'd never see them as "alive" with the way they're acting. Markus has a permanent scowl on his face and has been through absolutely NOTHING to justify him leading the revolution. He's a pathetically written and weak-willed Martin Luther King Jr. wannabe.- The romance with North was forced and annoying; especially in the peaceful revolution. It's been like 6 days bruh, you're not in love; You're traumabonding. This would've been the case in every romance because it's been SIX. DAYS. But with her, it was worse. She sees him as some sort of symbol and leader, and I can see them (if romanced in the peaceful revolution) breaking up after the revolution because they have nothing in common and disagree on everything all the time. Simon should've been romanceable, and ♥♥♥♥ it- Josh too, I guess. But Simon mainly, because he was the backbone of the group who would've done everything for Markus. Hence all the damn sacrifices. Even gave that useless Markus a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ heart, despite not being romanceable. North gave it to him so he could continue slaughtering humans, like she always wanted: it was never about equality for her, just about being on top, and being in charge. She completely ♥♥♥♥♥ up his legacy when he dies while trying to do a peaceful revolution. Her being the leader causes an instant game over for the deviants.. Only Connor can save them - if it's not already too late.- North should've had an option to die SOONER. Annoying from the get-go and I don't wanna wait a decade to finally get her killed. Had to kill Josh too, even though I like him, because the automatic cutscene for Markus where he's like "SHE MEANT EVERYTHING TO ME" despite, in my playthrough, her being hostile towards him. You never even opened up to her. Had like maybe two conversations in total. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ simp, Markus is so stupid, playing as him was torture, and once again: FORCED. ROMANCE. Once you start forcing a relationship in a game, despite the game not being about said relationship, it's over.- Simon deserved more screentime. While North and Josh argued the whole time over who's right, and Markus being a little ♥♥♥♥♥ who can't stand up for himself, Simon managed to calm them down, and usually had the most rational responses. He cared about Jericho, he was one of (if not THE) the oldest members there, and he cared about Markus and his safety, to the point where he neglected his own. He's a great and handsome character who deserved SO much better. Can't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ listen to Josh and North constantly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ arguing like go argue somewhere else or lead your own damn revolution. Such annoying characters. If it wasn't for the forced romance, they're literally just fillers. I can see the game without those two and just with Simon, and nothing would change: except I'd have peace and quiet to THINK and look at Simon's pretty face.- SIX. DAYS? FOR A REVOLUTION? Or however long it was - no longer than a full week. That's ridiculous in it of itself.- Connor was the only android who we saw that experienced the software instability, and we saw him progressively get more distressed over his emotions even BEFORE deviating. Now, why the hell did Markus make him deviate? It should've been Hank. It made it so lackluster and uninteresting to watch. _childDocuments_.review: I'm really upset that this style of game never really took off. I mean sure, we have a couple of games that most people agree are good, but they are typically seen in a niche spotlight instead of being the grand titans that would rival RPG's and FPS's. The way this game plays hits hard, and it hits well, because it really reflects who you are in this type of situation. Would you truly choose between your fellow races, or would you fight for a righteous cause?  But this style of storytelling has always left a sour taste in certain people's mouths due to its past. Games like Beyond Two Souls, Telltale's Borderlands, or the infamous pres X to fight bolder certainly were not helping to the power of a game like this' potential, despite the style having a very powerful past in the games of Heavy Rain, The Evil Within, The Walking Dead, The Cabin, and Until Dawn. Personally, this game is the gold standard for this format. Huge decisions hidden in the middle of seemingly meaningless or moot choices, all characters are relatable and lovable because they are who you make them to be, and he quick time events/inspection events are enough to keep the action flowing very very well; if there were a cherry on top of this cake, it would be the buddy cop/look into morality the game poses with  Now, would you like this game? Well, try the demo, first off. Second off, yes if you like the subjects of morality and liability challenged. To me, the answer is yes. To you? Well, I cant force you to answer that. Or will you answer because I said yes? Has that affected your answer in any way?Now the question is, whos side are you on? Human's, or androids? How do you know I'm not an android?

_childDocuments_.review: is my first Quantic Dream game, and I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed playing it – knowing the reputation of their polarizing previous titles, such as 2005’s  (aka ) or 2010’s .Much of my enjoyment stems from the game's focus on choices and their consequences – putting it all out there through detailed flowcharts that accompany the end of every chapter, detailing the (in)direct consequences of your nearly every action. Even after three full playthroughs, there are so many things I still haven’t seen and may not even know are possible through the countless branching paths available to you. lives and dies by its characters, and whether you'll enjoy the experience or not rests largely on their shoulders as you experience the story through three sets of biomechanical eyes: A cutting-edge detective Android—and clear fan-favorite of the three—Connor's story involves questions of morality and identity as the player is tasked with hunting down rogue Androids known as “deviants.”Bryan Dechart’s performance as Connor deserves mention, as the chemistry and buddy-cop dynamic between him and Clancy Brown as his "partner" Hank is one of the game’s many highlights. A housekeeper turned deviant, Kara's story thrusts you into a more personal affair; asking how far you would go to protect the one(s) you love. Valorie Curry’s performance absolutely sells this, and immediately had me invested in doing everything to get Kara and her adoptive daughter Alice through to the end in one piece. While perhaps the most disconnected from the main plot of , Kara's story may be the most central to its core themes and philosophy – as well as my personal favorite of the three.Deviant, and a caretaker turned revolutionary, Markus’ story is the most central to the game’s main plot of the Android uprising set to shock the city of Detroit and the world at large. While his story starts off very slow and more linear than Connor or Kara’s, once it gets going, it . As Markus is burdened with leading the revolution, your choices will determine the very course of the Androids’ future.While these stories all stand on their own two feet, they slowly but surely begin intersecting and intertwining, and that’s when things truly start to click into place. By the end, whether they all make it there in one piece rests on your decisions as well as your ability to think and act quickly under pressure, with much of the action involving your standard Quantic Dream QTE-sequences which, while relatively easy, are sure to get your blood pumping. makes for a great experience, and even if your first time through is likely to be the most memorable and effectful, the game encourages, hell, it actively incentivizes you to play through it multiple times to see every different version of events, taking the protagonists down different routes, and finding your perfect way to see it all through. Give it a chance, and you’re sure to enjoy it.Score: 3,5/5

_childDocuments_.review: To Dear Fellow Steamers and Who Is Interested in This Amazing Title,Hello :DThis is my first time ever writing a review for a game. I just want to pay my most sincere respect to the Quantic Dream, to all the creators and all those who have dedicated themselves to make this marvellous dream-like experience a reality, and to those who wrote great reviews and comments that made Steam a great place for articulating your opinions and ideas as rightfully conducting your right of free speech.Enjoying the Detroit: Become Human has been a great journey and such an immersive experience for me; I was deeply moved by it so much that I burst into tears many times.I had written some art critiques before, and this title does have the familiar resonance as how great artworks do to my heart – all the shapes and forms and sounds and vibrations will inevitably gradually fade from you once the show is finished and as the time passes, but there always will be a part of them becoming a part of who you are.This is an art piece.The branching storytelling as an essential structural system in this title had once been very popular in the 80s, especially in some puzzling Noire and Science Fiction novels for teens. They used to list charts and diagrams in the appendix of the book to visualize the options of the alternative story lines, and I have always been fascinated by their intriguing plots and designs. The reason is actually quite simple yet fundamental: You are holding a torch in the dark – you will explore. It is in our basic instinct, just as any living beings; it is at least as potent as arousal, if not stronger. As long as you have that courage in your mind and being determined, you will always be able to hold the most versatile, robust and valuable tool of a live being, curiosity, in your hand, and the torch never quenches, the light never fades.By then, the authors who tried to wield the art of integrating splitting consequences in their creations were highly restricted by the lack of technological means to fully elaborate on the intrinsic power of this expression; but now, everything is different. Every word in a script, every letter now can fully release its power along the timeline. Even some predictable dialogue options and cliché that had been adopted in this work, as to how it is like in a lot of Holly Wood movies, are emanating an enlightening aura because they fit the sceneries so well; and it strangely reminded me how their primitive forms had been created in the heroic poems at the first place, why they have been kept as a drama tradition in the history and since then been polished again and again along the shores, in the books, and on stages.Now creative artists can do so much more, the synchronizing of all of the component elements of this work is at a state-of-the-art level:a. One of the best sincere and heartful sound-acting in game history to date.b. Top-notch human facial expression capturing technique with unbelievably amazing credible micro-expressions and their corresponding post scene effects were done by the pure talent and hard works.c. The innate logic of the social background and the fulfillment of the concept-art designs are very believable.d. Extremely gorgeous and realistic environment texture which concords very much to their contexts.e. Right-on-spot sound effects with dynamic rhythms, smooth transitions and oh my music that absolutely elevate the atmosphere of the whole work, from the beginning to the end.f. Perfect optimization for the hardware and operating systems.What strikes me the most still is how sincere this work is! I truly believe, having that passionate sincerity is a very, very rare, yet the key quality for any kind of creation of art. Yet this work goes even further, once I started to play, it only took me very few minutes to forget about to notice that I was noticing that kind of passion and sincerity been sculpted and invested in it, and just became a part of the plot, I think that should be called a total-immersion. That is how good it is.That is the reason why it really is a masterpiece. That is the reason for all masterpieces being recognised as they are.Oh, it seems I forgot to mention its crucial key traits as being deeply philosophical and aesthetically emotional, well, they are everywhere. They are there even you don’t play it, or even haven’t heard of it and never have read this review. Because it exists, and that fact itself changes the world.Despite taking the multiverse theory into consideration of the current context, we are creating the story lines for ourselves every single moment in uncountable split seconds. Yes, it might seem that sometimes we don’t have many choices, but actually there are – not to mention in an anatomical or microscopic term – the options are truly infinite. We are creating reality at every moment.The word “game” or any of its current subdivided genre might just not clearly enough to properly categorize what this masterpiece really is. I can’t imagine how many sleepless nights, how many hours in total, all the immense energy of its creators that had been contributed into this wonderful art piece, I just want to say I am really, really grateful that I had the privilege to enjoy this art piece that all of you have put your lives into.Thank you.Sincere regards,:D

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: 8/10I honestly believe that Detroit: Become Human is Quantic Dream's best game to date. First off, these games have always been more narrative/cinematic focused than gameplay focused, and pretty much everyone should understand what they're getting into with these kind of games by now. That being said, the three intertwining stories this game tells are incredibly emotional and thought provoking in regard to the near future of AI, as well as the morality and potential sentience of androids who were designed to do nothing more than mindlessly serve their owners. The amount of choices this game gives you in each character's journey is impressive, and how each potential choice could play into the ending you get gives this title endless replayability. All this without even mentioning how remarkably every character is acted. I was genuinely impressed by pretty much every character, from the three main characters all the way to the one deviant android you could only see for one scene. The story as an idea alone brings a lot of moral questions to the front of your mind, but when preformed by such a talented cast of actors, it brings a whole different feeling to you while progressing. The beautifully composed soundtrack also attributes to this very heavily. The music in Detroit sets up each scene almost perfectly, subtly instilling specific vibes and telling you how to feel, without outright spoon-feeding it to you. This game also graphically benefits from being heavily focused on the narrative experience, as the massive effort put into lighting, level design, character design, and general cinematic scenes stand the test of time and hold up exceptionally well. I'd go as far as to say it still looks better than some more modern releases.TL;DR: I think Detroit: Become Human is an amazingly heart-wrenching and thought provoking game that is exceptionally acted, composed, and graphically designed and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys this style of "Interactive Movie" games, or has never tried them before, because this is one of the best!

_childDocuments_.review: Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep AGAIN?Funny thing about Quantic Dream games is that when they pick up setting, it would be absolutely classic and timeproof. I'm sure if you ask them to tell you a fairytale, it would be about knight, princess and dragon. But their games are still magnetic and interesting. And this one is the most.What this movie is about? In 20 years everyone can buy himself not distinguishable from human android for a price of an average laptop. And what androids do? All the dirty and hard work. Yeah, I know, you saw it hundreds of times. Meet our three heroes, which accidentally developed self-consciousness and feelings, and now they fight for their life and a place in this world.If you're familiar with TV-show "Humans", thats exactly what this game is about. QD just picked up the idea, shake off most of stupidity and sillyness and wrap it up in a shiny package.Why watch this movie?+ despite being not very original, the story is still interesting, characters are alive, you will feel for them, hate them, help them, worry about them.+ development of the story is non linear. Yes, there are two main "trunks" of the story and lots of smaller intertwined branches. You can deside the outcome as you like for any of our heroes and their companions.+ character models, animation and acting are outstanding!+ QTE's are manageble.+ graphics (excluding characters) is simple and mediocre, but well hidden under thick fat layers of "depth of field" and "motion blur".+ I want an AX400 robot.There are many plotholes and "deus ex machinas", but they don't ruin the story much.Sadly, there is one terrible thing that almost ruined the game: -  Constant stutters, fps drops, crashes, freezes... It's hideous! I hope androids, responsible for this inferior work, will be switched off and disassembled.So, check your systems, find a loophole in your program, go out to the snowy Detroit and fight for your robotic future, or end it if you're still just a machine...

_childDocuments_.review: For the most part, the best games are those that don't really have any rivals. The ones that scratch an itch you never even knew you had - the ones that keep you up all night. This is one of those games. The ones you wish you could play again for the first time. If you've played similar games before like Life is Strange, you might be thinking this is somewhat similar, maybe just in high definition. It isn't. The complexity this game provides is unmatched by any other. You are forced to make fast and hard decisions sometimes relying on nothing but emotion to guide you through events that may permanently alter the timeline and ending of the game. Someone spared might come back to haunt you. A detail you missed might force your hands later. A slight misstep and you've just ended the entire story line of someones life or even a main character. The harsh penalties really add a challenge into this game, and It draws scarily accurate parallels to unfortunately very real events on planet earth, as you experience the suffering through the eyes of Androids subjected to abuse, torture, experimentation and slavery. It's really hard not to be captivated by this game. Some games offer exploration of a world, I'd like to think that this one offers exploration of different narratives. With beautiful animations, music, scenery, story lines, and actors, this was a masterpiece of a game. It sets a precedent that will be challenging to reach again, although I hope someone does. My advice for people who try this game is to resist all temptation to meta-game. Some decisions are extremely painful as you become attached to the characters, or strive to pick the correct action in a tricky situation. Just play the best you can, and leave the meta gaming to the second play through. Sometimes it will all be okay, even if you were unsure. You only get to play it for the first time once.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard of this game when it was released as a console exclusive back in 2018. Of course, I didn't have said console, so I had to wait. It was when I saw this game on the store only a short time before writing this review that I decided to finally play this game, as Quantic Dream had recently ported more of its popular console exclusive games over to Windows, such as Heavy Rain or Beyond: Two Souls.The game is a great representation of what is happening with the Black Lives Matter movements spurring up across the country. However, it also talks about the sentience of artificial intelligence, and the question of whether A.I. that can emulate human emotions and patterns be recognized amongst humans. You play as three characters; Connor, a prototype of a detective android made to help investigate cases of androids that are dubbed "deviants";Kara, a household android that is owned by a somewhat abusive and aggressive single father;and Markus, an android owned by a artist who has grown old, and gets support from Markus.This three character dynamic may seem confusing at first, but you will get used to it.Except for when you get to the parts where they meet, those parts always confused me.There are some claimed issues with the game, mostly that it has to keep up to date with the constantly updating graphics cards industry, where new cards are released as close as months apart. It is not optimized for the most recent graphics cards, and as such need patches to run properly. However, if you have a graphics card the game supports, you should have no problem with the game. Overall score: 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is somewhere on the border between being a game and being an interactive movie. The story / stories are well told and gripping. It's no less visceral or horrible for that. You will care more for the fate of a single person and the results of a single gunshot in Detroit than a hundred slaughtered mooks in other titles. This is good and thoughtful scifi.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful. Actually, I was looking for a stronger word to describe my emotions, but failed to express my feelings with words. I loved it immensely. At first, I had some doubts about whether I should buy the game, because the question of AI and androids in particular is not new in science fiction and much has already been said about it. But as soon as I started playing, I thought: "Why didn't I buy it earlier?". I became so completely engrossed in the game that I couldn't stop thinking about it even when I was doing other things.The narrative and the way the events are presented couldn't be better. The game is centered on a very philosophical and controversial issue, and the developers created an awesome story around it. The music is great. The actors are perfect for their roles and they did really amazing work playing their characters. The graphics are very nice, facial animation is outstanding.The characters are... — well — I just "felt" every one of them. They were almost alive, I saw their development and personal growth throughout the game. At first, they were nothing to me — just androids, obeying commands, but then I started to fall for them. Connor, Markus, Kara, old buddy Frank — I really felt I should help them, I wanted them to live.In this game, choices do matter. I almost always sticked to my initial choices and never replayed the chapters (well, only once, but then it was not a wrong choice, but just a silly mistake). I recommend not remaking your choices, because that really makes the game more interesting, when you see the consequences of your actions in the following chapters. This also makes you want to replay the game another time with different decisions. I personally really would like to play the game again and try a different path (although I am completely satisfied with my ending as it is — and a big thanks to the developers for this ending).In short, I strongly recommend playing this game. Seriously, Detroit is one of the best games I've ever played. Don't miss on it, you won't regret buying it.PS: Connor, you are my personal favourite. I am going to replay the game for you (among other reasons =)

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Boomer is a game about the destruction of human society as we know it. Set in the nuclear post-apocalyptic wasteland of Detroit, the game is a story of how botched metaphors and ideas stolen from the social issues of the 1960s are sufficient to destroy humanity. You play as one of three characters. The first character is Markus, the most boring domestic terrorist to ever exist. Markus's story is, in my opinion, the worst, as it lacks any of the humor and great emotion of the other two stories and simply features really butchered analogies to the civil rights movement. The second character is Car, an android Karen who decides to speak to the manager of humanity after Todd Howard refuses to eat her spaghetti. Kara's story involves fun American pastimes such as homicide, domestic violence and illegal immigration to Canada. Finally, you can play as Connor, who has objectively the best story, fight me. Connor's story features actually good messages, funny moments, dogs, and the voice actor for Mr Krabs. If you, like me, want to wake up Lieutenant Anderson, shoot Todd Howard and nuke Detroit, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed Detroit: Become Human quite a lot. I am already a big fan of these story, decision oriented games where simple options overtake the actual gameplay. I know these aren't everyone's cup of tea and those that don't enjoy these types of experiences are completely justified, however I always end up having a great time with them. So if you have a similar taste for these narrative games, I think you will enjoy it too.I am always easily fascinated with branching plots and seeing where my decisions take me, and then I also like going back and trying to achieve different outcomes and scenarios. While nothing presented here was perfect and with a rather topical subject matter like robotics and artificial intelligence/sentience, I was still quite wrapped up in the story. I can't say I agreed with every ideological approach being presented in many of my story lines, but I was still moved enough by keeping things purely fictional in my head and enjoyed how everything was presented here as if it was just a television series or movie.Like many others, I also have the fears of artificial intelligence taking over, becoming misaligned with our needs, and possibly fooling us into thinking it shares our values, and my fears were brought up very frequently in this game and it did hinder my experience a bit because of the negative view it was giving me of the real world. However I do supposed that an argument could be made about how giving me this effect means this is profound storytelling, but for me it just instilled more unease into my daily life which I am not after in my video games. I still can't fault it too harshly though since that is the subjective approach they clearly wanted to take with this game, and they have every right to tell the story how they want.Aside from my ideological diatribes above, I liked all the other aspects of Detroit: Become Human. I enjoyed the characters, I had fun seeing how my actions changed their opinions on each other and their current stakes, the graphics were gorgeous, the music and soundscapes are a great wallpaper to help set the mood/tone, and I thought the acting was charming. I am also always impressed with the writing and acting in these branching games because I do start thinking of how many possibilities had to be taken into account and acted out. The controls were also easy enough, though I did play on the default "Casual" setting, and I am not entirely sure how it should become more difficult on the "Experienced" setting.In the end I loved my time with Detroit: Become Human, I liked the world that it put me in when I wasn't thinking about any real world projection, I liked the decision making and its possibilities, I appreciated the presentation and style, and if any of these factors sound enticing to you, I would recommend giving it a chance. Like before I know these storybook type games are looked down upon by many, and that's fair, but I'm casual enough to enjoy that time. Also my distaste for the current possibilities of artificial intelligence does taint my views on the themes a bit, but I still liked the decisions I made with these androids and getting to see what future I created for them. I thought it was great.

_childDocuments_.review: Please look at my screenshots of the game in order to truly understand how bad my visual glitches are. Please note that it is not static geometry it's sporadically moving and flashing about the screen. If you are having issues viewing my screenshots please comment.I remember in 2012 when the "Kara" by Quantic Dream short was released and despite not having a Playstation it was something that captured my attention. It was a very interesting short depicting what would later become one of three main characters and although I quickly forgot about it I was extremely excited when I saw the E3 2016 Showcase trailer for Detroit. It was an extremely unique idea based around what it means to be alive and 'the butterfly effect' with the main selling point being the ability to REPLAY the story a multitude of times, your decisions, greatly affecting how the characters will interact in the future and obviously the outcome of the game. Being a PS4 exclusive was disappointing, to say the least, but I held out hope that one day it would come to pc. Honestly, I would rather it stay a PS exclusive. The PC port of this game was poorly handled, with my i7-8700k CPU, ROG STRIX Z390-E motherboard, 32 Gigs of ram, and a GTX 1080 3GB graphics card it can hardly hold a consistent 30fps with medium settings in standard 1920. This is extremely frustrating because my specs surpass the recommended hardware requirements listed on the steam store page. Not only does the game perform poorly but the textures/geometry in the game break and the game becomes unplayable as it blocks vision. If I can play the game for 5-10 minutes without the visuals breaking the game I consider that particular play session a success. However, the game's story saves upon the completion of the chapters, and if at any point before the end of a chapter the textures break then I MUST exit the game and relaunch causing me to lose the progress. And if at any time during my replay of the mission this happens again then I must repeat it all over again. This makes what would be an engaging and captivating story tedious and annoying to play. As I continue to play it feels like the game is getting worse and more unstable. With the game in its current state, I am unable to experience the butterfly effect and feel like the product does not live up to the promises of replayability. I purchased the game one day after its PC release, the game coming to steam on June 18th of this year and despite the awful flaws, I figured that if given enough time the game would be stable and I would actually get to enjoy the product I bought. However, the game has been out for 2 months (75 days as of my writing this) and has received one "Steam Published - Regular Update" on August 5th in which they added simplified Chinese into the game but have no patch notes describing any work on the technical instability of the game. Despite the fact I want to experience all the game has to offer its clear to me that there will be no end to the technical problems any time soon.TL;DR: Gamebreaking visual bugs render it unplayable, my steam requirements are above the recommended, and yet the game struggles to perform, and I am unable to experience the replayability that is one of the games main selling points.

_childDocuments_.review: QTEs are fairly bad if you're on PC, quite the opposite of the Dead Walking series - it doesn't feel intense, but abstract and confusing, awful controls and even worse movement and camera.Plot is decent (sometimes enthralling, but YMMV), but the implementation of consequences that degenerate the plot (especially if on desktop) over infuriating gameplay mechanics worsens enjoyment (you should lower by one difficulty level if you're on desktop if you don't like QTEs), some interesting possibilities are not fully explored and dialogue options can be misleading on a few occasions. The topics of the game are poorly researched, especially on sociology and psychology (there'd definitely be a lot more humans on the android side, especially early on in the game, what with how the androids look human, and all of this goes on in a USA that appears to be a functioning democracy... are we supposed to believe that with a vanishingly few examples, that humans will hang out with creatures that look exactly like them except for some LED, and act like good servants, children and even lovers? Humans will form bonds with animals and even inanimate objects that give them no affection, and with androids looking less different than historically racially segregated slave societies, there'd be a lot more outcry than for other slave owning societies which often freed, or even fought civil wars to free them.The authors are clearly not futurists (it's not that they bend facts like setting the game far too early for the sake of it feeling relevant, but that they seem outright ignorant of basic ones like the economic, humanitarian and environmental importance of space exploration to Earth (without it we'd be much poorer, rural and poorer countries areas would be more impoverished and vulnerable due to lack of weather and environmental satellites and spin-off technologies), they don't understand basic military or policing tactics, and just generally get a lot of technology wrong. They're not historians either, as there's a very factually incorrect statement in one game ending, it's obvious not even a single search and wiki click was prioritized when writing this game. It's all put into the feel, which at least they manage very well.Oh, and the game takes itself extremely seriously and is therefore ENTIRELY UNSKIPPABLE, and you're not even allowed to fast move/jog anywhere unless it's a few special scenes. You may do chapters over again, but you've got to remove files manually with File Explorer to make save files, and there's only a few checkpoints, and even if you remove the files the game has a second way of saving game data, so your new save gets messed up. The strong parts of the story are very strong, and that's why I showed this game to others and found out about the save files, but if you haven't gotten into it then just watch an LP, it's not worth your money or full game time.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great game, overall score of a 9/10. One point off for being frequently depressing - the content is 'heavy' if you're not the sort that enjoys an emotional wringer. This game showed me what a good branching narrative with multiple endings absolutely should be, and it punches you a lot in the feels. A single playthrough is ~15 hours. The Good- Excellent quality of the game in general transports you into the game environment in a visceral way. I constantly admired the UI work, along with the many details in the environmental art. Overall, the animation was pretty good as well.  - The characters felt well-written and generally well-rounded. While there are a couple of predictable moments, for the most part the story is unique and extremely interesting. There's a lot of use of inference in the story, letting the player read between the lines too.- The outcome of choices is usually appropriate to the choice, and generally the story played smoothly with very few detectable rough patches. - I love that they give you a display of the story graph so that you can see the options that you did not take.- There are some cute Easter Eggs, and the choices generally feel meaningful throughout.- There are a lot of endings and variations to them. - The story was of extremely high quality on the whole.The Neutral- Depending on your taste, this game may not be for everyone. While it's definitely a great game, it's not at all lighthearted fun, and it touches heavily on bigotry, social injustice, and choosing between multiple 'evils'. There's very little moral high ground, and most of the endings aren't happy.- If you're a Twitch player who enjoys pressure, you'll be in hog heaven. If you're a slower paced player, it may irritate you (it did me). The Bad- Towards the end of the game, especially in the last major encounter/story beats after Jericho's outcome, the game devs introduced new control sequences in two high pressure situations where you're pretty much set up to fail, even on easy/casual mode. It is a classic 'poor' choice that game devs do to artificially make something harder, and it's just crappy.- You can miss choices simply by not looking around enough, or by finding things in the wrong order with no warning - like stepping into a room too soon can cut off previous choices. While it's mildly annoying, it doesn't happen too often, at least, if you become aware and cautious of it.- No accessibility accommodations in the configuration. There's just 'easy' and 'difficult' options for play, not really anything you can do about problems you might experience. This impacted me, so there are some chapters I doubt I'll ever be able to get through successfully because I physically cannot do what the controls required of me.- Real time saving - once something happens, you're stuck with it. There's no going back and exploring other options without another full PT to 'redo' a failure that was important to you simply because you pressed a wrong button. I personally really dislike it when game devs think their idea of how I ought to experience the game supersedes my desires and personal play style.- There are some stats in the game that no one bothers telling you the significance of, like how and why public opinion matters.- I have a fairly high end gaming machine that I built myself, and I experienced a few stability issues/crashes while playing. Nothing that blocked progress or ruined anything, but mildly annoying. Regardless, if you like branching narrative RPGs, you're missing out on a true gem if you don't play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sooo... Death Road to Canada with roided up graphics??Seriously though. This is a disturbingly immersive game. It's not a very interactive game compared to other video games, but that is to be expected from the story/investigative genre.Some jump scares here and there. The story is amazing but there are levels where it drags a bit. The dialogue parts of the game is what makes this such an amazing experience. It drags when you are just poking around searching for clues. I suppose that's the genre.I really wanted to recommend this game. But there are game breaking bugs in this PC port. Bugs where you cannot progress down certain paths, and unfortunately these bugs exist early in the game so they cut out massive portions of the story.Technical gripes:- My main technical gripe is with Alice at the start of the chapter where they are attempting to find a place to squat for the night after getting off the bus. The Alice model doesn't follow Kara, and Kara can't go back and trigger Alice moving so they can start probing different squat locations. This cuts off 3/4 of the story from there. This bug persists after multiple restarts of the application.- The clockwise and counterclockwise rotation of the mouse movements are very buggy. Sometimes I will left click and nothing will happen, even with the correct motion. It legit took a few minutes for me to open a door.- The action binding to the mouse movements cannot be rebound. This sucks. I would rather just hit a key on my keyboard or swivel a joystick or something. If the mouse motions weren't broken this wouldn't be an issue though.- I can't see any autosave notifications, even though there clearly is autosave. Was confusing when playing through for the first time, had no idea if I was going to lose my place. No manual save function whatsoever. This should be added, as currently you can't save mid level and have to restart again from last autosave every time.- Movement and re-positioning of third person camera shots are a bit tricky, compared to other third person view games.- There are some graphical static noise and missing textures, particularly relating to hair models in the early missions. RX 5700 XT running v21.2.2 Radeon software, i5-9600K with 16GB DDR4. Installed on an m.2 1TB SSD.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game this was and is. Managed to play through the whole thing in 12 hours and ended up getting the good ending which I enjoyed personally. There are many different endings to the game which gives you every play through a unique ending. I did have some problems with the fps at times during cut scenes, etc. and was running this game on an RTX 2080 but other then that the graphics were phenomenal, playing through this was like a movie experience as if you were watching the Lord of The Rings Trilogy. The game play felt unique and different to many other similar games, having multiple different stories with different characters felt refreshing and made sure that you didn't get bored of the same story line for too long. Don't get me wrong, some of the cut scenes in this game felt long and drawn out which kind of took me out of the immersion for a bit but bought me back with some hard choices to make and some heartwarming dialogue. The game felt short but enough fit into the time. By the end I felt attached the characters and I was left with the feeling that I wanted to play through this game multiple times to see the different endings. Personally my favourite relationship was between Connor and Hank which grows throughout the story if you make the right choices.The fight sequences are quite intense as you've got to make sure you hit the right buttons in the mix but it was quite simply just pressing D and S at the right time yet it didn't take away from how the fights ended. The story tree in this game is one of the best as it shows you where your choices have lead to and which different ways you could of took. It also offers for you to go back if you had mad what you feel to be a bad choice or if you accidentally killed your character off which happened a few times to myself.Overall an immersive, fun, emotional game which I couldn't recommend enough to someone that enjoys these time of choice choosing games. 9/10

And I'm still giving it a thumbs up. The controls border on horrendous. And I'm still giving it a thumbs up. The writing starts off incredible, and then, at the very end, delivers some really cheesy one-liners. And I'm still giving it a thumbs up. Why? But that's above 5, so it gets the thumbs up.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a review coming from someone who runs somewhere either a little above min or between optimal and minimum specs, so if you're one of those people who are unsure, hear me out.This game is BEAUTIFUL, the graphics are stunning, I love the gameplay and how my choices really matter. In terms of story, I wish it moved just a little slower, the game is excited to bring you to the juiciest parts the fastest, but I think it needs just a tad more setup storyline wise, but that's just a personal opinion. I do really love the tones and themes of the story however.In terms of performance on my PC, it took FOREVER to find a darn way to play the game. I literally spent days scouring the web looking for solutions to why I was getting a "your graphics card doesn't support vulkan 1.1" because unlike most people, my PC runs an AMD ryzen, and not Nvidia. Everywhere I looked was a fix for Nvidia, but not for AMD, and what was even crazier was my PC DID say it actively was supporting Vulkan, but it was Vulkan 2.0. Anyways, I'm a brain dead dummy when it comes to PC talk so it's probably why it took me days of search rather than a few hours which thankfully my boyfriend put in for me to fix. I had to go through updating my drivers, going through waves of files to figure out what was wrong, until my BF just took over and solved it. I wish I could say how as to offer help to others, but again, I am super not smart especially regarding PC talk. Though, many in the comments sections of this game already recommend a lot of fixes so shout out to those people that helped and if you're curious about how to fix or make your game work, scroll through them and see what helps.On occasion the game will crash but that's what happens when your specs don't meet recommended and go above minimum. Overall, recommend buying the game, but for the PC port, be prepared to visit Quantic's site or steam threads before purchasing to MAKE SURE everything is good to go. Maybe even try to run the demo for this game first if possible. (My personal experience, I hope others have had a much smoother time with running this game)

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great. The plot is well constructed, appealing and nuanced. The graphics are astounding and the acting is spectacular. However, this game is so poorly optimized that I just cannot recommend it. A top of the line, brand new gaming PC can still encounter massive FPS drops, which results in latency (lag) between audio and video. The game drops suddenly from 60 frames to 5 frames which can last between 2 seconds and 30 seconds, greatly diminishing the gameplay quality. This game spikes my 16Gb graphics card to 100% usage and my i9 processor too, meaning this is an optimization problem and not a hardware problem.I would definitely recommend this game if they reoptimize it, but until then I can't say that this thrilling, insightful and absolutely amazing game can be properly enjoyed. I realize that my experience is not universal and that it is more than likely that I am one in a minority who this is happening to, however, consider this a note of caution rather than advice to spend your money elsewhere. Check if your hardware matches that of those who are experiencing this issue before you buy it, is all the advice I can give.

_childDocuments_.review: If you read any part of this review read this: Buy This Game.Detroit: Become Human is probably the greatest game i have ever played. It is filled to the brim with superior writing, emotion, world building, characters and story that surpasses every game, every movie and every story, it is the greatest narrative experience I have ever had the honour of experiencing.Experiencing, I most definitely believe is the correct word. Unlike a traditional story  you do in this game effects the story, from making a decision like shooting someone or not shooting them, or what you look at while walking around an area, to almost every single dialog choice you make in a decision.  , either directly effecting what immediately happens or ever so slightly changing how a character thinks of you (This is shown as a negative or positive change in your levels of friendship or hostility with a character, the size of the change depends on your action.)(also these levels can make the difference between a character saving you life, or the same character literally stabbing you in the back.)You might think that with so many choices (and there are SO many) and so many consequences because of them that some portions of the story that you end up with are less interesting, exciting or well written. although you would be completely wrong, all of the many possible events within the story fit together and are amazing. For example in the first time I played the very first mission I failed the goal massively and ended up with a terrible ending that i think only 3% of people got, BUT despite the "bad" ending the final words of the ending stuck with me and left me considering them for days later. Because despite my failure I ending up with an indescribable feeling made of some sort of combination of melancholy, depression and wonder. A wonderful and terrible feeling created by this game's terrific 3 dimensional characters and story that I felt a great many times through out this incredible game.A amazing aspect of this game is death. From the start the game lets you know that each of the 3 main characters that you play as can die, and unlike most games death is permanent.This incredible decision means that during every choice and every combat encounter, you are aware that if you mess up too badly or make the wrong decision you can die, losing one third of the game. This knowledge means that the game is filled with the amazing, terrible and realistic fear of death.Negatives, probably the one aspect that the game is lacking in. all that I can think of that sometimes (although rarely) I felt that in a conversation there was not enough dialog choices or the names of the choices weren't descriptive enough and I ended up with a piece of dialog I didn't mean to or wanted to use.The story of Detroit: Become Human is nothing short of a 12 hour long cinematic masterpiece.The impeccable, beautiful and awe-inspiring story is filled with surprising, shocking and abrupt twists that make you question the meaning of humanity, life and what it means to exist. A incredibly interesting question this masterpiece asks is: What is more likely an AI so powerful that it becomes alive, or just advanced enough to imitate the human wish of freedom?Innovative and incredible features are the backbone that which the truly beautiful story is built upon.I will not tell you all the many innovative ideas as I probably could not remember a fraction of them. At the end of every level you are shown a tree like chart of the level that shows the many branching choices you chose and the percentage of people that chose them. the decisions that you chose are coloured and explained while the events you did not chose are greyed out and mysterious, This leaves you with a knowledge of what you missed out on but not really enough to spoil what it really is.Also as you play through the game you unlock "bonus points" that you can use to "buy"  the original art works of the game, the sound tracks, videos about the making of the game and shorts about the story.Scattered through out the levels of the game there are magazines that have articles that describe the world of 2038. These articles show everything about the world from the geopolitical climate, or the effects andoids have on the music, sports, job market or human psychology to how other technological advancements effect peoples lives.This is the is a 40 dollar game that is often on sale for 20 but is worth so so much more so i beg of  you to make the decision to buy this incredible work of art, or at least play the demo.

_childDocuments_.review: wow, wow, WOW. I can absolutely tell why there had been a lot of attention to this game. I know I'm kinda late to the party (since this came out in 2018) but still, this game is a MUST to play even after those years. And it still remains (and will remain) very recent.So, why should this game deserve your attention? Well, first off all, it looks absolutely flippin' fantastic. And I don't think that's just because I'm not used to good graphics. No, the people that made this game hired actual ACTORS so that the characters would seem as natural as possible. And it paid off. Many characters in other games just feel a bit off and you can't quite figure out why. You won't get that feeling here. The characters here are charismatic, lively, diverse and it's easy to sympathize with their issues and feelings.Fine, the game looks good, what about the gameplay, then? The game didn't disappoint in that regards either. It is a storytelling game, but it manages to blend the cinematics of a movie with thrilling action. You won't even feel bored during cutscenes, not only because the game is so engaging, but also because the game oftentimes actually requires you to take action during those cutscenes which can possibly affect destinies of the respective characters.There are several factors that make this game distinctively special compared to other storytelling games. Firstly, you play as 3 separate characters so you get to experience the problems the game portrays from the perspective of 3 different people (well, androids, actually.) I was also surprised by the amount of choices and outcomes of these choices you can experience. And those choices you make don't all actually all lead to the same ending as it is with many other games, in Detroit: Become Human there are supposedly 85 different endings, although many of them do overlap. That doesn't, however, change the fact that every time you do a replay you can experience a different story with a whole different ending.Overall, I was very surprised by the quality of this game. It is well worth the price (the developers really deserve it,) it is engaging, full of action, bonding with characters and tough decisions that impact the outcome of your choices. Go play it, you won't regret it.

It has stunning visuals and music, it has characters for whom you'd do anything just to pull them through the game and get them see the end of all things. Concept-wise, the game offers nothing too new, it covers topics we're all familiar with (looking at you, R.U.R., this is totally you, and I'll be getting you asap), but its way of putting you into the mains' shoes, not leaving you there just as a bystander, opens new spaces for new questions...... and will leave you scarred for the rest of your life, if you happen to be a softie just like me.100/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a pleasant surprise. I didn't expect to like this game all that much but I really did.However my playthrough was far from perfect and there are a few things you need to know before buying.First of all, the optimization is not great. My PC is way above the minimal specs and really close to those recommended but I couldn't go above medium graphics and even ended up playing on low for more stability. My game still crashed at some point and I had to run both Steam and Detroit as administrator and make an exception for Detroit in my antivirus. Only then did the game run but I still had quite a lot of small yet bothering stutters.Second of all, while the game does not have blatant playability issues, it has quirks here and there. The QTE's appear at different places on your screen and it can sometimes be hard to see them and react in time in action sequences. Similarly, if you play with a Xbox controller, the buttons for RB, RT, LB and LT that appear during QTE's are almost identical, and it becomes all the more confusing, again, in action sequences; fortunately, the game is pretty forgiving. Also, the characters are hard to control sometimes, but the sequences during which you have to run are well designed and the timed ones are not too tight. So these few issues are not that big of a deal in the end.Finally, while the story, the characters and level of control I had over both really hooked me up, the writing often lacked subtlety. I'm not going into details since I don't want to spoil anything (btw, avoid guides and discussions even if you just want to fix your game since the title of one of the community discussion spoiled me one plot twist). It was often insanely obvious what the game was trying to say. It wouldn't be a problem if the game wasn't constantly, clearly, openly and literally explaining the moral of the story. In addition to that, the game is a patchwork of sci-fi/dystopia/cyberpunk references and commonplaces, which, again, wouldn't be a problem if the game wasn't so convinced that it is telling something absolutely groundbreaking all the time.Despite all of that, I really liked the Detroit: Become Human, as it had lots of striking moments. It is probably a solid 8/10. But, I'm talking about these flaws because I feel like Quantic Dream was, and hopefully still is, close to making a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Usually I'm not much of a fan of games like this... where most of the interaction with the game world is like "press X to look at this crap" or "press this stupid series of buttons on your controller to simulate some action"... but with this game it is a bit different. The story of this game is absolutely gripping. This is a game that makes you feel things, makes you make hard choices, and makes those choices matter in ways that influence the entire plot and how the characters develop. The gameplay of Detroit is so plain... walk here, look at that, choose this dialog or that... but the compelling story this game tells is incredible, and masterfully composed. I enjoyed this game immensely, and am looking forward to playing through it again making different choices along the way to see what other plot developments might arise.

_childDocuments_.review: This is truly the first create your own story game I have ever played.  I am not that familiar with David Cage's work, I've played a little bit of Heavy Rain and Beyond Two souls but never got into them much.  Detorit: Become Human is a masterpiece in the fact that the decisions you make really do effect your outcome.  This game is divided into three stories and I liked almost all of it.  You got Conner who is android detective and his story is literally Blade Runner in almost every way, he hunts down Deviant androids with his partner Mr. Krabs.  Markus who is my favorite character, that I don't really want to spoil because his story is done so well.  You also have Kara who is the weakest of the three, her story in all honesty doesn't impact the overall narrative.  Kara's story isn't exactly bad, it's just my least favorite of the three.  The game uses your choices to make relationships with the characters in your stories, and influence the opinion the public will have of you.  Instead of just effecting your outcome characters will see you differently depending on your decisions.  The gameplay is nothing special to be honest, it kind of plays the same way as Heavy Rain or a bit more advanced version of a Telltale game.  Some people hate on this game because it is just a metaphor for slavery/civil rights, and while this is true using a real life scenario makes for great story telling in my opinion.  I played this game all the way through and also watched clips of other play thoughs, and hot damn does that game feel different based on your choices... I don't wanna get into spoiler territory, but i can't stress enough how much this game can change depending on how you play.  It's also not just the fact that the story changes to your liking, It's also just a really good story.  The voice acting in this game is crazy, and some of the best I've seen period.  The character development in this game is 10/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I've not finished yet the game, and I need to write this. Detroit: Become Human is not just a masterpiece. It's a work of love. Every good and bad decision, every mistake, every little error I made following my impulses, my instinct, my ideas, just like you do in real life, really made me feel genuinely good and genuinely bad. Not as a player, but as a human. I love and have loved every characters, and every time I felt that, because of me, something harmed them, something prevented them from being closer to their happiness, to their freedom, all because of my decisions, I felt like a piece of trash.However, that's life. And this game reflects it just as well. Not everything is rational decisions, and even those that are, often have unpredictable consequences. This game has made me feel peace, love, but it has also broken my heart. This game has made me feel closer to their characters than many of my friends in the real world. It has made me live a revolution that I would really like to live. This game has not only taken me away from a reality, from a world that is mostly grey and hostile, but it has also taken me to an alternative reality in which I can actually intervene in that same grey and hostile world (Detroit: Become Human is a masterpiece when it comes to creating a transhumanist science fiction worldbuilding, with its political, social and economic aspects), a reality in which I am not alone, in which I see people grow, creating relationships.Normally, when you finish a game that you have enjoyed, a void remains inside you for a while. The void that will remain when I will finish this game I think will never close.Excuse my English, it is not my native language.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent experience. The story is fantastic, the motion capture is amazing and the soundtrack is epic. It has been a while since I have been sucked into a game like this. Definitely worth every penny and every minute. I typically don't go for story type games like this, but after following it for a while I tried the demo and was immediately sucked in. Just try the demo.The game is almost entirely dialogue and QTE's however they are exciting and keep the pace well, so I think it works great to keep the player engaged. There are lots of choice options throughout the game. They claim 80+ endings but it realistically its one good and one bad ending with subtle dialogue/cut-scene variations based on your decisions throughout the chapters. But that said there is easily 3-4 playthroughs here and you still wont get 100%. Lots of replay-ability.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a good story, music wasnt really memorable, but some dialogue options were very vague so I often angered other characters without even meaning to, which is an easy to fix problem, but I guess they wanted to keep it vague.Either way I do like the story but 2 out of 3 main characters have a quite bland story.Markus is the classic underdog becoming the leader of a revolution, but he has the most difficult decisions to make.Kara is the typical mother wanting the best for her child, the decisions were often quite dumb and unnecessary, im sorry but questions like "do you accept ..." almost sound like a rhetorical question.Connor is the only one that feels like he was a well written and round character. Connor is between being a machine and becoming a deviant, which is an interesting choice because you have to determine who he is. That also means he's the only one where you can decide by your own values if an android is a machine or a person.I wish there was a human character tho, I think a contrast is necessary to see how humans think of the whole revolution going on.Either way, I enjoyed the game, but I really have to admit that this one opened my eyes, I don't like games which focus on story while gameplay seems very basic. Press a few buttons, find something by touching everything and you can decide about things, thats it. The gameplay aspect seems almost like filler while the QTEs are alright. Don't play the game if you didn't memorize your controllers layout, I suck with left, right  and the controllers back buttons so I may have lost a character at the end which made me a bit salty...Either way, its worth it, graphics are nice and if you enjoy interactive movie games this is probably the best you can get.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, so this game had a rough start for me. I was playing on 20-30 frames sometimes dipping to 10s and having constant freezing and crashes. Now you may be wondering why I'm still recommending this game, despite all of this. I have found the solution. So NVIDIA did a stupid and broke this game in future game-ready drivers for their cards. If you want to play this game, you have to install the 446.14 Game Ready Driver from NVIDIA and play through this game to the end before you go back to another game. Then, once you've finished, reinstall the new GRD and you'll be all set. I know it seems stupid to have to fix a game to play it, but honestly this game is worth it, and I don't think it's too much of a hassle to have this be the only game you play for a couple of days. Also, after installing the GRD, if you already set up the shaders by playing it without this version, then delete all of the files located in the ShaderCache folder in Steam/Steamapps/Common/Detroit Become Human. After this fix my game now runs at a solid 60fps and has most of the graphical settings to max, aside from cpu dependent options, since that's my bottleneck.Anyways, onto the review section:I have not finished this game. I got it recently. The only thing I knew about this game was androids and the memes that came out about the game. If you like Life is Strange or Telltale games, then I think you'll enjoy it. Ill update this review once I've actually finished so I can give a proper review. For now: RecommendEDIT: I have now finished the game once. And the playtime at editing reflects a single playthrough of this game without going back. I think I got two good endings and one bad, though I'm sure I missed a lot of things. Honestly, this game is good. It is beautiful and tells a great story, though maybe a bit cliche. Everything you do really does have an effect, even reaching as far as changes to the main menu of the game. If you're willing to put the time in to roll back your drivers and binge this game, it's worth it. If not, then I'm sorry that it's too much effort. At this point, try to get it on sale, as with any game, but especially since you have to do some extra lifting to get this to work.FINAL REVIEW SCORE: 8.5/10 Would have been 9/10 if not for driver issue
_childDocuments_.name: Detroit: Become Human

_childDocuments_.review: A narrative, artistic and visual masterpiece. I enjoyed it a lot, the story is captivating and timely in today's age when AI is becoming a relevant shaping force of our lives. The graphics are beautiful, the mechanics are simple but fit for purpose and I really liked the attention to detail in the menu and even in the extras section. It is a narrative exploration heaven with many decision making points and outcomes, but it does not feel overwhelming, very well executed, surely opens possibilities for replaying.The game reflects on some of the most important questions of our lives, what it means to be alive, what it means to love and what it means to have a "soul" with very relatable characters and storytelling. Is there a uniqueness to our biological design or can AI or any other form of intelligence exhibit the same traits? Enjoy the game and form your own opinions, I think they might become relevant questions for our own lives soon.
